Talking to Putin: Europe seeks a negotiator-in-chief for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:42:30 UTC
04:42:30 KST

Russia's President Vladimir Putin attends a meeting with US special envoy in Saint Petersburg on October 21, 2026. | Pool photo by Kristina Solovyova/Sputnik/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — There is a growing realization among European governments that they may soon need to nominate someone to face Russian leader Vladimir Putin in direct talks on a peace deal for Ukraine.
The main problem is deciding who should take on such a hazardous task.
The question gained urgency this week after U.S. presidential envoy Steve Witkoff traveled to Russia to offer Putin a three-way summit with Donald Trump and Ukraine’s leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy, in an effort to press for a ceasefire.
Advertisement
“President Putin disregards the European Union as an authority,” Czech President Petr Pavel said Tuesday in an interview with the Axel Springer Global Reporters’ Network, of which POLITICO is a part. “He doesn’t want to talk to Ursula von der Leyen, he doesn’t talk to Kaja Kallas. He stopped talking to other European leaders, including Emmanuel Macron.”
He added that the EU should “identify a person or a group of people who would speak for Europe. Not necessarily representatives of the EU or NATO, but simply leaders who would be given a mandate by the others to negotiate.”
In recent days, Trump has dismayed Ukraine and its European allies by talking over their heads with Putin and appearing increasingly willing to take Russia’s side in the almost five-year war.
That has reignited debate in Brussels and beyond about the need for Europe to have its own direct line to the Kremlin to safeguard the region’s interests and bolster Ukraine’s ability to resist a lopsided deal.
“Much as it sticks in the craw, I do think a channel of some kind to Putin would be a good thing to have,” said David Lidington, a distinguished fellow at the Royal United Services Institute in London. “I am not optimistic that it would achieve anything much in the short term, but to have a channel which can then be used as and when an opportunity arises is not a bad thing.”
Diplomats and officials disagree on who would be the best person to represent Europe.
Advertisement
Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, has negotiated directly with Trump on trade, while the president of the European Council, António Costa, has previously opened a line of communication with the Kremlin through his office. EU High Representative Kaja Kallas is another potential player who speaks for European interests as a whole.
But the Brussels bubble needs to accept that a deal with Putin and Trump won’t be dictated by EU protocols, in the view of a diplomat from a European Union country who, like others in this article, was granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.
“We cannot show up with two or three people all speaking on behalf of the EU,” the diplomat said. “The choice of who ends up representing the EU will be based on what would provide the most value, not personal power struggles or narcissistic preferences.”
Will Stubb step up?
One name outside the EU’s machinery that is gaining attention is Alexander Stubb, the president of Finland. Two key factors count in his favor: He has arguably the best relationship with Trump among EU leaders, and Finland has long experience of dealing with Russia — the two countries share a 1,300 kilometer border and have been at war in the past.
“Stubb is of interest because of Finnish knowledge of and traditional dialogue with Russia,” the diplomat said. “They know more than anyone on our side [about] what it takes to feel secure in such a situation.”
A second EU diplomat noted that Stubb was “the only person who has come forward so far” to show high-level political leadership, and could serve as a European envoy at a future peace summit. Stubb was in Norway with Zelenskyy and Witkoff on Tuesday for negotiations ahead of the U.S. envoy’s visit to Russia to meet Putin.
Advertisement
Also attending the gathering in Oslo was von der Leyen’s most senior aide, Bjoern Seibert, who has joined meetings of national security advisers as part of the Coalition of the Willing to support Ukraine.
A third European diplomat said it was vital that the EU itself be represented in the talks, instead of a small grouping of powerful countries such as Germany, France and the U.K.
That means both Seibert and Pedro Lourtie, the top aide to Costa, must have seats at the table during preparatory talks, the diplomat said, and that EU member countries must be properly updated on progress.
Calling Costa
According to a fourth EU diplomat, European leaders asked Costa at last week’s summit in Brussels whether it might be time for him to talk to Putin. “Costa said, no, he’s not going to talk to Putin now,” they said. “But Costa should start talking to Putin if we want to play a role in the negotiations. By not speaking, we are playing into the hands of our opponents.”
The fourth diplomat said Costa would be a better choice than von der Leyen or Kallas, who are both seen as too invested in the Ukrainian side to represent the EU effectively at leader level. Kallas in particular has been outspoken in her criticism of Trump. “Costa comes across as more of an honest broker,” they summarized.
The European Commission insists the EU is already present at the peace talks, flagging Seibert’s presence in Oslo on Tuesday. “The main aim [in Oslo] was to explore if the parameters are there for a possible move to trilateral or even multilateral talks with Ukraine and Russia present at the same table,” European Commission spokesperson Paula Pinho told reporters on Wednesday.
She said the talks had focused on territory, security and post-war prosperity for Ukraine; Witkoff is expected to debrief Ukraine and the Europeans after his trip to meet Putin. “What is very important is that we are sitting at the table, that we are able to present our position, and that we can engage in what is a shared objective to put an end to this horrific war,” she added.
Gerardo Fortuna and Paul Ronzheimer contributed to this report.

Lithuania seizes major synthetic drugs lab run by Dutch national
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:41:15 UTC
04:41:15 KST

Police recover more than 500kg of methamphetamine and 300kg of amphetamine in a three-day operation targeting a suspected international supply network.
Lithuanian authorities have uncovered one of the largest synthetic drugs laboratories in the Baltics, seizing hundreds of kilograms of drugs and thousands of litres of chemical precursors at a site near Vilnius allegedly run by a Dutch national of Turkish origin.
“[Drugs] were being produced on an almost industrial scale,” Saulius Briginas, Deputy Chief of the Lithuanian Criminal Police Bureau, told journalists during a press briefing on Wednesday.
Investigators believe the Dutch citizen organised the laboratory's work and coordinated its illegal activities alongside three other members who were all Lithuanian nationals.
Preliminary figures indicate that police recovered more than 3,000 litres of BMK, a chemical precursor used in the production of amphetamines; more than 500kg of methamphetamine; more than 300kg of amphetamine; and around 4.5kg of the synthetic cathinone 3-CMC. This amounts to over 4 million single doses, Briginas said.
“On the wholesale illicit market, the drugs would be worth more than €2 million,” he said. “At street level, the value could be ten times higher.”
Such figures, Lithuanian authorities believe, indicate that the drugs could not have been intended solely for the Lithuanian market.
Instead, the operation was geared towards markets across Europe, with the Netherlands, Germany, Belgium and the Czech Republic among the countries to which the drugs may have been destined.
The investigation also uncovered the industrial-scale procurement of chemicals needed to manufacture synthetic drugs. The group sourced laboratory equipment and chemical substances from China, India and several European countries, while also purchasing some uncontrolled substances from specialist suppliers in Lithuania.
Police found 380 cylinders of hydrogen originating from China at the laboratory. Hydrogen is used in the manufacture of synthetic drugs, while sulphuric acid was reportedly purchased in quantities of one tonne per transaction.
The operation extended beyond the laboratory itself. Police intercepted a shipment intended for the Czech Republic after finding 17kg of amphetamine crystals in two plastic containers inside cargo handled by a Lithuanian logistics company.
Under Lithuanian law, offences involving the illegal production, possession and smuggling of particularly large quantities of narcotic or psychotropic substances can carry prison sentences of up to 18 years.

Estonia Plans to Send Significant Number of Locomotives to Boost Ukraine Railway System
Estonia is currently working on transferring a significant number of locomotives to Ukraine, according to Minister of Foreign Affairs Andrii Sybiha following a discussion with his Estonian counterpart, Margus Tsahkna.
During the conversation, Sybiha briefed Tsahkna on recent attacks by Russia, the situation on the battlefield, and developments regarding peace efforts.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Sybiha also detailed Ukraine’s urgent defense and resilience needs ahead of the winter season, drawing specific focus to Russian strikes targeting Ukrainian railway infrastructure since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“I am deeply grateful to Margus and Estonia for today’s confirmation that they are working on sending a significant number of locomotives to Ukraine. We deeply appreciate this support for vital transport arteries that ensure the functioning of our economy and the lives of our citizens,” Sybiha stated.
Additionally, both ministers discussed the upcoming Ukraine Recovery Conference scheduled in Tallinn and its expected outcomes.
“Pressure on Moscow needs to be increased sharply, not gradually. Margus and I share this approach. We discussed next steps on strengthening EU sanctions against Russia, increasing defense assistance to Ukraine, particularly within the NATO PURL initiative, and ensuring accountability for Russian crimes,” Sybiha added.
As a harsh winter looms, Ukraine’s air defenses are dangerously depleted as the country prepares for an expected surge in Russian energy strikes.
International supplies of Patriot interceptors are severely constrained, leaving Kyiv scrambling alongside European allies to secure hundreds of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles before the cold sets in.
With Ukrainian air defense intercepting only a fraction of incoming ballistic missiles, experts and officials warn that the upcoming winter threatens to bring severe energy disruptions and critical infrastructure challenges across the country.

Why are some Israelis paying thousands of dollars to fly home and vote?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:39:01 UTC
04:39:01 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel elections 2026
- Israelis living abroad are paying thousands of dollars to fly home and vote
Israelis living abroad are paying thousands of dollars to fly home and vote
Many Israelis view this election as a sliding doors moment, and are willing to fork out on flight fees and hotel costs to make a difference.
Around 1 million Israelis eligible to vote in the October 27 parliamentary election live outside the country. Yet Israel is one of the few democracies that requires citizens to be physically present to cast a ballot, with no general postal or proxy voting and no voting at embassies except for diplomats and official emissaries.
That has not stopped tens of thousands from making the trip. The AID Coalition’s Fly & Vote initiative estimates that more than 50,000 Israelis living abroad, many of them in the United States, plan to return to Israel to vote, often at a cost of thousands of dollars. For a large proportion of them, this is their first time doing so.
“It’s my duty”
Revital Ganon Baruch moved to California in 2011 with her husband and two children. She had never felt the need to return to vote, but this year she is taking a 14-hour flight because she believes Israel needs change.
“I think the elections are very crucial,” she said. “I felt that if I won’t do it, I would feel bad with myself,”
“It’s an effort of time and money, but if I feel as Israeli as I feel, it’s my duty to do it now.”
She added that she once questioned whether she had the right to vote from abroad. “But the way this government is running Israel is affecting people outside of Israel too.”
Why this election feels different
For many expatriates, the election has become a pivotal moment for Israel’s future, shaped by demographic change, the October 7 massacre, the war in Gaza, the hostage crisis and years of political division.
Ido Kadman, an Israeli living in New York who left the country in 1994, pointed to the growing political influence of ultra-Orthodox communities. “We have generations and decades of Hasidic Jews coming in droves to vote,” he said, arguing that many had “never served in the military, paid taxes, or done anything to actually contribute to this country.”
Others say October 7 was the catalyst. Many are angry at Benjamin Netanyahu’s government over its handling of the attack, the hostages and the war, as well as its judicial overhaul plans and dependence on far-right coalition partners.
Every vote counts
If around 50,000 expatriates vote, their ballots could be worth roughly two Knesset seats. With polls suggesting a close race, organizers believe the number, and the influence that could reach, could be higher.
Nadav Nir, an Israeli living in Berlin, said the tightness of the race made the journey worthwhile. “With the two blocs and everything being so close, I would say every vote counts,” he said.
Nadav, an active climate campaigner, acknowledged the environmental cost of flying, but said he saw it as a necessary trade-off. “Letting go a little of my climate-related worldview, to be a tiny help in this huge crisis that Israel is facing, was obvious for me.”
Who can vote?
Israeli citizens can vote as long as they are in Israel on election day, regardless of how long they have lived outside of the country.
Maya Gur Arieh was born in Israel, moved to Canada as a child and later returned to Israel as a young adult. She moved to London a month ago for her studies, but she and family members in Canada who have not lived in Israel for years are flying back to vote.
“We’re all angry Israelis living abroad,” she said. “It’s still very much our home, and we just want the future of the country to be much brighter.”
Israel’s Law of Return allows any Jew to obtain citizenship, preserving voting rights even for people who have spent most of their lives abroad.
Marco Greenberg, an American-Israeli living in New York, was born in Hollywood and lived in Israel for only three years, between 1993 and 1996. He sees no contradiction in returning to vote.
“I think it’s the right of being a citizen,” he said. “I was granted citizenship. I have every right to take full advantage of that.”
Many believe that it is unfair to that people can vote in elections in countries they were not born in, and have not lived in for a long time.
Marco said reactions within his own family had been mixed. “Some say, all the honor to you, it’s so patriotic. Others don’t say that. They say, WTF.”
He argued, however, that the connection between Israel and its diaspora citizens strengthens the country. “Having a strong relationship between the Jewish people in Israel and Israeli citizens around the globe is only an advantage to the state of Israel.”
Will the laws ever change?
Every expatriate interviewed for this report, both on and off the record, said they planned to vote for parties in the opposition bloc seeking to unseat Netanyahu.
That may explain why the prime minister has shown little interest in changing Israel’s voting rules. Many Israelis left the country in recent years amid dissatisfaction with his government, and making it easier for them to vote from abroad would likely benefit the opposition.
The issue is also legally and politically sensitive. Likud challenged Fly & Vote, an initiative that made it easier for Israelis living in the U.S. to fly to Israel for the October election, arguing that it amounted to improper election interference, before withdrawing its petition under a compromise that bars the group from subsidizing tickets or adding group flights.
And while the opposition may be tempted to loosen the rules if it takes power, the combination of Israel’s Law of Return and overseas voting could open the door to foreign interference. The concern among politicians is that a foreign group or organisation could encourage Jews abroad to obtain Israeli citizenship, remain outside the country, and vote according to that group’s agenda.
For now, Israelis abroad must pay their own way home. But for the tens of thousands making that journey, the cost is an investment in what they see as the future of their homeland.

Ukraine's Zelenskiy hopes for new talks with Russia, US by early November
Oct 21 - President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Wednesday that Ukraine supported a US proposal for three-way talks with Russia and the United States at the level of negotiators to be held as soon as possible, preferably no later than early November.
Zelenskiy, speaking to journalists on WhatsApp as he returned to Kyiv from Norway, said he had spoken to US officials after presidential envoy Steve Witkoff's talks in St Petersburg with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"We have received feedback that...Russia supports a trilateral meeting at the level of our (negotiating) teams," Zelenskiy said.
"The American side has proposed holding it as soon as possible and we support that...The Ukrainian side has been in contact with its American partners. They will do everything to ensure that the meeting takes place as early as possible, in November. I think no later than early November."
Zelenskiy said that Kyiv supported "any proposals for a ceasefire, an end to the war, an energy ceasefire as well as humanitarian initiatives".
Earlier, the Kremlin said Putin has agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine as soon as next month.
Witkoff met Putin a day after holding talks with Zelenskiy in Norway amid concerns in Kyiv and among its allies that the United States was backing away from Ukraine. REUTERS

What China wants from a Trump-Putin summit on Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:32:00 UTC
04:32:00 KST

What China wants from a Trump-Putin summit on Ukraine
October 21, 2026
The administration of US President Donald Trump has stepped up diplomatic efforts this autumn to revive stalled negotiations aimed at ending Russia's war in Ukraine.
Washington has increased pressure on Kyiv and its European partners while seeking to draw Moscow back to the negotiating table through a series of concessions, including a deal involving Russian diesel exports to the US and the temporary easing of some sanctions.
Yet the Kremlin appears in no hurry to resume meaningful peace talks. Moscow is ready to hold negotiations with Ukraine at a technical level next month, the Kremlin said after the meeting between US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on November 21.
Putin agreed to resume the peace talks mediated by Washington after November 10, his aide Yury Ushakov said after the meeting. He added that the next round of negotiations could take place in Abu Dhabi and would focus on "building the security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the war."
According to his aide, Putin also shared some thoughts with Witkoff on the possible trilateral summit involving US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Ushakov pointed out that Beijing is already preparing the meeting.
Trilateral summit in China without Ukraine
Moscow proposed to hold a three-way meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, scheduled for November 18-19 in Shenzhen, China, The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this week. According to WSJ sources, Putin hopes to reach an agreement with Trump and Xi on ending the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Russia.
Moscow's proposal for the three-way summit involving Russia, the United States and China — but excluding Ukraine and the European Union — offers a glimpse of the negotiating format the Kremlin would prefer. Russia insists that Ukraine must be prepared to make territorial concessions before negotiations can move forward. Putin has also repeatedly stressed that he is willing to negotiate only if Russian interests are taken into account.
According to the WSJ, Putin views the proposed gathering in Shenzhen as a potential new Yalta Conference, referring to the 1945 meeting of the leaders of the United States, Great Britain and the Soviet Union to discuss the defeat of Nazi Germany and the postwar order in Europe.
The newspaper reported that Chinese officials had indicated through diplomatic channels that Beijing would not object to the three-way format if Trump agreed to participate. Trump, whose relations with Kyiv have deteriorated significantly in recent weeks, has also expressed openness to such talks.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy pointed out during his visit in Oslo on October 20 that talks concerning the future of his country will be acceptable only if Ukraine gets a seat at the negotiating table.
What does China stand to gain from the talks?
Temur Umarov, a researcher at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center in Berlin who specializes in China-Russia relations, is not surprised by the Kremlin's proposal. He told DW that Moscow wants to feel respected by Washington and treated as a major international power.
The previous US administration was unwilling to discuss questions affecting Ukraine's sovereignty with Russia without Kyiv's participation. Now, Umarov said, the Kremlin believes such negotiations may have become possible.
Moscow apparently hopes that any agreement reached at the proposed meeting would prompt the White House to pressure Ukraine and the EU into accepting its terms. But what role would China actually play?
Umarov believes Beijing would participate largely as a symbolic partner, rather than as an active mediator responsible for the outcome. "Beijing has no intention of taking responsibility for Ukraine's future," he said.
Simply attending the summit would not impose any additional obligations on China. "It is hardly surprising that the Kremlin insists on this format," Umarov explained. "Russia wants to demonstrate that it is on an equal footing not only with the United States, but also with China. Yet, objectively speaking, Moscow is not the senior partner in that relationship."
Umarov believes China has little direct interest in such negotiations. Even if the leaders issued a joint statement, Beijing would seek language that was as vague and noncommittal as possible, he said. That would allow China to present almost any subsequent development in the war as consistent with the understanding reached at the summit. For Umarov, such flexibility would be essential to Beijing's participation.
However, Yurii Poita, a senior associate researcher at the Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), offers a different assessment. He believes China and Russia have overlapping strategic interests, particularly in their efforts to promote an alternative security architecture across Eurasia.
Both countries, he argues, would benefit from a reduction in Western military presence in Europe and Asia and from a weakening of NATO's influence. "If Russia and China manage to convince the United States to reduce its military presence in Europe and military assistance to Ukraine, Russia would gain additional advantages on the battlefield," Poita told DW.
He added that such a development would further undermine the EU's confidence in the United States as a NATO ally. Poita believes Moscow and Beijing would seek precisely these outcomes in any negotiations with Washington.
Is Putin's political survival crucial for China?
Michael Kimmage, director of the Kennan Institute in the United States, also doubts that Beijing is preparing to take a more active diplomatic role in ending the war.
Speaking to DW, Kimmage said China may see the conflict as destabilizing and would prefer to maintain trade relations with Ukraine and other countries in the region. But he believes another priority outweighs those concerns. "More important to China is the political survival of Vladimir Putin," he said.
According to Kimmage, Russia provides China with several geopolitical advantages, including low-cost energy and a foreign policy partner that rarely stands in Beijing's way.
He believes China will continue indirectly supporting Russia's military efforts to prevent a Russian defeat. An outright Russian victory may not necessarily be Beijing's objective, he said, but ensuring Putin does not lose is crucial. For that reason, Kimmage does not expect China to pressure the Russian president into ending the war if Putin is unwilling to do so.
Does excluding Europe reveal the EU's weakness?
Neither Ukraine nor the European Union would be part of the proposed talks in China.
Kateryna Krasina, a junior researcher at the Kyiv-based New Geopolitics Network, believes their exclusion could reveal how Beijing actually views their international influence.
In her assessment, China's approach suggests that it does not regard Ukraine as an independent player in the negotiations and considers Europe relatively weak.
Kimmage, however, argues that excluding Europe from the summit would not necessarily diminish its influence over the course of the negotiations.
He acknowledged that European governments may have little power to prevent a meeting between Trump, Putin and Xi. But he pointed to European efforts surrounding the 2025 Alaska summit between Trump and Putin, which he believes helped prevent outcomes that would have been unfavorable to Europe.
Kimmage said Europe's influence has grown through financial assistance to Ukraine and extensive defense industry cooperation, particularly involving Germany and other European countries.
He argued that European support has played an important role in Ukraine's ability to resist Russian advances. "And that support equals leverage," Kimmage said.
He believes Russia, China and the United States may all be interested in portraying Europe as a secondary power, but that such a portrayal would overlook Europe's actual influence.
"The optics and the reality are not quite the same," he said, drawing a distinction between the appearance of great-power diplomacy resembling the Yalta Conference and Europe's role in supporting Ukraine.
Umarov offers another perspective.
He believes that any diplomatic agreement between the US, Russia and China would face the reality on the ground.
"China understands that whatever the outcome of negotiations with the United States and Russia, the reality on the ground will be very different and will depend above all on Ukraine," he said.
"Whether the Kremlin likes it or not, Ukraine has agency of its own. Neither the United States nor Western countries can fully determine what happens on the battlefield through diplomatic pressure alone."

Türkiye-Libya maritime deal 'entirely legitimate,' says Turkish foreign minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:31:16 UTC
04:31:16 KST

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on Wednesday said that the 2019 maritime agreement between Türkiye and Libya was "entirely legitimate" under international law and from a political perspective.
"This is an entirely legitimate agreement, both from a legal and a political perspective. There is no need to debate it," Fidan told Anadolu during a visit to Brussels.
His remarks followed the Libyan House of Representatives' acceptance of the 2019 memorandum of understanding on the delimitation of maritime jurisdiction areas between Türkiye and Libya.
Fidan described the development as a diplomatic achievement resulting from the foreign policy pursued under President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's leadership.
He said the agreement reflected Türkiye's foreign policy principles of supporting peace and stability through mutually beneficial cooperation.
"The trust that our Libyan brothers have placed in Türkiye, as well as the stability this agreement will bring to the Eastern Mediterranean, is of tremendous importance," he said.
Addressing reactions from other countries, Fidan said some governments felt compelled to respond, while others had genuine strategic concerns.
"We understand why these countries are reacting. Some are reacting because they feel they are expected to do so, while others genuinely have strategic concerns regarding this issue," he said.
Fidan said Turkish legal experts considered the agreement valid since its signing in 2019 because of its legal structure.
"According to our legal experts, what took place in the Libyan House of Representatives was essentially an act of acceptance rather than ratification," he said.
"From our perspective, we have regarded this as a valid agreement since 2019," he added.
Fidan reaffirmed Türkiye's determination to pursue diplomatic initiatives aimed at promoting peace, security, stability and prosperity in the Mediterranean.
"Our diplomacy has no other purpose than this," he said.
Fidan holds talks with Belgian, NATO and EU officials
Fidan said he held an “intensive series of meetings” in Brussels, covering the ties between the Turkish and Belgian governments, along with Ankara's relations with NATO and the EU.
He said discussions with his Belgian counterpart addressed bilateral and regional issues.
Fidan also attended a meeting involving the foreign, justice and interior ministers of Türkiye and Belgium, alongside Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek and Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci.
He said the discussions covered matters related to the responsibilities of all three ministries.
Fidan described the consultation mechanism, established in 2016, as highly beneficial.
Recalling Belgian Queen Mathilde's visit to Türkiye with a large economic and trade delegation, Fidan said the visit had strengthened bilateral relations.
"This clearly elevated our bilateral relations to another level, and we are continuing to build on that foundation," he said.
Fidan also met with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte to discuss Türkiye-NATO relations and follow-up efforts concerning decisions made at the NATO summit in Ankara in July.
He said their discussions also covered the Russia-Ukraine war, developments in the Gulf region, NATO institutional matters and various crisis areas.
During talks with EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, Fidan said they discussed obstacles in Türkiye-EU relations and regional and global challenges.
These included the Russia-Ukraine war, the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, energy challenges and disruptions to grain shipments from the Black Sea.
"We also reviewed the areas where Türkiye-EU relations have reached a deadlock, as well as the areas where progress has been made," he said.
Fidan said he also held extensive talks with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on trade, political relations and Türkiye's EU candidate status.
"It is essential to continue substantive, well-planned, and persistent discussions on these matters," he said.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:28:58 UTC
04:28:58 KST

Two people were killed in a drone attack targeting Saudi Arabia's Shaybah oilfield on Wednesday, despite the interception of the incoming aircraft by Saudi air defenses, the Saudi Press Agency reported, citing an Energy Ministry official.
The drone was attempting to strike a facility at the oilfield in the kingdom's Eastern Province when it was intercepted, according to the official. Despite the fatalities, operations at the field were not affected.
The report did not provide details about the identities of those killed or the circumstances of their deaths. It also did not identify those responsible for launching the drone.
Shaybah, operated by Saudi Aramco, is one of the kingdom's major oil-producing facilities, located deep in the Empty Quarter desert near the border with the United Arab Emirates. The remote field has a production capacity of approximately 1 million barrels per day, making it an important component of Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure.
The facility has been targeted before. In August 2019, a drone attack claimed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels caused a fire at Shaybah's natural gas liquids processing facility. Saudi Aramco reported no casualties at the time.
Wednesday's deadly incident comes amid a sharp escalation in Houthi missile and drone attacks against Saudi Arabia, including strikes targeting airports, military installations and energy facilities.
On Monday, the Houthis claimed to have carried out attacks against several Saudi targets, including the Shaybah oilfield, an Aramco facility in Yanbu and airports in Riyadh and Abha. Reuters reported at the time that Saudi authorities had not immediately confirmed the claims and that it could not independently verify them. It was not immediately clear whether the earlier claim was connected to Wednesday's incident.
Saudi Arabia has faced repeated attacks on its main international airport in Riyadh, which resumed limited domestic flights on Wednesday after being shut down earlier this month. International services remain severely disrupted, with several major airlines suspending flights.
The worsening security situation has also prompted additional international military support for Saudi Arabia. Britain announced Tuesday that Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets would be deployed on defensive missions to help protect Saudi cities and critical infrastructure against Houthi missiles and drones.
US prepares Gulf embassy departures amid escalation
In a separate development Wednesday, the U.S. State Department was preparing to order some diplomatic personnel and family members to leave American embassies across the Gulf region, three U.S. officials told Reuters.
Two of the officials said the preparations were prompted by concerns about a possible resumption of hostilities, particularly involving Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.
The planned measure, known as an "ordered departure," would require designated personnel and eligible family members to leave their diplomatic posts as a security precaution. Reuters did not specify which embassies would be affected or when the order might be issued.
The preparations followed coordinated security warnings issued by U.S. diplomatic missions across the Middle East earlier this week. The alerts cautioned American citizens that fighting involving the Houthis could spread rapidly beyond areas already affected by the conflict.
The State Department has warned of a growing threat to Americans throughout the region as the Houthis continue targeting Saudi infrastructure. Washington has provided Saudi Arabia with intelligence and other military assistance but has so far avoided direct intervention against the Yemeni group in the latest fighting.
The two deaths at Shaybah underscore the continuing danger to Saudi energy facilities, even as the kingdom reports successful interceptions and maintains that oil production has not been disrupted.

Trump uses France riots to push false immigration claims ahead of midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:28:54 UTC
04:28:54 KST

Trump exploits France riots to push false immigration claims ahead of midterms
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
Donald Trump and his inner circle are using unrest in France to push unsubstantiated claims blaming the riots on immigration, even showing French protest footage at midterm rallies. But there is no evidence linking immigration to the unrest, and it's prompted French President Emmanuel Macron to accuse world leaders of making “stupid comments” at France’s expense. Trump’s focus comes as Republicans face mounting pressure ahead of the midterms and his approval rating hits a reported record low.
In recent days, Trump and members of his inner circle have repeatedly invoked the unrest in France to push unsubstantiated claims blaming immigrants for the violence, and rally his MAGA base.
At a midterm campaign rally in Kansas this week, Trump even broadcast footage of the protests, and warned that the United States could become “like France” if Democrats win the elections, and that it is a once-great nation that had been "conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists".
He's also criticised French President Emmanuel Macron, claiming Macron had failed to get the situation under control: “The whole world was coming in, and as you know, Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon, and that wasn’t the deal,”
Other Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, have echoed claims blaming immigrants for the violence.
But there is no evidence linking the unrest in France to immigration.
France does not collect official statistics on the racial or ethnic backgrounds of people arrested, making it impossible to establish the demographic makeup of protesters detained on those grounds. Nor is there evidence that immigrants, whether documented or undocumented, are responsible for the violence.
It's also important to remember how the protests manifested: demonstrations began with student protests calling for more teachers and improved school conditions. They subsequently widened to include other groups expressing frustration over the cost of living and high fuel prices.
Trump may have highlighted images of people of colour in footage of the unrest, calling them "migrants, jihadists and communists who hate Christianity". But France is a diverse society, shaped in part by its colonial history, particularly in the two largest Paris and Marseille, where the largest demonstrations have taken place. The presence of people of colour in protest footage does not establish a link between immigration and the violence.
Macron has criticised foreign leaders for making "stupid comments" to advance their own political agendas, saying "We saw AI-generated images showing scenes that never happened in France. We had people claiming that we had been invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false."
Trump’s focus on France comes as Republicans face mounting political pressure ahead of the midterm elections, which are just weeks away. A Reuters/Ipsos poll put Trump’s approval rating at 31%, reportedly a record low. The president has also faced criticism from within his own party, as Republicans seek to address growing concerns among voters.
It remains unclear whether using the unrest in France to reinforce his immigration message will resonate with American voters. US media reports suggest the cost of living and the war in Iran are among the issues weighing heavily on voters’ minds.
As the midterms loom, Trump is holding up France as a "warning" to American voters and rally his MAGA base against rising political headwinds, but the claims linking the unrest to immigration are not supported by any available evidence.

US sanctions law firm, shipping agents for alleged Iranian shadow fleet links
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:27:44 UTC
04:27:44 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
The US Treasury Department announced sanctions Wednesday against a Panama-and Greece-based law firm, shipping agents in Singapore and the United Arab Emirates, and multiple cargo vessels for their alleged role in helping Iran evade sanctions and transport oil, petrochemicals and other commodities.
The measures, announced under Washington’s Operation Economic Outcast, target networks that the Treasury Department said generate revenue for Tehran’s military, weapons and nuclear programs.
“Whether you are conducting illegal oil transfers at sea or sitting in the corner office of a law firm, if you are supporting the Iranian regime, we will find you and sanction you,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. “Iran’s facilitators must make a choice: Either you are with us or against us.”
The Treasury Department designated Karnakis and Karnakis, a law firm operating in Panama and Greece, accusing it of establishing shipping companies used to transport hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of Iranian steel, petroleum and petrochemical products.
Washington also sanctioned Singapore-based Amigoz Singapore PTE. Ltd. and Dubai-based Whales Shipping Line LLC, alleging that the companies provided services supporting Iranian oil and petrochemical shipments.
Seven Panama-flagged cargo vessels operated or managed by Roxette Maritime Shipping and Trading S.A. were also targeted. The vessels had transported Iranian-origin goods, including petrochemicals and steel, according to the Treasury Department.
Separately, the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network is coordinating with European partners to investigate a Greek bank’s potential links to Iran and its proxies, including through an administrative subpoena issued under the Bank Secrecy Act.
Operation Economic Outcast, launched in August, aims to disrupt Iran’s remaining financial channels and increase the risks for foreign entities involved in sanctions evasion.
Under the measures, assets belonging to designated entities within US jurisdiction are blocked, while transactions involving them are generally prohibited.

Meta ordered to pay $25 billion in Cambridge Analytica case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:27:00 UTC
04:27:00 KST

Meta ordered to pay $25 billion in Cambridge Analytica case
October 21, 2026
US tech giant Meta, owner of Facebook, was ordered to pay $25 billion (around €22.5 billion) to the US state of New Mexico after a jury found Facebook deceived its users over privacy and content moderation.
"Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data. This was false," Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order following the Wednesday verdict.
The case links back to the 2016 Cambridge Analytica scandal, when a third-party quiz harvested the data of some 87 million Facebook profiles and sold it to the UK-based political consulting firm. The firm used the data for targeted ads, including campaign ads for Donald Trump's first presidential run.
New Mexico rejects deal with Meta
Nearly all US states agreed to settle with Facebook over a myriad of legal issues for an overall payment of $18 billion in August. This included releasing the company from future liability for the Cambridge Analytica breach.
New Mexico refused to settle and filed a lawsuit against the platform. Prosecutors claimed that the social network deceived the state's entire population of some 2.1 million people by its public statements on privacy. The US state also argued that Facebook allowed the spread of misinformation and violent content.
In turn, the company's lawyers said the state failed to prove people were actually harmed by Facebook's statements, and claimed the platform had robust content moderation.
In September, a jury found Facebook liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws. Meta pledged to "continue to defend ourselves against efforts to distort our record."
Meta's billions could go to New Mexico's education system
Following the jury's decision last month, it was up to the court to determine how much Meta would pay the state. While the $25 billion fine is lower than the $35 billion to $40 billion demanded by the New Mexico prosecutors, it far exceeds the cap of $3.45 billion suggested by Meta's lawyers.
"This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is money, and the value of its stock price," New Mexico attorney Randi McGinn said during the trial.
On Wednesday, New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez said the outcome should be "an unambiguous message" to Silicon Valley.
While noting that the money will likely be tied up due to appeals, Torrez also noted that the fine is legally due to be paid into New Mexico's education fund.
"We may have paid for the construction of schools for the next 100 years," he said.
The case is the latest in the string of legal challenges large social media companies face in the US and other parts of the world, including the separate August verdict in New Mexico ordering Facebook to pay $567 million over harm to children.

Who are the terrorists? J&amp;K and Ladakh high court questions ‘vague’ detention order

SRINAGAR: J&K and Ladakh HC has summoned the Srinagar deputy commissioner for a personal appearance over a “vague” preventive detention order under Public Safety Act that accused a 28-year-old man of supporting “aforementioned terrorists” without identifying a single one, prompting the court to question whether the officer had independently assessed the case or merely reproduced a police dossier.A single bench of Justice Wasim Nargal said preventive detention, which allows authorities to deprive a person of liberty without a regular criminal trial, demands the “highest degree of constitutional responsibility and procedural diligence”.“The safeguards embodied in Articles 21 and 22 of the Constitution of India are not empty formalities,” the court said, adding that the detaining authority must independently assess the material and satisfy itself that legal conditions for detention are met.The court directed the DC to appear with the detention order, police dossier, material placed before him and records showing his consideration of the case and subjective satisfaction before ordering detention under PSA.HC was hearing a habeas corpus petition filed by Zubair Amin Bangroo of Srinagar, challenging his detention under an order dated Jan 13, 2026. However, Nazir said it neither identified the terrorists nor named the network or associates with whom Bangroo was allegedly in contact.
HC found that the detention grounds referred to “aforementioned terrorists” without any preceding reference identifying a terrorist. The phrase raised a compelling question about whether the DC had independently formulated the grounds or simply reproduced the police dossier, the court said.“Personal liberty occupies a position of paramount importance in the constitutional scheme. Its deprivation, even for a single day, constitutes an injury which cannot subsequently be undone by the mere restoration of liberty,” the court said.

A US Department of State spokesperson told the AFP news agency that Washington was “closely tracking the situation”.
“The [President Donald] Trump Administration has no higher priority than the safety and security of American citizens,” he said.
Rights groups have criticised Saied, accusing him of rolling back freedoms in a 2021 power grab.
Thousands of Tunisians joined the largest protest against Saied in years on Saturday, accusing him of undermining democracy and mishandling the economy. Opposition leaders, activists and journalists have been imprisoned during his rule.
Saied rejects accusations that he is targeting political opponents and critics, saying the law applies to everyone regardless of their position.

US busts ring accused of arranging hundreds of sham marriages in Massachusetts

US busts ring accused of arranging hundreds of sham marriages in Massachusetts
- Federal prosecutors charged six people over a 12-year scheme in Massachusetts that allegedly arranged hundreds of sham marriages to help immigrants get green cards and possible US citizenship.
- US Attorney Leah Foley said Jennifer Gonzalez was the alleged mastermind, charging US$38,000 to US$40,000 per marriage and making over US$6 million in profit.
- The Justice Department said the case fits President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, and the investigation may lead to more charges against people who gained legal status through the scheme.
AI generated
BOSTON - Federal prosecutors on Oct 21 charged six people with participating in a long-running scheme to allegedly arrange hundreds of sham marriages in Massachusetts, in order to help immigrants unlawfully obtain green cards and potential US citizenship.
US Attorney Leah Foley during a press conference in Boston said the scheme’s alleged mastermind, Jennifer Gonzalez, helped organise sham marriages for over a decade in Massachusetts, a Democratic-led state the defendant described as a “sanctuary” jurisdiction where “you get a lot of help as an immigrant.”
It marked the latest such case by the US Department of Justice as part of Republican President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown. In August, it brought one of the largest such cases when in New York it charged 11 people over a scheme prosecutors said facilitated about 1,000 sham marriages.
Gonzalez, 43, told a cooperating witness posing as a client that her group helped obtain hundreds of permanent resident cards, or green cards, for non-citizens living illegally in Massachusetts, charging US$38,000 to US$40,000 (S$48,000 to S$51,000) for marriages to US citizens, according to a criminal complaint.
Authorities said the operation ran about 12 years and averaged about 18 to 20 fraudulent marriages annually, generating over US$6 million in profits.
Gonzalez, a US-born citizen, told the witness her goal was “for you to get the American Dream,” but that her business had become more difficult after Trump in 2025 returned to office, the complaint said.
Foley, whom the Trump administration appointed as the state’s top federal prosecutor, called it a sophisticated scheme that Gonzalez was “operating with impunity under the last administration.”
“My hope is that today the charged defendants and others like them realize that the American dream is not for sale,” Foley said.
“It is earned. And when you try to pilfer it for profit, we will hold you accountable.”
Gonzalez is charged with harbouring immigrants living illegally in the United States and marriage fraud. Her lawyer did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Other defendants include people accused of aiding Gonzalez’s scheme or entering into sham marriages with immigrants.
Foley said Gonzalez entered such a marriage herself and obtained food stamp benefits from Massachusetts without listing any income from her scheme, which she used to buy property in the Dominican Republic.
Foley said the investigation was ongoing and could result in future charges against anyone found to have obtained legal status through the scheme. REUTERS

Kazakhstan to introduce two-stage military service model under army reform
President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has chaired a meeting of the Security Council of Kazakhstan, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the press service of Akorda.
During the meeting, Deputy Chairperson of the Security Council Aida Balayeva presented the key provisions of the Army Reform Plan, developed in consideration of international experience in military development, modern methods of warfare, and proposals from domestic experts.
The document provides for institutional reforms aimed at enhancing the effectiveness of the country’s entire military establishment.
Plans include reviewing the structure and composition of the Armed Forces, improving command and defense planning systems, establishing unmanned systems forces, and strengthening key components of the army.
A key aspect of the military reform is the transition to a two-stage model of compulsory military service. During the first six months, conscripts will undergo training at training centers, while the following six months will be spent serving directly in military units, with a focus on combat training and carrying out missions as part of their units.
Particular attention will be paid to ensuring the safety of military personnel and protecting their rights.
Plans also include establishing military adviser positions and a Military Ombudsman, as well as taking measures to prevent hazing and strengthen military discipline.
The plan also provides for the development of the unified Zhas Aibyn military-patriotic training system based on the Adal Azamat concept, expanding the network of specialized military schools, and improving basic military training.
Earlier, the Head of State instructed officials to prepare and submit defense overhaul proposals to the Security Council, taking into account ongoing nationwide reforms.

Meta Platforms was ordered to pay a groundbreaking US$25 billion civil penalty to the state of New Mexico in a consumer deception case spurred by the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

Bundeswehr Raises Threat Level, Warns of Potential Russian Attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:08:08 UTC
04:08:08 KST

The German public broadcaster WDR and newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung reported on Wednesday that the Bundeswehr, Germany’s military, has raised its threat level to “Erheblich (Serious),” its second-highest level. It warns that not only could military facilities be subjected to Russian-inspired sabotage attacks, but serving personnel could face attacks at home.
According to a classified internal security report, seen by the media outlets, the German military has revised its previous threat assessments which focused on locations where Ukrainian troops were training or logistics bases forwarding weapons and equipment to Kyiv.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The catalyst for the change was the discovery of an explosive-carrying drone in a wooded area close to the Wunstorf air base in mid-September, as previously reported, which followed shortly after similar devices were intercepted in a planned August attack on Ukrainian cargo planes at Leipzig/Halle airport, which Germany attributed to Russia after an investigation.
Berlin’s security reassessment of the risk concluded that the Wunstorf drone was likely to have been intended to target military aircraft rather than civilian cargo planes; the air base is home to Germany’s strategic Airbus A400M transport fleet part of NATO’s strategic airlift capabilities.
Technical analysis of the Wunstorf drone by Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office highlighted many similarities to those recovered in Leipzig which contained around 1.8 kilograms (4 pounds) of high explosives in tin cans attached to the drones. The investigators assessed that the drone had pre-dated the earlier discovery by as much as two years.
Putin ‘Ready’ for Three-Way Ukraine Talks in November, Kremlin Says
In addition to these specific incidents, suspicious drone incursions occurred over sites associated with Germany’s air defense systems in January, and Patriot maintenance facilities in August, which are also suspected to have been instigated by Russian agents.
The Bundeswehr assessment said: “These incidents underline that Russia has, for some time, almost certainly possessed the capability and very likely now also the increased intention to take action against forces and facilities of the German Armed Forces as well as partners based in Germany, including Ukraine.”
Russia “has crossed a red line”
The assessment also said that the threat from Russian sabotage can no longer be ignored and that a “short-term escalation of the situation is to be expected, and actions are anticipated in the near future.”
It concluded that the use of drones as potentially lethal weapons by Moscow’s agents had crossed a “red line,” and was intended to weaken political and public support for Ukraine in Germany and to disrupt equipment deliveries and training for Ukraine.
WDR cited an Operational Command spokesperson who said as a result of raising the threat level, the German military is strengthening its protective measures at its installations to safeguard personnel and facilities.
Russia has consistently denied involvement in sabotage and hybrid attacks in Europe, and has accused Germany of staging these incidents to engender anti-Russian sentiment. Moscow’s ambassador to Berlin dismissed Germany’s allegations over Leipzig as “absurd” and described the incident as a “provocation.”

France unveils AI literary prize amid debate over authorship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:03:43 UTC
04:03:43 KST

Three tech entrepreneurs in France on Wednesday said they had launched what they claimed was the first literary prize for books written with artificial intelligence.
Named the "Prix Pascal", it does not have a jury yet or declared prize money, but the initiative is intended to challenge other prizes which are struggling with how to regulate AI and its use by authors.
"The prize is open to anyone who writes in French, anywhere in the French-speaking world, with no requirement of nationality or residence, and without a publisher," said the three entrepreneurs, Philippe Rodriguez, Albin Serviant and Gilles Mentre, in a statement sent to AFP.
"Only the work itself matters: an unpublished work of fiction, in French, co-written with an artificial intelligence, that dares to do what has never been read before," they added.
France's literary world has been roiled since September by allegations that top-selling debut novelist Thelyson Orelien used AI to write his book "It was Either That or Die".
It won the prestigious FNAC prize in early September before Orelien was accused of cheating, which led to him being ejected from the shortlist for the Goncourt, France's top prize.
After weeks of denials, Orelien's original publisher in Canada, Boreal, said on Wednesday that it had "confirmed" that he had used artificial intelligence in the writing process.
Initiatives to label books as written by humans are gaining ground in the industry, while the organisers of established literary prizes are rewriting their rules to exclude AI-generated submissions.
But the issue poses thorny questions: will authors be allowed to use services such as ChatGPT or Claude for research or writing advice? When does AI-assisted research become AI writing?
Submissions for the debut Prix Pascal will be accepted until November 30 with the prize set to be handed out in mid-December, the organisers said.

Albares and his Thai counterpart strengthen bilateral relations at the 4th Spain–Thailand Forum

The Minister for Foreign Affairs, European Union and Cooperation, José Manuel Albares, met on Wednesday with his Thai counterpart, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Sihasak Phuangketkeow, with whom he discussed bilateral relations, the EU’s agenda with Thailand and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), and the regional and global situation. The meeting between the two Ministers took place within the framework of the annual Political Consultations mechanism, which the two countries have maintained since 2017 and which is being held at ministerial level for the first time.
Albares welcomed his counterpart, highlighting the growing exchanges between Spain and Thailand and their shared commitment to further strengthening bilateral relations in areas such as political dialogue, multilateralism, connectivity and the energy transition. In the Minister’s words, the meeting “seeks to lay the foundations for a closer and more strategic partnership”, in line with Spain’s Asia-Pacific Strategy 2026–2029. In this spirit, the two Ministers signed two agreements during their meeting.
The two Ministers also inaugurated the 4th Spain–Thailand Forum, held at the headquarters of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, European Union and Cooperation and co-organised by Casa Asia.
Signing of agreements
Before holding the consultations, the Ministers signed an agreement waiving visa requirements for holders of official and service passports, aimed at facilitating exchanges of visits, and a memorandum of cooperation between their diplomatic schools, which provides, among other areas, for Spanish-language training for members of the Thai foreign service and the exchange of experts.
4th Spain–Thailand Forum and bilateral relations

This year’s edition is being held under the theme “Innovation, Technology and Cooperation for a Shared Digital Future”.

This priority is reflected in Spain’s new Strategy, which identifies Thailand as a key partner within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). Bilateral relations are currently excellent, driven by record levels of trade, a growing presence of Thai investment in Spain and extensive opportunities for cooperation in key sectors such as energy, infrastructure and technology.

US judge orders Meta to pay $25B in data privacy case: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:00:43 UTC
04:00:43 KST

Ahmet Salih Alacaci and Mucahithan Avcioglu
21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
A US judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in penalties over Facebook's handling of user data in a case involving political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica nearly a decade ago, the New Mexico Department of Justice announced Wednesday.
The ruling follows a September jury verdict in New Mexico that found the social media giant liable for more than 43 million violations of the state's consumer protection law.
The case stems from the 2018 scandal related to Cambridge Analytica, which improperly accessed personal information belonging to approximately 87 million Facebook users.
New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew said the violations were willful and systematic, citing repeated misleading statements by Facebook and the involvement of senior company executives.
The judge reduced an initial assessment of $219.5 billion to $25 billion and ordered that the penalty accrue annual interest of 15% until paid in full, CNBC reported.
The New Mexico Department of Justice said the case extended beyond Cambridge Analytica to Facebook's representations about its data practices and efforts to tackle misinformation and hate speech.
The trial examined statements about user privacy, third-party access to personal information and the handling of harmful content.
New Mexico pursued the litigation independently rather than joining a multistate settlement, the department said.
“Today’s result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable,” New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez said in the statement.

Putin praised Washington’s mediation efforts, Ushakov said. The Vesti news outlet also quoted the Kremlin aide as saying the talks could take place in the Emirati capital, Abu Dhabi.
Moscow and Kiev held three rounds of US-mediated negotiations earlier this year, on January 23–24, February 4–5 and February 17–18. Abu Dhabi hosted the first two rounds, while the third took place in Geneva.
Diplomacy on Iran
Ushakov said Putin also confirmed Russia’s willingness to help find political and diplomatic solutions concerning Iran.
“Vladimir Putin emphasised that diplomatic opportunities are far from exhausted. And that it is possible and necessary to reach an agreement with Tehran, our strategic partner,” he said.
He also said Witkoff briefed Putin on the substance of talks he took part in on Tuesday in Oslo, which included Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and leaders of Finland and Norway, and that the US sensed "some new nuances in the behaviour of the European leaders."
“They mentioned this to us, but, truth be told, these nuances do not entirely satisfy us,” he said.
The discussions also covered the implementation of agreements on Russian diesel supplies to the US and global markets following a phone call between Putin and US President Donald Trump earlier this month.
“The parties also held a detailed discussion on other large-scale joint economic projects, which offer significant prospects for cooperation between the two nations. Some of these initiatives are now nearing the implementation stage,” Ushakov said.
American prisoner released
During the meeting at Constantine Palace, Witkoff announced that Russia had released 73-year-old American Stephen Hubbard.
Hubbard was sentenced by the Moscow City Court on October 7, 2024, to six years and 10 months in a penal colony after being convicted of fighting alongside Ukrainian forces.
Ushakov said Russian officials handed Hubbard over to Witkoff at St Petersburg’s Pulkovo Airport for his return to the US.
The envoy thanked Putin on Trump’s behalf for the “gesture of goodwill”, saying the release would be appreciated by the US president and the American public, Ushakov added.

Could software cloning change the way we use the internet?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

An AI-cloned free tool is being dubbed 'the end of software'
It's being called "the end of software" and the dawn of a new era of AI-powered piracy.
New AI tools are disrupting the tech industry itself, making it relatively easy and quick to clone an existing piece of software and replicate its features.
Earlier this month, a small team of developers used AI tools to create near-identical, free versions of two commonly used products: Microsoft Office, think programs like Word and Excel, and Adobe Creative, which includes Photoshop.
Around the same time, a different tool called Reverse Engineer Anything that helps developers use AI to deconstruct and replicate features in other pieces of software shot to the top of trending projects on software repository GitHub.
For some, this new generation of tools will disrupt software in the same way MP3 file-sharing networks in the late 1990s changed how we listened to music and watched movies, replacing CDs and DVDs with streaming.
But whether this will give more power to users or further concentrate power in the hands of AI companies remains to be seen.
'Set the clock back' to the 1990s internet
Brandon Thomas is one of the developers who recently announced they had used AI tools to copy the Microsoft Office and Adobe Creative suites.
A 15-year veteran of the US tech industry, he sees himself fighting a "war" for the future of the internet.
In the 1990s, "everything [online] was nerdy, hackable, and weird," he told the ABC.
"Everything in this era could be inspected, copied, shared with friends, remixed. It was amazing."
But over time, the internet became more standardised and bland. Spaces for innovation and personalisation, like Geocities or Myspace, were replaced by closed ecosystems that tightly controlled user access.
"Everything became a walled garden fiefdom, extractive, and rent seeking,"
he said.
This is "enshittification", a term coined by writer Cory Doctorow in 2022 to describe the perceived decline of online spaces.
Social media platforms like Facebook initially attracted users with clean, chronological feeds and personal connections, then pivoted to intrusive ads and sponsored content.
Search engines became crowded with sponsored ads and affiliate-marketing spam, pushing out organic search results.
Software makers shifted to subscription-only models with automated billing and predatory cancellation fees, in some cases worth 50 per cent of the annual contract.
For some, AI is part of the problem, as "slop" content floods online spaces.
But for Mr Thomas, AI is the solution.
"AI flips the tide of this war in a way legislation never did," he said.
"We can build anything, even triple-A video games and operating systems.
"This is the most excited I've felt for the future in a long time.
"I think we have a great opportunity to take back the internet from the monopolistic platforms that became rent-seekers and behaved badly to us as users and customers."
How AI is making software easier to copy
Think of a piece of software like a cake from a bakery.
To copy the recipe, you could break into the bakery and steal the list of ingredients (the source code), for which you would be quickly prosecuted.
Or you could reverse engineer the cake by tearing it apart, tasting it, and studying it under a microscope. This is known as "decompiling".
You can then bake the cake based on what you learned. Each time you bake the cake, you tweak the recipe so the result more closely matches your description.
Marek Kowalkiewicz, an expert on the digital economy at Queensland University of Technology, said AI dramatically sped up this process.
"[AI-powered reverse engineering] is not very different from having a bunch of human software developers doing the same thing, but it's way faster and cheaper," Professor Kowalkiewicz told the ABC.
"In the past, I could have hired 100 developers to create a copy. Now it's not expensive anymore."
Reverse Engineer Anything, the viral tool on GitHub, dramatically streamlines the reverse-engineering process by allowing a user without coding skills to replicate features from other software at no cost.
The mood is giddy and chaotic in reverse-engineering forums where users share their projects.
These include hacking into the control systems of cars to replace factory dashboards, playing old games that have lost vendor support, or just figuring out ways to remove ads popping up on their smart TVs. One user wants to make a free version of their therapy practice's management software. Someone else wants their printer to accept less expensive third-party ink cartridges.
One user writes:
"I'm so excited for all the good and bad stuff that will happen onward."
Software could be recreated legally
AI-generated software cloning means some tech companies face similar issues to musicians, authors and artists who have seen big tech steal their work to train AI.
These tech companies have trained the AI models being used to reverse engineer their own software.
"All those big players will be probably now be lobbying for legislative change and more protection of software," Professor Kowalkiewicz said.
"It's an arms race."
But copyright law was not equipped to deal with the emerging scale of the software cloning issue, Malcolm Burrows, a lawyer at Dundas Lawyers said.
Software in Australia is protected under copyright as a class of literary work.
Reverse-engineered software is illegal where it is a "substantial reproduction" of an original.
But this will be hard to prove where AI tools have been used to copy software without access to the source code.
"It's going to get very grey in terms of source code and reproduction of software," Mr Burrows said.
Tool "devalues work of developers"
While Brandon Thomas and others dream of a retro internet, some fear a dystopian future.
The new AI tools may further entrench the power of AI companies and generate a rash of low-quality "slop" software.
Aaron Snoswell, a computer scientist at QUT, said the tools devalued the work of developers and would lead to more cost cutting and worse software.
"I think for the software industry it creates more of the same headaches and exacerbates the existing AI pain points," Dr Snoswell said.
"Companies are probably going to try to automate even more software development labour with AI."
This trend was already apparent among independent game developers.
"I'm seeing all these indie game developers who have spent 14 years developing their dream game … and then someone in one weekend can create a functional copy," Dr Snoswell said.
"What point is there in building with human effort, with human soul, if if can be stolen like that?"

Iran determined to keep uranium amid increased war odds, flurry of meetings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:58:29 UTC
03:58:29 KST

Iran determined to keep uranium amid increased war odds, flurry of meetings
Tehran had ‘nothing new’ to tell Washington after latest nuclear proposals reportedly offered by mediators.
Tehran, Iran – There has been a flurry of diplomatic activity in the Middle East in recent days, with hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough to end the United States and Israel war on Iran.
Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir was in Tehran on Wednesday to discuss the war and recent tensions in Yemen. It comes against the backdrop of fears of a new breakout in conflict in the region.
Despite this, Tehran has held firm to its position that the war will not end, and the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen, until the US accepts its conditions.
Iran maintains an unyielding stance on its contentious nuclear programme, which was a factor in the Trump administration’s decision to launch the war on February 28.
“Not a single gram of enriched uranium will be removed from Iran,” Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said late Tuesday after meeting Munir.
But he did not rule out downblending the highly enriched uranium inside the country under supervision from monitors, something Iran has offered before.
Iran’s authorities present the decades-old nuclear programme as a sovereign right and an achievement gained despite strikes, sabotage and assassinations. Rezaei described it as “national wealth” on Tuesday.
Iran has also used low-enriched uranium for civilian purposes like manufacturing radiopharmaceuticals and for power generation at the Bushehr plant in cooperation with Russia.
The authorities argue that surrendering the nuclear programme under military pressure would amount to capitulation, if it did not guarantee that Iran would not be left exposed to more attacks.
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly emphasised since the start of the war that he wanted to dismantle the Iranian nuclear programme. US Vice President JD Vance, however, suggested earlier this month that a “meaningful” reduction in the level of enrichment capacity may satisfy US demands.
Nuclear issue
Before Israeli and US attacks on Iran’s nuclear facilities in June 2025, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) estimated that Tehran possessed 440 kilogrammes (970 pounds) of uranium enriched up to 60 percent. A nuclear bomb would need enrichment of more than 90 percent.
The attacks, followed by further US-Israeli strikes on nuclear sites in 2026, severely damaged Iran’s nuclear infrastructure. With the IAEA unable to inspect key facilities, the current size, condition and whereabouts of much of Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile remain unverified.
Tehran has refused access to the IAEA to inspect its nuclear facilities since the war started, accusing the agency of advancing Western interests through adopting resolutions and referring the nuclear file to the United Nations Security Council.
Iranian authorities maintain they are not pursuing a bomb. But senior Iranian officials, like Rezaei, have publicly questioned the validity of being a party to the international nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty if Iran’s nuclear facilities and other infrastructure continue to be attacked.
Still, Iranian officials have hosted numerous foreign diplomats this week. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov was in Tehran on Monday after attending a meeting with Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries a day earlier. There were also indications of visits to Tehran by other Arab officials.
US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth is also reported to have met Israeli security officials earlier this week. These meetings did not appear to have decreased the prospects of renewed war.
But speaking at a conference for Iranian exporters in Tehran on Wednesday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi cautioned that the country faces threats of more attacks and expansive economic sanctions.
“The reality is that the country is truly in war conditions and the war continues. We have not reached peace conditions and are away from it, so all decisions must be made within war conditions,” he said.
Parliament speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf told Munir that Iran had “nothing new” to tell Washington and expected realisation of conditions offered in New York last month to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days.
Mediators did not publicly divulge details of their proposals to Tehran this week, but were told the US needed to build trust by accepting Iran’s conditions. These include returning to the June memorandum of understanding and recognising an Iran-Oman deal over temporary transit in the Strait of Hormuz.
In addition to a pledge for immediate talks on a bigger deal regarding Iran’s nuclear issue, the memorandum included removing the US naval blockade on southern Iranian ports, waivers for oil sanctions, unfreezing Iranian assets and halting military action in Lebanon and other regional hotspots.
Ellie Geranmayeh, a senior policy fellow and deputy head of the Middle East and North Africa programme at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said it was clear that Tehran would be unwilling to give up its enriched uranium without guarantees of sanctions relief.
“The Iranians have made it very clear, and I see no evidence that’s changing, that they are willing to negotiate over the fate of the highly enriched uranium or access for international monitors, but that has to be directly linked with a very clear implementation protocol for US sanctions relief,” she told Al Jazeera. “We are very far from those types of negotiations at this stage.”
US media cited unnamed officials as saying on Tuesday that the Pentagon was sending the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and a Marine unit to the Middle East. That would present President Trump with a range of strike options after the US midterm elections on November 3.
Over recent weeks, Trump and his officials have further discussed a range of military operations, including hitting Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain to diminish nuclear facilities inside, and dropping the “mother of all bombs” on nuclear and energy facilities. They have also previously raised the idea of seizing Iran’s southern islands on the Strait of Hormuz and assassinating more Iranian officials.
Iran’s state-run Press TV cited an unnamed security official as saying on Wednesday that decision-makers in Tehran have chosen to advance “without any limitations or restraint” if there are more US and Israeli attacks or assassinations.
Geranmayeh pointed out that Tehran had also helped its ally, the Houthis in Yemen, with their advances along the Bab al-Mandeb strait, and even considered potential preemptive strikes to rattle the US ahead of the election.
“One thing we should be watching out for is Israel and the US combining forces on military attacks after the Israeli elections and the US midterms,” she said, after Trump backed Netanyahu’s election bid.

Italian authorities are investigating whether Russia or other foreign actors had a role in the violent cost-of-living protests that swept Milan and other European cities over the weekend, as concerns rise across the EU over Moscow’s escalating hybrid warfare.
Italy’s government, led by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, has reportedly requested a briefing over what role – if any – foreign provocateurs may have played, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday, Oct. 21, citing people familiar with the matter.

The scale of the violence and the apparent coordination of some attacks led officials to question whether the unrest was entirely spontaneous.
“The events in Milan and elsewhere in Italy are fundamentally different from those seen in other periods,” Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said in Rome on Tuesday.
“They are the product of what I call ‘hybrid warfare,’ which someone is bringing into our countries with unconventional tools that are called TikTok, social media and YouTube, without the West realizing or reacting,” he continued, according to Bloomberg.
Meloni’s spokesperson had declined the request to comment.
Weekend unrest in Milan
