- One of Ukraine's best and fastest interceptor drones is an air-to-air version of the Bars one-way attack drone
- Bars are some of the best defenses against Russia's fastest Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones
- But there may be too few small jet engines to rapidly scale up Bars production
Russia's latest jet-propelled Geran-4 and Geran-5 one-way attack drones fly at 500 km/h or more, nearly three times as fast as an older, propeller-driven Geran-2.
That's too fast for many of Ukraine's air defenses. In particular, the inexpensive interceptor drones that Ukrainian forces deploy by the thousand.
Russia launched more than 2,700 jet Gerans at Ukraine in September, and Ukraine is shooting down only about 55% of them, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. The speed disparity is a big part of the problem.
Ukrainian forces are scrambling for new defenses against the speedy Gerans. Among the best is actually a Ukrainian take on the Geran-4 and Geran-5: a fast, jet-propelled one-way attack drone that the Ukrainians have modified for air-to-air use.
Against jet drones, the air-to-air Bars have a hit rate of around 30%, Zelensky said during a joint press conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv on 4 October. "The Bars have shown positive results," Zelensky said. "They currently have the highest percentage. Others are also catching up."
Did Ukraine just unleash its first Bars cruise missiles? A 500 km strike deep inside Russia suggests it
In July, Ukraine and Germany agreed to jointly produce Bars, with Germany financing the first phase. Ukraine has reportedly been launching Bars at targets on the ground since at least the summer of 2025. But it was only recently that clear photos and videos of the drones have circulated.
Over the weekend, Ukraine’s 1021st Anti-Aircraft Missile and Artillery Brigade released footage of one jet drone hunting another. Observers identified the interceptor as a Bars and its target as a Geran-5. After launching from an elevated ramp with help from a rocket booster, the drone's operator—seeing what the drone saw through a front-facing infrared camera—steered the drone toward the Russian drone, possibly destroying it.
Exactly how the operator controlled the Bars—whether by satellite or mesh radio or some other command and control system—is unclear. Equally unclear: what kind of warhead a Bars would employ in the air-to-air role. Many smaller interceptor drones lack warheads. Instead, they simply slam directly into their targets, wrecking them in the collision.
Mystery drone
Trending Now
Bars isn't small. It likely packs an explosive warhead. Potentially one that the operator can remotely trigger when the interceptor passes near its target.
Bars is adaptable. Its maker has reworked it from a 22-kg warhead and a 700-km range to a 60-kg warhead and a stated range of more than 1,000 km, and a heavier variant can carry a 105-kg warhead.
In the air-to-air interceptor role, long range is terribly important but speed is everything. There's an obvious way for the Ukrainians to boost the Bars' speed from its reported 700 km/h top speed to potentially even faster. They could shrink the drone's warhead and its fuel load, making it lighter in order to make it faster.
That may explain how a Bars can chase down a Geran-5 even as the Russians, by one Ukrainian analyst's estimate, try to push the Geran-5 toward 700 km/h or more.
Turkey’s Korkut guns now shoot down Russian drones over Ukraine. Almost half of the jet-powered Shaheds still get through
Cost is important, too. Russia churns out Gerans for an estimated $100,000 or so per drone. The cheaper the drone, the more copies the Russians can fling at Ukrainian cities. If it takes three or more interceptor drones to take down each of those 2,700 jet Gerans, Ukraine may need to deploy 8,000 to 10,000 interceptors a month.
Ukraine already builds more than 2,000 Bars a month, its maker says, but mostly in strike versions. How many go to air defense, and how much each costs, isn't public.
The supply of small jet engines could be a constraint. “Engines are a key element; we really import them in large quantities,” Zelensky said in an interview with Financial Times. "There are also domestically produced engines, but there are not enough of them.” A Ukrainian-made engine for Bars passed final tests in September.

The Baffling Gender Politics of Netflix’s New Stanford Prison Experiment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:23:27 UTC
03:23:27 KST

This article discusses all six episodes of Netflix’s The New Stanford Prison Experiment.
For decades now, scholars have argued over what—if anything—we should have gleaned from the Stanford Prison Experiment. That it was unethical to place two dozen male college students in a university basement repurposed as a prison, designate a few of them guards and the rest prisoners, and encourage the former to discipline the latter, was apparent by the time its mastermind, Stanford psychology professor Philip Zimbardo, ended what was supposed to be a two-week exercise after only six days. As the extent of Zimbardo’s manipulation came to light, the 1971 study lost credibility in academic circles, even as its pop-cultural legend kept growing. Fifty-five years after it was conducted, perhaps the only definitive conclusion to draw from the Stanford Prison Experiment is that the Stanford Prison Experiment is not worth repeating.
But just try telling that to the reality-TV machine, let alone a platform currently at work on the third, all-celebrity season of a competition series that cheerfully (and, of course, non-lethally) recreates the horrors of its international hit anticapitalist battle royale thriller Squid Game. The New Stanford Prison Experiment, Netflix’s take on a project that was always more convincing as improvisational theater than as scientific research, isn’t even television’s first crack at Zimbardo’s study. The BBC got there first with The Experiment, in 2002, whose earnest attempts to correct for the original’s missteps yielded a more nuanced, if still inherently flawed, look at authority. That the Netflix version of what can now be best understood as a reboot of a famous franchise feels less like social psychology and more like a high-concept season of Big Brother is no surprise. What’s most perplexing is its choice to incorporate female participants in a limited way—and its failure to make any real sense out of what they bring to the experience.
Aware that the televised resurrection of a notoriously inhumane experiment was bound to draw scrutiny (the mere announcement of the show’s existence touched off a wave of incredulity), the producers of the six-episode series take pains to make both their safety precautions and their high-mindedness visible. Instead of a retrofitted academic building, the inmates are sequestered in a real housing pod of a Georgia correctional facility. The 30 voluntary participants are said to come from all walks of life, though what we find out about their backgrounds is generally limited to hometown, racial identity, and line of work. According to executive producer Jane Lipsitz, each “underwent psychological screenings prior to entering the experiment.” There’s a safe word any of the participants can, and some do, use to leave the roleplay early.
The appearance of legitimacy is further reinforced by a panel of three experts who provide commentary on what’s happening in the pod. Michael Cantrell, who brings 30 years of experience working in federal corrections, games out the results of the guards’ strategies. Journalist Trymaine Lee, who has covered stories ranging from Hurricane Katrina to the power of the Black electorate, was presumably tapped to bring insight into big-picture issues such as race, violence, and the justice system. But the show keeps the experts’ interjections so brief that he’s rarely afforded more than a quick sound bite. Filling a limited version of the host role is Alison Wood Brooks, a behavioral scientist on the faculty of Harvard Business School. It’s she who introduces the series with a speed-run summary of Zimbardo’s study and its “ethical breaches,” as well as the true but comically vague observation that “in today’s world, the study of power couldn’t be more relevant.” So, Brooks says, it seemed like the right time to retry the experiment in hopes of more accurately answering its original question: “Does power corrupt?”
It doesn’t take long to notice that only three of the 30 participants are women—and all of them join the five men selected as guards. It’s not hard to guess why there are no female inmates. Correctional facilities are segregated by sex. Throwing men and women together in close quarters for 14 long, monotonous days is a recipe for uncomfortable, sexually charged interactions, if not full-on harassment or assault. Of course, similar dangers exist in single-sex environments. Abuse of power seems particularly likely when male guards are put in charge of female prisoners, yet precisely this dynamic is the reality in many American prisons. I suppose untrained, inexperienced guards might be expected to pose a greater threat. But you would think that the same safeguards put in place to protect participants’ physical and mental health could be extended to enable a truly coed experiment. (The show doesn’t have much to say about the existence of transgender, nonbinary, or even queer people behind bars.)
The architects of New Stanford might’ve avoided all of the above and still meaningfully included women by running parallel exercises in separate pods. Instead, they only examine the behavior of three women—a number so small, it precludes any claim of representativeness—in positions of authority over men. One of them, Laura Berens, is the CEO of her own business and thus presumably comfortable in a leadership role. Shavonnah Jefferson, whose background as a security guard also seems relevant here, has no trouble asserting herself. “You have to speak up,” she says. “Because if you do not, people will run you over.” Yet only Kiana Gaona, a young, devoutly Christian social media manager elected head guard by her shiftmates, gets much screen time in early episodes. Professing to believe in gender equality despite her choice to submit to her husband, she’s a bit erratic. She makes the extreme decision to give an outcast inmate a position of power, then veers dramatically in the opposite direction, punishing him and a fellow dissident with 23 hours of confinement to a cell for talking about a rebellion.
It’s these scheming inmates and the two male guards who initially claim control of their respective shifts who dominate the show for most of the season. There’s an interesting, if under-analyzed, contrast between the latter men’s leadership styles. Chris Lee, a prototypical new-school executive, wants to wield influence by inspiring his charges, while Chet Hudson, an oil rig supervisor, likens his new job to breaking horses. The resulting inconsistency fosters a bit of unrest. But it’s only after an extremely reality TV plot twist in which Lee, Hudson, and their fellow male guards switch roles with the most rebellious prisoners that a truly telling storyline emerges. Hudson, who as a guard had been the strongest proponent of a strict hierarchy, starts saying things like: “When people unite, no matter what, they’re in control of the power.” Then he makes a big deal of leaving the experiment early, claiming that he has nothing to learn from being a prisoner. For a certain kind of person, one that’s really having a moment right now in American politics, inequality only becomes a concern once they lose their place at the top.
Although the men’s role reversal remains the dominant drama, the shakeup also puts a new spotlight on the women, who are reassigned to an all-female shift. They quickly settle on Berens as head guard, citing her leadership experience. (It’s worth noting that neither of the two Black guards, Jefferson and Nicholas Washington, are shown to be considered by their peers for head guard.) “The female shift gave me an opportunity,” Berens reflects. “Obviously, the guys on my shift weren’t treating me super equal.” Unfortunately, this isn’t obvious based on the footage we’re shown, and it certainly doesn’t explain why Berens, the sole woman on her original shift, joined the majority that elected Hudson head guard. Regardless, she proves to be the most competent leader in the experiment, striking the right balance between firm rules and humane treatment. Her best moment happens when the shift made up of rebellious ex-prisoners loses control and she steps in to quiet the inmates and advise her counterpart to protect his guards.
Aside from the self-evident notion that some women make strong leaders (and some men weak ones), it’s hard to know what the takeaway from the introduction of an all-female shift is supposed to be. Maybe because they really do all respect women in positions of authority, or more likely because they don’t want millions of people watching them act sexist on TV, the inmates barely adjust their behavior when Berens’ team walks in. Another probable reason for their compliance is that they’re so intent on antagonizing the ex-inmate shift, which many feel is being rewarded for bad behavior. The women don’t come into the pod with the same baggage.
The expert commentators don’t really help make sense of the situation. When it comes to the gender issue, they could’ve supplied context about differences in how men and women typically wield authority or how men tend to perceive women in power. Maybe they did and that footage didn’t make it into the final edit. Either way, we see a lot of the experts noting that the all-female shift is fascinating without digging into specifics. The closest we get to synthesis comes from Berens. “I guess I really did have 22 men listening to me,” she marvels, attributing her success to kindness, humor, and mutual respect. “What if there are more women leaders who can lead in this type of way?” This is a subject far older than this Lean-In-era epiphany, yet New Stanford stops short at gesturing faintly in the direction of conversations that could theoretically be had.
The series’ shallow approach to gender doesn’t just weaken its depiction of the three female participants. It also neglects to acknowledge the explicitly gendered aspects of the male hierarchy, with its charismatic, physically strong leaders and smaller, less socially adept outcasts. In that sense, New Stanford replicates an ancient form of patriarchal bias that casts men as the norm and women as an atypical other. Maybe it’s silly to criticize something as inherently unserious as a reality show for failing to internalize the lessons of The Second Sex. But this particular reality show tries to justify its controversial existence by proclaiming its seriousness with regards to psychology, philosophy, and current events. So it seems fair to judge it by those lofty ambitions.
To that end, it isn’t only gender that the series glosses over. Racial disparities occasionally surface—one Black inmate justifies his obedience to authority by explaining that for his community, fighting back might result in an “accidental shooting”—yet go largely unexamined. Anyone hoping for timely debate over the purpose or efficacy of the criminal justice system is bound to be disappointed. By the time the guards are dismissed, in the finale, so that the prisoners can take responsibility for their own fates, the whole “experiment” feels like a bait-and-switch. New Stanford wants to reel in viewers with the notoriety of the original study and the promise that hot buttons will be pushed. But then, perhaps because the producers are afraid to alienate any segment of Netflix’s diverse audience, it shrinks from every opportunity to make meaning out of what happens in that housing pod. And so, as different as the two exercises are, this latest Stanford Prison Experiment becomes as pointless as the first one.

Russian strikes close plant of Ukraine’s biggest aid backer. Its 3,600 workers and millions in taxes now hang in balance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:22:34 UTC
03:22:34 KST

Russia is now hitting the German investment that helps keep Ukraine’s economy running. Russian strikes have forced one of the Zhytomyr Oblast's largest employers, the German-invested Kromberg & Schubert plant, to shut down completely, putting 3,600 jobs at risk, the Zhytomyr Regional Military Administration said.
Germany is Ukraine’s single biggest partner by volume of security aid, providing about a third of all support the country receives, according to Ukraine. Russia’s destruction of a German-owned factory strikes at the economic ties Kyiv most depends on.
The plant produced electrical onboard cable systems for world-class cars. Its closure will cost the region millions of hryvnias in tax revenue. Some of its workers may leave the country, while others move to company sites in other cities.
Regional Administration Head Vitalii Bunechko said the plant’s management and owners are working out options for the workers’ future. The authorities also promise maximum support if a decision is made to restart operations.
A war that now reaches every corner of the economy
The factory is one loss in a campaign that has widened far beyond the front. Russia has escalated its drone and missile attacks through 2026, striking first at power plants and residential blocks, then trains, factories, retailer warehouses and medicine depots across Ukraine.
Ukraine’s Economy Ministry expects losses from Russian strikes to reach up to $10 billion this year, the same report noted. By late August, officials said Russia had destroyed about 90% of retail chains’ food logistics, a measure of how deep into civilian commerce the attacks now cut.
The slow bleed on businesses that survive
Even companies left standing lose working days to the strikes. Russia’s air war cost the average Ukrainian shopping mall 166.8 working days between 2022 and mid-2026, more than eight months of closed floors.
For Zhytomyr, the Kromberg & Schubert shutdown turns that slow erosion into an outright closure, removing a budget-forming employer at a stroke.

New Poland-Ukraine dispute looms as local authorities move to honor UPA military leader
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:21:37 UTC
03:21:37 KST

New Poland-Ukraine dispute looms as local authorities move to honor UPA military leader
The monument to Roman Shukhevych, the military leader of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), is pictured on the 74th anniversary of his death at the Shukhevych Museum. (Anastasiia Smolienko / Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images)
Warsaw has denounced Lviv Oblast authorities' plans to honor the World War II-era Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and its military leader, Roman Shukhevych.
The move signals a fresh rift in the already strained Kyiv-Warsaw ties just days after President Volodymyr Zelensky said the relations had finally improved.
The council of the western Ukrainian region adopted decrees on Oct. 20 symbolically declaring 2027 as the Year of the UPA, the Year of Shukhevych, and the Year of Oleh Olzhych, a Ukrainian poet and political activist.
Poland’s charge d'affaires in Kyiv, Piotr Lukasiewicz, immediately reacted by saying that "glorifying the UPA and criminal figures runs counter to European values and the strategic and neighborly relations between Ukraine and Poland." Poland’s defense and foreign ministries also decried the decision, saying it "does not build mutual trust."
The episode marks another chapter in the Ukrainian-Polish dispute over the legacy of the UPA, a resistance organization that fought for Ukrainian independence from Soviet rule.
In Poland, the group is primarily remembered for its role in the 1943-1945 Volyn massacres — killings of tens of thousands of Poles in what is today western Ukraine, then under Nazi occupation.
Thousands of Ukrainians were killed in retaliatory attacks, making the massacres one of the most painful chapters in the two nations' shared history.
Shukhevych was a Ukrainian nationalist and the supreme commander of the UPA from 1943 until his death during a gunfight with Soviet security forces near Lviv in 1950.
As Warsaw sharply denounced the Lviv Oblast authorities' decision, the government in Kyiv moved to distance itself from the step to avoid derailing the restoration of ties with its western neighbor.
"The recent decision by the Lviv Oblast Council... is counterproductive to our current efforts to further develop Ukrainian-Polish relations and resolve contentious issues amid Russia's full-scale aggression," Ukraine’s foreign ministry said in a statement shared with journalists.
Contentious shared history
Shukhevych’s legacy remains deeply contentious in Ukrainian-Polish relations, with historians in both countries offering differing views on it.
The UPA was established in 1942 as a military arm of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists — specifically, the faction led by Stepan Bandera, OUN-B. Shukhevych officially assumed the leadership of the UPA in November 1943, several months after the start of the initial wave of the Volyn massacres.
Poland's Institute of National Remembrance has named Shukhevych "an architect" of the Volyn massacres and "co-founder of collaborationist units operating alongside Germany." Shukhevych was one of the commanders of the Nachtigall Battalion — a short-lived unit staffed by Ukrainians and organized by German military intelligence — in 1941.
In 1941, as Germany invaded the Soviet Union, the OUN-B leadership hoped Berlin would tolerate a Ukrainian state and proclaimed one in Lviv. Germany rejected it, arrested Bandera and other leaders, and cracked down on the organization.
Many Ukrainian historians debate the extent of Shukhevych's personal role in the Volyn massacres and point out that under Shukhevych's command, the UPA fought both Soviet and Nazi forces.
"Some Ukrainian historians have suggested that the order of ethnic cleansing in Volyn did not come directly from Shukhevych, but was an initiative of the local UPA leadership," Myroslav Shkandrij, a professor at the University of Manitoba, told the Kyiv Independent.
"The problem, however, is that Shukhevych has become a symbol, and symbols, whether they represent heroism or villainy, are resistant to facts."
Kyiv and Warsaw also hold different perspectives on the Volyn massacres themselves.
The Polish parliament recognized the killings as a genocide against Poles committed by Ukrainian nationalists, while Kyiv views them as a two-sided tragedy.
Olesia Isaiuk, a historian at the Center for Research on the Liberation Movement, a Ukrainian research institution, frames the Volyn massacres as part of a broader Polish-Ukrainian conflict, stretching back to the Ukrainian war of independence in the wake of World War I.
"For the Ukrainian side, the Volyn event is… one of the biggest and most tragic parts of the continued Ukrainian-Polish conflict… And Roman Shukhevych is a national hero for Ukrainians because he fought against the Nazis and the Soviets," Isaiuk told the Kyiv Independent.
But as Skhandrij notes, real history often evades easy classification.
"The histories of the OUN, UPA, and Shukhevych are complex. They include both heroic and shameful episodes," he says.
"It is not easy to tell the whole truth in a simple narrative, and even more so during wartime."
read also
Tense year for Ukraine-Poland relations
The Polish envoy in Kyiv noted that while the leaders in Kyiv and Warsaw made progress on resolving historical issues, "irresponsible local officials are meanwhile undermining the relations we have worked to build."
Earlier this year, tensions erupted between the two countries when Zelensky conferred a title on a military unit in honor of the UPA.
In response, Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped Zelensky of Poland's highest honor, the Order of the White Eagle, awarded by his predecessor.
After a period of tensions, Zelensky said on Oct. 18 that bilateral relations had finally improved. The latest episode risks reversing that progress.
"Such a decision does not build mutual trust between nations but strengthens divisions. It is necessary for the Ukrainian authorities to distance themselves from this position," Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Oct. 20.
Ukraine's foreign ministry has done just that, sharing a statement that criticized the Lviv Council decision as “counterproductive to our current efforts to further develop Ukrainian-Polish relations and resolve contentious issues.”
The ministry stressed that the decision was taken at the regional level by council members who did not consult the foreign ministry or the central government.
"At the same time, we call on the Polish side to refrain from rash steps that could undermine the normalization of our relations."
The proposals on the UPA, Shukhevych, and Olzhych were put forward by the head of the regional council's cultural committee, Sviatoslav Sheremeta.
"This is our history, our heroes, and we must duly honor their memory. I thank the councilors for their support," Sheremeta said, according to the local outlet Sokal Voice.
In response, Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said on Oct. 21 that he had requested that Sheremeta be placed on Poland's list of undesirable persons, potentially barring him from the entire Schengen area for five years.
The developments also come a year before Poland's parliamentary elections, in which the coalition led by centrist Prime Minister Donald Tusk faces a growing challenge from right-wing and far-right parties.
Historical grievances play an increasingly important role in Polish public debate ahead of the elections, with right-wing forces adopting a tougher line on Ukraine.
And it also arrives at a critical time for Kyiv.
"Additional foreign policy challenges are the last thing Ukraine needs today," says Sergiy Solodkyy, director of the New Europe Center think tank in Kyiv.
"At a time when Kyiv is engaged in a difficult dialogue with the United States and European support is becoming even more critical, Ukrainians have a particular interest in preserving a spirit of partnership with all EU member states," he told the Kyiv Independent.
As Ukraine's relations with neighbors were finally beginning to move in a positive direction, "opening another dispute would clearly run counter to Ukraine’s strategic interests," the expert said.
And Zelensky's deputy chief of staff, Iryna Vereshchuk, warned: "The only winner from the tension in Ukraine-Poland relations is Russia."

Flaw in PHP computer language leads to shutdown of websites around world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:20:30 UTC
03:20:30 KST

Websites around the globe have gone dark after a serious vulnerability was found in a computer language used to build much of the world wide web.
Belgian, Dutch, Finnish, French and German sites were among those that governments took down temporarily as they scrambled to patch the critical weakness in PHP, a language used by almost 70% of websites.
The vulnerability in the programming language, which became public on Tuesday, sparked warnings from national security agencies in Washington and London. It means millions of websites will need to be fixed. One internet infrastructure expert said Russian state actors or organised criminals could exploit the flaw to carry out cyber-attacks.
Wordpress, one of the most common website systems, uses PHP, as does Wikipedia, the messaging software Slack and – at least historically – much of Facebook. The Wikimedia Foundation said it had taken down several systems on Wednesday as a precautionary measure until they could be patched.
The organisation behind the language issued a patch on Wednesday after researchers testing cyberdefences discovered the flaw. The US National Security Agency told all organisations using PHP to take their systems offline if they were unable to patch them immediately. It said the vulnerability could “provide a direct path to the server’s file system or database”.
The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for “backdoors installed by an attacker”.
Prof Alan Woodward, a cybersecurity expert at Surrey University, said: “It was very surprising and troubling because of the extent to which PHP was used around the world. PHP issued a patch very quickly. The big thing is for everyone using it to get that in to make sure their systems are safe.
“The troubling part is there is going to be a long tail of websites who may not be maintained as well and they are going to remain vulnerable, which means we may see weeks and months of ongoing attacks. For the big juicy targets, I hope to goodness they are being patched quickly.”
Woodward said there was a window of opportunity for bad actors. “There is this race and some people unfortunately don’t even know they are in the race.”
OpenAI said it led a coalition of researchers that discovered the flaw and claimed “frontier AI” had been key. The researcher who found the weakness, however, said they did not use models that were not available to the general public.
In the UK, websites belonging to Edinburgh, Bristol and Oxford councils were taken offline. In France, local government websites including that of the Paris police prefecture went offline on Wednesday, as did in the Netherlands the national digital identity service, the website of the house of representatives and the site of the national cybersecurity centre.
Michał Woźniak, an internet infrastructure expert, said: “There’s going to be a lot of automatic exploitation of this.” The bug might allow cryptocurrency miners to exploit vulnerable servers at other people’s expense, he said.
He also said large crime organisations and Russian state actors could use the vulnerable sites as a launching pad from which to conduct distributed denial of service (DDoS) and other cyber-attacks.
The issue highlighted the poor state of internet infrastructure, Woźniak said, something that was being brought to light by advancing AI models but that had been a long-developing problem. The underlying vulnerabilities the researcher found were decades old.
“This is an environmental problem in an industry where there’s an incentive to move fast and make changes,” he said. “There’s an incentive to deploy a thing and then never update it and not think about maintenance.”

Ukraine Conflict Freeze Without Security Guarantees and Legitimacy Solutions is Pointless – Expert
Unknown

Bulgaria halts funding for arms purchases for Ukraine through the EPF: what is the reason
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:18:34 EEST
03:18:34 KST

Bulgaria halts funding for arms purchases for Ukraine through the EPF: what is the reason
Kyiv • UNN
Bulgaria is maintaining its contributions to the European Peace Facility but will direct them only toward non-lethal aid for Ukraine. Sofia supports negotiations.
Bulgaria will no longer participate in financing the procurement of new lethal weapons for Ukraine through the European Peace Facility (EPF). The national government adopted the relevant decision on October 21, UNN reports, citing the NOVA television channel.
At the same time, the country will continue to provide funding for non-lethal assistance
Details
The Bulgarian Council of Ministers approved a position on so-called "constructive abstention" from financing the procurement of new lethal weapons for Ukraine through the European Peace Facility. This mechanism allows an EU member state not to support individual decisions in the area of the common foreign and security policy, while not blocking their adoption by other countries.
The Bulgarian government emphasized that Sofia would continue to fulfill its financial obligations to the facility, but the funds would be directed exclusively toward non-lethal assistance to Ukraine.
"The financial contribution of the Republic of Bulgaria to the European Peace Facility for the benefit of Ukraine will be used exclusively for measures related to the provision of non-lethal assistance," the government statement says.
In addition, Bulgaria will insist that its funding be directed as a priority to Ukrainian regions where members of the Bulgarian national minority live. The possibility of such a distribution of funds is currently being discussed with the European Commission. The government of Prime Minister Rumen Radev has already explained the decision as being driven by Bulgaria's strategic interest in ending the hostilities in the Black Sea region.
Sofia said that it continues to support Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity, but opposes a protracted military confrontation and supports the opening of diplomatic channels for negotiations.
According to media reports, Bulgaria's contribution to the European Peace Facility in 2026 amounts to more than €9 million. At the same time, the specific amount that was to be allocated for the procurement of lethal weapons for Ukraine has not been determined.
Context
The European Peace Facility was established in 2021 to finance EU defense and security initiatives, including military assistance to Ukraine. Contributions from member states are calculated according to the size of their gross domestic product.
Earlier, Rumen Radev's government had already halted the free transfer of weapons and ammunition from the stocks of the Bulgarian army to Ukraine. At the same time, the restriction does not mean an automatic ban on the commercial export of weapons by Bulgarian manufacturers.
Reminder
EU leaders will discuss funding for Ukraine for 2027 on November 26–27.

Solzhenitsyn Statue Temporarily Returned to Original Vladivostok Site After Relocation Mishap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:16:38 UTC
03:16:38 KST

Authorities in the Far Eastern port city of Vladivostok have temporarily returned a controversial monument to Nobel Prize-winning Soviet dissident Alexander Solzhenitsyn to its original location after a failed attempt to relocate it.
The statue was dismantled from the waterfront promenade in central Vladivostok on Tuesday, with plans to place it in a nearby, smaller square.
However, on Wednesday, the Vladivostok city hall’s press service told Interfax that workers realized the statue was too large for the smaller square when attempting to install it there.
“The monument visually overloads the small recreational zone,” a press spokesperson was quoted as saying.
Officials confirmed that the Solzhenitsyn monument will remain at the original Ship Embankment until architects finish modifying the Faith and Hope Square, where it was intended to be moved. They did not provide a timeframe.
Solzhenitsyn, the Soviet Union’s most famous literary dissident who spent years in prison camps before being exiled to the United States, passed through Vladivostok when he returned back to Russia by plane in May 1994.
Some local activists have criticized the statue, which was installed in 2015, for depicting Solzhenitsyn stepping off a ship gangway.
Vladivostok’s city hall had agreed in March to move the Solzhenitsyn monument following complaints from the Russian Navy’s Pacific Fleet, which argued that a statue dedicated to a Soviet dissident was out of place on a waterfront reserved for World War II memorials and warships.

Netanyahu's empty Jerusalem home gets anti-drone nets as neighbors ask: ‘What about us?’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:15:43 UTC
03:15:43 KST

Extensive work has been underway over the past two days at Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's private residence on Gaza Street in Jerusalem, which has been designated an alternative official residence, even though Netanyahu and his wife do not live there. Two cranes blocked the street, a major thoroughfare in the Rehavia neighborhood, while at least 10 workers installed protective netting designed to defend against drones.
For about a year and a half, the Gaza Street residence has undergone extensive renovations, including the construction of an elevator, replacement of a bathtub, installation of metal scaffolding and placement of a protective shelter on the property. In addition, traffic barriers and concrete barricades have been installed along the street.
Throughout this period, Netanyahu and his wife have been living at another property in the same area rather than at the Gaza Street residence. Meanwhile, major renovations are also underway at the official prime minister's residence on Balfour Street, with work not expected to be completed before early 2027.
"Speaking of protection against drones, this is a middle-class neighborhood in the heart of the capital, with very densely packed buildings," one Gaza Street resident told ynet. "If you're worried about drones, maybe you could do us a favor and protect the neighbors too, instead of causing unnecessary anxiety? All this protective equipment is really frightening. What about us?"
About a week ago, it was revealed that the Prime Minister's Office spent 127,432,277 shekels (about $41 million) on security projects at prime ministerial residences between 2023 and 2026, during Netanyahu's current term in office. The properties include the official residence on Balfour Street in Jerusalem, his private home on Gaza Street, which has been designated an alternative official residence, and his private home in Caesarea.
According to the figures, 10.9 million shekels (about $3.5 million) was paid in 2023, rising to 27.8 million (nearly $9 million) in 2024. Spending then surged to 72.5 million (about $23.4) shekels in 2025, approximately six times the amount paid in 2022. A further 16.2 million shekels (about $5.2 million) was paid between January and October 2026.
When the figures were released, the Prime Minister's Office said they covered all residences under its responsibility, both official and private, belonging to current and former prime ministers.
The office attributed much of the increase since 2024 to changes in the security threat level that required substantial investment in protecting the official residence. The explanation appears to refer, at least in part, to the threat posed by explosive drones following the October 2024 drone strike on Netanyahu's private residence in Caesarea.
A month ago, it was reported that the Shin Bet and the Prime Minister's Office security division had constructed a 15- to 20-meter (50- to 65-foot) enclosed, secured passageway before Yom Kippur, connecting the Gaza Street residence to the Yad Tamar synagogue on HaAri Street in Rehavia.
The passageway, described as a "secret tunnel," was intended to allow Netanyahu to walk from his home to the synagogue for prayers. Air conditioners were also installed inside.
However, construction was halted midway, and Netanyahu ultimately did not attend services at the synagogue on Yom Kippur. The project nevertheless incurred costs and caused considerable distress to nearby residents during construction.

Why social media has become an election issue in Brazil’s presidential race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:14:02 UTC
03:14:02 KST

Why social media has become an election issue in Brazil’s presidential race
Critics have accused the tech giant Meta of censoring the political campaign of President Lula and favouring Bolsonaro.
In the race to be Brazil’s next president, the final two candidates are appealing to voters not only at rallies but online as well.
On Sunday, incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva will face right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in the final round of the election.
The race is expected to be tight. But in its final days, questions have festered over whether the digital arena has been a level playing field for the two candidates.
The social media giant Meta, which owns Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram, has faced accusations before Brazil’s top election authority, the Superior Electoral Court (TSE), that it suppressed Lula’s content and favoured material promoting Bolsonaro.
Meta’s products rank among the most popular social media platforms in Brazil, and political ad spending on its sites has grown at a breakneck pace.
An analysis from the Brazilian news outlet G1 found that Meta received at least 288m Brazilian reais ($57m) in direct campaign spending in 2026, double what it received during the 2022 presidential race.
That increase marks a shift in how Brazil runs elections. More than 76 percent of Brazilian voters now get their news online, said Andre K Rodarte, a researcher at the Digital Democracy Centre at the University of Southern Denmark.
With social media eclipsing traditional advertising, Rodarte explained that a growing class of politicians is using provocative, viral messaging to connect with voters.
He pointed to the success of online influencers like right-wing personality Nikolas Ferreira and left-wing activist Erika Hilton, who each were reelected this year to Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies with record numbers of votes.
“You are seeing people transitioning from information-producer roles to politics, and they are just getting more and more power, more and more votes,” Rodarte told Al Jazeera. “If this is the media landscape they are dealing with, it’s unlikely they will adopt a different campaign style, or different style of politics.”
But critics warn that this shift to online campaigning has put political hopefuls at the mercy of Big Tech corporations and their biases.
Effort to regulate
In Brazil, the reliance on online campaigning first took off in 2018, with the election of President Jair Bolsonaro, according to Leticia Cesarino, an anthropologist at the Federal University of Santa Catarina who studies far-right politics online.
Jair, a far-right leader, is the father of this year’s presidential frontrunner, Flavio Bolsonaro.
When Jair first ran for president eight years ago, his platform promised tough-on-crime tactics and a return to traditional Christian family values, which he spread through bite-sized social media posts.
At his 2019 inauguration, supporters chanted “Facebook!” and “WhatsApp!” in unison to show their support for his online presence.
“Since then, the left and pro-democracy actors have slowly come to recognise the importance of such media for elections and learned how to deploy it strategically,” Cesarino told Al Jazeera.
“They still lag significantly behind the far right when it comes to digital communication, though, especially since the kind of logic that underlies the attention economy is structurally beneficial to the kind of alarmistic, simplistic, affect-laden far-right discourse.”
But during his presidential term, Jair used his social media platforms to cast doubt on the accuracy of Brazil’s election system.
After losing the 2022 election, Jair continued to spread false claims that the vote had been rigged. His supporters ultimately stormed three buildings – Congress, the Supreme Court and the presidential palace – in the capital, Brasilia, on January 8, 2023, after Lula was sworn in.
In the aftermath, the TSE ruled that Jair had abused his position to undermine the election and prohibited him from holding public office for eight years.
He is currently serving a separate 27-year sentence for plotting a coup. He is also barred from using social media.
The scandal “really shocked a lot of policymakers and political elites to act”, said Vicky Wyatt, a campaign director at Eko, a coalition advocating for more accountability from tech companies.
Although Brazil had already passed some data privacy and data protection laws, leaders added a slew of new regulations after Jair’s presidency.
Brazilian law now bans depictions of electoral candidates generated by artificial intelligence (AI), and it also requires any political ads using AI to carry a disclaimer. Content that advocates violence, hate speech or gender-based discrimination is also considered illegal.
Only those with official campaign backing are supposed to be able to run ads on platforms like Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp.
The country, said Wyatt, now has “some of the strictest laws in the world when it comes to guardrails around the use of AI on tech platforms”.
But those laws have been the source of pushback. In a statement to Al Jazeera, a Meta spokesperson framed the restrictions as a potential threat to free speech.
“Meta has long warned that Brazil’s strict digital-content rules increase the risk of over-enforcement and threaten free expression,” the company said.
Meta accused of flouting regulations
Tech companies like Meta are supposed to walk regulators through their plans to comply with Brazil’s laws. However, evidence suggests Meta has not met its obligations.
Daniela da Silva, executive director of CTRL+Z, a nonprofit digital rights group, said some campaign coordinators have found their posts are not being shared as widely as they expected.
“They find their organic reach has decreased since the beginning of the elections, and they need to boost their posts,” da Silva told Al Jazeera. She added that some coordinators reported spending more than 70 percent of their budgets for such boosts on Meta.
As of October, CTRL+Z says it has collected 1,100 reports this year of accounts being taken down or having their reach restricted.
It determined that “the cases are mainly related to profiles supporting Lula”, who saw his own advertising account briefly suspended last month.
Lula’s campaign has cited studies by Eko, CTRL+Z and other groups to petition the TSE to intervene and enforce rules that require equal treatment for political campaigns.
Watchdog groups have also questioned whether social media platforms are complying with regulations that require them to remove false information and restrict AI-generated content.
One test, conducted by Eko, asked Meta to approve 15 election-season ads that included AI-generated content promoting violence and disinformation. In 13 cases, the social media platform approved them.
In another study, NetLab, a research group at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, found that Meta had allowed more than 1,600 political ads to run on its services, even though they were paid for by companies outside the country.
The group concluded that malicious actors appeared able to submit ads and tag them as non-political, allowing them to run on Meta’s services with little scrutiny, said Debora Gomes Salles, NetLab’s research head.
Meta made 2 million Brazilian reais ($400,000) from those ads, which, as far as Salles could tell, were meant to sow disinformation in the country.
Some told voters, for instance, that they could cast ballots online through a website that collected their private data. Voting online is not allowed at all in Brazil, Salles pointed out.
“Meta wasn’t really able to prevent these operations from happening, and even when it did do something and moderated this content, these ads were still a source of revenue for the company, and they already reached millions of Brazilians,” Salles said. “The damage was already done.”
Meta has repeatedly denied favouring any of this year’s presidential candidates on its platforms.
In a statement to Al Jazeera, a spokesperson said that technical errors were to blame for incidents like Lula’s campaign ads being taken offline temporarily.
The company also disputed the Eko report that suggested shortcomings in how it moderates campaign advertisements. The spokesperson said Meta’s system had correctly identified “content about social issues, elections or politics”.
“We removed ads that violated our policies,” the spokesperson said. The report’s small sample size, “out of millions in our Ad Library, does not reflect the scale of this work”.
Cesarino, the anthropologist who studies the far right online, said digital platforms will likely continue to spread problematic content.
The popularity of such content, she added, has contributed to the rise of far-right figures across the globe.
“It is not by chance that other far-right ‘populists’ rose at around the same time as Jair Bolsonaro in Brazil, such as Donald Trump in the US or Narendra Modi in India,” Cesarino told Al Jazeera.

A former Conservative election candidate has been suspended from the party after he was seemingly filmed discussing the cost of hiring contract killers and offering to “broker” the services of a far-right activist with alleged paramilitary links.
Jack Ross was filmed apparently asking an undercover reporter “What do you want done?” before listing the type of violent options that could be bought.
Ross appeared to tell the Al Jazeera journalist: “They can just kick the fuck out of someone. That’s a certain amount. They can start cutting people’s faces up, that’s another amount. And they can stab someone. They can shoot someone. They can kill someone.”
Police in Scotland say they will be reviewing and assessing the Al Jazeera documentary – Contract Killers and the Far Right – for any criminality.
Ross is the chief executive of Turning Point UK, a spin-off from the campaign group founded by the murdered US Republican commentator Charlie Kirk.
Footage released by TPUK last year showed Ross and others from the group meeting Kemi Badenoch, the Tory leader, after Kirk’s death.
A profile page for Ross on the website of the Bow Group, a Conservative thinktank that lists him as a research fellow, states he has advised MPs and candidates on political and digital strategy. He has been pictured alongside Boris Johnson and other high-profile figures including James Cleverly, Jacob Rees-Mogg and Liam Fox.
Ross was reported by Al Jazeera to have introduced an undercover reporter to a violent criminal from Glasgow with links to the paramilitary Ulster Volunteer Force, who offers to have people killed for money.
Al Jazeera approached Ross with a fictitious family problem where a deceased uncle’s business was at risk of being taken over by a gang, whose members were supposedly warned they would “get fucked” if anything happened.
Ross replied to this: “Yeah, you have to deliver on that as well. You’ve got to explain to me what’s needed … I can then go and broker from there. But I’ve got to say, even to myself … if there’s lashback I’ve got to keep my name out of it.”
The Scottish paramilitary contact was then filmed at a London hotel offering to arrange different types of killings, ranging from a hit-and-run that could be made to look like drink-driving to a stabbing.
The meeting took place after Ross, apparently acting on behalf of the Zimbabwean government, had reportedly paid thousands of pounds to the Glasgow activist to organise a fake political rally in support of lifting UK sanctions imposed on the African country.
Ross said: “I have had a few things and some of the Zims [Zimbabweans] have said to me they want stuff done. They wanted a fucking shooter.”
He said he had asked them to talk to the paramilitary, adding: “I said I was not putting fucking prints on anything.”
While TPUK was launched as a student movement, it has become increasingly involved in anti-migrant street protests. Its chief operating officer is Nick Tenconi, the leader of the far-right UK Independence party, who visited the Conservative conference in 2022 with Ross.
Ross was filmed in 2022 telling an undercover reporter they should chat to him about what they wanted, adding “keep it simple” and then listing the various violent options that could be bought for cash, including murder.
A Conservative party spokesperson said: “Mr Ross’s membership of the Conservative party has been suspended with immediate effect pending an investigation. We cannot comment further while the investigation is ongoing.”
At another point, Ross expressed concerns that journalists could be recording the sort of things he was saying and could pass them to police.
“The journalist will put it out there and then the police will pick it up and fuck you,” he said. “You’ve got to think that what we were talking about and had someone film it we’d be fucking done for conspiracy.”
Tenconi was filmed alongside Ross as they outlined a plan to use football hooligans to stir up trouble.
Tenconi said: “So let Labour get in. So we build the new right and we have these armies … so, three-pronged. We keep winning MPs over. Then we build the second prong, we build an army, and that’s street demos, protest, just fuck things up, basically.”
A Police Scotland spokesperson said: “We’re aware of the documentary. It will be reviewed and assessed for any criminality.”
Al Jazeera reported that Ross had “completely” denied its investigation’s findings, claiming that everything he said to the undercover reporter was not meant seriously.
Ross, who was a local elections candidate for the Conservatives, was approached by the Guardian for comment through TPUK. Tenconi was also approached for comment via his party.

Russian leader Vladimir Putin is “in principle” ready for Moscow to resume talks with Washington and Kyiv, the Kremlin said Wednesday.
During a meeting in St. Petersburg with U.S. President Donald Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, Putin said Moscow is ready to restart trilateral negotiations in November, Yuri Ushakov, a senior Putin aide, told reporters.

Advertisement

Earlier this week, the Wall Street Journal reported Moscow proposed a potential high-level summit with China and the U.S. to negotiate a deal on ending the war in Ukraine.

Sisi says Egypt would defend Saudi territory but rules out attack on Houthis in Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

18:12:27 UTC
03:12:27 KST

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said Egypt's military support for Saudi Arabia would be limited to defending the kingdom's territory and borders and would not include an attack on Yemen, the presidency said on Wednesday, as the Iran-backed Houthis intensify attacks on the kingdom.
Sisi's comments came as Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and intelligence chief Hassan Rashad met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Riyadh, Saudi state news agency SPA said. Abdelatty delivered a written message from Sisi to King Salman, and the two sides discussed bilateral ties and regional developments, SPA said.
Any Egyptian military backing for Saudi Arabia could mark a significant escalation in the broader Middle East conflict, which has threatened global energy supplies and pushed oil prices higher since the US and Israel struck Iran in February.
Egypt would also defend the territory of any other Arab country if asked, Sisi said, but its military effort would not extend beyond Egyptian territory or that of an Arab state whose security and stability Cairo was seeking to protect.
On Monday, Egypt's parliament delayed until October 26 a vote on authorizing the armed forces to support Saudi Arabia if requested, lawmakers said.
Saudi-Houthi conflict escalates over recent weeks
Fighting between the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognized government and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa and much of the north, has escalated in recent weeks.
Egypt and Saudi Arabia are close strategic and economic partners. Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states, including the United Arab Emirates, provided Egypt with billions of dollars in aid, central bank deposits and investments after the 2013 military overthrow of Islamist President Mohamed Mursi. Sisi became president a year later.
Egypt, a regional military power, previously joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015 in support of the government against the Houthis, though it played a limited combat role in the civil war.

Israel bans United Airlines pilot over Iran sympathies weeks after flydubai hijacking attempt

The Transportation Ministry has notified United Airlines on Wednesday that one of its pilots has been barred from entry to Israel as a crew member because of his history of Iranian sympathies.
The Diaspora Affairs and Combatting Antisemitism Ministry forwarded information that the pilot, Sina Amjadian, shared political and pro-Iranian regime posts on his social media accounts.
The case raises new questions regarding the vetting process for foreign airline crews, coming just weeks after an attempted hijacking aboard a flydubai flight en route to Israel.
Amjadian - a pilot of Iranian descent employed by United Airlines - shared images on social media featuring Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, alongside Islamic Republic flags, while criticizing Israeli military strikes in Iran.
Recent reports indicate that the pilot currently resides in Dubai. His LinkedIn profile states that he previously worked for flydubai before joining United.
Vetting process, security protocol
Transportation Ministry officials stated that the information uncovered by the Diaspora Affairs Ministry was initially passed to the Transportation Ministry's Security Department, which then forwarded it to Israeli intelligence and defense agencies. After reviewing the findings, security officials recommended prohibiting Amjadian from entering Israel as flight crew.
A formal notice was then sent to United Airlines, and the pilot's details were submitted to both the Israeli Aviation Security Center and the Population and Immigration Authority to block his air entry.
However, the Transportation Ministry clarified that following inquiries with United, it was determined that Amjadian does not operate international routes. Instead, he flies domestic routes within the United States and Canada. Consequently, the directive does not alter any existing flight assignments to Israel.
Khamenei imagery and criticism of Israeli strikes
Among the content Amjadian shared was a video showing people carrying portraits of Khamenei alongside Iranian flags and a black heart emoji. In an Instagram story dated June 15, 2025, he shared a memorial post for a Mahan Air flight attendant and her family members who were allegedly killed in an Israeli strike on their home in Tehran. Alongside the post, he wrote in English: "Since when did aircrew become military targets?!"
Reports from that period identified the flight attendant as Mahnoosh Haji Soltani, who was killed on the night of June 14 in Tehran's Narmak neighborhood. Citing the Iranian aviation news site Can News, the outlet IranWire reported that her home was destroyed by the blast wave during Israeli strikes.
In another Farsi post, Amjadian accused an unidentified entity of hypocrisy and of disrespecting others' beliefs. In a separate story, he shared an edited image depicting young girls with wings alongside soccer players, captioned in English: "We will never forget Minab." The post was timestamped June 27, without specifying the year.
Minab is a city in southern Iran where the "Shajareh Tayyiba" girls' primary school was struck on February 28, 2026. According to Iranian authorities, 168 children - mostly young girls - were killed in the attack. In March, Reuters cited US officials indicating that preliminary findings pointed to potential American involvement in the strike. However, due to the lack of a year on the story timestamp, it cannot be definitively confirmed whether the post referred to that specific incident.
Open-source intelligence (OSINT) researcher Travis Hawley also published a thread attributing expressions of support for the Iranian regime and Hezbollah to Amjadian. Among other claims, Hawley alleged that the pilot shared a video in which he kisses the emblem of the Islamic Republic and salutes. These claims have not been independently verified.
Who is responsible for vetting foreign flight crews?
The incident has reopened debate over who is responsible for screening foreign airline personnel entering Israel. According to Dani Shenar, who headed the Security Department at the Ministry of Transport from 1987 to 2017, a 2003 government decision assigned the department full responsibility for vetting foreign aircrews. Under this agreement, airlines are required to submit personnel data as part of the landing permit authorization process.
However, in this instance, as in previous cases, the Diaspora Affairs Ministry raised the initial red flags about the pilot rather than the Transportation Ministry's Security Department. Only after the information was handed over did authorized agencies initiate a background check, culminating in the directive sent to United.
This oversight issue previously surfaced following an attempted hijacking on a flydubai flight on September 30, when an Omani first officer attacked the captain during a flight from Dubai to Israel. The aircraft entered a steep dive before crew members and passengers managed to subdue the attacker and avert a catastrophe. The flight made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
That incident triggered harsh criticism of the security clearance apparatus for foreign aircrews. At the time, the Transportation Ministry's Security Department argued that intelligence background checks fell outside its scope and noted that it had not been provided with the names of flydubai pilots in advance. A senior department official explained that the ministry relies on background checks conducted by the airlines themselves and by security authorities in the countries of departure.
Police inquiry into senior Transport Ministry officials
Alongside public scrutiny over aviation security procedures, Israel Police have launched an inquiry into two senior officials within the Transportation Ministry’s Security Department: Avri Cohen, head of the Security, Emergency, and Cyber Division, and Dvir Rubinstein, manager of the Aviation Security Operations Center.
Reports indicate that Rubinstein is under investigation for a potential conflict of interest after it emerged that he provided paid training modules to foreign airlines, including flydubai and Emirates, while overseeing their security protocol compliance. Rubinstein works for the ministry as an external contractor, not a state employee.
Cohen is under review for secondary employment in foreign aviation security operations without the required clearance from the Civil Service Commission. Authorities emphasized that these are preliminary inquiries and do not constitute formal charges or findings of wrongdoing. The Transport Ministry previously stated that Rubinstein's side contracts were fully authorized under the law and carried out outside his official working hours.
According to recent reports, Transportation Minister Miri Regev insisted that responsibility for vetting foreign flight crews remain with her ministry's Security Department rather than being transferred to the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA). The decision adds to lingering questions about agency jurisdiction and Israel's ability to detect internal crew threats on incoming flights.
Transportation Ministry: 'We acted immediately'
In response to the report, the Transportation Ministry stated that it is not an intelligence agency and is not responsible for monitoring social media networks. It noted that the information regarding Amjadian was flagged by the Diaspora Affairs Ministry and was acted upon immediately once received.
The ministry added that its Security Department passed the information to the relevant Israeli security and intelligence agencies, conducted a direct inquiry with United Airlines management, and reviewed the case details. Following the presentation of findings to defense officials, a recommendation was issued to bar the pilot from flying into Israel as a crew member, and formal notification was sent to the airline accordingly.
While the incident highlights gaps in early warning systems for foreign flight crews, there is no evidence linking Amjadian to the flydubai hijacking attempt, nor do his social media posts directly prove involvement in terror activities.
The flydubai hijacking attempt
The directive regarding Amjadian comes approximately three weeks after the attempted hijacking of the flydubai flight from Dubai to Israel, which ended in an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. On September 30, the first officer assaulted the captain inside the cockpit, causing the aircraft to rapidly lose altitude until crew members regained control.
According to a reconstruction published by Walla, the plane was carrying roughly 170 passengers, almost all of whom were Israeli citizens. During the cockpit struggle, the aircraft plummeted more than 4,000 meters (13,000 feet) in under a minute. Once the crew re-established control, they broadcast emergency squawk code 7500, indicating unlawful interference or a hijacking in progress.
Following the event, Israeli defense officials recommended pausing flydubai flights to Israel pending the conclusion of the investigation. The crisis fueled widespread criticism of foreign aircrew vetting procedures and brought renewed scrutiny to the Transportation Ministry's oversight division.
No information links Amjadian to the flydubai incident, and authorities have not indicated that the ban against him was directly triggered by that event.

What happens next in court case for Helen Haines's accused attacker?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:11:22 UTC
03:11:22 KST

In short:
The man accused of attacking Indi MP Helen Haines made his first court appearance on Wednesday.
Brendan Nugent was brought into the Wangaratta Magistrates' Court dock by security guards, but was not required to speak or enter a plea.
The 43-year-old was remanded in custody and taken to the Melbourne Assessment Prison.
It could be close to four months until the man accused of attacking Indi MP Helen Haines faces court again.
In the meantime, police and lawyers are likely to be very busy.
Brendan Nugent's first court appearance on Wednesday played out in similar fashion to most filing hearings in Victorian magistrates courts.
The 43-year-old was brought into the Wangaratta Magistrates' Court dock by security guards, but was not required to speak or enter a plea.
No details of his alleged offending were aired and the charges were not even read out in open court.
He was remanded in custody and taken to the Melbourne Assessment Prison.
No application for bail was made on Wednesday.
If one was made, Mr Nugent's lawyers would need to prove there were compelling reasons for his release and the risk to the community was not unacceptable.
What do we know about the police brief of evidence?
On Wednesday, Magistrate Allison Vaughan gave police a Christmas Eve deadline to serve the brief of evidence on the defence.
A committal mention hearing was set for February 4, 2027.
Mr Nugent's lawyer, Chirag Patel, told the court his client had a rare neurological condition and orders were made so that Mr Nugent could be seen by a doctor.
Victoria Police's Special Investigation Unit is in charge of the case, and the brief of evidence it submits could be lengthy.
Typically, briefs contain police interviews, witness statements, security footage, downloads of mobile phone and computer data, and extracts of phone cell tower records. In Mr Nugent's case, it is likely police will scour the internet for his online posts.
Police can continue investigating and updating the brief past the December 24 deadline, especially if they need to order reports from specialists or request information from tech companies.
Usually, all relevant material gathered by police should be provided in full to the defence. That includes evidence which may weaken the prosecution case.
Once the defence has the brief, an accused person can decide how to plead to the charges.
What do we know about the charges Brendan Nugent is facing?
After holding Mr Nugent in custody for about a day, Victoria Police charged him with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official.
He is also facing charges of possessing and cultivating cannabis.
Even though the court process has begun, police are able to add, remove or modify charges.
At a media conference yesterday morning, Victoria Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush said further serious charges in relation to the alleged attack on Ms Haines were being considered.
Specifically, the Chief Commissioner was asked about a charge of attempted murder.
"That's always a consideration. Of course we have to locate and follow the evidence,"
Chief Commissioner Bush said.
To prove a charge of attempted murder, the prosecution must show beyond reasonable doubt that the accused intended to kill, their actions went beyond mere preparation, and they had no lawful excuse for their actions.
The state charges, dangerous driving causing serious injury and intentionally causing serious injury, are offences under Victoria's Crimes Act 1958.
A person convicted of intentionally causing serious injury faces the potential of a 20-year jail term. The dangerous driving charge carries a maximum penalty of five years' jail.
The causing harm to a Commonwealth public official offence is a federal crime.
Under the federal Criminal Code, the offence can be summarised as an offender intending to harm a Commonwealth official because of their role or something they did in it.
An attack on a politician carries a maximum of 10 years. It is a 13-year maximum if the victim is a federal judge, law enforcement officer or frontline worker.
What happens in a committal mention hearing in Victoria?
Given the nature of the allegations against Mr Nugent, it is highly unlikely the case will be finalised in the Magistrates' Court, which usually deals with less serious charges.
Mr Nugent has a committal mention hearing scheduled for February 4, 2027, at the Wangaratta Magistrates' Court.
However, it is possible the matter could be brought back for mention hearings beforehand, where updates on the legal case could be provided to the court.
At the end of the committal mention, a magistrate must ask Mr Nugent how he pleads to the charges before transferring the case to a higher court.
There is no guarantee that will happen on February 4, though.
Adjournments are common, often because police need more time to gather evidence, legal issues arise or the parties are negotiating.
Once the case has been transferred to the higher court, an accused person formally enters their plea again.
Committal mentions have taken on added significance in Victoria because law changes mean committal hearings rarely occur.
Committals served as "mini trials", with defence lawyers cross-examining witnesses and a magistrate assessing the prosecution evidence, before deciding whether it met the threshold to be sent to a higher court for trial.
Committals often revealed new details of prosecution cases, even though the material was sometimes highly prejudicial and had not been admitted at trial.
The law changes mean the prosecution case may only become clearer to the public once the trial begins or at a pre-sentence hearing.
The charges Mr Nugent is facing would likely be finalised in the County Court.
If he pleads guilty, more administrative court dates would be set before a pre-sentence hearing, where legal arguments are put forward and victim impact statements are read out. Afterwards, a judge would hand down a sentence.
If Mr Nugent pleads not guilty, pre-trial hearings would need to occur in the County Court ahead of a jury trial.
The same process would occur if police charged Mr Nugent with attempted murder, though that would result in the Helen Haines attack-related charges being moved to the Supreme Court.
Mr Nugent's case is well into the sub judice period, given police have laid charges and his first court appearance is complete.
There are limits on what the media can report about the allegations because a jury could one day have to decide the case.

No surprise and lasting anger: families of people who died in care homes react to Covid inquiry report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
18:11:16 UTC
03:11:16 KST

“At the time it felt like a devil’s bargain – it was horrible, but it was what [we thought] we had to do to keep people safe,” says Amy of the “devastating” and “terrifying” restrictions that led to her maternal grandparents being locked down in separate care homes during the early days of the Covid-19 pandemic.
Eva and Eric had been married for more than 60 years when her dementia and his increased frailty meant they needed separate residential support. When the first lockdown was announced in March 2020, however, it in effect cut them off from each other and their granddaughter, to whom they had been especially close after the early death of Amy’s mother.
“I spoke to Grandad on the phone when it was possible – it often wasn’t possible due to staff not being able to take him a phone – and he was desperately lonely, isolated in his room, unable to talk to anyone because they were worried about [the spread of Covid],” says Amy, 39, who lives in Milton Keynes and works for a large software company. “I consoled myself that they were keeping him safe. That all the isolation was necessary.”
Instead, she says, he was depressed and very afraid until he finally caught the virus in 2022. Amy saw him for the first time on a Covid ward, “when I had to beg and beg and beg the hospital staff to let me visit him”. Eric died shortly afterwards.
Six years after Covid struck, the latest report from the public inquiry into the pandemic, published this week, has convinced Amy that the policy of isolating residents was “cruel and pointless”, she says. “I want to smash something. I can never get that time with them back.
“The impression I had at the time was that [the government] were doing their best in the face of an unstoppable tidal wave, but it sounds like they put out a hand and expected it to stop the ocean.”
The inquiry concluded that the entire care sector had been an “afterthought” to government planners, and that a claim by the then health secretary, Matt Hancock, to have put a “protective ring” around residents was entirely unfounded. Instead, the decision to discharge untested patients from hospitals into care homes led to the virus spreading “like wildfire”, while blanket restrictions on outside contact led to “immense emotional harm” and “profound isolation” for vulnerable residents.
The findings are no surprise to the family members of care home residents, many of whom have told the Guardian of the immense distress their loved ones went through. Roger Dennison’s father, Lucius, was a sprightly 90-year-old care home resident when the first reports of the coronavirus emerged; they watched the news together in Lucius’s room and wondered how quickly it would peter out.
Weeks later, Lucius’s care home had firmly locked down, and the only way Dennison could talk to his dad was through a window that had been opened a few inches at the top. “You’re standing on tiptoe, trying to shout in and then be heard on the other side,” he says. “It was very confusing. It wasn’t very happy as an experience.” They tried it just once but stopped because it was too distressing for Lucius.
After that, Dennison, who had previously visited every other day, was reliant on passing messages through staff, while Lucius was “in his room, largely on his own”. The disease “became a growing apprehension for me once it became clear people were coming into the home and bringing it with them”, says his son. “I think there was a sense of inevitability.” Lucius caught Covid in the first wave and died in hospital in April 2020.
To care workers, too, the situation was terrifying and immensely distressing, says Nick (not his real name), who was a senior worker at a home in West Yorkshire. “The situation from the very start was frightening because we all thought that if you got Covid, you died or were going to be seriously unwell. I remember having to strip naked at the back door of my house because we had a resident return from hospital who had shared a ward with Covid patients. As a care home, we tried to refuse their return based on the risk of infection but were told [by the hospital] that we couldn’t.”
From that point, he says, “all hell broke loose”. “Our first case of Covid was about a week later.” They had already run out of personal protective equipment, he says.
“The mental health impact on all staff was huge. Watching people die at such a high rate in such a small space of time; having to say goodbye to so many people we came to know and love; putting our own health on the line every day and then quite possibly carrying that home to your family. Mentally, we were all spent.”
Like many, Catherine Bennett, a retired teacher from Lewes in East Sussex, says she was not shocked by the inquiry’s findings: “We knew what was happening. I am, however, very angry.” Her father, who had been in a care home since 2018, “felt a terrible sense of abandonment” that no one was able to visit and became paralysingly afraid of catching the virus.
“For a long time he didn’t go down for meals; he stopped doing all his activities so he wouldn’t meet anybody.” After some months, she says, the care home built a room where residents could talk to relatives through a glass panel and speakers. It was, she says, “very distressing for a man of his age to be separated from his loved ones in that way, to be able to see us through the glass but not be able to touch us or have any meaningful contact”. Her father died in the home in 2022.
Diana, a retired social worker from Derby, feels a similar lasting anger about the experience of her sister, Helen, whose mental health needs meant she was living in a care home in Carlisle when the pandemic struck, and who experienced a similar bewilderment at her sudden isolation. The first time Diana was able to sit with her was after a year of lockdown when Helen was very unwell; she died the same day.
“I just think they threw care homes under a bus while they partied in Downing Street, and I do feel rather cross about that,” says Diana. “I think it is a major trauma for this country and I think it should never be forgotten.”
