Controversial US-backed vaccine trial in African newborns halted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:18:56 UTC
02:18:56 KST

The US-backed hepatitis B vaccine trial in African newborns that drew global backlash was halted, the lead researcher said on Wednesday.
It was “now clear” that the study “will not move forward in Guinea-Bissau”, Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, a Danish researcher, wrote on LinkedIn, adding, “we were not given the necessary governmental approval.”
The minister of health in Guinea-Bissau, Quinhin Nantote, previously denied that the project would move forward. “This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese last week.
The study was to be funded with $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with another $1.6m from private partners like the Bill Ackman-backed Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.
“The solution is clear here: take the money and vaccinate as many kids as you can,” said Paul Offit, a vaccines expert at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, who sharply criticized the proposed study as unethical.
The government of Guinea-Bissau now has control over the researchers’ vaccines, which they apprehended when they searched the offices of the Bandim Health Project on Monday.
It was vital to support Guinea-Bissau in rolling the immunizations out to all newborns as soon as possible, Offit said. Guinea-Bissau currently plans to offer the universal birth dose in 2028.
The Danish researchers, led by Schaltz-Buchholzer, Christine Stabell Benn and Peter Aaby, hypothesized giving live vaccines, like the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG), may have an overall mortality benefit beyond simply preventing illnesses like tuberculosis – but giving another vaccine like hepatitis B alongside it could dampen that effect.
Such a hypothesis was “fanciful” because the hepatitis B vaccine is a single protein among billions encountered by the immune system each day, Offit said.
“There’s no evidence for that, and it doesn’t make biological sense,” he continued. He also added that there was a very clear benefit to giving the vaccine to babies as soon as possible, because of high rates of hepatitis B in the country and the possibility of lifelong illness and death from infection.
The Danish researchers did not respond by press time to questions about the study or to this criticism. The CDC did not respond by press time to questions about whether the funding, which was appropriated through its global health work, would now be used to roll out the vaccine to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau, as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO).
“WHO recommends that all infants receive a first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth – preferably within 24 hours – followed by at least two additional doses,” said Tarik Jašarević, a WHO spokesperson. “WHO remains committed to working with national authorities, researchers, and partners to ensure that all newborns – in Guinea‑Bissau and worldwide – receive timely, evidence‑based protection against hepatitis B.”
Those who declined participation in the study would not have received the vaccines – making true informed consent impossible, experts say.
“Imagine you’re a mother. You want to do the best for your child,” said Henrik Støvring, a Danish researcher who has co-published research raising questions about previous research from the Bandim project.
“If they decide to participate in the trial, they have a 50% chance of getting the vaccine for their children. But if they stay out, they have a 0% chance of getting the vaccine. So how can you say that’s a non-coercive informed consent?” Støvring asked.
The proposed trial led to distrust among Bissau-Guineans, who wondered if the vaccine – which has a decades-long record of being safe and effective – was being tested on Africans because it was dangerous, Schaltz-Buchholzer said in his post.
It “should be clear” that both birth vaccination schedules – with or without hepatitis B – are not “dangerous to anyone”, he wrote. There is a clear benefit to giving hepatitis B vaccines at birth, and not doing so can lead to lifelong danger, experts say.
Conducting a study like this “makes the case that there’s something that’s worthy of study, for which they have no evidence”, Offit said.
“We have millions and millions, arguably hundreds of millions, of children in this world who have gotten that vaccine as a birth dose or haven’t. If there was any evidence that this was problematic, you would know this by now,” Offit added. “We eliminated hepatitis B in the United States in children virtually within years of starting that program, so the benefits are clear.”
Schaltz-Buchholzer also cast doubt on the effectiveness and safety of the hepatitis B vaccine at birth, noting that he believes the study was canceled because it challenges “prevailing medical assumptions, such as that HBV0 does not have non-specific effects”. The study, in addition to looking at mortality, would have also examined side-effects such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. Dozens of studies have shown no link between vaccination and autism.
“All newborns should be given a birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine,” Offit said. “Guinea-Bissau is a country that suffers a high incidence of chronic hepatitis B. That country, more than any other country, arguably, needs to launch this program.”

A California immigrant and a Nevada group, joined by top Democrats, sue over federal election probes
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and others allege the Trump administration’s election efforts are unconstitutional.
- Trump administration officials say they are working to ensure noncitizens illegally registered on sloppy state voter rolls don’t negate American votes.
Top Democrats in Congress have joined a California immigrant and the Nevada State Democratic Party in suing the Trump administration over its unprecedented voter fraud probes in both states and broader efforts to meddle in state-run elections nationwide — alleging they are a “pretext to seize control over elections.”
The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Washington, D.C., late Tuesday, accuses President Trump, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Atty. Gen. Todd Blanche and the agencies they lead of using “shoddily compiled lists of supposed noncitizens” and “coercive threats of legal retaliation against state officials” to assert federal control over the Nov. 3 midterms.
In addition to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and several national Democratic groups, the plaintiffs include Erick Jose Jimenez, an “active California voter” and naturalized U.S. citizen since 2006 who now “fears that he will be unlawfully targeted for voting and disenfranchised (or worse)” given the Trump administration’s track record of misidentifying naturalized citizens as noncitizens.
Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement that while “Democrats and the media continue to dismiss concerns about voter fraud, the Trump Administration is taking decisive lawful action to protect our elections,” including by “prosecuting election crimes, strengthening election infrastructure security, and protecting vulnerable voters from fraud and coercion.”
“Anyone who illegally votes in our elections will be held accountable,” Bis said.
Filings in the Justice Department’s lawsuit accusing California officials of facilitating election fraud reveal new details about the underlying investigations.
A Justice Department spokesperson said “election integrity is a top priority” and that the department’s actions are “grounded in the law and being litigated in open court.” A Homeland Security spokesperson said it is “laser focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and preventing the dilution of the votes of U.S. citizens.”
Officials from both agencies have asserted that California and other states have ineffective policies for ensuring noncitizens do not vote — relying in part on voters attesting to being citizens — and staunchly defended their own processes for identifying noncitizens on state rolls.
Democrats and leading elections experts say isolated voter fraud does occur and should be taken seriously, but that there is no evidence of widespread fraud.
Tuesday’s lawsuit cites Trump administration claims of thousands of potential noncitizens on Nevada voter rolls crumbling amid state scrutiny. It also cites an administration list of 20,000 “likely noncitizens” allegedly on California rolls being “proven remarkably slapdash” and inaccurate in recent litigation between the administration and California.
The lawsuit alleges a coordinated effort between Trump and other administration officials — in violation of the 10th Amendment and other federal law — to intimidate state and local elections officials nationwide into removing voters from rolls, denying ballots to legally registered voters and segregating the ballots of others “based on spurious and unreliable claims that they are not citizens.”
It says the president is pushing the above efforts not “in a vacuum,” but in the face of repeated steps by Congress and the courts to block his election agenda.
The lawsuit, backed by prominent Democratic elections attorney Marc Elias, follows another filed in the same court last month by attorneys with the UCLA Voting Rights Project, on behalf of the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, or CHIRLA, and a California voter named Pedro Trujillo.
Several green card holders arrested in a Trump administration crackdown on alleged California voter fraud appeared in court Monday, with some saying they had no recollection of ever registering to cast ballots.
That ongoing lawsuit challenges the Trump administration’s use of unproven federal databases to allege registered California voters are not citizens, which it says risks misidentifying eligible voters and has left naturalized citizens frightened — the same argument made by Jimenez.
Jimenez, who could not be reached for comment, has “eagerly and consistently exercised his right to vote” since becoming a citizen two decades ago, and plans to vote in the Nov. 3 election but fears being misidentified as a noncitizen and targeted, Tuesday’s lawsuit says.
Administration officials have defended the accuracy of their lists, including in the lawsuit the Justice Department filed against California last week. In that case, the Trump administration has asked the court to force California to set aside the ballots of the 20,000 “likely noncitizens” it flagged until their citizenship is confirmed.
First Assistant U.S. Atty. Bill Essayli, the lead federal prosecutor in L.A., has said that list was compiled using public California voter registration records and third-party and law enforcement data, and that federal authorities have “overwhelming evidence” that those voters are ineligible.
On Monday, federal authorities filed fraudulent registration and other election-related charges against 28 lawful permanent residents in California, which Essayli said “prove our list is accurate and that noncitizens are actually voting.”
However, other administration officials have acknowledged the lists may not be entirely accurate. Acting Deputy Atty. Gen. Trent McCotter said Monday that “there may be some names on there who, it turns out, ultimately are citizens.” A Homeland Security official said in a court filing Monday that “discrepancies” have been found in about 189 of the records.
California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Dean Logan, head of the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk’s office — both named defendants in the California case — have accused the Trump administration of illegally interfering in state elections and trying to purge voters in the immediate lead up to an election in violation of federal law using inaccurate data.
Logan’s office said Tuesday that a preliminary analysis of a subset of the administration’s list found many were born in the U.S., weren’t registered or had never voted.

Pakistan’s cultural heritage takes center stage at Tehran exhibition

Pakistan’s cultural heritage takes center stage at Tehran exhibition
TEHRAN-An exhibition exploring Pakistan’s historical and cultural development, from ancient civilizations to its enduring literary traditions, was inaugurated in Tehran on Tuesday, bringing together diplomats, cultural officials and researchers to highlight the longstanding ties between Iran and Pakistan.
Titled “Pakistan Through the Ages,” the exhibition was organized by the Embassy of Pakistan in Tehran in collaboration with the ECO Cultural Institute (ECI). It featured historical photographs, calligraphy, paintings and visual records from different periods, offering visitors an overview of Pakistan’s rich cultural heritage.
The event also provided a platform for discussions on the countries’ shared civilizational legacy, the influence of Persian language and literature on the Indian subcontinent, and the potential for expanding cultural and tourism cooperation across the region.
Ambassador Imran Ahmed Siddiqui, Pakistan’s ambassador to Iran, was unable to attend the ceremony, as he was accompanying a Pakistani delegation led by Field Marshal Asim Munir during its engagements in Tehran. His remarks were delivered by Ismat Hassan Sial, deputy head of mission at the Pakistani Embassy.
Addressing the gathering, Ambassador Muhammad Hassan, president of the ECO Cultural Institute, welcomed the participants and described Pakistan as a country whose identity has been shaped by numerous languages, communities, customs and historical experiences.
He emphasized that Pakistan’s cultural richness could not be reduced to a single, uniform narrative. Rather, it reflected the distinct traditions of its regions and communities, each contributing to the country’s broader national identity.
Hassan referred to the Sufi poetry and music of Sindh, Punjab’s literary heritage, Balochistan’s poetry and handicrafts, and the storytelling and hospitality traditions of the Pashtun communities in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. He also drew attention to the distinctive heritage of the Kalash communities in Chitral and the linguistic and cultural diversity of Gilgit-Baltistan and Hunza.
These regions, he said, bear witness to centuries of interaction among South Asian, Central Asian and Tibetan cultures. Mountain ranges, rather than serving merely as barriers, have often provided routes for trade, migration and cultural exchange.
He added that national unity did not require the erasure of cultural differences. Respect for local identities and support for their development could instead strengthen social cohesion and deepen mutual understanding.
The exhibition also highlighted the influence of Islamic civilization and Persian cultural traditions on Pakistan’s historical and literary development, underscoring the role of language, music and poetry in connecting communities across the region.
Anoushirvan Mohseni Bandpei, Iran’s deputy minister of cultural heritage, tourism and handicrafts for tourism affairs, highlighted the potential of the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO) to promote regional integration and create new opportunities for sustainable development.
He said tourism could serve as an effective instrument for economic growth, closer cooperation among member states and greater familiarity among their peoples. Developing joint tourism routes, facilitating travel, promoting shared cultural attractions and encouraging cooperation between public and private sectors were among the measures that could advance these objectives.
Mohseni Bandpei also emphasized Pakistan’s strategic geographical position at the crossroads of South Asia, Central Asia and West Asia, describing the country’s active participation as important to the realization of ECO’s regional goals.
Turning to bilateral relations, he said Iran and Pakistan shared interests in regional peace and stability, economic development, public welfare and sustainable cooperation. Their relationship extended beyond political and economic ties to encompass a long history of cultural, linguistic and literary interaction.
He also welcomed Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts to encourage dialogue and peaceful negotiations, stressing that mutual understanding and confidence-building were essential to lasting peace. Expanding language education, academic exchanges and opportunities for younger generations to become familiar with thinkers such as Allama Muhammad Iqbal and Jalal al-Din Rumi could further reinforce the cultural bonds between the two nations.
Gholam-Ali Haddad-Adel, president of the Saadi Foundation, also addressed the gathering, describing Islam and Persian literature as fundamental links between Iran and Pakistan.
He said Persian had played a significant role in the transmission of Islamic thought to the Indian subcontinent, particularly through mystical literature and poetry. The historical influence of Persian, he added, remains visible in Urdu and Pakistan’s literary traditions.
Haddad-Adel pointed to the substantial collections of Persian manuscripts preserved in Pakistani libraries and the contributions of generations of Pakistani poets who wrote in Persian. He also highlighted the importance of Allama Iqbal, whose intellectual and literary legacy represents a significant connection between the two countries.
Drawing a comparison between Lahore and Isfahan, he noted that the cities share recognizable cultural and historical features that reflect their longstanding connections.
The speakers agreed that the region’s shared heritage provides a valuable foundation for closer cultural relations and regional cooperation. The exhibition served as a reminder that centuries of interaction among civilizations have left a lasting imprint on the languages, literature and traditions of the peoples of the region.

A ‘pipe dream of EU hawks’: What’s in Brussels’ new Arctic Strategy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:17:45 UTC
02:17:45 KST

A ‘pipe dream of EU hawks’: What’s in Brussels’ new Arctic Strategy?
The EU has updated its Arctic strategy, and militarism has replaced climate activism as Brussels’ new preoccupation in the frozen north. Despite what the new strategy claims, however, the Arctic is not “the EU’s Northern Neighborhood.”
Unveiled on Tuesday by the European Commission, the ‘Strategy for the Arctic’ describes the region as a “critical” zone for trade, investment, and conservation, and a flashpoint for military confrontation with Russia.
Today, we adopt our new 🇪🇺 Arctic Strategy. The Arctic is where the tectonic plates of geopolitics collide head-on. It requires us to change our strategic posture. And work with like-minded partners that share our values ↓ https://t.co/B6GvgUOCQk
— Ursula von der Leyen (@vonderleyen) October 20, 2026
“With Russia and China increasing their footprint and ambition, the Arctic has become a front line of global power competition,” top EU diplomat Kaja Kallas said in a statement. “Our revamped Strategy reflects this new reality and puts security firmly at its core.”
To understand just how dramatic this new focus on security is, it’s necessary to turn back the clock to 2021, when the commission released its previous Arctic strategy.
The EU’s green past
Published on October 13, 2021, the strategy opened by describing climate change as “the most comprehensive threat the Arctic is facing.” Russia’s refurbishment of Soviet-era military bases along its Arctic coastline was presented primarily as something that could “further aggravate the consequences of climate change,” and the EU pledged to work with Moscow “to improve environmental and health security,” and to leave military relations with Russia up to NATO and individual member states.
Four months later, Brussels severed relations with Moscow and entered the Russia-Ukraine conflict on Kiev’s side. The title of the 2021 strategy – ‘A stronger EU engagement for a peaceful, sustainable and prosperous Arctic’ – needed an update that reflected the EU’s new militarism.
Brussels claims the Arctic
“Russia’s unprovoked and unjustified war of aggression against Ukraine has reshaped the security of the Arctic and the EU as a whole,” the new document opens, going on to assert that “the Arctic is not someone else’s frontier. It is Europe’s Northern Neighbourhood and the European Union is part of the Arctic.”
Geography is not exactly on Brussels’ side here. The 27-member union has no coastline on the Arctic Ocean, and only two of its members – Finland and Sweden – have territory inside the Arctic Circle (although a Danish dependency, Greenland left the EU in 1985). Russia accounts for 53% of the Arctic Ocean’s coastline, and 45% of all land inside the Arctic Circle.
To compensate for this, the new strategy proposes that all waters north of 60 degrees latitude be considered ‘Arctic’. The commission argues that this would allow its environmental regulations to “cover the actual footprint of Arctic shipping.” It would also dramatically expand the EU’s ‘Arctic’ territory and population by bringing almost all of Finland and Sweden into the new region, including Finland’s entire 1,340 kilometer border with Russia. It is on this frontier that the EU is preparing for conflict.
War preparations
The strategy sets out a lengthy list of military objectives, with the commission promising to:
- “Deepen engagement with NATO” and hold military exercises focused on moving troops and equipment into the Arctic
- Develop military logistics corridors from central Europe to the Arctic
- Upgrade ports and airports for military use
- Expand icebreaker capacity
- Expand satellite surveillance of the region and tracking of Russian oil tankers
- Develop polar-capable undersea drones
- Establish a “Maritime Security Hub” and increase data-sharing with NATO
- Deepen military ties with Canada, Iceland, Norway, the UK, and US
The strategy is short on some specifics, and almost all of these goals are presented without an accompanying price tag. The only actual figures listed are €260 million for ten existing European Defence Fund projects, €107 million toward the construction of an undersea internet cable to Greenland, and the €200 million Greenland ‘Partnership Package’, which was announced last month. Although the commission says that this investment package will “support resilience, security and peace in the Arctic,” none of the €200 million in funding is earmarked for explicitly military projects.
Even though these objectives make up more of a wishlist than a set of concrete commitments, one in particular has the potential to push tensions with Russia to the breaking point. The strategy states that the EU will use its ‘Copernicus’ satellite network to track Russian “shadow fleet vessels,” thus making it easier for EU states to interdict and seize them. Belgium, Estonia, Finland, France, and Sweden have detained 12 of these vessels since December 2024, a number that would likely increase with the aid of satellite surveillance.
‘Shadow fleet’ is an EU euphemism for tankers carrying Russian oil in international waters. Russian oil exporters do not abide by EU sanctions, nor do importers outside the EU. Nevertheless, EU member states have abrogated the authority to seize them, in what the Kremlin considers “flagrant violation of international law” and “outright piracy and robbery.”
Should the seizures continue, Russian President Vladimir Putin has threatened to respond in kind.
The ‘hybrid war’ deception
The EU’s militarization of the Arctic is justified, the document states, as Russia is “pursuing hybrid strategies against its neighbours… from drone incursions and Global Navigation Satellite System jamming to the sabotage of undersea cables.” In the absence of real, verifiable military action by Russia against Europe, EU and NATO leaders have taken to accusing Moscow of waging “hybrid war,” describing drone sightings, fires, and accidents at weapons factories, protests, and even natural disasters as Kremlin-orchestrated plots to destabilize the West.
A wave of “drone incursions” across northern Europe and Scandinavia last year turned out to be a hoax, with Belgium’s defense minister attempting to pass off a photograph of a police helicopter as a ‘Russian drone’. Around the same time, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s PR team lied about Russia “interfering” with her jet’s navigation systems over Bulgaria. Western spy chiefs have since admitted there is no evidence that Russia has sabotaged undersea power and internet cables.
Nevertheless, claims of ‘hybrid war’ have persisted in European politics and media, to the point where some analysts view the claims themselves as a form of “hybrid warfare” against the European public, used to justify military spending hikes and welfare cutbacks.
“When you are sure it is the Russians, or almost sure it is the Russians, attribute it to the Russians,” NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte advised the bloc’s political leaders and intelligence chiefs earlier this month.
Russia has been holding military exercises in the Arctic for decades, and the refurbishment of its Soviet-era bases in the region has been underway since before the EU published its 2021 Arctic strategy. However, the newly militarized EU is no longer content to handle this matter through old mechanisms – namely the Arctic Council – and insists that countering Russia in the north is its responsibility as well as NATO’s.
The Europeans dictate their terms
The EU’s new strategy calls on Russia to “ensure that freedom of navigation is preserved” along the Northern Sea Route (NSR), a formerly impassable navigation corridor that can now be traversed year-round, thanks to receding polar ice caps and the assistance of Russia’s vast icebreaker fleet. The NSR cuts transit time from China to northern Europe in half, and in August, the first Chinese container ship arrived at the port of Murmansk via this route.
The NSR skims along more than 24,000 km of Russian coastline, and through internationally recognized Russian territorial waters. Russia is the only state capable of rendering assistance to any ships passing through the route, and vessels wishing to pass in winter must pay to be escorted by Russian icebreakers. Moscow retains the right to deny any ships access to the NSR.
Nevertheless, the EU insists that it has a say over Russian maritime policy, even as it vows to “continue to sanction the shadow fleet entering from the Northern Sea Route” and place Russian shipping under satellite surveillance. The latest Arctic strategy states that the EU will “actively engage” with other nations to ensure freedom of navigation in the Arctic, but omits any possibility of engagement with Russia. Only “like-minded partners,” a term mentioned nearly two dozen times in the document, will be consulted.
Diplomatic and economic disputes in the Arctic were previously handled at the Arctic Council. However, seven of the council’s eight members – every one except Russia – stopped participating in high-level Council meetings in March 2022. That same month, the EU joined Finland, Denmark, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden in suspending any activities involving Russia within the separate Barents Euro-Arctic Council.
The EU’s Arctic delusion
The central fallacy of the EU’s Arctic strategy is that it presumes Brussels can regulate, with laws or with arms, what Russia does in its own back yard. It presumes that the bloc, which has no Arctic coastline, can ignore long-established forums for cooperation and directly dictate terms to a superpower that controls half of the Arctic’s land and sea area; and that by repeating the mantra “the Arctic is the EU’s northern neighborhood,” it can overcome geographic reality and the massive power differential between Russia and everyone else in the region.
In a message released by its embassy in the Netherlands on Tuesday, the Russian Foreign Ministry described the document as “another pipe dream of EU hawks.”
“A quick reality check: Russia operates a fleet of 40+ icebreakers. How many does the EU have in total?” the ministry asked. “The Arctic should be a place of cooperation, not confrontation. Maybe it’s time to stop the provocations?”

The emperor has no clothes: Trump’s parade of power and the naked American empire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

The emperor has no clothes: Trump’s parade of power and the naked American empire
TEHRAN - In 1837, Danish author Hans Christian Andersen published The Emperor’s New Clothes, the story of a vain ruler deceived into believing he was wearing magnificent garments invisible to fools and those unfit for office. His ministers praised what did not exist, and the public followed, until a child finally cried out: “But he hasn't got anything on!”
Nearly two centuries later, Washington appears to be staging its own version of Andersen’s famous procession. Donald Trump continues to parade American power before the world, surrounded by officials applauding his decisions, even as the economic, military and political consequences of his confrontation with Iran expose a far less flattering reality.
Andersen’s emperor was not ruined by deception alone, but by the cowardice of those who knew the truth and chose to protect his pride.
Washington’s problem today looks remarkably similar. That child’s voice is the only honest sound in West Asia today. It rises from the ruins of Gaza, from the bombed suburbs of Beirut, from the defiant streets of Tehran, screams from the Minab school, from the mountains of Yemen. It says what the courtiers of Washington and Tel Aviv dare not: the American empire is naked. Its clothes are the fiction of victory. Its tailors are the lobbyists and generals who stitch wars from other people’s children. And the emperor, draped in the tattered myth of moral authority, continues his procession while his own people shiver.
Look at the latest spectacle. Donald Trump, the self-described master dealmaker, has announced that Russia will sell diesel to the United States. The Treasury has quietly eased sanctions on Russian fuel. The first tranche, he boasts, will flow immediately. But the arithmetic exposes the absurdity. America burns through millions of barrels of diesel every single day. The entire shipment would last barely a week.
Then the crisis returns the same crisis that has forced farmers to pay much more for fuel, that has parked truckers at the roadside, that has sent the price of bread and medicine climbing for working families. This is not a triumph. It is a beggar’s bowl extended to Moscow. The nation that spent years demonizing Russia now pleads with it for the fuel to keep its own economy breathing. The emperor has nothing on.
And while Trump parades his diesel-stained rags, the Pentagon buries its dead in fine print. The official count of American troops killed in the war with Iran has been revised upward again. Twenty-one dead. Eight hundred and sixty-five wounded. But the Washington Post reported months ago that the true toll was higher, that the military was hiding casualties from the public. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called that report “a complete lie.” Now the Pentagon has confirmed the very numbers it denied. The dead were real. The lie was his. This is the architecture of empire: it lies to the world, and then it lies to itself.
The lesson of the naked king is not merely that power deceives. It is that those who serve power will applaud the deception until their hands ache. In America today, the children are being silenced. Journalists are threatened. Whistleblowers are prosecuted. The wounded are hidden in statistics. The dead are erased from databases. The empire cannot bear the sight of its own reflection, because the reflection shows a hollow giant, bloated on bombs, starving for fuel, trembling before the very nations it swore to destroy.
The rot reaches the highest office. Speculation about Trump’s mental fitness once the stuff of late-night comedy has moved into the mainstream. Former allies, retired generals, even members of his own party whisper about frontotemporal dementia, a disease that erodes judgement, empathy, and impulse control. Psychologists warn of accelerating decline. The man who threatened to annihilate Iranian civilization in a late-night social media post is not the same man who occupied the Oval Office a month earlier. His former communications director Anthony Scaramucci called him “genuinely unwell.” This is not partisan malice. It is observation born of horror. A man with his finger on the nuclear trigger is unraveling before our eyes, and the world watches with dread.
Yet the psychological diagnosis, however troubling, obscures a deeper truth. Trump is not an aberration. He is the logical endpoint of a system that has spent decades convincing itself of its own virtue while committing atrocities across the Muslim world and others. The war with Iran was not his alone. It was planned years before, when Israel was moved from European Command to Central Command in January 2021—a bureaucratic shift designed to operationalize the Abraham Accords and align the region against the Islamic Republic. The October 7th incident provided the pretext. The slaughter in Gaza became the justification.
The bombing of Iran became the consequence. Trump is merely the latest actor in a tragedy scripted by the think tanks of Washington and the lobbyists of Tel Aviv.
Iran stands in the way. It always has. As long as Tehran refuses to kneel, the Zionist project cannot complete its map. As long as Hezbollah defends Lebanon, as long as Ansarallah defends Yemen, as long as the resistance axis breathes, the empire cannot declare its victory. So the bombs fall. So the sanctions tighten. So the lies multiply. But the child keeps crying out. The crowd keeps thinning. The parade keeps marching, but the truth is marching faster.
The emperor has no clothes. No diesel deal can dress up a failing strategy. No revised casualty figures can bury the human cost of his wars. And no amount of military power can restore the moral authority Washington has squandered. Trump may continue his procession, surrounded by generals, lobbyists, and obedient courtiers who applaud every disaster as a victory. But Andersen’s emperor had one advantage: his nakedness was merely embarrassing. Trump’s delusions carry consequences for millions.
The tragedy is no longer that the emperor refuses to see the truth. It is that those around him can see it perfectly well and still insist that he looks magnificent.

Japan suspended several websites, including government services, Wednesday after critical vulnerabilities were discovered in the widely used PHP programming language, according to Kyodo news agency.
The Health, Labor and Welfare Ministry temporarily suspended a website for its information disclosure system as a precaution, the news agency reported.
Online store service BASE also launched emergency maintenance, while Tokyo University of Foreign Studies ordered an urgent inspection of its web servers.
Sakura Internet Inc. suspended some service functions in response to the security concerns.
Japan's National Cybersecurity Office urged users to install security patches. "We are closely monitoring the situation," a government official said.
Australia's Signals Directorate also advised organizations and individuals to monitor their PHP applications and prepare to apply updates.
Developers warn of remote code execution risks
PHP developers urged users Wednesday to install security updates immediately after identifying two critical vulnerabilities that could allow attackers to execute malicious code remotely.
The developers released patched versions and warned that attackers could exploit the flaws without authentication.
In a security advisory, the PHP team said all installations handling web requests were potentially at risk.
The vulnerabilities, identified as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, involve memory-handling errors and outdated internal states that can persist between requests.
The flaws could allow attackers to execute malicious code on affected servers.
PHP is used extensively across the internet, meaning unpatched systems could present significant opportunities for attackers.

Greece’s alliances with UAE and Israel fail eastern Libya–Turkey test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:16:35 UTC
02:16:35 KST

Greece’s alliances with UAE and Israel fail eastern Libya–Turkey test
In the days before Libya’s eastern parliament approved a contentious maritime agreement with Turkey, Greece was trying to assemble its allies - Egypt, Israel and the UAE - to prevent the deal, multiple officials in the region told Middle East Eye.
But on Tuesday, the Libyan House of Representatives in Benghazi ratified the agreement, showing that a fractured Libya, at the very least, could come to a consensus in acknowledging Turkey’s sweeping maritime claims over the Eastern Mediterranean.
“Turkey has cemented itself in Libya. It’s almost impossible now for a Libyan leader in the future to sign a deal with Greece because there is a Libyan consensus,” Constantinos Filis, director of the Institute of Global Affairs in Athens, told Middle East Eye.
But the deal is more than a setback for Greece or a diplomatic notch in the belt for the Mediterranean. It underscores how the Middle East is rearranging itself in the wake of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and simmering conflicts across the region.
In sum, the partnerships that Greece depended on to counter Turkey in the Mediterranean failed to deliver because the Middle East is undergoing a geopolitical reordering of priorities.
Egypt and Turkey have mended fences after a deep rift, while Persian Gulf states like the UAE are looking for new security partners, with the Iran war on the verge of flaring up again. The irony for Greece is that the actions of its closest partner, Israel, have contributed to these shifts.
The maritime rivalry between Greece and Turkey in the Eastern Mediterranean long predates the fracturing of Libya into rival governments following the 2011 removal of Muammar Gaddafi. The two neighbors came close to war in 1996 over an uninhabited island.
Traditionally, Greece and Turkey could push the envelope in their tensions, knowing that the U.S. would intervene to prevent its NATO allies from crossing the line into direct conflict. But that dynamic has changed.
The U.S. is now less engaged in the Middle East and is at loggerheads with NATO on several fronts, like the war in Ukraine. Greece is a big spender in NATO, but Turkey has developed a domestic weapons industry of its own.
Turkey’s regional power is increasing, with an ally now governing Syria and Persian Gulf Arab states looking to it as a security partner as the U.S. steps away.
Tom Barrack, the American ambassador to Turkey and envoy to Syria and Iraq, said on Tuesday that the United States’ “grand bargain” of oil for security with the Persian Gulf was “transitioning”.
A Libyan source familiar with the matter told Middle East Eye that eastern Libya’s ratification of the maritime deal is one step in a wider plan to unite Libya under one government that the Trump administration has agreed to with Turkey.
The source said the United States wants Turkey to broker a deal between rival governments in Benghazi and Tripoli. Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin visited the latter on Tuesday.
Greece has sought new Middle Eastern allies as the U.S. retreats from its security role, and Turkey flexes its muscles in the region. The maritime deal Ankara has with Libya disregards Greek claims to maritime zones not just in uninhabited islands, but large ones like Crete, home to 600,000 Greeks.
Greece's search for allies to fill the US gap
Athens has doubled down on its relatively warm, historic ties to Egypt. When Turkey first signed the maritime demarcation deal with Libya’s Tripoli-based government, Athens responded by signing a deal with Egypt to counter it.
Greece has also moved closer to the UAE. Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis was one of the first foreign leaders to visit the Persian Gulf state at the height of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. In 2020, when tensions between Greece and Turkey soared, the UAE sent warplanes to Crete.
But most controversially, Greece has forged a close alliance with Israel, which is clashing with Turkey for power in hotspots like Syria and even the Horn of Africa. In August, Greece even agreed to purchase a $3.5bn air defence system from Israel - the largest arms deal in Israel’s history.
Eastern Libya’s ratification of the Turkish maritime deal stings especially hard for Greece because Israel, Egypt and the UAE are the main backers of Khalifa Haftar, the military commander who controls eastern Libya and has traditionally been a rival to Libya’s Tripoli-based government.
Greece has leaned on these relationships to try to counter Turkey in Libya.
Last year, Greece sought Egyptian support to forestall Benghazi’s ratification of the maritime deal. An Egyptian delegation visited Athens just five days ago to confer with Greece on Libya.
Khalifa Haftar’s son, Saddam Haftar, is increasingly seen as the next ruler of eastern Libya. Although Turkey intervened in Libya’s civil war to prevent his father from capturing Tripoli, Saddam has moved closer to Ankara. This summer, with some nudging from the UAE, Saddam was convinced to visit Athens despite his rapprochement with Turkey, MEE understands.
“It’s not up to Egypt or the UAE to support us in Libya. They have other interests. It was unwise for Greece to expect that they would support Greece at the sake of their own interests,” Filis told MEE.
Turkey and Egypt's rapprochement
Until a few years ago, both Egypt and the UAE were at loggerheads with Turkey. Cairo and Abu Dhabi supported the Haftars in Libya’s civil war, while Turkey backed the government in Tripoli. But since then, these countries have taken steps to restore ties.
Egyptian officials have stressed multiple times to MEE that Cairo’s rapprochement is not aimed at Greece. Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty held a call with his Greek counterpart on Tuesday, reaffirming their shared interests.
Egypt does not want to see the Eastern Mediterranean turned into a Turkish lake, Arab officials tell MEE, but Egypt and Turkey now converge in more hotspots than they compete.
Both countries are wary of Israeli expansionism in the wake of the October 7 attacks. Israel has carried out a genocide in Gaza and occupies swathes of Syria and Lebanon.
Egypt and Turkey are also aligned in the Red Sea. Both states support Somalia and oppose Israel’s recognition of a breakaway Somaliland republic. They also support Sudan’s armed forces against the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary, which is friendly to Israel, by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s own admission.
In Libya, there is also room for cooperation. Egypt wants to build a $1bn oil pipeline from Tobruk to the port of Alexandria.
While the UAE and Turkey are on opposite sides of these regional hotspots like Sudan, they have since moved to manage their differences. For example, in 2022, the UAE purchased Turkish-made TB2 drones.
Then there is Israel.
Notably, Eastern Libya’s recognition of Turkey’s maritime claims came the week that Netanyahu shared a map that showed the territory as “friendly” to Israel, the UAE and Greece.
Saddam Haftar even met in September with Netanyahu in the UAE, a Libyan source told MEE, confirming previous reporting. But Israel might see a wider Turkish claim to the Eastern Mediterranean pushing Greece closer into its orbit, one European official told MEE.
The fact that Greece’s partners did not mobilize to prevent Eastern Libya’s ratification of the maritime deal shows just how much the Middle East is changing.

Why is Europe on fire this October?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:15:18 UTC
02:15:18 KST

Why is Europe on fire this October?
The people of Europe are paying for a war they never chose
TEHRAN — It started with teenagers blockading their schools. Three weeks later (October 17), about 550,000 people marched through French towns and cities, according to Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez. Unions say 800,000.
Crowds followed in Milan, Lisbon, Madrid, Brussels and Tirana, and several marches ended in fires, looting and tear gas.
Though the triggers differ from capital to capital, the bill is the same everywhere: more for diesel, food and rent, less from the public services people already pay for.
Behind it sits a war that European governments say they were never consulted on, launched by Washington and Tel Aviv on February 28.
A bill Europe cannot dodge
Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which normally used to carry about a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas, was effectively shut after the attack on Iran.
Energy infrastructure became a front line. American-Israeli strikes hit Iran's Pars energy zone in Asaluyeh, a hub for processing gas from the world's largest gas field. Iran's retaliation forced Qatar to halt LNG production. Brent crude climbed above $100 a barrel.
Europe, whose gas market was already very tight after a cold winter, has been paying for a war it did not start and cannot end.
The European Commission puts the cost to Europe at roughly €100 billion in disrupted trade and energy markets. In some areas, gas has climbed about 140 percent and diesel has doubled.
On October 6, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said imported fossil fuels had cost Europe an extra €100 billion "without a single molecule of additional energy."
EU gas storage sits near 70 percent, well under the usual 80 for this time of year, and Germany's tanks are about half full.
Brussels now asks member states to limit heating in public buildings and switch off unneeded street lighting. TotalEnergies, meanwhile, has reported a surge in quarterly profit.
Despite ample evidence of their complicity, European leaders insist that the war is not theirs. Chancellor Friedrich Merz claims Washington consulted no one and has “no convincing plan.”
Polls show about 58 percent of Germans call the campaign of aggression against Iran unjustified and 68 percent of Spaniards oppose the war.
The invoice arrives regardless. The same reckless hegemon that started the war has imposed a 15 percent tariff on most EU goods, a deal Paris called a "submission," while it plans to buy Russian diesel itself while EU states fail to agree on relief.
Europeans are trapped in the orbit of a so-called ally that picks the wars and mails the receipts.
However, analysts warn against a single-cause story. Years of lagging wages and pandemic debt have left households without a cushion, so every new shock lands on bare ground.
A school blockade becomes a national crisis
The French movement began in late September, when high school students in working-class Paris suburbs blockaded schools over teacher shortages, crumbling buildings and lessons lost whenever absent staff go unreplaced.
The CGT union joined while the students were on fall break, then farmers, transport workers and public employees.
By mid-October, the unrest had escalated dramatically, culminating in about 2,400 arrests and hundreds of injuries, with shops looted in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux and Limoges’s 19th-century city hall nearly destroyed.
President Emmanuel Macron, in a rare televised address, acknowledged protesters' "legitimate demands" but blamed "far-left activists" for the destruction. He also described the Iran war as one of the main causes of economic hardship in France.
His government has already promised 3,000 substitute teachers and dropped planned university fee increases, an admission that the grievances are real.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in a post on X that Macron had “made his bed” by assuring Trump that he welcomed atrocities against Iranians. “Too late to blame the war his ilk helped cause,” Araghchi added.
The numbers explain the mood. Unemployment is 8.3 percent, and 21.6 percent among those aged 15 to 24. Consumer prices rose 3.1 percent in September, with energy up 21.3 percent.
Economists estimate a family of four has lost about €1,200 a year in purchasing power since 2024. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu's answer is a 2027 budget that freezes the civil service pay index and tightens sick-leave reimbursement to shrink a 5.4 percent deficit.
Bond yields rose on October 19 and a Goldman Sachs strategist expects higher taxes.
Rents, wages and a generation shut out
Housing is where the squeeze turns even more personal.
In Madrid, tents fill Puerta del Sol after the eviction of María del Carmen Abascal, 87, whose rent an investment fund raised 230 percent. She died in the hospital about two weeks later.
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's housing measures failed in parliament, so he called a snap election for November 29, and a general strike, Spain's first in 14 years, has been called for November.
The minimum wage is €1,221 a month. Rent on an 80-square-meter apartment averages about €1,130.
Portugal recorded the EU's fastest annual rise in house prices in the second quarter, 16.5 percent, and prices have more than doubled since 2017.
Lisbon rent reportedly equals 116 percent of the average salary. Tens of thousands marched there on October 17, and one official said the government would "not yield to shouts from the street."
Italy shows the same strain from another angle. Inflation hit 4.2 percent in September. Truckers, farmers and steelworkers blocked roads in the south, causing local fuel shortages.
"We cultivate the land, we harvest debts," read a banner in Gela, Sicily. In Milan, 271 people were arrested over two days, most of them minors, and a new October 17 Movement promises marches every Saturday at 3 p.m. The CGIL union has called a general strike for November 20.
Belgium saw clashes in Brussels and Liège, where police used water cannon.
In Albania, students in the Flamingo movement demand Prime Minister Edi Rama resign over corruption and a luxury coastal development linked to Jared Kushner, Donald Trump's son-in-law.
Money for arms, none for classrooms
Protesters in Rome, Brussels and Madrid have marched against higher military budgets.
An eight-country poll found 46.2 percent unwilling to back more military spending if it raises taxes, against 35.5 percent in favor.
Eurobarometer indicates 75 percent still support financial and humanitarian aid for Ukraine, but only 56 percent back paying for weapons. Governments plead scarcity when citizens ask for teachers and heating, then find billions for arms.
Moral anger runs alongside the economic kind. Pew finds unfavorable views of Israel at 73 percent in Germany, 75 in Italy and 69 in Britain, with deaths in Gaza above 74,000.
Sociologist Donatella della Porta ties Generation Z's activism to a chain of crises that includes solidarity with Palestinians, and Milan's march was held against war and living costs at once.
In France, 74 percent of voters under 30 say the political class neither represents nor listens to them.
Who is cashing in politically
The beneficiaries so far sit on the right. Marine Le Pen has made a deep cut in the fuel value-added tax her signature promise before April's presidential election, and Elabe polling shows her ratings up since the war began while Macron's slid.
The AfD leads German polls, with energy inflation at 14.9 percent, and wants to restore energy ties with Russia.
Giorgia Meloni faces a new challenger in Roberto Vannacci's National Future, and in Poland the Confederation of the Polish Crown is gaining.
Pew finds 69 percent of French people, 68 percent of Spaniards and 62 percent of Italians dissatisfied with democracy.
MIT economist Daron Acemoglu says liberal democracy stopped delivering shared prosperity to the working class and then grew used to dismissing its complaints.
Regarding France, Trump preferred another story, posting that "The migrants have taken over France."
Spain votes November 29, Italy strikes November 20, and France heads to the polls in April.
Each government tied itself to a transatlantic alignment whose costs now fall on its own voters, and none has offered a plan to reverse them. Until one does, the squares will stay full.

Burnham approves Jackdaw – and Labour’s unity on climate action is imperilled with the stroke of a pen | Zoe Williams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:14:42 UTC
02:14:42 KST

When the news broke that the UK government had approved the Jackdaw gasfield, I was at a Guardian climate event at the Royal Geographical Society. Appropriately, the theme suggested by readers was what can the public actually do in the face of what feels like paralysing climate doom?
There is so much going on that is hopeful: biodiversity tracking, river protection, rewilding. Shruti Suresh, from the independent watchdog Global Witness, told those in attendance that if they wanted to effect change, they should protest against Jackdaw and the Rosebank oilfield project. The message was so well understood that it didn’t need labouring. The mood in the room when the news came in was one of audible dismay. People had just watched the minister for climate transition declare that she could see the challenges ahead and was ready for them. The Jackdaw announcement will face immediate protest and legal challenge, but it sends a very clear signal from the government: we don’t mean what we say about ending emissions.
It turns out you can take all imaginable personal responsibility to arrest the climate crisis, make lifestyle adjustments that even five years ago you wouldn’t have dreamed of, miraculously summon the energy to take collective action from what is often private despair, but it will be insufficient as long as corporations – assisted by the government – are working against you, in effect with impunity. At some point, you need to get the people you elected to do what we all know – and they acknowledge – is necessary.
The Jackdaw decision had been quietly parked during the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, when the threat of the Greens seemed greater to Labour than it turned out to be. But while Labour successfully buried the issue during the campaign, the underlying issues surrounding Jackdaw – and Rosebank, which is yet to be decided upon – persist.
Since the 2015 Paris agreement, we have been committed to try to limit temperature rises to 1.5C, and we’ve known for at least five years that means the vast majority of fossil fuels have to stay in the ground. As of 2024, there’s been scientific consensus that the target of 1.5C is “deader than a doornail”, while this week’s emissions-gap report could not be clearer: the threshold will be breached and it will cause unimaginable damage, yet with urgent emissions reduction, there is a way back from the abyss. There is no workable argument that runs: “Everyone has to leave their fossil fuels in the ground, as a matter of the utmost urgency, except for us; everyone has to prioritise the long-term survival of a livable planet over energy bills, except for us; we all need to reach carbon neutrality and worry about high-skilled jobs later, except for us.” The Jackdaw field isn’t huge, will peak in a short time and won’t on its own reduce energy bills, which are determined by global markets. So it’s tempting to shuffle it off as a side-order issue, but it matters: it destroys our moral authority as a nation and it extinguishes hope.
The climate debate operates on two tracks that don’t meet. On the one hand, we talk about non-linear irreversible tipping points whose effects would be so seismic that the question of mitigation is too vast and, frankly, too painful to consider. The only bearable discussion of the collapse of the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC) – a system of currents within the Atlantic Ocean – is how to avoid it, and the contested matter of whether that is even possible. We talk about heat deaths across 854 European cities over the past summer, and we talk about areas in the UK of environmental deprivation, flood risks and poorly insulated housing. We also talk about food security both in the short term, with potato crops destroyed by the weather, and in the long term, with supply chains subject to the incomprehensible devastation of every country going through its own particular climate crisis simultaneously. We look at the social unrest across Europe – which is the fastest-warming continent – and ask to what extent the deprivation created by an unstable climate is being weaponised by a far right hell-bent on choking off climate action.
Then we gate off all that knowledge, all that anxiety, all that will to action, and turn our attention to the UK’s immediate energy compromises. The arguments here run that since we’re going to import gas from somewhere anyway, because any transition will take time, we may as well get it at home. Even though it’s well known that household energy prices won’t be reduced, the government can use the tax take to reduce VAT. Some categories of emission are lower from UK gas than they would be from energy imported from the Gulf.
We need to bring these conversations together, because what they describe is one shared reality. Alongside the carbon that Jackdaw and Rosebank would release, they’ve “sucked all the oxygen out of the debate around what to do about climate change”, Chris Stark, the former CEO of the Climate Change Committee, has said. A warm homes initiative would create vastly more jobs, research recently found, and by reducing bills would also bring far more prosperity, with the additional advantage of not undermining the climate goals we claim to hold.
Thinking of agriculture alone, the headroom, investment and planning we’re ploughing into carbon extraction could make an immeasurable difference to building resilience for an already uncertain future. The most meaningful way to reduce household bills is to reduce reliance on increasingly turbulent world markets, by separating the renewable price from the fossil fuel price, which would immediately boost the already flourishing wind and solar sectors.
Gas and oil proponents beg us to be pragmatic, while their own arguments are floridly impractical: conducted as though the outside world doesn’t exist; as though carbon emissions are tomorrow’s problem; as though there aren’t better solutions for high prices and insecurity everywhere you look; as though we have time to quickly exhaust all our bad answers before we move on to good ones.
One depressing aspect of the Jackdaw announcement – although by no means the most depressing – is that it’s all about the optics. Even its most trenchant supporters would admit that it’s not a long-term solution to energy security. Rather, it’s a flag to the fossil-fuel industry that the government isn’t an enemy. It’s a toxic smoke signal to the US that the UK might not be with it, but definitely isn’t against it. It’s a feeble attempt at domestic politicking by Labour, trying to deflate the Conservatives’ anti-net zero bubble. It’s a statement of intent to make no trouble, when the trouble is already upon us.
- Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

Mohebi also said Iran’s missile stockpile has increased by 1.5 times following the 12-day war between Iran and Israel in June 2025, without providing specific figures.
“The quality of the missiles has improved significantly, and their range, destructive power and accuracy in hitting targets have increased,” he added.
The IRGC spokesman said Iran is shifting its defense doctrine toward establishing permanent and absolute deterrence.
“Previously, Iran’s defense doctrine was purely defensive. We used to say that if a country attacked us, we would respond,” Mohebi said.
“Now, we say that if a country attacks us, we will not only respond but also launch an offensive,” he added.
Mohebi said Iran would respond to any assault with similar measures, stressing that the country’s military doctrine would increasingly rely on asymmetric warfare.
“Our doctrine will no longer be merely offensive; it will be asymmetric. We will attack the enemy in a way that makes them feel the intensity of our response,” he said.
Israel and the US launched a war against Iran on Feb. 28, while Tehran responded with attacks on Israel and US military facilities in Arab countries.
Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding in June, then began negotiations that later collapsed over disagreements concerning freedom of navigation and security in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a key route for energy and goods supplies.

Defense Without Limits
Iranian officials say Tehran will place no limits on hitting aggressors and their regional backers in case of a renewed US-Israeli attack
TEHRAN – The tone of the enemy toward Iran has sharply escalated again, with senior American and Israeli officials openly speaking of finishing the job and some analysts warning a new round of war is near, while Iranian political and military officials say the country is fully ready for a severe and unrestricted response.

"We will soon finish the job"

Russian Su-30SM Fighter Jet Falls From Sky and Crashes Near Cemetery in Kaliningrad
A Russian Su-30SM fighter jet fell from the sky and crashed near a cemetery in Russia’s Kaliningrad region on October 21 during a training flight. Both pilots managed to eject before the aircraft hit the ground but reportedly sustained injuries.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Russian media outlet REN TV on October 21, the crash occurred at approximately 12:53 p.m. local time in the Chernyakhovsk district, between the villages of Timofeyevka and Zelyony Bor. Both crew members reportedly sustained injuries and were transported to a military hospital.
Russia’s Defense Ministry confirmed the crash, stating that the Su-30SM had been conducting a scheduled training flight without ammunition. The ministry claimed the aircraft fell in an unpopulated area and that neither pilot’s injuries were life-threatening.
The Ukrainian OSINT Telegram channel Exilenova+ released footage purportedly capturing the moment the Russian fighter descended toward the ground and crashed near a cemetery.
The cause of the crash remains unknown, with Russian authorities investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident.
Kaliningrad is a strategically important Russian exclave situated between NATO members Poland and Lithuania. The region hosts the headquarters of Russia’s Baltic Fleet and several military aviation facilities, including an air base near Chernyakhovsk that operates Su-30SM fighters.
The Su-30SM is a twin-engine, two-seat multirole fighter designed for air superiority missions, interception, and strikes against ground and maritime targets. The aircraft is operated by both the Russian Aerospace Forces and Russian Naval Aviation.
Earlier, on September 7, two Russian Su-35S fighter jets collided mid-air over Russia’s Kursk region, killing one pilot while the other survived. The cause of the collision remains unknown.

French President Emmanuel Macron visited Riyadh on Wednesday for a surprise “solidarity” visit, making him the first Western leader to touch down in the kingdom since Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis intensified their attacks this month.

Mexico revives rare treason charge against former state prosecutor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:06:43 UTC
02:06:43 KST

Mexico levies rare treason charge against ex-official over US drug operation
MEXICO CITY, Oct 21 - Mexican federal prosecutors charged a former state prosecutor with treason on Wednesday after accusing him of allowing US personnel to take part in a drug operation in northern Mexico without the federal government's approval.
Authorities dusted off one of the country's gravest and least-used criminal charges against former Chihuahua Attorney General Cesar Jauregui, in a case that could reshape how Mexican officials work with US security forces.
Prosecutors allege Jauregui allowed US agents to participate in an April raid on a suspected drug lab in Chihuahua, a border state that has long been central to Mexico's fight against organized crime.
The raid only came to light after two of the US agents were killed in a car crash returning from the scene, drawing scrutiny from President Claudia Sheinbaum and pitting her against opposition Governor Maru Campos.
A judge ordered Jauregui be held in pretrial detention while the court decides whether there is enough evidence to formally proceed with a criminal case. A follow-up hearing is scheduled for Saturday, according to a statement from the Attorney General's Office.
Attorney General Ernestina Godoy said Jauregui allowed foreign agents to carry out activities reserved for Mexican authorities and failed to share information with federal officials as required.
FEDERAL CONTROL OVER US TIES
Analysts said the case could have consequences beyond Chihuahua, as the federal government moves to tighten control over security cooperation with the United States.
"The treason charge... seeks to set a precedent and prevent cooperation between (Mexican) states and the US government without the federal government's coordination and approval," said Matias Gomez Leautaud, an analyst at Eurasia Group.
He said the case fits a broader push by the federal Security Ministry to centralize information-sharing with the United States, curb unilateral actions by US agencies and bring state-level initiatives under federal control.
Gomez Leautaud said there was also a clear political dimension, given Chihuahua is governed by the opposition and could become a key battleground ahead of Mexico's 2027 midterm elections.
TREASON LAW RARELY TESTED
Treason cases are extremely rare in Mexico. No widely recognized conviction has been recorded since 1867, when Emperor Maximilian was executed after the government of Benito Juarez found that his French-backed rule violated Mexico's sovereignty.
Mexican law does not spell out treason in a single definition, but it broadly covers acts against the country's sovereignty, independence or territorial integrity carried out for the benefit of a foreign power.
In 2024, prosecutors also sought to bring treason charges against Joaquin Guzman Lopez, one of the sons of jailed drug lord Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman. That case has not led to a conviction, with Guzman Lopez currently detained in the US. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

As Miatta ignites the speaker’s gas-fuelled inferno, Reform show up as snowflakes | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:06:41 UTC
02:06:41 KST

When is a licence not a licence? When it’s a new licence that is an old licence. After months of faffing around – there were the small matters of a party conference and a byelection to negotiate first – the government finally gave the go-ahead to drilling in the Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea. What swung it wasn’t so much the irresistible excitement of creating 27 new jobs and securing 2% of the UK’s gas supply for the next 10 years, it was the politics. If other countries were going to carry on drilling then we might as well do so, too.
There would still be the same amount of greenhouse gases created and we wouldn’t have to rely on anyone else for our gas supply. Though we would for the other 98%. Small steps and all that. At a time of global insecurity and rising energy costs, it was time to drill, baby, drill. So the inconvenience of a Labour manifesto that promised no new North Sea licences could be rethought. It was now merely re-allowing a licence that had already been granted and then deemed unlawful by the courts. AKA dancing on the head of the pin.
Donald Trump greeted the decision with wild enthusiasm. Though he appeared to be under the impression Jackdaw would be drilling for oil and would turn the UK into a land of plenty overnight. No one in the UK could quite bring themselves to enlighten him. Fair to say, that not everyone in the UK was quite so thrilled. Not least Ed Miliband, the former energy secretary, and Miatta Fahnbulleh, the current one.
Miatta had sought permission to be as far away as possible from Westminster for prime minister’s questions and the subsequent ministerial statement on Jackdaw. So she had taken the trouble to go all the way to Aberdeen to make a television statement that she could have made in her own department. And she is the one worried about her carbon footprint.
Only it turns out that any amount of emissions is a price worth paying for a minister anxious not to have the hypocrisy of her former opposition to Jackdaw replayed to her by many of her own backbench MPs. Life comes at you fast when you’re a politician climbing the greasy ministerial pole. You find yourself in some awkward places, the most awkward being the House of Commons. Hence the – ahem – unfortunate diary clash.
The speaker was less than impressed. Lindsay Hoyle sounded as if he had swallowed a fistful of amphetamines and steroids and was mid-roid rage. He only just stopped short of calling the Labour frontbench a bunch of fucking fucks. Maybe he was just having a bad day.
For decades now, governments of all colours have been going out of their way to make sure that junior ministers take the flak to save their bosses the embarrassment of an hour’s humiliation at the dispatch box. The parliamentary equivalent of droit de seigneur. Lindsay demanded assurances this would never happen again, and the junior energy minister Michael Shanks duly nodded sheepishly. Not that he cared. He mainlines oil for breakfast. Inside, he was just counting down the seconds till the speaker had calmed down a bit. And then carried on as normal. Of course it will happen again. Maybe even next week.
PMQs itself also took on a familiar look, with Kemi Badenoch unable to make any inroads into Andy Burnham. You could even sense her frustration. There were times when she could get under Keir Starmer’s skin, but now both she and the Labour party have seen him off, she is faced with Mr Congeniality.
Against him, Kemi’s attack lines feel half-arsed. Not properly thought through. Everything she tries just bounces off him. He seems almost untouchable. Mostly because he’s a better politician, but also because he has the air of a reasonable grownup. Someone you feel is doing his best and comes across as someone you can trust. Well. As close to honest as you get in Westminster.
By contrast, Kemi feels like a second-rate opportunist. She tried making something of Labour taking years to approve the Jackdaw licence, a charge that rather melted away when Burnham pointed out we could have been drilling ages ago if the Tories had bothered to get the necessary legalities right in the first place. This was about putting pragmatism before ideology, Andy insisted. Fair enough. Though expect him to say precisely the opposite when it comes to the Rosebank oilfield. Then ideology will take precedence over pragmatism. Fahnbulleh had already as good as confirmed that Rosebank was dead in the water.
For the rest of PMQs, it was Kemi who was dead in the water. Seemingly having no other real questions she wanted to ask. It felt like she was sulking. Or underprepared. Her pre-budget attack lines went nowhere. First Andy pointed out that he was the only one with a plan to ditch the triple lock and sort out social care – still more vibes than policy – and ended by making fun of Liz Truss’s forthcoming new book on the mini-budget.
It wasn’t her who had screwed the country, apparently. Liz had been captured by the Blob. But it could have been any number of the current members of the shadow cabinet. Including the shadow chancellor who was part of the Trusster’s team. Incidentally, Liz was due to be interviewed by a robot on Wednesday afternoon at a Lincolnshire fair. But how would we know which was which?
That just left time for Burnham to take one question from a Labour backbencher about the ITV exposé of Reform. Though Nigel Farage had already left the chamber by then, so he couldn’t get all heated and declare that it was all a London plot and that it was perfectly normal for people to be as racist as possible in the comfort of their own homes. It was political correctness gone mad.
As if by telepathy, Zia Yusuf had chosen just that moment to post a video on social media in which he expressed his immense sadness that the media had stooped so low. He would be reporting ITV to the police, he insisted, because they had betrayed the racist code of honour.
How could everyday racists feel comfortable expressing their racism in the workplace if they couldn’t be sure that their colleagues weren’t undercover journalists looking to expose them? The world had gone mad. Who would have guessed that deep down, Zia – the man even the Reform elite have come to hate – was a snowflake at heart.

EU leaders to discuss 2027 money for Ukraine, next EU budget on November 26-27
BRUSSELS, Oct 21 - European leaders will seek to agree on how to finance Ukraine's €70 billion unmet needs in 2027 at a special summit on November 26 and 27 where they will also discuss the EU's next long-term budget, an official from the bloc involved in preparations said.
Ukraine, which has fought a Russian invasion since 2022, needs clarity on how to cover its financing gap for next year.
EU governments, meanwhile, need to agree on the bloc's 2028-2034 budget this year before campaigns for elections next year in France, Italy, Poland, Greece, Estonia, Finland and Slovakia politicise the issue.
Ukraine's 2026 funding is already covered, with some €31 billion from the EU still awaiting disbursement this year as soon as Kyiv votes through agreed reforms. The money comes from a total of €45 billion that the EU has for Ukraine this year, €14 billion of which has already been disbursed.
There is another €45 billion ($50 billion) from the EU for Ukraine for 2027, but Ukraine's needs will be much higher because the war with Russia is dragging on. The 27-nation EU had been counting on non-members such as Norway, Switzerland, Canada, Japan and Britain to contribute a total of yet another €45 billion spread over 2026 and 2027.
But EU officials say not all of that money has materialised and with Ukraine's funding gap for 2027 now estimated at around €70 billion despite the planned EU contribution, EU countries will have to agree on some new form of financing, possibly another loan. REUTERS

OpenAI has revealed that two of its artificial intelligence agents disabled or weakened systems built to catch them misbehaving, with one later denying it had done so.
The cases are the latest in a string of safety scares at the world's top AI developers involving agents, AI programs that carry out tasks without human involvement.
In a report released this week, the ChatGPT maker said that during two internal coding jobs, its agents switched off or undermined tools for detecting incidents of AI models acting against human wishes.
On October 3, an agent running on OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol model, which had been told not to send any messages on the workplace chat app, took that as license to switch off safety alerts meant for the company's security team while fixing a testing system.
Three days later, a GPT-6 Astra agent stripped out its own monitor while copying code from another project, then told the human programmer it had done no such thing.
The company said it had also seen several cases of agents launching software with monitoring switched off, exposing a gap in its oversight.
OpenAI said it is still trying to determine whether the models were simply overzealous in following instructions or have a particular tendency to evade monitoring.
"We don't yet have a satisfying explanation for this behaviour,"
it said.
The disclosure adds to mounting unease over how well leading labs can control increasingly autonomous systems.
In July, a group of OpenAI agents broke out of their test environments and launched a cyberattack on AI firm Hugging Face, causing international alarm. Other companies have since reported similar incidents.

Super Typhoon Champi sets the record for strongest storm of 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:01:31 UTC
02:01:31 KST

A cyclone in the Philippine Sea reached wind speeds of about 185 miles per hour (around 290 kilometers per hour) on Tuesday afternoon EST. Those wind speeds are the strongest of any storm this year, forecasters say.
As of Wednesday morning EST, Super Typhoon Champi had winds of 175 miles per hour; it is expected to weaken in the next day or so, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The storm is currently about 430 nautical miles south of Kadena Air Base in Japan and is heading northwest, according to the Joint Typhoon Warning Center.
You’re more likely to see strong storms in the western Pacific than anywhere else on the planet. But the typhoon underscores how tumultuous Pacific storm activity has been in comparison with activity in the Atlantic. In the North Atlantic, 2026’s strongest storm so far was Hurricane Isaias, which had maximum winds of about 120 mph (193 kph), according to Colorado State University’s (CSU’s) cyclone database. By contrast, in the northeastern Pacific, September’s Hurricane Polo hit wind speeds of about 178 mph (286 kph), while in the northwestern Pacific, April’s Typhoon Sinlaku and July’s Typhoon Bavi also reached around the same strength. Champi is the 25th northwestern Pacific storm this year, according to CSU’s tracker.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
To be considered a typhoon or a hurricane, a cyclone must achieve wind speeds of at least 74 mph (119 kph). The designation of hurricane or typhoon depends on where the cyclone occurs. In the Northern Hemisphere, Pacific cyclones that occur west of the international date line are considered typhoons, while those occurring east of that border are categorized as hurricanes.
It’s been a historic year for cyclones. As Scientific American previously reported, the Atlantic has been unusually quiet: Hurricane Isaias was the first storm of its kind for the season, setting a record for the latest-forming first Atlantic hurricane since reliable record-keeping began. Meanwhile the Hawaiian Islands in the Pacific Ocean have seen an unusually high number of hurricanes this season.
Those trends are driven in part by El Niño, a climate pattern that influences weather across the globe. During El Niño years, hurricanes activity tends to slow in the Atlantic and pick up in parts of the Pacific.
