It became like a ghost town, because nobody lives in the old town any more.”
Alice believes dark tourism helps a country reconcile with its past, even if the government decides what can be remembered.

TASA launches two more satellites in CubeSat program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:44 UTC
01:42:44 KST

The Taiwan Space Agency’s (TASA) Startup CubeSat Program has launched two more satellites to test technologies for a future low-Earth orbit communications network. Both spacecraft established preliminary contact with ground stations after liftoff aboard a SpaceX rideshare mission.
The two 8U CubeSats, T.MicroSat-3 and T.MicroSat-4, developed by Tron Future Tech Inc, were launched at 7:04pm on Tuesday aboard SpaceX’s Bandwagon-5 mission, which deployed satellites into a mid-inclination orbit, TASA said yesterday.
The satellites established preliminary communications with ground stations in Chile and Azerbaijan before 3am yesterday, and were in good condition with sufficient power reserves, the agency said.
Photo courtesy of Taiwan Space Agency
The launch marked the third batch of satellites under the Startup CubeSat Program, which follows a constellation-development strategy. By launching multiple satellites in stages, domestic companies can refine their designs based on the in-orbit performance of earlier spacecraft while progressively testing more advanced technologies, TASA said.
The two satellites would test beam-hopping technology, which allows them to adjust beam service times and coverage areas according to communications demand, improving the efficiency of satellite resources.
They would also test an intersatellite link to verify their ability to establish two-way communications and exchange data directly.
The team would further assess end-to-end data relay between the spacecraft to determine whether multiple satellites can work together to provide communications services, TASA said.
The tests aim to advance key technologies for low-Earth orbit broadband communications and coordinated satellite operations, the agency said, adding that other teams in the program are preparing additional launches.
Two more satellites in the Black Kite series, developed by Radiant Tech, and two in Fang Hsing Technology’s Albatross series are scheduled to launch in the first quarter of next year.
Those missions would continue testing satellite Internet of Things and ocean remote-sensing technologies, expanding opportunities for Taiwan’s space industry, TASA said.

Stuck shark in Busan finally returns to sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:41 UTC
01:42:41 KST

A shark that became a sensation after spending more than a month in a canal in the South Korean port city of Busan was yesterday guided back into the open sea, following two failed rescue attempts, the South Korean Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries said.
The shark, affectionately nicknamed “Bukhangi,” was first spotted in a narrow waterway at North Port on Sept. 18.
More than 1.6 million people visited the waterfront park through Tuesday to catch a glimpse of the animal, the Busan Infrastructure Corp said.
Photo: Reuters
The South Korean National Institute of Fisheries Science confirmed that Bukhangi is a female dusky shark measuring about 3m in length.
The species, which inhabits tropical, subtropical and temperate waters, is classified as endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
The shark’s prolonged stay drew particular attention because of the unusual location. The narrow canal is close to high-rise buildings and a major high-speed rail station in the heart of Busan.
Authorities on Sept. 29 first attempted to guide the shark toward the sea using vessels equipped with water jets, but the shark swam away and remained in the canal.
A second attempt on Oct. 2 involved a 50m-long and 6.8m-high net, but rescuers had to end the operation after the net was caught on rocks on the canal floor.
For yesterday’s attempt, authorities used a net attached to floating platforms, along with divers, to overcome difficulties posed by the canal’s underwater terrain and varying depths.
Workers moved the net toward the open sea while preventing the shark from swimming back into the canal. Drones were also mobilized to track its movements.
Busan livestreamed the operation as curious onlookers gathered along the canal for another glimpse of the shark.
The shark has been celebrated for its unexpected boost to the local economy, with Busan Mayor Chun Jae-soo thanking it for generating publicity he said would otherwise have cost “trillions.”
However, environmental groups said the shark’s appearance should be seen as a warning of the climate crisis, rather than a spectacle or economic boost.
They linked its arrival to warming seas, saying rising temperatures are pushing warm-water fish northward — and subtropical sharks in pursuit.

Mapping beaches for mine plans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:39 UTC
01:42:39 KST

The navy IS planning to hire fishers (“Military to enlist civilians to map coast,” Oct. 18, page 1). The Ministry of National Defense’s Defense Innovation Division is to contract private survey firms to fit civilian fishing boats with multibeam echo sounders to map the seabed to depths of up to 3m off “red beaches” where the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) would be most likely to land in a hypothetical invasion. Chartered aircraft carrying Lidar would map the sand above and below the waterline.
A senior official called the effort a first-of-its-kind initiative and said the data could show where to lay mines and place obstacles.
The move is overdue. The navy’s 192nd and 151st fleets have gathered hydrographic data on their own during exercises, but that method cannot keep up with near-shore topography reshaped every season and by every typhoon.
The ministry, US think tanks and the Institute for National Defense and Security Research have identified four to 20 potential landing sites, among them Jhuwei (竹圍) in Taoyuan, Wazihwei (挖子尾) in New Taipei City and Sishu (喜樹) in Tainan. Knowing the lay of those beaches is a precondition for denying access.
A survey is not a defense. It answers where to put mines, but it does not answer with what, by whom or on whose order, and the reports give no budget, no schedule and no list of which beaches come first.
Taiwan should treat the survey as the first line item in a funded mining plan for its red beaches. Otherwise it will end up with nothing more than an excellent set of maps.
The mine-warfare force Taiwan has was not built for the surf zone. The navy’s four Min Jiang-class minelayers, with six more due by the end of this year, carry 32 to 64 mines each. They draw about 1.6m, which lets them work up to the edge of the 0m to 3m band the survey boats will map, but not its inner reaches. Public reporting describes no surf-zone mine, and no public inventory of any kind exists.
“Delay, Disrupt, Degrade: Mine Warfare in Taiwan’s Porcupine Defense — an assessment by Jonathan Dorsey, Kelly Grieco and Jennifer Kavanagh published online by War on the Rocks on March 21, 2024 — said that Taiwan’s mine stock was relatively small and old.
The army has a partial answer on land. Taiwan News on Oct. 7 reported that the military is to take delivery of 14 Volcano systems, each able to carry 960 anti-tank mines, next year under a revised delivery schedule. The vehicles can seed beaches above the waterline, but nothing comparable has been described for near-shore waters.
The picture is bleaker when it comes to the issue of mine clearance. The navy’s six minehunters are four Yung Feng-class ships built in Germany in 1991 and two secondhand Yung Jin-class ships from the US. They can conduct limited clearance in calm seas against known minefields.
The NT$35.85 billion (US$1.1 billion) Ching Fu program meant to replace them collapsed in a corruption scandal in 2017, as I have written (“Mine strategy needs an exit plan,” Aug. 12, page 8), and no successor has been announced.
The Taiwan Security Monitor has described this gap between concept and capability in detail.
None of this makes the survey program a mistake, but it does make it a forcing function. The navy has to decide how it would use bathymetry at that resolution: bottom mines in deep channels and moored mines at varied depths to build the layered curtain that War on the Rocks describes, and decoys among the real mines to multiply clearance time.
Each choice implies a purchase and the survey sets the clock for making the decisions.
The case for mining beaches is strong. Geography helps: Taiwan has a limited number of landing beaches, and many are narrow and steep, which lets the defender concentrate its mining in a few places.
Timing helps too. During operations focused on Wonsan in 1950 during the Korean War, mines cost a US-led amphibious force eight days and four ships. China’s roughly 40 operational mine countermeasure ships might clear 32 to 80 mines a day between them, so cutting a passage through even a field containing 600 mines might take 0.75 to 1.8 days or longer.
Simple moored contact mines can cost as little as US$2,000 each. They target landing craft and hovercraft that are worth far more.
Mining can also tell the defender where an attack is coming. The War on the Rocks assessment said that clearing efforts are easy to detect and that China likely lacks the capacity for multiple feints, so the location of Chinese sweeping would be one of the most reliable indicators of intent.
Taiwan could reinforce the one or two beaches being swept instead of spreading thin across 20.
Officials say the data from the Defense Innovation Division program would identify deep channels for mines and reefs for obstacles, blocking routes that Chinese craft would use.
However, Taiwan is also not the only party mapping its seafloor. On Oct. 18, National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu (吳釗燮) said that there were six survey vessels among 16 Chinese ships detected near Taiwan.
The implications of the program to collect the data raises several issues:
The first issue is authority. Would Taiwan’s leaders authorize mining before the first shots are fired?
Pre-conflict mining is far more effective than mining under fire, but it risks escalation, and the question has not been tested in a public drill.
A plan has to name who makes the decision to act, when and on what warning. The Han Kuang exercises should rehearse that decision with real survey data on the table.
The second issue is mine clearance. A beach barrier that buys time should not become a self-imposed blockade of nearby ports.
Taiwan needs funding and a timeline to replace its minehunters, because mines that cannot be cleared constrain Taiwan’s own navy and shipping.
The third issue is civilian risk. Surf zones are fishing areas. The crews who survey them will know where mines might be and will not want to work the same water afterward.
A plan needs notice procedures, charts and a clearance commitment, or Taiwan will have mined its own fishers.
The fourth issue is data security. Defense officials say that civilian boats and aircraft collect only raw data, and that noise reduction, integration and the military’s tactical linkage would be conducted by the Naval Meteorological and Oceanographic Office.
That is a sound design on paper. It becomes a policy only when the contracts spell it out, particularly when Chinese survey ships, and by Wu’s count four suspected maritime militia vessels, are already working the waters around Taiwan.
The last issue is that the PLA might not land on beaches at all.
Planners already speak of “composite red beaches” that combine port facilities with terrain suited to airborne operations. That is an argument for extending the survey to port approaches, not for skipping the beaches.
The ministry should prepare the outline of a mine-warfare plan: how many mines, which types, laid at what depths, and from which platforms.
It should fund a replacement minehunting fleet and give the legislature a deadline for completion.
It should test the authorization chain in the Han Kuang exercises, assessing every facet of the process from collecting survey data to issuing orders to lay mines.
Mapping a beach is the easy part. The navy has shown it can pay fishers to do it. The harder test is whether it would pay for what goes in the water.
Ethan Connell is an assistant director at Taiwan Security Monitor and a graduate student at George Mason University’s Schar School of Policy and Government. His research focuses on maritime security and cross-Strait military affairs.
The most troubling message coming out of Washington for Taipei is not any single statement but the cumulative effect of a series of signals suggesting that US President Donald Trump is rethinking Taiwan’s strategic value while viewing the US-China relationship through the lens of a transactional great-power bargain. The danger behind Trump’s new softness toward Beijing is a potential US-China bargain that undermines Taiwan’s core interests. Brewers’ ‘Timeless Ticket’ deal upsets some fans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:37 UTC
01:42:37 KST

The Milwaukee Brewers ran a promotion over a decade ago offering fans a “Timeless Ticket” granting them admission to any game in the future if they paid US$1,000.
Now that the Brewers are in the MLB World Series for the first time since 1982, fans who took that deal are eager to redeem those tickets they bought in 2015. That has led to some complications.
Brewers president of business operations Rick Schlesinger said on Tuesday that several hundred fans had indicated they wanted to redeem their Timeless Tickets for a World Series game.
Photo: Getty Images, AFP
Schlesinger said that “we subsequently erred in our internal communications on the logistics of fulfilling the requests.”
“While we were able to accommodate all with seats, we received feedback from some that they were unhappy with their seat locations,” he said. “Clearly, even with extraordinary limitations on available seats, we did not live up to the spirit of the program, and we have been working through a resolution.”
Danny Fochesato of Milwaukee bought a Timeless Ticket on his 27th birthday, planning all along to redeem it whenever the Brewers reached the World Series.
Photo: Getty Images via AFP
The promotion enabled a Timeless Ticket holder to redeem that ticket and become eligible to buy three additional tickets to that game for the full retail price. The offer said the tickets “may be redeemed for the best available seat locations, subject to ticket availability at the time of redemption.”
“Back in 2015, that was a big selling point from the sales people about this,” Fochesato said. “They really touted: ‘Hey, this is going to be the best available seats. You’re getting the priority just behind season ticket holders. Anything the season ticket holders don’t have, you’ll have dibs at it for the World Series.’ That’s kind of the story they sold.”
That would have worked out fine when Fochesato tried redeeming his Timeless Ticket for a potential World Series game in 2018, when the Brewers reached the National League Championship Series.
Fochesato said he got four tickets in the 100 level behind home plate that he could have used if the Brewers had made the World Series that year, when they ended up losing to the Los Angeles Dodgers in Game 7 of the NLCS.
This time, he was not as fortunate.
“We had a form, and it only had 400-level or standing-room options,” Fochesato said. “We couldn’t even know what game we had. We just had to put a preference of which ones we wanted, and then we had to submit the form, and just sit and wait for them what we got. I immediately was like: ‘No, that’s bogus.’”
Fochesato said he bargained his way to three 400-level seats for Saturday’s Game 2 with the Tampa Bay Rays and one lower-level seat in the right-field corner for tomorrow’s Game 1.
He said he was in line for the public sale of tickets and saw better seats were available than those that were offered to him under the Timeless Ticket program.
The Brewers are trying to make amends.
Schlesinger said any Timeless Ticket holder who applied for World Series tickets before the deadline will now get to keep those World Series tickets while also being able to retain their Timeless Ticket to redeem for another game in any future season.
“We regret our mistake and look forward to welcoming them to American Family Field for their World Series experience,” Schlesinger said.

Photo: Chen Yu-fu, Taipei Times

Meanwhile, a national security expert warned that Beijing’s celebrations for Retrocession Day on Sunday and the anniversary of Sun Yat-sen’s (孫逸仙) birth next month are a bid to rewrite history to legitimize Chinese claims on Taiwan.
China over the past few years has repeatedly attempted to establish legal justifications for its claims over Taiwan through reframing World War II history, the Central News Agency cited the expert as saying in a government brief.
Beijing had commemorated Retrocession Day no more than once every five years until last year, when the Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress declared it an annual holiday, they said.
Similarly, China’s move to celebrate the 160th anniversary of Sun’s birth with fanfare next month is an effort to rewrite history with the narrative that the People’s Republic of China (PRC) is the Republic of China’s legal successor and therefore Taiwan’s rightful owner, the expert said.
Beijing is inserting the PRC into historical events that predated the communist state’s founding in 1949, they said.
China is uninterested in history, save for the advantages that come with being its author: the ability to control perceptions, dominate the narrative and provide legal cover for its ambitions to annex Taiwan, they added.

Typhoon Champi is forecast to have the greatest effect on Taiwan tomorrow and on Saturday, with a sea warning issued late last night and a land warning expected afternoon today, the Central Weather Administration (CWA) said yesterday.
The storm’s projected track has shifted slightly westward and it could begin moving away from Taiwan toward Japan’s Kyushu island on Saturday, with the warnings potentially lifted as early as Saturday afternoon, CWA forecaster Chang Cheng-chuan (張承傳) said.
As of yesterday afternoon, Champi was about 910km east-southeast of Oluanpi (鵝鑾鼻), Taiwan proper’s southernmost point, CWA data showed.
Photo: CNA
Its maximum sustained winds had weakened slightly to 209kph from 216kph, but its storm radius is expected to expand to up to 300km as it approaches Taiwan, Chang said.
The typhoon could weaken to the lower end of a severe typhoon or the upper end of a moderate typhoon over the next few days, as conditions are expected to become less favorable for its development after it turns north, he said.
Rain is forecast across Taiwan tomorrow, with localized heavy or extremely heavy rain possible in mountainous areas of northern Taiwan, while Taichung and mountainous areas in eastern Taiwan could have localized heavy rain, the CWA said.
Photo: Screen grab from the Central Weather Administration’s Web site
Other areas could experience scattered brief showers, it said.
On Saturday, brief showers and localized heavy rain is forecast for northern Taiwan, while eastern Taiwan and mountainous areas of central Taiwan are expected to have isolated showers, it said.
The storm is expected to move farther away on Sunday and Monday, although localized brief showers could persist in areas north of Taoyuan, eastern Taiwan and the Hengchun Peninsula, with scattered afternoon showers in mountainous areas elsewhere, it said.
The northeasterly monsoon is expected to bring cooler weather to northern Taiwan and Yilan County today, with daytime highs of about 24°C and lows of 21°C, Chang said.
Temperatures are forecast to rise slightly from Saturday to Monday, with highs of 29°C to 34°C nationwide, before another strengthening of the monsoon brings cooler conditions to northern Taiwan and Yilan on Tuesday, he said.
The public should beware of large waves from today through Saturday along the Keelung coast, northern and central coastal areas, the eastern coast, the Hengchun Peninsula, and Penghu and Lienchiang counties, as well as around Orchid Island (Lanyu, 蘭嶼) and Green Island, he said.
Foehn winds could push temperatures above 36°C in southeastern Taiwan tomorrow and on Saturday, the CWA said.
As Champi is approaching Taiwan, government agencies have stepped up disaster preparations, suspending some transport services and closing several tourist destinations, while airlines have canceled flights between Taiwan and Okinawa scheduled for today.
China Airlines (CAL) canceled six flights between Taiwan and Okinawa today, including services linking Taoyuan, Taichung and Kaohsiung with the Japanese island, and brought forward two other Taichung-Okinawa flights.
Tigerair Taiwan canceled several flights connecting Taoyuan, Kaohsiung, Taichung and Tainan with Okinawa.
Starlux Airlines and EVA Airways said their international flights had not yet been affected, but warned that weather conditions could prompt schedule changes.
Domestic carriers Mandarin Airlines and Uni Air also announced cancelations on several routes, while some services would be adjusted.
The Maritime and Port Bureau said several domestic ferry routes, including Keelung-Lienchiang and Kaohsiung-Magong, would be suspended today.
The Kinmen-Xiamen ferry service would also stop operating in both directions from 8:30am today, it said.
The Coast Guard Administration warned that coastal conditions are expected to deteriorate, with long-period swells already occurring.
People who enter restricted coastal areas could face fines of up to NT$250,000, it said.
Several tourist attractions are to close from noon today, including Wuling (武陵) and Fushoushan (福壽山) farms in central Taiwan and Taipingshan (太平山) National Forest Recreation Area in Yilan County.
Gueishan Island (龜山島) will also be closed for three days.
An army open-house event originally scheduled for Saturday at Chengkungling in Taichung has been postponed to Oct. 31, while a riverside arts event and water fireworks display in New Taipei City’s Yonghe District (永和) have been rescheduled for Saturday next week.
The Water Resources Agency has ordered river management offices to coordinate with local governments on flood preparations, including clearing drainage systems and checking flood-control equipment.
New Taipei City is deploying additional mobile pumps in low-lying areas of Wanli (萬里), Jinshan (金山) and Shimen (石門) districts.
President William Lai (賴清德) urged the public not to underestimate the storm even if it does not make landfall, while the Executive Yuan’s disaster response office called on central and local authorities to prepare for heavy rain, flooding, landslides, strong winds and dangerous waves.

Celebrity exorcist priest to take 1-year ‘media fast’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:35 UTC
01:42:35 KST

At the urging of his archbishop, a prominent Catholic exorcist in the Denver Archdiocese is taking a one-year break from public speaking and interviews, which have garnered millions of views on social media.
Instead, the Reverend Chad Ripperger would use his “one-year fast” to devote himself to the Society of the Most Sorrowful Mother, the semi-contemplative religious community he founded and the people it serves, the archdiocese announced in a statement on Monday.
The decision arose from a meeting Ripperger had with Denver Archbishop James Golka, who asked the Catholic priest to consider taking the break.
Photo: AP
“Father Ripperger readily agreed,” the statement said, adding that Golka is grateful for Ripperger’s “priestly service, exorcism ministry and for the generous spirit in which he received this request.”
It also said they would revisit this arrangement together at the end of the year.
Efforts to reach Ripperger through the archdiocese were not immediately successful, and the archdiocese declined to provide more details, including what led to the archbishop’s request.
Ripperger’s year-long fast comes about four months after Monsignor Stephen Rossetti, another Catholic exorcist who gained notoriety on social media, was removed by Cardinal Robert McElroy after serving as the exorcist for the Washington Archdiocese for 19 years. That decision followed a viral video Rossetti posted on social media, expressing his personal belief that many UFO sightings are demonic manifestations.
Ripperger said that aliens are “just demons” during a nearly three-hour interview on the Shawn Ryan Show, a wide-ranging conversation that racked up about 2.8 million views.
Ripperger said that famed inventor Nikola Tesla probably received messages from demons, and dismissed evolution as scientifically, theologically and philosophically problematic.
He has also made appearances on other high-profile conservative media platforms, including The Tucker Carlson Show.
Interest in exorcisms has spurred a recent memo to priests in the Archdiocese of Newark, New Jersey. In response to priests’ queries about the possible use of the Rite of Exorcism, they were instructed to treat distressed parishioners with respect and urge them to participate fully in Catholic worship while avoiding involvement with occult practices.
The protocol said that if a parishioner was still suffering from demonic influence after “prudent spiritual care,” priests should contact the Vicar General’s Office to launch an evaluation of whether an exorcism is warranted.
It also said that popular culture has reduced exorcism to a movie and fiction genre rather than what it truly is — “a pastoral act of the Church.”
The Catholic Church recognizes and authorizes the use of exorcism as a spiritual ministry, but dealing with Catholic exorcists with large online followings is a delicate matter for bishops and other church leaders, Villanova University theology professor Massimo Faggioli said.
“There is no canon law that is clear on this,” he said. The bishops “know that the online clergy have a following they can’t afford to alienate. It’s an area with not just a legal vacuum, but also a lack of understanding of what it means for the church to be present on the Internet.”
Celebrity priests can present big theological challenges for those who have spiritual authority over them.
These bishops tend to “embody a church that might be boring, but reliable,” Faggioli said, adding that it can also be theologically dangerous for online Catholic personalities to possess an influence that can be easily monetized.

Nvidia CEO encourages Europe’s lagging AI sector and offers tools to accelerate data center buildout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:35 UTC
01:42:35 KST

Nvidia Corp chief executive officer Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) urged players in Europe’s lagging artificial intelligence (AI) industry to get going and touted a modular system to quickly build AI data centers with the massive computing capacity the continent’s developers need but currently lack.
In an upbeat speech on Wednesday at the company’s GTC conference for developers and investors in Berlin, Huang also laid out tools to keep AI applications from running amok by confining them in a digital “sandbox.”
“Europe’s AI economy is starting, and it’s accelerating, and it’s great to see,” Huang, striding across the stage in his trademark leather jacket and sneakers, said in front of some 3,000 developers, analysts and journalists at Berlin’s Tempodrom auditorium.
Photo: Reuters
Huang, whose company designs the computer chips and software used by AI developers like Anthropic PBC and OpenAI, frequently name-checked European partner companies such as Siemens AG, Mercedes-Benz AG and Volkswagen AG’s Audi.
“Europe is building its AI economy” as the technology moves from language models to so-called physical AI in manufacturing, Huang said. “Every company in the future will be an AI company.”
Mercedes-Benz CEO Ola Kallenius, whose company is working on developing autonomous driving technology with Nvidia, said that the technology could reduce the number of auto fatalities caused by human error “down to zero... we will have safer streets once we have full autonomy.”
Huang said Nvidia’s design for the Vera Rubin DSK Pod, a ready-made modular computing center that is delivered in a shipping-container like box, will reduce the time needed to set up a data center from months to days. The pod “will change the way people build AI centers,” he said. Nvidia has invested US$10 billion in European start-ups and partners in the past year, Huang said.
Building out data centers is key for Europe, which has only about 5 percent of the world’s AI computing capacity, compared to 75 percent in the US. Lack of the massive computing power, or “compute” in digital jargon, needed to train AI applications is a key obstacle for European developers.
“The big bottleneck is compute,” General Catalyst Partners LLC president and managing director Jeannette zu Furstenberg said ahead of the speech. General Catalyst invests in AI companies.
Huang was briefly interrupted by protesters who stood up with a banner urging him to “clean up” his business. Huang promised “to talk to you later” and urged security to avoid rough handling as they removed the protesters.
Huang also addressed concerns about safety by talking about the company’s OpenShell open-source software designed to exert external control over what AI applications are doing and block them if they violate company policy.
The event is part of a tour through Europe by Huang, who has been signing deals with local companies and trying to persuade the continent’s political and business leaders that AI is safe. His trip comes at a delicate moment for the industry. AI stocks have been battered during the past two weeks, and the closely watched Philadelphia semiconductor index suffered its longest losing streak since 2008.
Nvidia, the world’s most valuable publicly traded company, has frequently cited supply chain constraints as an impediment to its growth. To combat that, Ibiden Co, Samsung Electro-Mechanics Co and Unimicron Technology Corp (欣興電子) will help it get more substrates — the materials used to house other components.
Amkor Technology Inc will help increase the amount of chip packaging available by fourfold by the end of 2028. That material is used to encase semiconductors and connect them with other components. KYEC Microelectronics Co, a subsidiary of King Yuan Electronics Co (京元電子), will increase testing capacity. Nvidia is also helping to boost the availability of on-package optical connections, which will speed up communication between components.

Five indicted over China-linked attack on comedian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:34 UTC
01:42:34 KST

Five Taiwanese men have been indicted for hitting comedian Huang Yi-hao (黃逸豪) with a car last month in an alleged act of transnational repression, after the entertainer made comments critical of the Chinese Communist Party.
In its indictment released yesterday, the New Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office said a Chinese national, identified by the nickname “K,” offered a Taiwanese man, surnamed Cheng (鄭), NT$450,000 to seriously injure Huang so he could not give a scheduled performance on Sept. 20.
Huang was hit by the vehicle near his home in New Taipei City on Sept. 11.
Photo courtesy of a Liberty Times reader
The five suspects have been indicted on charges including attempted grievous bodily harm under the Criminal Code and contravening the Personal Data Protection Act (個人資料保護法), the office said.
Prosecutors said they are seeking a minimum sentence of five-and-a-half years for the primary suspect, describing the alleged offenses as showing a disregard for human life, while also posing a threat to national security and social stability.
In a separate attack on May 29, two men threw a mixture of paint and human feces at the Comedy Club (卡米地) in Taipei, where Huang in December last year made comments mocking Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) during a performance.
The two men were indicted on charges including intimidation and property damage.
Between July and August, Cheng installed a GPS tracker on Huang’s scooter to monitor his whereabouts and record his daily routine, and found Huang’s home address and vehicle registration number, prosecutors said.
Cheng passed this information along to K in exchange for an advance payment of NT$250,000, they said.
He then conspired with a man surnamed Yu (游) to stage a traffic collision and another man surnamed Huang (黃) to purchase the vehicle and carry out the attack, prosecutors said.
Two other men, surnamed Fan (范) and Liao (廖), were also recruited to help in the attack, they said.
Liao filmed the attack from the front passenger seat as evidence for payment, they said.
Suspect Huang attempted to stop the attack after hearing Huang Yi-hao scream, although the comedian still sustained a contusion to his right pelvis, they said.
After the attack, the group obtained a medical certificate with Huang Yi-hao’s personal information, including his name, date of birth and national identification number, under the pretext of helping him apply for traffic accident compensation, prosecutors said.
They photographed that document and sent it to K, although he was allegedly dissatisfied that Huang Yi-hao had only sustained minor injuries and refused to pay the remaining NT$200,000, they said.
Prosecutors are seeking prison sentences of at least five years and six months for Cheng, five years for Yu, four years for Huang, three years and six months for Fan and two years and seven months for Liao.
The prosecutors urged the court to impose severe sentences as a deterrent to others.
Huang Yi-hao yesterday thanked investigators and police in a post on Facebook.
“I simply mocked Xi Jinping for two-and-a-half minutes on a stage in Taiwan, and was subsequently targeted in a feces-splashing attack and a deliberate vehicle collision,” he wrote.
Huang Yi-hao, who is from Hualien County, urged Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Legislator Fu Kun-chi (傅?萁), who represents Hualien, to support legislation protecting Taiwanese from politically motivated violence and show that he supports freedom of speech.
The Mainland Affairs Council condemned the attack, saying it would hold anyone involved accountable and bolster measures to protect Taiwanese from intimidation and violence by foreign hostile forces.

US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff yesterday urged Russian President Vladimir Putin to consider resuming US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine and to review new ideas on ending the war amid Washington’s latest push to stop Europe’s bloodiest conflict since World War II.
The talks in a grand imperial palace in St Petersburg, the ninth time that Witkoff has met Putin in person, began with a goodwill gesture from Russia — the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired US school teacher held in Russia.
Putin also offered to help US President Donald Trump in dealing with Iran, saying Russia had a decades-long relationship with Tehran, which it has repeatedly offered to leverage to address US concerns about Iran’s nuclear program.
Photo: Kristina Solovyova, Sputnik via Reuters
Russia could also supply large quantities of fertilizer to the US to help US farmers, the Russian president told Witkoff, saying he wanted to discuss a potential meeting in China next month with Trump, which the Kremlin has suggested could also include Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平).
The encounter comes amid concerns in Kyiv and among its allies that the US is backing away from Ukraine, at times holding back real-time intelligence on Russian attacks and hobbling Ukraine’s military communications.
The latest talks also come more than two years since Trump promised in his election campaign to end the Ukraine war within 24 hours.
“One thing that I hope to accomplish today is to have some good conversation between us about the resumption potentially of trilateral talks between Ukraine and Russia and the United States,” Witkoff told Putin.
“Even if we don’t have a resolution today, if we just talk about and sort of consider what that next step might be I think that would be important and the world is waiting to hear that,” he said.
Witkoff flew into Russia’s second city a day after conducting talks in Oslo with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, the leaders of Finland and Norway and European and NATO representatives.
Witkoff said he would brief Putin on the Oslo talks which he described as productive and said had been characterized by “some degree of momentum.”
A US official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said Ukraine had brought new ideas and proposals to the Oslo talks, which had made “meaningful progress” toward a coordinated approach to engaging with Russia.
The official said the talks covered “key elements of a comprehensive peace framework,” including security guarantees for Ukraine, a postwar economic plan and a broader European security architecture.
Zelenskiy said he hoped to discuss key issues on how to end the war during a trilateral meeting with Putin and Trump.
The Kremlin has repeatedly said that any Putin-Zelenskiy meeting would need to be painstakingly prepared in advance by aides to make it worthwhile.

Regulator blocks Grab’s merger with Foodpanda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:30 UTC
01:42:30 KST

The Fair Trade Commission (FTC) today blocked Grab Holdings Ltd’s proposed acquisition of Delivery Hero SE’s Foodpanda operations in Taiwan, citing concerns that the deal would negatively impact competition in Taiwan’s food delivery market.
Uber, the parent company of Taiwan’s leading food delivery platform Uber Eats, holds 13.1 percent of Grab’s shares and has close ties with the company in other markets, the regulator said.
Although Grab limits Uber’s voting rights to 3.9 percent, Uber’s stake in the firm, and the companies’ shared board members and past business partnerships could still affect how they interact and make Grab less likely to compete aggressively, it said.
Photo: CNA
Three of the five commissioners voted to block the deal, one voted to allow it and one abstained.
If Uber Eats cut prices or offered discounts to compete with Grab, it would boost its own sales, but hurt Grab’s profits, affecting Uber’s investment returns, the FTC said.
Their years of working together in other markets would increase the risk they would coordinate rather than compete, it said.
Taiwan’s food delivery market has high barriers to entry, as new platforms need substantial investment and must attract enough restaurants, delivery workers and customers to compete, it said.
However, restaurants and customers lack the bargaining power to counter major platforms, leaving little to prevent Grab and Uber from coordinating rather than competing, it added.
Uber would need to significantly reduce its stake in Grab or even sell all its shares to reduce the risk of coordinating after the merger, the FTC said.
Although Grab has proposed reducing Uber’s stake, restricting Uber personnel from serving on its board and limiting the exchange of sensitive business information, the measures would be difficult to enforce and insufficient to address competition concerns, it said.
The disadvantages outweigh the potential benefits in this merger, the FTC said, blocking it under Article 13 of the Fair Trade Act (公平交易法).
Asked whether denying the acquisition could inadvertently strengthen Uber’s market position by triggering Foodpanda’s exit from Taiwan, FTC spokesman Hsin Chih-chung (辛志中) said the commission does not make decisions on hypotheticals.
The FTC’s standard for permitting or halting a merger is whether it would negatively impact free-market mechanisms, not what would happen if its antitrust authority is enforced, he said.
Grab and Delivery Hero have a legal right to reapply for approval after proposing changes to their deal or their finances, Hsin said.
Asked if the decision would affect foreign investors’ confidence in Taiwan’s business environment, he said the FTC makes its ruling to protect fair trade without distinctions between foreign and domestic companies.
“We are disappointed with the outcome, as it means we will not be able to bring innovative services, fair earning opportunities and improved service standards to Taiwanese consumers, delivery partners and merchants as planned,” Grab said in a statement.
“Grab’s core businesses across Southeast Asia remain strong. We will continue to invest capital and resources to pursue our established growth plans and support the continued development of local communities across the markets in which we operate in Southeast Asia,” it said.

Mexico, last bastion of the vanishing left, faces the populist tide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:29 UTC
01:42:29 KST

Latin America’s political map has been redrawn with remarkable speed. Since April last year, center or far-right forces have won power in Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Honduras and Peru. In Argentina, President Javier Milei’s populist party secured a decisive victory in midterm elections last October. And in Brazil, the right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro finished ahead of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in the first round of the recent presidential election 47 to 45 percent.
Should Bolsonaro prevail in the runoff on Sunday, Mexico will be the only large country in Latin America still governed by the left. However, for how long? With midterms set for June next year, some commentators think Mexico would soon be swept up by the regional political tide. I doubt it, although that does not mean the country will not feel the effects of a Bolsonaro victory in Brazil.
The case for contagion rests on the observation that voters are punishing incumbents for insecurity, corruption and stagnant living standards. However, a shared grievance is not a causal chain.
Mexico has long been out of sync with South American political cycles: It elected its first leftist government only in 2018, as the “pink tide” was ebbing. Today, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum’s approval rating remains high, thanks partly to the ruling Morena party’s vast cash transfer programs, and the opposition remains fragmented. While the midterms might well end Morena’s qualified majority in the lower house, a rightward swing propelled by regional forces appears unlikely.
The real risk to Mexico lies in Washington. A Bolsonaro victory would leave Latin America governed largely by leaders who regard US President Donald Trump as an ally and, in many cases, partly credit him for their electoral success.
Trump openly backed Milei ahead of Argentina’s midterms. He pardoned former Honduran president Juan Orlando Hernandez, who was serving a 45-year prison term for cocaine trafficking, on the eve of an election Hernandez’s party went on to win. He endorsed new Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella. In Brazil, the US suspended consular services two days before the first round, prompting Lula’s campaign to request a probe into possible election interference.
As the outsider in the new Latin American order Trump is seeking to construct, Mexico stands to face his ire alone. The groundwork for a campaign of intimidation has already been laid. The US Department of State has designated Mexico’s drug cartels as foreign terrorist organizations with which the US is engaged in “armed conflict.”
The US Drug Enforcement Administration has alleged that the Sheinbaum government has links to organized crime, and the US Department of Justice has indicted 10 current and former Mexican officials on charges of aiding narcotics trafficking into the US.
At last month’s UN General Assembly, Trump called Mexico “the epicenter of cartel violence” and a territory “controlled by enemy cartels.” The Mexican delegation, which did not include Sheinbaum, sat through the speech without protest. Mexican Secretary of Foreign Affairs Roberto Velasco Alvarez’s own address three days later barely touched the subject. It was a low point for Mexican diplomacy, but at least Brazil joined Mexico in refusing to join Trump’s anti-cartel coalition. Soon, Mexico might be on its own.
There is good reason to think that Trump would escalate his attacks. The Iran war has pushed his approval rating down to 33 percent, a new low. If, as seems likely, Republicans lose ground in next month’s midterms, a weakened Trump would be desperate for cheap and flashy foreign policy victories. In Mexico, he can concoct a narrative in which he “takes down” the “narco-politicians” who are supposedly poisoning Americans with fentanyl.
Trump’s arsenal is formidable, with tariffs, visa revocations, indictments of more politicians and even unilateral military action on the table. The US-Mexico-Canada agreement, which the US declined to renew in July, is now subject to annual reviews that hang over every investment decision in Mexico. The risk that the Trump administration would find ways to put its thumb on the scale during Mexico’s midterms — as it has done in Argentina, Brazil and Honduras — cannot be discounted.
Without Brazil on its side, Mexico would find itself with no major Latin American ally. Regional leaders might even applaud Trump. Against this backdrop, Mexico would find it increasingly difficult to address its stagnant growth and falling private investment, which partly reflects loss of faith in the rule of law following Morena’s controversial judicial overhaul.
Instead of loudly condemning US violations of Latin American sovereignty, Sheinbaum’s government should deprive Trump of a pretext to commit such violations in Mexico. This means restoring judicial independence and putting forward a verifiable security agenda that can withstand scrutiny. It also means investigating and prosecuting politicians linked to organized crime, beginning with those in Morena’s own ranks.
Investigating Andres Manuel Lopez Beltran — the son of Morena founder and former Mexican president Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador, Sheinbaum’s mentor — would be a good place to start. Lopez Beltran, who is seeking a seat in the Mexican Congress, is one of more than 50 Mexican politicians who have been stripped of their US visas over allegations related to fuel smuggling and tax fraud.
So far, Sheinbaum has rejected the opposition’s calls for an inquiry, but she can distance her government from Lopez Obrador’s circle without breaking with her mentor. Letting independent prosecutors investigate the allegations on Mexico’s terms would show that no one is above the law and affirm Sheinbaum’s authority. It would also deprive Trump of a convenient narrative.
Sheinbaum’s government has delivered a significant decline in homicides. The challenge is to show that the Mexican state, not the cartels, is in charge. At the same time, Sheinbaum should stop viewing her regional counterparts through an ideological lens and instead pursue pragmatic working relationships with them.
A Mexico perceived as the standard-bearer of a vanishing left would be far easier to isolate — and far more vulnerable to Trump’s wrath.
Guillermo Ortiz, a former Mexican minister of finance and Banco de Mexico governor, is treasurer of the G30.
Copyright: Project Syndicate

North Korea has moved new units into “firing positions,” the sister of leader Kim Jong-un said yesterday, days after Pyongyang warned it was considering deploying additional strike means to its border with South Korea.
Tensions between Seoul and Pyongyang have soared since the South last month blamed an explosion inside the heavily fortified demilitarized zone (DMZ) separating the two countries on landmines laid by North Korea, an accusation it has rejected.
“Our military leadership underlined the need to make those rogues aware that our new firepower units have taken their firing positions,” state media cited Kim Yo-jong as saying.
Photo: AFP
Her statement came a day after Seoul warned of a “firm” response to further North Korean provocations.
She added that Kim Jong-un had “issued an order to fortify the border with an enemy state to be eternally impregnable.”
The statement came as the Korea Central News Agency said the North Korean Marshal Pak Jong-chon had inspected “pivotal positions” on the border, stressing to troops it was “time to organize the firepower strong enough to strike terror into the enemy’s heart.”
“If the enemy troops make a provocation actually threatening the safety of our service personnel ... the border forces of the DPRK [Democratic People’s Republic of Korea] must take very proficient, specialized and overwhelming military action,” he said.
Korea Institute for Military Affairs senior researcher Hong Sung-pyo said that the claimed troop movements should be taken seriously.
“These are small military positions — essentially guard posts or fighting positions for units armed with individual firearms — and it looks like North Korea has been moving them forward,” he said.
“Of the developments we have seen so far, this appears to be among the most serious. North Korea has conducted various demonstrations of its firepower, but this now appears to be about operational deployment,” he added.
North Korea has separately tested a slew of weapons in the past few months, including a “new-type” precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile, both of which were said to employ artificial intelligence technology.
Seoul’s military on Tuesday accused Pyongyang of attempting to shift the blame for escalating military tensions, while confirming the use of loudspeakers and warning shots as “legitimate defensive measures to prevent North Korean troops from crossing the MDL [military demarcation line] and to drive back troops that have crossed it.”
South Korean Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Jin Young-seung also ordered the military to “respond with firm resolve” should North Korea use Seoul’s actions as a pretext for aggressive action.
Kim Yo-jong a day earlier said that the South’s use of loudspeaker broadcasts and warning shots had “gone beyond the red line,” while threatening the deployment of “more tactical strike means along the southern border.”

Ex-Taitung commissioner freed on bail of NT$5m
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:22 UTC
01:42:22 KST

The Taitung District Court yesterday granted a NT$5 million (US$153,903) bail, imposed travel restrictions and ordered electronic monitoring for former Taitung County commissioner Wu Chun-li (吳俊立) after prosecutors sought his detention over alleged corruption.
The Taitung District Prosecutors’ Office said in a statement it would immediately appeal the ruling, citing concerns that Wu might flee or collude with witnesses, while the accused questioned whether prosecutors were playing political games.
The move came less than six weeks before the elections for city mayors and county commissioners.
Photo: Liu Jen-wei, Taipei Times
Wu’s younger sister, Taitung County Council Speaker Wu Hsiu-hua (吳秀華) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), is running for county commissioner.
Prosecutors filed the request at about 1am after questioning Wu, alleging that he had sought unlawful gains in matters under his authority or supervision.
They also cited the risk of flight and collusion, saying that suspected accomplices had not yet been brought before the authorities.
The statement did not offer any further details on the case or on what evidence of suspected wrongdoing there might be.
Wu’s corruption case centers on an agricultural road-widening project suspected of unlawfully benefiting a project linked to the Wu family’s interests.
The investigation began in May after independent Taitung County Councilor Lin Tsan-tien (林參天) alleged that the county government had used public funds to build a road serving the resort.
The agricultural road, which was supposed to be 3m wide, was allegedly widened to more than 9m, with state-owned land also involved in the project.
Prosecutors did not say when the road-widening project occurred, but sources indicated that it happened sometime in the past two to three years.
Prosecutors began questioning witnesses and suspects on July 16.
They have since detained several suspects, including Taitung County Agriculture Department head Hsu Chia-hao (許家豪) and then-section chief Tsai Ming-han (蔡明翰).
Also detained was Chiu Chia-ping (邱嘉平), who was Wu Hsiu-hua’s publicly funded assistant, Wu Chun-li’s secretary and a staff member at the resort involved in the case, prosecutors said.
Several county councilors, who are thought to have used their discretionary funds to finance the project, have also been implicated in the investigation, but were not summoned during the county council’s month-long regular session that began last month.
On Tuesday, Wu Chun-li was stopped from boarding a flight out of Taitung (Taitung Airport only offers domestic flights), while prosecutors searched 11 locations, including Wu Hsiu-hua’s office.
“Everyone knows what is happening when you play these games before elections,” Wu told reporters when he arrived at the prosecutors’ office on Tuesday, and urged authorities to clarify the facts of the case as soon as possible.
The Wu family is prominent in Taitung politics. Wu Chun-li’s wife, Kuang Li-chen (鄺麗貞), served as county commissioner from 2006 to 2009.
Wu Chun-li was elected county commissioner in 2005, but resigned about a month later after being convicted of corruption.
Higher courts later acquitted him for lack of evidence. In 2012, he was convicted of vote-buying in connection with his 2005 magistrate campaign and served a prison sentence.
He has not held any formal political position in the past few years, but local media reports said Wu Chun-li has recently ventured into stock market investments and land development.

The ambassador of St. Vincent and the Grenadines (SVG) to Taiwan yesterday called Taiwan a “faithful partner” that has helped his country develop and prosper, as the Caribbean nation marked the 47th anniversary of its independence at a reception in Taipei.
“Today, we pay tribute to our developmental partners, the countries, international agencies and organizations that have contributed and continue to contribute to our development over the last 47 years,” Ambassador Kenton Chance said in his address.
“In this regard, I express particular gratitude to the Republic of China (Taiwan), which has been a faithful partner over the last 45 years,” he said.
Photo: CNA
Chance also urged his compatriots to learn from Taiwan’s success.
“My fellow Vincentians, Taiwanese today enjoy the fruits of the hard work of their forebears while building an even more resilient and prosperous country for the next generation,” he said.
“I urge every Vincentian in Taiwan to take inspiration from our host and build sacrificially so the next generation can experience in St. Vincent and the Grenadines a level of development similar to what we enjoy now in Taiwan,” he added.
Representing the Taiwanese government at the reception, Deputy Foreign Minister Chen Ming-chi (陳明祺) wished the Caribbean ally a happy Independence Day.
Chen said 2026 also marks the 45th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries.
“Throughout these years, our two nations have developed a close friendship built on mutual trust, shared values, and meaningful cooperation,” he said.
Looking ahead, Chen said Taiwan was committed to deepening its partnership with SVG, particularly in economic cooperation, tourism and agriculture.
“By working together in these areas, we hope to create new opportunities for our local businesses, support economic growth, and bring lasting benefits to both our peoples,” Chen added.
SVG is one of 12 countries that maintain diplomatic relations with the Republic of China, Taiwan’s official name. The two countries established diplomatic ties on Aug. 15, 1981.

Powerchip expects more price hikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:21 UTC
01:42:21 KST

Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corp (力積電) is negotiating with customers to further hike prices by 10 to 20 percent next year, the logic and memory chipmaker said yesterday, citing persistent capacity constraints across the industry.
The company said it would prioritize capacity allocation for customers under long-term supply agreements with fixed volumes and pricing.
Last quarter, Powerchip raised prices by 23 percent from the previous quarter, and expects another 30 percent increase this quarter, it said.
Photo: Grace Hung, Taipei Times
“Provided that artificial intelligence [AI] momentum remains strong, we hold a highly optimistic outlook for 2027 revenue and profitability,” Powerchip president Martin Chu (朱憲國) said at an earnings conference.
The company also unveiled a new capacity expansion plan for the next three to five years, saying that it is scouting a site to build a small-scale chip facility in Taiwan, Japan or Singapore.
The new plant would focus on expanding advanced packaging-related technologies, including post-wafer-finish (PWF) service, interposers used in advanced chip-on-wafer-on-substrate packaging and integrated passive devices (IPD), which are used in AI-related applications, it said.
“We have to expand clean room space to address strong customer demand for those technologies,” Powerchip chairman Brian Shieh (謝再居) said.
Demand for IPD would surge to as many as 50,000 wafers a month in the second half of next year, exceeding its current capacity of 10,000 wafers per month, he said.
To mitigate capital expenditure risks, the company aims to secure 30 to 60 percent of funding for new production line expansions from customers via leasing or prepayments, Shieh said.
Micron Technology Inc has set a precedent by fully funding the manufacturing equipment for Taiwan’s PWF mid-to-back-end packaging expansion through prepayments, he said.
Powerchip is poised to become the world’s sole memory manufacturer producing legacy DRAM from DDR1 to DDR3, utilizing 63-nanometer to 20-nanometer process technologies, Shieh said.
Those technologies are projected to have an extended lifecycle of 10 to 15 years, he said.
The company attributed the ongoing supply crunch to aggressive AI server buildouts, which have spurred massive demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and squeezed mature DDR3 and DDR4 DRAM production.
“As major memory makers aggressively reallocate capacity to HBM and exit mature DRAM, we expect supply tightness for customers,” Chu said. “We anticipate that our niche DRAM foundry pricing will remain robust, showing no signs of a downward adjustment.”
Powerchip attributed the mild pricing weakness in DDR3 DRAM to a temporary supply influx, driven by an enterprise refresh cycle where outdated computers were replaced with AI-capable models.
This pricing softness is expected to be short-lived, the company said.
The company expects revenue to expand by a double-digit percentage sequentially this quarter, after revenue expanded 23 percent last quarter.
Net profit last quarter almost doubled to NT$6.5 billion (US$200 million), from NT$3.29 billion in the previous quarter. That reversed a loss of NT$2.73 billion in the third quarter last year.
Earnings per share rose to NT$1.38 last quarter from NT$0.76 in the previous quarter, while gross margin improved to 48 percent from 28 percent a quarter earlier.

Mpox cases hit two-year high, CDC data show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:17 UTC
01:42:17 KST

As of Monday, 18 new cases of mpox had been reported this month, topping the highest monthly number in two years, with local cases having been reported weekly for seven consecutive weeks, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said on Tuesday.
CDC data showed that 52 mpox cases had been reported so far this year as of Monday, comprising 41 locally acquired cases and 11 imported.
CDC Epidemic Intelligence Center Director Guo Hung-wei (郭宏偉) said 18 cases were reported in the first 19 days of this month alone, including 16 with the Clade 1b mpox virus, a variant first identified in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in September 2023.
Photo: Lo Pi, Taipei Times
Contact tracing showed that the 16 cases were aged between 20 and 50, with all of them having had unsafe sex and only two having received an mpox vaccine, Guo said.
Thirty people have tested positive for Clade 1b mpox so far this year, with 22 local cases and eight imported — six from Thailand and two from Hong Kong, he said.
The risk of cross-border Clade 1b mpox viral transmission is increasing, with 68 countries and areas having reported confirmed cases, while mpox cases have been rising in parts of the WHO’s Western Pacific Region, Guo said.
A WHO assessment report published in August showed that overall global public health risk is “moderate” for “individuals with multiple sexual partners,” and “low” for all other individuals, he said.
CDC Deputy Director-General and spokesman Lin Min-cheng (林明誠) said that local mpox cases have been reported weekly for seven consecutive weeks.
The 52 local mpox cases reported so far this year is about 20 percent higher than the same period last year, Lin said.
“We continue to urge people who are eligible for [mpox] vaccination to get fully vaccinated with two doses for full protection,” he said.
Vaccination is the most effective method of preventing mpox infection, the CDC said, adding that getting the full two-dose regimen provides about 90 percent protection, while one dose provides about 40 to 80 percent.
There are 327 healthcare facilities across Taiwan that provide publicly funded mpox vaccinations, so people who have engaged in high-risk sexual behavior, such as having multiple sexual partners, engaged in sex work or had sex at commercial venues should get vaccinated, it said.

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:17 UTC
01:42:17 KST

Australian lawmaker Helen Haines has had both legs amputated after being rammed by a car outside her electoral office, her husband said yesterday, as the man accused of the attack appeared in court.
Doctors amputated Haines’ left leg after the alleged attacker struck her twice with his car in Wangaratta, northeast of Melbourne, on Monday, Phil Haines said.
They worked for days to save her right leg, but were ultimately unsuccessful, he told a news conference in Melbourne.
Photo: EPA
“The good news in all this is Helen is alive and she’s stable. That is the most important thing for our family,” he said.
Brendan Nugent, a 43-year-old resident of the rural town of Tarrawingee within Helen Haines’ electorate, was charged with three offenses: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and causing harm to a public official.
Additional charges of cannabis cultivation and possession have also been laid against Nugent, court filings showed.
The suspect was restrained by members of the public at the scene before being arrested.
Helen Haines, an independent lawmaker who has championed causes including climate change and regional housing, remains in critical condition.
Police are still investigating the motive for the attack.
During a brief court appearance yesterday, the accused’s lawyer said his client suffers from a rare neurological condition called idiopathic transverse myelitis and was also being treated for concussion, the Australian Broadcasting Corp reported.
His lawyer told the magistrate his client had some mental health concerns and that it was his first time in custody.
There was no application for bail, and the case was deferred until Feb. 4.
Anti-terrorism police are among the agencies investigating the incident. While police allege the attack was “targeted,” they believe it was an isolated incident.
There was no intelligence to suggest any threat to Helen Haines, and the Australian Federal Police received no warning of any imminent danger from the alleged attacker, Commissioner Krissy Barrett told reporters.
“What I can say is we didn’t have any specific intelligence that would have indicated something as atrocious as happened on Monday afternoon,” she said.
Victoria Police said they could not find any direct past contact between Helen Haines and the accused, with the motive still unknown.
“Motivation is one of these things that we absolutely need to explore. His motivation for this, what we allege is a deliberate attack, is very much a centerpiece of the investigation,” Victoria Police Chief Mike Bush said.
Bush declined to comment on the man’s mental health, saying the matter was before the court.
The alleged attack has sparked soul-searching in a country where political violence is rare, but where police have documented a steady rise in threats and abuse toward elected officials in the past few years.
Australian Governor-General Sam Mostyn — King Charles III’s official representative in Australia — said the nation was crying out for “decency” following the attack.
“Australians are yearning for kindness and care, and they’re asking us why we’ve lost the great skill of disagreeing well,” Mostyn said alongside Phil Haines.
Helen Haines had worked in nursing, midwifery and academia before being elected to parliament in 2019 for the rural seat of Indi, which she retained in both 2022 and last year.

US Army details First Island Chain preparations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:09 UTC
01:42:09 KST

The US Army would improve its warfighting infrastructure in the Pacific with its forward-deployed “inside forces” ready to act immediately on day one of a conflict in the First Island Chain, which includes Taiwan, it said in a report released this month.
How the Army Fights, an operational warfare guidance report released on Oct. 7, states that the US Army would counterbalance “the pacing threat,” which it defines as the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA), by improving its warfighting infrastructure across the region.
Because of China’s “rapid deployment capabilities,” the US Army is “developing the infrastructure to support forward-positioned multidomain capabilities and munitions, starting in the” First Island Chain, it said.
Photo: screen grab from US Army’s Facebook page
The US Army must “organize, train and equip against” the PLA “with the same institutional focus that the Cold War generations brought to the Soviet Army.”
“The Homeland is no longer a sanctuary, and peer adversaries can disrupt our ability to generate and project combat power before our formations close with the enemy,” US Army Acting Chief of Staff Christopher LaNeve, who previously commanded the US Eighth Army in South Korea, wrote in the foreword.
Military experts in Taiwan have interpreted the document as reflecting a Pentagon expectation of enemy strikes against railroads and harbors on US soil to delay US reinforcements in a conflict abroad.
To counter such possibilities, the US Army should reposition its “land power stocks and forward sites” to enable “inside forces” to overcome anti-access/area-denial capabilities, “deny a fait accompli, and win the first battle.”
The US Army plans to implement four operational elements: convergence, strike, close battle and endurance.
Under that protocol, the army would first combine electronic warfare, cyberwarfare and space-based capabilities to jam communications and disrupt air defenses, it said.
The forces would then use medium and long-range precision fire and uncrewed systems to degrade and dislocate the enemy and its supply lines before it can deploy ground forces, the report said.
The Russia-Ukraine war highlights the need to develop advanced capabilities in deception, concealment and counter-reconnaissance to disrupt an enemy’s “operating picture” of the battlefield, it said.
The report presents a hypothetical scenario in which the US Army Multi-Domain Task Force is deployed in the Luzon Strait within the First Island Chain, which includes Taiwan and stretches to the southern Kyushu in Japan.
That region is within the operational range of the PLA Navy.
The US Army is hardening logistics across the Second Island Chain — which includes Japanese islands, Guam and Palau — with fuel stockpiles, and engineering, medical and air defense assets to sustain operations in the region, the report said.
In Europe, the US Army would maintain a “relevant posture,” providing limited, but critical capabilities needed to support NATO-led deterrence, it said.
The army would “support a modernized, warfighting-focused NATO, where European allies assume primary responsibility for conventional ground defense,” it added.

Swift passage of supplementary budget urged to keep energy prices in check
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:07 UTC
01:42:07 KST

State-owned CPC Corp, Taiwan (CPC, 台灣中油) and Taiwan Power Co (Taipower, 台電) could struggle to keep domestic energy prices in check if a supplementary budget to cover rising energy costs fails to pass the Legislative Yuan, Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS) Minister Chen Shu-tzu (陳淑姿) said yesterday.
Without additional government funding, CPC’s cumulative losses could reach NT$127.6 billion (US$3.93 billion) by the end of this year, Chen said at a meeting of the legislature’s Finance Committee in Taipei.
Taipower’s accumulated losses have totaled NT$371.2 billion since 2020, the Ministry of Economic Affairs’ data showed.
Photo: Liu Hsin-de, Taipei Times
Both CPC and Taipower have been absorbing higher international oil and natural gas costs to help stabilize domestic energy prices, putting mounting pressure on their finances, Chen said.
The Cabinet proposed a supplementary budget of NT$607.6 billion that includes subsidies for the two companies. The proposal would lapse if lawmakers do not pass it by the end of this year.
However, subsidies alone would not be enough to offset CPC’s accumulated losses, making a planned capital injection of NT$233.8 billion into the company necessary, Chen said.
The company has a paid-in capital of about NT$130.1 billion. Without additional funding, CPC’s projected losses would nearly wipe out that amount, potentially undermining its ability to maintain the current pricing policy and making it more difficult to secure bank financing, she said.
Deterioration in CPC’s financial position could also weaken its creditworthiness and disrupt crude oil procurement, threatening domestic energy supplies and adding to inflationary pressures, Chen warned.
Lawmakers also questioned whether the proposed capital increase would help fund CPC’s planned investment in a liquefied natural gas (LNG)project in Alaska.
CPC is negotiating a deal to purchase 6 million tonnes of LNG annually from the project, with the investment potentially reaching US$4.4 billion, the ministry said last week.
Deliveries could start as early as 2032 if the project develops on schedule, though purchase and investment details are still being negotiated, the ministry said.
Chen said the proposed capital injection includes funding for urgent, necessary natural gas infrastructure projects.
However, CPC’s planned investment in the LNG project in Alaska remains under negotiation and has not been finalized, she said.
Whether funding would come through the annual budget or a special budget depends on CPC’s financial structure, she added.
Opposition parties, which hold a majority in the Legislative Yuan, have been reluctant to provide additional funding for CPC and Taipower because they object to the Democratic Progressive Party’s energy policy since it took power in 2016.
The policy stressed phasing out nuclear power while supporting renewable energy development, while relying heavily on fossil fuels, especially LNG.
Fossil fuels accounted for over 85 percent of Taiwan’s electricity generation in the first eight months of this year, according to Energy Administration figures.

Academia Sinica’s Institute of Modern History and Stanford University’s Hoover Institution on Oct. 8 signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to share archived primary sources for historical research.
The deal promotes archival sharing, joint research and researcher exchanges, with the institutions hoping eventually to deposit copies of selected materials in each other’s collections, officials said at a signing ceremony.
The agreement came three years after a California court ordered the California-based Hoover Institution think tank to end its decades-long legal battle with Academia Historica by returning Chiang Kai-shek’s (蔣介石) personal diaries to the nation.
Photo courtesy of Academia Sinica
Institute of Modern History director Sean Lei (雷祥麟) said the agreement would significantly ease research work by saving time and resources that would have been spent on traveling between Taiwan and the US.
The Taiwanese institution looks forward to copying and sharing documents, which would make the invaluable academic resource more accessible to researchers and create new opportunities for transnational history, Lei said.
Hoover Institution deputy director Eric Wakin, the director of its library and archives, said that archives should be a common good, not hoarded by any one group or place.
The MOU’s mandate for the two institutions to share resources would open doors for historians hailing from both institutions and enhance global collaboration in scholarship, Wakin said.
The Institute of Modern History, which conducts research on modern Taiwanese, Chinese and East Asian history, runs one of the most important archives in the nation, Academia Sinica said in a statement.
The institute’s archive has gathered more than 5 million hard-copy documents, ranging from diplomatic and economic reports, personal letters and diaries, government internal communiques and maps, the statement said.
More than 17 million digital images are also in the archive’s collection, it said.
The Hoover Institution Library and Archives at Stanford University is dedicated to collecting materials relevant to the study of peace and war and revolutions, the statement said.
The Hoover Institution’s archive contains nearly 7,000 collections from 171 countries, about 1 million volumes of books and journals, and 100 terabytes of digital documents, Academia Sinica said.
The collection includes documents pertinent to the history of Taiwan and modern China, it said.

US Supreme Court rulings have been ‘destructive:’ justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:42:04 UTC

US Supreme Court Justice Elena Kagan on Tuesday said the court’s conservative majority has undermined democracy and “created a race to the bottom” in how congressional districts are drawn.
Kagan, one of the court’s three liberals, told students at Catholic University of America’s law school that the conservatives have enabled increased political polarization by not reining in partisan gerrymandering, which involves states redrawing the boundaries of electoral districts based on the partisan leanings of voters to boost a political party’s candidates.
In the past few years, “both political parties have been engaged in a race to the bottom in terms of doing these partisan gerrymanders, effectively depriving masses of citizens of their rights to voting equality,” she said.
Photo: Bloomberg
Partisan gerrymandering is driving political candidates “toward the extremes, because the only thing anybody has to worry about anymore is being primaried,” Kagan said.
“It is making what I think is unfortunately a too polarized country even more so,” she said. “In this election, and the next election, we are seeing large states with substantial numbers of people who vote for Republicans and who vote for Democrats, and the states are going to be tried to turn all red or all blue in a way that I think is very destructive to our democracy.”
The court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority, in April gutted a pillar of the Voting Rights Act, a landmark 1965 civil rights law that aimed to prevent racial discrimination in voting.
That ruling prompted a frenzied round of redistricting across the South to eliminate US House of Representatives districts where black voters make up a majority or near-majority, as Republican-led states scrambled to take advantage of the decision.
Republican-governed Texas last year redrew its electoral map in an effort to flip Democratic-held US House seats, while Democratic-led California reconfigured its map to target Republican-held House seats.
Kagan, an appointee of former US president Barack Obama, said the court’s conservatives did not appreciate the real-world impact of their April voting rights decision, or their June decision that struck down a cap on the amount of money parties can spend on campaigns with input from candidates.
“I think part of the reason why the court got it wrong was a lack of the appropriate concern or understanding of the consequences of their decisions,” Kagan said.
“I do think in all these areas the court has blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political system works and has created a democracy that doesn’t work as well as it should,” she added.
The June decision on campaign finance regulation has created opportunities for donors to corrupt candidates.
“The one place where the court has allowed campaign finance regulation to operate is to prevent quid pro quo corruption, kind of money for favors, and the court never seems to see the opportunities for doing exactly that,” Kagan said.
“I think you know the people of America look around this political system and think that all this money, chasing all these political candidates, is a nightmare, and they’re right,” she added.
