How Egypt's Saudi pledge aims to curb Israel's Gulf ambitions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:29:22 UTC
01:29:22 KST

Breadcrumb
How Egypt's Saudi pledge aims to curb Israel's Gulf ambitions
Egypt, a regional military power, has pledged to provide all forms of assistance to defend Saudi Arabia amid escalating Houthi attacks from Yemen, in a move aimed at maintaining its strategic position in the Gulf.
But analysts view another geopolitical objective behind the Egyptian support for Riyadh: countering Israel’s bid to play a security role in a region vital to Cairo’s political and economic interests.
On 17 October, President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said Egypt would take any necessary measures to protect Saudi Arabia if Riyadh requested assistance. He called an emergency parliamentary session to authorise possible troop deployment.
The following day, the National Defence Council, Egypt’s top security body, pledged to provide all necessary and possible support to safeguard Saudi Arabia’s security, stability, and territorial integrity.
The Egyptian pledge came after US President Donald Trump said on 16 October that Israel had been helping Saudi Arabia counter Houthi attacks from Yemen and suggested Riyadh should accept further Israeli assistance.
It followed Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s visit to Cairo last month to seek support against the Iran-backed Houthis. The visit highlighted the importance of Egyptian-Saudi coordination on issues affecting the Red Sea and wider regional stability.
For Cairo, which has longstanding strategic ties with Riyadh, the prospect of Israel becoming a more prominent security partner for the kingdom adds urgency to its efforts to reinforce its role in regional security.
“Egypt’s interest lies in doing everything possible to strengthen its ties with Saudi Arabia, or at least to ensure that its relationship with Riyadh is closer than Israel’s,” Ahmed Aboudouh, an associate fellow at Chatham House in London, told The New Arab.
Strengthening ties with Saudi Arabia offers Egypt significant economic and geopolitical benefits as Cairo seeks foreign investment, financial support, and foreign currency. The kingdom is also important for millions of Egyptians working there, whose remittances provide a vital source of foreign currency.
Closer coordination with Riyadh also helps Egypt protect its interests in the Red Sea, particularly shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key route to the Suez Canal and a major source of revenue for Cairo.
During Trump’s first term, the US brokered the Abraham Accords in 2020 to normalise relations between Israel and Arab countries, including Saudi Arabia’s neighbours, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Bahrain, allowing Tel Aviv to expand its economic, diplomatic, and security partnerships in the Gulf.
The American president has also pushed for normalising ties between Saudi Arabia and Israel, but Riyadh insists that any normalisation depends on resolving the Palestinian issue, including the establishment of a Palestinian state.
If Riyadh accepts any Israeli assistance against Houthi attacks, cooperation in areas such as intelligence sharing and air defence could expand, potentially giving Israel a greater role in Gulf security.
For Egypt, that possibility raises concerns about a changing regional balance in which Israel could become a more influential security partner for Arab states traditionally linked to Cairo.
Cairo's bid to keep Israel at bay
“Egypt would oppose any attempt by Israel to become a player in the Arab world’s collective security, regardless of who was involved, and Saudi Arabia would certainly stand with Cairo. This means keeping Israel out of regional military and intelligence cooperation,” Egyptian military expert Samir Ragheb told The New Arab.
Egypt was the first Arab country to sign a peace treaty with Israel in 1979, following decades of conflict and several wars, but their relations have remained largely cold despite formal diplomatic ties.
The relationship has been marked by mutual distrust, periodic tensions, and regional competition, particularly over Gaza and broader Middle East security arrangements.
Egyptian political analyst Mokhtar Ghobashi said Egypt’s pledge to defend Saudi Arabia could deter Israel from seeking a security role in the Gulf.
“Relying on Israel as a security guarantor for a country in the Arab world, amid divisions and conflicts between Arab states, is an extremely dangerous proposition,” he told The New Arab.
Since the 2020 Abraham Accords, security cooperation between Israel and some Gulf states has expanded, including arms sales and coordination on air and missile defence amid shared concerns over Iran.
Egypt’s support for Saudi Arabia reflects its interest in preserving its regional influence and maintaining a central role in shaping the security arrangements in the Middle East.
Cairo could face greater competition for influence if Riyadh turns to Israel for certain defence capabilities. While this would not necessarily weaken Egyptian-Saudi relations, it could reduce Egypt’s role in shaping the kingdom’s security policy.
The implications extend beyond bilateral relations. Closer security ties between Israel and Saudi Arabia could give Tel Aviv a greater role in shaping regional responses to threats, from Yemen’s Houthis to Iran.
Protecting Egypt's strategic interests
Red Sea security is another concern for Cairo. A broader Israeli security role in the Gulf could give Tel Aviv greater influence over decisions affecting the Bab el-Mandeb, a vital maritime corridor central to Egypt’s national interests.
Aboudouh said another objective behind Egypt’s pledge to defend Saudi Arabia is to protect its strategic interests in the Red Sea and around Bab el-Mandeb.
“Egyptian officials may have concluded that expanding the country’s regional role is now crucial to protecting maritime traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait against any Houthi attempt to exploit a conflict with Saudi Arabia to disrupt shipping, as they have done in the past,” he told The New Arab.
Egypt has been hard-hit by regional instability following Israel’s war on the Gaza Strip and Houthi attacks on shipping in the Red Sea since 2023, losing an estimated around $20 billion in Suez Canal revenues.
Sisi framed Egypt’s potential role in Saudi Arabia as defensive, saying Cairo had no intention of attacking any party but was prepared to defend Saudi Arabia if requested. “We do not want to fight or attack anyone. We will only defend Saudi Arabia,” he said.
Egypt joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen against the Houthis in 2015, but its role remained limited. A deeper commitment now could expose Cairo to a costly conflict, particularly if operations extend beyond the defence of Saudi territory.
It could also strain Egypt’s resources and increase its exposure to instability along the Red Sea.
The extent and form of any Egyptian assistance will therefore be crucial. Intelligence-sharing, logistical support and maritime security cooperation would carry different risks from deploying troops to Yemen.
Cairo may seek to bolster Saudi Arabia’s defences while avoiding involvement in an open-ended conflict.
Mohamed Sabry is an Egyptian journalist based in Cairo with over two decades of experience covering Egypt, regional politics, foreign policy, and diplomacy. His work has appeared in Al-Monitor and InsideOver

Sahin Demir

Army spokesman Majed Abdullah al-Nuzayli said in a statement on US social media company X that the operations involved fighter jets, drones, field artillery, rocket launchers and sniper units.
The strikes targeted Houthi troop movements, gatherings, reinforcements, weapons, armored vehicles, firing positions, fortifications and supply routes, according to the statement.
The military claimed that approximately 285 Houthi fighters and commanders were neutralized, while around 190 military vehicles, pieces of equipment and drones were destroyed or damaged.

Al-Nuzayli said the operations were continuing in accordance with the military’s operational plans.

Meanwhile, Al-Jumhuriya TV reported heavy clashes between government forces and Houthi fighters near the old airport and Mount Han, west of Taiz city.
On Tuesday, the Yemeni army said it had carried out 744 attacks against Houthi positions over the previous 24 hours, neutralizing around 200 fighters and destroying or damaging 90 military vehicles and other assets.
The latest developments come amid an offensive launched by Yemen’s internationally recognized government earlier this month to recapture Houthi-held areas, including the capital Sanaa, with support from the Saudi-led coalition.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several other provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.
The Houthis control much of northern and western Yemen, while government forces and their allies hold Aden and large parts of the country’s southern and eastern provinces.

Ukrainian energy companies urge international partners to speed up aid ahead of winter
That is according to a joint statement issued by Naftogaz Group, Ukrenergo, Energoatom, the Gas Transmission System Operator of Ukraine (GTSOU), and Ukrhydroenergo, Ukrinform reports.
The energy companies stressed that Russia continues its systematic attacks on Ukraine's electricity generation and transmission infrastructure, gas production, storage and transportation facilities, and heating systems.
These attacks also pose serious nuclear and radiological safety risks by threatening reliable off-site power supplies, which are essential for the safe operation of Ukraine's nuclear power plants. The coming winter could also be one of the most difficult since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion.
"Ukrainian energy companies and their employees continue to restore damaged facilities and maintain energy supplies under extremely difficult conditions. However, the fact that Ukraine's energy system continues to function does not mean it is safe. Each new attack deepens the destruction and increases the strain on equipment, personnel, and financial resources," the statement said.
The companies noted that restoration work alone cannot indefinitely compensate for the consequences of systematic destruction. At the same time, energy security does not stop at national borders, meaning that protecting Ukraine's energy infrastructure will strengthen Europe's collective security.
The companies identified five priority areas for assistance. The first is to "protect critical energy infrastructure by strengthening air defense and physical protection, particularly at facilities essential to nuclear and radiological safety."
The second priority is to accelerate emergency assistance through funding, equipment supplies, and installation and connection of equipment. The energy companies also called on partners to ensure that gas and electricity can be imported during the winter.
In addition, they urged partners to mobilize grants, concessional financing, guarantees, and war-risk insurance to support urgent repairs and investment.
Another separate priority is strengthening sanctions against Russia, particularly targeting its oil and gas sector.
"We are deeply grateful to the governments, international organizations, financial institutions, and private partners whose support has helped keep Ukraine's energy system running. The scale and speed of international assistance must match the scale and pace of Russian attacks, as well as the urgency of Ukraine's needs," the statement's authors added.

Germany's military warns of 'significant' Russian sabotage threat, raising alert level
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21

01:27:29 KST

Germany's armed forces classified the threat of Russian sabotage against their own troops and facilities as "significant" for the first time, the second-highest level on their internal threat scale, according to a Bundeswehr assessment reported by German broadcasters WDR and the Sueddeutsche Zeitung on Wednesday.
A defense ministry spokesperson confirmed the assessment, telling reporters: "We are noting that we face a significant sabotage threat overall for the Bundeswehr."
The reassessment was triggered by the discovery in mid-September of a crashed drone carrying a tin of high explosives near the Wunstorf air base in Lower Saxony, WDR and Sueddeutsche Zeitung reported.
Russia accused of crossing 'red line of harmful intent'
The internal document, seen by WDR and the Sueddeutsche Zeitung, said Russia had crossed "a previously anticipated red line of harmful intent involving kinetic and/or lethal effects" against Germany and the Bundeswehr through the use of weaponized drones.
The Wunstorf drone resembles one laden with explosives that was used in a failed attack at Leipzig/Halle airport in August. But unlike the Leipzig incident, which authorities said targeted civilian cargo aircraft, investigators believe the Wunstorf drone was aimed at Bundeswehr aircraft, the document is cited as saying.
Germany has blamed Russia for the Leipzig attack.
Moscow denied involvement and has consistently rejected accusations of carrying out sabotage or hybrid attacks in Europe.
The report also cited a pattern of suspected Russian reconnaissance across Germany, including drone overflights of the Arrow 3 missile defense site in Saxony-Anhalt, and a camouflaged camera found filming a strategically important railway station in Minden, Westphalia.
Situation expected to worsen if no action taken
Intelligence services expect the situation to worsen in the short term, with further actions likely in the near future, the document says, according to WDR and Sueddeutsche Zeitung.
The defense ministry spokesperson said preventive measures were being tailored to individual sites and could range from increased guard patrols to additional technical security such as infrared cameras and fence surveillance systems.
The assessment comes just over a week after German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Germany faced a "shadow war" and called for expanded intelligence powers.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Wednesday that Russian disinformation and hybrid attacks posed the biggest threat to Germany. "My view is that our people are still underestimating this big threat to our society... This is a fundamental attack against the entire political order we achieved after 1990."

France's Macron calls for order, says foreign criticism of unrest 'stupid'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:27:06 UTC
01:27:06 KST

President Emmanuel Macron vowed on Wednesday to prevent a repeat of last weekend's violence at protests planned in the coming days, and dismissed as "stupid" and "unacceptable" comments from some foreign leaders about the unrest.
France's main student union, UNEF, has called for further rallies on Saturday, while the Yellow Vest group, which emerged as a potent anti-establishment movement in 2018, has filed plans for a march through central Paris the same day.
Efforts to ease social tensions showed little sign of progress, as unions pledged to press ahead with a general strike on November 5 to denounce the high cost of living and cuts to public services after government talks ended inconclusively.
France was hit by some of the worst urban tumult in years on October 17 on the fringe of nationwide protests, shocking the nation both because of its scale and the apparent inability of police to contain it.
Macron said he would meet intelligence officials and senior ministers on Thursday to discuss the crisis.
"Those who want to cause disorder in city centers next Saturday will be prevented from doing so," Macron told reporters during a visit to Qatar, where he has been seeking energy deals as France grapples with rising fuel costs.
He also accused some foreign leaders of spreading misinformation about what had happened. US President Donald Trump in particular has blamed immigrants and radical Islam, without providing evidence, and said the turbulence was a warning for Americans.
Asked whether he was referring to Trump, Macron said: "Among others," adding that some foreign politicians were looking to make political capital at the expense of France.
"There was foreign disinformation in the aftermath, which prompted comments that were as unacceptable as they were stupid from many people, including foreign leaders," he said.
Borrowing costs rise as investors' fears grow
Highlighting investor concern over the situation, French government borrowing costs have jumped this week, pushing benchmark 10-year bond yields to 5%, their highest level since July 2002.
Analysts said the move reflected worries that the unrest could complicate government efforts to repair strained public finances at a time of already mounting budget pressures.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu met union leaders in an effort to defuse the crisis, but there was no sign of a breakthrough, with labor groups saying they had received no concrete response to their demands on wages and public services.
"There has been no consideration whatsoever of our demands," said Sophie Binet, head of the left-wing CGT group.
"The time has come to take the mobilization to the next level," she added, confirming next month's national strike.
The protests reflect a deeper malaise in France, where high energy costs, pressure on household budgets and concerns about the state of public services have fed a growing sense of frustration among workers and young people.
A second consecutive night of local curfews passed without major incidents in areas hit by the mayhem, offering the government some respite as it prepared for fresh demonstrations.
Government ministers have promised a vastly reinforced security operation this coming Saturday after acknowledging shortcomings in their initial response, with troops expected to be deployed alongside additional police.
Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said on Wednesday around 2,500 people had been taken into custody following the October 17 protests, adding that 917 suspects had been referred for prosecution and 174 people already jailed.
Protests spread across Europe
The unrest has triggered a political backlash ahead of presidential elections next year, with candidates from the far right and hard left performing strongly in polls.
"The government has lost control of everything," far-right leader Marine Le Pen told Franceinfo radio.
The hard-left France Unbowed (LFI), which has denied allegations by ministers of fueling the unrest, criticized plans to deploy troops on the streets of Paris.
"Demonstrators are not enemies within. The French government must not go to war against its own people," LFI's parliamentary group said in a statement.
Protests in other European countries have added to concerns that anger over living standards risks spreading at a time when many nations are struggling with budget woes.
In Greece, thousands of students and teachers took to the streets on Wednesday, demanding higher state funding for education, better facilities and less-crowded classrooms, echoing protesters in other European countries.
Meanwhile, Italy approved a raft of security measures on Tuesday, including a new offense of violent participation in a demonstration and tougher penalties for rioters in response to turbulence last weekend.

Libya's HoR ratifying Turkey maritime deal 'very troubling' for Israeli security, expert to 'Post'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:26:56 UTC
01:26:56 KST

Turkey and Libya’s maritime boundary deal is a “very troubling” development for Israel, Colonel (res.) Eran Lerman, vice president of the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security and a lecturer in Middle Eastern and Islamic Studies at Shalem College, told The Jerusalem Post on Wednesday.
The deal, agreed upon by the Tripoli-based, internationally recognized western Libyan government in 2019, was approved by the eastern Libya's legislature, the House of Representatives (HoR), on Tuesday, drawing criticism from Cyprus, Egypt, Greece and Israel.
Eastern Libyan authorities breaking boycott of Ankara
The move marks a significant shift in regional alignments, with Khalifa Haftar, commander of the Benghazi-based Libyan National Army, breaking with the boycott of Ankara that had been in place since 2020.
While Lerman said he was unsure what prompted HoR to approve the long-delayed agreement, he warned it could threaten Israel’s ability to develop underwater infrastructure connections and create more serious maritime security challenges.
Israel has been working in recent years on an ambitious project to connect its electricity grid to Cyprus and Greece, and from there to mainland Europe. Ankara has opposed the project, disputing the maritime boundaries claimed by Greece under international law.
Turkey, which runs a military occupation of Northern Cyprus, is not a signatory to the Convention on the Continental Shelf or the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, and has sought to claim Greek islands as an extension of its territory.
“I’m not sure the Turks will actually intervene to disrupt the laying of an electricity connector. It is not entirely clear whether they have the authority to do so in their exclusive economic zone, but this is going to be a source of growing tension in the coming years,” Lerman predicted.
Egypt and Greece had previously opposed the Turkish-Libyan alignment, and any fracturing of the established alignment would give Ankara an opportunity to further pursue its neo-Ottoman aspirations, he continued. Egypt’s orientation toward the Mecca defense pact could bring it closer to Turkey, strengthening a country that has already made clear its aspirations to regain the imperial power it once wielded.
“The common interests of Israel, Egypt, Cyprus, and Greece were very much at play against the neo-Ottoman ambitions of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and that created an important commonality. Over the past decade, we saw parallel tripartite summits of Greece, Cyprus, and Israel, and of Greece, Cyprus, and Egypt. We also saw the creation of secretariats in Lefkosia, Cyprus, to manage these parallel tripartite relations,” Lerman said.
“We were looking at this as essentially the emergence of an alignment of interests and forces in the Eastern Mediterranean. If Egypt is sliding out of this alignment, despite the recent summit that Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi held with the leaders of Greece and Cyprus at El Alamein, and is increasingly moving toward accepting the Turkish position, that would be highly problematic from an Israeli perspective,” he added.
Israel's maritime security comes under risk
There is also the issue of Israel’s maritime security. The vast majority of Israel's international trade is conducted by sea, and the ports of Haifa, Ashdod and Eilat handle 98% of the country's import and export volume. The Houthis already pose a threat to the Eilat port, Lerman highlighted, and “the last thing we need is a problem also with our Western maritime approaches.”
Turkey maintains a significant naval presence in the Mediterranean and has increasingly asserted its claims under the Mavi Vatan (Blue Homeland) doctrine, which challenges maritime boundaries claimed under UNCLOS. Introduced in 2006, the doctrine seeks to assert Turkish sovereign rights and jurisdiction over a 462,000-square-kilometer maritime area spanning the Black Sea, Aegean Sea, and eastern Mediterranean.
“Of course, they have the naval capacity, the military capacity to back this [strategy] up. Of course, Israel is not without its own capabilities, but nobody, under the circumstances under which we live, nobody is looking for another major front of tension and confrontation,” he continued.
Warning that Israel needed to do what it could to keep Egypt from fully aligning with Turkey, Lerman advised Jerusalem to strengthen cooperation with Athens and Nicosia.

Independent review finds extensive antisemitism in English schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:26:52 UTC
01:26:52 KST

Schools and colleges across England must recognize antisemitism as a distinct category of harm following a major independent review published on Wednesday.
Launched by the Department for Education in March 2026, the government-commissioned review was led by former Ofsted chief Sir David Bell and set out 27 recommendations after finding that three-in-five Jewish students in England have experienced prejudice.
The review revealed that one-in-five students overall reported witnessing antisemitism, while many cases went entirely unreported by students and teachers due to a lack of confidence that the incidents would be properly addressed.
Discussing the findings in a statement to the BBC, Bell explained that existing approaches to general racism had failed to identify anti-Jewish hatred clearly enough.
“We do need to name antisemitism as a particular kind of prejudice and hate because I think if you don’t name it, you don’t actually know what you’re tackling or what you’re going to be able to do to respond to it,” Bell said.
Elaborating further in an interview with Sky News, he pointed out that a broad commitment to tackling racism has historically fallen short of addressing anti-Jewish hatred effectively.
“I think what this review has demonstrated is that a general commitment to tackling racism or prejudice or hate has not properly identified antisemitism as a particular kind of hate,” Bell told Sky News.
Sharp rise in antisemitic incidents in the UK
The findings follow a sharp rise in recorded antisemitic incidents within educational settings, with data from the Community Security Trust showing that reports reached record highs earlier this year, jumping from 112 incidents in the first half of 2025 to 178 during the same period in 2026.
The review calls for schools and colleges to officially track and treat antisemitism as a distinct category of harm rather than grouping it under general racism, establishing an explicit safeguarding duty to protect students.
It also urges educational institutions to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) working definition of antisemitism and recommends enhanced teacher training, clearer guidance on political impartiality during sensitive global discussions, and better educational resources to help students identify and challenge prejudice.
Addressing the House of Commons on Wednesday, Secretary of State for Education Lucy Powell presented the formal review and announced that the government has accepted all 27 recommendations from Sir David Bell’s review.
Outlining the challenges contributing to the crisis, Powell told MPs that “old tropes have found new life in the modern world” and warned that antisemitism is “now normalized and amplified in the echo chambers online, reaching directly into children’s bedrooms.”
She stressed the urgent need for a broader cultural shift, stating that society requires “this big conversation, this national conversation about what contemporary antisemitism looks like, where it is appearing, why it is appearing; calling it out, and explaining to the next generation what happens, what goes wrong in a country and a society when we fail to do that.”
Powell noted that, in the report, a survey of secondary school teachers who teach about the Holocaust found that “40% reported encountering antisemitism coming into those classes and amongst their students.”
Detailing the educational reforms tied to the review, she confirmed that while Holocaust education will remain compulsory in the national curriculum, instruction will be strengthened, and schools will move beyond solely studying the Holocaust to ensure proper education regarding Jewish life.
“As part of the curriculum, we will ensure the contribution, the culture, and the history of Jewish people in Britain is well understood and appreciated. Judaism is a diverse, modern, and generous faith tradition, and the curriculum should reflect that too,” Powell said.
He added that “blaming British Jews for the actions of the Israeli government is antisemitism” and noted that “targeting British Jews out of concern for Palestine is antisemitism.”
She also directly addressed the definition of Zionism and recent political controversies, stating, “Zionism is not racism, and that is why the motion passed by the Green Party is so wholly wrong and is antisemitic. And I want people to hear that loudly and clearly. And in the IHRA definition of antisemitism, it is clear that denying the right to Jewish people to self-determination is antisemitic, and that’s why it’s really important that schools adopt it.”
Warnings of attempts to isolate Jewish communities
The Green Party’s motion and its broader cultural impact were also condemned by other parliamentarians, including Conservative MP Sir Iain Duncan Smith, who warned that actions to isolate and attack Jewish communities mirror historical warnings and point to broader societal failures.
When pressed by MPs regarding financial support for the implementation of the sweeping changes, Powell confirmed to the House that “there will be funding attached to what we’ve outlined today” and explicitly clarified during subsequent questioning that schools will receive “new funding, as well as new resources for training for suggested classroom resources and so on, so that will be available, and hopefully schools will feel fully supported in taking this forward.”
Jewish community leaders welcomed the news of recommendations following publication of the independent review on Wednesday.
“We welcome the recommendations of Sir David Bell to tackle antisemitism in schools and colleges and the commitment of the Secretary of State for Education to implement them. The struggle against extremism and antisemitism begins with education, so we must get this right in schools,” Board of Deputies Vice President Karen Newman said.
“This is not just about protecting Jewish pupils and staff but [also about] protecting all our children from hateful and extremist ideas and supporting schools to tackle them where they arise. The evidence gathered by Sir David Bell showing the scale of the challenges is sobering, and makes clear the need for a determined and consistent approach,” Newman added.
“Treating antisemitism in schools as a safeguarding issue will have the benefit of creating an explicit duty on all schools to address this as they would any other threat to children’s safety, and will strengthen accountability,” she said.
Newman also pointed to specific measures within the report, addressing institutional guidance and external pressures.
“We particularly welcome the clear recommendations that schools and local authorities follow government guidelines by adopting the IHRA Working Definition of Antisemitism as a tool to deepen understanding of contemporary antisemitism. We further welcome recommendations relating to improving education about Jewish life, as well as antisemitism, and ensuring schools maintain their duties in relation to political impartiality,” she noted.
“We remain concerned about undue external influence on schools driven by narrow political agendas; and tendentious materials seeping into schools and increasing disharmony, and we will continue to press for vigilance against this,” Newman added.
'CST welcomes the recommendations of the Bell Review'
The Community Security Trust (CST) also praised the publication of the Bell's recommendations.
“CST welcomes the recommendations of the Bell Review into antisemitism in schools and colleges and hopes that this is the first step towards meaningful action to tackle anti-Jewish hatred in our education establishments,” the CST stated.
“Sir David Bell’s report details the damaging impact that the growth in antisemitism has had on Jewish school children and staff. Schools should be places where every child feels safe, included and able to learn without fear because of who they are. Instead, too often, Jewish children and staff have their educational experience marred by racist harassment, intimidation and extremism. This cannot continue,” the organization added.
“We thank Sir David Bell for producing this thorough review and welcome the government’s decision to accept its recommendations.
“The report provides an important acknowledgment that antisemitism has not been properly addressed through existing structures to tackle discrimination and that it requires dedicated, focused efforts to tackle it,” the trust noted.
“Too often, anti-Jewish prejudice is misunderstood or overlooked, leaving Jewish pupils feeling isolated and unsupported. Ensuring that school leaders and staff have the confidence, understanding, and training to recognize antisemitism and respond appropriately will be essential,” CST said.
“The priority now must be to ensure that these recommendations are implemented effectively, with clear guidance, appropriate training, and consistent action whenever antisemitism occurs.
“Jewish children should be able to attend school, learn, and thrive in the same safety and security that every child deserves. There can be no place for antisemitism in our education system,” CST emphasized.

Why Netanyahu is making the Iranian regime’s overthrow a personal promise - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:26:45 UTC
01:26:45 KST

Amid all the speculation about renewed military confrontation with Iran before next week’s elections or just after the US midterms, one shift in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s rhetoric is clear: he moved from promising to create the conditions for the Iranian regime’s overthrow to pledging to bring it down.
“The regime must fall, and I will bring it down,” he said on Sunday in a briefing with journalists.
“Our plan is a very comprehensive and very determined plan to bring about the fall of the regime. That is my plan. That is the directive I have given all the security agencies, and that is what will happen.”
On Tuesday, at the opening of the academic year at Tel-Hai University in Kiryat Shmona, Netanyahu expanded on that commitment and explained the rationale.
“We must complete the elimination of the Iranian regime; that is the primary objective,” he said. “I have spoken about this with President Trump more than once, including the day before yesterday [Sunday].”
Netanyahu says the regime will try again to produce a nuclear bomb
He argued that any agreement or accommodation leaving the regime in power would leave it determined to pursue a nuclear bomb and rebuild its network of proxies surrounding Israel.
Even a regime that is “battered, wounded, and beaten,” he said, would try again to produce nuclear weapons and reconstruct its regional axis.
“Therefore, the only way to prevent this is to bring down this regime, and then the elimination of Hezbollah will follow.”
Israel has long made clear that it would welcome the fall of a regime committed to its destruction. What stands out now is Netanyahu’s explicit, personal commitment to bringing that fall about.
Consider what he said in June 2025, during the ‘12-day war’.
“The matter of changing the regime or the fall of this regime is first and foremost a matter for the Iranian people. There is no substitute for this.”
Speaking to Kan television at the time, Netanyahu drew a clear distinction between a possible outcome of the war and its declared objectives. Regime change “could be a result, but it’s not a stated or formal goal that we have,” he said. Both he and the IDF stressed that the campaign’s purpose was to dismantle Iran’s nuclear and ballistic missile programs.
His position subsequently evolved.
'I will bring it down'
During the war that began on February 28, Netanyahu differentiated between what Israel could accomplish militarily and what the Iranian people would have to do themselves. At a March 12 press conference, he described preventing Iran from developing nuclear weapons and threatening ballistic missiles as the campaign’s purposes, alongside “another goal” of creating the conditions for Iranians to remove their rulers.
The distinction was consequential. Israel could strike the regime’s capabilities and weaken its grip. The Iranian people would have to seize the opportunity.
Now the language is more categorical: “I will bring it down.”
So what changed? Why is Netanyahu personally promising an outcome he previously said Israel could help the Iranian people achieve?
Part of the answer lies in the distinction he is drawing between damaging Iran’s capabilities and ending the threat it poses.
Israel can destroy centrifuges, hit missile factories and kill commanders. However, if the regime survives, Netanyahu argues, so will its determination to rebuild. Another successful military campaign may buy Israel time, but it will not spare the country another campaign down the road; only overthrowing the regime can do that.
This helps explain the rationale. It does not, by itself, explain the timing.
For that, look at the two political clocks ticking in the background: Israel’s election next week and the remaining time in Trump’s presidency.
The electoral logic is clear. One of Netanyahu’s central campaign themes is that he has changed the Middle East and must remain in office to complete the task.
An Iran that has been weakened but remains dangerous fits neatly into that argument: much has been accomplished, much remains to be done, and changing leaders now would put those gains at risk. At Sunday’s briefing, he explicitly linked finishing the job to the election.
This also gives him an answer to an uncomfortable question. If the campaigns against Iran were as successful as he maintains, why is another confrontation looming?
His answer is that military success has brought Israel closer to its destination, but the destination has yet to be reached. The regime’s survival explains the ongoing danger; overthrowing it promises the finally remove it.
For a public that wants to see an end to more than three years of wars, that is a powerful proposition. Netanyahu is offering the prospect that the sacrifices of recent years can produce a fundamentally different security reality, one in which Israel is no longer required to fight the same enemies every few months.
It also places his opponents in a difficult position. They can question his ability to fulfill the promise, but few Israeli voters need convincing that the fall of the Iranian regime would be welcome. The political argument shifts toward who can deliver that outcome, and whether Netanyahu’s confidence is justified.
Then there is the American clock.
Netanyahu's warnings of an anti-Israel US president in the future
In presenting his security doctrine on Sunday, Netanyahu warned that a future American president could be hostile to Israel and stressed the importance of the coming years. The implication is that he sees the remaining Trump years as a window of opportunity Israel cannot assume will remain open under the next administration.
That adds urgency to his argument. If Israel has weakened its enemies and has a supportive president in Washington, Netanyahu’s case is that it should use that combination to secure lasting results.
Yet an opportunity to act does not necessarily translate into an ability to achieve the desired outcome. And a conversation with Trump about bringing down the regime does not establish that the American president has signed on to that objective.
The same distinction applies to Israel’s military capabilities. The ability to destroy facilities, eliminate senior figures, and disrupt a country’s defenses is something we have all seen. The ability to translate all of that into regime change is something else entirely.
Netanyahu does not need to disclose operational plans to explain the basis for his confidence. But there is a legitimate question about what would make another effort succeed where earlier blows failed to produce an uprising capable of toppling the ayatollahs.
The prime minister’s rationale for wanting the regime gone is clear, and the election helps explain why he has moved its overthrow to the top of his rhetorical agenda. What remains missing is an explanation of how he intends to deliver on what increasingly sounds like a campaign promise–and one whose feasibility he has yet to demonstrate.

Israel music showcase struggles as Gaza genocide fuels boycott
Israel’s annual music showcase is struggling to attract international guests ahead of its November edition, with organisers citing a growing cultural boycott amid the genocidal war on Gaza.
The Israel Music Showcase Festival, held annually in Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, expects to welcome half as many international guests as last year, according to Israeli media reports on Wednesday.
The festival, which connects Israeli musicians with international music industry professionals, receives backing from Israeli state institutions, including the Foreign Ministry’s Cultural Diplomacy Division, the Culture Ministry and the Jerusalem Municipality.
As the event prepares for its November edition, organisers have acknowledged the growing impact of the cultural boycott amid continued international condemnation of Israel’s devastating military campaigns in Gaza, Lebanon and elsewhere in the Middle East.
Hadas Vanunu, the festival’s artistic director, told Israeli media that around 30 international guests were expected to attend this year, half the number who travelled from abroad last year.
Vanunu described the anticipated turnout as “both surprising and not surprising”.
The growing cultural boycott comes amid recent backlash against UK rapper Russ Millions, who cancelled his scheduled performance at the Boomerang Music Festival in Tel Aviv on Wednesday.
The rapper, known for hits including “Gun Lean” and “Body”, had been advertised as performing at the event.
His booking prompted criticism online, with fans and social media users questioning why a prominent British artist would perform in Israel amid its ongoing genocidal war on Gaza.
Russ Millions addressed the controversy during an Instagram Live session, saying: “If I was aware of any form of people killing, children or women I wouldn’t even have accepted any show.”
The growing international isolation of Israel’s music industry reflects a wider campaign by artists and cultural workers to oppose what they view as the normalisation of Israel’s actions against Palestinians through international cultural participation.
Long supported by pro-Palestine advocates, including the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement, the campaign has gained greater visibility since Israel launched its assault on Gaza in October 2023.
Musicians have withdrawn from performances, filmmakers have pulled their work from Israeli festivals, and industry figures have urged cultural organisations to sever institutional ties with Israel.
Israel’s continued participation in the Eurovision Song Contest has also prompted a backlash, with the Netherlands, Ireland, Spain, Iceland and Slovenia withdrawing from the 2026 competition.
Israel’s inclusion has additionally sparked protests from critics opposing its participation.
Israel’s offensive has displaced nearly the entire population of Gaza and killed more than 74,450 people, according to the territory’s health ministry.
Israeli forces have continued to carry out near-daily strikes on Gaza, with the health ministry reporting that at least 1,500 people have been killed in attacks since the ceasefire came into effect in October 2025.
The UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry, chaired by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Navi Pillay, concluded that Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

Slovakia resumes talks with russia on energy supplies, moving away from the position of its EU allies - media
Kyiv • UNN
For the first time since 2022, a meeting of the Russian-Slovak commission will take place in Moscow. They will discuss gas, oil, nuclear energy and cooperation.
Next week in Moscow, Slovakia will discuss the supply of Russian energy resources, resuming cooperation that was suspended after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. This step is another indication of the country’s departure from the position of its allies in the European Union and NATO, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
As Slovakia’s Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs reported late on Tuesday, a meeting of the Russian-Slovak intergovernmental commission on economic, scientific and technical cooperation will be held in Moscow on October 26. It will be the first such meeting since Russia’s attack on Ukraine in 2022.
According to ministry representatives, the meeting will focus on energy issues (including nuclear energy), as well as agriculture, environmental protection, sports and culture.
The publication notes that the resumption of consultations comes after several visits by Prime Minister Robert Fico to Moscow, including in May this year. Fico’s position stands out against the backdrop of the other 27 EU member states—especially after Hungary’s pro-Russian leader Viktor Orbán suffered defeat in the elections in April.
"Energy and opportunities for cooperation in ensuring the supply of strategic resources will be the key topic," the ministry said. "The Slovak side is also interested in discussing gas supplies and continuing oil supplies."
Slovakia, which purchases Russian oil and gas, is required under the EU plan to stop purchasing gas by the end of 2027. The plan is aimed at depriving Russia of the financial resources it uses to finance the war in Ukraine.
The ministry said that, while developing relations with Russia, Slovakia "continues to build its approach based on its membership in the European Union and the North Atlantic Alliance, as well as on fulfilling the obligations arising from that membership," but seeks to create space for dialogue.
In addition
Robert Fico—a populist and nationalist politician who is serving as prime minister of this Central European country for the fourth time—has repeatedly criticized EU sanctions against Russia. He also blamed Ukraine for disruptions in oil supplies to Slovakia that occurred earlier this year (while Kyiv said they were caused by Russian attacks).
Fico halted Slovakia’s provision of military aid to Ukraine, but the export of ammunition and military equipment continues on a commercial basis—including through state-owned companies. Fico said he would prefer Slovakia to be a neutral state rather than a member of NATO; he also said he does not want Slovak troops to take part in a war with Russia that could begin through the invocation of NATO’s collective defense provision.
In addition, he expressed the view that the West could provoke a confrontation with Russia, while Western intelligence services assert that the West’s actions are exclusively defensive in nature and warn of possible escalation by Russia.

Kuznetsova soon received a notice from Roskomnadzor demanding that she delete the post for spreading false information on a matter of public importance.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

leather octopuses and mohair whales by cosima von bonin take over paris’ petit palais
Unknown

01:19:24 KST

leather octopuses and mohair whales by cosima von bonin take over paris’ petit palais
within the historic galleries during art basel 2026, padded animal sculptures interrupt the solemn company of classical figures.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
cosima von bonin’s plush animals arrive at paris’ petit palais
Paris’ Petit Palais has acquired some unusual residents for Art Basel Paris 2026. A velvet St. Bernard has joined the figures in its historic sculpture gallery, while leather octopuses and mohair whales occupy the same grand setting. The animals belong to Dollys & Beaux, an installation by Cologne-based artist Cosima von Bonin, whose oversized fabric creatures, created first for LOEWE, bring a peculiar sense of humor to the museum’s collection of classical sculpture.
The gathering includes a bulldog and a pair of scallops, along with hermit crabs that extend the artist’s strange little animal kingdom. Some have been dressed in silk scarves, while others sport tartan textiles added especially for their appearance in Paris. Their soft, exaggerated bodies seem perfectly comfortable sharing the gallery with their more solemn neighbors. It’s an amusing encounter between materials, with floppy fabric creatures taking their place among figures traditionally carved to endure.
from LOEWE’s runway to the petit palais
The animals have already enjoyed a rather fashionable debut. Earlier this year, Cosima von Bonin was invited by Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez, creative directors of LOEWE, to create sculptures for the house‘s Fall/Winter 2026 show. At the Château de Vincennes in March, her plush creatures occupied seats alongside the runway, perched on oversized white shoeboxes as models passed along a bright yellow catwalk. Their presence extended into the collection itself, with the artist‘s imagery appearing across garments and accessories.
For Art Basel Paris, the same cast has been given a new setting and a few changes of costume. The silk scarves and tartan additions are a playful continuation of the fashion collaboration, although the creatures now find themselves surrounded by the permanent collection of a fine arts museum. Their placement among historic works gives them a different kind of presence. Without a runway to watch, the animals become part of the gathering themselves.
a soft interruption among the classics
Animals have appeared throughout von Bonin’s practice, particularly marine creatures and dogs that she renders in fabric with distinctly human attitudes. Working with found objects and familiar imagery from popular culture, the artist uses humor to examine social relationships and the conventions surrounding them. Her sculptures have a way of appearing both endearing and faintly ridiculous, with oversized features and relaxed postures that give each creature its own personality.
The Petit Palais offers an especially entertaining setting for this work. Visitors can move among the textile figures while the museum’s existing sculptures remain in place, creating unexpected encounters across the gallery. There is something funny about a plush whale occupying a room built for the formal display of art, particularly when its companions have arrived wearing silk accessories. The installation is presented by Petzel, Gaga, and Galerie Neu as part of Art Basel Paris’ public program, and is open with free admission from October 20th to 25th, 2026.
project info:
name: Dollys & Beaux (2026)
artist: Cosima von Bonin
location: Petit Palais
event: Art Basel Paris 2026
dates: October 20th — 25th, 2026
original commission: Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez for LOEWE Fall/Winter 2026

Raids at far-right group's offices at European Parliament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:14:00 UTC
01:14:00 KST

Raids at Patriots for Europe offices in Brussels, Strasbourg
October 21, 2026
The third-largest alliance of parties in the European Parliament, the right-wing nationalist Patriots for Europe (PfE) group, on Wednesday said searches had been carried out at "administrative offices" at the European Parliament buildings in Brussels and Strasbourg.
PfE said the searches appeared to be tied to the long-running probe into alleged misuse of funds by members of the now-disbanded Identity and Democracy (ID) Group.
PfE formed out of the ashes of ID, losing and gaining some members along the way, after the last European Parliament elections in 2024.
What did the investigative body say about the searches?
The European Public Prosecutor's Office — the independent body that investigates and prosecutes crimes against the EU budget, such as corruption or misuse of EU funds — said it searched premises in France and Belgium.
It said this was part of an ongoing investigation into the use of European Union funds by a former European Parliament group.
EPPO did not say which group was involved and said it would not publish further details for now for fear of compromising the investigation.
What did the PfE say about the searches?
PfE, meanwhile, confirmed the activity around its offices but also tried to stress its distance from the case since its rebrand and reformation — even though its constituent political parties are largely the same with the notable exception of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) now being excluded.
"Since this morning, the European Public Prosecutor's Office has been carrying out searches in administrative offices at the European Parliament in Brussels and Strasbourg. It would appear that these searches are linked to the complaint lodged against the Identity and Democracy Group (ID) dissolved in 2024," it wrote in a statement.
"The Patriots for Europe Group emphasizes that there is no legal continuity with the ID Group and that it is not involved in the ongoing investigations," it said.
A French member of the European Parliament for the Rassemblement National or National Rally (RN) party, Jean-Paul Garraud, said that "the offices of staff members of the former Identity and Democracy group" were targeted.
What were the details of the ID misuse of funds probe?
European Parliament auditors concluded last year that ID members had misused at least €4.3 million (roughly $4.8 million) in EU funds during the previous legislative term from 2019 to 2024.
According to their report, the money flowed to companies close to the group and to associations supporting anti-abortion campaigners.
The case was reminiscent of, but separate from, the conviction against RN leader Marine Le Pen, herself a former MEP, that for a time looked set to stifle her bid for the French presidency.
The ID group existed for one term in the European Parliament, from 2019 to 2024. It included France's RN, Germany's AfD, Austria's Freedom Party (FPÖ) and Italy's Lega, among other members.
It fell apart after major internal friction during the 2024 European election campaign, not least because of dissatisfaction within the group with their lead candidate Maximilian Krah of the AfD over a number of issues — from controversial remarks about Nazi Germany through to allegations of his close allies being Russian and Chinese influence, with one of Krah's aides since convicted of spying for China.
RN, FPÖ and Lega are part of the new PfE group, which claims "no legal continuity" to the dissolved ID alliance, but the AfD was not invited to join the PfE.
PfE has 85 seats in the 719-seat European Parliament, making it the third-largest group in the chamber, but a rather distant third behind the center-right European People's Party (184) and the center-left Socialists and Democrats (135).
The European Parliament relies heavily on such groupings, which try to unite political parties from various member states with broadly comparable policy positions and political alignment.
The AfD set up a much smaller splinter far-right grouping called Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN), with just 27 seats, 15 of them held by the AfD.

These are the most exciting potential human landing sites across the moon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:13:05 UTC
01:13:05 KST

The biggest “land rush” of the 21st century is underway—but not on Earth.
Together with multiple international partners, the U.S. and China are racing each other to build crewed outposts around the moon’s south pole, a region rich with water ice and other resources that could be used to kick-start an otherworldly economy and strengthen humanity’s expansion deeper into space. NASA’s Artemis IV mission seeks to send astronauts to the lunar south pole in 2028, and China is targeting human landings there by 2030.
But the clamor to capitalize on that prized patch of lunar real estate shouldn’t overlook other areas on the moon that could be even more valuable for science, according to an authoritative new report. Convened by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, a blue-ribbon panel of experts contends that human sorties to nonpolar regions of the moon hold great promise for resolving long-standing mysteries about Earth’s nearest celestial neighbor, the solar system and the universe at large.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Better yet, the report offers a short list of destinations to prioritize.
The NASA-sponsored report comes from the National Academy of Sciences (NAS) Committee on Key Nonpolar Destinations across the Moon, and it flags four places to send future human missions: Bhabha Crater, Mons Hadley, the Orientale Basin and the Aristarchus Plateau.
“Returning to the moon will be a great achievement for humanity—and setting foot where we never have before will be a major moment for science,” says James Day, co-chair of the committee and a professor at the University of California, San Diego’s Scripps Institution of Oceanography.
Visiting these four sites would add immense scientific value to whatever will be learned from any sequence of U.S. and Chinese crewed missions to the lunar south pole, adds committee co-chair Daniel Dumbacher, a professor of engineering practice in the School of Aeronautics and Astronautics at Purdue University.
Dumbacher and Day both discussed their findings in-depth during a webinar shortly after the report’s release.
Location, Location, Location
Bhabha Crater, the report notes, is on the lunar farside and would give astronaut expeditions the ability to access material from the moon’s oldest known preserved impact basin and to deploy ultrasensitive radio and optical astronomy experiments shielded from Earth’s noisy emissions.
The Mons Hadley region, part of which was previously explored by Apollo 15 moonwalkers, is a prime location for a space weather observatory. This site, the report says, could also host experiments to assess how piled-up regolith—impact-pulverized rocks that make up the lunar “soil”—could shield against radiation hazards.
The moon’s Orientale Basin is one of the largest and best-preserved multiringed impact crater in the solar system; going there would give unprecedented looks into the deep structure and origin of our natural satellite. Mission crews, the report adds, should return samples from the basin to Earth to reveal exactly how the basin was formed; while they’re there, they could also deploy a gravitational-wave observatory.
Lastly, the moon’s Aristarchus Plateau is a geologically rich volcanic landscape. Collecting samples there would help researchers understand volcanic processes that have shaped the moon and identify potentially important resources that could support future exploration.
The NAS panel also notes that the moon’s accessibility and sterility make it “an excellent testbed” for refining “planetary protection” procedures—that is, for finding ways to avoid Earth life contaminating other potentially habitable places in the solar system (and ensuring any alien biology doesn’t catastrophically contaminate Earth). Crewed dry runs at lunar test beds could help establish the rules of the road before sending humans to more biologically sensitive environments.
“Practicing planetary protection protocols on the moon will lead to greater confidence in the successful execution of these on other planetary bodies, such as Mars, where life may exist or may once have existed and the stakes are significantly higher,” the report states.
Adding a whole swath of extra proposed crewed lunar landing sites in addition to already planned human forays to the moon’s south pole may seem like overkill, says committee member Clive Neal, a professor of civil and environmental engineering and Earth Sciences at the University of Notre Dame. But the exercise is meant “to be enabling for Artemis and not a distraction.”
“There are four examples given for different missions, but it comes back and feeds into [NASA’s] developing moon base,” he says. One overlooked concept that the report seeks to highlight, Neal adds, is “the idea of a ‘distributed’ moon base”—a network of interlinked sites that can be more than the sum of their parts, providing far more value overall than any solitary outpost.
That’s because the moon probably has much more to offer than just the resources at its shadowy south pole—and figuring out the specifics is a long-term project with far-reaching implications. “There’s both science that enables exploration as well as exploration-driven science that enables a long-term human presence on the moon,” Neal says. “Achieving a permanent human presence on the moon is akin to now having a permanent human presence in low-Earth orbit,” he adds, and the lessons learned will feed forward for future crewed voyages to Mars.
A “History Book” for the Entire Universe
Jack Burns, a professor emeritus of astrophysics at the University of Colorado Boulder, is delighted by the report’s recommendations. He briefed the specially convened panel regarding a proposed array of low-frequency radio telescopes on the lunar farside.
Called FarView, this facility makes use of the moon’s radio-quiet environment to open the last unexplored electromagnetic window for astrophysics, delivering breakthrough science across astronomy, astrophysics, cosmology, heliophysics and planetary science, he tells Scientific American.
“Astronauts could play a crucial role in the early stages of that array, helping in site surveys, as well as setting up power stations and communications and the basic electronics to get started,” Burns says. The primary science driver for FarView, he adds, is the exploration of the cosmic dark ages, a mysterious era shortly after the big bang and before the formation of the first stars.
As for astronauts conducting such duties versus robots, “the modern way of looking at it is not either; it’s both,” Burns observes.
The NAS report underscores the need to explore the whole moon, not just its south pole, he adds. “The moon is our history book. With Apollo, we just thumbed through the first few pages. But there’s much more to delve into, as the moon is a unique learning tool, not only to understand that body but also to help unwrap the history of our Earth.”
Erica Jawin, a research scientist at the Planetary Science Institute, who was not part of the NAS panel, agrees. Answering questions such as why the moon’s nearside looks so different from its farside, when the giant lunar impact basins formed, and how much water and other “volatile” materials may lurk in the lunar interior would help reveal otherwise-hidden chapters of our planet’s and our solar system’s deepest history.
“These questions, among many others, can be addressed by exploring nonpolar locations,” Jawin says. “The scientific community has repeatedly discussed locations of high scientific value for surface exploration.” The Aristarchus Plateau has been of particular interest.
“The Aristarchus Plateau has been consistently recognized for its scientific value in the form of diverse volcanism and the young, bright Aristarchus Crater, as well as its exploration potential for everything from resource prospecting for water to manufacturing building materials using the thick pyroclastic deposit,” Jawin says.
A robust and successful lunar exploration program, Jawin continues, should leverage the unique role humans can play in conjunction with robotic assets. In particular, it is critical to understand specific locations where scientific exploration would benefit from having a human-crewed component, she said.
“Humans have unique skills for exploration and observation that differ from robotic surface or orbital assets. Particularly, humans excel in visual analyses such as assessing geologic setting and diversity across a landing site, as well as in complex decision-making and confronting unexpected obstacles,” Jawin notes.
With proper investment into scientific and technological capabilities, Jawin concludes, “the coming years could be a renaissance for human exploration of the moon, allowing us to answer scientific questions that have persisted for decades.”

Former Palestinian envoy to be freed and expelled from Lebanon

Breadcrumb
Former Palestinian envoy to be freed and expelled from Lebanon
Lebanese judicial authorities have ordered the release of former Palestinian ambassador to Lebanon Ashraf Dabbour under a settlement requiring him to leave the country, the Almodon news site reported on Tuesday.
Security forces were expected to escort Dabbour to Beirut Airport for departure to Bulgaria, bringing to a close a judicial case that involved his detention and questioning. It was not clear exactly when he would be required to leave Lebanon.
The agreement, according to Almodon, includes halting all media campaigns waged by both his supporters and those aligned with his rival, Mazen Abbas, son of Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas.
Sources close to Dabbour stressed that the agreement did not involve any financial settlement. The sources said several factors had contributed to his release, including a firm position by Lebanese Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri against allowing the dispute to escalate, as well as repeated interventions by former Progressive Socialist Party leader Walid Jumblatt, who questioned the legal grounds for Dabbour's detention.
There were also concerns among Palestinian and Lebanese figures that handing Dabbour over to the Palestinian Authority (PA), if carried out, would set a legal precedent that could trigger further disputes and potentially prompt the authority to seek the detention of other Palestinians in Lebanon, the sources said.
Fatah leaders also played an important role in containing the dispute, which had begun to affect the movement's internal cohesion. Several messages were reportedly sent by senior Fatah figures to President Abbas, urging him to intervene and prevent the situation from escalating further.
Lebanese security forces arrested Dabbour in April, acting on an Interpol arrest warrant tied to financial corruption allegations. He was detained upon his arrival at Beirut Airport from Jordan, in implementation of a Red Notice issued in absentia.
In July 2025, Abbas relieved Dabbour of his duties as deputy to the general supervisor of the Palestinian file in Lebanon, reportedly as part of broader organisational and security changes within Fatah.
He later faced multiple financial allegations, including corruption and illicit enrichment.
Dabbour had been under scrutiny over his alleged role in the sale of properties in Beirut owned by the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO), which maintained a significant presence in Lebanon until Israel’s 1982 invasion.
Jumblatt had close and direct ties to the PLO during the Lebanese civil war.
During his tenure as ambassador from 2012 to 2015, Dabbour is accused of approving real estate deals for personal gain, including the purchase of a PLO-owned building in Beirut’s Corniche al-Mazraa area, and of transferring funds from embassy accounts into his personal bank accounts.
After refusing to appear before Palestinian judicial authorities, an arrest warrant was issued against him through Interpol.

Women entrepreneurs in frontline regions receive nearly UAH 20 mln in grants under Oschadbank initiative
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:10:00 EEST
01:10:00 KST

KYIV. Oct 21 (Energy Reform) - The Move Forward programme, which provides grants and consulting to microenterprises and is funded by the German government and jointly implemented by GIZ and the National Development Institution (NDI), has provided nearly UAH 20 million to 51 women entrepreneurs in frontline regions to develop their businesses, NDI First Deputy Chairman of the Management Board Valeriy Maiboroda said.
"The programme launched in May 2026. We received nearly 500 applications from women entrepreneurs in frontline regions. We selected 51 winners and provided almost UAH 20 million in funding," Maiboroda said at a presentation in Kyiv of Oschadbank's Women's Business initiative, launched jointly with international partners. The event took place at the OschadBusiness Hub.
Maiboroda said that 71% of the projects supported were aimed at improving energy resilience.
"I'm glad we managed to support our women entrepreneurs ahead of winter in equipping their businesses for energy resilience, including through energy storage systems and energy-efficient equipment," he said.
In addition to financial support, the selected entrepreneurs received individual consultations from NDI and Oschadbank, including assistance with developing business plans and other necessary tools.
As reported, Oschadbank's Women's Business initiative to support women entrepreneurs envisages approximately EUR 2 million in grants, alongside preferential lending and training.
Other partners in the initiative include Prosper Global, the European Fund for Southeast Europe (EFSE), the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), Germany's German Sparkassenstiftung for International Cooperation (DSIK), and the Move Forward programme for grants and consulting to microenterprises, funded by the German government and jointly implemented by GIZ and NDI.

Russia believes the war in Ukraine is moving closer to a resolution, but it remains difficult to determine how soon a settlement could be reached, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Wednesday.
"I don’t know how close we’re getting, but things are heading in that direction,” Ushakov said, responding to a question by the Vesti news outlet about how close the over-four-year war in Ukraine is to reaching a conclusion.
Ushakov’s remarks come amid his commentary to reporters following a meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff in the city of St. Petersburg earlier in the day.
In his remarks, the Russian presidential aide stated that Putin conveyed to Witkoff Moscow’s readiness "in principle” to resume trilateral Ukraine talks "around the 10th of November,” particularly on the issue of building a post-war "security system” for Moscow and Kyiv.
Moscow and Kyiv last held U.S.-mediated peace negotiations earlier this year, with three rounds of talks on Jan. 23-24, Feb. 4-5, and Feb. 17-18. The first two rounds were held in Abu Dhabi, while the third took place in Geneva.

The Hidden Economy of Iran’s VOD Market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

The Hidden Economy of Iran’s VOD Market
Reaching an aggregate industry revenue of 13 trillion Tomans in 1403, Iran’s Video-on-Demand (VOD) sector operates on a distinct financial model: unlike the subscription-first global benchmark set by Netflix, domestic streaming economics are fundamentally anchored in telecom data traffic sharing and advertising capacity.
A financial breakdown of Iran's streaming industry highlights how bandwidth consumption and corporate sponsorships outweigh direct retail subscriptions:
1. Revenue Share Breakdown Across a 13-Trillion-Toman Market:
- Telecom Data Traffic (~5.0T Tomans / 38.5%): Data-traffic revenue sharing with telecom operators serves as the primary revenue driver across major streaming platforms.
- Ads & Corporate Sponsorships (~4.3T Tomans / 33.1%): In-app advertising and corporate sponsorships represent the second-largest revenue pillar.
- Direct User Subscriptions (~3.7T Tomans / 28.4%): Retail subscription purchases rank third, accounting for less than one-third of total industry income.
2. The Real Cost per User:
The total average monthly cost incurred by an active user is estimated between 579,000 and 766,000 Tomans. This total expenditure reflects the combined cost of the direct platform subscription fee alongside the necessary internet bandwidth usage required for streaming.
3. Market Competition and Industry Leadership:
Across the primary platforms analyzed—Filimo, Namava, Filmnet, Sheyda, and Namafilm—Filimo maintains the dominant market share across all monetization verticals, leading in user subscriptions, data traffic yields, in-app ad volume, and external sponsorships.
4. Platform Spotlight: Sheyda:
Backed by Tourism Financial Group, emerging platform Sheyda has structured its subscription plans at 140,000 Tomans for 1 month, 395,000 Tomans for 3 months, 690,000 Tomans for 6 months, and 990,000 Tomans for a 1-year plan. Consistent with broader market dynamics, traffic-revenue sharing functions as its core monetization engine.
Unlike subscription-first international models, Iran’s streaming economy expands through cumulative watch hours, bandwidth volume, and ad delivery, tying platform financial sustainability directly to telecommunication infrastructure.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned that Iran and its regional proxies have been considering ways to influence the upcoming election in a Wednesday interview with The Jerusalem Post.
“We have clear warnings from military intelligence and the Mossad that Iran and its proxies are considering ways to influence the elections,” Netanyahu told the Post.
“If they do, it’ll be a big mistake for them because we’ll respond with force and might they can’t even imagine,” he warned.
The prime minister added that Iran and its allies could seek to undermine public confidence in Israel’s security by staging attacks intended to suggest that the country’s military achievements had not fundamentally changed the regional balance of power.
“We’ve had an amazing success story,” Netanyahu said, describing Israel’s transformation since the October 7, 2023, Hamas massacre.
“We went from October 7 to being the most powerful force in the Middle East, clearly, the most powerful country in the Middle East,” he repeated.
According to Netanyahu, Israel has completed “90% of the job” against Iran and its proxies, but the remaining challenge is preventing the Islamic Republic from rebuilding its capabilities.
Netanyahu names 'enemies that want Israel to lose,' including Erdogan, Mamdani, Hamas, Hezbollah, Iran, Abbas
The prime minister framed the election as a strategic contest, naming Iranian leaders, Hamas, Hezbollah, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas among those he said wanted him defeated.
“All the enemies of Israel want me to lose,” he said.
Netanyahu identified Iran’s nuclear ambitions as the most consequential security threat currently facing Israel, arguing that Israeli military operations had addressed an immediate danger but had not eliminated the underlying threat.
“About a year ago, Iran was on the verge of developing several atomic bombs,” he said. “If we hadn’t acted in Operation Rising Lion and after that with Operation Roaring Lion, they’d have atomic bombs to destroy us.”
As long as the current regime remained in power, Netanyahu said, Iran will seek to rebuild its nuclear program and ballistic missile capabilities.
Iran plans to acquire 20,000 ballistic missiles, Netanyahu claims
During the interview, Netanyahu claimed that the Islamic Republic had planned to acquire 20,000 ballistic missiles, describing such an arsenal as an existential threat to Israel. He estimated that Iran still possessed over 1,000 missiles.
According to the defense establishment’s assessment, Iran possesses 1,600 missiles.
Asked whether he and US President Donald Trump were aligned on potential targets for another operation against Iran, Netanyahu said he believed the two leaders shared an understanding of the strategic stakes.
“President Trump recognizes what I recognize,” he said, without specifying which targets might be considered in any future military action.
“As long as the Iranian regime is there, they’ll reconstitute themselves,” he said.
Asked whether a name had already been chosen for a potential third operation against Iran, Netanyahu pointed to the lion-themed names of the previous campaigns, Rising Lion and Roaring Lion.
“We’re dealing with lions,” he said. “This generation – lions. Lions and lionesses.”
