Kremlin payment firm A7 has been pumping billions in ‘untraceable’ cash into global financial system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:08:13 UTC
01:08:13 KST

RUSSIA
Kremlin payment firm A7 has been pumping billions in ‘untraceable’ cash into global financial system
Documents show the sanctioned payments firm has handled at least 283 tons of rubles gathered in Moscow’s giant trading halls, processed and trucked to Russia’s main defense bank.
At the sprawling Sadovod market in southeast Moscow, among the 160 acres of clothing, jewelry and appliance booths, at least eight teams are spotted, working apart from the everyday hustle and bustle of the market.
Throughout a business day, these teams, known in confidential records as “departments,” receive a steady stream of customers, almost always carrying bags of various shapes and sizes.
And inside the bags are piles and piles of cash – Russian rubles. These departments, staffed by payment brokers, are a key intake point for one of the largest, and most secretive, cash-processing operations in the world.
Welcome to the industrial cash machine that is A7, the payments giant backed by the Russian state.
Between November 2024 and July 2025, A7 processed at least 283 tons of cash rubles — equal to more than $14 billion U.S. dollars, an investigation by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists and Russian independent media Proekt has found.
For A7, ICIJ discovered, cash is king, the jet fuel for a firm now under scrutiny as a “shadow banking network” designed to evade Western sanctions at scale, according to U.S. authorities.
On Oct. 1, the U.S. Treasury sanctioned A7 as a “significant transnational criminal organization,” which “utilizes money laundering methodologies to fraudulently move vast sums of money in violation of sanctions and other laws in the jurisdictions in which it operates.”
But while Western governments and banks scramble to trace A7 money flows through the international financial system, ICIJ’s investigation reveals that the origins of the bulk of A7 transmissions are, in fact, untraceable.
According to internal A7 records seen by ICIJ, and people familiar with the matter, a huge portion of A7’s payments do not stem from conventional bank transfers by clients inside Russia, but literally from hundreds of tons of cash rubles.
Leaked internal records allowed ICIJ to identify that a handful of wholesale markets and other businesses around the Russian capital, including Sadovod, where much of the business is done in cash, made up a significant share of the cash A7 processed.
The records show that while the source of the cash is untraceable, its destination is not: Most of the cash is bound not for Western markets, but for China.
A7 did not return ICIJ’s requests for comment.
In public statements, A7 has strongly rejected the U.S. allegations of wrongdoing, saying that it “employs a modern, multi-tiered compliance system” and that it was “established to ensure uninterrupted settlements for the Russian market, which has been subjected to unlawful restrictive measures.”
“All clients undergo screening to identify risks and prevent the servicing of individuals or organizations whose activities violate regulatory requirements,” it continued.
Experts say the fact that cash drives A7 raises the spectre of a money laundering operation limited only by the size of the market and A7’s capacity to physically handle the cash. As such, A7’s cash-based model presents challenges not previously understood both to the conventional banking system and to law enforcement.
“Cash is considered one of the highest risk methods of payment and store of value because it’s anonymous, it can travel across borders, and it doesn’t attach to any specific individual or company,” anti-financial crime expert George Voloshin told ICIJ in an interview.
“The A7 network not only helps Russia circumvent Western sanctions and export controls,” Voloshin continued. The fact that A7 takes massive volumes of cash from Moscow’s wholesale markets suggests that the company “is also likely to facilitate cash-based money laundering by effectively legitimizing potential proceeds of crime,” he said.
Voloshin added that international banks bear an additional burden of tracing payments emanating from A7. “The main risk is that [foreign] intermediary or beneficiary banks become complicit in [a] form of criminal activity that they know nothing about, because they don’t have any visibility into what’s happening in Russia where the money originates from.”
Cash by the ton, bound for China
On its launch in late 2024, A7 touted itself as a sanctions-proof payments system, and has come under increasing scrutiny for its role as one of the Kremlin’s principal channels for laundering billions of dollars worth of payments out of Russia and into the global financial system, via a global network of shell companies, often with accounts at major international banks.
As part of its launch, A7 integrated into its business a hodgepodge of informal payment brokers at Moscow markets, including Sadovod, according to internal A7 records seen by ICIJ.
“For [A7], Sadovod is simply a big client base — a big, aggregated pile of clients,” a person familiar with the matter, who requested anonymity due to security concerns, told ICIJ. “And that’s exactly what they go there for: the money and the profit.”
For years, this ecosystem of market brokers converted importers’ cash into conventional bank transfers or crypto, most often bound for China. This informal system was upended by Western sanctions, which barred Russian businesses from the SWIFT system, the international messaging network that allows banks to exchange transactions. The threat of U.S. secondary sanctions — which target entities for doing business with sanctioned states or businesses — made Chinese banks more cautious when dealing with Russia.
The informal cash payment system at Moscow’s wholesale markets “depends on trusted intermediaries, established relationships and confidence that money will arrive,” Ilia Shumanov, managing partner of Russia-focused due diligence firm Tri-Trace Investigations, told ICIJ. “Its international reach can be extensive, while outsiders have limited visibility into the underlying transactions.”
Under A7’s new, supercharged system, a platoon of market brokers takes in the bags of cash brought by vendors and makes an initial count.
The brokers then stuff the rubles into numbered bags to be loaded, along with clients’ payment orders, into vans bound for an A7 processing office elsewhere in the Russian capital, according to leaked internal payment and cash management records.
A review of cash deposit and internal payment records shows that a small army of 50 or so A7 cashiers feeds the cash into a counting system where the amounts are verified; A7 enters the bag number, ruble amount and the client’s payment order into a bespoke payment management system, then trucks the cash on to Promsvyazbank, or PSB, the Russian state defense bank, a co-owner of the company. PSB puts it in a vault and credits A7 accounts. PSB acknowledged ICIJ’s request for comment, but did not provide a response.
Records show that A7 then orders one of a network of shell companies registered outside Russia to make a payment on behalf of an A7 client to a beneficiary’s account, often a Chinese exporter, at another bank outside Russia – without any trace of the cash, or Russian origin, of the funds surfacing on the wire transfer or supporting documentation. The shell companies are advanced funds from A7 in Russia which pass through Kyrgyzstan on their way to the payee.
“The only bank that sees [where the funds come from] is Promsvyazbank,” Voloshin commented. “And the only company that sees everything is A7 itself.”
With A7’s role in sanctions evasion increasingly in the spotlight of Western authorities, understanding the source of A7 payments will become a central challenge for Western sanctions enforcers and international banks charged with know your customer (KYC) and other anti money-laundering obligations.
The scale of A7’s cash intake is visible in a series of leaked documents reviewed by ICIJ, including a cash deposit ledger dated to shortly after the company’s launch in late 2024. Over a six-week period between November and December 2024, that ledger and other documents provide a running total of A7’s incoming cash at that time, some 126 billion rubles ($1.2 billion).
A leaked A7 promissory note register reviewed by ICIJ reveals that A7’s cash intake at PSB only rose in 2025, reaching 195 billion rubles ($2.3 billion) in a single month by April 2025, and 250 billion rubles ($3.1 billion) in June 2025. At its peak, A7 was processing at least 58 tons of cash per month.
The only company that sees everything is A7 itself.
—anti-financial crime expert George Voloshin
PSB, which serves as a bank for all payments routed through the company inside Russia, typically has to give approval to process market payments made by A7, likely because of the size of this channel, according to a leaked A7 document seen by reporters.
It is unclear what checks, if any, A7 or the brokers at Sadovod and other markets perform on these funds.
“Sadovod is quite a chaotic place, I can’t imagine [the brokers] do all the checks required – KYC, source of wealth, source of funds,” Voloshin continued. “They may check your passport. But where the money comes from, that’s the biggest question.”
The problem of undeclared cash circulating at Moscow’s wholesale markets has also been flagged by Russian financial authorities, including its Central Bank.
“Where do [cash] funds of unknown origin come from?” a senior Central Bank official asked during remarks at a banking conference in Moscow on Sept. 23. “I won’t be revealing anything new here,” he said, “but primarily they come from wholesale and retail markets, mostly in Moscow, and illegal crypto exchanges.”
Sadovod did not respond to ICIJ requests for comment. There is no allegation of wrongdoing by the market.
One A7 payment register, dated late 2024, as well as other payment records, suggests that A7’s market payments are mostly bound for China. Chinese exports to Russia have surged since the Kremlin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as Russia’s industrial and consumer economy has searched for new inputs to replace Western goods.
The payment register showed approximately 2,300 proposed and in many cases documented transfers for different Sadovod brokerage teams — numbered one to six and called “otdely,” or “departments” — destined for their clients’ suppliers, or further intermediaries, in Hong Kong and mainland China.
The person familiar with the markets payment business told ICIJ that the brokerage teams typically operate from offices close to the market administration offices.
These payments, the register shows, were routed predominantly through the bank accounts of a Kyrgyz state-owned company, the Trading Company of the Kyrgyz Republic, as well as several trading companies in Turkey and Hong Kong. The Kyrgyz Ministry of Economy acknowledged ICIJ’s request for comment, but did not respond.
And the destinations for the bulk of these market payment requests, records show, are accounts owned by Chinese export companies at major Chinese banks. Among these are: Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC), Bank of China, Agricultural Bank of China and China Construction Bank. ICBC, for example, was the destination for at least 72 market payment requests, in both U.S. dollars and Chinese yuan, worth the equivalent of $11 million, according to A7 internal records. Neither ICBC, nor the other banks responded to ICIJ’s questions about their knowledge of the payments.
In the wake of the U.S. Treasury’s threat to impose secondary sanctions, in December 2023, Chinese banks started refusing payments from Russian banks, as well as payments they suspected could be related to exports to Russia, according to Russian media reports.
The A7 system, including its use of shell companies, is designed to effectively strip Russian funds of their origin, making them easier for Chinese banks to accept, says illicit finance expert Zachary Tvarozna, co-author of a recent investigation into A7 with the Open Source Centre, a U.K. non-profit.
“By the time [an A7 payment] is received, nobody in the chain, from the U.S. clearing bank to the Chinese supplier, knows where it came from,” Tvarozna said. “Washington kind of created a market for A7 and then didn’t really do anything about it.”
Leaked records allowed reporters to see the scale of payments made by A7 on behalf of the clients of Sadovod brokers, which were ultimately converted to yuan or U.S. dollars. It’s not known how the currencies are converted.
The records show, for example, that A7 received a total of 314 payment requests from Sadovod brokers worth $76 million, made in U.S. dollars and yuan, to be made to a Hong Kong export company called Yiton Trading Ltd. in late 2024.
Each payment logged in A7’s payment management system includes an amount, currency, beneficiary details, proposed payment route and a unique identifying number.
While most of the payments to Yiton Trading – which has since been dissolved – were routed through the Trading Company of the Kyrgyz Republic, on Nov. 22 that year, for example, the A7 records also include a dollar-denominated payment to Yiton Trading via a Hong Kong intermediary.
According to a payment authorization contained within leaked A7 records, the transfer amounted to $287,000 made by the intermediary from its account at the Hong Kong branch of British multinational bank Standard Chartered to an account held by Yiton Trading at the same bank. Standard Chartered declined ICIJ’s request for comment.
That payment, according to its unique reference number within A7’s payment management system, declared its client in the payment register as “Sadovod.”

A Texas husband and wife are facing criminal charges following the fatal shooting of a 17-year-old girl who was driving to a Halloween celebration at the St Louis zoo when gunfire struck her vehicle on a Missouri highway.
St Louis county prosecutor Melissa Price Smith announced on Monday that Willie Herndon, 43, has been charged with first-degree murder and armed criminal action in connection with the death of Alyssa Wilson. His wife, 45-year-old Taiya Herndon, is also facing a charge of hindering prosecution.
The charges follow an investigation into the deadly 14 October shooting along Interstate 170 in Overland, Missouri, a community north-west of St Louis.
Wilson was traveling southbound at about 7pm, heading to meet a friend for the zoo’s Halloween festivities, known as Boo at the Zoo, when the shooting occurred.
Court documents reveal that at least one bullet was fired into the back of the teenager’s vehicle.
The gunfire left Wilson “incapacitated,” according to court records, and her vehicle subsequently slammed into a concrete median barrier. Emergency responders transported the teenager to the Barnes-Jewish hospital, where she was pronounced dead.
Investigators say security footage captured crucial details that helped authorities identify the suspects.
Jack Abell, chief deputy commander of the region’s major case squad, said during a news conference that Wilson had just driven past a white Buick Enclave parked along the highway shoulder when a single gunshot could be heard.
“A person exited the vehicle and stood outside for a short period of time,” he said. “There was a gunshot, got back in the vehicle. The vehicle turned its hazards off and continued on.”
Authorities used surveillance footage and automated license plate readers to trace the Buick, which carried an out-of-state registration, which ultimately led authorities to the Texas couple.
During Monday’s press conference, Wilson’s father, Robert Hickman, spoke about the devastating loss of his daughter and the future she will never get to experience.
“Alyssa was 17, excited about her life, excited about her future,” he said. “She had 60 days until she turned 18, and we were getting ready to take our first family vacation together to go to Disney for her to see her favorite person in the world, Princess Tiana, and unfortunately, she’s not going to get to do that any more. This was a senseless act.”
Investigators did not disclose what may have prompted the deadly encounter. Abell confirmed that Wilson had no relationship with either of the accused individuals.
Willie Herndon now faces first-degree murder and armed criminal action charges, while Taiya Herndon has been charged with hindering prosecution in connection with the teenager’s death.

In the mining sector, China will strengthen work safety accountability at all levels and accelerate the shift toward a preventive approach to safety management, said Zhang Ruiting, deputy administrator of the National Mine Safety Administration.
China will leverage digital and intelligent technologies to improve mine safety and upgrade equipment used in challenging mining environments, to strengthen disaster prevention and control, Zhang said. ■

====================================================================================================

Xinhua Headlines: Xi Jinping's new Long March
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
00:07:03 CST
01:07:03 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- On the banks of the Yudu River in east China, a choir sang of soldiers leaving home more than nine decades ago. Beside the singers, eight large red Chinese characters proclaimed: "May the spirit of the Long March shine forever."
In October 1934, some 86,000 Red Army soldiers crossed the river, little knowing that they were embarking on a grueling 12,500-kilometer journey, which American journalist Edgar Snow hailed as "an odyssey unequaled in modern times." In October 1936, three main Red Army forces converged in northwestern China, marking the end of the Long March.
As China commemorates the 90th anniversary of the Long March's victorious conclusion this year, visitors have traveled to the mountainous county of Yudu in Jiangxi Province to see where it all began.
Yudu's visitors number in the millions each year. Among those who have made the trip is Chinese President Xi Jinping.
During his visit in May 2019, Xi laid a floral basket at a Long March departure monument, went to the river crossing used by Red Army soldiers and met their descendants.
"I have come here to let people across the country know that the Party has not forgotten its original aspiration," said Xi, who is also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission.
"We must build on the past, pack our bags and set out again," he said.
CARRY THE BATON FORWARD
The Long March was a strategic shift. In 1934, the fledgling CPC was forced to abandon its main base in the provinces of Jiangxi and Fujian after failing to repel the Kuomintang regime's fifth encirclement and suppression campaign.
The maneuver took the Red Army across nearly 100 rivers and more than 40 towering mountains, and through marshland known as a "death zone." The troops fought more than 600 battles. Many lost their lives along the way.
Far in the northwest, Xi's father, Xi Zhongxun, and his comrades Liu Zhidan and Xie Zichang established the Shaanxi-Gansu revolutionary base. The existence of the base was an important factor in Mao Zedong's decision to make it the Long March's final destination.
After the Long March, the Party established a firm foothold in northern Shaanxi, with Yan'an as its headquarters for more than a decade. From there, it grew in strength, led the Chinese people in fighting against Japanese invasion and eventually overthrew the Kuomintang regime.
Growing up in such a revolutionary family, Xi developed a deep connection to the Long March and the region. He was not yet 16 when he left Beijing for a village in Yan'an, where he spent seven years living and working alongside farmers. There, he joined the Party, became the village Party chief, forged close ties with local people, and made a commitment to serving the people through public office.
Yan'an, the Chinese revolution's foothold after the Long March and its springboard for national victory, was thus the starting point of Xi's political journey.
"Whenever I went to Yan'an in those years, I felt a deep sense of reverence and excitement," Xi recalled.
As a young man, Xi was deeply fascinated by the history of the Long March. In the 1980s, he was acquainted with writer Wang Yuanjian, who devoted himself to chronicling the Red Army's heroism. Wang had interviewed many Long March veterans. As he recounted their stories, Xi would pull a notebook from his pocket and carefully take notes, Wang's wife recalled in an article.
In 1996, while serving as Fujian's deputy Party secretary, Xi joined a 1,000-person torch relay marking the Long March's 60th anniversary. He set off at the front alongside an 82-year-old Red Army veteran.
In 2006, as Party secretary of Zhejiang, Xi visited a photo exhibition marking the 70th anniversary of the Long March. He described the Long March as both an extraordinary test of the human spirit and will, and a journey in pursuit of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.
Since taking the top office in late 2012, Xi has retraced the Long March routes on visits across the country: from Yudu, where the Central Red Army assembled and set out, to Quanzhou, where soldiers fought the bloody Battle of the Xiangjiang River; Zunyi, the site of a decisive turning point; and Jiangtaibu, where Red Army forces joined up at the end of the Long March.
At museums, Xi studied artifacts and asked questions. At monuments, he paid tribute to revolutionary martyrs by presenting flower baskets and bowing. He also instructed authorities to recover and properly bury soldiers' remains and build memorial facilities.
On one visit, he paused before a painting of Chen Shuxiang, whose division served as the Red Army's rear guard. Captured after covering the main force's river crossing, Chen refused to surrender and died after tearing open his abdominal wound.
Xi asked how the Red Army had broken through encirclement and held together despite devastating losses, then offered his answer: the power of conviction.
For generations of Chinese leaders, the Long March is not just a military campaign, but a metaphor for the ongoing task of transforming China.
In 1949, more than a decade after the Long March ended, the People's Republic was founded. Earlier that year, with victory in sight, Mao said that winning the revolution "would be only the first step of the Long March." The journey of building a new China had just begun.
It significantly gained pace with the launch of the reform and opening up in 1978. Deng Xiaoping, a Long March veteran, proposed a three-step strategy for China's modernization, which was later elaborated as follows: meet the people's basic needs of food and clothing by 1990, achieve moderate prosperity by the end of the 20th century, and basically attain modernization by the middle of the 21st century. This modernization drive came to be known as the new Long March.
"The Long March of our generation is to attain the 'two centenary goals' and realize the Chinese Dream -- the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation," Xi said.
The two goals refer to achieving moderate prosperity in all respects by the Party's centenary in 2021 and building a great modern socialist country in all respects by the centenary of the People's Republic around the middle of the century.
In 2017, Xi brought forward the timetable for basically achieving modernization under Deng's three-step strategy by 15 years to 2035.
"Every generation must undertake its own Long March," Xi said.
BRAVE THROUGH ALL ODDS
When the Long March began, the Red Army faced an enemy superior in both numbers and weaponry. Kuomintang forces pursued it from behind and blocked the routes ahead, seeking to encircle and destroy it. Breaking through meant fighting for every chance of survival.
In the winter of 1934, the struggle reached a critical point at the Xiangjiang River. Under heavy bombardment, Red Army troops fought their way toward the crossing points. By the time the army broke through, its ranks had dwindled from some 86,000 at the start of the march to just over 30,000.
The new Long March Xi is leading would test the Party's resolve against a different set of challenges. When he was elected the Party's top leader in 2012, China had become the world's second-largest economy and largest manufacturer after more than three decades of rapid economic growth.
That transformation also brought new challenges. China needed to sustain its economic momentum while narrowing regional disparities, tackling corruption, eradicating absolute poverty, and easing mounting environmental pressures. Meanwhile, the international community's expectations for China were rising.
Talking about "today's Long March," Xi said that although the conditions and tasks differ greatly, it remains "a pioneering, arduous and complex undertaking."
The modernization drive Xi now leads is unprecedented in human history. A population exceeding 1.4 billion is collectively advancing toward modernity on a scale surpassing the combined populations of existing developed nations. His goal is common prosperity for all, encompassing both material wealth and cultural-ethical advancement. Harmony between humanity and nature is emphasized. China also pursues rejuvenation through peaceful development.
None of these is easy.
Xi believes that overcoming the risks and challenges on the new journey requires the same revolutionary will forged during the Long March. "No matter how great the difficulties, think of the Red Army's Long March, and think of the bloody battle at the Xiangjiang River," he said.
He put forward a series of visionary strategies to ensure the march proceeds in the right direction. These include an extensive reform package -- the most comprehensive in history -- that gives the market a "decisive" role in allocating resources while making sure the government better fulfills its role. He promises broader market access for foreign investors. Since 2013, the number of pilot free trade zones in China has expanded from one to the current total of 23.
He put forward a new development philosophy that places greater emphasis on innovation, coordination, green development, openness and shared benefits. All these echo the important experience drawn from the Long March -- acting on one's own initiative, seeking truth from facts, and proceeding from reality.
More recently, Xi introduced "new quality productive forces" -- his term for growth driven by technological advances and industrial upgrading. Like his predecessors during the Long March, Xi leads from the front, demonstrating his strategic vision and decisiveness.
Upon visiting an automobile factory years ago, he called for a shift from conventional fuel-powered vehicles to new-energy vehicles, identifying the transition as the future of China's auto industry. Over a decade ago, Xi urged China's top scientists to pay attention to a "robot revolution" that could reshape global manufacturing, emphasizing the need for China to strengthen its robotics capabilities and compete for a larger share of the market.
During the Long March, the Red Army fought the enemy with outdated weapons. Today, the challenge is different: keeping pace with the scientific revolution and the explosion of technological innovation. As the pressure of overseas technology restrictions and trade barriers rises, Xi directs the country to strengthen independent innovation and the resilience of industrial and supply chains, and ensure both development and security.
He spearheaded a campaign to build China into a sci-tech powerhouse, elevating the country to the world's forefront in fields such as artificial intelligence, quantum technology and new energy.
From carrier rockets to nuclear submarines, China has named some of its major technological achievements after the Long March, honoring a history of self-reliance and perseverance while inspiring new technological advances.
In 2014, Xi led high-ranking generals to Gutian in Fujian, where a 1929 Red Army meeting established the principle of the Party's absolute leadership over the army, to reinforce that principle. He initiated a sweeping military reform, laying the groundwork for achieving the goals for the centenary of the People's Liberation Army in 2027 and building world-class armed forces.
The new Long March is progressing steadily with significant results. From 2012 to 2025, China's GDP grew from about 54 trillion yuan to more than 140 trillion yuan, while per capita GDP rose from just over 6,000 to nearly 14,000 U.S. dollars. The country has built a complete industrial system covering all industrial categories in the United Nations classification.
China's economy remains the largest engine of global growth, accounting for roughly one-third of the increase in global output in recent years, according to data from the Chinese government and international institutes. China's technology and cultural influence are also increasingly viewed positively around the world.
A global survey released by the Pew Research Center in July found that views of China had improved in many countries in recent years. For the first time, China was viewed more favorably than the United States in a majority of the countries surveyed.
Yet, as the 2035 modernization target draws closer, Xi has warned against complacency. "There are still many 'snowy mountains' and 'grasslands' for us to cross," Xi said.
Meeting those challenges hinges above all on strengthening the Party's leadership. The historical parallel is explicit. The Long March helped form a new central leadership with Mao at its core and opened a period in which the Party increasingly found its own answers to the problems the Chinese revolution faced.
"After the Long March, the Party and the Red Army were stronger, not weaker," Xi said. "This is because they had found the right path and the theory to guide them."
In the new era, the Party established Xi's core position on the Party Central Committee and in the Party as a whole and established the guiding role of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era.
Lu Yi, a professor at the Party School of the CPC Central Committee, said navigating the challenges of the new Long March requires sound strategic direction from the Party's leadership, unity within the CPC and across the country, as well as discipline, commitment and dedication among all Party members.
"This is how the steel was tempered," said Yuri Tavrovsky, a Russian expert on China. "The dramatic events of 1934-1936 brought to the fore and strengthened the CPC's finest qualities, enabling it to unite a divided country and build a great one."
ALL FOR THE PEOPLE
In his masterpiece "Red Star Over China," first published in 1937, Snow recorded a Red Army soldier's simple explanation of what he and his comrades were fighting for: "Here everybody fights to help the poor, and to save China."
Lu, the Party school professor, said that the history of the Red Army's epic march is also a history of the deep bonds between the army and the people, and of how the Party relied on the very people it sought to serve.
In Yudu, residents took down doors and dismantled beds to build makeshift bridges that carried the Red Army across the river. Along the Long March, local people supplied them with food, served as guides and sheltered the wounded.
"Back then, we relied on the people at every turn. We relied on them for food, and to fight our battles we had to mobilize them and rely on their support. Without them, we could not have accomplished anything," said Xi's father, Xi Zhongxun, when recalling his early revolutionary years.
That reliance on the people remains central to Xi's approach to governance. He has stressed that the Party must work for the people and draw on their wisdom and initiative, grounding its policies in their needs and experience.
Xi called on officials to draw inspiration from the Long March spirit and better understand the Party's original mission, which is "to seek happiness for the Chinese people and rejuvenation for the Chinese nation."
He once recounted the story of "half a quilt." During the Long March, three Red Army soldiers slept at a villager's home, where the family lacked adequate bedding. Before leaving, they cut their only quilt in half and gave one half to the family to help them keep warm.
When Xi took the top office, the Party had been in power for more than six decades, and some of its members had increasingly strayed from the traditions forged during the revolutionary years.
Xi condemned some officials for being so brazen in their misconduct, including cronyism, factionalism, dangling official posts and feigned compliance -- practices that alienated the Party from the people.
Xi warned that unchecked corruption could spell the end of both the Party and the state. He soon introduced a code of conduct known as the eight-point rules to curb official extravagance. He launched the largest anti-corruption drive in the Party's history, which has seen millions of people investigated for disciplinary violations. He also led improvements to the internal Party regulatory framework and established supervision commissions, all to "confine power to an institutional cage."
Earlier this year, Xi initiated a Party-wide study campaign, prodding Party members to fix their mindset regarding governance performance. A key target is to stamp out the tendency among some officials to sacrifice public well-being in seeking to polish their performance records.
"Ultimately, the Long March succeeded because the Party and the Red Army stood together with the people, maintained a close bond with the people, and shared weal and woe with the people. This is also a fundamental guarantee that enables us to overcome all difficulties and dangers," Xi said.
Sustaining that bond means understanding what people hope for and acting on their most urgent concerns.
Xi spearheaded an unprecedented poverty alleviation campaign that lifted nearly 100 million rural residents out of absolute poverty over eight years. Since the start of reform and opening up in 1978, over 70 percent of the world's poverty reduction has been attributed to China.
Xi used Long March metaphors for the tough battle against poverty. "Just as Liupan Mountain was the last high peak the Red Army had to cross during the Long March, lifting all people out of poverty is the final summit we must overcome to build a moderately prosperous society in all respects," he said.
Xi's anti-poverty war was vast in scale but granular in its approach, reaching into individual households to identify what kept them poor. Aid was tailored accordingly -- fostering industries suited to local conditions and relocating villagers out of inhospitable places. Over eight years, more than 3 million cadres were sent to villages to work on the frontline of fighting extreme poverty.
As in the Long March, some never lived to see the victory: more than 1,800 Party members and officials died in the line of duty. Xi has described the willingness to make sacrifices for the country and its people, whatever the hardship, as central to the spirit of the Long March.
The snow-capped mountains and grasslands that the Red Army had to surmount on foot are now linked by highways and railways. China has built the world's largest expressway and high-speed railway networks, which have brought agricultural products out of remote villages to boost income for local residents.
Ecological restoration is another feat. China has become the country with the largest and fastest increase in forest area worldwide. At the foot of the mountains along the Long March routes, ordinary visitors today may encounter giant pandas and other wild animals. Photovoltaic and wind power installations rise from the grasslands. Kerosene lamps that herders once provided to the Red Army are now mostly seen in museums.
The country has also built the world's largest education, social security and health-care systems. Life expectancy reached 79.25 years in 2025. China now ranks among the best in upper-middle-income countries on major health indicators.
The Long March China pursues today requires no less effort than the historic Long March, British scholar Martin Jacques said.
"It's a complicated challenge, but there's so much possibility and so much potential in that. And the rewards will be enormous," he said.
ECHO ACROSS THE WORLD
The international community, according to Xi, increasingly believes that the Long March was one of the key events that shaped world history in the 20th century, regarding it as an epic of ideals, devotion, willpower, and bravery whose inspirational power has transcended time and borders.
In the 1930s, Snow anticipated that someone would one day write the full epic of the Long March. In the decades since, many people have retraced its path, sought out survivors and written their own accounts. Among the best-known was American journalist Harrison Salisbury, who in his 1985 book "The Long March: The Untold Story" described the Long March as "sui generis," with its heroism firing the dreams of a huge nation and setting it moving toward a destiny no man can yet divine.
Kenyan military officer Felix Gitaari Njage, among more than 100 officers from over 80 countries and regions who were studying in China, visited sites along the Long March routes this summer. He said the Long March spirit is a precious asset for the world, offering lessons for military personnel across nations.
"Its underlying spirit offers countries of the Global South strategic wisdom and intellectual strength for achieving unity and self-reliance and overcoming adversity," he said.
The Long March continues to draw interest from scholars in both developed and developing countries. They believe China's success in the new Long March would benefit people beyond its borders as well as its own population.
In 2013, Xi put forward the vision of a "community with a shared future for humanity." The vision, together with the initiatives he later proposed on global development, security, civilization and governance, set out China's proposals and solutions to tackle shared challenges in a world marked by wealth gaps, conflicts, mistrust, unilateralism and bullying.
In September, at the BRICS summit in India, Xi urged the grouping to take the lead in promoting innovation, peace and stability, exchanges between civilizations, and reform of global governance.
Kirill Babaev, director of the Institute of China and Modern Asia at the Russian Academy of Sciences, interpreted China's message as a call for other major countries to join a "new Long March" toward an international order based on equality and mutual respect. Its outcome, in his assessment, would matter to all humanity, not only to China.
Keith Bennett, vice chairman of Britain's 48 Group, has drawn a similar connection between revolutionary memory and international cooperation. Writing in "China Today" in July, he said that the spirit of the Long March now finds expression in projects such as the Belt and Road Initiative, which connects countries through infrastructure, trade and development.
The Long March, he wrote, remains a guiding force in tackling difficult and complex tasks, overcoming development bottlenecks, and pressing ahead with long-term national goals.
For countries that look to China's experience, its efforts to combine development with security, shift toward cleaner energy, and advocate common prosperity may offer insights into addressing challenges such as climate change, public health emergencies, food and energy insecurity, and inequality.
The Long March stands as a powerful testament to the boundless strength of the human spirit once awakened, said Professor Lu. "It offers confidence to developing countries and hope to all humanity, affirming that even in a world rife with uncertainties, there are still forces steadfastly defending justice and striving toward a brighter future," he said.
The horizon stretches far ahead. The first of China's "two centenary goals" has been achieved. The second, tied to the People's Republic's centenary in 2049, still lies ahead.
"Today, we are closer, more confident, and more capable than ever of reaching the goal of rejuvenating the Chinese nation," Xi said.
"We will strive to safeguard world peace and development as we pursue our own development," he added. ■

International experts convene in London to tackle evolving chemical weapons threats
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:06:59 BST
01:06:59 KST

International experts convene in London to tackle evolving chemical weapons threats
International experts gathered in London for the 28th Chemical Weapons Demilitarisation Conference, bringing together policy, scientific and technical expertise to address current and future chemical weapons challenges.
- Discussions ranged from efforts to address Assad’s legacy chemical weapons programme in Syria and wider chemical weapons destruction challenges to chemical forensics, emerging technologies and future chemical security.
- Experts shared lessons from chemical weapons destruction programmes and explored the technologies and capabilities needed for future chemical security.
Hosted by the Ministry of Defence and the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory (Dstl), the conference, which has been running since 1998, provided an international forum for exchanging expertise, sharing lessons from chemical weapons destruction programmes and developing practical responses to current and emerging chemical weapons challenges.
Opening the conference, keynote speakers included Damian Johnson, Director for Homeland Defence and Strategic Threats at the Ministry of Defence; Sabrina Dallafior, Director-General of the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW); Cassandra Simmons-Brown, Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear Defense Programs (Acting); and Dr Paul Hollinshead, Chief Executive of Dstl.
The opening address reflected on the changing chemical weapons landscape, including the opportunity to address the legacy of the Assad chemical weapons programme in Syria, the continuing threat posed by chemical weapons use by Russia, and the importance of maintaining momentum and preserving expertise to ensure the international norm against chemical weapons is protected, strengthened and enforced.
Ministry of Defence’s Director for Homeland Defence and Strategic Threats, Damian Johnson said:
  Chemical weapons demilitarisation is one of the great success stories of international arms control. But we cannot be complacent. The international community must help Syria to eradicate the Assad regime’s legacy chemical weapons programme. Russia must be held accountable for its continued use of chemical weapons in direct violation of the Chemical Weapons Convention. And we must continue to evolve our detection, identification, attribution and destruction methods to strengthen deterrence and prevent the future use of chemical weapons. State and non-state actors must know that they will not be allowed to act with impunity.
The conference’s opening sessions placed particular emphasis on Syria. A dedicated panel, Syria 2.0: A New Challenge for a New Syria, examined the challenges and opportunities presented by the country’s changed circumstances and efforts to address the legacy of the Assad chemical weapons programme.
OPCW Director-General Sabrina Dallafior said:
  The progress made in Syria shows successful multilateralism in action. It demonstrates how political will, technical expertise and international cooperation can deliver tangible results in addressing the legacy of chemical weapons. Preserving and developing that expertise is precisely why conferences such as this remain so important.
Alongside these current challenges, delegates considered the considerable experience accumulated through previous and ongoing chemical weapons destruction programmes.
Sessions covered progress in Japan’s work to destroy Japanese abandoned chemical weapons left in China after the Second World War and technical specialists also shared experience of destruction technologies and the practical lessons developed through their use.
US Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear Defense Programs (Acting) Cassandra Simmons-Brown said:
  The integration of super intelligent systems, automated chemistry, additive manufacturing, and drone delivery systems is rapidly lowering traditional barriers to chemical weapon acquisition and use, making proactive, creative collaboration with industry partners our team’s highest priority.
Attention then turned towards the capabilities that will be required to meet future chemical security challenges, including how specialists identify unknown chemicals in complex samples, chemical forensics and source attribution, the application of artificial intelligence and machine learning to chemical analysis, analytical technologies, capacity building and knowledge management. The conference also considered the practical engineering challenges that can arise when dealing with unfamiliar chemical weapons destruction scenarios.
A dedicated Early Careers session showcased work from the next generation of scientists and practitioners. Presentations ranged from portable chemical threat screening and the analysis of biomarkers of chemical exposure to advances in chemical forensics, chlorine exposure analysis and work relevant to OPCW verification.
Dr Paul Hollinshead OBE MBA, Chief Executive of the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory (Dstl), said:
  Scientific expertise is critical to addressing the evolving chemical weapons challenges we face today and in the future.
As threats and technologies emerge and change, the role of designated laboratories such as Dstl remains vital in preserving expertise, advancing scientific capabilities and ensuring that the global norm against chemical weapons remains strong, credible and enforceable.

South Africa lowers 2026 growth forecast, cuts fuel levies to ease cost pressures
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
00:06:53 CST
01:06:53 KST

CAPE TOWN, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- South Africa has lowered its economic growth forecast for 2026 to 1.2 percent and announced temporary fuel levy cuts to ease cost-of-living pressures, Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana said on Wednesday.
Godongwana made the announcement while presenting the Medium-Term Budget Policy Statement to Parliament in Cape Town, outlining the country's economic outlook, fiscal position and spending priorities amid heightened global uncertainty.
According to Godongwana, domestic economic activity has lost momentum, particularly in export-linked sectors, as geopolitical conflicts push up global oil prices and raise costs for households and businesses.
"A prolonged conflict in the Middle East, alongside El Nino and its likely impact on producer costs and output, could further weaken domestic growth," he said. Economic growth is forecast at 1.2 percent in 2026, down from the 1.6 percent projected in February, before rising to 1.6 percent in 2027 and 2 percent by 2029.
To ease pressure on consumers and businesses, the government will reduce the fuel levy by 3 rand (18 U.S. cents) per liter for diesel and 1.50 rand per liter for petrol from Nov. 4 to Dec. 1, followed by smaller reductions until Jan. 5, 2027, Godongwana said.
The measures will provide 10 billion rand in support, at a fiscal cost of 10 billion rand in foregone revenue, he noted.
"Because we have rebuilt fiscal buffers, government is in a stronger position to respond, including by providing a temporary fuel levy again," he said.
The 10 billion rand previously transferred to the Central Energy Fund will be returned to the National Revenue Fund and placed in the contingency reserve to finance the relief.
"This intervention will help ease cost of living pressures without compromising the sustainability of the budget," Godongwana said.
Despite the weaker growth outlook, the country's public finances have improved, he noted. The consolidated budget deficit is projected at 3.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in the current fiscal year, down from the 4 percent forecast in February.
For the first time in nearly two decades, South Africa's debt-to-GDP ratio stabilized at 78.4 percent in the 2025/26 fiscal year, the minister said.
The revenue outlook has also strengthened, with gross tax revenue for 2026/27 revised upward by 17.1 billion rand from the February estimate, largely due to higher collections from corporate tax, dividends tax and value-added tax, Godongwana said.
He said fiscal discipline had helped restore confidence in public finances, creating room to respond to economic pressures while maintaining budget sustainability.
The government will continue prioritizing structural reforms, stronger state capacity and growth-enhancing infrastructure investment to support faster and more inclusive economic growth, he added. ■

US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia as Trump envoy meets Putin
- Published
Russia released a 74-year-old American citizen who was jailed for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine, as President Vladimir Putin met US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg for talks.
Stephen Hubbard had been taken to the city's Pulkovo Airport, Putin said during the meeting early on Wednesday.
President Donald Trump later said the former teacher was "on his way back home" and "there was no 'swap' necessary". Following the release, Witkoff called Putin a humanitarian.
Hubbard, who was sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony in 2024, was accused of serving in a defence unit in eastern Ukraine when he was captured in 2022, shortly after Russia's full-scale invasion.
CBS News, the BBC's US media partner, reported that Hubbard had been in poor health and was expected to be flown to Texas for treatment.
Witkoff gave praise to Putin for releasing Hubbard, saying: "You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian - you are a humanitarian also sir, and I salute that. I commend you."
His comments sparked a backlash from lawmakers in the Republican party, with Representative Don Bacon posting on social media that it was "another embarrassment". Senator John Cornyn said Putin "is a stone cold killer".
In response to a question from the BBC about the backlash, Vice President JD Vance said Witkoff's "job is to go over there and get a job done".
"I care much less about what Steve said than about the fact that he is bringing an American hostage home to his family," he said during a press conference in Ohio on Wednesday.
Hubbard was later seen thanking Witkoff as they met separately. Putin's financial adviser Kirill Dmitriev was also present.
Writing on social media after Russian state media reported the release, Trump said it had followed a request he "made directly" to Putin last week.
In the past, detained Americans have primarily been released from Russia through prisoner swaps.
Trump also appeared to defend his recent decision to suspend sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to come into force, writing that "if sanctions would have been placed", negotiations for Hubbard's release "would have come to a complete and total halt".
The US state department had previously classified Hubbard, from Michigan, as "wrongfully detained" and Trump on Tuesday had suggested that his release may be imminent.
"Watch what happens," Trump told reporters, "we have been focused on Hubbard".
The state department said in a statement that the release was "a welcome step that we hope leads to the release of all Americans unjustly held in Russia". It also said that "there are currently no Americans determined to be wrongfully detained in Russia".
Russian prosecutors had accused Hubbard of joining a Ukrainian military unit and receiving training and weapons. But his sister, Patricia Fox Hubbard, previously told Reuters that this was unlikely because of his older age and his disinterest in the military.
Hubbard's son, Joseph Coleman, who is an Orthodox priest, said in a statement that he had prayed for many years for his father's release.
"As I await the blessing of embracing him again, I receive his freedom not as a political victory, but as a gift of mercy," Coleman said.
A lawyer for Hubbard, Martin De Luca, posted on social media on Wednesday: "The road to peace is difficult, but its human dividends need not wait for a final agreement."
A spokesman for Putin, Dmitry Peskov, told Russian media that American officials had been seeking Hubbard's for some time, and Putin decided to do it for humanitarian reasons.

As Russia penalises European firms over Ukraine, US rivals largely spared
MOSCOW, Oct 21 - Russia has deepened a crackdown on European companies in response to Europe's support for Ukraine, while largely sparing US firms as Moscow courts business ties with Washington, Russian officials and US business people said.
Of 20 foreign-owned firms that Russian President Vladimir Putin has placed under temporary administration since Donald Trump's inauguration as US president in January 2025, only three were linked to the US, with the remainder controlled by European companies, a Reuters analysis of official data shows.
A person close to Russian financial regulators said that while business negotiations were underway with Washington, it was not in Moscow's interest to take as tough a line on US firms as the Kremlin was adopting towards those from Europe.
US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday for talks aimed at resolving the war in Ukraine. Russian news agencies reported Putin told Witkoff he was interested in restoring economic ties with the United States.
Ukraine and its allies have voiced concerns that the US is backing away from Kyiv, and Trump has criticized Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries even as European leaders have lined up behind Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy.
Russia, citing Europe's wartime support for Ukraine and involvement in "direct battlefield hostilities", has since last month taken control of local units of Swiss food group Nestle and retailers Auchan and Metro.
Last week it seized control of the local assets of four smaller companies from France, Germany, Sweden and Belgium.
"Their country of origin was one of the factors taken into account in making the decision," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, adding that these countries were involved in "illegal expropriations of Russian property".
Nestle, which said in September it would take steps to protect its rights in Russia, declined to comment further. The other companies did not respond to requests for comment.
A spokesperson for Switzerland's State Secretariat for Economic Affairs said that the available information supported the perception that more European than US firms were being hit.
The Kremlin declined to comment on how it was treating US and European companies in Russia, while the White House did not respond to a request for comment.
'WE HAVE TRUMP'
Russia's relations with the Trump administration, meanwhile, have warmed. The US announced a deal this month to buy Russian diesel and other deals, including on gas, have been discussed at meetings in recent months. Trump signed an executive order on Saturday waiving key sanctions and tariffs on Russian goods.
Russian negotiator Kirill Dmitriev, a US-educated investment banker who heads the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) and has pushed in talks for the return and expansion of US firms, hailed the move as a "historic moment".
Trump's envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner have used the prospect of multibillion-dollar deals with Russia as an incentive to push Putin toward a peaceful settlement since the start of talks in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, in February 2025.
Dmitriev said last week Russia and the US would soon announce new joint initiatives that could move ahead before the war ends. The US has previously signalled that deals are unlikely while the conflict continues.
One person familiar with the situation said that some Russian officials who do not support peace efforts could yet push for the Kremlin's actions to include more US companies.
The RDIF's only current partnership with a US company is a joint investment with New York-listed Titan International in a tyre factory in Volgograd.
Another person familiar with the situation said Dmitriev has in private highlighted this as an example of a thriving US business in Russia.
Titan did not respond to a request for comment.
Trump's commitment to economic cooperation with Russia and ongoing talks have helped to protect the interests of US companies, two US business people in Moscow said.
American Chamber of Commerce Russia President Robert Agee said in December last year that European firms in Russia were less optimistic than American ones, citing European policy. The chamber estimates there are some 300 US firms left in Russia.
"We have Trump and they don't, and our hopes are linked to him," Agee told Russian media last year. Agee and the chamber declined to comment further for this story.
Russia did target some mid-sized US firms during its property redistribution drive after the start of the war. One report estimated Moscow seized more than $50 billion worth of private property from both Russian and foreign owners.
The European Commission in Brussels declined to comment on the number of EU firms being targeted relative to US ones, but said the recent asset seizures were without due process and amounted to "forced expropriation in all but name".
"This follows a clear pattern of economic retaliation," a Commission spokesperson told Reuters, adding that the moves showed that "Russia is not a safe environment for business".
"The EU has measures in place to respond. We can sanction those profiting from forced expropriations," they added. REUTERS

2026-10-21

01:06:26 KST

Reform UK has been fined more than £2,000 for failing to declare it was the publisher of campaign material seen by voters – including an additional penalty for failing to pay on time.
Nigel Farage’s party was sanctioned by the Electoral Commission after four items of election material were missing an “imprint” – a declaration of the publisher so voters know who has paid for the promotional message.
It was due to pay £1,750 on 23 September, but the fine was increased by a quarter to £2,187 because Reform missed the payment deadline. The penalty was eventually paid on Tuesday.
Jackie Killeen, the commission’s director of electoral administration and regulation, said: “The UK’s political finance and imprints laws are there to ensure transparency in both the finances of political parties and the materials produced to influence voters.
“As a regulator, we take proportionate action based on the facts and circumstances of each case, as set out in our enforcement policy. We seek to support compliance and deliver transparency, and we will take enforcement action where necessary.”
The fine related to three social media accounts run by Reform, on X, Instagram and LinkedIn, that did not have digital imprints between at least November 2025 and January 2026.
The party also published an advertisement in the Telegraph in February 2026 without an imprint, promoting its shadow chancellor, Robert Jenrick. The watchdog’s investigation found that the purpose of the advertisement was to promote Reform and its electoral success in the May 2026 elections, so the ad required an imprint.
There has also been a separate complaint about the Reform candidate’s election material in the Gorton and Denton byelection in February this year.
On that occasion, the party sent out a letter designed to look as if it had been handwritten by the local resident Patricia Clegg, who said she no longer wanted to vote Labour, but who was in fact working for Reform – without including an imprint.
The party said it was caused by a printing error, and that the company had accidentally left the imprint off the material.
Reform’s censure from the Electoral Commission came as the party said it had reported ITV to the police after the broadcaster’s exposé which revealed racist remarks by members of the party.
Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, announced it would also launch a legal challenge against the ITV journalists involved and the broadcaster’s board of directors.
The channel’s undercover investigation included footage of Reform councillors and candidates using racist language.
In one excerpt, black children were referred to as animals, while in another a Reform member said his area had become infested with Asian families.
In a social media video, Yusuf said: “We have reported multiple ITV journalists and their board of directors to the police, and will be taking legal action against all of them. Journalists are supposed to report the news. These ones set out to create it.”
He claimed that the undercover ITV reporter who became employed as a Reform press officer had “doctored” her passport to gain the job.
He also said two undercover reporters who joined Reform members campaigning in Portsmouth had been reported to the police, as it is illegal to pay someone to canvass for a candidate.
An ITV spokesperson said: “ITV stands by its journalism. The programme Undercover: A Year In Reform was produced in compliance with the Ofcom broadcasting code, relevant laws, and its broadcast is in the public interest.
“All journalists were instructed to operate within this framework and did so under the supervision of the programme’s producers. Should the police get in touch, we would fully cooperate.”

Sisi-GPT: Egypt launches AI 'fact-checker' amid press crackdown
Egypt has launched an AI-powered tool for countering disinformation, days after security forces detained journalists working for the independent fact-checking outlet Matsad2sh.
The Chat Egypt app, unveiled at the 2026 Egypt Forum on Monday, draws on state-owned media and official communications to counter information designated as false news published outside official channels.
The government describes the app as the "first unified platform to combat rumours using artificial intelligence".
Its algorithm screens text, images and video and flags content it identifies as misleading or manipulated, the cabinet's media centre said.
It also tracks the spread of rumours and their circulation rates, and enables users to report potentially false content to authorities.
Statements by government officials are uploaded to the platform daily, along with information published in state media.
The app appears to have had a rocky launch, with local news outlet Almanasa reporting that the image and video verification feature was disabled a day after it went live.
The platform warns users that its answers may contain errors, omissions and outdated information.
Chat Egypt's launch came less than three weeks after security forces forcibly disappeared Matsad2sh's entire editorial team.
Prosecutors charged the six journalists with terror offences after they were held incommunicado for almost a week. They allege that the platform, whose name means 'Don't Believe It' in Arabic, has links to the Muslim Brotherhood and receives foreign funding to spread disinformation.
Lawyers representing the journalists say they reported being subjected to "various forms of torture and mistreatment".
The arrests triggered protests by dozens of local reporters at the Journalists Syndicate and were condemned by dozens of international organisations.
Egypt ranks 169th out of 180 countries on the 2026 World Press Freedom Index.
It is one of the world's leading jailers of media workers, with more than two dozen currently behind bars, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists.

European Parliament Vice President Declares a Hunger Strike in Solidarity With Oleshky Residents

European Parliament Vice President Pina Picierno declared a hunger strike on Tuesday, Oct. 20 in protest over the humanitarian catastrophe Russia’s occupation has created in Oleshky, where thousands of civilians have been facing starvation for months.
Picierno, who also leads Spazio Pubblico – a reformist, pro-European Italian political movement, announced the strike in an interview with Italian newspaper La Repubblica. She said it was a response to Pope Leo XIV’s appeal for a truce in the town, located in the Kherson region, and hoped other leaders would join her.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Words are not enough, we must also put our bodies on the line to save the Ukrainians of Oleshky,” Picierno told La Repubblica, calling the fast “a gesture of anger and hope.”
Responding to growing calls in Italy for fewer weapons deliveries to Ukraine and increased diplomacy, she described her hunger strike as a “diplomatic and nonviolent initiative,” adding that “diplomacy without defense has another name: surrender.”
Residents cut off for months
Oleshky is located on the left bank of the Dnipro River in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region, roughly 5 kilometers (3 miles) southeast of Kherson city. It has been under Russian occupation since the opening days of the full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Picierno called the town a symbol “of the inhumanity of the murderer who sits in the Kremlin,” pointing to Russian President Vladimir Putin who, according to senior Ukrainian authorities, recently ordered Russia’s military to abandon previous constraints and intensify attacks on civilian sites.
‘We Need to Move On’: Zelensky Won’t Wait in Oslo for Witkoff After Putin Meeting
According to her estimates, roughly 1,700 people remain in the city from a prewar population of 24,000, including 47 children.
Her figure matches that of Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha but differs from the estimates of Dmytro Lubinets, Ukrainian parliament commissioner for human rights, who has said about 6,000 people, including some 200 children, remain across Oleshky and the surrounding settlements. In his view, up to 2,000 people could remain in Oleshky itself.
However, neither figure could be independently verified, particularly because Russian occupation authorities narrowly restrict access to information from the area.
What we do know is that the town’s residents hadn’t received any food or medicine deliveries for months, forcing some to to barter for basic goods. Tetiana Hasanenko, head of the Oleshky City Military Administration, said on July 10 that no vehicles had entered or left the town since May 26.
The town’s only pharmacy has also reportedly run out of essential medications months ago, while overall medical care has been significantly complicated due to power cuts and lack of fuel as the city remains isolated.
Residents also cannot access their bank accounts nor withdraw cash as that would require leaving the town – which is nearly impossible.
“Those who stay risk starving to death; those who try to flee risk stepping on a mine,” Picierno said, echoing previous warnings of Ukrainian authorities who have been appealing to international organizations for months to help secure an evacuation corridor for the town and provide much needed additional humanitarian access.
“Families are starving, surviving on leftover garden vegetables, canned goods, and even snails. Residents say that Russian soldiers have threatened them at gunpoint to seize their food,” Sybiha said.
In a statement on Sept. 16, Lubinets said that the residents had started escaping on foot independently across mined fields and under threat of constant Russian drone attacks, simply because they saw no other way out.
“They see no other way to escape this hell,” Lubinets said, adding that his office had received 176 appeals regarding the humanitarian situation in Oleshky, and had already verified at least 358 people who urgently need assistance to leave safely.
Pope spoke to Putin and Zelensky
Pope Leo XIV held a telephone discussion with Putin on Oct. 16, in what marked the second phone call between the two, following their first conversation on June 4, 2025 that also focused on the war in Ukraine.
The pope had expressed his deep concern about the humanitarian situation in Oleshky, urging the Russian president to agree to an immediate ceasefire and allow the delivery of food and medical assistance to the city.
He also called for a safe evacuation of the civilians.
While the Kremlin backed Vatican’s initiative and agreed to cooperate, it again pinned the blame for the crisis on Ukraine, despite Kyiv’s repeated appeals to Russian authorities and international partners to secure humanitarian access to the town.
The pontiff then spoke to President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday, Oct. 19, reiterating his earlier request for a humanitarian ceasefire. He expressed hope for a cooperation between Kyiv and Moscow which would allow for the desperately needed food and medical supplies to reach trapped civilians.
“We are working to help our people there. We are preparing decisions,” Zelensky said, confirming the conversation.
Evacuation talks finally move forward
As of Oct. 19, Kyiv and Moscow are now in daily contact over a possible evacuation, Lubinets told Espreso TV, confirming that the Russian side had taken up all proposals previously submitted by Ukraine.
“I cannot disclose many details, but I will say this: In my view, we have made significant progress,” Lubinets said, while acknowledging that difficult issues remain.
No evacuation date has so far been announced.
Picierno urged that the talks be concluded without further delay. “The negotiation must be closed immediately,” she said, “food and medicine must be let in, and those who want to leave must be let out.”
