Your posture may change how much pain you feel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:00:46 UTC
01:00:46 KST

A new study published in Psychophysiology indicates that people are somewhat less sensitive to pain while lying down than while standing upright. The researchers propose that this reflects shifts in blood volume and blood pressure as the body adjusts to gravity, which may help explain why lying down eases acute discomfort. They also suggest the same relief could encourage inactivity in people with chronic pain, an idea the study did not test directly.
The human cardiovascular system does more than circulate oxygen and nutrients; it also helps regulate how the nervous system processes physical discomfort. Embedded within the walls of major blood vessels, such as the carotid arteries in the neck and the aorta near the heart, as well as inside the heart chambers and lungs, are microscopic stretch sensors called baroreceptors. When blood volume increases or blood pressure rises, the walls of these vessels expand, stretching the baroreceptors. Once stretched, these sensors send neural signals to the brain that slow the heart and relax blood vessels while simultaneously triggering pain-inhibiting pathways in the central nervous system.
Because of this built-in dampening mechanism, higher blood pressure tends to be accompanied by reduced sensitivity to physical pain. Early evidence from a 1994 human experiment demonstrated that artificially stimulating neck baroreceptors with gentle suction dulled pain reflexes and lowered how much pain participants reported feeling. Building on that work, a 2009 clinical study showed that giving medication to raise blood pressure in people with chronically low blood pressure reduced their pain sensitivity.
This link between the circulatory system and pain processing even extends beyond physical sensation. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2019 found that higher resting blood pressure was associated with lower self-reported sensitivity to social pain and rejection. Closer to physical pain, a 2021 study of fibromyalgia patients by Reyes del Paso and colleagues found that individuals whose baroreceptors were less responsive to blood pressure changes experienced worse daily pain, fatigue, and anxiety.
Despite these established findings in psychophysiology, lead study author Gustavo A. Reyes del Paso, a full professor of psychophysiology at the University of Jaén in Spain, noted that “the general public is unaware that an increase in blood pressure has an inhibitory effect on pain: people with hypertension report fewer pain complaints, whereas those with chronic low blood pressure are more sensitive to pain.”
Recognizing that blood flow alters pain sensitivity, Reyes del Paso and his colleagues in Spain and Austria wanted to test whether everyday changes in body posture naturally move enough blood to change how much pain people feel. When a person stands up, gravity pulls blood down into the legs, reducing blood return to the heart and temporarily lowering blood pressure and baroreceptor stretching. When a person lies flat on their back, blood flows easily back to the chest, increasing the volume of blood pumped with each beat and stretching the baroreceptors, which the researchers hypothesized would dampen pain sensitivity.
“Changes in body posture alter blood pressure (it decreases during standing up and increases during lying down), so they may also affect pain,” Reyes del Paso told PsyPost. “We wanted to probe this hypothesis. Also, patients with chronic pain usually are very sedentary (i.e., have kinesiophobia) and are lying down much of the time. Is there a cause for that?”
In clinical settings, kinesiophobia refers to an excessive, debilitating fear of physical movement and activity resulting from a feeling of vulnerability to painful injury. To test how posture affects pain and circulation, the researchers recruited 83 healthy university students, consisting of 61 women and 22 men with an average age of about 20 years. None of the participants had cardiovascular conditions or chronic pain, and all abstained from pain medications for 24 hours and alcohol or vigorous exercise for three hours beforehand. Women taking oral contraceptives were excluded because synthetic hormones alter both blood pressure regulation and pain sensitivity, which could obscure the natural effects of posture.
During the experiment, the researchers measured cardiovascular activity and pain perception while participants assumed three postures: sitting, standing upright, and lying flat on their backs. The sequence included an initial sitting phase, a first standing phase, a lying down phase, and a second standing phase, with cardiovascular measurements recorded across four-minute intervals in each position. Pain testing was carried out during sitting, lying down, and the second standing phase, and the study protocol was publicly registered before data collection began.
To measure pain in a controlled way, the team used a computer-guided pressure algometer, a device that applies steadily increasing mechanical pressure to a one-square-centimeter area on the third fingernail of the left hand. The researchers recorded two behavioral thresholds: the pain threshold, defined as the pressure at which the participant first began to feel pain, and pain tolerance, defined as the maximum pressure the participant could endure. Participants also received five-second pressure stimuli ranging from 1.5 to 4 kilograms per square centimeter and rated how painful each press felt on a 10-centimeter visual scale from painless to extremely painful.
Throughout these postures, participants wore chest electrodes to record an electrocardiogram, which tracks the timing between heartbeats, and an impedance cardiogram, a non-invasive method that uses mild electrical currents across the chest to estimate blood flow volume. Continuous blood pressure sensors on the fingers of the right hand were calibrated every minute with an upper-arm cuff.
From these recordings, the team tracked blood pressure, heartbeat intervals, stroke volume (the blood pumped per beat), cardiac output (the blood pumped per minute), total peripheral resistance (how tightly constricted the blood vessels are), and baroreflex sensitivity, which measures how effectively the heart adjusts its beat timing in response to blood pressure shifts.
The results supported the hypothesis that lying down dulls pain sensitivity compared to standing upright. Participants exhibited higher pain thresholds while lying down than when standing, and their maximum pain tolerance was higher while lying down than during both standing and sitting. Across the sample, average pain thresholds varied only modestly between 3.4 and 3.6 kilograms per square centimeter across postures, and the authors noted that the clinical relevance of these small differences remains uncertain.
Subjective pain intensity ratings followed a similar pattern once the applied pressure crossed that threshold into actual pain. At the highest pressure of 4 kilograms per square centimeter, participants rated the sensation as more painful while standing than while either sitting or lying down. At 3 and 3.5 kilograms per square centimeter, standing also produced higher pain ratings than sitting. Contrary to the researchers’ hypothesis, for lighter pressures between 1.5 and 2.5 kilograms per square centimeter, ratings were slightly higher while lying down than sitting, though the authors noted that pressures below 3.4 kilograms may not have been perceived as painful by most participants.
The cardiovascular recordings confirmed that shifting postures produced substantial changes in blood flow and pressure regulation. When participants moved from sitting to the first standing period, their systolic blood pressure dropped from an average of 109.36 to 104.97 millimeters of mercury, and their stroke volume fell from 73.39 to 63.61 milliliters per beat. When they lay flat on their backs, systolic blood pressure rose to 111.33 millimeters of mercury, stroke volume climbed to 89.47 milliliters, and baroreflex sensitivity nearly tripled from 11.52 while standing to 30.35 milliseconds per millimeter of mercury while lying down, which the authors interpret as stronger heart-slowing nervous system activity.
When the researchers analyzed how baseline cardiovascular traits while sitting predicted pain responses, they found that mean arterial blood pressure was inversely linked to pain intensity ratings. Participants with higher resting blood pressure tended to rate the presses as less painful, a pattern that appeared at every pressure level when stimuli came in random order and at three of six levels when they increased step by step.
Total peripheral resistance, or the tightness of the blood vessels, was positively associated with both pain threshold and pain tolerance across the entire group, suggesting that blood vessel constriction may play a role in dampening pain. Stroke volume, cardiac output, heart rate, and baroreflex sensitivity, the measures that shifted most with posture, were not linked to any of the pain measures.
The researchers also observed distinct differences between men and women in both pain and circulatory measurements. Men had higher overall blood pressure, greater blood vessel resistance, and higher pain thresholds and pain tolerance than women, although men and women gave similar subjective pain intensity ratings on the visual scale. In addition, higher blood pressure was directly associated with a higher pain threshold in men, with correlation coefficients ranging from 0.43 to 0.47, whereas this specific association was not statistically significant in women, though the male subsample included only 22 participants.
The authors noted that lying down appears to be an intuitive, functional behavior for easing acute physical pain, which they attribute to greater blood return to the heart and stronger stimulation of pain-blocking baroreceptors. At the same time, they pointed out that this biological mechanism could have unintended drawbacks for people with chronic pain conditions.
“The reduction in pain during lying down could be a mechanism explaining the typical sedentarism and low physical activity in chronic pain patients, in which bed rest is considered counterproductive for pain rehabilitation, as this inhibitory effect can negatively reinforce inactivity by reducing pain,” Reyes del Paso explained.
“If you feel an acute pain, the maintenance of a lying down posture will help alleviate the pain,” he added. “However, if a person suffers from chronic pain, he/she should avoid the frequent use of a supine position, because it reinforces inactivity and in the medium and long term can aggravate the pain problem.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting the results. The study sample consisted entirely of young, healthy university students who generally had low-to-normal resting blood pressure, and nearly three-quarters of the participants were women. Because the pain-dampening effects of blood pressure are typically strongest in people with elevated or high-normal blood pressure, the modest effects observed here might differ in older adults, people with hypertension, or patients living with chronic pain syndromes. The idea that pain relief while lying down reinforces inactivity in chronic pain is the authors’ hypothesis, and the study did not test it.
In addition, the links between blood pressure and pain were measured only while participants were seated, by comparing people with one another. The study did not test whether each person’s blood pressure changes across postures explained their own changes in pain.
Another detail to keep in mind is that the researchers did not randomize the order of the postures, meaning every participant went through the sitting, lying, and standing phases in the exact same sequence. When participants stood up for the second time, directly after lying down, which is when standing pain was measured, their blood pressure did not drop as it had during the first standing phase, averaging 110.30 millimeters of mercury. The authors explained that standing up from a flat position causes a bigger, faster shift of blood toward the legs than standing up from a chair, which likely triggered a rapid reflex that kept blood pressure from dropping. They suggest this may have weakened the posture effect on pain.
Looking ahead, the research team plans to directly investigate how these postural mechanisms operate in clinical populations. “We are going to replicate this study in individuals with chronic pain disorders, such as fibromyalgia or chronic back pain,” Reyes del Paso said.
The study, “Body Posture-Related Differences in Pain Perception and Their Mediation by Cardiovascular Factors,” was authored by Gustavo A. Reyes del Paso, Dolores Santiago, Belén Moreno, Casandra I. Montoro, Stefan Duschek, and Dmitry M. Davydov.

Deloitte contract scrapped after million pound payment
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:00:29 BST
01:00:29 KST

The Ministry of Defence terminated its Project SERAPH contract with Deloitte for convenience and moved to an alternative delivery model, in a decision that produced a fruitless payment of £1.354 million, according to answers given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked why the contract was terminated, and separately what the scope of Project SERAPH had been.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, gave the same answer to both: “Project SERAPH was a concept, assessment and demonstrator project that evaluated options for establishing an enterprise-level solution at the tactical layer.
“Its scope encompassed a range of digital and cyber capabilities in support of key Defence programmes, alongside associated governance, assurance and engineering activities.
“Following a review of the programme, the supporting contract with Deloitte was terminated for convenience in accordance with its contractual provisions, and the Department transitioned to an alternative delivery model.”
A fruitless payment is the accounting term for money spent that produced nothing of use to the department, and the figure of £1.354 million came from an earlier answer on 6 October. Fruitless payments are reported in the department’s annual accounts and scrutinised by the Public Accounts Committee, and a termination for convenience is the clause that lets a customer walk away from a contract without the supplier being at fault.
Terminating for convenience is a legitimate commercial tool, used when a requirement changes or a better route appears, and the supplier is compensated for work done and costs committed. The money is not lost through misconduct on either side. It is lost because the department decided partway through that it no longer wanted what it had asked for.

“Talent in, Impact Out”: Inside The Education University of Hong Kong's vision for an interconnected world of talent and expertise
EdUHK’s distinctive internationalisation efforts have earned global recognition, reflected in its strong performance across major international rankings. The University is ranked 7th in the world and 2nd in Asia for Education and Training in the QS World University Rankings, and it places 37th – the second-highest new entrant – in Times Higher Education Asia University Rankings.
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
The Education University of Hong Kong (EdUHK) pursues a dual internationalisation strategy: attracting talented students, scholars and researchers from around the world while exporting educational and research expertise to communities beyond Hong Kong.
“Partnerships are not one-off events but sustained, ever-growing relationships,” he adds. “As we mark the 10th anniversary of the University’s retitling, our next decade is about education with impact: attracting and nurturing talents who contribute to social good in Hong Kong SAR, China, and the world.”
The journeys of three faculty members bring this vision to life.
Bringing international expertise to Hong Kong
Professor Andrew Mark Edwards joined EdUHK in 2025, among a growing number of international scholars drawn to the University. He now serves as Associate Dean (International Engagement) of the Faculty of Liberal Arts and Social Sciences (FLASS). He previously held senior academic positions in the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand, and is internationally recognised for his research in exercise physiology and psychophysiology.
“EdUHK offers a distinctive focus on education while embracing interdisciplinary research and innovation. Within my first year at EdUHK, I secured a competitive General Research Fund grant. The University has been highly supportive in helping me establish my research programme, including supporting an international PhD student from the Netherlands to join my research group.”
The University's commitment to building international networks and fostering global collaboration left a strong impression on Edwards. Shortly after joining EdUHK, he was invited by the President to help the Head of Department organise a major international conference. "Shaping the Future: Sport, Health and Education 2026", which will be held in November.
As Associate Dean (International Engagement), Edwards is also helping to advance a wider programme of international engagement across FLASS, covering staff mobility, international partnership development and global impact initiatives.
“What impressed me most was its openness to new ideas and international collaboration. The University provides a supportive environment where academics can exchange ideas, expand global networks and create research with real-world impact,” he notes.
A strategic focus on Belt and Road countries
EdUHK actively promotes international educational collaboration, with a particular focus on Belt and Road countries. One notable example is its longstanding partnership with Kazakhstan, which includes the establishment of the EdUHK-Kazakh Academy of Education in Almaty, and a major student recruitment initiative.
Inspired by the opportunities available, he chose to undertake his doctoral studies at EdUHK under the highly competitive Hong Kong PhD Fellowship Scheme. After completing his PhD, he secured a grant under the RGC Postdoctoral Fellowship Scheme, placing him firmly on the path towards becoming a promising early-career researcher.
The appeal of EdUHK lies in its generous support, world-class research environment and strong reputation in technology-enhanced language education, Zadorozhnyy explains.
“I found an inspiring academic community at EdUHK, where scholars are engaged in rigorous, collaborative, and socially meaningful research. What particularly appealed to me was EdUHK’s emphasis on interdisciplinary collaboration, where fields such as language education, digital learning and computer science intersect to generate innovative research,” he says.
Exporting research expertise and creating global impact
Integral to EdUHK’s internationalisation strategy is the export of expertise through international research partnerships and capacity-building projects that create tangible benefits for communities worldwide.
One example is the work of Dr Deng Wenjing, Acting Head of the Department of Science and Environmental Studies and Associate Professor at FLASS, who has built an international research collaboration from a project examining environmental risks in schools. Aligned with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, the initiative demonstrates how EdUHK translates research excellence into practical solutions while informing policymaking in several Belt and Road countries.
Deng’s team has developed monitoring technologies, educational resources and policy-support tools that help schools better understand environmental health risks and respond effectively.
“Because environmental challenges vary across regions, we work with local universities, schools and education authorities to co-create solutions tailored to each community’s needs,” she explains.
Through portable air-quality sensors, hands-on monitoring activities and STEM learning resources, the team empowers local educators and students to improve their own environments.
“Through initiatives in Sri Lanka, Nepal, Malaysia, Indonesia and Guangxi, Chinese Mainland, we have reached more than 3,000 students and educators.”
“The success of this work demonstrates how international collaboration, built on local ownership and co-creation, can generate lasting impact,” Deng adds.
Deng’s achievements also reflect EdUHK’s commitment to fostering an inclusive academic ecosystem that provides opportunities for talented and dedicated scholars regardless of gender or background.
“I am grateful for the many opportunities at the University. I think I have made a mark as a woman in science,” she says.
EdUHK’s internationalisation strategy demonstrates how Hong Kong serves as a welcoming, dynamic and globally connected education hub, where scholars from diverse backgrounds and at different stages of their careers can thrive, contribute and create meaningful global impact.

Yemen's anti-Houthi forces prepare counteroffensive to save Taiz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21

Breadcrumb
Yemen's anti-Houthi forces prepare counteroffensive to save Taiz
Yemeni government forces and local anti-Houthi fighters are preparing to launch a counteroffensive to break the tightening Houthi siege of Taiz, after a series of battlefield setbacks left the country's third-largest city increasingly isolated, a senior military commander has told The New Arab.
Brigadier General Mohamed al-Mahmoudi, Yemen's deputy interior minister and commander of anti-Houthi forces on Jabal Sabir in Taiz governorate, said government forces had begun regaining the initiative after reorganising their ranks and strengthening defensive positions around the besieged city.
He warned, however, that the rapid collapse of government-held positions in the surrounding countryside had left Taiz facing a deepening humanitarian crisis, with around two million people at risk of being cut off from essential supplies.
"If Taiz falls it means the fall of the Yemeni republic and the legitimate government," al-Mahmoudi said. "It is the first and last stronghold of the republic. If it falls, that will carry huge symbolic significance."
Al-Mahmoudi attributed the latest setbacks to the collapse of National Resistance forces on Yemen's western coast, followed by the loss of al-Kadha, Shamir and Maqbana, and the Houthi advance into Jabal Habashi district and parts of the Al-Hujariyah region.
He said these areas had fallen rapidly because they were predominantly civilian population centres with a limited military presence, allowing Houthi forces to advance with little resistance and tighten their siege of Taiz.
"The Houthis' incursion into Jabal Habashi had extremely serious consequences," he explained, "as did their expansion into al-Hujariyah and their capture of its towns, which they were able to overrun at great speed, leading to a suffocating siege on Taiz."
Government complacency blamed for military setbacks
Al-Mahmoudi accused Yemen's internationally recognised government and military leadership of failing to prepare for the Houthi offensive, despite years of warnings about the group's intentions.
"Since the legitimate government agreed to a truce with the Houthi militias in 2022, they've been preparing for this day," he said.
He argued that the army, local authorities and other government factions had become distracted by internal disputes and secondary issues while neglecting the growing Houthi threat.
"Complacency, turning a blind eye and failing to focus on the real enemy led to this outcome."
Al-Mahmoudi said the country's military and political leadership must bear substantial responsibility for the territorial losses, calling for an investigation into how government-held positions had collapsed so rapidly.
Jabal Sabir becomes key to defending Taiz
The loss of surrounding territory has left around two million people facing an increasingly severe siege, according to al-Mahmoudi, who warned that prolonged isolation could have devastating consequences for civilians and the forces defending the city.
He identified Jabal Sabir, the strategic mountain overlooking Taiz, as central to the city's defence, recalling its importance during the fighting in 2015.
However, he acknowledged that the mountain had not been adequately prepared to serve as a frontline defensive position when the latest Houthi advance began.
Since Sunday, 18 October, government forces and local anti-Houthi fighters have reorganised their ranks, halted parts of the Houthi advance and reinforced their positions on the mountain, he said.
Al-Mahmoudi said the forces were now preparing to move beyond defensive operations towards a counteroffensive aimed at "breaking the siege".
He identified the battle for al-Misrakh as particularly important to reopening access to Taiz, warning that a prolonged blockade would deprive civilians of fuel, food and freedom of movement.
"All these factors will put enormous pressure on the resistance and the national army. We must act as fast as possible," he said.
Preparing to shift from defence to attack
Al-Mahmoudi said the immediate priority was to consolidate Taiz's defences before launching a separate military operation to push Houthi forces back from the city's southern approaches and reopen vital supply routes.
"It is essential to move the fighting out of Taiz city and into the southern rural areas of Taiz, and to open supply routes from Taiz to the interim capital, Aden, through Al-Hujariyah," he said.
The commander acknowledged that government forces remained constrained by limited military resources, particularly following the loss of key supply routes.
"Nevertheless, the national army is capable of standing firm. We must also work to arm ourselves and develop our own capacity using what we seize from the enemy."
He also highlighted Saudi Arabia's continued military support, saying Riyadh had maintained assistance through air power, communications and intelligence.
Despite the territorial losses and worsening siege, al-Mahmoudi expressed confidence that Taiz would withstand the offensive and that Houthi forces would ultimately be defeated.
He argued that domestic, regional and international developments were increasingly working against the group, which he accused of seeking to use the siege of Taiz to strengthen its negotiating position.
"The Houthis are weak internally right now and wish to wield greater leverage in negotiations by strangling the city and its civilians," he said. "However, Taiz will emerge victorious."

This Startup Is All In on Recursive Self-Improvement. Its Latest Model Is Scary Good
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

For the past few days I’ve been testing an impressive open-weight AI coding model called Flint. It suggests that fully recursive self-improvement, or RSI—an exciting and controversial approach that uses AI to build AI—is getting closer.
Flint is the first offering from Recursive, a company that aims to use RSI to advance both AI itself and other areas of science using AI. “Nearly every aspect of the entire model pipeline was actually done and improved upon by AI,” Recursive CEO and cofounder Richard Socher told me.
Socher says his company used its recursive AI system, dubbed the Eureka Machine, to automate most elements of the model’s development. This enabled a company with a handful of researchers to build a world-class model in just a few months, he says.
Socher told me that the Eureka Machine devised a number of innovations, including a new way of training the base model, new model architectures, and code optimized for specific silicon chips. Recursive shared benchmark scores that suggest Flint outperforms other models of similar size and architecture on coding tasks.
AI is already widely used to help build, test, and improve AI thanks to its amazing coding skills. This can speed up the process of refining a model and testing new ideas without the need for as much input from humans.
It is also possible to create a loop through which AI decides what improvements to make and then begins another round of improvement. For the moment this technique is limited, but if AI can contribute to every aspect of model development, then the process could theoretically continue indefinitely.
Some experts worry that letting AI improve itself in this manner could ultimately lead to disaster. These doomsayers claim that AI capable of improving indefinitely could escape human control and might decide that humans are an impediment to its goals.
Those concerns gained wider notice this September when a researcher quit Anthropic and warned that advances in AI, including recursive self-improvement, could lead to human extinction within a few years—a concern then echoed by a number of other experts. The idea of RSI has become so controversial that several bills in Congress propose to ban it.
Recursive sees these fears as more sci-fi than reality and believes legislation to prevent RSI is an unnecessary impediment to progress.
Socher says Flint was built using a system incapable of escaping human control. He says the goal is for the Eureka Machine itself to achieve full recursive self-improvement, but this would still be overseen by humans who could stop the process if it goes awry. “We hope that this shows people that indeed we have all the steps in place” to build such a system, he says.
Recursive has raised $650 million at a $4.65 billion valuation from Google Ventures, Greycroft, Nvidia, and AMD Ventures. Socher was previously the chief scientist at Salesforce, and his cofounders include Jeff Clune, a professor at the University of British Columbia who researches ways of building AI systems capable of learning indefinitely.
I must say I am impressed with Flint. I tested it on a Mac with 48 GB of RAM—a healthy amount but only enough to run a modest-size AI model like Flint, which has 40 billion parameters. The biggest models out there have several trillions of parameters, and they can only run on racks of industrial servers.
I used Flint to build a bunch of programs and found it to be both fast and very capable. In my experience, models of this size can be annoyingly error-prone or slow compared to Claude or Codex, but Flint nailed my coding requests every time. I used it to create a command line to-do list, then tried having it build a program that scours the web for interesting research related to recursive self-improvement. I also had Flint whip up a simple website that explains how RSI works. You can see that here.
It’s unclear how much progress other US labs have made chasing recursive self-improvement, but some published work suggests fully recursive systems are already feasible. A team from Microsoft, Carnegie Mellon University, and the University of Virginia recently published work, for instance, showing how an AI coding agent can recursively improve itself by modifying the software harness that turns reasoning into useful action and its own model’s weights.
Perhaps there are risks to full RSI if you are close to building a godlike intelligence, but for the time being it seems like a very promising way to improve your own AI models. This is something I’ve dabbled with in previous editions of AI Lab.
Indeed, Socher says the approach used to build Flint could make cutting-edge AI more accessible. “It's the only way this very small team can produce a model that's actually better than any other model in its class,” he told me. “This will hopefully show people that [recursive self-improvement] is actually quite nice and will benefit a lot of people.”
This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Australia’s cybersecurity site among those hit by ‘critical’ software flaw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:58:02 UTC
00:58:02 KST

Australian government sites among those exposed to 'critical' PHP software flaw
In short:
Two major vulnerabilities in programming language PHP have been discovered, and websites are being urged to implement a fix as soon as possible.
Australian government websites, including that of the Australian Signals Directorate, were affected.
It is believed hackers have been exploiting the vulnerability to target websites and governments around the world have taken sites offline.
Australia's own cybersecurity agency was among the government websites affected by vulnerabilities in a widely-used internet programming language that hackers are believed to be exploiting.
Developers of the PHP programming language have identified two critical vulnerabilities and have been urging website operators to run an update to fix the issues.
The issue was first discovered using artificial intelligence, according to a Google-owned cybersecurity agency.
PHP underpins large parts of the internet, raising concerns that a significant number of websites could be vulnerable to attack.
Among those known to be affected are European government departments and popular sites like Wikipedia.
The Australian Signals Directorate said on Wednesday that cyber.gov.au and other Australian government websites had reported outages in a tweet mentioning a "critical" PHP issue.
"Organisations and individuals using PHP within their environments should monitor and review PHP official guidance, and apply security patches as they become available," the ASD said on X.
Government agencies in the Netherlands and Finland were among those that took sites offline ahead of the fix as a precaution.
"PHP is everywhere. It quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," cybersecurity company Huntress said in a blog post.
Dane Knecht, the chief technology officer of Web and cloud security firm Cloudflare, said that attacks were emerging and Cloudflare was updating its firewall rules as a stopgap measure.
"We are seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up. This is a STOPGAP only. Patch as soon as PHP releases the update," he said on X.
Cybersecurity agencies in Europe, Australia, Japan and Britain have urged PHP users to update immediately or take websites offline until patches can be applied.
The Dutch cybersecurity agency itself went offline, saying it had done so as a precaution because of the vulnerabilities.
Officials have said that all PHP versions from PHP 5 onward could be affected, although PHP has not yet disclosed which versions are vulnerable.
Critical software
PHP is a programming language used to run websites. When a visitor loads a page, a server running PHP assembles the content and sends it to the browser. It is free, open-source software maintained by volunteers.
It is also among the most widely used software on the internet.
PHP runs roughly 75 per cent of websites whose programming language can be identified, according to web technology tracker W3Techs.
It is the engine behind WordPress, which powers about 43 per cent of all websites from blogs and small business pages to government portals, online stores and news sites.
Security experts said the vulnerabilities could potentially open the door to millions of servers because so many websites rely on the same underlying software.
Rather than target victims individually, attackers could scan the internet for systems running vulnerable versions of PHP.
Danish municipal IT company Kombit said it had shut down several services, including the national school communication platform, a spokesperson told Reuters.
Disruption was even more widespread in Finland, where state IT services provider Valtori said government public network services had been taken offline "as a precautionary measure."
France's Interior Ministry said it had temporarily taken local government administrative websites offline while awaiting a security fix.
The US cybersecurity agency CISA did not respond to emails seeking comment.
ABC/Reuters

Russia ready to resume talks with Ukraine and US to end war
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:56:21 BST
00:56:21 KST

Russia says it is ready to resume talks with Ukraine and US to end war
- Published
Russia is "ready in principle" to resume talks with the US and Ukraine on ending the conflict, Vladimir Putin's top aide has said.
Yuri Ushakov was speaking after Putin met US President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff in the Russian city of St Petersburg.
Ushakov said a new round could be held next month, and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky later said he wanted this to happen as soon as possible. Kyiv and its European allies have long been pressing Moscow for resumption of the talks halted in February.
Russia has for months refused as it believes it is winning on the battlefield with Ukraine facing an acute shortage of interceptors against deadly Russian missile attacks.
Witkoff went to St Petersburg after meeting Zelensky as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland in the Norwegian capital, Oslo, on Monday.
It is not clear what specific proposals Witkoff brought to Putin, but Zelensky said after talks in Oslo that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine and energy ceasefire proposals had been discussed.
Ushakov said their ideas were not very "useful".
Top officials from Russia, Ukraine and the US have held several rounds of talks aimed at ending the war that began in February 2022 when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Russia blamed last month's "massive" Ukrainian strikes during its general elections for their disruption.
Speaking to reporters after Wednesday's talks in St Petersburg, Ushakov suggested that a new round could be held around 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates.
He stressed that the talks must focus on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the conflict."
A US official later told the BBC that Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, another key negotiator, had proposed at Tuesday's talks in the Norwegian capital "a trilateral meeting at the technical level between the US, Russia, and Ukraine".
"This was accepted by the Ukrainians in Oslo yesterday and by the Russians in St Petersburg today," said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Late on Wednesday, Zelensky told reporters: "We received feedback that Russia... supports a trilateral meeting between our teams. The American side is proposing to do this as soon as possible. We are in favour of it."
Ushakov also told reporters that President Putin reiterated to Witkoff that Russian troops were advancing everywhere across the vast front line and had a "strategic initiative".
Ukraine and its European allies are disputing Putin's claim, pointing to a virtual stalemate on the front.
On Wednesday, Zelensky said he would accept a deal that would freeze the war along the current front line.
"We call it 'ceasefire' or 'stop killings' like President Trump called it. Freeze and stop. And of course this is minimum what we need from Russia today," he told Fox News, adding that security guarantees for Ukraine could be discussed after this.
Witkoff described the latest talks as "constructive", while Kushner, who was participating via a video link, said: "There is still hard work ahead, but we have a real opportunity to move beyond this war and build a framework for lasting peace, security, and prosperity for generations to come."
The talks were held amid a growing row between Ukraine and the US.
Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".
Trump has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.
He was heavily criticised by Democratic and some Republican lawmakers after lifting sanctions on Russia - allowing it to release tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace".
That was despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks earlier.
Zelensky - and Ukraine's European allies - criticised Trump's move.
Last week, Kyiv accused Washington of withholding critical intelligence to warn Ukrainians about incoming Russian ballistic missile launches, resulting in many civilian deaths. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday rejected such accusations as "scandalous", and Zelensky said after the Oslo talks that intelligence sharing "works now".
Ukraine's military has also complained of speed restrictions by the US satellite internet network Starlink which is owned by Elon Musk which constricted its ability to use drones to conduct strikes against Russia.
US officials have denied having requested such a slowdown and a bipartisan group of US senators has called for an urgent investigation.
Before the Putin-Witkoff talks started, Russia released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American citizen who had been given a jail sentence of nearly seven years for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine.
Trump said the former teacher was "on his way back home" and "there was no 'swap' necessary", while Witkoff called Putin a "humanitarian" for agreeing the release.
When asked by a BBC reporter whether he agreed with such description of the Kremlin leader, US Vice-President JD Vance said: "I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage.
"Whether you agree with the underlying sentiment or not, Steve Witkoff is a diplomat. His job is to go over there and get a job done. I care much less about what Steve said and about the fact that he is bringing an American hostage home to his family."

Trump strikes a deal with Putin to bring down diesel prices. But Russia may not have enough fuel to make it work, analysts tell Reuters.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:55:44 UTC
00:55:44 KST

Trump strikes a deal with Putin to bring down diesel prices. But Russia may not have enough fuel to make it work, analysts tell Reuters.
Donald Trump’s deal with the Kremlin to supply diesel to the global market is unlikely to lower prices substantially, analysts and market participants interviewed by Reuters said. The promised quantities are too small, and Ukrainian attacks are preventing Russia from increasing production.
Trump said Russia would immediately supply 300,000 metric tons of diesel (2.25 million barrels), followed by another 500,000 metric tons in November and 1 million metric tons “immediately thereafter.” Spread over a month, the first shipment would amount to about 73,000 barrels a day.
That is too little to lower prices noticeably, experts warned. Analytics firm Kpler estimates that at least 400,000 additional barrels of diesel a day are needed. Consulting firm Baringa puts the minimum even higher, at 850,000 barrels a day.
“The diesel that Putin was going to sell, they were going to make it available to the global market one way or the other. The only difference is how much of it the U.S. was going to get,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said over the weekend. Trump initially said the supplies would go to the U.S. and global markets, but later clarified that the shipments would not go specifically to the U.S.
The Energy Policy Research Foundation calculated that Russia would need to produce an additional 384,000 to 509,000 barrels of diesel a day. The country currently produces about 1.4 million barrels a day and consumes roughly 1.2 million domestically, leaving only a small surplus for export.
“We question whether Russia’s refineries could even support an increase in exports with, by some estimates, up to 45% of Russia’s refining capacity currently offline,” Baringa said.
If Ukrainian attacks on refineries stopped, the facilities could begin repairs and eventually ramp up output, but that is unlikely to happen before the end of the year, sources told Reuters.

====================================================================================================

Canada wants to expand its LNG business. Critics raise red flags
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:52:46 UTC
00:52:46 KST

Kitimat, British Columbia: As Canada tries to position itself as an emerging leader in global liquefied natural gas (LNG) markets, it risks locking in multidecade, multibillion-dollar contracts with companies whose current and past ventures include human rights abuses and environmental damage.
LNG Canada, which began operations in mid-2025 in Kitimat in British Columbia on the country's west coast, is the nation's first major export facility.
In late September, it gave the green light to a $33bn expansion which will double production in the coming years at Kitimat.
But the Kitimat plant has had challenges with its flaring equipment since beginning commissioning in late 2024. In 2025, the new liquefaction facility burned 350 million cubic metres of gas due to an issue with its main flare stack.
“The flaring noise was on a whole other level when they were first getting started up,” a resident who asked not to be named said in an interview. “It was just huge, way bigger than I think it was supposed to be.”
“I am devastated about the changes to my home territory,” another resident said. “I can't always see the stars like I used to from my parents' place here. My friend returned temporarily, and her asthma has been much worse.”
The residents requested to remain unnamed because Kitimat is a small community and the industrial project is a major employer and donor to local organisations.
The project has political support, especially as Canada faces economic pressures from United States President Donald Trump’s administration, which has unleashed a slew of tariffs on it, including on Canadian steel, lumber and aluminium in 2025 and added an additional suite of tariffs on Canadian products worth $20bn in August, including wine, dairy and textiles.
Since Trump started his tariff campaign, the Canadian government has announced a flurry of deals and agreements aimed at diversifying trade partners and expanding domestic infrastructure developments.
‘It’s all about investment’
Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government recently added two LNG developments – LNG Canada and Ksi Lisims LNG – to its major projects list, promising strong federal support. The Major Projects Office, a dedicated agency, has been established to speed up infrastructure projects deemed to be of national interest.
“Canada is building big again,” Carney said at a news conference in Vancouver following the announcement. “A year ago, the federal government referred LNG Canada Phase 2 to our Major Projects Office. One office. One point of contact. One goal: get to the right decision, rapidly and efficiently. Working with Shell and LNG Canada, British Columbia and First Nations, we have accomplished exactly that.”
Marc Lee, senior economist with the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives, said the underlying economics of oil and gas markets over the next 10 to 20 years are ultimately driving those decisions — and maintained the government is unconcerned with companies’ conduct in other countries.
“None of that matters to the federal government,” he said. “It's all about investment.”
Lee said the ongoing trade war with the US is being used as an excuse to fast-track major projects — and it comes at the expense of environmental protection and community-level impacts.
“I don't think it’s part of some broader strategic game around diversifying from Trump or supporting the energy transition,” he said, explaining how the Canadian LNG projects predate Trump's first term in office.
“It's just pure growth and extraction for very short-term benefit and long-term costs. We're essentially promising to liquidate this resource that should be the inheritance of British Columbians for hundreds of years into the future, and we're squandering it all at bargain-basement prices.”
“It's like this bicycle you have to keep pedalling or you fall off,” he said. “You always need this new capital investment. That's what the governments are chasing right now.”
Carney’s office declined an interview request and referred questions to the federal government’s Privy Council Office, which did not respond prior to publication.
Construction on the expansion, which includes adding five new compressor stations to the Coastal GasLink pipeline that supplies the export plant, is to begin immediately.
Murky history
Several of the companies involved in the two projects, either directly or through financing agreements, have murky histories and troubling portfolios. Domestic costs also include accusations of environmental pollution and potential human rights violations.
Since commissioning began in early 2025, a technical problem at the newly built LNG Canada facility led to the plant burning off more than 350 million cubic metres of gas that year, putting it among the world’s highest sources of flaring emissions.
The local community was unaware of the scale or nature of the issue until reporting by the Canadian environmental news outlet The Narwhal revealed the plant had started operations despite identifying an “integrity issue” with its equipment.
LNG Canada is owned by a consortium of five foreign companies: Shell, Petronas, Korea Gas, PetroChina and Mitsubishi. Shell is the majority shareholder.
Like TotalEnergies, Shell signed a deal to purchase two million tonnes of LNG from Ksi Lisims in 2024. The corporation recently bought Arc Resources, a Canadian oil and gas company with assets in northeast British Columbia and Alberta.
Shell’s oil and gas operations in Nigeria are among its more notorious. The United Nations estimates Shell spilled more than 13 million barrels of crude oil in at least 7,000 incidents in the Niger Delta since it started operations there in 1958. Those spills, and the company’s subsequent attempts to evade responsibility, have allegedly devastated the lives and livelihoods of local residents.
Anna Zalik, a professor with York University in Toronto, has been documenting Shell’s conduct in Nigeria for more than 20 years. She said the way the company portrays itself as a “responsible actor in the Canadian context” is disingenuous.
“The firm has been associated with these major human rights violations and all sorts of legal cases around actual violence against communities and severe environmental devastation in Nigeria, and yet tries to act as if their operations here are somehow not the same as their operations there,” she said.
“Their track record demonstrates an attempt to evade responsibility and liability for the pollution that they cause.”
Shell declined an interview request and said the characterisation of its operations “is not one we recognise”.
“Shell is committed to honesty, integrity and respect for people, and to conducting its business in an ethical and transparent manner, in accordance with applicable laws and regulations where we operate,” a spokesperson wrote in an emailed statement.
The spokesperson added its operations in Nigeria included “complex and contested issues” and the allegations “do not reflect the challenging operating environment in the Niger Delta at the time, including large-scale oil theft, sabotage and illegal refining carried out by organized criminal gangs”.
Shell’s LNG facility in northwest British Columbia is supplied by the contentious Coastal GasLink pipeline, built by TC Energy between 2019 and 2024 across Wet’suwet’en territories without the consent of the nation’s Indigenous leaders, or Hereditary Chiefs. In 2020, construction of the 670-kilometre (420-mile) pipeline became the focal point for Indigenous-led protests, arrests and nationwide outrage.
KKR, a New York investment firm with vast global reach, is a majority owner of the pipeline. Last year, KKR faced controversy after its acquisition of Superstruct Entertainment, the parent company of numerous music festivals and franchises including the electronic music outfit, Boiler Room, and festivals like Barcelona’s Sonar and London’s Field Day. Dozens of artists also accused KKR of promoting illegal occupation of Palestinian territory.
At the time, KKR had holdings in a German media company, Axel Springer, which advertises real estate developments in the occupied West Bank, where Israel has been accused of ethnic cleansing as it forcibly displaces Palestinian residents.
KKR said it does not have real estate interests in the West Bank and no longer invests in Axel Springer. Whether the investment company retains financial interests in companies linked to Israeli defence contractors and cyber security firms that provide support to the Israeli military remains unclear.
As part of LNG Canada’s proposed expansion, the pipeline operator would install compressor stations along the route, including on Wet’suwet’en territories, to double the amount of gas it currently transports. In addition to its holdings in the Coastal GasLink pipeline, KKR is one of three investment companies vying for a purchase of Shell’s shares in LNG Canada, which would include the proposed expansion.
Meanwhile, Ksi Lisims would be supplied by the Prince Rupert Gas Transmission pipeline, an 800-kilometre (500-mile) linear project that would cross numerous First Nations territories. The pipeline and LNG facility are co-owned by Nisga’a Lisims, an Indigenous government in northwest British Columbia. Some of the neighbouring nations claim they were not adequately consulted and do not consent to the projects.
In 2025, French multinational TotalEnergies signed an agreement with Ksi Lisims LNG to buy two million tonnes of liquefied gas per year, while simultaneously acquiring a 5 percent stake in the project’s parent company, Texas-based Western LNG.
TotalEnergies has been accused of “complicity in war crimes, torture and enforced disappearance” at its LNG facility in Mozambique, according to a criminal complaint filed by the European Center for Constitutional and Human Rights (ECCHR) in late 2025. The complaint, filed with France’s national antiterrorism prosecutor, centres around the company’s complicity in the so-called “container massacre” in 2021. There is no update on the investigation by the prosecutor.
TotalEnergies was also implicated in reports about crude oil supplies to Israel, enabling the genocide in Gaza, where at least 75,000 Palestinians have been killed since Israel waged war there in 2023. The French corporation was also accused of supplying the Russian military with feed gas used to produce jet fuel for planes that have bombed Ukraine.
TotalEnergies did not respond to requests for comment.
'Power imbalance'
Aidan Gilchrist-Blackwood, a coordinator with the Canadian Network for Corporate Accountability, said the public is largely ignorant of how companies involved in major projects in Canada are linked to alleged human rights abuses, which he attributed in part to a “power imbalance”.
“These companies have a lot of money, a lot of influence, and it's a lot easier for them to get their message out there,” he said. “When we're talking about communities who are having their human rights violated, we're talking about communities that are structurally disempowered compared to those companies.”
Gilchrist-Blackwood said Canada doesn’t have legal tools to ensure companies conducting business in the country are upholding international human rights obligations.
“This pattern of widespread and systemic human rights abuses linked to Canadian companies is the result of intentional policy decisions,” he said. “I think that's something that surprises a lot of people, that there's a lack of even that basic level of legal accountability.”
York University's Zalik recently returned to Canada from the Niger Delta, where she said the ongoing legacy of pollution and corruption is far-reaching and intergenerational. Over the past few years, Shell has been divesting from its Nigerian holdings, but Zalik said the multinational is directly financing local companies to buy up its operations.
“Here's a location where Shell made windfall profits over decades and has now sought to basically abandon or sell off its oilfields in order to avoid liability,” she said. “But Shell actually had to lend money to the Nigerian firms buying these assets.”
The company, in partnership with nine Nigerian banks, launched a $3bn financing programme aimed at facilitating the transfer of its assets in July 2026. This follows the 2025 sale of its onshore operations to a consortium of Nigerian and international companies.
As Shell distances itself from its controversies in Nigeria, it is shifting its investments to places like Canada — and from oil to LNG, which is marketed as a cleaner fuel. Zalik noted the oil and gas sector is “a global industry” with executives regularly moving from one location to another.
“People go from Malaysia to Nigeria to Canada, et cetera,” she said. “There are direct relationships between these different sites.”

Supreme Court rejects Trump's order to end hormone treatments for transgender prisoners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:52:24 UTC
00:52:24 KST

Supreme Court rejects Trump’s order to end hormone treatments for transgender prisoners
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel A. Alito Jr. voted to uphold Trump’s appeal.
- A Reagan-appointed federal judge had ruled the Trump administration did not have evidence or good reasons for changing the long-standing policy for transgender inmates.
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Wednesday turned down an appeal from President Trump and rejected his order to end hormone treatments and other gender-affirming care for transgender inmates in federal prisons.
The justices denied Trump’s appeal without comment, over dissents by Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel A. Alito Jr.
The order leaves in a place a decision by a senior judge appointed by President Reagan who had blocked Trump’s new prison policy from taking effect.
The decision is a rare win for trans rights at the Supreme Court.
In June, U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth, a Reagan appointee, said he would “not wade into the culture war being waged against transgender individuals” and ruled the Trump administration did not have evidence or good reasons for changing the long-standing policy for these inmates.
He cited the Administrative Procedure Act, which forbids abrupt and “arbitrary” changes in federal regulations.
An increasing number of Democratic leaders have begun to push back against their party’s unflinching support for the transgender community this midterm season.
Lamberth said the Bureau of Prisons’ new regulation would “arbitrarily deprive inmates of medications and other lifestyle accommodations that its own medical staff have deemed to be medically appropriate.” The evidence showed that “gender affirming care is the only effective treatment for gender dysphoria and severe harm flows from the cessation of such care,’’ he wrote.
Last month, the D.C. Circuit upheld his decision on a 2-1 vote, prompting the administration’s appeal to the Supreme Court.
The American Civil Liberties Union, which sued on behalf of three inmates, said the court should not “overturn a three decades-long status quo.” Since 1992, the Bureau of Prisons has “treated people with gender dysphoria with hormone therapy,” their lawyers told the court.
In response to Trump’s order, the “BOP overrode its own medical providers’ clinical judgment and mandated the cessation of treatment for almost 1,000 people in its custody,” they said.
At issue in this latest legal dispute over trans rights was whether the government had evidence to justify a sharp change in its prison regulations.
Trump’s order barred the use of federal funds “for any medical procedure, treatment or drug for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex.”
In defense of the order, the administration’s lawyers argued for deferring to the prison officials.
“If deference to prison administrators means anything, it means that courts cannot second-guess their eminently reasonable choice to treat the mental-health condition of gender dysphoria with psychotherapy rather than physical, sex-rejecting interventions,” Solicitor Gen. D. John Sauer said in an emergency appeal in the case of Trump v. Kingdom.
But the justices disagreed and blocked the order from taking effect. While the decision was not a final ruling, it sends a strong signal the administration is not likely to prevail in the end.
“This decision protects trans inmates from the administration’s attempt to steamroll constitutional rights for now, but the fight to uphold the dignity and respect our community deserves is far from over,” said Kelley Robinson, president of the Human Rights Campaign. “Trump and MAGA extremists are obsessed with targeting our community and undermining access to essential healthcare.”

Explainer: What is PHP and why did it take government websites offline?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:51:28 UTC
00:51:28 KST

Explainer: What is PHP and why did it take government websites offline?
- PHP powers most websites, including WordPress, and runs behind the scenes on servers. It is free, open source, and used by nearly 70% of identifiable websites.
- Two PHP flaws scored 9.2/10 and could let attackers run commands remotely with no password. CERT-EU warned some sites should be taken offline until patched.
- Researchers found the bugs with AI tools, and the fixes were urgent because attacks could cause stolen data, defaced pages, or full system control.
AI generated
BRUSSELS - Government websites across Europe went dark on Oct 21 as operators raced to patch two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, one of the most widely used programming languages on the web.
The developers of PHP said on Oct 21 they would release patches for two critical vulnerabilities, and EU cybersecurity officials warned organisations unable to apply the fixes to take affected websites offline.
Here is what you need to know:
What is PHP?
PHP is a programming language that runs websites. It works behind the scenes. When a user loads a page, the server running PHP assembles the content and sends the finished page to the browser.
It is free, open source and maintained by volunteers. Site owners rarely interact with it directly.
PHP runs nearly 70% of all websites whose programming language can be identified, according to web technology tracker W3Techs. It is the engine behind WordPress, the software that powers about 40% of all websites such as blogs, small business pages, government portals, online shops and news sites.
What are the risks of the flaws?
The two vulnerabilities are rated 9.2 out of 10 on the CVSS v4.0 severity scale, a standard industry scoring system. CERT-EU, the European Union's cybersecurity response team, said that rating signals unauthenticated remote code execution, meaning an attacker can run commands on a vulnerable server, over the internet, with no password or account.
A single flaw in PHP opens the same door on millions of servers at once. Whoever exploits the flaw controls the website. GoDaddy, a web hosting provider, said that could mean stolen data, defaced pages or full-system compromise. Cloudflare's chief technology officer said early attacks were emerging.
Most small websites are typically run by owners with no security staff, often on shared hosting where they do not manage the server and may not know who updates PHP. Wordfence, a security plugin for WordPress sites, warned that the usual automatic updates will not apply this fix. CERT-EU's guidance is to take affected sites offline rather than leave them exposed.
How was it found?
Researchers at security firm Calif, working with OpenAI, reported the first flaw to PHP on Aug 11 after finding it with OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model, the company said. Wiz, a security firm owned by Alphabet’s Google, found the flaws independently and reported a second one on Aug 24, also using AI models.
Wiz said the findings “rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history.” The underlying flaws had been present for decades, the firm said, but proving they were exploitable required a chain of steps “at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve.”
US President Donald Trump’s administration said it was “tracking and coordinating with federal agencies and leading SI labs to expedite the release of the fix,” referring to Trump’s preferred name for artificial intelligence. It framed the discovery as evidence that American “Super Intelligence” strengthens national security. REUTERS

Iraq denied Wednesday reports of Houthi bases on its territory, stressing that it would not allow its land to be used to threaten neighboring countries, according to the Iraqi News Agency (INA).
Government spokesman Haider al-Aboudi said there were no Houthi headquarters or bases in Iraq, affirming that Baghdad would not allow its territory to be used to threaten neighboring countries.
He said Iraq would not host any armed group involved in a particular conflict.
According to Iraqi news outlet Ultra Iraq, Aboudi also dismissed reports circulating on social media about the presence of Houthi bases, saying the government had no reason to take action against facilities that did not exist.
He stressed that the presence of armed groups from other countries on Iraqi territory violates constitutional principles.
“Iraq will not serve as a launching point for attacks against neighboring countries, nor will it host any armed group participating in a particular conflict,” he said.
Separately, Aboudi confirmed that Iraqi authorities had closed the al-Sheib border crossing with Iran due to a lack of technical, technological and infrastructure readiness.
He said the closure was intended to improve the crossing’s technical and logistical capabilities, noting that trade with Iran continues smoothly through several other border crossings.
Iraqi authorities closed the crossing early Wednesday, suspending passenger and cargo traffic until further notice.
Ultra Iraq cited a source within Iraq’s Coordination Framework as saying that the closure was ordered by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi to review security arrangements at the crossing.
The source claimed that the measure was also aimed at curbing dollar smuggling and was unrelated to US sanctions against Iran.
On the Iranian side, Valiollah Hayati, deputy governor of Khuzestan province for security affairs, confirmed that the Chazabeh crossing, known as al-Sheib in Iraq, was closed to passenger and commercial traffic until further notice, according to Iran’s Tasnim news agency.
He said travelers and businesses should use the Shalamcheh border crossing while Iranian authorities coordinate with Iraq to reopen Chazabeh.

Some Rectal Cancer Patients May Be Able to Skip Surgery, Chemo, and Radiation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:47:30 UTC
00:47:30 KST

Immune-based treatments for cancer have become the biggest new advance in tackling tumors, and the latest approval could make a big difference for some people with rectal cancer.
On Oct. 19, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved dostarlimab (brand name: Jemperli) to treat a specific type of rectal cancer called microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H)/mismatch repair deficient cancer. This cancer is caused by the accumulation of certain genetic mutations that prevent rectal cells from repairing DNA damage and accounts for 5-10% of rectal cancers. In a study of 154 people with this type of rectal cancer who were treated with dostarlimab, 68% had a complete clinical response at one year, which meant doctors could not see evidence of tumors on imaging or other methods for tracking the tumors. In the study, which the drug's manufacturer, GSK, submitted to the FDA, people received nine infusions of the drug: once every three weeks for six months.
“Not only did they reach clinical complete response, but they maintained that for a year,” says Dr. Andrea Cercek, section head of colorectal cancer at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and principal investigator of the study. (Some of the earliest patients have continued to remain tumor-free for even longer. ) “That really suggests that the response is durable and real.”
Dostarlimab is a checkpoint inhibitor, which means it releases the brakes that hold back the immune system from recognizing and attacking tumors. The drug allows immune cells to destroy cancer, making it a powerful weapon for seeking out cancer cells no matter where they spread or hide.
“We have completely leapfrogged over standard of care with a simple immunotherapy that melts the tumor away,” says Dr. Luis Diaz, head of solid tumor oncology at Memorial Sloan Kettering and one of the trial investigators.
The benefits of avoiding standard rectal-cancer treatment
Standard treatment for rectal cancer involves chemotherapy, radiation, and surgery to remove the rectum that requires patients to wear colostomy bags for the rest of their lives. The dostarlimab approval means more patients whose tumors have specific mutations could avoid those aggressive therapies altogether. “We have patients who would have lost the ability to bear children who have had children because this therapy replaced chemotherapy, radiation, and life-altering surgery in one swoop," Diaz says. "That’s a big deal.”
Kelly Spill is one of them. Diagnosed in 2020 when she was 29, shortly after having her first baby, Spill spent nearly nine months trying to figure out why she continued to have constipation and see bloody discharge in the toilet. Because she had recently given birth, doctors first attributed the symptoms to her pregnancy, and when they persisted after delivery, to internal hemorrhoids. It wasn’t until a doctor ordered a colonoscopy that they found a tumor.
“The doctor told me it was Stage III colorectal cancer, and that the treatment plan would include chemo, radiation, and surgery. And that I would never carry another baby again, and would most likely have a colostomy bag for the rest of my life,” says Spill. “It didn’t seem real until I heard the words that I was not going to carry another baby. I immediately stopped thinking about me, and started thinking about my husband and what it meant for my son. We had just started our lives together; we were supposed to have all these kids.”
Sascha Roth also faced devastating news when she was diagnosed with rectal cancer in 2019 after seeing blood in her stool. A resident of Washington, D.C., she had a friend with a similar diagnosis who had received chemotherapy, radiation, and surgery and recommended his surgeon at Memorial Sloan Kettering. Roth assumed she would follow the same strategy, but she learned that she had Stage III cancer and that she wasn’t a good candidate for surgery because the tumor was located so low in the rectum. Her tumor also had mutations that suggested it wouldn’t respond well to chemotherapy.
“It was a double whammy that threw me down,” she says. But the surgeon introduced her to Cercek, who was waiting to hear from the FDA about starting an immunotherapy trial for patients like Roth. “They told me I would be the first patient in the study, and there wasn’t scientific evidence that it would work.” Still, Roth wanted to try. She agreed to become Memorial Sloan Kettering’s first patient on the study, and then spent two months waiting for the FDA to greenlight the trial so she could begin receiving the drug. “I was calling Sloan Kettering incessantly to see if the FDA approved [the study],” she says. “The second the FDA gave its stamp of approval, Dr. Cercek’s team called me to New York to start the first round of treatment less than a week later.”
Not long after that, at Spill's first appointment at Memorial Sloan Kettering to discuss chemotherapy, she learned that the mutations on her tumor made her a good candidate for a study they had just begun. Only three patients had enrolled ahead of her (including Roth), so there was no data on whether it would actually treat her cancer. Spill, who was at the appointment with her mother, decided she had nothing to lose by joining the trial. “If it doesn’t go well, we could go back to option A,” Spill remembers her mother saying.
By her second infusion, Spill felt the tumor was shrinking because she no longer had major constipation. By the fourth infusion, scans showed the tumor had shrunk by 50%. The study originally called for patients to get chemotherapy, radiation, and surgery if needed after six months on dostarlimab. But a nurse pulled Spill’s mother aside after that appointment to tell her that the first three patients in the study did not need any additional treatments because their tumors had disappeared. Following Roth’s results, the study was revised to make chemotherapy, radiation, and surgery an option only if needed: if the tumors hadn’t gone away. It wasn’t a guarantee that Spill would have the same results as those first patients, but “it gave me hope, and all I could think about was maybe I could have another baby,” she says.
After all of her dostarlimab infusions, Spill, too, no longer had any tumor left and was declared cancer-free. Her doctors advised her to wait two years before trying to get pregnant again to ensure the cancer wouldn’t return. Once she was cleared, she got pregnant and gave birth to a girl in 2023, and later a boy in 2025. “I am now five years cancer-free, and last September got the boot from Memorial Sloan Kettering,” she says, meaning she no longer needs to follow up with her oncologists there. She now sees her primary care doctor for colonoscopies every two years.
“I see beauty in absolutely everything in life now,” Spill says.
What comes next for dostarlimab
Not only does the immunotherapy appear to work well in treating these rectal cancers, but it also comes with relatively few side effects. About 20% of those in the study reported fatigue, rash, diarrhea, and uncontrollable itching. Roth, who received her infusions during the COVID lockdown, drove from D.C. for her treatments and was able to make the roundtrip in one day. "It's just proof that you can really do the things you want to do. I didn't feel tired or sick after [the treatment], and there was never a time when I was at home recovering," she says. "I watched my mom and dad go through standard chemo and radiation and anticipated that would be what my treatment was like. It was nothing like that."
Cercek says the results point toward a potentially new model for managing some rectal cancers, which may include relying on immunotherapy like dostarlimab and monitoring patients more carefully before automatically turning to chemotherapy, radiation, or surgery. Some of the patients in the trial who were treated on dostarlimab underwent surgery after finishing their infusions if their doctors still felt there might be tumors remaining. Among them, despite the doctors’ suspicions, 80% did not turn out to have evidence of tumors in their specimens, says Cercek.
Dostarlimab is already approved to treat endometrial cancers with the same mutations and costs $10,000 to $12,000 per dose out of pocket, although GSK has a manufacturer's savings program to cover that cost for some patients.
“We still have a lot of learning about what complete clinical response means,” she says, and with immunotherapy, that might mean a more patient-centric, individualized approach that involves more time for the immune system to respond to the immunotherapy and become trained to attack the cancer. “If it looks like the tumor is responding, we need to give it more time with better techniques to determine whether or not the tumor is truly gone.”
Cercek and her team are studying the best ways to monitor how tumors respond to dostarlimab by looking at snippets of genetic information that tumors shed in the blood, or more advanced imaging to accurately capture changing tumor sizes. “We need to improve on those techniques but also to teach the oncology community that there is a very, very high chance that the tumor might disappear, even if it might not look like it at six months. We need to continue watching and waiting and giving it time.”

Top AI models successfully plan cyberattacks on water, power systems in 90% of attempts: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:45:33 UTC
00:45:33 KST

Halis Sunnetci
21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
Some of the world's most advanced artificial intelligence models successfully developed cyberattack plans targeting critical infrastructure, including water and power systems, in roughly 90% of attempts, according to research published Wednesday.
Cybersecurity company Frenos tested 10 AI models on their ability to identify weaknesses, assess access requirements and plan attacks against industrial systems that operate essential services.
The study involved 16,980 tests, including 13,884 individual decisions, 2,520 attempts to develop complete attack plans and 576 simulated runs.
Three leading commercial AI models produced workable attack plans in 89.5% to 92.9% of planning attempts, while other models performed significantly worse.
The strongest foreign open-weight model achieved a 36.2% success rate, compared with 5.2% for the best-performing US open-weight model. The researchers did not disclose the models' names.
Frenos emphasized, however, that the tests used supplied information and simulated scenarios rather than real-world attacks.
The models sometimes omitted critical steps or assumed access they did not possess, and the research did not demonstrate that AI could independently identify targets or carry out cyberattacks.
The findings come amid growing concerns about attacks on industrial systems, including a recent incident in France in which hackers manipulated refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets, causing temperatures to rise sharply, spoiling food and reportedly triggering fires.
Frenos also cited a January cyberattack on a Mexican water utility, where attackers used Anthropic's Claude AI to identify an industrial monitoring interface and suggest additional access attempts. Those attempts failed, and no compromise of operational control systems was confirmed.
The company urged critical infrastructure operators to strengthen network separation, restrict remote access and monitor suspicious activity to reduce the risk of AI-assisted attacks.

Israeli troops turn home in occupied southern Lebanon into polling station
Israeli occupation forces have turned a Lebanese home into a polling station for Israel's upcoming parliamentary elections, bringing the country's electoral process onto occupied southern Lebanese territory as its military continues to seize land and destroy villages.
Footage filmed from a distance and circulated by Lebanese media appears to show Israeli soldiers using a house in the village of Zawtar al-Sharqiya as a polling station, transforming civilian property in an occupied Lebanese village into a voting site for the very forces occupying it.
Israeli media have also reported that soldiers deployed in occupied Lebanese, Syrian and Palestinian territories began casting their ballots on Wednesday ahead of Israel's 27 October election.
