Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported earlier this month that the military was preparing more than 800 polling stations, including sites in occupied lands in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, as thousands of Israeli soldiers remain deployed beyond the country's borders.
Around 850 polling stations had been established, including mobile voting facilities serving Israeli forces stationed at 40 military outposts in Gaza, numerous positions in southern Lebanon and nine outposts in souhwesern Syria, according to Israeli media reports.
The military has deployed approximately 3,000 soldiers to administer the voting process, which began on Wednesday and will continue until election day.
"Our mission is to enable all IDF service members to exercise their democratic right to a secret ballot, including during operational activities and combat beyond the border," Israeli Colonel Vered Ben Yehuda, who oversees the military's election preparations, told the Times of Israel.
The Israeli military's invocation of democratic rights stands in stark contrast to the reality in southern Lebanon, where occupation forces are using seized territory to hold their own elections while hundreds of thousands of Lebanese civilians remain displaced and unable to return to their homes.
Meanwhile, Lebanon itself has been forced to postpone its parliamentary elections amid the devastation and disruption caused by Israel's war.
Occupation and destruction of Lebanese homes
Israel has maintained a military presence in parts of southern Lebanon since its October 2024 invasion. Since March this year, it has significantly expanded its occupation, establishing a so-called security zone while destroying dozens of towns and villages.
Against this backdrop, the apparent use of a Lebanese house for an Israeli election illustrates how occupation forces are treating territory belonging to another country as an extension of their own military infrastructure.
Numerous videos have surfaced showing Israeli troops occupying and destroying Lebanese civilian property, often filmed by the soldiers themselves.
In one video that went viral on Tuesday, Israeli soldiers were seen boasting as they rigged a house with explosives at an undisclosed location in southern Lebanon.
Other footage has repeatedly shown entire neighbourhoods being demolished, with Israeli forces systematically reducing residential areas to rubble.
The reported use of a Lebanese home as a polling station comes as Israeli officials continue to insist that their forces will remain in occupied southern Lebanon, despite repeated demands from Beirut for their withdrawal.
Israeli elections extend into occupied Arab territories
The voting arrangements are not limited to Lebanon, with Israeli soldiers also casting ballots at military positions in occupied Palestinian and Syrian territories.
In Syria, Israeli forces crossed the armistice line and seized additional territory in the country's southwest, including the Syrian side of Mount Hermon, immediately after the collapse of Bashar al-Assad's regime in December 2024.
Israel has also occupied Syria's Golan Heights since 1967, with its annexation of the territory rejected under international law.
In Gaza, Israeli forces currently occupy close to 70 percent of the territory following three years of genocidal warfare that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and devastated much of the enclave.
The Israeli military has established polling arrangements at 40 outposts inside Gaza, allowing soldiers involved in the occupation to participate in Israel's elections from within the devastated Palestinian enclave.
The West Bank, meanwhile, has remained under Israeli occupation since 1967, with illegal settlement construction accelerating alongside increasingly frequent and violent settler attacks against Palestinian communities.
Israeli officials have repeatedly warned that their forces will remain in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, citing security threats to justify their continued military presence.
Beirut and Damascus have demanded that Israel withdraw its forces from their territories, maintaining that they seek no further conflict.

France has launched an award for books written with AI

France has launched an award for books written with AI
Kyiv • UNN
The Prix Pascal competition accepts French-language manuscripts of 10,000–50,000 words created in collaboration with AI. The winner will receive publication.
This week, a prize was launched for books written with the help of artificial intelligence (AI). The Prix Pascal de Littérature IA ("Pascal Prize for Literature Created with the Help of AI") accepts manuscripts written in collaboration with artificial intelligence tools, with the winner guaranteed publication of their work, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Details
Participants must submit an unpublished manuscript of between 10,000 and 50,000 words, as well as provide information about which AI model and which prompts were used to create the text. Any leading language models may be used, including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and LLaMA. Participants may be located in any country in the world, but the entries must be written in French.
The prize is named after Blaise Pascal, a French thinker and encyclopedist who took part in the creation of one of the first mechanical calculators and also wrote theological works. These include "Pensées," which Pope Francis praised for their "philosophical depth and literary charm."
Although the competition rules call for the submission of a work of fiction, the organizers also state that the text must contribute to solving a particular ethical, social or environmental problem that threatens humanity. The prize was founded by technology entrepreneurs Philippe Rodriguez, Albin Serviant and Gilles Mantre.
OpenAI AI agents bypassed their internal monitoring system twice21.10.26, 13:10 • 3126 views
Rodriguez is a founding partner of Avolta, a consulting firm specializing in mergers and acquisitions; on the company’s website, he is described as a "leading figure in the European cryptocurrency and blockchain industry." Serviant is a digital media entrepreneur and former head of the LGBTQ+ magazine Têtu. Gilles Mantre is a former civil servant and PhD who teaches at Harvard University and Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne University. He is also a co-founder of the online voting platform Electis.
The establishment of the Prix Pascal came amid ongoing discussions about the possible use of AI by finalists and winners of a number of literary prizes this year—including the Commonwealth Short Story Prize, the Caine Prize and the Prix Goncourt (France’s most prestigious literary award).
Applications for the Prix Pascal opened on Tuesday; participants can submit their works through the prize’s website. Registration will remain open until the end of November. A shortlist of 10 candidates will subsequently be drawn up, and the winner’s name will be announced in early December. The jury will consist of five or six writers, critics, journalists, philosophers and publishers; their names will be announced in early November.

MasterZoo invests over $130,000 in website upgrade, mobile app development

2026-10-21

00:42:35 KST

Ukrainian pet store chain MasterZoo has launched an upgraded online store at masterzoo.ua and its first mobile app, investing $100,000 in the website upgrade and more than $30,000 in app development, the company’s press service told Interfax-Ukraine.
"We are investing in building a digital ecosystem that will meet pet owners' varied needs, from regular purchases to discovering new products and getting professional advice. At the same time, we recognize the specifics of pet retail. In some categories, pet owners need to see products in person, try clothing or accessories on their pets, or receive in-person consultations. Our task is therefore not to pit online against offline, but to combine their advantages and create a seamless customer experience. For us, investment in technology is a strategic investment in MasterZoo's future," MasterZoo CEO Oksana Kyrychenko said.
The new platform offers product recommendations based on a pet's species and breed, expanded customer account features, an auto-subscription service offering a 10% discount on repeat orders, and other personalized offers. The upgraded platform lists more than 18,000 SKUs from over 350 brands. The mobile app is available for download from the App Store and Google Play.
The chain is developing an omnichannel model in which physical pet stores and digital services complement each other. Its more than 200 stores in 40 cities are gradually becoming part of its e-commerce infrastructure, serving as pickup and product reservation points. In the future, some stores are expected to function as "dark stores" for picking and dispatching online orders through postal operators or MasterZoo's own delivery service.
MasterZoo aims to make shopping convenient and personalized regardless of how customers interact with the brand. Online sales accounted for an average of 15% of the company's total sales in 2024, rising to 18% in 2025 and reaching 25% in 2026.
Company data show that customers increasingly combine online and offline channels. One in three to four buyers of dry pet food already uses multiple sales channels. The average online order value is 2.5 times the average purchase value at physical stores, while the lifetime value (LTV) of omnichannel customers is almost four times that of customers who shop exclusively at physical locations.
Pickup plays an important role in this model, accounting for about 35% of all MasterZoo online orders. More than 40% of pickup orders are placed in Kyiv. Kharkiv, Lviv, Dnipro and Odesa follow in terms of order volume.
"We see the habits of Ukrainian pet owners changing. Online shopping is becoming increasingly common not only in major cities but also in smaller communities. The share of orders from outside regional centers has increased from 26.4% to 29.7%, while the number of orders delivered by MasterZoo's own courier service has nearly tripled in a year, rising 182%. Delivery preferences also vary by location. In smaller communities, Nova Poshta handles about 80% of orders, compared with 39% in Kyiv. That is why our goal is not simply to develop an online store, but to create a flexible system that allows every customer to choose the most convenient way to shop and receive products, regardless of where they live," MasterZoo e-commerce director Alisa Dashevska said.
MasterZoo, operated by Petmaster LLC, is Ukraine's largest pet retail chain, with more than 200 stores in 40 cities and 19 grooming salons in seven cities. The chain has opened 15 new stores in 2026, including in Pryluky and Kamianets-Podilskyi, where it had not previously operated. MasterZoo is part of the Ukrainian family-owned Suziria Group. Its range includes more than 18,000 SKUs from over 350 brands.
According to Opendatabot, Petmaster LLC's revenue increased by 18.81% to UAH 2.282 billion in 2025, while net profit fell by 24% to UAH 6.256 million from UAH 8.234 million in 2024.

Catalonia’s new far right: How anti-Muslim sentiment is reshaping politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:36:42 UTC
00:36:42 KST

Catalonia’s new far right: How anti-Muslim sentiment is reshaping politics
The rise of Catalan Alliance is causing alarm among Muslims ahead of Spain’s snap election in November.
Barcelona, Spain – Almost a decade after a failed independence bid in Catalonia, anti-migration and anti-Muslim sentiment has replaced secession as the driving force among voters in this wealthy region.
A new far-right party, Alianca Catalana, or Catalan Alliance (AC), which wants a crackdown on migration and has targeted Islam as a threat to society, has surged in the polls in a region with the largest Muslim population in Spain.
The party is on course to become the second biggest political force in Catalonia after the Socialists at the next Catalan regional election in 2028, polls predict.
It has capitalised on the anti-migrant sentiment sweeping Europe, which has seen victories for the far-right in Germany, Italy, and France.
The rise of Catalan Alliance has alarmed Muslims, who fear a backlash in a country which has previously seemed welcoming.
“This has surprised all of us,” said Soukayna El Abdi, president of the Young Moroccans of Ripoll, referring to the party’s growth.
“Most people come to integrate, to work and live among others. The rise of [Catalan] Alliance is about unfounded hate. They spread lots of things about our community which are not true.”
Spain will vote in a snap election in November. Polls show the conservative People’s Party and the far-right Vox gaining support. The rise of the Catalan Alliance shows a shift towards the right in the fourth biggest economy in the eurozone.
The party backs independence and has taken support from the other secessionist parties, Together for Catalonia and Catalan Republican Left, which were behind the failed bid to break away from Spain in 2017.
“All my friends support Catalan Alliance. There are too many migrants around now and Islam is a threat,” Eduard Lopez, a businessman from Molins de Rei near Barcelona, told Al Jazeera. “These other independence parties are from the past. They failed to do what they said they would.”
A fifth of Spain’s population of nearly 50 million was born outside the country, according to the Spanish National Statistics Institute (INE). Colombians, Venezuelans and Moroccans are the three largest groups by nationality.
Catalan Alliance started in Ripoll, a small town near the French border. It was where members of a cell plotted an attack on Barcelona in 2017 which killed 16 people and was claimed by ISIL.
‘No substantial change’
Silvia Orriols, leader of Catalan Alliance, is also mayor of the town.
After the 2017 attack, she became fervently anti-Muslim.
“If there is no substantial change, the prospects for Catalonia are bleak,” Orriols told Al Jazeera.
“The decline in the use of our own language, the depersonalisation of neighbourhoods, the rise in insecurity and crime, the fraudulent use of public services, the mass and invasive immigration, the demographic growth of those who advocate [Islamic] law, the fiscal plundering we suffer by Spain, threaten the welfare state and the rights and freedoms we have achieved up to now.”
She said her party was for “those who have not surrendered to globalisation and barbarism”.
There are 2.4 million Muslims living in Spain, with the largest community in Catalonia, according to the Union of Islamic Federations of Spain.
El Abdi of the Young Moroccans of Ripoll said, “I am very scared. I fear for my parents and my two brothers who still live there. This racism affects all Muslims. It started after the 2017 attack in Barcelona.”
Ironically, she said, Orriols’ daughters used to be friends with her cousins, but this changed after the Catalan Alliance leader went into politics.
The party currently has just two seats in the Catalan parliament, but polls predict it is set to rival the Socialists to run a region which accounts for 20 percent of the Spanish economy.
A poll for El Mundo newspaper, published in September, found the Catalan Alliance would win 25-28 seats, with 16.7 percent of votes if there were an election. The Socialists would be the largest party but would lose 10 seats, garnering 23.3 percent of support and 19-22 seats. All other secessionist parties would lose out.
Juan Ignacio Castien Maestro, a specialist in Islamic affairs at the Complutense University in Madrid, said anti-Muslim feeling is on the rise in Spain.
“People are focusing on Islamophobia, which has existed for centuries but has risen in Spain in recent years. The Muslim migrant is seen as the symbol of many ills such as the housing crisis, unemployment and other problems. It plays on feelings of insecurity,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Catalonia is a special case in that some Catalan [nationalist] parties were already Islamophobic.”
Jose Pablo Martínez, a specialist in migration at the Real Elcano Institute, a think tank in Madrid, said the left-wing Spanish government, unlike many other European countries, is applying a policy which is more favourable towards migration.
But “certain sections of the population consider migrants to be competing for their jobs and housing,” he said.

AAIB asks Alliance Air to ‘strengthen simulator training’ for pilots in serious incident probe report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:36:12 UTC
00:36:12 KST

AAIB has listed these among the contributory factors, including weather conditions, wind shear characterised by rapid transition from headwind to tailwind close to the ground
NEW DELHI: The Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) has asked Alliance Air to “strengthen simulator training requirements for flight crew by incorporating advanced scenarios involving heavy rain, low-visibility approaches, and rapidly deteriorating weather conditions.” This recommendation has been made in the final report of a serious incident on Oct 8, 2024, when an Alliance ATR (VT-RKF) with 47 people on board had undershot the runway at Bhubaneswar during landing in “severe” rain.It had “made ground contact approximately 100 metres before the runway threshold.” Luckily there were no injuries to the 43 passengers and four crew members. Also there was no fire on the aircraft which had flown in from Rourkela.
“Inadequate communication, cross-checking, mutual intervention, and challenge-response coordination between the pilots contributed to the ineffective management of deteriorating approach conditions and the failure to initiate a timely go-Around. After landing, the pilot-in-command informed ATC that the aircraft had landed on Runway 51 instead of Runway 14, possibly due to nervousness, stress, and confusion following the serious incident, indicating a temporary lapse in situational awareness,” says the report.
AAIB has listed these among the contributory factors: “Severe convective weather conditions include heavy rain, turbulence, downdrafts, and low visibility in the runway environment. Presence of significant low-level wind shear characterised by rapid transition from headwind to tailwind close to the ground.”AAIB has recommended that Alliance Air should place “special emphasis on pilots who have recorded operational exceedances within a six-month period, with mandatory recurrent simulator sessions and targeted remedial training to enhance decision-making, situational awareness, and adherence to standard operating procedures during adverse weather operations.”

What are Italy’s new measures against violent protests?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:35:54 UTC
00:35:54 KST

What are Italy’s new measures against violent protests?
The government has unveiled a new offence of ‘violent participation in public demonstrations’, among other measures.
The right-wing government of Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has approved a raft of security measures, including the deployment of 500 troops in the financial capital Milan, to curb youth-led protests that turned chaotic over the weekend.
“There is nothing revolutionary about vandalising and stealing. Vandalism and theft are not protest, they are criminality,” Meloni wrote on social media on Tuesday, unveiling the decree.
Unrest broke out on Saturday in Milan during a peaceful rally over rising living costs and poor school conditions inspired by similar mobilisations in neighbouring Spain and France.
Groups of mainly young people looted shops, smashed windows and clashed with the police again on Sunday, with riots also reported in Bologna and Turin.
Here’s what we know about the new measures.
What measures have been announced?
The Italian cabinet approved sending 500 troops to Milan until the end of the year to maintain security at key sites, step up surveillance of sensitive locations, and enhance monitoring across the area, the Defence Ministry said in a statement.
It is unclear what the army will be able to do, given that the cabinet stopped short of granting soldiers additional policing powers following opposition from President Sergio Mattarella. In Italy, the army is responsible for national defence while police carry out investigations and arrest duties.
As part of the new legal measures, which take effect immediately, the government has also introduced a new offence of “violent participation in public demonstrations” targeting people gathering in groups of more than five who use potentially harmful objects including stones, sticks and fireworks.
The offence is punishable with up to five years in prison and a fine up to 20,000 euros ($22,440).
The text of the decree also cites the saying “You break it, you buy it” as grounds for making the parents of minors financially liable for the damage caused by their children. The state can claim damages for any resulting loss against parents’ properties or by deducting public subsidies received by the family.
Children and young people aged 14 to 18 will also be subject to administrative detention, even if they have not committed a crime, provided there is evidence they pose a danger, extending powers that previously applied only to adults.
Additional measures include longer prison sentences of up to 12 years for individuals who use social media or online tools to organise groups for violent public demonstrations.
Gregorio Sorgona, a historian at the University of Palermo, said the measures do not take into account growing discontent among young people, sparked by a “fundamental contradiction”: “On one hand, the ostentatiousness of wealth and richness as a model of success; on the other, a profound crisis marked by economic precariousness.”
“For the youth who live in poverty, the impossibility of accessing those symbols of wealth can spark violent behaviour and looting,” Sorgona told Al Jazeera. “Before tackling the effects, one should act on the causes, starting with growing social inequality.”
What happened over the weekend?
Hundreds of thousands of Europeans took to the streets in Italy, France, Spain, Belgium and Portugal on Saturday in largely uncoordinated demonstrations to protest against the rising cost of living in their countries.
In Milan, rioters clashed with police, looted stores and set property on fire in the city centre, emptying Piazza del Duomo and a luxury arcade that would usually be full of shoppers.
A march against wars and rising living costs began peacefully, but masked protesters threw stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and set fire to barricades made from bar tables.
Police used water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds. At least two police officers were injured, and about 50 demonstrators – many of them minors – were detained, the Italian LaPresse news agency reported.
In Bologna, police also reported that, alongside peaceful rallies, protesters threw stones and clashed with officers. In Turin, hooded protesters used bins and outdoor furniture to set up barricades, and threw firecrackers, sticks and stones at police.
What have the reactions to the new measures been?
Protesters say the measures fail to address the root cause of the violence, namely rising prices that are pushing families into poverty. A lack of affordable housing, rising household costs, and failing public services have led many young people to say they no longer expect to be better off than their parents.
Prices rose by about 2 percent a year on average, but jumped in 2022, when annual inflation hit 8.7 percent in Italy. The surge was driven mainly by energy costs, which soared following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Between 2000 and 2025, the cost of everyday necessities such as food, energy, transport and household bills has risen by 68 percent in Italy, while the average full-time wage has fallen by almost 5 percent.
Genoa Mayor Silvia Salis said: “Young people must be listened to, but in Milan and Turin we have seen violence with the sole aim of destruction.”
“The response, however, should be inclusion,” she said, according to Italian newspaper La Repubblica.
NGOs including Associazione Antigone, which promotes human rights within the prison system, warned that arresting young people en masse will only add to pre-existing problems. More and longer prison sentences, it said, will worsen overcrowding. According to government data, the prison population in Italy has already increased by more than 17 percent over four years.
The organisation said in a Facebook post that while roughly one child in seven (13.8 percent) lives in poverty, the government has not formed any policies to tackle this.
Sorgona said, therefore, that these latest measures are unlikely to prevent further protests and violence, as they failed to do in Genoa against G8 anti-globalisation demonstrators in 2001, when 300,000 protesters marched and police responded with tear gas and rubber bullets.
“Deterrence is not necessarily a valid tool to prevent the radicalisation of conflict, especially in a society that is swept by poverty and social segregation,” Sorgona said.
“The decree risks intensifying the protests and leading to the arrest of thousands of suspects on the basis of ill-defined legal grounds.”

Yemen: People are facing displacement again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:35:46 UTC
00:35:46 KST

Since September 2026, the military escalation in Yemen between Ansar Allah forces and the internationally recognised government backed by Saudi Arabia has plunged people back into uncertainty. More than 230,000 people have been displaced from the western coast of Yemen, seeking refuge as far as possible from the frontline amid insecurity and uncertainty about how the situation will unfold.
For many, this is not the first time they have had to flee for their lives since the start of the war in 2015. The story repeats in a country facing a worsening and chronically underfunded humanitarian crisis, with malnutrition and cholera on the rise.
Maher was a fisherman in Mocha before he had to flee last month, together with five other families.
“We fled by a miracle; the roads were already closed,” he says. “It was a long distance; we walked almost a day and a half and took a bus.”
Maher is currently residing in Atira displacement camp, Lahj governorate, around 250 kilometres from Mocha.
“We sought refuge in the camp, but there were no tents,” Maher says. “We stayed under the trees for almost a week in the middle of the wind before they could give us a tent.”
An extension was built at Atira camp to host the 150 newly displaced families. Today, around 310 families who have been displaced over the past decade of war live together in this desert-like land, which is kilometres away from any infrastructure and exposed to the burning sun.
“Displaced people are in critical need of medical and humanitarian support,” says Itta Helland-Hansen, MSF country coordinator in Yemen. “MSF has been conducting assessments and carrying out medical activities in different informal settlements and displaced camps and has witnessed the extremely difficult conditions displaced people are living in.”
“We see pregnant women who have not had access to a single antenatal care consultation and who had to deliver in unequipped and unsanitary places; we keep referring acutely malnourished children to hospitals that are already reaching their full capacity; and we see how medical complications increase due to the limited access to healthcare,” says Helland-Hansen.
Many displaced people are running low on their medications, especially those living with chronic diseases.
“Our teams are seeing patients with empty boxes of medication for epilepsy, hypertension, and diabetes, desperately asking for more,” Helland-Hansen says.
According to the World Health Oragnization (WHO), only US$3.78 million has been secured of the US$31 million needed to fund a 90-day emergency response in Yemen. Before the latest military escalation, efforts to address Yemen's general humanitarian crisis were severely underfunded, with only 22 per cent of necessary funds secured.
Fatima and her eight children fled Mocha at night, in a hurry, because of the shelling. She reached Atira camp with almost nothing at hand
“Our main issue here is access to drinking water,” she says. “I do not have money to buy bottles, and my kids are thirsty. The water available in the tanks is salty. I am very tired; I suffer from heart and hypertension issues and had to push my kid, who uses a wheelchair, for long distances.”
Latrines are not yet available for the newly displaced people in Atira, increasing the risk of cholera spreading; cases have tripled in the past three weeks, the WHO has warned.
In Mocha, western Yemen, the context remains volatile as the fighting continues. Our teams are maintaining their paediatric and maternal activities at Mocha General hospital, and continue to support a general healthcare centre in Khokha, 50 kilometres north of Mocha. We also restarted our support in Mafraq Al-Mocha's general healthcare centre, 40 kilometres northeast of Mocha, after two weeks of disruption due to violence.
Patients’ medical needs may be exacerbated by a context in which humanitarian and medical organisations struggle to respond, and access to supplies, such as ready-to-use therapeutic food for malnourished children, becomes increasingly difficult. In Khokha, cases of acute watery diarrhoea have almost doubled in the past week, from 28 to 52.
“In this context, an urgent scale-up and inclusive response to displacement needs, including water and sanitation, the improvement of living conditions, and outbreak prevention, must be prioritised,” says Helland-Hansen.
Since 15 September, MSF has carried out more than 1,000 consultations in mobile clinics across Aden and Lahj governorates. The most common health conditions teams have seen, such as upper respiratory tract infections (245 cases), urinary tract infections (127), and gastritis (79), were linked to poor living conditions.

Leipzig Was Only the Beginning—Putin Reportedly Orders New Sabotage Campaign Against NATO
Russian leader Vladimir Putin has ordered an escalation of sabotage operations against NATO countries, potentially setting the stage for a new wave of hybrid attacks across Europe, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported on October 20, citing three European officials familiar with US intelligence.
According to the officials, the Kremlin’s decision is linked to Russia’s limited battlefield gains in Ukraine, increasingly damaging Ukrainian strikes against military and strategic targets inside Russia, and Kyiv’s refusal to accept Moscow’s terms for ending the war.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Western intelligence reportedly assesses that the August 5 incident in Leipzig, Germany, may have served as a test for a broader campaign. One European official told the Journal that after the incident, an informal contact in Moscow warned that similar operations were likely to follow.
The expectation, according to the report, is that future sabotage would be intended not only to cause physical disruption but also to destabilize European societies and strengthen political movements opposed to continued military support for Ukraine.
The investigation into the Leipzig incident has already helped Western security services uncover what authorities describe as a Moscow-linked covert network operating across Europe.
Investigators reportedly identified safe houses and weapons caches in several European cities, while members of the network were suspected of moving explosives, drones, and weapons across borders.
Investigators believe the operation was coordinated by Oleg Levushkin, a former Russian serviceman who was allegedly recruited by Russia’s GRU military intelligence service.
According to the investigation, Levushkin oversaw a network that used Serbia as a transit point for moving drones and explosives toward Germany.
Serbian prosecutors have since announced the arrests of seven people, including one dual Russian-Serbian citizen, on suspicion of involvement in the group allegedly directed by Levushkin.
The reported order would mark another escalation in Russia’s broader hybrid campaign against European countries, which Western governments have already linked to sabotage, cyberattacks, arson plots, disinformation operations, and other covert activity.

A lifesaving medication is not behind the drop in U.S. overdose deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:33:50 UTC
00:33:50 KST

A lifesaving medication is not behind the drop in U.S. overdose deaths
New research suggests the use of naloxone, which reverses opioid overdoses, also fell
Drug overdose deaths unexpectedly took a nosedive in the United States a few years ago. But it doesn’t appear to be due to more people being revived than before.
At the peak in mid-2023, there were around 111,000 drug overdose deaths per year in the United States. By the end of 2025, the number had fallen to under 71,000 per year, and researchers are still piecing together why. One theory: The wider availability of naloxone, a medication that reverses opioid overdoses, made it possible to revive more people than before.
But a study of U.S. emergency medical services agencies found that emergency medical responses for nonfatal overdoses dropped along with deaths, and the use of naloxone also declined. That suggests that fewer overdoses overall occurred, not that naloxone stopped deaths more often, researchers report October 21 in the Journal of the American Medical Association.
“Naloxone still saves lives every day,” says Michael Barnett, a health services researcher at Brown University School of Public Health in Providence, R.I. “But it doesn’t look like the reason for the sudden turn” in overdose deaths.
State policies, community distribution programs and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s approval of the nasal spray version of naloxone as an over-the counter drug have expanded access.
Barnett and colleagues analyzed nearly 186 million emergency medical service activations — an ambulance or other EMS response after a 911 call — nationwide that occurred from May 2020 through December 2025. Of 2.5 million responses for nonfatal drug overdoses, 40.5 percent involved opioids.
From May of 2023 onward, EMS activations for nonfatal opioid overdoses fell on average by about 6,000, or around 33 percent, below what was expected. Total administrations of naloxone dropped as well, by around 4,700 on average, or 21 percent below what was expected. The study suggests that naloxone was not used more often than before by bystanders prior to the EMS response, but did not include data on cases when a bystander provided naloxone and no one called 911.
Additional possibilities to explain the steep drop in overdose deaths — which followed a three-decade increase — include changes to the illicit opioid supply or with the population of people at risk for overdoses. “My own read is that a disruption in the fentanyl supply best explains how sudden and widespread the turn was,” Barnett says. “Underneath it, the population at risk has probably been shrinking for years.”
But “a supply-driven decline can reverse,” Barnett says, noting that the decline in overdose deaths slowed in 2025. Traffickers can adapt “by finding new chemical sources or turning to more potent synthetic opioids.”

Kazakhstan-EU trade tops $26 billion as investment ties deepen
Bilateral trade between Kazakhstan and the European Union reached $26.4 billion in the first seven months of 2026, up 3% year-on-year, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the Kazakh Foreign Ministry.
The Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Kazakhstan, Ardak Zebeshev, met with the Ambassador of the European Union to the Republic of Kazakhstan, Aleška Simkić, in Astana.
The parties discussed the implementation of agreements reached during the official visit of the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan, Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, to Brussels, as well as prospects for expanding trade, economic, investment, and transport cooperation.
“The European Union remains Kazakhstan’s largest trade and investment partner. In 2025, bilateral trade exceeded USD 45 billion, while cumulative investment from EU countries since 2005 has surpassed USD 200 billion. Our priorities remain unchanged: trade and investment, transport connectivity, energy, the green and digital transitions, critical raw materials, environmental protection and climate action,” said Ardak Zebeshev.
In January–July 2026, bilateral trade rose 3% year on year to USD 26.4 billion, compared with USD 25.6 billion in 2025. Kazakhstan’s exports to EU countries increased by 5.9% to USD 20.8 billion, while imports from the EU declined by 6.5% to USD 5.6 billion.
The Deputy Minister outlined measures to improve the investment climate and mitigate administrative risks. Investors have access to investment agreements, tax and customs incentives, state in-kind grants and opportunities offered by special economic zones. Investment protection and support are ensured by the Investment Ombudsman, a dedicated investment prosecutor, the National Digital Investment Platform and the “green corridor” mechanism.
The parties also discussed the Global Gateway Investment Hub, launched by the European Commission to facilitate investment projects in partner countries. The Kazakh side emphasised that the mechanism’s practical value would depend on its ability to help move projects from the conceptual stage to implementation.
Another key topic was the development of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, one of Kazakhstan’s strategic priorities. The Kazakh side welcomed the signing, with EU support, of loan agreements with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and the European Investment Bank (EIB), including agreements aimed at modernising the Port of Aktau and developing sustainable transport infrastructure in Kazakhstan.
Following the meeting, the parties agreed to maintain close cooperation to advance joint projects.
Earlier, Qazinform reported that Kazakhstan is strengthening the Middle Corridor role as President Tokayev advances Caspian cooperation.

'Lefty and proud': Spain's Sánchez hits back at Argentina's Milei in Madrid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:30:33 UTC
00:30:33 KST

Javier Milei has reignited his war of words with Pedro Sánchez during a visit to Madrid, as the Spanish prime minister declared himself “leftie and proud”.
Javier Milei let it be known he had arrived in Madrid.
The Argentine libertarian launched a tirade against Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez as he began a visit to the Spanish capital. Milei, who has blamed socialism for Argentina’s economic malaise and cultural decline, accused Sánchez of acting like a dictator.
His visit comes amid a highly polarising political campaign ahead of the 29 November election, with Sánchez positioning himself as the last bastion against what he calls the ultra-right and a coalition of reactionary forces, including Milei.
At a breakfast event, the Argentine president called Sánchez a “shameless dictator” and suggested the Spanish prime minister was fuelling an “invasion” in Ceuta, the Spanish enclave that saw a mass border breach from neighbouring Morocco in July.
"The socialists would rather reign in hell than serve in heaven. That is why they encourage the invasion. Every immigrant is a vote. If the price to pay is the destruction of the country, they are more than willing to pay it,” he said.
While more than 70,000 migrants crossed illegally into Ceuta, the vast majority returned to Morocco within 48 hours. Some 7,000 remain, although they would not be eligible to vote.
Milei, known for his chainsaw economics and sweeping cuts to public spending, saw his verbal acrobatics reach a crescendo as the day progressed.
He urged Spanish voters to oust the Socialist government “a patadas” — literally, “by kicking them out” — if necessary.
Milei and Sánchez have clashed in the past and see each other as polar opposites.
In 2024, during a visit to Madrid, Milei called Sánchez’s wife, Begoña Gómez, “corrupt”. Gómez is under investigation and faces trial, but denies any wrongdoing.
The remarks triggered a diplomatic spat between Buenos Aires and Madrid, prompting Spain to recall its ambassador over what it described as “unacceptable” remarks.
With the campaign underway, Sánchez got ahead of the attacks from his Argentine counterpart, tweeting that he was “leftie — and proud” before the visit. He also shared a screenshot showing his iPhone playing “Fanático” (fanatic) by Lali Espósito, an Argentine singer and outspoken critic of Milei.
While Spanish sources described Milei’s latest comments as completely out of place, his attacks may play into the hands of Sánchez, who faces an uphill battle ahead of the November election.
Chainsaw politics
Sánchez is running an aggressive campaign, positioning himself as the only candidate able to “safeguard the social rights” of the majority.
He has also warned that a government led by the mainstream conservative Partido Popular (PP) and far-right Vox would undo years of progress. The PP is leading in the polls, with several opinion surveys suggesting the two parties could secure a governing majority.
At a rally, Sánchez told supporters that "a chainsaw cannot build anything, it destroys" and suggested PP-Vox would do the same. "If there's a lesson from Milei's visit, it's that they will do to Spain what Milei is unfortunately doing to Argentina."
Chainsaw, or la motosierra, is a campaign slogan used by Milei to describe budget cuts.
For the Spanish Socialists, the aim is to dominate the progressive camp by rallying all forces to its left. But that alone would not guarantee a return to government, as Spain’s parliamentary system requires sufficient support in parliament to form a government.
“If raising pensions, increasing the minimum wage or defending the right to abortion makes me a leftie, then I am a leftie,” the Spanish prime minister said, concluding: “Yes, I am a leftie, and proud of it.”
Sánchez also replaced his picture on social media with an image bearing the slogan “Leftie and proud” against a red background.
As Milei landed in Madrid, a banner appeared outside the PSOE’s headquarters on Calle Ferraz, the party’s historic base in the Spanish capital.
It read: “The lefties, men and women, welcome you to Spain.”
Milei, polarising to the right too
With the general election only weeks away, PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, who has cultivated an image of a moderate conservative, did not meet Milei.
The two men have never been photographed together.
Milei did, however, meet Madrid regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso, a trailblazer on the right whose political style is far more combative.
For Feijóo, Milei's visit represents a delicate balancing act, as he seeks to project a more institutional, statesmanlike image.
To govern in Spain, Feijóo will most likely have to enter a formal coalition with Vox.
While the two parties have forged alliances at regional level, they have yet to do so nationally. Vox’s group in the European Parliament, Patriots for Europe, is seen by Feijóo’s European political family, the European People’s Party (EPP), as lying outside the pro-European consensus.
Asked by reporters whether his visit to Madrid had put anyone in an awkward position, Milei rejected the premise, telling journalists: “That’s a view held by people who are intellectually limited, which is your case.”

From dust to dirt: Australians to become compost after death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:29:04 UTC
00:29:04 KST

From dust to dirt: Australians to become compost after death
Residents of New South Wales, Australia could soon have the option to make a final contribution to their garden upon death, after the state’s parliament approved turning human remains into compost as an alternative to burial and cremation.
The bill, introduced by Independent Sydney MP Alex Greenwich, cleared the upper house on Wednesday after passing the lower house unanimously last week. It now awaits assent, with a minimum two-year wait before going into force.
Known as ‘terramation’ or natural organic reduction, a body is placed in a vessel with wood chips, straw, and other plant material. Microbes break down the remains, producing material that can eventually nourish trees and gardens.
US operator Recompose says its process takes 8-12 weeks, including a curing period. Remaining bones are mechanically ground down and mixed back in, and artificial implants are removed.
Under the NSW bill, families can take the resulting compost home to nourish a memorial tree or garden, or arrange for it to be placed elsewhere. However, choosing to become garden material remains a personal decision; operators are barred from turning a deceased person’s remains into compost against their written wishes.
Supporters of the method say the method uses less land and energy than conventional burial and cremation and could ease the financial and environmental burden of dying.
“We are running out of burial space [and] that space can cost as much as $50,000 [Australian dollars],” Greenwich told ABC in June. He predicted that composting will become cheaper than cremation, although local prices have yet to be established.
Not everyone is pleased with the proposal. NSW Premier Chris Minns said in June that he felt “a bit weird about it.” Catholic Weekly columnist Michael Cook described it as a “bizarre solution to saving the planet,” arguing that composting conflicts with religious respect for the human body.
Similar human composting practices have already been approved in several US states and part of Germany. England and Wales are considering rules that could eventually allow it.

Nuclear collaboration completes its mission
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:28:18 BST
00:28:18 KST

Nuclear collaboration completes its mission
Cross-industry programme set up to safeguard skills has concluded its work
The UK Alpha Resilience and Capability (ARC) Programme has formally closed.
It leaves a positive legacy of technical products, standards, knowledge, teamwork, and lasting relationships.
Since it began, the programme has united organisations from the civil and defence nuclear sectors.
Its aims were to tackle common challenges, boost resilience and capability, and speed up the sharing of knowledge and expertise across the sector.
By working together, partners found ways to create shared solutions, creating greater benefits than if each organisation worked alone.
Its success was built on the commitment and expertise of partner organisations including:
- Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ)
- Nuclear Decommissioning Authority (NDA)
- AWE Nuclear Security Technologies
- Office for Nuclear Regulation (ONR)
- Sellafield Ltd
- Ministry of Defence (MoD)
- UK National Nuclear Laboratory (UKNNL)
- Nuclear Restoration Services (NRS)
- Nuclear Transport Solutions (NTS)
They provided expert knowledge, resources, and leadership. This helped create solutions that improve capability throughout the UK nuclear industry.
The programme’s biggest success may be the strong professional networks and the culture of collaboration now found across the sector.
Investments and interventions from all organisations involved helped the programme deliver a portfolio of products. They included standards, frameworks, training solutions, and Communities of Practice to support current and future Alpha programmes.
Key achievements included:
- Development of sector-wide engineering standards and guidance, de-risking our national programmes
- Delivery of the non-active Glovebox Training Facility, accelerating capability development
- Development of collaborative platforms and digital knowledge-sharing tools, building resilience across the sector
Dale McQueen, UK ARC Programme senior sponsor, said:
  ARC has shown the power of enterprise-wide collaboration.
By bringing together expertise from across the UK nuclear sector, the programme has delivered solutions that no single organisation could have achieved alone.
The legacy of ARC includes not just its products and standards. It also involves the relationships, knowledge-sharing communities, and collaborative behaviours that will keep strengthening the sector for years.
Scott Bazley, programme manager for the UK ARC Programme said:
  ARC has shown what’s possible when civil and defence organisations unite for a common goal.
In the last six years, we have provided standards, guidance, collaboration tools, and lasting networks. These will keep adding value even after the programme ends.
Most importantly, ARC has built a culture of collaboration and trust. This strong foundation supports future cross-sector initiatives.
Richard Gibson, vice president for legacy sites at UKNNL, said:
  We are proud to have been a key partner to ARC since its inception in 2020.
It’s a ground-breaking partnership between civil and defence nuclear groups for the UK’s alpha missions.
It has provided real benefits, such as shared engineering standards and strong Communities of Practice and knowledge management.

Turkey to try Netanyahu, 34 Israelis over Gaza flotilla attacks
A Turkish court will begin proceedings on Friday against 35 Israeli political and military officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, over attacks on humanitarian aid flotillas attempting to break Israel's blockade of the Gaza Strip.
The first hearing will take place on 23 October at Istanbul's 11th High Criminal Court, with defendants facing charges including torture, unlawful deprivation of liberty, armed robbery, hijacking of vessels, genocide and crimes against humanity.
The Global Sumud Flotilla movement announced the proceedings on Tuesday, saying the case seeks to hold Israeli officials accountable for intercepting civilian aid vessels in international waters, detaining their passengers and allegedly subjecting them to violence and mistreatment.
Among those named in the indictment are Netanyahu, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, Defence Minister Israel Katz and several senior military commanders.
The indictment was prepared in April and subsequently accepted by the court, which is examining the case under the principle of universal jurisdiction.
Turkish authorities have already issued arrest warrants for suspects in the case and completed the necessary legal procedures to request Interpol red notices, according to the movement.
The proceedings concern Israeli military operations against flotillas attempting to deliver humanitarian assistance to Gaza and challenge the naval blockade imposed on the Palestinian territory.
Italian prosecutors expand investigations
The Istanbul proceedings come as Italian prosecutors have expanded a separate investigation into alleged abuses against 50 Italian civilians who participated in Global Sumud Flotilla missions in 2025 and 2026.
According to the movement, Italian prosecutors announced on 16 October that their investigation, which initially examined Ben-Gvir's suspected involvement in torture, unlawful detention, deliberate injury, looting and damage to vessels, had been expanded to include Katz, Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir and 11 senior officials from the military, police and prison authorities.
Italian investigators also found that alleged abuses had been repeated during the April and May 2026 flotilla mission, with more severe methods reportedly employed, including electric shocks and rubber bullets.
The movement said judicial authorities investigating similar incidents had participated in a coordination meeting at Eurojust, the European Union's criminal justice cooperation agency, in The Hague.
Citing Italian newspaper La Repubblica, it said representatives from ten other countries attended the meeting, including Portugal, Spain, France, Sweden, Poland, Belgium, the Netherlands, Australia, Finland and Slovakia.
The developments indicate a growing international effort to investigate alleged Israeli violations against humanitarian activists attempting to reach Gaza.
The Global Sumud Flotilla movement said the legal proceedings in Turkey and Italy demonstrated that the interception of its vessels was no longer the end of the matter, but the beginning of criminal proceedings against Israeli decision-makers.
It also cited a UN investigative report issued on 9 September, which it said concluded that flotilla vessels had been unlawfully intercepted in international waters, with hundreds of participants arbitrarily arrested, forcibly transferred to Israel and detained.
Allegations of systematic violence
The Istanbul case covers alleged Israeli attacks on the vessel Conscience, its eight accompanying boats and the wider Global Sumud Flotilla.
According to the movement, evidence submitted to the court includes drone attacks on the Alma and Familia Madeira vessels near Tunisia, as well as the interception of 42 humanitarian boats carrying 462 civilian volunteers, including healthcare workers, parliamentarians, lawyers and journalists.
The movement said the evidence documented a pattern of violence, including drone attacks on civilian vessels near Malta and Tunisia, attacks on boats off Crete, forced deportations, physical assaults and humiliating searches.
Activists also reported degrading treatment in Israeli detention facilities, including Ketziot prison.
The organisation said the court proceedings represented a direct challenge to what it described as unlawful military interventions against unarmed civilians attempting to deliver aid to Gaza.
Push for accountability
Lawyers Without Borders International, an organisation established in Turkey in 2016 that is supporting victims in the case, said the proceedings concerned not only the 101 victims identified in the court file but also the broader question of accountability for alleged Israeli abuses.
The organisation argued that when states use armed force against unarmed civilians attempting to deliver essential assistance to people facing hunger, those responsible throughout the chain of command must be held accountable under international law.
The Global Sumud Flotilla movement said it would continue pursuing legal action through national courts, European judicial institutions and international mechanisms.
Its planned efforts include seeking the return of confiscated vessels and submitting a request to the Office of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court.
The movement said its ultimate objectives were to secure accountability for those responsible for alleged abuses, recover seized ships and bring about the permanent lifting of Israel's blockade of Gaza.

The Long March spirit will always serve as a source of inspiration for China to march toward its great goals with confidence, unity and resolve.

An Indian court has ordered the release of two leaders of India’s Cockroach movement who were jailed last week amid a mounting state crackdown on youth-led protests.
The two leaders of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) movement, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, had spent a week in Delhi’s Tihar jail after being arrested by Delhi police last week.
On Wednesday, a special magistrate ordered that Das and Ranka be released, despite efforts by police to keep them in prison. They were made to sign a bond pledging no further breach of peace.
Their arrest came after a draconian police crackdown on a CJP march held in the capital two weeks ago to protest alleged manipulation of the country’s electoral roll, which led to the barricading of central Delhi and thousands of young people being detained.
Das and Ranka were taken into custody for a second time days later after they jumped police barricades and held up an Indian flag at a site in central Delhi that police had cordoned off.
The pair were charged with trespass and violating the peace and sent to jail for five days, which was then extended by two further days. Their detention had provoked outrage among leaders and supporters of the youth movement, who accused the government of “cowardice” for jailing CJP leaders for holding a peaceful protest.
After the magistrate’s ruling on Wednesday evening, Das said that “truth has triumphed”.
The release of the two leaders is likely to come as a blow to the ruling Narendra Modi government, which has implemented an unforgiving crackdown on recent protests that have erupted across India.
The CJP, alongside the opposition alliance, student groups and civil society, have been calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of the electoral roll that benefits Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) and has led to more than 130 million names being deleted from the voter register. The BJP has denied any interference.
The CJP began as an online satire earlier this year, but has since grown into a fully fledged political movement, challenging the powerful Modi government. Over the summer, it was Cockroach-led protests that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister after sustained demonstrations.
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the CJP movement, vowed over the weekend that the Modi regime and threat of jail would not intimidate the Cockroaches. Dipke was also detained on Friday after he called for a peaceful demonstration in central Delhi where CJP supporters would gather and wave the Indian flag in solidarity with Das and Ranka.
He had said that, once his fellow Cockroach leaders were released, they would “gather, re-strategise, and determine how to move forward”.
“The illegal arrests and detentions we have witnessed over the past few days indicate an attempt to intimidate us,” said Dipke. “But we will not be cowed down or retreat. This is a long battle and we are prepared for it.”

The Kremlin wants Russian media to call attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ‘Putin strikes.’ The inspiration? Stalin.
Russia’s Presidential Administration has ordered state and Kremlin-aligned media outlets to begin writing about “Putin strikes” on Ukraine, two employees at such outlets told Meduza.
The Presidential Administration’s political bloc sent loyalist media recommendations advising them to report that “the effectiveness and efficiency of Russia’s strikes far exceed what the Ukrainian military has achieved.”
“Our ballistic weapons have performed flawlessly. The Ukrainian regime has lost its most important production and storage sites, where cruise missiles and drones, along with their components, were assembled and stored. ‘Putin strikes’ are far larger in scale and more effective than enemy attacks. We are shutting down the militants’ missile programs, which helps keep Russia’s regions secure,” the guidance document says.
Headlines, comments from servicemen, and articles using the phrase “Putin strikes” indeed appeared this week in major Russian media outlets.
For example, the Russian news website Gazeta.ru published an article with the following subheadline:
“SVO” veteran Konovalov: “Putin strikes” deprive the Ukrainian military of the ability to fight.
The outlet cites Vitaly Konovalov, head of the Association of Veterans of the Russia-Ukraine War in Stavropol Krai, who says the strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure are allegedly aimed at undermining supplies to the Ukrainian military. Notably, Konovalov himself never uses the phrase “Putin strikes.” It appears in the connecting phrases and generalizations added by propagandists.
Novye Izvestia published an article titled “Putin Strikes on Ukraine: Ukrainian Military Left Without Electricity and Weapons.” Rosbalt used the phrase in the headline of a news item titled “Putin Strikes on Ukraine: Ukrainian Military Losing Logistics Hubs, Substations, and Vessels.” It also appears in headlines and articles from Fedpress. Segodnia.ru writes about a “series of “Putin strikes.”” The phrase has even appeared in pro-government Instagram accounts.
A political consultant who works with the Presidential Administration’s political bloc said directly linking Putin to the strikes on Ukraine is meant to try to boost the president’s approval ratings.
According to polls by the Public Opinion Foundation (FOM), Putin’s approval rating fell from 75% in July to 71% in early October, while trust in him fell from 74% to 70% over the same period.
“In this case, [the idea is to raise the ratings] among the pro-war, ultra-patriotic segment of society, who need to be shown some successes from the war. To the question “What has been accomplished?” [at the front], the suggested answer is “Putin strikes,” by analogy with the “Stalinist strikes,”” the consultant said.
During Joseph Stalin’s rule, the term “Ten Stalinist Strikes” referred to 10 major Soviet army operations during World War II.
The source told Meduza that it is hard to assess how effective the appearance of “Putin strikes” in the press has been: “Maybe it will have some effect on the older segment [of society].”
Speaking at a press conference in Bishkek on September 1, following the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit, Vladimir Putin said he had ordered the Russian military to prepare and carry out massive strikes on Ukraine’s energy facilities. “They’re striking our people, so they’ll get a response,” he added.
In mid-October, discussing the Russian army’s strikes on Ukraine, Putin said:
They took the first step. We started responding. Now they’re whining about energy facilities too, and about other targets, including data centers and so on. They started it. They shouldn’t have started it.

Five bullets and a broken promise: Israel's forgotten political assassination
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:25:23 UTC
00:25:23 KST

On the evening of January 12, 1981, a security guard outside Jerusalem's Holyland Hotel heard gunfire. Looking toward the entrance, he saw a military jeep speeding away against the direction of traffic. Nearby, inside a bullet-riddled Peugeot 504, Israeli lawmaker Hamad Abu Rabia lay dead. He had been struck by five bullets. 
The killing made him the first serving member of Israel's Knesset to be assassinated. The motive was extraordinary: Abu Rabia had refused to surrender his parliamentary seat under a political rotation agreement, and the men responsible for his murder were the sons of the politician who stood to replace him.
Abu Rabia's life had begun far from the corridors of the Knesset. Born in 1929 in a Bedouin tent near Tel Malhata, in what is now the southern Negev between Arad and Dimona, he attended elementary school in Beersheba and later studied in Hebron. At just 18, he became sheikh of the Abu Rabia tribe and worked to expand educational opportunities for its children. In the 1973 election, he headed the Arab List for Bedouins and Villagers, becoming the first Bedouin elected to Israel's parliament when the eighth Knesset convened in 1974. His election was celebrated with a gathering of some 2,000 guests at his tribe's encampment. Among those attending were senior politician Yigal Allon and Druze lawmaker Jaber Muadi, who would later become his political rival.
Abu Rabia's early parliamentary career was closely tied to the political representation of Israel's Bedouin population. His faction joined the Labor Alignment before breaking away and eventually becoming part of the United Arab List, a small Arab party affiliated with the Alignment, then led by Shimon Peres. In the 1977 election, the United Arab List won just one seat, prompting its three senior figures to agree to share it through a rotation arrangement. Saif al-Din al-Zoubi, a former mayor of Nazareth, served first, resigning after approximately two years. Abu Rabia replaced him in April 1979, with Muadi, from the northern Druze village of Yarka, next in line.
But when Abu Rabia's allotted time expired, he refused to step aside. His decision was not simply a dispute over political status. Following the peace treaty with Egypt, Israel planned new military airfields in the Negev to replace installations in Sinai, raising concerns over the displacement of Bedouin communities and the expropriation of their land. Abu Rabia argued that he needed to remain in parliament to defend his community's interests. "I must continue being a member of the Knesset to protect the Bedouins," he explained at the time. Muadi, however, insisted that the rotation agreement obligated Abu Rabia to resign. He pursued the matter through parliamentary channels and the courts, but efforts to compel the resignation failed.
The dispute grew increasingly bitter. In the months before his murder, Abu Rabia feared for his safety and was occasionally accompanied by armed bodyguards. He also carried a pistol, which was found in his possession after the assassination. On January 12, he spent the day at the Knesset, briefly speaking with Labor politicians Shimon Peres and Moshe Shahal before driving to the Holyland Hotel in Jerusalem's Bayit Vegan neighborhood, where lawmakers frequently stayed during parliamentary sessions. At approximately 8:30 p.m., attackers waiting near the hotel opened fire as he arrived, killing him inside his car before escaping in a jeep.
Muadi initially denied any connection to the killing. He acknowledged that he and Abu Rabia had quarreled but maintained that they had reconciled. Asked whether he knew who might have murdered his colleague, he replied: "How could I know? It hurts me very much." As suspicion increasingly focused on his family, Muadi rejected suggestions that he had been involved. "Would I kill a man just to get into the Knesset?" he asked, according to contemporary reporting in Yedioth Ahronoth. He nevertheless continued to criticize Abu Rabia for breaking their agreement, saying the murdered lawmaker had sworn on the Quran to honor it. Muadi acknowledged telling him that God would take revenge on him and his children, but insisted the remark had not been a threat.
Police arrested six suspects, several of them members of Muadi's family. Investigators established that three of his sons had traveled to Jerusalem and waited near the Holyland Hotel for Abu Rabia to arrive. According to the reconstruction presented during the investigation, Saif Muadi fired the fatal shots before fleeing with his brothers. In January 1982, all three brothers were convicted of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment. The court accepted the prosecution's account that they had acted to secure their father's place in the Knesset, regarding Abu Rabia's refusal to honor the agreement as an affront to their family's honor. In 1984, however, the Supreme Court overturned the murder conviction of the third brother, Dahash Muadi, who had served as deputy commander of Nablus Prison. He was released after being acquitted of murder, although he had been convicted of other offenses.
The assassination also had an immediate political consequence. Muadi took Abu Rabia's place in the Knesset just days after the killing, in a swearing-in ceremony held under heavy security. He remained in parliament until the ninth Knesset was dissolved about six months later but did not regain his seat in the subsequent election. Throughout the investigation and trial, he maintained that he had no involvement in the murder, despite acknowledging the bitter dispute with Abu Rabia and the exchanges that had preceded it.
The two convicted brothers remained imprisoned until January 10, 1991, when President Chaim Herzog granted them pardons following sustained political pressure from members of the Druze community. Their release was celebrated in Yarka with a large gathering. According to reports from the time, 130 sheep were slaughtered and half a ton of baklava and other sweets were served to guests welcoming the brothers home.

Rare 700-year-old Quran manuscript to be auctioned in London
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:24:52 UTC
00:24:52 KST

Breadcrumb
Rare 700-year-old Quran manuscript to be auctioned in London
A rare Quran manuscript page dating back more than 700 years to medieval Baghdad is set to go under the hammer at Christie's in London next month, with an estimated value of between £50,000 and £70,000.
The elaborately decorated folio, believed to have been produced around 1310 during the Ilkhanid period, features verses from the Quran written in gold and surrounded by intricate Islamic ornamentation.
The manuscript will be offered as part of Christie's Art of the Islamic and Indian Worlds auction on 12 November, which will feature more than 230 historical objects, including manuscripts, ceramics, paintings, metalwork and textiles.
According to Christie's, the page contains the opening three verses of Surah al-Humazah, the Quran's 104th chapter, written in four lines of gold muhaqqaq script, a distinctive style of Arabic calligraphy associated with monumental manuscripts.
The lettering is outlined in gold, silver and black ink, while individual verses are separated by decorative rosettes featuring gold and multiple colours.
The chapter heading appears in black Kufic script outlined in gold, surrounded by an elaborate panel of interlacing arabesque patterns and a decorated marginal medallion.
Measuring approximately 57.7 by 42.6 centimetres, the unusually large folio reflects the importance attached to the production of luxury Qurans under the Ilkhanids, the Mongol dynasty that ruled much of Iran and Iraq between the 13th and 14th centuries.
The manuscript's illumination, or decorative artwork, has been attributed to Muhammad ibn Aybak ibn Abdullah, regarded as one of the leading manuscript illuminators working in Baghdad during the early 14th century.
Ibn Aybak is associated with two monumental Qurans produced for the Ilkhanid royal court, one probably commissioned for Sultan Ghazan, who ruled from 1295 to 1304, and another for his successor, Sultan Uljaytu.
Both rulers belonged to the Mongol dynasty that emerged following the conquests of Genghis Khan's descendants, with Ghazan's conversion to Islam helping consolidate the religion's position within the Ilkhanid state.
The period witnessed significant developments in Islamic manuscript production, particularly in Baghdad, where calligraphers and illuminators developed elaborate styles combining Arabic lettering with colourful decorative motifs.
Christie's says the manuscript closely resembles pages associated with Ibn Aybak's royal commissions, although the identity of the calligrapher responsible for its lettering remains uncertain.
The auction house notes that the decorative style incorporates Chinese-inspired details, reflecting artistic exchanges across the territories once connected by the Mongol Empire.
A comparable folio held by the Museum of Islamic Art in Doha is believed to have originated from the same manuscript, offering further evidence of the artistic traditions associated with Ibn Aybak's workshop.
The page's known ownership history is limited, with Christie's listing it as having belonged to a private collection in the UK, reportedly by 1971.
Its appearance at auction highlights the continuing international market for historic Islamic manuscripts, particularly examples associated with major centres of medieval Islamic scholarship and artistic production.
Christie's November sale will also include works from across the Islamic world and Indian subcontinent, with objects representing artistic traditions stretching from North Africa and Spain to Central Asia.
The auction is scheduled for 12 November in London, following a public exhibition running from 7 to 11 November.

Ukraine’s top war charity names only way to save $25,000 to $4 million each time cheap Russian jet-powered drone is shot down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:19:43 UTC
00:19:43 KST

Intercepting a jet-powered Geran can cost anywhere from $2,000 to $4 million depending on the weapon used. Cheap interceptor drones are the only option that keeps air defense affordable, the foundation of Ukrainian top war volunteer Serhii Sternenko said on Telegram.
Russia’s jet Gerans now carry every characteristic of a small cruise missile, and Russians keep raising their speed in answer to each Ukrainian countermeasure. Former commander-in-chief Valerii Zaluzhnyi has framed the shift bluntly: an expensive Cold War missile has become a cheap weapon fired in bulk, and the drone is now “a missile in all but name,” affordable to any side, not only wealthy countries.
Sternenko heads a charitable foundation that has purchased 291,502 FPV drones, which have helped Ukraine’s military down more than 12,954 aerial targets. Also, has advised the team of former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov.
Three ways to kill a jet Geran, and what each costs
The foundation laid out the price of each method:
- Aircraft (F-16, MiG-29, Su-27, Mirage 2000): $25,000 to $1.2 million per kill. Effective, but the stock of missiles is critically low, and some air-to-air types are no longer being replenished.
- Surface-to-air and shoulder-fired systems (IRIS-T, NASAMS, Vampire, Avenger): about $30,000 to $4 million. Good for shielding key sites, but a missile capable of reaching a jet Geran at 6 to 7 kilometers costs $0.5 million to $4 million.
- Interceptor drones (makers undisclosed): from $2,000. Cheap, with trained operators ready, but not yet scalable.
Why the cheapest option is the one that matters
No single tool is enough, the foundation stresses. Downing jet Gerans still needs aircraft, small aviation and missile systems together, but it is the interceptors that make the defense affordable, taking out the cheaper Shaheds and saving costly missiles for targets nothing else can reach.
The foundation says it has found a way to counter drones that already match small cruise missiles, working with Ukrainian manufacturers, without disclosing details. The method is far cheaper than other ways of downing jet Gerans and significantly strengthens air defense, it says, as part of a wider Ukrainian push to field interceptor drones fast enough to catch Russia’s fastest weapons.

Physicists trap a single antimatter particle for a month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:19:14 UTC
00:19:14 KST

You can’t hold antimatter in your hand or even in a regular laboratory apparatus. As soon as antimatter meets matter, the two tend to annihilate each other. This makes studying antimatter tricky. But now physicists have managed to trap a single subatomic particle of the stuff for months at a time in a way that allows them to study its quantum states.
Further investigations using the trap might reveal the secret of why the world around us is made of matter and not antimatter, when things could have presumably gone either way.
Every normal particle of matter has an antimatter counterpart with equal mass but opposite charge. To build their trap, physicists started with atoms of sodium 22, a radioactive isotope with a half-life of about two and a half years. When one of these atoms decays, it emits a positron—the antimatter counterpart of the electron.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“The big challenge is to persuade these positrons to slow down and then capture them,” says Gerald Gabrielse, a physicist at Northwestern University, who oversaw the project. The team reported its achievement on Wednesday in Physical Review Letters.
The first step is to send the positrons through the crystal lattice of a sliver of cold tungsten. As the particles go pinballing through the material, they slow down and lose energy. “Every time they bang into something, there’s a chance of annihilation, but it doesn’t always happen,” Gabrielse says. “If they make it to the end, they get popped out.”
Next, the physicists steer the positrons along a channel using electromagnetic fields. Eventually the particles end up in a vacuum, just three tenths of a degree Celsius above absolute zero, trapped by an electric field on top and bottom and a magnetic field on the sides. “If you want to hold on to antimatter, you have to hold it in a container without walls,” Gabrielse says.
This method allowed the researchers to isolate and study a solitary, lone positron for a month—and could let them do so indefinitely.
The researchers intend to use their trap to make precise measurements of the positron’s magnetic moment—basically the strength and orientation of its magnetic field. To do this, they must determine two things: the energy needed to flip the direction of the positron’s spin and the energy needed to make it jump from its ground state to its first excited state.
Using a similar trap setup, Gabrielse and his team have already measured the magnetic moment of an electron to a precision of one part in 10 trillion. Taking the equivalent measurement for a positron will allow them to make a crucial comparison. “We’re looking to see if they have an exactly opposite magnetic moment,” Gabrielse says. That’s the prediction of the Standard Model of particle physics. If the two have different values, however, this could help explain why our universe is made of matter instead of antimatter.
Just after the Big Bang, scientists think there were roughly equal amounts of the two. Most of the matter and antimatter must have annihilated, but a small excess of matter was somehow left over to seed the stars and planets we see. The magnetic moment measurement is just one of many realms where physicists are seeking differences between matter and antimatter to account for this profound discrepancy.
“Turn every particle to its antiparticle, look at physics through a mirror (flipping left and right) and press the ‘rewind button’ to reverse the flow of time,” says Roni Harnik, a theoretical physicist at the Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory in Batavia, Ill., who was not involved in the project. “Our most basic theories say that physics stays the same.”
If it turns out things are different—that the positron, for instance, has a different magnetic moment than the electron—then we’d have a hint about how matter won out.
“This is an exciting development,” Harnik says, “that will enable us to test a basic symmetry.”
