Poland’s parliament votes to ease abortion ban but faces likely veto from president
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:56:46 UTC
23:56:46 KST

Poland’s lower house of parliament has approved two bills aimed at loosening a near-total ban on abortions, in what campaigners have described as a “small-scale step” ahead of protests calling on the government to fulfil its promises to overhaul the country’s laws.
The new measures, which are likely to be vetoed by Poland’s nationalist president, would remove some of the criminal penalties for those who help women to access abortion care and allow terminations in cases of foetal abnormalities.
Leah Hoctor, of the Center for Reproductive Rights, said: “These bills represent a very small-scale change. Even if these pieces of legislation are ratified and signed into law by the Polish president – which remains to be seen – they would change very little for most women in Poland who need abortion care.”
This view was echoed by the NGO Legalna Aborcja (Legal Abortion), a reproductive rights and advocacy initiative. “What does this mean for women who need an abortion right now? Nothing, because none of these bills would help them,” said a spokesperson.
The Fundacja Widzialne (Visible Foundation) asked people to keep up the pressure on the government by taking to the streets on Thursday. “Poland still has an inhumane abortion law,” it wrote on social media as it announced rallies in 27 cities. “We demand the full decriminalisation of abortion and access to abortion covered by the National Health Fund!”
The rallies, backed by a range of groups across Poland, mark the sixth anniversary of a 2020 ruling that tightened the country’s already-restrictive abortion rules. The ruling prompted the largest protests in Poland since the fall of communism as people poured into the streets wielding placards that read “The revolution has a uterus” and “My body, my choice”.
The protests were later credited with helping to propel Donald Tusk into power in 2023, with promises to overhaul abortion laws within 100 days. Last year Tusk backtracked on the pledge to legalise abortions until the 12th week of pregnancy, saying there was “simply no majority” to reform the laws.
Even if the two bills passed this week are signed into law, Poland would remain “completely out of step with the rest of its EU peers”, said Hoctor. Currently, abortion is only legal in Poland when a pregnancy results from a criminal act, such as rape or incest, or when it threatens the life or health of the mother.
The Center for Reproductive Rights instead called on Tusk to skirt around Poland’s polarised politics by putting in place an interim moratorium on the application of all criminal law provisions concerning abortion. “This would ensure that those caring for women no longer do so under the threat of criminal investigation and prosecution,” Hoctor said.
The idea was first floated by the UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women, which in 2024 concluded that women in Poland faced severe human rights violations due to restrictive abortion laws.
Hoctor said: “The reality is that thousands of women in Poland every year access abortion care. So they are doing that illegally, or they’re travelling for it. That’s not what a modern European country needs to be. They’re not living up to the promise of what it is to be a modern healthcare system and a modern democracy.”

During the journey, cadets from the Baltic Naval Institute continued their practical training, taking part in navigation watches, plotting courses using onboard instruments, and practicing maneuvers through narrow waterways. They also received instruction in ship operations and damage control.
The vessel was welcomed in Walvis Bay by representatives of the Russian Embassy and the Namibian navу. The visitors who toured the ship were briefed on its operations and the training program for future naval officers. The crew and cadets are also to visit local attractions during their stay.
Earlier in October, ‘Perekop’ called at the port of Maputo, Mozambique’s capital. The vessel also made stops in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, and Victoria, the capital of Seychelles, in September as part of its ongoing voyage.
According to Sputnik, the voyage is scheduled to conclude on December 9, 2026, after taking the vessel through four oceans, 14 seas, 23 straits, nine bays, and two rivers, with calls at 20 ports, including 12 overseas.
The ‘Perekop’ is not the first Russian naval ship to visit Africa. In July 2025, another Baltic Fleet vessel, the ‘Smolny’, visited the Republic of the Congo as part of a regional tour that also included Equatorial Guinea and São Tomé and Príncipe. The ship had previously called at several African ports in 2024, including in Namibia, Angola, and South Africa.
Russia previously deployed warships to South Africa for joint naval exercises. In January 2026, the Russian Navy’s ‘Stoikiy’ corvette and ‘Yelnya’ tanker took part in the multinational Will for Peace drills off the South African coast.

Russia to send first diesel tanker to the US amid Trump deal

Russia to send first diesel tanker to the US amid Trump deal
Russia will send on Thursday its first diesel tanker to the US to an undisclosed port.
Russia will send its first tanker of diesel fuel to the United States on Thursday, Russia’s Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters amid a deal with US President Donald Trump.
The vessel will have 40,000 tonnes of fuel, but Novak, who made his remarks on Wednesday, did not name which US port the fuel would be delivered to.
Russia lifted its ban on diesel exports on October 9, which Moscow originally put in place to tackle the country’s shortages as Ukrainian-led drone strikes hindered production capacity.
The shipment comes despite setbacks for Russia’s diesel output. Earlier this month, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence said that drone strikes knocked out at least half of Russia’s oil refining capacity, forcing cuts at Russia’s top diesel-producing refineries.
“Additional shipments will follow, of course. There were agreements reached between the two leaders. We will meet the United States’ needs, to the extent of our capabilities,” the RIA Novosti news agency quoted Novak as saying.
That was echoed by US special envoy Steve Witkoff, who has been meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin for talks in St Petersburg.
“We are preparing deliveries of several vessels, the tankers, right now. They will go one after another. The financial component should be provided,” he said, adding that Russia would also be able to supply fertilisers in “large quantities” to the US market.
US President Donald Trump had previously said that Moscow would export 300,000 tonnes, or 2.25 million barrels, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and 1 million tonnes “immediately thereafter”.
US consumers have continued to face high prices at the petrol station, particularly for diesel fuel, a pressing point as the country heads into midterm elections in less than two weeks. The average price for a gallon of diesel is $6.31 ($1.70 per litre), according to the American Automobile Association (AAA). While prices remain well over the $6 mark, they are on the downturn. The average price a month ago was $6.51.

Ships and hydrofoils at risk in Gulf of Naples
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:54:04 CEST
23:54:04 KST

Maritime connections in the Gulf of
Naples are at risk of grinding to a halt over the next two days
due to a fuel shortage caused by striking truckers.
                                    
Supplies of diesel for ships and hydrofoils are running
critically low, and the shipping companies that provide services
to Ischia, Capri, and Procida are notifying authorities and
passengers of an impending suspension of some routes.
                                    
Already today, several connections from Capri have been
cancelled, and by tomorrow morning, other vessels may remain
docked in port; unless fuel supplies are replenished, the
shutdown could progressively extend to most maritime services.
                                    
Caremar was the first company to report the emergency to the
Prefecture, noting that its fuel reserves are nearing
exhaustion. Medmar has also issued a similar statement,
clarifying that while services from Naples and Pozzuoli to
Ischia and Procida can be maintained until tomorrow evening at
the latest, some vessels will be forced to stop operating as
early as tomorrow.
                                    
The situation for high-speed ferry services is much the same.
                                    
Alilauro has issued an advisory to customers warning of
potential cancellations and schedule changes in the coming days,
and Gestur has released a similar notice.
                                    
The emergency could soon affect Capri as well; while Snav
currently rules out a total suspension of service, it has
announced the need to adjust schedules and reduce the number of
daily crossings.
                                    
The company warns that, without new supplies by the weekend, it
will no longer be possible to guarantee regular service.
                                    
A potential halt to maritime transport threatens to have serious
repercussions for tourism, which remains active on the islands
in the Gulf despite the arrival of autumn.
                                    
On Ischia, nearly one hundred accommodation facilities are still
open, and there is a significant number of foreign
visitors—particularly Americans.
                                    
For them, as well as for the islanders, any disruptions to
maritime connections could be compounded by issues with local
land-based public transport: EAV Bus has stated that it can
maintain service only until next Monday, while on Procida, bus
services could come to a standstill as early as Saturday.
                                    
There are also concerns on Capri, where about twenty hotels
remain open and hundreds of day-trippers continue to arrive
daily.
                                    
Any reduction in ferry or hydrofoil services could create
difficulties for both arrivals and departures.
                                    
Finally, on top of the transport crisis, there is the risk that
food supplies on the three islands could gradually run out,
given that the last shipments arrived last weekend.

UN warns El Nino could be strongest on record as it urges world to prepare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:53:37 UTC
23:53:37 KST

The UN's aid chief says the humanitarian system cannot cope alone, as $50 million is released for 11 frontline countries including Chad and Somalia.
The current El Nino could reach a strength never seen in modern records, United Nations officials warned on Wednesday, calling on governments to act now to limit the damage.
"The current El Nino event could be unprecedented in strength. Literally off the monitoring charts that we have used for the past four decades," Celeste Saulo, secretary-general of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), told reporters in Geneva.
"El Nino will peak towards the end of 2026, but its impacts will be felt long after that," she added.
According to the WMO's latest global seasonal climate updates, sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific, where the phenomenon originates, could climb as high as 3.8C above average between November and January. That would be far beyond what is normally seen during an El Nino.
"This will have far-reaching consequences for weather patterns across the world," Saulo said.
The agency expects the event to push up temperatures across much of the globe, adding to the warming already driven by human-caused climate change.
A call for early action
Saulo appeared alongside Tom Fletcher, the UN's under-secretary-general for humanitarian affairs.
"Today, we are issuing a joint call for urgent and coordinated anticipatory action... We cannot stop El Nino, but we can prevent many of its worst human consequences," she said.
Fletcher described the coming El Nino as a "wrecking ball" of extreme heat, drought and flooding, warning it would bring "massive humanitarian consequences".
"The damage will not stay in the countries in the immediate path of this El Nino," he said. "It will create economic shocks for the global economy and drive further conflict, displacement, migration.
"I am sounding the alarm that the humanitarian system... cannot alone cope with a threat on this scale." He urged governments, development banks and international financial institutions to release funding "before that damage is done, not afterwards".
"The choice is clear: we can wait for disaster or we can invest in resilience. We cannot prevent El Nino but we can be serious about the challenges ahead."
Fletcher said he had already released $50 million to support 11 of the most exposed countries, among them Chad, El Salvador, Ethiopia, Somalia and South Sudan.
What is El Nino?
El Nino is a naturally occurring climate pattern in which surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific become unusually warm. This shifts winds, air pressure and rainfall around the world. It usually returns every two to seven years and lasts between nine and 12 months.
The climate swings between El Nino and its cooler counterpart, La Nina, with neutral periods in between.

Sevilla filed a formal complaint with LaLiga over what it described as “unequal and “inadequate” television coverage of key incidents during Sunday's 4-1 defeat to Real Madrid, the club said Tuesday.
The Spanish club said it was "deeply dissatisfied" with the audiovisual production of the Oct. 18 match at Santiago Bernabeu Stadium.
Sevilla also raised concerns over comments made by LaLiga's head of production and editorial, Sergio Carranza Lezcano, on Spanish radio program El Partidazo de COPE.
Sevilla coach Luis Garcia Plaza criticized an incident involving Real Madrid's Arda Guler and Gerard "Peque" Fernandez while the score was 0-0.
Guler appeared to elbow Peque but was not sent off. He later opened the scoring in the 30th minute.
Garcia Plaza said Sevilla had been "denied the chance to play another game, 11 against 10."
In its complaint, signed by club president Jose Maria del Nido Carrasco, Sevilla questioned how four incidents were broadcast and replayed.
The club cited an alleged foul by Cucurella on Peque that it believed could have resulted in a penalty, saying broadcasters failed to provide adequate replays.
Sevilla also criticized the coverage of Guler's alleged elbow, saying the incident was shown only from distant angles without zoom or magnification.
The club questioned the lack of sufficient television analysis of an alleged foul by Konate on Robbie Ure before Real Madrid's second goal.
By contrast, Sevilla said Real Madrid's penalty following a foul on Kylian Mbappe was shown through multiple replays from different angles.
Sevilla demands footage, investigation
Sevilla rejected criteria it attributed to LaLiga production officials, including reliance on player protests, the referee's initial decision and broadcasters' subjective judgment.
The club also questioned considerations related to live coverage and the video assistant referee system.
It called on LaLiga to publish the protocols governing match broadcasts and clarify the extent of editorial discretion.
Sevilla alleged that three disputed incidents were deliberately omitted from the official match highlights, despite footage later being broadcast by Movistar Plus+ and DAZN.
The club requested detailed documentation covering the production plan, camera positions, blind spots and personnel responsible for broadcast decisions.
It also demanded the immediate release of complete original footage of the four incidents.
Sevilla called for the preservation of technical records and independent camera recordings in case of potential legal action.
The club also sought access to LaLiga's audiovisual production guidelines and called for an investigation and corrective measures to ensure equitable treatment of all teams.
Sevilla said it also disagreed with the criteria presented by the Technical Committee of Referees during a meeting Tuesday concerning the controversial incidents.
The club said the meeting involved a respectful exchange but that the two sides maintained clearly divergent views over the decisions.

EU prosecutors raid far-right group's offices in €4 million funds scandal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:52:30 UTC
23:52:30 KST

The searches are linked to an probe into the alleged misuse of more than €4 million by the now-defunct Identity and Democracy group, whose debts Patriots for Europe could be forced to repay.
The European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) raided the offices of the far-right Patriots for Europe (PfE) group in Brussels and Strasbourg on Wednesday as part of an investigation into the alleged misuse of millions of euros in EU funds.
The searches at the European Parliament’s two main seats are linked to an investigation into the former Identity and Democracy (ID) group, the Parliament confirmed to Euronews.
PfE, which includes France’s National Rally, led by Marine Le Pen; Italy’s The League, led by Matteo Salvini; and Hungary’s Fidesz, led by Viktor Orbán, could be ordered to repay more than €4 million allegedly misspent by its predecessor.
“It would appear that these searches are linked to the complaint lodged against the Identity and Democracy group, which dissolved in 2024,” the PfE group said in a statement, insisting that it has no “legal continuity” with ID and is therefore “not involved in the ongoing investigation”.
Neither the EPPO nor the Parliament has released further details about the searches.
The Parliament “cooperates with relevant authorities” and “does not have any additional comment,” its press service said.
Jean-Paul Garraud, an MEP who leads the National Rally delegation in the Parliament, wrote on X that the searches targeted “the offices of former ID staff members”.
The anti-graft body has been investigating since last July the alleged misappropriation of EU funds by ID between 2019 and 2024. The group brought together MEPs from far-right parties such as France’s National Rally, Italy’s Lega and the Alternative for Germany (AfD).
ID dissolved after the 2024 European elections, and many of its parties went on to form PfE, which also includes newcomers Spain’s Vox and Hungary's Fidesz.
An opinion approved by the Parliament’s Committee on Budgetary Control (CONT) last September argued that EU funds wrongly spent by ID during the previous term should be repaid by PfE once the investigation is closed.
Under the Parliament’s rules, a political group is treated as “the successor” of a dissolved one, and therefore liable for any remaining debt, if certain conditions are met.
These include “a decisive share of the former group’s members moved together into the new formation”, “premises, IT systems, bank accounts or other assets passed to the new structure”, and “the new name and public messaging presenting the entity as the direct heir of the dissolved group, or following so closely in time that the rebranding appears designed mainly to shed liabilities.”

AI generated
BRUSSELS - Developers of the PHP programming language said a set of new updates fixing two previously identified critical vulnerabilities was now live, and acknowledged a delay in addressing a previously identified flaw.
Government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline on Oct 21 after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in PHP sent website operators around the world scrambling to protect their systems.
PHP underpins large parts of the internet and the vulnerabilities had raised concerns that a significant number of websites could be vulnerable to attack. The developers issued four patches to address two “critical” vulnerabilities that could allow hackers to execute code on vulnerable systems.
It said users were strongly encouraged to update immediately.
The PHP Foundation, which oversees development and maintenance of the software, said in a blog post that a security researcher in 2024 found the first signs of a flaw that led to one of the vulnerabilities, but that the issue was “theorised, but no concrete vectors were found and other concrete issues with clear impact overshadowed these concerns.”
The delay in addressing the flaw “was a structural failure,” the foundation said.
The programming language’s developers had earlier said they had identified two critical vulnerabilities and urged users to update their sites as soon as a fix was released. Security experts warned that hackers would quickly reverse engineer the patches and race to exploit unpatched systems.
The US National Security Agency said in a statement that the vulnerabilities “often provide a direct path to the server’s file system or database,” and that if an immediate update was not feasible, organisations should take systems offline for full mitigation.
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) said in an advisory that organisations “should immediately update” their PHP installations.
“While CISA has not observed exploitation of these vulnerabilities as of the time of publication, they pose a risk to organisations if left unpatched,” the agency said in an advisory. REUTERS

Adel Abdelrheem and Ikram Kouachi
21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
The death toll from a drone attack on a market in the disputed Abyei area between South Sudan and Sudan rose to 153, a South Sudanese government official said Wednesday.
Yohana Akol Ngor, acting information minister in the Abyei Special Administrative Area government, told Radio Tamazuj that 153 people had been killed in the attack on Amiet Market, also known as the “Ostrich Market,” in Abyei.
Ngor said the toll included people whose bodies had been buried, while others remained missing, indicating that the number of casualties could rise further.
“The total number of people who died as a result of the drone attacks is 153. These are the people whose bodies have been buried, but there are still people missing,” he said.
Ngor accused the Sudanese army of carrying out Monday’s attack on the market, located about 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) north of Abyei town.
The Sudanese army has not commented on the allegations.
Ngor said the victims were buried in two mass graves, one east of the market and the other nearby, adding that some bodies had been charred in the attack.
He added that 30 injured people were receiving treatment at a hospital, some of them in critical condition.
On Monday, Sudanese media reported that civilians had been killed and injured in a drone attack targeting the northern entrance of Amiet Market, locally known as the “Ostrich Market,” in Abyei.
The reports said the victims included South Sudanese nationals and members of Sudan’s Misseriya tribe.
On the same day, South Sudan’s Foreign Ministry summoned Sudanese Ambassador to Juba Isam Karar to protest the attack on the market.
Abyei, an oil-rich area, was granted special status under the Comprehensive Peace Agreement signed by Khartoum and Juba on Sept. 25, 2003.
The area serves as a bridge between northern and southern Sudan. The Arab Misseriya tribes live in the north, while African Dinka communities inhabit the south.
The attack comes amid Sudan’s ongoing war between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, which began in April 2023 over a dispute about integrating the latter into the military.
The war has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced about 13 million, while worsening famine and a humanitarian crisis considered among the world’s worst.

&quot;Destructive force&quot; of El Niño could cause record temperature rise in the Pacific Ocean - UN
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
17:50:51 EEST
23:50:51 KST

"Destructive force" of El Niño could cause record temperature rise in the Pacific Ocean - UN
Kyiv • UNN
The WMO forecasts an extremely strong El Niño peaking in December. The phenomenon could cause floods, droughts and famine for 50 million people.
As UN representatives reported on Wednesday, the weather phenomenon "El Niño" could cause a record increase in ocean temperatures in the Pacific Ocean. It is moving across the planet like a "wrecking ball," causing floods and droughts, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
According to the new seasonal forecast by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the "El Niño" phenomenon will reach exceptional strength: between November and January, temperatures in the central Pacific Ocean will exceed the norm by approximately 3.8 degrees Celsius, with the peak expected in December.
"Our archives have never recorded a figure of 3.8. During previous record El Niño events, we recorded values of around 3 degrees, which already had very serious consequences worldwide. So, we have gone beyond that level," said WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo.
"El Niño" is the warm phase of the natural "El Niño–Southern Oscillation" cycle; it is a climate phenomenon that affects weather around the world.
It usually leads to a rise in global temperatures and disrupts precipitation patterns across large regions: droughts occur in some places, while others experience heavy rainfall.
This is a natural climate phenomenon that is not caused by climate change. However, global warming may make "El Niño" more intense.
According to the WMO, extreme weather conditions associated with "El Niño" may increase pressure on the housing sector, water supply and sanitation systems, as well as healthcare. In particular, the risk of flooding in southern Africa will increase from November.
In Southeast Asia, the WMO notes, warmer conditions and a lack of precipitation may negatively affect agriculture and water supplies, while in Latin America, by contrast, increased rainfall is expected.
The WMO and UN Deputy Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator Tom Fletcher called for urgent preparedness measures.
"This El Niño is a true giant, a real 'wrecking ball.' It will sweep through Latin America, East and Southern Africa, Asia and the Pacific region, bringing extreme heat, droughts and floods," Fletcher said, warning of extensive humanitarian consequences.
According to him, around 50 million people may face a worsening hunger crisis.

A Russian Su-30 fighter jet crashed in the Kaliningrad region on Wednesday, Oct. 21, with both pilots ejecting before the aircraft came down in Russia’s Baltic exclave between two NATO countries.
Russia’s defense ministry confirmed the crash during a scheduled training flight, according to RIA News. The ministry said a ground search-and-rescue team evacuated the crew and that neither pilots were in danger.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The aircraft crashed in an uninhabited area. The flight was conducted without ammunition,” the ministry said. It did not specify what caused the accident.
Russian broadcaster REN TV, citing an unnamed source, identified the aircraft as a Su-30SM and reported that both pilots suffered injuries of varying severity and were hospitalized.
According to the report, cited by RBC-Ukraine, the aircraft crashed in the Chernyakhovsk district, between the settlements of Timofeyevka and Zelyony Bor.
The ministry’s statement confirmed that the crew survived but did not provide details about injuries or hospital treatment. The reported hospitalization therefore remains attributed to Russian media.
The official account also identified the aircraft only as a Su-30, without specifying the SM variant named in the initial reports. Neither account established the cause of the crash.
Another Russian military aircraft crashes
The incident follows several other reported Russian military aviation accidents this year, involving both fighter jets and a strategic bomber.
Ukraine May Have 300-500 Russian Spies Working for Kyiv
On April 3, a Russian Su-30 crashed during a training flight in occupied Crimea. Russia’s defense ministry said that the aircraft was also flying without weapons and that its crew ejected before being evacuated by a search-and-rescue team.
The Su-30SM is a two-seat multirole fighter derived from the Su-27. Its NATO reporting name is Flanker-H.
On Sept. 7, Russian military bloggers reported that two Su-35S fighters collided over the Kursk region. Pro-war aviation blogger Ilya Tumanov, who runs the Fighterbomber Telegram channel, reported the collision, with other Russian military bloggers subsequently describing the loss.
One pilot was reportedly killed, while the other escaped. Russia’s defense ministry had not commented at the time of those reports, and the circumstances remained unclear.
The Su-35S is another fighter developed from the Su-27 family. Russian forces use it for missions including escorting Su-34 fighter-bombers, intercepting drones and missiles, and engaging Ukrainian air defenses.
Later that month, a Tu-95 strategic bomber crashed in Russia’s Amur region during a training exercise. Russian Telegram channel Baza reported that six crew members were killed and one person was hospitalized after the Sept. 29 crash near Krasnoyanovo.
Initial reports incorrectly identified that aircraft as a Tu-154 transport plane before Russia’s defense ministry confirmed that it was a Tu-95. The cause was not immediately established.
The Tu-95 forms a central part of Russia’s strategic bomber fleet and has been used to launch missiles against Ukrainian cities.
Kaliningrad’s military significance
Wednesday’s crash occurred in Russia’s heavily militarized Baltic exclave, which borders Poland and Lithuania, both NATO members, and has no direct land connection to mainland Russia.
Kaliningrad hosts the headquarters of Russia’s Baltic Fleet. Moscow has also deployed Iskander tactical missile systems there, making the territory an important part of Russia’s military posture in the Baltic region.
The exclave was at the center of renewed tensions in September, when Russia’s embassy in Belgium warned that Moscow could use its entire arsenal if NATO countries attempted to isolate the territory.
NATO rejected the warning and described the alliance as defensive, saying its exercises and other activities posed no threat to Russia. The alliance also condemned Moscow’s threats of force and nuclear rhetoric.

Time still open to prepare for powerful El Nino; humanitarian system cannot cope alone: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:47:23 UTC
23:47:23 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
The window to prepare for an exceptionally powerful El Nino remains open in many regions, but UN officials warned Wednesday that the humanitarian system cannot cope with a threat of this scale alone, as they urged wider global mobilization.
"The window for preparedness is still open in many regions. Extreme weather conditions do not need to translate into humanitarian emergencies or into casualties, but this window will not remain open indefinitely," World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Secretary-General Celeste Saulo told reporters in Geneva.
Saulo said the current El Nino event could be unprecedented in strength, potentially exceeding monitoring scales used for the last four decades.
The WMO forecasts that sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific could rise to 3.8C (6.84F) above average between November 2026 and January 2027, bringing droughts, floods and extreme heat to different regions.
UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher said it could expose 50 million people to increased hunger, with consequences extending across Latin America, Africa, Asia and the Pacific.
"I'm sounding the alarm that the humanitarian system, this community of ours, cannot alone cope with a threat on this scale," Fletcher said alongside Saulo.
He urged broader international mobilization involving governments, development banks, scientists, civil society and businesses.
"The next two weeks are the critical window to act before that damage is done," he stressed.
Fletcher said the UN Central Emergency Response Fund has released more than $50 million to support preparedness in 11 countries, including Chad, El Salvador, Ethiopia, Somalia and South Sudan.
He also announced that the UN's disaster readiness network was on full alert.
Fletcher said countries must provide funding and practical support before extreme weather strikes, including helping farmers protect crops and livestock, and moving supplies before roads become inaccessible.
Saulo stressed that forecasts and early warning systems could help governments and humanitarian organizations protect vulnerable populations, particularly those already affected by conflict and displacement.
"What we need now is decisive action, especially to protect the most vulnerable communities," she said. "We cannot stop El Nino, but we can prevent many of its worst human consequences."

Shares in Ukrainian milk producer IMC dropped 9.21%, while Ukrainian agro holdings Agroton, KSG Agro and Milkiland recorded smaller losses, according to Interfax-Ukraine.
The sharp drop comes as Astarta reports weaker financial results. For Astarta, whether the fall reflects a temporary reaction to a bad half-year or deeper doubts about the company’s outlook will depend on its next results and on conditions in Ukraine.
Astarta reported a net loss of 14.07 million euros ($15.8 million) in the first half of 2026, compared with a net profit of 42.27 million euros ($47.5 million) in the same period in 2025.
Revenue remained broadly unchanged at 226.5 million euros ($254 million). The loss came mainly from lower sugar and milk prices and higher logistics costs for its soybean business, which offset growth in crop production.
Astarta is a vertically integrated agricultural group with operations spanning crop production, sugar manufacturing, soybean processing and dairy farming. Listed on the Warsaw Stock Exchange since 2006, the company provides international investors with exposure to Ukraine’s agricultural sector.
Exports accounted for 62% of revenue, according to the company’s first-half 2026 financial report.

Eurozone government debt climbs to 88.8% of GDP as Italy closes in on Greece
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:45:53 UTC
23:45:53 KST

Government debt in the eurozone rose to 88.8% of GDP in the second quarter of 2026, with Italy closing in on Greece, the most indebted member state, and France's debt climbing to 119.1% as its borrowing costs topped 5%.
Public debt across the 21 countries of the eurozone reached 88.8% of their combined economic output between April and June, up from 87.3% a year earlier, the EU's statistics office, Eurostat, said on Wednesday.
Italy's debt ratio is now less than one percentage point below Greece's, while France's has climbed to 119.1% as its borrowing costs rose above 5%.
The debt-to-GDP ratio compares what governments owe with the size of their economies. Under EU rules, debt should not exceed 60% of GDP, and annual budget deficits should not exceed 3%.
Across the wider EU, government debt rose to 82.9% of GDP in the second quarter, from 81.4% a year earlier. In cash terms, eurozone governments owed some €14.4 trillion.
Full-year figures, also published on Wednesday, show EU debt rose to 81.5% of GDP in 2025 from 80.3% in 2024, while the bloc's budget deficit held at 3.1%, just above the EU's 3% limit.
EU debt has stayed above 80% of GDP since the COVID-19 pandemic, when it peaked at 89.5% in 2020.
For the eurozone, Eurostat's headline full-year figures still cover the 20 countries that used the euro last year, as Bulgaria joined on 1 January 2026. Their debt rose to 87.7% of GDP from 86.6%.
Eurostat also expressed a reservation about the quality of Bulgaria’s 2025 data on how it records spending by its road infrastructure agency.
Germany, the bloc's largest economy, saw its debt ratio rise to 62.8% from 61.4% as its deficit widened to 2.9%.
Deficits are also increasing again this year. Adjusted for seasonal swings, the combined deficit of eurozone governments edged up to 3.3% of GDP in the second quarter from 3.2% in the first, while the figure for EU governments rose to 3.5% from 3.1%.
Last year, 12 member states had debt above the EU’s 60% ceiling, and 11 ran deficits of 3% or more.
Italy closes in on Greece while France's debt and yields climb
Greece remained the most indebted EU country at 140.8% of GDP in the second quarter, but Italy was just behind at 139.9%.
Greece's ratio has fallen by 11.2 percentage points in a year as the country runs budget surpluses, while Italy's rose by 1.3 percentage points in the second quarter alone.
In 2022, Greece's debt stood at 177.8% of GDP, against 138.4% for Italy.
France has the third-highest debt-to-GDP ratio, at 119.1%, up 3.7 percentage points in a year, one of the steepest rises in the bloc. Debt also remained above 100% of GDP in Belgium and Spain, at 110.2% and 101.4%, respectively.
Estonia had the lowest ratio, at 26.1%, followed by Denmark and Luxembourg, while Poland recorded the sharpest increase in its debt ratio, up 6.7 percentage points from a year earlier.
The figures landed on the same day the yield on France's 10-year government bond rose above 5% for the first time since 2002, as investors demanded more to hold French debt.
France's deficit was 5.1% of GDP last year, the fourth-largest in the EU after Romania, Poland and Belgium.
A divided French parliament is debating the 2027 budget, which aims to bring the deficit down to 5% of GDP, while Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu lacks a majority to pass his spending cuts.
Ratings agency Moody’s is due to review France’s credit rating on Friday, with most economists expecting a downgrade that could push its borrowing costs higher still.

UN agency warns nearly 874,000 could be displaced by floods in Somalia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:44:00 UTC
23:44:00 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
Nearly 874,000 people could be displaced in Somalia over the next three months as heavy rainfall and rising rivers threaten communities already affected by drought and repeated displacement, the UN migration agency warned Wednesday.
In a statement, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said projections developed with the Danish Refugee Council estimate that 874,319 people could be displaced between October and December, with flooding accounting for 92% of the total.
“We are looking at the possibility of hundreds of thousands of people losing their homes in just a matter of weeks,” said Manuel Marques Pereira, IOM Somalia chief of mission.
The warning comes as Somalia enters a rainy season forecast to bring above-normal rainfall amid strengthening El Nino conditions.
IOM said it has secured only 14.4% of the $16.62 million required to prepare for and respond to flooding, with the funding intended to assist more than 517,000 people.
Beletweyne and Gaalkacyo face particularly “greatest threat,” with nearly 229,000 and 82,000 people, respectively, at risk of displacement.
The agency said rising river levels and heavy rainfall are already threatening communities, while flooding could destroy crops, contaminate water sources and disrupt access to healthcare.
IOM urged immediate international funding to strengthen early warning systems, prepare evacuation routes and provide emergency shelter, clean water and sanitation.

Progress on a sore point for Ukraine and Poland: remains of over 40 Ukrainians killed by Polish WWII units found in Łasków
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:43:33 UTC
23:43:33 KST

During an expedition from 2 to 16 October in the Polish village of Łasków, a Ukrainian team uncovered the remains of more than 40 Ukrainians, including women, men, and children, the Ukrainian Institute of National Memory, which commissioned the search, said on 20 October.
Ukraine and Poland disagree over how to interpret their shared history. One of the most contentious issues is the Volhynia tragedy, a series of massacres of Polish and Ukrainian civilians during World War II, the largest of which took place in Volhynia. Amid unresolved disputes over this history, Ukraine halted Polish search and exhumation work on its territory. Both sides have since resumed the work, and Łasków is the first Ukrainian search in Poland to find remains since 2016, the institute said.
During Poland’s 2025 presidential campaign, Karol Nawrocki said that unresolved historical issues could stand in the way of Ukraine's accession to the EU and NATO. The dispute is still live: on 20 October, Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz called on Kyiv to distance itself from the Lviv Oblast Council’s decision to declare 2027 the year of the UPA and Shukhevych. The searches, meanwhile, continue on both sides of the border.
More than 300 Ukrainians were killed in Łasków
On the final day of the investigation, specialists partially uncovered a mass grave containing the remains of eight people and documented all the findings. The victims’ ages, sexes, and causes of death will be established during exhumation work planned for spring 2027.
“According to witness accounts, a large number of the Ukrainian victims were buried—or, in fact, simply covered with a thin layer of soil—in hiding places, fields, and the yards of their own homes in the village of Łasków. They were buried only 10 days later by Ukrainians from the neighboring village of Smolihiv, who were then also killed and shot near the forest,” director of the Dolia memorial search center Sviatoslav Sheremeta said, according to Istorychna Pravda.
The Ukrainians were killed in an attack by units of the Polish Home Army (Armia Krajowa) and the Peasants’ Battalions (Bataliony Chłopskie), the institute said when the search began.
“Most of the graves are located at a depth of 40–70 centimeters from the ground surface,” Sheremeta said.
Historical records indicate that more than 300 people were killed in the Polish village of Łasków on 10 March 1944, the media outlet reported. Ukrainian and Polish historians and experts have identified 327 village residents who were killed, although some researchers estimate the death toll at around 350, the report said. Further historical research and search operations may help establish the final number of victims.
Ukraine imposed a ban on exhumations but allowed the work to resume several years later
In response to the widespread destruction of Ukrainian monuments in Poland between 2015 and 2017, and what the Ukrainian side considered an inadequate investigation into these incidents, Ukraine imposed a moratorium on search operations and the exhumation of Poles killed by Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) fighters in 1943–1945, Ukrainska Pravda reported.
In January 2025, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced a “breakthrough,” saying there was a decision on the first exhumations of Polish victims of the UPA.
By April 2025, exhumations of Polish residents killed in 1945 had begun in Ukraine’s Ternopil Oblast. A joint Polish-Ukrainian team of experts took part in the work.
Searches in Ukraine have found mostly Polish soldiers from 1939, while Ukraine waits for permits in Poland
Most of the Polish remains recovered in Ukraine since the moratorium ended belong to soldiers killed fighting the Germans in September 1939, not to victims of the Volhynia killings. In Lviv, searchers exhumed at least 31 soldiers at Zboiska in 2025 and found 113 more at Holosko this autumn.
Of the 1943–1945 victims, joint Polish-Ukrainian teams have recovered 42 in Puzhnyky, Ternopil Oblast, which were reburied in September 2025, and 55 in Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka in Volyn Oblast, which they found this summer. Polish historians attribute the Puzhnyky killings to a UPA unit. Ukraine’s Institute of National Memory first described the dead as victims of Soviet repression, then changed the wording to victims who died in 1945 after Poland’s Foreign Ministry objected. A search in Uhly, Rivne Oblast, this spring found no mass grave.
Ukraine’s first search in Poland in years, for UPA fighters in Jureczkowa in autumn 2025, found no remains. The Ukrainian team waited more than a year for permission to work in Łasków, which came on 31 August. Its requests for Sahryń, where Home Army units killed between 200 and 800 people on the same day, according to PAP, and for Przemyśl were still pending in July, with Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance asking for more documents.
The history row reaches the search permits
Kyiv has said it will keep issuing permits for Polish searches despite the tensions. In August, before the Łasków permit came through, Ukraine’s ambassador to Poland, Vasyl Bodnar, said Ukraine could not get a single permit to search for its dead in Poland while it kept approving Polish work in Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Warsaw has kept raising the stakes over how Ukraine remembers the UPA. Nawrocki stripped President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of Poland’s Order of the White Eagle in June after Zelenskyy named a military unit after the “Heroes of the UPA.” In July, the head of Nawrocki’s chancellery, Zbigniew Bogucki, spoke in the Sejm of genocide “in Volhynia and Eastern Lesser Poland,” using the interwar Polish name for what is now western Ukraine. In August, Deputy Foreign Minister Marcin Bosacki warned that placing Stepan Bandera or Roman Shukhevych in Ukraine’s National Pantheon would damage relations with Poland and Europe.
Nawrocki has also sent the Sejm a bill that would punish promoting the ideology of the OUN and the UPA, which had its first reading on 3 July. Polish members of the European Parliament proposed adding the Volhynia tragedy and the UPA to the parliament’s report on Ukraine’s progress toward EU membership.
The two sides also disagree on the numbers the exhumations are meant to help settle. Polish estimates put the number of Poles killed in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia at about 100,000. Ukraine’s Institute of National Memory counts about 30,000 Polish and 10,000 Ukrainian victims identified so far.

I&amp;B ministry warns TV channels over communal rhetoric, violent visuals, AI use

(Representative image): The committee stressed that “inappropriate behaviour or language should not be normalised in telecast”, and urged broadcasters to follow both the letter and spirit of existing rules.
NEW DELHI: Flagging repeated lapses in television content, the information and broadcasting ministry has asked private satellite channels to check communal rhetoric, sensational coverage of crime and violence and the misuse of artificial intelligence in news production, warning that violations of the Programme Code could invite action.In an advisory issued on Wednesday, the ministry said its Inter-Departmental Committee had found content aired by various channels “not in conformity with the spirit of the Programme Code”. It also noted instances of similar news and visuals being broadcast across multiple channels on the same subjects.The committee stressed that “inappropriate behaviour or language should not be normalised in telecast”, and urged broadcasters to follow both the letter and spirit of existing rules.Taking particular note of television debates, the advisory said channels must ensure that discussions do not “promote or encourage communal or anti-national attitudes”. It called for careful selection and prior sensitisation of panellists, adequate editorial control and, where necessary, “immediate remedial measures such as muting, disclaimers, interruption or discontinuation of feed” to stop derogatory, abusive or inflammatory content from being aired.
On AI, the ministry asked broadcasters to exercise caution while using it, including generative tools, for graphics and virtual news presentations. “The use of AI tools may be limited to assistive capacity,” it said, stressing that accuracy, authenticity and sensitivity must not be compromised.The advisory reiterated the prohibition on live coverage of anti-terror operations by security forces, restricting such reporting to periodic briefings by authorised officers. Telecasts of related visuals should be time-stamped wherever necessary to avoid misleading viewers.It also urged channels to avoid graphic or disturbing visuals, unverified and sensationalised crime reports, excessive replay of violent footage and coverage that might glorify unlawful behaviour. Images from disasters and major accidents, it said, should be time-stamped where necessary to prevent panic.
Broadcasters were further reminded to use only authentic maps issued by the Survey of India and protect the identities of sexual offence victims, including through indirect details.The ministry asked channels to strengthen editorial reviews and train news, production and transmission staff in the Programme Code.

Renowned for his incisive coverage of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, accreditation reforms, and skilling initiatives, he has also reported on student politics, urban policy, and social movements. His political reportage—both reflective and news-driven—adds depth to his writing, bridging policy with public impact. Through his 2,500 articles and related outlets, he has emerged as a trusted voice in national discourse, particularly in linking education reform to broader societal change.

Musk pledges $10bn in SpaceX shares for US children: Who really gains?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:41:03 UTC
23:41:03 KST

Musk pledges $10bn in SpaceX shares for US children: Who really gains?
The pledge, which Trump says will go through accounts with his name, comes two weeks before the US midterms.
Elon Musk has pledged to give one SpaceX share to every child in the United States next year – a gift that could be worth more than $10bn.
“This will be the first of many,” the world’s richest man wrote on X on Monday.
About 73 million children under 18 live in the US, according to US Census Bureau data.
At Friday’s closing price of $146.03, the pledge would be worth about $10.7bn.
President Donald Trump thanked Musk on his Truth Social platform, and claimed the shares would be given to children “through TRUMP ACCOUNTS”, the tax-friendly investment accounts for children created under his signature tax and spending law last year.
The pledge comes two weeks before the November 3 midterm elections.
Musk is the biggest known donor in the run-up to those elections, having given more than $276m to Republican groups since July.
Musk has not said which children will qualify, when the shares will be handed over, or how.
So how might the giveaway work, and who stands to gain?
Here’s what you need to know:
How much is a SpaceX share worth, and how much is Musk giving away?
SpaceX, the world’s seventh-largest company, began trading on the Nasdaq in June at an initial public offering price of $135 per share.
That price has been volatile. SpaceX shares have fallen 35.3 percent since peaking days after the listing.
The shares are currently trading at around $146 a share. Every $1 move in the share price will change the gift’s value by about $73m.
Musk owns 4.8 billion shares in SpaceX outright, according to a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) in August.
Including unvested awards and stock options, his stake rises to about 6.4 billion shares, or 48.4 percent of the company.
Giving away 73 million shares would reduce his outright holding by about 1.5 percent, barely affecting his control of the company. That’s because his voting power, which is currently about 82 percent because SpaceX has two classes of shares, would fall by only 0.1 percentage points, according to a Bloomberg Opinion calculation.
It would be the largest single gift linked to Trump accounts so far.
How would the shares reach children?
Musk has not said.
Trump said the shares would be held in Trump accounts, and Musk thanked Brad Gerstner, the tech investor behind the accounts, for “helping enable this”.
Nearly 70 million Trump accounts have been opened, one for every child under 18 with a Social Security number, according to the White House. Investments held in Trump accounts can roll up with tax deferred until they are withdrawn when a child turns 18. Alternatively, they can be rolled into a tax-friendly IRA – a retirement account for adults – and continue with the tax-friendly status.
Under Treasury rules published on September 30, donors can now gift individual company stock to children via the accounts. Families and friends making regular contributions to a child’s Trump account are limited to investing low-risk index funds.
Families cannot refuse the shares on behalf of their children and generally cannot sell them for five years, or until the end of the year the child turns 17 if that comes sooner.
Musk cannot sell or trade most of his SpaceX shares until June 2027, the Wall Street Journal reported.
Who gains?
The accounts carry the president’s name, and Trump has tied himself closely to the gift.
He thanked Musk on Truth Social, saying the pledge was “exactly what was envisioned when we created TRUMP ACCOUNTS”.
The White House has presented the accounts as a signature achievement of Trump’s tax law, noting that “every single Democrat voted against” the legislation.
The pledge also marks a public reconciliation. Musk and Trump fell out in 2025 over Trump’s tax-and-spending bill, a rift Trump later called a “little dispute”.
Children will be gaining a share for free, but the gift could also save Musk money.
Donors who give appreciated stock to charity avoid capital gains tax and can usually claim a deduction, the US broadcaster CNBC reported.
As SpaceX’s founder, Musk paid very little for his shares, and selling $10.7bn of them could mean a tax bill of up to about $2.5bn.
It is “a popular practice for particularly high-income taxpayers that would otherwise be paying a high rate”, Will McBride, chief economist at the Tax Foundation, told the broadcaster in May.
Ann Lipton, a law professor at the University of Colorado Boulder, told Inc. magazine that millions of shareholders unable to sell would also have an interest in SpaceX’s success and in “minimising its regulatory burdens”.
For Mitchell Downey, an economist at Stockholm University’s Institute for International Economic Studies who studies political influence in the US, the more striking part of the pledge is what he called “the horseshoe aspect of this” – the idea that right-wing and left-wing policies can curve around and meet.
For decades, progressives have backed the concept of Child Development Accounts, investment accounts for every newborn designed to reduce inequality in wealth, he said. The idea was associated with groups such as the Democracy Collaborative but struggled to gain federal support. Now the idea may become more mainstream as a result of Musk’s gift and Trump accounts.
“It always felt like it might be out of reach,” Downey said. “But I don’t see how Musk’s proposal would be possible without building some infrastructure like this.”
Why is the timing important?
The pledge comes just two weeks before the November 3 midterm elections, which will decide control of the two houses of Congress. All seats in the House of Representatives and one-third of the Senate are up for re-election.
Trump’s approval rating has meanwhile fallen to a record low of 33 percent, according to a Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll, with many political observers expecting to see the Republicans lose seats to the Democratic Party as a result.
Musk, who campaigned with Trump in 2024 and spearheaded the president’s Department of Government Efficiency initiative to reduce the size of the federal workforce, has contributed heavily to Republican candidates in advance of the midterm elections.
Is this legal, and why is it controversial?
Downey said he does not believe the pledge raises legal concerns.
“Individuals are allowed to spend their money in support of a politician,” he told Al Jazeera. “The law only gets violated when either it isn’t publicly reported, or it is part of an explicit and documented quid-pro-quo.”
But he said it does raise ethical concerns, though not ones unique to Musk’s approach.
Those concerns relate to “the outsized role that external donors play in US elections”, Downey said. In his view, they apply much like when someone spends heavily on television advertisements for a candidate.
Has anyone done this before?
Downey said the precedent was “hard to assess”.
Because Musk is the richest person in modern history, he said, it is perhaps unsurprising that he is “doing something that involves more money than other very rich people have done”.
He pointed to the Gates Foundation’s spending over the past three decades as “a different type of ‘gift to the public’”. The difference, he said, is that the Gates Foundation focuses funding on health crises in countries in Africa and South Asia – not on voters in the US.
Last year, Gates pledged to “give away virtually all my wealth through the Gates Foundation over the next 20 years to the cause of saving and improving lives around the world”.

A new security doctrine for Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21

A new security doctrine for Israel
MADRID - Israel has a new security doctrine. It has never been published, never presented to the public, and never formally adopted by the military establishment. And yet, since October 7, 2023, it is this unwritten concept, not the doctrine forged over decades, that has shaped Israeli decision-making and now dictates the country’s entire approach to security.
On Monday, Tamir Hayman, former military intelligence chief, set out the principles that, he argued, can be inferred from the policy Israel is actually applying.
The document makes clear that “Jewish identity” must prevail over “its democratic system of government”. This primacy is conceived to guarantee the survival of Israel as a Jewish state, even at the cost of eroding its “democratic values”.
This is nothing new. Modern Zionism was born among the liberal-nationalist currents of nineteenth-century Europe. But unlike the emancipatory nationalisms that sought integration into Europe, Zionism organised a colonisation outwards: a population transfer articulated more as demographic engineering than as an “ancestral return”. Herzl himself considered founding a Jewish state in Argentina or East Africa. Palestine was finally chosen, but the logic was the same: build a homogeneous space for a diaspora. The “return” narrative disguised a colonial settlement project — not merely occupying a land, but displacing and replacing those who inhabited it. The premise became explicit with Vladimir Jabotinsky in The Iron Wall (1923): no Arab people would voluntarily accept being colonised; force was the only way. Therein lies the nucleus of “Greater Israel” — a project that does not contemplate coexistence, but the definitive subordination of the other.
“Democracy” in Israel was established for the Jews after the Zionists expelled 90 percent of the Palestinian population. It makes no sense, then, to speak of “democratic decline”: the foundations on which Israel rests today are racial, and they have always been there for anyone who wished to see them.
Hayman linked this to another principle: security pursued through the establishment of “communities and forward positions in all friction zones with the Arab population, in the occupied West Bank, and in the security zones of Syria, Lebanon and Gaza”.
Under this new approach, aspiring to peace is considered a repetition of the error of the “conceptzia”, the Hebrew label for the strategic assumptions widely blamed for Israel’s failure to foresee the attack of October 7. A meaningful peace agreement in the Middle East is deemed unattainable: peace accords are mere technical, temporary arrangements requiring constant reevaluation. Peace, here, is not an intrinsic value that generates security, but an instrument for other political ends.
“War is necessary, and preventive war is preferable because it allows significant gains from the outset. Its intensity may vary, but its constant presence constitutes an asset for national security,” Hayman wrote. Surprise attacks are the only path to victory; offence takes priority over defence. If Israel cannot withstand a surprise attack or guarantee reliable early warning, the conclusion is foreordained: a standing policy of preventive attacks and preventive wars. This doctrine is no longer hypothetical: Israel applied it in its attacks on Iran in June 2025, and it leaves the door open to future unilateral action.
The document also describes the United States as a “declining power” that “will soon abandon Israel in any case”, and holds that breaking ties with Washington is “essential for Israel’s independence”. Given current social and political shifts in the United States, above all, the majority of the American public’s rejection of the genocide in Gaza, Washington will drop Israel soon regardless, the text concludes.
Arab countries, meanwhile, are treated not as authentic nations but as “collections of tribes and ethnic groups lacking a common history and a foundational national perspective”. Their destabilisation is a natural process, one Israel can manage far more effectively than confronting powerful nation-states, and one it should actively encourage.
The throughline is plain. Israel’s goal has always been to destroy the sovereignty of regioal countries, one after another. Its failure in Iran has forced its strategists to admit they cannot impose their political will everywhere, and to adjust.
On the “Palestinian question”, the document is explicit once more: the solution runs through the deployment of Zionist ideology and its pursuit of the total colonisation of the territory. Hence principled opposition to any political, geographical or security separation between Israel and a Palestinian entity, and to a Palestinian state itself.
Other listed priorities include national arms production, artificial intelligence, quantum computing and the expansion of illegal settlements in the occupied territories.
Israel’s new security doctrine is marked by the current regional landscape, the memory of Hamas’s operation of October 7, and Iran, whose military capacity stands as the symbol of the limit of Israeli power.
Finally, it is worth recalling the roots of Zionism: contrary to what its most obstinate and ignorant defenders claim, it has never been anything but an ideology and a movement of colonial character.

Melike Pala

Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever said Wednesday he was certain the European Commission would not propose using frozen Russian assets held in Belgium to finance Ukraine.
Speaking before the Federal Advisory Committee on European Affairs, De Wever said the issue had been discussed at last week's EU summit, according to Belga news agency.
He said the commission had assured leaders that it would not reopen the debate over Russian assets held at Brussels-based Euroclear.
"I am certain that the European Commission will not make proposals to meet Ukraine's financing needs through a new operation linked to Russian assets. I am certain of that, because that is what was said," he said.
De Wever strongly opposed a proposal last year to use approximately €185 billion ($207 billion) in frozen Russian assets held at Euroclear to support Ukraine.
Instead, EU leaders agreed on a €90 billion loan for Ukraine covering this year and next.
However, the funding is expected to fall short of Kyiv's needs.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy requested an additional €70 billion in support for next year during last week's summit.
De Wever did not rule out the possibility that other EU member states could raise the issue of using frozen Russian assets again.
He criticized Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten for publicly supporting the seizure of the funds.
"Not everyone took part in last year's debate. New leaders have emerged who are developing a line of argument that I managed to nip in the bud last year," De Wever said.
The Belgian premier also warned that even public statements supporting the seizure of Russian assets could have legal consequences.
According to De Wever, his warning had an impact on other leaders during the summit.
He said there was no longer "overwhelming enthusiasm" among EU leaders for pursuing the proposal.

First Deputy Prime Minister Nurlybek Nalibayev paid a working visit to the Aktobe region, where he participated in the opening of the 28-kilometer section of the Aktobe-Ulgaisyn (791 - 819km) highway, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The highway is an important part of the Western Europe – Western China transport corridor.
In August of this year, Head of State Kassym-Jomart, via a teleconference, launched the construction of three large projects in the Aktobe, Mangystau, and Kyzylorda regions. These are the Aktobe-Ulgaisyn, Ulgaisyn-Sekseuil, and Sekseuil-Kyzylorda highways.
Under the Aktobe-Ulgaisyn project, a 262-kilometer section of highway is to be reconstructed, with its technical category upgraded from Category II to Category I.
A new highway is being built through sandy terrain between Sekseuil and Beineu.
Approximately 3 trillion tenge has been allocated for the three projects, which will involve the construction and reconstruction of more than 1,900 kilometers of roads. The work is scheduled to be completed within the next three years. At the same time, contractors have been tasked with making every effort to complete the projects ahead of schedule, Nurlybek Naliyev said.
To ensure the quality of road construction, a special commission has been established on the instructions of the Prime Minister. It comprises scientists, road industry experts, government officials and members of parliament. The commission is examining the quality of construction materials, including bitumen, crushed stone and other components, as well as measures to regulate the weight loads imposed on road surfaces by heavy vehicles.
Construction work has been completed on the 28-kilometer section that has been opened to traffic. Street lighting and road barriers are scheduled to be installed within the next two weeks.

The China-US Quantum Computing Contest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:40:00 UTC
23:40:00 KST

The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Matt Kinsella – the CEO of Infleqtion, a leading U.S. quantum technology company – is the 531st in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”
Briefly describe U.S. advancements in quantum computing technology.
The United States is moving from experimental quantum systems toward logical, fault-tolerant computing. The key measure is no longer the number of physical qubits, but whether those qubits can be organized into reliable logical qubits and used for meaningful applications.
Infleqtion is at the forefront of that shift. Our neutral-atom platform has demonstrated 12 logical qubits with error detection and loss correction, a 99.73 percent two-qubit gate fidelity, and arrays of up to 1,600 neutral-atom sites. With Nvidia, we published a materials-science demonstration in which logical encoding reduced error approximately sixfold compared with physical-qubit execution.
Our roadmap achieves 30 logical qubits later this year, 100 by 2028, and 1,000 by 2030. We see approximately 100 high-quality logical qubits as the threshold for outperforming classical systems on selected valuable problems.
Hardware alone will not get us there. As our CTO, Pranav Gokhale, has emphasized, hardware-aware software can force-multiply quantum performance. Infleqtion is developing the complete stack – from atoms, photonics, and control systems to error correction, Superstaq compilation, resource estimation, and integration with GPU-accelerated computing. That full-system approach is how quantum computing becomes useful.
In what ways is the U.S. collaborating with partners in the Asia Pacific in developing quantum computing technology?
The United States is building a trusted quantum ecosystem with Asia-Pacific partners through joint research, technology development, workforce training, and access to advanced systems.
Japan provides a strong example. Japan’s Science and Technology Agency selected Infleqtion as the first foreign company – and the only foreign quantum-computing partner – to participate in its Quantum Moonshot program. In a consortium led by Professor Kenji Ohmori of the Institute for Molecular Science, we are contributing neutral-atom technology, photonics expertise, and systems engineering to the development of a large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computer based on atomic qubits.
This is more than a research exchange. It combines an American commercial platform with Japanese leadership in ultrafast atomic control and aligns both countries around a shared technical objective. To this end, Infleqtion has delivered neutral-atom systems, helping researchers build the practical experience required to operate and develop applications for advanced quantum machines.
In Australia, Infleqtion has established an Asia-Pacific presence at Swinburne University of Technology and worked with the Australian Army and Australian industry on trustworthy quantum computation. One collaboration with Australian quantum company Diraq explored quantum physically unclonable functions intended to help verify the identity and integrity of remotely accessed quantum computers.
We are also engaging Australian leaders on the future use of quantum computing in energy and infrastructure. This application-led approach is essential: allied programs should begin with consequential problems and jointly determine the hardware, software, and classical resources required to address them.
These partnerships expand the talent, facilities, test environments, and applications available to the United States. Our alliances are not simply diplomatic relationships; they are a practical technology advantage.
Analyze the scope and scale of the U.S.-China quantum computing competition.
The U.S.-China quantum competition is not a single race. It spans computing architecture, logical reliability, software, photonics, manufacturing, talent, supply chains, data-center integration, and applications.
China can concentrate substantial state resources behind selected national programs. The United States operates through a more distributed system of companies, universities, federal laboratories, private capital, and international partners. That diversity supports several technical pathways while creating strong pressure to demonstrate practical results.
Infleqtion represents the strength of the American model. We are advancing a vertically integrated neutral-atom platform while expanding from research milestones into deployed systems and application centers. Our technology is operational in national institutions, and our teams are working with government and industry on energy, materials, AI, and scientific discovery.
We have delivered a 100-physical-qubit system to the U.K. National Quantum Computing Centre, announced a fault-tolerant system for Illinois, opened a Chicago Quantum Innovation Center, and expanded our U.K. engineering and manufacturing presence. These are signs of an industry developing the infrastructure to scale – not merely producing individual experiments.
The competition will be decided by sustained execution: who can build dependable logical systems, reduce resource overhead, manufacture them, connect them to classical supercomputers, and solve consequential problems. The United States has a powerful innovation network, and Infleqtion is rapidly converting that advantage into operating capability.
Examine China’s quantum computing technology developments.
China has demonstrated credible progress in superconducting and photonic quantum computing, supported by centralized programs that coordinate across universities, national laboratories, and state-linked companies. In particular, the University of Science and Technology of China’s Zuchongzhi 3.0 superconducting processor and Jiuzhang 4.0 photonic system have now achieved world-leading results.
These are technically impressive demonstrations, but more consequential questions concern logical error rates, programmable circuit depth, application performance, system availability, and the resources required to outperform the best classical alternative. Of note, China’s leading results in neutral atom quantum computing have lagged developments here in the U.S., though there have been recent accelerations in China’s efforts over the past year.
China is also building domestic control electronics, cloud platforms, software, and industrial capacity. Its 2026-2030 planning framework treats quantum technology as a strategic emerging field, so the United States should expect continued progress.
The appropriate response is disciplined acceleration. We should measure China’s achievements accurately while investing in the capabilities that determine practical advantage: logical qubits, efficient error correction, hardware-aware software, advanced manufacturing, and application deployment. Those are the areas where Infleqtion is concentrating its computing roadmap.
Assess how quantum computing technology is integrated into U.S. national security and defense systems and its implications for the U.S.-China tech race.
Large-scale quantum computers are not yet embedded in operational defense systems. Current integration is occurring through research programs, independent technical validation, hybrid computing infrastructure, and development of mission-relevant applications.
An exemplar is DARPA’s HARQ program exploring heterogeneous systems that combine different quantum processors with classical resources. To meet that demand, Infleqtion is developing Multistaq, a software layer designed to compile and coordinate workloads across multiple qubit technologies.
Infleqtion is also supporting three Department of Energy Genesis Mission projects involving AI-optimized quantum circuits for nuclear applications, fusion research, and deployable atomic sensing. Our planned Illinois system will connect a neutral-atom QPU with Nvidia GPU infrastructure, providing a test environment for quantum-classical workflows and real-time error correction. The associated Chicago center is initially focused on energy-grid and nuclear optimization problems with direct implications for national resilience.
Quantum sensing and timing are closer to field deployment than fault-tolerant computing. Infleqtion’s work in GPS-independent navigation, spectrum awareness, precision timing, gravity sensing, and space systems gives the company operating experience with government missions while strengthening the shared photonics, controls, software, and manufacturing base behind our computers.
For the U.S.-China competition, the objective should be clear: move quantum computing from scientific potential to trusted national infrastructure. Infleqtion is helping the United States do that by combining technical progress, deployed systems, application development, and allied partnerships on one scalable neutral-atom platform.
