The Houthi war machine is evolving. Can Saudi Arabia keep pace?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:30:38 UTC
23:30:38 KST

Breadcrumb
The Houthi war machine is evolving. Can Saudi Arabia keep pace?
The Houthis are seeking to manufacture parts of advanced Iranian-designed medium-range ballistic missiles inside Yemen, according to new research that raises questions about how effectively Saudi Arabia can interrupt the group’s ability to sustain its attacks.
In a report published on 14 October and previewed by The Wall Street Journal, Conflict Armament Research (CAR) identified components associated with the Iranian-designed Kheibar Shekan missile family alongside industrial equipment and raw materials in shipments intended for Houthi-controlled territory.
Shipping documents identified a Chinese supplier, suggesting that the group is expanding its procurement beyond Iran-linked networks.
The findings come as Riyadh faces repeated attacks on airports and other critical infrastructure. The strikes have disrupted aviation and exposed the costs of protecting a vast country against an adversary whose arsenal and methods have developed through years of war.
For Saudi Arabia, the concern extends beyond the specifications of an individual missile. A growing ability to source components, manufacture selected parts and adapt how different weapons are used could make the Houthi strike campaign more difficult to contain.
Beyond imported missile kits
The October report concerns four containers documented by Yemeni authorities in July 2026. They had arrived in Aden’s free zone aboard two vessels in June and October 2025, carrying shipments from China whose intended destination was the Houthi-controlled port of Hodeidah.
The cargo included machined components associated with the airframe and rocket motor of the Kheibar Shekan series, one of Iran’s most advanced and longest-range ballistic missiles, together with materials and machinery potentially useful for manufacturing and testing.
Their presence points towards an effort to produce parts locally, beyond reassembling weapons delivered in separate packages.
“Inspection of the cargo revealed Houthi ambitions to at least partially manufacture medium-range ballistic missiles inside Yemen,” Fabian Hinz, a senior analyst at CAR, told The New Arab. “Whether that effort has succeeded, remains a work in progress or has met major obstacles remains difficult to determine.”
Douglas Barrie, senior fellow for military aerospace at the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), outlined a more limited scenario. “Final local assembly with domestic manufacturing of some components I think is most likely,” he told The New Arab.
The systems involved nevertheless represent a substantial ambition. Iran unveiled the original solid-propellant Kheibar Shekan in 2022, with a reported range of 1,450 kilometres. The missile was first used against targets in Syria in January 2024, and later against Israel and US bases in the MENA region.
CAR identifies several related variants in Houthi service, giving the group access to designs intended for long-range strikes and equipped with manoeuvring features that could complicate interception.
Earlier seizures show that the supply chain encompasses both weapons and the means to assemble or produce them. A shipment intercepted in Aden in August 2025, for example, included drone and propulsion-related equipment and advanced control components, according to US Central Command.
A separate CAR briefing, published in September, described missile kits bearing assembly labels that used Iranian rather than Houthi designations, suggesting they were produced in Iran. Broadening the supplier base would loosen that dependence.
“Sourcing components and raw materials from suppliers beyond Iran-linked networks can reduce dependence and potentially eliminate bottlenecks,” Hinz said. He cautioned that independence depends on the weapons involved: small drones built largely from commercial components are easier to manufacture than systems requiring specialised parts.
“For the more advanced weapons, the Houthis will likely continue to rely on the import of key subsystems, but further developing a domestic capability could increasingly allow for the manufacture of less sophisticated guided weapons. This would reduce dependency on external actors,” Barrie added.
Farzin Nadimi, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute, sees the Chinese supply chain as a substitute for “the Iranian one, which has been severely hampered by the US naval blockade”.
The cargo documented by CAR arrived in 2025, before the current blockade, so such channels were already in use; they are likely to matter more now that Iranian routes are under pressure. Replacement has limits, however. “Houthis still depend on Iran for critical missile subsystems and guidance components,” Nadimi told The New Arab. “The Houthis cannot get those from China.”
Chinese suppliers, in other words, can provide raw materials and machined parts, but not the most sensitive components. Nor is the technology itself new. Kheibar Shekan and Fattah technology, Nadimi said, “has been transferred to Houthis for quite some time now”, though he could not say whether the group has incorporated “the latest upgrade kits”.
Iran unveiled the Fattah, which it describes as hypersonic, in 2023. The new evidence therefore concerns ambitions to manufacture parts locally, rather than the first acquisition of those technologies.
The concern predates CAR’s latest findings. On 11 September 2025, the US Treasury sanctioned Hubei Chica Industrial Co., Ltd., accusing the China-based supplier of coordinating with Houthi procurement operatives to provide chemical precursors used to manufacture ballistic missiles, explosives and other weapons inside Yemen.
The US Treasury also accused China-based Shenzhen Shengnan Trading of shipping dual-use electronics to Houthi front companies.
CAR’s evidence requires qualification. Shipping documents identified a Chinese precision-metal producer advertising custom aerospace components, but investigators have not traced the items with the manufacturer or independently verified the documentation. The findings do not establish Chinese government involvement, production volumes or a link to specific attacks on Saudi Arabia.
For Riyadh, this widens the interdiction challenge to commercial suppliers and intermediaries beyond Iran. It also gives the kingdom an incentive to seek Beijing’s cooperation on export controls and end-use checks.
An evolving strike campaign
The industrial investigation coincides with indications that the Houthis are refining how they employ their weapons. According to the Gulf Research Center, as of 15 October, the Houthis have staged at least 42 attacks on Saudi territory, including nine targeting Riyadh and five targeting energy infrastructure in the Eastern Province. At least one third of these raids involved ballistic missiles.
The Associated Press reported on 12 October that regional officials described drones preceding cruise and ballistic missiles in an attack on Riyadh airport. The sequence suggests an effort to combine weapons with different flight characteristics, although it remains unclear whether the drones acted as decoys.
“Houthis and Iranians have both tested hybrid tactics, and I am sure they compare notes too,” Nadimi told The New Arab.
Iran’s April 2024 attack on Israel combined drones, cruise missiles, and ballistic missiles, while its October 2024 attack relied exclusively on ballistic missiles. The strike on Riyadh airport followed the first pattern.
Mixed attacks require defenders to track threats across different altitudes and speeds, while repeated strikes keep personnel and equipment under pressure. Barrie cautioned that Kheibar Shekan-family missiles must be accounted for even if their actual performance falls short of advertised capabilities, “further complicating the challenges facing a defender”.
CAR’s September briefing identified another operational development: a reconnaissance drone helped cue a close-range ballistic missile against a time-sensitive target. This points to improvements in battlefield targeting, alongside the group’s expanding long-range strike capabilities.
Against Saudi Arabia, repeated attacks on airports and energy infrastructure aim to raise the costs of Riyadh’s intervention in Yemen, pressing the kingdom to scale back support for anti-Houthi forces and ease restrictions on Houthi-controlled ports and airports. The goal is bargaining power, without having to defeat Saudi forces directly.
Inside Yemen, the 15 October attack on Aden, which hit the presidential palace, exposed the internationally recognised government’s vulnerability at its own seat of power, while strikes on Marib appear intended to disrupt preparations for counteroffensives.
In the Red Sea, the threat to shipping gives the Houthis leverage over Riyadh and outside powers weighing intervention, on a trade route made more important by insecurity around the Strait of Hormuz. Their declared blockade of Saudi Arabia ties this maritime pressure to the campaign against the kingdom’s airports.
Together, these operations seek to protect Houthi territorial gains while raising the costs of attempts to reverse them. Greater military reach does not guarantee political concessions, however: attacks causing civilian casualties could instead harden Saudi resolve and draw greater external assistance.
Riyadh's containment dilemma
“They are already changing the battlefield around KSA,” Nadimi told The New Arab. For Saudi Arabia, the challenge is both immediate and cumulative: preventing the next strike while reducing the Houthis’ ability to keep launching them.
ACLED reported on 12 October that Houthi strikes and attempted strikes on Saudi territory had more than doubled over the preceding week. An airport need not be destroyed for airlines to suspend services.
Interception also consumes finite resources. Regional officials have reported pressure on Saudi interceptor stocks during the wider Iran war, making replenishment and outside assistance central to sustaining the defensive effort.
Offensive operations face a different problem: airstrikes can destroy launchers, depots and workshops, but suppressing the campaign means repeatedly locating assets that may be mobile, concealed or dispersed. Nor have Houthi air defences closed Yemeni airspace: CTP-ISW assessed on 15 October that the group’s occasional successful engagements had not significantly disrupted the Saudi air campaign.
Wider procurement networks and partial local manufacturing could make replenishment harder to interrupt, even without making the Houthis self-sufficient, while imported subsystems remain a point of vulnerability.
Riyadh’s challenge is to reduce both the group’s ability to rebuild its arsenal and the political leverage it derives from using it.
Francesco Salesio Schiavi is an Italian specialist in the Middle East. His focus lies in the security architecture of the Levant and the Gulf, with a particular emphasis on Iraq, Iran, and the Arab Peninsula, as well as military and diplomatic interventions by international actors

The vehicles were delivered to Kyiv in several batches from September 2025 to June 2026.

Our Friends in the North: The Thatcher Years review – old pals back on the toon as TV series gets squished
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:30:20 UTC
23:30:20 KST

The four thwarted, postwar north-eastern dreamers created by dramatist Peter Flannery have now played more than a whole day of drama across different formats. The 1982 RSC world premiere of Our Friends in the North featured almost four hours in the lives of lawyer-councillor Mary, drifting philanderer Tosker, photo-journalist Nicky and petty criminal Geordie. The award-winning 1996 BBC Two version ran 10 hours, as did the 2022 Radio 4 adaptation. Now Flannery brings the quartet home to the stage and to Newcastle (where the first version toured) in another play.
Starting in 1964, with Labour PM Harold Wilson promising a new Britain, the first stage version ended in 1979, as Margaret Thatcher’s victory heralded a rightwing transformation. Exploiting the way that saga dramas test characters against landmark events, the TV version took them to 1995 (brink of Blair) and the radio one to 2020 (Boris Johnson and Covid). It would be intriguing to know if the idealism of these now triple-locked pensioner characters burns again under Burnham, but Flannery has tracked back to 1979-85, adapting the sixth (Thatcher in) and seventh (miners out) TV episodes.
A piece begun when he was an RSC writer in residence always had Shakespearean ambitions and these continue with the tremendous Trevor Fox, like the Chorus in Henry V, galvanising our imaginations and dropping historical footnotes. Fox, who starred in the TV and radio series, doubles as Nicky’s dementia-affected dad, Felix, a subplot especially poignant in what will be a memory play for much of the audience.
All forms of the story have used soap opera domestic tension to offset socialist history and here the epic courtship of Sam Neale’s Mary and Ryan Nolan’s Nicky affectingly shows campaigners for social change yearning for romantic conformity. The largely wasted lives – the piece’s bleak sub-theme – of Tosker and Geordie are caught by Jack Robertson, pointlessly optimistic, and Scott Turnbull, accepting defeat. Jude Nelson makes a small part large as a Tory MP who achieves a prophetic early breach in Labour’s “red wall”. The politics are Kinnockian, accusing Labour’s Militant tendency and miners’ union leader Arthur Scargill of swelling a rightwing electorate that led to 18 years of Tory rule.
The different Our Friends in the North directors have tended to panic at its politically expository dialogue and in this case it sometimes feels as if director Jack McNamara is searching for action such as slow-motion strobing for clashes between colliery pickets and riot squads.
For completists, this is a must-see but, paradoxically, it feels incomplete. In all media, the story has had length and breadth and, though these two episodes were a logical choice, Flannery perhaps acknowledges losses from selection and compression when Fox’s Chorus laments: “There’s always so much more to say.” The events depicted partly explain why a regional theatre would struggle to put on an all-day epic, but this dramatically immortal foursome needs it.

A roughly 350-year-old oak in the village of Klykiai, in eastern Lithuania, has been named the country’s Tree of the Year for 2026.
The Klykiai Oak, located in Utena district, received about 2,800 votes in the public poll. It will represent Lithuania in the 2027 European Tree of the Year competition.
The award ceremony was held Wednesday at the Lithuanian Parliament.
The oak is 18.5 metres tall, with a crown approximately 23 metres wide. Its trunk measures 4.15 metres in circumference at a height of 1.3 metres above the ground.
The competition aims to highlight Lithuania’s exceptional trees and their natural, historical and cultural value, as well as their importance to local communities, organisers said.
Twelve trees from across Lithuania reached the final, including centuries-old oaks, an old poplar, a chestnut, a linden, a sweet cherry and a pear tree.
“Each of these trees tells a unique story, bearing witness to nature’s strength and longevity and to people’s connection with their surroundings, local history and community,” the organisers said.
The competition was organised by the Lithuanian Arboriculture Centre. A special panel comprising representatives of the organisers, environmental groups and community organisations initially selected the finalists from submitted applications. The public then chose the winner through an online vote.
The Laukiai Oak, in the northwestern Skuodas district, was named the 2026 European Tree of the Year.

‘Developing trade relations with Africa requires results-oriented economic diplomacy’

‘Developing trade relations with Africa requires results-oriented economic diplomacy’
TEHRAN- The Advisor to the President for Economic Cooperation, referring to the importance of coordination among government institutions, the private sector, and academic centers, said: “Developing trade relations with Africa requires moving from preliminary and ceremonial talks toward results-oriented economic diplomacy.”
According to IRNA, Masoumeh Aghapour said on Wednesday at the second course of the Iran-Africa Chamber of Commerce, aimed at empowering the younger generation to enter international trade: “To achieve this goal, the government must facilitate the ground for the activity and presence of the private sector; universities and academic centers must provide the necessary knowledge and specialized support; and economic actors, relying on their understanding of the market and their capabilities, must take on the main responsibility for advancing trade projects.”
Aghapour added: “None of these sectors alone can actualize all existing capacities. Cooperation and division of responsibility among the government, universities, and the private sector will pave the way for the formation of an efficient system for developing foreign trade.”
The Advisor to the President for Economic Cooperation, emphasizing the necessity of changing Iran’s approach to developing trade relations with the African continent, said: “Success in African markets will not be achieved by increasing the number of trips and signing memoranda of understanding; rather, we must seek the implementation of real projects, the formation of capable companies, the conclusion of operational contracts, and the training of a new generation of international trade actors.”
He added: “Africa is not merely a market for supplying Iranian goods; it is a strategic horizon for the future of Iran’s economy and an important platform for the effective presence of the new generation in the field of international trade.”
Aghapour, referring to the government’s special attention to the capacities of the younger generation, said: “Belief in the capabilities of young people and their role-playing in the country’s economic transformations is one of the important issues on the path of Iran’s economy transitioning from traditional structures toward a modern economy and broader international interactions.”
He said: “The younger generation, especially young people familiar with modern technologies and global economic developments, can play a role in designing new paths for foreign trade, identifying international opportunities, creating innovative businesses, and developing Iran’s economic relations with other countries.”
The Advisor to the President for Economic Cooperation, referring to the demographic, economic, and trade capacities of the African continent, stated: “Africa, with its young population, broad production and consumption capacities, and developing markets, is one of the important areas for expanding Iran’s economic cooperation. Therefore, the view toward this continent must change from a short-term approach limited to case-by-case interactions to a long-term and targeted strategy.”
He stated: “To effectively exploit these capacities, economic actors’ view of Africa must be based on precise market knowledge, assessment of opportunities, and the design of executive plans. Therefore, success in international markets becomes meaningful when initial contacts lead to sustainable economic cooperation, joint projects, export development, and the creation of added value for the country’s economy.”
Aghapour, referring to the complexities of economic activity in foreign markets, said: “Successful presence in African markets requires precise knowledge of the economic conditions, regulations, and trade mechanisms of destination countries. Before entering any market, economic actors must professionally examine potential risks, the supply chain, laws and regulations, the banking and foreign exchange system, and the methods of conducting trade transactions.”
The Advisor to the President for Economic Cooperation added: “Iranian exporters must carefully study the destination market before offering their products, and by understanding distribution methods, retail shelves, household preferences, and consumer expectations, they must design and offer products suited to market needs.”
Aghapour considered the establishment of a specialized department for trade with Africa and the training of specialized personnel to be among the important steps toward developing economic cooperation with this continent, and stated: “One of the country’s fundamental needs is cultivating human resources familiar with the characteristics of African markets and equipped with specialized knowledge of international trade.”
He added: “Specialized training must be linked with operational experience so that young people can, in addition to becoming familiar with the theoretical foundations of trade, gain experience in real processes of negotiation, marketing, identifying business partners, and implementing contracts.”
The Advisor to the President for Economic Cooperation said: “Developing cooperation with this continent should not be limited to exporting traditional goods; rather, the ground must also be provided for the presence of Iranian technology companies, knowledge-based firms, and providers of specialized services. Therefore, identifying the real needs of destination countries and matching the capabilities of Iranian companies with these needs must be at the center of trade planning.”

Benin, Ghana, Rwanda advance cross-border digital ID pilot
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
22:29:18 CST
23:29:18 KST

KIGALI, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Benin, Ghana and Rwanda have established initial connectivity to the Smart Africa Data Exchange (SADX), a trusted infrastructure that allows their national systems to securely exchange and verify information, authorities have said.
A statement issued Tuesday in Kigali by the Smart Africa Secretariat said the move marked a key technical milestone in a cross-border digital identity pilot.
Coordinated by the Smart Africa Secretariat, the initiative combines two complementary mechanisms: the Smart Africa Trust Alliance, the common framework of trust, governance and cooperation between participating countries, and the SADX.
Together, they enable cross-border digital interoperability without centralizing identity databases or surrendering control over national data.
The three countries are therefore pioneering a country-led approach to continental digital interoperability, demonstrating how sovereign national systems can progressively establish trusted connections without compromising national control over data, according to the secretariat.
Lacina Kone, chief executive officer of Smart Africa, mentioned that Africa's digital future cannot be built on fragmented national systems.
"Our ambition is to connect our digital economies while preserving the sovereignty of every nation. With Benin, Ghana and Rwanda taking this important first technical step, we are demonstrating that interoperability does not require centralization, and integration does not mean surrendering sovereignty," he said.
The initiative's first use case focuses on cross-border digital identity verification, whereby a traveler from one participating country could have their identity checked directly against their home country's official records, for example at an automated airport e-gate. ■

====================================================================================================

Interview: World Rowing president confident in beach sprint's Olympic future
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
22:28:59 CST
23:28:59 KST

QINGDAO, China, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- With music playing, waves breaking and athletes sprinting across the sand, the 2026 World Rowing Beach Sprint Finals in Qingdao offered a glimpse of how one of the world's oldest sports is reinventing itself ahead of its Olympic debut at Los Angeles 2028.
For World Rowing President Jean-Christophe Rolland, the event marked an important step in the development of a discipline designed to bring rowing to new audiences through shorter races, unpredictable conditions and a more accessible setting.
In an interview with Xinhua during the competition, Rolland discussed beach sprint rowing's growing appeal, preparations for its Olympic debut and China's increasingly prominent role in the sport.
STILL ROWING, "BUT COMPLETELY DIFFERENT"
Beach sprint is a short, head-to-head knockout format of coastal rowing, the open-water branch of the rowing family.
While classic rowing takes place on flat water with specialized boats, coastal rowing is raced at sea where waves demand sturdier craft. Beach sprint adds a third dimension: athletes start by running on the beach, jump into their boats, race through two 250-meter sections around buoys and sprint back across the sand to hit the finish button.
"It is still rowing because we have a boat, a sliding seat and oars. But the concept, the environment and the rules are completely different," he said.
That difference, he argued, is exactly its appeal. Music, the beach setting, running on sand and jumping into the boat make it "a little more fun," while the waves inject an element of uncertainty.
"Depending on how athletes ride the waves, they are affected by the surrounding conditions. That makes the sport a little unpredictable. For the public and spectators, it is probably more fun and faster-paced."
He also drew a clear line between the two coastal formats held in Qingdao: last week's World Rowing Coastal Championships is a six-kilometer endurance race with all crews starting together, while beach sprint is a compact knockout competition, the exact format that will appear at the Los Angeles Olympics.
READY FOR THE OLYMPIC STAGE
Rowing has been part of the Olympic program since the first modern Games in 1896, while coastal rowing only took shape about two decades ago. In October 2023, the IOC Executive Board approved coastal rowing beach sprints for LA 2028, where men's solo, women's solo and mixed double sculls will award three sets of medals.
"It allows us to reach different territories and different audiences, and the environment is completely different from classic rowing," Rolland said. "At the Olympic Games, we can benefit from sharing a venue with other sports rather than needing a standalone venue."
With two years to go, he said the discipline is still maturing. "When the discipline started, it was limited to a very small number of countries. Now its inclusion in the Olympic program has encouraged countries to invest in it. I would not say that we have reached maturity yet, but it is absolutely clear that this discipline really matters in rowing. It continues to grow year after year."
World Rowing is refining the rules to keep them simple. A World Beach Sprint Series will be launched in 2027, with stops in Türkiye and China.
Rolland called the Qingdao finals "a key milestone" on the road to the Olympics. "They allow us to keep improving the event and to show that we have reached the Olympic standard, both in the product we deliver and in the quality and performance of the athletes."
CHINA, "A VERY ACTIVE CONTRIBUTOR"
This was Rolland's first visit to Qingdao, a city known worldwide for its beer. "But there is much more to the city than beer," he said, "The athletes from around the world who are here are very pleased and happy, because we have a very good environment for these world championships."
His bond with China dates back nearly 30 years, to when he first visited as an athlete after the Atlanta Games. "Since then, I have seen the incredible development of rowing in the country," he said, citing the support of the water sports administration and the Chinese Rowing Association, which he described as "one of the most contributive member federations worldwide."
In 2025, China hosted the World Rowing Championships for the first time in Shanghai, followed by the Shanghai Sprint, the coastal championships and now the beach sprint finals. "This shows how active China has become in rowing and how much it contributes to the sport."
He recalled China's women's rowing medals at the Tokyo Olympics and his visit to China's National Games last year, where he was impressed by young athletes. "China has a large number of athletes and the capacity to perform at the highest level," he said.
For China's young rowers, his advice was simple: "Train, train, train. There is no other path to performance than training and making the effort."
"Sport is about respect, respecting one another, respecting the rules and doing your very best to perform," he said. "There is also friendship and the relationships we build with other athletes. We are a family. Competition is competition, but we can still create very good relationships among athletes." ■

National Export Day ceremony held with President Pezeshkian in attendance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:28:54 UTC
23:28:54 KST

National Export Day ceremony held with President Pezeshkian in attendance
TEHRAN- The National Export Day ceremony was held on Wednesday morning, October 21, at the Summit Hall, with the attendance of President Masoud Pezeshkian; Foreign Affairs Minister Abbas Araghchi; Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade Seyed Mohammad Atabak; Head of the Trade Promotion Organization Mohammad Ali Dehghan Dehnavi; Head of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines, and Agriculture Samad Hassanzadeh; those active in the field of foreign trade, and related experts, to honor national exemplary exporters.
At the 30th National Export Day ceremony, the Export Atlas system was unveiled, and 13 national premium companies and 43 national exemplary companies were honored.
A joint committee should be formed to quickly remove export barriers
The Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade, emphasizing the need to accelerate the removal of export barriers, called for the formation of a joint committee with the participation of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, the Ministry of Industry, Mining and Trade, and the Central Bank to quickly resolve exporters’ problems.
Seyed Mohammad Atabak, Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade, speaking at the National Export Day ceremony and referring to the presence of private-sector representatives in the Supreme Council for Non-Oil Exports, stated: “Given the multiplicity of government bodies present in this council, it is necessary to form a specialized committee before issues are raised at the highest level, so that the required matters are examined there and, as far as possible, decided.”
Addressing the President, the Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade added: “In the current situation, especially given hour-by-hour changes in the status of some borders, decisions must be made more quickly. Accordingly, I propose that a committee be formed with the membership of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, the Ministry of Industry, Mining and Trade, and the Central Bank so that it can decide on the current issues and problems of exporters. In cases requiring decision-making at a higher level, the approvals of this working group would be submitted to the Supreme Council for Non-Oil Exports for final approval.”
Atabak, referring to the unveiling of the comprehensive atlas of the country’s official foreign trade gateways at the ceremony, said: “It is expected that this atlas will become a reference for foreign trade actors. Of course, to maintain its effectiveness, the information must be continuously updated, and this can be pursued under the stewardship of the Trade Promotion Organization of Iran.”
He also emphasized the need to strengthen the presence of Iranian traders in target markets and referred to the capacities of the country’s trade agreements, saying: “In some markets, including the Eurasian Economic Union, there are fewer barriers to trade development, but the presence of Iranian traders in these markets still needs strengthening.”
The Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade, referring to last week’s meeting with officials of the Eurasian Economic Union, stated: “At this meeting, the Union’s officials did not consider the number of Iranian traders active in the Union’s market to be proportionate to existing capacities. This is while the efforts of the country’s exporters have placed Iran among the top countries in this field; nevertheless, increasing the presence of Iranian traders in the markets of member states remains necessary.”
Atabak also announced agreements in the field of standards and said: “It was agreed that, to prevent export stoppages due to standards issues, the country’s prevailing standards and certificates of origin would be used so that the export process continues and exported goods do not face stoppage due to these barriers.”
He emphasized the need to follow up on the agreements made, continuously update the comprehensive atlas of the country’s official foreign trade gateways, and strengthen decision-making mechanisms to remove export barriers.
Drafting of 10 proposals to remove trade barriers and develop value-creating exports / Necessity of compensating for increased transportation costs
The Head of the Trade Promotion Organization of Iran, while emphasizing the need to facilitate regulations, compensate for increased transportation costs, and strengthen the presence of Iranian firms in global markets, announced the drafting of 10 proposals aimed at entering the decision-making cycle and facilitating the path of exporters’ activity.
Mohammad Ali Dehghan Dehnavi, at the 30th National Export Day ceremony, emphasized the necessity of supporting exporters, removing domestic barriers, and strengthening the infrastructure for export development.
Dehghan Dehnavi, referring to the position of exporters in the country’s economy, said: “National Export Day is not a day for stating numbers and lists of actions; rather, it is a day to appreciate those who have created and maintained a link between the domestic market and foreign customers.”
He added that exporters did not stop the trade process under the difficult conditions caused by war, sanctions, and economic blockade: “Despite problems in transferring funds, exporters remained committed to their obligations and worked to sustain employment. This resilience demonstrates their decisive role in maintaining the flow of trade and the continuity of the country’s economic activities.”
The Head of the Trade Promotion Organization of Iran, referring to the slogan “Dynamic Trade, Value-Creating Exports,” stated: “This year’s slogan cannot be reduced to a mere title; rather, it is a criterion for measuring the performance of actors in the non-oil export field.”
The Head of the Trade Promotion Organization of Iran, referring to the importance of transportation routes in the country’s foreign trade, stated: “Seventy-five percent of the country’s foreign trade was conducted via sea, but with the efforts of various agencies, especially the private sector, we were able to redefine alternative routes during this period and continue the trade process.”
Dehghan Dehnavi, emphasizing Iran’s capacities for trade development, added: “The country possesses capabilities, knowledge, skills, and specialized human resources that can be used to increase trade volume and raise it from one billion dollars a week to one billion dollars a day.”
The Deputy Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade called exporters the front line of the economic war and stated: “It is our duty to remove the domestic barriers facing exporters and facilitate the path of exporters’ activity.”
Dehghan Dehnavi, referring to the increase in transportation costs under current conditions, considered the allocation of appropriate incentives to be one of the solutions for compensating for the increased costs and said: “We must remove the existing barriers in the path of trade, facilitate regulations, and develop the necessary executive capacities for the effective presence of economic actors in global markets.”
He further stated, emphasizing the preservation of target markets and the achievement of value-creating exports: “Exporters have guaranteed the sustainability of the country’s trade despite numerous pressures. On this path, we must, by strengthening export capacities and focusing on creating added value, provide the ground for a more sustainable presence of Iranian products and services in global markets.”
The Head of the Trade Promotion Organization of Iran also emphasized the necessity of making solution-oriented decisions and announced the drafting of 10 proposals, expressing hope that by placing these proposals in the decision-making cycle, the process of addressing issues and removing barriers to export development would be accelerated.
Dehghan Dehnavi, in conclusion, expressed gratitude for the efforts of economic actors and those involved in the country’s export development.
Iran Chamber president urges unified, programmatic trade strategy to counter external pressure
Speaking at the same ceremony, Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture (ICCIMA) President Samad Hassanzadeh praised exporters for maintaining export flows despite difficult economic and wartime conditions and for resisting enemy intentions. He said protecting exports during the recent critical war conditions was a strategic necessity for employment, foreign-exchange earnings, and Iran’s economic credibility, and commended the Ministry of Industry, Mining and Trade, the Trade Promotion Organization, and other agencies for pursuing barriers and supporting trade routes.
Hassanzadeh said Iran remains in a “neither war, nor peace” situation marked by uncertainty, economic pressure, trade restrictions, and threats to transport routes. Foreign trade is increasingly affected, and the enemy seeks to weaken Iran’s economic competitiveness by raising transaction costs. The response, he argued, must be a unified message from government officials and the private sector: turn external pressure into a coherent will to keep trade flowing, remove domestic barriers, and neutralize the cost of foreign pressure through rationality, pragmatism, and decisions based on national interests.
He called for moving from day-to-day crisis management to sustainable trade mechanisms and for redefining export’s place in macro-economic policy. This requires coordination among foreign-exchange, industrial, financial, and trade policies and avoiding decisions that raise the cost of Iranian firms’ presence in markets. He proposed a Foreign Trade Continuity Headquarters, with government and private-sector participation, customs, the Central Bank, and other agencies, to draft an operational plan. Priorities included diversifying transport routes, easing customs and border procedures, strengthening trade insurance and risk management, and improving inter-agency coordination.
On forex policy, Hassanzadeh urged aligning currency-repatriation and working-capital mechanisms with trade realities. He called for reviewing restrictive business-card procedures, distinguishing intentional violations from limited and recoverable obligations, giving proportionate time to meet foreign-exchange commitments, and avoiding punitive measures against reputable exporters.
He stressed that preserving traditional markets and developing new ones requires attention to costs, payment terms, tariffs, and freight. Without logical support, Iranian exporters cannot compete with regional and international rivals, and lost markets are not easily regained. He urged making economic diplomacy operational—pursuing tariff and transport agreements, removing customs obstacles, and expanding cooperation with neighbors, with greater coordination between relevant agencies, ICCIMA, and joint chambers.
Finally, Hassanzadeh called for moving from sporadic exports to sustainable market presence through value added, quality, completed production chains, and stronger Iranian brands, while supporting downstream industries, technical and engineering services, knowledge-based products, and service exports. He also urged redefining government–private sector relations based on trust, partnership, and responsibility, and turning private-sector demands into a prioritized, time-bound action plan.

Uganda's economy shows resilience amid global shocks: ministry
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
22:28:53 CST
23:28:53 KST

KAMPALA, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Uganda's economy continues to show resilience amid global economic shocks and geopolitical uncertainties, the Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development said Wednesday.
The ministry's Performance of the Economy Report for September 2026 said high-frequency indicators of economic activity and business sentiment pointed to continued economic growth, with output and demand improving since the start of the 2026/27 financial year on July 1.
The Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) stood at 53.0 in September, above the 50-point threshold that separates expansion from contraction. The reading indicated improving private-sector business conditions, as firms continued to report increased output and new orders amid sustained customer demand, the report said.
The Composite Index of Economic Activity rose by 0.3 percent to 193.87 in August from 193.30 in July, reflecting an increase in economic activity over the previous month.
Business sentiment also remained positive, with the Business Tendency Index reaching 55.80 in September, above the 50-point threshold.
However, annual headline inflation rose to 4.6 percent in the year to September, up from 4.1 percent in the year to August, according to the report. The increase reflected higher prices across various categories of goods and services, driven by unfavorable weather conditions that affected food crop supplies. Higher transportation and energy costs, amid continued increases in international oil prices, further pushed up production costs.
Uganda's trade deficit with the rest of the world also widened by 151 percent to 817.03 million U.S. dollars in August 2026, from 325.53 million dollars in the same month of 2025.
The government is undertaking various initiatives to reverse this trend, including enhancing economic and commercial diplomacy through facilitating our missions and embassies abroad to promote our exports and tourism attractions while also sourcing investments into the economy, prioritizing value addition to export products through agro-processing and mineral development, the report said. ■

China's economic powerhouse province steps up integration of AI, IP protection
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
22:28:50 CST
23:28:50 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- East China's economic powerhouse Jiangsu Province on Wednesday outlined efforts to integrate artificial intelligence (AI) and intellectual property (IP) protection, aiming to foster innovation and improve efficiency.
According to provincial IP authorities, Jiangsu has 68,000 invention patents in the AI sector. By 2025, the province had 292,000 high-value invention patents, accounting for 12.7 percent of China's national total.
Jiangsu has strengthened IP protection for AI research and businesses. IP protection centers across the province have established expedited pre-examination procedures for AI patent applications, reducing the average approval time from 22 months to just three months. It has also issued guidelines to help AI companies operated by one person, or OPCs, comply with IP-related requirements.
Meanwhile, Jiangsu is applying AI to improve IP services. It has developed AI infrastructure, such as a digital innovation laboratory, and created AI models and application scenarios to boost the efficiency of IP-related work.
"We should both make good use of AI as a powerful tool and provide institutional support for the development of the AI industry," said Zhang Chuanbo, a senior provincial IP official, at a press conference held by the China National Intellectual Property Administration (CNIPA) in Beijing.
Jiangsu has long been a major manufacturing and foreign trade hub in China, while several of its cities have emerged as centers of technological innovation. Suzhou, Nanjing and Zhenjiang were included in the World Intellectual Property Organization's ranking of the top 100 innovation clusters this year.
The 15th China International Patent Fair will be held in Jiangsu's Wuxi in November, according to the CNIPA. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- China put a total of 1,625 kilometers of new railway lines into operation in the first three quarters of 2026 as the country, home to the world's largest high-speed rail network, speeds up efforts to build a modern railway infrastructure system.

With the newly opened lines and continuing investment, the overall efficiency of the railway network has continued to improve and new momentum has been injected into economic and social development, the company said.
During the period, a number of new lines and stations were put into operation. On Sept. 28 this year, China opened four high-speed rail sections, connecting Xiongan in north China's Hebei Province with Shangqiu in Henan Province in central China, Xi'an with Ankang in Shaanxi Province in northwest China, Yichang with Xingshan in central China's Hubei Province, and Harbin with Yichun in Heilongjiang Province in the country's northeast.
"These projects have further optimized regional railway networks, improved overall transport efficiency, and made travel more convenient for people along the routes," the company said, adding that they have also driven industrial upgrading and resource development, becoming a new engine for high-quality regional economic and social development.
By the end of 2025, the country's total operating railway mileage had reached 165,000 km, which included more than 50,000 km of high-speed rail.
China's high-speed rail network is projected to hit 70,000 km by 2035, featuring eight north-south vertical lines and eight east-west horizontal lines. Once complete, the network will connect major cities, city clusters and key economic zones across the country.
Continued investment in the sector reflects the growing demand for railway travel in the world's second-largest economy.
Railway passenger trips hit a record high in the first three quarters in the country, totaling 3.71 billion passenger trips in the period, up 4.8 percent year on year, China Railway data showed.
Earlier this month, the National Railway Administration released a plan that proposes to basically establish a science and technology innovation system that leads railway modernization by 2030.
The plan envisions no fewer than 20 typical application scenarios or demonstration projects in areas such as the 400 km/h high-speed train operating system. Regarding technical equipment, it proposes to advance research on 600 km/h high-speed maglev technology as well as testing and verification of key technologies for domestic production. ■

====================================================================================================

Africa faces most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak on record as DR Congo cases near 10,000
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
22:28:35 CST
23:28:35 KST

KINSHASA, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Africa is grappling with "the most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak in history", according to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), as infections in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) approach 10,000 and newly reported cases in Kenya and Nigeria raise concerns over the virus's spread across borders.
Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya warned Tuesday that the outbreak had already affected multiple countries across three regions of Africa, calling for urgent international support to contain further transmission.
Nearly five months after the outbreak was declared in the DRC, the epidemic has claimed more than 4,600 lives in the country and spread to eight of its 26 provinces, while imported infections have exposed vulnerabilities in cross-border disease surveillance.
CROSS-BORDER SPREAD RAISES ALARM
Nigeria on Tuesday confirmed its first case of Ebola caused by the Bundibugyo virus, the same strain responsible for the ongoing epidemic in the DRC, becoming the fifth country to detect the virus since the outbreak began in May, according to the Nigerian health authorities.
The patient, a woman who had recently traveled through Uganda, developed symptoms on Oct. 7 and sought medical care at a private hospital in Abuja four days later. Her infection was confirmed on Oct. 20. Nigerian authorities have identified 44 contacts for monitoring, while the patient remains in isolation and is receiving medical care.
Uganda's Ministry of Health said the woman had traveled to eastern DRC for business before transiting through Uganda in early October without symptoms. It stressed that her travel through Uganda did not establish where she contracted the virus, with investigations still underway.
Uganda, which previously reported 20 confirmed Ebola cases and two deaths linked to the DRC outbreak, was declared Ebola-free on Aug. 27 after completing a 42-day monitoring period without new infections.
The ministry reiterated Tuesday that Uganda still had "no confirmed active Ebola cases" and pledged to strengthen health screening and surveillance at points of entry.
Meanwhile, Kenya reported its ninth confirmed Ebola case on Tuesday, with all infections linked to an initial imported case involving a Kenyan national who had traveled from the DRC through Uganda and died in Nairobi on Oct. 5.
The latest patient was already in quarantine when symptoms developed. Kenyan health authorities said there was no evidence of transmission beyond the identified cluster, while 134 of 135 identified contacts had been placed under quarantine.
DR CONGO OUTBREAK NEARS GRIM MILESTONE
In the DRC, the outbreak continues to take a heavy toll despite signs of slowing transmission in some areas.
The country had recorded 9,637 confirmed cases and 4,646 deaths as of Oct. 19, representing a case fatality rate of 48.2 percent, according to the latest situation report released Wednesday by the country's health authorities.
The eastern province of Ituri remains the epicenter, accounting for 72.7 percent of cumulative infections. Neighboring North Kivu has also emerged as a major transmission hotspot, recording 2,117 confirmed cases and 1,191 deaths, with a case fatality rate of 56.3 percent.
The virus has also recently reached the northern province of Nord-Ubangi, bringing the number of affected provinces to eight and the number of affected health zones to 66.
The outbreak's geographical expansion has also raised concerns over the risk of the virus reaching Kinshasa, the country's densely populated capital of nearly 20 million people.
Former health minister Jean-Jacques Mbungani Mbanda warned Tuesday that the detection of infections in the northern provinces of Sud-Ubangi and Nord-Ubangi had heightened the risk of imported cases reaching the capital through river transport, air travel and road networks.
He urged authorities to strengthen surveillance at airports, river ports and other entry points, warning that temperature screening alone could not identify infected travelers during the incubation period.
Mbungani also called for stronger community surveillance and infection prevention measures in healthcare facilities, stressing that Kinshasa should reinforce its preparedness before recording its first confirmed case.
AFRICA CDC CALLS FOR URGENT GLOBAL ACTION
Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya warned Tuesday that the continued geographical spread of the outbreak, coupled with a case fatality rate approaching 50 percent in the DRC, posed an extremely serious public health threat.
In a statement following Nigeria's confirmation of its first case, Kaseya said Africa CDC has begun mobilizing support for Nigeria while intensifying its response in the DRC and Kenya and maintaining heightened vigilance in Uganda.
Calling for urgent international support, Kaseya appealed for flexible financing, medical supplies, diagnostic tools, trained responders and stronger community-based surveillance.
"We cannot allow this outbreak to spread to more countries or continue for another year," he warned.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus also called for sustained regional preparedness following Nigeria's confirmation of its first Bundibugyo Ebola case.
In a social media statement Wednesday, Tedros urged countries across the region to maintain a high level of readiness to detect cases early, prevent further transmission and protect healthcare workers and communities.
The outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo virus, for which no vaccine or specific treatment has yet been approved, making early detection, supportive care and effective infection control crucial to reducing deaths and interrupting transmission.
The epidemic was declared in the DRC on May 15 and designated a public health emergency of international concern by WHO two days later. Africa CDC subsequently declared it a public health emergency of continental security.
The current Ebola outbreak has become the largest and deadliest ever recorded in the DRC and the second-largest Ebola outbreak globally, after the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic. ■

Donald Trump’s approval rating sank to 36% just two weeks before the midterm elections, the lowest recorded in a poll by the New York Times/Siena College, with most respondents expressing frustration over his handling of the US economy, cost of living and Iran war.
In an October survey of approximately 3,494 likely voters, 59% said they disapproved of Trump’s handling of his job, and 52% said they planned to vote for the Democratic candidate in the upcoming election.
Much of the disapproval toward the US president was associated with frustrations over Trump’s handling of economic and cost-of-living-related issues. On gas prices, 73% of registered voters said they disapproved; on the cost of living, 69% said they disapproved, and on the economy, 64% said they disapproved.
Approximately 65% said they disapproved of Trump’s handling of the Iran war, which has dragged on for nearly eight months and pushed gas and oil prices up.
The new polling numbers paint a gloomy picture for Trump and Republicans, who have embarked on an uphill battle to defeat Democrats in the upcoming midterms to maintain their majority control in Congress.
Trump, whose name recognition has largely helped Republican candidates in past elections, has been on the road campaigning for Maga-aligned candidates. However, some candidates have sought to distance themselves from the president, who has become increasingly unpopular over his economic policies.
In 2024, Trump promised to lower everyday costs for Americans, keep inflation low and to keep the US from starting more wars abroad.
But as of 21 October, gas prices were more than $4.25 a gallon, inflation increased to 3.7% last month and the president’s war with Iran remained steady.
Between September and October, the US president’s approval rating decreased by two percentage points in the New York Times/Siena College polls.
Democratic candidates, meanwhile, have seized on the cost-of-living issues to appeal to independents and undecided voters, promising to rein in the president’s policies that have pushed costs up, such as tariffs.
While polling from the New York Times/Siena College indicates Democrats have the upper hand headed into next month’s election, the party is still fighting against a massive financial war chest in competitive races in Texas, Ohio, New York, Alaska and Iowa.
The Guardian has asked the White House for comment.

Ukraine’s interceptor crews destroyed thousands of Russian aerial targets during Vivaldi. Jet-powered Shaheds remain a challenge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:27:34 UTC
23:27:34 KST

The commander of an interceptor battalion in Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps said his unit destroyed several thousand Russian aerial targets during Operation Vivaldi, ArmyInform, the Defense Ministry’s news agency, reported on 21 October.
Operation Vivaldi is a Ukrainian counteroffensive north of Lyman in Donetsk Oblast, where the 3rd Army Corps has reported liberating settlements. In its third phase, Ukrainian forces reclaimed five settlements and expanded their gains to 176 square kilometers. Strikes on Russian logistics and electronic warfare likely neutralized Russia’s drone defenses before Ukraine sent in armor, the Institute for the Study of War assessed.
The commander, who uses the callsign “Betsyk,” leads the interceptor battalion of the 1030th Anti-Aircraft Missile-Artillery Regiment “Aquila,” part of the 3rd Army Corps. He said Russian forces deployed large numbers of reconnaissance drones to locate Ukrainian positions after the corps began advancing.
Betsyk named Zala, Orlan, Supercam, Merlin, and Knyaz Veshchiy Oleg among the reconnaissance drones used by Russian forces.
Russia also brought in reinforcements and units operating strike drones, including first-person-view (FPV) quadcopters, Molniya fixed-wing FPV drones, and Lancet crews, he said. At one stage, Russian forces deployed crews from their Rubicon drone unit to disrupt the advance, but the move did not change the situation.
Ukraine retook Kolodiazi north of Lyman as its drones hit 200-plus Russian vehicles in Operation Vivaldi’s last phase, Ukrainian drone officer says
Betsyk said his battalion’s work deprived Russian forces of the ability to strike Ukrainian troops and track their movements.
Jet-powered Shaheds: speed is the main challenge
The regiment also works against Russian strike drones heading for targets behind the front line. Betsyk said interceptor crews had destroyed some jet-powered drones, but not in significant numbers.
The main difficulty is speed, he said. Interceptor drones need to reach 500–600 km/h to intercept Russian jet-powered attack drones, according to Betsyk.
For now, the regiment mainly uses conventional air-defense systems against these targets: self-propelled anti-aircraft systems, surface-to-air missile systems, and portable surface-to-air missile systems. Betsyk said these systems were historically designed to engage jet-powered targets.
He compared the current challenge with the early use of piston-powered Shaheds. Those drones initially posed a serious threat but later became easier for Ukrainian air defenses to counter. Russia has largely stopped using piston-powered Shaheds on most fronts since summer, he said, but continues to use piston-powered Gerbera drones, which are relatively cheap and can partly exhaust Ukrainian air defenses. The main drones Russian forces use now are jet-powered Shaheds, he said.
Betsyk expects Russian forces to adapt if Ukraine fields effective interceptors against jet-powered drones. They will seek ways to evade the interceptors, increase speed, improve navigation, and change their tactics, he said. However, he added that the battalion had not observed a major evolution so far and did not expect the drones’ speed to double.
What the corps says Vivaldi achieved
Separately, 3rd Army Corps commander Andrii Biletskyi said Ukrainian forces retook 277 square kilometers and 16 settlements during Operation Vivaldi, Ukrainska Pravda reported. Biletskyi also said Russian losses exceeded 8,000 personnel, according to ArmyInform. These figures are Ukrainian claims and have not been independently verified.

====================================================================================================

‘This Is Not a Drill’: Critical PHP Vulnerabilities Are Setting the Internet on Fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:26:19 UTC
23:26:19 KST

Internet security and web administration teams around the world are scrambling to prevent widespread disaster. On Wednesday, the developers behind the much-used PHP programming language released emergency security updates designed to fix critical flaws that could be exploited to allow attackers to gain dangerous remote control of victim systems.
The PHP Foundation detailed the two critical vulnerabilities—CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619—which impact “all PHP installations serving web requests” going back to PHP version 5, released in July 2004. However, only PHP 8.2 and newer are still supported and will receive patches, according to the alert. The PHP Foundation noted, though, that some PHP distributions and third-party vendors still produce legacy fixes. The caveat is significant because ubiquitous and foundational web layers like PHP can persist forgotten and un-updated in historic internet infrastructure.
“There are no complete mitigations, updating is the only safe choice,” the PHP Foundation wrote in its advisories. Security experts warn of the potential dire consequences of overlooking unpatched systems.
“This is not a drill,” says Lukasz Olejnik, an independent security consultant and visiting senior research fellow at King’s College London. Since its development in the 1990s, PHP has evolved into an essential scripting language for web development and is used across vast swaths of the internet in websites and software. Everything from publishing systems like WordPress and Drupal to e-commerce platforms like Adobe’s Magento are built on PHP.
Olejnik likens the widespread use of the programming language to critical infrastructure.
“The impact is enormous,” he says of PHP’s security flaws, adding that millions of systems could be impacted. “Especially if attackers would turn to exploiting these vulnerabilities fast. Worst case is wormable malware affecting big chunks of the internet.”
The overriding fear for security teams and developers is that malicious hackers could quickly jump upon the vulnerabilities and begin exploiting deployments before they are fixed. Internet infrastructure company Cloudflare reported it was “seeing early attacks emerging” before the PHP Foundation had detailed the vulnerabilities and released fixes. “We expect mass attacks to start within 15 minutes of the release,” security firm Sansec wrote ahead of the fixes, which were released just before 10 am ET on Wednesday.
“Most of the web runs on PHP and this bug is in a file upload interface that’s like a front door with no lock,” says longtime security and compliance consultant Davi Ottenheimer. “An attacker does not need to know which site they are hitting or even the actual software it runs. They send one crafted upload to any server they can find, and that is the entire attack.”
Ahead of the updated versions of PHP becoming available, some organizations took their websites offline as a precautionary measure. Multiple sites belonging to the Finnish government, including the National Land Survey, were inaccessible, according to reports. French government websites and the Port of Rotterdam’s website were also offline, according to Reuters.
“Everybody should patch immediately, exploitation may happen very fast and at a scale,” says Olejnik. “AI makes exploiting such vulnerabilities of immediate importance. Like, indeed, a minute or so.”
Security company Wiz, which is owned by Google, claimed its researchers discovered the vulnerabilities in PHP partially using AI tools, while OpenAI and security firm Calif also say they independently discovered the issues and worked together. Dubbing an exploitation demonstration php2shell , the Wiz researchers write that in some cases the vulnerabilities can be exploited “fairly easily.”
“The vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers or read sensitive process memory,” Wiz writes in its research. “That memory may contain passwords, authentication tokens, API keys and certificates belonging to other requests or the server itself.”
Details of the upcoming vulnerabilities first appeared from the maintainers behind PHP on October 20. In a short post on the PHP website, the PHP Foundation wrote it was giving “advance notice” of the security flaws and upcoming release of the fixes. While omitting specific details about the vulnerabilities or the versions impacted, it said both flaws are considered to have a “critical” 9.2 score out of 10 on the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS).
“We reserve the right to release earlier should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild,” the security warning on the PHP site said ahead of Wednesday’s release. According to reports from Bleeping Computer and Ars Technica, some details about the vulnerabilities may have leaked before they were due to officially be published.
The early warning from the PHP Foundation may have given some developers, security teams, and companies enough of a heads up to start preparing to update systems using PHP. Ahead of the details being published, warnings from the EU’s Computer Emergency Response Team (EU-CERT) and Australia's cybersecurity agency said IT teams should be prepared to update their systems as soon as possible, with the potential for websites to be taken offline while fixes are applied.
Similarly, the UK’s National Cyber Security Center (NCSC) published an alert saying organizations should “prepare for immediate updating of systems” using PHP. “Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organizations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated,” the agency wrote online.
The NCSC advises that organizations and businesses should identify systems running PHP across their tech infrastructure. There should be a particular focus on systems using PHP that are connected to the internet, including monitoring them for any potential exploitation. The next step is applying PHP updates as they are available and monitoring for updates from software companies as they may use PHP within their apps or services.
“If you find signs of compromise, isolate the system, preserve your web server and PHP logs, and report it to your local FBI field office,” Brett Leatherman, the FBI’s cyber assistant director posted online. “Those reports help us identify the actors involved and warn other organizations before they become victims.”

Finnish President Alexander Stubb has called for direct negotiations between Ukraine, Russia and the United States over disputed territories and security guarantees, as US President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday, to discuss proposals for ending the war.
Stubb outlined Europe's priorities during a speech at the University of Helsinki, a day after participating in eight hours of discussions in Oslo involving Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Witkoff and representatives from NATO and the European Union.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
According to Stubb, the Oslo meeting sought to ease tensions between Washington and Kyiv, establish European and Ukrainian priorities ahead of Witkoff's meeting with Putin, and agree on the next steps towards negotiations.
The Finnish president said the central objective was to arrange bilateral or trilateral talks addressing territorial disputes, which remain among the main obstacles to an agreement.
He identified US security guarantees for Ukraine and Europe's security arrangements after the war as further priorities. Negotiators would also need to address ceasefire monitoring, the location of military contact lines, energy security, food supplies and prisoner exchanges.
Stubb said the eventual agreement would involve compromises concerning territory and security guarantees, including the question of whether Ukraine receives bilateral US commitments or NATO membership.
Speaking about the Oslo discussions, Stubb said negotiations behind closed doors differed considerably from the public exchanges between Washington and Kyiv.
Witkoff subsequently travelled to St Petersburg for his ninth meeting with Putin, carrying documents outlining proposals for a possible peace settlement.
"One thing that I hope to accomplish today is to have some good conversation between us about the resumption potentially of trilateral talks between Ukraine and Russia and the United States," Witkoff told Putin, according to Reuters.
A US official told Reuters that the Oslo discussions had produced "meaningful progress" towards a coordinated approach to Russia, including proposals covering Ukrainian security guarantees, economic reconstruction and European security.
The meeting in Russia also coincided with the release of Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired American teacher imprisoned in Russia on charges of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine.
According to The Guardian, Putin ordered Hubbard's release following a personal request from Trump. The release did not involve a prisoner exchange.
Trump confirmed on Truth Social that Russia had released Hubbard without requiring concessions from Washington.
Witkoff praised Putin during their meeting, describing him as a humanitarian and thanking him for the gesture.
The discussions took place amid tensions between Washington and Kyiv following Trump's agreement to resume Russian diesel imports and Ukrainian complaints about restrictions on US intelligence sharing and military satellite communications.
Zelenskyy said Tuesday's Oslo meeting had helped resolve some intelligence-sharing problems.
Russia continues to demand control over the entire Donetsk region and opposes Ukrainian NATO membership, while Kyiv seeks security guarantees and an end to Russian attacks.
Putin also raised prospects for economic cooperation with Washington, including fertiliser exports, and offered Russian assistance concerning Iran.
In Helsinki, Stubb addressed the wider implications of changes in US foreign policy, warning that relations between Europe and Washington had undergone a lasting transformation.
"There is no return to the old transatlantic relationship," Stubb said.

Airbnb bans check-out chores like stripping the bed or taking the bins out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:24:27 UTC
23:24:27 KST

Hosts can no longer ask guests to do anything that would take “significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner”.
A common complaint around staying at an Airbnb is the dreaded check-out chores, like stripping the bed linen or taking the bins out.
But now the short-term rental service has updated its rules to prevent hosts from including such tasks in their house rules.
According to its community policy update, guests can’t be asked to do things that require “significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner”.
As an example, hosts can’t ask you to wash and put away dishes, but they can ask you to put used tableware in the sink.
In a statement shared with Euronews Travel, Airbnb said: “House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we've heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage.
“So we've redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises.”
Airbnb’s house rules updates
As part of the update, house rules are now shared on the listing page, in the trips tab, and in reservation reminders.
There are seven standard house rules hosts can share, which cover check-in and check-out times, the number of approved guests, smoking, approval for pets, designated quiet hours, and commercial film and photography.
Hosts will also be able to add “reasonable” requests, and these can be updated at any time.
Airbnb will flag any requests that do not fall in line with the new policy, and the host will need to remove them, or make an appeal.
The cleaning fee should only cover a standard tidy up between guests, and hosts are not allowed to charge guests for not doing something listed in the checkout tasks.

Besieged Yemeni city on verge of ‘unmanageable’ crisis, aid workers warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:24:02 UTC
23:24:02 KST

The humanitarian crisis in the besieged Yemeni city of Taiz is becoming unmanageable as the city runs out of water, fuel and fresh food, Oxfam aid workers in the country have warned.
Iran-allied Houthi forces have largely encircled the city of more than 900,000 people, cutting it off from most supply routes. This week, heavy fighting has raged around the city’s old airport, causing extensive damage in a densely populated residential area.
The conflict has intensified since forces loyal to the internationally recognised government and the Saudi-led coalition launched airstrikes on the Houthi-held airport in Sana’a in July, shattering a 2022 ceasefire deal that had largely stopped the fighting.
The UN has called for aid workers to be given access to Taiz. Oxfam in London called for the UK to send extra humanitarian aid to the country. The UK has allocated just £104m in aid to Yemen for each of the next three years, down from the £196m allocated in 2020. US aid to the stricken country has been virtually wiped out, and Germany, another leading funder, has halved its aid programme.
Donor countries have subscribed to only 23% of the cost of the UN humanitarian relief programme for Yemen this year, and pressure is growing on Saudi Arabia – itself cash-strapped by the cost of war – to make up the shortfall. The World Food Programme said wheat flour reserves in the city were nearly exhausted as of mid-October.
On Tuesday the UK government allocated an unspecified sum in extra military help to Saudi Arabia to help protect its airports and infrastructure, but London has yet to decide on whether to back a much more robust military response, including supporting the possible deployment of foreign ground troops to Yemen.
Fatma Jaffar, a Yemen-based advocacy manager for Oxfam, said local staff described an almost total siege of Taiz.
“All the main entrances [to the city] have been blocked. The clashes are continuing and the casualties are very high,” she said. “Even people that have money are not able to buy food. Supplies are becoming very limited in the markets. No fuel has entered Taiz for two or three weeks. Drinking water is a massive issue. Even our staff are struggling to buy water.
“Hospitals are struggling without medicines and a lot of people as a result are dying. Those that have been wounded by missiles – there have been attempts to get them out of the city, but because of the blockade they are not able to transfer anyone. Prices have rocketed.
“Our staff told me that people are even searching for apples right now and they cannot find any fresh fruit, and basic commodities are not found inside the city. Garbage is piling up since they are not able to transfer the waste outside the city. They are trying to burn it, but we can only anticipate there will be diseases such as cholera in the near future. If this goes on much longer and access remains blocked, there will be casualties from missiles, hunger and disease from lack of water right across the city.
“The situation was bad before the escalation – Yemen is one of the poorest countries on Earth – and now it is becoming unmanageable.”
Prices have rocketed: a 20-litre container of petrol that cost about $20 (£15) before the crisis is now worth $80 on the hidden market. Potato prices have doubled.
The Houthi focus on Taiz reflects the city’s strategic importance, but the level of resistance inside the city may swallow the group’s resources, weakening its response elsewhere.
Oxfam has been forced to transfer its limited resources from development to emergency humanitarian work, including offering cash transfers.
The Halo Trust, the world’s largest humanitarian landmine-clearance organisation, said 30 of its staff were among hundreds of thousands of civilians trapped inside the city.
In the Trump administration’s fiscal year 2027 budget request to Congress, the US state department has requested no economic support or development assistance specifically for Yemen. By comparison, the US committed roughly $760m in total aid to Yemen during the last year of Joe Biden’s presidency.
UN diplomats are still mediating between the two sides, but there is no sign that either the Houthis or the internationally recognised government are ready for a ceasefire, let alone a long-term settlement.

14:21:39 UTC

SpaceX stock jumped 10% Wednesday after the company reported surging revenue growth in its third quarter, and owner Elon Musk floated a potential SpaceX-Tesla merger.
The space company, which made its debut on the Nasdaq in the biggest initial public offering ever in June, reported third-quarter revenue on Tuesday of $14.6 billion, up 161% from the previous year, and beating LSEG consensus estimates of $12.72 billion.
Meanwhile, its operating income came in at $2.8 billion, with net income of $4.4 billion, after reporting a net loss of $1.05 billion in the same period a year earlier.
On an earnings call, Musk said he's considering a combination with Tesla — which would mark the largest merger in history — and that the boards of both companies have created specific committees to discuss a consolidation.
"I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained from cooperating," Musk said on the call. Tesla is set to report third-quarter earnings after the closing bell on Wednesday.
Shares of other space stocks, including Rocket Lab, Intuitive Machines and AST SpaceMobile climbed on Wednesday.
SpaceX forecasts first-quarter 2027 revenue between $33 billion and $37 billion, beating the average analyst estimate of $22.2 billion, according to LSEG.
"We delivered another strong quarter in Q3. Revenue grew an impressive 161% year-over-year, fueled by continued momentum in Connectivity and a clear inflection in our Super Intelligence business," SpaceX's chief financial officer, Bret Johnsen, said in the earnings release.
Johnsen pinned the strong results on recurring revenue from its satellite internet business, Starlink, and significant expansion of its Super Intelligence [SI] infrastructure.
The company has dived into artificial intelligence this year, which it's now calling SI. The segment is its largest business unit, with revenue soaring ninefold to $7.56 billion from $813 million in the same quarter last year.
Bull case for AI cloud providers
Commentary on computing during the earnings call supported "continued pricing power and shorter payback periods" for AI cloud providers, Truist Securities analysts said in a Tuesday note.
"Despite market concerns relating to financing for AI cloud providers this past week, we believe SpaceX's third-quarter 2026 represents the first data point during the earnings season to support the bull case for AI cloud providers," they added.
They explained that demand appears "insatiable," with SpaceX noting that it could rent out its capacity several times over. The analysts said Coreweave and Nebius are set to benefit and capture demand as "pricing power will more than offset higher rates."
The shares of neoclouds Nebius and Coreweave traded marginally lower, while Iren and Applied Digital climbed in early trading on Wednesday.
— CNBC's Lora Kolodny contributed to this report.
