Thousands of students, teachers, parents and workers demonstrated across Greece on Wednesday, demanding more funding for public education and measures to ease rising living and study costs, public broadcaster ERT reported.
Around 10,000 people joined a march in Athens, while an estimated 2,000 to 2,500 demonstrated in Thessaloniki and more than 3,000 took to the streets in Patras, according to ERT.
Rallies were also held in Larissa and other cities.
Protesters demanded that thousands of teaching vacancies be filled, substitute teachers receive permanent positions, class sizes be reduced and school buildings be made safer.
University students called for lower rents, increased housing allowances, more places in student dormitories and the repeal of legislation on student expulsions.
Primary school teachers held a 24-hour strike, while secondary school teachers staged a three-hour work stoppage. Public sector workers and other unions also joined the demonstrations.
In Athens, protesters gathered at the Propylaea before marching to Syntagma Square and returning to their starting point.
The main march ended peacefully shortly before 2 pm local time, ERT reported.
However, disturbances were reported in the nearby Omonia area, including stone-throwing and damage to electric scooters.
Police used stun grenades, while Molotov cocktails were reportedly thrown.
According to the report, police detained 21 people during preventive checks in Athens, where more than 3,000 officers were deployed across central areas, including shopping streets.
In Thessaloniki, police took 10 people in for questioning.
The march there ended without further incidents after some participants lit flares outside the US Consulate.
Students occupied 18 schools in Thessaloniki, bringing the total number of occupied schools across Central Macedonia to 30.
The demonstration in Patras ended peacefully, while participants at the Larissa rally expressed solidarity with protesters in France.
"From Greece to France, we are fighting for free public education," read a slogan at the rally.

Ukraine steps up fight against shadow economy, PM Koretskyi outlines priorities
Prime Minister of Ukraine Sergii Koretskyi announced this on Telegram, Ukrinform reports.
“Together with government officials, members of parliament, and the heads of the Bureau of Economic Security, the National Police, the tax service and the customs service, we have identified priority measures to eliminate/reduce the shadow economy,” the statement said.

The priority measures include:
- Combating the illegal production and circulation of tobacco products, as well as taxation of electronic cigarettes and e-liquids;

- Eliminating tax evasion schemes;
- Tackling fraud in the gambling industry, among other measures.
Particular and detailed attention was paid at the meeting to strengthening oversight of the import, registration and intended use of humanitarian aid brought into Ukraine.

The Ministry of Social Policy, together with the relevant government agencies, will prepare amendments to the applicable regulations.
The participants also considered introducing electronic contracts and invoices for formalizing agreements and billing, as well as enabling automatic data exchange. The necessary legislative amendments will be prepared to this end.
The Prime Minister emphasized that specific tasks, deadlines and responsible parties had been established for each area. Progress reports are to be submitted monthly.
As reported, the Bureau of Economic Security of Ukraine, together with the State Tax Service and the Main Service Center of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, has introduced an analytical tool to detect tax evasion schemes involving the import and sale of cars.

Burnham backs mandatory suicide prevention training for social workers after parent-carer Matilda Davis’s death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:18:58 UTC
23:18:58 KST

Andy Burnham has backed mandatory suicide prevention training for social workers after the “devastating” death of Matilda Davis, a parent-carer who killed herself minutes after meeting professionals.
The Guardian revealed in August how the “absolutely inspirational” 36-year-old had taken her life after feeling “completely exhausted” and failed by England’s social care system.
Davis, a former art teacher, had told multiple professionals she was struggling to cope with the significant care for her seven-year-old son and “paralysed with anxiety” about her looming divorce from her estranged husband.
She died on 3 October last year, minutes after an emotional meeting with social workers who had not received suicide prevention training.
Burnham was asked about Davis’s case at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday and said he supported the extension of this training to all local authorities in England.
Manuela Perteghella, the Liberal Democrat MP for Stratford-upon-Avon, where Davis lived, said: “My constituent Matilda Davis was a wonderful and devoted mum and a full-time carer for her disabled seven-year-old child. Despite providing round the clock care, she received almost no support leaving her physically and emotionally exhausted.
“Last October, social workers visited Matilda and she took her own life 15 minutes after they left. She was 36.”
Perteghella highlighted University of Birmingham research showing that 41% of parent-carers have contemplated suicide, and asked Burnham to meet her and Matilda’s family to discuss “mandatory suicide prevention training for local authorities and other measures so that no more normal families suffer such a devastating loss”.
Burnham replied: “I will ensure that a minister meets the honourable lady to discuss that proposal because I find myself in agreement with it.”
The prime minister praised the Lib Dem leader, Ed Davey, for his work campaigning on behalf of unpaid carers, whose failure by the state has been brought into light by an award-winning Guardian investigation into the carer’s allowance scandal.
Burnham said these carers, who often gave up work and other commitments while saving the government billions of pounds to look after severely disabled loved ones, could often “sink under their responsibilities and find it very, very difficult”.
He added: “Sadly in the case of Matilda, [Perteghella’s] constituent, obviously a devastating situation. I will arrange that meeting and I thank [Perteghella] for raising it in the House [of Commons] today.”
At Davis’s inquest in March, social workers admitted they did not ask her whether she had thoughts of suicide despite knowing she was in significant distress, nor was she directed to crisis organisations.
As a result, the coroner, Deborah Sewell, issued a rare prevention of future deaths notice ordering Warwickshire council to make suicide prevention training mandatory for 600 members of staff, primarily social workers.
Davis’s brother, Joel Harley-Davis, said the family was “really reassured” by Burnham’s response and that his sister would have been “proud” to make a positive difference.
“We all believe that this training would have been enough to save Matilda’s life,” he said. “If those social workers had asked her [whether she was considering ending her life] Matilda was so honest she would have said yes.
“This needs to be made mandatory – you can’t leave it up to councils to decide whether to put it in place because it creates a postcode lottery. It doesn’t need to be this really expensive thing. All the literature and advice says that if in doubt about whether someone is suicidal, ask that direct difficult question.”
Guidance issued by the mental health charity Mind states that it is best practice not to “skirt around the topic of suicide” and instead ask direct questions such as: “Are you having suicidal thoughts?” when speaking to someone who might want to kill themselves.
Harley-Davis, 30, said his sister felt “failed and let down” by England’s social care system and was passionate about advocating on behalf of other parent-carers. He added: “Matilda was an incredibly stoic individual but that’s not to say she didn’t need someone to offer that respite.
“Matilda needed that professional support and a degree of empathy and I don’t think she got that, especially on the day she died.”
In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline on 988, chat on 988lifeline.org, or text HOME to 741741 to connect with a crisis counsellor. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

“During its 96th year of activity, Magen David Adom is inaugurating 96 new ambulances, which will join the fleet of approximately 2,000 ambulances already operating across the country to save lives,” Bin said.
“Although 96 is a mature age, Israel’s national emergency medical service is young and strong, and brings exceptional modern lifesaving capabilities that enable it to meet the challenges, scenarios and emergency incidents that arise in Israel,” he continued.
“I would like to thank the generous donors and the friends’ associations around the world, which do outstanding work to strengthen Magen David Adom in its primary mission: saving lives,” Bin said.

Russia arrests German man, calls him a 'mercenary' for Ukraine
October 21, 2026
Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) domestic intelligence agency said on Wednesday that it had arrested a German national on allegations of mercenary activity, calling him an "active member of the Ukrainian armed forces."
The news came on the same day that Russia released a retired teacher from the US, Stephen Hubbard, after years in detention on similar mercenary charges, which he denied.
Russia has detained a number of foreign nationals since its 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, accusing them of assisting Kyiv in some way or another.
There was no immediate comment from Germany's government, besides acknowledging that it had seen the reports and was pursuing them.
What did the FSB say about the arrest?
The FSB said in a statement carried widely by Russian media that the man was a former Bundeswehr soldier and trained sniper. It did not issue his name but published a short video in which he could be heard speaking German.
According to the FSB, the man was a Bundeswehr soldier from 1996 to 2010, who served in Afghanistan and Somalia between 2004 and 2010.
They alleged that he later operated as a mercenary fighter in Syria's civil war.
From 2016 to 2018, according to the Russian spy agency, he fought in Ukraine against the Russian-backed rebels in eastern states, prior to Moscow's full-scale invasion in 2022.
The FSB claimed that he returned to Ukraine as a "mercenary" in 2025 and was fighting in the contested region of Donetsk, but then deserted over non-payment of wages.
They did not comment on why or how the man, whom they said was born in 1976, had come to be in Russia. Nor did they say where or under what circumstances they arrested him.
How did German authorities respond?
A spokesperson at the German Foreign Ministry only initially responded by saying that Berlin was aware of the reports from Russia.
The spokesperson said the ministry would not comment on the individual case or specifics for the time being.
Similar Swedish arrest last week, US prisoner freed
Russia has arrested hundreds of foreign nationals on charges like espionage, sabotage and treason amid its invasion of neighboring Ukraine. The charges can carry lengthy prison sentences.
A smaller number have also been accused of mercenary activity.
The FSB last week arrested a Swedish national, again accusing him of fighting on Kyiv's behalf.
In his case, they said he was operating as the commander of a drone unit and that he was detained attempting to illegally cross the border in the western Pskov region.
A Japanese journalist was also arrested last week, accused of espionage, prompting sharp criticism from Tokyo.
Also on Wednesday, Russia released a retired US teacher, Stephen Hubbard, who had been arrested in 2024 on comparable allegations.
This took place as US negotiator Steve Witkoff was visiting St. Petersburg and after a series of recent concessions to Russia and criticisms of Ukraine from US President Donald Trump.
Trump claimed there was no quid pro quo involved in the release, but later said Hubbard would not be free if he had not eased sanctions on Russian diesel shipments.

MSM ‘sources’ contradict Musk on Starlink for Ukraine

MSM ‘sources’ contradict Musk on Starlink for Ukraine
The Wall Street Journal has challenged Elon Musk’s denials over alleged restrictions on satellite services used for Ukrainian drone strikes deep inside Russia. The outlet has cited anonymous White House sources who have claimed that the SpaceX founder and Starlink owner had personally ordered restricting the service.
Ukrainian officials last week claimed that SpaceX’s Starlink satellite communications service and its military-grade version, Starshield, which Kiev uses for frontline drone operations, stopped working on drones traveling faster than 160 kph (100 mph). Neither Starlink nor SpaceX has publicly acknowledged a technical “signal or service failure,” leaving the questions of whether an actual service restriction took place, and if so what could have caused it, unconfirmed.
What has Ukraine claimed about Starshield?
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky initially claimed, without evidence, that Kiev had been told “technical malfunctions” had caused a service slowdown. He later shifted the blame to Washington. On NBC’s ‘Meet the Press’ on Sunday Zelensky claimed, again without citing evidence nor being asked to provide it, that an order had come from the US government. According to Zelensky, Kiev had even secretly despatched cars to the EU, where they could drive "legally" at 180kph (110mph) where tests allegedly surfaced discrepancies in Starlink performance between the EU and Ukraine.
What has Musk said about Starshield?
Musk has categorically denied that he instructed SpaceX to restrict either service, nor has he confirmed that any restriction or slowdown took place.
The WSJ cited anonymous sources who contradicted him, alleging on Tuesday that he personally ordered speed limits on Ukrainian hardware connected to the satellite network.
Even the WSJ's sources accounts differed. Some claimed that Musk acted unilaterally; others said he consulted senior administration officials, including President Donald Trump, before making the decision. The outlet also claimed that SpaceX representatives contacted the White House to coordinate their accounts of whether the restrictions had been agreed on with the administration.
What has the US government said about Starshield?
Musk earlier insisted that Starshield is owned and controlled by the US government, meaning any speed or usage restrictions are determined by the US military and ultimately Trump – who denied that he ordered the restrictions, though he said on Monday he “would like to find out” who did. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent both said the administration was not behind the restrictions, with Bessent rebuking Zelensky for making “reckless” allegations.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio also rejected the claims. Questioned about the allegation during a visit to India on Wednesday, he warned Kiev against escalating the dispute, saying Ukraine “would not exist” as a sovereign state without US support.
Relations between Zelensky and Washington have effectively collapsed in recent weeks over sanctions on Russia and Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure. Both Musk and Trump have sharply criticized Ukraine’s attacks on Russian diesel refineries, blaming them for global fuel shortages and soaring prices at the pump.
Speaking at the Oval Office on Tuesday, Trump warned Zelensky that he is “going to have to want to make a deal.” He also criticized the cost of supporting Kiev, saying the US has received “absolutely nothing back” except “grief, death and tremendous monetary loss.”
What did Kiev say about Starshield?
Despite Zelensky’s evidence-free assertions and there being no record in the public sphere to support it, the Western press and Ukrainian diplomats are echoing the claims regardless. Ukraine’s ambassador in Washington, Denis Senik, said on Tuesday that Kiev is still “waiting for the official response from contacts with the Pentagon and SpaceX” to understand what happened.
What did the Kremlin say about Starshield?
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said last week that Moscow is unaware of the reported Starlink restrictions, but stressed that “overall, of course, it would be better if such amazing technology… was not used for military purposes at all.” Moscow has condemned Western military assistance for Kiev, arguing that it only prolongs the conflict and obstructs peace efforts.
Is there any proof Starshield was slowed down?
There is no proof on the public record or in the public domain that the Starshield was affected. The only suggestions supporting the idea such an incident took place are Vladimir Zelensky's uncontested claim that Ukrainians sent cars to the EU with Starlink terminals to compare data and the claims of an anonymous Ukrainian officer who told German media giant Axel Springer's Global Reporter's Network, seemingly during the alleged service restriction, that all operations were on hold.

'I didn’t know it was theft': Trials begin in Paris following October 17 violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

'I didn’t know it was theft': Trials begin in Paris following October 17 violence
Those arrested during the October 17 rallies filed into the dock at Paris’s Judicial Court on Tuesday, accused of a broad range of offences – from assault against police officers to resisting arrest and handling stolen goods. The courtroom’s charged atmosphere was palpable amid the justice minister’s call for the law to respond with “utmost firmness”.
A tightly packed crowd waits patiently outside a courtroom half an hour before the hearing begins at the Paris Judicial Court. “You’re keen, aren’t you!” a police officer jeers at the front of the queue. “You’re right to be, there won’t be room for everyone.”
On Tuesday, October 20, a horde of journalists, students and curious onlookers arrived in the early afternoon to watch the trials of those arrested during the October 17 riots. Proceedings began the previous day, mainly involving participants arrested prior to the action – notably for carrying weapons.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Special arrangements were put in place to cope with the mass influx of defendants; according to the authorities, 2,513 people were taken into police custody on October 17 alone. These involved the use of four – rather than the usual one or two – courtrooms to fast-track trials, as well as “additional screening” upon entry to the courthouse to prevent potential trouble, a police officer explained.
Before the hearings began, a group of representatives from several lawyers' collectives delivered a message to the presiding judge, protesting the handling of the demonstrations and condemning “repression as the sole response”.
Read moreHow French police are harnessing social media to identify looters
“Our role as lawyers is to reject any interference by a minister who might seek to steer the outcome of any ruling in the coming days,” said lawyer Arié Alimi. His indignation follows a call by Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin for “utmost firmness” in response to the events of October 17 – a demand he made during his visit to the Lille Judicial Court, also on Tuesday.
Earlier that morning Darmanin welcomed the imprisonment of 149 rioters and looters, adding that more than 800 people had been “brought before a court” to stand trial.
'These are weapons? A mask and a smoke canister?'
The first defendant enters the courtroom: Victor B, a young lanky figure wearing a t-shirt and black jeans, with a black eye on his left side. The 21-year-old audiovisual production student from Sartrouville in the Paris region is accused of being one of several hundred who helped erect barricades and threw paving stones and other projectiles at police while shouting “ACAB” – an acronym for “All Cops Are Bastards”. In their reports, the arresting officers described him as “very hostile and violent”.
In a weak voice, Victor presents a very different account. He said he came to the demonstrations with his girlfriend, who he lost among the crowds before becoming startled when riot police charged. He said he fell to the ground and was struck on the head repeatedly by police with batons.
“The doctor recorded ‘superficial injuries’,” the presiding judge noted.
“I never threw a paving stone or shouted ‘ACAB’”, he insisted. And the barricade? The young man explained he merely moved a wooden plank lying across a burning rubbish bin. Arrested while carrying a pull-pin smoke canister, Victor said his intention was to use it with friends who had brought their camera to make a short film.
“Perhaps you should have thought that through a little more,” the judge remarked.
Read moreFrench PM blames 'ultra-left' groups for weekend riots, promises 'massive' security deployment
“I would never have thrown it at the riot police,” Victor stammered in response.
His father – also present in the courtroom – is invited to say a few words. “He’s a good lad. I don’t know what he’s doing here. To be honest, I’m quite astounded,” he professes. Victor sheds a tear.
For her part, the prosecutor highlighted “the defendant’s preparation and determination”, noting he arrived on the scene masked and carrying a weapon. Despite his clean criminal record, she seeks a conviction: a five-month prison sentence, with immediate imprisonment.
He was “in the wrong place at the wrong time”, argued his lawyer, who maintains that his client came to demonstrate peacefully. “These constitute weapons? A mask and a smoke grenade? We’d better go and arrest every football supporter!” he exclaimed, before requesting an acquittal.
Arrested wearing trainers – security tag still attached
Next up are 38-year-old Lamine B and 34-year-old Sofiane R. The two friends are jointly accused of theft and damage to the Louis Vuitton concession in Printemps department store on Boulevard Haussmann. Both were found inside the shop at 7am on October 18 after it was broken into overnight.
In a somewhat curious turn of events, Sofiane was found to be wearing a pair of the luxury brand’s trainers and a black jacket – complete with security tags. He admitted the theft but declined the opportunity to speak.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
His friend, however, denies the allegations. Lamine said he wanted to buy clothes for his children and found himself locked inside the store against his will. Unable to leave, he went to the toilets to smoke before drinking heavily from bottles of whisky and vodka he had brought with him. He said he doesn’t remember much of what happened next.
“You bring alcohol with you when shopping for your children?” the judge enquired.
“They let us in with them!” he retorted.
Lamine insists that he approached a member of security staff of his own accord early that morning, after having tried – and failed – to reach the police by phone on two occasions.
Read moreAnger at rising fuel prices bolsters Europe's far right as unrest sweeps France
The judge reviews Lamine’s troubled history: A criminal record tallying 22 offences including violence, theft, resisting arrest, insulting public officials and driving without a licence.
The father of five – soon to be six – acknowledges a small “problem with alcohol”. Above all, he emphasises his new job: he has been working in construction via a temporary employment agency for two months.
Sofiane, who has spent the last year working as a forklift operator at Amazon, also has a criminal record, but insists on having stayed out of trouble since leaving prison in 2018.
The prosecutor describes the two men as having succumbed to the lure of easy gain, “tempted to take advantage of the weekend’s sad events” and requests sentences tailored to each defendant.
In contrast, the defendents' lawyer characterises the episode as a “daydream” involving two people “trying out the clothes and sitting on the armchairs” of the luxury brand. He requests an acquittal.
'I found them on the ground'
Defendants appear one after another in the dock. The presiding judge begins each hearing with the same question: "Do you wish to be tried immediately?"
Following time spent in custody, defendants must be brought before a judge within 20 hours. Some, however, ask for more time to prepare their defence, including Blairda M, who is accused of acts of violence on the sidelines of the demonstrations. The question then becomes whether the alleged perpetrators should be held in custody or released pending trial.
Blairda’s lawyer argues he has well-established ties to the community and is employed. The prosecutor, meanwhile, requests pretrial detention because of the seriousness of the allegations against him.
Others want to be tried immediately, but their lawyers can’t be found because they are busy in other courtrooms. This is the case for Moustafa D, whose trial finally takes place at the end of the day. The 18-year-old, who is training to become a construction site supervisor and has no previous convictions, is accused of throwing projectiles at police officers, resisting arrest and handling stolen goods. He was caught in possession of seven pairs of sunglasses and a Nike t-shirt.
Moustafa denies any acts violence, saying he struggled during his arrest because he could not breathe, and he maintains he picked up the items without any criminal intent.
Read moreFrance faces reckoning with public order policing after violent protest weekend
“I found them on the ground. I didn’t know it was theft,” he says.
“There’s chaos all around you, and these are what you notice?” the judge asks. “You know perfectly well the glasses came from a looted shop,” she continues.
He nods almost imperceptibly. Once again, given the allegations, the prosecutor requests a prison sentence.
It is then time for the judges to deliberate. The courtroom empties. In the corridor, a man paces back and forth. He is looking desperately for his son, a young man who was also arrested over the weekend in the Les Halles district. “A friend of his told me he’d been taken away. I had to keep pestering police stations to find out he would be brought before the court today. I understand that the police get a lot of calls, but still!” he said irritably. A lawyer tries to help him, with little success.
Back in the courtroom, the judges return to deliver their decisions.
Victor B, the audiovisual production student, and Moustafa D, the trainee construction site supervisor, are found guilty but are spared imprisonment given their clean criminal records. Instead, they receive six-month and ten-month suspended prison sentences, respectively.
For the incident at Louis Vuitton, Lamine B receives a ten-month prison sentence under a day-release arrangement which the judge noted would enable him ‘to continue working during the day” while spending his nights in prison. His friend Sofiane receives a six-month sentence to be served under electronic tag monitoring. A civil hearing at a later date will determine the financial damages incurred by the French luxury brand.
Finally, Blairda avoids detention pending trial. Released under judicial supervision, he is required to report to the police station every week until his hearing.

Global diesel prices seen staying high despite Trump’s deal with Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:15:00 UTC
23:15:00 KST

Global diesel prices seen staying high despite Trump’s deal with Russia
- Trump’s deal with Russia is unlikely to cut diesel prices much. Analysts said the promised volumes are too small to ease the global supply squeeze.
- US diesel prices have stayed above US$6 a gallon since September. The issue has become a political risk for Trump and Republicans before the Nov 3 midterm elections.
- Russia may struggle to deliver the extra fuel because of weak refining, high freight costs and sanctions. The International Energy Agency warned shortages could last until 2027.
AI generated
NEW YORK - US President Donald Trump’s deal with Russia to supply diesel to US and global markets is unlikely to meaningfully lower diesel prices, market watchers and analysts said, noting that the promised volumes are too small to ease a global supply squeeze.
Diesel prices have shot to record highs during the US-Israeli war on Iran, creating a political liability for Trump and his Republican party as they campaign to maintain thin majorities in the US Congress in the Nov 3 midterm elections.
Critics of Trump’s move said lifting sanctions on Russian diesel could help Moscow fund further attacks on Ukraine, undermining years of efforts to curb Russian energy revenues and raising the risk the Kremlin could profit while consumers get little relief from high fuel prices.
Trump said Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric tons, or 2.25 million barrels, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter”.
Analysts have said it may not be possible for Russia to produce enough excess diesel in the near-term to meet those ambitious goals, while a strained global tanker market may also make timely shipments difficult.
Analysts also said the announced volumes are unlikely to meaningfully lower diesel prices.
US retail diesel prices topped US$6 a gallon in September for the first time ever and have remained above that level since.
Big promises, limited impact
Michelle Brouhard, head of policy and geopolitical risk at Kpler, said it would take an additional 400,000 barrels per day of diesel supply to materially ease prices in the current market.
But the initial shipment of roughly 2.2 million barrels would amount to only about 73,000 bpd if distributed over a month.
She said that volume on its own would probably not significantly affect global diesel prices.
Caspian Conran, lead economist at consulting firm Baringa, estimated that the market would require an additional 850,000 bpd of supply to produce an immediate softening in prices.
Trump initially said Russia would immediately supply diesel to the US and global markets to help bring down fuel prices, but later said the Russian cargoes would be released to global markets rather than shipped to the US.
This raised questions about whether the deal will deliver the domestic supply relief the president promised.
“The diesel that Putin was going to sell, they were going to make it available to the global market one way or the other,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said over the weekend. “The only difference is how much of it the US was going to get.”
White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said Trump announced that “massive amounts” of Russian diesel will supply the global markets and will lower prices at home and abroad.
“President Trump continues to secure good deals, not just for the United States, but for the world,” Rogers said.
Strained refining system, high freight rates
It was unclear whether Russia can substantially increase diesel exports in the near term due to limited Russian export availability and elevated freight costs.
Shipping data on Oct 20 showed some Russian diesel cargoes were returning to their traditional destinations after the US suspended sanctions and secured the lifting of an export ban.
At least two tankers were signalling trips to Turkey and Brazil.
Data also showed Russia has resumed diesel export loadings from the Baltic port of Primorsk following an agreement between Washington and Moscow to supply fuel to global markets.
Disruptions to diesel exports from Russia, the world’s second-largest diesel exporter after the US, and the Middle East reached 1.3 million barrels per day in September, about 4.5% of global diesel and gasoil demand.
The International Energy Agency has warned shortages could persist into 2027.
“We question whether Russia’s refineries could even support an increase in exports with, by some estimates, up to 45% of Russia’s refining capacity currently offline,” said Mary Melton, an analyst with tanker company Braemar.
Delivering the announced volumes in addition to existing exports would require Russia to produce roughly 384,000 to 509,000 barrels per day of diesel, the Energy Policy Research Foundation said in a note.
Russia currently produces about 1.4 million barrels per day and consumes roughly 1.2 million barrels per day domestically, leaving little surplus available for export.
Traders noted the country is currently importing distillates and lacks sufficient production and surplus volumes.
While an end to attacks could allow damaged facilities to begin repairs and eventually return to international markets, sources said that is unlikely to happen before the end of the year, a view widely shared across the market.
Ukraine resumed its attacks on Russian refineries last week with a strike on a plant in the Ryazan region.
Moreover, freight rates for Russian oil and fuel exports have also risen sharply amid heightened security risks in the Black Sea.
A tight global tanker market has also raised the cost of moving cargoes.
Many tanker owners and operators are probably reluctant to move Russian diesel on their ships, fearing future customers may shun the ships due to worries of having moved sanctioned cargoes, a source at a tanker owner said.
While Trump has temporarily removed US sanctions, he noted, other Western nations still have sanctions in place. REUTERS

Araghchi warns of further escalation around Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:14:46 UTC
23:14:46 KST

In an article published in the Financial Times, Araghchi also revealed that Iran had submitted a seven-day proposal to the United States through mediators, outlining steps to end the war, reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume negotiations toward a final agreement.
Referring to his meetings with several foreign ministers on the sidelines of last month’s United Nations General Assembly, Araghchi said that although the discussions covered different issues, they conveyed a common message: Iran wants a fair and dignified agreement with the United States.
He said reaching such an agreement would require the White House to demonstrate genuine seriousness and resolve to permanently end its acts of aggression against Iran.
Araghchi stressed that Iran was firmly pursuing a peaceful and dignified solution to the conflict while remaining fully prepared to defend itself.
He said U.S. President Donald Trump entered the war based on fundamentally mistaken assumptions about Iran’s resilience and endurance. According to Araghchi, Trump appears to continue receiving misinformation suggesting that Iran’s armed forces are incapable of defending the country, an assessment that, he said, is contradicted by the available evidence.
He added that Iran’s armed forces had learned valuable lessons from Israeli and U.S. military actions against the country since 2025.
Araghchi said Iran had absolutely no confidence in the U.S. government’s stated desire for peace.
To explain Tehran’s position, he pointed to military attacks in June 2025 and February 2026, saying they took place while negotiations were actively underway.
He also said Iran came under attack for a third time in June this year, shortly after an agreement had been signed by Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Trump.
Asking how Iran could trust the U.S. president again, Araghchi said there was little reason to expect progress under current circumstances, given that the White House had shown neither a willingness to reach an understanding on the way forward nor any intention of abandoning threats to use further force.
Araghchi said the recent escalation across the region demonstrated how quickly the conflict could spread and how far-reaching its consequences could become, posing a serious threat to international peace and security.
Despite these circumstances, he said, his responsibility as a professional diplomat was to make every possible effort to give diplomacy a chance, even when the prospects for success were limited.
The Iranian foreign minister revealed that, through mediators, he had presented Washington with a seven-day proposal on the sidelines of the recent UN General Assembly session. The plan outlines steps both sides would need to take to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Araghchi stressed that the proposal did not require the United States to take any action to which it had not already agreed.
Under the proposed timeline, the Strait of Hormuz would reopen on the sixth day, while negotiations toward a final agreement would resume on the seventh day. Araghchi said implementing the plan could gradually restore normal life across the region.
Araghchi also addressed the economic consequences of the war for the United States, saying the White House was refusing to acknowledge the mounting costs borne by ordinary Americans.
Citing an estimate by credit rating agency Moody’s, he wrote that U.S. military action against Iran had cost American consumers approximately $265 billion in the current year alone, equivalent to about $2,000 per household.
He said the sharp increase in energy prices accounted for nearly half of that amount, while the estimate did not include the much greater damage inflicted on the global economy.
Araghchi added that damage to numerous U.S. military bases across the region and the loss of substantial quantities of military equipment further highlighted the consequences of the war for American interests.
Referring to Iran’s geographical position, Araghchi said the country would always have significant leverage over maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz because of its location.
He argued that, despite discussions about alternative routes, the waterway could not be replaced for either the region or the global economy.
At the same time, he said Iran intended to remain committed to its historic role in safeguarding the Strait of Hormuz and protecting vessels that pass through it lawfully.
Araghchi said a way out of the crisis remained possible, but it would require the U.S. government to sincerely acknowledge that military options were no longer effective.
Referring to nearly eight months of war, he said none of the objectives Washington had publicly announced for its attacks on Iran had been achieved.
In conclusion, Araghchi reiterated his warning that any further escalation around the Strait of Hormuz or elsewhere in the region would seriously threaten civilian lives, the security and prosperity of regional countries, and the global economy.
He warned that if the United States once again chose military action over diplomacy, the outcome would be a far greater strategic defeat.
Emphasizing Iran’s long and proud history, Araghchi said the country would not bow to any power. He added that Tehran remained prepared to give diplomacy another chance if it saw clear evidence that Washington was genuinely willing to pursue a fair and dignified solution aimed at permanently ending the conflict.
Araghchi concluded that repeating the miscalculations Trump made about Iran at the start of the war would lead to far more painful consequences under the current circumstances.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Foreign players exploiting “home-grown protest movement”
According to the Disinformation Commission’s report, findings that were also shared by French and European intelligence agencies according to the FT, the unrest in France originally stemmed from domestic dissatisfaction, particularly the Sept. 17 teachers’ strike.
According to the watchdog’s report, there is no evidence that it was instigated, controlled, or directed by foreign states. It does say, however, that there is strong evidence that Russia and Iran, along with foreign far-left and far-right influencers, are actively exploiting and attempting to inflame the protests.
Both the Disinformation Commission report and the FT article say social media has been flooded with videos of rioting and looting that portray France as descending into chaos and on the brink of a civil war.
Russian Ports Lose Up to 100% of Cargo, Seek Government Bailout After Drone Strikes
Analysis of much of the footage by the disinformation watchdog shows that, at the start, these were often scenes taken from previous instances of public unrest. This included old footage of a 2022 Kurdish protest, 2024 demonstrations in Tbilisi, Georgia, and celebrations following Paris Saint-Germain’s Champions League victory last year, all of which were presented as current rioting in France. The videos garnered several million online views.
As the French protests grew, these “historic” scenes were replaced with fresh footage from the actual rioting that was now taking place in several cities, further inflaming an already spiraling situation.
While the formal EU investigation was described as being at its early stages, others are in no doubt that Russia and, to a lesser extent Iran and Algeria are intent on making the situation worse. Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto described the unrest as “a manifestation of a hybrid war being waged against European countries via TikTok, YouTube, and social media.” He also attributed weekend riots in Milan as being exacerbated by the same exploitative methods.
Evidence against Russian bots
According to the Disinformation Commission’s report, Russian “Matryoshka” bots impersonated established news organizations, including AFP, DW, and Le Monde, to produce almost two dozen fake reports in just two daythat claimed the deaths of 54 schoolteachers and an attack by Muslim pupils on the Pope.
The assessment was that: “This is Matryoshka’s usual method: impersonate trusted media, then tag fact-checkers to draw attention.” The group has repeatedly carried out activities aimed at undermining support for Ukraine, but have been accused of carrying out disinformation campaigns in Europe for more than 10 years. This includes the “Star of David” graffiti campaign that beset Paris in 2023 and most recently AI attacks on Democrats during the US mid-term election campaigns.
Separately, the disinformation watchdog says the Russian Pravda/Portal Kombat propaganda network published more than 20 items across two French-language websites about the Oct. 17 disturbances. Much of the material originated from pro-Kremlin milbloggers, including Rybar, Readovka, and Zakharova, as well as state media and other Russian commentators.
However, the FT cites an unnamed European intelligence official as saying: “It would be too simplistic to say that the Russians are to blame for everything.”
More may come
The rioting and protests began on Oct. 17, when more than half a million people took to the streets to protest rising prices, teacher shortages, and poor school conditions, according to France’s Interior Ministry.
As the protests spread, they became increasingly violent, with clashes between demonstrators and police, widespread looting, and arson attacks in Paris, Lyon, Marseille, and other cities. During the unrest in Limoges, the historic City Hall building was destroyed by fire. In response, authorities imposed nighttime curfews in parts of Paris and other cities, while more than 2,400 people were arrested.
According to the FT, the EU’s diplomatic service says that France, after Ukraine, is the second most targeted country in continental Europe when it comes to state-sponsored manipulation of information. The newspaper reported that representatives of digital regulatory authorities from all EU member states met on Tuesday to discuss the situation.
More protests are planned for Saturday, Oct. 24.

US congressional candidate Brad Lander detained in West Bank
Lander says dozens remain in Israeli custody after being detained while helping Palestinian farmers harvest olives.
United States Democratic congressional candidate Brad Lander says he has been released from Israeli military custody with a warning after being detained alongside dozens of volunteers helping Palestinian farmers harvest olives in the occupied West Bank.
But several dozen others, including rabbis and international volunteers, remain in detention, according to Lander, who called for them to be released immediately after the incident Wednesday.
“I’ve been released from [Israeli army] custody with a ‘warning,’ apparently because of my public profile,” Lander wrote on X. “I told them I wasn’t even a congressmember yet, just a nominee.”
Lander, a Jewish American and former New York City comptroller, was among approximately 80 volunteers detained by Israeli soldiers and police near the village of Nahalin, outside Bethlehem, according to the Israeli organisation Rabbis for Human Rights.
The group included American, Israeli, Palestinian, British and Canadian volunteers.
Becca Strober, a representative of the Protect the Harvest Coalition, which helped organise the olive harvest, told Al Jazeera that the group had been picking olives at the invitation of a Palestinian family for several hours when the Israeli army arrived.
“It was a nice, peaceful day,” he said. “There was no conflict. There was no settler violence. There was no violence of any kind.”
According to Strober, after a while, soldiers began checking the volunteers’ IDs, and soon after, issued an order declaring the area a closed military zone. They then detained the group, first in the field and later at a police station.
“To this moment, everyone’s still detained except for Brad Lander,” said Strober. “They very clearly told him that they allowed him to be released because he’s likely to be in Congress very soon.”
Israel’s Foreign Ministry, meanwhile, accused Lander of staging a “calculated political provocation,” alleging that he’d deliberately entered a restricted security area without approval.
“This was not about harvesting olives. It was about harvesting headlines,” the ministry said in a statement on X, alleging that Lander’s team and reached out to Israeli representatives in the US in advance of the visit and had been told it would require coordination with relevant authorities, but that Lander ignored those instructions.
“Brad Lander came looking for a confrontation,” said the statement. “Now he is pretending to be its victim.”
Anton Goodman, acting director for Rabbis for Human Rights, told Reuters that volunteers who were neither Israeli nor Palestinian citizens were expected to be transferred to an Israeli military base.
In a video posted on X from one of the buses, Lander said Israeli forces had detained the group after apparently being called to the area by settlement security personnel.
“We’ve been detained by the Israeli military for harvesting olives,” he said. “And let’s be clear, occupation is a crime under international law. Harvesting olives is not a crime under any law.”
It’s not clear why the area was declared a closed military zone. Rabbis for Human Rights said the olive pickers had no way of knowing about the order and had offered to leave voluntarily when they were told.
Lander said the volunteers had been taken away for processing, but had not been told whether they were under arrest.
Lander, a vocal critic of Israel’s war on Gaza, is a former New York City mayoral candidate and an ally of Mayor Zohran Mamdani. He’s now running as the Democratic nominee for New York’s 10th Congressional District in the US’s November 3 midterm elections.
Writing on X after his release, Lander said Palestinians face worse consequences every day.
“These detentions by the [Israeli army] are one more attempt to undermine Palestinians’ right to harvest their olive groves, travel on their roads, and live in their homes,” he wrote. “Yet one more element of escalating, and very clearly state-sponsored, ethnic cleansing.”
Neither the Israeli government nor the US Embassy in Jerusalem immediately responded to a request for comment.
The volunteers had travelled to the West Bank to support Palestinian farmers during the annual olive harvest, amid a surge in settler violence, including several attacks in recent days targeting Palestinians and international observers.
Strober said Wednesday was the first time the Palestinian family picking olives had been able to access its own land since October 7, 2023 because violence in the area had made it too dangerous to return.
“The fact that Brad was there, of course, made the situation more newsworthy, but we’ve been seeing this happen in the West Bank for years,” she said.
On Friday, an American photojournalist working for The Washington Post was beaten by Israeli settlers while covering the olive harvest. The following day, European diplomats and a French mayor were attacked by settlers during another harvest. Palestinians were also attacked in both incidents.
Israeli police said on Tuesday that they had arrested 10 people in connection with the attacks.

Russian Su-30 fighter jet crashes in Kaliningrad Oblast during training exercises, Moscow says
A Russian Su-30 fighter jet crashed during a scheduled training flight in Kaliningrad Oblast, a heavily militarized Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea bordering Poland and Lithuania, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Oct. 21.
Moscow has not elaborated on the reason for the plane crash. The Russian Defense Ministry said the crew ejected and evacuated by a ground search-and-rescue team, without disclosing whether they were injured.
The jet crashed near the town of Chernyakhovsk, about 90 kilometers (about 56 miles) east of Kaliningrad, according to the pro-Kremlin Mash Telegram channel. It said that both pilots were injured and were taken to a military hospital.
The Su-30 is a two-seat, multirole fighter for air-to-air and air-to-ground missions. Moscow said that the jet was not carrying any weapons at the time of the crash.
Russia has had multiple instances of a aircraft crashing during training exercises, including ones that led to the death of crew members aboard. In September, a Russian Tu-95 aircraft crashed in Russia's Amur Oblast during training, killing six crew members and injuring one, the Kremlin-controlled Interfax news agency said on Sept. 29, citing the Russian Defense Ministry.
The crash also occurred amid escalating tensions between Russia and NATO over Kaliningrad, prompting Lithuania's Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas to call for troops to be deployed to the country's border with the Russian exclave.

Feeding Our Tomorrow: how India’s women-led, sustainable farming is reaching Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:11:44 UTC
23:11:44 KST

At SIAL Paris 2026, the India Trade Promotion Organisation put sustainable agriculture, women’s empowerment and a changing relationship with Europe at the heart of India’s food story.
When Jawed Ashraf took to the stage at the opening of SIAL Paris 2026, in the presence of French Minister Anne Genevard and an international audience, he described an agricultural revolution taking place across India. Led by small farmers, he said, it rests on diversity, resilience, sustainability and greater self-sufficiency. These themes defined the India pavilion, which carried a simple title: “Feeding Our Tomorrow”.
As Chairman of the India Trade Promotion Organisation (ITPO), Ashraf led India’s presence as Partner Country at the exhibition, held at Paris Nord Villepinte from 17 to 21 October 2026. He knows the French capital well: he was India’s ambassador to France and Monaco from 2020 to 2024 and received the Commander de la Légion d’honneur for his service. More than 140 Indian exporters joined the pavilion, with live culinary masterclasses and a programme on plant protein, women-led agriculture and rice exports.
A farm sector built on sustainability
Ashraf described a shift towards more sustainable, climate-resilient farming, with less chemical use and better traceability. Drones, sensors, artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things (IoT) help farmers manage water, fertilisers and crop protection more efficiently, a growing advantage as extreme weather puts pressure on food production.
The stakes are global. Feeding a growing population amid climate pressure, trade disruption and inflation will demand change. India already produces grains, fruit, vegetables, dairy, meat and seafood for roughly one sixth of humanity, and Ashraf sees that capacity, paired with more sustainable methods, as part of the answer.
2026: the year of the woman farmer
The UN has designated 2026 the International Year of the Woman Farmer, and Ashraf used the occasion to highlight the role women play in India’s agricultural transformation. Many farmer/producer organisations are founded and run by women, raising household incomes and giving women greater independence and influence in their communities.
One of those women travelled to Paris. Priyanka Rhushikesh Mohite, from Nashik in Maharashtra, is a certified agricultural drone pilot. Her husband, an agricultural adviser, heard about a Government of India scheme training rural women to operate drones, the Namo Drone Didi Scheme. She applied, won a place and completed a month of training in Pune. She has flown since August 2024.
The practical gains are striking. Her drone sprays nano fertilisers and spreads seeds. Watering an acre once took a full day and around 200 litres of water. With the drone, she says, it takes seven to eight minutes and 10 litres.
Yet technology is only part of her story. “I am a simple housewife,” she says. Becoming a pilot has given her an identity of her own, respect in her community and the chance to encourage other women to follow. Before 2024, she could never have imagined travelling to Paris, and she thanked ITPO for the opportunity.
A trade deal with wider reach
A free trade agreement (FTA) reduces or removes customs duties on many traded goods and sets rules to ease cross-border commerce. The EU-India FTA was concluded in January 2026 and is expected to be signed by the end of the year. It builds on India’s arrangements with the UK and the European Free Trade Association, which have opened further opportunities for Indian food products through zero or reduced tariffs.
Ashraf believes the benefits could reach farmers and small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), provided they meet market requirements and reach European buyers. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has called the agreement the “mother of all deals”. Ashraf sees a partnership between economies representing around two billion people, with democracy and the rule of law as shared foundations.
Its reach extends well beyond food. According to Ashraf, India’s exports to Europe have grown by more than 100% in a decade, led by electronics, machinery, electrical goods and mobile phones. Future cooperation could span artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing equipment for data centres, clean energy, green mobility, biopharmaceuticals and critical minerals, alongside digital technology, defence, education and science. Energy security is a shared concern, and he sees nuclear power as one area for closer work.
He says trade between India and Europe has nearly doubled in a decade and that European investment in India has risen from 80 billion to 140 billion in four years. In France, bilateral goods trade stood at around €13.6 billion in 2025-26, and 38 CAC 40 companies operate in India.
“An FTA is an enabler,” Ashraf says. Exporters and trade agencies must now turn it into business.
From commodities to brands
For food exporters, that means thinking beyond volume and price. Ashraf wants more Indian products to build a recognisable presence in Europe, which requires understanding European standards, strengthening logistics and creating products that stand out on the shelf. At SIAL the emphasis was on packaged, ready-to-eat and premium foods, backed by traceability and geographical indication tags for products tied to particular places, such as Naga chilli and Mithila makhana, the edible seeds of the fox nut plant.
ITPO is also considering offices in several European cities, with Frankfurt, Paris, Milan and Rotterdam among the options.
Taking flight
Priyanka Rhushikesh Mohite’s journey to become a drone pilot is one example of what that change can look like. Her drone is a practical tool for farming. It has also given her a profession, a public voice and a reason to imagine new possibilities for other women in her community.
For India, the challenge now is to turn that kind of progress into something more widespread, while building a stronger presence for its food producers in European markets.

What to Say When Someone Cuts in Line in Front of You
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:05:54 UTC
23:05:54 KST

Wait a second. You’ve been standing in line for 20 minutes, famished and desperate to order one of the viral bagels that keep selling out—or for six hours outside a concert venue, determined to claim a spot at the barricade to see your favorite band.
And then someone strolls up and slips in line ahead of you. Apparently, the rest of you have been standing around for the ambiance.
How much of a sin are line-cutters committing? “You are ripping the fabric of society apart,” says Nick Leighton, an etiquette expert and co-host of the podcast Were You Raised by Wolves? Queue-jumpers have to live with that, he adds. “But worse, we have to live with you.”
Here’s exactly how to handle this maddening situation—including when and how best to speak up.
When to speak up about someone cutting in line
If a stranger jumping ahead of you feels strangely personal, Richard C. Larson, a professor emeritus of data, systems, and society at MIT who has studied queuing, understands why. “We only have a finite number of minutes of life on Earth,” he says. The cutter’s implied message: “A minute of my life is worth more than a minute of yours.”
Before you decide whether to confront the offender, think about what speaking up would accomplish. Are you trying to reclaim your turn or get revenge? Sometimes, the impulse is “to sort of let them know you think they’re a jerk,” says Ryan Martin, a professor of psychology and dean of the College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences at the University of Wisconsin–Green Bay, known online as the Anger Professor because he studies strong emotions.
Martin would speak up to help someone recognize “that what they did wasn’t OK and that I wanted them to go to the back of the line,” he says. But he’d also consider: “What is going to allow me to have the kind of night I want to have?” If you spend the concert replaying a confrontation instead of singing your happy heart out, you’ve lost more than your place in line.
Leighton's gut check for situations like these is to ask yourself: Is this the hill you want to die on? “That’s always a good etiquette question,” he says.
Consider your safety, too. If the person seems hostile or you feel uneasy approaching them, you can ask staff for help or let the cut go. “Health and safety always trumps etiquette,” Leighton says.
What to say—if you do decide to say something
Marie Helweg-Larsen, a professor of psychology at Dickinson College who studies social norms, has explored what makes line-cutting so rage-inducing. For a 2008 study, she and a colleague surveyed U2 fans waiting for prime concert-floor spots, asking how they would react to hypothetical line-cutting scenarios.
Interestingly, fans reacted just as negatively to someone cutting behind them as ahead of them—even though their own place wasn’t affected. “You have to have people follow the rules,” she says, “or your investment into the line falls apart.” Helweg-Larsen’s co-author also heard fans invoke a higher authority when someone misbehaved: “Bono wouldn’t like that!”
You don’t need a rock star’s moral authority—or a grand speech—to point out where the line starts. Helweg-Larsen’s suggested opener: “Excuse me, but the line starts down there.” Aim for an “‘I’m just trying to be helpful’ kind of vibe,” she says.
That approach gives the person a chance to correct their mistake without having to defend their character. And you don’t have to believe it was an innocent oversight to deliver the message graciously. “Even if they’re doing it on purpose, you still need to use that tone,” Leighton says.
He’s been on the receiving end of a polite correction himself: At a deli, he once joined what he thought was the back of the line, only to discover he’d guessed wrong. He was happy for someone to point him in the right direction.
If you decide to speak up, do it promptly. “Your window of opportunity is short,” Leighton says. “As soon as it happens, that’s when you need to say something.” Waiting until you’ve spent five minutes glaring at the back of someone’s head won’t make the conversation any easier.
For a line that represents a serious investment of time, Martin suggests spelling that out: “Hey, I’m not sure you noticed, but there’s actually a really long line here, and people have been waiting all day.” You’ve identified the problem and given them an opening to say “Oops.”
Of course, some situations are murkier than a stranger breezing past the entire queue. Someone returning from a bathroom break is different from four friends arriving hours later to join the person who saved their places. Leighton is sympathetic to a water or restroom run. Holding spots all day for a last-minute entourage? “I don’t love that,” he says.
What to do if a line-cutter won’t move
Sometimes, your kind reminder won’t be met with the same level of helpfulness: They saw the line. They’re staying put. Now what?
If you feel comfortable continuing, Martin suggests a firmer follow-up: “I really think you should go back to the back of the line.” You’re making a direct request without adding an insult.
Larson advises skipping any confrontational nicknames or demands—like “What do you think you’re doing, bud?” You’re pointing someone toward the back of the line, not challenging them to a duel.
If the person still refuses to move, resist the urge to keep arguing. “We can’t control everybody,” Martin says. Continuing to push someone who’s already refused could lead to “a more significant confrontation.”
At a concert venue, amusement park, or other staffed location, you can ask an employee or security person to step in. “You can always appeal to a higher authority,” Leighton says. Whether they’ll enforce the rules is another question, but it’s an option worth trying when the cutting is particularly egregious.
If you decide to drop it, drop the parting shot, too. A sarcastic “Must be nice!” might feel irresistible, but Leighton advises against adding more rudeness to the encounter. “It will not achieve anything,” he says.
As Larson puts it, “A fight can ruin your whole day—or life.”

Eight hearings postponed in a row: who is stalling the case concerning medical negligence by Odrex doctors?
Kyiv • UNN
On October 21, the Kyivskyi District Court of Odesa was again unable to hold a hearing in the case concerning medical negligence by Odrex doctors due to the continuation of the sick leave of the accused, Vitaliy Rusakov. The hearing scheduled for October 22 will also not take place. Thus, all three hearings scheduled for this week have been postponed.
On October 21, the Kyivskyi District Court of Odesa once again failed to continue hearing the case concerning medical negligence by doctors at the private Odrex clinic. One of the defendants, Vitalii Rusakov, did not appear in court and filed a motion to postpone the hearing due to the extension of his sick leave. The next hearing is scheduled for October 27, UNN reports.
Details
As a result, the court held none of the three hearings scheduled for the current week. Overall, in October, seven consecutive hearings have already failed to take place because of motions filed by the defense. The eighth hearing, scheduled for October 22, was canceled for the same reason.
According to UNN's sources familiar with the case, the participants in the proceedings expected Vitalii Rusakov to join the court hearing remotely via videoconference. However, this did not happen.
The case concerns criminal proceedings against surgeon Vitalii Rusakov and oncologist Maryna Bielotserkovska, who have been charged under Part 1 of Article 140 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine — improper performance of professional duties by a medical worker that caused grave consequences for a patient.
The case concerns the death of Odesa businessman Adnan Kivan, who died on October 27, 2024, while being treated for cancer at the private Odrex clinic. According to the investigation, after surgery, the doctors may have failed to prescribe the necessary antibacterial therapy to the patient and may have responded inadequately to postoperative complications. This could have led to the development of sepsis, which, against the background of the cancer, may have caused the businessman's death. The defendants do not admit their guilt. The court must provide the final assessment of their actions.
Reminder
The trial in the case concerning medical negligence by Odrex doctors has been ongoing for almost a year. During this time, the proceedings have been accompanied by numerous motions from the defense, motions to recuse judges, and systematic postponements of hearings.
Systematic postponements create a risk that the statute of limitations will expire. Part 1 of Article 140 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine provides, in particular, for up to two years of imprisonment, while the statute of limitations for such an offense is three years. If the actions attributed to the doctors took place in October 2024, the relevant period may expire as early as autumn 2027 in the absence of statutory grounds for its suspension or interruption.

====================================================================================================

Extraversion is linked to faster relief from depressive symptoms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:00:45 UTC
23:00:45 KST

As patients receive inpatient treatment for depression, their personality traits often shift in tandem with their recovering mood, pointing to a deeply intertwined relationship between character and mental health. Individuals with higher average levels of neuroticism experience a slower recovery across a wide range of depressive symptoms, while those who lean toward extraversion or agreeableness tend to bounce back faster. These findings were recently published in the Journal of Affective Disorders.
Mental health professionals classify human personality into five broad domains, often called the Big Five. Neuroticism involves a tendency to experience negative emotions like sadness and worry. Extraversion reflects how outgoing, enthusiastic, and socially engaged a person is. Openness describes a willingness to try new things and embrace novel ideas.
Agreeableness involves being cooperative, empathetic, and trusting. Finally, conscientiousness is characterized by being organized, reliable, and goal-oriented. Together, these traits shape how individuals perceive the world and interact with others.
Depression is a highly varied condition. Two people diagnosed with major depressive disorder might experience entirely different challenges. One might sleep too much and feel constantly guilty, while another might suffer from insomnia and a total loss of appetite. Standard therapies help many people, but about one third of patients do not see their symptoms improve.
Researchers want to know why some people respond well to therapy while others do not. Personality is a prime suspect in this investigation. Prior studies have established a strong link between personality dimensions and psychiatric conditions. Neuroticism is generally viewed as a risk factor for mental health struggles, whereas extraversion and conscientiousness are often seen as protective traits.
Mara Carlotta Berg and Maike Richter, along with senior authors Mitja Back and Nils Opel, led the new investigation. The team includes researchers from the University of Münster and Charité Universitätsmedizin Berlin in Germany. They wanted to understand how personality and depression evolve together over time. They also wanted to look beyond total depression scores to see how specific symptoms respond to treatment in people with different personality profiles.
The research team recruited 334 psychiatric patients receiving care at a German university hospital. The participants had been diagnosed with affective or psychotic disorders, such as major depressive disorder or bipolar disorder. To be included in the analysis, patients needed to stay in the hospital for at least four weeks. This minimum duration allowed the research team to track their progress over a meaningful timeframe.
Patients completed digital questionnaires upon admission and then again roughly every two weeks. The final assessment took place shortly before they were discharged from the hospital. One questionnaire measured the severity of 21 different depressive symptoms experienced over the previous two weeks. This assessment included questions about mood, suicidal thoughts, and physical complaints.
A second questionnaire assessed the Big Five personality traits. The researchers opted for a very brief, 15-item version of a standard personality test. This shortened format reduced the burden on patients who were already dealing with severe mental health challenges. The research team then used statistical models to track how these scores shifted and interacted from admission to discharge.
The overall severity of depression dropped substantially across the study population as patients received inpatient care. Alongside this clinical improvement, the researchers observed coordinated shifts in how patients described their own personalities. Neuroticism scores went down over the course of the hospital stay. At the same time, scores for conscientiousness and extraversion went up.
The statistical models revealed a synchronized relationship between personality and mood. Patients who reported the steepest drops in neuroticism also experienced the largest reductions in their overall depression scores. The reverse was true for agreeableness, conscientiousness, and extraversion. For those three traits, greater increases over the course of treatment were tied to larger mood improvements.
The researchers then broke the depression data down to the level of individual symptoms. They wanted to see if a patient’s average personality profile during their stay influenced the speed of their recovery for specific issues. They found that higher average neuroticism was associated with slower improvement across 14 distinct symptoms.
These lingering issues spanned emotional problems like sadness, irritability, and suicidal thoughts, to physical complaints like insomnia, appetite loss, and somatic worries. The broad impact of neuroticism aligns with its reputation as a general vulnerability factor in mental health. Patients with high neuroticism often experience heightened emotional reactivity and persistent rumination, which might make these symptoms harder to shake.
Other personality traits were linked to faster recovery in specific areas. Patients with higher average extraversion saw quicker relief from seven symptoms, including work difficulty, indecisiveness, and pessimism. Higher average agreeableness mapped onto faster improvements in self-blame, guilt, and body image concerns. Openness was associated with a quicker return of sexual interest and a faster reduction in feelings of guilt.
Conscientiousness was the only trait that did not show these item-by-item associations with recovery speed. While conscientiousness increased overall as patients felt better, it did not seem to dictate the pace at which individual depressive symptoms faded. The researchers suspect that the benefits of conscientiousness might operate through broader behavioral habits that are not captured by specific symptom questions.
The study relies on observational data gathered during naturalistic treatment. Because patients received different types of therapy for varying lengths of time, the results cannot establish that personality directly caused the symptoms to change. The researchers note that the brief personality questionnaire used in the study has limited precision. The short test may have reduced the reliability of the measurements, particularly for the extraversion trait.
It is also difficult to separate true personality changes from a recovering mood. When people are deeply depressed, they often view themselves through a negative lens. The observed changes in personality traits might reflect enduring psychological growth. Alternatively, they might simply represent a return to the patient’s normal baseline as their depression lifts.
Future studies could track patients for months or years after discharge to see if the personality changes stick. Researchers could also use more comprehensive personality tests to confirm the symptom-specific findings. Understanding these patterns could eventually help mental health professionals design more personalized treatments.
Psychiatry is gradually moving toward precision medicine, where care is tailored to the individual rather than the diagnosis alone. If a clinician knows a patient has high neuroticism, they might anticipate a slower recovery and deploy targeted interventions earlier. These targeted interventions could focus specifically on emotion regulation or persistent rumination. Conversely, highly extraverted patients might benefit most from socially engaging group therapies.
The study, “Big Five personality dimensions and their association with depressive symptom severity over the treatment course,” was authored by Mara Carlotta Berg, Maike Richter, Marius Gruber, Janik Goltermann, Luise Victoria Claaß, Julian Herpertz, Ramona Leenings, Lara Gutfleisch, Jonathan Mathias Fasshauer, Michael Storck, Rogério Blitz, Udo Dannlowski, Mitja Back, and Nils Opel.

Military satellites could be refuelled in orbit
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher

15:00:44 BST
23:00:44 KST

Life extension of the in-service SKYNET 5 military communications satellites would use in-orbit servicing, assembly and manufacturing technologies, and any requirement for future defence satellites to be capable of refuelling will be considered on a capability-by-capability basis, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Olly Glover, the Liberal Democrat member for Didcot and Wantage, asked whether the Secretary of State will set out whether future defence satellites will be required to be refuelled.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence, said: “In-Orbit Servicing, Assembly and Manufacturing was one of four prioritised sub-sectors in the UK’s National Space Strategy. As part of our Defence Investment Plan the life extension of the in-service SKYNET 5 military communications satellites, would utilise ISAM technologies. The Ministry of Defence continues to consider the potential benefits of emerging in-orbit servicing technologies, including satellite refuelling, which could enhance the resilience, flexibility and operational life of Defence space capabilities. Any requirement for future Defence satellites to be capable of refuelling would be considered on a capability-by-capability basis, taking account of operational requirements, technological maturity and value for money.”
A geostationary communications satellite spends most of its propellant on station keeping, nudging itself back into position against the pull of the sun and moon, and it dies when the tanks run dry even though the radios still work.
SKYNET 5 was launched between 2007 and 2012 and built by Airbus, carrying British secure military communications across most of the globe, and the fleet has already run well past its original design life. SKYNET 6A is under construction with Airbus for launch later this decade, and this publication reported when the contract was awarded, with the wider SKYNET Enduring Capability programme covering the ground segment and future spacecraft.
