Peek into hidden worlds revealed by the 2026 Nikon Small World contest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:00:31 UTC
23:00:31 KST

Peek into hidden worlds revealed by the 2026 Nikon Small World contest
Winners include ink droplets frozen in flight and what a molting tardigrade leaves behind
Nestled within a rebuilt inkjet printer, droplets of ink hang suspended above a page. Seen through a microscope, the droplets reveal how an inkjet printer produces crisp, uniform letters.
Ole Bielfeldt, a design student in Cologne, Germany, has been photographing the microscopic world since about 2021. His interest began as a quarantine hobby, when an old school microscope from his attic gave him a way to explore while stuck at home during the pandemic.
His printer image won first place in the 2026 Nikon Small World photomicrography competition. To capture the winning photo, he built a custom rig that moved the paper instead of the printer’s ink nozzles, keeping the nozzles stationary and in focus.
The mini side of ‘macro’
Ole Bielfeldt created this custom rig to catch impossibly fast ink droplets midflight. The contraption is only a bit larger than his head. Swipe through to see what word the printer was spitting out ink to spell.
Bielfeldt estimates that the droplets traveled at nearly 20 meters per second — too fast for even his best slow-motion camera to resolve. To freeze their motion, Bielfeldt worked in darkness, illuminating the scene with a single brief flash. He instructed the printer to repeatedly spell out “macro,” a nod to his social media handle, macrofying.
Before this project, a printer was “like magic,” Bielfeldt says. Photographing its inner workings helped him understand how it operates.
Bielfeldt no longer takes the magic printers spit out for granted. “It’s so, so advanced technically, but at the same time it’s so, so common,” he says.
His photograph is one of 86 images recognized in this year’s competition, whose winners were announced October 21. Here are some of our other favorites.
Did you capture my jumping side?
This pollen-dusted jumping spider offers a close look at the bristling hairs and some of its eight eyes that are easy to miss with the naked eye.
John-Oliver Dum’s fascination with spiders began as a childhood fear. Dum says he suffered a particularly painful arachnid-inflicted bite when he was young. Several years ago, when he was inspired to study the movements of a curly hair tarantula (Tliltocatl albopilosus), Dum became passionate about capturing their beauty.
Preparations for his photographs can begin years before he submits them to a competition. His wife grows plants selected for their pollen, which Dum uses in his images.
“The biggest challenge was finding a spider like this on the right plants, with the right pollen attached to it, at exactly the right time of year and at exactly the right moment,” he says. “You need to understand not only the spider’s behavior, but also the surrounding insect and plant life and their seasonal rhythms.”
Dum hopes the photograph, which won second place, encourages viewers to look more closely, too. “We first have to see the beauty of this largely unknown world before we can truly understand what we may be destroying,” he says.
Seeing a mouse eye in a new way
It’s not a leaf and it’s not a flower. This cross section of a mouse eye is crisscrossed in fractals of blood vessels and tethered by the optic nerve.
Cell biologists Sinem Karaman and Satu Paavonsalo at the University of Helsinki visualize vascular networks, like blood vessels, to study how they work within tissues. The arrangement, Paavonsalo says, could even point to mechanisms underlying how these systems stop working in obesity and diabetes.
Paavonsalo says the duo set out to capture a mouse eye in 3-D, different from the flattened retinas typically used in her research. After meticulous mounting which required several attempts for an arrangement she was satisfied with, Paavonsalo still didn’t know for certain the image would turn out right.
“I had to hope that the sample was correctly positioned and that the staining was detected throughout the sample,” Paavonsalo says, which made her excitement upon seeing the image even more pronounced. The image won 19th place in the competition.
A tardigrade Easter egg
A water bear emerges from its shed cuticle, and oh! What’s that left behind? This egg will be protected by its mother’s discarded skin.
The tardigrade (Hypsibius exemplaris) is one of nature’s toughest creatures, able to survive space by going into a state of suspended animation. This species, emerging from its former skin, is only about two-and-a-half times as wide as a strand of hair. Evolutionary developmental biologist Gonzalo Quiroga-Artigas captured the image during his studies of these tiny wonders at the University of Montpellier in France.
In the tardigrade life cycle, “egg laying is closely synchronized with molting,” says Quiroga-Artigas. Tardigrades can lay up to about a dozen eggs at once, and the moment one sheds its old cuticle happens quickly enough that it’s easy to miss.
Snapping this image demanded painstaking mounting and imaging of many specimens. Quiroga-Artigas chose this particular one, which won 12th, because “the egg looks almost like a precious gem being left behind by its mother.”
The stretch of a slime mold
This slime mold (Hemitrichia sp.) was found in the heart of Brooklyn, N.Y., sprouting from a decaying log in Prospect Park. The image features the mold’s gelatinous fruiting bodies, which release spores as part of reproduction. To bring the delicate structures into sharp detail, Eric Epstein stacked 240 images.
First, Epstein searched local parks for slime molds to photograph, carefully cutting pieces of waterlogged wood free without disturbing his subjects. “In this liquidy state, any touch would demolish” the fruiting bodies, he says.
One species of slime mold closely mirrors the cosmic web of gas and dark matter connecting galaxies, which helps scientists to more accurately map the cosmos. Another species has fascinated researchers for its ability to pack a store of bacteria to feed the next generation, when it’s near death.
Epstein hopes the photograph hints “at [a] vast array of activity beyond our unaided perception.” The image won sixth place in the competition.
A brain full of stars
This cell could have become anything in the body. Through some scientific nudging, it burst into a brilliant neuron.
Clusters of nuclei, looking like flashpoints in an intricate web, were captured by undergraduate student Faith Fernandes and structural cell biologist James Glover at the University of California, Berkeley.
The image commemorates the team’s first attempt at crafting neurons from a particular kind of stem cell. “I was so instantly enamored with this piece that I made it my computer wallpaper as soon as it was taken,” Fernandes says.
The eruption of color depicts human induced pluripotent stem cells, which can become any type of cell in the body, that have developed into neurons. The neurotubules, which contribute to the structure of and transportation of intracellular molecules, appear blue. Orange indicates where the DNA is located.
The stem cells are created by reprogramming adult cells to a stage before the cell was locked into a path to become a specific type of cell. They are studied for their many potential applications in regenerative medicine.
Fernandes says she hopes that studying these cells will illuminate ways to address neurodegeneration in diseases such as Parkinson’s disease. Already, researchers have used these cells to regrow eye tissue, address premature aging in mouse studies and grow organs. The shot won an Image of Distinction title in the competition.

AI Guardrails Aren’t Stopping Criminal Hackers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

As AI adoption spreads among both malicious hackers and defenders, even relatively unsophisticated cybercriminals are incorporating agentic AI into their campaigns and getting around model safeguards, according to new details published on Wednesday about recent successful attacks by four different threat groups.
Researchers from the threat intelligence firm CrowdStrike looked at the AI infrastructure powering attacks perpetrated between May and August by four previously unreported groups—one that operates in Chinese, one in Spanish and English, one in Indonesian, and one in Russian. The former two exhibited sophisticated AI “harnesses,” the software that supports and guides a model to carry out tasks. The latter two showed less technical prowess, researchers found, but were still able to compromise multiple targets. All had left their AI infrastructure openly accessible on web servers, allowing the researchers to analyze their activity and which models they used—largely versions of Anthropic’s Claude as well as versions of the open-weight Deepseek models. All the actors devised ways to allow their campaigns to run autonomously over relatively long periods of time.
“You can leverage different models for different aspects in the operation. Model routing and selection is very important because it’s expensive and a lot of times would be overkill to use newer models,” says Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike's senior vice president of counter adversary work. The researchers observed the attackers using both open- and closed-weight models; in almost all cases, they were using older versions rather than working with frontier models. Meyers notes that doing as much as possible with older models is common in legitimate AI usage, too, as costs mount.
The attackers also used multiple models to take advantage of differences in the guardrails meant to prevent people from using AI to carry out digital attacks.
“The models don't all have equivalent guardrails and protections, even from one company,” Meyers says. He adds about the sophistication of the hacking campaigns overall that “these attacks are not using new exploits or novel vulnerabilities. They’re really just taking advantage of the speed and the volume that you can use AI for in conducting these operations targeting the bulk of security hygiene issues in a lot of these environments—things that were preventable but weren’t prevented.”
The researchers found that all four threat actors circumvented AI safeguards, often by convincing a model that the activity was all legitimate and authorized, often for penetration testing or other security evaluation. One method used by many of the groups involves adding files to an agent’s working directory to try to show that tasks are approved and authorized. The attackers also used traditional jailbreaking methods, crafting prompts and narratives framing their hacking as authorized and benign, and proactively addressing potential questions or concerns the models might raise. The more sophisticated actors were typically more strategic in their world-building, while the less sophisticated actors sometimes resorted to more crude and aggressive prompts that tried to bully the models into accepting that the activity was legitimate.
The Chinese-speaking actor also used what's known as a “run time patch,” in this case a tool known as ClawGod, to add functionality on top of Claude Code and attempt to remove the “CYBER_RISK_INSTRUCTION” from the Claude Code system prompt, an instruction directing Claude Code to only participate in authorized security testing, not abusive or destructive hacking.
The actor that worked in Spanish and English targeted Argentine health care entities and successfully compromised at least 15 organizations. CrowdStrike researchers see evidence that the actor stole credentials and medical records from at least one of these victims. The actor special built a penetration testing harness, the kind an organization would use to test its own infrastructure, to find and fix vulnerabilities. Using models including Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Haiku 4.5, and Deepseek V4 Pro, the group set up a full infrastructure for autonomous attacks involving a “Supervisor” Claude Code agent to direct the steps of an attack and an “Executor” agent to carry them out.
The attacker working in Chinese also built penetration testing harnesses to guide Claude Code in reconnaissance and then autonomously attack once a human had selected a course of action. The researchers found that the actor successfully compromised government targets in both Brazil and Colombia and also targeted private organizations in Brazil and the United States in a range of sectors that include biotech, healthcare, food and beverage, retail, technology, and travel.
According to the researchers, the Chinese-speaking actor primarily relied on Claude Opus 4.8, but also used other models including Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Deepseek Chat. The actor accessed Claude through an AI proxy service based in China but set up multiple fallbacks to other AI tools if Claude was not available through the proxy.
Anthropic did not provide comment ahead of publication, and Deepseek did not immediately respond to WIRED's requests for comment.
The researchers say that both the Russian-speaking actor, which seems to have been focused on financially motivated “e-crime,” and the Indonesian-speaking actor (the least sophisticated of the four) used more basic, publicly available skills and harnesses to carry out their attacks. But both were still successful at compromising targets. This included multiple Indonesian government domains, a Bangladeshi government domain, and some private-sector targets, in the case of the Indonesian-speaking actor.
“What we are seeing is humans are doing some of the initial probing in these situations and then they’re engaging the AI for the hacking at scale,” CrowdStrike’s Meyers says. “I find it interesting that even with agentic attacks with all of these capabilities, we could still see that there’s a human behind it and what they’re up to.”

How a bizarre phrase became France's new protest slogan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:59:31 UTC
22:59:31 KST

Breadcrumb
'Bismillah, c'est les ténèbres': How a bizarre phrase became France's new protest slogan
Across France, the phrase "Bismillah, c'est les ténèbres" has appeared on placards at demonstrations, posters and social media, becoming an unlikely rallying cry for a nationwide protest movement.
The phrase, which means "in the name of God, it's the darkness", makes little sense on its own, but has become a symbol of the generational divide between young protesters and the French authorities, as well as a way of mocking racial stereotypes held by police.
"Bismillah, c'est les ténèbres", which combines French and Arabic, appears to have originated on Snapchat, where someone attempted to join a private group of students organising protests and school blockades.
The message, sent under names including Mamadou and Abdellah and accompanied by Algerian flag emojis, used an awkward mixture of French slang and Arabic expressions commonly used by young people in France.
Students suspected the messages came from undercover police officers unsuccessfully attempting to infiltrate their protest groups by imitating the language of young French people.
Screenshots of the messages began circulating on social media in early October, and student protesters quickly adopted the phrase as a mocking slogan of resistance.
The slogan ridicules what protesters see as the authorities' racial stereotyping of young people, particularly those of Arab and African descent, and their failure to understand the generation leading the demonstrations.
"No young person talks like that," Sabrine Kharbach, a spokeswoman for a French student union, told The New York Times.
"Young people have reclaimed this phrase to point out that attempts to monitor and infiltrate their movements do not go unnoticed, and to assert their ability to organise in spite of them," she added.
Another student, Phèdre Quémener, said the phrase had become a national joke because it was "such a terrible impersonation of a young person".
"This is seen as an example of racism because it implies that the people who are going to vandalize property are Arab," she added.
Students across France have been protesting since September, demanding better conditions in schools and universities. The demonstrations have since grown into a wider movement involving parents, teachers, trade unions and other groups protesting against rising living costs and inequality.
The protesters are calling for smaller class sizes, more teachers, shorter school days and improvements to deteriorating school facilities.
Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets across France over the weekend in the largest mobilisation since the protests began.
In response to the unrest, French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu pledged on Tuesday that curfews would be imposed where necessary.
Protests have largely been peaceful, but some have descended into violence, with fires, looting and attacks on school buildings reported across the country.
According to government figures, at least 24 schools have been set alight or ransacked, while roughly 8,000 people have been arrested.
French police have responded forcefully to demonstrations, using tear gas and rubber bullets against protesters, many of whom are children. This response has further inflamed tensions.
France's police watchdog, the IGPN, is investigating at least 34 allegations of police misconduct since the protests began, including a case involving a 14-year-old boy who was severely injured by a tear-gas grenade fired at close range.
Rights group Amnesty International has condemned the police response and urged authorities to de-escalate tensions without the use of excessive force.
French police had already faced accusations of targeting Black and Arab young people before the recent outbreak of protests.
In June, Human Rights Watch reported that French police disproportionately targeted Black and Arab young people with fines, identity checks and searches.
The far right in France and beyond has sought to blame immigrant and Muslim students for the unrest, despite the protesters coming from a wide range of religious and ethnic backgrounds.
British far-right activist Tommy Robinson shared a video of riot police in Paris, blaming a "green/islamic unholy alliance" for supposedly destroying the French capital in a post on X.
However, the footage Robinson shared was not from the current protests and had been circulating online since 2022.
US President Donald Trump also weighed in on the unrest, claiming on his Truth Social platform that migrants had taken over France.
The slogan has since spread beyond France, appearing at demonstrations in Belgium, Germany and Italy, while Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg repeated it in a video expressing solidarity with the student movement.
"Bismillah, c'est les ténèbres" has become more than a viral joke, mocking far-right stereotypes of Muslims in France and the racial prejudices of the police, while serving as a rallying cry for a generation increasingly frustrated with the authorities.

Russia willing to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine – Moscow

Russia willing to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine – Moscow
Russia is ready to resume three-way negotiations with the US and Ukraine to discuss security arrangements for when the conflict has ended, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov has said.
The announcement followed nearly three hours of talks between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff at Constantine Palace in St. Petersburg on Wednesday. Jared Kushner joined by video link after illness prevented him from traveling.
Ushakov said Putin told Witkoff that Moscow was “in principle, ready to resume” trilateral negotiations in mid-November, with the main topic being a post-conflict security system for Russia and Ukraine. Witkoff indicated that Trump would welcome the proposal, the aide added.
The presidential aide noted that earlier attempts to restart trilateral talks were derailed by Kiev having carried out massive attacks on Moscow and other cities during Russia’s recent parliamentary elections. Polling stations were targeted on the main voting day, with election commission personnel killed.
However, the situation has since been “re-evaluated, taking into account the signals received from the Americans,” Ushakov said, adding that Putin had praised the mediation efforts of Trump, his administration, and special representatives in seeking mutually acceptable solutions.
The Russian president also presented an “objective picture of the situation along the line of contact, where Russian troops hold complete strategic initiative,” and noted that Moscow’s forces are conducting a “relentless offensive in all key areas” and effectively destroying military-industrial, energy, and logistics facilities in Ukraine.
Beyond Ukraine, the participants discussed the October diesel agreement, under which Washington eased sanctions on Russian fuel exports. Both sides said the deal served their interests and would help stabilize global fuel markets. Other joint economic projects are also approaching implementation, Ushakov added.
Russia, Ukraine and the US last held talks in Geneva in February, following two rounds in Abu Dhabi. Further negotiations, however, were put on hold after the US and Israel launched their war against Iran, disrupting access to the UAE.
Ushakov told Russian media that Abu Dhabi was again being examined as a possible venue for renewed talks, noting that Putin has yet to choose the members of a future Russian delegation.
Asked by reporters whether the Ukraine conflict was approaching its end, Ushakov suggested it is “moving in that direction.”

How Qatar, Turkiye, Pakistan and Indonesia are deepening defence ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:58:17 UTC
22:58:17 KST

How Qatar, Turkiye, Pakistan and Indonesia are deepening defence ties
Experts say conflicts and uncertainty are accelerating efforts to strengthen regional military capacity.
Qatar, Turkiye, Pakistan and Indonesia signed a deal on Wednesday to deepen their defence industry cooperation, reflecting a broader effort by countries in the region to widen their network of security partners amid the prolonged US-Israel war with Iran.
The four countries signed the memorandum of understanding in Doha, building on existing military projects through joint production, technology transfers and more closely integrated supply chains.
The initiative comes as the failure of the United States and Iran to reach a concrete peace agreement pushes countries in the region to diversify their defence partnerships and look beyond what experts described as an overreliance on Washington for their security. But they stress that closer cooperation does not mean abandoning long-standing alliances. Instead, the ambition is to gain greater control over their own security while strengthening pre-existing partnerships.
Arda Mevlutoglu, a defence industry analyst and managing director of Mergen Analytical Strategies, told Al Jazeera that the implications could extend well beyond the four participants.
“We may be witnessing the emergence of an interconnected network of defence and security arrangements extending from the Gulf to South and Southeast Asia, rather than a single formal alliance,” he said.
What would the agreement do?
In a statement, the Qatari Defence Ministry said the “Badr” Memorandum of Understanding “aims to foster cooperation in the field of defence manufacturing, enhance defence capabilities among the four countries, and promote collaboration in technical defence training, as well as in research and development areas, thereby contributing to the creation of solutions and industries worthy of the evolution of modern defences”.
Experts say that under the agreement, each country will bring its own resources or set of skills to the table. “Turkiye contributes technological expertise, systems integration and a mature defence industry; Pakistan and Indonesia offer manufacturing capacity, skilled workforces and sizeable domestic markets; and Qatar provides investment potential and demand,” said Mevlutoglu.
Together, the four nations could “establish integrated supply chains, allowing these countries to jointly develop, manufacture and sustain defence systems”, he told Al Jazeera.
Such arrangements could give buyers a larger role in producing and supporting their own equipment, while providing manufacturers with longer-term orders and investment. Albert Vidal, a research associate at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, told Al Jazeera that Pakistan and Indonesia were both willing to purchase Turkish weapons and locate part of their production at home.
This could bring down costs for Turkish companies and bring jobs to Pakistan and Indonesia, while Qatar brings “financial depth”, he said.
Building on existing partnerships
Turkiye, home to one of the world’s most advanced defence sectors, already has military manufacturing ties with Qatar, Pakistan and Indonesia separately. Qatar and Turkiye, for instance, signed a bilateral defence industry memorandum in October 2025.
But Vidal says that the new agreement, bringing together all four nations, points to a strategic calculation alongside an industrial one. Closer relationships could give more countries a stake in each other’s security. He pointed to Qatar’s investment in the Turkish defence industry over more than a decade and Ankara’s deployment of forces to Doha during the 2017 diplomatic crisis.
Pakistan’s existing naval manufacturing project with Turkiye, meanwhile, shows how weapons purchases can support domestic manufacturing. Of the four ships announced under the project, two are to be built in Istanbul and two at Karachi Shipyard.
Indonesia and Turkiye, meanwhile, are jointly building a tank.
“The rationale is to streamline these distinct defence export and joint production agreements under a more structured and resilient networked hub, rather than reinvent the wheel with each new defence agreement,” Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, told Al Jazeera.
Less dependence on Washington?
The US-Israeli war with Iran and recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have heightened regional security concerns, analysts say, while reported US weapons shortages may be adding urgency to efforts to strengthen pre-existing partners and bolster domestic arms-building capacity.
“Diversification is a major driver, particularly as recent conflicts have exposed vulnerabilities associated with dependence on foreign suppliers, technology restrictions and supply chain disruptions,” Mevlutoglu said.
But he cautioned against interpreting the memorandum as a break with Washington. “Qatar is unlikely to abandon its strategic relationship with Washington, while Turkiye seeks greater technological independence within NATO, not autonomy from it,” he said.
According to Bader Mousa Al-Saif, an associate fellow with Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa Programme and an assistant professor at Kuwait University, the initiative reflects Gulf countries increasingly looking towards the Global South and fellow Muslim countries.
It also complements a separate effort to formalise military cooperation across the region, analysts say. Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, establishing a mutual defence commitment. Ankara submitted the agreement to parliament for ratification on Wednesday, although deploying Turkish troops abroad would require separate parliamentary approval.
The Doha memorandum concerns industrial cooperation rather than a mutual defence pledge, but Mevlutoglu sees a connection between the two initiatives. “While Mecca focuses on collective deterrence and military cooperation, Doha could provide the industrial and technological foundations for such partnerships,” he said.

The company said it had installed 434 mobile shelters in total since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion.
The shelters are being installed at the most dangerous locations, the company said, including near critical facilities essential to train operations and at stations where Ukrzaliznytsia has no other designated protective structures.
The previous day, Deputy Minister for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport Volodymyr Shemaiev said Ukrzaliznytsia had installed 281 mobile shelters for employees at stations, depots and production units, including 214 this year, and that one of the objectives was to increase the number to 800.
He said mobile shelters had been installed in Kyiv and Kyiv region at Darnytsia, Pochaina, Boryspil, Vasylkiv-1 and Brovary stops and platforms.

Von der Leyen signals new EU trade measures against China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:55:32 UTC
22:55:32 KST

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has announced plans for new trade measures aimed at addressing what she describes as unfair competition from China.
Speaking at the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Wednesday, von der Leyen said Chinese companies receive up to eight times as much state aid as comparable European companies, giving them an unfair competitive advantage.
“Our companies must be able to compete on fair terms globally. Let me take China as an example. In 2025, our trade deficit with China was one billion euros a day. That is not sustainable,” she said.
“Industrial overcapacity and unfair market practices distort competition, and our companies are paying the price,” von der Leyen added.
China was also discussed at last week’s EU summit in Brussels, where leaders from the 27 member states backed the European Commission’s efforts to seek results through dialogue with Beijing.
Those efforts have already produced agreements in some areas. In October, EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič reached an agreement on hybrid cars intended to reduce Chinese exports to the EU. The EU has also secured greater certainty for European companies seeking access to Chinese rare earth elements and magnets, which are important for manufacturing.
“Dialogue has delivered. It is an important first step, but one agreement cannot solve an overall structural imbalance,” von der Leyen said.
EU leaders also expressed support for taking action if negotiations with China fail to produce results, including the use of additional trade tools.
The EU already has defensive trade instruments that can be used if China, for example, suddenly floods the European market with large quantities of cheap goods. These measures include additional tariffs, which make imported Chinese products more expensive.
“The leaders of the EU countries gave a clear, positive signal of support for this last week. We are already working closely with the chemicals and machinery industries, which face growing concerns,” von der Leyen said.
The Commission also plans to introduce measures designed to make the EU less vulnerable to external pressure.
“We must reduce our vulnerabilities. In December, we will present a package that we call ‘Diversify EU’. It will help European companies diversify their supply chains,” von der Leyen said.
The Commission will also propose a new defensive trade instrument that would allow it to restrict access to the EU single market “immediately,” according to von der Leyen.
“Deterrence works when others know that we are ready to act,” she said.
Finally, the Commission plans to propose measures to strengthen solidarity between EU countries when trade pressure threatens a particular industry or member state.
“Economic threats are designed to divide us. Therefore, we will present a solidarity package so that no member state will stand alone against the pressure,” von der Leyen said.

Russia has released American citizen Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan who had been detained for more than four years after Russian forces captured him in Ukraine.

“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanist,” Witkoff said, according to NBC News.
“You are also a humanist,” he told Putin.

“Stephen is on his way home and will soon be back with his family,” Trump wrote.
Trump said Tuesday that he had asked Putin to release Hubbard.
“I have spoken with him for a long time. I have asked him to release him. Let’s see what happens,” Trump told journalists in Washington, according to AFP.
Hubbard had lived in the eastern Ukrainian city of Izium since 2014, according to CNN. He had worked as an English teacher outside the United States for decades.
Russian forces occupied Izium in February 2022, at the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Ukrainian forces recaptured the city in September that year, but Hubbard had been captured by Russian forces in the meantime.
Russian prosecutors accused him of fighting for Ukraine as a mercenary. In October 2024, he was sentenced to six years and 10 months in prison.
Hubbard’s sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox, told CNN that the accusations against him were false.
Russian state media have reported that Hubbard admitted guilt, according to Reuters. However, the U.S. government classified him as “wrongfully detained.”
The circumstances surrounding his capture and detention have not been fully detailed in the information released about the case.

Hungary’s former central bank governor György Matolcsy was arrested Wednesday on suspicion of financial fraud linked to his time in office, according to news agency AFP.
Matolcsy, 71, led the Hungarian National Bank from 2013 to 2025 and was a close ally of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.
His lawyer, Pat Batki, told Hungarian news outlet Telex that the pretrial detention relates to Matolcsy’s tenure as central bank governor, AFP reported.
“My client is suspected of financial fraud,” Batki said.
According to AFP, assets belonging to the central bank went missing in connection with a series of investment and real estate transactions. The losses to public funds are estimated at around 500 million euros, equivalent to more than 3.7 billion kroner.
An investigation into the case began last year.
Other people have also been arrested in connection with the alleged financial fraud, AFP reported, citing Telex.
Those arrested reportedly include a lawyer and the owner of a construction company that renovated a villa on a Greek island. The property has been linked in reports to Matolcsy’s son.
Orbán previously described Matolcsy as his right-hand man, AFP reported. Their relationship reportedly became more distant as the former central bank governor came under scrutiny over corruption allegations.
The arrests come after a major political shift in Hungary. In the April election, Orbán and his Fidesz party lost to Péter Magyar and his Tisza party, which won a landslide victory.
Orbán and Fidesz emphasized national conservatism, criticism of the European Union and opposition to liberal values during their time in power.
Magyar also previously belonged to Fidesz but broke with the party in 2024. He subsequently helped bring Tisza to national prominence by campaigning against corruption, calling for democratic reforms and promising to rebuild Hungary’s strained relationship with the EU.
Magyar has repeatedly criticized prosecutors for moving too slowly in pursuing corruption cases.

Denmark guarantees 750 million kroner loan for Ukrainian rocket fuel factory in Vojens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:55:12 UTC
22:55:12 KST

Denmark will guarantee a loan worth 750 million kroner ($110 million) for a Danish subsidiary of Ukrainian defense company Fire Point to establish a rocket fuel factory in southern Jutland.
The Ministry of Industry, Business and Financial Affairs announced the state-backed guarantee in a press release, saying the support was necessary because the war in Ukraine makes it difficult for Fire Point to secure financing through conventional Danish lending arrangements.
The factory will be built in Vojens, near Skrydstrup Air Base. Production is now expected to begin in late 2027, a year later than originally planned.
Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh announced the delay in August, citing slower-than-expected construction.
Business Minister Martin Lidegaard said the project would strengthen Ukraine’s defense capabilities while supporting Denmark’s defense industry and European security.
Denmark invited Fire Point to establish production in the country in September 2025, becoming the first NATO member to welcome Ukrainian weapons manufacturing on its territory.
That same month, the Danish Parliament passed legislation allowing the defense minister to waive certain regulations for military projects considered nationally important.
Under the legislation, Fire Point can temporarily bypass more than 20 laws and regulations, including rules covering environmental protection, planning and nature conservation.
The company must eventually comply with the standard regulations governing such facilities.
Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus said manufacturing military equipment outside Ukraine would help protect supply chains from Russian attacks.
He added that access to secure production facilities and critical defense technology was essential to Ukraine’s ability to defend itself.

Denmark’s power grid operator will answer hundreds of connection requests in November while big data centers face long delays.
Energinet, the Danish state-owned electricity transmission company, has now mapped out the capacity needs on the country’s strained electricity grid, the company said in a press release on Wednesday.
With this overview finished, the company will be able to answer applications from several hundred electricity consumers and power producers in November about whether they can connect to the grid.
“In a time of sharply rising demand for electricity, we unfortunately cannot give connection to everyone at the pace they desire,” said Soren Dupont Kristensen, the acting chief executive officer of Energinet.
“But there is room in the transmission grid to cover the electricity needs of ordinary households, smaller businesses, and critical societal functions such as healthcare, defense, and emergency preparedness, both now and in the years to come,” Kristensen said.
Customers will be sorted into four priority categories that were recently passed by a broad political majority as part of an emergency plan for the power network.
Projects placed in Category 1 and Category 2 will get their answers first. These two groups include critical public services, as well as green transition and electrification projects.
Category 3 includes energy storage systems, such as large battery facilities. Category 4 covers major electricity users, including data centers.
“We do not have all the results in place, but it looks difficult to give full grid access to projects in categories 3 and 4,” Kristensen said in Wednesday’s statement.
The political emergency plan was designed to let Energinet and local electricity companies choose who gets hooked up to the power lines. Under this plan, large data centers are pushed to the back of the line because the grid does not have room for huge new projects.
Energinet has faced heavy criticism for expanding the Danish electricity network too slowly. This criticism has come from several groups, including Rigsrevisionen, the National Audit Office of Denmark.
In March, the state company stopped connecting new projects. At that time, Energinet announced that no new connection contracts would be signed until the autumn.
In May, the company stated that very large connection projects could face waiting times of five to ten years. At that point, Energinet also admitted that demand for power had grown at an unexpectedly rapid speed.
Several business groups say it is good news that applicants will soon get answers, but they stress that Denmark still has a real shortage of space on its power grid.
This warning came from DI, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, which is the main employers’ and business association in Denmark; Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, an employers’ organization representing businesses; and Green Power Denmark, the business and trade group for the green energy sector.
Ulrich Bang, the deputy director for climate, energy, environment, and building at Dansk Erhverv, said the likely lack of space for Category 3 and Category 4 projects shows how serious the situation is.
“Denmark cannot build the industries, business community, and jobs of the future in a waiting room,” Bang said.
“Therefore, action must be taken now, and we look forward to dialogue with authorities and grid companies on how room can be made for more on the electricity grid in the very short term,” Bang said.

====================================================================================================

New partnership aims to connect lonely patients with social activities through their GPs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:54:56 UTC
22:54:56 KST

A new partnership in Denmark aims to help people experiencing loneliness and social isolation access community activities through referrals from their general practitioners.
Many people visit their doctors because they feel lonely, but their needs cannot always be addressed through medical treatment, said David Vincent Nielsen, a loneliness consultant at Ældre Sagen, a Danish association for older people, and chairman of Folkebevægelsen mod Ensomhed, a national movement against loneliness.
“There are a lot of people who seek out the healthcare and care system because they experience loneliness and social isolation.
“Most often, they cannot get help from the healthcare system because they need companionship and social relationships,” he said.
Under the proposed system, a doctor could issue a social referral for a patient. A professional or volunteer would then contact the patient and help identify activities and community groups suited to their needs.
The professional, known as a bridge-builder, would discuss the patient’s situation and help them find relevant offers from local organizations and municipalities.
These could include knitting groups, card game clubs or local exercise groups. Patients could also be encouraged to become volunteers themselves.
Nielsen said many people experiencing loneliness face barriers that make it difficult for them to seek out social activities and build relationships on their own.
For social referrals to become a regular part of Denmark’s health care system, however, the public sector would need to fund the service, he said.
“In 2017, the University of Southern Denmark calculated that loneliness cost 5.5 billion kroner, but since then, the prevalence of loneliness has increased by 42 percent, so around 10 billion kroner would be a qualified estimate today,” Nielsen said.
He argued that social referrals could also help reduce health care costs by addressing loneliness before people repeatedly seek medical assistance.
“But social referrals will not necessarily be an expense. Right now, there are at least 500,000 extra visits to general practice each year that are due to loneliness and paid for by the regions,” he said.
Pilot projects are already underway, Nielsen said. The new partnership aims to bring the existing efforts together into a coordinated model that could eventually be introduced nationwide.
The World Health Organization recognizes social referrals as a way to connect people with nonmedical support. According to the organization, one in five doctor visits is prompted by problems that cannot be resolved through clinical treatment.
The United Kingdom was the first country to incorporate social referrals into its health care policy. The WHO says there are now 3,300 active bridge-builders in the country.
The Danish partnership brings together Ældre Sagen, the Danish Red Cross, Social Sundhed, DGI, Sund By Netværket, Not a Box, and Frivilligcentre og Selvhjælp Danmark, an organization representing volunteer centers and self-help initiatives in Denmark.

Venstre and other opposition parties expect to be left out of Denmark’s 2027 budget deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:54:48 UTC
22:54:48 KST

Venstre does not expect to be included in an agreement with the government on Denmark’s 2027 national budget, party chairman Troels Lund Poulsen said after an introductory meeting on Wednesday.
“There is no willingness to listen to our views. It is a budget that has been agreed upon in advance with the government’s support parties. And that is just how it is,” Lund Poulsen said, according to Danish public broadcaster DR.
The government’s support parties are Enhedslisten, the Red-Green Alliance, and Alternativet, a green political party. Both are expected to reach a budget agreement with the government, particularly as it is the first national budget deal since the general election earlier this year.
Lund Poulsen said Venstre would be willing to attend further negotiations if the government invited the party.
Other opposition parties also expressed doubts about their chances of joining the agreement after meeting with Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard, a member of the Social Democrats, on Wednesday.
Dansk Folkeparti, the Danish People’s Party, does not expect to receive further invitations, according to its finance spokesperson, Anders Vistisen, who spoke to DR.
The same applies to De Konservative, the Conservative People’s Party.
“That is what I think. Because regarding the wishes we have for the budget, we have not been accommodated,” party chairman Mona Juul said.
The Conservatives were the only opposition party included in last year’s budget agreement, when the government consisted of the Social Democrats, Venstre and Moderaterne, the Moderates.
Liberal Alliance also took part in negotiations on Wednesday. Its political leader, Alex Vanopslagh, does not expect the party to be included in the final budget agreement, according to DR.
Danmarksdemokraterne, another opposition party, also attended negotiations on Wednesday.
The budget negotiations follow a setback for the government on Tuesday, when it had to abandon a proposal to tighten the eligibility requirements for senior pensions after failing to secure support from the parties involved in the negotiations.
The decision was welcomed by Pelle Dragsted, Enhedslisten’s political spokesperson.
“We are very happy about that. It was antisocial to cut the opportunities of worn-out workers to be able to retire,” he said on Tuesday.
Under its budget proposal, the government had planned to save 200 million kroner in 2028, 500 million kroner in 2029 and 800 million kroner in 2030 by tightening the requirements for senior pensions.
Enhedslisten and Alternativet held their budget negotiations with the government on Tuesday.

Danish municipalities shut down IT systems after potential security risk
Kombit, the IT organization serving Denmark’s municipalities, has shut down several of its digital services, either fully or partially, after identifying a potential technical security risk.
The shutdown began Wednesday afternoon and affects services including Aula, the digital communication platform used by schools and parents, and the municipal library system, Lars Skov Granerud, Kombit’s press manager, told news agency Ritzau.
“We have been made aware of a potential technical security risk in an underlying element of several of our solutions,” he said.
“Therefore, we decided a short while ago to shut down several of them.”
Kombit does not yet have a complete overview of the situation, Granerud said.
The disruption also affects several municipal systems used by local government employees in their daily work, including systems for processing benefit payments.
Aula has been shut down completely, while the library system is only partially affected, Granerud said.
Kombit has not disclosed which other digital services have been affected.
Unauthorized people have gained access to parts of the computer systems of the Danish department store chain.
Magasin reported the incident in an email to DR, the Danish public broadcaster.
Following the breach, Magasin warned members of its customer loyalty club, named Goodie, that their personal details may have been compromised. The exposed data includes names, addresses, and purchase history.
“We are working dedicatedly with external experts to handle the incident, including re-establishing our access to the systems. In addition, we have reported the incident to both the police and Datatilsynet,” Magasin stated in the email. Datatilsynet is the Danish Data Protection Agency, the national authority that oversees data privacy rules.
Magasin warned that the compromised details could be used to make phishing scams look more believable.
Phishing is a deceptive practice where scammers try to trick individuals into handing over personal information. This often happens through fake emails designed to steal login details for MitID, the official digital identification system used across Denmark for banking and public services.
Magasin stressed in its message to club members that the security breach did not include any credit card information.
“We want to emphasize that we are working to limit the scope of the breach and to ensure that something similar does not happen again,” the email said.
The incident follows a similar alert sent to shoppers a few weeks ago by the British online retailer Asos.
In that case, Asos stated that an unauthorized person managed to enter an employee account. The intruder used that account to pull information from external platforms that Asos works with.
That breach allowed the unauthorized user to access customer names and contact details.
Following the incident, Asos told its customers to be cautious of unexpected phone calls and messages from individuals pretending to work for the company. Asos also reported its security breach to the police.
Foreign workers and older employees fuel Denmark’s job market growth
The Danish labor market added 3,600 wage earners in August, according to a report published Wednesday morning by Danmarks Statistik, the national statistical authority of Denmark.
The increase follows a July that showed signs of a small slowdown.
The new numbers support the view held by financial group Nykredit that the Danish job market remains active.
Palle Sørensen, who serves as chief economist at Nykredit, noted that the trend is clear over a longer period.
“It is completely clear when you look at the development over a slightly longer horizon. In the past 12 months alone, there have been 29,638 more wage earners,” Sørensen said in a written comment.
He added that the job market matches the general economy.
“The development in the labor market matches well with the general economic development. Activity is increasing, and it is therefore not surprising that more people are entering employment,” Sørensen said.
There are multiple reasons for the increase in employed people.
One of the main reasons is foreign labor, according to Jesper Grunnet-Lauridsen. He works as chief analyst at 3F, Fagligt Fælles Forbund, which is the United Federation of Danish Workers and the largest trade union in Denmark.
“An important explanation is that more foreign employees have arrived, at the same time as more seniors are staying longer in the labor market,” Grunnet-Lauridsen said in a written comment.
He explained that these groups have helped employers find staff.
“This has made it possible for employment to continue to rise without companies having a correspondingly harder time finding employees,” Grunnet-Lauridsen said.
Neither Nykredit nor 3F expects the Danish labor market to slow down in the near future.
Sørensen said that recent experience shows that later retirement and foreign workers make the size of the total workforce more flexible.
“This is somewhat of an innovation compared to previously, where employment growth was often assumed to be temporary,” Sørensen said.

The payment company Nets has lost a court case against Konkurrencerådet, the Danish Competition Council, which serves as the public competition authority in Denmark.
The ruling was delivered Wednesday by Sø- og Handelsretten, the Danish Maritime and Commercial Court.
Nets had asked the court to set aside a decision made by the Competition Council. That decision concluded that Nets abused its dominant position in the market for payment solutions between the years 2012 and 2016.
The case involves the company Teller, which was a subsidiary under Nets during that period. Teller offered what were described as exclusivity discounts to a number of large customers. The competition authorities determined that this practice broke legal rules meant to secure free competition, and they made their official decision on the case back in 2018.
The legal process has taken several years. Alongside the civil lawsuit, police have also run an investigation into Nets. That investigation led to criminal charges against the company, with authorities seeking a fine. The criminal case was put on hold to wait for the result of the civil case, and it has not yet gone to trial.
The specific legal reasons behind the court decision are not yet known. In a brief summary published on its website, the Maritime and Commercial Court stated that the full ruling will be released within four weeks.
The court noted that the delay is needed because the text of the ruling may contain business secrets that cannot be made public.
Share of 21-year-olds living at home in Denmark nearly doubles since 2011
More young adults in Denmark are choosing to stay in their family homes, with the share of 21-year-olds living with their parents rising from 32 percent in 2011 to 57 percent in 2025.
The figures come from Statistics Denmark and are highlighted in a new study by Realdania, a Danish philanthropic association focused on the built environment.
Henrik Mahncke, Realdania’s head of analysis, says high housing prices could partly explain the trend. Another possible reason is that many young people enjoy living with their parents.
However, where young people grow up also influences when they move out.
In Albertslund, a municipality near Copenhagen, 61 percent of 21-year-olds still live at home. On the island of Læsø, the figure is just 14 percent.
According to Statistics Denmark, distance to educational institutions is an important factor. Young people who live farther from places of study are more likely to move out.
Cultural background also plays a role, with young people from non-Western backgrounds generally staying at home longer.
Housing availability and prices may also influence their decisions.
Mette Mechlenborg, a senior researcher at Aalborg University who studies housing, points to another explanation: the design of modern family homes.
Many young people grow up in spacious houses with separate areas for parents and children, giving them greater privacy and independence.
This can make staying at home more attractive than moving into a small, expensive room.
Realdania’s study also found no overall difference in quality of life between young adults living with their parents and those who have moved out.

The government has abandoned proposed changes to Denmark’s senior pension scheme after failing to secure support from parties behind the existing agreement.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen announced the decision Tuesday following a meeting with the parties involved.
The changes were part of the government’s proposed 2027 budget and were expected to save 200 million DKK in 2028, 500 million DKK in 2029 and 800 million DKK in 2030.
Under the proposal, applicants would have needed to prove that their ability to work was limited to 15 hours a week or less across all types of jobs, rather than just their most recent job.

The scheme was introduced through a political agreement in 2019. Its signatories include the Danish People’s Party, the Social Democrats, the Socialist People’s Party, the Moderates and the Social Liberal Party.
Changes to the agreement require approval from all participating parties during the parliamentary term.
Several center-right parties opposed the proposal, while the Red-Green Alliance also rejected changes.
“We respect the agreements we have. It has not been my intention to terminate any agreement,” Halsboe-Jørgensen said.
“On the contrary. The fact that I called the colleagues from the other parties together today was precisely an expression of the fact that I actually wanted to discuss it with them, and that I respect that the agreement we have with each other gives all of them a veto right against changes in this area,” she added.
Dropping the proposal leaves a gap in the government’s budget plans.
Halsboe-Jørgensen said spending priorities would need to change but did not specify where the missing funds would come from.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard will now have to address the shortfall during negotiations on the 2027 Finance Act.

Economic and Interior Affairs Minister Pia Olsen Dyhr will convene labor unions, employer organizations and other groups for talks on preventing work-related stress.
The first roundtable discussion will take place Friday following a new report from the Danish Economic Council’s independent economic advisers.
The report estimates that severe work-related stress reduces Denmark’s labor supply by between 16,000 and 39,000 people.
More than one in 10 people affected by severe stress do not return to employment, while more than one in three disability pension recipients receive the benefit after a stress reaction, according to the report.
“Stress makes us poorer,” Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party said. “This applies both to the individual person who becomes ill with stress and their family, but it also matters for our society.”
Chief Economic Adviser Jakob Roland Munch said severe stress has long-lasting effects on people’s connection to the labor market.
However, the report found no evidence that the number of severe stress cases has increased during the past 15 to 20 years.
Dyhr said Denmark must place greater emphasis on preventing stress instead of responding only after people become ill.
The government’s proposed 2027 budget includes 50 million DKK for a prevention fund intended to help people remain healthy and employed.
Dyhr said the government wants stronger evidence about which preventive measures work before deciding how to prioritize future efforts.
The European Commission has made security the main focus of its new Arctic strategy as Russia and China expand their activity in the region.
The approach marks a significant shift from the European Union’s 2021 strategy, which concentrated primarily on international cooperation, climate and environmental protection.
“As Russia and China increase their presence and ambitions, the Arctic has become a frontline in the global power competition,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.
The Commission fears the Arctic could become a major source of conflict with Russia after the war in Ukraine ends.
The strategy proposes expanding Europe’s icebreaker capacity and strengthening protection of northern maritime borders and critical undersea infrastructure.
The EU’s 27 countries collectively have about 10 icebreakers, compared with an estimated 40 operated by Russia.
The Commission also proposes creating a maritime security center to monitor activity in the Arctic.
A separate Arctic cable center would monitor, protect and repair undersea cables in the North Atlantic and Arctic. It could later track ships belonging to Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, which transports sanctioned oil and gas.
Western intelligence services also suspect that Russia has used shadow fleet vessels in hybrid attacks.
The strategy contains no spending figures and must now be discussed with EU governments.
Kallas said Arctic security was a European concern because Denmark, Sweden and Finland are Arctic countries and more than 500,000 EU citizens live in the region.
Record trout catch in Varde River follows restoration efforts
Anglers caught a record 1,400 large trout in Denmark’s Varde River during 2025, according to science news outlet Videnskab.dk.
Researchers have also found trout fry at more locations in the river system than at any point during the past 40 years.
“It is good to see that efforts to remove obstacles to fish movement are beginning to work in Varde Å,” said Bjarke Ibsen Dehli, a fish conservation adviser at DTU Aqua, the National Institute of Aquatic Resources.
However, he said Denmark remained far behind in restoring healthy, natural river systems.
Rivers have historically been straightened, widened and deepened to drain surrounding farmland. Stones and gravel were removed, despite fish such as trout and salmon relying on gravel for spawning.
Aquatic plants have also been removed, reducing places where fish can hide.
Sluices, dams, water mills, fish farms, bridges and pipes can block migrating fish. Fish gathered near such barriers may become easier prey for cormorants, herons, otters and seals.
DTU Aqua’s latest survey found healthy trout populations along 14 percent of the examined stretches of the Varde River system. That was up from five percent in 2016.
Associations can apply for funding to restore local waterways, including grants from DTU Aqua for spawning gravel and shelter stones.
Dehli encouraged residents to join local organizations working to improve rivers and streams.

The City of Copenhagen began installing separate waste bins for used diapers in residential courtyards and municipal day-care centers Monday.

The city estimates that between 85 and 94 percent of diaper waste, including liquids and feces, can be converted into new materials.

The bins will accept diapers for children and adults, incontinence pads, paper-based cloths and wet wipes without plastic or bamboo. Menstrual hygiene products are excluded.
Diaper waste must be placed in an ordinary plastic trash bag sealed with a tight knot.
Study finds misogynistic TikTok content can appear within minutes
Young male TikTok users can encounter misogynistic content within minutes, even when they do not actively search for it, according to a Danish study.
Researchers from the Center for Digital Pedagogy and Analyse & Tal created eight fictional profiles representing men ages 16 to 19 interested in fitness, dating, investing and gaming.
After the profiles interacted with videos about those subjects, researchers allowed them to scroll automatically for one hour.
Content associated with the “manosphere” appeared after an average of three minutes. In one case, it appeared after 21 seconds.
The manosphere refers to online communities and content that degrade women or support restricting their rights and opportunities.
Researchers also examined one year of viewing data provided by 29 men ages 15 to 22. They identified an average of five to six manosphere videos in each participant’s weekly feed.
The researchers said this was a minimum estimate but emphasized that the 29 participants were not representative of all young men.
Employment and Equality Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen of the Social Democrats called for stronger social media regulation and more discussion in schools and homes.
TikTok said it takes the findings seriously.
“We proactively remove 98.1 percent of the videos that violate our rules on hate and hateful behavior,” Nordic communications director Lukasz Lindell said.
TikTok said it was also working to diversify recommendations and interrupt repetitive content patterns.

Denmark’s shift from fossil fuels to electricity is accelerating
Electric cars, heat pumps and electric boilers are driving a sharp increase in the share of Denmark’s energy consumption covered by electricity.
Denmark is becoming increasingly electrified as electric cars, heat pumps and electric boilers replace fossil fuels.
Electricity accounted for 23.4 percent of Denmark’s total energy consumption in 2025, according to figures highlighted by industry organisation Green Power Denmark.
That was an increase of 1.5 percentage points in just one year.
The increase is significant. Between 2016 and 2024, the share of electricity in Denmark’s total energy consumption rose by only 3.8 percentage points.
The acceleration is being driven particularly by the growing number of electric cars and by district heating companies investing in electric boilers and heat pumps.
Kristian Jensen, CEO of Green Power Denmark, says the development will gradually make Denmark less dependent on imported oil and natural gas – and therefore less exposed to international energy prices and geopolitical developments.
“We are freeing ourselves from what is going on in the Middle East and American politics,” Jensen told Ritzau.
“When Danes experience that gasoline, diesel and electricity have become more expensive than they were a year ago, it is because we are still dependent on the price set in the rest of the world.”
Target: 60 percent by 2035
Green Power Denmark wants electricity to account for 60 percent of Denmark’s total energy consumption by 2035.
Reaching that level will require a much faster transition in Danish industry, according to Jensen.
He points to heat pumps as one of the technologies that can help companies replace natural gas with electricity. Iron foundries and food producers, including dairy group Arla, have already demonstrated that large heat pumps can be used in industrial production.
Jensen argues that other companies should follow their example.
“It will not only reduce the companies’ CO2 emissions, it will also reduce energy expenses and thereby improve their competitiveness,” he said.
Figures for Denmark’s electrification rate in 2026 are not yet available, but Green Power Denmark expects the shift towards electricity to continue.

Denmark’s oldest-ever person was a member of the Danish Nazi party
Records show that 112-year-old Kirsten Schwalbe joined Denmark’s Nazi party during the German occupation. She says she did so at her husband’s request and did not sympathise with Nazism.
Kirsten Schwalbe, who this week became the longest-living Dane in recorded history, was a member of Denmark’s Nazi party during the German occupation.
The 112-year-old joined the National Socialist Workers’ Party of Denmark (DNSAP) in August 1941, according to Kristeligt Dagblad.
Her name appears in the Bovrup registry, a record of people who were members of DNSAP. Two historians have independently confirmed to the newspaper that the entry matches Schwalbe’s date of birth and address, although her surname is misspelled as “Schalbe”.
Schwalbe has confirmed that both she and her former husband were members of the party, but says she only joined because her husband urged her to do so.
She rejected the suggestion that she had sided with Nazi Germany.
“Not at all. I barely knew what it was, because I have never taken an interest in politics,” she told TV Midtvest when asked whether she had sympathised with the Nazis.
Schwalbe said she found it unfair that she should have to “pay for it” more than 70 years later, adding that “back then, wives didn’t look into such things”.
Membership does not show level of involvement
DNSAP was founded in 1930 and was strongly inspired by Adolf Hitler’s German Nazi Party, the NSDAP.
But Charlie Krautwald, a historian at the University of Copenhagen, cautioned against drawing conclusions about Schwalbe’s level of involvement from the registry alone.
The record shows that a person joined the party, he told Kristeligt Dagblad, but not why they joined, how long they remained a member or whether they paid membership fees.
A person could therefore appear in the registry without having been active in the party.
TV Midtvest has followed Schwalbe for several years and manages an Instagram account about her life. Two of the broadcaster’s employees have also recently published a book about her.
Her membership of DNSAP had not previously been mentioned. TV Midtvest editor-in-chief Marc Killigren Akselsen told Kristeligt Dagblad that the broadcaster had not known about it.
Schwalbe, who lives in Struer in western Jutland, became the longest-living Dane on record on Wednesday, when she reached the age of 112 years and 218 days.

Lidl has Denmark’s cheapest basket of organic groceries, analysis finds
Lidl offers the lowest prices on a selected basket of organic groceries among seven Danish supermarket chains, according to an analysis by price-monitoring service Madprisluppen.
A basket containing 22 organic products cost 355.20 DKK at Lidl. The same basket cost 449.60 DKK at Meny, the most expensive chain in the comparison.
Madprisluppen said the Lidl basket was 26 percent cheaper than the one at Meny.
“We want to make it easier for Danes to make room for organics in everyday life, and here price plays an important role,” Lidl Denmark purchasing director Peer Sandtner said.
Rema 1000 was the second-cheapest supermarket, with its basket costing only 5 DKK more than Lidl’s.
SuperBrugsen was the second-most expensive, though its total was almost 35 DKK below Meny’s.
The analysis also included Netto, 365discount and Føtex. Prices were recorded from October 9 through October 12.
Products included milk, eggs, vegetables and dry goods. Meat was excluded because Madprisluppen found it difficult to identify comparable products across the chains.
The monitoring service also found that supermarkets carry fewer organic products than they did six years ago. Organic prices have increased, and such products appear in special offers less frequently than non-organic groceries.
Norway to lend 10-meter Viking boat to Danish museum for 10 years
A Norwegian Viking boat will be displayed at Moesgaard Museum near Aarhus under an unusual 10-year loan agreement.
The oak boat is almost 10 meters long and nearly two meters wide. It was among three smaller vessels discovered when archaeologists excavated Norway’s Gokstad ship in 1880.
The Gokstad ship is Norway’s largest preserved Viking ship.
“The boat is a very important cultural treasure from the Viking Age, and it is not an everyday occurrence that we grant permission for such a boat to be taken out of the country,” Kaare Stang of Riksantikvaren, Norway’s cultural heritage authority, said.
The three smaller boats had been chopped into pieces, possibly as part of a burial ritual, according to archaeologists.
The Museum of Cultural History in Norway owns the boat and applied for permission to lend it to Moesgaard Museum for a new exhibition.
Norwegian authorities normally approve loans for no more than three years. Moesgaard Museum must therefore submit a report on the boat’s condition every three years during the loan period.
Stang said Norwegian authorities trusted the Danish museum to protect the boat but emphasized that it must eventually return to Norway.
No arrival date has been announced.
Moesgaard Museum already displays a 6.5-meter Gokstad boat that was used to transport crews and exchange orders between warships.
Copenhagen establishes support groups for parents of children missing school
A new parents’ association has signed a four-year agreement with the City of Copenhagen to establish support groups for families whose children experience prolonged, involuntary school absence.
Such absence is often connected to poor well-being and is considered concerning when a pupil misses at least 20 percent of school for two consecutive quarters. That corresponds to about 10 days per quarter.
The first groups will be funded by Copenhagen and include eight to nine parents who meet approximately once a month, education news outlet Folkeskolen.dk reported.
A family therapist will lead the meetings, with a parent from Forældrekommissionen, or the Parents’ Commission, also participating.
Louise Gielov and Jens Langorn helped establish the association after their family appeared in the Danish public broadcaster DR documentary “Skolens tabte børn,” which showed daily life with children unable to attend school.
The couple received more than 1,000 messages from parents in similar situations after the documentary aired.
The association now has 2,545 members and aims to establish parent groups across Denmark. It also plans to use families’ experiences to promote earlier intervention and broader changes to prevent school absence.
The proportion of pupils with prolonged concerning absence increased from 2.4 percent in the 2019-2020 school year to 5.1 percent in 2024-2025.
The association has also secured 7 million DKK from foundations.
Dane becomes first European participant to receive combined flu and Covid vaccine
A 65-year-old Dane will become the first person in Europe to receive a new combined influenza and Covid-19 vaccine as part of a clinical trial Friday.
The trial will examine whether one injection can protect against both diseases as effectively as, or better than, the two separate vaccines currently used, Danish public broadcaster DR reported.
The first participant will receive the vaccine at Gentofte Hospital.
“We are investigating whether one shot with this new vaccine is just as effective or potentially better than the two shots given today at preventing hospitalizations with influenza and Covid-19,” said Tor Biering-Sørensen, a professor and senior physician at Herlev and Gentofte Hospital who is leading the trial.
About 165,000 Danes have agreed to participate. More than 300,000 people are expected to join over the next two years.
Half of the participants will receive one dose of the combined vaccine. The other half will receive separate influenza and Covid-19 vaccinations.
People age 65 and older in Denmark are automatically invited to receive free vaccinations against both diseases. The Danish Health Authority said about 1.3 million residents received invitations in September.
People with chronic illnesses or other conditions placing them at increased risk are also eligible for the free program.
The vaccines are intended to reduce the risk of severe illness and hospitalization during the winter respiratory infection season.

Archaeologists uncover more than 1,000 graves in Copenhagen park
Archaeologists have excavated more than 1,000 graves containing human remains beneath Hans Tavsens Park in Copenhagen’s Nørrebro district.
The park, located next to Assistens Cemetery, was previously used as a burial ground for Copenhagen’s poorest residents. Victims of the city’s 1853 cholera epidemic are among those buried there.
“We can use it to gain insight into the poor population from this period and Copenhagen’s history,” Museum of Copenhagen archaeologist Olivia Persson told Danish public broadcaster DR.
The excavation is taking place before Hans Tavsens Park and the neighboring Hans Tavsens Gade are redeveloped into a connected green space.
The project will also allow the park to collect water during cloudbursts, helping prevent flooding of nearby roads and basements as Denmark experiences wetter weather.
Construction began in autumn 2025 as part of the City of Copenhagen’s plan for managing extreme rainfall. The redevelopment is expected to be completed in spring 2028.
Most of the remains will be transferred to the University of Copenhagen’s Anthropological Laboratory for storage and examination. Some will undergo additional analysis, while the remainder will be reburied in the park.
Researchers will examine the health of selected individuals. They will also study how the graves were arranged to better understand religious and cultural attitudes toward death among Copenhagen’s poorer population at the time.

Greenland’s parliament unanimously adopted a resolution Thursday directing the government to draft legislation temporarily banning deep-sea mining.

The ban must therefore pass as legislation before taking effect.

Denmark’s power grid operator will answer hundreds of connection requests in November while big data centers face long delays.
Energinet, the Danish state-owned electricity transmission company, has now mapped out the capacity needs on the country’s strained electricity grid, the company said in a press release on Wednesday.
With this overview finished, the company will be able to answer applications from several hundred electricity consumers and power producers in November about whether they can connect to the grid.
“In a time of sharply rising demand for electricity, we unfortunately cannot give connection to everyone at the pace they desire,” said Soren Dupont Kristensen, the acting chief executive officer of Energinet.
“But there is room in the transmission grid to cover the electricity needs of ordinary households, smaller businesses, and critical societal functions such as healthcare, defense, and emergency preparedness, both now and in the years to come,” Kristensen said.
Customers will be sorted into four priority categories that were recently passed by a broad political majority as part of an emergency plan for the power network.
Projects placed in Category 1 and Category 2 will get their answers first. These two groups include critical public services, as well as green transition and electrification projects.
Category 3 includes energy storage systems, such as large battery facilities. Category 4 covers major electricity users, including data centers.
“We do not have all the results in place, but it looks difficult to give full grid access to projects in categories 3 and 4,” Kristensen said in Wednesday’s statement.
The political emergency plan was designed to let Energinet and local electricity companies choose who gets hooked up to the power lines. Under this plan, large data centers are pushed to the back of the line because the grid does not have room for huge new projects.
Energinet has faced heavy criticism for expanding the Danish electricity network too slowly. This criticism has come from several groups, including Rigsrevisionen, the National Audit Office of Denmark.
In March, the state company stopped connecting new projects. At that time, Energinet announced that no new connection contracts would be signed until the autumn.
In May, the company stated that very large connection projects could face waiting times of five to ten years. At that point, Energinet also admitted that demand for power had grown at an unexpectedly rapid speed.
Several business groups say it is good news that applicants will soon get answers, but they stress that Denmark still has a real shortage of space on its power grid.
This warning came from DI, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, which is the main employers’ and business association in Denmark; Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, an employers’ organization representing businesses; and Green Power Denmark, the business and trade group for the green energy sector.
Ulrich Bang, the deputy director for climate, energy, environment, and building at Dansk Erhverv, said the likely lack of space for Category 3 and Category 4 projects shows how serious the situation is.
“Denmark cannot build the industries, business community, and jobs of the future in a waiting room,” Bang said.
“Therefore, action must be taken now, and we look forward to dialogue with authorities and grid companies on how room can be made for more on the electricity grid in the very short term,” Bang said.
