EU leaders to discuss funding for Ukraine at special meeting
Pedro Lourtie, Head of the Cabinet of the President of the European Council António Costa, presented plans for upcoming European Council meetings to EU ambassadors on 21 October, including a special meeting dedicated to the EU budget and funding for Ukraine.
Source: European Pravda, citing an informed EU official on condition of anonymity
Details: EU leaders will gather for a special meeting on 26-27 November, the main focus of which will be the EU's Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) for 2028-2034 and funding for Ukraine in 2027.
The European Pravda source said that EU ambassadors discussed the outcome of the European Council summit of 15-16 October on 21 October. During the Coreper meeting, Pedro Lourtie, Head of the Cabinet of the President of the European Council, presented plans for the preparation of upcoming meetings of EU leaders.
He stated that the next European Council meeting will take place in an informal format in Dublin on 13 November. The main topic of discussion will be artificial intelligence.
Quote from the EU official to European Pravda: "The special European Council meeting on 26-27 November will be dedicated to the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) and funding for Ukraine."
Details: The European Pravda source explained that over the next few weeks, the team of European Council President António Costa will hold separate consultations with representatives of each of the 27 member states. Based on these discussions, an updated negotiating document on the EU's Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) is planned to be prepared and presented before the start of the November summit.
In addition, Costa plans to hold another informal meeting of European leaders in Alden Biesen, Belgium. It will be a continuation of two previous meetings in this format, during which EU defence and competitiveness issues were discussed. The preliminary date for the meeting, which is already being called Alden Biesen 2, is set for 5 February 2027.
Another initiative by Costa concerns the March European Council summit. The president of the European Council proposes holding it on 18-19 March 2027 in Rome rather than Brussels, timing the meeting to coincide with the 70th anniversary of the signing of the Treaty of Rome.
However, as the European Pravda source specified, moving the summit to the Italian capital is only possible with the unanimous support of all EU member states.
Background:
- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated at a summit in Brussels that the war will cost Ukraine €155 billion next year. He appealed to EU presidents and prime ministers to find another €70 billion to support Ukraine.
- The European Commission has acknowledged that the Ukrainian budget for 2027 indeed lacks €70 billion, which must be covered by international partners.
- The European Council has tasked the European Commission with preparing proposals to cover the €70 billion shortfall in Ukraine's budget for 2027.

Mourning Air: Leena Magdi on grief, loss and Sudan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:52:44 UTC
22:52:44 KST

Breadcrumb
Mourning Air: How Leena Magdi's brother's death changed her understanding of grief, loss and Sudan
How does the sudden death of a sibling change the way we perceive our lives and our understanding of everything around us? In her memoir, Mourning Air, Leena Magdi shares her personal experience of grief and its lasting impact on her soul.
"The loss of my younger brother is a tragedy that uprooted systems of imbedded beliefs about how the world operates."
Leena Magdi is a Sudanese immigrant who has lived in the United States since she was five years old. She has two sisters and a younger brother named Hamoodi, to whom she was very close. Yet, his sudden death while on summer vacation in Sudan changed her life forever.
Faced with such a profound loss, Leena finds that expressing grief in any form, whether through painting or writing, helps ease the sadness. So she chose to write her memoir as a letter to the world, sharing her personal experience.
"My hope for this book is that it will paint a picture of a mind in grief."
Sudden loss and permanent grief
"After loss, the air changes around us. It’s heavier and lighter at the same time. It’s like a veil is lifted. It seems impossible to keep going. It feels like we have to try to keep living. But we don’t. We keep breathing, and we don’t even notice it."
Throughout her memoir, Leena explains how grief isn’t temporary. It lives inside us for a long time as we carry it forever. Losing her brother felt as if part of her had been taken away.
At first, she lost the ability to talk to others, laugh with someone, or feel normal again. Even fleeing Sudan during the war was harder because she was leaving her brother buried there.
In the book, Leena addresses him in emotional verses:
"I’ve only ever carried you
I’ve only ever cradled you
And watched you grow
I never thought I’d watch you go."
As she continues to live with his loss, Leena also expresses the permanent sadness that she feels every day. She writes: "Grief does not know logic. There is no beginning, middle and end. It is all present still. That is the reality of grief. It is every day renewed."
But as time passes, Hamoodi’s death makes her rethink her existence and redefine the way she perceives it. She starts treating people with a little more love, enjoying her time with her kids, appreciating happy moments, and letting things be. She believes that even in death, clarity can change us for the better.
War, betrayal, and belonging
"This is my story of escaping a forgotten war. Mourning a forgotten country. And grieving as a forgotten mourner."
Once the war erupted in Sudan back in 2023, Leena Magdi and her family had to flee the country and head to Egypt.
In her memoir, she describes what they went through during those horrifying moments: "One bomb. And then another. The walls shaking. Wondering if the next one would come through the bedroom wall, or the roof, or the living room […] We couldn’t quite see where it was coming from, but death seemed unescapable."
According to her, the war in Sudan was terribly dismissed and left without any media coverage, with an "international silence."
Both the experience of war and the loss of her brother became deeply connected to a feeling of betrayal. Losing her younger brother made her feel as if she had been betrayed by everything and everyone around her: time, homeland, and life itself.
"Betrayed by the men claiming to stand for security and freedom. Betrayed by the country he proudly and bravely stood for."
This sense of betrayal also leads her to question the system that allowed Hamoodi’s death to happen. Leena puts the blame on a corrupt political system for killing him: "A corrupt system allowed a trained officer to believe he could purposely shoot and kill my brother, an innocent, unarmed civilian. A corrupt system allowed him to believe whatever he did was justified."
Yet, Leena’s relationship with Sudan begins to change. Before Hamoodi’s death, she felt no sense of belonging to her homeland. Later, she feels a deeper connection to Sudan and embraces the idea of having two homes and two cultures.
"This is my Sudan. The soil that held my brother. It is the land that witnessed his last steps. The air that carried his last breath."
Synchrony of life
Throughout her memoir, Leena Magdi emphasises the synchrony between good and bad. Her main belief is that peace and pain coexist.
"I realise that I can be dressed in layers of hurt and still carry pockets of laughter. I can flow in rivers of happiness and still feel the ripples of stones. I do not have to be one or the other. Most days, I am both. That is the beauty of being, it is all encompassing."
She believes we are always living in both states, good and bad, happiness and sadness, in synchrony.
At the same time, she emphasises the beauty that exists around us. Even in bad times, beauty is always there. "In that, we see the synchrony that has always been there." She further adds: "Life and death exist in synchrony."
So, finding synchrony in life means understanding how both states carry lessons that push us forward and help us accept things as they are.
Ultimately, Leena highlights the inner strength that lets us stand firm and not let grief or any other trauma determine our future. She still grieves for her brother, but she looks ahead and sees her children and the life that awaits her.
Joyce Bou Charaa is a Lebanese freelance writer and book editor, with a keen interest in writing about literature, culture, and history
Follow her on Instagram: @joyboucharaa

Merz Says Forcing Ukraine to Surrender Would Be a Defeat for All of Europe

Merz Says Forcing Ukraine to Surrender Would Be a Defeat for All of Europe
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said continued support for Ukraine is firmly in Germany’s own national interest and is intended to bring Russia’s war of aggression to an end as quickly as possible—not prolong it.
But forcing Kyiv to surrender, he warned, would amount to a defeat for Europe as a whole.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We support Ukraine not to prolong this war. We are doing so to end it as quickly as possible. But capitulation, or even unconditional capitulation, by Ukraine is not an option, because that would mean the capitulation of all of us,” Merz said during a discussion at the Berlin Global Dialogue, according to Ukrinform on October 21.
The chancellor said Germany therefore intends to continue providing substantial support to Ukraine, framing that assistance not simply as solidarity with Kyiv but as a direct investment in Germany’s own security.
“That is precisely why I support Ukraine so decisively. It is in our own interest. It is absolutely in our own interest,” Merz said.
His remarks came as diplomatic efforts to end the war continue. Merz referred to talks held the previous evening in Oslo involving President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, US representatives, and European officials, saying the discussions had produced some movement.
“Yesterday evening in Oslo, there was a meeting with Zelenskyy, with our representatives from Europe, and we made some progress in this discussion. We are always ready for negotiations,” he said.
Merz stressed, however, that Europe cannot view Russia’s aggression as a problem limited to Ukraine. In his assessment, Moscow is challenging the broader European political and security system that emerged after the Cold War.
“This is not just a war in Ukraine. It is a fundamental attack against the entire political order that we achieved after 1990,” the German chancellor said.
He also warned that Russia poses a wider threat to security and freedom across Europe through hybrid operations, including sabotage, cyberattacks, drone activity, and disinformation.
For Berlin, Merz argued, supporting Ukraine is therefore inseparable from defending Europe’s own political order and security. Ending the war remains the goal—but not on terms that leave Ukraine forced into surrender and Russia rewarded for aggression.
Previously, Merz warned against complacency over the threat from Moscow, saying Russian leader Vladimir Putin aims not only to defeat Ukraine but also to undermine democracy across Europe.

Russia to Build $815 Million Arctic Shipyard for Its Growing Fleet of Floating Nuclear Reactors

Russia to Build $815 Million Arctic Shipyard for Its Growing Fleet of Floating Nuclear Reactors
Russia plans to begin construction of a new $815 million shipyard in Murmansk in 2027 to service its expanding fleet of floating nuclear power plants, as Moscow seeks to strengthen its nuclear energy infrastructure in the Arctic and promote the technology to foreign markets.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Barents Observer on October 20, Rosatom subsidiary Energoflot Murmansk is seeking a contractor to develop the shipyard, which will be located on the eastern shore of Kola Bay, north of Atomflot’s existing base for Russia’s nuclear-powered icebreaker fleet.
The project is estimated to cost 65 billion rubles (approximately $815 million) and will include docking facilities for floating nuclear power plants, equipment installation, utility systems, and new road and railway connections.
Russia currently operates one floating nuclear power plant, the Akademik Lomonosov, which has supplied electricity to Pevek in the Russian Far East since 2020.
However, Moscow is preparing to expand its fleet significantly. A second floating nuclear power plant, equipped with larger reactors, is being outfitted at the Baltic Shipyard in St. Petersburg, while three additional units are under development, with their hulls being constructed in China.
All four new plants are intended to supply electricity to the Baimsky copper and gold mining complex in Russia’s Arctic region, approximately 400 kilometers inland from Pevek.
Although floating reactors can be refueled at their operating locations, they require specialized docking facilities for major maintenance and repairs. According to the report, no existing shipyard along Russia’s Northern Sea Route can accommodate vessels of this size, making Murmansk a key location for the project.
Beyond domestic energy production, Rosatom is seeking to export floating nuclear power plants to international customers.
In April, Rosatom chief executive Alexey Likhachev said negotiations with Indonesia over a potential floating nuclear power plant had reached their final stage. Russia has also discussed similar projects with Brazil, Argentina, Malaysia, and Cuba.
Despite these ambitions, Rosatom has yet to secure its first international contract for a floating nuclear power plant.
Earlier, leaked internal correspondence revealed reported delays, financial irregularities, and corruption allegations surrounding Rosatom’s Paks II nuclear power plant project in Hungary, raising questions about the Russian state corporation’s ability to deliver major nuclear infrastructure projects abroad.

Russia’s Next Fighter Jet Could Be Designed With a Banking Chatbot
Russia is turning to artificial intelligence developed by its largest bank to help design future aircraft, potentially including fighter jets, as Western sanctions continue to restrict access to engineering software previously used by the country’s aerospace industry.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defence Blog on October 21, Russia’s state-owned United Aircraft Corporation (UAC), which manufactures Su-57 and Su-35 fighter jets, has begun testing Sberbank’s GigaChat AI system to assist engineers in developing new aircraft.
The initiative could eventually bring technology developed by a banking institution into the design process for Russia’s next generation of military aircraft, although UAC has not confirmed that its current AI-assisted project involves a fighter jet.
In May 2026, UAC chief executive Vadim Badekha revealed that the company had launched a pilot program with Sberbank to explore generative aircraft design using GigaChat. The initial testing focuses on early-stage aircraft development, with plans to expand the technology’s role into structural strength assessments and aerodynamic calculations.
UAC says artificial intelligence could allow engineers to examine more design alternatives, process larger volumes of technical data, and reduce the time and expense required to develop new aircraft or modify existing models.
On October 13, UAC general designer Sergey Korotkov also supported introducing AI into aircraft development, provided the technology delivers practical engineering benefits.
The company’s growing interest in artificial intelligence comes after Western software developers, including Dassault Systèmes, Siemens, and Autodesk, withdrew from Russia following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
These companies previously supplied engineering and design tools used throughout Russia’s aerospace industry, forcing domestic manufacturers to accelerate the transition toward Russian-made alternatives.
According to Defence Blog, UAC claims to have replaced nine major aircraft lifecycle management software modules and equipped approximately 4,000 engineering workstations with domestic programs.
The corporation also reported that digital engineering technologies have reduced certain aircraft system calculations, including hydraulic networks and cabin thermal balance, from months to days. However, Russia’s efforts to replace Western aviation technologies have not eliminated problems affecting its aircraft development programs.
Russia’s push to adopt AI comes amid persistent difficulties replacing Western aviation technology. In July 2026, Russia’s Ministry of Industry and Trade sought to recover $3.2 million from a domestic manufacturer that had failed to develop replacements for US-made military aircraft displays, with the project running nearly six and a half years behind schedule.

Prosecutor searches far-right group offices in EU Parliament

STRASBOURG — Officials acting on behalf of the European Public Prosecutor’s Office searched the offices of staff of the far-right Patriots group in the European Parliament on Wednesday morning.
The searches are part of an investigation into allegations that the now-defunct Identity and Democracy group mismanaged EU funds. In 2025, the Parliament’s finance department found that ID misspent €4.3 million between 2019 and 2024 in irregular donations and public tenders. The EPPO, which investigates financial crimes involving the EU budget, opened a probe based on the Parliament’s reports.
“Since this morning, searches have been underway at the European Parliament in Strasbourg — where we are currently located — targeting the offices of staff members of the former Identity and Democracy Group,” said France’s National Rally chief in the Parliament, Jean-Paul Garraud.
Advertisement
The EPPO confirmed it carried out searches in the Parliament’s buildings in France and Belgium “as part of an ongoing investigation into the use of European funds by a former political group in the European Parliament.”
The searches took place at the group’s secretariat offices, according to two officials, granted anonymity to speak about the ongoing investigation.
When ID dissolved in 2024, many of its staff moved to the Patriots, including lawmakers from France’s National Rally, Austria’s Freedom Party, Hungary’s Fidesz, Spain’s Vox, Belgium’s Flemish Interest and Czechia’s ANO 2011.
In their statement, the group insisted “there is no legal continuity with the ID Group” and that “it is not involved in the ongoing investigations.”
The allegations of mismanagement of funds relate to the budget allocated annually by the Parliament for political groups to spend on administrative and operative costs. EPPO is probing whether ID made irregular donations to regional organizations in several EU countries, and whether the group breached tender rules in contracts awarded to companies friendly to the group.
In 2025, the finance department ordered the Patriots to give back €276,967 in EU funds it says the group misused during the second half of 2024, related to similar irregular tender procedures.

“As always when requested Parliament cooperates with relevant authorities — we don’t have additional comment,” a Parliament spokesperson said via a text message.

CERT-UA sees signs of possible AI use by cybercriminals in Jan-Sept 2026 – State Special Communications Service
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:51:35 EEST
22:51:35 KST

Specialists from CERT-UA, which operates under Ukraine's State Service for Special Communications and Information Protection, recorded signs of possible use of artificial intelligence (AI) by cybercriminals in preparing phishing messages, creating fake web pages and developing software code in January-September 2026.
"At the same time, identifying individual indicators does not make it possible to conclusively establish that artificial intelligence was used and requires additional technical analysis," Dmytro Pakholchenko, director of the Cyber Protection Department of the Administration of the State Service for Special Communications and Information Protection of Ukraine, told Interfax-Ukraine in a blitz interview.
Although there is no separate tracking of AI use, the agency's specialists' experience indicates that cybercriminals are resorting to AI tools significantly more often than last year, he said.
The State Special Communications Service also explained that AI allows cybercriminals to automate certain stages of attacks and create convincing texts in any language.
"In addition, these technologies lower the barrier to entry, making it possible for even insufficiently qualified individuals to carry out attacks," Pakholchenko said.
Earlier, Vitaliy Balashov, deputy minister for digital transformation for cybersecurity and cloud technologies, told Interfax-Ukraine that some cyberattacks observed by the specialized Security Operations Center unit of the state-owned Diia enterprise may be carried out using AI. The technology can enhance the capabilities of both attackers and those defending against attacks, enabling them to work faster, automate a large number of processes and increase the number of simultaneous actions.
At the same time, the deputy minister said AI in cybersecurity can primarily speed up processes and reduce operational workloads by automating established procedures. These include analyzing event logs, identifying patterns of potential attacks and responding to threats quickly.
The full text of the blitz interview with Dmytro Pakholchenko, director of the Cyber Protection Department of the Administration of the State Service for Special Communications and Information Protection of Ukraine, will be published on the Interfax-Ukraine website.

Deputy Justice Chancellor: Police acted lawfully in not pursuing Finns Party MP's conspiracy theory comments
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:50:39 EEST
22:50:39 KST

The Deputy Chancellor of Justice says a Helsinki detective chief inspector acted lawfully when he decided last September not to open a preliminary investigation into MP Teemu Keskisarja's (Finns) comments on Yle's A-studio talk show.
In August 2025, Keskisarja, an MP and the Finns Party's first deputy chair, spoke on A-studio about "population replacement" as if it were fact and described immigrants as "mostly low quality."
A private citizen complained to the Chancellor of Justice about how the police handled the case. They argued that the department had already decided to start an investigation, but the case was taken off the first head of investigation and handed to another officer, who saw no reason to suspect a crime.
Prosecutor General would not have pressed charges
Prosecutor General Ari-Pekka Koivisto ruled in June that ordering a criminal investigation was ultimately unnecessary, because he would most likely not have pressed charges.
According to Koivisto, Keskisarja was not criticising immigrants' innate or genetic traits, but their level of education, culture and professional skills, which immigrants can themselves influence.
"The statements were generalising, but they were not made with the intention of insulting or treating people unequally, and Keskisarja has not denied immigrants their human dignity," Koivisto said.

Live Updates: Iran says indirect talks with U.S. on ceasefire proposal continue
What to know about the Iran war today:
- Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday that indirect negotiations with the U.S. continue over a seven-day ceasefire proposal that President Trump initially rejected last month, with the U.S. seeking new clauses.
- A senior official with Iran's Revolutionary Guard threatened Wednesday to target undersea internet cables in the Strait of Hormuz and other U.S. "investments" if the U.S. launches new strikes on Iranian infrastructure.
- Despite global oil prices remaining near five-month highs, President Trump insisted Tuesday that "we're doing very well" with Iran, adding that he was yet to "make a final decision of which way do we want to win" the war, "the nice way or the not nice way."
State Department orders some U.S. government employees and family members to leave Saudi Arabia
The U.S. has ordered all non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as the kingdom faces escalating attacks by Houthi militants.
"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a social media post Wednesday.
The order came a few days after the U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and several other countries warned that hostilities could rapidly and without warning spread beyond areas already affected by the fighting.
"The safety and security of Department personnel and their families remain our highest priority, and we will continue to take all necessary steps to protect and support them," Pigott added.
U.S. will suffer "even greater strategic failure" if it chooses war over diplomacy, Iranian FM says
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi issued a warning to the U.S. on Wednesday afternoon, saying it should choose diplomacy over returning to war.
"Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance if we see strong evidence of a sincere desire by US to build trust & reach a just solution," he wrote on X, sharing a link to an opinion piece in the Financial Times. "But if US chooses war over diplomacy, it'll certainly result in an even greater strategic failure."
Araghchi said earlier in the day that Iran and the U.S. were still involved in indirect negotiations via mediators over the seven-day ceasefire proposal from September. The proposal was outright rejected by President Trump, but Araghchi said the U.S. was trying to add further clauses to the agreement.
U.S. sanctions Greek law firm for alleged involvement in Iranian "shadow fleet"
The U.S. Treasury announced new sanctions on the Panamanian-Greek law firm Karnakis and Karnakis for involvement in Iran's "shadow fleet" as part of its Operation Economic Outcast.
The U.S. accuses Karnakis and Karnakis of being indirectly involved in Iran's illicit shipping operations for years. A "shadow fleet" refers to oil tankers that hide their true ownership in order to evade sanctions.
"Whether you are conducting illegal oil transfers at sea or sitting in the corner office of a law firm, if you are supporting the Iranian regime, we will find you and sanction you," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. "Iran's facilitators must make a choice: Either you are with us or against us. We know who you are, we know what you're doing, and we will continue to take action."
The Treasury also said it sanctioned Singapore- and UAE-based shipping agents, including a fleet of cargo vessels that has directly taken part in Iran's "shadow fleet" and "helped generate substantial revenue for the Iranian regime."
Riyadh airport partially reopens after deadly Houthi strike
A limited number of Saudi airlines took off and landed at the country's main airport on Wednesday, two days after authorities notified airlines that they could resume operations with prior permission.
Saudia and FlyNas were operating flights Wednesday, according to flight-tracking data published by FlightAware. Major carriers, including Lufthansa and Air France, have canceled flights through mid-November.
Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport has been hit multiple times this month by Yemen's Houthi rebels and shut down on Oct. 10. A strike two weeks ago killed 13 people and injured hundreds more.
The Houthis have acknowledged attacking the airport, claiming without evidence that Saudi Arabia provided military equipment to government forces through the facility.
Iran criticizes potential Egyptian involvement in Yemen war; Sisi promises only defensive actions
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said any interference in the Yemen war by Egypt or any other country would make the situation "more difficult."
"Egypt has sufficient experience to avoid entangling itself in such a highly complex conflict," said Iran's top diplomat in an interview with Iraqi state broadcaster Al-Iraqiya aired on Tuesday.
"We believe that any foreign presence or interference will only make resolving this issue more difficult," Araghchi noted.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Wednesday that Cairo's proposed military support for Riyadh was to "defend Saudi territory, and does not include an attack on Yemen," according to a statement from his office.
At a government event titled Egypt Forum 2026, Sisi said the "objective is to defend the kingdom's lands and borders, as well as those of any other Arab state, should it be requested of Egypt," his spokesman said in a statement.
Sisi on Saturday had asked parliament to authorize support for Saudi Arabia in its war with the Houthis, "if requested."
The parliament, which is stacked with supporters of the president, has since held two rare secret sessions, before postponing deliberations until next week.
Iran's new defense minister says first priority is meeting air force needs
Iran's newly appointed defense minister, Mehrdad Akhlaghi, said Wednesday his first hours in office were devoted to meeting the requirements of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' Aerospace Force and the army's air defense units.
"We are not in a war of rhetoric in response to repeated threats; we are turning threats into greater readiness and more effective defensive power," he wrote in his first post on X since taking office.
Akhlaghi added Iran was concentrating on its objectives through the use of new technologies.
"We may eat dirt, but we will not give up our soil," he concluded.
Trump blocked Netanyahu's plan for multiday strikes on Iran, report says
President Trump blocked a planned Israeli multiday operation that would have resumed strikes against Iran on the weekend of Oct. 10, according to the Financial Times.
The plan was designed to exceed the intensity of the joint U.S.-Israeli military offensive launched in February, three people familiar with the matter told the paper, and would have struck Iranian nuclear sites, regime targets and civilian infrastructure such as power plants.
The president blocked the strike to avoid escalating conflict before the U.S. midterm elections, according to the report.
Iranian regime needs to be toppled, Netanyahu says
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Wednesday he had directed the Israeli army and intelligence services to topple the Iranian regime.
"The regime in Iran has still not learned the lesson," Netanyahu told a graduation ceremony at an officer training school in the country's southern Negev desert.
"Mojtaba Khamenei, the current tyrant, has decided to follow in his father's footsteps," he said, referring to the country's supreme leader, who replaced his father Ali Khamenei after he was killed in a U.S.-Israeli airstrike on Feb. 28.
"He has taken the safety off, and Iran is once again attempting to develop 'death bombs,'" he added, without giving details on what exactly he was referring to.
"There is only one way to remove this threat once and for all," Netanyahu said, "by toppling the regime in Iran. And that is my directive to the [Israel Defense Forces], the Mossad, and the security services."
He did not expand on how he expected the military or intelligence services to carry out the directive.
Saudi Arabia discusses deployment of up to 10,000 Syrian troops to Yemen
Saudi Arabia has held talks with a senior Syrian military delegation on arrangements to transfer up to 10,000 Syrian fighters to take part in the war against Yemen's Houthi movement, according to a report by the Lebanese Hezbollah-owned Al-Akhbar newspaper, citing Yemeni intelligence sources.
The report claims Syrian military officials visited Saudi Arabia's southern regions of Najran and Asir to inspect sites prepared to receive the fighters, while discussions in Riyadh covered transport logistics, financing and military assignments.
The Syrian delegation included Brig. Gen. Khaled Khattab, former commander of the Ansar al-Tawhid faction and current commander of the 82nd Division in the new Syrian army; and Brig. Gen.Haitham al-Ali, also known as Abu Muslim, commander of the army's Third Corps and a former leader in Hayat Tahrir al-Sham.
Khattab reportedly spent four days in southern Saudi Arabia, accompanied by Saudi officers, visiting sites in the regions of Asir and Najran being prepared to receive Syrian fighters. Meanwhile, al-Ali held several meetings with Saudi officers at the Defense Ministry in Riyadh to discuss the costs of transferring around 10,000 fighters, financial arrangements, additional benefits and their intended military tasks. The delegation reportedly finalized logistical arrangements for the transfer.
The report also raises the possibility that foreign fighters currently in Syria, including Uyghurs, Uzbeks, Tajiks and other nationalities, could be transferred to Yemen.
Iran taps missile industry figure as new defense chief, highlighting focus on weapons production
A missile industry veteran has been tapped as Iran's new defense minister, replacing the previous minister who was killed on Feb. 28, the first day of U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran.
Iranian parliamentarians overwhelmingly approved the appointment of Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi, 68, as the country's new defense chief on Sunday.
Akhlaghi studied chemical engineering at Amirkabir University of Technology and then spent more than four decades working in Iran's military industries, holding senior positions in the Shahid Bagheri Industrial Group, the Aerospace Industries Organization – which has worked on missile development in cooperation with Russia, China and North Korea – and the Defense Industries Organization.
He worked with Hassan Tehrani Moghaddam, a senior Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commander widely regarded as the father of Iran's missile industry.
Akhlaghi has been under international sanctions since 2007 because of his involvement in Iran's missile programs.
His appointment comes as Iran works to rebuild its military facilities and replenish weapons lost during the war. He has pledged to strengthen domestic arms production, and his background suggests rebuilding Iran's missile programs will be a priority for the ministry.
Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia has claimed repeatedly since late August that Iran has rebuilt its weapons manufacturing capacity, including last week, when it said the country was now able to make more arms than "even before it [the war] began."
Early in the war, the U.S. military said it had destroyed more than 85% of Iran's "defense industrial base," and President Trump had previously claimed Iran's military capabilities were destroyed by U.S. strikes, but experts have questioned that assessment, and Iran has demonstrated an ongoing capacity to launch attacks on ships in the region.

American regime change ops cause chaos every time – US ambassador

US ambassador makes regime change ‘disaster’ confession
Washington has been involved in nearly two dozen regime change operations across the Middle East, each ending in disaster, US Ambassador to Türkiye Tom Barrack has said.
Barrack criticized American efforts to manipulate the region and impose change through military force during an interview at the Global Security Forum in Qatar on Tuesday. He warned that his remarks would be “real” rather than “diplomatic.”
“If you take the greater Middle East, including the Levant, the Gulf, the Caucases, Central Asia, North Africa, we’ve had 23 regime changes. None of them have worked,” he said, stressing that the US had been involved in all of them in one way or another and bore responsibility for the outcomes.
The diplomat added that “kinetic reactions have never worked” either, referring to US military interventions and their “unintended consequences.” The latest US-Israeli war on Iran, which began in late February, has also plunged the region into chaos.
Barrack acknowledged that fomenting “conflict and controversy” had previously benefited Washington because “the more off base the region was, the more [Washington] could manipulate fossil fuels for its own benefit.” That is no longer the case, he said.
According to Barrack, the US “no longer wants to own [what it] doesn’t need to own” and envisions a different role for itself in the Middle East. “The bargain is not to own, not to control, but to tend, not to leave,” he said.
The envoy contrasted the proposed approach with the arrangement Washington reached with Saudi Arabia in 1974 following the oil shock triggered by the Yom Kippur War between Israel and several Arab nations.
Under the old arrangement, Saudi Arabia continued pricing its oil exclusively in US dollars and invested much of its revenues in American assets, while also purchasing US weapons and expecting American troops stationed in the region to rescue it in case of a major conflict.
The US confrontation with Iran, culminating in two open wars since 2025, has crumbled the foundations of that relationship.
Barrack urged friendly Middle Eastern nations to temper their expectations of American assistance, saying the US is not offering “a commitment to open seas and open trade at any cost.” Washington should “do a better job of defining: here’s what we’re willing to do, here’s what we’re not willing to do,” he added.
The diplomat repeatedly deflected questions critical of Israel, its regional policies, and its role in pushing Washington toward war with Iran.
“We leave Israel out of this because it’s so delicate to talk about,” Barrack said.
He also acknowledged that the Israeli government was reluctant to make any concessions on national security and described a “failure” of the Abraham Accords, a series of normalization agreements Israel signed with several Arab nations in 2020.

Apple Day festival in Almaty brings together over 500 guests
Almaty Resort, a branch of Medical and Wellness Complex Okzhhetpes JSC, hosted a festival on Wednesday to mark Apple Day, Qazinform New Agency reports.
More than 500 guests gathered at the festival, which featured live music, traditional games, dance performances, and a wide variety of apple-themed dishes.
A central feature was a tasting of sweet and savory creations prepared by the resort's kitchen staff. Over two days, a 15-person team under chef de cuisine Madiyar Kydyrbayev crafted a menu centered on fresh, locally grown apples.
The festive buffet featured apple puff pastry roses, strudels, donuts, muffins, pastries, buns, fruit marmalade, and other desserts. The highlight was a braised-apple pilaf, anchored by a display centerpiece sculpted from 100 kg of apples.
“We prepared for the festival well in advance, selecting recipes, testing new pairings, and creating dishes to surprise our guests,” said restaurant head chef Madiyar Kydyrbayev. “Some ideas were born right here in our kitchen, for example, the pilaf with braised apples. For us, this is a chance to show the sheer variety of dishes that can be made from local ingredients.”
The event also featured an artisan craft market, interactive photo booths, and an art exhibition of apple-themed drawings created by children of the resort’s employees.
Almaty Resort Director Gulzhanat Bugubayeva emphasized the event's health aspect.
"For our resort, national health is the core value. Apple Day is especially meaningful to us because the apple is a true source of vitamins and essential nutrients. Our chefs created a wide array of pastries this year, and we strive to innovate each time to delight our guests. It is wonderful to see Almaty residents embracing this tradition and attending with their families," said Gulzhanat Bugubayeva.
The festival culminated in a concert featuring Kazakh performers and creative ensembles, including singers Nurlan Yespanov, Anara Ayazbayeva, and Daniyar Karabalayev, as well as State Dance Ensemble Saltanat and a local senior women's folk group.
Organizers note that the apple’s central role in the celebration reflects the region’s botanical heritage. The foothills of the Trans-Ili Alatau range are home to Malus sieversii, the wild apple species widely recognized as the primary ancestor of modern cultivated apples. For Almaty Resort, the annual Apple Day festival has become an established tradition, bringing together the local community to celebrate regional natural heritage and wellness.

Justice minister: Worst AI offenses should be equated with crimes against humanity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:49:00 UTC
22:49:00 KST

Justice minister: Worst AI offenses should be equated with crimes against humanity
Justice and Digital Affairs Minister Liisa Pakosta calls for stronger international regulation of AI to protect national sovereignty, smaller languages and cultures.
Justice and Digital Affairs Minister Liisa Pakosta spoke Wednesday on ERR's "Otse uudistemajast" webcast about regulating artificial intelligence, protecting children's rights, safeguarding privacy, reducing bureaucracy, restricting overly powerful electric scooters, sex offender registries and the future of her party, Eesti 200.
The global push to regulate AI
Pakosta compared the challenges posed by artificial intelligence to those associated with nuclear energy, stressing the need for international regulation.
"Broadly speaking, the situation is more or less the same as with nuclear energy. Nuclear energy has positive aspects, but it also has the potential to cause catastrophes. And although it took some time in that case, from August 1945 until 1970, to establish international rules, we need to move faster here. We don't have that many years," she said.
Pakosta outlined three areas Estonia wants to prioritize in international AI regulation.
"First, we have proposed that the most harmful impacts of artificial intelligence should be treated as crimes against humanity. We already have that entire framework in place and we would extend it to cover AI's extremely harmful and destructive capabilities," she said.
Second, Estonia must ensure its digital infrastructure does not become dependent on technology controlled by foreign providers.
"We cannot build the Estonian state around AI solutions when someone in a third country could suddenly decide not to provide them to us or to add two zeros to the price, for example. This has become a matter of national sovereignty, which means that AI systems with a significant impact must have open-source options that we can build our services on," Pakosta said.
Her third priority is protecting smaller languages and cultures in major AI systems.
"Large systems must be required to include small languages and cultures. This is something we are genuinely fighting for. Otherwise, the Estonian language and culture will disappear from the world," she said.
Pakosta also warned that Russia is deliberately financing automated online activity to influence the information used by AI systems.
"Russia is deliberately using and funding bots to ensure that its interpretation of imperialist history and everything associated with it is represented in AI systems, while Estonia's perspective is not," she said.
"Russia is not only destroying cultures with bombs on Ukrainian territory; it is also destroying our culture, our narratives, our stories and our identity in AI environments."
The minister warned that younger generations increasingly rely on AI rather than history books for information, making such manipulation a potentially effective investment for Russia.
She called for international agreements requiring AI systems to incorporate safeguards against disinformation and the distortion of historical narratives.
Pakosta also defended digital regulation, arguing that clear rules encourage rather than hinder innovation.
"When you have clear rules, you can build innovation around them. And businesses actually support this, too," she said, pointing to Estonia's experience with the EU's General Data Protection Regulation.
Businesses investing heavily in AI need predictable regulations to protect their investments, she added.
Another priority is developing sovereign AI solutions to protect Estonian residents' personal information.
"There are some very impressive large models in third countries, but we don't know exactly how our data moves through those systems. We don't know exactly what happens to that data afterward," Pakosta said.
She emphasized that Estonia has made a fundamental decision not to use AI for surveillance activities that would otherwise be considered unacceptable.
"We have decided not to use AI to surveil people in ways that technology makes possible but that we would not otherwise do as human beings. That is a very fundamental decision," she said.
Estonia currently uses AI in approximately 260 public sector services, relying on public or non-sensitive information, according to the minister.
As an example of locally developed technology, she highlighted an Estonian legal advice service that automatically deletes sensitive personal information entered by users seeking assistance.
Protecting children
Turning to children's rights, Pakosta discussed legislative proposals being prepared by her ministry based on research conducted under the Mudila project.
The goal is to make it easier for parents and others to find assistance for children, something she described as currently "terribly complicated."
"This is not just about preventing crime. That is only a very small part of it. It is about the broader question of how, in a small, lovely country like Estonia, we can make sure help reaches every child," she said.
Pakosta said the aim is to prevent children from falling through gaps between different services and ensure they receive help as early as possible, potentially immediately after birth.
Containing red tape
On reducing bureaucracy, the minister said Estonia has made substantial progress, introducing a "one in, one out" principle in lawmaking and repealing or simplifying nearly one-fifth of legal acts.
She also highlighted efforts to prohibit the practice of "gold-plating" EU legislation where additional domestic requirements are attached to European rules.
According to Pakosta, this practice has allowed extra regulations to pass through the Riigikogu without sufficient democratic scrutiny.
"We have been successful both in Estonia and in Brussels in not only putting an end to this insane proliferation of bureaucracy, but actually beginning to reduce it," she said.
Illegal electric scooters
Discussing police proposals to confiscate electric scooters exceeding legal power limits, Pakosta acknowledged that legislative changes would be necessary but said they should follow public debate.
She raised the example of parents purchasing excessively powerful scooters for their children, potentially endangering both the children and other road users.
"The parent is putting the child's life at risk, but also endangering other people, including pedestrians. Would the right solution be to fine the parent? That would lead to enormous disputes, with parents saying, 'No, I only bought it for myself to ride somewhere on an off-road track and my child secretly took the scooter. I'm not to blame.' After all, we cannot really punish a younger child, and rightly so. Or do we place greater emphasis on protecting not only the life of the child, for whom the parent is responsible, but also the lives of other road users?
This is where society needs to discuss how to strike the right balance," she said.
Private offender lists
Pakosta also addressed controversy surrounding a privately created registry of sex offenders and domestic abusers launched at ettevaatust.ee by content creator Mallu Mariann Treimann-Legrant and her husband, Tomas Märten Legrant.
She encouraged people to report problems with existing government registries, saying Estonia has the most transparent and accessible criminal records registry among democratic countries.
She warned that privately maintained criminal records databases can contain inaccurate information, cause lasting harm to innocent people and victims and create a false sense of security.
"That registry contained around 400 people, but our national criminal records registry actually contains more than 11,000 people who are prohibited from having contact with children," she said.
The minister also announced that the government was expected to consider legislation Thursday extending the time available for victims of childhood sexual offenses to report crimes.
Currently, such offenses become time-barred when the victim turns 28. For the most serious offenses, the proposed amendment would extend that deadline until age 50.
"Victims need time to gather themselves, process what happened and report to the police that such a vile crime was committed against them," Pakosta said.
Sensitive health data
On medical privacy, Pakosta discussed a bill already before the Riigikogu that would allow investigative authorities to obtain certain medical information during criminal proceedings, subject to court authorization and strict conditions.
She emphasized that investigators would only be permitted to access technical descriptions of injuries, not patients' personal accounts of how those injuries occurred.
For example, authorities could obtain information about the depth of a knife wound or the path of a bullet, but not statements a patient made about a domestic dispute or other circumstances.
"People must be able to tell their doctors openly and honestly what actually happened. That is essential because it is the only way a doctor can properly treat them," she said.
Hospitals and doctors would use a separate form to ensure that patients' accounts are not passed to investigators.
Pakosta also stressed that competent, sober adults who are not under guardianship would retain the right to refuse such disclosures and investigations, citing the privilege against self-incrimination. Different rules would apply to children, while exceptions would also exist in cases of suspected fraud by doctors or patients.
Eesti 200 and elections
Turning to politics, Pakosta declined to reveal her views on the future of Eesti 200, saying decisions rested with the party's board, of which she is not a member.
Her comments followed Sunday's decision by Eesti 200's council not to pursue a merger with the Estonian Greens ahead of the Riigikogu elections.
Nevertheless, Pakosta expressed support for party mergers, arguing that smaller parties can strengthen their influence and broaden their representation by joining forces.
"All the major parties we have today were formed from several parties coming together. There is nothing bad about it. In fact, it is entirely positive," she said.
She argued that parliamentary parties need sufficient size and geographic reach to represent voters effectively, including strong connections with local governments.
Although Eesti 200 has rejected a merger for now, Pakosta said she believes one will eventually take place.
Asked whether she would run in the next Riigikogu elections, Pakosta said the question was premature, noting that Eesti 200 had not yet decided whether it would participate.
"There are a whole range of other issues that I also feel very passionate about. It is not just politics," she added.
Pakosta also declined to express a preference on whether Eesti 200 should participate in the elections, saying she did not want to pressure the party's leadership.
She concluded by defending politicians across party lines, emphasizing the personal sacrifices and hostility that often accompany political work.
"I have seen how difficult it is to work as a politician. No matter which party you belong to, it is very difficult. You face a great deal of hostility, even physical attacks," she said.
"I respect every person who is willing to devote their time to participating in Estonian politics and doing this difficult work. Every person who does this work deserves respect."

Swiss barn owls are changing colour, study shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:48:00 UTC
22:48:00 KST

Swiss barn owls are changing colour, study shows
Over the course of thirty years, the plumage of Swiss barn owls has become more reddish-brown and spotted. A long-term study by the University of Lausanne interprets this as a sign of rapidly advancing evolution, as it announced on Wednesday.
According to the study report, published in the journal Nature Communications, alongside owls with immaculate white plumage, the scientists had observed an increasing number of specimens with plumage ranging from golden-brown to deep red. This was neither a chance finding nor purely cosmetic in nature.
According to the long-term study, the colour change is the result of a rapidly advancing evolutionary process. It is linked to fertility and hunting strategies, and thus also to food intake.
More
Almost extinct owl is making a comeback in Switzerland
The scientists have identified a gene that could be linked to traits such as stress management or aggression, whilst also playing a role in pigmentation. Ultimately, however, it remains difficult to determine exactly which ecological factors account for the varying colouration.
White barn owls use moonlight to hunt their prey – mostly field mice. The red owls, on the other hand, feed predominantly on voles. The mottled plumage, in turn, is linked to immunity and the ability to cope better with stressful situations such as food shortages or parasite infestations.
Not least, the study demonstrates that evolution does not only take place over millions of years, but also within timeframes of just a few decades. Against the backdrop of climate change, this is seen as an encouraging sign. The ability to adapt quickly could help living organisms cope swiftly with environmental changes.

Government websites go dark as vulnerabilities in programming language send shudder across internet
Oct 21 - Government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline on Wednesday after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in a widely used programming language sent website operators scrambling to protect their systems.
Developers of the PHP programming language said Tuesday they had identified two critical vulnerabilities and urged users to update their sites as soon as a fix was released. With reports that hackers were already exploiting the flaws to break into websites, government agencies in the Netherlands and Finland were among those that took sites offline as a precaution.
PHP underpins large parts of the internet, raising concerns that a significant number of websites could be vulnerable to attack.
"PHP is everywhere. It quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," cybersecurity company Huntress said in a blog post.
Dane Knecht, the chief technology officer of Web and cloud security firm Cloudflare, said that attacks were emerging and Cloudflare was updating its firewall rules as a stopgap measure.
"We are seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up. This is a STOPGAP only. Patch as soon as PHP releases the update," he said on X.
Wordfence, a security plugin that protects WordPress websites, said all WordPress sites run on a PHP-installed server. It warned that automatic updates would not apply the fix and advised site owners to find out who is responsible for updating PHP on their sites.
Cybersecurity agencies in Europe, Australia, Japan and Britain have urged PHP users to update immediately or take websites offline until patches can be applied. The Dutch cybersecurity agency itself went offline, saying it had done so as a precaution because of the vulnerabilities.
Officials have said that all PHP versions from PHP 5 onward could be affected, although PHP has not yet disclosed which versions are vulnerable. REUTERS

Investors are questioning neoclouds' business model but Nebius says AI computing prices are rising
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:44:12 UTC
22:44:12 KST

BERLIN — Nebius is seeing AI computing prices rise more than expected, a top executive told CNBC on Wednesday, offering a bullish view as neocloud firms' business model comes under increasing scrutiny.
Investors have grown wary after CoreWeave, one of the biggest neocloud players, saw the spread on its five-year credit default swaps hit levels generally viewed as signs of distress. The yields on CoreWeave's bonds also climbed.
The CoreWeave developments and questions around the amount of debt being used to fund the data center buildout have weighed heavily on other neoclouds like Iren and Nebius, whose stocks have dropped sharply over the last month.
Marc Boroditsky, chief revenue officer at Nebius, said his company wasn't in CoreWeave's position because "we're not carrying the kind of debt that they are."
He also said that if the AI infrastructure company brought its 2027 capacity online, it would sell out. There could be "the same type of dynamic" in 2028, supporting a positive longer-term demand outlook, he said, as companies race to secure access to computing power.
When asked whether he sees the price per megawatt continuing to rise ahead of expectations, Boroditsky replied: "Yeah."
Nebius is among a new wave of Neocloud companies that are investing billions to buy up Nvidia's graphics processing units, build data centers and rent that capacity.
Nebius ran an auction for computing capacity on Tuesday, which showed continued price rises, the revenue chief said. "We're seeing continued upward mobility in terms of the kind of price per megawatt," he told CNBC.
Price per megawatt, a key measure among new cloud companies, shows how much a company can charge customers for a certain amount of computing capacity.
Chase Lochmiller, CEO of Crusoe, an Nvidia-backed AI company that is building data centers, was also bullish on pricing, saying the company was seeing rising prices for GPUs, including older Nvidia chips.
"We're seeing higher pricing today for A100s than we saw in 2020 or 2021. We're seeing higher pricing for H100s than what we saw when they were first deployed in 2023," Lochmiller said.
"There's tremendous demand and a lot of it is because the underlying model capabilities have gotten so much more advanced that people are just creating so much more value out of the compute infrastructure."
The comments come amid an investor debate over how quickly Nvidia's GPUs lose their economic value as more powerful chips enter the market.
The ability to continue renting out older chips at attractive prices is crucial to AI infrastructure companies that need to recover their investments and generate profits, while spending billions on GPUs.
Lochmiller's comments suggest that, at least for Crusoe, older generations of Nvidia chips are commanding higher rental prices than when they were first deployed, potentially strengthening the economics of its AI cloud business.
SpaceX boost
Nebius stock rose on Wednesday after SpaceX reported revenue at its AI business jumped ninefold to $7.56 billion. SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen said pricing is "currently tracking slightly above the high end of the $30 to $50 per watt range," underscoring the pricing power for those renting out compute capacity.
Cloud providers CoreWeave, Iren, and Applied Digital also rose in premarket trading on Wednesday following Johnsen's comments.
"I'm thrilled by SpaceX's results. It's confirming what we already know, which is that it's a very dynamic market and that supply continues to fall far behind demand," Boroditsky said.

Jordan, Saudi Arabia upgrade coordination council as Amman condemns Houthi attacks

2026-10-21
13:42:12 UTC
22:42:12 KST

Laith Al-jnaidi and Ikram Kouachi
21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
Jordan and Saudi Arabia signed an amended protocol Wednesday to restructure their Supreme Coordination Council and strengthen its role in expanding bilateral cooperation, under the leadership of Jordan’s King Abdullah II and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
The agreement was signed during expanded talks in Riyadh between Jordanian Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi and his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin Farhan, Jordan’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
The protocol aims to “strengthen the council’s role in institutionalizing and expanding cooperation and coordination between the two countries,” replacing the Jordanian-Saudi Joint Committee, it said.
The two foreign ministers will head the council’s general secretariat, and their ministries will follow up on its work, including preparations for its meetings and those of its affiliated committees and working groups.
The council was established in 2016, when King Abdullah and Saudi King Salman bin Abdulaziz witnessed the signing of its founding agreement in Riyadh to strengthen cooperation and coordination across various fields.
During the talks, Safadi affirmed Jordan’s “absolute solidarity with Saudi Arabia in confronting attacks by the Houthi group,” saying his country stood alongside the kingdom in its efforts to protect its security, stability, sovereignty and the safety of its citizens and residents.
He reiterated Jordan’s condemnation of attacks targeting civilians and civilian and economic facilities as a “blatant violation of international law and the UN Charter” and a violation of Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty, security and stability.
On regional developments, Safadi and bin Farhan discussed efforts to end the escalation, contain its regional and international repercussions, and restore calm on foundations that guarantee lasting security and stability, the statement said.
Their talks also covered respect for international law, good-neighborly relations, non-interference in the affairs of other countries, and “freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.”
On the economic front, trade between the two countries exceeded $4 billion in 2025, accounting for 14% of Jordan’s total trade, making Saudi Arabia the kingdom’s second-largest trading partner, according to the statement.
Saudi investments in Jordan amounted to around $16 billion in sectors including transport, tourism, financial services and trade, it said, noting that the number of Saudi tourists visiting Jordan also increased by about 14% in 2025.
The two ministers said the signing of the protocol would provide additional momentum to bilateral cooperation, reaffirming their commitment to further developing relations and maintaining coordination and consultations on shared regional and international issues.

EU plans to spend over €200 billion in 2027: where the money will go and how much will be allocated to Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
16:41:48 EEST
22:41:48 KST

EU plans to spend over €200 billion in 2027: where the money will go and how much will be allocated to Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
The EU is considering the bloc’s budget for 2027 and support for Ukraine. The member states have still not agreed on the amount of future funding.
On October 21, the European Parliament is considering the results of the European Council summit held on October 15–16 in Brussels, as well as the European Union’s budget for 2027. Key issues include financial support for Ukraine, defense spending, the competitiveness of the European economy, and the future of the EU’s multiannual budget.
However, it is already known that, despite confirming common priorities, the member states have not yet reached a compromise on the amount of funding for the coming years.
UNN explains how everything unfolded and why the European Parliament’s budget decisions are currently extremely important for Ukraine.
The European Parliament discussed the summit’s results — which issues became key
During the plenary session in Strasbourg on October 21, MEPs returned to the issues discussed by the leaders of the 27 EU member states at the October 15–16 summit.
One of the central topics was the EU’s economic competitiveness. European leaders examined the consequences of rising energy prices, the need to support industry, reducing the administrative burden on businesses, and accelerating investment. According to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, European gas prices have risen by 140% since the end of February, while diesel fuel has doubled in price. Additional costs for importing fossil fuels amounted to approximately €100 billion. Against this backdrop, EU leaders called on the European Commission to consider short-term measures to contain energy prices while maintaining the strategic course toward the development of renewable energy.
The EU’s future spending was no less important an issue. The states must simultaneously finance defense, economic development, social programs, and support for Ukraine. However, some national governments are already insisting on limiting budget expenditures, resulting in heated debates.
Support for Ukraine after the summit — what decisions did the European leaders make
Following the meeting, the European Council reaffirmed its readiness to continue political, financial, economic, humanitarian, and military support for Ukraine.
Particular attention was paid to preparations for winter, the protection of energy infrastructure, and strengthening air defense following large-scale Russian attacks. EU leaders welcomed the continuation of payments under the €90 billion Ukraine support loan mechanism for 2026–2027. They also supported the decision to allocate €6.6 billion under the European Peace Facility (EPF).
However, despite these optimistic developments, Ukraine’s financial needs for 2027 remain substantial. Therefore, during the summit, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy appealed to European partners to provide an additional €70 billion. Following this, the European Council instructed the European Commission, together with the International Monetary Fund, to update its assessment of Ukraine’s financial and defense needs and prepare concrete financing proposals.
The EU budget for 2027 — how much money is proposed for allocation
The draft European Union budget for 2027, presented by the European Commission, provides for approximately €199.9 billion in commitment appropriations and €212 billion in payment appropriations, taking special instruments into account. Commitment appropriations determine the amount of financial commitments the EU may enter into during the year. Payments are the funds actually planned to be disbursed, including under programs from previous years.
However, the Council of the EU proposed reducing the initial draft by approximately €1 billion in commitment appropriations and €500 million in payment appropriations. Its budget position provides for €191.88 billion in commitments and €202.07 billion in payments, excluding special instruments outside the multiannual financial framework. Meanwhile, the European Parliament’s Budget Committee opposed the proposed cuts. The committee set expenditure within the main budget headings at €194 billion in commitments and €203.3 billion in payments.
MEPs also proposed increasing funding for priority programs by €1.17 billion compared with the European Commission's initial draft. These discrepancies became the basis for further budget disputes between the European Parliament and the member states.
What the European Parliament wants to allocate additional funds to
The European Parliament's Budget Committee proposes directing the largest share of additional funding to economic development, infrastructure, and scientific research. In particular, €376.7 million has been earmarked for programs related to competitiveness. Of this amount, €260.5 million is proposed for addition to the Connecting Europe Facility, which supports the development of European transport and energy networks. Another €63 million is planned for Horizon Europe, while €31.6 million is intended for the Single Market Programme.
An additional €275.1 million is proposed for social and humanitarian priorities. In particular, €96 million is earmarked for Erasmus+, €80 million for the civil protection mechanism, and €50 million for EU4Health.
An additional €182.5 million will be allocated to agriculture, environmental protection programs, and support for young farmers.
Funding for border management and migration programs is to be increased by €72.9 million, while funding for security and defense is to rise by €66.3 million, of which €20 million is earmarked for military mobility.
Another €139 million is proposed for addition to funding for foreign-policy programs, including humanitarian aid and support for the EU's eastern and southern neighbors.
EU long-term budget for 2028-2034 - why member states cannot reach agreement
The EU's long-term budget (MFF) for 2028-2034 remains a separate subject of dispute. Unlike the annual budget, it sets the bloc's main financial priorities for the next seven years.
The European Commission proposed a long-term financial plan worth approximately €1.76 trillion. However, Ireland, which holds the presidency of the Council of the EU, presented a compromise option involving a reduction in spending of approximately €141 billion, or 8%. The proposed total is approximately €1.62 trillion.
Despite the cuts, a number of countries, including Sweden, Germany, and the Netherlands, consider the financial commitments excessive. At the same time, other states advocate maintaining sufficient funding for agriculture, regional development, and social programs.
The European Parliament, for its part, criticizes the proposed restrictions. According to its representatives, taking inflation and the costs of repaying common debt into account, the new budget's real purchasing power could decline by approximately 10% compared with the current financial period.
Another problem is the lack of agreement on new sources of EU revenue. Possible options under discussion include additional levies on large digital platforms and other Europe-wide revenues. The October 15-16 summit did not ensure any significant convergence of positions, so further negotiations were entrusted to European Council President António Costa.
What the European Union's budget decisions mean for Ukraine
For Ukraine, the consequences of the European budget negotiations extend far beyond ordinary state expenditure planning. At a minimum, the stability of international budget support, defense procurement, infrastructure reconstruction, and the implementation of joint economic programs will depend on the availability of EU financial resources.
Ensuring Ukraine's financial needs for 2027 is of particular importance. It is the European institutions that must determine the sources of funding, the conditions for raising it, and possible mechanisms for distributing the financial burden among partners.
It should also be noted that the European Parliament's Budget Committee separately proposed earmarking €1.1 billion to cover the cost of borrowing under the Ukraine Loan Cooperation Mechanism.
At the same time, the EU links the timely disbursement of part of the funding to Ukraine's implementation of the agreed reforms, particularly in the area of the rule of law and its commitments under the Ukraine Plan.
When will the EU budget for 2027 be finally approved?
The review of the European Union's annual budget is now entering its final phase. Following discussions on October 20, the European Parliament's vote on budget amendments and its own position for 2027 is scheduled for October 21.
Since the positions of the European Parliament and the Council of the EU differ, the next step should be a conciliation procedure involving representatives of both institutions. The first meeting of the conciliation committee is scheduled for November 3, while the 21-day period allotted for reaching an agreement is due to end on November 16.
If a compromise is reached, the agreed budget must be approved by both sides. If the negotiations fail, the European Commission must present a new draft budget.
The EU's key financial decisions by the end of 2026 — what to expect next
By the end of the year, the European Union must resolve several strategic financial issues. The most immediate task will be approving the annual budget for 2027, on which funding for current European programs will depend. In parallel, the European Commission must determine the possibilities for additional support for Ukraine, based on updated calculations of its needs.
In November, António Costa is expected to present a new basis for negotiations on the multiannual budget.
A special European Council summit devoted to the 2028–2034 financial framework is scheduled for November 26–27. The next discussion is expected on December 17–18.
European leaders aim to reach a political agreement by the end of 2026 so that the necessary legislation can be adopted during 2027 and uninterrupted funding for programs can be ensured from January 2028. However, reaching a compromise is complicated by disputes over member states' contributions, defense spending, agricultural subsidies, and the search for additional sources of budget revenue.
Recall
Earlier, UNN reported that EU leaders had failed to reach an agreement on the long-term budget at a summit in Brussels. The countries are arguing over whether to cut spending or increase the budget.
