Israel's olive oil harvest set to nearly double, but farmers warn of a hidden problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:41:00 UTC
22:41:00 KST

After one of the worst olive harvests in recent memory, Israeli farmers are finally seeing signs of recovery. Last year, the country's olive oil production reached an estimated 8,000 tons, far below the anticipated 15,000 tons. This season, however, the outlook is considerably brighter, with production expected to rebound to approximately 15,000 tons of olive oil and another 10,000 tons of table olives. But beneath the encouraging figures lies an unexpected problem: Israel's olive trees are bearing plenty of fruit, yet the olives contain unusually little oil.
According to the Agriculture and Food Security Ministry, Israel has between 310,000 and 350,000 dunams of olive groves, more than 75% of them in Arab communities. Most groves in the Arab sector are rain-fed, including those growing the traditional Syrian olive variety. In the Jewish agricultural sector, groves are generally irrigated, largely using treated wastewater and recycled water. Approximately 15,000 dunams are devoted to table olives, while 120 olive presses operate across the country.
Agronomist Ayala Neubauer, a resident of Moshav Tzipori in northern Israel, previously headed the Agriculture Ministry's olive oil tasting panel and now manages her family's Rish Lakish olive grove. She has recently focused on restoring ancient orchard trees and established an organization dedicated to saving agricultural produce and promoting Israeli farming.
"Unlike last year, which was particularly bad, this season we're seeing an abundance of fruit," she explained. "However, the oil content of the olives is very low."
According to Neubauer, climate change and extreme summer temperatures have placed olive trees under considerable stress. Although the trees have produced fruit, they have not accumulated oil efficiently. Many growers, including farmers in Arab communities, are waiting for substantial rainfall and lower temperatures, hoping the change will help the fruit develop more oil and make extraction easier.
The situation has been complicated by delayed ripening, a problem also affecting Israel's wine industry. Growers are concerned that heavy rainfall during November and December, particularly if unusually strong El Niño conditions develop, could make it difficult to enter groves with heavy harvesting equipment. Stormy weather could also cause more sensitive olive varieties, including Italy's Coratina, to shed their fruit before harvesting.
Last year's harvest was so disappointing that producers remain reluctant to discuss the figures. Neubauer says one difficulty is that olive oil production is difficult to measure accurately because much of the oil is sold directly at olive presses rather than through supermarket chains. As a result, industry estimates can sometimes be inflated.
She believes farmers should consider delaying the harvest until conditions improve. When olives yield only 10% oil, production becomes significantly more expensive, making it harder for growers to remain profitable.
"I really recommend that farmers wait a little before harvesting," she said. "Consumers should also wait. Everyone would benefit from waiting a little."
For Raviv Avshalom, 55, from Moshav Sde Moshe near Kiryat Gat, this year's harvest represents a welcome turnaround after the difficulties of 2025. His family's agricultural story began in 1956, when his wife's grandparents established their farm. The property later passed to her parents but was abandoned following the death of her father. Several years ago, when agricultural land in the moshav was redistributed, Avshalom and his wife, Mor, received their first olive grove.
Neither had previously worked in agriculture, but they returned to the moshav and began growing olives. Avshalom quickly discovered that growing fruit alone was not enough to make a living.
"In the olive industry, you can make a living only if you grow the olives, produce the oil and sell the finished product directly to consumers," he explained.
Their experience has been shaped by both weather and war. In October 2023, the couple began harvesting on a Thursday, just two days before the Hamas-led October 7 attack and the outbreak of war. Overnight, their agricultural workforce disappeared. With the help of friends, relatives and volunteers, they managed to complete the season.
Today, Avshalom relies mainly on Israeli workers, occasionally employing Bedouin laborers from nearby communities. He remembers 2023 as an exceptionally productive season, when the groves yielded large quantities of olives with oil content reaching 20%.
"Last year, many plots weren't harvested because there simply wasn't any fruit," he said. "This year, many trees needed support because of the enormous weight of the olives."
The contrast between seasons is particularly striking in northern Israel, where farmers are returning to groves that have suffered years of neglect and damage from nearby fighting.
In Metula, just 180 meters from the Lebanese border, 79-year-old olive grower Roni Bakhmotsky returned to harvest his trees this week after three years of warfare, fallen missile fragments and interrupted agricultural work. His 18-dunam grove, described as Israel's northernmost olive orchard, stands on land his family received from Baron Rothschild. Bakhmotsky planted the trees himself in 1988, when the land was still barren.
During the fighting, maintaining the grove became both dangerous and emotionally exhausting.
"We had interceptor fragments and pieces of missiles falling around us while we worked, and we had to stop," he recalled. "A great deal of fruit was lost, and it was heartbreaking. Even during the war, I worked under fire. I came to the grove to take care of the trees because otherwise everything would have been lost."
The inability to reach his land regularly took a particularly heavy toll on the plots closest to the border fence. The October 2025 harvest produced disappointing results because years of interrupted maintenance had weakened the grove.
"Unfortunately, the grove still hadn't been properly cared for," Bakhmotsky explained. "I hadn't pruned it for two years because of the war."
The problems extended beyond the orchard. His private home was also damaged during the fighting, and dealing with property tax officials over compensation for his losses consumed time and attention that might otherwise have gone toward restoring the farm.
"This year, I hope that once the harvest is over, I'll finally be able to prune the trees and take proper care of them," he said.
Yet despite the expectation of a particularly abundant harvest, Bakhmotsky is not necessarily celebrating the quantity of olives on his trees. For him, producing high-quality extra virgin olive oil matters more than maximizing the amount of fruit.
"Personally, I don't like having too much fruit," he explained. "When there are too many olives, I thin the trees because the oil content is lower. The fruit is smaller, and the trees attract pests."
He estimates that his approach may cost him between 100 and 200 kilograms of olive oil, but considers that an acceptable price for maintaining the quality of his product. He also prefers to begin harvesting slightly earlier, helping preserve the characteristics required for high-quality extra virgin olive oil rather than allowing the fruit to develop further at the expense of quality.
But alongside the challenges of extreme weather and war damage, olive growers face another threat: counterfeit oil being marketed as locally produced Israeli olive oil.
The Plants Production and Marketing Board warns that consumers seeking authentic Israeli olive oil should look for the industry's official quality seal, which is backed by laboratory testing and strict supervision. The certification is intended to help distinguish genuine locally produced oil from counterfeit or adulterated products, including imported oil sold under misleading labels.
Bakhmotsky knows the problem firsthand. His family's olive oil has a recognizable label featuring an image of his late father at a threshing floor. According to the farmer, fraudsters have exploited his farm's reputation by selling products that customers believed came from him.
"I came across five families who told me they had bought my olive oil. But it was nothing of the sort," he said angrily. "I contacted the Plants Production and Marketing Board, which involved the police. These things make me very angry because there are con artists out there."
For Israeli olive growers, the promising 2026 harvest may offer a chance to recover from an exceptionally difficult year. But as farmers contend with changing weather patterns, damaged groves and fraudulent competition, the abundance of olives on the trees tells only part of the story. The real measure of recovery will be how much quality oil they can produce and whether they can earn a sustainable living from it.

Why Haaretz called Israel's first election in 1949 a 'failure of the extremists'

Why Haaretz Called Israel's First Election in 1949 a 'Failure of the Extremists'

====================================================================================================

China Focus: Panda homeland takes a new path amid changing times
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:38:07 CST
22:38:07 KST

CHENGDU, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Deep in the mountains of southwest China's Sichuan Province stands a Catholic church that looks like a traditional wooden Chinese courtyard house, yet its interior follows Gothic design.
Visitors flock to the Dengchigou church in Baoxing County year-round, but most are not there to pray. They come for the giant panda, an animal that continues to shape the memories, identity and economic profile of the region.
In 1869, French missionary and naturalist Armand David arrived in Muping, as Baoxing was then called, and spent more than eight months at the Dengchigou church. There, he encountered an animal known locally as the "black-and-white bear," which was found to belong to a species totally new to science -- the giant panda.
For Li Yunjun, 48, who grew up in these mountains, giant pandas have always been part of life. He recalls how his parents' generation rescued starving pandas during widespread bamboo flowering in the 1980s, carrying weakened animals on makeshift stretchers for treatment.
Back then, wild pandas occasionally wandered near villagers' homes in search of food. "If one came to our home looking for food, we'd just let it eat whatever it wanted," Li said.
Li and other villagers were relocated from the mountains to a new village in 2016, but pandas still occasionally paid a visit. In July 2021, villagers spotted one near a riverbank and watched from a distance without disturbing it. The animal eventually returned to the forest.
If a panda is found injured or ill, villagers report it to local authorities, who arrange for experts to examine the animal before it is taken by "panda ambulance" to a veterinary hospital, Li said.
The peaceful encounters contrast with a darker chapter of the panda's history, documented at the Dengchigou church, part of which now serves as the giant panda origins museum.
Among its exhibits are photographs of Western expeditions in the 1920s and 1930s, when pandas were hunted for foreign museum collections.
The images recall an era of foreign aggression and domestic turmoil in China, when another chapter of history was unfolding in the same mountains.
In June 1935, the Communist Party of China (CPC)-led Red Army reached Baoxing after crossing the Dadu River and capturing the Luding Bridge. The soldiers then climbed Jiajin Mountain, the first major snow-capped mountain on their Long March.
The Long March, an epic military trek from 1934 to 1936, saw Red Army troops cross mountains and marshlands while battling better-armed Kuomintang forces, some marching as far as 12,500 kilometers.
The journey preserved the Red Army and gave the CPC a new foothold in northwest China, from which it built up its strength, fought back against invading Japanese troops and eventually toppled the corrupt Kuomintang regime, leading to the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949.
There are no known records of Red Army soldiers encountering giant pandas, but the animals, too, would see their fortunes change dramatically in the decades ahead.
For years, Baoxing relied heavily on white marble mining, logging and small hydropower projects, which provided jobs but put pressure on the environment.
That development model began to shift in 1998 when China banned commercial logging in natural forests along the upper Yangtze River. Dan Zhaohui, who had built roads for timber transport in Baoxing, joined reforestation efforts.
Three years later, he became a forest ranger, patrolling 1,250 hectares of mountainous terrain. "Over the years, I have encountered giant pandas, golden snub-nosed monkeys and other wildlife," he said. "The animals have come back."
Decades of conservation efforts have helped bring giant pandas back from the brink. Sichuan's wild panda population rose from 909 in the 1980s to 1,387 in the fourth national survey released in 2015, while their habitat expanded to more than 2 million hectares. The International Union for Conservation of Nature has reclassified the giant panda from "endangered" to "vulnerable."
At the 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics, panda mascot Bing Dwen Dwen became a sensation, with souvenirs quickly selling out. Once hunted for foreign museum collections, giant pandas have become a global symbol of friendship and conservation.
Protecting the animals and their habitat, however, has required difficult economic trade-offs.
Nearly 40 percent of Ya'an, the city that administers Baoxing, now lies inside the Giant Panda National Park. In Baoxing itself, more than 80 percent of the territory is included in the park.
The closure of mines and small hydropower facilities in protected areas has forced Baoxing to seek new sources of growth.
"The transition has been painful, but moving away from the old economic model is necessary. We must find new paths toward greener, higher-quality development," said Li Lun, director of Baoxing County's bureau of economy, commerce and technology.
Tourism has emerged as a source of growth. In 2025, Baoxing received 4.63 million tourist visits, up 10.28 percent year on year, while tourism revenue rose 10.41 percent to 4.09 billion yuan (about 608.7 million U.S. dollars), according to local authorities.
For Li Yunjun, the shift has meant leaving behind the marble trucks he once drove through the mountains.
He used to earn about 60,000 to 70,000 yuan a year hauling marble. He remembers the dust from blasting and the muddy Baoxing River during the mining boom.
In 2016, he sold his truck and opened a guesthouse in Dengchigou. Its seven rooms are often booked ahead of holidays, and his family's annual income now exceeds 100,000 yuan.
"Instead of hauling stone out of the mountains, I now welcome visitors drawn by giant pandas and the surrounding forests," he said.
But pandas are not the only draw for travelers to Baoxing. Many also come to trace the Long March. The Memorial Hall of the Red Army Crossing Jiajin Mountain receives over 300,000 visits annually, according to guide He Mengyu.
She said more student groups are coming from outside Sichuan, while foreign visitors who come for the pandas often extend their trips to Long March sites too. Some even ask where they can try making the straw sandals once worn by Red Army soldiers, an experience available in Dengchigou.
Jiajin Mountain, at the border of Baoxing and Xiaojin counties, has become a hiking destination for outdoor enthusiasts. As of August 2026, the Jiajin Mountain scenic area had recorded 13,327 tourist visits so far this year, up 1.45 percent year on year.
For Li Yunjun, the transformation is visible much closer to home.
"The Baoxing River has become clear again," he said. "The mountains are still the same, but the way we live with them has changed." ■

====================================================================================================

From Israel's youngest prime minister to oldest candidate: Netanyahu's new record at 77
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:37:35 UTC
22:37:35 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu celebrated his 77th birthday on Wednesday, receiving a cake during a visit to the southern Israeli city of Dimona. But next Tuesday, October 27, he will mark another milestone: At 77 years and six days old, he will become the oldest candidate for prime minister in Israel's history.
The previous record was held by former Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir, who led the Likud party into the 1992 election at the age of 76 years and eight months, ultimately losing to Yitzhak Rabin. Netanyahu, already Israel's longest-serving prime minister in terms of cumulative time in office, is now poised to claim another historical distinction.
There is, however, an important difference between being the oldest candidate and the oldest person to hold the office. That record still belongs to Ariel Sharon, who formally remained prime minister until April 2006, when he was 78 years and one month old.
Netanyahu's new milestone is particularly striking given how his political career began. In 1996, at just 46, he defeated Shimon Peres in Israel's first direct election for prime minister, becoming the youngest person ever to lead the country. Three decades later, he is about to set a record at the opposite end of the age spectrum.
A look back at Israel's leaders reveals how the ages of its prime ministers have varied throughout the country's history. David Ben-Gurion, Israel's founding prime minister, was 61 when he declared independence in May 1948. Despite his nickname, "the Old Man," he was considerably younger than Netanyahu is today.
Ben-Gurion served as prime minister almost continuously until June 1963, when he stepped down at 76. He remained politically active as a member of the Knesset, Israel's parliament, before finally retiring in 1970 at the age of 83.
His successor, Levi Eshkol, was 67 when he took office. Eshkol led his party to victory in the 1965 election and was prime minister during the Six-Day War in 1967. He died in office in February 1969 at the age of 73.
Eshkol was succeeded by Golda Meir, who became Israel's first female prime minister at the age of 70. She remains the only woman to have held the position. Meir led her party to election victories in 1969 and 1973, when she was 75. But growing public criticism of the government's handling of the Yom Kippur War prompted her resignation in April 1974 and eventual retirement from political life.
Yitzhak Rabin succeeded Meir at the age of 52, becoming Israel's first native-born prime minister. His relatively young age stood in contrast to several of his predecessors.
The historic political upheaval of 1977 brought Menachem Begin to power, ending nearly three decades of Labor-led governments. Begin, who had spent decades leading the opposition, became the first Likud prime minister at 63.
Following Begin's resignation in 1983, Yitzhak Shamir took over. He celebrated his 68th birthday just 12 days after assuming office.
The national unity government established after the 1984 election introduced a rotation agreement between Israel's two major political blocs. Shimon Peres became prime minister first, at 61, before handing the position back to Shamir two years later. Shamir returned to office just two days before his 71st birthday.
Shamir remained prime minister following the 1988 election, but his political career reached its turning point in 1992. At 76 years and eight months, he led Likud into another election, only to lose to Rabin, who returned to the premiership at the age of 70.
After Rabin was assassinated on November 4, 1995, Peres again assumed the premiership, this time at 72. The following year, he faced Netanyahu in a direct contest for the country's leadership and lost to the 46-year-old Likud leader.
Netanyahu served until 1999, when he was defeated by Ehud Barak, who was then 57. Less than two years later, Barak was replaced by Ariel Sharon, who took office in March 2001 at the age of 73.
Sharon secured another election victory in 2003, less than a month before his 75th birthday. He continued serving until suffering a severe stroke in January 2006 that left him in a coma. Although Ehud Olmert assumed his duties, Sharon formally retained the title of prime minister until April 14, 2006, making him the oldest person ever to hold the position, at 78 years and one month.
Olmert, who succeeded Sharon, was 60 when he assumed office. In March 2009, Netanyahu returned as prime minister at 59, beginning more than 12 consecutive years in power. That period ended in June 2021, when Naftali Bennett replaced him at the age of 49.
Bennett served for just over a year before handing the premiership to Yair Lapid in July 2022. Lapid was 58 when he took office. Netanyahu subsequently returned to power in December 2022.
As Israel prepares for its October 27 election, the ages of the leading political figures span more than three decades. Netanyahu, at 77, is the oldest among the party leaders listed in the current race, followed by Avigdor Liberman, 68; Aryeh Deri, 67; Gadi Eisenkot, 66; and Yair Golan, 64.
Other figures include Yaakov Asher, 61; Ofer Winter, 55; Naftali Bennett and Yousef Jabareen, both 54; Mansour Abbas, 52; Yoaz Hendel, 51; Itamar Ben-Gvir, 50; and Bezalel Smotrich, 46.
For comparison, U.S. President Donald Trump celebrated his 80th birthday in June. Trump was 78 when he won his second, nonconsecutive presidential term in November 2024 and is expected to be 82 when his current term ends in January 2029.
Netanyahu's approaching election record requires no victory at the ballot box. Regardless of the outcome, he will surpass Shamir as the oldest person to seek Israel's premiership in a national election. Whether he will eventually surpass Sharon's record as the oldest serving prime minister is another question entirely.

That said, we believe in the wisdom of crowds, have heard them loud and clear, and removed the market."
Some of the recent outcry over the Polymarket contract has been aimed at its celebrity promoters. Polymarket also has partnership agreements with the NHL, Major League Baseball, Major League Soccer, the UFC and ATP Tour.
A woman identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit last month alleging that seven fraternity members sexually assaulted or exploited her in October 2024 and that Cornell mishandled her complaint. Australian researchers suggest gut's nervous system evolved before brain
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:37:26 CST
22:37:26 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Australian researchers have proposed that the nervous system in the gut may have evolved before the brain, challenging traditional theories about the evolution of the nervous system.
Researchers from Flinders University in South Australia argue that the gut's nervous system may have served as the body's original "brain," with the brain evolving later to support its functions, according to a university statement released on Wednesday.
The theory, published in The Journal of Physiology, draws on evidence from physiology and evolutionary biology to suggest that the nervous system may have originated in the gut to help early organisms obtain the energy needed for survival.
The enteric nervous system, often referred to as the body's "second brain," can sense its environment, process information and coordinate complex responses independently, according to the researchers.
The researchers said the theory could open up new avenues for studying conditions linked to the gut and nervous system, including obesity, diabetes, Parkinson's disease and digestive disorders. ■

China Focus: China makes significant progress in climate action, charts green path
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:37:25 CST
22:37:25 KST

The State Council Information Office (SCIO) holds a press conference on China's proactive efforts in addressing climate change and leading global climate governance, in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 21, 2026. (Xinhua/Pan Xu)
BEIJING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- China has achieved significant results in tackling climate change in recent years, gradually forging a green and low-carbon development path, a senior environment official said on Wednesday.
Li Gao, vice minister of ecology and environment, made the remarks at a news conference, where an annual report on China's policies and actions on climate change was released by the Ministry of Ecology and Environment.
The report showed that in 2025, China's carbon dioxide emissions per unit of GDP fell by 17.7 percent compared with 2020 levels. Non-fossil energy accounted for 21.7 percent of total energy consumption last year, while combined installed capacity of wind and solar power reached 1.84 billion kilowatts. Forest stock volume stood at 20.99 billion cubic meters in 2025.
This progress is backed by the country's sustained efforts to accelerate its green and low-carbon transformation.
China has built the world's largest and most complete clean energy industrial chain, with green and low-carbon industries becoming an important engine of economic growth, Li said.
By mid-2026, the country's total installed renewable energy capacity had reached 2.46 billion kilowatts, accounting for 60.7 percent of total national power generation capacity. At the end of July, installed solar power capacity had surpassed coal power for the first time in China's history, making it the country's largest single power source.
Moreover, China's combined installed capacity of operational and approved nuclear power units has risen to first place globally. New energy vehicle production and sales, meanwhile, have ranked first in the world for 11 consecutive years.
Li noted that the country has established the world's largest carbon emission trading market, covering about 8.3 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide, or more than 65 percent of the country's total emissions. Cumulative allowance trading volume recently surpassed 1 billion tonnes.
China has long placed high importance on addressing climate change. It has set the dual carbon goals of peaking carbon dioxide emissions before 2030 and achieving carbon neutrality before 2060.
China last year announced its 2035 nationally determined contributions, including a target of reducing economy-wide net greenhouse gas emissions by 7 percent to 10 percent from peak levels, while striving to do better.
It represented the first time China had put forward an absolute emission reduction target covering all greenhouse gases across the entire economy, Li said.
The country is also actively participating in and leading global climate governance while helping other developing countries build their capacity to address climate change.
China has signed South-South cooperation memoranda of understanding on climate change with 46 developing countries, helped build low-carbon demonstration zones, implemented a series of flagship climate projects, and trained more than 10,000 officials and technical personnel from over 120 developing countries.
China in 2023 launched the "Africa Solar Belt" photovoltaic project, which has helped nearly 20,000 households in five African countries gain access to electricity and lighting. By 2027, this flagship project is expected to benefit 50,000 African households.
Looking ahead, China's commitment to addressing climate change will not waver.
In July, the government released a national climate change plan for the 2026-2030 period, targeting a 17-percent reduction in carbon dioxide emissions per unit of GDP by 2030 compared with 2025 levels. The plan also vowed to deliver the country's carbon peaking target on schedule and fulfill the 2030 nationally determined contributions.
Li said China will promote green and low-carbon development in key sectors including energy, industry, transport, and urban and rural construction, accelerate the development of the national carbon market, and advance the building of a climate adaptive society.
Also on Wednesday, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology released an action plan on controlling both the total amount and intensity of carbon emissions across the industrial and information technology sectors for the 2026-2030 period to speed up China's green and low-carbon transition.
The plan called for improving carbon emission management in key industries, accelerating the development of zero-carbon factories, zero-carbon computing facilities and low-carbon supply chains, establishing a carbon footprint management system for industrial products, and setting up carbon accounting mechanisms.
By 2030, the plan targeted the formulation and implementation of around 400 carbon footprint accounting standards for key industrial products, the establishment of roughly 500 national-level zero-carbon factories and zero-carbon computing facilities, and an over 10-percent reduction in energy consumption per unit of value-added output of major industrial enterprises. ■

Across China: Extended-stay travel gains ground among China's older people
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
21:37:24 CST
22:37:24 KST

HEFEI, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- On a recent autumn morning in Xiongcun Village in east China's Anhui Province, Bi Sheng sipped coffee in his small studio while answering emails.
A short walk away, craftsmen were renovating an old house, waiting for the 55-year-old to review designs and select timber.
A native of Beijing, Bi first visited villages in Shexian County of Huangshan City, southern Anhui, more than a decade ago for a design project. Drawn to the area's rich cultural heritage, he eventually bought a house there and embraced what he described as a semi-retired life.
"Every village has its own stories, and history is everywhere. That was beyond my expectations," he said.
His new life has given Bi something he missed in the city: close-knit neighborhood ties. His new neighbors sometimes bring him freshly caught fish or vegetables they have grown themselves.
"In cities, many people don't even know their neighbors," he said.
Bi is part of a growing trend in China, where many older people are traveling to spend extended periods in places with beautiful scenery, rich culture and opportunities to build social connections, particularly after retirement.
From July 2024 to June 2025, China recorded more than 84.3 million extended-stay visits by older travelers, averaging more than 7 million a month, according to a report released by the China Association of Ageing.
To cash in on this fast-growing market, many regions offer services tailored to older travelers, ranging from age-friendly accommodations and traditional wellness treatments to activities that help newcomers build social connections.
In Shexian County, at the foot of Mount Huangshan and within easy reach of major eastern cities such as Shanghai and Hangzhou, local authorities have developed eight wellness-themed guesthouses, said Xu Yuhong, deputy director of the county's health commission. These guesthouses received 13,300 guests from January to July this year, he said.
Wu Zenghe is one of the guesthouse managers. He converted three traditional Huizhou-style buildings into a guesthouse catering to older travelers.
"People who travel after retirement are more interested in in-depth experiences than in simply rushing from one tourist attraction to another," Wu said.
His guesthouse features specially designed doors and windows to block noise and light, as well as herbal sachets intended to aid sleep. It also offers an artificial intelligence-powered health consultation device, acupuncture, moxibustion and medicinal baths.
So far this year, it has welcomed several thousand older visitors from across China, including hundreds who stayed for more than a week.
In Yunnan Province in southwest China, some markets have been renovated to better accommodate older people, while eligible visitors can receive discounts at tourist attractions and use public services such as universities for older adults. In Heilongjiang Province in northeast China, localities are exploring cross-border extended-stay and wellness initiatives for older visitors.
At the same time, as older travelers spend weeks or months away from home, many want a stable social network and a sense of belonging.
About 2,600 older people from across China live in the Huangshan mutual aid community in Huangshan District, Huangshan City.
Li Jiankang, a 66-year-old from Nanjing, capital of neighboring Jiangsu Province, was among the community's first residents. His daily routine includes running, tending a vegetable garden, playing the saxophone, and joining other residents for table tennis or swimming.
He said he has made many friends and found a fulfilling rhythm to life in Huangshan.
The community has established more than 20 interest groups covering sports, agriculture and music, giving residents opportunities to connect through shared interests. It has also set up mutual aid groups so residents can care for one another.
"Many older people who live alone can feel isolated, and some may even struggle with their mental health. That is why we hope to help them find comfort and companionship through mutual support," said Li Junping, manager of the community. "A sense of being needed is often the main reason residents choose to stay."
For Li Jiankang, this sense of connection is central to the experience.
"To me, the Chinese character for 'mutual' looks like two hands clasped together," he said. "Everyone here extends a hand to help others, and people can feel the bonds between us." ■

Gaza’s fragile internet lifeline: Nattat’s battle to keep his neighbourhood connected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:35:03 UTC
22:35:03 KST

For Ali Nattat, the day begins with a look at the sky. In Gaza, the sunlight falling on his solar panels determines whether he can keep his neighbourhood connected to the outside world.
Unlike many homes nearby, Nattat’s modest house survived the airstrikes. It now houses a small internet network that supports his family and provides work for five employees. For displaced families and people working remotely on his street, it also provides a vital means of communication.
The network runs entirely on solar energy. Nattat has four small panels of his own and uses additional panels borrowed from a neighbour in exchange for free electricity. Together, they charge salvaged batteries that keep the equipment running after sunset.
But the system is fragile. Cloudy weather limits how much electricity the panels generate, leaving less power available at night.
“When my system abruptly dies at night, it doesn’t just cut my income; it paralyses the entire neighborhood,” Nattat said.
A connection to an injured daughter
For Abu Firas, 50, the network allows him to stay in touch with his daughter, who is receiving medical treatment in Egypt.
An airstrike destroyed his home and killed his wife. He now lives alone in the kitchen where he works, while the rest of his family have fled to Egypt.
He relies on Nattat’s network to make daily video calls to his daughter. When the batteries run out and the connection fails, Abu Firas must turn to expensive international mobile roaming to hear her voice, adding to his financial difficulties.
His dependence on the network is one reason Nattat feels unable to step away from it, even during the night.
Sharing limited power
The electricity generated by the panels must also meet the needs of Nattat’s household.
His wife, Areej, said the family uses some of the power to run a small freezer, allowing them to sell chilled water to people living in a nearby displacement camp. The sales provide an additional income.
Nattat’s parents and other relatives also rely on the system to charge their phones and power essential lights. As the batteries run low, he switches off other electrical appliances to keep the internet equipment working for as long as possible.
READ: UN: 950,000 displaced people in Gaza face flood risks this winter
“My dream is simply to achieve basic electrical stability for my network,” he said. “This internet business doesn’t just feed my immediate family; it is the sole source of income for five workers I employ.”
Yet replacing worn-out equipment or buying a more reliable system is costly.
Prices are at approximately $970 and a lithium-based solar power system at around $25,900. A basic installation also requires a panel and wiring, adding to the expense.
Those unable to afford their own equipment must pay for access to electricity. Charges cited for solar-powered phone-charging services range from approximately $0.32 to $0.65 per phone, while electricity supplied by private neighbourhood diesel generators can cost up to $11.30 per kilowatt-hour.
For families with little income, even charging a phone becomes another expense competing with daily necessities.
Broken sleep to keep the network running
Nattat’s mornings are divided between household responsibilities and earning a living. He collects water from a distribution truck, goes to the market and opens his small shop. Alongside those tasks, he manages the internet network from his living room.
“Almost everyone on my block relies solely on me to check if their families are safe,” he said.
After sunset, his attention turns to the batteries. He must balance keeping the network available against preserving enough charge to restart it the following morning.
He describes going to bed around midnight and waking again at 2.30am to inspect the system. When the remaining charge falls too low, he has to switch off the equipment.
“Flicking that switch feels like cutting a medical lifeline,” he said.
By 6.30am, Nattat is awake again to prepare the system for the day as the panels begin generating electricity. He aims to have the full network running about an hour and a half later, when residents need it for work and contact with their families.
The routine leaves him with little uninterrupted sleep. Each evening brings the same uncertainty: whether the batteries will last, when he will need to disconnect the network and who will be waiting to make a call.
For Nattat, a reliable electricity supply would mean a more secure livelihood and a chance to rest. For Abu Firas, it would mean being able to check on his injured daughter without worrying that the connection will disappear.

====================================================================================================

U.S. Midterms Loom Over a Deadlock Between Trump and Tehran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:35:00 UTC
22:35:00 KST

Iran may have found a weapon in the American electoral calendar. With the midterm elections two weeks away, Tehran is intensifying attacks on shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, calculating that higher energy prices will deepen President Donald Trump’s political troubles and make another U.S. military campaign too costly to contemplate.
The wager is seductive: an American president anxious about diesel prices and his party’s prospects in the midterms, Iran seems to believe, will have little appetite for another major war.
Trump’s declaration that he will refrain from striking Iran before the Nov. 3 vote appears to vindicate this view, even as he periodically threatens to use force again. Having survived two rounds of war and absorbed punishing economic losses, Iran’s leaders believe they can endure a little longer. By disrupting Gulf commerce, they gain leverage their conventional forces cannot provide. They also hope to make that leverage permanent and compel Washington to accept Tehran’s authority over passage through the world’s most important energy chokepoint.
Yet the past nine months of war against Iran have made it clear that renewed military conflict before the midterms or after the elections is unlikely to resolve the disputes between the U.S. and Iran. The two countries will eventually have to sit across the negotiating table to resolve their long-running disputes.
Miscalculations in Tehran and Washington
Tehran may be misreading how political peril shapes an adversary’s decisions. Trump could decide that appearing powerless as Iranian attacks push up prices is more damaging than another round of military strikes. Reports that his administration has considered fresh strikes suggest the military option remains in play. A serious attack on American forces could turn Trump’s promise of restraint into a political liability overnight.
The political situation in Israel adds a combustible variable. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces an Oct. 27 election with his bloc struggling to secure a majority. He has staked his political reputation on the claim that only he can neutralize the Iranian threat.
With Tehran rebuilding its missile and drone capabilities and uncertainty surrounding its nuclear program, Netanyahu may see renewed strikes as both a strategic opportunity and a means of restoring his standing at home. Such a gamble could deepen Israel’s insecurity, but electoral desperation seldom improves anyone’s judgment.
The convergence of these calculations makes the coming weeks particularly perilous. Iran thinks Trump’s electoral weakness will constrain him. Trump and Netanyahu might each conclude that a show of force could rescue their political fortunes. Each side imagines it can calibrate the violence and manage the aftermath. The experience of this year’s conflict, in which successive rounds of fighting outran diplomatic efforts to contain them, offers little reason for that confidence.
Even if October passes without another conflagration, November brings its own hazards. After the midterm elections, the political constraints Trump has publicly imposed on himself will disappear. With substantial American forces already positioned in the region, Washington may be tempted to break the deadlock through another round of attacks. Tehran, fearing another surprise attack, might choose to strike Israel or U.S. military assets in the region first. What might seem like prudent preparation in Washington or Tehran could help bring about the war it is meant to deter.
The underlying impasse is as stubborn as ever. Washington wants a nuclear agreement and believes its blockade will ultimately compel Iran to negotiate. Tehran insists on upfront economic relief and an end to the war before substantive talks on the nuclear issue can begin.
America can point to tankers still transiting Hormuz, but shipping that depends on costly military protection and remains under threat is a poor substitute for normal trade. Iran can inflict considerable damage on the oil exports of its Gulf neighbors, but it has so far failed to turn that leverage into meaningful American concessions.
Dangers of a wider war
Another surge in hostilities would widen this gulf rather than bridge it. American and Israeli aircraft can destroy missile launchers, production facilities, and infrastructure, but Iran has repeatedly demonstrated that it can retaliate and survive. Iran’s response could extend further to target Gulf energy infrastructure, maritime commerce, data centers, and other critical networks.
The Houthi confrontation with Saudi Arabia already offers a grim illustration of how quickly the costs can spread. The war in Yemen has been reignited with devastating consequences, including deadly attacks on civilian airports and a spiraling cycle of retaliation. The fighting now threatens to draw in Turkey and Pakistan to support Saudi Arabia, as the three countries recently signed a mutual security pact known as the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement.
A new campaign could leave Iran poorer, Israel more exposed, and the U.S. burdened with an even more expensive regional commitment, while markets around the world absorb another shock.
The outlines of a diplomatic bargain have been visible for months: reciprocal steps to reopen Hormuz, calibrated sanctions relief, and a resumption of nuclear negotiations. The difficulty lies in sequencing and trust. Tehran fears that surrendering its maritime leverage first would invite fresh demands; Washington worries that easing pressure would reward coercion without securing lasting constraints on Iran’s nuclear program. Addressing those fears will require reciprocal steps and credible verification. More bombing won’t help.
Leaders contemplating an October surprise or an offensive after the midterms must remember that uncomfortable truth. Military force may alter the balance of pain without resolving the disputes each side will eventually have to confront across the negotiating table.
After another round of death and destruction, they could find themselves negotiating over the same issues, with less trust, greater bitterness, and far fewer resources to rebuild what they have broken. Their choices will be no easier then; the cost of reaching an agreement will be far greater.

The Indian Government’s Job Statistics Are Misleading
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:35:00 UTC
22:35:00 KST

The Indian government claims that the formal job market in the country is booming. It cites as proof payroll data from the Employees’ Provident Fund Organization (EPFO).
The Employees’ Provident Fund is a mandatory government-backed retirement savings scheme in India for salaried workers. The question, however, is: does a rising EPFO count really amount to more good jobs?
The official story goes as follows. The Economic Survey 2023-24 reported that net EPFO payroll additions more than doubled, from 6.11 million in FY2018-19 to 13.15 million. The survey called it “healthy growth in formal employment.” The Union Labor Ministry hailed it as a “growing formal employment landscape.”
The Indian government has now gone further and linked formalization of employment directly to “quality jobs.” In August 2026, it promoted the Pradhan Mantri Viksit Bharat Rozgar Yojana as a scheme to expand formal employment, designed to encourage first-time employment and to reward employers for creating new formal jobs through EPFO.
Formalization is valuable. A worker brought under EPF coverage gains access to an institutional mechanism for retirement savings and social security. An enterprise complying with labor regulations represents progress over one that does not.
However, these claims ignore reality. An EPFO “net subscriber addition” is not a net new job. It can include a person moving from one EPFO-covered employer to another; an existing worker newly brought into EPFO coverage; a worker previously outside formal coverage becoming covered; workers rejoining after an employment break; changes resulting from EPFO administrative coverage; and, importantly, formalization of an already existing informal job.
September 2026 EPFO data showed contributors in 12 traditionally labor-intensive sectors (garments, textiles, leather, jute, beedi, tea, brick-making, cashew, coir, cotton ginning, diamond cutting, and others) fell 1.3 percent, from 5,536,000 in 2023-24 to 5,464,000 in 2025-26. These are precisely the sectors India must expand to absorb workers leaving agriculture.
There is a further fundamental statistical problem.
EPFO payroll statistics measure movements into and out of the EPF system. The monthly payroll series records first-time subscribers, members exiting coverage, and earlier members who rejoin. The government itself cautions that the numbers are provisional because employee records are continuously updated.
The Economic Survey 2025-26 carried the government’s claims further: organized manufacturing added 5.7 million jobs. This is potentially more interesting because it is not based on EPFO figures.
The National Sample Survey or NSS Survey uses Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) data and says organized manufacturing employment increased by more than 5.7 million between FY2015 and FY2024; grew at about 4 percent compounded annual growth rate (CAGR); and increased by more than 1 million in FY2024 alone, a 6 percent year-on-year increase.
This is probably the strongest official evidence currently being cited for actual employment expansion in the organized sector, rather than simply formalization. But there is a major definitional qualification: The ASI’s “persons engaged” category includes working proprietors, family members, and unpaid workers, as well as employees. So it is not synonymous with regular wage/salaried formal jobs.
The government is also pointing to the rise in regular salaried employment. Regular wage/salaried employment increased from 22.4 percent of workers in 2024 to 23.6 percent in 2025. That is a meaningful movement toward wage employment, although it is still very far from the claim that most new employment is formal.
In fact, what takes the wind out of the government’s claims is that the increase in organized manufacturing has been accompanied by growing contractualization. According to ASI, contract workers accounted for only about 13 percent of the formal manufacturing workforce in 1993-94. However, this share rose sharply to 20 percent by 1999-2000 and further to 37.8 percent in 2018-19. As per the latest ASI data (2022-23), it has reached 40.7 percent. So much for the claim of formalization – the ILO defines it as work with social security, and contract work does not offer that.
The percentage share of contract labor in capital-intensive industries has increased from 19.5 percent in 1999-2000 to 46 percent in 2018-2019, whereas it has increased from 22 percent in 1999-2000 to 33 percent in 2018-2019 in labor-intensive enterprises.
As though that is not enough, if EPFO was really creating so many new jobs, how is it that India’s Periodic Labor Force Survey (PLFS) continues to show that India’s share of informal workers without social insurance (i.e. pensions, death/disability insurance, maternity benefits, etc.) was 90 percent in 2004-5, 90 percent in 2017-18, and still 90 percent in 2024.
Job quality also matters: duration, earnings, working conditions, social protection, security of tenure, and prospects for advancement. India’s employment challenge has historically been not only unemployment but also underemployment, low productivity, and poor-quality work.
The latest PLFS data illustrate this complexity. Even after the increase in regular wage employment, 56.2 percent of workers in 2025 remained self-employed (mostly own-account and unpaid family labor) and another 20.20 percent were casual wage laborers. Agriculture still accounted for 43 percent of employment in 2025 (42 percent in 2019). The largest addition to the workforce since 2020 has been in agriculture (rising from 200 million to 280 million in 2024).
This matters most for the young. A graduate in a low-paid, insecure job is technically employed but not upwardly mobile. As we estimate in our new book, “India Out of Work,” real wages for casual and regular workers, and for the 53 percent of workers who are self-employed, have stagnated for 12 years. If non-farm jobs have grown at half the required rate (12 million a year) for a dozen years the Modi government has been in power, leaving youth unemployment double its 2012 level, from 6 percent to 12 percent in 2024, how can real wages rise, however loudly the government touts its low inflation?
The real test of India’s labor market is not how many names enter an EPFO database but whether the economy creates enough stable, productive, and decently paid jobs. If it did, the youth (those aged 15-29 years) not in education, employment, and training, would not have jumped from 50 million in 2012 to 100 million in 2024. Clearly, many became “discouraged workers” who stopped looking for work.

Telehealth Giant Hims Wants to Test Every Dude for Low Testosterone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:34:37 UTC
22:34:37 KST

Talk of testosterone deficiency is hard to escape these days, with podcasters and politicians obsessing over how to avoid a “low T” lifestyle.
As the hormone’s cultural salience deepens, demand is growing. In a timely move, telehealth giant Hims just launched a testosterone replacement therapy service for cisgender men.
The direct-to-consumer juggernaut will offer two types of injectable treatments, as well as an oral pill option that can be sent to patients after they take an at-home capillary blood test. Peter Stahl, a urologist and a senior vice president of men’s health at Hims, wants to “cast as wide a net, and get as many people tested, as possible.”
Hims, which started out selling erectile dysfunction medications, has expanded into women’s health and grown from a startup to a publicly traded company serving 2.9 million customers since it launched in 2017. Offering testosterone replacement therapy, or TRT, is both a new phase for the health platform and a doubling down on men’s health care. “When we first started, we didn't have the capabilities to take care of a complex condition like testosterone deficiency,” Stahl says. “We've finally grown up.”
The company will compete with a wide array of online clinics offering testosterone therapy, many of which have cropped up in the past few years using turnkey telehealth services to launch quickly. Many of these services market the medication as a lifestyle enhancer or anti-aging solution.
Stahl sees testosterone deficiency as a medical condition that’s “really underdiagnosed” and “really misunderstood.” Testosterone became a controlled substance following the 1990 Anabolic Steroids Control Act, and for decades, taking it has carried an association with muscle-obsessed gym rats. “That created a lot of stigma,” he says. Older research also showed that testosterone therapy came with cardiovascular risks, though more recent findings suggest those concerns were overestimated.
Testosterone levels have become a MAGA fixation. This fall, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth announced a mandatory testosterone deficiency screening for most male troops in the US armed services. Texas Republicans have been hurling the phrase “low T” as a masculinity-questioning insult in a hotly contested Senate midterm race between Ken Paxton and James Talarico.
A survey of 2,000 American men this summer commissioned by Hims indicates that they are increasingly willing to talk to one another about testosterone treatment, but the stigma persists around taking medication to address low levels.
Because testosterone is a controlled substance, it can’t be dispensed like many other treatments popular with digital clinics. Unlike GLP-1s and estrogen-based hormone replacement therapy, which are now often prescribed by clinicians after patients simply fill out a quick questionnaire, TRT requires "synchronous" care. That means any would-be users have to have a video chat with a clinician before getting a prescription, and for ongoing monitoring.
“It's important to remember that testosterone therapy can cause infertility, and you don't give it to someone trying to conceive,” says urologist Mohit Khera, the director of Baylor College of Medicine’s Laboratory for Andrology Research at McNair Medical Institute. Khera sees telehealth TRT services as promising ways to expand access to the medication, “as long as it’s monitored appropriately.”
While laboratory testing can show whether testosterone levels are below thresholds set by groups like the American Urological Association to indicate potential issues, diagnoses aren’t made based on bloodwork alone. Instead, clinicians assess labs along with patients’ symptoms and medical history. Common symptoms of hypogonadism (the technical term for the diagnosis) include sexual dysfunction and muscle loss. Stahl calls it a “powerful biomarker” for understanding someone’s health.
“Quite frankly, it’s underutilized,” he says, noting that men with low testosterone have a 35 percent increased risk in overall mortality.
The test doesn’t require a standard blood draw. Instead, Hims will send patients a Tasso blood collection device, a round single-use wearable that sticks to the upper arm and punctures the skin with microneedles to collect a small sample. (It may sound suspiciously like Theranos, but Tasso devices have a solid track record.) From there, the patient sends the collection off to a lab that will conduct an analysis of a broad selection of 21 different biomarkers to assess health, including triglycerides and thyroid hormones as well as testosterone.
Based on the results, a patient might be prescribed a compounded injectable testosterone, a commercially available injectable testosterone, an oral pill—or something else entirely, if their testosterone levels are not low. Stahl sees hormone testing as a way to persuade otherwise-reticent men to go see a doctor. “Getting screened for testosterone deficiency is much more exciting to a young man who's feeling good than getting tested for high cholesterol,” he says. “So we're trying to leverage that opportunity as much as we possibly can.”
Hims’ expansion comes at a Wild West moment for online testosterone sales. In 2022, urology researchers went undercover to test how digital clinics prescribed the medication, and found that six of seven platforms in the analysis offered testosterone replacement therapy despite reported normal levels of the hormone.
Although he wants to test people widely, Stahl has a more conservative philosophy about who should actually get a prescription for testosterone, especially in comparison to digital clinics that explicitly offer it as an anti-aging treatment or lifestyle enhancement: “If you're asymptomatic, it doesn't matter what your testosterone level is, you're not going to get treated on our platform.”

Poland's defence minister in touch with Lithuania over drone incursion
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Monday that he is in contact with his Lithuanian counterpart over an incident involving a drone that entered Lithuanian airspace on Sunday.
The advisor on national security to the President of Lithuania, Deividas Matulionis, cited by the Baltic News Service (BNS) on Monday, said: "I can state unequivocally that we have credible data indicating the drone crossed the Polish border." He added that the government in Vilnius has not yet received any official information from Warsaw and urged that media reports not be treated as confirmed findings.
The Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius, speaking after a National Security Commission meeting later on Monday, echoed Matulionis' words. "There is no doubt that the drone entered ... from the direction of Poland," he said, adding that Lithuanian hardware explicitly registered the moment of entry.
According to the Chief of the Defence Staff of the Lithuanian Armed Forces, Giedrius Premeneckas, radars first detected the object at 05:47am local time inside Polish territory, 30–40 kilometres from the border. The drone crossed into Lithuania at 06:02. Although NATO fighter jets were scrambled at 06:40, pilots could not establish visual contact due to poor weather conditions.
Kosiniak-Kamysz said at a conference in Lapanow, southern Poland, that various scenarios were being investigated and that he expected the military to provide an explanation. He added that one possibility initially considered by investigators was that the unmanned aerial vehicle that had violated Lithuanian airspace was a drone used for smuggling.
He further said that, according to the latest information, it was a Ukrainian military drone. "The Ukrainian side has apologised to the Lithuanian side." "I am in contact with the Lithuanian Minister of Defence [Robertas Kaunas] regarding this matter," added Kosiniak-Kamysz.
On Sunday, Lithuanian authorities issued a red alert for two regions in the north of the country due to an unidentified object in their airspace. In Latvia, a yellow alert was issued for three regions. In both countries, the alerts remained in effect for approximately 30 minutes. Sinkevicius said that because the drone arrived from Poland - a NATO, EU, and Schengen partner - it was not automatically flagged as an immediate hostile threat.
According to Kaunas, the object was a Ukrainian FPV-type drone carrying an explosive payload that had veered off course while en route to an attack on St. Petersburg. The drone exploded over Lithuania's Pasvalys district, and its debris damaged a civilian vehicle. The driver was unharmed. The exact cause of the explosion is still unknown, with technical failure, fuel depletion, or impact with trees being considered.
Lithuanian authorities strongly rejected reports in some Polish media suggesting the drone had been launched from Lithuanian territory without entering Polish airspace, arguing that Lithuania does not permit third-party military operations from its soil.
Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi apologised for any disruption, threat or anxiety that this incident may have caused. He added that Ukraine is committed to providing its Lithuanian partners with all relevant information to establish the full circumstances of the incident. (PAP)

How Israel’s war on Lebanon has cost young people with autism and ADHD
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:32:57 UTC
22:32:57 KST

How war in Lebanon has cost young people with autism and ADHD
Experts warn that war takes a heavy toll on neurodivergent people, who often rely on routine.
Beirut, Lebanon – After her husband died from COVID-19 in 2020, Lena Kouyoumjian moved back to her parents’ house in Mazraat Yachouh, a village 20 minutes’ drive from Beirut. For Lena, energetic and outgoing, the move was difficult, but she accepted that she needed help to care for her 20-year-old daughter, Vana, who is autistic and non-verbal.
Lena first noticed her daughter’s symptoms when she was two years old. Vana is still unable to communicate verbally how she feels, but her mother does her best to understand her.
Like many autistic individuals – and neurodivergent people in general – Vana needs a supportive and stable environment, alongside a structured routine, to feel well.
Lebanon has been engulfed in war since October 2023, with bombings across the country and an economic crisis continuing to impact all Lebanese, particularly neurodivergent people.
When Israel escalated its attacks on southern Lebanon in March, as a trainer for children with disabilities, Lena understood that this could impact her autistic daughter.
“Any sudden change in routine, loud noises, fear, or uncertainty can increase their anxiety and make them feel unsafe,” Lena told Al Jazeera.
“I can see this in my daughter. Since the situation became more difficult, she has become more anxious and sensitive to the changes happening around her.”
Challenging a social stigma
The symptoms of autism and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) vary depending on the person and condition, but they frequently include sensory issues and emotional dysregulation. ADHD and autism often occur together, combining to make AuDHD, where traits from both conditions can be seen.
People with these neurodevelopmental conditions are often stigmatised by societies that do not fully understand them, including in Lebanon.
While the pressures caused by Israel’s war on Lebanon and mass displacement have led to psychological issues for many, neurodivergent people are more vulnerable due to their need for consistent support and routine.
“Being a parent of an autistic child isn’t something every parent can handle. A challenge I often face is deciding the amount of time and energy I should allocate to my child,” said Lena.
Lebanon’s Autism Awareness Association (AAA) has provided support for both mother and child. Vana has attended classes at AAA, a nonprofit based in Antelias, outside Beirut, for the past six years, which serves as an alternative school for young autistic people.
But rising costs in Lebanon during the war have prevented Vana from attending classes regularly. “Even transportation to her centre became very difficult, especially with the increasing financial challenges. At times, it became impossible for her to go, so she had to stay home,” Lena said.
Ghada Hayek Makhoul, who co-founded AAA with other parents of autistic children in 2015, said the group has made constant efforts to increase awareness about the condition in Lebanon.
“Many people don’t know what autism really is. They don’t know the spectrum; how it can vary from mild to moderate to severe,” Ghada told Al Jazeera.
Sensory overload
Ghada’s son, Anthony, is a calm 27-year-old autistic, non-verbal man who relies heavily on helpers. Although he is unable to speak, his mother said it is clear when he is distressed, putting his hands over his ears when he is in pain due to sensory discomfort.
Autistic people can be more sensitive to noises than neurotypical people. During the war, people in Lebanon have been subjected to a harrowing range of sounds, from Israeli bombs exploding on the ground to the sonic booms of warplanes flying overhead.
“So, imagine the drones all the time [for autistic people], the bombs, and the vibration of the bombs … all of this that we were hearing, so of course it affected him a lot,” Ghada said.
“My son can’t listen to the TV any more due to the news. He switches it off and removes the remote control. It’s too triggering for him.”
Anthony’s mother said he senses tension and anxiety, even if his understanding of what is being said or happening is limited.
“[It affects] all the senses, everything. He doesn’t want to go into a pool any more. He used to love the water. And now, he doesn’t want to go into the pool any more,” Ghada said.
“I don’t know what changed. Because it’s outside? Because of the sound? I don’t know.”
Mental health support as a luxury
Israel’s war on Lebanon has had a direct economic impact on the AAA and other organisations providing neurodivergent or psychological support.
Lebanon’s economic crisis, with inflation potentially reaching 17 percent this year, has also led to a brain drain of professionals who could support neurodivergent people.
AAA is a crucial support base for families with autistic children. But it comes at a significant cost of $700 per month for children attending five days a week. With 80 percent of the population living in poverty, few can afford such services.
“We need more trained staff, and we also need to keep the staff that are leaving the country. So, we need to have better salaries, but we cannot afford it, because we will have to increase the load on the parents,” said Ghada. “Things are in crisis mode for everybody during the war.”
The same thing is being seen with other mental health services. While many nongovernmental organisations (NGOs) provide free therapy, private consultations can cost more than $100 for a single 50-minute session.
Nour Toukan, a public health researcher at Enmaeya, a media platform focused on sustainable development, told Al Jazeera that care for people with autism or even for ADHD is “very much an out-of-pocket expense.”
While the government did launch a National Disability Allowance in 2023, with funding from the European Union and the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), the allowance of $40 per month is not enough to cover even the basics in Lebanon. People with autism can get a personal disability card, issued by the Ministry of Social Affairs, making them eligible for support, but those with ADHD cannot.
Lebanon’s National Mental Health Programme, established in 2014 by the Ministry of Public Health, is trying to bridge gaps in support caused by economic and geographic variables.
Dr Rabih El Chammay, the founder and director of the programme, told Al Jazeera a national mental health strategy for children and teenagers is being finalised.
“National studies addressing autism and ADHD have also been conducted, providing evidence to inform this work. We are meeting with several organisations, particularly organisations representing families of persons with autism, to understand priorities and build momentum for further coordinated action,” Dr Rabih said. “War makes this work more difficult because it can increase support needs while disrupting the services people depend on.”
Developmental regression
Displaced people have been the most impacted, but all of those in Lebanon whose schooling and routines have been disrupted are affected.
Adham Faraj, a 23-year-old psychology student at the Lebanese American University in Beirut, who was diagnosed with ADHD in 2024, said that when his classes moved online due to the war, he found himself staying at home more and more.
“It’s less engaging, especially if you struggle with attention. You’re less motivated to go out, so you just attend classes from bed,” Adham said.
Adham said the intensity of Israeli air strikes in Lebanon unsettled him, along with concerns about the rising price of medicine.
“There’s always a cheaper alternative, but it depends on people’s social class. Maybe an $11 box of medication is affordable for some, but not for everyone,” he said.
Rim Ajjour, a psychologist and psychotherapist in Beirut, whose work focuses on young people with autism, has seen that many of the skills neurodivergent people learned before the war are now being lost.
“With the limited resources available in Lebanon and the shift in people’s priorities, there has been more limited access to therapy,” she said.
Rim said that her clinic and others are doing their utmost to keep therapy accessible by freezing consultation fees, even when their own expenses are increasing.
With Israeli attacks continuing in southern Lebanon, which remains occupied by Israeli forces, in violation of a US-brokered June ceasefire, many fear the impact on their work in case of a return to full-scale war.
“I don’t know how we’ll be able to take it again,” Rim said.

Vereshchuk on Lviv Regional Council decision: Only RF stands to gain from tension in our relations with Poland

Deputy Head of the Office of the President Iryna Vereschuk has urged deputies of Lviv Regional Council to refrain from decisions that could harm relations with Poland.
"I am from Lviv region myself. Moreover, I once worked in local government, just as you do. I therefore understand well what local self-government entails, and I have great respect for the rights of territorial communities. At the same time, the local authorities of Lviv region cannot disregard the foreign policy interests of the Ukrainian state. I am referring to certain decisions of yours that damage our relations with Poland—one of our key allies in the war against Russia," Vereschuk wrote on Facebook on Wednesday, without specifying which particular decision she meant.
She emphasized that Ukraine’s military and economic logistics depend heavily on Poland; that Ukraine’s European and Euro-Atlantic integration also relies on Polish support; and that nearly a million Ukrainian citizens currently reside in Poland.
"Consequently, we cannot afford to disregard the Poles, especially during wartime, and even more so when it comes to sensitive issues of historical memory. Only Russia stands to gain from tension in our relations with Poland. That must not be allowed to happen. I urge you to exercise pragmatism and a sense of responsibility toward the state. I hope you will hear me," Vereschuk added.
As previously reported, on October 20, Lviv Regional Council voted to designate 2027 as the "Year of Roman Shukhevych, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), and Oleh Olzhych." The decision in question was approved during a meeting of Lviv Regional Council’s commission on culture, information policy, and promotion on July 6 shortly after Karol Nawrocki (a Polish official) announced a move to strip Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of the Order of the White Eagle. This followed Zelenskyy’s decision to bestow the honorary title "Named After the Heroes of the UPA" upon the Pivnich (North) Separate Special Operations Center of the Special Operations Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. The incident led to tensions in Ukrainian-Polish relations, though on October 17, Zelenskyy indicated that the situation had improved.
On October 20, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk criticized Lviv Regional Council’s decision, noting that it serves the interests of Ukraine’s enemies. Meanwhile, Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz stated that the move harms relations between the two nations. "Such a decision does not foster mutual trust between our peoples; on the contrary, it deepens divisions. It is essential that the Ukrainian authorities distance themselves from this position," he wrote.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine issued a statement emphasizing the importance of fostering friendly bilateral relations with Poland and described Lviv Regional Council’s recent decision as counterproductive to ongoing efforts. "We believe that the recent decision by the Lviv Regional Council, which touches upon sensitive historical issues within the bilateral agenda, is counterproductive to our current efforts aimed at further developing Ukrainian-Polish relations and addressing problematic issues, especially amid the full-scale Russian aggression and the unprecedented security threats facing both our countries and the region as a whole," the message reads.

The Israeli military has detained about 80 US, Israeli and British volunteers helping Palestinians harvest olives near Bethlehem, including the New York Democratic congressional nominee Brad Lander, several rabbis and Israel’s former deputy attorney general.
“I’ve been detained by the IDF, along with a group of rabbis and volunteers,” Lander posted from a bus taking him to a police station. “We were simply harvesting olives in a grove near Nahalin in the West Bank. The occupation is a crime under international law. Harvesting olives isn’t a crime under any law I know.”
Lander, who is Jewish and an outspoken critic of the Israeli government, describes himself as a liberal Zionist. He believes in the vision of Israel as a safe, Jewish home, but argues that it cannot be a true democracy while it denies Palestinians their human rights and freedom.
An ally of the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, Lander’s critical approach to Israel was a key factor in his resounding primary victory against Dan Goldman, a prominent supporter of Israel.
He condemns Israel’s continued occupation of the West Bank and Gaza, supported the restriction of US military aid to Israel and believes that Israel’s military campaign in Gaza after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks amounts to genocide.
Settler militants have unleashed extreme violence on Palestinians attempting to harvest olives from their trees across the occupied West Bank, and anyone accompanying them.
A vicious assault on a US photojournalist and attacks on European diplomats and a French mayor over the weekend drew international condemnation and calls for the Israeli government to crack down on militants.
Wednesday’s olive-picking from trees outside the village of Nahalin was uneventful until a large contingent of Israeli security forces arrived, the organisers Protect the Harvest said in a statement.
“All volunteers were peacefully harvesting on the private land of a Palestinian family who had invited them. For reasons that remain unclear, the Israeli army showed up and detained approximately 80 people who were present.”
Soldiers said the area had been declared a closed military zone, separated the group by nationality and drove them to a nearby police station in minibuses for the Israelis and a larger bus for Americans.
Joshua Schoffman, who served as Israel’s deputy attorney general for more than a decade, described the mass detention as a “complete hallucination” in a post on social media.
“Just now, they told me that I’m being detained for the crime of olive harvesting,” he wrote. “We were asked to stop, and everyone complied. There was no friction whatsoever with settlers or with the security forces.”
Lander was released with a warning but all the others were still being held, Protect the Harvest said. Detainees include Jill Jacobs, the chief executive of T’ruah: The Rabbinic Call for Human Rights, and 11 other American rabbis affiliated with the group.
The detainees have been given water but no food. The Israeli military and police did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
On Monday, Lander made a first post about his journey to Palestine. “Our goals for the trip are to help protect the olive harvest – and to shed a light on the reality of the occupation,” he wrote. “Thankfully, our corner of today’s harvest was peaceful and successful. But violence unfortunately is never far away.”
