How to eat at a Danish restaurant like a Dane
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

Have you ever been to a Danish restaurant?
Wait, we are not talking about a restaurant in Denmark. We mean a Danish restaurant: a place that follows local traditions and, perhaps more importantly, serves traditional Danish food.
No? You are not the only one.
Many internationals live in Denmark for years while eating almost exclusively at international restaurants, leaving the “local experience” for some unspecified point in the future. But this is one experience you may not want to miss.
So, here are a few tips on how to really enjoy a restaurant experience in Denmark like a Dane.
What is Danish and what is trendy in Denmark
Traditional Danish cuisine and Denmark’s modern dining scene are two completely different things.
The latter is usually fancier and more international, often with several courses, ingredients from around the world and a quieter, more polished atmosphere.
Traditional Danish food is something else entirely.
Many internationals live in the country for years before trying it, and some never do. But by skipping it, you also miss one of the most genuinely Danish dining experiences you can have.
Traditional Danish cooking is simpler, more straightforward and more rustic. It is often based around a large meat-based main course, especially pork. The presentation and combinations may sometimes look unsophisticated, but this is where a lot of the flavour of traditional Denmark lies.
There are not many traditional Danish restaurants left in the largest Danish cities. They are more common outside the major urban areas, particularly in Jutland, but you can still find them if you look.
Book!
We will never repeat this enough: in Denmark, booking is often essential.
This is particularly true if you are going to a high-end restaurant or a traditional Danish restaurant. It tends to matter less at casual international restaurants or fast-food-style places, unless they are especially popular.
How far in advance should you book? As a general rule, two weeks is a good idea.
Unless, of course, there is a special occasion.
For example, some Danes start booking their tables well in advance for julefrokost, the traditional Christmas lunches and dinners that begin filling restaurants from late November and December.
So, what are you waiting for?
Pay attention to special occasions
When you book, make sure you know exactly what you are booking.
Christmas lunches are a good example. Many restaurants offer special menus that you have to request when reserving, while others temporarily replace their normal menu with a Christmas buffet.
Read the restaurant’s website carefully or ask when you book by phone.
The two-hour time limit
At many Danish restaurants, particularly in larger cities, your reservation may be for a fixed two-hour slot.
That means you are expected to arrive on time and, in principle, leave when your slot ends.
Of course, if the restaurant is half empty, nobody is likely to rush you out. But on a busy Saturday night, you should expect the two-hour limit to matter.
No tips
Tipping is not traditionally expected in Denmark.
Restaurant staff receive wages rather than relying on tips as the only part of their income. In recent years, some restaurants and payment terminals have started asking or suggesting that customers leave a tip, but many Danes would still find this unusual.
As a general rule, you should not feel obliged to tip in Denmark, even if the card terminal asks you.
How a traditional Danish dinner works
Now we are entering slightly tricky territory, because different restaurants naturally have different menus and offer different experiences.
If you are going to an Italian restaurant, a New Nordic restaurant or a Lebanese restaurant, things will work differently. Here, we are talking specifically about a traditional Danish restaurant.
Do not expect the classic structure of a starter, first course and second course. Usually, you order one main course, generally based around meat, with one or several side dishes already included.
Portions are often generous, so unless you have a big appetite, the main course may be enough.
If you are particularly hungry, you can start with an appetizer. After the main course, you may also find cheese or dessert on the menu.
And what should you drink?
Beer is the traditional choice, although most restaurants today also offer a decent selection of wine.
In more old-fashioned Danish restaurants, finishing the meal with a small glass of liquor, perhaps a snaps, followed by coffee is a very traditional combination.

Moldova is considering moving Ukrainian border checkpoints onto its territory to reduce the risk of Russian attacks near the Ukrainian border, Chișinău’s Interior Minister Daniela Misail-Nikitin said in comments published Wednesday.
Speaking on TV channel Moldova 1, Misail-Nikitin said Moldova has withdrawn its border guards and customs officers from four crossings on Ukrainian soil, adding that Chișinău is negotiating for Ukrainian border guards to work on the Moldovan side so the two countries can exercise joint control, as reported by Moldovan outlet NewsMaker.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
She said arrangements have already been reached with Kyiv for two crossings, and others will be assessed in the medium term depending on the risk of incidents.
Ukrainian Deputy Minister for Communities and Territories Development Serhiy Derkach told Radio Liberty in early October that Kyiv was working on the plans. He said he expects several pilot projects in three months, supported by an existing agreement with Moldova on joint checkpoints.
Neither government has said which crossings would be relocated first or when.
On Sept. 12, Moldova’s Customs Service said staff at three joint crossings, including the Giurgiulești-Reni checkpoint, had returned to Moldovan territory for 90 days.
Strikes on crossings
The talks follow a series of Russian drone strikes on crossings in Ukraine’s Odesa region, with the checkpoints directly targeted.
Drone Attacks on Cargo Ships in the Black Sea
On Sept. 9, a strike on the Starokozache crossing killed two civilians and wounded three, Ukrainian officials said. The checkpoint is about a kilometer from Moldovan territory, and Moldovan officials said traffic was halted. Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan said on X that the war was increasingly endangering Moldovan citizens.
On Aug. 21, Ukraine’s State Border Guard Service (DPSU) said Russian drones had hit the Tabaki crossing, damaging buildings and forcing it to close. On Oct. 5, Moldova’s Border Police said a drone debris ricocheted into a bus at the Palanca crossing and lightly injured a Moldovan border guard.
The Moldovan police attributed it to Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, with Chișinău accusing Moscow of deliberate strikes. Russia claimed the checkpoints were used to supply weapons to Ukraine, a claim rejected by Chișinău.
Moldova, a former Soviet republic, fought a short war with its breakaway eastern region of Transnistria in 1992 that ended with a Russia-mediated settlement enforced by Russian troops already stationed there.
The Foreign Policy Research Institute said former Soviet troops under Russian Federation control armed and trained the Transnistrian militias. Moldova says those troops violate its territorial integrity.

Doctors, engineers and computer scientists leave Israel. Researchers sound alarm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:27:37 UTC
22:27:37 KST

Seven years ago, when Benjamin Netanyahu celebrated his 70th birthday, one of the people who came to wish him well him was May Golan – then a Knesset member and now the social equality minister. At the time Netanyahu was the leader of the opposition, having failed to form a coalition after the 2021 election.
Golan ceremoniously proclaimed to Netanyahu that masses of Israelis would leave the country if he weren't the prime minister. "Young people in Israel don't see their future and their children's future in the country if you don't continue to lead it," she told him.
Netanyahu was elected for a sixth term as prime minister at the end of 2022 and since 2023, there has been a dramatic increase in the number of Israelis who left the country. This number reached almost 70,000 in 2025, compared to less than 40,000 in 2009-2023, a jump of dozens of percent. The emigrants were primarily young families with children. Concurrently, the number of returning Israelis has fallen to a low not seen in many years.
Researchers at Tel Aviv University warn of a loss of equilibrium and damage that will lead to the collapse of the Israeli economy if the emigration trend continues. They note that while the current situation is not dangerous, it could quickly spiral into an extreme scenario.
According to a forthcoming report on the subject by Prof. Itai Ater of the School of Management, Prof. Netai Bergman, head of the School of Economics, and Doron Zamir of the School of Economics, emigration from Israel is particularly pronounced in several groups: those with a bachelor's degree or higher, those with degrees in science, engineering or computer science, and doctors.
"The continuation of the emigration trend could lead to a dangerous decline in the stock of skilled human capital available to the Israeli economy, which is the State of Israel's primary resource," the report states.
The researchers warn that additional negative shocks could lead to a surge in the number of emigrants. "Every additional emigrant increases the incentive for others to leave, due to the growth of networks of Israeli immigrants abroad and due to the consequences for the Israeli economy, social cohesion and public service. This will have severe macroeconomic consequences," they write.
'A stream that will become a flood'
The researchers have been tracking trends in emigration from Israel in recent years. According to the report, the number of Israelis who returned home in 2023-2024 is the lowest since 2009. Israel's negative migration balance (the number of those leaving minus the number of those returning) is also the highest since 2009.
According to Central Bureau of Statistics definitions, emigrants are defined as Israeli residents who spent 12 full months abroad, with three of those months being consecutive. The researchers excluded from the data new immigrants to Israel who emigrated within three years of making aliyah, thereby nullifying the excuse for the high figures that Netanyahu gave in the Knesset in January when he said that that a large portion of those leaving Israel are immigrants from Ukraine who returned to their country.
According to Central Bureau of Statistics data analyzed in the report, an average of 32,000 Israelis left Israel each year between 2009 and 2019, but in 2023-2024 the number jumped to about 50,000 per year (an increase of more than 50 percent); in 2025 that number reached 69,000. Concurrently, in 2024, the number of returning Israelis fell below 20,000 per year for the first time since 2009. Israel's negative migration balance rose from an average of 10,500 people in the previous decade examined (2010-2019) to about 30,000 people in 2024 – almost threefold.
An extended analysis by the researchers shows that the emigration rate (emigrants per 1,000 people in the population) of those who have a higher education (bachelor's degree or higher), doctors, engineers and those with science degrees almost doubled between 2019 and 2024, and increased at a faster rate than the increase in the emigration rate in the general population.
While the emigration rate in the general population increased 1.74-fold during these years, it increased 1.75-fold among doctors, 1.87-fold among those with a bachelor's degree, 1.9-fold among engineers, and almost doubled among those with technological qualifications. According to another publication by the researchers from September, close to 1,400 doctors left Israel in 2023-2025 – almost double the number from the corresponding period a decade earlier (2013-2015).
"The great concern stems from the fact that the people leaving are Israel's best human capital, who contribute to society and to the economy," Ater says. "If the trend is not stopped, this stream will become a flood that will endanger Israel's ability to exist as an independent and advanced state."
"We know of countries like Turkey, Iran, Russia, Venezuela and South Africa that have undergone similar processes and have not managed to recover," Ater adds. "In Israel, there is also a large, unskilled ultra-Orthodox group that doesn't study the core curriculum and puts Israel's ability to survive a large wave of emigration of skilled Israelis at risk. As a country that relies on high-tech, our greatest resource is human capital. A large emigration rate will also harm security, not just the economy."
"This is not just about the brain drain and the weakening of research and development, but also a real blow to the country's security and resilience," says Prof. David Harel, president of the National Academy of Sciences. "Israel's scientific and technological capabilities in engineering, cybersecurity and computer science are a vital component of national security, from the development of advanced defense systems to Israel's cyber capabilities."
The Tel Aviv University researchers say the increase in the number of Israelis who left was already noticeable in the third quarter of 2023 – before the October 7 massacre. According to Ater, it's still too early to determine whether the end of the Gaza war led to a decrease in the number of emigrants or an increase in the number of returnees. "The election is a pivotal event," he says. "For many people, the results will influence the decision of whether to leave or to stay."
Young people, families with children
The researchers say a particularly significant change occurred among young families. The main increase in emigration rates was among adults aged 35 to 45 and children aged 0-14 – families with children. The emigration rate in these groups almost doubled.
High-income earners are more prominent among emigrants from Israel. The share of highest earners (in the upper third) among emigrants increased from 24.5 percent in 2009 to 33.5 percent in 2024; close to half of those leaving earned above the median wage. The researchers noted, however, that education and skillset predict emigration more than income.
"The loss of high-value human capital has a real economic cost," the report states. According to an Israel Tax Authority report published this year, the loss of tax revenue from emigration increased from half a billion shekels ($161 million in today's dollars) in 2019 to 1.2 billion shekels in 2024. If the emigration trend continues, the tax loss is expected to reach 3.5 billion shekels per year within five years.

Center for Defense Investments sells Seli Manor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:27:00 UTC
22:27:00 KST

Center for Defense Investments sells Seli Manor
The Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) has sold the Seli manor complex at auction. The new owner plans to preserve the manor estate and find a suitable use for it.
The Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) sold the Seli manor complex in Rapla County at auction for €380,000, the starting price.
The Seli Manor property came under RKIK's management in 2019 when the Seli Health Center ceased operating as an independent institution and was merged with the Estonian Defense Forces. As the health center relocated to Raadi in Tartu, there was no longer a need to use the manor complex and it was put up for sale, RKIK media relations specialist Andra Nõlvak told ERR.
The complex was purchased by Eksfisk, whose owner, Maria Peetri, told ERR that the company views Seli Manor primarily as a long-term development project.
"The first priority, once the transaction is finalized, is to properly take over the manor complex, gain a comprehensive overview of the buildings' technical condition and initially focus on the work needed to preserve the property," she said.
Going forward, the new owner hopes to find a use and development strategy for the complex that will allow the historic manor estate to be preserved and gradually brought back into active use.
"It is still too early to announce more specific plans, as some matters require design work, planning reviews and approvals. This is not a project we want to rush through, but a long-term development where we want to do things in the right order," Peetri said.
Peetri added that although the auction has ended, the notarized sale transaction has yet to take place.
Eksfisk, which operates Peetri Lõheäri, is engaged in the retail and wholesale sale of fish products. The company posted a profit of €330,000 last year, compared with nearly €280,000 the previous year. According to its annual report for last year, the company had more than €1 million in retained earnings.
The manor complex includes the main building and several outbuildings, including servants' quarters and a hydrotherapy facility.
The earliest records of Seli Manor date back to 1474. The first buildings were wooden structures with straw or reed roofs, none of which have survived. The first limestone buildings at Seli Manor were not constructed until the mid-to-late 18th century. Of these, the manor house or main building, the estate manager's house and the horse stable remain standing today.

Germany's military warns of 'significant' Russian sabotage threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Germany's military warns of 'significant' Russian sabotage threat
BERLIN, Oct 21 - Germany's armed forces classified the threat of Russian sabotage against their own troops and facilities as "significant" for the first time, the second-highest level on their internal threat scale, according to a Bundeswehr assessment reported by German broadcasters WDR and the Sueddeutsche Zeitung on Wednesday.
A defence ministry spokesperson confirmed the assessment, telling reporters: "We are noting that we face a significant sabotage threat overall for the Bundeswehr."
The reassessment was triggered by the discovery in mid-September of a crashed drone carrying a tin of high explosives near the Wunstorf air base in Lower Saxony, WDR and Sueddeutsche Zeitung reported.
CROSSED 'RED LINE'
The internal document, seen by WDR and the Sueddeutsche Zeitung, said Russia had crossed "a previously anticipated red line of harmful intent involving kinetic and/or lethal effects" against Germany and the Bundeswehr through the use of weaponised drones.
The Wunstorf drone resembles one laden with explosives that was used in a failed attack at Leipzig/Halle airport in August. But unlike the Leipzig incident, which authorities said targeted civilian cargo aircraft, investigators believe the Wunstorf drone was aimed at Bundeswehr aircraft, the document is cited as saying.
Germany has blamed Russia for the Leipzig attack.
Moscow denied involvement and has consistently rejected accusations of carrying out sabotage or hybrid attacks in Europe.
The report also cited a pattern of suspected Russian reconnaissance across Germany, including drone overflights of the Arrow 3 missile defence site in Saxony-Anhalt, and a camouflaged camera found filming a strategically important railway station in Minden, Westphalia.
Intelligence services expect the situation to worsen in the short term, with further actions likely in the near future, the document says, according to WDR and Sueddeutsche Zeitung.
The defence ministry spokesperson said preventive measures were being tailored to individual sites and could range from increased guard patrols to additional technical security such as infrared cameras and fence surveillance systems.
The assessment comes just over a week after German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Germany faced a "shadow war" and called for expanded intelligence powers.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Wednesday that Russian disinformation and hybrid attacks posed the biggest threat to Germany. "My view is that our people are still underestimating this big threat to our society... This is a fundamental attack against the entire political order we achieved after 1990." REUTERS

Are the UK, France being pulled into the Saudi-Houthi conflict?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:25:50 UTC
22:25:50 KST

Are the UK, France being pulled into the Saudi-Houthi conflict?
The European states say their support for Riyadh is ‘defensive’, but analysts warn Houthi reaction may complicate that.
France and the United Kingdom have both moved to deploy military assets to Saudi Arabia, deepening their defence ties with the kingdom as its conflict with the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), in Yemen escalates.
Paris last week said it had begun sending assets to Saudi Arabia as part of a previously announced agreement, after President Emmanuel Macron committed to deploying troops and air defence systems to help protect the Red Sea port city of Yanbu, which has come under attack from the Iran-backed Houthis.
The UK, for its part, on Tuesday announced plans to deploy fighter jets to help shield Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks.
Both countries stressed that their support would be defensive.
Analysts say the European moves serve several geopolitical purposes: protecting Saudi oil exports that are important to European energy markets, shoring up their strategic alliance in the Gulf amid US reluctance to offer direct military assistance to Saudi Arabia, and strengthening deterrence against future Houthi attacks.
But the deployments also carry significant risks, many analysts say, potentially drawing the two European states more directly into the protracted Saudi-Houthi conflict.
“If insufficiently deterred, the Houthis may decide that the moment is ripe to test the resolve and resilience of Saudi Arabia’s defensive posture, and attempt to draw Saudi Arabia’s allies even further into the Yemen-Saudi confrontation,” Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow for Middle East Security at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told Al Jazeera.
‘Support during crisis’
The British and French military support measures come as Saudi Arabia faces a sustained Houthi missile and drone campaign against it, including targeting energy and transport infrastructure.
Houthi attacks targeting Saudi airports in Riyadh and Abha this month have killed 19 people and injured more than 300 others, according to the Saudi-led coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki.
Addressing the UK’s stepped-up military support for Saudi Arabia, UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting called recent Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia “absolutely despicable”, specifically condemning the group’s targeting of Riyadh airport.
The UK Ministry of Defence said it would deploy Typhoon fighter jets to fly “defensive counter air missions” in Saudi Arabia, send UK military advisers to work with Saudi staff officers and provide an A400M transport aircraft to help move defence material within the kingdom.
French support for Saudi Arabia would include soldiers, radars and defence systems, Macron has said, without detailing the scale of the support.
Urban Coningham, a research fellow at RUSI, noted differences in the British and French roles, with the French mainly limited to protecting Saudi export infrastructure. The British, by contrast, will conduct “defensive patrols where they would shoot down incoming missiles or drones” in Saudi Arabia, as well as provide air-to-air refuelling support for Saudi bombers and jets heading into Yemeni airspace, he said.
Camille Lons, policy fellow and deputy head of the Paris office at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said France is limited in what it can provide to Saudi Arabia, particularly given the demands on European defences amid the war in Ukraine. Still, Paris sees its assistance as a way to “show support [for Saudi Arabia] in times of crisis, and a way to deepen the defence partnership”, Lons told Al Jazeera.
‘Freeing up’ Saudi aircraft
Saudi Arabia will welcome the European deployments, as it has struggled to translate some of its security partnerships into high-level military support.
In September, US President Donald Trump rejected multiple Saudi requests to participate in strikes on the Houthis, agreeing only to provide intelligence and targeting support, the news agency Reuters cited informed sources saying.
Turkiye and Pakistan have committed to “collective deterrence measures”, including potential troop deployments, under the newly signed Mecca defence pact with Saudi Arabia, but the agreement has yet to be ratified in Turkiye.
Egypt’s parliament has also postponed a vote that would authorise its armed forces to support Saudi Arabia.
Nawaf Obaid, a senior fellow at King’s College War Studies Department, called the UK and French deployments “militarily valuable and politically significant”, saying they could help shield the kingdom’s sprawling territory from persistent Houthi air attacks while giving Riyadh more room to focus its own assets on offensive operations.
“The British Typhoons can reinforce Saudi air defences and, crucially, free up Saudi Eurofighters for offensive operations,” Obaid told Al Jazeera. “France’s contribution is particularly important for protecting Yanbu.”
Saudi Arabia “does not need foreign assistance to conduct air strikes”, Obaid added, noting that the kingdom has its own powerful combat aircraft fleet. “What it needs is additional defensive coverage across its enormous territory, particularly for critical energy infrastructure.”
Ozcelik said the recent British move was “not insignificant”, but its deterrent impact was not immediately clear.
“The question remains whether the UK air missions will move the dial in deterring sustained Houthi attacks while Saudi air defences and interceptor stockpiles are stretched,” said Ozcelik. “The difference between deterrence and interdiction is an important one.”
‘Dragged into protracted conflict’
What also remains to be seen is whether the UK and France will maintain a purely defensive posture – and whether the Houthis will recognise that distinction at all.
Coningham said the Houthis could interpret European military involvement, especially the UK’s air-to-air support for Saudi bombers and jets, as “offensive” rather than defensive, leading the group to view those countries as belligerents and their forces as targets.
As a result, Coningham said, the Houthis could strike at British forces stationed in the region – whether in Saudi Arabia or elsewhere, such as Cyprus – or reverse their position on allowing free transit to non-Saudi vessels, including European ships, in the Bab al-Mandeb strait – a key maritime route in the world.
Another potential flashpoint would be a Houthi attack in Saudi Arabia that kills British or French personnel, analysts noted.
“Whether it’s a direct attack planned by the Houthis or collateral damage, if the British or French have any casualties … then there becomes a pointed debate in those countries as to whether they should then retaliate,” said Coningham.
Ozcelik said the UK could face pressure to play a more offensive role in the event of a “mass civilian casualty event” caused by the Houthis or “debilitating attacks on Saudi’s energy infrastructure”, although London would likely view such a scenario as a “last resort”.
“Neither the Mecca signatories nor the UK are inclined to get dragged into deeper and likely protracted conflict inside Yemen,” said Ozcelik.

The Ukrainian airline "Constanta" won a lawsuit against Russia for nearly UAH 30 million over destroyed property
Kyiv • UNN
A Russian attack destroyed Constanta’s base, aircraft, and equipment in Zaporizhzhia. The court awarded the airline UAH 28.95 million in compensation.
The Commercial Court of Zaporizhzhia Region upheld the claim of the Ukrainian airline "Constanta" against the Russian Federation and ordered the aggressor state to pay nearly UAH 30 million in damages caused by the occupiers' shelling of Zaporizhzhia. The company called the ruling an important step toward restoring justice, UNN writes.
Details
In July 2025, Russian forces attacked Zaporizhzhia with strike drones. As a result of the shelling and the fire it caused, the aviation and technical base of PJSC "Constanta Airline" suffered significant destruction.
A rented hangar containing An-74T-100 and An-28 aircraft was destroyed on the company's premises. In addition to the aircraft, the company also lost capital investments and more than 3,000 pieces of equipment necessary for its operations.
As a result of the Russian attack, Constanta Airline suffered not only direct material losses but also lost the ability to fully conduct its business activities for the following six months.
In its claim filed with the Commercial Court of Zaporizhzhia Region against Russia, the airline demanded compensation for destroyed and damaged property, as well as compensation for lost profits.
The claim shall be upheld. The Russian Federation, represented by the Ministry of Justice of the Russian Federation, shall pay PJSC "CONSTANТA AIRLINE" damages in the amount of USD 683,065 (USD 580,292.00 in actual damages and USD 102,773.00 in lost profits), which as of 31.12.2025 (the valuation date) is equivalent to 28,953,668. Issue a writ of execution
In addition, the court ruled that Russia must pay court fees amounting to UAH 347,444.02.
Constanta Airline emphasizes that the court ruling is of fundamental importance not only for the company itself but also for Ukrainian businesses suffering losses as a result of Russian aggression.
This is an important decision for us on the path to restoring justice. Russia destroyed our aviation and technical base, damaged and destroyed aircraft, and caused significant losses to the company. There must be accountability for this destruction. Ukrainian businesses must not accept the aggressor destroying their property with impunity and depriving them of the ability to operate. We are convinced that every Ukrainian enterprise affected by Russian attacks must defend its interests and demand compensation. The fight against Russia must be waged by all available lawful means, including in the courts
Background
PJSC "Constanta Airline" is a Ukrainian air carrier founded in 1998 in Zaporizhzhia that specializes in charter cargo and passenger transportation, including providing support for international humanitarian and peacekeeping missions in difficult and hard-to-reach regions of the world.
The company is one of Ukraine's leading operators of Antonov aircraft. In addition to air transportation, Constanta Airline performs maintenance, restoration, and modernization of AN-family aircraft in cooperation with Ukrainian aircraft-manufacturing enterprises.
In 2023, Constanta was officially recognized as an enterprise critically important to the functioning of Ukraine's economy during a special period, as well as an operator of critical infrastructure facilities in the air transport sector.
Background
European countries are considering the modernization of Ukrainian An-124-100 "Ruslan" transport aircraft as the most realistic short-term solution for transporting heavy and oversized military cargo. During 18 months of research, specialists effectively found no full-fledged alternative to these aircraft.

Dialogue in the dark: David Bowie meets Nina Simone at Steve McQueen's exhibition at Guggenheim Bilbao
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:25:40 UTC
22:25:40 KST

Steve McQueen’s exhibition “66–76–26” at Guggenheim Bilbao Museum is a sound sculpture with no image. It is a link between the decades, the emotion of love and understanding, and it also stars David Bowie and Nina Simone.
When you enter the room it is dark. Only a few light spots, fluffy carpet and an amazing sound. One corner belongs to Nina Simone. She sings acapella, separated from her daughter’s friend, David Bowie, who responds to her with the same words of the same song from another corner.
It is almost like listening to your own family as we all know Simone and Bowie’s voices so well. They share something special with visitors. Two voices, one emotion. Love. But this duet never happened.
Be present and receive
The Oscar-winning filmmaker and artist Steve McQueen heard Wild is the Wind for the first time 30 years ago. The song was written by composer Dmitri Tiomkin and lyricist Ned Washington for the 1957 film of the same name. Later, it was taken to another register entirely by Nina Simone in 1966 and then a decade later, David Bowie paid tribute to her version. What McQueen appreciated the most in those two performances is the pure yearning – the want, the need, the must.
Knowing the lyrics are so important to the artist, visitors don't need to be familiar with either the song, Simone, Bowie or McQueen at all to enjoy the exhibition, according to its curator, Lekha Hileman: “This is an exhibition that’s very experiential. It's about feeling, it's about being present," she told Euronews Culture. "It's about slowing down and just receiving something. So in that way, it's very universal.”
As McQueen said, the viewer is the other voice in the work.
How David met Nina
Steve McQueen was inspired not only by the song, but by the way it had so many new lives thanks to the next generations of artists. He likes the story about how Bowie met Simone in 1975.
“[Nina Simone’s] daughter wanted to go to David Bowie's concert, so she dragged her mother to take her, and they met afterwards. I think [that] Bowie version is almost homage to Nina. There's a certain kind of imitation of her voice, but then it goes somewhere,” said McQueen.
The original version was a Johnny Mathis song, sang in 1957, which was nothing like Nina Simone’s.
“She took that song and took it to another stratosphere. So by putting these two versions together, it's complimentary," said McQueen. "They're both singing A major. And it's one of those things where I just felt that by putting those two things together, these two stones, it makes fire. And I know for sure they would be extraordinary, happy with this collaboration, with this duet.”
Tension and love
The title “66–76–26” refers to the years in which Simone and Bowie respectively recorded the song, as well as to the year of the exhibition at Guggenheim Bilbao itself.
Both recordings, in 1966 and 1976, came out in moments of political tension. The work invites reflection not only on the song’s enduring power but also on the social and political conditions through which these recordings have travelled.
Created during periods marked by upheaval, uncertainty, and transformation – the civil rights movement, Vietnam, Watergate – the performances speak with particular force to the present moment.
“Particularly now things seem very turbulent. And I think when things are very turbulent, the things that you hold on to are the things which are precious to you, which is love," said McQueen. "And again, I know it sounds sort of corny, but it's important because that's the basis of us all in one way, shape, form or the other.
"That's what we crave and that's what we need. So to come back to some kind of understanding of love is important, at least for me,” explained McQueen.
Between work in cinema and the gallery
The plan of having Steve McQueen at Guggenheim Bilbao Museum began six years ago and the exhibition opened on the 9th of October, on his 57th birthday.
Perhaps best known for his work as a filmmaker, McQueen won an Oscar, a Golden Globe and a BAFTA for his movie 12 Years a Slave. He also won several plaudits for Hunger including the Caméra d’Or at the Cannes Film Festival.
But prior to those landmark works, McQueen made his name as a pioneering contemporary artist, who represented Great Britain at the Venice Biennale and has had shows at the Tate museums in London among others.
In parallel with the exhibition, the Guggenheim Bilbao will present a film programme dedicated to McQueen’s cinematic work, offering audiences an opportunity to consider the relationship between his work in cinema and the gallery.
“66–76–26” highlights the concerns that have long animated his artistic practice: perception, embodiment, memory, duration, and the capacity of art to create spaces for reflection and encounter.
Steve McQueen's sound installation "66-76-26" at Guggenheim Bilbao Museum is open until 13 February 2027.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Line launched Line Touch on Wednesday, letting users access coupons, loyalty points, and digital services by tapping their phones instead of scanning QR codes.
The near-field communication, or NFC-enabled service works with compatible devices installed at stores, restaurants, and event venues, per CNA. Users can access Line Official Accounts for coupons and membership services, or Line Mini Apps for ordering, check-in, and registration.

Line Touch is available in adhesive NFC tags priced at NT$69 (US$2) and acrylic stands priced at NT$249. Businesses can purchase and configure them through the account manager settings.

Cartel-linked mom wanted for child's 1997 murder caught in Mexico
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:25:11 UTC
22:25:11 KST

Cartel-linked woman wanted in brutal 1997 murder of her child in Arizona is captured in Mexico
A woman linked to drug cartels and accused of torturing and murdering her daughter in Arizona in 1997 has been captured in Mexico nearly 30 years after the crime, officials said Wednesday.
Anna Marlene Somoza was connected to a "major transnational drug trafficking network" along the Arizona border through the 1980s and 1990s, the U.S. Marshals Service said in a news release. She was arrested for selling and transporting marijuana in 1993, and agreed to act as a confidential informant for Arizona law enforcement.
In November 1993, Somoza had a daughter, Crystal Reyes. The child was born in Nogales, Mexico. Her father was Darren Stockwell, a law enforcement officer and U.S. citizen, the U.S. Marshals said.
Somoza and Crystal then moved to Ahwatukee, Arizona, to live with her boyfriend, narcotics detective Avelino Tamala. The U.S. Marshals Service said that Somoza and Tamala began an "improper romantic relationship" while she was a law enforcement source.
While living with Somoza and Tamala, Crystal was allegedly subject to "severe physical abuse," including being bound and gagged in a small dog kennel for weeks at a time, the U.S. Marshals said. The abuse "escalated fatally" on January 30, 1997, when Crystal suffocated inside a sealed cardboard box, the agency said.
Nearly a year later, in November 1998, human bone fragments were found in Mobile, Arizona. The bones could not be identified. In 1999, Somoza and Tamala were arrested on drug and weapon offenses. DNA was collected. When compared to the bones, the analysis "could not eliminate Somoza as the maternal source," the U.S. Marshals said. But without a paternal DNA source, an identification could not be made. In 2008, Somoza was released from prison.
The case went cold until 2014, when Stockwell was located and interviewed by cold case detectives. A sample of his DNA was collected and analyzed, allowing investigators to identify the bone fragments as Crystal's.
Somoza and Tamala were indicted on charges of first-degree murder on December 12, 2014. Arrest warrants were issued. Tamala was arrested that day by the U.S. Marshals and Arizona's WANTED Violent Offender Task Force. The task force quickly determined that Somoza had fled to Mexico. They began collaborating with the U.S. Marshal Service Mexico Foreign Field Office, but Somoza could not be found. In 2016, Tamala was sentenced to life in prison.
Federal, state and local officials continued to investigate the case for the next 12 years, the U.S. Marshals said. "Extensive investigative efforts" were taken to locate Somoza, but law enforcement found that she "had taken deliberate and extensive measures to evade detection by law enforcement." The long search was also "affected by her close connections with cartels," officials said.
In September 2026, members of a U.S. Marshals task force became aware that Somoza was in Cernavaca, Mexico. On Sunday, Mexican police and Interpol officers were able to arrest Somoza in Xochitepec, Mexico.
Efforts to extradite Somoza are underway. She will face charges in Arizona, the U.S. Marshals said.
Attorney Juan Rocha, who teaches at Arizona State University, told CBS affiliate KPHO-TV that Mexico often seeks assurance the death penalty will not be pursued. Prosecutors have not publicly said whether they will seek the death penalty against Somoza.
"No one can hide from American justice forever," said Timothy Courchaine, U.S. Attorney for the District of Arizona, in the news release. "The United States Attorney's office stands in partnership with both our federal and critically our state partners to ensure defendants have their day in court. We look forward to now working alongside our Mexican partners to bring this fugitive back to Arizona."

Water rationing, garbage pile-up raise disease fears in Yemen's besieged Taiz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:24:13 UTC
22:24:13 KST

Families have started rationing water in and around Yemen's Taiz city, where renewed fighting has disrupted fuel supplies and access to water systems serving 3 million people, aid groups and UN agencies said.
Meanwhile, mounting piles of garbage along major roads are raising fears of disease outbreaks in the city, Yemen's third-largest.
Fighting between the Saudi-backed government and the Iran-backed Houthis since September has cut key supply routes, including the Taiz-Aden corridor, worsening shortages of water, food and fuel in and around the city.
The lack of fuel is hampering the operation of water pumps and hospitals, while disruption to waste collection has left garbage piled along roads of the city, a stronghold of anti-Houthi forces which is now under siege by the Houthis.
The Taiz governorate hosts nearly half of the 250,000 people displaced by the latest escalation, aid groups said.
"The state of the garbage in the city is very wretched, and the build-up is terrible, like nothing before,” Taiz resident Abdelbari al-Qadi told Reuters.
Sanitation worker Ali Ahmed said authorities could no longer go to the main dumping site because of clashes, and they were forced to burn it in the streets.
'Extremely dangerous situation' for children, says relief official
Families are rationing drinking water as diesel shortages hobble pumping stations and sanitation systems, said Akhil Iyer, UNICEF's representative in Yemen.
"I get the water with difficulty. We wait in queues from the morning until our turn comes,” Alaa Khalil told Reuters while people queued to fill jerry cans in Taiz, where most residents depend on trucked water.
Access to the Al-Dhubab aquifer, a major source of trucked water for Taiz, has been restricted, while fuel disruptions have affected pumps, creating a severe water crisis, said Wathiq Aghbari, director general of the Local Water and Sanitation Authority in the governorate.
Water production in Taiz has fallen by about 50%, according to Save the Children.
“We find children in an extremely dangerous situation where they are not able to have their basic needs satisfied. They are not able to access sufficient food and water and healthcare,” said Rishana Haniffa, Save the Children's country director for Yemen.
Aid groups are exploring other sources, including a shallow aquifer west of the city. The cost of a water truck has tripled from about 23,000 Yemeni rials ($14.80) before the latest escalation to about 70,000 rials ($45), according to UNICEF.
CARE International says cash assistance is buying less food and water as prices rise.
“We feel the situation is really getting out of hand unless we able to negotiate access to have water tankers come in to the city,” said Iman Abdullahi, CARE Yemen country director.
Garbage build-up 'will cause diseases,' says health official
"The build-up of garbage is very harmful and will cause diseases, whether respiratory or otherwise," said Abdulrahman al-Sabri, director of Taiz Governorate's Health Office, adding that dengue fever and cholera cases were spreading.
Cholera cases have tripled since early September from 221 to 683 this month, while hospitals face medicine shortages and 12 facilities have fuel supplies sufficient for only about four days, the World Health Organization said.
A doctor who asked not to be named for security reasons said some families could not reach healthcare facilities because of fighting around the city.
The Danish Refugee Council said the impact of deteriorating water and sanitation conditions could spread beyond Taiz city. It pointed to overstretched resources in crowded displacement sites across the governorates of Taiz, Lahj, Abyan and Aden.
The spread of disease could also worsen hunger in Taiz governorate, UNICEF said. It has identified 52,000 acutely malnourished children in Taiz so far this year. Road closures have halted UNICEF's deliveries of a therapeutic food for severely malnourished children in Taiz.

In this Florida district, politicians battle over who most loves Israel

Rep. Jared Moskowitz said that he is “proud to be known as the most pro-Israel Jewish Democrat in Congress” during a synagogue event in one of the country’s most Jewish congressional districts on Tuesday evening.
The comment came during a one-hour candidates’ forum featuring Moskowitz and his Republican challenger, Scott Singer, both Jewish and wearing kippahs, that largely centered on Israel and grew testy at times.
Moskowitz said he is “proud to have AIPAC’s endorsement” at a moment when the popularity of Israel and the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC has plummeted among Democratic voters amid Israel’s military campaign in Gaza and the war with Iran.
But the crowd at the Reform synagogue Congregation B’nai Israel in Boca Raton was, like Florida’s 25th Congressional District, split across party lines and staunchly pro-Israel.
“This isn’t New York, this isn’t Boston, this is South Florida,” attendee Edward Kone told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency.
Florida's recently redrawn 25th Congressional District
Moskowitz soundly defeated Democratic Socialist challenger Oliver Larkin, a sharp Israel critic, in August. As Democrats look to take control of the House of Representatives, Florida’s recently redrawn 25th Congressional District, which would have favored Trump by 9 percentage points in 2024 but backed Joe Biden in 2020 under its new boundaries, is being closely watched ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Despite some tense moments between Moskowitz and Singer, who was Boca Raton’s mayor until earlier this year, the two politicians have been largely aligned on the issue of Israel.
Both have condemned accusations that Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. They each oppose any effort to condition or cut off US military aid to Israel. Both supported Israel’s strikes on Iranian facilities in 2025, though Moskowitz has since called for the US to end its war with Iran.
Moskowitz referenced his and Singer’s shared pro-Israel viewpoints on Tuesday during the forum moderated by South Florida Sun Sentinel journalist Anthony Man.
“This is exactly why nothing gets done in Washington. This is exactly why nothing is functioning: Because literally two people who agree on 99% of this stuff want to take this 1% and try to ram it down people’s throats,” Moskowitz said.
Singer, however, emphasized where the two candidates differ on Israel. He criticized Moskowitz for voting for the March 2026 war powers resolution in response to the Trump administration ordering strikes on Iran without congressional authorization. While Moskowitz has called for the administration to end the war, Singer argued that the threat of Iran must be thoroughly dealt with. “We have to ensure victory here,” he said.
'America first, but Israel is extremely important to me'
For siblings Edward and Susan Kone, both Jewish Republican voters who attended the forum, Moskowitz’s record on Israel does not stack up against Singer’s positions. They also criticized Moskowitz for voting to end the Iran war and for his 2023 vote to keep Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar on the Foreign Affairs Committee.
“I’m America first, but Israel is extremely important to me. And on Israel, Jared Moskowitz just doesn’t add up,” Edward Kone said. Omar is among a number of pro-Palestinian Democrats whom Republicans say are leading the party’s left-wing flank in turning it against Israel.
Singer himself blasted Moskowitz for voting against removing Omar and tied him to the left flank of the Democratic Party.
“The strategy is adjective, verb, Ilhan Omar, I got it. Let’s move on to the next topic,” Moskowitz responded, drawing some groans from the audience.
Others in the room had voted for Moskowitz in previous elections, and said they were likely to do so again, at least in part because of his Israel stance.
“He has a good track record with Israel, and as an American Jew I appreciate that,” said Peter Davidson, an independent who is a member of Congregation B’nai Israel.
Moskowitz pointed to AIPAC's endorsement and Singer’s lack of an endorsement from Rep. Randy Fine, a fellow Jewish Republican from Florida, as evidence that he is seen as sufficiently pro-Israel across parts of the political spectrum. He also pointed to a post on X by Jeff Miller, an RJC board member, who wrote that he has “zero interest in tearing down one of the few Democrats left willing to stand unapologetically with America and Israel.”
“They’re staying out,” Moskowitz said. “They’re specifically saying, ‘We’re not going to oppose Jared Moskowitz because of his record fighting antisemitism and fighting for the State of Israel.’”
Singer has the endorsement of the RJC and Trump as well. He admitted during the forum that he had reached out to Fine for an endorsement and was rejected.
Earlier this year, Singer downplayed anti-Israel trends on the right as “a few fringe commentators” who are out of step with Trump. Moskowitz challenged him to name three of those figures: Tucker Carlson, Candace Owens and Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback.
Singer named all three and said “I gladly, shamelessly condemn” them, but countered that Democrats are voting in anti-Israel voices while Republicans cast theirs aside.
Man also asked Singer about President Donald Trump’s use of the term “Shylock” on Monday, a term that references a character from the play “The Merchant of Venice,” which is rooted in an antisemitic trope.
“I think that’s an ill-advised term,” Singer said, before pivoting to praise of Trump and urging the audience to focus on what the president has done for Israel rather than his choice of words.
“‘Merchant of Venice’ happens to be my favorite Shakespeare play. That term has multiple meanings. But let’s look at the real record beyond an offhand comment: No president has been better for the State of Israel than President Trump,” Singer said, drawing applause.
As for the upcoming Israeli elections, which Trump recently weighed in on, Singer told reporters after the event that he was too busy with his own race to endorse candidates and has no preferred candidate.
“To be candid, I have some awareness of it, but I’m not following it intently,” he said.
Singer’s attacks on Tuesday often focused on Moskowitz’s Democratic Party, which he says will drown out the congressman’s pro-Israel views as it takes its cues from its left-wing flank. He pointed to Moskowitz’s quote from last month, when he said that pro-Israel voices are being “ostracized” in the party.
“It’s great that he says these things, but he’s also voted to empower Ilhan Omar twice,” Singer said. “He’s tried to go along to get along with the Squad, and it’s not working.”
But for some in the crowd, that attack didn’t quite land.
Davidson, an independent, said he is “not a great fan” of the Democratic Party. But for him, Moskowitz is an exception.
“He’s more of an independent thinker,” Davidson said. “Crosses a lot of party lines.”

Christiane Amanpour exits CNN with a legacy shaped by the debate over Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:23:35 UTC
22:23:35 KST

Christiane Amanpour, CNN’s chief international anchor, is leaving the network after 43 years, closing a chapter in a career that made her one of television journalism’s most celebrated war correspondents and, among Jewish and pro-Israel viewers, one of its most controversial figures.
For many viewers, Amanpour’s legacy is that of a fearless correspondent who brought the human costs of war into American living rooms, from the first Gulf War to Bosnia, Rwanda and Ukraine.
But her coverage of Israel and the Palestinians has long drawn sharp criticism from some Jewish viewers, who accused her of giving insufficient weight to Israeli security concerns, mischaracterizing events and disproportionately presenting Israeli religious nationalism in an especially unflattering light.
Amanpour, 68, announced Monday that she will wind down her daily CNN International program early next year, conclude its weekly successor in May and leave the network in June 2027. Her PBS program, “Amanpour & Company,” will end at the close of this year. However, she will continue her podcast, “The Ex Files,” with her ex-husband, Jamie Rubin, a former State Department official.
'Always be truthful, not neutral': Amanpour's farewell
Amanpour did not give a specific reason for her departure, which comes as CNN enters a new era under Paramount Skydance ownership.
“Always be truthful, not neutral,” Amanpour wrote in her farewell message, summing up a philosophy that has animated her reporting and helped make her a polarizing figure.
Amanpour’s admirers would argue that the same qualities that make her coverage uncomfortable for some Jewish viewers- skepticism toward official accounts, attention to civilian suffering, and a willingness to challenge powerful governments- are essential to journalism.
When the National Press Foundation honored her in 2025 with its Sol Taishoff Award for Excellence in Broadcast Journalism, its judges called her “a gold standard for international broadcast journalism” and praised her tough questioning of world leaders. The Committee to Protect Journalists, which honored her in 2016, likewise celebrated her commitment to press freedom.
Amanpour, who was raised in Iran and England by her Iranian Muslim father and British Roman Catholic mother, joined CNN in 1983 as a desk assistant and rose through the ranks to become one of its most prominent correspondents. Her reporting from the Bosnian war in the 1990s helped establish her reputation for confronting officials and challenging the language governments use to justify military action.
Some of the sharpest criticism of her work came in 2007, when Amanpour hosted “God’s Jewish Warriors,” the opening installment of a three-part CNN documentary series examining the role of religion in politics and conflict.
Andrea Levin, president of the Committee for Accuracy in Middle East Reporting and Analysis, or CAMERA, condemned the program as a biased portrayal of Jewish religious life and Israeli settlers. A 2010 Jewish Telegraphic Agency commentary revisited the controversy, with Ron Kampeas noting that “the only explicitly religious people she interviewed were ultranationalist settlers,” and that Amanpour ignored religious Jews who opposed the settlements.
Kampeas also said the program’s treatment of the pro-Israel lobby in Washington exaggerated the power of groups like AIPAC and downplayed the shared strategic and moral imperatives that drove the US-Israel alliance.
“God’s Jewish Warriors” became Exhibit A in the case against Amanpour’s work. Legitimate criticism of Israeli policy, her detractors asserted, was framed in a way that left Jewish viewers feeling that Jewish religious identity, political advocacy, or national aspirations were inherently suspect.
Critics of Amanpour's coverage of Lebanon in 2006
Reporting from Lebanon during the 2006 war between Israel and Hezbollah, Amanpour was part of a CNN team whose work rekindled a longstanding debate over how journalists should cover conflicts in which a state military fights an armed group embedded in civilian areas.
Even as Amanpour at times acknowledged the difficulty of covering such “asymmetrical warfare,” Israeli officials and supporters argued at the time that images of destruction and civilian suffering in Lebanon obscured Hezbollah’s role in initiating and sustaining the conflict. Those objections anticipated similar complaints, aimed at CNN and other outlets, over coverage of Israel’s devastating war in Gaza after the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023.
Critics have continued to document what they see as a pattern. CAMERA has maintained a collection of complaints about Amanpour’s reporting, while HonestReporting, another pro-Israel media-monitoring organization, has accused her of repeated anti-Israel distortions.
Although both organizations have a clear advocacy perspective, they often provide specific examples of errors and request corrections.
One example came in April 2023, when Amanpour described the killing of Israeli Lucy Dee and her daughters Maia and Rina in a Hamas-linked West Bank terrorist attack as a “shootout.” The women were driving on a highway when Palestinian gunmen opened fire on their vehicle. Amanpour subsequently apologized on air for her inaccurate characterization.
In 2024, Amanpour also drew criticism for a social media post about Marwan Barghouti, the imprisoned Palestinian political leader convicted by an Israeli court of involvement in deadly attacks. “To many Israelis, he’s a terrorist. To many Palestinians, he’s their Mandela,” she wrote.
The comparison accurately captured Barghouti’s sharply different reputations among Israelis and Palestinians, but critics argued that it risked reducing the gravity of the attacks for which he was convicted.
Complaints about CNN’s Gaza coverage gained a striking new dimension in February 2024, when Amanpour reportedly joined CNN colleagues in accusing the network of a pro-Israel bias in its coverage of the Israel-Hamas war.
'Double standards' in CNN's coverage of Israel
According to reporting by The Intercept and The Guardian, journalists at an internal CNN meeting raised concerns that the network’s editorial procedures were favoring official Israeli narratives and making it harder to convey Palestinian perspectives. CNN’s process required coverage of the conflict to pass through its Jerusalem bureau; Amanpour was heard on tape saying that the process led to “changing copy, double standards, and all the rest.”
At the same time, some pro-Israel viewers saw CNN and Amanpour as too willing to accept Palestinian claims and too quick to foreground Gaza’s devastation.
In response to the reports, CNN defended its coverage of the conflict. “We remain absolutely committed to reporting all sides of this immensely challenging, complex and emotive story,” it said in a statement. “We absolutely reject the notion that any of our journalists treat Israeli officials differently to other officials.”
Amanpour again apologized on air in October 2025 for having said that surviving Israeli hostages released from Hamas captivity were “probably being treated better than the average Gazan, because they are the pawns and the chips that Hamas had.” Following backlash from political figures and organizations, Amanpour retracted the statement, calling her remarks “insensitive and wrong.”
Amanpour's telling of Israel-Hamas war since 2023
Last month, in a rare long-form interview about her career with the podcaster Sam Fragoso, Amanpour discussed CNN’s coverage of the Gaza war. In the immediate aftermath of the October 7 attacks, she said, the network was “practically wall to wall with horrendous stories from the victims in Israel. I mean, just horrendous.”
But as Israel’s military response ground on, “the story flipped,” she said. “As the destruction of Gaza took place and the bodies piled up, most particularly the women and the children, the tone of the coverage reflected the reality.” At the February 2024 meeting with CNN executives, she said her colleagues expressed frustration that the network took too long to cover the Palestinian side.
In the same interview, Amanpour also walked back an apology she made in 2020, not about CNN’s Mideast coverage, but for a commentary on the 82nd anniversary of the Kristallnacht attacks. In that segment, she juxtaposed the Nazis’ anti-Jewish pogrom with what she called President Donald Trump’s “attacks on history, facts, knowledge and truth.” After Jewish groups, including the American Jewish Committee, complained that she had “instrumentalized” the Holocaust with a faulty comparison, Amanpour said on air that she regretted any pain her statement may have caused.
Speaking last month with Fragoso, Amanpour said that she stands by her assertion that Kristallnacht demonstrated how quickly “democratic values can slowly slip away.” She also suggested that her employers had bowed to outside pressure and instructed her to apologize.
“There were people, you know, in various communities in regard to this,” she said, referring to her critics, “who decided that I need to be slapped around and pulled down a peg. But I think that’s just because some people are afraid of the truth.”
Amanpour’s departure comes at a moment of uncertainty about CNN’s future under its new corporate owner. Paramount Skydance’s $110 billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery, CNN’s parent company, has raised concerns among journalists about political influence and editorial independence, particularly given new owner David Ellison’s ties to Trump and the changes he has overseen at CBS News.
Amanpour herself expressed concern in May about what she called an “ideological realignment” at CBS News under its new leadership. “So clearly, obviously, I’m concerned,” she said, speaking at an investigative journalism conference in London. “I would like to think that we would have the very basic, which is editorial independence. I’m hoping for that. I know many of us at CNN are incredibly, including leadership, very, very committed to that, clearly.”
For some Jewish and pro-Israel observers, however, the same changes have raised hopes that CNN’s coverage of Israel might become more favorable. Bari Weiss, who became CBS News editor-in-chief after Paramount acquired her strongly pro-Israel publication, The Free Press, has long argued that mainstream news organizations have mishandled Israel and antisemitism.
Amanpour didn’t mention the merger in her announcement. But she noted how her background shaped her perspective.
“Because of my upbringing, I’m half-Iranian and half-British, I’ve had the great privilege of being able to see the world from two very distinct perspectives,” she said. “I’ve always spoken out about the need to bridge gaps. I know we can live in a world that’s not 100% tribalized.”

EXPLAINER – EU’s new Arctic strategy: What changes and why it matters?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:23:33 UTC
22:23:33 KST

- ‘Northern Neighbourhood’ framework placed at heart of new approach
- EU plans stronger satellite surveillance, protection of undersea cables, closer cooperation with Arctic partners 
The European Union unveiled a new Arctic strategy on Tuesday, shifting toward a more security-focused approach while maintaining its commitment to climate protection and regional cooperation.
The strategy builds on the bloc’s 2021 Arctic policy but places greater emphasis on surveillance, critical infrastructure protection, economic security and strategic autonomy.
Titled Europe's Northern Neighborhood: A New Strategy for the Arctic, the framework is built around four priorities: security, climate, economy and people.
According to the European Commission, increased military activity, pressure on infrastructure, changing access routes and growing economic interest are reshaping the region.
The strategy also comes as the Arctic becomes increasingly accessible, creating economic opportunities in renewable energy, critical raw materials, transport and digital connectivity.
Here are three key questions that explain the EU’s new Arctic strategy.
 
What's the new policy?
The strategy introduces a political cooperation framework called the “Northern Neighborhood,” aimed at strengthening ties between the EU, its member states, Arctic partners and other like-minded countries.
The framework seeks to improve coordination, support the development and financing of joint projects, strengthen connectivity and facilitate regular high-level political exchanges.
It is also intended to complement existing regional cooperation structures, including the Arctic Council.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the Arctic was “close, connected and critical to our future,” highlighting the growing significance of the region.
“With our new strategy, we are investing in stronger security, resilient infrastructure and economic opportunities,” von der Leyen added.
Security and infrastructure resilience are central to the new approach. A dedicated Arctic surveillance pilot is planned for 2027 to improve situational awareness and maritime monitoring. The EU also intends to develop a Maritime Security Hub to facilitate information-sharing.
The bloc also plans to expand its icebreaker capacity through joint procurement, resource-sharing and technological development. According to the commission, these measures will be pursued in cooperation with member states and Arctic partners, in complementarity with NATO.
The strategy also seeks to strengthen the EU's economic presence and connectivity in the region, focusing on renewable energy, critical raw materials, transport, digital connectivity and sustainable marine industries.
Among the proposed projects is the Pan-Arctic Cable, which would establish a direct submarine cable connection between Greenland and Europe, with potential future extensions toward Canada and Japan. 
The IRIS2 Arctic Connectivity initiative also aims to provide secure satellite communications for government use, with additional satellites planned to expand coverage across the region.
Research and environmental monitoring form another part of the strategy. A new EU Polar Research Hub will aim to connect research, observation and scientific infrastructure, while the OceanEye initiative will bring together EU member states and partners, including Canada and Norway, to collect and share ocean data to improve climate predictions and maritime safety.
The strategy also maintains a focus on climate protection and Arctic communities, with plans to expand climate observation and support education, employment, skills development and social inclusion, including through expanded Erasmus+ opportunities.
How is it different from the 2021 strategy?
The EU's previous Arctic policy, adopted in October 2021, focused more on peaceful cooperation, addressing climate change and environmental challenges, and promoting sustainable development.
Although security concerns were already part of the earlier policy, the new strategy gives them greater prominence, with specific initiatives focused on surveillance, critical infrastructure protection and operational capabilities.
According to the commission, the new document responds to geopolitical, security and environmental changes since 2021.
“The new strategy reflects a different political, security and economic environment: stronger geopolitical competition, rising pressure on critical infrastructure, faster environmental change and new economic dynamics,” it said.
Economic security also receives greater attention. Critical raw materials, transport infrastructure and digital connections are linked to efforts to strengthen resilient supply chains and strategic autonomy.
Why it matters?
The commission says the Arctic is directly linked to Europe's security, climate, prosperity and resilience, with more than 500,000 EU citizens living in the region.
Andreas Raspotnik, a senior fellow and leadership group member at The Arctic Institute, noted in an analysis published Tuesday, that the Arctic was not simply a matter of foreign policy for the EU but rather a “domestic policy wearing a diplomatic coat.”
“The 2026 Joint Communication is unusually direct on this point. Its introduction declares that ‘Europe’s strategic autonomy is inseparable from the Arctic’ – the clearest formulation yet of why a policy exists,” he said.
He noted that it also “explicitly” framed this change as a “rupture” with 2021, redefining what Arctic means for Europe.
“That self-conscious break is itself analytically significant: it is not about updating a policy anymore but claiming that the terms of engagement have changed,” Raspotnik said.
According to Raspotnik, the effectiveness of the new approach will depend on adequate resources, institutional coordination and clear priorities.
“The test of this new strategy is whether it finally makes clear what it intends to do there – and whether it is willing to match its institutional architecture and resources to the ambition it has now declared,” he added.

Publishers want Brussels and London to stop Meta’s new AI terms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:23:02 UTC
22:23:02 KST

This photograph, taken on Jan. 20, 2026, shows signage bearing the Meta logo during the World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, Switzerland. | Ina Fassbender/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — Europe’s biggest media companies have asked regulators in Brussels and London to stop Meta from introducing new terms they say would let it copy publishers’ websites to build artificial intelligence, as a backlash that began in the U.S. spreads across Europe.
In a letter Monday, the European Publishers Council, whose members include POLITICO’s owner Axel Springer, called on EU competition boss Teresa Ribera and tech chief Henna Virkkunen to press Meta to put the terms on hold before they take effect Oct. 30.
The group wants Brussels to check them against EU copyright and competition law, and has requested an urgent meeting with the teams of both commissioners.
Advertisement
“The Commission remains committed to ensure that Meta’s practices fully comply with all applicable obligations under EU law, including competition rules and the Digital Markets Act,” Commission spokesperson Ricardo Cardoso told POLITICO, referring to the EU’s rulebook for Big Tech. He said Brussels was aware of both Meta’s changes and publishers’ concerns.
The U.K. competition watchdog has moved as well. British publishers have complained to the Competition and Markets Authority that Meta is so dominant they are compelled to accept its terms.
The watchdog’s chief, Sarah Cardell, told British lawmakers on Tuesday that it had asked Meta to explain the changes and would meet the company on Wednesday. She named Meta as a possible candidate for Britain’s new rules for tech giants.
Sarah Cardell, Chief Executive of the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), speaks in a panel discussion during the Annual CBI Conference, at Queen Elizabeth II Centre on November 25, 2024 in London. | Leon Neal/Getty Images
The terms cover businesses that use Meta’s tools to run Facebook pages, Instagram accounts or ads, which includes almost every newsroom.
The fight began in the U.S. last week, when Nieman Lab, a journalism research outlet at Harvard, reported on the terms after receiving a tip from a small business owner.
As first written, they let Meta send automated programs to copy websites linked to those accounts and use the material to “train” its products, Nieman Lab concluded. There is no opt-out, and a business that continues to use Meta’s tools after Oct. 30 will be deemed to have consented.
Advertisement
Publishers say the terms would hand Meta content for free that other AI companies pay to license.
Rapid reaction
On Friday, Meta communications chief Andy Stone responded on X that the Nieman Lab report was “false” and that there was “no change to how Meta uses web crawlers.”
Stone said the update aimed to let Meta pull accurate product information from shopping sites for ads, not to scrape news sites. The company also said the crawling language already existed in other Meta terms and was just being gathered in one place.
Late Friday, however, Meta revised the terms and deleted the word “train,” saying the terms cover only its advertising and business products.
“We’ve heard you and want to clarify,” a spokesperson for Meta told POLITICO over the weekend, adding the change was “not about scraping news sites.”
Publishers say that changes little, however.
Advertisement
Meta has given them verbal assurances that they can keep using its tools without surrendering their content to AI, but the terms themselves don’t guarantee that, the European Publishers Council’s letter says.
“Meta’s supposed Friday night correction is a farce,” said Jason Kint, who heads Digital Content Next, a U.S. publisher group whose members include Axel Springer. “Exactly what you’d expect from a gatekeeper notorious for abusing its market power.”
Others have gone further.
“This is unscrupulous theft,” Germany’s newspaper and magazine associations said in a joint statement on Tuesday. They want Brussels to block the terms while it reviews them, warning that once articles are copied into AI systems, they can’t be clawed back.

Russian leader Vladimir Putin said on Wednesday, Oct. 21, that the first tanker under the Kremlin’s diesel agreement with the White House would sail in two to three days, revising an earlier announcement that it would depart on Thursday.
The ship will carry 40,000 metric tons (about 44,100 US tons) of diesel, Putin said during talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg, according to Russian state news agency TASS.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The first tanker will leave in 2-3 days,” Putin said, adding that more tankers would follow.
He also said the financial arrangements needed to be in place for the shipments to work. He did not announce a departure port or an arrival date in the US in the quoted remarks.
Earlier on Wednesday, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said the first tanker was scheduled to leave for the US on Thursday, Oct. 22, with supply contracts in the final stages of signing.
Novak said Russia could fully restore diesel export volumes by the end of the year, depending on its refineries’ capabilities. Other countries could also receive additional supplies as production recovered and Russia met the Trump representatives’ request.
Novak described the vessel’s displacement as 40,000 metric tons (about 44,100 US tons). Putin separately referred to that quantity as the diesel cargo.
Putin’s subsequent estimate of two-to-three days indicates instead a departure around Oct. 23-24.
‘He Just Doesn’t Like Him’: Trump’s Personal Animosity Toward Zelensky May Be Shaping US Policy on Ukraine
First cargo is a fraction of Trump’s initial pledge
The shipment amounts to approximately 13 percent of the initial 300,000 metric tons (about 330,700 US tons) that President Donald Trump said Russia would release immediately under the agreement.
Trump announced the arrangement on Oct. 9, saying larger volumes would follow in November and afterward. He claimed the deal is a way to bring down fuel prices for American farmers, truckers and consumers.
Putin said Russia was preparing several tankers, indicating that the first cargo would be part of a wider sequence of shipments.
The timing he gave refers to departure, rather than delivery to an American buyer. Shipping and unloading would still have to take place after the vessel sails.
Ukraine’s sanctions envoy calls cargo a “rounding error”
Ukraine’s presidential sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk said the announced 40,000-metric-ton diesel cargo would cover less than two hours of American diesel consumption.
He estimated that the voyage would take approximately three weeks, during which the US would export around 100 times as much diesel of its own.
“A rounding error for the market. A sanctions loophole for the Kremlin,” Vlasiuk wrote.
His post referred to the earlier announcement of an Oct. 22 departure, before Putin gave a revised timeline.
For context, US Energy Information Administration data shows domestic distillate fuel supplied averaged 4.323 million barrels per day in the week ending Oct. 9. That category includes both diesel and heating oil.
Sanctions relief draws criticism from Kyiv and Congress
The diesel agreement has become a source of friction between Washington and Kyiv.
After Trump announced the deal, the US Treasury authorized transactions involving Russian diesel through April 7, 2027, easing restrictions imposed over Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Trump later signed an Oct. 16 executive order waiving sweeping new Russia-related sanctions and tariffs shortly before they were scheduled to take effect.
The suspended measures included additional 500% tariffs on Russian imports and 100% duties targeting major buyers of Russian oil and gas.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has criticized the diesel arrangement and broader sanctions relief, arguing that additional energy revenues would help Russia finance its war rather than persuade Putin to stop it.
Opposition has also come from US lawmakers. A bipartisan group of 12 senators urged Trump to rescind the diesel agreement, warning that it would reward Moscow while offering limited relief to Americans.
The senators called for stronger enforcement of economic pressure on Russia as attacks on Ukraine continued.
