Why the US Needs Ukraine as Much as Ukraine Needs the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:12:57 UTC
22:12:57 KST

The US appears to have picked a side over Ukraine, and it’s not Kyiv.
As President Volodymyr Zelensky not so subtly called on US President Donald Trump to “stay in the middle,” Trump has pursued deals with Moscow and has ostensibly chosen Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s side – that of a man who, according to Ukraine, has been responsible for 228,992 war crimes committed by the Russian army as of Oct. 12, 2026.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, a total of 17,605 civilians have been killed and more than 55,000 injured as a result of the war. Among them, 760 children have been killed and 2,950 injured.
And that is on top of more than 114,000 Ukrainian civilians, including over 2,000 children, who are considered missing due to Russia’s war in Ukraine. The largest group, estimated at between 20,000 and 40,000 people, consists primarily of those killed in Russian bombardments of Mariupol, a city leveled in the initial days of the 2022 invasion.
One of the latest victims was a one-year-old girl killed while sitting in her stroller, when Russia struck a park in eastern Ukraine’s Kharkiv region on Monday, killing six locals.
The attack coincided with Trump’s statement about the war, which, perhaps unsurprisingly, was not taken kindly by Ukrainians:
“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven’t been doing much.”
‘He Just Doesn’t Like Him’: Trump’s Personal Animosity Toward Zelensky May Be Shaping US Policy on Ukraine
That, on top of his administration’s recent plan to exempt Russian shadow fleets from sanctions and its decision to throttle Starlink access for Kyiv, which crippled Ukraine’s ability to conduct deep strikes and intercept incoming drones, raises one simple question.
Why?
The most logical and straightforward explanation is that the US wants to end the war as early as possible, and it’s easier to pressure a non-nuclear nation than a nuclear power. And business deals, of course.
But for a country working hard to rebuild its democracy from the ashes of the USSR, establish anti-corruption institutions and an independent judiciary, and align itself with the best examples of democracy, these developments are nothing short of a betrayal.
Moral questions aside, foresight is also a good thing to have for any government, and here’s why aiding Russia can backfire on Washington long after Trump is gone.
Russia is not a friend
The central issue behind Trump’s seemingly misguided shift toward Russia is that Russia has never been an ally of the United States – and never will be.
In Russia’s national mindset, the US is an adversary and its principal global competitor, even during Trump’s presidency and despite the fact that the US has come to Russia’s aid numerous times.
The Lend-Lease program during World War II is just one example. More recently, Dmitry Medvedev, Russia’s former president and close Putin ally who sits on Russia’s Security Council, put it plainly.
“We have been, are, and will remain systemic adversaries,” he wrote on Tuesday.
Second, Russians themselves believe that the United States should become Russia’s next target after Ukraine. In 2014, Kremlin mouthpiece Vladimir Solovyov threatened to turn “Washington into radioactive ash,” and the latest polls on the street indicate that Russians view the US as an enemy and NATO countries as US proxies.
Moscow’s values are also far removed from those of the US. Democracy, freedom, an independent judiciary and parliament are not considered core values in Russia – just look at how Putin’s term limit was removed in 2021 and how anti-war parties were simply barred from running in this year’s elections.
Unlike democratic countries, autocrats do not remember acts of goodwill. They exploit them.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has spent 35 years steadily building democratic institutions and working with the US on a range of issues, particularly reforms and improvements to its legislation. There are hiccups, of course, but big changes come in small steps, and the Ukrainian people have kept marching in the streets, rallying against corruption, war or not.
Relations with Kyiv have always been a two-way street
Speaking to journalists on Monday, Trump claimed, among other things, that Ukraine had received a great deal from the US but had contributed little during the war.
Neither claim is true.
Ukraine received not simply cash from the US, but weapons and equipment, not “$350 billion,” as Trump claimed and debunked by Kyiv Post; it received only $66 billion, much of it drawn from old Cold War-era stockpiles that would otherwise have needed to be disposed of.
It’s also worth noting that restocking US arms means jobs at the factories making those weapons.
Beyond that, Ukraine has given the US two of the most valuable things in this war: real-world combat data on US weapons and air defense systems against a world power, and time to rearm and prepare for a major conflict that is now looming among the world’s powers.
The US can use these lessons, and it has gained this experience without losing a single soldier.
The Ukrainian military, with its invaluable combat experience in modern warfare, could also become a genuine pillar of European security and NATO’s eastern flank should the day come.
Ukraine today, US and Europe tomorrow
Russia’s ambitions extend beyond eastern Ukraine.
By Putin’s 2022 decree, Russia incorporated four Ukrainian regions into its constitution, including Kherson and Zaporizhzhia, which Russian forces do not fully control. If Russia were to achieve its objectives, it would become the dominant power in the Black Sea.
Russia has also openly called for a government change in Ukraine, with its advance on Kyiv in the spring of 2022 showing that it does not just seek to subjugate a part of Ukraine, but the entire country, either as part of Russia or as a puppet state.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has considerable industrial potential, a strong base of educated engineers, and a population with combat experience. If defeated and then used by Russia as a battering ram against its Western neighbors, Ukraine could become a threat to NATO.
Russia has also long portrayed NATO as an ideological enemy, calling not only for Ukraine’s membership ban but the alliance’s withdrawal from the entire eastern flank in its pre-2022 invasion ultimatum.
Without an eastern flank, the problem is no longer a Ukraine problem; it becomes a NATO problem, and, under the Article 5 mutual defense clause, also a US problem after Trump leaves office.
Ukraine is preventing that with the lives of its people, and NATO’s cost for helping Ukraine is nothing more than financial contributions and weapons drawn from its stockpiles.
With power comes responsibility
Turning its back on Ukraine – a victim of aggression – does not bode well for global trust in Washington.
Just as Americans once fought for independence from British rule, Ukraine is fighting to break free of Moscow’s sphere of influence, which plagued the country throughout the Russian Empire and the USSR.
These are not merely lofty words – the US is long seen as a bastion of democracy, and the success of US companies around the world stems not only from Washington’s economic and military power, but primarily from the perception of the US as a reliable partner.
Eroded trust is not easily restored, as recent examples show when the US, whether the White House or billionaire Elon Musk, flipped the switch on Ukrainian access to Starlink and Starshield during the latest row, with Europe now seeking alternatives worth billions in government contracts.
Betraying allies, refusing them support promised under previous commitments, and siding with autocrats and dictators undermines the most valuable form of capital the US possessed until recently: trust, and the expectation that its words are backed by the principles of freedom and solidarity with everyone fighting for that freedom.
It’s also worth noting the commitments made when Ukraine gained independence.
On Dec. 8, 1994, Ukraine, the US, the UK and Russia signed the Budapest Memorandum, under which Ukraine voluntarily gave up the world’s third-largest nuclear arsenal at the time in exchange for security assurances and guarantees respecting its borders from Britain, the US and Russia.
Ukraine was still invaded.

UN warns climate pledges leave world far off track for 1.5°C goal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:10:37 UTC
22:10:37 KST

Current climate pledges would cut global greenhouse gas emissions by only 11 percent to 15 percent by 2035, far short of the 45 percent reduction needed to help bring warming back below 1.5°C by the end of the century, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) warned Wednesday.
In its Emissions Gap Report 2026, UNEP said emissions must fall 18 percent by 2030, 45 percent by 2035 and 69 percent by 2040 from 2025 levels to limit peak warming to around 1.7°C-1.8°C before potentially returning to 1.5°C or below by 2100.
However, fully implementing countries' existing climate pledges would cut emissions by only 5 percent to 8 percent by 2030 and 11 percent to 15 percent by 2035.
The report found that current climate policies could lead to 2.8°C of global warming this century, while fulfilling all national climate commitments would limit warming to 2.6°C.
Even meeting additional net-zero targets alongside national climate commitments would limit warming to only 2.1°C, according to UNEP.
"Every additional fraction of a degree and additional year of warming above 1.5°C increases climate impacts and risks, such as the deadly floods, heatwaves and wildfires that have plagued many nations this year," UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen said in the report.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres stressed that exceeding the 1.5°C threshold does not mean abandoning efforts to reverse warming.
"Overshoot is not surrender. We can still keep it as small and as short as possible — and bring temperatures back below 1.°C degrees by the end of the century," he said.
The report also found that returning to 1.5°C would require removing and permanently storing approximately 320 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere this century, a task facing significant technological and economic challenges.
Despite the warnings, UNEP noted that renewable energy expansion and climate policies have already reduced emissions in several countries.
"It is now up to nations to urgently put in place policies that spark fast, deep and sustained emissions reductions, and put the world on track for a more stable climate and more stable economies and societies," Andersen said.
The report warned that without urgent action, keeping peak warming below 1.7-1.8°C "will quickly become impossible."

World falling ‘dangerously short’ on climate action, UN chief warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:09:58 UTC
22:09:58 KST

World falling ‘dangerously short’ on climate action, UN chief warns
- UN report says current climate pledges are far too weak, putting the world on track for 2.6 deg C warming by 2100 and missing the Paris goals.
- UN chief Antonio Guterres warned that 1.5 deg C is already out of reach, with record emissions causing floods, heatwaves, wildfires and rising inequality.
- The report says 2025 emissions stayed near record highs, with the US the biggest driver of increases, and calls for urgent cuts and 5,000 gigawatts more renewables.
AI generated
PARIS – Global commitments to cut planet-heating emissions are falling far short of the Paris climate goals and put the world on course for 2.6 deg C warming this century, the UN warned on Oct 21.
The report by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) lays bare the chasm between rhetoric and action when it comes to tackling global warming, and the challenge before political leaders at November’s COP31 climate summit.
Even if countries deliver their latest climate pledges in full, global temperatures could still rise 2.6 deg C above pre-industrial levels by 2100, said the annual Emissions Gap Report.
That would blow past the historic goal agreed in 2015 in Paris: keeping warming well below 2 deg C while striving for a safer 1.5 deg C. Any chance of keeping to 1.5 deg C has been “lost” due to decades of insufficient action, the report said.
“The world can no longer avoid overshooting the 1.5 degree limit, and the consequences are already devastating,” said UN chief Antonio Guterres in a statement to launch the closely watched report.
“Deadly floods, brutal heatwaves, raging wildfires, lost lives, crippled economies, deepening inequalities, and those least responsible are suffering first and worst,” he said.
Overall, global greenhouse gas emissions in 2025 were broadly on a par with record levels in 2024, with the difference between the two years too small to call, the report said.
Carbon emissions just from burning coal, oil and gas – the main driver of climate change – rose slightly in 2025 compared to the previous year.
Guterres said deep and immediate cuts were needed to protect humanity from worsening impacts, but instead “emissions remain at record levels, and national climate plans and current policies fall dangerously short”.
Sticking just with current policies would see warming hit 2.8 deg C by the end of the century, the report said.
No country immune
Scientists warn that every additional fraction of a degree above 1.5 deg C increases extreme weather events and the likelihood of irreversible changes to the planet, from dying coral reefs to melting permafrost.
The world has already warmed roughly 1.4 deg C relative to pre-industrial times, and crossing 1.5 deg C is expected in a matter of years.
This latest UNEP warming outlook is worse than in 2025 because of the formal withdrawal of the United States from the Paris accord and upward revisions of historical emissions, said report co-author Anne Olhoff.
Emissions growth slowed among the G-20, but the US was a “major exception”, it added.
The Group of 20 major economies (G-20) accounts for three-quarters of global emissions.
Among the world’s top six emitters, preliminary data for 2025 showed emissions increases in the US, Indonesia and China, and decreases in India, Russia and the European Union.
But the US increase of 133 megatonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent “far exceeded” that of any other country, driven by higher electricity demand and a rebound of coal power generation.
The next-largest increase was recorded in Turkey, which is hosting the UN climate summit in Antalya from Nov 9 to 20.
The US is the world’s second-largest polluter, behind China.
US President Donald Trump has called climate change a hoax and rolled back clean energy policies while boosting fossil fuel production.
UNEP executive secretary Inger Andersen said she would not put the blame “squarely on one nation”, saying every country, especially those in the G-20, has “a specific duty to find a way to phase down their carbon emissions”.
To limit the overshoot beyond 1.5 deg C, Andersen said the world has an “urgent to-do item”: adding another 5,000 gigawatts of renewable energy over the next five years.
‘Historic failure’
The report details a scenario with a 50% chance of bringing global warming back down to 1.5 deg C by 2100.
To get there, warming must peak around 1.8 deg C by 2050, and vast amounts of carbon dioxide would have to be removed from the atmosphere to bring temperatures down further.
But this scenario assumes immediate emissions cuts of 6% per year, every year, until 2035, nowhere near current projections.
Some climate-vulnerable developing nations have accused bigger emitters of abandoning the Paris goals, and a showdown over the 1.5 deg C target is expected at COP31.
“This is a historic failure of political leadership,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Kenya-based think tank Power Shift Africa.
“The science has been clear for decades, but governments have chosen delay over action,” Adow said. “The consequences will be measured in lives lost, not just degrees of warming.” AFP

Latvia ranks among top five importers of Russian grain this season as Moscow’s exports pivot toward Baltic ports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:09:02 UTC
22:09:02 KST

Latvia, a member of the European Union and NATO, has become one of the five largest importers of Russian grain in the current agricultural season despite strained political relations with Moscow, according to a Reuters report citing an agricultural consultancy firm.
The shift comes as Russia redirects grain exports from the Azov-Black Sea basin to ports in the Baltic Sea.
According to agricultural consultancy ProZerno, Latvia imported 431,700 metric tons of Russian grain from July through October.
Iran remained the largest buyer, importing 1.7 million metric tons, driven largely by major purchases of barley and corn. Egypt, once the biggest buyer of Russian wheat, remains one of the main destinations for Black Sea shipments, importing 1.35 million metric tons.
Azerbaijan, with 545,000 metric tons, and Nigeria, with 420,900 metric tons, also ranked among the five largest importers.
Russia has been restructuring its grain export routes since shipments through the Azov-Black Sea basin — its main export corridor — nearly came to a halt in mid-August.
Deepwater Baltic ports have since become the main route, particularly for wheat exports. According to calculations by rail freight operator Rusagrotrans, the Baltic accounted for 65% of Russian grain exports in September.
Cargo is being shipped both through Russian Baltic ports and through ports in the Baltic states, especially Latvia.
Shipments across the Caspian Sea have also risen sharply, with most of that grain bound for Iran.
Estonia, meanwhile, has banned the transit of Russian grain through its territory. In early October, the Baltic states proposed introducing a similar ban across the entire European Union.
At the same time, Latvia has been tightening its policies toward Russian citizens.
On Oct. 1, the Latvian parliament referred proposed amendments to its Legal Affairs Committee. The changes to Latvia’s citizenship law would impose a complete ban on holding Russian citizenship as a second nationality.
Dual Latvian-Russian citizenship is already effectively prohibited, but exceptions remain — with billionaire former Alfa-Bank head Petr Aven being the most notable among them. The amendments were drafted after Latvia’s Interior Ministry was unable to find a legal way to strip Aven of his Latvian citizenship.

Adoption of the UNESCO-endorsed Call by Young People for a New Culture of Peace UNESCO Statement On : October 20th 2026 France welcomes the endorsement today by the Executive Board of UNESCO of the Call by Young People for a New Culture of Peace in the Minds of Women and Men for the 21st Century. This summer, 145 young people from 135 countries proposed practical recommendations to UNESCO for strengthening its action and impact to build the defences of peace in the minds of men and women. On 3 September 2026, M. Jean-Noël Barrot, Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs, was officially handed the text by young people at UNESCO headquarters in Paris. Young people are asking to have some power of decision, with representation in decision-making, conflict-prevention and mediation mechanisms, and above all they are asking for a public follow-up of the recommendations and their implementation. It is not a traditional call for peace centred solely on war and armed conflict. The text considers that the new threats to peace are also played out in classrooms, social media, information, memory, science and now artificial intelligence. It explicitly links conflicts, polarization, disinformation, discrimination, the digital divide and technology. The Call is intended to feed into UNESCO’s strategic thinking, particularly the UNESCO80 Roadmap, whose goal is to reform the organization to make it more effective and agile. On 20 October, to respond to the Call, UNESCO’s Executive Board decided to launch a process towards issuing, in 2027, a Recommendation on youth and digital environments in the age of AI, in coordination with the Coalition for Children’s Rights and Protection in the Age of Artificial Intelligence. France will continue mobilizing States and international organizations to ensure that young people all over the world are listened to and fully take part in a more effective multilateralism.

Faheem Akram has been charged with several offences including conspiracy to defraud the United States.
Pakistani authorities have arrested a man accused of masterminding an online counterfeit operation that United States prosecutors say resulted in more than $125m of losses to the US Postal Service.
Faheem Akram, 33, was arrested on Tuesday after an expansive search operation and raids across Pakistan, a senior official at the Pakistani National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency told reporters.
Akram was indicted last month by a federal grand jury in the Southern District of Florida, and is accused of operating a fraudulent website where he sold more than 5.1 million counterfeit stamps in the US.
The stamps, which cost about $2 each, allowed customers to ship their packages at a lower price than official postal rates, causing significant losses to the Postal Service, according to the US Attorney’s office.
The estimate of more than $124m however, represents the losses to the Postal Service and not the proceeds from the website, officials said.
Pakistani investigators discovered that Akram has been operating the website since August 2023 and used 16 bank accounts, including his own and several family members’, for the operation.
Akram has been charged with several offences, including conspiracy to defraud the US and the making and selling of fake postage stamps, as well as four counts of wire fraud, according to the US Postal Service.
He could face 20 years in prison on each count of wire fraud, as well as five years in prison for conspiracy.
Akram is currently in custody in Pakistan, but it is unclear whether he will face trial in the country or be extradited to the US.

The net gun built for civilians in Ukraine’s kill zone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:04:10 UTC
22:04:10 KST

The net gun built for civilians in Ukraine’s kill zone
A soldier with the call sign Poliak from the National Guard's Omega unit holds an first-person-view drone caught in a net during a training exercise in an unnamed location, Ukraine, on Oct. 20, 2026. (Jakub Laichter/The Kyiv Independent)
At a training with the Ukrainian National Guard’s Omega unit, engineers from the defense tech company BlueBird Tech describe how to use their net gun, named Chipa, to entangle an approaching drone’s propellers.
The soldiers rehearse encounters with approaching first-person-view (FPV) drones, monitoring a handheld detector as they walk. Once they spot a drone, one soldier who goes by the callsign Poliak (Ukrainian for "Pole"), pulls the safety pin and takes aim with the net gun, while the others take cover in the bushes.
With a loud boom Poliak fires, and the net spreads through the air, catching the drone and tangling in its propellers.
Chipa was originally designed for civilians living in the expanding "kill zone" on the front lines where Russian soldiers target people shopping, civilian vehicles, and even ambulances in what has become known as a "human safari."
As the danger spreads into roads and neighborhoods behind the front, the appearance of the net gun shows just how the threats usually associated with battlefields are becoming a part of everyday civilian life in Ukraine.
"FPV drones now threaten everyone in the front line areas," says Eduard, an engineer from BlueBird Tech who asked to be identified by first name only for security reasons.
"The enemy does not distinguish between civilians and soldiers now," Poliak says.
While a drone detector can give civilians warning and time to seek cover, the net gun is intended for the moment when the drone is already close. Each launcher costs around Hr 3,000 (around $67) and can be fired only once, according to Eduard.
It was important for them that Chipa was classified as a non-firearm, which allows civilians to buy it without a firearms permit, he said.
The soldiers from the Omega unit are leaving for the front line the next day. Poliak has been fighting since 2015 and describes how the pace of change on Ukraine’s battlefields had accelerated in recent years. The dangerous part of any mission comes mostly from moving between positions.
"When you have to move out in the open, the enemy can see you from drones," he says.
In combat, Poliak’s unit carries the net guns alongside shotguns. At longer distances, he prefers the shotgun, he says. Close in, he said, the net’s wider coverage offered a better chance of stopping a drone. Eduard put its most effective range at 10 to 20 meters, depending on wind, and the drone speed.
But there is little room for error, because a drone caught in a net can still explode. Poliak said some intercepted drones had detonated, putting nearby soldiers at risk from the blast and shrapnel. A drone exploding a few meters away instead of hitting someone directly can still mean the difference between life and death.
Asked about the danger from a drone’s explosive payload, Poliak’s answer was simple: "The farther away, the better."

Too much RNA can starve cells of energy, scientists discover
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:02:34 UTC
22:02:34 KST

Too much RNA can starve cells of energy, scientists discover
- Date:
- October 21, 2026
- Source:
- Texas A&M University
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered an unexpected danger lurking inside cells: too much RNA can damage the structures responsible for producing energy. A new study found that excess RNA, including the normally essential messenger RNA (mRNA), can directly disrupt mitochondria without relying on the immune system. The discovery could help explain how viral infections and certain aging-related diseases damage cells.
- Share:
Scientists have uncovered a surprising way that viruses can interfere with the body's cells. When too much RNA accumulates inside a cell, it can damage the structures that produce energy, potentially leaving the cell struggling to function normally.
A new study led by researchers at the Texas A&M College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences (VMBS) found that excess RNA produced during poxvirus infections can impair mitochondria, the tiny structures responsible for generating most of the energy cells need to survive.
Published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the research reveals an unexpected connection between RNA buildup and cellular energy production. The findings could have implications far beyond viral infections, potentially helping scientists better understand aging-related diseases and improve RNA-based medical treatments, including mRNA vaccines.
"Scientists have long known that RNA degradation helps control protein production and remove defective RNA," said Dr. Zhilong Yang, a professor in VMBS' Department of Veterinary Pathobiology. "Our study reveals another important role: it helps cells maintain the energy they need to function properly."
Cells constantly produce and break down RNA as part of their normal activities. This cleanup process, known as RNA degradation, helps regulate protein production, eliminate faulty RNA, and control immune responses. The new findings suggest it also performs another essential function by protecting the cell's energy supply.
Why Too Much RNA Can Damage Cells
RNA plays several important roles in keeping cells functioning. Messenger RNA (mRNA), for example, carries genetic instructions that tell cells which proteins to produce. These proteins are needed for nearly everything cells do, from maintaining their structure to carrying out essential chemical reactions.
Another type, double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), frequently appears during viral infections. Its presence can serve as a warning signal, alerting the immune system that a virus may have entered the cell.
Viruses often generate large quantities of RNA as they reproduce inside infected cells. Ordinarily, cellular cleanup systems help prevent RNA from accumulating to harmful levels. However, when RNA production exceeds the cell's ability to break it down, the excess material can interfere with mitochondria and reduce energy production.
Scientists already understood that excessive double-stranded RNA could provoke potentially harmful immune responses. What surprised the researchers was discovering that too much ordinary messenger RNA could also damage mitochondria.
"MRNA is a normal component of our cells, but it seems like with many good things, if we get too much, that can become a problem for the cell," Yang said. "When too much RNA builds up, including mRNA, it can damage the mitochondria and interfere with the cell's ability to produce energy."
This creates an unusual challenge for viruses. Although viruses depend entirely on the cells they infect to supply energy and manufacture proteins, producing excessive amounts of viral RNA can damage the very machinery they need to reproduce.
According to Yang, poxviruses, a group that includes the viruses responsible for smallpox and mpox, appear to have ways of managing this problem. They use RNA cleanup mechanisms to remove excess RNA, helping infected cells remain functional long enough for viral replication to continue.
"If the cell is not healthy, the virus would not replicate well," Yang said. "The virus needs to keep RNA levels balanced inside the cell."
Scientists Discover RNA Can Directly Damage Mitochondria
One of the study's most unexpected findings emerged when researchers investigated exactly how excess RNA affects mitochondria.
Initially, the team suspected that RNA buildup was damaging these cellular powerhouses indirectly by activating the immune system. Certain types of RNA are known to trigger defensive responses, which can place additional stress on infected cells.
However, experiments revealed that the damage did not require an immune response.
"When we isolated only the mitochondria and added RNA, we still saw mitochondrial damage," said Dr. Djamal Brahim Belhaouari, the study's first author. "That was the moment we realized this could be a previously unknown cellular response to RNA."
The researchers also observed that mitochondrial problems developed before substantial immune activation occurred. Furthermore, the damage did not depend on the immune pathways normally activated during infection.
Together, these results indicate that excess RNA itself can interfere with mitochondrial function, rather than simply causing damage through the body's response to a virus.
The precise mechanism remains unclear, but the researchers have proposed a possible explanation involving electrical charges.
Mitochondria produce energy by maintaining an electrical and chemical difference across their inner membranes. This difference helps drive the production of ATP, the molecule cells use as their primary energy source.
RNA carries a negative electrical charge. The researchers suspect that when unusually large amounts accumulate near mitochondria, they may disturb the electrical conditions required for efficient energy production.
"We think the negatively charged RNA may accumulate around mitochondria and disrupt the electrical balance needed for energy production, although how it happens is unknown," Yang said. "This is a new concept that we are continuing to explore."
What the Discovery Could Mean for Aging and Disease
Although the experiments focused on viral infections, the findings raise questions about whether RNA buildup might contribute to other health problems.
Abnormal RNA accumulation has been observed in several conditions, including certain cancers, neurodegenerative diseases, and disorders associated with aging. Neurodegenerative diseases involve the progressive deterioration of nerve cells, as occurs in conditions such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease.
Because mitochondria are essential for maintaining healthy cells, disruptions to their energy production could potentially contribute to cellular dysfunction in some of these conditions.
The researchers suggest that excess RNA may represent one previously unrecognized source of mitochondrial stress. However, further studies are needed to determine how broadly this mechanism operates and whether it directly contributes to these diseases.
"We think this has quite broad translational implications," Brahim Belhaouari said. "Too much double-stranded RNA or mRNA that cannot be degraded effectively may contribute to disease processes in some contexts."
Potential Implications for mRNA Vaccines and Future Treatments
The discovery could also provide useful information for scientists developing medicines that rely on RNA.
RNA-based therapies, including mRNA vaccines, work by introducing RNA instructions into cells to produce specific proteins. Understanding how cells respond to RNA, process it, and eventually break it down is important for designing these treatments.
By identifying another way excessive RNA can affect cellular health, the findings may help researchers optimize future RNA-based therapies and vaccines. The study does not establish that existing mRNA vaccines cause mitochondrial damage in people.
"Understanding this mechanism could help researchers design and optimize future RNA-based therapeutics and vaccines by better understanding how cells respond to large amounts of RNA," Yang said.
More broadly, the research suggests that controlling RNA levels is important for more than maintaining accurate protein production or managing immune activity. It may also be essential for keeping mitochondria functioning and ensuring cells have enough energy.
For the scientists, the most striking result was that even a molecule cells depend on every day can become harmful when it accumulates beyond normal levels.
"Scientists already knew that too much double-stranded RNA can be harmful," Yang said. "What surprised us was finding out that too much mRNA -- something cells normally need every day -- can also damage mitochondria and interfere with the cell's ability to produce energy."
Research reported in this study was supported, in part, by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (R01AI143709 to Z.Y.) and Texas A&M University. The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official views of the NIH.

Perturbation of RNA homeostasis impairs mitochondrial respiration during poxvirus infection through excess RNA accumulation. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2026; 123 (22) DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2605194123

Libya’s maritime deal with Türkiye angers EU states
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21

22:01:36 KST

Libya’s maritime deal with Türkiye angers EU states
Libya’s eastern-based parliament has approved a disputed maritime agreement with Türkiye, drawing condemnation from Greece and Cyprus over competing boundaries and energy rights in the Mediterranean.
The House of Representatives voted unanimously on Tuesday to endorse the agreement, which was first signed in November 2019 between Ankara and Libya’s internationally recognized government in Tripoli. Lawmakers also overturned a 2020 decision to sever political ties with Türkiye.
The agreement demarcates maritime jurisdiction between the two countries in an area contested by Greece, Egypt, and Cyprus.
The Greek Foreign Ministry called the parliamentary decision “unilateral [and] legally unfounded,” saying the deal disregards Greek islands’ rights to maritime zones between the Turkish and Libyan coasts.
“The memorandum remains illegal, null and void, contravenes international law of the sea, and infringes upon the sovereign rights of states in the region,” the ministry said in a statement.
It argued that Türkiye and Libya lack opposite or adjacent coastlines providing a lawful basis for the boundary, warning that Greece would take action to defend its sovereign rights. Cyprus also condemned the decision, calling the memorandum “illegal, null and void.”
Ankara welcomed the vote, saying the agreement safeguards “the mutual rights and interests” of both countries under international law and the principle of equity, while deepening cooperation between Türkiye and Libya. “Türkiye will continue to work with all partners to foster trust, stability and peace in the Mediterranean basin, in line with its commitment to international law,” the Foreign Ministry stated.
The eastern Mediterranean has seen a wave of offshore gas discoveries since 2009, opening new export opportunities while intensifying disputes over maritime boundaries and drilling rights. Major finds off Israel, Cyprus, and Egypt have attracted international energy companies, including Chevron and Eni, to the region, according to a US Energy Information Administration report.
Greece and Egypt signed an overlapping maritime agreement in 2020, which Türkiye rejects. Athens also approved offshore exploration south of Crete by a consortium led by Chevron last year, prompting Turkish objections.
The move on Tuesday comes amid improving ties between Türkiye and Libya’s eastern authorities, who are aligned with military commander Khalifa Haftar. Ankara helped Tripoli repel his forces’ 2019-2020 campaign to capture the capital, but has since expanded diplomatic contacts and investment in the east. The country remains divided between Abdul Hamid Dbeibah’s government in the capital, Tripoli, in western Libya, and an eastern administration led by Osama Hammad and backed by Haftar.
Officials from both rival administrations welcomed the parliamentary approval. The Tripoli-based Foreign Ministry called it a “positive development toward strengthening bilateral relations” with Türkiye. Haftar’s son Saddam, the deputy commander of the Libyan National Army, called it a move toward overcoming past differences, putting Libya’s national interests first.

House prices across capitals post steepest quarterly decline ever: Domain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:01:00 UTC
22:01:00 KST

House values drop in all capital cities for first time in 15 years, Domain says
In short:
House prices have fallen across every capital city for the first time in 15 years, Domain reports.
Data shows Australia's most expensive homes have recorded the biggest drops this year, while lower-value homes have remained largely stable.
Experts say rising interest rates and lower market confidence are driving the downturn.
House prices have fallen 4.7 per cent, the steepest quarterly drop on record, according to new data from Domain.
Prices dropped in every capital city in the September quarter, the first time in 15 years and only the second time on record.
The real estate platform's data showed the sharpest decline was in Perth, where prices dropped 7.4 per cent.
Combined capital city house prices fell to $1,226,566. Domain said markets that started the year in very different positions "are now moving in the same direction".
Australia's biggest property markets, Sydney and Melbourne, recorded their largest quarterly house price drop in four years, falling 4.7 per cent and 3.3 per cent, respectively.
Unit prices also fell 3.5 per cent, marking the second consecutive quarter both property types declined.
It marked a clear shift in the housing cycle, according to Nicola Powell, Domain's chief residential economist.
"What began as weakness concentrated in some cities has broadened considerably," Dr Powell said.
"The balance of power has shifted towards buyers.
"Homes are taking longer to sell, there is greater scope to negotiate, and sellers are having to be more realistic about price expectations."
The cumulative impact of rising rates, lower affordability, and cost-of-living pressures has reduced demand, according to Gerard Burg of data firm Cotality.
"It's been a demand-led downturn," Mr Burg said.
Australia's most valuable homes falling the most
While all major markets across the country have joined the downturn, prices have not been dropping equally within cities.
Australia's most valuable homes are dropping the most, while lower value homes were relatively stable in three months to September, according to property data firm Cotality.
In Sydney, the most valuable quartile of homes dropped more than twice as much as the least valuable quartile.
Nationwide, lower-value homes have seen a much slower price drop, Cotality said.
Prices grew in Darwin's lowest value quartile.
The sharper downturn in more expensive properties reflects fewer buyers and higher borrowing costs, according to property economist Cameron Kusher.
"They've typically seen larger increases in values over recent years and when you see that market slowdown, there's overall fewer buyers for those properties," he said.
However, he said the ultra-top end of the market had remained largely stable.
Mr Burg agreed, saying lower-priced homes remained affordable to more buyers.
"The median house really appears kind of out of reach of the median income household across much of the country," he said.
Prices were falling before federal budget
The federal budget was a factor, but not the only factor, in house price falls, according to Mr Kusher.
House prices peaked last year and had already begun to drop before the changes to investment taxes in May's federal budget, Mr Kusher and Mr Burg both noted.
Mr Burg said prices were already falling in many capital cities, and three consecutive interest rate hikes had dampened market confidence.
Auction activity, a common gauge of market confidence, has roughly halved from last year, with 1,423 auctions across capital cities last week, according to Cotality.
"Confidence has really evaporated. Affordability is very stretched and borrowing capacity is reduced dramatically," Mr Kusher said.
"People just aren't in a position or able to pay the prices that a lot of these properties are worth at the moment."
He said home ownership rates had not moved much since the May budget changes, due to lower buyer confidence and stretched affordability.
"The first time is pretty scary as it is, and I think a lot of them are looking at it and saying, 'Well, prices are falling, why would I jump in now when there's quite a lot for sale, if I wait another six or 12 months properties will probably be cheaper,'" he said.
"I just don't think first home buyers have that urgency anymore."
He said prices would be unlikely to return to their previous heights, at least not in the short term.
"I think this downturn is probably going to drag on a bit longer than people expect, and it probably will until it looks like interest rates are going to actually be reduced again," he said.

E-scooter hospitalisations more than tripled since 2019
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:01:00 UTC
22:01:00 KST

E-scooter and e-bike hospitalisations on the rise in Australia, report finds
In short:
A report from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) has found e-scooter hospitalisations have more than tripled since 2019.
There were 4,089 hospitalisations involving e-scooter in the 2024-25 compared to 1,291 in 2019-20.
Two-thirds of those hospitalised in 2024-25 were male with largest increase in young boys aged between 12 and 15.
Teenage boys riding e-scooters drove a sharp rise in hospitalisations over the last five years, according to a report from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW).
The number of boys aged 12 to 15 hospitalised following e-scooter falls saw a 15-fold increase between 2019/20 and 2024/25.
Boys in that cohort were four times more likely than girls to end up in hospital because of an e-scooter fall.
It also found hospitalisation rates increased for e-bike riders, but these data were harder to capture because of how these injuries were classified.
The report found e-scooter-related deaths increased over the last decade from seven in 2014/15 to 20 in 2024/25; however, the proportion of deaths was stable.
New codes introduced in July this year will help better differentiate between e-mobility devices such as e-scooters and e-bikes, the report said.
AIHW spokesperson Jacqueline Rek said the improved data will help better understand the risks surrounding e-mobility devices.
"Meaning these findings should not be interpreted as precise counts of injuries involving e-scooters or e-bikes alone," Ms Rek said.
"This report provides the first national view on this topic, while also highlighting where more data is needed."
What can improve safety?
E-bikes and e-scooters are now mainstream, with almost 1 million privately owned by Queenslanders, according to University of Queensland research.
Richard J Buning, who worked on the research, said improving safety was crucial given the growth.
"Every single year over the last five years, the growth in e-mobility device purchases has risen by 30 per cent," he said.
Dr Buning said unsafe devices such as over-powered e-bikes were among his chief concerns.
Last year, the federal government introduced stronger e-bike import standards similar to those in the European Union (EU), limiting access to unsafe devices.
"It's these unsafe, uncompliant, illegal devices that are creating much of the problems of people riding really fast on high-powered devices," Dr Buning said.
"But the safe, compliant devices, they don't provide more power than just a normal typical average fit person can provide."
Dr Buning highlighted Queensland as one jurisdiction in the country leading e-mobility device regulation.
People riding e-bikes in the state must be 16 or older and hold a valid driver's licence, including a learner licence.
Children aged between 12 and 17 (where 16- and 17-year-olds do not hold a driver's licence) will only be able to ride an e-bike or e-scooter with parental supervision.
Dr Buning disagreed with licensing e-bikes but praised the state's e-bike assurance scheme, which followed EU regulations.
It will mean from March 2027, all e-bikes in the state must have a compliance label to ride in public.
"So stopping those things from being sold and making sure that the public knows if they buy one of these devices that are uncompliant, they cannot legally ride it on the road," he said.
Dr Buning also suggested more targeted initiatives to better educate those who are riding unsafely, which was mostly younger people.
"Ideally we can get into schools and teach them how to ride a device safely. That's probably going to take out the majority of the problematic behaviour,"
he said.
"Because the vast majority of people that use e-bikes are actually much older, 70 per cent of e-mobility device users are over the age of 40.
"That highly visible behaviour may be obscuring public perception of an overall quite inclusive and sustainable transport mode."

Older adults tell the story of their lives differently, and it may not be a sign of decline, new psychology study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:00:44 UTC
22:00:44 KST

A new study published in Psychology and Aging indicates that having to switch between recalling different types of personal memories makes it harder for both young and older adults to follow instructions accurately. Beyond the mental effort of juggling changing rules, the findings suggest that older adults tend to include more general personal facts and fewer specific details than younger adults, whether they are recalling a one-time event or a recurring routine.
Autobiographical memory is the mental system that allows people to recollect their own life history. It encompasses two main kinds of information: episodic memory and personal semantic memory. Episodic memories are rich recollections of unique events tied to a specific time and place, such as a particular birthday dinner last month. Personal semantic memories are broader facts about one’s life that are not tied to a single episode, such as general self-knowledge. Falling between the two are memories of repeated events, like a weekly habit of cooking with a friend, which summarize many similar occasions while still carrying some sensory and contextual detail.
As people age, the balance between these forms of recall tends to change. A benchmark 2002 study of younger and older adults found that when asked to describe past life events, younger adults mostly shared specific details about what happened, where they were, and how they felt, whereas older adults shared fewer time-and-place details and favored general, factual knowledge.
“A typical example would be that if a young adult is telling you about their last birthday party, they are more likely to include specific contextual and perceptual details (such as the specific time and place, what clothes people wore at that party, or specific details about what they said),” senior author Louis Renoult, a professor of cognitive neuroscience and the postgraduate research director in the School of Psychology at the University of East Anglia, told PsyPost. “In contrast, when remembering the same event, older adults would typically provide more factual background knowledge about similar birthday parties or other celebrations they would have attended, or more general knowledge they have about the people involved, for example.”
This pattern raised questions about whether the shift toward general memories comes from changes in how memories are stored or from age-related declines in executive control, which is the set of mental skills used to manage goals, stay focused, and filter out irrelevant thoughts. A 2013 study explored this by changing how instructions were given while participants listened to musical clips, finding that younger adults adjusted how specific their memories were to match the rules, while older adults did not adjust their recall as much when task demands grew more complex.
To test how mental flexibility affects memory recall, another 2013 study of university students introduced a test requiring participants to rapidly alternate between recalling unique, one-time events and repeated routines. The students were less accurate at providing specific memories when they had to switch back and forth compared to when they followed a single rule at a time.
“In the field, people generally assume that the greater reliance on factual knowledge (and semantic memory) in aging would constitute a compensation, due to a less efficient episodic memory,” explained Renoult, who also recently discussed memory and aging on a podcast episode. “However, tests commonly used to assess semantic and episodic memory are rarely well matched in difficulty, and most tests of autobiographical memory focus on episodic memory only. Due to these issues, my research group has developed new memory tests to study semantic and episodic memory in parallel, in conditions where they are well matched experimentally to better understand memory changes as we get older.”
To examine whether mental switching places an extra burden on older adults during memory recall and how it interacts with the broader shift toward factual details, Renoult and his colleagues carried out the new study. The work was led by Greta Melega while she was completing her doctorate at the University of East Anglia; she is now a postdoctoral researcher at Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin (“and also an elite European Ultimate Frisbee player (!),” Renoult noted).
The researchers recruited 45 younger adults and 45 older adults, all of whom were native English speakers without psychiatric or neurological conditions. After excluding participants who did not finish the study, had poor audio recordings, fell below a cognitive screening threshold, or did not pass an initial training check, the final sample included 37 older adults aged 60 to 85 and 37 younger adults aged 18 to 33.
The two age groups had similar levels of education and did not differ in self-reported symptoms of depression or anxiety, which the authors measured because mood can influence how specifically people recall the past. A subset of 30 younger and 30 older participants also completed standard tests of attention and working memory, showing no statistically significant differences between the age groups.
Participants completed an online memory task where they saw 21 neutral, easy-to-visualize cue words on a screen, one at a time. Depending on the prompt, they had up to one minute to think of either a specific memory (a unique event lasting less than a day, such as having “a good time at Jane’s party last month in London”) or a categoric memory (a repeated event that happened multiple times in a similar way, such as “When I go to Jane’s house, we usually cook together and watch a movie afterwards”).
Once a memory came to mind, they pressed a button and spoke aloud for up to two minutes to describe it in as much detail as possible. After each description, participants had five seconds per question to rate how vivid and emotional the memory was, whether they saw it through their own eyes or as an outside observer, and how long ago it took place.
The experiment was divided into two parts: a baseline block and a switching block. In the baseline block, participants followed one instruction at a time, recalling three specific memories in a row and three categoric memories in a row. In the 14-trial switching block, the instructions to recall specific or categoric memories changed unpredictably every two or three trials. This allowed the scientists to compare “switch trials,” where the rule had just changed from the previous prompt, with “remain trials,” where the rule stayed the same as the prompt right before it.
The research team evaluated the recorded narratives in two ways. First, they measured accuracy, defined as the percentage of memories that matched the prompt given on that trial. Second, for the memories that matched the instructions, the researchers broke the transcripts down to count the exact types of details produced: episodic details (specific sights, times, and feelings of a one-time event), repeated event details (context and sensory details of a recurring routine), semantic details (general facts and personal background knowledge), and other statements like repetitions. Because older adults spoke longer on average than younger adults (about 45 seconds versus 27 seconds) and produced more total details per memory (an average of 11.00 details compared to 7.41), the authors analyzed the proportion of each detail type rather than raw counts.
When looking at overall accuracy, both younger and older participants had a harder time following instructions when they had to juggle both rules in the switching block, dropping from 82 percent accuracy in the baseline block to 73 percent in the switching block. Within the switching block itself, accuracy did not differ between switch trials and remain trials, suggesting that the mental cost came from keeping two different rules in mind at once rather than the immediate act of switching from one trial to the next.
Older adults were not disproportionately harmed by the switching block compared to younger adults. Across the experiment, the two age groups were equally accurate when asked to recall specific, one-time events, with older adults succeeding on 81 percent of trials and younger adults on 80 percent. However, older adults were less accurate than younger adults when instructed to recall categoric, repeated events, matching the instructions 68 percent of the time compared to 81 percent for younger adults. When participants failed to provide a proper categoric memory, they most often defaulted to sharing general personal facts instead of an actual recurring event.
When the researchers examined how participants elaborated on their accurate memories, strong age differences appeared regardless of whether participants were in the baseline or switching block. Even when older adults successfully recalled a unique, one-time event, only 66 percent of the details they shared were specific episodic details, compared to 79 percent for younger adults. In turn, general semantic facts made up 18 percent of older adults’ descriptions of unique events, compared to 13 percent for younger adults.
A similar pattern emerged for categoric memories: older adults included a smaller proportion of on-target repeated event details than younger adults (48 percent versus 72 percent) and a much larger proportion of general semantic information across both blocks (40 to 42 percent for older adults, versus 15 to 24 percent for younger adults).
“As observed previously, older adults consistently produced more semantic (factual) details but less episodic (specific) elements than young adults,” Renoult said. “However, crucially, this was not only observed under specific (episodic) instructions, but also under categoric (semantic) instructions. This suggests that remembering the past using more factual knowledge is adaptive and meaningful to older adults, and not necessarily the result of a compensation, or of a general decline in their memory abilities.”
The study itself did not test what purpose, if any, this narrative style serves.
Increased task demands in the switching block also altered the makeup of memory details. Under categoric instructions, moving to the switching block reduced the proportion of target repeated event details from 67 percent to 54 percent across participants. The paper reports a similar shift under specific instructions, but its figures for that comparison duplicate those given elsewhere, so the size of that effect is uncertain.
The subjective ratings highlighted additional differences in how the two age groups experienced their memories. Even though older adults included proportionally fewer specific details in their stories, they rated their specific memories as more vivid than younger adults did (an average of 3.81 versus 3.53 on a 5-point scale) and rated their memories overall as more emotional (2.92 versus 2.46). Regarding the age of the memories, younger adults mostly drew from the past five years, especially the past year, whereas older adults recalled memories from more than 10 years ago on 39 percent of specific trials and 48 percent of categoric trials, compared to just 15 percent and 7 percent for younger adults.
“It is important to realize that, even though young and older adults remember their past differently (with different narrative style), in these studies participants of both age groups are able to follow the overall instructions and retrieve the relevant type of information in most trials (i.e., they produce the correct type of memory, even if with different amount of details),” Renoult noted. “Nonetheless, the results that we report in this study are consistent with previous findings from our group using different methods.”
Renoult also emphasized that differences in how older adults recount their past should not be mistaken for a broad loss of memory function. “Sometimes people have gloomy views of aging, but not all types of memory decline when we get older, as shown in studies such as ours: Semantic memory (general knowledge of the world) is well preserved in older adults (who sometimes outperform young adults in these tasks).”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. The study’s design and analysis plan were not preregistered. Because the baseline block was always completed before the switching block so participants could learn the rules, fatigue or the possibility that the easiest memories were used up first could have contributed to the drop in performance during the switching phase. The number of trials was also kept relatively small to prevent tiredness during online testing, which meant the authors could not separately test whether switching rules hurt one memory type more than the other.
In addition, the older adults in this sample performed just as well as the younger undergraduate students on standard cognitive tests of working memory and attention. Because executive control often declines with age, this high-performing group of older adults might not reflect the broader aging population, which could explain why they had no trouble finding specific memories when prompted. The participants were also predominantly female, and they were allowed to choose memories from any point in their lives; future studies could restrict recall to specific time periods and use standardized follow-up prompts to see if older adults can retrieve more specific sensory details when encouraged to do so.
Looking ahead, the research team plans to explore how the social context of a conversation shapes the way people recount their lives. “We are interested to investigate social elements that may influence memory retrieval in aging, such as with whom one is sharing their memories,” Renoult said. “One related bias in the literature is that older adults are typically interviewed by a young adult (e.g., a PhD student, or a research assistant). It is possible that, in such cases, older adults include more general knowledge to provide additional background information for someone of a different age group.”
The study, “Age-Related Differences in Autobiographical Memory Recall: Impact of Retrieval Mode Switching,” was authored by Greta Melega, Alice Bush, Tabitha James, Riccardo Sacripante, and Louis Renoult.

North Korea will deploy loudspeakers along the border for "psychological warfare" against South Korea
Kyiv • UNN
Kim Yo Jong announced the deployment of loudspeakers for propaganda along the border with South Korea by the end of October. Tensions are rising.
Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of North Korea’s leader, said on Wednesday that by the end of October, the DPRK would deploy loudspeakers for anti-South Korean propaganda along the entire border. The move will lead to a further escalation of tensions along the heavily fortified border, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
The publication notes that this development threatens one of the achievements of which the South Korean president’s administration was most proud. It concerns the suspension of South Korean broadcasts and the dismantling of fixed loudspeakers, carried out last year.
In a sharply worded statement released by the state news agency KCNA after visiting the border area, Kim said that North Korean tactical units were taking up new positions. She called the deployment of loudspeakers along the entire border “the most legitimate measure and an adequate response” to South Korea’s actions.
“Our tactical groups are taking up new positions, and during October, loudspeakers for psychological warfare against the Republic of Korea will operate along the entire border,” she said, using South Korea’s official name.
According to her, on Wednesday morning she and Marshal of the North Korean Army Pak Jong Chon visited several sections of the border and confirmed that the border area was completely blocked off and being actively fortified.
Kim accused the South Korean military of using loudspeakers to issue warnings in at least two locations on Wednesday, as well as firing warning shots. She noted that North Korean troops were currently showing restraint while carefully preparing for any possible development.
“If the enemy’s provocative warning fire goes beyond its stated purpose and causes real harm to the security of our territory or our soldiers, our border troops will mercilessly destroy the armed bandits who have lost their minds,” she said.
The statement came a day after Seoul promised to “resolutely” punish Pyongyang for any further provocations if the DPRK moved to implement its threats to strengthen its military presence along the border.
According to KCNA, Kim said that new fire units had already “taken up their combat positions” along the border. The military leader called for turning the border into an “impregnable fortress.”
Additionally
Tensions between North and South Korea have risen since Pyongyang began fortifying its border in April 2024. The two countries are separated by a demilitarized zone established after the end of the Korean War, when an armistice agreement was signed in 1953.
According to Seoul, this year Pyongyang sent up to 7,000 workers to the border; around 50 instances were recorded in which they crossed the Military Demarcation Line — the boundary running through the middle of the demilitarized zone — toward South Korea.

This country aims to attract €18B in cleaner energy investment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:00:17 UTC
22:00:17 KST

Kazakhstan aims to mobilise €18 billion in investment in cleaner energy through its just energy transition platform, QaJET, with support from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD).
The initiative targets renewable power and grid upgrades while addressing the impact on workers and coal-dependent communities.
Fossil fuels still supply around 85% of Kazakhstan’s electricity, according to LowCarbonPower. The country wants to expand renewable power, but that will also require upgrades to its electricity networks and support for workers in regions that depend on coal.
To help finance that shift, Kazakhstan aims to attract $20bn (€17.4bn) through QaJET, its just energy transition platform. Backed by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), the initiative brings together public and private investment.
The platform is already operational and is due to be officially launched at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, in November.
It supports Kazakhstan’s goal of carbon neutrality by 2060 and its commitment to cut net greenhouse gas emissions by up to 25% by 2030 compared with 1990 levels, subject to international support.
Kazakhstan’s Just Energy Transition platform QaJET
According to the platform’s investment breakdown, around half of the funding, approximately €8.7bn, is intended to support 10 GW of new renewable energy capacity by 2035.
A further quarter, around €4.35bn, is earmarked for integrating renewables into the power system and improving its reliability. The remaining quarter will support electrification in transport, industry and small and medium-sized enterprises, alongside upgrades to electricity networks and smart energy systems.
The platform is expected to reduce annual greenhouse gas emissions by more than 20 million tonnes, equivalent to around 7% of Kazakhstan’s energy-related emissions.
Projects already in the pipeline
QaJET already includes projects worth more than €1bn, including a major wind farm in the Zhambyl region and an electricity infrastructure upgrade in Almaty.
The Mirny wind farm, scheduled to enter operation in 2028, will have a capacity of 1 GW and include 150 turbines, alongside a battery energy storage system with a capacity of 600 MWh.
The project, developed by TotalEnergies and its Kazakh partners, is expected to generate around 4 TWh of renewable electricity annually. Its output will be sold to Kazakhstan’s state-owned Financial Settlement Centre for Renewable Energy under a 25-year agreement.
The project is expected to avoid up to 3.5 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions a year.
The second project focuses on modernising electricity distribution infrastructure in Almaty and the surrounding region. The EBRD is providing a loan of up to 102 bn tenge (€194m) to Alatau Zharyk Company, which serves around 50,000 commercial customers in Almaty and the surrounding region.
The funding will help the company install automated metering and remote-control equipment and upgrade its low- and medium-voltage distribution networks.
Investment opportunities
Beyond the projects already in the pipeline, Kazakhstan faces the challenge of modernising its existing energy infrastructure and preparing workers for the transition.
“We are a carbon-dependent country, with large combined heat and power plants and power stations. These facilities and the energy networks need to be modernised. Workers in the energy sector also need to be retrained as part of the energy transition,” said Saule Sabieva, Climate Policy Director at the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources.
The government is seeking support from international partners, including the European Union, the United Kingdom, the Green Climate Fund, the Global Environment Facility and the Climate Investment Funds.
Ensuring a just energy transition
Moving away from coal also presents social and economic challenges, particularly in regions where employment and local economies depend heavily on conventional energy production.
Before major changes are made, QaJET’s partners are expected to assess the regions most exposed to the risks of decarbonisation and identify ways to ensure people have access to new economic opportunities.
“We are expecting these findings. After that, we will be able to assess our major infrastructure projects and calculate their costs for inclusion in the project portfolio,” Sabieva said.
She identified Karaganda, North Kazakhstan and East Kazakhstan regions as likely to face some of the greatest challenges.
More broadly, she said, the difficulties would affect regions where electricity is generated by large combined heat and power plants and major power stations.
Attracting renewable energy investment
The EBRD says Kazakhstan has many of the prerequisites for expanding renewable energy, including strong natural resources and a government seeking to improve the regulatory environment.
“Kazakhstan is blessed with the natural resources needed for renewable energy projects,” said Yerlan Ramazanov, the EBRD’s Deputy Head of Kazakhstan and Regional Head of Energy.
He pointed to regulatory changes, competitive auctions and long-term power purchase agreements as factors helping to attract investors.
These agreements provide greater predictability for developers and help lenders assess the risks associated with renewable energy projects.
Referring to the electricity buyer, Ramazanov said, “Over 11 years of experience, I would say that the agreements are being honoured and the off-taker is paying in full and on time.”
Renewable energy auction tariffs have also fallen since the system was introduced in 2018. Kazakhstan is developing domestic expertise, with local companies increasingly involved in building and operating renewable energy projects.
Remaining barriers
Despite progress, several obstacles remain. Ramazanov highlighted limitations in grid capacity and stability, as well as the challenge of balancing electricity supply as more renewable energy comes online.
The EBRD is already working with officials to develop the regulatory framework for battery storage and pumped-storage projects.
For investors, stable rules and a clear long-term outlook are essential. QaJET’s target of adding 10 GW of renewable energy capacity by 2035 could help provide that direction, setting out the scale of Kazakhstan’s ambitions.
With its renewable energy ambitions, growing project pipeline under QaJET and support from the EBRD, Kazakhstan is working to create new opportunities for investors to build a cleaner, more resilient energy system.

United Kingdom

The Jet Training System programme is ongoing and no final procurement decisions have been made, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what comparative assessment the Secretary of State has made of the effectiveness of the Collins Aerospace ACES 5 ejection seat fitted to the Boeing T-7A Red Hawk against the Martin-Baker seats used across the rest of the RAF fleet.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “The Jet Training System programme is ongoing and no final procurement decisions have been made.”
The Jet Training System will replace the Hawk T2 that trains fast jet pilots at RAF Valley, with the older Hawk T1 already retired and the T2 fleet running towards the end of the decade. A competition is expected, and Boeing, Saab and BAE Systems have offered the T-7A Red Hawk with local assembly in the United Kingdom, with Leonardo’s M-346 among the alternatives.
Ejection seats carry unusual weight in a British competition because Martin-Baker is a British company that has equipped almost every RAF type since the 1940s and holds a worldwide position built on that record. Choosing an airframe fitted with the American ACES 5 would move that work, and swapping a seat into an airframe designed around a different one is a design and certification exercise in its own right.
The T-7A’s escape system drew sustained criticism during American testing, with problems identified around the performance of the seat and canopy for pilots at the light end of the weight range and around the sequencing of the escape itself, and Boeing has worked through a series of modifications. Programme delays in the United States have pushed initial operating capability for the American air force to the end of the decade.
Martin-Baker’s Mk16 variants are fitted to Typhoon, the F-35 and the Hawk, which means an RAF trainer on a different seat would put student pilots through a different escape system from the one they meet on the front line.

Poland has no Patriot missiles to spare for Ukraine
Poland does not have enough Patriot air defense missiles to hand over to Ukraine, Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski has said, urging other NATO members to supply Kiev with the scarce interceptors.
In an interview with the Polish Press Agency published on Monday, Sikorski warned of growing pressure on Western air defenses, citing the US-Israeli bombing campaign against Iran.
“Following the attacks on Iran, the shortage of interceptor missiles has indeed increased, and Russia is producing more missiles than we have interceptors to neutralize them. This is a real problem,” he said.
“There are NATO countries that still have such resources to contribute, but Poland is not one of them,” Sikorski said, adding that Warsaw “can only join the calls for countries possessing Patriot missiles to share them with Ukraine.”
The issue sparked a political scandal in Poland in July, when the government came under fire over the transfer of Patriot interceptors to Ukraine as part of a wider NATO-backed aid package. Opposition politicians accused Warsaw of sacrificing its own security to arm Kiev, while Prime Minister Donald Tusk insisted the deliveries would not compromise the country’s defenses.
Poland has emerged as one of the EU’s most rapidly militarizing nations, with defense spending reaching 4.7% of GDP. Warsaw has also been one of Kiev’s staunchest backers, pouring billions into military and other aid while serving as a crucial hub for Western arms shipments.
Yet Poland now faces delays in replenishing its own arsenal, with deliveries of US-made PAC-3 MSE Patriot interceptors pushed back as the war with Iran drains American weapons stocks, Polish General Ireneusz Nowak warned earlier this month.
Relations with Kiev have also soured over Ukraine’s honoring of Nazi collaborators linked to the World War II-era Volhynia massacres, in which Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) militants associated with the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN) killed an estimated 100,000 ethnic Poles. Warsaw recognizes the killings as genocide, while Kiev continues to honor figures including OUN leader Stepan Bandera.
Tensions flared again this year after Zelensky awarded a Ukrainian military unit the honorary title “Heroes of the UPA.” Polish President Karol Nawrocki subsequently stripped him of the country’s highest honor, politicians on both sides renounced state decorations, and Warsaw threatened to obstruct Ukraine’s EU accession.
The ammunition crunch is spreading across NATO. In July, the Netherlands said it had exhausted its capacity to supply Ukraine with Patriot missiles from its own stocks, having already provided interceptors and helped assemble a complete Patriot system for Kiev.
Meanwhile, Kiev is facing a critical shortage of air defense ammunition as Russia intensifies strikes on Ukrainian military and energy infrastructure. Moscow has said the attacks are in retaliation for Kiev’s continued strikes on Russian territory, including civilian targets and energy facilities.
Vladimir Zelensky has requested 300 Patriot interceptors from European backers and complained that Washington has approved only some of the missiles purchased through a NATO-backed initiative. The White House has also delayed approving additional transfers as US President Donald Trump presses Ukraine to reach a negotiated settlement with Russia.
Moscow has repeatedly maintained that Western weapons deliveries prolong the conflict, obstruct peace efforts, and risk drawing NATO countries into a direct confrontation with Russia.

Turkish Cypriot President Tufan Erhürman has rejected a Greek Cypriot proposal linking U.N. administration of Maraş to direct EU trade through Mağusa port under the bloc’s control, saying the arrangement offers no balanced exchange.

“Twenty years have passed. It has been brought back as a new formula after 20 years,” he said.

On broader Cyprus talks, Erhürman said negotiations must be aimed at reaching a settlement, explaining his decision not to attend a proposed three-way meeting in New York.
“I will not negotiate for the sake of negotiating,” he said.
