CERT-UA handles 22.4% more cyber incidents in Jan-Sept 2026 year-on-year - State Special Communications Service
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:57:12 EEST
21:57:12 KST

Ukraine's national Computer Emergency Response Team, CERT-UA, operating under the State Service of Special Communications and Information Protection, recorded and handled 4,800 cyber incidents in January-September 2026, up 22.4% from 3,900 in the same period last year.
"Government bodies, local authorities, security and defense sector institutions, critical infrastructure enterprises and commercial sector representatives were among the main targets of cyberattacks," Dmytro Pakholchenko, director of the Cyber Protection Department at the administration of the State Service of Special Communications and Information Protection of Ukraine, told Interfax-Ukraine in a blitz interview.
Incidents involving malicious code accounted for the largest share of cases, at 44.9%, followed by information gathering, including phishing, at 24.2%, he said.
"Incidents involving interference with or attempts to interfere with information systems, the distribution of malicious content and fraud were also recorded," Pakholchenko said.
The State Special Communications Service said attackers focused mainly on stealing credentials and information, gaining unauthorized access to information systems and maintaining a presence in compromised environments.
Compared with last year, attackers have been updating their malware tools and increasingly using legitimate software and web services to carry out cyberattacks, Pakholchenko said.
Another trend identified by the agency is the increasingly frequent use of techniques that induce users to execute malicious commands themselves, under the pretext of fixing technical problems or completing a verification procedure.
Emails containing malicious attachments and links also remain a concern, he said.
Earlier in October, the Microsoft Digital Defense Report 2026 said Ukraine ranked third worldwide and first in Europe in the first half of 2026 among countries whose organizations and users were most frequently targeted by cyberattacks. In 2025, Ukraine ranked fifth globally and third in Europe.
According to the report, Ukraine accounted for 4.8% of victims worldwide, with only the United States and Israel ranking higher.
The Microsoft report also highlighted that Ukraine remains a major focus of activity by Russian state actors, accounting for 14% of their recorded activity.
The full text of the blitz interview with Dmytro Pakholchenko, director of the Cyber Protection Department at the administration of the State Service of Special Communications and Information Protection of Ukraine, will be published on the Interfax-Ukraine website.

Up to 12,000 North Koreans work under conditions of forced labor at Russia’s Alabuga drone plant, CSIS report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:57:07 UTC
21:57:07 KST

A factory in Russia’s Alabuga special economic zone in Tatarstan, where Shahed-type attack drones are assembled, is using labor from victims of human trafficking, according to a report by Victor Cha of the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) and Joseph Kim of the George W. Bush Institute.
The authors said the drones are assembled by Russian teenagers, foreign workers from countries of the Global South, and citizens of North Korea.
Ukrainian intelligence estimates that as many as 12,000 North Koreans have been sent to Alabuga. They are paid around $2.50 an hour, with the regime of Kim Jong Un taking between 70% and 90% of their earnings.
Women ages 16 to 22 from Africa, Latin America, and Asia are recruited with promises of service-sector jobs paying salaries starting from $500 a month. After arriving, their passports are confiscated, and about 90% are sent to assemble drones, according to the report.
Students at Alabuga Polytech college are also put to work from the age of 15 under the guise of earning “work experience,” with shifts lasting as long as 12 hours.
The report’s authors write:
“North Korean laborers have their wages confiscated by the state that sent them. This is the definition of forced labor.”
The Alabuga factory is capable of producing more than 5,500 drones a month, according to the report. Ukrainian intelligence estimates that its workforce is planned to expand from about 1,000 people to 40,000.
The authors called on the U.S. Treasury Department to impose sanctions on companies and educational institutions involved in recruitment for the facility and urged Washington to establish a multilateral investigative group through the United Nations. In September, the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT), a group made up of the United States and allied countries, reported that as many as 25,000 North Koreans were working in Russian drone production. According to the group, the workers are registered as students in order to circumvent sanctions.

Emily Feng on the Uyghur fighters who helped topple Assad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:57:04 UTC
21:57:04 KST

Breadcrumb
Our Hearts Burned For Home: Emily Feng on the Uyghur fighters who fought Assad for a homeland of their own
How did a few thousand Uyghur hairdressers and farmers, shoe salesmen and writers, become part of an elite fighting troop, a pivotal force in overthrowing Syria's brutal dictator Bashar al-Assad?
That is the question at the centre of this remarkable, rarely-told story. Journalist Emily Feng had gone to cover the Israel-Lebanon ceasefire in December 2024, but instead made her way to Syria as Assad fell.
In 2025, she found Central Asian fighters everywhere she went. With the help of exiled Uyghur writer Abduweli Ayup, essential when the new regime banned her from interviewing them directly, they tracked down some five dozen fighters and families from a 20,000-strong Uyghur community that had made Syria home.
About 4,000 of them took up arms. But why would stateless people endure hardship and martyrdom for a country that was not their own?
The answer is that Syria was never the point. The history of this rebel movement is not straightforward. Feng's candid interviews shed light on their complicated, fractured story. Our Hearts Burned For Home: Uyghur militants in Syria’s Civil War is the result.
A revolution within a revolution
Their presence in Syria was almost accidental; a mix of China's crackdown after the 1990s protests and 2009 Ürümqi riots, geographical chance, and revenge.
Unwilling to live in what they called the prison of Xinjiang, they made their way, some via Afghanistan to Syria, not to save Syrians but to learn how to fight for Hotan and Kashgar.
With no Arabic and no war experience, they typically got three months of training and were sent straight to the front.
In Jisr al-Shughur, in houses emptied by war, they built a state within a state: schools, businesses, their own security, raising children for the next war.
"We are raising our own army," one commander tells Feng. They decorated classrooms with cardboard tanks and anti-aircraft rockets to "acclimatise" children to war.
Never losing sight of that goal, they avoided joining other rebel groups and insisted on fighting as Uyghurs. But ideologically, things got complicated and fractured.
From 2014, ISIS/ISIS-K tried to recruit Uyghurs for a global caliphate. Most Turkestan Independence Party (TIP) Uyghurs rejected it; they wanted a Uyghur state, not a caliphate. Those who joined ISIS were arrested and became enemies.
When East Turkestan Islamic Movement (ETIM) leader Abdul Haq in Afghanistan pressed them toward al-Qaeda and the Taliban, they split from the Afghan Uyghurs in 2018, swapped the black Islamist flag for the blue flag of East Turkestan, and recast themselves as nationalists.
As far as the new regime-in-waiting was concerned, it made them rather unreliable allies. In 2016-17 they refused to formally merge into Ahmed al-Sharaa’s Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS). Their goal was Xinjiang, not Syria, and joining HTS meant mission creep.
And yet they fought against the regime. Ferociously.
From neutral newcomers, they were dragged into the rebel independence fray in 2015, earning a fearsome reputation for holding the northern front against Russian bombardment for a decade.
They lived off savings brought from Xinjiang and weapons captured from regime forces. Forced to learn fast, they fashioned shoulder-launched rockets from scrap canisters and mixed their own explosives.
"War became free training," one says, for the future war with China.
Feng is compelling on the brutal reality of that training. The rebel regime was punishing and relentless as it hammered the motley band of volunteers into disciplined soldiers versed in intelligence, strategy and logistics.
Bilal, a former hairdresser, says, "Sometimes, I was so sad I cried.” Revenge pulled him through.
The book's heart is how they fought. After ten gruelling years of fighting hand-to-mouth, the book builds to its climax: Operation Deterrence of Aggression in November 2024.
Triggered by a regime strike that killed children in Ariha, the Uyghurs used a disused tunnel at Dadikh to penetrate Assad's stronghold.
Tragically, digging 500 metres short of their target, they pushed on regardless to break the line to Aleppo. Half their team was stuck with a jammed motorcycle in the tunnel, and one of their tanks was lost to a minefield.
But by November 30, thanks to a rebel-negotiated ceasefire with Russia, Aleppo finally fell. Days later, rebel troops stormed Damascus, and Uyghur fighters waving blue East Turkestan flags rolled into town, earning the respect of the new regime and a place in Syria’s independence struggle.
A new Syria, an uncertain future
It should have been triumphant. But it was hollow.
Feng captures the mood perfectly. They had fought tooth and nail for ten years, losing hundreds of kin. But this was not their war. They wept — not for Syria, but for home. They preferred to save their tears for Hotan or Kashgar one day.
What comes next is the book's most painful part. Where do 20,000 stateless Uyghurs fit in a new Syria when their loyalty lies 4,500 km away?
There are almost as many answers as there are Uyghurs.
Some Uyghur children feel no affinity with East Turkestan and want to become Syrian.
Others, with their long black beards and children who call Alawites and Christians "infidels," frighten locals and want to remain a state within a state independent of Syrian state institutions.
Neutrality, however, might have made them good wartime partners, but how could political independence work in the new Syria?
For many others, comfortable inertia has set in, and the debate over whether to settle or keep fighting for a liberated East Turkestan now dominates.
The new Syria is moving forward anyway, with or without the Uyghurs, and it has big decisions to make.
The TIP has been disbanded into the Syrian Army’s 84th Brigade, and Uyghur commanders have been given posts in the Defence Ministry.
Many hope for citizenship and schooling. But as one interviewee tells Feng: "I hope this exile does not last very long, because they will become more and more Syrian. I hope at the end, when we have our own land back, maybe they at least will still want to visit me in East Turkestan."
Debates about their future rumble on both inside Syria and among the exiled faithful marooned in Turkey.
Many of those in Turkey are de facto stateless after Ankara refused passports over their East Turkestan independence activism.
Living under a cloud of frequent threats of repatriation to China, Syria looks like the perfect place to raise children free to study the Quran and practise their faith.
Squeezed from all sides, the Uyghurs are threatened not only by Turkey but also by Beijing, determined to drag them back to the homeland.
Radicalised Syrian Uyghur fighters have been in China's sights for years, and the fear they might stir trouble in Xinjiang is never far from the surface.
One way for Beijing to solve that problem is to use them as a bargaining chip in Syria's desperate need for reconstruction. Rumours of such a deal abound, but Damascus has denied them for now.
What comes after victory?
Feng and Ayup have done something extraordinary in Our Hearts Burned For Home. This is not just a war story, but one of exile, ideology and what happens when a displaced people borrows another people’s revolution to train for their own.
Their story is not without controversy.
Some Uyghurs fear their militancy is justified, while others find it distasteful. They fear being tarred with the terrorist brush and thereby vindicating Beijing in its crackdown in the Uyghur region.
Feng was drawn to the sheer improbability of Assad's overthrow: some 30,000 rebels in fractious bands up against the Goliaths of Iran, Turkey and Russia. And winning.
In her conclusion, she hints their story might not be over: "What several thousand highly motivated, highly experienced Uyghur fighters can do may end up surprising us all. They have already surprised me."
The author is writing under a pseudonym to protect her identity

Elon Musk Ordered Ukraine Starlink Slowdown Despite Saying US Military Controls Limits, Says WSJ
Elon Musk personally ordered restrictions on Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink service used by Ukraine, on October 14, disrupting Ukrainian drone operations, The Wall Street Journal reported on October 20.
The outlet disclosed the development, citing US officials and people familiar with the decision. According to the newspaper, Musk imposed speed limits on Ukrainian equipment connected to the satellite network, reportedly rendering some Ukrainian strike drones and aerial interceptors virtually unusable.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Journal's sources, Musk and US President Donald Trump discussed the restrictions in a telephone conversation shortly after the slowdown became public. One person familiar with the situation also claimed the two discussed the matter before the restrictions were imposed. However, other US officials maintained that Musk acted independently and that Trump had not explicitly ordered punitive measures against Ukraine.
The restrictions reportedly triggered alarm in Kyiv and confusion within the Trump administration. According to the Journal, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's warnings that the disruption could cost Ukrainian lives prompted an informal White House investigation into who authorized the decision.
SpaceX representatives also reportedly contacted White House officials to coordinate their understanding and public messaging about the restrictions.
Musk subsequently wrote on X that "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," according to the newspaper. Trump, meanwhile, denied knowing who was responsible for the slowdown and said he wanted to determine what had happened.
According to the Journal, some US officials maintained that Musk had acted unilaterally. Another person familiar with the matter claimed that he had consulted several senior administration officials, including Trump, before introducing the restrictions. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio subsequently denied that the administration had requested the slowdown.
The reported operational consequences extended to Ukrainian air defense. Michael Kofman of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace told the Journal that Ukrainian strike and interceptor drones remained subject to a 160 km/h speed cap, while in practice reliable connectivity could be lost at speeds above roughly 130 km/h.
Zelenskyy separately said Ukraine does not use Starlink for strikes inside Russia, including attacks on Russian oil infrastructure. During an October 16 press conference in Brussels, he explained that Ukraine instead relies on the system to operate interceptor drones protecting civilians from Russian Shahed attacks.
"We do not use Starlink to attack or respond within the territory of the Russian Federation," Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated, according to Ukrinform. He added that Kyiv had previously asked SpaceX and the White House to provide such capabilities, indicating that they were not available to Ukrainian forces.
According to Zelenskyy, reducing Starlink connection speeds prevented Ukrainian interceptors from engaging some high-speed Russian Shahed-type drones. He described the restrictions as a dangerous surprise, explaining that certain Russian jet-powered drones were traveling at speeds exceeding 400 kilometers per hour. Ukrainian units reportedly encountered severe connection limitations while attempting to intercept those threats.
SpaceX has not publicly explained the restrictions or responded to the Journal’s report that Musk personally ordered them.
The restrictions disrupted frontline drone units within hours of taking effect. Overnight on October 14, units of the 7th Air Assault Corps in the Huliaipole sector of the Zaporizhzhia region began losing drone connections for 10–20 seconds at speeds of roughly 110–120 km/h.
Medium-range strike drones, which must accelerate rapidly at launch, faced the greatest risk of failing to take off or complete their missions. Slowing down to stay connected left aircraft more exposed to Russian forces, and one drone unit in the sector canceled several missions that day as Ukraine's Defense Ministry began investigating the cause.

El Nino could be 'literally off the monitoring charts': UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:56:33 UTC
21:56:33 KST

Breadcrumb
El Nino could be 'literally off the monitoring charts', 'unprecedented in strength': UN
The El Nino weather phenomenon gripping the planet could be off the charts, the United Nations warned Wednesday, saying countries should take urgent action to prepare for the worst.
"The current El Nino event could be unprecedented in strength. Literally off the monitoring charts that we have used for the past four decades," Celeste Saulo, head of the UN's World Meteorological Organization, told a press conference in Geneva. "El Nino will peak towards the end of 2026, but its impacts will be felt long after that."
She said the WMO's latest global seasonal climate updates forecast that sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific Ocean—the epicentre of El Nino—may rise to 3.8C above average during November to January: way out of line with typical El Nino figures.
"This will have far-reaching consequences for weather patterns across the world," said Saulo.
The naturally occurring weather phenomenon is set to bring higher temperatures to much of the planet, the UN's weather and climate agency said, with its impact compounding the effects of man-made climate change.
Saulo was joined by the UN aid chief Tom Fletcher.
"Today, we are issuing a joint call for urgent and coordinated anticipatory action... We cannot stop El Nino, but we can prevent many of its worst human consequences," she said.
Fletcher said El Nino was set to be a "wrecking ball" of extreme heat, droughts and floods in different parts of the world, triggering "massive humanitarian consequences".
"The damage will not stay in the countries in the immediate path of this El Nino," he warned. "It will create economic shocks for the global economy and drive further conflict, displacement, migration. I am sounding the alarm that the humanitarian system... cannot alone cope with a threat on this scale."
He called on countries, development banks and international financial institutions to get money moving "before that damage is done, not afterwards".
"The choice is clear: we can wait for disaster or we can invest in resilience. We cannot prevent El Nino but we can be serious about the challenges ahead," he added.
Fletcher said he had released $50 million to help 11 countries on the frontline, including Chad, El Salvador, Ethiopia, Somalia and South Sudan.
El Nino warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns.
It typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months.
Conditions oscillate between El Nino and its opposite La Nina, with neutral conditions in between.

China launches satellite for low-inclination remote sensing net
A CERES-1S Y8 carrier rocket blasted off at 11:39 am Beijing time on Wednesday from waters near east China's Shandong Province, delivering the Xiguang-4 01 satellite into a 541 km-altitude low Earth orbit, CGTN reports.
Xiguang-4 01 is the pilot satellite of the Wuyang Constellation, the world's first low-inclination remote sensing constellation. A mysterious metal object discovered floating in the sea near Helsinki earlier this month has been identified as part of a Soviet naval torpedo dating from the Second World War, Finnish police confirmed on Tuesday. The Finnish Defence Forces have since destroyed the object, bringing the investigation to an end.
A fisherman spotted the cylindrical object on 3 October near Suomenlinna, an island fortress off Helsinki, in a shipping channel used by passenger ferries.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The discovery prompted a police operation involving the Finnish Border Guard and the Gulf of Finland Coast Guard, which temporarily closed the waterway while authorities recovered the object.
The metal cylinder measured 4.2 metres in length and 53.48 centimetres in diameter. Investigators initially considered whether it belonged to the machinery of an old shipwreck.
Police subsequently asked the Finnish Heritage Agency to examine the object. Working with maritime specialists, the agency identified it as the central section of what appears to have been a Soviet navy torpedo from the Second World War.
The torpedo's warhead and rear section were missing. Its central compartment contained tanks designed to hold compressed air, water and fuel.
Helsinki police confirmed that the object posed no danger when recovered and that investigators found no evidence of criminal activity.

Married couples can use double surnames from 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:54:00 UTC
21:54:00 KST

Married couples can use double surnames from 2027
From January 1, 2027, married couples will once again be able to use a double surname in Switzerland. The government will bring this amendment to the Civil Code, which was passed by parliament, into force on that date.
From next year spouses will once again be able to use a double surname with or without a hyphen. However children will not be allowed this privilege.
Double surnames were allowed in Switzerland until an amendment to the Civil Code in 2013. From that year onwards, couples intending to marry had to choose a shared surname or retain their respective surnames. Only an unofficial “alliance name” was permitted. This refers to the unofficial double surname with a hyphen.
More
Why double surnames are stirring controversy in Switzerland
Under the amendments adopted by the government, people who are already married will be able to apply to the registry office for an official double surname from 2027 onwards. In future, the alliance name – which differs from the official surname – will no longer be included in passports or on identity cards.
However, a transitional period will continue to allow the alliance name to be recorded in identity documents to enable the authorities to make the necessary technical adjustments.
The governing Federal Council has not yet determined the duration of this transitional period. It will bring the relevant amendment to the Identification Documents Act into force in due course and announce the end of the period well in advance.

She said: “I got a phone call at home from somebody I know through the sport that I play. This man said to me: ‘Pippa, I don’t want you to worry, but you’ve got cancer.’ I just couldn’t really believe it.”

She told the BBC: “It really distresses me people can’t see just how invasive and intrusive it is if somebody looks at your information and then shares it inappropriately.”
A spokesperson for the Royal Cornwall hospitals trust said: “We are truly sorry that Ms Boardman was contacted in this way. Whilst the member of staff had legitimate access to her records as part of their work, it was outside of their role to contact her and discuss her diagnosis. This should not have happened, and we recognise the distress and concern it will have caused.
“Appropriate action was taken following our investigation, which was carried out immediately after Ms Boardman raised her concern. While we cannot disclose the details of individual employment matters, we want to reassure Ms Boardman that we have treated this extremely seriously.
“We have reminded all our staff of their responsibility to protect patient confidentiality and that records must only ever be accessed for a legitimate work-related reason. We are also reviewing our policies and processes in light of the strengthened NHS England guidance on inappropriate access to patient information.
“We sincerely apologise to Ms Boardman for what happened and for the time she has had to wait for answers.”

New report points to widespread and systematic Israeli sexual violence against Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:52:26 UTC
21:52:26 KST

Content warning: This article contains descriptions of sexual violence and abuse that readers may find distressing.
Sexual violence against Palestinians has become part of a widespread and systematic pattern of abuse under Israeli occupation, with a new report laying out incidents of rape, genital torture, forced nudity and sexual humiliation across detention facilities, military operations and displacement sites.
The report in the British Medical Journal collates evidence from medical, humanitarian, and human rights organisations and examines the scale of the abuses to highlight the failure to secure accountability.
The report comes a few weeks after the third anniversary of the start of Israel’s genocidal war against Palestine that has killed more than 75,000 people and displaced millions in the devastated enclave of Gaza.
Sexual violence is part of a wider campaign of abuse that terrorises Palestinian communities and helps drive their forced displacement, according to Dr Nick Maynard, an Oxford-based consultant surgeon who has travelled to Gaza multiple times to provide medical care and co-author of the new report.
“It is important to understand that the evidence we have provided of sexual violence against Palestinians must not be considered as isolated incidents but a part of a widespread systematic pattern of severe physical and sexual abuse of Palestinians throughout the (occupied) West Bank and in Gaza,” Maynard tells TRT World.
“This behaviour is designed to break the will of the Palestinian people and clearly represents a fundamental and core part of their policy of forced displacement of Palestinian people and ethnic cleansing,” he adds.
In March 2025, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry concluded that sexual and gender-based violence against Palestinians was increasingly being used as a method of war.
It found that forced public stripping, sexual harassment and assault formed part of Israeli security forces’ standard operating procedures, with sexualised torture committed with explicit orders or implicit encouragement from senior civilian and military leadership.
The Commission documented a pattern of sexual violence, torture and other inhumane acts amounting to war crimes and crimes against humanity.
The evidence includes rape and sexual assault against Palestinian detainees, attacks targeting their genitals, threats of rape against detainees and their family members, and repeated strip searches conducted in degrading circumstances.
Life-altering injuries
The documented abuse against Palestinian detainees includes sexual violence and beatings that have left them with devastating and sometimes permanent injuries.
In one documented case, a Palestinian detainee suffered a rectal rupture requiring surgery and the formation of a stoma.
Other accounts describe detainees losing one or both testicles after beatings targeting their genitals.
The abuse has also extended beyond detention.
Palestinian men, women and children in Gaza were subjected to prolonged forced nudity during Israeli military operations, including being forced to walk naked in public.
Israeli soldiers also photographed and filmed Palestinian women’s underwear in homes they had raided, posting images online to humiliate them.
The UN’s 2026 report on conflict-related sexual violence verified sexual violence against 31 Palestinian men, women and children in Gaza and the occupied West Bank across 2023 to 2025.
Nine victims were subjected to rape or gang rape, in some cases repeatedly. The documented abuses included genital violence, forced nudity, threats of rape and invasive searches without apparent security justification.
Maynard, who has travelled to Gaza repeatedly since 2010, including on three occasions since October 7, 2023, says he witnessed appalling atrocities including mass casualties caused by bombings in densely populated civilian areas, with children among those killed.
During his work, Maynard collected detailed testimonies from two healthcare workers and one civilian who had been abducted and detained in Israeli prisons. Their accounts included descriptions of torture and sexual violence.
“I have worked in the hospitals with many patients who died because of the lack of resources, and clearly many of them would have survived if we had had adequate resources.”
“The lack of adequate medical resources, as a direct result of the direct targeting of healthcare facilities and the Israeli blockade stopping adequate aid and resources coming into Gaza, meant that patients suffering from trauma often were not able to get adequate medical care and support and this applied to those with trauma from sexual violence,” Maynard says.
“Those who were tortured and underwent sexual violence in Israeli detention centres and prisons were also denied medical care while in custody,” he adds.
Sexual violence drives fear and displacement
For Palestinians, sexual violence and threats have also shaped everyday life under occupation, including during military raids, at checkpoints and in displacement sites.
Reports document women being forced to undress in front of soldiers, subjected to sexual assault and threatened with rape, sometimes in front of their children.
Other accounts describe Israeli soldiers exposing their genitals to women and girls, while Palestinian women in the occupied West Bank have faced sexual harassment and threats from Israeli settlers.
In one study involving 39 displaced households in Area C of the occupied West Bank, more than 70 percent identified threats to women and children, particularly sexualised violence, as a decisive reason for leaving their homes.
The findings illustrate how sexual violence can contribute to an environment of coercion and displacement, alongside other forms of violence and intimidation faced by Palestinian communities.
Children are also among those affected.
In 2025, more than half of 165 Palestinian children aged 12 to 17 who had been detained by Israeli authorities reported witnessing or experiencing sexual violence in detention, including rape threats, forced stripping and genital assault, according to research cited in the BMJ article.
Underreporting and impunity
The scale of documented abuse is compounded by the barriers survivors face in reporting violence and obtaining care.
Fear of reprisals, shame, stigma, and distrust of complaint mechanisms can keep survivors from coming forward. Limited access for independent investigators also limits evidence collection and verification.
“We believe these abuses are greatly underreported for many reasons. Victims frequently refuse to report their injuries out of fear of further abuse and attacks on themselves and their families,” Maynard says.
“It is challenging to document the full extent of sexual violence as Israel has repeatedly refused to allow independent investigators to review what is going on,” he adds.
The accountability record is also troubling.
The UN Commission found that the Israeli civilian and military justice systems had failed to ensure accountability for sexual crimes against Palestinians.
Of 1,260 cases of offences by Israeli soldiers against Palestinians known to the military law enforcement system between 2017 and 2021, only 11 resulted in indictments.
Neve Gordon, professor of human rights and humanitarian law at Queen Mary University of London, said credible allegations required independent investigation, including into those who ordered or enabled the abuse.
Sexual violence can constitute a war crime and, where the legal requirements are met, a crime against humanity.
Establishing criminal responsibility requires investigators to examine individual incidents, preserve evidence and determine the roles of direct perpetrators and those in positions of command.
“The UN needs to be allowed to send in independent teams to investigate such reports of sexual violence and ensure not only that victims of this violence have access to all appropriate specialist medical care but also that perpetrators must be held accountable,” Maynard says.
“Western governments such as the UK government have an obligation under international law to prevent these violations and to make sure international humanitarian law is upheld.”
“These governments must do more to protect Palestinians and must insist on independent monitoring and investigation,” he adds.

Israel’s election may change its leader, but not Iran war policy

- Netanyahu and his rivals both oppose a Palestinian state. Most see only small style changes, not a real shift, on settlements and the West Bank.
- The Iran conflict may deepen. Netanyahu talks of toppling Tehran’s rulers, while analysts warn of a long, risky struggle that could drive Iran towards nuclear deterrence.
AI generated
DUBAI - Israel’s election next week may change its leader, but not its strategy: Iran will remain its chief adversary, military force will continue to be its preferred tool and Palestinian statehood a distant prospect, regional policymakers and analysts say.
That is because the strategic assumptions underpinning Israeli policy were hardened by the Oct 7, 2023, attacks on southern Israeli communities by Palestinian militant group Hamas and by the wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
If anything, Israel could toughen its security policy, the analysts said, as victory for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu with the backing of far-right coalition partners could embolden him to step up the war with Iran, tighten Israel’s grip on the occupied West Bank and push diplomacy further to the margins.
Israel’s security doctrine now rests on three pillars: breaking Iran, holding buffer zones beyond its borders and using force to deter enemies.
The real divide is one of degree rather than direction – how aggressively Israel fights its wars, how far it expands Jewish settlements in the West Bank and whether any leader opts for diplomacy, the analysts said.
From Tehran to Riyadh, the Oct 27 election is not seen as a potential turning point but as a test of whether the Middle East is settling into a long confrontation, where wars ebb and flow while the underlying conflicts are unresolved.
“If Netanyahu is elected, he’ll do whatever he thinks he wants to do,” said Aviv Bushinsky, a former adviser to Netanyahu. “Expansion of the settlements will continue. The wars against Iran, Hamas and Hezbollah will continue.”
“What you see now is what you’ll see after the election, maybe even more aggressively,” he said. “As long as Iran is in such a situation, it’s a waste of time talking about Palestine.”
Netanyahu said on Oct 18 that Israel must prioritise “prevention and offence over containment and defence”, including pre-emptive strikes to thwart emerging threats, while establishing Israel as a regional power and maximising its independence in armaments.
Why the course is unlikely to change
The election pits Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud and its ultra nationalist allies against an opposition led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party.
Palestinian analyst Ghassan al-Khatib sees no prospect of a fundamental shift in policy towards the Palestinians, with Israeli political parties competing to project harder-line positions as public opinion moves further to the right.
“The substance of the policy remains the same: No to a Palestinian state and yes to further settlement expansion. On this, they are all in agreement,” he said.
A government led by Netanyahu’s opponents might seek to repair Israel’s international standing by curbing some settler violence or pursuing settlement expansion with less fanfare.
But such changes would be a shift in style rather than substance, al-Khatib said.
Michael Young of the Carnegie Middle East Center said Israel’s security establishment and much of its political class share a common strategic outlook, centred on confronting Iran, maintaining “forward defence” and preserving military deterrence, reducing the scope for big policy shifts.
Joost Hiltermann of the International Crisis Group, who has conducted research in the West Bank, said growing settler violence, mounting Palestinian frustration and the absence of a “political horizon” had created combustible conditions, where even a minor trigger could spark a wider uprising.
‘Venomous octopus’
Some regional policymakers ask whether Israel’s confrontation with Iran has become the organising principle of Middle East security, regardless of who wins the election.
US President Donald Trump’s praise of Netanyahu as a “great warrior prime minister” has reinforced expectations that the Israeli leader will try to finish the campaign against Tehran if he retains power.
Netanyahu has made clear his ambitions extend beyond containing Iran to toppling its clerical rulers.
“Completing the task means toppling the terrorist regime in Iran, the head of the venomous octopus,” he said in a speech this week.
But military and political analysts question whether anything short of a US-Israeli ground invasion would force Tehran to abandon what it views as its core security interests in what it sees as an existential fight.
After surviving months of war, Iran may be betting it can outlast its opponents while continuing to exert pressure through regional allies.
“This is a quagmire,” Young said. “The Iranians can outlast Trump.”
Hezbollah in Lebanon and Hamas in Gaza have been weakened, but the broader network of Iran-aligned groups has survived and the conflict could strengthen Tehran’s determination to pursue a nuclear deterrent, the analysts said.
For all the alarm Netanyahu causes in the Arab world, some Gulf leaders still see him as the Israeli politician most likely to keep Iran under pressure.
This creates a dilemma for them. They oppose what they view as his expansionist policies but want Iranian influence curbed.
“Netanyahu’s policies in Gaza, the West Bank, Syria and Lebanon are damaging,” said Abdulaziz Sager, chairman of the Gulf Research Centre.
“As for Iran, a settlement is needed before the conflict escalates further. If Iran’s role is not curbed, the region could be heading toward 50 years of Iranian hegemony.” REUTERS

UN warns world on course for 2.6 C warming this century
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:51:00 UTC
21:51:00 KST

Current global commitments to cut greenhouse gas emissions fall far short of Paris Agreement goals, putting the world on track for 2.6 degrees Celsius of warming this century, the U.N. warned Wednesday.
The report by the U.N. Environment Programme (UNEP) highlights the gap between rhetoric and action on global warming and the challenge facing political leaders at November's COP31 climate summit.
Even if countries deliver their latest climate pledges in full, global temperatures could still rise 2.6 C above preindustrial levels by 2100, the annual Emissions Gap Report said.
That would blow past the historic goal agreed to in Paris: keeping warming well below 2 C while striving for a safer 1.5 C. Any chance of meeting the 1.5 C target had been "lost" due to decades of insufficient climate action, the report said.
"The world can no longer avoid overshooting the 1.5-C limit, and the consequences are already devastating," U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said in a statement launching the closely watched report.
"Deadly floods, brutal heatwaves, raging wildfires, lost lives, crippled economies, deepening inequalities, and those least responsible are suffering first and worst," he added.
Overall, global greenhouse gas emissions in 2025 were broadly on par with record levels in 2024. The difference between the two years was insignificant, the report said.
Carbon emissions from burning coal, oil and gas – the main driver of climate change – rose slightly in 2025 compared to the previous year.
Guterres said deep, immediate cuts were needed to protect humanity from worsening impacts, but instead, emissions remain at record levels, and national climate plans and current policies fall dangerously short.
Sticking with current policies would result in warming hitting 2.8 C, the report said.
Scientists warn that every additional fraction of a degree Celsius above 1.5 C increases extreme weather events and the likelihood of irreversible changes to the planet, from dying coral reefs to melting permafrost.
The world has already warmed roughly 1.4 C relative to preindustrial times, and crossing 1.5 C is expected in a matter of years.
The G-20 accounts for three-fourths of global emissions, but Guterres said "all countries, especially the big emitters, must do more" to stop heating the planet.
This latest UNEP warming outlook is worse than last year's due to the formal withdrawal of the U.S. from the Paris accord and upward revisions of historical emissions, report co-author Anne Olhoff said.
Emissions growth slowed among the G-20, but the U.S. was a "major exception," the report added.
Among the world's top-six emitters, preliminary data for 2025 showed emissions increases in the U.S., Indonesia and China and decreases in India, Russia and the European Union.
But in terms of magnitude, the U.S. increase of 133 megatons of carbon dioxide equivalent "far exceeded" that of any other country, driven by higher electricity demand and a rebound of coal power generation.
The next-largest increase was recorded in Turkey, which is hosting the U.N. climate summit in Antalya from Nov. 9-20.
The U.S. is the world's second-largest polluter, behind China. President Donald Trump has called climate change a hoax and rolled back clean energy policies while boosting fossil fuel production.
UNEP Executive Secretary Inger Andersen told reporters that no country was shielded from climate change, and impacts were being felt "on every nation on the planet, including the U.S."
The report details a scenario with a 50% chance of bringing global warming back down to 1.5 C by 2100.
To get there, warming must peak around 1.8 C by 2050, and vast amounts of CO2 would have to be removed from the atmosphere to bring temperatures down further.
But this scenario assumes immediate emissions cuts of 6% annually until 2035 – nowhere near current projections.
"The main takeaway is simple – governments need to get on with enacting policies that cut fossil fuel use as soon as possible," Bill Hare, CEO of global policy institute Climate Analytics, said.
Some climate-vulnerable developing nations have accused bigger emitters of abandoning the Paris goals, and a showdown over the 1.5 C target is expected at COP31.
"This is a historic failure of political leadership. The science has been clear for decades, but governments have chosen delay over action. The consequences will be measured in lives lost, not just degrees of warming," Mohamed Adow, director of Kenya-based think tank Power Shift Africa, said.
Guterres agreed there was a climate "leadership gap" but said overshooting 1.5 C "is not surrender."

Student who stabbed housemate to death in Gloucestershire jailed for life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:50:55 UTC
21:50:55 KST

A university student who lay in wait for his housemate to return home before stabbing him 30 times has been jailed for life with a minimum term of 28 years.
Zack Coughlan, 23, dressed in black and wore a mask and gloves to ambush Jamie Collins, 21, in the garden of their home in Filton, South Gloucestershire.
Bristol crown court heard Collins was stabbed repeatedly and Coughlan left him dying in an alleyway as he cycled away on his housemate’s bike.
Coughlan had denied murder and a trial was under way at Bristol crown court but he changed his plea to guilty on Tuesday.
Sentencing Coughlan on Wednesday, Mr Justice Linden said: “He [Collins] was caught totally unaware by you and was utterly defenceless.”
He dismissed Coughlan’s evidence in court that Collins had previously threatened him, describing Collins as a “gentle soul”.
The judge said no one would know why Coughlan killed Collins.
Collins was attacked shortly before 6pm on 8 April this year after cycling home from University of the West of England (UWE) Bristol where he was studying robotics alongside his killer.
Adam Vaitilingam KC, prosecuting, told the jury: “This was a carefully planned and cold-blooded execution.”
Coughlan dumped the bike at a nearby retail park, bought a change of clothes and threw his bloodstained clothing in a pond, in carrier bags weighed down with bricks.
He returned to the house they shared at about 9pm, put a pizza in the oven and did some online gaming with friends.
At around 2am, Coughlan dialled 999 claiming he had just found Collins’s body in the garden.
The attack was caught on CCTV installed at the house they shared, which Coughlan showed the attending police officers who initially treated him as a witness.
The defendant’s blood had been found on Collins’s bike, and analysis of his mobile phone matched the killer’s movements afterwards captured on CCTV.
Coughlan also had injuries to his hands, and he told people who saw him bleeding that he had been climbing trees and had fallen and hurt himself.
After the murder, Coughlan told a university friend he wanted to hold a memorial for his housemate.
Coughlan and Collins, originally from Swansea, were both final year students and lived together in a £300,000 three-bedroom house owned by the defendant.
The defendant is half Danish and grew up with his family in Cork, Ireland, before moving to Bristol to study robotics at the age of 19.
In a statement issued following Coughlan’s change of plea, Collins’s family said his death had “affected our family in a deep, profound, and lasting way”.
“As a family we have had to explain repeatedly to people what has happened,” they said. “Every time we do so it reinforces the pain of him having been killed so suddenly, and in such a senseless and brutal way.
“Our family has been sickened that Zack Coughlan pretended to help Jamie when in fact he is responsible for killing him.”

MOSCOW, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Russia can resume natural gas supplies to Europe via an intact Nord Stream pipeline if Europeans are willing, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Wednesday.
"One line out of four remains operational. If European consumers, European countries and politicians are willing, gas can be supplied through this line," Novak said when asked whether it would be possible to resume Russian gas supplies to Europe.

21:49:01 KST

NEW DELHI, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- The Delhi government on Wednesday imposed restrictions on burning coal or firewood, and using diesel-based generators, in restaurants, hotels, etc., as the air quality deteriorated into the "Poor" category.
The Air Quality Index (AQI) jumped from nearly 180 to about 300 in and around the national capital city in the past 24 hours, said media reports. Though in some areas, like Gurugram city adjoining the national capital, the AQI was recorded at 313 on Wednesday evening.
The worsening of air quality was attributed to the bursting of firecrackers on the "Dussehra" festival. Delhi's air quality was expected to further deteriorate in the coming days, as people would indulge in bursting firecrackers in the run-up to the "Diwali" festival, which falls on Nov. 8.
Announcing the restrictions, Delhi's Environment Minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa said, "GRAP-1 (Graded Response Action Plan Stage-1) has been invoked today."
GRAP-1 restrictions involved a ban on using coal or firewood in hotels, restaurants, and roadside eateries, besides a total ban on the open burning of garbage, plastics, and municipal solid waste.
The minister said all government and private offices were required to implement a 50 percent "Work from Home" policy. ■

Malaysia's 2026 inflation outlook steady, but upside risks loom in 2027

2026-10-21
20:48:59 CST
21:48:59 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Economists largely maintained their inflation forecasts for Malaysia in 2026 on Tuesday, as fuel subsidies and electricity bill protections continue to contain consumer price pressures, but rising energy costs, geopolitical tensions and potential weather-related food supply disruptions could push inflation higher in 2027.
Hong Leong Investment Bank Research has revised down its 2026 consumer price index (CPI) forecast to 1.9 percent from 2 percent previously, citing continued petrol subsidies, electricity bill protections and the limited pass-through of higher input costs to consumer prices.
However, escalating geopolitical tensions and the lagged impact of El Nino could exert stronger inflationary pressures, prompting the research house to maintain its 2027 inflation forecast at 2.1 percent.
UOB Global Economics and Markets Research retained its 2026 inflation forecast at 2 percent, despite softer inflation in September and average inflation of 1.8 percent in the first nine months of 2026, compared with 1.4 percent in the corresponding period last year.
The research house said targeted fuel subsidies, price stabilization measures and a stable ringgit should help contain cost pass-through. However, adverse weather conditions, sustained energy price shocks and fading base effects remain key upside risks.
UOB also maintained its 2027 inflation forecast at 2 percent, within the government's projected range of 1.8 percent to 2.8 percent.
Kenanga Research likewise kept its inflation forecasts unchanged at 1.9 percent for 2026 and 2 percent for 2027, although it expects risks to remain tilted to the upside.
Kenanga expects inflation to pick up in early 2027 as higher energy, food and input costs feed through the economy with a lag. ■

China Focus: China-initiated Luban Workshops empower global youth with practical skills
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:48:57 CST
21:48:57 KST

TIANJIN, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- At an automotive industrial park in north China's Tianjin Municipality, Egyptian students Abdelrahman Ayman Zaky and Adham Ayman are gaining hands-on experience in new energy vehicle (NEV) chassis systems alongside their Chinese peers.
Having acquired vocational skills at an Egyptian Luban Workshop, the two came to China to deepen their expertise. Adham, 20, hopes to improve his Chinese and vehicle maintenance skills before returning to Egypt to pursue a career as an automotive engineer.
Their experience highlights the mission of the China-initiated Luban Workshops, which over the past decade have equipped young people worldwide with useful skills, fostered local talent, and supported industrial development.
Named after Luban, an ancient Chinese craftsman and inventor who lived more than 2,500 years ago, the initiative draws on a longstanding Chinese tradition of craftsmanship and innovation.
Jointly established by Chinese and foreign educational institutions, Luban Workshops now offer vocational education and skills-training programs in 32 countries.
In Egypt, Luban Workshops are helping students like Adham translate classroom learning into engineering capabilities.
Mohamed Mostafa, a student at an Egyptian Luban Workshop now studying at Tianjin Light Industry Vocational Technical College, said hands-on practice has strengthened his ability to tackle real-world engineering challenges.
"In the EPIP (Engineering Practice and Innovation Project) classroom, we don't just work on simulated problems. We work on real-world engineering problems in teams, discussing solutions, refining our techniques and testing them again and again. We break down complex challenges to achieve the best results and meet engineering standards," Mostafa said.
He added that he has shared the approach with students in Egypt, where they have applied the same methods to develop their own projects.
The two Egyptian Luban Workshops have provided formal education to more than 3,100 people and skills training on over 4,000 occasions, creating new opportunities for industrial cooperation.
Wang Baolong, dean of the School of Mechanical Engineering at Tianjin Light Industry Vocational Technical College, said graduates trained in advanced technologies can meet the needs of local businesses, strengthening Chinese companies' confidence in investing in and establishing factories in Egypt while supporting local economic development.
An employment training base jointly established by the Egyptian Luban Workshops and the China-Egypt TEDA Suez Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone has provided young Egyptians with a direct pathway to employment.
"After receiving professional technical training, these young people can operate production equipment proficiently. They are exactly the kind of skilled workers that companies need," Wang added.
Beyond teaching technical skills, the workshops also help build local capacity for sustained vocational training. While setting up training centers and supplying advanced equipment, Chinese partners send teachers and technicians to train local instructors and arrange exchanges and learning opportunities in China.
In 2016, the Tianjin Bohai Vocational Technical College and the Ayutthaya Technical College in Thailand jointly established the world's first Luban Workshop. Over the past decade, all six of the workshop's internationalized majors have been incorporated into Thailand's national education system.
"We are not just cultivating talent for the local area, but leaving the whole system behind. Chinese standards and models are truly integrating into and promoting local development," said Mei Wentao, a staff member at the Tianjin Bohai Vocational Technical College.
More than 100 Chinese companies in Thailand operate businesses ranging from NEV components to vehicle distribution. In August 2025, the China-Thailand automotive intelligent manufacturing industry-education integration community was established in Thailand. With a steady supply of skilled graduates, companies can recruit directly from schools, helping young Thai people find jobs more easily and quickly.
In Central Asia, the Tajik Luban Workshop is helping local young people explore new career opportunities. In nearly four years of operation, it has provided learning and training opportunities to more than 3,600 undergraduate and postgraduate students.
When Bakhtiyor Bozorzoda enrolled at the Tajik Technical University, he was uncertain about his chosen major in geodesy and cartography. Advanced surveying equipment, digital mapping technologies, and virtual simulation courses at the Tajik Luban Workshop helped him recognize the field's potential and develop a stronger interest in surveying.
During his studies, Bozorzoda gained hands-on experience with high-precision instruments and digital mapping technologies.
"I hope to continue my studies in China in the future, learn more advanced surveying technologies and contribute to infrastructure development in Tajikistan," he said.
Today, Luban Workshops have become a hallmark of China's international vocational education cooperation. Data from China's Ministry of Education show that the country has established 38 Luban Workshops in 32 countries, providing formal education to more than 30,000 students and non-degree training to over 160,000 people.
The Luban Workshops reflect a commitment to harmony, coexistence and the common good in Chinese cultural tradition. By responding to local needs, they help young people in different countries acquire skills that can benefit them throughout their careers, said Tian Xuejun, president of the China Education Association for International Exchange, at the 2026 World Vocational and Technical Education Development Conference, held in Tianjin from Oct. 15 to 17.
China has the world's largest vocational education system, with 9,151 secondary vocational schools, 1,554 higher vocational colleges and 124 vocational undergraduate institutions.
As of the end of 2025, China's vocational education catalog covered 19 major categories, 97 subcategories and 1,491 majors, spanning virtually all sectors of the national economy and all 41 major industrial categories.
China is continuing to strengthen its vocational education system to support the development of emerging industries and expand opportunities for people both at home and abroad. At the 2026 World Vocational and Technical Education Development Conference, representatives from 45 countries jointly released the Framework of World Vocational and Technical Education Standards developed under China's leadership.
The framework calls for improving vocational school systems, establishing lifelong education and training opportunities for all, developing teaching materials through industry-education collaboration, building teaching teams through school-enterprise partnerships, and using artificial intelligence to drive reform in education and teaching. ■

The event, organized by the Kazakhstan Tennis Federation in partnership with the Bulat Utemuratov Foundation, brought together Rublev and children from the foundation's Asyl Miras Autism Center at Almaty's Alatau Tennis Center.
Held on the sidelines of the ATP 250 tournament, the session featured adapted ball-and-racket exercises, accuracy drills and other activities designed to introduce the children to tennis in a relaxed environment.

The Russian, whose mother is a tennis coach, said he had grown up watching how coaches worked with young children.
"Every charitable initiative is incredibly meaningful, and everyone connects with it in their own way. But the most important thing is simply to do something good," he added.
The initiative forms part of the Kazakhstan Tennis Federation's efforts to encourage wider participation in the sport, which has undergone significant development in the country under federation president Bulat Utemuratov.
Ainur Karbozova, CEO of the Bulat Utemuratov Foundation, said sporting activities could help create a more inclusive environment for children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).
"It is particularly important to us that children with ASD have the opportunity to participate in all aspects of life, including sports," she said.
"Meetings like these help broaden the understanding of inclusion not only among children but also throughout society."
The initiative has previously attracted leading players including Novak Djokovic, Carlos Alcaraz, Elena Rybakina and Daniil Medvedev.
The Almaty Open, which runs through Sunday, is one of Kazakhstan's leading international tennis tournaments. ■

Malaysia's coral reefs at risk over climate change, says official
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:48:37 CST
21:48:37 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Rising sea temperatures of up to 35 degrees Celsius have caused increased coral deaths and bleaching at six popular island destinations in Malaysia, a Malaysian official said on Tuesday.
Monitoring by the Fisheries Department at 32 islands in Malaysia's marine parks found serious environmental pressure and worsening reef health at six islands, Agriculture and Food Security Minister Mohamad Sabu told parliament.
"Monitoring found a drop in live coral cover and a higher rate of coral deaths after bleaching, caused by sea-surface temperatures reaching between 32 degrees Celsius and 35 degrees Celsius," he said.
Mohamad said coral reefs are important marine habitats, providing shelter and breeding grounds for sea life, while supporting the country's fisheries resources.
He said the ministry is carrying out a climate action plan for the fisheries sector for 2024 to 2030, which includes efforts to reduce the effects of climate change on coral reefs, adding that 4 million ringgit (980,000 U.S. dollars) has been allocated toward rehabilitation programs.
The government is also strengthening enforcement under the Fisheries Act 1985 against activities that damage coral reefs.
These include taking corals, dumping pollutants, destroying marine habitats and anchoring vessels in prohibited ways within marine parks and marine reserves without written permission. ■

Ruined by NATO, divided without Gaddafi: Can Libya’s new deal hold?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:48:31 UTC
21:48:31 KST

Ruined by NATO, divided without Gaddafi: Can Libya’s new deal hold?
The long-awaited agreement between Libya’s rival factions was finally signed on August 30 under the auspices of the United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL). On that day, the mission gathered the two negotiating delegations at its Tripoli headquarters to formalize the text ironed out during earlier rounds of talks in Rome and Tunis. UNSMIL invited foreign diplomats, media representatives, and Libyan delegations to the event, where UN Special Representative Hanna Tetteh hailed the accord in her opening remarks as “another important milestone in Libya’s journey toward stability and national unity.”
This, however, bore a resemblance to previous diplomatic milestones – most notably the 2015 Libyan Political Agreement (LPA) signed in Skhirat, Morocco. The LPA established the rules of the political game in the fractured country; rules to which none of the domestic political actors seem fully committed, yet from which none completely depart. In a sense, Skhirat remains the ultimate reference point for every subsequent UN roadmap in Libya.
In the vacuum left by the 2011 NATO intervention and the brutal murder of Muammar Gaddafi, Libya has seen a continuous parade of diplomatic accords. Yet the fundamental problem has never been a shortage of roadmaps, but rather their consolidation into nationally accepted political facts that elites cannot simply manipulate at will.
The August 30 agreement has two main parts. The first is restructuring the High National Elections Commission (HNEC), the agency in charge of organizing elections. In practice, this means replacing its leadership to settle disputes over appointments and regional representation. Although these changes were long delayed by regional quotas and political patronage stemming from the 2015 Skhirat agreement, rivals can still negotiate them with relative ease.
The 24-month timeline to hold elections was also established. However, the countdown is designed to govern the transition only once a single, unified executive authority and unified national institutions are established to oversee the voting process.
The second component concerns the central objective of UNSMIL’s latest roadmap: agreeing on viable election laws, an issue on which the UN has failed to make meaningful progress since the collapse of the planned 2021 elections.
Libya remains divided between rival power centers: the Government of National Unity (GNU), led by Abdul Hamid Dbeibah in Tripoli, the western part of the country, and the Libyan National Army (LNA) command in the east led by General Khalifa Haftar. These exist alongside two political institutions: the Tripoli-based High Council of state (HCS) and the eastern-based House of Representatives (HoR). To break the deadlock, UNSMIL established a smaller negotiating group known as the ‘Smaller Convening’, or the ‘4+4’. It brings together eight representatives from the GNU, Haftar’s military command, the HCS, and the HoR.
This mechanism directly mirrors the ill-fated 2021 Geneva process, Libyan Political Dialogue Framework, which ultimately hardened Libya’s institutional divide and brought the country closer to a permanent de facto partition than at any point since its formal unification in 1951. The UN Security Council issued a delayed presidential statement endorsing the deal, and thus repeating a familiar ritual that seems to elevates elite compromise over structural reform. Seeking to seize the political initiative, Speaker Aguila Saleh brought the 4+4 framework to the HoR floor for an immediate vote where it was approved by the majority of members.
The ‘4+4’ format developed alongside (and ultimately eclipsed) UNSMIL’s broader Structured Dialogue. Even before those conclusions were finalized, UNSMIL was already facilitating a parallel ‘Smaller Convening’ behind closed doors – the 4+4 was born. As Hanna Tetteh told the Security Council on June 18, the explicit goal of this smaller format was to bypass the paralysis between the legislative bodies and force an accord on the roadmap’s first two steps: reconstituting the elections commission’s board and resolving the contested electoral framework. Thus, the ‘4+4’ was a deliberate strategy to concentrate decision-making among the political and military figures deemed capable of enforcing an outcome.
After the HoR approved the agreement on September 14, the HCS formally rejected it on October 5, along with the related laws and decisions issued by the House, arguing that they bypassed the constitutional, legal and consensual frameworks governing the political process. In her October 14 briefing to the UN Security Council, Tetteh acknowledged this rejection but maintained that the agreement offers an actionable path to presidential and legislative elections under a single, unified executive authority within 24 months.
She also announced that UNSMIL would meet members of the 4+4 committee later this month to examine the possibility of establishing a broadly representative national mechanism under Article 5 of the agreement in consultation with the Security Council. This proposal implicitly acknowledges that the 4+4 mini-dialogue alone may not be sufficient to advance the roadmap.
Another significant development is the removal of Aguila Saleh as speaker of the HoR after 12 years in office. On October 7, the eastern-based parliament elected Al-Salhin Abdulnabi as his successor, ending Saleh’s long tenure amid growing discontent over his leadership. The change is particularly significant because Saleh had been accused of being a prominent obstacle to previous attempts to move Libya’s political process forward. Tetteh acknowledged the transition, expressing her appreciation to Saleh for “his leadership and engagement over his 12-year tenure of service.” Her emphasis on the change in parliamentary leadership is noteworthy: The departure of a figure long associated with resistance to political roadmaps could create new room for maneuver, although it does not by itself guarantee that the House will cooperate with the UN initiative or that the entrenched political divisions will be overcome.
Ultimately, the structural core of the August 30 agreement rests on a fundamental contradiction: 4+4 does not equal 1. Combining four delegates from Tripoli’s political-institutional structures, including representatives of the HCS, with four delegates representing the eastern power structure in Benghazi does not produce a unified state. Instead, it seems to function as a shared enterprise in which rival political elites, rather than competing to build a single nation, recognize that their mutual survival depends on dividing power and maintaining exclusive control over the state apparatus.
Setting a 24-month timetable neither offers a guarantee that elections will actually occur; instead, it grants entrenched factions another two years of status quo protection without imposing any penalty for non-compliance.
Still, the UN Security Council appeared to endorse the latest UNSMIL plan. Following Tetteh’s briefing on October 14, the Council reaffirmed its support for the agreement, despite concerns over its implementation and the High Council of State’s rejection.
By prioritizing elite consensus over an enforceable constitutional baseline, the international community risks continuing to repeat a flawed equation. Until UNSMIL and foreign powers break this cycle and align their strategy with the Libyan public’s demand for genuine democratic renewal, every new agreement risks becoming another monument to the status quo. In the end, the ‘4+4’ framework offers no viable fallback or alternative path forward if it fails.
Last week, the UNSC did not vote to extend UNSMIL’s mandate, which expires on October 31. However, this is largely a technicality, since the Council has already approved UNSMIL’s roadmap.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

The findings, released Tuesday, show that Laos has an estimated combined resident and non-resident population of 7.55 million, including 7.24 million people living in the country and 313,766 Lao citizens residing abroad. In terms of education, the overall literacy rate for individuals aged six and above has risen to 83.6 percent.
For the first time, the census employed modern technologies, including electronic maps to define survey areas, digital devices for data collection through computer-assisted personal interviewing, and real-time data monitoring to improve efficiency and accuracy. ■

MADRID, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Spain's historic pottery city of Talavera de la Reina is seeking to strengthen cultural and commercial ties with China through its participation in the Jingdezhen International Ceramic Fair, the city's mayor has said to Xinhua.
The fair is being held from Oct. 17 to 22 in Jingdezhen, in east China's Jiangxi Province, with five Spanish ceramic artists attending the event.
"We're very happy because this international fair is perhaps the most important one worldwide in terms of ceramics. The fact that we have 48 pieces from 18 workshops in Talavera is a challenge, and it is also a source of pride for me as mayor of this city," Jose Julian Gregorio Lopez, mayor of Talavera, told Xinhua on Tuesday.
Renowned for its ornate glazed pottery, Talavera has a centuries-old ceramic tradition that flourished in the 16th century. Its traditional ceramic-making processes were inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2019, alongside those of two Mexican communities.
The pieces selected for the exhibition feature a range of designs and techniques reflecting the diversity of contemporary Talavera pottery. According to the local council, participating artists were given complete freedom to choose works that best represent their artistic identities.
"The ceramics we have at the fair are contemporary, artistic but within the traditional ceramics of Talavera, so that our exhibition is very complete, and our ceramicists will be able to meet their counterparts from China and other countries at this major fair, and see how they work," said the mayor.
In 2025, Talavera hosted a touring exhibition of Dehua white porcelain, known internationally as "Blanc de Chine," from southeast China's Fujian Province. During the exhibition, Dehua officials expressed hopes of establishing sister-city ties with Talavera and expanding cooperation in ceramic craftsmanship, culture and trade.
Talavera's participation in Jingdezhen this year reflects the two-way nature of these exchanges, with Talavera now bringing its own ceramic heritage to Chinese audiences.
"We're doing this exhibition, but then we will also have exhibitions here in Talavera from China, showing their porcelain and their ceramics. It is a two-way street," said the mayor.
Beyond cultural exchanges, Talavera is also seeking to create new commercial opportunities for its ceramic artists and workshops in the Chinese market.
According to the local council, the works displayed at the fair will remain in China after the event, while Talavera will establish a permanent official sales point at the Jingdezhen Official Ceramic Flagship Store, providing a lasting platform for Spanish ceramic products in China. ■

Across China: East China's Liangzhu offers Chinese wisdom for sustainable tourism
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
20:48:22 CST
21:48:22 KST

HANGZHOU, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- A silver self-driving shuttle glided past golden rice fields on the outskirts of Hangzhou in east China's Zhejiang Province, linking several cultural landmarks, including the Liangzhu ruins, where an early regional state flourished over five millennia ago.
This route, launched earlier this month, points to a question facing many World Heritage sites: how to protect fragile ruins without turning them into isolated monuments, and how to let surrounding communities share in their value without putting the heritage at risk.
This year marks 90 years since the Liangzhu ruins were first discovered. From Oct. 18 to 20, the fourth Liangzhu Forum brought together officials, archaeologists and scholars from about 60 countries and regions in Hangzhou to discuss issues including advances in technologies for protecting and utilizing cultural relics and sustainable tourism.
"UNESCO believes that sustainable tourism can help safeguard cultural heritage by raising awareness of the importance of heritage for future generations, improving cultural understanding and strengthening local livelihoods," said Nayef Al-Fayez, UNESCO assistant director-general for culture, in his video speech.
"Liangzhu was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2019. Much of Liangzhu's ancient city layout and its water conservancy system lie beneath the surface, so non-specialist visitors may easily miss what makes the site remarkable," said Wang Shu, director of the Hangzhou Liangzhu Archaeological Site Administrative District Management Committee.
"If the public cannot see or understand it, the social value of the heritage cannot be fully realized. Our focus is on how to translate archaeological evidence into cultural experiences that the public can understand, participate in and share," Wang added.
Technology is helping make such translation possible. At the Liangzhu Museum, visitors can put on augmented reality glasses and watch a virtual exhibit appear to float out of its display case, revealing intricate carvings from every angle without touching the original.
In the virtual reality experience at the ruins, tourists can drift through ancient waterways on a bamboo raft, stand atop the palace to take in the city's grand layout, or walk into a virtual altar to witness a sacred ceremony firsthand.
"Just as tourism needs heritage, heritage also needs tourism," said Michael David Robinson, vice chair and non-executive director for culture, UK National Commission for UNESCO, adding that management plans and clear rules are needed to prevent excessive damage. "You have to ensure that the tourists understand how sensitive some of the archaeology is."
At many sites, conservation has focused on the ruins themselves and the museums built to tell their stories, while development in surrounding areas has followed a separate course. Residents may live alongside extraordinary cultural heritage yet have few opportunities to benefit from it.
Liangzhu's efforts have offered a window into China's practice regarding this global issue.
That effort now stretches across a 634-square-kilometer cultural corridor linking the Liangzhu ruins with the nearby Grand Canal, the world's oldest artificial waterway system and a UNESCO World Heritage Site inscribed in 2014, and with surrounding hills, waterways, woodlands and cultural institutions.
"Archaeology shows that over 5,000 years ago, Liangzhu was an early thriving regional state. Today, the same land is still buzzing with innovation and entrepreneurship," Wang said. "Liangzhu is using a corridor-style development approach to strike a balance between protection and growth."
"We have been trying to bring rural communities, urban centers and industry together to let culture benefit people," said Yao Huimin, deputy director of the Liangzhu Museum.
Driven by Liangzhu's cultural resources, the corridor has gathered more than 1,000 cultural enterprises above the designated size. In the first half of 2026, it added 50 such enterprises, with combined revenue exceeding 89.1 billion yuan (around 13.26 billion U.S. dollars), up 37 percent year on year.
Rather than simply restricting construction, Liangzhu has sought ways to turn protection into opportunity for its villages, which are home to residents who have lived on the heritage belt for generations.
In Xin'gang Village, idle land left by the closure of six furniture and brick factories in 2016 was transformed into a standard football pitch. This field quickly drew city dwellers to the countryside, hosting 12 corporate league matches in its first year.
This single move set off a chain reaction. Xin'gang has since built more sports venues, becoming a sports hub on Hangzhou's outskirts. The model is spreading across villages in Liangzhu, with softball, rugby, archery, tennis and pickleball centers now in use.
Raphael Callou Neves Barros, director general for culture, Organization of Ibero-American States, emphasized the need for continuous dialogue with local communities and to ensure tourism does not undermine the sustainability of culture and heritage.
The deeper value of sustainable tourism lies in what visitors take away and what they leave behind, Barros added. They take away not just a sightseeing experience, but an understanding of a civilization. And they leave behind not only short-term consumption, but a positive force supporting heritage protection, community development and the continuation of local culture.
"Heritage conservation does not end at the fence. Its true destination is people's hearts," said Liu Jiecheng, deputy director of Peking University's Institute for Cultural Innovation. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- A mainland spokesperson on Wednesday said attempts by Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities to decouple the island's industries from the mainland market are doomed to fail.
Speaking at a regular press briefing, Zhang Han, a spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said the DPP authorities had been desperately obstructing economic exchanges across the Taiwan Strait and catering to external forces.
According to official data, trade between the mainland and Taiwan totaled 301.2 billion U.S. dollars in the first nine months of this year, up 30.3 percent year on year. Mainland imports from Taiwan reached 216.3 billion U.S. dollars, an increase of 27.8 percent.
