The spokesperson also responded to recent remarks by a Taiwan economic official regarding plans by the island's authorities to tighten controls on AI chip exports to the mainland and launch restriction measures that "correspond to U.S. ones."
She criticized the DPP authorities for disregarding the interests of Taiwan's industries and businesses, while following the United States in lockstep to pursue their own political interests, obstructing and restricting normal business operations.
"The mainland is committed to greater self-reliance and strength in science and technology," Zhang said. "External blockades have never been able to hold back our progress, and they will be even less able to do so in the future."
The Chinese mainland's AI core industry was estimated to have exceeded 1.2 trillion yuan in 2025. By the end of September, its smart computing power reached 2,592 EFLOPS, up 146 percent year on year -- EFLOPS refers to a unit measuring computing performance, with each unit representing 1 quintillion floating-point operations per second.
Zhang warned that the DPP authorities' restriction measures would only benefit opportunists pursuing "Taiwan independence" at the expense of Taiwan's industries and ordinary people, as they are squandering the competitive strengths of the island's industries built through generations of hard work by professionals, entrepreneurs and researchers. ■

19 dead at Kolkata pandal, SIT tasked with probing tragedy and safety lapses
NEW DELHI: The West Bengal government, in consultation with the Calcutta High Court, has constituted a Special Investigation Team (SIT) to probe the October 17 stampede at the Chorbagan Durga Puja pandal in Kolkata that claimed 19 lives and left 25 people injured.The SIT will investigate the circumstances leading to the incident and recommend measures to prevent similar tragedies. Its members include the Principal Secretary of the Disaster Management and Civil Defence Department, the Director General and Inspector General of Police of the Special Task Force (STF), a police representative of at least Additional Director General rank, a Home and Hill Affairs Department representative of at least Joint Secretary rank, and a representative of the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) based in Kolkata.
Preliminary findings indicate that the victims sustained multiple traumatic injuries as the crowd surged towards the pandal’s exit during evening rain. The deceased included 13 women and six minors. The youngest victim was seven-year-old Aayansh Srivastava, who had travelled from Bihar with his family.The victims came from Kolkata, neighbouring districts and other parts of West Bengal. Among them were 14-year-old Sandip Bej from Purba Bardhaman, 13-year-old Pranjal Sarkar from Agarpara, and teenagers Priya Samaddar, 18, from New Barrackpore, Akriti Kumari, 17, from Bally, and Barnali Haldar, 17, and Tania Biswas, 18, from New Town.
Meanwhile, the Kolkata Fire Department has placed five Durga Puja pandals in South Kolkata under special scrutiny following the tragedy. The department has issued written instructions to the committees of Chetla, Tridhara, Deshapriya Park and Tollygunge Cultural, directing them to pay particular attention to entry and exit routes and implement additional fire safety measures.
The state government has announced compensation of Rs 25 lakh and a job for the family of each deceased victim. The Special Task Force has also begun an investigation to establish accountability for the incident.Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari, along with the Chief Secretary, Home Secretary, Director General of Police and Commissioner of Police, is closely monitoring the situation.Hospitals have begun discharging injured survivors in phases. Fourteen patients were shifted to a private hospital off EM Bypass after initially receiving treatment at Medical College and Hospital and RG Kar Medical College and Hospital.

'Avoid airing anti-national content': Govt warns TV channels against inflammatory debates and AI misuse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:48:06 UTC
21:48:06 KST

NEW DELHI: The ministry of information and broadcasting on Wednesday issued an advisory to satellite TV channels, asking them to avoid live coverage of anti-terror operations, exercise caution while broadcasting violent visuals and refrain from airing anti-national content.In its advisory, the ministry asked channels to strictly adhere to the Programme Code prescribed under the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995, and the Cable Television Networks Rules, 1994."The ministry of information & broadcasting has observed instances of non-compliance with the provisions of the Programme Code prescribed under the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995, and the Cable Television Networks Rules, 1994, by various private satellite television channels," the ministry said."Instances of similar news/visuals broadcast on multiple channels on similar topics were observed during the meeting of IDC. Therefore, IDC recommended that all private satellite television channels be advised to strictly adhere to the statutory provisions governing content broadcast on television. The committee also emphasised that inappropriate behaviour or language should not be normalized in telecast," it added.
The guidelines cover live coverage of anti-terror operations, violent visuals, crime reporting, natural disasters, the use of authentic maps of India, communal harmony and the protection of sexual assault victims' identities.On communal harmony and debate programmes, the ministry said channels must ensure that programmes, including live debates and panel discussions, "do not promote or encourage communal or anti-national attitudes".
Broadcasters have also been cautioned to exercise due care while using artificial intelligence, including generative AI, in programmes such as graphics and virtual news presentations.The ministry said AI tools "may be limited to assistive capacity" without compromising the "accuracy, authenticity, or sensitivity" of news content.The ministry further asked broadcasters to strengthen their editorial and content-review mechanisms and regularly sensitise and train personnel involved in news gathering, editing, production, transmission and telecast.The ministry said violations of these guidelines may invite action under the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995.
Rohitashwa Ranjan is a digital journalist with The Times of India, where he decodes Indian politics as a carefully staged production with scripts, subtext and everything behind. His stories track elections, party dynamics and the things that often are buried beneath the headlines. When not parsing vote shares or alliances, he is usually reading between the lines, where the real story tends to reside.

Japan-US exercise Keen Sword poses security risks to Russia — MFA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:47:46 UTC
21:47:46 KST

MOSCOW, October 21. /TASS/. The joint Japanese-US military exercise Keen Sword poses security risks to Russia’s Far Eastern borders, Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said at a news briefing.
"Amid Japan’s current course toward remilitarization, this military activity, like many others, has lost its original, strictly defensive character as previously defined in Japanese legislation," she said.
"We have repeatedly conveyed to the Japanese side our serious concern over this trend, as such actions create additional security risks along Russia’s Far Eastern borders. In light of historical realities, these concerns are well founded," Zakharova concluded.
The joint US-Japanese military exercise Keen Sword is taking place in Japan and surrounding waters from October 19 to 29. It involves approximately 45,000 Japanese military personnel and 12,000 US troops.

Documents
Details
Timetables for operational low flying (OLF) training by RAF fast jets and Hercules aircraft. These timetables cover 3 tactical training areas (TTA) only. These are:
- LFA 7(T): central Wales
- LFA 14(T): northern Scotland
- LFA 20(T): the borders of southern Scotland and northern England
When the TTA is not in use, there may be other flying activity in the area. The MOD is unable to provide a timetable for all low flying activity as the information can very quickly become outdated due to weather conditions and training requirements.

How Israel's election could play out as polls forecast deadlock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:47:39 UTC
21:47:39 KST

Breadcrumb
How Israel's election could play out as polls forecast deadlock
Israel could be heading towards another political crisis after its general election on 27 October, with neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his main rival, retired general Gadi Eisenkot, expected to secure a parliamentary majority.
With the two rival blocs neck and neck in the polls, the vote could trigger weeks of difficult coalition negotiations, leaving the country without a new government and potentially forcing another election.
The stakes are particularly high as Israel remains embroiled in regional conflicts, while deep divisions over military conscription, Palestinian statehood and the role of the far right threaten to complicate efforts to form a government.
Netanyahu's far-right bloc and Eisenkot's opposition coalition both face significant obstacles to securing the 61 seats needed to control the 120-member Knesset.
As Israel prepares to head to the polls on Tuesday, several scenarios could determine who governs the country next.
A Knesset majority
The simplest outcome would be for either the pro-Netanyahu group or Eisenkot's coalition to win more than 60 seats in the vote.
Current polling indicates that this is unlikely. An average of polls tracked by The New Arab over the past week shows that both sides are likely to fall short of a majority by around 10 seats.
Nevertheless, with a week to go before the vote, there is plenty of time for something dramatic to happen that alters the course of the race. US news reports suggest that Netanyahu and Trump have been discussing a renewed attack on Iran, while both leaders have escalated their rhetoric against Tehran in recent days. Few would be surprised if the two made a move against Iran if Netanyahu's position remains shaky ahead of election day.
That said, a majority doesn't necessarily ensure the quick formation of a government given the frictions among both coalitions.
While considered allies of Netanyahu, neither of the Haredi parties is guaranteed to go back into government with him given the continued tensions over the conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jews. Shas and United Torah Judaism, which quit the coalition last year over the issue, will want commitments that religious Jews will remain exempt from military service before entering the next government.
Meanwhile, the Eisenkot coalition is united on its opposition to Netanyahu and a Palestinian state but little else. Its members range from the hardline ultranationalist Yisrael Beiteinu to the Democrats party led by Yair Golan. Golan, a former general, doesn't support a two-state solution but is against the annexation of the West Bank and supports negotiations with the Palestinians, putting him at odds with the rest of the coalition.
Coalition horse-trading
In the likely event that the vote produces a stalemate, it will fall to both sides to negotiate with other parties to expand their coalitions.
The Arab parties – which include the Joint List, an alliance of Palestinian parties spanning nationalist, secular and communist traditions, and the conservative Ra'am – are projected to win 14 seats between them, potentially leaving them holding the balance of power.
Between them, Ra'am's Mansour Abbas is most likely to do a deal to enter government with Eisenkot, in a repeat of his agreement with hardliner Naftali Bennett in 2021. There are potential roadblocks from within the coalition, with Yashar members opposing a deal with the party.
Assuming a deal can be done, including Ra'am in the coalition would only get Eisenkot so far. The party is expected to win only five seats, leaving him short of a majority.
That leaves the Joint List and the Haredi parties as potential pathways to government. Cooperating with the Joint List – which includes Sami Abu Shehadeh's nationalist Balad, Yousef Jabareen's left-wing Hadash and Ahmed Tibi's Ta'al – is scarcely thinkable, given the chasm that separates the two sides.
Alternatively, Eisenkot could look to enter talks with Shas and UTJ, which are projected to win 15-16 seats. That, theoretically, would get him over the line but would likely come with the cost of fracturing his existing coalition. Such a deal would require them to make a huge compromise over the draft – one which they are unlikely to swallow. Yisrael Beiteinu's Avigdor Lieberman is particularly hardline on this issue and has long refused to enter government with Shas or UTJ.
Minority government
Should negotiations stall, one side could decide to govern as a minority. This has never happened after an election in the country's history and would be a recipe for political instability.
It is also an option for Eisenkot if he can convince his coalition to make an informal arrangement with the Joint List. Jabareen said this month that he could agree to provide backing in the Knesset to an Eisenkot minority government if it means keeping Netanyahu out of power.
Such support would not necessarily require the Joint List to join the government or formally back it in every parliamentary vote. It could instead involve abstaining from confidence votes to allow a minority administration to take office.
But it's a big if. Jabareen has outlined conditions for the group's support, including commitments to combating spiralling crime in Arab communities and supporting a Palestinian state, the latter of which is anathema to every party in Eisenkot's coalition. Any arrangement would therefore depend on negotiations rather than unconditional or automatic backing.
National unity government
Given the potential for a post-election political crisis, speculation has increased in recent days about whether Netanyahu and Eisenkot could come together to form a unity administration and block the Kahanist right from staying in power.
Both leaders have flatly rejected the possibility of going into government with each other, though President Isaac Herzog is reportedly trying to bring them together.
Assuming the Likud leader were to cut ties with the extreme right, such an arrangement would still require the backing of most of Eisenkot's coalition, all of whom have staked out stridently anti-Netanyahu positions.
The record shows that such an administration is unlikely to last long. The most recent unity government - between Netanyahu and Benny Gantz in 2020 - barely lasted six months before it collapsed and new elections were called.
A new election
If all efforts to form a government fail, Israel could be forced to hold another election, raising the prospect of a return to the political paralysis of 2019 to 2021, when the country held four elections in just two years.
A prolonged deadlock in 2026 could prove even more destabilising, with the Israeli military engaged in conflicts on multiple fronts and social tensions continuing to rise.
With Trump threatening to relaunch the war on Iran next month and Israeli settler violence escalating across the occupied West Bank, a political vacuum could provide Netanyahu's Likud party and the increasingly powerful far right with an opportunity to advance their ambitions at home and abroad.

German sniper detained after deserting Ukrainian Army – FSB
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:47:04 UTC
21:47:04 KST

German sniper detained after deserting Ukrainian Army – FSB
A German sniper who deserted the Ukrainian military after failing to receive a promised payment has been detained by Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), the agency announced on Wednesday.
In footage released by the agency, the man said he had served with German forces in Afghanistan between 2004 and 2010, took part in fighting in Somalia from 2006 to 2008, and later fought as a mercenary in Syria between 2008 and 2010.
The former Bundeswehr soldier said he then served as a sniper with Ukraine’s 25th Territorial Defense Battalion near Donetsk between 2016 and 2018, alongside fighters mainly from Britain and Georgia.
He later moved to Switzerland before returning to Ukraine in November 2025 to sign another three-year military contract the following month. The man said he held the rank of corporal and served as a sniper.
“After signing the contract, I was promised a payment of 100,000 hryvnias ($2,200). However, I did not receive this money and was forced to flee the Ukrainian armed forces,” he said in the testimony.
The FSB released copies of the German national’s military documents and contracts, with his identity concealed, as well as photographs showing him alongside other fighters. The agency said he could face criminal charges for mercenary activity under Russian law.
The detention comes a week after the FSB apprehended Swedish national Freddy Mikael Stalkrantz Lindholm in Russia’s Pskov Region. According to the agency, he crossed the border illegally to carry out sabotage and terrorist attacks on Russian military facilities, posing as a prospective recruit for the Russian Army.
Lindholm previously commanded a drone unit in Ukraine’s Aidar battalion, which Russia has designated a terrorist organization. He faces charges of illegally crossing the border, while investigators are considering additional charges related to terrorism and mercenary activity.
US investigators have also reportedly uncovered a scheme in which Mexican drug cartels sent their members to Ukraine to gain battlefield experience and paid officials close to Vladimir Zelensky for their “training,” Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service said on Tuesday.
Kiev has increasingly turned to foreign fighters as its military struggles with manpower shortages, draft evasion, and desertion. In March, then-Defense Minister Mikhail Fedorov identified the recruitment of more foreigners as one of the measures aimed at tackling Ukraine’s mobilization crisis.
At least 20,000 foreign mercenaries have fought for Kiev since 2022, Russian diplomat Yulia Zhdanova told the OSCE Forum for Security Co-operation earlier this month, saying most came from the US, UK, Canada, and Georgia.
Moscow has repeatedly pursued criminal cases against foreign fighters fighting for Kiev, including prosecutions in absentia, and has warned that mercenaries are not entitled to prisoner-of-war protections under the Geneva Conventions.

Israel's Foreign Ministry released a statement on Wednesday condemning the Libyan House of Representatives (HoR) for ratifying a maritime jurisdiction memorandum with Turkey.
"Israel strongly condemns the decision of the Libyan House of Representatives to ratify the Maritime Jurisdiction Memorandum between Turkey and Libya. This agreement infringes upon the sovereign rights of our close allies in the region. Regretfully, once again, we see Turkey working to destabilize the eastern Mediterranean region," the ministry wrote on X/Twitter.
Egypt's Foreign Ministry also rejected the deal, saying in a statement that the ratification will have no legal impact on Cairo. The deal approved on Tuesday is part of a years-old dispute over competing claims to sea borders and energy exploration rights in the eastern Mediterranean.
The HoR is the legislative body representing eastern Libya, based out of Benghazi and Tobruk.
HoR backed the maritime deal with Turkey to "bring strategic economic, political, and national security advantages," according to two lawmakers who spoke with Reuters. The backing of the deal overturns a 2020 decision to cut political ties with Ankara.
Control of Libya is split between rival western and eastern administrations, with the east under Libyan National Army Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar. Turkey has in the past been a major backer of the internationally recognized Government of National Accord (GNA) in the west, succeeded by the Government of National Unity, which still holds de facto international recognition and rules from Tripoli.
'Some countries may be upset,' but Libya follows national interest
The maritime deal covering claims in the eastern Mediterranean had been agreed to by the GNA with Turkey in 2019, but was rejected by authorities in eastern Libya, as well as by Egypt and Greece, sparking a boycott.
Libyan lawmaker Tarek al-Jeroushi told Reuters the agreement would strengthen Libya's position as a political, military and economic partner to major powers.
"Some countries may be upset by this agreement, but what matters to us is our national interest," he said.
Lawmaker Aisha al-Tabalqi told Reuters the agreement was approved after specialized committees presented a full and detailed explanation of its provisions.
The parliament unanimously revoked two decisions issued in 2020: one rejecting the ratification of maritime and security memorandums signed by Libya's GNA and Turkey, and another cutting political relations with Ankara.
Greece on Tuesday rejected the decision, saying the deal was without legal effect.
James Genn contributed to this report.

Nvidia announces plug and play Vera Rubin racks that can be shipped on a truck
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:43:49 UTC
21:43:49 KST

Nvidia announced Wednesday a new product that will put seven of its Vera Rubin AI racks into a shipping container, the company's latest effort to move up the stack and offer complete systems for artificial intelligence computing.
The DSX Pod AI Factory is roughly the size of a standard shipping container and weighs about 28,000 kilograms (nearly 62,000 pounds), Nvidia said. It's designed to be shipped on a truck on normal roads and all the cabling and liquid cooling for the Pod are assembled at the factory, the company said.
"The only thing that has to happen when it gets to the site is it's placed in its location, connected to the rest of the other containers, and validated through final burning and testing," Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale computing at Nvidia, said on a call with reporters this week.
The DSX Pod AI factory will reduce the time for a new AI data center to start serving tokens from six months to 14 days, according to the company. Nvidia said the pod is intended for customers worldwide and could help address deployment challenges faced by European customers.
Nvidia did not announce a price for the system, but analysts say a single Vera Rubin rack can cost more than $7 million.
The DSX Pod is a reference design that will ship from Nvidia's manufacturing partners. Nvidia said it was working with manufacturers including Foxconn, Gigabyte, Lenovo, HPE, Quanta and Pegatron. Nvidia expects deliveries to start in early 2027.
Nvidia, once a chip company, now offers networking, storage and other data center needs to its customers. Its AI systems have evolved from single graphics processing unit chips to servers with four or eight GPUs, then to entire racks and now to the DSX Pod, a containerized building block with several racks already integrated.
"What we offer into one gigawatt went from about $18 billion or so per gigawatt, to $20-something billion per gigawatt, to now $40-plus billion per gigawatt," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said recently on a podcast. Gigawatts refer to the size of data center infrastructure by how much power is used. "My sense is that's going to keep going up."

See one of the most iconic meteor showers at its peak this week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:43:17 UTC
21:43:17 KST

Bright flashes of shooting stars are set to streak across the night sky this week as the Orionids meteor shower hits its peak—and if you’re lucky (and patient), you could spot dozens of these meteors.
NASA estimates stargazers might see three to six meteors per hour in suburban areas, with even more shooting stars likely to be seen in rural areas with less light pollution. Night owls can rejoice: the “prime viewing window” will occur after the moon sets around 3 A.M. over the nights of October 21 and October 22, NASA says.
The Orionids’ shooting stars are particularly fast and bright. They travel at around 41 miles per second, and the fastest ones can leave fiery trails of debris in their wake or even ignite into fireballs.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Meteor showers are the beautiful remains of debris trailing from comets and asteroids. As that debris hits our atmosphere, it burns up, creating the light shows we know as meteor showers and love to view. The Orionids gets their name from the constellation Orion because the shower seems to flow from that direction, but that’s not their true origin. These meteors were once part of Halley’s Comet.
The comet sheds rock, dust and ice as it shoots through the solar system. This iconic space rock is visible from Earth once every 75 to 76 years or so—it is famous for its brightness, appearing in historical records stretching back for millennia. Although we won’t see Halley’s again until 2061, the Orionids offer a glimpse of its leftovers.
If you can’t catch the Orionids, look out for a spooky full moon that’s traditionally called the “hunter’s moon” next week, on October 26. Plus, the Taurid meteor showers, which have been shooting across the sky since September, are set to peak next month: you can catch the Southern Taurids’ peak on November 4–5 and the Northern Taurids’ peak on November 11–12.

France Protests: How Fuel Prices, Student Anger are Driving Riots and Unrest

France Protests: How Fuel Prices, Student Anger are Driving Riots and Unrest

====================================================================================================

Why Europe's student protests signal a deeper education crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:40:03 UTC
21:40:03 KST

A wave of youth-led protests has swept across Europe, from France and Belgium to Spain, Portugal, Germany, Italy, Albania, and Greece, reflecting growing frustration among young people who feel the political establishment is increasingly ignoring their educational needs.
The protest in France began at the Saint-Exupéry high school in a Paris suburb before spreading to schools across the country.
French high school students and their peers across Europe have demanded better educational facilities, more teachers, smaller classes and adequate funding and learning resources.
While university students, trade unions, and other parts of French society have backed the protests and consider the demands legitimate, the demonstrations have also been marked by looting and violence, prompting President Emmanuel Macron to call on security forces to restore “calm and order”.
Emmanuel Dupuy, a French political scientist at the Catholic University of Lille, which has also witnessed these protests, says there is "a big difference" between earlier student protests and the violence that erupted over the weekend, when more than 3,000 stores were damaged or looted across France.
Videos also showed Limoges' historic town hall in flames.
While Dupuy describes the latest violent protests as riots, he sees student protests, from high schools to universities, as driven by legitimate demands over poor school conditions, from infrastructure to teacher shortages, and growing concerns about whether their education will help them secure jobs.
"The same sort of resentment" has become a powerful trend not only in France but also among young people in other European countries, the French professor tells TRT World
Beyond France, massive student protests erupted in Italy, with more than 400,000 people participating over the weekend, while similar protests against education budget cuts turned violent in Belgium.
“France reflects a wider European challenge affecting students, teachers and families,” Riyad Rogiest, a Ghent-based Belgian teacher, tells TRT World, referring to a growing education crisis across Europe.
This challenge is “particularly visible in schools serving socially disadvantaged communities”, where problems often accumulate, he adds.
“The anger we see in France is not simply about education budgets. It is also about young people who feel increasingly abandoned by the system.”
Education ‘falls victim’ to economics
Under Macron, a former Rothschild investment banker, the government has cut public spending, reduced corporate taxes and employer social contributions, and replaced the wealth tax with a narrower levy on property assets.
But France continues to face sluggish economic growth and mounting public debt, which reached 119.1 percent of GDP in the second quarter of 2026.
From the COVID-19 crisis to recent US-Europe tensions over NATO defence spending and ongoing escalations in the Strait of Hormuz, which have driven up energy prices, successive crises have put additional pressure on public finances, raising questions about governments' spending priorities, including investment in education.
These policies “have had some consequences and education is one of their victims,” Dupuy tells TRT World, referring to education spending cuts.
He says the current Macron government has not sufficiently considered the need to invest in education.
Dupuy also believes that the French education crisis extends beyond Macron’s governments.
“We haven't sufficiently invested in education over the last 20 years, and we're paying the price for that,” he says. “It has collapsed and is in very poor shape.”
While France and many developed European countries have long been admired by non-Western populations for their educational, economic and political standards, the current protests have shocked many international observers.
This international perception no longer reflects the realities on the ground in Europe, as "a sort of dream land" for non-European education "no longer exists in our countries," says Dupuy.
He also points to how the rise of AI has contributed to the decline of French education.
"New specialities like artificial intelligence are more linked to human resources, or management, which has never been a sort of French excellency," he says, noting that France has traditionally excelled in law and other social sciences.
Like France, other European countries also suffer from "the same reasons of shifting priorities" from education to sectors such as health, defence and AI, Dupuy adds.
"We didn't understand how low our investment was in education. But the situation is now so dire that there was an obligation to improve conditions for the sake of the new generation," he says.
‘Teachers are overwhelmed’
Among other measures, France's draft 2027 budget, which proposes eliminating 1,588 teaching posts in a country already facing overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages, has drawn criticism from teachers' unions amid growing student unrest.
In 2019, Macron's proposed pension reforms sparked widespread protests, adding to public anger after the Yellow Vest movement began in 2018 over fuel tax increases.
Despite continued opposition, Macron's government enacted a new pension reform in 2023, gradually raising the retirement age from 62 to 64, although the timetable was subsequently suspended until 2028.
But Macron’s position has been significantly weakened in recent years, as his decision to call snap elections in 2024 led to a divided parliament and further weakened his centrist allies. Since then, France has seen repeated changes of prime minister, with successive governments struggling to secure parliamentary support.
Amid growing protests, Education Minister Édouard Geffray announced plans to deploy 3,000 substitute teachers to schools facing shortages, a measure backed by Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu.
But experts say this may not resolve the structural problems facing education systems in France and other European countries.
“We are facing a serious teacher shortage, while the teaching profession is becoming less attractive. Teachers are increasingly expected to be educators, psychologists, social workers, mediators and administrators simultaneously. Many experience exhaustion or burnout,” Rogiest says.
On the other hand, many young people carry frustrations from home into the classroom, as financial difficulties, family conflicts, parental separation, social media and a lack of emotional support deeply affect their behaviour and motivation, he adds.
These behavioural problems require additional meetings, administrative reports, and constant follow-up, leaving less time for teaching and personal interaction with students.
In Belgium, for example, new rules introduced in September 2026 require secondary schools, in principle, to organise supervision or alternative activities when lessons are cancelled.
Although limited exceptions exist, Rogiest says this creates additional organisational pressure on teachers.
He also notes that the current digital age makes his job difficult in certain ways, as students are increasingly influenced by social media and constant digital stimulation, which creates unrealistic teaching expectations.
“We expect teachers to solve society's problems inside the classroom, while giving them fewer resources and less time to build relationships with their students,” he says.
“This is neither fair to teachers nor beneficial to children.”
Future of European education
Europe has been facing not only rising inflation, which has increased the cost of living, but also growing political divisions between left-wing and far-right groups, both of which accuse mainstream politics of social and economic problems.
While worsening economic conditions hit classrooms, leading to various cuts in the educational sector, political divisions do not help countries meet the new generation’s demands, exposing deep social insecurity in the new digital age.
“European education has many strengths, but I am deeply concerned about its increasing focus on economic productivity rather than human development,” Rogiest says.
“Historically, we spoke about the humaniora: an educational tradition that sought to develop the whole human being, intellectually, morally, culturally and socially.”
But today, education is increasingly reduced to obtaining qualifications, entering the labour market, becoming economically productive, and paying taxes, he adds.
While earning a decent salary is important for a decent life, education must be much more than professional training, according to Rogiest.
“We should not only ask what profession our students will have, but what kind of human beings they will become.”
From this perspective, Rogiest says the future of European education depends on restoring its human dimension.
“We need smaller classes, better support for teachers, more investment in mental health and stronger cooperation between schools and families.”
While digital education and artificial intelligence offer enormous opportunities, young people “need guidance in developing concentration, discipline, empathy, responsibility and critical thinking,” he says.
Without these fundamental skills, modern technologies will help students little, he adds. This also requires restoring the dignity and attractiveness of the teaching profession.
“Education should not simply produce skilled workers for the economy,” Rogiest tells TRT World.
“It should develop responsible, compassionate and thoughtful human beings who can contribute positively to society. That is the educational vision Europe needs to rediscover.”

Ukraine’s MFA says Lviv Regional Council’s UPA decision counterproductive
The Ukrainian Foreign Ministry said this in response to a query from journalists, Ukrinform reports.
The ministry noted that in recent years, significant progress had been made in developing the strategic partnership with Poland, conducting search and exhumation efforts, and establishing a historical dialogue. Defense cooperation has also been developing.
“In this context, we consider the recent decision by the Lviv Regional Council, which touches on sensitive historical issues on the bilateral agenda, counterproductive to our current efforts aimed at further developing Ukrainian-Polish relations, resolving problematic issues amid Russia’s full-scale aggression and unprecedented security threats to our two countries and the region as a whole,” the Foreign Ministry said.
The ministry stressed that the decision was adopted by a local government body and that the lawmakers had not consulted the Foreign Ministry or other central government bodies before the vote to assess the possible consequences for bilateral relations with Poland.
The Foreign Ministry said it believes that the strategic partnership between Ukraine and Poland requires restraint, predictability, professional and open dialogue, and confidence-building, while political decisions by regional local government bodies should not harm Ukraine’s national interests, particularly in the areas of security and European integration.
At the same time, Ukraine called on Poland to refrain from drastic steps that could undermine the trend toward normalization of bilateral relations.
“For our part, we reaffirm our commitment to resolving all problematic issues in bilateral relations constructively through diplomatic channels and in the spirit of good neighborly relations,” the Foreign Ministry said.
As reported by Ukrinform, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk criticized the recent decision by the Lviv Regional Council to declare 2027 the Year of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and Roman Shukhevych, saying that such actions harm Ukraine itself and complicate Polish-Ukrainian cooperation.

21:40:00 KST

On October 4, Taliban officials inaugurated the 121-kilometer-long Wakhan Transit Road connecting Afghanistan to China via the Wakhan Corridor after approximately three years of construction work. The road stretches from Afghanistan’s Broghil border area, on the Afghanistan-Pakistan border, along Badakhshan province’s Wakhan district, finally reaching the border with China. According to Afghanistan’s de facto government under the Taliban, beyond China, the road will connect the country with third parties like Central Asian countries and global markets.
This corridor is expected to play a significant role for Afghanistan’s trade as well as its regional transit. Its opening marks an important milestone for the Taliban since the corridor was ignored for years due to security concerns.
A remote region in northeast Afghanistan, the Wakhan Corridor is 350 kilometers long and 13 to 65 km wide. The corridor, which shares borders with Pakistan (through the Durand Line, which the Taliban has started referring to as a “hypothetical” line), Tajikistan, and China, was created as a buffer zone between the Russian and British empires in 1895-96 when the Anglo-Russian Boundary Commission awarded the area to Afghanistan. Once a part of the famous Silk Road trade route, the Wakhan Corridor has been closed for regular transit for almost a century now.
Taliban Minister of Rural Rehabilitation and Development Abdul Latif Mansour, speaking at the inauguration ceremony, said that the road held “political, economic, and strategic significance” for Afghanistan. “The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan has prioritized such public projects, especially in provinces that are most in need,” Mansour said, according to Tolo News. He further emphasized the homegrown nature of the project, saying, “There are no foreign engineers or advisers; all the engineers are Afghans.”
Governor of Badakhshan Rahmatullah Najib highlighted the road’s opening as a milestone. “After 45 years of war in the country, the Afghan people are witnessing the completion of such a major project in one of Afghanistan’s most remote areas,” Tolo News paraphrased Najib as saying.
This project is said to have cost 365 million Afghanis ($5.6 million) and was funded by the Taliban’s Ministry of Rural Rehabilitation and Development.
According to Afghanistan’s Deputy Prime Minister for Economic Affairs’ website, this trade route will benefit Afghanistan by providing direct access to imports from and exports to China. The minister highlighted that China is Afghanistan’s largest trading partner, with annual trade exceeding $1 billion between the two countries. The website claimed that the Wakhan Corridor is now the “closest, safest, and most reliable” route for China to export its goods not only to Afghanistan, but to the Central Asian countries, and beyond: to the Arab world, Turkiye, Iran, and the European countries.
That assumption is questionable; China has direct borders with three Central Asian countries – Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan – and has invested millions in upgrading its trade and transit infrastructure to the region. China already has well-developed rail links with Kazakhstan. The Khorgos Gateway, which opened for operations in 2012 on the China-Kazakhstan border, is the world’s largest dry port. And construction on the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan (CKU) railway is underway. It’s unclear why China would choose to route exports to Central Asia via Afghanistan.
The benefits for Afghanistan are more obvious. Due to the ongoing conflict between Afghanistan and Pakistan, trade across their border has come to a halt. That cuts off landlocked Afghanistan’s primary trade and transit route for reaching third countries. If the Wakhan Corridor route becomes fully operational, it will provide an alternative route for Afghanistan to trade with the regional countries, particularly with China. Afghanistan could then connect directly with China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), rather than linking itself to the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) as previously discussed.
In 2016, Afghanistan – then under the Republic government – and China signed a memorandum of understanding to integrate Afghanistan into the BRI. The following year in December, foreign ministers from Afghanistan, China, and Pakistan agreed to discuss ways to extend the CPEC to Afghanistan. In 2023, Afghanistan – now ruled by the Taliban – again reiterated its intention to join CPEC. This was also discussed during last year’s trilateral foreign ministers’ dialogue in Kabul. However, there has been no further progress in this regard due to the ongoing conflict between Pakistan and Afghanistan.
The Taliban government views the new road via the Wakhan Corridor as an opportunity to lessen Pakistan’s leverage. Islamabad has a history of closing the border crossings between the countries, affecting trade and inflicting heavy losses on Afghanistan’s economy. Thus, the de facto regime is jubilant with the inauguration of the Wakhan transit road.
As per Afghanistan’s Deputy Minister for Economic Affairs’ website, “With the opening of the Wakhan Corridor, Afghanistan will be forever freed from the pressure of neighboring countries, which often exploit the Karachi route, Gwadar Port, and Chabahar for political purposes and cause heavy financial losses to our traders and compatriots every year.”
Even though the inauguration of the route is expected to alleviate the transportation challenges for the residents of Pamir and Wakhan, its role as a trans-regional route, or even just connecting Afghanistan to China, seems to be a distant dream.
Despite the Taliban regime’s completion of the road, China still has not opened its border with Afghanistan, arguably due to security concerns vis-à-vis the crossing. Moreover, China neither sent its representative to the inaugural ceremony on October 4, nor did it acknowledge the road’s completion diplomatically.
China built the road that the Taliban’s Wakhan transit road aimed to link up with over a decade ago. The goal wasn’t to increase trade, but to secure its militarized border with Afghanistan by advancing access for its armed patrols. The Taliban refer to the transit route as a trading link to gain access to Chinese markets; Chinese media refers to this approximately 76-kilometer-long border as a “major counterterrorism front line.” This media framing aligns with Chinese officials’ narrative that Uyghurs in the region have frequently visited the corridor in order to “return to Xinjiang for Jihad.”
China’s major security concern in Afghanistan is the potential threat from the members of the East Turkestan Islamic Movement (ETIM), a group that seeks self-determination for the Uyghurs and independence of Xinjiang province from the Chinese government.
According to some estimates, there are over 3,000 Uyghurs living in Afghanistan. China has asked the Taliban to ensure that Uyghur separatists would not be allowed to use Afghan soil as a base for their activities in Xinjiang. Besides this, China wants the Taliban to extradite Uyghurs affiliated with ETIM to China.
China’s lukewarm reaction to the Taliban’s completion of the Wakhan transit route emanates mainly from its security concerns. Until the Taliban completely secure the route and convince Beijing that it will not be used as a route by ETIM members to infiltrate Xinjiang, the use of the Wakhan Corridor as a trade route between the two countries will remain a distant dream.

The US Army Looks to the Pacific – and Space – for Future Relevance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:38:00 UTC
21:38:00 KST

The U.S. Army sees its future as preparing for a fight in the Pacific, and it’s taking lessons from both the current fight in the Middle East and Russia’s ongoing war with Ukraine. In addition to missiles, drones, and electronic warfare, that means an increasing presence for the land service in the space domain. The effort represents an attempt by the Army to maintain its relevance under geographical constraints that are less than ideal, and in an institutional context that increasingly favors long-range, high-end unmanned systems.
Both the U.S. Navy and the U.S. Air Force have experienced embarrassing setbacks in the present war against Iran, the former because of an overcommitment of its aircraft carrier fleet and the latter because of the loss of several key assets in combat. Nevertheless, both services have contributed immensely to ongoing operations. The contribution of the U.S. Army has been more limited and less visible, in large part because of the reluctance of the Trump administration to develop serious plans for an invasion of Iran.
Given the geography and the strategic issues at stake, a war in the Pacific is likely to resemble the Iran War much more than the Wars on Terror, which highlighted the Army’s strengths. Given this, Army leadership has focused on developing tools to contribute to a potential fight against China. The most recent and notable of these efforts is the stand up of a new Indo-Pacific task force, designed to conduct long-range missile combat and defeat area denial networks. The 4th Multi Domain Task Force is expected to integrate long-range strike with intelligence gathering and air defense capabilities in an effort to threaten and defeat efforts to impede the entry of the U.S. Navy and the U.S. Air Force into the Western Pacific. The 7th Infantry Division Multi-Domain Command has concentrated on developing plans for long-range drone and electronic warfare (EW) combat in the Western Pacific, assisted by AI tools that will manage data flow and the sequencing of targets.
These efforts build upon the Army’s work to establish itself in space and to institutionalize networked warfare. Space assets act as the connective tissue for all of the elements that the Army is attempting to integrate into a cohesive whole with a standard operational logic. The steadily increasing profile of the U.S. Space Force complicates the institutional landscape by creating overlapping claims of bureaucratic authority.
All of this is an artifact of the way that the U.S. military does business. Although the geography of the Western Pacific (like the Persian Gulf) favors air and sea power, the Army must be involved because its funding and future depend on its ability to contribute in critical sectors. That Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has made reforming the Army’s senior leadership a focus of his tenure only makes the situation more urgent for the organization. In a sense, what the Army is preparing to fight in the Western Pacific in order to preserve its ability to fight in the halls of Congress and the Pentagon.
Arguably, the Army’s relatively low level of commitment in the Middle East may work to the Army’s advantage, as it can commit its focus and attention to fighting the next fight instead of an intractable slog against Iran. But new technological realities always require time, experience, and a careful negotiation with institutional reality. Whether Hegseth’s Army is capable of that negotiation remains open to question.

Hungary is considering replacing Rosatom in the Paks nuclear power plant expansion project - media

Hungary is considering replacing Rosatom in the Paks nuclear power plant expansion project - media
Kyiv • UNN
Hungary is studying alternatives to Rosatom for the expansion of the Paks nuclear power plant. A final decision is expected at the end of this year or at the beginning of next year.
Hungary is considering replacing Russia’s "Rosatom" as the general contractor for the expansion of the "Paks" Nuclear Power Plant and has already begun examining options involving alternative suppliers as part of a review of the project. This was reported by two informed sources, according to UNN, citing Reuters.
Details
The publication notes that the project, which Viktor Orbán awarded to "Rosatom" in 2014 without a tender, is politically sensitive and extremely expensive. The situation is further complicated by the fact that in August, drought brought the plant’s operating reactors to the brink of shutdown.
The expansion of the "Paks" Nuclear Power Plant is "Rosatom’s" largest nuclear project in the European Union—especially after Finland terminated its contract with the Russian company in May 2022. Since then, the parties have been involved in legal disputes.
During Orbán’s tenure, Hungary opposed any sanctions against Russia’s nuclear energy sector.
The government of Prime Minister Péter Magyar (who won a convincing victory in the April election) is expected to make a final decision on the expansion of the "Paks" Nuclear Power Plant later this year or early next year.
The project’s cost, initially estimated at €12.5 billion, had already cost Hungary more than €2 billion ($2.24 billion) by the time the first concrete was poured in February.
Asked whether this could lead to a change of general contractor, a source familiar with the project review said that all possible scenarios were being considered.
According to the source, the review will analyze the legal, technical, financial and time-related consequences of changing the supplier, as well as assess the project’s financial viability.
In addition
According to Reuters, the initial contract with "Rosatom" has already been amended five times; a sixth version of the amendments was prepared but never signed.
Another obstacle was a decision by the European Court of Justice (the EU’s highest court), which annulled the European Commission’s approval of state aid for the project. A second source close to the administration said that the government "is leaning toward the conclusion that the expansion of the \"Paks\" Nuclear Power Plant is necessary," but believes that "Rosatom" should not participate in it.
Nuclear energy can provide substantial amounts of baseload electricity with almost no carbon emissions. However, nuclear power plants usually require large volumes of cooling water, making them vulnerable to droughts and heatwaves—phenomena that are becoming increasingly frequent as a result of climate change.
Despite the high cost and complexity, Hungary’s pro-European government strongly supports the development of nuclear energy. It is necessary for the country to meet growing electricity demand, as well as to balance an energy system that uses intermittent renewable energy sources.
"Nuclear energy and its associated industrial value chains have enormous potential—including at the European level—to guarantee and strengthen our own capacities," said Zsuzsa Beres, Deputy State Secretary at the Ministry of Economy and Energy, responsible for nuclear energy and international relations.
"In the future, we will continue to rely heavily on nuclear energy," she said at a conference held last week.
As a temporary measure while awaiting the expansion of the "Paks" Nuclear Power Plant, Budapest is considering seeking permission to extend the operating life of the plant’s four existing Russian-made reactors by 20 years. Their licenses expire between 2032 and 2037.
Context
Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, EU member states reduced their imports of Russian oil and gas.
However, Rosatom managed to avoid EU sanctions. According to the World Nuclear Association, in 2025 Russia supplied around 23% of the EU’s uranium enrichment services and 16% of its natural uranium supplies.
If, following the government review, a decision is made that is unfavorable to Rosatom, Hungary may have to cover the €1.1 billion already paid to the Russian corporation, as well as pay penalties for breaching the contract terms.
The sources did not name any potential new suppliers, although one of them noted that bringing in a European supplier would simplify the foreign-policy situation and matters related to sanctions. At the same time, the difficulties associated with managing the project would remain unchanged.
Earlier this month, speaking to journalists in Moscow, Rosatom CEO Alexei Likhachev said that the company was awaiting the completion of the review being conducted by the Hungarian side.
He also said that he had approached the new Hungarian government with a proposal to hold talks, but had not yet received a response.

The European Investment Bank (EIB) Group is providing EUR 60 million in financing to Ukraine to modernize checkpoints on the country's western border, the EIB press service told Interfax-Ukraine.
"Ukraine's border crossing points are gateways to the EU, connecting businesses, people and markets. Removing each bottleneck means faster freight deliveries, stronger supply chains and greater opportunities for Ukrainian businesses. These investments are aimed at strengthening Ukraine's economic resilience and bringing it closer to the EU," EIB Vice President Karl Nehammer said, announcing the signing of the loan agreement during his visit to Ukraine.
The EIB Group funding will be used to equip terminals and buildings, including waiting areas, service and sanitary facilities and canopies, improve access roads, and purchase equipment and software for customs control at Ukraine's borders with the European Union and Moldova. The project is expected to increase capacity, reduce trade costs and facilitate the safe movement of goods and people between Ukraine, the EU and Moldova.
The EIB Group is providing the financing as a loan to the Ukrainian government through the Ministry for Communities, Territories and Infrastructure Development of Ukraine.
"Modernizing the infrastructure at our border checkpoints is a priority. With financing from the EIB Group, we will increase capacity, reduce delays and strengthen key logistics routes connecting Ukraine with the EU and Moldova. These investments will contribute to our economic recovery and further integration into the European transport network," Deputy Minister for Communities, Territories and Infrastructure Development Mykola Kalashnyk said.
The project is the first under the Security and Connectivity Initiative launched by the EIB, the European Commission and the Ukrainian government. The initiative aims to accelerate Ukraine's strategic investments in transport, energy and digital infrastructure, ensuring reliable and efficient connections between Ukraine and the EU.
The loan announced on Tuesday is part of coordinated efforts under the Team Europe approach. The European Commission is providing a guarantee for EIB Group financing under the Ukraine Investment Framework (UIF).
The EUR 60 million loan is also expected to be supplemented by a EUR 6 million EU investment grant and EUR 2.5 million in EU technical assistance to support project implementation.
The planned modernization of Ukrainian border checkpoints concerns roads forming part of the European Union's priority Trans-European Transport Network (TEN-T). The State Agency for Restoration and Infrastructure Development of Ukraine will implement the project.
The EIB Group has operated in Ukraine since 2007. Following Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, it significantly increased financial support for the country's resilience and modernization. Since then, EIB financing for Ukraine has exceeded EUR 4.5 billion.
Through the EU for Ukraine (EU4U) initiative and its key role in implementing a dedicated component of the Ukraine Facility, the EIB is committed to scaling up and accelerating its activities. This is in line with the mandate set by EU leaders and is being carried out in close cooperation with the European Commission, the European Parliament, EU member states and international partners.

Russian Su-30 fighter jet crashes in Kaliningrad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

12:36:00 UTC
21:36:00 KST

- A Russian Su-30SM fighter crashed during a training flight in Kaliningrad’s Chernyakhovsk district, between the villages of Timofeyevka and Zelyony Bor.
- Both pilots ejected, were injured and were taken to a military hospital.
A Russian Su-30SM fighter jet crashed during a training flight in the Chernyakhovsk district of Russia’s Kaliningrad region, coming down between the villages of Timofeyevka and Zelyony Bor, and both pilots ejected before impact.
The two crew members were injured and taken to a military hospital, and Russian outlets published the first details of the crash, including the location of the wreckage.
The Chernyakhovsk district lies in the east of the Russian exclave, which sits on the Baltic coast between NATO members Poland and Lithuania and is home to the headquarters of Russia’s Baltic Fleet. The area hosts a military air base used by Baltic Fleet naval aviation, which operates Su-30SM fighters alongside other combat aircraft, and the jets regularly fly training sorties over the region and the Baltic Sea.
The Su-30SM is a two-seat multirole fighter built by Irkut, part of the state-owned United Aircraft Corporation, and it serves with both the Russian Aerospace Forces and Russian Naval Aviation in air defense, strike and maritime attack roles. Its two-seat cockpit carries a pilot and a weapon systems officer, both equipped with ejection seats, which allowed the crew to escape the aircraft before it hit the ground.
The crash is the latest in a series of Su-30 losses in noncombat flights over the past year. In April, a Su-30 went down in Crimea during a scheduled training flight, the Russian Defense Ministry said at the time, and in November 2025 a Su-30 crashed in the Prionezhsky district of Karelia, killing both crew members.
Russia’s Su-30 fleet has been flying at a high tempo since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, both in combat missions over Ukraine and the Black Sea and in training and patrol flights elsewhere, and Russian Naval Aviation has lost several of the jets during that period. A commission will investigate the cause of the Kaliningrad crash, with technical failure and pilot error typically among the first lines of inquiry in Russian military aviation accidents.

A train was delayed by a solar storm. But something didn't add up.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:35:57 UTC
21:35:57 KST

A train was delayed by a solar storm. But something didn't add up.
- Date:
- October 21, 2026
- Source:
- RMIT University
- Summary:
- Scientists have cracked a 178-year-old mystery surrounding a train delayed by a solar storm, revealing that the famous incident happened in 1848 rather than 1841. The discovery rewrites the early history of space weather and highlights a threat that still endangers modern power grids, satellites, and communication systems.
- Share:
A mysterious train delay nearly 180 years ago has led scientists to uncover a surprising mistake in the history of space weather. An international research team has solved a 178-year-old mystery involving one of the earliest documented cases of solar activity interfering with electrical technology.
The incident dates back to the 1840s, when electric telegraph networks were beginning to transform long-distance communication. As these early systems expanded, operators occasionally encountered strange electrical disturbances that could disrupt their equipment. Scientists now understand that some of these problems were caused by changes in Earth's magnetic field triggered by activity on the Sun.
Researchers led by Lancaster University have revisited a historical account of a train delayed in Exeter, England, when solar activity interfered with the railway's telegraph system. The investigation involved scientists from RMIT University, the British Geological Survey, Natural Resources Canada, Baylor University, and the UK's national space laboratory, RAL Space.
By piecing together historical documents and scientific observations, the team uncovered an error that changes the timeline of the earliest known technological disruptions caused by space weather.
How Solar Storms First Disrupted Technology
One of history's most dramatic examples of space weather affecting technology occurred in 1859. Known as the Carrington Event, the powerful solar storm involved a massive solar flare and a coronal mass ejection, an enormous eruption of charged particles and magnetic fields from the Sun.
The resulting disturbances produced spectacular auroras, commonly known as the northern lights, that appeared as far south as Hawaii and Central America. In some locations, the sky glowed brightly enough for people to read newspapers at night. The unusual illumination even fooled gold miners into thinking morning had arrived, prompting them to prepare breakfast shortly after midnight.
The storm also wreaked havoc on telegraph networks around the world. Electrical surges caused equipment failures, sent sparks flying from wires, shocked operators, and even started fires. In some cases, the electrical currents generated by the disturbance were so powerful that telegraph systems continued operating without batteries.
Although the Carrington Event remains the most famous example from this period, evidence of solar activity interfering with electrical systems stretches back even further.
In 1871, an anonymous author published an account in the scientific journal Nature describing a "very intense magnetic disturbance" that supposedly occurred on October 18, 1841. According to the report, the disturbance interfered with railway signals in Exeter and delayed the scheduled 10:05 p.m. train departure by 16 minutes.
If the date had been correct, the event would have represented the earliest known instance of space weather disrupting human technology.
However, a new investigation published in the American Geophysical Union journal Space Weather has revealed that the original account contained a significant historical error.
The Railway Mystery That Changed Solar Storm History
Associate Professor Brett Carter, a space weather researcher at RMIT University, helped investigate the historical records. During the investigation, the team noticed a problem that immediately called the original timeline into question.
The Exeter-to-Starcross railway line mentioned in the report did not open until 1846, almost five years after the event supposedly occurred.
"In this study, we effectively investigated what had to be a typo in a Nature paper from 1871. We know it was a typo because the Exeter-to-Starcross train line mentioned in that paper didn't exist until 1846, which is 5 years afterwards," he said.
To establish when the train delay actually happened, the researchers examined a wide range of historical evidence. They compared railway timetables and newspaper reports with observations of solar activity, accounts of auroras, and digitized measurements of Earth's magnetic field.
Together, these records pointed to a different date: October 18, 1848, exactly seven years later than originally reported.
The revised timeline resolves the apparent contradiction and places the incident during an important period in technological history, when electrical communication systems were becoming increasingly widespread.
Carter explained that the 1840s marked a turning point in humanity's relationship with space weather. Solar disturbances had always occurred, but the emergence of electrical technology meant that their effects could now interfere directly with everyday human activities.
"Understanding this historical event is important because the 1840s mark the intersection between the rise of our technological age and space weather, which has always been around," Carter says.
"Since this line was crossed, humans have not looked back."
The findings also change the incident's place in the historical record. Although the Exeter disruption remains one of the earliest credible examples of space weather affecting technology, it can no longer be considered the first.
That distinction now belongs to an earlier documented incident involving telegraph interference on Britain's Midland Railway in March 1847.
Why the 178-Year-Old Discovery Matters
Professor Jim Wild of Lancaster University, who led the study, said the findings demonstrate that the dangers associated with space weather began affecting society long before the development of modern power grids, satellites, and electronic communication networks.
"What this research highlights is that space weather is not a new threat but a long-standing natural hazard. Society has been experiencing the effects of space weather on technology for almost as long as electrical technologies have existed," Wild said.
The Exeter incident is especially significant because it occurred when electrical technology was still in its infancy. Early railway operators were beginning to rely on telegraph systems, creating new opportunities for solar disturbances to interfere with essential infrastructure.
"The Exeter train delay is a fascinating story because it sits right at the point where emerging technologies first began to encounter the realities of the space environment. By combining historical archives with scientific observations, we've been able to show that the event almost certainly happened in 1848 rather than 1841.
"Although this means it is not the earliest recorded space weather impact, it remains one of the first clear examples of solar activity disrupting critical infrastructure," he said.
The investigation also shows how historical scientific records can be used alongside newspapers and other archival materials to reconstruct events that occurred long before modern monitoring instruments became available.
"It also demonstrates the value of combining scientific records with contemporary newspaper reports and archival documents when reconstructing historic space weather events."
Dr. Mike Hapgood, a Visiting Scientist and space weather expert at the UK's national space laboratory, RAL Space, described the research process as something resembling a detective investigation.
"It highlights the importance of preserving these older records, which give us the evidence base we need to interpret past events and strengthen future predictions," he said.
Modern Technology Still Faces the Threat of Solar Storms
Almost two centuries after the Exeter train delay, solar storms continue to pose risks to railways and other essential infrastructure. The technologies involved have changed dramatically, but they remain susceptible to disturbances originating from the Sun.
Today, space weather can interfere with electrical power systems, railway signaling equipment, satellite navigation, and communication networks. Powerful solar events can disturb Earth's magnetic field, potentially generating unwanted electrical currents in infrastructure and affecting systems that depend on reliable satellite signals.
Scientists now have far more sophisticated instruments and forecasting methods than were available in the 19th century. However, Hapgood emphasized that modern society's growing dependence on interconnected electrical and space technologies also creates new vulnerabilities.
Understanding how past solar storms affected infrastructure can help researchers assess the dangers posed by future events and develop better ways to reduce potential disruptions.
"Deepening our understanding of these events is essential for preparing for, and mitigating, the impacts of space weather - especially as we look forward to a decade of exciting space developments that will face the challenge of a new solar cycle in the 2030s," he said.

A Design Flaw in Share Links Exposes Users’ Personal Conversations With Meta’s Muse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:35:00 UTC
21:35:00 KST

Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through web links, researchers reported Monday. In response to questions from Ars about the behavior, Meta said it’s suspending the sharing feature while the company reviews it and considers making changes.
Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed.
Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. After opening a few hundred of them, the researchers found information that was clearly not intended to be publicly available, including:
- a candidate’s notes preparing for a confidential executive-search call with a frontier AI lab, naming the lab’s internal contact and the meeting time;
- a national marketing company’s internal revenue review, marked for its CEO;
- a small-business owner’s loan application, with the amount requested;
- a to-do list that included a bank fraud alert, with a partial account number and a transaction amount and time;
- a real-estate investor’s internal performance report, with two property addresses and exact return, income, and mortgage figures;
- a workplace’s full-year staff vacation calendar, listing dozens of employees against the week each one would be away;
“If you had asked us beforehand, we would have guessed that gathering these would take real effort,” the researchers wrote. “It took one query.”
In an emailed statement responding to questions from Ars, Meta said: “We opened the Muse bug bounty program so researchers could raise different scenarios and help us continue improving the product. People have the ability to share specific Muse artifacts, which creates a page that can be accessed by those with the link. However, we’ve paused this functionality while we review this report and consider changes to how these links can be discovered.”
Asaf Aprozper, a cofounder and CTO of Claroc, said he reported the findings through Meta’s bug bounty program on October 8 and also tried reaching people at Meta on LinkedIn but got no reply either way.
The easiest way to discover the URLs is to perform a passive DNS search through one of many available commercial services. Passive DNS records store the historical resolution of domain names to IP addresses, as well as nameserver, and mail-server records over time. Passive DNS systems typically collect DNS responses from sensors positioned at recursive DNS resolvers or other infrastructure. A passive DNS record is generally created when a monitoring system observes a DNS response. In the case here, once the intended party clicks on the share link, the DNS information is recorded in a searchable database.
Claroc researchers were able to discover the Muse share links because all of them use the domain name cf.metaaiusercontent.com. Discovery is further made easy by the decision to add the conversation name to the URL, along with a long string of text. Simplified examples of such links are home-sale-budget-9f21c8a3.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, q3-revenue-review-7b1e42f0.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, and loan-application-draft-a4c9e2.cf.metaaiusercontent.com. It’s this last design decision, putting the conversation title in the subdomain rather than in the URL path, that makes public discovery possible.
“Plenty of AI assistants share by public link,” Claroc said. “What makes Muse’s shares easy to find is the title sitting inside the web address, where public DNS records it for anyone to search. We call these GhostShares: pages that open for people who were never handed the link, and that those people can find on their own.”
Muse quickly catapulted to one of the top spots in Apple’s App Store. The assistant autonomously fills out forms, books appointments, makes purchases, creates documents, and carries out all kinds of other actions. To work as intended, Muse requires access to most of a user’s accounts. Meta has heavily marketed the assistant as a platform that’s worthy of the extraordinary trust it needs to work as intended.
Three weeks after the Muse launch, macOS security expert Patrick Wardle discovered a zero-day vulnerability that allowed any other app installed on the same device to gain complete control of the user’s Muse account. Meta downplayed the severity of the vulnerability on the grounds that exploitation wasn’t possible unless a device was already compromised. The company didn’t acknowledge Wardle’s finding that a simple ClickFix attack was all that was needed to hijack an account. The ease in discovering share links further justifies asking if Muse is worthy of the access it requires.
With Meta’s suspension of the feature, Muse users no longer face this particular threat, at least for now.
This story originally appeared on Ars Technica.
