Energy secretary leaning towards rejecting Rosebank oilfield
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:31:05 UTC
21:31:05 KST

Miatta Fahnbulleh is minded to reject the giant Rosebank oilfield, sources have told the Guardian, in what would be a blow for the North Sea energy industry and a major victory for climate campaigners.
After approving the smaller Jackdaw gasfield on Wednesday, officials say the energy secretary is leaning towards refusing approval for what would be one of the biggest oilfields in the North Sea.
But she could still be overruled by Andy Burnham, who may hear different representations from the chancellor, John Healey. A final decision is expected before the end of this year.
In comments that will be read as a signal of her intent, Fahnbulleh told the Guardian that the rationale behind Jackdaw did not apply to Rosebank, saying the UK would rely on gas as it made the transition to net zero and that it would be better to take it from relatively low-carbon sources in the North Sea than importing it.
“One is a gasfield that caters for the domestic market, while the other is an oilfield that is mainly for export,” she said. “It is right that we judge each application in its own right, and it is absolutely critical that the decision is consistent with our climate obligations, our carbon budgets and the end destination we need to get to with the energy transition.”
In contrast, Healey told ITV he expected “oil and gas” revenues to contribute to a new energy wealth fund, a suggestion he is anticipating new oil revenues. Burnham would be expected to make the final call if there is conflict on the decision.
Labour MPs warned on Wednesday there would be a major pushback in the party if Rosebank was approved, though most are prepared to accept the arguments that Jackdaw was a necessity as part of the transition to net zero.
MPs are understood to have discussed ways of forcing or encouraging a parliamentary vote on Rosebank should it be approved, as a way of expressing dissent.
Officials say Fahnbulleh has not yet taken a final decision on Rosebank. The field would emit about seven times the carbon of Jackdaw and Fahnbulleh is understood to believe that it would do less for UK energy security, given most of the oil would be exported.
A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “This is speculation. As the energy secretary has said, each project will be assessed on its own merits.”
On a visit to Aberdeen, Fahnbulleh said she had been satisfied that Jackdaw, which is due to begin producing gas within weeks and will add an estimated 36m tonnes of carbon emissions, would not violate the UK’s climate commitments.
“As we make the transition, we are going to need gas,” she said. “At a point when we have got conflict in the Middle East that is triggering an energy crisis, energy security is vital, and homegrown energy is key.”
She admitted, however, it would not help achieve the government’s main energy target of bringing down bills, saying: “This is not about bills.”
The UN Environment Programme has recommended that global carbon emissions be cut by nearly a fifth in the next four years, and by close to half within a decade, to avoid overshooting climate targets by a disastrous margin.
The Jackdaw announcement could boost Labour’s position in north-east Scotland, where much of the industry is based and where unions have been campaigning heavily for the permits to be granted.
But it is likely to cause angst among some Labour MPs, especially those in seats where they face a challenge from the Green party.
One Labour MP close to the energy secretary said she knew her credibility was “on the line” and that she was able to show she was pragmatic by approving Jackdaw but drawing the line at Rosebank. “She’s putting up a fight and I want to be supportive of Miatta – I understand what she is fighting,” they said.
But they said the decision would ultimately come down to Burnham. “Andy is not a climate guy – he is under pressure. If he wants to do it, he’ll do it.”
Several serving ministers have said they would find Rosebank a more difficult decision to back and it would cause greater problems in their constituencies.
The former minister Catherine West said climate change “is not a future threat but a present reality” and that the answer to job losses in the North Sea was not to “double down on new fossil fuel developments”.
Afzal Khan, the Labour MP for Manchester Rusholme and chair of the all-party parliamentary group on climate change, said: “Approving projects on the scale of Rosebank, on top of today’s decision to approve Jackdaw, cannot be justified.”
Burnham is seeking more ways to lower energy bills, telling MPs on Wednesday that ministers would consider whether standing charges could be removed from gas bills to ease cost pressures on households.
While Labour’s 2024 election manifesto committed to a ban on new drilling licences in the North Sea, the companies behind Jackdaw and Rosebank oilfield project have sought approval for existing licences.
The Greens said on Wednesday they intended to fight seats directly on the issue of Jackdaw and Rosebank. The Green MP Carla Denyer said: “We have identified dozens of seats where we are Labour’s main challenger and the climate is one of the top issues and voters have been mobilised by the heatwave and wildfires.
“Our strong advice to Labour MPs is to stand up to Andy Burnham and his act of climate violence, both to save your seats and, far more importantly, to protect the planet for future generations.”
Fahnbulleh has promised that future revenues from the North Sea will be spent on green energy projects through a new energy wealth fund. She said the fund would be given £2bn in the budget.
“When we have tax revenues that are coming from the oil and gas industry, it is right that we invest that in the transition we need to make in energy,” she said, adding that the money would be spent on renewables, nuclear and other clean energy schemes.
However, she could not say exactly which tax revenues would be given to the new fund, or how much that might generate. “The chancellor will make those details clear in the budget,” she said.

5 indicted over China-linked attack on Taiwanese comedian

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — New Taipei prosecutors indicted five men Wednesday for allegedly carrying out a car attack on comedian Huang Yi-hao (黃逸豪) under orders from a person in China.
CNA reported that an individual in China known as "K" allegedly offered NT$450,000 (US$14,000) to arrange the attack. Prosecutors said K was upset by Huang's performances mocking the Chinese Communist Party.
A suspect surnamed Cheng (鄭) was hired to gather Huang's personal information and arrange an attack that would leave him hospitalized. The goal was to prevent Huang from performing at Taipei's Comedy Club on Sept. 20, per Taisounds.
Between July and August, Cheng allegedly attached a GPS tracker to Huang's scooter and monitored his movements. He collected the comedian's home address, license plate number, and daily routines before sending the information to K and receiving NT$250,000.
Cheng then worked with a man surnamed Yu (游) to stage a traffic accident intended to break Huang's arms or legs. Yu recruited a man surnamed Huang (黃), who brought in Fan (范) and Liao (廖) to carry out the attack.
On Sept. 11, the three men waited near the comedian's home in New Taipei. Fan alerted the driver, Huang, when the comedian returned, while Liao filmed from the passenger seat as the car struck him.
Prosecutors said the driver stopped after hearing the comedian scream in pain. Huang Yi-hao suffered bruising to his right pelvis but escaped serious injury, per PTS News.
After the attack, three suspects allegedly obtained the comedian's medical records by claiming they were helping with an insurance claim. They sent images of the records to K, who refused to pay the remaining NT$200,000 because the injuries were not serious enough.
Prosecutors charged all five men with attempted serious bodily injury and violations of the Personal Data Protection Act. Cheng also faces a charge of unlawfully recording another person's private activities.
Prosecutors sought prison terms of at least five years and six months for Cheng and five years for Yu. They also recommended at least four years for the suspect surnamed Huang, three years and six months for Fan, and two years and seven months for Liao.
The case followed a May 29 attack on Taipei's Comedy Club, where Huang was scheduled to perform material mocking Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Taipei prosecutors previously indicted two men for allegedly throwing paint and feces at the venue under instructions from China.
New Taipei prosecutors described the latest attack as another suspected case of China's cross-border repression of government critics. They warned that such violence threatened public safety and freedom of expression.

France and Italy blame foreign powers for riots – but where's the evidence?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:30:09 UTC
21:30:09 KST

There is so far no evidence that foreign powers caused Europe’s riots, only that they exploited them, despite politicians blaming online manipulation for them. Brussels has refused to act, citing a lack of evidence.
There is no conclusive evidence that foreign powers fuelled riots in France, Italy and other European countries through social media, although some have exploited the unrest to push their own narratives.
The European Commission has faced pressure to act against suspected disinformation campaigns by countries such as Russia, but has so far held back, citing a lack of evidence.
“There is no evidence of foreign interference in the events that took place. However, there has been foreign manipulation of information in the aftermath; that much is true,” French President Emmanuel Macron told reporters on the sidelines of his visit to Qatar.
“But there are many people who have sought to exploit the situation. There are people campaigning at France’s expense,” he said.
The distinction matters. Other European officials have gone further, blaming foreign powers for the unrest that has gripped cities in France, Italy, Belgium and Spain.
Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto said at a conference on Tuesday that the riots in Milan were “the result of what I call a ‘hybrid war’ that someone is waging in our nations by resorting to unconventional tools such as TikTok, social media, YouTube”.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot made a more limited claim at an OECD-hosted conference last week. “A few days ago, the high school student protests in France were themselves exploited by hostile narratives emanating from Russia, China, Iran, and the MAGA community. We see them, we denounce them, and we respond,” he said.
National regulators, including France’s Arcom and Italy’s AGCOM, have extensive powers to tackle potential disinformation operations under the Digital Services Act (DSA). They work closely with the Commission, with their most recent meeting taking place on Tuesday.
However, while regulators have urged the Commission to launch a formal investigation, the EU executive says there is insufficient evidence to justify one.
“We don’t have any information or definitive confirmation that foreign information manipulation is behind the events in France and elsewhere,” an EU official with direct knowledge of the matter told Euronews on condition of anonymity.
The disagreement highlights a gap between the accusations made publicly by some national politicians and the evidence available to the authorities.
“The situation is unfolding at national level, and the Commission is definitely ready to assist and support the national authorities,” Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said. “Let the French authorities carry out their work first. We are ready to assist where we can.”
The DSA also provides for a crisis response mechanism that can be activated in the event of a serious threat to public security or public health in the EU. This would give the Commission emergency powers over online platforms.
So far, however, there has been no move to activate it.
Meanwhile, law enforcement authorities have asked online platforms to provide information to help identify those involved in vandalism and looting.
In France, looters have attempted to sell stolen goods on the second-hand marketplace Vinted, prompting police to ask the platform for help identifying those responsible.
"We are actively collaborating with law enforcement and the French authorities, and we continually adapt our processes to detect and counter emerging risks and malicious behaviour," a Vinted spokesperson told Euronews.
There is evidence that Russia-linked disinformation networks, including those behind Operation Overload and Doppelgänger, have seized on the violence to amplify their online campaigns.
However, unlike during the Ceuta migration crisis this summer, when extensive evidence showed that thousands of people had been mobilised by false information circulated online, the protests in France, Italy and elsewhere appear, so far, to have been exploited by foreign actors rather than driven by them.

Twice recently, Israeli Jewish mob terror in the occupied West Bank broke through the international media’s wall of self-censorship: first, when the mobs attacked Israeli soldiers, and again when they brutally beat The Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine. The irony is damning. Attacking Israeli soldiers is news; violence against a Western journalist becomes international headlines and may even force Israel to stage a token, rotating door arrest, for PR consumption. But when Israeli soldiers and Jewish mobs terrorize Palestinian farmers, torch their cars, burn their olive trees, and drive them from their land, coverage too often disappears into the background.
The day following the vicious attack on the American journalist, another Israeli Jewish mob attacked a delegation of European diplomats in the Palestinian Christian village of Taybeh.
They smashed the window of a consular vehicle and beat a French mayor with iron bars. The Israeli army sought to bury the incident in the same talking points: it would investigate. Benjamin Netanyahu’s office urged “caution,” suggesting the reports were part of a “coordinated campaign to smear Israel,” and Jews in the West Bank.
When the world witnesses Israeli Jewish mob terror firsthand, Zionist defenders deflect, portray themselves as perpetual victims, and cry conspiracy against Jews.
Worse, these attacks unfold under the watchful eye of Israeli soldiers, who not only stand by as settlers terrorize Palestinians but at times join in the abuse themselves. And when a Palestinian is murdered by these mobs, the community is denied, by the occupying Israeli military, to mourn their dead. The question is not why these hateful Jewish mobs are violent, but why they are allowed to act with complete impunity.
The campaign to dispossess Palestinian farmers from their land has now acquired a religious imprimatur.
On the first day of the olive harvest season, October 16, Rabbi Dov Lior, a prominent religious authority among the illegal West Bank Jewish colonizers, issued a religious Halakha ruling on Teshuva, declaring it “permissible and virtuous” for Jewish colonizers to steal Palestinian olives, pontificating that harvesting the crop constitutes an exercise of Jewish ownership.
The Polish-born rabbi’s edict rests on the premise that Palestinians cannot claim ownership of their land without a deed from (European) Jews. Under the protection of an occupying army and a culture of religious impunity, the Israeli Jewish mobs’ theft becomes an instrument of the broader Zionist project of ethnic cleansing. This is not merely a theological dispute over land. It is a religious license for dispossession, a sanction for kosher theft.
On the same day the Rabbi Koshered the theft of non-Jewish property, mobs descended on Palestinian villages. They attacked farmers, stole their harvest, burned vehicles, trees, and injured residents across at least eight villages. In Abu Falah, Israeli rights activist described soldiers standing “literally shoulder-to-shoulder with settlers as they attacked Palestinians.”

The Israeli military provides security to protect “Jews” in the occupied West Bank. Its soldiers possess the authority, weapons, and institutional power to intervene, only on their behalf. They watch Jewish mobs operating with no fear of consequences. The Israeli army assists and protects Israeli Jewish settler mobs, or stands by as they attack Palestinians, only to arrest the assaulted Palestinians if they dare to fight back.
Jewish colonizers have found an almost absurdly “animal” way to steal Palestinian land: sheep. As a recent 60 Minutes report highlighted, settlers establish so-called “shepherding outposts” on hilltops, then graze their flocks on land Palestinians have farmed and herded for generations. A flock of “Jewish” sheep are used as a tool to reclaim the new “Jewish land” title. According to a report by the Israeli watchdog groups Peace Now and Kerem Navot, the “Jewish” shepherding outposts have so far seized nearly 200,000 acres or 14% of the West Bank’s total area for the exclusive benefit of “Jewish-only” grazing. When Palestinians are the victims, and the destruction is carried out by Zionist mobs in the name of Judaism, imposing economic suffocation and territorial dispossession to achieve their delusional “biblical” objectives, organized Jewish mob terror is reduced to a “handful,” their terror is euphemized as “alleged,” and their violence is relegated to an “investigation.”

Destroying people’s livelihood is not a random act of vandalism. A burned mature olive tree represents generations of accumulated labor and investment. A missed harvest means lost a year’s income. It is the systematic campaign, ideologically rooted to make Palestinian life economically unsustainable, sever Palestinians from their land, and ultimately drive them out.
U.S. Representative Rosa DeLauro captured this in a single question after a masked Israeli Jewish mob attacked Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine, breaking four vertebrae and a rib. “If the settlers will do this to an American journalist on camera, in broad daylight, imagine what Palestinian families face when no one is watching,” DeLauro said.

Palestinians are left to suffer in silence as systematic destruction continues, and the impunity of Jewish apartheid emboldens the machinery of Zionist hate and terror.
Unlike the Washington Post reporter or the European diplomats, the Palestinian suffering generates no headlines, their torment goes unreported, their Israeli Jewish attackers face no accountability, and no one is watching.

Estonian and Helsinki art academies hold joint exhibition in Finland
A group exhibition will open at the Kuva/Tila exhibition space, bringing together students' work from the Estonian Academy of Arts (EKA) and the Academy of Fine Arts (KuvA) at the University of the Arts Helsinki.
The exhibition opens on Thursday (October 22) and is titled "Sild/Silta", meaning bridge in both Estonian and Finnish.
The gallery will showcase work from 22 students, and the idea behind the art show is to build relationships between the two neighboring countries.
The collaboration will continue in January 2027, when the same group of students will open a second exhibition at the EKA Gallery in Tallinn.
The organizers say the two exhibitions form a conceptual bridge between Finland and Estonia, allowing artistic ideas, working methods and cultural experiences to flow in both directions.
Participating artists: Eeva-Liisa Anttila, Cecilia Ebbe Belinskij, Vita Edvards, Denis Kudrjašov, Anetta Lukjanova, Sandra Marins, Daniel Niittymäki, Liisa Nurklik, Anna Ovtšinnikova, Jaakko Pennanen, Viljamaria Raittila, Ella Rahkonen, Paul Rannik, Kertu Rannula, Mahmood Salim, Kertu-Liisa Sarap, Marc Léger Sauvageot, Nora Schmelter, Kati Silo, Yiyang Sun, Hanna Vinter, Maria Wrang-Rasmussen.
The exhibition is curated by Merike Estna, Kristi Kongi, Kaisa Maasik, Päivi Takala, Salla Tykkä and Laura Wesamaa.

Georgian court begins hearing lawsuit seeking ban on major opposition parties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21

Georgian court begins hearing lawsuit seeking ban on major opposition parties
TBILISI, Oct 21 - A court in Georgia opened hearings on Wednesday in a lawsuit filed by the government seeking outright bans on the five main opposition parties, in a move that civil society groups say presages the beginning of one-party rule in the South Caucasus country.
The Constitutional Court in the Black Sea city of Batumi will meet for three days to review the suit, first filed by the ruling Georgian Dream party a year ago. The court, whose ruling is final and cannot be appealed in Georgia, must give its decision by June 2027.
The lawsuit marks the culmination of government efforts to crack down on the political opposition since Georgian Dream clinched victory in a 2024 parliamentary election that the opposition says was rigged.
Georgian Dream, in power since 2012, is seeking to outlaw the five parties on the grounds that they pose "a real threat to the constitutional order".
The ruling is about "depriving a large part of Georgian society of genuine political choice and fundamentally changing the nature of the country's political system," said Giorgi Butikashvili, the foreign secretary of the Ahali-Coalition for Change, a party named in the lawsuit.
Rights groups and the European Union, which Georgia is seeking to join, have also condemned Georgian Dream's move.
'CONSOLIDATION OF AUTHORITARIANISM'
Once among the most democratic and pro-Western of the successor states to emerge from the Soviet Union, Georgia has turned increasingly authoritarian and deepened ties with Moscow since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Georgian Dream says it is protecting the country from opposition figures who it says are trying to seize power and foment a catastrophic war with Russia, which fought and won a short war with Georgia in 2008.
The country received EU candidate status in 2023 but Brussels now says it has backslid on its democratic reforms so far that it is considered a candidate country "in name only".
Kornely Kakachia, a political science professor at Tbilisi State University, said the ban would challenge the minimum standards of political pluralism expected of an EU candidate country.
"Georgia is moving from democratic backsliding towards the potential consolidation of authoritarianism," he said.
The government's lawsuit was initially filed against three opposition groups but has since been widened to five, all of them pro-Western. Only one, For Georgia, has seats in parliament.
The case is based partially on an extensive report prepared by a parliamentary investigative commission looking into alleged crimes and human rights violations carried out under the previous government, led by former President Mikheil Saakashvili. REUTERS

Türkiye, Qatar, Indonesia and Pakistan have signed a memorandum to strengthen defense cooperation and develop strategic partnerships, the Turkish Defense Ministry said in a statement on Oct. 21.
The agreement was signed in the Qatari capital Doha by the defense ministers of the four countries.
The signatories were Turkish Defense Minister Yaşar Güler, Qatar’s Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Sheikh Saud bin Abdulrahman bin Hasan Al Thani, Indonesian Deputy Defense Minister Yusuf Jauhari and Pakistani Defense Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif.
The ceremony was also attended by Haluk Görgün, head of Türkiye’s Defense Industries Presidency (SSB).
Named “Badr,” meaning “full moon,” the agreement aims to promote cooperation in military production, strengthen military capabilities, and support collaboration in technical military training, research and development, the ministry said.
The initiative would help develop solutions and industrial sectors aligned with advances in modern defense systems, it added.
The memorandum also carries significant economic importance for the signatories by combining their respective military production capabilities, improving integration and strengthening their defense industries to meet the needs of allied and friendly countries.
It is also expected to expand military cooperation among the participating countries, deepen ties in the defense industry, and strengthen multilateral collaboration in support of security, stability and shared objectives, the ministry said.
Türkiye, which has NATO’s second-largest army, has been helping Gulf nations, including Qatar, where it has a military base, and bolster their defenses amid the Iran war.
In August, Ankara signed a mutual defense pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, under which an attack on one party constitutes an attack on all.
The Turkish government on Oct. 20 submitted the Mecca pact to parliament for ratification.
The move came after President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan signaled that the parliament will first ratify the agreement for Türkiye to consider supplying military support to Saudi Arabia in its conflict with Iran-backed Houthi groups in Yemen.
“The submission of the bill regarding the approval of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement... to the Turkish Parliament marks an important milestone toward the institutionalization of strategic cooperation among the three brotherly countries,” Communications Director Burhanettin Duran said in statement.
“Based on the principle that regional issues should be addressed through the responsibility of regional countries, the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement is the manifestation of a shared will prioritizing security and solidarity.”
Ankara also has close ties with Indonesia, notably in the defense industry.

TEL AVIV – Brad Lander, a US Democratic Party candidate for Congress, was detained by Israeli forces in the occupied West Bank on Oct 21, along with other Americans and Israelis harvesting olives alongside Palestinian farmers, rights groups said.

Lander was among a group of international volunteers, which one organiser said also included British and Canadian citizens, accompanying local Palestinian farmers, who often face the threat of violence from Israeli settlers, as an act of solidarity in what is known as protective presence.
Lander is a former New York City comptroller and mayoral candidate who is running for New York’s 10th Congressional District in the US House of Representatives in the Nov 3 midterm elections. He is an ally of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and is critical of Israel’s conduct in the war in Gaza.

Israel’s foreign ministry accused Lander of “looking for a confrontation” and said that he had ignored advice ahead of his visit that coordination with Israeli authorities was required.
The incident took place in Nahalin, a village south of Bethlehem, as Palestinians were gathering olives accompanied by around 80 volunteers, according to Israeli organisation Rabbis for Human Rights and Jewish North American organisation T’ruah.
Israeli police said it had detained Palestinian olive harvesters and dozens of Israeli and foreign activists gathering olives near the fence of an Israeli settlement, saying it was prohibited. One of the foreign nationals was later released once it became known he was a congressional candidate, police said.
‘Harvesting olives is not illegal’
The military said harvesting in that area, which is located near the Israeli settlement of Beitar Illit, required prior coordination, which had not happened, and that those present had been detained. It did not say harvesting there was prohibited.

“Harvesting olives is not illegal. The occupation is,” he said, accusing Israel of genocide, and demanding the release of the other New Yorkers and an end to the Israeli occupation.
Israel’s government has denied accusations, including by a UN commission, and international and Israeli rights groups, that it is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Police later said 72 people had been released, some on condition that they stay away from the harvest area. It also said four foreign nationals would remain in custody until a hearing on Oct 22 to determine whether they would be deported.
Rabbis for Human Rights and T’ruah said Israeli military and police forces arrived around two hours after the Palestinians and volunteers began gathering olives, and informed them that they were in a closed military zone and would be detained.
The participants were not aware it was a closed military zone and offered to leave, Rabbis for Human Rights acting director Anton Goodman told Reuters by phone from the Beitar Illit police station, where he was being detained.
He said the Israeli forces accused the participants of disturbing the public and took them by bus to the station.

‘They try to break us’: Pro-Palestine activists in Czech custody
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:24:23 UTC
21:24:23 KST

‘They try to break us’: Pro-Palestine activists in Czech custody
As a group is accused of an attack on a weapons factory, activists allege a growing crackdown on the solidarity movement.
Prague, Czech Republic – Youssef Moursi, a 25-year-old Egyptian university student and activist in Prague, has spent the last six months in pre-trial detention, accused of an arson attack in March against a Czech weapons factory with alleged ties to Israel.
Moursi is one of 11 people being charged with “terrorism” for the attack and could face up to 20 years in prison if convicted.
The case has echoes of legal battles in the United Kingdom, where Palestine Action activists have been sentenced under terrorism laws, and Germany, where five people accused of targeting a site linked to Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest weapons maker, are on trial.
Moursi, a humanities student at Charles University, said in a statement to Al Jazeera that “a group of armed and masked policemen smashed down [my] front door”, two days after the alleged attack, in which he denies any involvement.
He spent the first three months of his detention in solitary confinement, according to his lawyer. Today, he is allowed one hour outside his cell and 20 minutes on the phone a day, with visits from friends and family every two weeks.
“[There] is the psychological front being waged against us, where [the police] deliberately try to break us by putting some of us in solitary confinement for months, denying us visits, blocking correspondence, or spreading fear,” Moursi said. “Putting people in custody and prolonging it time and time again without direct evidence, mainly based on a mix of inclinations, activism, racism, and an attempted blurring of freedom of speech, is unacceptable.”
Moursi and his lawyer, Pavel Cizinsky, believe he has been targeted because of his involvement in pro-Palestine activism in Prague.
Cizinsky said part of the evidence police have against Moursi is that on the day after the fire, he posted advice for pro-Palestinian activists on social media, should they be approached by officers. Cizinsky called this “ridiculous.”
“If you put into Google what to do when interviewed by the police, the first advice is wait for your lawyer. But if you say it as a pro-Palestinian activist, if you write it to your friends, then it’s reason against you that you are guilty,” Cizinsky said.
At the beginning of the investigation, Cizinsky said he faced pressure from the authorities not to take the case. As a result, he was not present during the initial interrogation and house raid on Moursi’s flat.
“It is clear that there is extraordinary attention to this investigation by the police, and really great resources dedicated to this case,” Cizinsky said. “But the fact that he is already five months in prison is surely a breach of law.”
Under Czech law, individuals held in pre-trial detention who have not been convicted must have their detention reviewed by a court every three months. Moursi’s detention has so far been reviewed twice, with the court deciding each time that he must stay in prison.
His detention will be reviewed again in early December, and the trial is expected to start within a year.
The fire broke out in the early hours of March 20 at LPP Holding, a Czech weapons factory in Pardubice, about 120km (75 miles) east of Prague.
No one was injured but police said the building was destroyed, with damage estimates reaching hundreds of millions of crowns, or at least four million euros.
A previously unknown pro-Palestinian group called The Earthquake Faction claimed responsibility and posted videos of the fire, saying it targeted LPP Holding for its cooperation with Elbit Systems, an Israeli weapons company.
In 2023, LPP Holding and Elbit Systems announced a partnership to build drones in the Czech Republic. But on the day of the fire, an LPP Holding spokesperson told Czech media the collaboration never happened.
In the weeks following the attack, police launched a manhunt and arrested several foreign nationals including Ukrainian, Czech, Slovak, Polish and American citizens. Of the 10 other individuals accused, three are under house arrest in Poland and seven remain behind bars in the Czech Republic.
Over the past two years, Elbit Systems has become a primary target for pro-Palestine activists across Europe.
In June, a UK court convicted four imprisoned Palestine Action members of criminal damage with a “terrorist connection” after a raid on an Elbit Systems factory in Filton, near Bristol. In September last year, police in Poland arrested protesters at an arms fair for throwing red liquid over an Elbit Systems stand. This week, an elderly man in Germany was arrested after protesting against the Israeli weapons giant.
In Prague, the atmosphere for pro-Palestinian activists has grown increasingly tense.
A collective called Prague 4 Palestine Youth stopped organising demonstrations and charity events after police investigations into dozens of its members in the months following the arson attack.
Rue, a 25-year-old Czech activist who requested anonymity, said that friends of those detained in the arson case and fellow activists are being subjected to interrogations, house raids, and indefinite confiscations of their devices as the investigation continues.
Nine days after the fire, Rue said, “[The police] interrogated us, and then they took us back to [our] apartment where they did a search of the house. They kept us awake for more than 24 hours. I was having panic attacks for a week straight after it happened.”
After the interrogation and house search, Rue was told they were being treated as a witness to the arson attack. The police confiscated their phone and computer, which have not been returned.
Rue believes they were investigated because of their friendship with suspects in the arson case. They have visited two in prison; one is in solitary confinement for 23 hours a day, Rue said.
“When it comes to the end of the visit, the tears come,” Rue added. “You’re free to go anywhere and do anything, and they go back to being in those four walls.”
The individuals detained in the Czech Republic could remain in prison for up to four years without being convicted, according to their lawyers.
Police confirmed they have arrested and charged suspects of several different nationalities and remanded them in custody.
“Given the gravity of the case and the ongoing investigation into terrorism-related offences, the supervising public prosecutor’s office has assumed exclusive authority to release information,” the police said.

She also questioned the effectiveness of nighttime curfews introduced in several cities, including Paris, Lyon and Marseille, following the unrest. “I’m not at all sure that the curfew is the cause of this lull,” she said.
Asked about Thursday’s meeting between Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu and political parties, Le Pen said National Rally would send representatives, rejecting suggestions that it was boycotting the talks.
The Yellow Vests, backed by students, held nationwide protests on Oct. 17 against high living costs and fuel prices. Around 2,500 people were detained and more than 1,000 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters were injured.
About 3,000 businesses were damaged or looted, while public buildings were attacked, including Limoges town hall and Lyon’s tourist office, which were set ablaze.
Business owners criticized the government’s handling of the crisis, prompting authorities to introduce localized curfews from Oct. 19 in several cities, including Paris, Lille, Lyon, Marseille and Nice.
The movement has planned new protests on Oct. 24.

Türkiye, Qatar, Indonesia and Pakistan sign 'Badr' defence cooperation accord
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:20:37 UTC
21:20:37 KST

Türkiye, Qatar, Indonesia and Pakistan have signed the Badr memorandum to strengthen defence cooperation and develop strategic partnerships, the Turkish National Defence Ministry said in a statement on Wednesday.
The agreement was signed on Wednesday in Doha, the capital of Qatar, by the defence ministers of the four countries.
The signatories were Turkish National Defence Minister Yasar Guler, Qatar’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of State for Defence Affairs Sheikh Saud bin Abdulrahman bin Hasan Al Thani, Indonesian Deputy Defence Minister Yusuf Jauhari and Pakistani Defence Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif.
The ceremony was also attended by Haluk Gorgun, head of Türkiye’s Presidency of Defence Industries.
Multi-layered cooperation
Named “Badr,” meaning “full moon,” the agreement aims to promote cooperation in military production, strengthen military capabilities, and support collaboration in technical military training, research and development, the ministry said.
The ministry added that the initiative would help develop solutions and industrial sectors aligned with advances in modern defence systems.
The memorandum also carries significant economic importance for the signatories by combining their respective military production capabilities, improving integration and strengthening their defence industries to meet the needs of allied and friendly countries.
It is also expected to expand military cooperation among the participating countries, deepen ties in the defence industry, and strengthen multilateral collaboration in support of security, stability and shared objectives, the ministry said.

OpenAI to bring AI models to Google's cloud, in further expansion beyond Microsoft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:20:13 UTC
21:20:13 KST

OpenAI will make its artificial intelligence models available for developers through Google's cloud, following years of competition between the two companies.
For OpenAI, the effort reflects a growing push to expand distribution of its technology to enterprise developers. That's critical as the ChatGPT creator looks to build its business beyond its consumer roots, and the move puts OpenAI's models on all three of the top cloud infrastructure providers.
Less than six months ago, OpenAI said Microsoft would no longer have the exclusive license on its intellectual property. The day after that ended, cloud leader Amazon unveiled plans to host OpenAI models.
Now Google is getting its shot, bringing OpenAI's GPT products to its cloud's model garden and Antigravity coding tool in the coming weeks.
"Google Cloud's longstanding investment in machine learning and AI has made it a destination for AI workloads and the developers and data scientists building them," OpenAI said in a blog post.
Google has been on a run in cloud computing this year. Annualized revenue growth in the segment accelerated to about 82% in the second quarter from 63% in the first quarter, thanks partly to strong demand for AI models and custom chips. Amazon and Microsoft posted second-quarter cloud growth of 37% and 42%, respectively. All three report quarterly results next week.
Most business spending on AI is on OpenAI and Anthropic, according to data from corporate card issuer Ramp, though some corporate IT departments have integrated Google's Gemini models into their systems. In September, Google announced its next-generation Gemini 4 Argon model.
OpenAI was founded in 2015 partly as a counterweight to the concentration of AI research at companies like Google. Two years later, Google employees submitted the influential Transformer academic paper that propelled AI, but it was OpenAI that helped bring the technology forward with ChatGPT. Now OpenAI is courting investors at a $1.4 trillion valuation and targeting an initial public offering.
Google and OpenAI previously partnered last year, when the AI lab said it was using Google's cloud to run ChatGPT and its application programming interface.

Witkoff says he hopes Ukraine included in U.S., Russia talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:19:43 UTC
21:19:43 KST

Russia says Ukraine must make "necessary decisions" to end war as Witkoff meets Putin
Progress toward a negotiated resolution to Russia's war on Ukraine is "theoretically possible," Kremlin officials said Wednesday as U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, but any headway will require Ukraine's leaders to make "necessary decisions," according to Russian state media.
If Ukraine fails to make those decisions, the situation for the country "will be worse," the officials said, according to Russian state news agency TASS.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted by Russian news agencies as saying Moscow would study proposals on the Ukraine war brought to St. Petersburg by Witkoff, but that the talks would take a long time.
During Witkoff's meeting with Putin, he and the Russian leader confirmed that Stephen Hubbard, a U.S. citizen jailed in Russia for more than four years, had been released from custody. President Trump said Putin agreed to free the American with "no 'swap' necessary," but he also said it wouldn't have happened had the U.S. not prevented new sanctions against Moscow from taking effect last week. Witkoff told Putin he was a "humanitarian" for releasing Hubbard, sparking backlash in the U.S.
State media said Russian officials told Witkoff on Wednesday that a meeting between Mr. Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping was "possible," referring to an idea the White House has also floated, but Ukrainian officials have balked at as it would sideline them from talks on their own country's fate.
After Putin and Witkoff's meeting, a U.S. official told CBS News that the Russians and Ukrainians had agreed to the resumption of trilateral talks with the U.S. at the technical level.
According to a Kremlin transcript, Putin's senior foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov said that the Russian leader told Witkoff that Moscow was prepared, in principle, to resume the talks in early November. Ushakov also said the talks would involve building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the war.
But Ushakov also said that the proposals brought to St. Petersburg by Witkoff, which he attributed to Ukraine and the European Union, "contained little that was useful in the context of resolving the Ukrainian crisis."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Fox News on Wednesday that he believed trilateral talks between himself, Mr. Trump and Putin were the best way to resolve the conflict, and that he would not accept any resolution crafted by China, Russia and the U.S., saying: "Don't talk about us without us."
Zelenskyy also said any negotiated end to the war would need to be approved by Ukraine's Parliament.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio told journalists on a separate trip Wednesday that Witkoff held "positive" talks with Zelenskyy on Tuesday in Oslo before traveling to Russia, and that he would share ideas discussed with Zelenskyy with the Russian side in an attempt to "make some progress."
After that meeting with Witkoff in Oslo, Zelenskyy thanked Washington for restoring U.S. intelligence sharing on Russian strikes, after saying this week that his country had stopped receiving advance warnings of imminent Russian missile strikes.
"We are thankful that intelligence works," Zelenskyy told reporters in Oslo. He said the early warnings for ballistic missiles were "very, very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians."
Zelenskyy told Fox on Wednesday, however, that access to data from the Starshield satellite network, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink system, remained "limited" in Ukraine, but that Rubio was working on it and expected full access to be restored.
Witkoff planned to return to Oslo for more consultations with European officials following his visit to Russia, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said.
"I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy," Støre told Norwegian broadcaster NRK on Wednesday morning.
Zelenskyy was still in Oslo on Wednesday, where he said "a lot depends on whether the American side manages to hear something new from Russia today."
The diplomacy comes after weeks of friction between Kyiv and Washington, with Mr. Trump criticizing Zelenskyy for Ukraine's continued response to relentless, deadly Russian strikes on energy and civilian infrastructure with Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil infrastructure.
Mr. Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" earlier in the month, claiming both sides had agreed to halt strikes on each other's energy infrastructure, but within hours Russia launched new missile attacks on Ukrainian refineries and other sites, and neither Ukraine nor Russia ever confirmed agreeing to a truce of any kind.
The U.S. president also announced a deal with Moscow on Oct. 10 for Russia to release millions of tons of diesel fuel over the next several months, which Zelenskyy labeled a sign of "weakness."
Russian state media said the first shipment of diesel had been dispatched for the U.S. on Wednesday.

NEW DELHI: Stating that peace had been established in the country's three primary hotspots -- Jammu and Kashmir, northeast region and areas affected by Left-wing extremism -- home minister Amit Shah on Wednesday said the home ministry is now focused on the next big challenge, the drug menace, and aims to make the country completely narcotics-free by Dec 31, 2029.Addressing an event here to mark the Police Commemoration Day, Shah said 2026 has been an extremely significant year for the Indian police, as they successfully freed the country from the decades-old stranglehold of violent Naxalism by March 31. "From 1981 to March 2026, the country had endured numerous hardships due to Naxalism....more than 3,600 security personnel were martyred, and nearly 13,700 innocent civilians also lost their lives," he recalled and said the sacrifices of 3,600 police personnel have laid the foundation of progress "as the country moves forward on the path of development".
The Police Commemoration Day event was attended by Members of Parliament Krishna Prasad Tenneti and Rajiv Kumar, home secretary Govind Mohan, Intelligence Bureau director Mahesh Dixit and the Directors-General of various Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs).Stating that an environment conducive to development has emerged in Kashmir, northeast and LWE-hit regions, which now compete with the rest of the country in terms of development, Shah particularly thanked the CRPF and its CoBRA battalion as well as the Chhattisgarh police for their role in the decisive fight against LWE.

Noting that drug abuse and trafficking undermine the future of coming generations, place an unnecessary burden on the economy and often provide financial support to organisations with anti-national intentions, Shah called upon police forces across the country to wholeheartedly join in implementing the 'nasha-mukt Bharat' roadmap.
Meanwhile, to spread the message regarding the govt's time-bound war on drugs, the home minister flagged off a nationwide motorcycle rally on Wednesday with the theme 'fight against drugs'. On Wednesday, Shah placed a wreath at the National Police Memorial to honour the service and sacrifice by 36,852 police personnel who have made the supreme sacrifice thus far.

Iran’s enriched uranium re-emerges as point of contention in US talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:18:10 UTC
21:18:10 KST

Iran’s enriched uranium re-emerges as point of contention in US talks
Iran’s nuclear enrichment has emerged as a major point of contention amid diplomatic push to end the war.
The renewed diplomatic push to end the United States-Israel war on Iran is facing headwinds as Tehran’s nuclear programme, which the two countries invoked to launch the war in February, has once again emerged as one of the biggest stumbling blocks in reaching a ceasefire.
Nearly eight months into the war, which has caused a global energy crisis, a deal to ensure a permanent ceasefire remains elusive. Moreover, the war has since spilled into a regional conflict, with Yemen emerging as its latest theatre.
The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz – a global oil chokepoint – was the focus of the June Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed between the US and Iran.
The MoU had also stated that Iran “shall not procure or develop nuclear weapons”, but a comprehensive deal, including the nuclear issue, could not be thrashed out within the stipulated 60-day period. Analysts said that differing interpretations of the agreement clauses caused the MoU to fall apart.
Now the nuclear issue has once again emerged as the central point of contention, with Tehran insisting that uranium enrichment is a right guaranteed under the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT).
US President Donald Trump, on the other hand, has called for “zero uranium enrichment”. His ally, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, on Sunday reiterated his pledge to topple the Iranian government, which he said is key to preventing it from developing nuclear weapons.
Earlier this week, US Vice President JD Vance appeared to offer concessions on the nuclear doctrine to reach a deal.
While Qatar and Pakistan are engaged in mediation efforts, how will they get the sides to agree on the nuclear enrichment issue?
What is Iran saying?
Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir, who is also a key negotiator in the conflict, is currently in Tehran, where he met Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei on Tuesday.
In the meeting, Rezaei said “even a particle of enriched uranium will not exit Iran at all,” according to comments carried by Iran’s semi-official Fars news agency, describing the material as a major national asset that would remain in the country for domestic use.
His response came amid media reports that the US wants Iran to transfer part of its enriched uranium out of the country. Trump has previously called for the removal of the enriched uranium stockpile from Iran.
Rezaei also said negotiations with the US would not begin until Washington fulfils trust-building measures, including meeting the latest conditions Iran has set.
Iran wants the US to lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waive sanctions, and release frozen Iranian assets as part of its latest terms to end the war. In return, Iran has promised to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Another Iranian lawmaker, Alaeddin Boroujerdi, also a member of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, reiterated that Iran is not seeking the production of nuclear weapons.
“Iran’s enrichment activities are unrelated to the US, and Washington should focus on fulfilling its own obligations regarding nuclear arms reduction,” he said.
Where does the US stand?
Addressing a Republican Party campaign rally earlier this week, Trump claimed that the US bombing had destroyed Iran’s nuclear facilities and that he would not allow Tehran to rebuild them.
“They cannot have a nuclear weapon,” Trump told his supporters at a rally at Northern Kentucky University.
Vice President Vance said earlier this week that the US has “in some ways decisively won” the war on Iran and has destroyed the country’s nuclear programme.
He told a town hall hosted by CBS News that the US was now focused on ensuring that Iran makes a “long-term” and “verifiable commitment” not to rebuild its nuclear programme.
“Not over the administration of Donald Trump … but five years from now, could the Iranians rebuild that nuclear arsenal? Could they try to rebuild that enrichment capacity?” he asked.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said this week that a decision to end the war finally rests with Trump. “The US will not support any deal that creates a pathway for Iran to have a nuclear weapon. As long as President Trump is in office, they will not have a nuclear weapon,” he reiterated.
Last month, Vance told the Reuters news agency in an interview that Tehran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the war.
“If you don’t want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60 percent enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don’t build highly enriched fuel. That’s a very basic threshold issue,” Vance said.
“I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity,” he added.
What the MoU says about Iran’s uranium programme
The MoU signed on June 17 left the future of Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile to further negotiations, but identified downblending under international supervision of the International Atomic Energy Agency as the minimum approach to resolving the issue.
Downblending involves mixing highly enriched uranium with lower-enriched material, making it less suitable for rapid conversion into weapons-grade material.
The MoU left room for Iran to reduce the material’s enrichment domestically rather than surrender it. However, it did not specify the quantity to be downblended, a target enrichment level or a detailed implementation timetable.
“The two parties also agreed to discuss the issue of enrichment and other mutually agreed matters related to the Islamic Republic of Iran’s nuclear needs, based on a satisfactory framework being agreed upon in the final deal,” the MoU clause reads.
That final deal, of course, could not be reached as the MoU expired in mid-August.
The Trump administration invoked the imminent threat of Iran acquiring nuclear weapons to launch the war on February 28, 2026. On the first day of the war, US-Israel strikes killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who had banned the development of nuclear weapons in a fatwa, or religious edict.
President Trump has often argued that Iran would use the nuclear weapon “within moments after getting it”, and then “the Middle East would be gone, Israel would be gone, and then hit Europe probably next.”
The US president has spoken out against Iran’s nuclear programme numerous times in the past.
As the war progressed over months, the US focus shifted gradually towards reopening the Strait of Hormuz as a base condition of the ongoing fighting.
Speaking in Alaska last week, Trump again falsely claimed that he had to start his war on Iran because, “[Iran was] two weeks away from having a nuclear weapon.”
In April, Trump had warned that “the enriched material, sometimes referred to as ‘Nuclear Dust,’ will be unearthed by the United States … and DESTROYED.” Later in the month, he told reporters on board Air Force One that the US would “go in with Iran, and we will take it together, and we will bring it back. 100 percent of it back to the United States.”
Mostafa Najafi, a foreign policy analyst based in Iran, noted that “despite [the US’s] insistence on nuclear negotiations and obtaining tangible concessions in this area, [Washington is] unwilling to offer significant concessions such as lifting sanctions.”
The US wants “to secure major concessions solely in exchange for lifting the blockade and releasing some of Iran’s assets”, he wrote in a post on X. “From Iran’s perspective, lifting the blockade and releasing assets is no longer a noteworthy concession for Tehran!”

Fire Point has received a Danish state guarantee for a $113 million loan
Ukraine

2026-10-21

Fire Point has received a Danish state guarantee for a $113 million loan
Kyiv • UNN
The financing will be provided through the Danish Export and Investment Fund.
Denmark will provide a state guarantee for a loan of 750 million Danish kroner (approximately $112 million) for the Danish subsidiary of Ukrainian drone and missile manufacturer Fire Point. Reuters reports this, citing the Danish government, according to UNN.
Details
As explained by the Danish government, the state guarantee is necessary because, due to the war in Ukraine, the company is unable to obtain financing in Denmark on normal market terms. The loan will be provided through the Danish Export and Investment Fund (EIFO).
According to Reuters, citing a statement by Danish Defence Minister Troels Lund Poulsen, locating production abroad enables Ukraine to protect supply chains from Russian attacks.
The Danish plant for producing rocket fuel is expected to begin operating by the end of 2027.
Let us remind you
As UNN reported, Fire Point is building a solid rocket fuel plant in the Danish town of Vojens in the south of the country, where FP-7 and FP-7.x missiles and boosters for Flamingo will be filled. This is the first case within NATO in which a member state has allowed a Ukrainian defence company to establish a production facility on its territory.
As Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh reported, the plant's total area will exceed 120,000 square metres, with a capacity ranging from 800 to more than 4,100 missiles per year, depending on demand. The construction process required a review of the regulations and expertise governing the construction of such large-scale facilities. In addition, the Danish authorities eliminated more than 20 legislative barriers overall.
During the war in Ukraine, the plant will operate to meet the needs of our Defence Forces; later, it is planned that the fuel will also be supplied to European partners.

DONETSK, October 21. /TASS/. Vladimir Zelensky is more afraid of peace than war, which is why he is rolling the dice, Alexey Muratov, head of the Donetsk People’s Republic’s (DPR) regional executive committee of the United Russia party, told TASS.
US President Donald Trump said earlier that Zelensky does not want to end the conflict with Russia, and probably never did. His adviser, Alex Bruesewitz, also pointed out that Zelensky’s inner circle benefits from the Ukrainian conflict, which is why he does not want to bring it to an end. According to Bruesewitz, ordinary Ukrainians, meanwhile, continue to endure immense suffering.
"Zelensky is not seeking peace because his conditions are impossible to meet. Peace means inevitable political, and, most likely, physical, death," Muratov said. "As long as Zelensky clings to power, conditions for him will only get worse. He understands this, but peace is more terrifying to him than war, so he’s gambling with his fate."
He added that Zelensky demands a strong army, NATO security guarantees, and a refusal by Russia to recognize Crimea, Donbass, and Novorossiya. "But no one is promising him NATO membership, and without it, any guarantees are just words on a piece of paper," the politician pointed out.
Muratov is convinced that Zelensky’s concerns about retaining power are precisely why he is linking the holding of presidential elections to the end of the conflict. "His approval rating is falling, his legitimacy is eroding, and elections can only be held ‘after the end of hostilities’ – that is, never, as long as he is in power. Peace would mean elections, and elections would mean defeat," he concluded.

Meeting Putin in St. Petersburg, Witkoff thanked the Russian leader for releasing American teacher Stephen Hubbard, whom Washington considered wrongfully detained, while presenting proposals aimed at securing a ceasefire in Ukraine.
“You often describe President Trump as a humanist. But you are a humanist too, sir. I give you credit, express my respect and thank you again,” Witkoff said.
The praise came against a sharply different assessment from UN human rights monitors, who have documented escalating civilian suffering as Russia intensifies attacks across Ukraine.
The UN verified that at least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 injured in Ukraine in September. In an update published Oct. 16, its monitoring mission said Russian attacks had continued to cause mass casualties into October, alongside renewed strikes on electricity and heating infrastructure as winter approaches.
Witkoff told Putin he had brought documents outlining possible approaches to a peace settlement and asked him to consider resuming negotiations involving the United States, Ukraine and Russia. He suggested that representatives of technical working groups could participate.
Putin Orders US Teacher’s Release as Witkoff Arrives for Talks
The envoy said there was a basis for moving toward a ceasefire and that he would brief Putin on discussions held in Oslo. He also asked to bring Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and a participant in the diplomatic effort, into the meeting by telephone.

Witkoff arrived in Russia from Norway, where he met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the meeting as positive, saying Witkoff would relay its outcomes to the Russian side.
Zelensky said on Tuesday that Ukraine and the US had agreed on a series of proposals to end the war during their meeting in Norway, including security guarantees for Kyiv.
He also confirmed that intelligence sharing with the US had resumed and said progress on Patriot interceptors and Starlink restrictions could come within 48 hours.
Notably, hours after Zelensky met Witkoff in Oslo, US President Donald Trump said Ukraine “has to want to make a deal” to end Russia’s war, claiming Washington and Europe had spent “a fortune” on Kyiv and that Europe was tired of the conflict.
Trump also said the US had received “nothing back other than high diesel,” apparently defending his recent moves to ease pressure on Moscow.
Kyiv has repeatedly rejected claims that it is obstructing peace efforts, saying it has supported ceasefire proposals and initiatives from international partners.
Zelensky has offered a full ceasefire and proposed direct talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, while 51 countries signed a joint statement at the UN General Assembly in September urging Moscow to accept an immediate truce.
Russia has rejected such proposals, with Lavrov saying the Kremlin would not pause its war even during potential negotiations.
Tensions between Kyiv and Washington escalated on Oct. 9, when Trump announced a diesel deal with Putin as a Ukrainian delegation was holding peace talks with US officials in Miami.
Zelensky later said Ukrainian officials had been warned that Washington could restrict intelligence sharing if Kyiv continued striking Russian oil facilities.
The Trump administration also reportedly threatened to suspend the PURL mechanism, which enables European countries to purchase US weapons for Ukraine, including Patriot air defense interceptors.
Trump subsequently called for Ukraine to elect a new president, prompting Zelensky to insist that his removal was a decision for Ukrainians alone.
Kyiv proposed a 60-day ceasefire to allow elections, but Moscow rejected the proposal, offering only a one-day truce. Trump then announced an immediate energy ceasefire on Oct. 11, claiming both sides had agreed to it.
Ukraine signaled its willingness to observe the energy truce and refrained from striking Russian energy facilities, but Moscow continued attacking targets across Ukraine.
Meanwhile, restrictions on Starlink terminals and a week-long suspension of US intelligence sharing reportedly left Kyiv without allied warnings of Russian ballistic missile attacks and vulnerable to attacks by jet-powered drones.

EU probes whether Booking.com is doing enough to tackle fake listings and phishing scams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:12:34 UTC
21:12:34 KST

There is no fixed legal deadline for the investigation to conclude, but Booking.com can propose measures to address the European Commission's concerns.
The European Union has launched an investigation into online travel platform Booking.com on Wednesday over concerns that it has failed to adequately address fake listings and phishing scams.
EU authorities suspect the company has underestimated the impact of fraud and unlicensed accommodation on its platform and has not done enough to prevent users' data from being exploited by scammers.
"Europeans should be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed," EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in a statement.
The EU said it was also looking into whether the firm breached rules "because it did not clearly label as ads those listings whose providers paid for a higher ranking in search results shown to users".
The probe marks the first investigation into Booking.com under the Digital Services Act (DSA), the EU's sweeping law regulating online platforms, including social media and digital marketplaces.
The DSA "sets clear responsibilities" and "we must ensure that the leading booking platform in Europe takes those responsibilities seriously", Virkkunen added.
Booking.com pledges to cooperate
Booking.com said it was "cooperating fully" with the investigation, adding that "security, trust and the protection of personal information are top priorities".
"We remain committed to working with relevant governments, regulators, law enforcement and industry partners to combat cybercrime and online fraud and protect travellers and partners," it added.
Under the DSA, Booking.com could face fines of up to 6% of its global annual turnover if violations are confirmed.

Government websites shut down in Finland over critical security flaws
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
15:12:26 EEST
21:12:26 KST

Government websites across Finland have been taken offline after authorities identified two critical security vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language used by websites worldwide. The precautionary shutdowns began on Wednesday, disrupting government services, public institutions and other organisations.
The Finnish Government ICT Centre, Valtori, began restricting incoming public internet traffic at 12.45 pm local time to protect government systems against potential cyberattacks.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
Finland's National Cyber Security Centre, which operates under the Finnish Transport and Communications Agency Traficom, classified both vulnerabilities as critical, assigning them a severity score of 9.2 out of 10.
The agency said there was no evidence that attackers had exploited the vulnerabilities, although the situation might change as information about the flaws becomes public.
Valtori stressed that the shutdowns were preventive measures rather than a response to a confirmed cyberattack or data breach. Internal government network traffic remains unaffected.
A software update addressing the vulnerabilities was scheduled for release at 5 pm Finnish time on Wednesday. Valtori said it would install the patches across the PHP applications it maintains and restore public access once security checks were complete.
The shutdowns have disrupted services across Finland. The National Land Survey of Finland experienced website outages, while Helsinki University reported disruptions linked to the security measures.
Finnish national broadcaster Yle also confirmed outages affecting several of its online services.
The interruptions extended beyond government agencies. The Finnish Film Foundation (SES) announced on Instagram that its website had been shut down.
Helsinki’s Messukeskus convention and exhibition centre also reported that its website, messukeskus.com, and event pages were temporarily unavailable. The centre said it expected services to resume at around 5 pm on Wednesday, once the necessary updates and security checks were completed.
Valtori director-general Hannu Naumanen told Finnish news agency STT that the shutdown process had begun shortly after 1 pm.
PHP supports websites, content management systems and online shopping platforms across the internet. The vulnerabilities therefore extend beyond Finland's government infrastructure.
The National Cyber Security Centre urged website administrators to install the security updates immediately after their release, prioritising systems accessible through the public internet.
Valtori said it would continue assessing affected services and restore connections once administrators had verified their security.

Politician who was intentionally hit by car loses both her legs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:10:14 UTC
21:10:14 KST

Australian politician who was intentionally hit by car loses both her legs
Australian lawmaker Helen Haines has had both legs amputated after being hit by a car, her husband said on Wednesday, hailing her as a "fighter" despite critical injuries sustained in what police described as a targeted attack.
Haines, 65, is now in a stable condition at a Melbourne hospital days after being struck by a car on Monday near her office in the town of Wangaratta, which is just over 200 kilometers, or 120 miles, northeast of the Victoria state capital.
The incident has prompted soul-searching in a country where political violence is rare but where police have documented a steady rise in threats and abuse toward elected officials in recent years.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has led tributes to Haines, an independent member of parliament and a passionate campaigner for transparency and against corruption. He has also acknowledged the need for Australians to turn down the temperature and embrace respectful disagreement over polarization.
Speaking at the hospital on Wednesday, Haines' husband of almost 40 years, Phil, said that after days in intensive care, surgeons had been forced to amputate both her legs.
"But the good news in all this is Helen is alive and she's stable. That is the most important thing for our family," he said, adding, "The two most important parts of Helen for us as a family are her heart and her mind."
Haines' husband went on to describe her as "a very compassionate, caring, loving person" with a "huge" heart.
"Helen's road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter," he said.
"Extremist views"
The man alleged to have wounded Haines in what police have called a "targeted" attack faced court for the first time earlier on Wednesday.
Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury and intentionally causing serious injury, as well as the federal crime of harming a public official, which carries a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison. He has also been charged with cultivating a cannabis plant and possession of the drug, according to court documents shared with AFP.
Nugent's initial hearing took place at a courthouse in Wangaratta, according to an AFP journalist at the scene. He didn't speak in court or apply for bail, and his next hearing is scheduled for Feb. 4.
In court, Nugent's lawyer Chirag Patel told Magistrate Allison Vaughan that his suffered from idiopathic transverse myelitis, a neurological condition, as well as a concussion. The lawyer didn't explain how Nugent had become concussed. Patel also said his client was suffering from potential mental health issues but had never been diagnosed with any mental health problem.
According to the Cleveland Clinic, idiopathic transverse myelitis is a rare condition that damages the spinal cord's protective myelin sheath and disrupts nerve signals between the brain and body, leading to rapid muscle weakness, sensory loss, pain, and bladder and bowel dysfunction.
The motive for the attack remains unknown, and authorities will not speculate while the investigation is ongoing. But police said Wednesday they were examining all possible leads, including that Nugent may have held radical anti-government views.
"We're examining social media associations, talking to witnesses, friends and colleagues," Victoria police commissioner Mike Bush told reporters. He said, however, that authorities had no intelligence on the suspect and hadn't seen anything to suggest he posed an immediate threat.
Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett pointed to a growing and concerning level of "extremist views" online, saying the incident was "what many had been dreading for some time."
World "more dangerous"
Helen Haines entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife, becoming known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action.
The independent lawmaker was standing near the trunk of her car when she was struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser on Monday afternoon. Witnesses told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation that they saw her pinned between the two vehicles.
Threats against Australian lawmakers and electorate offices doubled between 2021 and 2025, with 1,067 incidents reported to police last year.
Governor-General Sam Mostyn — King Charles III's official representative in Australia — said the nation was crying out for "decency" in the wake of the attack on Haines.
"Australians are yearning for kindness and care, and they're asking us why we've lost the great skill of disagreeing well," Mostyn said, speaking alongside Phil Haines.
Highlighting the tense climate, police in Western Australia charged a man late on Wednesday after he made threats and swung nunchucks at the office of state lawmaker Hannah Beazley, media said.
The incident has drawn comparisons to other acts of violence against elected officials elsewhere, most notably the killing of British lawmaker Jo Cox outside her office in 2016.
"It's a reminder that the world is a more dangerous and divided place than it was a generation ago," Prime Minister Albanese told ABC Melbourne radio.

Russia’s Novoshakhtinsk Oil Terminal Takes Heavy Damage as 8 of 12 Tanks Are Hit, Satellite Images Show
At least eight of the 12 large storage tanks at the oil-loading terminal of the Novoshakhtinsk Petroleum Products Plant (NZNP) in Russia’s Rostov-on-Don were damaged following a drone attack on October 10, according to satellite imagery published by the OSINT monitoring channel Exilenova+.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The extent of the damage was revealed in a satellite image released by Exilenova+, providing further evidence of the impact of the strike on the facility, which handles petroleum exports and reportedly supplies fuel to Russian military forces.
The facility was targeted overnight on October 10, when drones struck the oil-loading terminal, triggering a large fire.
The Novoshakhtinsk Petroleum Products Plant (NZNP) operates an oil-loading terminal in Rostov-on-Don’s Zheleznodorozhny district, formerly known as Yug Rusi.
The facility handles the storage and transportation of petroleum products, including shipments destined for export, and reportedly provides fuel supplies to Russian military forces. Its annual handling capacity is estimated at between 2.5 million and 3.5 million metric tons.
Petroleum products arrive at the site by rail and road before being transferred to storage tanks and subsequently loaded onto vessels. The facility’s infrastructure includes pumping stations, pipelines, and specialized berthing equipment to support these operations.
The terminal is part of NZNP’s broader logistics network, which incorporates railway facilities and a dedicated tanker fleet. According to the company, the fleet comprises five river-sea tankers and three floating storage vessels.
The reported damage in Rostov-on-Don comes amid further drone attacks targeting Russian oil infrastructure, including a separate incident in the Tambov region.
On October 20, a fire broke out at the Nikolskoye oil pumping station following a suspected Ukrainian drone strike. The facility is connected to the infrastructure supporting the Druzhba oil pipeline network.

Beskrestnov later clarified that information about the drone's designation, manufacturer, and technical specifications had already emerged. However, he emphasized that these details remained unconfirmed and would not be disclosed yet.
The aircraft's most notable reported difference from the Lancet is its propulsion system. While the Russian Lancet uses an electric motor, the unidentified drone reportedly operates on gasoline. Internal combustion engines can provide greater endurance than battery-powered systems, although the new aircraft's actual range and flight duration remain unknown.
The Lancet is a Russian-made loitering munition developed by ZALA Aero Group. It is designed to strike artillery systems, armored vehicles, radar installations, and other battlefield targets. The system uses electric propulsion and is launched from a catapult, with variants carrying different warheads.
The appearance of the unidentified aircraft follows earlier Russian efforts to modify the Lancet family. In September 2025, Militarnyi reported that Russian forces had introduced an updated Lancet featuring a redesigned antenna system. The modification potentially affected the drone's communication capabilities, although Ukrainian forces continued intercepting the upgraded systems.
The rapid evolution of Russian drone designs reflects a broader pace of change that Ukrainian commanders and defense specialists have repeatedly warned about.
At a defense forum in Kyiv on September 25, military officials and industry figures cautioned that frontline technology can now shift within just several months. They called for faster innovation, wider use of artificial intelligence and autonomous systems, and engineering forecasts able to anticipate Russian developments six months to a year in advance.
Ukraine has leaned heavily on its own industry to keep pace, with domestically produced systems accounting for 95% of unmanned aerial vehicles procured for its Defense Forces.

Ukraine’s German Gepard Goes Six for Six Against Jet-Powered Aerial Targets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
12:08:04 UTC
