Summit in Samarkand, a boon for child wellbeing and health
Representatives from across the international community are meeting in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, to ensure that children everywhere can thrive in a world marred by war, climate chaos and other fundamental challenges.
The UN-backed World Summit Investing in Children’s Wellbeing opened on Wednesday, bringing together more than 600 participants from over 100 countries.
A child’s wellbeing depends on many factors, including health, access to education, protection from violence, family support and access to help when they need it.
Progress in peril
In a message to the summit, UN Secretary-General António Guterres stressed that “when we invest in children, we invest in the future”.
The Secretary-General’s message was read at the opening by Sabine Mahl, the UN Resident Coordinator in Uzbekistan.
Mr. Guterres warned that progress on child wellbeing is under threat. Conflicts, economic pressures, health emergencies, poverty and climate-related shocks put children at risk, particularly those from vulnerable groups.
He also noted that humanitarian and development assistance is declining, while developing countries continue to carry heavy debt burdens, which is why the summit is focusing not on a single programme or service, but on systems that need to work together.
Put children before process
Addressing the summit, Khalilur Rahman, the President of the UN General Assembly, called for a sharper focus on turning commitments to children into tangible results, declaring that “a target matters when a child eats, learns, receives treatment and returns home safely.” With only 36 per cent of assessable Sustainable Development Goal (SDGs) targets on track or making moderate progress, he urged countries to accelerate collective action rather than lower their ambitions.
He set out four priorities: put children before process; build services and social protection around their needs; reach those furthest behind; and match political promises with financing, responsibility and deadlines. He also called for child-centred approaches to artificial intelligence and other technologies, saying digital transformation should expand opportunity while protecting children from exploitation, discrimination, manipulation and privacy violations.
The Assembly President argued that governments should judge progress not simply by improving averages but by closing gaps for children most at risk, including those living in poverty, with disabilities, on the move or affected by conflict and climate shocks. And he challenged governments to make their commitments visible in their budgets: “A declaration cannot vaccinate a child. A promise itself cannot pay a teacher. Applause itself cannot purchase cancer medicines.”
‘A serious warning’
The summit was organized by the Government of Uzbekistan in partnership with the Office of the UN Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Violence against Children, child rights agency UNICEF, the World Health Organization (WHO) and the World Bank.
Minsters, academics and experts are taking part along with civil society and business representatives – as well as children and adolescents themselves.
Uzbekistan’s First Lady Ziroat Mirziyoyeva said that, according to experts, amid a sharp decline in international humanitarian assistance, the number of deaths among children under five is expected to rise in 2025 for the first time this century.
“This is a serious warning to us all,” she said. Ms. Mirziyoyeva also noted that one billion children are growing up in countries most vulnerable to the effects of climate change.
National priority
In Uzbekistan, where more than half the population is under 30, children’s wellbeing is a government priority. This agenda, actively supported by UN agencies, is also linked to changes in social services and access to early education.
According to UN Resident Coordinator Mahl, preschool enrolment in Uzbekistan has risen from 27 per cent in 2017 to 78 per cent in 2026.
More than 10,000 children with disabilities attend mainstream schools and about 1.5 million families receive social assistance.
UNICEF says the share of children living in monetary poverty has fallen significantly, in part thanks to government social support.
In 2025, the country adopted a law to protect children from all forms of violence, as well as an action strategy for 2026–2030.
Childhood cancer: tackling inequality
The Samarkand summit also includes the Second International Congress on Childhood Cancer - “From Cure to Wellbeing” - dedicated to paediatric oncology and haematology.
According to WHO, more than 80 per cent of children with cancer are cured in high-income countries, while the figure is below 30 per cent in many low and middle-income countries.
In his message, the UN Secretary-General called this “an unacceptable inequality driven by inadequate investment and weak social services.”
Cancer is diagnosed in around 400,000 children and adolescents worldwide each year. WHO aims to increase the global survival rate to 60 per cent by 2030.
Children with cancer need more than medical treatment. The State-sponsored institution Mehrli Maktab – which means “caring school” in Uzbek – operates at the Scientific and Practical Medical Centre for Paediatric Oncology, Haematology and Immunology in the capital Tashkent.
Children aged two to 18 can continue their education there during lengthy treatment, studying mathematics, information technology, electronics, music and other subjects.
They make friends and can discover new interests – many return after completing treatment to see their former classmates. Some former students also attended the summit to share their experiences.
Organizers gave prominence to the voices of other children and adolescents. As Najat Maalla M’jid, the UN Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Violence against Children, put it: “They have voices, ideas, expertise, and urgency.”

UN agencies appeal for help to protect weakest from unprecedented El Niño

UN agencies appeal for help to protect weakest from unprecedented El Niño
Two UN agencies issued a powerful appeal on Wednesday for immediate assistance to help communities already being impacted by the strongest El Niño weather pattern on record.
“The current El Niño event could be unprecedented in strength – literally, off the monitoring charts that we have used for the past four decades – and will peak towards the end of 2026, but its impacts will be felt long after that,” said Celeste Saulo, Secretary-General of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).
According to the latest Global Seasonal Climate Update from WMO, sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific – the epicentre of the extreme El Niño weather phenomenon – may rise to 3.8℃ above average between November 2026 and January 2027.
While a Pacific Ocean surface temperature anomaly of 0.5℃ above normal is enough to trigger an El Niño alert by WMO, Ms. Saulo highlighted concerns that the impact of an El Niño fuelled by a 3.8℃ gap has no precedent.
Simply unprecedented
Previous El Niños linked to anomalies of 3℃ have brought “very substantive impacts across the world”, but “we are beyond that limit, out of our records, out of our statistics of what we can expect”, the agency chief stressed.
“We are already witnessing extreme weather events and expect this to multiply and cascade as El Niño intensifies,” Ms. Saulo noted.
“But a powerful El Niño does not have to be a recipe for humanitarian disaster. We have the science forecasts, the early warnings to save lives and protect livelihoods.”
Echoing Ms. Saulo’s appeal for prevention efforts to boost resilience among the world’s most vulnerable communities, the UN’s emergency relief chief, Tom Fletcher, described the new El Niño as a “behemoth…a wrecking ball that will likely tear through Latin America, eastern and southern Africa, Asia and the Pacific with extreme heat, droughts and floods”.
Funding to avert disaster
The next two weeks will be critical to averting a worsening humanitarian crisis linked to El Niño, Mr. Fletcher said, adding that Somalia, Ethiopia and Kenya urgently need funding and emergency supplies in place before heavy rains arrive.
In southern Africa, the priority is to deliver seeds and safeguard livestock, while Central America requires immediate support to protect livelihoods.
Across Asia and the Pacific, countries must brace for a range of climate shocks, including droughts, floods and cyclones.
“It would be an extraordinary failure to see this crisis coming, to hear the predictions from the experts, and yet still squander the opportunity to protect people in its path,” Mr. Fletcher warned.
Some 50 million people could face increased hunger because of the weather phenomenon, he stressed, before citing an African Development Bank estimate that it will cost African countries between $10 and $20 billion “and drive down GDP by between one and two per cent”.
UN cash injection
To support resilience efforts, the UN’s top aid official announced that he has released more than $50 million from the Central Emergency Response Fund to help 11 countries on the front line, including Chad, El Salvador, Ethiopia, Somalia and South Sudan.
The long-term impact “will be felt for months and potentially years to come”, Mr. Fletcher continued, citing the additional strains placed on the humanitarian system by the global supply chain crunch in the Strait of Hormuz and the Black Sea, respectively linked to war between Iran and the United States and the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
How is the UN helping the world brace for El Niño?
With a potentially devastating El Niño approaching, UN agencies are helping countries build disaster risk reduction into shelter and preparedness from the start, rather than reacting after disaster strikes. Here are some examples:
Chile: Shifting rainfall patterns have brought deadly floods to several regions. In northern Antofagasta, the UN Development Programme (UNDP) helped build massive barriers to hold back torrents of mud and debris.
Madagascar: Facing recurring cyclones, the national shelter cluster is developing a strategy that includes a five-year humanitarian action plan, with pilot projects running since early 2025 in the Atsimo Andrefana and Androy regions.
Nigeria: Despite aid cuts, the UN Disaster Risk Reduction office (UNDRR) and the Global Shelter Cluster brought government, humanitarian and environmental partners together in June 2025 to start work on a roadmap for safer shelter in areas hit by conflict and climate shocks.
Yemen: More than four million people are displaced, many of them on land prone to flooding, and flash floods hit over 100,000 households in 2024 alone. The UN refugee agency (UNHCR), UNDRR and partners have backed community-led defences, including a 2.5km flood diversion channel in the Al-Hazm district.

Migrants paid up to $500 million in smuggling fees on European sea routes
The price tag for smuggling on European sea routes reached up to half a billion dollars last year, the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) and the UN migration office, IOM, reported on Wednesday.
Key points
- Total fees paid to smugglers on sea routes to Europe reached between $388 and $509 million in 2025: UNODC estimates
- The busiest smuggling corridor was the Central Mediterranean route, where 84,000 to 100,400 people attempted a crossing
Almost half of migrants trying to get smuggled into Italy or Malta from North Africa or Türkiye reported paying fees of over $7,500 each, an IOM survey found.
Other routes are cheaper than this busy Central Mediterranean corridor.
Smugglers received as little as $170 per person for transport across the Northwest African Atlantic route, a dangerous maritime path where people travel in open boats from the coasts of Northwest Africa to Spain’s Canary Islands.
Read the full survey here.
Busy routes
The report found that around 190,000 to 209,000 people were smuggled along the four main sea routes to Europe in 2025.
The busiest smuggling route was the Central Mediterranean route (84,000 to 100,400 people), followed by the Eastern Mediterranean (48,400 to 51,300), which runs from Türkiye, Libya and the Middle East towards Greece, Cyprus and Bulgaria.
The Northwest African Atlantic came third, with 33,000 people smuggled, followed lastly by the Western Mediterranean route (24,500) which connects North and West Africa to Spain.
Destination not guaranteed
Many of the people who paid these fees to get smuggled to Europe did not arrive at the destination, according to the UN.
Among all those departing on the sea routes in 2025, 3,404 lost their lives or were reported missing.
Another 104,200 people were intercepted at sea and returned.
Smuggling not the only way
“Perpetrators commit smuggling offences to make a profit,” UNODC said. But, the agency stressed that not all those attempting irregular entry on sea routes are smuggled.
The UN office estimates that 72 to 86 per cent of people departing on the Central Mediterranean route in 2025 were smuggled, along with 73 to 83 per cent of people on the Northwest African Atlantic route.
On the Western Mediterranean route, 57 to 90 per cent were smuggled, and on the Eastern Mediterranean route, it oscillated between 75 and 90 per cent.

Fate unknown of many returned to DPR Korea from China: UN independent experts

Fate unknown of many returned to DPR Korea from China: UN independent experts
Three years on from the reported resumption of large-scale forcible returns of nationals of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) from China, serious concerns persist about their fate, according to a group of Human Rights Council-appointed independent experts.
There is no information on the whereabouts and treatment of those repatriated – or those who remain at risk of return – the experts said in a press release on Wednesday.
“These events form part of a longstanding pattern of serious human rights violations against individuals forcibly returned to the DPRK. In the absence of independent monitoring in either country, many returnees remain unaccounted for,” they said.
“For as long as their fate and whereabouts remain unknown, returnees are deprived of essential safeguards against enforced disappearance, arbitrary detention, execution, torture, forced labour, sexual and gender-based violence and other serious human rights violations,” the experts added.
Trafficked and exploited
Reports indicate that some women who left the DPRK – commonly known as North Korea – became victims of trafficking, forced marriage and sexual exploitation.
Among them is Kim Cheol-ok, who reportedly fled the DPRK during the 1990s famine and was trafficked into China as a child.
Forced into marriage at 14, she was subjected to sexual violence and forced pregnancy.
Despite living in China for about 25 years and establishing family ties, she reportedly faced harassment and restrictions due to her irregular status.
Detained by Chinese authorities in April 2023 without access to legal representation, she was forcibly returned in October 2023. Her fate and whereabouts remain unknown.
The Working Group on Arbitrary Detention found in 2024 that her detention by China and the DPRK was arbitrary.
Crime and punishment
Since 2023, reports have emerged of serious human rights violations against returnees, particularly those perceived as having sought asylum or who left the country without authorisation, raising concerns under the principle of non-refoulement.
The principle states that no one should be returned to a country where they face a real risk of persecution, torture or inhuman treatment.
“Irregular migration status does not diminish the obligation to respect the principle of non-refoulement,” the experts said.
“Given longstanding evidence that DPRK nationals who leave the country without authorisation, or seek protection abroad, may face severe punishment upon return,” they said, the reported mass returns “raise questions about whether their protection needs were adequately assessed before repatriation”.
‘Persistent obstacles’
The experts said “persistent obstacles continue to impede efforts to obtain information” on the fate and whereabouts of returnees – including those in political prison camps – as well as those who remain at risk of forcible return from China.
They called on China to respect the principle of non-refoulement, refrain from repatriating North Koreans “and ensure access to fair and effective procedures for assessing their international protection needs”.
They also called on Pyongyang to disclose the fate and whereabouts of returnees.
About the experts
Special Rapporteurs and other independent experts are appointed by the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva to monitor and report on specific human rights themes or country situations.
They serve in their individual capacity, are independent of any government or organization, are not UN staff and receive no salary for their work.

‘Ominous start’ to West Bank olive harvest amid settler attacks
The use of live ammunition, arson and the destruction of centuries-old olive trees have marked the opening weeks of this year’s harvest in the occupied West Bank.
At least 160 Israeli settler attacks linked to the olive harvest were recorded in the first two weeks of October, according to the UN aid coordination office (OCHA) – often under the protection of, or with the participation of, Israeli forces.
Settlers have also damaged Palestinian property and stolen harvested olives and farm equipment. Last Friday, they assaulted a Washington Post photojournalist covering the harvest and the following day attacked European diplomats visiting a Palestinian community.
On Thursday, the UN human rights office (OHCHR) in the Occupied Palestinian Territory urged states and donors to go beyond condemnation and take urgent action to protect Palestinian communities as the season gets off to an “ominous start”.
Cut off from their land
Thousands of Palestinian farmers are unable to reach their olive trees because of severe Israeli movement restrictions, which have dramatically worsened over the past three years. Meanwhile, according to OHCHR, settlers are being allowed onto Palestinians’ land to harvest their crops.
“Palestinians often say that olive trees are symbolic of their existence as a group and their connection to the land,” said Ajith Sunghay, Head of the UN human rights office in the Occupied Palestinian Territory.
“This is yet another tool of displacement and dispossession, adding to the suffering of communities whose rights are under attack on a daily basis.”
The toll on the olive sector has been heavy. The Palestinian Ministry of Agriculture estimates losses at $157 million since October 2023 and says 90 per cent of Gaza’s two million olive trees have been destroyed in that time.
In the West Bank, 286,000 olive trees were damaged between 2023 and the end of September 2026, including 100,000 this year, even before the harvest season began.
Call to action
Mr. Sunghay reiterated a call by the Protection Cluster – a network of more than 100 international and national organisations led by his office – for Member States to increase their diplomatic field presence in high-risk communities, particularly during harvest periods.
The Cluster urged national governments to press Israel to ensure Palestinians’ safe access to their agricultural land, protect farmers from violence and expulsion, strengthen accountability and end settler expansion.
It also called on donors to provide:
- timely and flexible funding for protective presence
- legal assistance
- food security
- livelihoods interventions
Amid Israeli settler attacks across the West Bank over the years, UN agencies have a long history of taking action to protect Palestinian farmers.
Staffers with the UN relief agency for Palestine refugees (UNRWA) have helped farmers harvest olives, including in Beit Surik, Biddu and Wadi Fukin.
UN officials have also met with communities to mitigate attacks, including allocating $750,000 from the Humanitarian Fund in 2024 to support olive farmers, saying they must have unimpeded and safe access to their groves.

World News in Brief: Aid for Ethiopia, Abyei drone strikes condemned, extreme heat and newborn health
The World Health Organization (WHO) is scaling up emergency health response operations across Afar, Amhara and Tigray in Ethiopia to address growing humanitarian and health needs resulting from ongoing hostilities.
The UN health agency has strengthened its emergency coordination, deployed technical teams and expanded operational support to keep essential health services running in conflict-affected areas of the north.
Working with regional authorities, WHO is supporting preparedness, response coordination, disease surveillance and lifesaving interventions in collaboration with a range of partners, including the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) and the UN refugee agency, UNHCR.
71 tonnes of supplies
WHO has delivered more than 71 metric tonnes of essential supplies to Tigray, Amhara and Afar.
Aid includes emergency health kits, cholera response materials, reproductive health kits and medicine for noncommunicable diseases.
The agency is also backing outbreak investigation, vaccine distribution and emergency referrals while strengthening public health monitoring in areas affected by insecurity and displacement.
Mobile teams and facilities continue to provide essential services, including primary care, disease prevention and maternal and reproductive health services.
Guterres deplores recent deadly attack in Abyei
UN Secretary-General António Guterres has urged authorities in Sudan and South Sudan to act to avert further attacks in the disputed Abyei border region.
The Secretary-General strongly condemned deadly drone strikes near a busy market on Monday that killed dozens of civilians, injured many others and set structures ablaze.
“I express my deepest and heartfelt condolences to the families of those who lost their lives and wish a swift recovery to the injured,” he said in a statement published late on Wednesday.
He noted that in the aftermath of the attack, the UN peacekeeping force in Abyei (UNISFA) deployed medical personnel, firefighting equipment and quick reaction forces to provide emergency treatment, support casualty evacuation and prevent the fire from spreading.
Respect and protect civilians
The strikes on Amiet Market and the Todach area are among the latest developments in the war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and former allies the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) that erupted in April 2023.
The Secretary-General stressed that attacks targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure are prohibited under international law.
“I remind that all parties to the armed conflict must comply with their obligations under international humanitarian law, including to respect and protect civilians at all times,” he said, underlining the need for accountability and calling on the Governments of South Sudan and Sudan “to take all steps possible to help prevent further attacks and uphold Abyei’s demilitarised status”.
New tool tracks heat’s impact on pregnancy, newborns and children
Extreme heat can put lives at risk even before birth. It also raises health risks during pregnancy and for newborns and young children.
To help countries track these dangers, a group of UN agencies has launched the first set of priority indicators focused on these vulnerable groups.
“Our health systems need the data to recognise this reality and take action,” said Bruce Gordon, interim director of environment, climate change, One Health and migration at the World Health Organization (WHO).
That means everything from protecting people during heatwaves to building climate risk into everyday health services, he added.
WHO, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), UNICEF and the UN reproductive health agency, UNFPA, launched the new framework designed to strengthen preparedness, improve monitoring and accelerate response.
Improved heat-health planning
The new report recommends that countries monitor pre-term births, stillbirths, low birthweight, pregnancy hypertension, child deaths and health-facility visits during extreme heat.
Monitoring school attendance can also help reveal how heat is disrupting children’s lives.
An estimated 1.5 billion children worldwide are exposed to heatwaves that are becoming more frequent, longer or more severe.
The new information can help health governments prepare facilities for rising demand, strengthen warnings to pregnant women and families, identify communities at greatest risk and improve planning, the agencies said.

Astronauts’ hearts just passed a surprising test for Mars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:59:14 UTC
20:59:14 KST

Astronauts’ hearts just passed a surprising test for Mars
- Date:
- October 21, 2026
- Source:
- Northwestern University
- Summary:
- A new study tracking 13 astronauts suggests that the human heart may be surprisingly well equipped for a journey to Mars, especially with regular exercise during spaceflight. Researchers found that astronauts' hearts adapted to months of weightlessness and handled simulated Martian gravity without major problems, offering new hope for future missions to the Red Planet.
- Share:
A journey to Mars may be less challenging for the human heart than scientists once feared. A new study suggests that astronauts can adapt remarkably well to months of weightlessness, offering encouraging evidence that humans could endure the long trip to the Red Planet and function under its weaker gravity.
Researchers from Northwestern Medicine, UT Southwestern, and UT Houston monitored the hearts of 13 astronauts who spent approximately six months aboard the International Space Station. Their findings showed that although spaceflight initially affected heart performance, the astronauts gradually adapted, with intensive daily exercise playing an important role in maintaining their cardiovascular health.
One of NASA's major concerns about sending humans to Mars is how astronauts' hearts and circulatory systems will respond when they leave the weightless conditions of spaceflight (known as microgravity) and encounter Martian gravity, which is only about one-third as strong as Earth's.
Encouragingly, the researchers found that the astronauts showed no significant signs of cardiovascular strain when exposed to simulated Martian gravity after returning to Earth.
"With our findings, there is now reason to think that we would be able to traverse to Mars, get there and actually work on the surface of Mars," said study senior author Dr. James Thomas, professor of medicine in the division of cardiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.
The study, published last month in the journal Circulation, is the first to investigate how the heart responds to simulated Martian gravity following an extended period in space.
How Daily Exercise Protects Astronauts' Hearts in Space
Living without gravity creates unusual challenges for the human body. On Earth, the heart constantly works against gravity to circulate blood, while muscles must support the body's weight. In space, those demands decrease substantially, allowing muscles and even the heart itself to shrink over time.
Returning to a gravitational environment can also be difficult. Astronauts on previous missions have frequently experienced dizziness or lightheadedness when standing after landing. This happens because gravity pulls blood toward the lower body, sometimes causing blood pressure to drop suddenly. The condition is called orthostatic hypotension. (If you've seen Sandra Bullock crawling after returning to Earth in "Gravity," you get the idea.)
However, the astronauts involved in the new study generally handled this transition well, potentially because they had maintained demanding exercise schedules throughout their missions.
As part of NASA's Exercise Countermeasures program, astronauts exercised for up to two hours each day. Their routines included 30 to 45 minutes of endurance training, which strengthens the cardiovascular system, along with 60 to 75 minutes of resistance training to help preserve muscle mass and strength.
"You lose muscle mass and cardiac mass when you're in a weightless environment because you are working less up there," explained Thomas, who also is a Northwestern Medicine cardiologist. "You're floating around in the air, and you give a little tap with your foot, and you can sail over to say hello to your buddy."
"To counter that, exercise is crucial when you're in space," Thomas added.
Heart Scans Reveal How the Body Adapts to Weightlessness
To understand what happens to the heart during prolonged spaceflight, the researchers collected echocardiograms before, during, and after each astronaut's mission. These ultrasound scans use sound waves to produce moving images of the heart, allowing doctors to examine its structure and measure how effectively it pumps blood.
While aboard the International Space Station, astronauts were trained to perform these scans on one another every few weeks. The recordings were transmitted to Earth, where researchers could monitor changes in heart function throughout the missions.
Thomas worked alongside Dr. Benjamin Levine of UT Southwestern Medical Center and Dr. Michael Bungo of the McGovern Medical School at UTHealth Houston.
"It would be typically about 3 a.m. for me because the space station runs on Greenwich Mean Time," Thomas said. "I would watch the recordings come in live and coach the astronauts in real time to improve the images."
The scans revealed that the astronauts' hearts initially struggled to adjust to their new environment. During the first two weeks in space, researchers observed declines in cardiac filling, stroke volume, and several other measures of cardiovascular performance.
Cardiac filling refers to how much blood enters the heart between beats, while stroke volume describes the amount of blood pumped out with each contraction. Both measurements decreased early in the missions, indicating that the astronauts' hearts were temporarily moving less blood with each beat.
But the changes did not persist.
As the astronauts spent more time in space, their cardiovascular systems adapted. Cardiac filling and stroke volume gradually improved, approaching the levels recorded before launch.
These results suggest that the heart can adjust to prolonged weightlessness more effectively than early measurements might indicate, particularly when astronauts maintain regular physical activity.
Astronauts' Hearts Pass a Simulated Mars Gravity Test
The researchers also wanted to answer a particularly important question for future Mars missions: What happens when an astronaut who has spent months in weightlessness suddenly encounters gravity again?
Mars has roughly 38% of Earth's surface gravity. Although this is considerably weaker than what people experience on Earth, it would still force astronauts' hearts to work differently after months of floating in space.
To reproduce some of these effects, the researchers conducted a simulated Martian gravity test after the astronauts returned to Earth.
Each astronaut was tilted upward by 22 degrees from a lying position. This posture caused blood to shift toward the lower body, approximating the circulatory effects of Martian gravity.
The results were encouraging. After spending about six months in space, the astronauts' hearts performed just as well under simulated Martian gravity as they had when standing upright on Earth before their missions.
This suggests that astronauts who maintain their cardiovascular fitness during spaceflight may be capable of transitioning to the weaker gravity of Mars without experiencing major cardiovascular difficulties.
Although the findings come from a relatively small group of astronauts and a simulation rather than an actual Mars landing, they provide valuable evidence for planning future missions.
Combined with the benefits of daily exercise, the heart's ability to adapt to weightlessness and respond well to simulated Martian gravity offers another reason to be optimistic about sending humans to the Red Planet.
The study is titled "Impact of Prolonged Spaceflight on Cardiac Structure and Function: An Exploratory Longitudinal Observational Study." Funding was provided by the National Space Biomedical Research Institute (grant NCC9-58), NASA (grant NNJ04HH01A), the IDP Foundation, Sandra Helton, and the National Heart Foundation of Australia.

Star Ferry fares are set to rise by as much as HK$1.80 (23 US cents) from January after Hong Kong authorities endorsed the operator’s application for an increase, taking the cost of a weekend cross-harbour trip to up to HK$8.30.
The operator, which last raised its fares in 2023, applied in March to increase charges on its two franchised routes by between 80 HK cents and HK$2 per journey.
Under a proposal approved by the Executive Council last Tuesday and announced on Wednesday, fares for the Central-Tsim Sha Tsui and Wan Chai-Tsim Sha Tsui routes will rise from January 25 next year.

EU Seeks More Ukraine Aid From Canada, UK as Kyiv Faces €70 Billion Funding Gap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:58:32 UTC
20:58:32 KST

Ukraine faces a €70 billion ($77 billion) funding shortfall next year, prompting the EU to seek greater financial commitments from countries outside the bloc as it struggles to cover Kyiv’s growing needs.
The issue is expected to feature in upcoming EU summits with Canada on Oct. 29-30 and the UK on Nov. 20. According to POLITICO, citing EU officials and diplomats, Brussels wants to use the meetings to encourage both countries to increase their contributions to Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The effort comes as the EU tries to secure long-term financing for Ukraine’s defense and state operations while Russia continues its war and the future of US support remains uncertain.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said last week that the EU and its member states provide 80% of Ukraine’s external aid.
“We urgently need other partners to step up,” she said.
The funding challenge follows the EU’s commitment to a €90 billion loan ($101 billion) for Ukraine covering 2026 and 2027. The package is expected to meet roughly two-thirds of Kyiv’s financial requirements, leaving a substantial amount to be secured elsewhere.
Brussels had expected non-EU partners, including Canada, Japan, South Korea, Australia, and Norway, to contribute another €45 billion ($50 billion). But some of the anticipated funding has yet to be finalized or disbursed, POLITICO reported.
Putin Orders US Teacher’s Release as Witkoff Arrives for Talks
The European Commission has also been tasked with exploring ways to bridge the financing gap.
Allies face growing pressure to contribute
The EU is seeking broader international support rather than relying increasingly on European taxpayers to cover Ukraine’s needs.
European Council President António Costa told the European Parliament on Wednesday, Oct. 21 that international partners must intensify their financial support for Kyiv.
European Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis also raised the issue during last week’s meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank in Bangkok, saying Ukraine’s 2027 financing needs were a prominent topic.
He called for “broad burden sharing” among international partners as Ukraine continues to resist Russian aggression.
EU officials stressed that the initiative was not intended as criticism of Canada or the UK, both longstanding supporters of Ukraine. They said the country’s financial requirements had grown and more partners would need to help cover them.
The UK says it has committed £25 billion ($33 billion) in support for Ukraine, according to its official government figures.
Canada has pledged the equivalent of €5.4 billion ($6 billion) in military assistance and €8.2 billion ($9 billion) in direct financial support, according to the Canadian government’s Ukraine assistance overview.
The EU and its member states say they have contributed more than €231 billion ($259 billion) since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.
That total includes military aid, budget support, guarantees, assistance for Ukrainians living in the bloc, and proceeds from immobilized Russian assets.
Funding push coincides with wider EU negotiations
The upcoming summits will also address broader economic and defense ties, giving Brussels an opportunity to discuss Ukraine alongside other priorities.
Von der Leyen has proposed making Canada the EU’s first “associate member.” Ottawa is also set to participate in the bloc’s SAFE defense procurement program, which finances joint weapons purchases and opens eligible contracts to Canadian companies.
Canada says it has committed nearly C$26 billion ($18 billion) in military, financial, development, and humanitarian assistance to Ukraine. Its support includes a military aid package worth $900 million, announced in July.
“Canada continues to stand by Ukraine and remains engaged with international partners on Ukraine’s needs,” Privy Council Office spokesperson Kathryn Serieux told POLITICO.
The Nov. 20 EU-UK summit is expected to advance British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s efforts to reset relations with the bloc.
London also wants British companies to qualify as European under the EU’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act, which would favor European-made goods in public procurement and industrial support.
British officials told POLITICO they were unaware of any request to link those benefits to increased aid for Ukraine.
An EU official said Ukraine was expected to feature in the summit’s joint declaration, but characterized it as recognition of both sides’ support for Kyiv rather than a demand for additional funding.
Brussels is also seeking greater contributions from Japan. One EU official described Tokyo’s 2026 support as lagging, although a person familiar with the Japanese government’s position disputed that assessment, citing around $20 billion already provided to Ukraine and saying further assistance could be considered if Kyiv requested it.
Australia said it had not received a request for additional funding for Ukraine in 2027. An Australian official suggested Canberra might be a lower priority after its leaders announced additional funding and a security agreement with Kyiv last month.
European support faces political uncertainty
The push for more international funding comes as support for Ukraine could face renewed political pressure in elections across Europe next year.
In France, Marine Le Pen has vowed to end aid to Ukraine if elected president in 2027. In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni faces a challenge from Russia-friendly politician Roberto Vannacci ahead of next year’s election.
Combined with uncertainty over Washington’s future commitments, those political risks are encouraging European officials to look beyond their own budgets.
The Commission is also urging Ukraine to seek more contributions directly from non-EU partners.

Putin, Witkoff meet in Russia for Ukraine war talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:58:13 UTC
20:58:13 KST

Breadcrumb
Putin, Witkoff meet in Russia for talks on Ukraine war
Russia's Vladimir Putin began talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff on ending the Ukraine war in Saint Petersburg on Wednesday, with the American official saying he had brought "ideas" for a possible peace deal.
Witkoff travelled to Russia from Norway, where he met Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky in talks Washington described as "positive."
The meeting is taking place as the United States pushes an end to Europe's worst conflict since World War II, with Russia pounding Ukrainian cities ahead of winter and amid a bitter feud between Donald Trump and Zelensky.
As Witkoff touched down in Putin's home city, Russia announced it would soon begin shipments of diesel to the United States under a deal with Trump, and that it had freed a US citizen—Stephen Hubbard—held by Moscow since the start of the war on allegations of fighting as a "mercenary" for Ukraine.
"We've brought some papers. It's really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you'll read that at your leisure," Witkoff—Trump's business partner and envoy—told Putin in Saint Petersburg's Konstantinovsky Palace.
Putin thanked Trump for his efforts to resolve the war and said he was eager to be informed about the US meeting with Zelensky.
The longtime Russian leader has repeatedly refused to hold face-to-face talks with Zelensky and said that Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine.
Witkoff told Putin he hoped trilateral talks can resume.
"I'm hoping that you might consider that as a next step in the peace process so we can begin to have technical teams discussing what are those next steps," he told the Russian leader.
Putin thanked Trump for his "attention" to the conflict and said the US leader had "insisted that it was necessary to end this conflict" in their last phone call.
Russia's war against Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands of troops on both sides as well as thousands of civilians.
As Witkoff arrived in Saint Petersburg, Kyiv said Moscow's strikes killed at least four people —including two in the capital and an elderly couple in the eastern Kharkiv region.
'Momentum' in talks
Meeting Putin, Witkoff described his talks with Zelensky as "productive."
"I think there's some degree of momentum and I hope that today can be another step forward in the peace process and discussing how we resolve the Ukrainian conflict," he said.
Zelensky on Tuesday thanked Washington for the resumption of US intelligence sharing on Russian strikes.
The Witkoff-Zelensky meeting in Norway followed days of friction between Washington and Kyiv, with Zelensky urging the US not to side with Russia and Trump calling for the Ukrainian leader to be replaced.
Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner is also due to participate in Wednesday's talks with Putin remotely.
US-led talks on the conflict have so far not led to a breakthrough and Moscow insists it intends to press on with its offensive.
Witkoff also told Putin that Washington was "grateful" for a diesel deal—met with astonishment in Kyiv and across Europe—that saw US sanctions on Moscow eased to allow Russian fuel to flow to the United States.
The deal has been seen as a way to try to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of testing midterm elections in the US next month.
Washington was interested in further "business and economic cooperation" with Russia when the war ends, Witkoff said.
"We even talk about it now openly with the Ukrainians to give them some sort of sense about what the possibilities will be when this whole conflict is over," he said.
Kyiv has pleaded with Western countries to put more pressure on Moscow and not lift sanctions.
Ahead of the talks, Putin announced that Stephen Hubbard, an American taken captive by Russian forces in Ukraine in 2022 and later sentenced to almost seven years in prison, had been freed.
Trump had asked the Russian leader to free Hubbard, a retired English teacher in his 70s who had always denied the charges he was a "mercenary" fighting for Ukraine.
Witkoff hailed the move and called Putin a "humanitarian".
Trump later said that Hubbard was on his way to the Unites States and that the release had not been part of a swap deal.

MOSCOW, October 21. /TASS/. Russia will respond firmly to a Japanese company’s supply of combat drones to Ukraine, Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said at a news briefing.
"Such hostile actions against Russia will not go unanswered. We will respond firmly, including through measures that Tokyo will feel in relevant areas. Our country has the means to ensure this," she said.

"I trust that Tokyo will hear us," Zakharova concluded.

Lithuanian Prime Minister: Russia is testing the limits of Article 5
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:56:49 UTC
20:56:49 KST

Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius has indicated that Russia is testing NATO’s collective defense by carrying out attacks that come very close to triggering the Alliance’s Article 5.
Sinkevičius noted that the phrase that Russia is testing boundaries appears with increasing frequency in political discussions—and this does not concern only Lithuania, Latvia, or other countries on the eastern flank. Russia is testing how far it can go without crossing the threshold that would necessitate the activation of NATO’s collective defense.
Referring to recent events in Europe, Sinkevičius pointed out that these pose serious challenges for the Alliance regarding the appropriate response. These are not classic, conventional attacks, nor are they direct and unambiguous border violations. Often, such acts are carried out by individuals hired specifically for the purpose, and investigations reveal that the party behind them is to be found in the East.
Sinkevičius stated that he will continue close cooperation with his Polish counterparts to accelerate response times and improve communication in the event of future incidents.
The most significant agreement reached is an arrangement for the heads of government to communicate directly with one another. He and Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk have exchanged private contact details, ensuring that in the event of incidents or the receipt of critical information—including intelligence—they can communicate immediately, rather than waiting for the offices of the prime ministers to make contact.

Ukraine plans to test the FREYJA anti-ballistic system by the end of 2026 - Zelenskyy
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:55:38 EEST
20:55:38 KST

Ukraine plans to test the FREYJA anti-ballistic system by the end of 2026 - Zelenskyy
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine and its European partners plan to test the FREYJA anti-ballistic system by the end of 2026. President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported on the initial results of the development and Norway’s active participation in the project.
Ukraine, together with its European partners, plans to conduct the first tests of the FREYJA anti-ballistic system by the end of 2026. As President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported, developers have already achieved the first results in creating individual components of the system, while Norway is actively involved in implementing the project, UNN writes.
Details
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported on a new stage in the implementation of the pan-European FREYJA anti-ballistic shield project following a meeting with Norway’s Minister of Defence Tore Sandvik, Kongsberg CEO Eirik Lie, and representatives of the corporation. According to the head of state, Norway is playing an active role in creating the future missile defence system.
Norway is also actively participating in our European FREYJA anti-ballistic programme. There are already initial results in creating individual elements of the system. Today, we determined where we can and must accelerate in order to begin testing by the end of this year. We also discussed in detail the launch of work on new satellite communications capabilities for our soldiers. We will involve partners that have the capabilities to provide support
Zelenskyy separately highlighted the contribution of Norwegian company Kongsberg, which manufactures NASAMS air defence systems. These systems protect Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure from Russian missile and drone attacks every day. The head of state also expressed hope that partners would provide additional packages of defence assistance next month.
Ukraine has already completed its part of the work on FREYJA
Earlier, Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported that Ukraine had completed its part of the work on the FREYJA anti-ballistic project. At the same time, European partners continue to carry out their own tasks.
The President of Ukraine stressed that creating anti-ballistic systems is an extremely complex technological process that usually takes decades. However, due to the ongoing threat of Russian ballistic strikes, Ukraine seeks to significantly shorten the development timeline.
Background
FREYJA is a Ukraine-initiated pan-European anti-ballistic shield project intended to protect Ukrainian cities from Russian ballistic missiles. To implement it, Ukraine and its European partners established the Anti-Ballistic Coalition, which brought together 10 countries and leading defence companies. The joint efforts are aimed at developing indigenous missile defence technologies and establishing their mass production.
The foundation of the future system is the Ukrainian FP-7.x interceptor missile, being developed by Ukrainian defence company Fire Point. The project envisages integrating the Ukrainian missile with European technologies, including German radar systems and Norwegian guidance technologies.
As UNN previously reported, Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh said that development of FREYJA had already moved to the stage of technical integration of the entire ecosystem—radars, the launcher, data transmission channels, and the command centre. According to her, technical tests of individual components are conducted up to twice a week.

Russia is losing almost US$2.5bn a month due to Ukrainian port blockade – Russian newspaper
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:55:00 EEST
20:55:00 KST

Russia is losing almost US$2.5bn a month due to Ukrainian port blockade – Russian newspaper
Operations have virtually ground to a halt at Russian ports on the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov due to drone and uncrewed surface vessel (USV) attacks, with industry players estimating that government budgets and businesses are losing out on more than RUB 200 billion (about US$2.43 billion) a month.
Source: the Russian newspaper Kommersant, citing sources, including OTEKO, which operates terminals in Taman
Details: Cargo handling at terminals in Russia's southern ports fell by 95-100% in September, and passenger traffic dropped by 85%. Cargo flows have been redirected to ports in northwestern Russia or overland routes.
Russian agricultural exports have also been affected. In July and August, 3.8 million tonnes of agricultural cargo passed through ports in Krasnodar Krai, compared with 7.9 million tonnes during the same period in 2025.
Kommersant reported that Russia's largest southern ports, including Novorossiysk, Taman and Tuapse, have begun cutting staff, with some employees forced to take unpaid leave or accept shorter working weeks.
Against this backdrop, Krasnodar Krai governor Veniamin Kondratyev has proposed that Russian Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Patrushev consider providing state subsidies to the region's ports along the same lines as those granted to airports in the region that have been closed.
Possible measures include subsidising employees' wages and the costs of maintaining and servicing equipment, silos, warehouses and berthing infrastructure, as well as covering electricity and utility bills.
The authorities are also considering reimbursing part of the interest on loans and borrowings intended to keep terminals ready to resume operations. On 6 October, Patrushev instructed the relevant ministries to consider the proposals.
Russia's Association of Commercial Sea Ports has also asked for government support, addressing its request to Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak.
The association has called for a deferral of taxes and lease payments on federal property, wage subsidies equivalent to one month's minimum wage per employee, and more favourable terms for war risk insurance.
Russia's southern ports employ around 20,000-25,000 people. Experts estimate that providing support equivalent to one month's minimum wage per employee would cost Russia RUB 550-670 million per month (US$6.67 million-US$8.13 million), or RUB 6.6-8 billion per year (US$80.0 million-US$97.0 million).
Background:
- Ukrainian agricultural producers managed to increase exports in September compared with August, although Russia's continuing blockade of Ukrainian seaports remains one of the main economic risks for the agricultural sector.
- In August, it was reported that Russian grain exports, which bring around US$15 billion into the Russian economy annually, had been almost completely paralysed by Ukrainian strikes on ports in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.

She said the initiative would help officials engage with AI confidently, use it responsibly and translate new capabilities into better public outcomes.Pragya Misra, head of strategy and government affairs, OpenAI India, said the country's AI opportunity depended not merely on access to technology but also on how effectively institutions and individuals used it.
"With more than 1.7 crore government employees across the Centre, States and Union Territories registered on iGOT Karmayogi, the platform offers a powerful way to build practical AI capability at scale," she said.The partnership comes amid the Centre's broader push to integrate AI into governance while developing skills needed to use the technology responsibly.

Speaking at a discussion at the Berlin Global Dialogue conference, Merz said Europe is supporting Ukraine to end the war, not prolong it.
“We are not supporting Ukraine in order to continue this war. We are doing this to end it as soon as possible,” he said, adding that there has been “some progress” in the Oslo talks without elaboration, as reported by Ukrainian state media Ukrinform.
The Kremlin has long accused Kyiv’s allies of prolonging the war by supporting Ukraine, while they argue they are supporting Kyiv’s right to defend itself from Moscow’s invasion.
Merz added that Ukraine’s surrender would mean “the capitulation of all of us,” adding that supporting Ukraine is “entirely in our own interests.”

Merz said Russia’s invasion represents an attack on “the entire political order that we have achieved since 1990.”
“This is not just a war in Ukraine,” he said, echoing European intelligence reports that Russia has stepped up hybrid attacks on Europe, with tactics ranging from drone incidents to assassinations against arms executives.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov reiterated Moscow’s rejection of Europe’s stance on Wednesday, arguing that, from Moscow’s perspective, the new proposals are “unlikely to be a constructive contribution to a settlement.”
The developments came as the US stepped up pressure on Kyiv toward a peace settlement after pursuing a diesel deal with Moscow, with Europe pushing back against the deal and Washington’s subsequent pressure on Kyiv.
Peace on whose terms?
While all parties – including the US and Europe – have called for peace in Ukraine, the terms have been polarizing.
Europe has sided with Kyiv, arguing that Russia is responsible for the invasion and that any peace should be just and lasting, rather than a temporary ceasefire.
Russia has long cast its own Ukraine invasion as a war against NATO, initially demanding that Ukraine be demilitarized and barred from joining the alliance, and recently reiterated demands for Kyiv to voluntarily withdraw from eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region, to which Moscow has laid claims via unrecognized referendums.
Kyiv, meanwhile, called for a freeze along the contact lines, arguing that ceding the Donbas region could weaken its own security and allow Russia to recuperate for another invasion against the rest of Ukraine; Ukraine’s recent Operation Vivaldi also reversed much of Russia’s gains in the region throughout 2026.
While the previous US administration backed Ukraine’s sovereignty, the current administration has pursued economic incentives to bring Moscow to the negotiating table, with President Volodymyr Zelensky saying in March that Washington had pressured Kyiv to give up the Donbas in exchange for security guarantees.

SUVA, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Fiji is bracing for worsening water shortages as a strengthening El Nino is expected to bring drier conditions in the coming months, the Fiji Meteorological Service has warned.
Shweta Shiwangni, a scientific officer at the service, told local media on Wednesday that the El Nino event had become established in the tropical Pacific and was expected to intensify, increasing the risk of prolonged dry conditions as Fiji enters the 2026-2027 tropical cyclone season, which runs from November to April.
Rainfall toward the end of November could ease dry conditions in the Western Division, but significant rainfall remains uncertain and may depend on the development of a low-pressure system or tropical disturbance near Fiji, she said.
Shiwangni urged communities already facing water shortages to seek water deliveries through relevant authorities and collect rainwater wherever possible.
Meanwhile, Fiji could be affected by two to three tropical cyclones during the upcoming season, with one or two potentially reaching Category Three or higher, according to the Meteorological Service.
The Northern and Eastern divisions have historically experienced greater cyclone impacts during El Nino conditions, Shiwangni said, while warning that all parts of the country could face destructive winds, heavy rainfall and flooding.
Authorities have urged residents to secure their homes, clear gutters and drains, prepare emergency supplies and identify evacuation centers.
Farmers have been advised to move livestock to higher ground when flooding threatens, while businesses in flood-prone areas should take steps to protect infrastructure. ■

CANBERRA, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- The Australian Capital Territory (ACT) Legislative Assembly passed new planning reforms to speed up housing approvals and increase housing supply in Canberra, the territory government announced on Wednesday.
The changes will simplify planning and leasing processes for smaller-scale housing developments, including townhouses, duplexes, terraces and secondary residences.
Under the reforms, assessment and approval timeframes for smaller-scale subdivisions and land consolidations will be reduced from 60 days to 30-45 working days.
Homeowners will also be automatically entitled to build secondary residences, such as granny flats, without requiring a Crown lease variation.
Minor lease variations, including changes to permitted dwelling numbers, will be processed through a streamlined pathway, reducing assessment times to 10 days.
ACT Minister for Planning and Sustainable Development Chris Steel said the reforms would make the planning process simpler and help deliver more housing choices for Canberra residents.
The reforms form part of the ACT government's broader housing strategy, which aims to enable the construction of 30,000 new homes by 2030. ■

The platform has maintained effective operations over the years through regular meetings, case referrals and other forms of cooperation, making itself an important channel for people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait to lodge complaints, seek advice and assistance, and protect their legitimate rights and interests, Zhang Han, a spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said at a regular news briefing.
Since the beginning of this year, the Taiwan Work Office of the CPC Central Committee and the KMT have held multiple consultations to improve the platform's operations and effectiveness, and they have reached a consensus on further cooperation, she said.
The two sides will maintain regular communication and provide timely feedback, and the platform will offer Taiwan residents professional legal services, Zhang said.
They will also work to enhance assistance for Taiwan residents facing temporary difficulties, help people search for missing relatives and provide humanitarian care, she added.
The two sides of the Strait established an investment dispute settlement mechanism in 2012 under a cross-Strait investment protection agreement reached on a common political foundation of the 1992 Consensus.
However, the mechanism was suspended in May 2016 because Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities refused to recognize the 1992 Consensus, which embodies the one-China principle, Zhang said.
The mainland is willing to engage in dialogue on resuming the mechanism's operations, provided that the DPP authorities recognize the 1992 Consensus, Zhang said.
The Taiwan question stems from a civil war fought between the forces led by the CPC and the KMT about eight decades ago. In 1949, the defeated KMT retreated to Taiwan, while the People's Republic of China was founded under the leadership of the CPC.
The unresolved civil war and foreign interference have left the two sides of the Strait in a prolonged state of political confrontation. However, the fact that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory has never changed. ■

Israeli patient receives new non-invasive treatment for epilepsy in first outside Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:52:46 UTC
20:52:46 KST

An Israeli patient received a non-invasive epilepsy treatment at Clalit-Beilinson Hospital, making her the first outside of Europe to use the technology.
The EASEE brain stimulation system, first developed in Germany by PRECISIS, is designed to treat epilepsy without opening the skull or inserting electrodes into the brain.
"This is the first time we can treat patients with epilepsy without penetrating the brain or inserting an electrode into it, while potentially achieving a significant reduction in the number of seizures," Dr. Idit Tamir, Director of the Functional Neurosurgery Unit at Clalit-Beilinson, said.
"The technology has demonstrated results comparable to the improvements seen with invasive neurostimulation devices. In appropriately selected patients, it offers a genuine alternative to these treatments."
Approximately one-third of the 100,000 people in Israel living with epilepsy do not achieve adequate seizure control through medication.
Israeli patient did not respond to medication for epilepsy
The first Israeli patient to undergo the treatment, 42-year-old Olga Moisa, has lived with epilepsy for 15 years and did not respond fully to medication.
"Some patients do not respond to medication. We sometimes try one drug after another, but none succeeds in controlling the seizures," Professor Felix Benninger, Director of the hospital’s Epilepsy Treatment Unit, explained.
On August 31, Moisa received treatment through the EASEE system, which electrically stimulates the seizure focus in the brain from outside the skull. Since then, she has not experienced any seizures, but it is still too early to fully determine its effectiveness.
"At the moment, the device is operating at a low stimulation level, allowing her body to gradually adjust to the stimulation. We still do not know what the outcome will be. We will only know in a few months," her son, Sasha, said. "Even if there is something that can reduce the seizures by 50%, that is already better."

====================================================================================================

Liberty, equality, impunity: France ignored the warnings. Now it’s paying for it - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:52:36 UTC
20:52:36 KST

There are moments when you wish you had been wrong.
Watching the images coming out of France since Saturday, October 17, has been one of those moments. And it has been painful.
What was meant to be a nationwide mobilization against the rising cost of living turned, in several cities, into a day of riots and looting. Streets ransacked, businesses plundered, buildings and cars set ablaze. It leaves a feeling hard to put into words.
Sadness, first. Shame, too. And above all, one question: How much longer will it take France to stop downplaying what is happening, acknowledge how serious the situation has become, and act accordingly?
This did not come out of nowhere. For years, voices have warned of the normalization of violence, the radicalization of rhetoric, the erosion of authority, and the growing reluctance of France’s leaders to draw clear red lines out of political calculation.
Those warnings were ignored, and those who voiced them were stigmatized. French Jews know this better than anyone: they were often the first to see those lines recede, and the first to be accused of overreacting.
Saturday’s scenes of chaos are what happens when those in charge refuse to listen, understand, or respond.
As a French woman living in Israel, I do not write these lines with the satisfaction of someone who has been proven right. There is no victory in watching my native country tear itself apart.
What is most alarming is no longer the violence; it is the way a society ends up getting used to it. Each new episode becomes one more crisis, a few days of outrage, then nothing. And it all starts again, in a spiral that keeps intensifying.
And always the same question: How far is France willing to go in accepting it?
When red lines disappear
A society does not slide into violence overnight. Limits shift. Words harden. Threats become slogans, intimidation is played down, and people sometimes end up working harder to justify the violence than to state that it is unacceptable.
In September 2024, Elias d’Imzalène, an Islamist activist described by French media as close to the Muslim Brotherhood, called on a crowd to “lead the intifada in Paris, in our banlieues, in our neighborhoods.”
“Intifada” is not an innocent word: it refers to a history marked, among other things, by deadly attacks against Israeli civilians.
In December 2024, he was given a five-month suspended sentence for public incitement to hatred or violence. That such calls can echo through France should make us ask what we have become capable of tolerating.
Then it was Gaza; on Saturday, the cost of living. The cause changes. The logic remains the same.
Responsibility does not end with those who call for violence or carry it out. It also lies with those in the political far-left who have spent years fueling confrontation, normalizing radical rhetoric, and excusing violence whenever it serves their ideological and political struggle.
When Ersilia Soudais, a lawmaker from La France Insoumise, visited d’Imzalène in police custody to express her “full support,” when her colleague Éric Coquerel called him more “respectable” than then-interior minister Bruno Retailleau, and when another La France Insoumise figure, MEP Rima Hassan, went on trial in Paris on October 19 for glorifying terrorism, the line between radical activism and elected office was not blurred. It was erased.
This is called islamo-gauchisme, the alliance between Islamist activists and parts of the radical Left. Shared enemies unite them: the Republic, the West, and, first in line as always, the Jews.
Words have consequences. When political leaders support those who demonize opponents, excuse extremist rhetoric, or legitimize violence in the name of a cause, they do more than express a political position: they help make that rhetoric acceptable.
They shift the boundaries of what can be said, justified, and ultimately tolerated. And when violence follows, those who helped create the climate in which it could be excused cannot claim innocence because they did not carry it out themselves.
The far-left is not the only one at fault. The responsibility also belongs to those whose job it was to stop it, like President Emmanuel Macron, who attributes the violence to “factions from ultra-left groups, joined by many delinquents.”
For years, successive governments have let the situation fester, condemning in words while rarely following through. When a call to “lead the intifada in Paris” ends with a suspended sentence, impunity itself becomes the message.
There is a bitter irony in all this. Macron and his ministers rarely miss an opportunity to lecture Israel on how it should fight its wars, govern its territory, and contain violence.
Yet those so eager to tell Israelis how to manage their society have presided over the unraveling of their own.
Watching from Israel, one cannot help but wonder whether France would be better served if its leaders devoted to its own streets a fraction of the attention they devote to ours.
The price of surrender
The question now is who is still willing to defend the rules of the Republic, and who pays when no one does.
France built part of its identity around a republican ideal: liberty, equality, and fraternity.
It was never perfectly realized, and it would be absurd to claim that the France of yesterday was free of injustice or tension. But it was the France I grew up believing in.
This weekend, that ideal was put to the test, and the first to pay were the shopkeepers.
Over 3,000 businesses were hit. Behind each one is someone who gets up every morning to go to work, pays ever-higher taxes year after year, and trusted that in return, the state would protect what they built.
In a single day, many of them lost everything. And the state that takes its share of their work every year failed to protect them.
There is something painfully familiar in their sense of abandonment. French Jews have lived with it for 20 years.
From Ilan Halimi to the Toulouse school shooting, from the Hyper Cacher to Sarah Halimi and Mireille Knoll, they sounded the alarm again and again. And that was before October 7.
Since then, France has recorded over a thousand antisemitic acts every year. French Jews no longer felt safe in their schools, synagogues, and streets. They were met with statements, vigils, and promises, rarely with action.
History offers a lesson France seems determined to forget: when a country lets its Jews feel threatened and does nothing, it is rarely the Jews alone who pay the price. The Republic is usually next.
On Saturday, the Republic paid.
The freedom to demonstrate does not grant the right to destroy. Anger does not excuse violence. And understanding why people are angry never exempts the state from holding accountable those who break the law.
This is not a radical position. It is the bare minimum a state owes to those who keep it running.
The sadness of having seen it coming
I watch these images from afar, like many others. It would be so much easier to keep that distance, as if France has become a problem that no longer concerns me. But one does not so easily detach oneself from a country that is part of who one is.
The revolting part is seeing a country that hesitates to defend what defines it, as if standing by its values had become riskier than letting them erode.
Nowhere is this clearer than in its foreign policy. In September 2025, the same president who now denounces the ultra-left recognized a Palestinian state. France called it a step toward peace; Hamas welcomed it as a victory.
It came as calls to “lead the intifada in Paris” still echoed in French streets, and as the Palestinian flag had become a fixture at protests where solidarity too often blurred into intimidation.
Perhaps he believed it would ease tensions at home. Saturday showed otherwise.
Of one thing I am certain: France has not finished paying the price.
Beneath the anger, there is something deeper: grief. Grief for a country that still proclaims “liberty, equality, fraternity” above the doors of its town halls, even as rioters set one of those very buildings ablaze in Limoges.
A Republic cannot survive on the words carved into its stone if it no longer has the resolve to defend what they stand for.
This spiral is not inevitable. But a state that cannot protect its shopkeepers, its Jews, its streets, or even its own buildings will not be saved by speeches.
France is quick to preach values to Israel. Israel, at least, knows which ones it is willing to fight for.
There are moments when you wish you had been wrong. Lately, France keeps giving me more of them. And the saddest thing of all would be if one day we reached a point where none of this made us sad anymore.
The writer is a public diplomacy consultant and content creator who explains Israel to French-speaking audiences on Instagram. A former Breaking News editor at The Jerusalem Post and adviser at Israel’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations, she recently launched Israel Compass, a nonpartisan platform for the Knesset elections.

Attending the Financial Street Forum for the second consecutive year, Ramos, also a member of the International Advisory Council of China's National Financial Regulatory Administration, welcomed the progress in China's financial-sector opening up, describing it as "encouraging."
She noted that China continues to expand institutional and two-way opening up, guided by market-oriented, law-based and internationally aligned principles. These efforts are making it easier for global investors to access the Chinese market while helping domestic investors connect with international markets, she said.
The country is also advancing renminbi (RMB) internationalization, strengthening Shanghai's role as an international financial center, and consolidating and enhancing Hong Kong's status as one. These efforts support more transparent, stable and predictable market rules, providing a stronger foundation for sustained confidence among long-term global investors, she said.
Ramos pointed out that China's economy is growing in a more innovation-driven and quality-oriented manner, and that the orderly advancement of financial opening up has created tangible opportunities for Standard Chartered's China-related business, particularly in RMB internationalization, the global expansion of Chinese corporates, cross-border trade, green finance and wealth management.
Citing examples, she said Standard Chartered has provided RMB-denominated cross-border receivables financing to a leading Chinese EV manufacturer to support its overseas expansion. The bank has also provided green project financing to a Chinese company for the construction of a battery gigafactory in Sunderland, Britain.
With a presence in China spanning nearly 170 years, Standard Chartered views the country as one of its most strategically important markets, Ramos said. The bank has been both a participant in and a beneficiary of China's reform and opening up, and remains firmly committed to the Chinese market over the long term.
Between 2020 and 2026, the bank invested almost 600 million U.S. dollars in China, and Ramos said it would continue to invest in its China franchise and technology. "We are aiming to turn our confidence in China into tangible action on the ground," she said. ■
