Across China: Young entrepreneurs give Xinjiang's cultural heritage modern makeover
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:52:33 CST
20:52:33 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- A slim, sky-blue scarf caught the eye of young visitors at an exhibition in downtown Beijing, with its contemporary zodiac motifs offering a fresh take on Xinjiang's traditional Atlas silk, known for its vivid colors and distinctive patterns.
The scarf was the work of designer Gong Yue, a young entrepreneur from Korla, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, at an exhibition showcasing specialty agricultural products and cultural and creative products from Bayingolin Mongolian Autonomous Prefecture.
Gong's booth features a wide range of creative cultural products designed and made by him and his team. Drawing on local materials and traditions, these products vary from Atlas silk tissue holders and mouse pads to refrigerator magnets with ethnic wedding themes, to cashmere scarves featuring contemporary interpretations of traditional Xinjiang motifs.
Born in 1996 in Korla, Gong used to work in a pharmaceutical firm in Shanghai. He later returned home and launched a business with two friends.
The idea grew out of his habit of bringing Xinjiang specialties and souvenirs to colleagues in Shanghai, whose positive responses convinced him that locally inspired products could appeal to consumers beyond the region.
Located in southeastern Xinjiang, Bayingolin Mongolian Autonomous Prefecture features diverse landscapes ranging from mountains and grasslands to deserts and lakes, and is home to numerous historical sites, including the ruins of the ancient city of Loulan, offering Gong a rich source of inspiration for his designs.
Among his team's newer products are ceramic plates and coffee cups made with sand from local desert and Gobi areas. After repeated trials, the team found that the sand and local water gave the ceramics a distinctive blue-green finish.
Beyond experimenting with local materials, Gong also draws on both technology and traditional craftsmanship to bring Xinjiang's cultural heritage into contemporary life. His AR fridge magnets, for instance, are inspired by the well-known Han Dynasty brocade armband inscribed with the Chinese characters "five stars rise in the East." Scanning a QR code takes users to a slideshow explaining the historical artifact and its cultural significance, adding context to the designs.
He has also reimagined traditional motifs for embroidered cashmere scarves and blankets, adapting clustered-grass, vine-and-grass and flame patterns to contemporary tastes. Gong develops the designs and works with local embroiderers, who bring them to life by hand.
"For example, I incorporated traditional motifs symbolizing flourishing growth and career advancement into the scarf design to resonate with young consumers' aspirations for success," Gong said.
Turning these designs into finished products requires close cooperation with traditional craftspeople. Gong's team now works with 13 family-run workshops in the region, and producing a single handmade blanket can involve 10 to 16 embroiderers.
In working with the artisans, Gong comes to appreciate the meticulousness of traditional handicrafts and the time and patience required to produce each piece. He realizes that bringing traditional crafts to a wider market is not simply a matter of scaling up production, but also of respecting the skills, working rhythms and craftsmanship of the artisans behind them.
Gong's designs speak to both tourists and local residents. Li, a Korla resident who has bought a pair of cups inspired by the city's signature fragrant pears, said the products capture her hometown's character while offering a fresh, fashionable take on local culture.
The stores have also gained followings on social media platform Xiaohongshu. As posts about the stores spread online, they become popular check-in spots in Korla. Gong's team now operates three stores and is collaborating with museums and galleries in Beijing's 798 Art District.
Gong is not alone in bringing Xinjiang's local culture to consumers. In Yili Old Town, Cao Hongbing's leathercraft workshop produces sheepskin pyrography artworks. The business has grown from two people to more than 10 employees, most of whom are local residents.
In Yuli County's Lop Nur Village scenic area, college students are turning local fishing and hunting traditions and folk culture into wood carvings, bookmarks and other souvenirs.
Local authorities are also helping young entrepreneurs bring Xinjiang's local products and cultural offerings to wider audiences. Gong's trip to Beijing, for example, was part of a promotional event by local authorities showcasing Bayingolin's specialty products and cultural and tourism resources. Other measures to support local businesses include startup loans, access to business premises and incubation services, as well as job fairs tailored to relevant industries.
Meanwhile, Xinjiang's booming tourism market offers further opportunities for local cultural and creative businesses. In 2025, the region received a record 323 million tourist visits, with tourism spending reaching 370 billion yuan (about 55 billion U.S. dollars).
Developing strong brands is key to preserving and advancing traditional crafts, while creative design and new technologies can help connect them with modern life, meet consumer needs and enhance their market value, said Huang Yonglin, head of the National Research Center of Cultural Industries under the Central China Normal University.
For Gong, the goal is to make Xinjiang's cultural traditions more tangible and accessible. "I hope my products will attract more people to visit Xinjiang in person to experience its flavors, breathtaking landscapes and exquisite handicrafts," he said. ■

EU opens probe into Booking.com over scams, advertising transparency
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:52:32 CST
20:52:32 KST

BRUSSELS, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- The European Commission on Wednesday opened a formal investigation into Booking.com over its possible failures to tackle fraudulent listings and phishing scams, and to clearly identify paid advertisements.
The investigation will examine whether the platform properly assessed and mitigated risks from fake accommodation listings, such as non-existent properties, impersonation fraud and offers that fail to comply with applicable rules under the European Union's Digital Services Act (DSA), the Commission said in a statement.
It will also scrutinize how reservation and guest data is shared with accommodation providers and how Booking.com operates its messaging service. Investigators will assess whether sufficient safeguards exist to prevent data misuse for phishing attacks and fraudulent payment requests.
According to the statement, accommodation providers pay higher commissions to secure greater visibility in search results on the platform, and the Commission will examine whether these boosted listings are clearly labeled as advertisements and whether users can easily identify who placed and paid for them.
Under the DSA, users should be able to distinguish between listings prominently displayed because they match a search and those promoted through payment, the Commission said.
If confirmed, the suspected failures would breach the DSA's obligations on systemic risk assessment, risk mitigation and advertising transparency.
The Commission said it would prioritize an in-depth investigation and gather further evidence through information requests, interviews or inspections. It may also impose interim measures or accept commitments from Booking.com to address the concerns.
The opening of proceedings does not prejudge the investigation's outcome, it added. Booking.com was designated as a Very Large Online Platform under the EU's DSA on 25 April 2023. ■

Turkey, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia sign defense pact

Maryland man pleads guilty to vandalizing Jewish cemetery, filming himself spray-painting swastikas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:52:24 UTC
20:52:24 KST

A Maryland man pleaded guilty in federal court on Tuesday to vandalizing 12 gravestones at a Jewish cemetery outside Baltimore, where he spray-painted swastikas and other antisemitic symbols, according to a plea agreement obtained by Walla.
George Horne, 36, of Dundalk, Maryland, admitted to targeting the Ohr Knesseth Israel Anshe Sfard Cemetery because it was Jewish.
The plea agreement revealed new details about the attack, including racist messages Horne exchanged before the vandalism, a video he recorded of himself carrying it out, and Nazi memorabilia and white supremacist literature discovered by investigators.
Among the materials recovered was an image of the Pokémon character Pikachu wearing a Nazi armband.
The FBI investigated the incident alongside the Baltimore County Police Department, with the US Attorney's Office for the District of Maryland prosecuting the case.
According to the investigation, Horne arrived at the Jewish cemetery on the night of July 16-17, 2023, after sending messages to two users of an encrypted messaging application indicating that he intended to visit a "rabbi graveyard."
He subsequently entered the cemetery and spray-painted swastikas in black paint on several gravestones.
Following the vandalism, Horne sent another individual a message describing his actions as a "secret, nonviolent Aryan protest."
He also complained that six Jewish cemeteries had been established along the street among the burial grounds of those he described as the "original white residents."
Dundalk, a longtime industrial suburb east of Baltimore, developed around the region's steel mills and port facilities.
The Ohr Knesseth Israel Anshe Sfard Cemetery is among the historic burial grounds serving Baltimore's Jewish community, whose roots date back to the 19th century.
Established in the late 1800s, the cemetery served longstanding Jewish congregations in the city and is managed by the Jewish Cemetery Association of Greater Baltimore.
The cemetery had previously been targeted in an antisemitic attack in 2021, when swastikas were spray-painted on more than a dozen gravestones.
Investigators found that Horne shared a link to a news article about the earlier vandalism, though authorities did not establish that he was involved in that incident.
Distinctive tattoo helped investigators identify suspect
A key piece of evidence against Horne was a nine-second video he recorded while committing the vandalism.
The footage showed his tattooed hand spray-painting a swastika onto a gravestone.
Investigators were able to connect Horne to the attack by matching a distinctive tattoo on the back of the hand visible in the video to a tattoo on his own hand.
Cemetery workers discovered the vandalism five days after the incident and identified 12 damaged gravestones.
Approximately $1,000 was spent attempting to remove the paint, but traces of the swastikas remained visible on some of the stones. Replacing the damaged gravestones is expected to cost several thousand dollars more.
Additional fencing and security cameras were installed at the cemetery following the attack.
Nazi memorabilia, white supremacist writings discovered
Searches of Horne's vehicle, phones, and a storage unit he used uncovered numerous items associated with Nazi ideology and white supremacy.
Among the materials recovered was a compact disc bearing the words "Warning: Extreme Nazism," along with a photograph of Horne wearing a hat displaying the Black Sun symbol, which is associated with neo-Nazi movements.
Investigators also found a phone wallpaper depicting Pikachu wearing a Nazi armband featuring a swastika.
Other materials included a translated copy of Adolf Hitler's Mein Kampf, messages in which Horne exchanged photographs of Nazi coins, and images and memes expressing support for Hitler and white supremacy.
Investigators also recovered a journal containing references to Nazism and the white supremacist slogan known as the "14 Words."
A sticker bearing the number 1488 was also discovered. The number is widely used as a code among neo-Nazi groups, with 14 referring to the white supremacist slogan and 88 representing the Nazi salute "Heil Hitler," based on the letter H being the eighth letter of the alphabet.
Under the plea agreement, Horne acknowledged that he had deliberately selected the cemetery because of its Jewish identity.
Horne and his defense attorney also stipulated that the facts outlined in the agreement were accurate and that prosecutors could have proven them beyond a reasonable doubt had the case proceeded to trial.
The offense to which Horne pleaded guilty carries a maximum sentence of three years in prison.
US District Judge Matthew Maddox scheduled sentencing for mid-January.

====================================================================================================

Current climate pledges fall far short of emissions cuts needed to return to 1.5C warming limit: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:51:05 UTC
20:51:05 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
Current climate pledges would cut global greenhouse gas emissions by only 11%-15% by 2035, far short of the 45% reduction needed to help bring warming back below 1.5C (2.7F) by the end of the century, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) warned Wednesday.
In its Emissions Gap Report 2026, UNEP said emissions must fall 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040 from 2025 levels to limit peak warming to around 1.7C-1.8C (3.1F-3.2F) before potentially returning to 1.5C (2.7F) or below by 2100.
However, fully implementing countries' existing climate pledges would cut emissions by only 5%-8% by 2030 and 11%-15% by 2035.
The report found that current climate policies could lead to 2.8C (5F) of global warming this century, while fulfilling all national climate commitments would limit warming to 2.6C (4.7F).
Even meeting additional net-zero targets alongside national climate commitments would limit warming to only 2.1C (3.8F), according to UNEP.
"Every additional fraction of a degree and additional year of warming above 1.5C increases climate impacts and risks, such as the deadly floods, heatwaves and wildfires that have plagued many nations this year," UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen said in the report.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres stressed that exceeding the 1.5C (2.7F) threshold does not mean abandoning efforts to reverse warming.
"Overshoot is not surrender. We can still keep it as small and as short as possible – and bring temperatures back below 1.5 degrees by the end of the century," he said.
The report also found that returning to 1.5C (2.7F) would require removing and permanently storing approximately 320 gigatons of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere this century, a task facing significant technological and economic challenges.
Despite the warnings, UNEP noted that renewable energy expansion and climate policies have already reduced emissions in several countries.
"It is now up to nations to urgently put in place policies that spark fast, deep and sustained emissions reductions, and put the world on track for a more stable climate and more stable economies and societies," Andersen said.
The report warned that without urgent action, keeping peak warming below 1.7-1.8C (3.1-3.2F) "will quickly become impossible."

Ukraine hits data center of Russia’s top bank
Ukraine continued striking Russian data centers this week, hitting one belonging to Sberbank, Russia’s largest bank. The state-owned lender is also a sweeping online conglomerate, developing its own artificial intelligence model and operating an extensive ecosystem of digital services. Although the strikes did not cause serious disruptions to banking services, the ongoing Ukrainian campaign could undermine Russians’ confidence in the banking system.
- Ukraine attacked a data center in the city of Balakovo, in the Saratov region, approximately 1,000 kilometres from Moscow. Sberbank has been building the facility since 2021 and described it as the largest in Russia. A week earlier, Ukrainian drones knocked out three of Yandex’s six major data centers. Yandex is one of Russia’s largest IT companies.
- Following the attack, users in Russia began complaining about problems with Sber’s services (the bank’s umbrella brand encompasses its digital products), the Samokat grocery delivery service, and the GigaChat AI service. Some other websites unrelated to Sber also experienced technical issues, including the Kontur business ecosystem and the Ozon marketplace. The disruptions peaked at 11:10 a.m. Moscow time on October 14, after which the number of error reports began to decline.
- Sberbank customers barely noticed the effects of Ukraine’s attack on the data center because the bank’s core banking systems are hosted at other sites, technology expert Anastasia Bezrukova told the business newspaper Vedomosti. According to her, the Balakovo data center was being built to expand existing infrastructure. It was also intended to house the country’s most powerful supercomputer and provide backup capacity for Gostekh, a cloud platform serving federal and regional government agencies. Sberbank has two other data centers that remain untouched: one in Moscow and another in Moscow Oblast.
- Earlier, following Ukrainian attacks on Yandex data centers, Russian users experienced serious disruptions to Yandex Pay, the company’s payment service. For several days, they were unable to make payments or transfers. Some users complained that the problems with Yandex Pay prevented them from making their monthly loan and mortgage payments.
- Strikes on data centers and the subsequent disruptions to banking services are unlikely to trigger a systemic crisis in Russia’s banking sector, but they could further erode public confidence in it. Amid mobile internet disruptions, rising taxes, and widespread anxiety fueled by rumors of a possible new wave of mobilization, Russians have been withdrawing increasing amounts of cash and using it to pay for purchases. According to September data from the central bank, the share of cashless transactions in retail turnover fell for the first time in the second quarter of 2026, dropping by 0.5 percentage points to 88.4%, the data shows. Previous crises — the pandemic, the beginning of the war against Ukraine, and Yevgeny Prigozhin’s attempted military mutiny in 2023 — led to noticeable increases in the amount of cash in circulation.
Why the world should care
A potential increase in cash in circulation could have two consequences. The first is an expansion of the shadow economy, which could potentially affect tax collection, although the impact is unlikely to be significant. The second is a liquidity shortage in the banking sector, which could affect banks’ financial results and slow the decline in lending rates as the key interest rate falls.

Swiss pharma will have to fund poisoning helpline
The Swiss government remains opposed to the national poison information centre being funded solely by the public sector. It now intends to use legislative amendments to compel the pharma and chemicals industry to contribute to the funding of Tox Info.

Putin orders release of jailed American as he meets Trump envoy for Ukraine talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:50:27 UTC
20:50:27 KST

Vladimir Putin ordered the release of an American man from a Russian jail as he met Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg on Wednesday for fresh talks on ending the war in Ukraine, amid increasingly close relations between Moscow and Washington.
Trump had previously asked Putin to free Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old former teacher who had spent more than four years in Russian jails on charges of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine.
His release appeared to be Moscow’s latest calculated move to bring Trump further into line with Putin’s position on Ukraine, while offering the US president a diplomatic victory before the midterm elections.
Hubbard was released unilaterally by Russia, rather than as part of a prisoner exchange as has often been the case with previous releases of Americans held in the country.
Writing on social media after the release was announced, Trump said it followed a request he had made “directly” to Putin last week.
He wrote on Truth Social: “The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return – an unprecedented situation for Russia … There was no ‘swap’ necessary for this release.”
Witkoff, meanwhile, lavished praise on Putin during their meeting at the grand Constantine Palace in St Petersburg, describing the Russian president as a humanitarian.
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Witkoff told Putin. He also conveyed Trump’s thanks for a deal to resume Russian diesel exports to the US.
The Russian president is wanted by the international criminal court (ICC) as a war criminal, in relation to the deportation of Ukrainian children to Russia during the war.
More than 17,500 civilians have been confirmed killed in Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to the UN, which says the true toll is likely to be significantly higher.
The warmth of Witkoff’s remarks stood in stark contrast to the increasingly hostile rhetoric directed at Volodymyr Zelenskyy by senior US officials, most notably Trump, who has called for the Ukrainian president to resign and portrayed him as the main obstacle to peace.
Witkoff travelled to Russia from Oslo, where he had met Zelenskyy and European leaders a day earlier in an attempt to inject momentum into stalled negotiations, with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine now in its fifth year.
Witkoff told Putin during a televised portion of their meeting: “We’ve brought some papers. It’s really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you’ll read that at your leisure.”
The visit was Witkoff’s ninth to Russia since Trump tasked him with brokering an end to the war.
Witkoff described his meeting with Putin as “constructive” but said “important work” remained and trilateral talks between the US, Russia and Ukraine “at the technical level” would follow.
The Kremlin said it had agreed “in principle” to the talks, which would focus on how to guarantee the security of Ukraine and Russia once the war ended.
The latest rupture in relations between Washington and Kyiv was triggered by Trump’s surprise decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel as part of a deal with Putin, followed by his call for Zelenskyy to be replaced after Ukraine refused to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Kyiv has since complained of disruptions to US intelligence-sharing and restrictions on its access to Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite network.
Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that Washington had resumed providing advance warnings of Russian missile attacks after his meeting with Witkoff in Oslo.
But Ukraine continues to face restrictions on Starshield, although it remains unclear who ordered them. The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk had personally ordered the slowdown, while Reuters, citing sources, said the directive had come from inside the White House.
During Wednesday’s meeting with Witkoff, Putin thanked Trump and his wife, Melania, for “their attention to efforts to end the war”.
Yet there are few signs of an imminent breakthrough. Despite repeated Ukrainian calls for a ceasefire, including a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure, Moscow has given little indication that it intends to end its bombardment of Ukraine as winter approaches, apparently confident that continued pressure will help it extract greater concessions from Kyiv.
The Russian leader remains intent on sticking to his maximalist war aims, including his demand for full Russian control of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region.
Putin also sought to emphasise the prospects for closer economic ties between Russia and the US once the war ends, suggesting that Moscow could significantly increase its exports of fertilisers to the American market.
Russian officials said the first tanker carrying diesel to the US would depart on Thursday as part of an initial shipment of about 300,000 tonnes.
Energy analysts and traders have questioned whether Trump’s agreement to temporarily resume Russian diesel imports will deliver meaningful relief to US consumers before the midterm elections, arguing that the volumes involved are too small to significantly ease the global supply squeeze.
The talks on Wednesday also touched on a possible meeting in China next month between Putin, Trump and the Chinese president, Xi Jinping. The Kremlin said Beijing was already making preparations for what it described as an unprecedented summit between the three leaders.

Dispute over teaching family values in Latvian schools – Education Ministry responds to criticism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:49:11 UTC
20:49:11 KST

Latvia’s Ministry of Education and Science (IZM) has denied using the controversial Teen Star programme or other religious or ideological approaches in its plans to introduce family values and health literacy education in schools, according to its response to a parliamentary inquiry submitted by the opposition Progressives party.
The ministry, currently overseen by the National Alliance (NA), has announced plans to incorporate family values and health literacy into the national education curriculum.
However, the proposal has attracted criticism amid concerns that the planned educational content could be partly influenced by ideas promoted by religiously conservative organisations.
The ministry emphasised that the family values and health literacy module has not yet been developed.
The informational report presented to the government in early October, along with the initial mapping of educational content, was prepared by Laura Joma, a national methodology specialist in social sciences education at the State Education Development Agency (VIAA).
According to the ministry, consultations were held with representatives of the University of Latvia and Riga Stradiņš University, social studies teachers, municipal education methodology specialists in social and civic education, as well as representatives of the Men's Health Alliance and the Latvian Association of Large Families.
The views gathered during these consultations were used to prepare the initial thematic framework and implementation roadmap.
As previously reported, Manuel Joaquín Fernández-González, a researcher at the University of Latvia with a background in the Catholic organisation Opus Dei, has been seeking to introduce new educational materials on moral and sexual education in Latvian schools.
Fernández-González's approach to sex education differs on several issues from that of Papardes zieds, an organisation that has long provided information and practical support to young people, parents and educators on sexual and reproductive health and rights.
The Education Ministry maintains that the planned curriculum is not based on any particular religious or ideological approach.
According to the ministry, its preliminary research included recommendations from the World Health Organization (WHO), UNESCO and the United Nations, alongside existing Latvian education standards, model subject curricula and 22 foreign educational programmes.
The international comparison examined Finland's approach to health education, Estonia's Human Studies subject, educational frameworks in Ireland, England and Wales, Ontario's Family Studies curriculum and the United States' Family and Consumer Sciences standards.
These sources were used to assess the scope of the proposed topics and their progression across different stages of education.
In matters relating to family relationships and development, the ministry referred to research on Bowen family systems theory, which considers the family an interconnected emotional system regardless of its composition.
The ministry also examined studies addressing personal boundaries, intergenerational influences, change and resilience.
For topics concerning human development, identity and health, the ministry cited James Gross's 2015 theoretical review of emotion regulation.
In the areas of relationships, sexuality and safety, the ministry examined a 2023 meta-analysis by Kang and colleagues covering 34 studies.
According to the ministry, this research supports a structured, age-appropriate approach to sexuality and reproductive health education.
It also referred to a 2021 literature review by Goldfarb and Lieberman addressing healthy relationships, violence prevention and media literacy.
Regarding parenting and children's needs, the ministry cited a 1983 paper by McCubbin and Patterson outlining a model of how families adapt to stressors, accumulated demands, available resources, interpretations of circumstances and coping strategies.
In its response, the ministry also confirmed that it had met with Fernández-González,
 who leads the project Promoting Values-Based Moral and Sexual Education for Family Formation in Latvia's Education System.
However, the ministry stated that only one recommendation from the project's policy proposals had been considered: strengthening values education within the framework of existing educational standards and upbringing guidelines.
According to the ministry, Fernández-González is not expected to participate as an author in the further development of the module.
The ministry pledged that the compulsory national curriculum would not promote any particular religious or ideological understanding of the family.
Instead, it would incorporate only values established in education standards and upbringing guidelines, together with learning outcomes supported by legal, scientific and pedagogical considerations.
Education specialists, sector experts, teachers, social partners and other stakeholders are expected to participate in developing and reviewing the curriculum.
The ministry said this process would ensure compliance with human rights, equality, non-discrimination and the principle of the best interests of the child.
It also referred to constitutional provisions guaranteeing freedom of religion and the separation of church and state, as well as provisions in Latvia's Education Law concerning the separation of education and religion.
At the conclusion of Wednesday's meeting of the Saeima's Public Requests Committee, MPs rejected the inquiry submitted by the Progressives.
As previously reported, the Education Ministry intends to continue improving Latvia's general education curriculum, including strengthening the teaching of family values and health literacy.
These plans were outlined in an informational report considered by the government in early October.
The family values and health literacy module is scheduled to be developed by 30 April 2027, in consultation with social partners and other stakeholders.
Relevant model subject curricula will subsequently be updated.
However, the proposal has faced opposition from representatives of the education sector.
During the government meeting, Inga Vanaga, head of the Latvian Trade Union of Education and Science Employees (LIZDA), called for the proposed family health education component to be removed.
She argued that the initiative appeared to reflect political and ideological influences and suggested that the ministry was promoting ideas associated with the Teen Star programme.
In a publication earlier in 2026, Latvian magazine Ir reported that Fernández-González's research on moral and sexual education for young people had highlighted Teen Star as a recommended educational resource.
According to the magazine, the programme promotes a critical attitude towards what it describes as the promotion of contraception and safe sex.
Fernández-González has developed methodological materials for teachers covering how to teach virtues to children from preschool through the final year of secondary school.
In a section titled Sex Education Toolbox, Teen Star is listed as the first recommended programme.
Teen Star is a sex education programme developed in the United States during the 1980s.
The magazine reported that the programme had faced criticism in several European countries over allegations that it reinforces gender stereotypes and promotes medically inaccurate educational content.
Critics have argued that such approaches could endanger young people's health and violate provisions of the European Social Charter.
In Bavaria, Germany, the programme has also faced accusations of homophobia and Christian fundamentalism.
Nevertheless, Latvia's Minister of Education and Science, Ilze Indriksone (National Alliance), has rejected claims that the planned educational changes are ideologically motivated.

The European Union says democratic backsliding under the government has brought Georgia’s accession process to an effective halt.

The chief of Europe’s biggest budget airline expects airfares to go up by as much as 20% in 2027 across Europe, as airlines are hit by higher jet fuel costs while the Iran war continues to drive up oil prices.
According to O'Leary, airlines are largely unhedged against higher jet fuel prices from April 2027.
Jet fuel prices in Europe and the CIS averaged $207.61 a barrel in the week ending 16 October, up almost 128% from a year earlier, according to the International Air Transport Association’s (IATA) monitor.
Many European airlines, including Ryanair, had strong hedge positions through 2026, O’Leary said, but their protection is much more limited from April 2027. He told Euronews that Ryanair had locked in fuel at about $67 a barrel this year, but he added, “our oil price will double” next year.
Speaking at a press conference in Brussels on Tuesday 20 October, he said: "You're going to see airfares rise next year in Europe, I think by 10, 15, maybe 20%. You're going to see the biggest increase in airfares, I would say, in history in Europe for the next 12 months."
“We’re 85% unhedged next year, and most of the other European airlines are in a similar position,” he said.
Higher jet fuel prices have squeezed margins for airlines without hedging protection.
Prices of crude oil and refined products, including jet fuel, rose rapidly following the outbreak of the Iran war and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, traded at $109.86 on Wednesday near a five-month high.
According to O'Leary, on top of the higher fuel costs, there will be fewer seats available in 2027 as a result of bankruptcies and takeovers in the European aviation market.
O'Leary was in Brussels to announce a major cut to the company’s operations in Belgium ahead of an increase in the country’s aviation tax from €2 to €7 in January 2027.
Ryanair is cutting 20 routes and 1.1 million seats from its Belgian winter schedule, blaming the tax rise. The airline said it was moving six aircraft to lower-cost European markets.

Ayhan Simsek
21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday called on US President Donald Trump to invite South Africa to the G20 summit in Miami in December.
Speaking at the Berlin Global Dialogue conference, Merz said anyone discussing the global economy’s future must involve all major partners. “Obviously, Africa belongs at the table,” he stressed.
“The African Union is a member of the G20. And so is South Africa. That’s why I urge that South Africa be represented at the G20 summit,” the chancellor said, referring to the summit of the world’s major industrial and emerging economies.
Trump earlier announced that South Africa would not receive an invitation to the 2026 summit. The decision followed Washington’s boycott of the Johannesburg summit and stemmed from Trump’s claims of persecution against white farmers in South Africa.
 
Europe seeks larger role
In his speech, Merz said the G20 remains a key platform for economic cooperation and global prosperity, and argued that Europe, as the world’s largest single market, should have a greater say in the group.
He thanked Trump for inviting EU members Spain, the Netherlands and Poland to take part as guests alongside regular members. “I will work to ensure that they remain part of the G20 loop in future,” he added.
Merz said this year’s G20 summit should focus on issues vital for the future of the world economy, including the opportunities and risks of artificial intelligence, a secure and affordable energy supply, how to address unfair trade practices, and rising public debt worldwide.
He also suggested prioritizing discussions on growth at the G20 summit in Miami. “Because today more than ever, economic stability and prosperity depend on the international environment,” he said. “To this end, we have proposed the Miami growth agenda to the US. We want to cut red tape jointly, drive necessary structural reforms and facilitate investment.”

Russia frees detained American Stephen Hubbard during US envoy's visit
Unknown

20:45:30 KST

Moscow says Putin, Trump and Xi will meet in Shenzhen next month after "constructive" talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff, while a US diesel deal easing sanctions on Russia has angered Kyiv and European capitals.
Russia is willing to return to three-way negotiations with the United States and Ukraine on ending the war, the Kremlin said on Wednesday after Vladimir Putin hosted US envoy Steve Witkoff in Saint Petersburg. However, it complained that recent Ukrainian and European proposals lacked "substance".
The talks, which lasted more than three hours in Putin's home city, coincided with the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired American teacher jailed in Russia for allegedly fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine. Witkoff announced the release during the meeting.
The Kremlin also said preparations were under way for a summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen next month between Putin, US President Donald Trump and China's Xi Jinping, describing it as "the first such meeting in history."
Witkoff said talks were "constructive" but that "important work" remained, as the Kremlin downplayed new Ukrainian and European approaches to ending the conflict.
"Discussions were constructive, and will continue with trilateral talks between the United States, Russia, and Ukraine at the technical level," Witkoff said on social media.
"While there is still important work left to do, President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end."
The US envoy, who has made several unsuccessful trips to Russia in pursuit of a settlement, arrived in Saint Petersburg a day after what he called a "productive" meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Norway.
He told Putin he saw "some degree of momentum" in the US-led talks.
Diesel deal angers Kyiv and Europe
Witkoff also told Putin that Washington was "grateful" for a recent diesel deal, under which US sanctions on Moscow were eased to allow Russian fuel to flow to the United States.
The arrangement has provoked outrage in Ukraine and across Europe. It is widely seen as an attempt to bring down fuel prices for American consumers ahead of next month's midterm elections, which are expected to be difficult for Trump's Republican Party.
The deal is one of several steps by the Trump administration seen as favourable to Moscow, at a time of growing tension between Washington and Kyiv.
Witkoff said the US was interested in further "business and economic cooperation" with Russia once the war ends. "We even talk about it now openly with the Ukrainians to give them some sort of sense about what the possibilities will be when this whole conflict is over," he said.
Hubbard freed without prisoner swap
Hubbard was first imprisoned by Russia in 2022 on charges that Hostage Aid Worldwide, a hostage advocacy group, has called bogus. He was sentenced to nearly seven years in prison following a closed-door trial in 2024.
Russian prosecutors accused him of joining the Ukrainian military after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022 and fighting alongside Ukrainian forces until his capture two months later.
The Biden administration had classified Hubbard as wrongfully detained.
He is the second American released by Russia in roughly two months, following the release in August of former US Marine Robert Gilman, who had been seriously ill and was jailed on contested charges of assaulting a police officer.
His release coincided with Witkoff's visit and came as Trump has taken several steps favourable to Moscow, amid growing tensions between Washington and Kyiv.
In an open letter to Trump published by Hostage Aid Worldwide in August, Hubbard's sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox, praised the president but also claimed her brother had endured "constant beatings, torture and starvation" while in detention.

National Museum of Iran pays tribute to renowned archaeologist Yousef Majidzadeh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21

National Museum of Iran pays tribute to renowned archaeologist Yousef Majidzadeh
TEHRAN - The National Museum of Iran has expressed its profound sorrow at the passing of Yousef Majidzadeh, one of Iran’s most distinguished archaeologists, whose research made significant contributions to the study of the country’s prehistoric cultures and early civilizations. Majidzadeh died in France on October 19, 2026, at the age of 90.
In a statement, Jebrael Nokandeh, Director General of the National Museum of Iran, extended his condolences to Majidzadeh’s family, colleagues, students, and the wider archaeological community, recognizing his important role in advancing archaeological research in Iran.
“Yousef Majidzadeh was an influential figure in Iranian archaeology, dedicating much of his academic career to investigating and interpreting the country’s archaeological heritage. His research on prehistoric societies, the emergence of complex communities, and the development of early civilizations made a substantial contribution to our understanding of Iran’s ancient past,” Nokandeh said.
Majidzadeh’s fieldwork encompassed several important archaeological sites, including Tepe Ghabristan in the Qazvin Plain, Tepe Ozbaki, and the sites of the Halil Rud basin in southeastern Iran. His excavations at Jiroft, particularly at Konar Sandal, brought international attention to the archaeological significance of the region and stimulated renewed discussion of southeastern Iran’s role in the development of complex societies in the ancient West Asia.
His scholarly publications also addressed the beginnings of urbanization in Iran, the history and civilization of Elam, and cultural relations between Iran and Mesopotamia. Alongside his fieldwork and writing, Majidzadeh contributed to the discipline through university teaching and the training of younger generations of archaeologists.
“The National Museum of Iran recognizes Majidzadeh’s substantial contributions to archaeological research and the study of Iran’s ancient civilizations. His fieldwork and publications remain important points of reference for scholars investigating the prehistoric and early historic periods of the Iranian plateau and the wider ancient Near East,” Nokandeh added.
The National Museum of Iran extends its condolences to Majidzadeh’s family, colleagues, former students, and the archaeological community.

Calls for Irish University to end its collaboration with Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:44:31 UTC
20:44:31 KST

The deep irony involved in studying human rights and international law in a university which continues to have a research partnership with an Israeli institute which collaborates closely with the Israel Defence Force (IDF) was highlighted during a sold-out conference on the west coast of Ireland this week.
The ‘Voices for Palestine’ conference at the Aras na nGael centre in Galway city centre was organised by the Campus Anti Genocide Coalition (CAGC) in opposition to the University of Galway’s continued research partnership with Technion, the Israeli public research university which maintains deep collaborative ties with Israel’s security forces.
Speakers at the event included three members of the Gaza Sumud Flotilla, all graduates of the University of Galway, who were abducted by Israeli forces in international waters as they tried to bring aid to Gaza in October of last year, and veteran campaigner for human rights Bernadette McAliskey (née Devlin), a former member of the British parliament from Northern Ireland.
All of the speakers called on the Galway institution to end its EU-funded research contract with Technion, which the University of Galway claims it cannot back out of due to contractual obligations and legal advice that it cannot do so.
The University of Galway is the home of the Irish Centre for Human Rights, attracting students from all over the world to study international law, and also hosts a Nelson Mandela Anti-Apartheid week in March each year. The former President of South Africa received an honorary degree there in 2003 and his legacy is invoked in Galway every year when high profile speakers visit the campus to celebrate its opposition to racism and Apartheid.
A Ph.D. scholar on genocide, Ramez Al Hayek, told the conference that he had spent much of the last three years researching the law of genocide and how international law can address the destruction of a people.
“Yet I have spent almost the same amount of time asking my own university to take seriously the very principles that we study and teach here,” said Al Hayek, a scholarship student from Palestine. “And that is a contradiction I find increasingly difficult to accept.”
READ: Ireland’s university leaders must step up where the Irish government has failed
Mr. Al Hayek, whose research focuses on genocide and settler-colonialism in Palestine, said the University of Galway has had two presidents and one interim president since October 2023. Students and staff at the University met with the then President, Ciaran O hOgartaigh, to discuss the university’s “deeply disappointing” response to the start of the onslaught in Gaza in late 2023.
“Three presidents, three years of meetings, statements, reviews, and promises. Yet here we are, still demanding that our university ends its institutional relationship with the Technion. In those three years, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza, over 175,000 injured, and approximately 82 per cent of Gaza’s structures damaged or destroyed. An entire education system has been devastated, with more than 95 per cent of schools and universities damaged,” said Mr. Al Hayek.
He said some progress had been made. In February 2024, the University called for a ceasefire in Gaza and, three months later, it proposed the adoption of a human rights policy and impact assessment, including a review of research collaborations. And in February 2026 it acknowledged that a genocide had been inflicted on the people of Palestine.
But he said that the “contradiction” between studying human rights in Galway and the university’s partnership with the Technion had been increasingly difficult to accept during three years of mass killings and destruction in Gaza and the on-going attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank.
Mr. Al Hayek said that there was shock among Palestinian students on the campus when the news broke in March 2025, via the Electronic Intifada news website, that the University of Galway had become the co-ordinator an EU-funded project known as ASTERISK, a green hydrogen initiative, and that its partners included Technion.
In September 2025, the university’s management said its interim human rights assessment process should not be used to end the Technion project because a formally approved policy and procedure was not in place.
The controversy led to the establishment of the CAGC, an alliance of students, academic staff, and trade unions on the Galway campus, leading to weekly protests at the entrance to the university, honorary degrees being refused, and Irish students even refusing to accept anti-racism awards.
In April of this year, brothers Dylan and Shane O’Halloran returned the Nelson Mandela Anti-Racism / Leadership Award in protest against the university’s refusal to end its research partnership with Technion.
“How can the university’s own failure to put a human rights mechanism in place become the justification for not applying one?” asked Mr. Al Hayek. “This is a fundamental problem of institutional accountability.”
Mr Al Hayek said the onus was on other states not to assist a state committing violations of fundamental rules of international law and that the International Court of Justice established obligations for other states, including Ireland, after ruling in July 2024 that Israel’s continuing presence in the occupied Palestinian territories is illegal.
READ: Palestine welcomes Ireland’s ban on Israeli settlement goods, urges others to follow
He said that Technion’s relationship with the Israeli military establishment was “extensively documented” and listed the Silon and Brakim programmes, which provide training for the Israeli defence forces, as clear examples from Technion’s own website.
“We are not demanding that individual Israeli academics be excluded because of their nationality, nor are we calling for restrictions on academic discussion or the exchange of ideas,” he said. “We are asking why the University of Galway continues to maintain a formal research relationship with an institution whose connections to the Israeli military are openly acknowledged. A contract cannot be treated as the final word on an institution’s responsibilities, especially when circumstances raise serious questions under international law.
“I think there is something deeply troubling about a situation in which the University of Galway proudly celebrates the expertise of its Irish Centre for Human Rights, yet continues to struggle to translate that expertise into institutional action. The university should now complete and publish a credible human rights policy, provide a transparent assessment of the Technion relationship, and pursue the necessary steps to end that institutional cooperation.”
Poet and human rights activist Sarah Clancy, a graduate of the University of Galway and member of the Global Sumud Flotilla detained by Israeli forces after being seized in international waters last year, told the conference that she was deeply ashamed by the University of Galway’s research partnership with the Technion.
Ms. Clancy said the Technion contract was just one of a number of ways in which the authorities in Ireland was complicit in the horrors unfolding in Gaza, including the use of Shannon Airport in Co. Clare by the US military, and the more general collaborations between the tech sectors in Ireland and Israel.
“I never thought I would be utterly ashamed of the institution in which I obtained a Master’s Degree,” she said. “Have no doubt, the University of Galway is complicit in genocide.”
Dr. Margaret Connolly, a sister of the President of Ireland, Catherine Connolly, also recalled her experiences with the Global Sumud Flotilla in 2025. She said that Irish people were particularly moved by the horrors unfolding in Palestine because of their own history of being colonised, occupied, and living through a man-made famine under the rule of the British Empire.
“As a mother, a woman, and a medical doctor, I cannot ignore the horrors of the occupation and Israel’s system of settler-colonialism and Apartheid in Palestine,” said Dr. Connolly. “Injustice is coded into the DNA of Irish people, but our government, and the governments of the western world, are shockingly complicit in what has been happening in Palestine.”

Turkey and Qatar lead push for four-nation defence partnership
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:44:25 UTC
20:44:25 KST

Breadcrumb
Turkey, Qatar, Pakistan and Indonesia eye joint weapons production
Turkey, Qatar, Pakistan and Indonesia are moving towards a new defence manufacturing partnership, with a memorandum of understanding expected to be signed in Doha to expand joint production and technology transfers.
The agreement will build on existing defence cooperation between the four countries and pave the way for closer collaboration in manufacturing, supply chains and military technology.
Turkey's Presidency of Defence Industries (SSB) said in a statement on Tuesday that the proposed agreement represented a new step in Ankara's approach to multilateral defence cooperation.
The agency said its efforts were increasingly focused on moving beyond the supply of defence equipment towards joint production, technology transfers, greater interoperability and the integration of supply chains.
It added that defence industry cooperation was a strategic component of Turkish foreign policy, with efforts to expand mass production and exports gaining momentum under SSB President Haluk Görgün.
The announcement coincided with an official visit to Qatar by Turkish Defence Minister Yaşar Güler, who arrived in Doha on Tuesday.
According to Turkey's Defence Ministry, Güler was received at the airport by Qatar's air force commander Faisal bin Khalid Al Ghanim, Turkish Ambassador to Qatar Yakup Caymazoğlu and Turkish military attachés stationed in Doha.
Turkey's defence exports surge
The proposed partnership comes amid rapid growth in Turkey's defence and aerospace industries, which have emerged as major contributors to the country's exports.
According to data from the Turkish Defence and Aerospace Industry Exporters' Association, the sector generated approximately $54 billion in exports between 2012 and the end of September 2026.
More than $30 billion of that total was recorded between 2023 and September 2026, accounting for over 55 percent of the sector's exports during the period.
Defence and aerospace exports rose by 48 percent in 2025 compared with the previous year, exceeding $10 billion.
Exports also surpassed $11 billion over the most recent 12-month period for the first time.
According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), Turkey's arms exports increased by 122 percent over the past five years, making it the world's sixth-largest arms supplier.
Around 56 percent of Turkey's defence and aerospace exports are destined for NATO member states.
Joint production and technology transfers with Qatar
Qatar has been a key partner in Turkey's defence industry for several years, with cooperation covering armed drones, armoured vehicles and naval equipment.
Among the Turkish-made systems already in service with Qatar's armed forces are Bayraktar TB2 armed drones, armoured vehicles and fast attack craft.
In recent years, Qatar's Barzan Holdings, which is affiliated with the country's Ministry of Defence, has signed cooperation agreements with several Turkish defence companies, including Aselsan, STM and MKE.
One of the most prominent examples is Barq, a joint venture established in Qatar by Aselsan and Barzan Holdings.
The company has begun assembling, manufacturing and calibrating SARP remotely controlled weapon systems and electro-optical equipment.
Turkish defence projects in Qatar have also created opportunities for the two countries to jointly provide defence industry solutions to third countries.
Warships with Pakistan, tanks with Indonesia
Turkey's defence cooperation with Pakistan has focused heavily on naval manufacturing, particularly the MILGEM warship project for the Pakistani navy.
The programme involves four Babur-class corvettes, with Turkish defence company ASFAT serving as the main contractor.
The first two vessels were built in Istanbul, while the remaining two were constructed at the Karachi Shipyard in Pakistan.
The project also involved upgrading production infrastructure at the Karachi facility and transferring shipbuilding and engineering expertise to Pakistani personnel.
These measures helped strengthen Pakistan's domestic naval manufacturing capabilities alongside the delivery of the vessels.
Meanwhile, Turkey's defence partnership with Indonesia has centred on the development of the Kaplan MT medium tank.
The tank was jointly designed by Turkish defence manufacturer FNSS and Indonesia's PT Pindad under an intergovernmental agreement between Turkey's Presidency of Defence Industries and Indonesia's Defence Ministry.
Following the delivery of prototypes and the first batches of tanks manufactured in Turkey, PT Pindad has continued local production under a technology transfer arrangement.

By the time the tanker carrying Russian diesel arrives, US will have managed to export 100 times more abroad, presidential adviser says

By the time the tanker carrying Russian diesel arrives, US will have managed to export 100 times more abroad, presidential adviser says
Kyiv • UNN
The first tanker carrying 40,000 tonnes of Russian diesel is heading to the United States. During that time, the country’s own exports will exceed the shipment volume 100-fold.
By the time the tanker announced by russia, carrying 40,000 tonnes of Russian diesel, reaches the United States, the U.S. will have managed to ship more than 4 million tonnes of its own diesel abroad. That is "one hundred times more" than the amount it will bring in. Presidential Adviser–Commissioner for Sanctions Policy Vladyslav Vlasiuk stated this on social media on October 21, UNN reports.
So, tomorrow the first tanker carrying 40,000 tonnes of Russian diesel is heading to the United States. Let’s do the math. 40,000 tonnes is approximately 300,000 barrels. The United States consumes about 4 million barrels of diesel fuel per day. That means this entire tanker covers "less than 2 hours" of U.S. consumption. At the same time, the U.S. itself exports ~1.5 million barrels of diesel per day. The tanker is equivalent to "4.5 hours" of U.S. exports. The journey from Ust-Luga to U.S. terminals takes 2.5–3 weeks. By the time the tanker arrives, the U.S. will have managed to ship more than 4 million tonnes of its own diesel abroad. That is "one hundred times more" than the amount it will bring in. So, is one of the world’s largest diesel exporters buying diesel from an aggressor country to cover two hours of its own demand?
According to him, "all the figures are taken from EIA data for September–October".
We remind you
Earlier, russia announced that it would send the first tanker carrying diesel to the United States on October 22. This happened after the deal announced by U.S. President Donald Trump.

Saudi Arabia Executes Two Bangladeshi Nationals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:42:00 UTC
20:42:00 KST

On October 13, Saudi Arabia’s Supreme Court set aside the death sentence of Sri Lankan migrant worker Anojan Sivarasa. Sivarasa had been sentenced to death over a Facebook post deemed insulting to Prophet Muhammad and blasphemous against Islam.
The following day, Saudi authorities executed two Bangladeshis, Nazrul Islam Abdul Basir and Suety Akhter (Sweety Akhtar, according to family), in the holy city of Makkah. According to their families, both had moved to Saudi Arabia for work nearly four years earlier. They had been convicted of what Saudi authorities described as an “immoral act” inside a mosque.
The two cases put Bangladesh’s protection of migrant workers in Saudi Arabia under scrutiny. Sri Lanka organized legal and diplomatic support for Sivarasa, winning a reprieve for its citizen. Bangladesh said it learned of the execution of its nationals only after it happened.
Sri Lanka’s success does not mean Bangladesh could have secured the same outcome; the allegations in the two cases were different. But the fact that Dhaka claimed not to know about the sentences until it was too late to intervene is concerning.
Saudi authorities described the death sentences of the Bangladeshis as ta’zir, a discretionary punishment, and said judicial review and a royal order preceded execution. The public statement did not explain the precise “immoral act,” identify the mosque, or disclose the arrest dates.
What evidence supported the conviction of the two Bangladeshis? Did the defendants have lawyers and interpreters? Could they understand the proceedings and challenge the charges?
Bangladesh’s claims are hard to accept without scrutiny. Media reports said the Bangladesh consulate general in Jeddah had sought prisoner information in September. Saudi authorities supplied a list containing the two names on September 30, but no details of their death sentences.
The Jeddah consulate sent a report to Bangladesh’s Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment on October 18. The Daily Star, a Bangladeshi daily, which obtained the report, says that the two Bangladeshis had been detained since August 2023. The list recorded cybercrime allegations against Nazrul and adultery allegations against Akhter.
The report also listed 306 Bangladeshis held in prisons across Saudi Arabia’s western region. Of them, 147 had received sentences ranging from one month to 15 years of jail time.
A Bangladeshi official said the consulate received no requests for assistance from the pair or their family members. Another official said following every case was impossible.
What the government said after the executions has also drawn criticism. Speaking to reporters on October 17, Bangladesh’s State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam described the executions as a lesson for Bangladesh and urged citizens abroad to follow their host countries’ laws. “When a law is violated, there is not much I can do for a Bangladeshi citizen,” she said.
However, Bangladesh could still have sought lawyers’ help and engaged in diplomatic discussions to help the two citizens appeal their sentences.
Did Bangladeshi officials ask for details of the charges or copies of the court records? Were cases that involved potentially severe punishment referred for legal advice? Who was responsible for following the cases? Bangladesh needs to explain what its officials did and when. The claim that the two citizens did not ask for help does not resolve questions about its own consular response.
Sri Lanka’s response shows what Bangladesh could have done. Sivarasa was arrested on July 1. A court initially imposed five years in prison and a fine of 3 million riyals (about $800,000) on him. On September 17, an appeals court increased the punishment to death. Amnesty International said he lacked access to a lawyer before his initial sentencing.
On September 18, Sri Lanka’s Foreign Ministry publicly confirmed that it was pursuing his case through diplomatic channels. Ambassador O. L. Ameer Ajwad visited him in prison on October 8 and provided contact details. A specialist Sri Lankan legal delegation supported the Supreme Court appeal.
The court overturned Sivarasa’s death sentence. That did not guarantee that he would be acquitted or could return home. Media reports also give little detail about why the court ruled in his favor. It is unclear how much the outcome was due to the legal appeal or Sri Lanka’s diplomatic efforts.
Still, Sri Lanka provided legal support, pursued the case through diplomatic channels, and visited its citizen in prison. Bangladesh has yet to provide evidence of comparable efforts in these two cases.
Saudi Arabia also needs to explain what happened. Both countries are parties to the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations. Article 36 requires authorities to inform detained foreigners promptly of their consular rights. If a detainee requests it, the consulate must be notified without delay. Consular officers have the right to visit, communicate, and arrange legal representation.
The convention does not expressly mention a duty to warn an embassy before every execution. Therefore, the absence of an advance warning alone cannot establish that Article 36 was breached. Even so, Saudi authorities could have taken greater care to inform Bangladesh of the death sentences while there was still time to seek legal help. Saudi authorities need to explain what the prisoners were told about contacting the Bangladeshi consulate. They also need to clarify what happened to any requests for help, and if consular officials were allowed to visit.
Bangladesh has strong reasons to preserve relations with Riyadh. More than 3 million Bangladeshis live in the kingdom. Protecting such a large community requires a large consular staff and a system for following serious criminal cases. Officials need to know which prisoners face severe punishment and when legal help is needed. That work cannot depend entirely on prisoners or their families knowing whom to contact.
Sri Lanka’s efforts helped its citizen challenge his death sentence. In Bangladesh’s case, it is still unclear whether officials could have acted in time. The executions have left Bangladesh’s diplomats facing a difficult question about whether they could have done more before they were executed.

Taiwan's WeiTzuYuan looks to nature and spiritual world for inspiration

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — WeiTzuYuan looks beyond the visible world for its spring/summer 2027 collection, drawing on monsoon winds and folk deities to shape its designs.
Titled “Silent and Subtle,” the collection explores the forces of nature and faith through three series: “Wind,” “Mountain Peak,” and “Fengdu.”
“Wind” takes its cue from the northeastern monsoon, which brings strong gusts around the ninth month of the lunar calendar. For generations, people have used these seasonal winds to dry food and fly kites, and wind power is now another way to make use of them, according to Hsing Tian Kong.
The series also draws on other cultural traditions, featuring Aeolus, ruler of the winds in Greek mythology, and Vayu, the Hindu god of wind. Purple hues and auspicious cloud motifs reflect traditional associations with blessings and prosperity.
In “Mountain Peak,” Taiwan’s rugged terrain meets the imagery of Tudigong, the Earth God traditionally worshipped as a protector of communities and a bringer of prosperity. Mountain-like textures appear in fabrics and shawls, bringing familiar symbols of folk religion into contemporary fashion.
“Fengdu” ventures into the underworld. It references the Great Emperor of Fengdu, a deity in Taoist mythology and Chinese folk belief who rules over the realm of the dead.
The series also incorporates elements of Indigenous ancestral spirituality and mythology, bringing different cultural traditions into the conversation. Loofah fiber and other composite materials are used in experimental garments and installation art, expanding the collection beyond conventional clothing.

Kulbergs’ government receives negative public rating – yet scores among Latvia’s highest in 18 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:41:27 UTC
20:41:27 KST

Public satisfaction with Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs’ (United List) government remained significantly negative more than a month before Latvia’s parliamentary elections. Nevertheless, its approval rating was among the highest recorded in the country in nearly two decades.
According to a survey conducted by research centre SKDS for the think tank Providus as part of its study Public Mandate: Governance Barometer (2026–2029), only 3% of respondents were completely satisfied with the government's performance in August, while 28% were somewhat satisfied. Meanwhile, 29% were completely dissatisfied and another 32% were somewhat dissatisfied.
The study found that the government's performance rating index stood at -27.8 points in August, measured on a scale ranging from -100 to +100. Despite remaining in negative territory, the result was among the highest recorded since 2008. For historical comparison, researchers used data from the SKDS Latvia Barometer surveys dating back to April 2008. Throughout this period, the government performance index has never reached a positive value. The lowest rating was recorded in January 2009, when the index fell to -76.9 points during the severe economic crisis that followed Latvia's years of rapid economic growth.
The study found that the government's performance index was negative across every demographic group analysed. The most pronounced differences were associated with the language spoken at home. Among Latvian-speaking respondents, 43% were satisfied with the government's performance, while 48% were dissatisfied. In contrast, only 11% of Russian-speaking respondents expressed satisfaction, compared with 82% who were dissatisfied. Men evaluated the government's performance somewhat more positively than women.
Residents aged 65 to 75 also expressed more favourable views than the population overall.
At the same time, the survey indicated that lower household income per person was associated with lower levels of satisfaction with the government's work.
The Providus study also examined the issues Latvian residents consider most important for the 15th Saeima. In a survey conducted in July, respondents were asked to identify, in their own words, the three most important problems the next parliament should address. No predefined answer options were provided.
Healthcare emerged as the leading priority, mentioned by 46% of respondents. Economic issues were identified by 28%, education by 25%, and national security and defence by 23%. Meanwhile, 18% highlighted public finances, government administration and bureaucracy, 17% mentioned demographic challenges, and 16% identified social protection, pensions and benefits.
Healthcare was the most frequently mentioned priority in 43 of the 46 demographic groups analysed.
Among men, however, economic issues ranked first, mentioned by 33%, while healthcare was identified by 32%. National security and defence were the most frequently mentioned concerns among young people aged 18 to 24, as well as among school pupils and university students.
Significant differences were also observed between women and men. Healthcare was identified as a priority by 60% of women, compared with 32% of men. Education was mentioned by 34% of women and 16% of men.
Differences were also evident between Latvian-speaking and Russian-speaking households. National security and defence were mentioned by 30% of Latvian-speaking respondents, compared with just 10% of Russian-speaking respondents. Conversely, economic issues were identified by 36% of Russian-speaking respondents and 22% of Latvian-speaking respondents.
Residents aged 25 to 34 were more likely than the population overall to highlight demographic challenges. Older residents, meanwhile, placed greater emphasis on education, the state budget and bureaucracy.
Both surveys were conducted by SKDS on behalf of Providus.
The survey examining public priorities took place between the 16th and the 21st of July, while the survey assessing government performance was conducted between the 10th and the 12th of August.
Each online survey involved 1,005 Latvian residents aged 18 to 75.
The Public Mandate: Governance Barometer (2026–2029) initiative is being implemented by Providus in cooperation with SKDS and the Friedrich Ebert Foundation's Baltic States Office.
The initiative will measure public satisfaction with the government's performance every quarter and assess residents' quality of life across seven areas once a year.

TSMC has already committed about NT$8.61 trillion to expand its manufacturing operations in Arizona. The chipmaker is also considering further investment in Texas as demand for advanced chips continues to grow, per The Independent.
TSMC remains a major supplier of advanced chips to US technology companies, including Nvidia and Apple. The company reported a 69% annual increase in third-quarter net profit last week, driven by strong demand for artificial intelligence chips, per the Financial Times.

Starlink slowdown makes Ukraine’s Shahed-hunting drone maker rethink air-launched interceptors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
11:36:39 UTC
20:36:39 KST

Ukrainian drone maker Wild Hornets is rethinking projects it is currently working on, including launching interceptors from aerial platforms, because of limits on SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet. Spokesman Mike Orliuk told The War Zone (TWZ) this on 20 October. The company builds Sting interceptors, which it says destroyed over 15,000 Shaheds and Gerberas, a cheaper Shahed lookalike, in a year. Orliuk said Sting’s current operations are unaffected.
The stakes rise as Russia shifts to faster drones. Ukrainian defense technology adviser Serhii Beskrestnov counted more than 2,500 jet-powered Gerans, Russia’s version of the Shahed, in August. President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 16 October that these drones fly faster than 400 km/h. He added that some Ukrainian interceptors chasing them work through Starlink. When the link was slowed, Ukraine could not intercept some of them, he said.
How Sting stays connected
“Our own communications system provides the basic connection to our interceptors,” Orliuk said. The company’s remote-control technology can draw on various internet sources, he added, though the military often uses Starlink. Even then, the terminal does not need to move at high speed. It only links the command center to a ground station, which Orliuk compared to a cell tower.
“For these needs, everything is operating normally with Starlink at the moment,” he said.
An air-launch project under review
“Some drones carry a terminal on board and need to fly at high speed with it,” Orliuk said. “In such cases, Starlink’s limitations make their operation impossible.”
That is why the company is rethinking the air-launch project. Wild Hornets has made no clear decision yet but will test alternatives, Orliuk said. He declined to describe them.
“I believe, in any case, depending on a single solution is very risky,” he said.
Musk pointed at the US military over Ukraine’s satellite limits. Now a US official says the administration had nothing to do with them
Other firms share the concern
Orliuk said he has spoken with other companies that rely far more on Starlink and have expressed concerns. He pointed to growing interest in Europe’s Eutelsat network, though “creating something like Starlink won’t be easy.”
Who ordered the slowdown remains unclear. The order to slow Ukraine’s Starshield service came from inside the White House, two US officials and a Western official said. A US official told TWZ the president never made such a request. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on 17 October that the slowdown had “nothing to do with the White House” and called “a report on that” “categorically false,” without saying which report he meant.

Secondary school pupils and teachers are protesting poor infrastructure, a shortage of staff and insufficient public spending on education.
The conservative Greek government has sought in recent days to avoid any parallel with the protests and violence in France.

French cities experienced some of the country's worst rioting in recent years Saturday, with public buildings torched, hundreds of shops looted and more than 2,000 people arrested.
According to EU data agency Eurostat, Greece in 2023 spent 3.3% of national output on education, among the lowest share in the bloc and far below the European average of 4.7%.

Greek education unions and student groups have long called for additional spending on dilapidated buildings and more staff.
“School buildings are terrible and poorly maintained,” said Yiannis Papanikolaou, a 17-year-old school pupil from the Athens district of Exarchia.

“I think something might change because of what France is doing. France will spur Greece,” he said.
Teachers' union OLME said there is a shortage of 15,000 secondary school teachers nationwide.
Earlier this month, falling roof plaster injured a 14-year-old schoolboy in a classroom in Thermi, near the city of Thessaloniki in northern Greece.
A similar incident occurred Monday at the entrance of an Athens school, outside operating hours. A major school complex in Athens has been closed for almost two weeks over a gas leak scare under investigation, affecting some 4,000 pupils.

Europe is the most represented region with 20 restaurants across 11 countries making the cut, followed by 17 from Asia, six from North America, three from South America, two from Africa and two from the Middle East.
