Nigeria reports Ebola case, fourth African country affected by outbreak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:41:25 UTC
19:41:25 KST

Nigeria reports Ebola case, fourth African country affected by outbreak
- Nigeria confirmed its first Ebola case in more than a decade. The patient is a Ugandan woman who arrived in Abuja on 5 October and was confirmed positive on 20 October.
- Health officials have traced 44 contacts, mostly healthcare workers, and the woman is in isolation receiving treatment. Nigeria says it has the systems to respond, after containing Ebola in 2014.
- The outbreak has spread to four African countries and killed 4,646 people since May in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Officials warn that misinformation and funding gaps could help it spread further.
AI generated
ABUJA - Nigeria reported its first Ebola case in more than a decade on Oct 20, becoming the fourth African country and the most populous yet to be affected by an outbreak that health officials have described as the fastest-spreading on record.
The Ebola species behind the outbreak kills about half of those infected and has no approved treatment or vaccine.
Since the first cases were confirmed in Democratic Republic of Congo in May, the disease has killed 4,646 people.
Health officials fear misinformation and funding shortfalls could fuel further spread within the region and across borders.
“Ebola is now affecting three regions of Africa. The situation demands urgent action and political leadership at the highest level,” Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention Director General Jean Kaseya said on X on Oct 21.
The Nigerian case involves a Ugandan woman who arrived in Nigeria’s capital Abuja via Addis Ababa on Oct 5, Odianosen Ehiakhamen of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control told Arise TV on Oct 20.
She began feeling unwell two days later and sought treatment at a private hospital in Abuja on Oct 11 with malaria-like symptoms, but her condition did not improve, Ehiakhamen said.
After health officials learned she had recently travelled to Uganda, one of the countries affected by the current outbreak, they tested her for Ebola on Oct 19.
The positive result was confirmed on Oct 20.
Authorities have identified 44 contacts, most of them healthcare workers.
They included the patient’s husband, a Swiss national who lives with her in Abuja.
Officials are also tracing passengers who travelled with her but do not believe she was symptomatic during the flight.
Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate told public broadcaster NTA that the woman was in isolation and receiving treatment.
Uganda says it has no active Ebola cases
Uganda’s health ministry said the woman had travelled to Congo, where more than 9,500 Ebola cases have been recorded across eight provinces.
It was not immediately clear where she had been in Congo.
“Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here,” Uganda’s health ministry said, adding that the country has no active Ebola cases.
Uganda reported 20 cases in May and June, mostly imported from Congo, but the World Health Organisation declared the country Ebola-free in August.
Earlier in October, Kenya reported its first Ebola case, involving a traveller who arrived from Congo via Uganda.
The country has since reported nine cases, all linked to the same patient.
The spread of Ebola to Kenya raised questions about the effectiveness of border screening systems designed to prevent cross-border transmission.
Pate, Nigeria’s health minister, said the country had successfully contained Ebola in 2014 during the West African epidemic, the largest outbreak on record.
He said Nigeria had the systems in place to respond to the new case. REUTERS

French President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday condemned “unacceptable and stupid comments” by foreign leaders about the Oct. 17 protests in France, after US President Donald Trump blamed the unrest on immigration.
Speaking to reporters in Doha, Macron accused foreign leaders facing elections of exploiting the unrest for political gain.
“When I see leaders campaigning in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic … they are campaigning at our expense,” he said, without naming Trump.
His remarks followed Trump’s assertion Tuesday that immigration, rather than education grievances, was behind the unrest.
“It’s not about education. It’s about immigration,” Trump said.
The demonstrations began as a student movement demanding better school funding before unions and other groups joined to protest high costs of living.
France will take all lawful measures to prevent unrest during further protests planned for Saturday, Oct. 24, Macron said, citing curfews and restrictions on gatherings already introduced after the violence.
“Those who want to cause disorder in city centers next Saturday will be prevented from doing so,” he said.
He added that a state of emergency was currently unnecessary, arguing that existing laws provided sufficient powers, while leaving the option open if circumstances warranted it.
Macron also denounced “foreign manipulation of information” following the unrest, saying artificial intelligence had been used to fabricate images.
“We have seen AI-generated images showing scenes that never happened in France,” he said.
“Some people have claimed that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false.”

Most young Arab Israelis are willing to vote for non-Arab parties, demand solution for crime - poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:39:41 UTC
19:39:41 KST

A majority of Arab Israeli young adults are open to voting for non-Arab parties in the upcoming Knesset elections, according to Arab-Jewish Center for Empowerment, Equality, and Cooperation – Negev Institute for Strategies of Peace and Economic Development (AJEEC-NISPED), citing a recent survey conducted by Dialog, an Israeli consulting firm.
AJEEC-NISPED, per the organization's website, is made up of a joint team of Arabs and Jews who work to create a society in which Arabs and Jews can coexist while preserving their identity and culture.
The poll, conducted in August, collected data from 257 Arab Israelis aged 18-26.
Sixty percent of respondents said they would consider voting for a non-Arab party if it presented a clear plan to address issues important to them.
Only 48% of respondents said they were loyal exclusively to Arab parties. About 20% said they had no preference regarding party identity, and 9% preferred an Arab party but were also willing to consider other parties.
What issues matter most to the younger generation in Arab society?
Violence and crime were the top concerns among young Arab Israelis, with 55% of respondents identifying them as a key priority when choosing whom to vote for. Employment and income opportunities followed at 22%, while 20% prioritized investment in education and higher education, and 19% cited housing solutions.
The surge in crime and violence across Arab towns and cities, with armed gangs controlling public space, has left many Arab Israeli citizens feeling helpless and under constant anxiety, several members of the Arab community in Israel told The Jerusalem Post in January.
The poll also found that 70% of respondents believe that political parties in Israel do not listen sufficiently to young people in Arab society.
"This survey should be a wake-up call for the entire political establishment," said Suleiman al-Amour, CEO of AJEEC. "Young Arabs in Israel are not asking for much...They want to know who intends to address the crime and violence threatening their personal safety...They are yearning for practical plans, with goals, budgets, and accountability for implementation."
"It is time for the political establishment to stop talking about Arab society and start talking with its young people and its leadership, and above all, to offer them a future," he concluded.
Dana Ben Shimon contributed to this report.

Some 90 volunteers with Rabbis for Human Rights were detained by the IDF in the West Bank on Wednesday, including congressional nominee Brad Lander (D-NY), sources told The Jerusalem Post.
"Following a joint investigation and review conducted by police investigators in coordination with the Foreign Ministry and relevant security and law enforcement agencies, 32 activists were questioned and released subject to restrictions prohibiting them from returning to the area," Israel Police said on Wednesday evening.
"In addition, the questioning of four foreign activists has been completed following the identification of their anti-Israel activity online. Some had also expressed support for organizations opposed to Israel," police continued.
"The remaining 40 individuals who had been detained were released from the police station during the afternoon after no grounds for further detention were found," police said.
Police initially took the foreign volunteers to the Etzion Regional Brigade headquarters for questioning, a source at the scene told the Post earlier on Wednesday. Sources added that no one was harmed in the incident.
"The police intend to complete the investigation into the four foreign nationals and transfer them to the Population and Immigration Authority tomorrow (Thursday) for hearings regarding their removal from Israel," the police said.
Authorities are inclined to deport the foreign activists, a source at the scene had told the Post earlier on Wednesday.
Lander was specifically released with a warning, he noted in a statement.
"I’ve been released from IDF custody with a 'warning,' apparently because of my public profile (I told them I wasn’t even a congressmember yet, just a nominee)," he wrote.
"But several dozen rabbis & participants harvesting olives with me are still in detention. For harvesting olives. They should all be released immediately," he said, adding that "Palestinians face far worse consequences every day."
Rabbis for Human Rights activists detained in West Bank
Rabbis for Human Rights said the volunteers worked in the village of Nahalin near Bethlehem, accompanying Palestinian farmers to groves during the olive harvest. According to the left-leaning activist group, Palestinian farmers in the area had been unable to access the groves for three years. Authorities say that olive harvesting in the area is prohibited without coordination with security services.
The IDF arrived two hours after the volunteers had begun working and declared the field a closed military zone. Activists told the Post that they complied with the military orders and agreed to leave the area, but were still detained.
KAN News later reported that the area that the volunteers were harvesting in does not require prior coordination with the IDF.
In a statement hours after the incident, the IDF said that the activists did not submit a request to harvest in advance.
"The landowner was informed that he must coordinate the olive harvest on his plot of land and was provided with the relevant contact information to arrange a harvest at a later date," the IDF said. "In areas designated for coordinated harvesting, only harvesters will be permitted to enter, solely for harvesting."
The IDF's Arabic Spokesperson's unit said that it will "not allow inciting elements to exploit civil activity to provoke violence or create disturbances. The olive harvest season is an agricultural activity; it must not be transformed into a period of violence and conflict."
The activist added that they did not get a response from the IDF, and that the group mainly corresponded with the owner of the olive grove because it is located on private property.
Leadership from Rabbis for Human Rights said that their work in the West Bank was peaceful, and that it was the organization's policy to comply with IDF orders.
"We came to accompany farmers to land they had been unable to access for three years, and after two hours of peaceful olive harvesting, large numbers of troops arrived and closed off the area. No one could have known about this order in advance. Instead of protecting people working their land, the army is keeping them away from it and detaining those who came to accompany them for identification,” acting executive director of Rabbis for Human Rights Anton Goodman said.
“The fact that Israeli and American rabbis are compelled to stand alongside Palestinian farmers to help them harvest their olives and protect them from settler violence is a damning indictment of the Israeli government. The fact that these same rabbis are detained by security forces, rather than the authorities protecting the farmers and taking action against those perpetrating the violence, is nothing short of a disgrace," said Dr. Yizhar Hess, Vice Chairman of the World Zionist Organization.
"But today’s events are not merely a moral failure; they are also a devastating blow to Israel–Diaspora relations. As a Zionist and as a Jew, I want to remind us all: a Jewish and democratic state is judged not only by its ability to protect its citizens, but also by how it treats those living under its control. We must not accept a reality in which those who act in the name of justice are arrested, while those who resort to violence enjoy de facto impunity. These values are not at odds with Zionism; they are the very values without which Zionism loses its soul," Hess added.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani called for the end of what he called genocide and occupation at the hands of the Israeli government, along with the release of several activists affiliated with Rabbis for Human Rights.
“Today, Brad Lander, rabbis, and other New Yorkers accompanied Palestinian farmers during the olive harvest. For that, they were detained by the Israeli government,” he wrote, specifically noting that Lander was released by Israel Police.

Putin claimed that he released the Michigan native, 74, “for humanitarian reasons.”
“Never once did we waver as we prayed for success in these negotiations, and we must acknowledge that this humanitarian move by President Putin in this matter is deeply appreciated,” Hubbard's son, John Coleman, said in a statement.
US President Donald Trump noted that there was no "swap" necessary for the release. However, the administration recently waived a round of sanctions against the Kremlin. Trump claimed that had he not waived the sanctions, "certainly those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt.”
The administration also recently announced a deal to import Russian diesel fuel, going against years of US foreign policy against Moscow.
Stephen Hubbard released from Russian prison
Hubbard was detained in Ukraine four years ago. Russia alleged in a closed trial in 2024 that he was fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine in the war. Prosecutors claimed that Hubbard signed a contract with the Ukrainian military at the start of the invasion, and that he was captured by Russian troops two months later.
His family and lawyer have denied the claims.
His sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox, has argued that Hubbard’s age made it unlikely that he would take up arms against Russian troops. Hubbard’s lawyer said that Russian troops entered his home and took him away.
The State Department maintained that Hubbard had been wrongfully detained since his sentencing in 2024. Officials also said that Russia refused to grant US officials consular access to Hubbard.
Ahead of Witkoff’s visit, a US official said that the envoy’s meeting with Putin is “expected to include efforts to seek the release of wrongfully detained American citizen Hubbard, reflecting President Trump’s continued commitment to bringing Americans home,” as per CNN.

After eight months of war and severe military and economic losses, the Islamic Republic continues to pursue its survival through nuclear blackmail, threats to global energy security, and protracted negotiations.
President Donald Trump faces a strategic choice: accept a deal that allows Tehran to rebuild or sustain pressure until its security threats are verifiably constrained. In this confrontation, the CIA and Mossad’s intelligence capabilities, particularly their ability to identify and assess vulnerabilities within Tehran’s security establishment, may prove decisive.

Mossad’s 2018 seizure of Iran’s nuclear archive, sabotage attributed to Israel at nuclear facilities, and the 2020 assassination of Mohsen Fakhrizadeh exposed serious weaknesses in the regime’s security defenses.
Although the CIA’s direct involvement in these operations remains publicly unverified, US-Israeli intelligence cooperation is well established. Their shared strategic interests, however, should not be confused with evidence of joint participation in every operation attributed to Mossad.
Iran’s greatest vulnerability
For Tehran’s Shi’ite caliphate, the greatest danger extends beyond American air superiority or Israeli missile capabilities.
It is the prospect of intelligence penetration into the institutions sustaining the regime: the IRGC, counterintelligence agencies, national security decision-making centers, nuclear networks, and the increasingly compromised Intelligence Ministry.
A regime unable to protect its secrets, personnel, and command structure remains strategically vulnerable regardless of its military arsenal. Ideological loyalty and internal repression cannot compensate for counterintelligence failures.
The Strait of Hormuz represents another dimension of this asymmetric confrontation. The IRGC claims Iranian naval mines blocked three oil tankers, although independent verification remains lacking. Tehran’s broader objective is to weaponize maritime insecurity and energy-market uncertainty.
It need not win a naval battle to impose economic costs on Washington; threats to shipping can raise insurance premiums, transportation costs, and oil prices. Accurate intelligence on Iran’s actual maritime capabilities is therefore essential to distinguishing credible threats from coercive bluffing and preventing strategic miscalculation.
The Islamic Republic’s asymmetric warfare extends far beyond the Persian Gulf. For decades, Tehran’s outlaw regime has relied on terrorist militias, intelligence networks, cyberoperations, and terrorist proxies to project power and threaten adversaries.
The Iranian and Russian efforts to fuel unrest in France, alongside British counterterrorism investigations into suspected Iranian intelligence connections, underscore Europe’s growing security concerns. While allegations must be distinguished from verified intelligence, Washington cannot afford to view Tehran’s transnational threat solely through the nuclear lens.
Tehran’s refusal to relinquish its enriched uranium raises a critical question: If the regime genuinely seeks to resolve international concerns, why preserve one of its most dangerous strategic bargaining chips?
Enrichment alone does not establish an intention to build nuclear weapons. Yet uranium stockpiles, centrifuge capacity, and independent verification remain central to assessing nuclear breakout risks. Any agreement that leaves these vulnerabilities unresolved risks granting Tehran the time and strategic breathing space to rebuild.
For the CIA and Mossad, the strategic imperative is to deliver precise, independent intelligence that exposes Tehran’s capabilities, vulnerabilities, and intentions. Covert operations, however successful, cannot replace a coherent national strategy or independently guarantee regime collapse.
Intelligence achievements can degrade an adversary’s capabilities, but lasting strategic change requires political, economic, social, and security pressure working together.
Trump must distinguish between ending military operations and neutralizing the Islamic Republic’s criminal ruling apparatus. Destroying weapons, damaging facilities, and degrading IRGC capabilities does not necessarily dismantle the regime’s command structure, political will, or capacity to regenerate.
Tehran has repeatedly exploited periods of reduced pressure to rebuild its military, intelligence services, and proxy networks. American success must therefore be measured not merely by silenced missiles or a temporarily reopened Strait of Hormuz, but by the enduring degradation of the regime’s capacity to threaten regional and international security.
One strategic distinction must remain clear: Iran is not the Islamic Republic. Iranians have endured decades of repression, systemic corruption, isolation, and the regime’s regional adventurism.
Washington must not mistake the regime’s survival for Iran’s stability or sacrifice the Iranian people’s right to determine their political future in a closed-door security bargain. The demand for regime change among significant elements of the Iranian opposition deserves consideration in any serious diplomatic assessment.
This does not justify an unlimited war. Washington must weigh the human, economic, and military costs of another prolonged conflict. But avoiding war must not mean accepting a weak agreement.
Any settlement requires verifiable nuclear restrictions, independent monitoring, maritime security guarantees, and enforceable consequences for violations. Diplomacy must reduce threats, not reward their continuation.
Tehran is betting that rising oil prices, public exhaustion, and approaching US elections will force Trump to concede. Yet its leadership cannot know the full extent of American and Israeli intelligence assessments or the options under consideration. That uncertainty is a strategic factor in itself.
Covert operations may already be underway, but their existence and scope cannot be established from publicly available evidence, nor is another war inevitable.
History will judge this confrontation not by bombs dropped or facilities destroyed, but by whether a persistent security threat was durably contained. Tehran must not regain through diplomacy what it lost militarily without meaningful security concessions.
Trump must ensure that ending the war does not allow the Islamic Republic to rebuild its capacity for aggression. The intelligence battle may precede the first missile, but strategic victory requires lasting results.
The CIA and Mossad’s intelligence capabilities remain central to understanding and confronting Tehran’s intelligence apparatus. Whether their operations contribute to regime change remains uncertain, but their documented achievements deserve serious recognition.
For those seeking an end to the Islamic Republic, dismantling its machinery of repression and external aggression remains a fundamental objective. The regime’s continued existence offers no inherent guarantee of regional peace, stability, or international security.

Swiss government wants CO2 levy on cement imports
The governing Federal Council wants to ensure a level playing field between Swiss cement and cement from abroad. To this end, a CO₂ compensation levy is to be imposed on cement imports above a certain quantity.
A CO₂ border adjustment mechanism is intended to offset differences in the CO₂ costs of cement production between Switzerland and third countries with less ambitious climate policies, the Federal Council announced on Wednesday. It recommends that parliament approve a corresponding bill from the National Council’s Environment Committee.
In Switzerland, cement production is integrated into an emissions trading scheme (ETS). The ETS sets a price on CO2 emissions, thereby creating an incentive to reduce CO2.

As Serbia votes, students emerge as greatest threat to Vucic’s long rule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:36:31 UTC
19:36:31 KST

As Serbia votes, students emerge as greatest threat to Vucic’s long rule
BELGRADE, Oct 21 - Aleksa Simic, a political science student at Belgrade University, did not hesitate when he learned that the collapse of a railway station canopy in the northern Serbian city of Novi Sad had killed 16 people in November 2024.
Demanding justice for the dead, and an end to the kind of corruption that many believed led to the station's shoddy construction, he and other students blockaded the political science faculty in protest. As Serbia mourned, sympathetic residents brought them homemade meals, mattresses and pillows. Many stopped by to discuss the students' demands.
"For the first time, I had a sense of belonging to a community. I realised that my voice mattered," Simic said.
Two years on, as Serbia prepares for elections on October 25, the student protest movement has ballooned to become one of the most powerful political forces in the country and poses the greatest threat yet to the rule of Aleksandar Vucic, who has dominated Serbian politics first as prime minister, then president, since 2014.
With protests raging in cities across Europe, fuelled by the high cost of living, a shortage of jobs and poor education standards, the Serbian students have shown what a force younger generations can be when they harness widespread discontent.
In interviews with Reuters, a dozen students and teachers described how a methodical countrywide door-knocking campaign, peaceful marches, a tightly controlled media message and a constant rotation of leaders to protect individuals from government smear campaigns have helped maintain momentum in Serbia.
Now, they have their own "Students Win" list of 250 candidates for Sunday's election, which includes university professors, actors, farmers and even a popular rapper.
The only poll published this month, by New Serbian Political Thought (NSPM) on October 20, showed the students' list of candidates edging ahead of Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) with 44.5% of the vote to 42.7%, although betting odds favour Vucic.
"The protests changed the society. It showed people they are not alone," said Florian Bieber, professor of Southeast European history and politics at the University of Graz.
UNKNOWNS SURROUND STUDENT MOVEMENT
The big question is how the students would govern should they win on Sunday.
Vucic is a significant international figure, managing a delicate balancing act that seeks closer ties with China, a major investor, and Russia, Serbia's traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas, while leaving the door open to joining the European Union even with the accession process stalled.
The students' list is headed by cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, although they have said this does not mean he would become prime minister should they win.
Some political analysts wonder how the country would fare on the international stage with an unknown at the helm, while there are scant details about how the students will set about fulfilling their pledges to fight corruption, promote transparency, create greater media freedom and enact education reform at home.
Critics also point to their silence on joining the EU and relations with the former province of Kosovo. Pro-European opponents of Vucic's government criticise them for saying that they would not introduce sanctions on Russia.
"A (student-led) government would pursue broad reforms to tackle corruption, overhaul key public institutions and companies, and dismantle patronage networks," consultancy Teneo said in an analyst note on Tuesday. "However, strong bureaucratic resistance could generate short-term institutional instability."
GROWING DISCONTENT WITH VUCIC RULE
Vucic, 56, stepped down as president in September to run again for prime minister in the snap election.
While he has overseen a period of strong economic growth and a fall in unemployment, critics blame him for democratic backsliding, the silencing of critics and the media, and hampering Serbia's EU accession by not undertaking necessary reforms. Police have beaten protesters and threatened people who voice opposition online, rights groups, activists and students told Reuters.
Simmering anger towards the government boiled over with the collapse of the station roof in Novi Sad. Vucic has sought to discredit the student movement, saying it is trying to destroy Serbia and accusing foreign agents from Croatia and Montenegro of financing it, but that has not dented their support.
Government representatives did not respond to a request for comment. Vucic and the authorities have repeatedly denied the allegations of corruption and violence and attempts to discredit the opposition. The students dismiss claims that they are being organised from abroad.
HOW A SMALL MOVEMENT GREW
The student protests were small to begin with: days after the canopy collapse, a few dozen people blocked traffic in Novi Sad and Belgrade for one minute for each person who was killed.
Less than three months later, in late January 2025, then prime minister and close Vucic ally Milos Vucevic resigned a day after tens of thousands of people blocked one of Belgrade's main junctions, joined by farmers in their tractors.
In March that year, the students led hundreds of thousands of people through Belgrade, the biggest anti-government march in a generation. By then, the movement had a symbol: a red handprint, representing the blood that the protesters say is on the government's hands.
"We felt we had importance and that we had a greater responsibility," Simic said.
University faculties across the country held plenums and working groups focused on media and social media strategies, and organising marches.
On the first anniversary of the roof collapse, the students walked from Belgrade to Novi Sad. People in small villages offered fruit. An image of a man with a traditional Serbian hat hugging a Muslim student in a headscarf flooded social media - which supporters hailed as an emblem of a young, progressive Serbia after the devastating Balkan wars of the 1990s.
Ahead of Sunday's vote, student groups have undergone training on election fraud and say teams plan to be present at polling stations.
Gavrilo Andric was a software engineer for a big company when the protests began. An amateur photographer, he watched the movement grow, eventually leaving his job to become its unofficial documenter.
"I finally realised that in our society we have a group of people who see things can be improved and want to work on it together with other people," he told Reuters. REUTERS

Why are French protesters chanting ‘Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres’?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:35:34 UTC
19:35:34 KST

Why are French protesters chanting ‘Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres’?
For students, the slogan has come to represent a whole array of grievances that lie at the heart of the protest movement.
As violent protests roil France, bringing together students demanding better educational conditions and groups rejecting the high cost of living, one chant has become an improbable rallying cry: “Bismillah, c’est les ténèbres”.
The unofficial slogan does not mean much taken literally, but students have channelled a whole array of grievances that lie at the heart of the protest movement into this nonsensical expression. It is meant to mock racial stereotyping by the police.
Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets nationwide over the weekend, in the largest mobilisation since protests over education reforms and rising prices began last month. The protest movement has been triggered by grievances ranging from overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages to systemic inequality and lack of opportunity.
Police conduct has also come under scrutiny. France’s police inspectorate, the IGPN, has opened dozens of investigations into alleged police violence since protests began.
What does the slogan mean?
“Bismillah” is Arabic for “in the name of God”, an expression used by Muslims before beginning an activity. In French slang, it has lost some of its original meaning, becoming more akin to “let’s do it”.
“C’est les ténèbres” literally translates as “it’s the darkness”, which alludes to a situation that is bleak and hopeless.
The slogan therefore translates as “In the name of God, it’s the darkness”, which does not convey a clear message in and of itself.
Where did the slogan come from?
Students say the phrase is a mockery of the police force, which tried to infiltrate social media chats used by protesters to coordinate.
The screenshot of a Snapchat conversation featuring the expression began circulating in early October. In it, a user named Mamadou requests to be added to a group, saying: “Hi, in the name of God, it’s the darkness. When’s the blockade, wallah, bro?”
The message also featured emojis with Algerian flags.
Students say the message was sent by undercover police officers attempting to infiltrate their chats by using an unconvincing mix of Arabic and slang. The claim has not been verified and French authorities have not issued any statement.
Youssef El Chazli, associate professor in Arab and Mediterranean sociology at Paris 8 University Vincennes – Saint-Denis, said the phrase “reinforces an image of out-of-touch policemen filled with stereotypes”.
“Such stereotypes appear to disproportionately aim at youths from Arab and African descent,” El Chazli told Al Jazeera. “This appears as one more example of how out-of-touch state agencies seem to be with the current movement.”
What does the slogan tell us about the protest movement?
The slogan has appeared on cardboard placards as a mockery of racial stereotypes and as a symbol of how authorities are out of touch with the realities of young people.
The slogan has spread as far as Italy and Belgium, where similar protests over the high cost of living and poor education also took place over the weekend.
El Chazli said satirical memes and internet trends have become tools to express political grievances during protests, which have traditionally been “inventive and creative”. “With youth mobilisations, protest creativity will draw heavily on youths’ subcultures,” he said.
Discussions around Islamophobia have also taken a front seat in public debate. French authorities have been reluctant to comment publicly on a significant spike in Islamophobic acts in France. One report cited by the Reuters news agency last year showed a 72 percent increase in such incidents during the January-March quarter of 2025 compared with the same period in 2024.
The French far right quickly resorted to racist language to blame Muslim youths for the violence, while United States President Donald Trump also chimed in, claiming that this is about “Islam wanting to take over”.
“What used to be a nonsubject 20 years ago is now a debated point,” El Chazli said. “For younger generations, Arab and African influences have been steadily mainstreaming in youth subcultures, owing to sports and arts figures, as well as new radio shows or social media content.”

Dutch workers more likely to stay on after state retirement age
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:35:23 UTC
19:35:23 KST

Dutch workers more likely to stay on after state retirement age
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The number of Dutch workers who stay in work beyond the statutory retirement age has increased by more 50% in eight years, according to latest figures from the statistics agency CBS.
In the second quarter of this year 152,000 people in work were over the age of 67, representing 1.7% of the working population.
In the first quarter of 2018 1.2% of workers were beyond the retirement age, which was then 66, equivalent to 96,000 people.
Men are more likely than women to keep going to work after drawing their pension, the figures show. In June 2.3% of men over 67 were working, compared to 1.1% of women.
The figures also revealed large differences between sectors, with 4.3% of people working in real estate after their 67th birthday compared to 0.6% of civil servants.
A study by the demographic institute NIDI in 2023 found that most people who kept working in retirement did so because they enjoyed their job or to feel useful. Just 10% said the need to earn money was a significant factor.
The Netherlands has the latest retirement age in the European Union, along with Denmark, Sweden, Italy and Greece. The state pension age is due to increase to 67 years and three months in 2028.

Pakistan-Taliban conflict: How India could benefit from shifting regional dynamics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:35:00 UTC
19:35:00 KST

Does Pakistan-Taliban conflict create a strategic opening for India?
October 21, 2026
Pakistan and Afghanistan right now are locked in a cycle of escalating tension. Repeated border clashes have strained ties between the two nations.
The current round of tensions began in February 2026, when Pakistan launched strikes into Afghanistan targeting Taliban militants. At one point in March, Pakistan's defense minister said the country was at "open war" with Afghanistan. Periodic bouts of violence have continued since then, with the latest Pakistani strikes targeting the Afghan Taliban's "terrorist hubs" reported earlier in October.
At the heart of the dispute is Pakistan's accusation that the Taliban authorities in Kabul allow the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), a militant group, to target Pakistan from Afghan territory. Kabul denies providing the group with sanctuary.
Where does India come into play?
As the two neighbors trade strikes, the escalating conflict "presents a significant diplomatic and strategic opportunity for India," Shanthie Mariet D'Souza, an Afghanistan expert and founder of the India-based Mantraya Institute for Strategic Studies, told DW.
D'Souza argues the confrontation has weakened Pakistan's traditional influence in Afghanistan and encouraged the Taliban to broaden its external relations.
"India can respond by expanding diplomatic engagement, humanitarian assistance, development projects and trade, while seeking assurances that Afghan territory will not be used by anti-India militant groups," she said.
However, D'Souza cautioned against interpreting the opening as a fundamental realignment.
"There is no ideological alignment between India and the Taliban," she said. Afghanistan under Taliban rule is likely to pursue a diversified foreign policy rather than align exclusively with New Delhi.
India also lacks the geographical advantages, economic leverage and security presence needed to replace Pakistan's influence, she notes. "The scenario of the Taliban becoming a strategic ally remains far-fetched."
Former Indian ambassador to Afghanistan Amar Sinha warned against viewing the conflict simply as an opportunity for New Delhi to gain at Pakistan's expense.
"The issues have very little to do with India," Sinha told DW, arguing that India was not seeking strategic advantage from the fighting. He also pointed to the consequences of Pakistan's military actions for Afghan civilians.
"Yet the rupture has made Kabul's search for alternative partners more pressing," he added.
For India, that creates an opening, but not necessarily a strategic alignment, Sinha notes. The Taliban can seek Indian assistance while maintaining relations with China, Russia, Iran and Gulf states, preserving its autonomy rather than exchanging dependence on Pakistan for dependence on India.
The cost of closer ties
Gautam Mukhopadhyaya, another former Indian ambassador to Afghanistan, sees the deterioration in relations between Pakistan and the Taliban as an opportunity for India to recover some of the strategic ground it lost when the Taliban returned to power in 2021.
"The crisis has allowed strategic openings for India," Mukhopadhyaya told DW. He warned, however, that New Delhi's own treatment of Afghans could undermine its efforts to build a durable relationship.
He pointed to restrictions affecting Afghans seeking Indian visas for education, scholarships, work and medical treatment.
"For all practical purposes, India's security establishment treats Afghans as proxy Pakistanis and 'terrorists' by default," he said.
Former Afghan partners had been left "disappointed, even bitter," Mukhopadhyaya added. "A strategic relationship built on the sands of oppression is not a sound foundation."
Trade cannot overcome geography
India has restored air freight links between Kabul and Delhi and between Kabul and Amritsar in northwestern India in December 2025.
Bilateral trade between India and Afghanistan stood at about $908 million (€807 million) in the 2025-26 fiscal year, while trade between Pakistan and Afghanistan fell sharply amid repeated border closures.
On October 14, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi stressed the importance of relations with India during talks with Indian charge d'affaires Yatin Patel, signaling Kabul's interest in expanding economic cooperation.
But air freight is expensive, and India cannot easily replace Pakistan as a transit route.
New Delhi has sought to use Iran's Chabahar port to improve access to Afghanistan and Central Asia, but regional instability and complications surrounding Iran have constrained those ambitions.
D'Souza cautioned that "the ongoing conflict in Iran" limits India's ability to use Chabahar as a crucial trade and connectivity hub.
Gulshan Sachdeva, a professor at Jawaharlal Nehru University specializing in Afghanistan and Eurasian connectivity, highlighted similar obstacles.
"In the last few decades, Islamabad has obstructed Kabul's efforts to gain access to the vast Indian market. However, political instability in Afghanistan and sanctions on Iran have undermined these efforts," Sachdeva told DW.
"Afghanistan's potential as a connector between regional markets remains considerable, but the infrastructure and political conditions needed to realize it are far from assured," he added.
Sachdeva also sees Russia and China as better positioned to shape Afghanistan's wider economic integration. Alternative routes may become more attractive to India, but they are not commercially viable overnight.
Islamabad's security fears
Pakistan has portrayed arch-rival India's growing engagement with the Taliban as a security threat. On October 7, Pakistani diplomat Muhammad Jawad Ajmal accused India at the United Nations of providing the Taliban with material and logistical support.
"Under the guise of humanitarian aid, they have been actively supporting the Taliban regime with material and logistical support for carrying out terrorist attacks against Pakistan," Ajmal said.
The allegation reflects Islamabad's position and has not been established as fact.
Pakistan has accused India of supporting the TTP and the Balochistan Liberation Army, a militant organization.
India rejects accusations of backing militant activity, while the Taliban denies allowing Afghan territory to be used for attacks against Pakistan.
Ayesha Siddiqa, a Pakistani expert on military and security affairs at King's College London, offered a more nuanced assessment of Pakistan's position.
"India has stepped into a space and is trying to exert its influence and feed anti-Pakistan groups intelligence," she told DW.
Siddiqa added that Pakistan's establishment continues to view the crisis through "a singular security lens."
"Islamabad feels physically squeezed from both sides," she said, adding that closer Kabul-New Delhi ties could create "a dangerous two-front security trap" for Pakistan.
India may gain more room to operate in Afghanistan as ties between Kabul and Islamabad deteriorate. But the Taliban is unlikely to put all its eggs in New Delhi's basket.

Data centers have become a hot-button issue ahead of the midterm elections in November. Public opposition to the buildout of the facilities and their environmental impact has been growing, with multiple states considering moratoriums.

Data center stocks have also come under pressure this week amid growing concerns about the financial health of the sector. As the AI infrastructure buildout grows more costly, companies are increasingly turning to debt markets to finance deals.

Access to power is a major constraint on the sector, as power grids in the U.S. and Europe become overwhelmed with applications from large energy users like data centers.

In fact, there could be a substantial decrease," Trump said, in a post around 1.37 a.m. ET.
In some cases, data centers can operate as flexible loads, adjusting their electricity use to help stabilize the grid.
Hyperscalers have secured deals where they agree to help finance badly needed updates to local power grids. However, some experts have warned that the AI boom will ultimately result in higher electricity prices.

Russia wants AI to help design its next aircraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:32:23 UTC
19:32:23 KST

- Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation said it is evaluating new software, including artificial intelligence, to speed up the design of future aircraft and modifications.
- UAC is already running a pilot project with Sberbank’s GigaChat AI for generative design at the early stage of a new aircraft.
Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation is looking at artificial intelligence and other new software to speed up the design of future aircraft and cut the cost of developing new versions of existing ones, the state-owned planemaker said in a statement on its social media.
UAC, which builds nearly all of Russia’s military and civil aircraft, from Su-57 and Su-35 fighters to the MC-21 airliner, said its engineers are evaluating new software products, including AI technologies, as the company moves its design work onto digital models.
The company said digital models let its engineers analyze far larger volumes of data and test many more aircraft layouts before choosing the best one, which makes developing new modifications faster and cheaper over an aircraft’s life cycle. UAC added that it is taking a measured approach to AI and will only use the new tools where they make sense and help solve specific engineering problems.
“Digital technology makes it possible to take a larger sample and understand a problem more deeply. Over the life cycle, this will be faster and cheaper when creating the next modifications,” UAC specialists said.
The statement follows remarks by UAC general designer Sergey Korotkov, who said on Oct. 13 that there is no reason not to use AI in aircraft design as long as it helps with the task at hand and is applied thoughtfully. UAC has already been testing the idea, and in May its chief executive, Vadim Badekha, said the company was running a pilot project with Sberbank to use the bank’s GigaChat AI model for generative design of a new aircraft at the early design stage, with plans to extend it later to strength and aerodynamic calculations.
The shift to domestic digital tools has been driven largely by sanctions, since Western design software vendors such as Dassault Systèmes, Siemens and Autodesk pulled out of Russia after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine and left the country’s aerospace industry without the programs it had relied on for decades. UAC says it has since replaced software at its design bureaus with Russian products, equipping about 4,000 engineering workstations and swapping out nine key product lifecycle management modules, and on Oct. 16 it said digital design had cut some aircraft system calculations, such as cabin heat balance and hydraulic networks, from months to days.
Those efforts come as UAC struggles with delays on its most important civil programs, which have had to replace Western parts and systems with Russian-made equivalents. President Vladimir Putin said in June that the MC-21 had been set back by almost two years, partly because of problems with the wing, and First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov said certification of the version built entirely with Russian components is now planned for the end of 2027.

Giant tunnel proposed to tackle Windermere sewage discharges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:32:12 UTC
19:32:12 KST

Plans are under way for a new giant tunnel to transport sewage away from Windermere, England’s largest lake.
Windermere, in the Lake District, has suffered from widespread raw sewage and bacterial pollution driven by discharges from United Utilities. Campaigners say this pollution has caused more frequent toxic blue-green algal blooms, with the public advised to avoid swimming in the lake.
Modelling indicates the climate crisis will exacerbate these challenges, with the catchment expected to experience more intense rainfall over the coming years, placing further pressure on the wastewater infrastructure.
A new project, backed by United Utilities, the Environment Agency and local campaigners, has set out a vision to end sewage discharges into the lake by building an 12-mile (19km) tunnel to transport sewage away from the lake.
The water company said the use of tunnelling techniques would minimise the disruption to local communities.
Windermere is at the heart of the Lake District Unesco world heritage site and has been the inspiration for poets, storytellers and lyricists for generations, with an estimated 17.7 million people visiting every year.
The treated effluent would then be discharged into either the River Leven or the Irish Sea at Ulverston. It is estimated the project will cost £3.6bn, with United Utilities to seek permission from the government to raise customer bills to pay for it. It said the programme could add up to £3.17 a month to water bills in 2035.
The project will now enter the detailed design phase during which specialised engineers will work out the technicalities of the build, which is expected to take two years.
If granted permission to raise bills to pay for the project, United Utilities said the project could be complete within seven years and would provide a “one and done” solution with an immediate impact.
Matt Staniek, a campaigner at Save Windermere, which is a partner on the project, said creating the feasibility report had involved weekly meetings over 15 months.
Staniek, who has been calling for the end of sewage discharges into the lake for more than five years, said he was concerned at first about partnering with the company causing the pollution, but said they were the only people who could actually fix it. “This has demonstrated that it is possible not to dump sewage in Lake Windermere,” he said.
In planning for the project, the team considered the transformation of Lake Annecy in France, which is widely recognised as one of the cleanest lakes in Europe. In the 1950s, Annecy faced similar pollution problems, but the authorities invested in long-term infrastructural improvements to eliminate the sewage discharges.
“This is up to the government now. The plan is there, it’s in place, we’re not going to stop until Andy Burnham is on the shores of Lake Windermere with a spade announcing that the construction has begun on this project,” Staniek said.

Trump Keeps Promising Cash on the Campaign Trail—but Has a Poor History of Following Through
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:31:17 UTC
19:31:17 KST

Donald Trump is betting that the promise of more money in Americans’ pockets will translate into support at the ballot box. With his approval ratings low and November’s midterms just weeks away, the President has made a series of financial pledges in a bid to preserve Republicans’ majorities in Congress.
At a Kansas rally on Monday, Trump announced that the Administration is offering an $8 billion aid package to help American farmers offset higher diesel costs in the current harvest season. Diesel has remained above $6 per gallon since mid-September, per the American Automobile Association, as oil prices have been pushed up by the war with Iran, which Trump started in late February.
Some rural voters, who helped elect Trump in 2024, have grown disillusioned with him, but he continued to court them in Kansas, adding: “When the Republicans win, we will pass even more funding for our farmers. We love our farmers.”
Several opinion polls show that rising costs of living are top of mind for voters ahead of the elections. Some polls rate the President’s handling of the U.S. economy as very poor. Disenchantment with the current political and economic system has also reached a point where socialism has grown more popular among Americans.
Trump’s efforts to woo voters with offers of cash gained attention in September, when he explicitly promised a Dallas crowd that his Administration would dole out a $5,000 dividend to every American adult if the GOP maintains its majorities in Congress. But with about 240 million adult citizens, the proposal would cost around $1.2 trillion—a gargantuan financial undertaking that even some in his own party questioned how the U.S. could afford. Democrats, meanwhile, called the dividend proposal a vote-buying scheme.
The same month, the Administration promised to refund more than 950,000 Obamacare enrollees in 30 states $500 each for “overcharges” collected by the Biden Administration. Earlier this month, it promised a one-time $90 payment per person to help more than 20 million enrollees pay for their Medicare premiums. Some voters have already reported receiving these payments.
While mentions of these handouts have earned cheers at Trump’s supporter-packed rallies, it is unclear if they will translate to any additional earned votes. Voter turnout in the U.S. is historically lower during midterm and off-year elections, and Trump, in a bid to boost the GOP’s chances, has repeatedly called on his supporters to imagine that he is on the ballot.
It’s also unclear if voters are sold on Trump’s cash-based solutions. For example, a Wall Street Journal poll in September found that 64% of respondents thought Trump’s proposed $5,000 checks were a “bad idea right now.” And even if Republicans won the election, an Economist/YouGov poll from September found that most voters are skeptical that Trump would deliver—and they have good reason to be.
What happened to Trump’s past cash proposals
Trump has made many big promises, but he hasn’t always kept them.
He has repeatedly floated the idea of giving a $2,000 stimulus check or tax rebate to most Americans, supposedly funded by revenue from the global tariffs he’s imposed throughout his second term. But since making that promise in November 2025, as of this month, such dividends have yet to materialize. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
When his on-and-off friend Elon Musk was implementing a cost-cutting initiative across the federal government last year, Trump said he was considering using some of the savings to give Americans cash. “We’re thinking about giving 20% back to the American citizens, and 20% down to pay back debt,” Trump said in February last year. That plan also never materialized.
During his first term, while he was seeking re-election in 2020, Trump promised that his Administration would send $200 discount cards to 33 million older Americans on Medicare to help them pay for prescription drugs. Critics slammed the plan for lack of a clear funding source and how it appeared to be designed just to court voters, but his term eventually ended without distributing those cards and he did not pursue the policy in his second term that began in 2025.
To save Americans in economic freefall during the COVID-19 pandemic, Trump in 2020 promised to get money to them “as quickly as possible.” It also coincided with his campaign for re-election. Eligible adults were able to receive as much as $1,200 as well as $500 per qualifying child. By October that year, the Internal Revenue Service delivered more than 160 million payments totaling over $270 billion. Although he did make good on his promise, the effort did not help Trump’s re-election, however, as he lost the 2020 presidential race to former Vice President Joe Biden.
Trump pours his own cash into election
Trump appears to be ramping up his own political spending to ensure the GOP’s political victory on Nov. 3. “I have spent, or will be spending, over 400 Million Dollars by Election Day,” he posted on Truth Social on Tuesday. “More than 300 Million Dollars has already been spent on Advertising, Direct and Indirect Voter Contact, Rallies, Rally Arenas, Telerallies, Get Out the Vote Programs, Election Integrity, and more.”
Trump’s super political action committee, MAGA Inc., allocated $277 million, a record amount for a second-term President, from the start of September through the first two weeks of October to help the GOP in the midterms, according to the latest Federal Election Commission filings.
The latest filings also show that MAGA Inc. received about $25 million in donations during that period. Some of the biggest donors include Trump-allied billionaire Diane Hendricks, Blackstone CEO Stephen Schwarzman, and casino-resort developer Steve Wynn.
MAGA Inc. has raised about $473 million since Trump’s re-election in 2024.

Dosorozco uses stone and blackened timber for textured home in Mexican forest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Dosorozco uses stone and blackened timber for textured home in Mexican forest
Architecture studio Dosorozco has used a palette of blackened timber, stonework and pale plaster at Casa Sima, a Mexican home designed to echo the textures and tones of its forest surroundings.
Named Casa Sima, the 150-square-metre dwelling sits on a sloping forest site in Sierra de Tapalpa in Jalisco, with panoramic views towards mountains in the distance.
Dosorozco’s decision to avoid excavation or tree removal informed the home’s elongated plan and the placement of its blocky volumes, which instead align with the contours of an existing clearing.
“Casa Sima started with something very simple, the place already had its own order before we arrived,” the studio’s creative director Guillermo R Orozco told Dezeen.
“One of the first decisions we made was that no existing trees would be removed. That sounds simple, but it affected almost every decision that came after,” he explained.
“Their position affects the geometry of the house, the views, the shadows, the terraces and even the points where the building can touch the ground.”
Casa Sima is accessed via a stepped walkway elevated above the forest floor, which leads from the base of its sloping site to the home’s rectilinear volumes perched at the top.
Marking the transition from the forest into the home is what Orozco calls an “elevated courtyard”, comprising a timber wall supported by a steel frame, positioned above this walkway.
This timber was finished with a local technique that uses oil and heat to weatherproof its surface, giving it a rough, blackened finish intended to blend with the surrounding trees.
“There is a brief moment there where you are not really outside anymore, but you are not inside either,” Orozco explained.
“You become aware of the ground below you, the structure around and above you, and the trees beyond it,” he continued.
“It is suspended above the terrain, framed by the structure and open to the forest, so it works almost like a vestibule without ever becoming a conventional room.”
The living spaces of Casa Sima are housed within two intersecting, rectilinear volumes, with the ground floor given over to a large living, dining and kitchen space flanked by two stone walls.
These stone walls are left visible, complemented by dark timber ceilings and fully-glazed walls that open onto two distinct terraces – one at ground level to the south and another elevated to the north.
A study and bathroom also occupy the ground floor, while above, the central cubic volume contains two bedrooms lined in timber and plaster. These both have access to rooftop terraces.
“The house is compact, but it doesn’t really feel compact when you are inside it,” said Orozco.
“The rotation between floors, the terraces, the diagonal views and the constant relationship with the exterior make the spaces feel much more open,” he added.
Other homes in Mexico recently featured on Dezeen include a lime-rendered home next to a wooded hillside in Cristóbal de las Casas by local studio Colar, and a holiday home in Valle de Bravo by Chain + Siman comprising a row of gabled forms.

OpenAI Invests in Startup That Uses Brain Implants to Detect Cancer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

OpenAI’s venture capital arm as well as Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund are investing in Coherence Neuro, a startup developing a brain implant to detect and treat cancer.
The investments are part of a $45 million seed funding round for Coherence and reflect Big Tech’s burgeoning interest in brain data. Coherence’s CEO and cofounder Ben Woodington says there is “growing synergy” between the big AI labs and companies building devices to decode the brain, known as brain-computer interfaces.
“The idea of capturing data to train better models and use it to optimize treatments is going to be super important,” he says. “The AI companies seem to be aligned with this thesis as well—that this novel data source is going to be valuable.”
Woodington says AI is a “perfect use case” for brain-computer interfaces because developers of these devices generate massive datasets that are too large for humans to analyze themselves. AI models can help read raw neural data and link it to actions, such as moving a computer cursor or producing synthesized speech.
In January, OpenAI announced that it was directly investing in a new brain-computer interface company, Merge Labs, cofounded by its billionaire CEO Sam Altman. Merge Labs came out of stealth with $252 million in initial funding to pursue ultrasound technology that can decode information from the brain. At the time, OpenAI said it was funding Merge Labs because of a belief that brain-computer interfaces “will create a natural, human-centered way for anyone to seamlessly interact with AI.” (The name Merge Labs comes from the idea popular in Silicon Valley that humans will eventually merge with machine intelligence.)
Thiel’s VC firm has also backed Elon Musk’s Neuralink as well as CTRL-labs, the creator of a wristband that translates neural signals from arm and hand movements that was acquired by Facebook in 2019.
Rather than focusing on restoring function for paralyzed individuals, San Francisco–based Coherence is developing AI models to decode subtle electrical signals associated with brain tumors. The company says it already knows how to detect these signals in animals to determine whether cancer is growing, shrinking, or recurring. The team is working to translate these findings for human research and, eventually, clinical trials.
This summer, Coherence briefly tested the recording ability of its implant in the brains of three people who were already undergoing brain tumor removal surgery at the Royal Melbourne Hospital in Australia. The implant was in place for roughly 30 minutes before being removed, providing an initial safety check. Next, Coherence is testing both the recording and stimulation capabilities of the device in an additional seven patients.
The implant is also designed to emit mild electrical stimulation to halt the growth of tumors. The idea is that over time, the device would learn to detect signals associated with cancer and provide real-time treatment. Coherence plans to use the new funding to launch a clinical trial to implant the device long-term in patients with glioblastoma, an aggressive type of brain cancer. The company also aims to develop implants to treat cancers in other parts of the body.
“Coherence's approach to developing a cancer therapy capable of improving from data is incredibly innovative,” Ian Hathaway, partner at the OpenAI Startup Fund, says in a statement. “We are proud to be backing them on this exciting mission.”
Woodington says that OpenAI will not have access to its data. “There's nothing in the contracts or arrangements that would mean that we would share, or they would have access to, any brain data or other health data that we're generating,” he says.
That is seemingly different from OpenAI’s relationship with Merge Labs. In its January announcement, OpenAI said it would “collaborate with Merge Labs on scientific foundation models and other frontier tools to accelerate progress.”

Fifth country reports Ebola case

Fifth country reports Ebola case
Nigeria has confirmed its first Ebola case in more than a decade after a woman who recently traveled through Uganda tested positive for the virus in the capital, Abuja.
The patient arrived in Nigeria in early October and began showing symptoms on October 7, the country’s Health Ministry said on Tuesday. The woman sought treatment at a private hospital on October 11 and was diagnosed with the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola on October 20, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). The woman remains in isolation and is receiving medical care. Health authorities have identified 44 people who may have been exposed to the infection.
The patient was initially treated for malaria-like symptoms, but doctors became concerned after her condition failed to improve, Odianosen Ehiakhamen, an official at the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC), told Arise TV, as reported by Punch.
“For the 44 contacts, they are majorly healthcare workers and support staff of the hospital, because everything has happened within the hospital,” Ehiakhamen said.
Uganda’s Health Ministry said the woman was a Nigerian national who had visited eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo) for business before passing through Uganda. The ministry stressed that the location of her infection remained unknown and that Uganda had no active Ebola cases.
Nigeria is the fifth country to report the Bundibugyo virus since the current outbreak began in DR Congo in May, following earlier cases in Uganda, France and Kenya, according to the WHO. Kenya has recorded nine infections linked to an imported case, while the outbreak in DR Congo continues to spread.
The Ebola outbreak in DR Congo has claimed 4,602 lives, with 9,552 confirmed infections recorded since it began in May, according to the country’s Health Ministry. As of October 18, the virus had affected eight provinces, with Ituri accounting for nearly 73% of all cases.
Nigeria previously contained an Ebola outbreak in 2014.
Meanwhile, the US State Department on Monday raised its travel advisory for Kenya from Level 2 to Level 3, urging Americans to reconsider visiting the country due to health risks linked to Ebola, as well as security concerns.

Wonderhaul: has Liam Gallagher really got into metal detecting?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:28:42 UTC
19:28:42 KST

Liam Gallagher is one of the country’s foremost trendsetters. When Oasis emerged in the 1990s, you couldn’t move for the sight of young men doing their darndest to look like him – wearing parkas and swaggering around as if they had just wolfed down a breakfast that didn’t agree with them.
Which is to say, we should probably expect stocks of metal detectors to run low in the coming days, because Gallagher has apparently outed himself as a keen detectorist. “I’m a big fan of the metal detector phenomenon,” he tweeted on Sunday, adding in a separate message that: “I do it for the buzz n the bing.”
Assuming that Gallagher is telling the truth here – and that’s a big assumption, given his tendency to tweet falsehoods about everything from the existence of a new Oasis album to the possibility that Peppa Pig would soon join them on drums – doesn’t it make perfect sense?
If nothing else, it means that he has finally found an appropriate pastime for his uniform. It’s a little ridiculous for him to wear big coats when he’s singing songs to thousands of people in a stadium, but stick him in a field on a drizzly Thursday afternoon and it suddenly all falls into context. Plus, you know, what is Oasis if not an exercise in getting stuck in the quagmire of the past?
And if it is real, it couldn’t be more timely. Metal detecting, by all accounts, is on the up and up. Not only do 1% of British adults say they have tried metal detecting in the last year, but they are finding things at an extraordinary rate. Last year the government released its reported treasure finds for 2023 and 2024, noting that a provisional 2,883 pieces of reported treasure were found across the UK (though not including Scotland) over those years – the highest figure since records began – with many of the finds being acquired by museums. And the overwhelming majority of these treasures were discovered by metal detecting.
Now, there is no point attributing this popularity solely to Gallagher, because he has only just jumped on to the bandwagon. More likely the rise is down to Detectorists, the bucolic comedy-drama written by Mackenzie Crook, and co-starring Toby Jones, which ran from 2014 until 2022. That show was so gentle, and painted such an idyllic picture of detecting, that membership of the National Council of Metal Detecting has reportedly quadrupled over the last decade.
And, excitingly, there is still plenty out there to be discovered. More than 800 iron age objects were unearthed in North Yorkshire’s Melsonby hoard in 2021. That same year, a medieval gold coin worth almost £650,000 was found in Devon. And two years before that came the Chew valley hoard, where seven Somerset detectorists found 2,584 silver coins that were subsequently valued at £4.3m.
With riches like this still lying beneath our feet, no wonder Gallagher has taken to the pursuit with such aplomb. Especially since, given the perennial palaver over his band’s ticket prices, he seems especially well versed at extracting every last penny from well hidden spots.

UK approves development of Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea

UK approves development of Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea
The decision has drawn sharp criticism from left-wing politicians and environmentalists.
The United Kingdom’s government has approved a natural gas project off the coast of Scotland, as the Labour government seeks to balance its climate goals with energy security concerns.
Energy Minister Miatta Fahnbulleh said on Wednesday that the Jackdaw gasfield would begin supplying energy to UK homes by the end of the month and would help to boost the country’s energy security.
The government said the North Sea project would increase UK gas production by about 6 percent at its peak.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the decision will “protect hundreds of jobs and help keep millions of homes warm”, but stressed it would not hinder the government’s targets on renewable energy.
The government also announced a New Energy Wealth Fund, which will invest in renewable and low-carbon energy projects as part of the green transition.
The fund has been established with an initial 2 billion pounds ($2.7bn), with plans to raise additional funds through tax revenues from North Sea oil and gas.
Higher energy prices amid the Russia-Ukraine war and the United States-Israel war on Iran have weighed on households and businesses, dragging on Britain’s economy.
Fahnbulleh told UK radio station LBC that the development of Jackdaw would not bring down household energy bills.
“I think it’s really important that we’re honest about this,” Fahnbulleh said.
“That was not a consideration in the decision because it won’t mean cheaper bills. This was about energy security.”
The announcement has drawn criticism from left-wing politicians and environmental groups.
Zack Polanski, the leader of the opposition Green Party, described the decision as “climate vandalism”.
“Surreal to hear [the] energy secretary try and say this is a ‘pragmatic decision’,” Polanski wrote in a post on X.
“It will do nothing to lower bills. It will do lots for the profits of the oil and gas companies. And will continue us further down the path of floods and wildfires.”
Environmental group Greenpeace said the decision showed “the toxic grip fossil fuel lobbyists still hold over our energy policy”.
“True pragmatism means severing our reliance on expensive oil and gas that leaves British households broke, supercharges extreme weather, and leaves our energy security at the mercy of petrostates,” said Ami McCarthy, head of politics at Greenpeace UK.
