what we learned: spectator and spectacle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:27:58 UTC
19:27:58 KST

what we learned: spectator and spectacle
in this chapter, we journeyed from underground nightclubs to cinematic illusions, wearable architectures, and sculptural mirrors, exploring how spectacle can challenge our perceptions and experience the world.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
WHAT HAPPENS WHEN WE STOP JUST WATCHING?
When Sofia Lekka Angelopoulou opened SPECTATOR AND SPECTACLE, she posed a question that challenged our relationship with the world around us: ‘What if we are not overwhelmed by spectacle, but starved of it?’ In her opening editorial, The Haçienda Must Be Built, she traced the history of the night, from radical discotheques to the increasingly measured and optimized rhythms of contemporary life, asking what happens when experiences become predictable and images lose their capacity to surprise us. Over the weeks that followed, the chapter explored how architecture, art, fashion, and design might recover that sense of wonder. Again and again, spectacle emerged not simply as something to observe, but as an experience capable of unsettling our habits, changing our behavior, and dissolving the boundary between those who watch and those who perform.
That conversation extended through a series of guest contributions and encounters with practitioners reconsidering what it means to create an experience. John Leo Gillen reflected on the disappearing architecture of the nightclub and the importance of moments that cannot be reproduced, while Łukasz Twarkowski blurred the boundaries between theater, cinema, and live images. Dennis Vanderbroeck considered how spatial design can create the conditions for collective experiences, while photographers David Altrath and François Prost approached the spectacle from different perspectives: one through the experience of architectural space, the other through the facades that promise extraordinary nights. Together, their perspectives revealed something that would return throughout the chapter: spectacle is not necessarily about what is in front of us, but about what happens when we encounter it.
THE CROWD IS PART OF THE ARCHITECTURE
Few spaces demonstrate the relationship between spectator and spectacle as clearly as the nightclub. Looking back at the history of nightlife architecture, from Italy’s radical discotheques of the 1960s to New York’s Studio 54 and Berlin’s industrial clubs, we discovered how these environments became laboratories for collective experience. At Florence’s Space Electronic, architecture, projections, music, and performance came together in an experimental setting, while the Haçienda in Manchester offered an industrial interior that its occupants could transform through their own presence. Later, Berlin’s Berghain introduced another dimension to this relationship by restricting photography, protecting an experience that cannot easily be consumed from a distance. These spaces reminded us that architecture can establish the conditions for spectacle, but the people occupying it ultimately determine what happens.
A similar understanding of collective performance emerged in our conversation with Leda Papaconstantinou, whose Spetses Players transformed a Greek island into an experimental stage during the 1970s. Rather than working with fixed scripts or conventional theatrical settings, the group developed performances around local stories, social realities, and the island’s existing architecture. Harbors, houses, and even a discotheque became temporary stages, while elaborate costumes and characters invited audiences into unfamiliar worlds. By the end of their performances, spectators would often join the performers in singing and dancing. The distinction between art and everyday life became increasingly difficult to maintain. What mattered was not simply the event itself, but the temporary community formed around it.
ILLUSION CAN CHANGE HOW WE SEE REALITY
Spectacle can also challenge the distance we maintain between fiction and the world we inhabit. In Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s Digger, production design becomes a central narrative instrument, constructing layers of reality that progressively undermine the audience’s certainty about what they are watching. Designed by Dennis Gassner and Richard Johnson, the film’s environments move between elaborate interiors, theatrical scenery, and carefully exposed artifices, making the process of constructing an illusion part of the story itself. As the boundaries between performance and reality begin to collapse, the viewer’s position becomes increasingly uncomfortable. The sets do more than establish atmosphere: they measure the distance between the audience and the catastrophe unfolding before them, until the possibility of remaining a detached observer begins to disappear.
In a very different way, Yeondoo Jung’s Wonderland revealed how the construction of an image can expose unexpected truths. The Korean artist collected 1,200 drawings by young children and selected 17 to recreate as meticulously staged photographs, using teenage models, costumes, props, and locations across Seoul. Impossible proportions, floating figures, and imaginary landscapes were brought into physical existence without correcting the peculiar logic of the original drawings. Yet beneath their playful appearance, these images revealed observations about the real world, from urban development to social inequality. Two decades later, in an age when similar scenes can be generated instantly through artificial intelligence, Jung’s painstaking process offers another perspective on spectacle. The wonder lies not only in the finished image, but in the human effort, negotiation, and material reality required to make imagination visible.
THE BODY BECOMES THE SPECTACLE
Throughout the chapter, the body repeatedly emerged as more than a passive observer. At London’s Tate Modern, HOMME PLISSÉ ISSEY MIYAKE’s OPEN STUDIO transformed Henri Matisse’s The Snail into a choreography of pleated garments, movement, and audience encounters. Inside the museum’s circular South Tank, dancers animated the colorful geometries of the painting, while individual visitors became part of improvised performances developed through eye contact and physical proximity. The audience was no longer positioned outside the work, but integrated into its changing composition. As the garments eventually returned to the floor to reconstruct Matisse’s original image, the performance revealed how an artwork can move between representation and lived experience. The body had temporarily become the medium through which the image existed.
For Lucy McRae, the body is also the starting point for imagining alternative futures. Moving between sculpture, film, fashion, and speculative technology, the artist approaches clothing and wearable objects as forms of invisible architecture capable of transforming how we perceive ourselves and relate to others. Her experiments question what happens when technological innovation becomes inseparable from physical experience, and how identity might be shaped through the things we wear. Rather than presenting the future as a distant spectacle to be observed, McRae creates scenarios that invite us to imagine inhabiting it ourselves. Her work suggests that some of the most profound transformations do not require an elaborate stage or monumental setting. They can begin with the body itself, and with the subtle ways its relationship to the surrounding world changes.
SPECTACLE DOES NOT HAVE TO BE LOUD
Not every spectacle requires an extraordinary setting or a dramatic performance. Sometimes, an everyday object can be enough to disrupt the familiar act of looking. French designer Jean-Baptiste Fastrez explored this possibility through his sculptural mirrors for Moustache, turning the form of an inflatable boat into a glossy ceramic frame and transforming ordinary mirror fittings into oversized chrome spheres. Both objects play with the paradox of the mirror: an object with a strong physical presence whose appearance depends almost entirely on its surroundings. Their surfaces reflect, distort, and incorporate the spaces and people around them, making the viewer an unavoidable part of the composition. Fastrez also challenges the conventional separation between function and ornament, suggesting that decoration can be as essential to an object’s purpose as its practical use. The spectacle, in this case, emerges from the act of looking itself.
That quieter understanding of spectacle also appeared in our conversation with Lausanne-based studio Panter&Tourron, whose work for brands including Balenciaga and Hermès questions the traditional codes of luxury. Rather than relying on extravagance, precious materials, or obvious displays of status, Stefano Panterotto and Alexis Tourron place emphasis on craftsmanship, material intelligence, performance, and the stories behind objects. Their designs demonstrate how something apparently restrained can still command attention, challenging the assumption that visibility must always come through excess. Perhaps this is where many of the ideas explored throughout SPECTATOR AND SPECTACLE eventually meet. Wonder cannot simply be manufactured through scale, novelty, or visual intensity. Sometimes it comes from entering a room that changes our behavior, recognizing reality inside an illusion, seeing ourselves reflected in an unexpected form, or encountering something familiar as though for the first time. The challenge may not be to make the world more spectacular, but to rediscover our capacity to be surprised by it.

World falling ‘dangerously short’ on climate action
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:26:39 UTC
19:26:39 KST

This aerial photograph shows the parched bed of the upper part of Lake Gruyere on October 19, 2026, near Morlon, as the region remains under a Level 4 ('High Danger') drought warning on Switzerland's National Drought Platform. (AFP Photo)
Global commitments to cut planet-heating emissions are falling far short of the Paris climate goals and put the world on course for 2.6 degrees Celsius warming this century, the U.N. warned on Oct. 21.
The report by the United Nations Environment Program (UNEP) lays bare the chasm between rhetoric and action when it comes to tackling global warming, and the challenge before political leaders at November’s COP31 climate summit in Antalya.
Even if countries deliver their latest climate pledges in full, global temperatures could still rise 2.6 degrees above pre-industrial levels by 2100, said the annual Emissions Gap Report.
That would blow past the historic goal agreed in Paris: keeping warming well below 2 degrees while striving for a safer 1.5 degrees. Any chance of keeping to 1.5 degrees had been “lost” due to decades of insufficient climate action, the report said.
“The world can no longer avoid overshooting the 1.5-degree limit, and the consequences are already devastating,” said U.N. chief Antonio Guterres in a statement to launch the closely-watched report.
“Deadly floods, brutal heatwaves, raging wildfires, lost lives, crippled economies, deepening inequalities, and those least responsible are suffering first and worst.”
Overall, global greenhouse gas emissions in 2025 were broadly on a par with record levels in 2024, with the difference between the two years too small to call, the report said.
Carbon emissions just from burning coal, oil and gas, the main driver of climate change, rose slightly in 2025 compared to the previous year.
Guterres said deep and immediate cuts were needed to protect humanity from worsening impacts but instead “emissions remain at record levels. And national climate plans and current policies fall dangerously short.”
Sticking just with current policies would see warming hit 2.8 degrees, the report said.
The G20 accounts for three-quarters of global emissions but Guterres said “all countries, especially the big emitters, must do more” to stop heating the planet.
Among the world’s top-six emitters, preliminary data for 2025 showed emissions increases in the U.S., Indonesia and China and decreases in India, Russia and the European Union.
The U.S. is the world’s second-largest polluter, behind China. U.S. President Donald Trump has called climate change a hoax and rolled back clean energy policies while boosting fossil fuel production.
UNEP executive secretary Inger Andersen told reporters that no country was shielded from climate change and impacts were being felt “on every nation on the planet, including the U.S.”
Guterres agreed there was a climate “leadership gap” but said overshooting 1.5 degrees “is not surrender.”

BRUSSELS – Government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline on Oct 21 after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in a widely used programming language sent website operators scrambling to protect their systems.
Developers of the PHP programming language said on Oct 20 they have identified two critical vulnerabilities and urged users to update their sites as soon as a fix is released.
With reports that hackers were already exploiting the flaws to break into websites, government agencies in the Netherlands and Finland were among those that took sites offline as a precaution.
PHP is used across large parts of the internet, and speculation has circulated over the past day that websites running the software could be exposed to serious cyber intrusions.
“PHP is everywhere. It quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful lot of software that doesn’t even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood,” cybersecurity company Huntress said in a blog post.
In a security update, PHP said both vulnerabilities were rated 9.2 on the CVSS v4.0 severity scale and urged users to “upgrade as soon as the release is available”.
It said a patch for both vulnerabilities was scheduled for 2pm GMT (10pm, Singapore time) on Oct 21.
Dane Knecht, chief technology officer of web and cloud security firm Cloudflare, said attacks were emerging, and Cloudflare was updating its firewall rules as a stopgap measure.
“We are seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up. This is a STOPGAP only. Patch as soon as PHP releases the update,” he said on X.
The European Union Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-EU) said on Oct 20 in an advisory that the 9.2 rating indicated a risk of unauthenticated remote code execution, a type of flaw that can allow attackers to run malicious code on vulnerable systems without logging in.
CERT-EU urged organisations to prepare for the immediate patching of affected assets. It said those unable to do so should consider taking affected sites offline.
The Australian Cyber Security Centre (ACSC) issued similar guidance, urging organisations to identify PHP systems in their environments, prepare to apply patches and monitor applications for signs of malicious activity.
“ACSC is currently not aware of active exploitation related to these vulnerabilities,” the agency said.
Web hosting provider GoDaddy said the flaws could allow attackers to execute code on affected servers over the internet, potentially leading to data theft, website defacement or full system compromise.
Wordfence, a security plugin that protects WordPress websites, said all WordPress sites run on a PHP-installed server. It warned that automatic updates would not apply the fix and advised site owners to find out who is responsible for updating PHP on their sites.
PHP’s security team said details of the vulnerabilities, affected versions and the fixed releases would be published when patches are issued.
CERT-EU and the ACSC said all PHP versions from PHP 5 onward could be affected, although PHP has not disclosed which versions are vulnerable. REUTERS

Exclusive: Corbyn vows to pursue Gaza inquiry despite UK refusal

Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Corbyn vows to pursue Gaza inquiry despite UK refusal
Jeremy Corbyn has vowed to continue pressing for an inquiry into Britain's possible complicity in Israel's genocide in Gaza after the UK government rejected his renewed calls for an investigation, the former Labour leader told The New Arab.
Corbyn, who now represents Islington North for Your Party, is seeking an independent public inquiry into Britain's military, economic and political cooperation with Israel since October 2023, including arms supplies, surveillance flights and the use of Royal Air Force (RAF) bases.
The former Labour leader first introduced the Gaza (Independent Public Inquiry) Bill in June 2025 before reintroducing the legislation in the 2026–27 parliamentary session. The latest version was published on 2 September and is awaiting its second reading.
However, the government has resisted calls to establish an inquiry, arguing that its policies and actions relating to Gaza have already undergone extensive parliamentary scrutiny.
"The UK's policy and actions relating to the conflict in Gaza have been subject of extensive parliamentary scrutiny through ministerial statements, debates, Select Committee scrutiny, and oral and written Parliamentary Questions," Middle East Minister Stephen Doughty said in a written response to Corbyn's request.
The refusal comes despite hopes that Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government would take a different approach after he apologised for his predecessor Keir Starmer's words and actions regarding Israel's genocide in Gaza.
"We're not going away, we're not giving up because I think this cause is far too important and far too great," Corbyn told The New Arab.
Corbyn said an inquiry could answer questions about Britain's supply of F-35 fighter jet components to Israel and RAF reconnaissance flights over Gaza.
UK companies manufacture around 15% of the components used in F-35 fighter jets, which Israel has deployed in its assault on Gaza, according to the Campaign Against Arms Trade.
Between December 2023 and July 2025, the RAF conducted more than 600 reconnaissance flights over Gaza, according to Action on Armed Violence (AOAV).
The Ministry of Defence maintained that the flights were conducted "solely to locate hostages", though AOAV questioned whether their scale and persistence were consistent with humanitarian aims.
"We do need a very profound apology to the Palestinian people for the way in which the British government has maintained a supply of arms and military corporation with Israeli Defence Force throughout this whole horrific period, particularly since October 2023," Corbyn said.
In 2016, while Labour leader, Corbyn apologised for the Labour Party's role in the Iraq War following the publication of the Chilcot inquiry's findings.
The inquiry found that Saddam Hussein did not pose an imminent threat to Britain at the time of the 2003 invasion and that intelligence about Iraq's alleged weapons of mass destruction had been presented with unjustified certainty.
Corbyn was among the Labour MPs who opposed the Iraq War and subsequently pushed for an inquiry into Britain's role in the invasion and its aftermath, which resulted in hundreds of thousands of deaths, according to various estimates.
"One day the British Prime Minister will say we need an inquiry. I hope it's soon," Corbyn told The New Arab.

WW1 to Houthis: British jets for Saudi Arabia build on long military bond
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:22:35 UTC
19:22:35 KST

WW1 to Houthis: British jets for Saudi Arabia build on long military bond
The UK’s deployment of jets to defend Saudi Arabia is the latest chapter in a military relationship older than the kingdom itself.
The United Kingdom has announced it will deploy Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets to help defend Saudi Arabia from missile and drone attacks by Yemen’s Houthis, the armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God).
The jets will play a “defensive role”, the British Ministry of Defence (MoD) said in a statement on Tuesday, adding that they will not carry out attacks against the Iranian-backed armed group.
The move comes amid heavy fighting between the Houthis and Yemen’s internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.
In recent weeks, the Houthis have carried out missile and drone attacks against the kingdom, including oil facilities and Riyadh’s main airport, while the Saudi-led coalition supporting the Yemeni government has launched air attacks on Houthi positions.
The UK’s decision to send jets to assist Saudi Arabia marks just the latest chapter in a partnership that stretches back more than a century, to a treaty signed during the First World War, years before the Saudi kingdom was founded.
So what is the UK sending, and how did the two countries become so closely bound?
Here’s what you need to know:
What is the UK sending?
Fighter jets, an A400M transport aircraft and advisers.
The ministry said it was also extending air-to-air refuelling, which it previously agreed to provide for Saudi air operations, including those to degrade Houthi military targets in Yemen.
How far back does the UK-Saudi relationship go?
To the First World War.
In December 1915, Sir Percy Cox, a senior British official in the Gulf, concluded the Treaty of Darin with King Abdulaziz Ibn Saud, then ruler of Nejd in central Arabia, according to India Office records held by the UK’s National Archives.
In return, he allied with Britain against the Ottoman Empire, and Britain backed him with cash and weapons.
In May 1927, Britain signed a new treaty with him at Jeddah, according to an India Office memorandum.
King Abdulaziz founded the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932.
When did UK-Saudi arms deals begin?
In the 1960s.
In May 1966, Saudi Arabia signed contracts to buy 40 Lightning fighter jets and 25 jet trainers from the British Aircraft Corporation, along with a radar system, according to a US Department of State memo from the time.
Even then, Yemen was part of the picture.
In 1962, the Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen was overthrown in a military coup and the Yemen Arab Republic was established. Egypt sent troops to back the republican government, while Saudi Arabia and Jordan armed and funded royalist forces trying to restore the Imam. By 1966, the civil war had reached a stalemate.
Meanwhile, Britain was facing rebellion from Soviet- and Egypt-backed nationalist groups over its control of Aden and southern Yemen. Britain ultimately withdrew in 1967.
In 1966, Saudi Arabia’s defence minister, Prince Sultan, asked the UK to supply an RAF fighter squadron to fly under Saudi colours if fighting resumed in Yemen, according to declassified US State Department records.
Britain instead offered fighter jets flown by British pilots, and said it was ready to send an RAF squadron of Lightning interceptors for a short period if required.
In the end, Saudi Arabia accepted the jets and civilian pilots, and the RAF squadron was not needed, the records show.
BAE Systems, then the British Aircraft Corporation, says its ties with Saudi Arabia date back to 1966, and in 1973, the two governments signed a memorandum of understanding naming the company as prime contractor.
1980s and the Al-Yamamah deal
In 1985, the two governments signed an oil-for-arms agreement, known as Al-Yamamah, for Tornado and Hawk jets.
The Reuters news agency has described the Al-Yamamah deals as the largest export contracts in British history.
Saudi Arabia set aside up to 600,000 barrels of oil a day to pay for Tornado jets and other equipment.
The UK’s Serious Fraud Office investigated corruption allegations linked to the deal from 2004, but dropped the inquiry in December 2006, according to a House of Lords judgement.
The attorney general, Lord Goldsmith, cited the need to safeguard national security.
Has Britain fought from Saudi soil before?
Yes.
When Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990, King Fahd of Saudi Arabia asked friendly governments for help.
On August 11, 12 RAF Tornado fighters flew from Akrotiri in Cyprus to Dhahran in Saudi Arabia, according to the RAF Museum.
Further RAF Tornado detachments were set up at Tabuk in Saudi Arabia in October 1990, and at Dhahran in January 1991, the museum’s records show.
During the war, then-Defence Secretary Tom King told Parliament that Saudi Arabia had provided the UK with host-nation support.
He also reported that a Tornado based in the kingdom had gone missing, the fourth lost in enemy action.
British aircraft then patrolled a no-fly zone over southern Iraq, alongside United States and French jets, flying from Saudi bases until 2003, according to the US Air Force.
Where do the Typhoons come in?
In September 2007, Saudi Arabia agreed to buy 72 Typhoons from Britain, the UK MoD said at the time. The jets were to replace Tornadoes and other aircraft in the Saudi air force.
The deal was worth 4.43 billion pounds (then about $8.9bn).
BAE Systems, which builds the jets, called it the Salam Project.
Further RAF Tornado detachments were set up at Tabuk in Saudi Arabia in October 1990 and at Dhahran in January 1991.
In March 2018, during Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s visit to London, the UK signed a memorandum of intent with Saudi Arabia to finalise the purchase of 48 more Typhoons, BAE Systems said in a statement to the London Stock Exchange.
But the deal stalled.
Germany, which helps build the Typhoon and has a veto over its exports, halted arms sales to Saudi Arabia after the killing of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi, a columnist for The Washington Post who wrote critically of the crown prince and his policies, in 2018.
Berlin dropped its objection in January 2024, with then-Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock saying the Middle East had become a completely different place since October 7, 2023, when southern Israel was attacked by Hamas and Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza.
BAE said that year it was supporting the UK government in discussions with Saudi Arabia.
What about Yemen?
In June 2019, five years after the Houthis seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, triggering a brutal civil war, the UK’s Court of Appeal ruled that the government had acted unlawfully by licensing arms sales to Saudi Arabia for possible use in Yemen without assessing whether past incidents had breached international humanitarian law.
New licences were halted. In July 2020, then-Trade Secretary Liz Truss told Parliament they would resume, saying there was not a clear risk the arms would be used in a serious violation of the law.
The UK has also struck the Houthis directly. RAF Typhoons joined US attacks on Yemen in 2024 following Houthi attacks on Israel-linked Red Sea shipping in response to the bombardment of Gaza, according to the MoD.
Then, in September this year, Britain sent a Voyager tanker to assist Saudi Arabia with air-to-air refuelling of fighter jets. The planes it refuels are British-built Typhoons flown by the Saudi air force.

Spotify removes 50 million AI spam tracks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:22:33 UTC
19:22:33 KST

Spotify removes 50 million AI spam tracks
The company announced the figures on October 20, marking one year since it outlined plans to tackle spam, impersonation and deception linked to AI.
The removals are separate from more than 75 million spam tracks that Spotify has taken off its platform entirely for serious or repeated violations of its rules.
Over the past 6 months, Spotify has updated its recommendation system to reduce the visibility of spam and low-quality content and promote music by human artists. The company said it had seen a marked decline in listener complaints about such tracks appearing in recommendations.
To identify unwanted content, Spotify combines listener feedback, engagement data, upload patterns, metadata and information from third-party AI detection tools. It also monitors tactics such as mass uploads, duplicate tracks, misleading search optimization and artificially short songs.
New tools
Spotify has also introduced several measures to improve transparency and give artists greater control over their music.
Since April, artists have been able to submit AI Credits that disclose which parts of a song, including instruments and creative roles, involved AI. The company said artists now submit tens of thousands of these credits daily.
More than 300,000 artists have received Spotify's verification badge. They account for more than 99% of the artists listeners search for on the platform, and more than 70% are independent musicians.
The platform has also labeled thousands of AI Personas, whose identities are generated by AI. By default, these profiles are excluded from editorial and algorithmic recommendations unless listeners follow them, for example.
Another tool, Artist Profile Protection, allows participating artists to review releases that list them as performers before those tracks appear on their profiles. Spotify plans to make the tool available to all artists by the end of 2026.
Spotify also pointed to its royalty eligibility rules, which require tracks to reach at least 1,000 streams within a specified period to qualify for recorded music royalties. Tracks showing strong indicators of AI generation are 10 times more likely than other tracks to fall below this threshold, according to the company.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that the Spotify app went down for US users.

Kazakhstan records lowest infant mortality rates in Central Asia
Unknown

Kazakhstan records lowest infant mortality rates in Central Asia
Kazakhstan reported the lowest infant mortality rates among Central Asian nations, Qazinform News Agency reports citing the Healthcare Ministry.
According to the ministry, infant mortality in Kazakhstan is 3 cases per 1,000 live births.
To note, Kazakhstan fulfilled ahead of time the UN SDGs to reduce infant mortality.
16 new children’s hospitals and perinatal centers will be built countrywide to further raise the availability of medical care.
Development of perinatal care, introduction of advanced technologies and improvement of medical support for maternal and child health led to a reduction in infant mortality.
Today, the survival rate of infants with extremely low birth weight reaches 57%. Further work will be aimed at raising this rate, developing specialized assistance and strengthening the material and technical base of healthcare facilities.
Utmost attention is paid to early detection of congenital diseases and pregnancy care, the ministry said in a statement.
Detection of congenital diseases rose by 12%, and infant mortality due to congenital anomalies declined by 15% thanks to the Analar saulygy (Maternal healthcare) program.
The authorities noted that further development of maternal and child healthcare protection services will be aimed at raising the quality of medical assistance, early detection of risks and ensuring nationwide availability of modern diagnostics and treatments.
Last year, thanks to the WHO and UNICEF recommendations, the country’s maternal mortality ratio decreased by 12% to 10.1 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2024, while infant mortality declined by 11% to 6.88 per 1,000 live births.

Putin welcomes Witkoff with fresh Ukraine peace talks in offing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:22:00 UTC
19:22:00 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin hosted U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff Wednesday to discuss new proposals for ending the war in Ukraine, amid Washington's latest push to stop Europe's bloodiest conflict since World War II.
The talks in St. Petersburg, Witkoff's ninth meeting with Putin, included a goodwill gesture from Russia: the release of a retired U.S. schoolteacher held in Russia.
The encounter prompted concerns in Kyiv and among its allies that the United States is backing away from Ukraine, at times holding back real-time intelligence on Russian attacks and hobbling Ukraine's military communications.
The latest talks came more than two years after President Donald Trump promised in his election campaign to end the Ukraine war within 24 hours.
Witkoff flew into St. Petersburg Wednesday morning, a day after conducting what a U.S. official called "constructive" talks in Oslo with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the leaders of Finland and Norway, and European and NATO representatives. President Donald Trump said it was time for Ukraine to end the war or face "a very bad thing."
U.S.-Ukraine ties have deteriorated sharply since Trump announced a diesel export deal with Russia earlier this month, which he said would help lower prices in the United States.
Since the diesel deal, Ukraine has complained of disruption to some intelligence sharing and to its use of the Starlink military satellite system, though Zelenskyy said Tuesday's Oslo meeting had reached an agreement to resolve those issues.
Citing U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that billionaire Elon Musk ordered last week the slowdown of a military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite service that Ukraine relies on to track Russian ballistic missile strikes.
Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
Musk has said any such decision is made by the U.S. military or the president. Trump has said he was not responsible. U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth signaled Tuesday that the problem lay in the terms of service Kyiv needed to comply with.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that Witkoff's meeting with Zelenskyy was positive and that Witkoff would share the results with Russia. He also reiterated that Washington had not pulled back Kyiv's ability to access Starlink.
"He will now, armed with those ideas, be able to go to St. Petersburg and share them with the Russian side, and let's see if we can make some progress," he said.
Despite the apparently cordial nature of Tuesday's meeting in Oslo, Trump, in comments Tuesday at the White House, remained frustrated with Zelenskyy, whom he has repeatedly rebuked and suggested should be replaced.
"He's going to have to want to make a deal, because I don't think his people are going to stand for it any longer," Trump told reporters on the eve of the talks in Russia.
Putin, who has shown few signs of compromising on his central war aims – which include full Russian control of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine and no NATO membership for Kyiv – received Witkoff in the Constantine Palace, an imperial edifice in his home city.
Kirill Dmitriev, Putin's special investment envoy and his key liaison for potential economic and financial deals with the U.S., also attended the meeting with Witkoff, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said.
A U.S. official said Ukraine brought new ideas and proposals to the Oslo talks, which made "meaningful progress" toward a coordinated approach to engaging with Russia.
The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the talks covered "key elements of a comprehensive peace framework," including security guarantees for Ukraine, a postwar economic plan and a broader European security architecture.
Witkoff aimed to "create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations," the official said. Zelenskyy said he hoped to discuss key issues on how to end the war during a trilateral meeting with Putin and Trump.
The Kremlin has repeatedly said that any Putin-Zelenskyy meeting would need to be painstakingly prepared by aides to make it worthwhile and that much legwork would be required for an overall agreement.
Trump said Tuesday he raised the idea with Putin of freeing Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired U.S. schoolteacher being held in Russia on mercenary charges he denies.
Putin told Witkoff that Hubbard was at the airport waiting to fly back to the U.S. with him. Witkoff thanked Putin for the goodwill gesture.
Hubbard was first detained in April 2022 and later sentenced to six years and 10 months on charges whose veracity his family and U.S.-based lawyer question.

Cabinet split widens as minister refuses to back Shabana Mahmood’s immigration plans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:21:18 UTC
19:21:18 KST

Shabana Mahmood has been urged to “read the room” on Labour opposition to her immigration policy, as No 10 declined to rule out watering down her plans to make foreign workers wait 15 years to get permanent residency.
Mahmood, the home secretary, is consulting on plans to increase the period before foreign workers can claim indefinite leave to remain from five to 15 years, backdated to apply to anyone arriving from 2021 onwards.
She has previously hinted that her plan to make it harder to claim permanent residence could be watered down by exempting care workers from the new rule.
However, there were reports on Tuesday that she was holding firm against making changes. A senior ally told the Times that she had the prime minister’s support, saying: “Andy has been on Shabana’s side throughout this row over ILR. He is holding the line.”
There is already a cabinet split over the policy, which deepened on Wednesday when Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, repeatedly refused to back the specific plans to make foreign workers wait 15 years to claim permanent residency in the UK.
This week it was reported that Fahnbulleh appeared to criticise the plans on her Peckham constituency website in a post about a community discussion that was later removed. She was quoted as saying: “If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.”
This year the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, publicly criticised the plans, and dozens of Labour MPs oppose the changes.
One of the leading opponents, Mike Tapp, a former immigration minister who clashed with Mahmood over the policy, said the home secretary should “read the room” in relation to the strength of feeling about the changes.
“It’s important we do the right thing. If people have come to the country and genuinely worked in the sector, they shouldn’t be punished and should have the right to apply for settlement after five years as they expected,” he said.
MPs campaigning for changes to Mahmood’s policies believe they have a chance of convincing Andy Burnham to exempt care workers, given reforming adult social care is an issue close to his heart. However, the Home Office has said that would lead to an exodus of foreign workers from the sector when they are no longer bound by the terms of their visa.
No 10 stressed on Wednesday that Mahmood was “carefully considering” more than 200,000 responses to a consultation before finalising the reforms.
Asked whether tweaks to the home secretary’s revamp – including no longer applying the policy retrospectively – could be ruled out, Burnham’s press secretary said: “We set out proposals for consultation. We’ve consulted on what the transition arrangement should look like for people already in the UK who have not received settled status.
“The home secretary is leading a thorough piece of work to ensure we get this right and have the right arrangements in place.”
In her interview with Sky News on Wednesday, Fahbulleh repeatedly avoided the question on whether she would back an increase in the waiting period for permanent residency to 15 years. She said: “We have got to reform our immigration system, and my view is that we need a system that is based on the principle of compassion, contribution. And so there is a package of reforms. The home secretary has been consulting on this. She’s looking at the range of responses, and she will come out with the measures that we take forward.
“No one can look at our immigration system – and I say this as someone that came to this country as a refugee – and not believe that it’s broken and not believe that we need to fundamentally reform it.
“But our principles has to be a system where we’ve got control, but ultimately a system that when people do come to this country, they are able to integrate, they are able to contribute, and that we both respect but also value that contribution.”
She said she supported “reforms that say that people have to contribute and make a contribution to this country in order to get citizenship”, adding: “I 100% back Shabana Mahmood and everything she is trying to do.”
But she avoided multiple questions on the prospect of a 15-year wait. When it was put to her that she did not back that specific proposal, Fahnbulleh said: “Don’t … put words in my mouth.”
A government source said that “the minister clearly supported the policy and process” in her interviews, “but while subject to review of the consultation, the final policy is not set – so ministers cannot offer opinions on specific parts of it”.
A Home Office spokesperson said: “This government has announced reforms that mean settlement must be earned and not automatic. We are currently considering responses to our consultation on elements of these reforms.”

Nearly half of Dutch lawmakers used AI-generated text in parliamentary speeches: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:21:05 UTC
19:21:05 KST

Melike Pala
21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
Nearly half of the members of the Dutch House of Representatives used artificial intelligence (AI) tools to prepare speeches delivered in parliament last year, according to an investigation by weekly De Groene Amsterdammer and investigative journalism platform Investico.
The investigation found that 68 of the 150 lawmakers delivered speeches containing text generated with AI tools, including ChatGPT and Claude.
Journalists analyzed speeches by all 150 MPs using Pangram, an AI-detection tool designed to identify texts generated by artificial intelligence.
Texts estimated to contain less than 50% AI-generated content were excluded from the findings, suggesting that the actual number of MPs using such tools could be higher.
The analysis focused on opening statements delivered by lawmakers during parliamentary debates, excluding interventions and motions.
The investigation also found that some lawmakers used AI-generated material in their maiden speeches, traditionally considered personal contributions marking an MP's first address to parliament.
All lawmakers identified in the investigation acknowledged using AI, but said they mainly relied on it to improve sentence structure, shorten texts, or refine arguments.
Previous reports revealed that Prime Minister Rob Jetten regularly uses AI to draft social media posts, while a separate investigation by public broadcaster NOS found that approximately a quarter of parliamentary written questions were prepared with AI assistance.

Paramilitary hitman linked to British right-wing group Turning Point UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:20:41 UTC
19:20:41 KST

Paramilitary hitman linked to British right-wing group Turning Point UK
Al Jazeera exposes UK far right's links to criminal underworld.
A violent paramilitary linked to a proscribed terror group has close ties to a right-wing student group in the United Kingdom, an Al Jazeera investigation has revealed.
Allan Nesbitt, a convicted criminal who is a member of the Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF), is linked to Turning Point UK (TPUK).
Our investigation, Contract Killers and the Far Right, began in 2021, when an undercover reporter from Al Jazeera joined TPUK, an independent offshoot of the right-wing US activist group Turning Point USA. TPUK has close ties to several senior British Conservative Party members, as well as to leaders of Reform UK.
TPUK’s CEO Jack Ross stood as a Conservative Party candidate in 2023. Ross introduced Al Jazeera’s undercover reporter to Nesbitt, who is from Glasgow, Scotland.
Ross made clear that he and Nesbitt had a long history together. Ross was filmed by our undercover reporter agreeing to pay Nesbitt thousands of pounds to stage a fake political rally designed to show support for the lifting of UK sanctions against Zimbabwe.
Ross also told Al Jazeera’s undercover operative that for “a certain amount”, Nesbitt and his contacts could arrange physical attacks, saying they could “kick the f*** out of someone. They can start cutting people’s faces up. That’s another amount. They can stab someone,” Ross said. “They can shoot someone. They could kill someone.”
Murder for hire, caught on tape
To test Ross’s claims about Nesbitt, Al Jazeera’s undercover operative devised a story about a business dispute with a fictional rival they wanted “dealt with”.
In a private meeting in a London hotel, Nesbitt told our reporters he could “arrange whatever you need done”, but “at a price”. This included killing the fictional person with the help of his UVF connections.
“He can have a bad accident,” Nesbitt said, confirming to Al Jazeera that the person would be “finished”.
“These c***s are terrorists. They’re f***ing trained killers,” Nesbitt added.
Nesbitt also claimed to have personally killed before.
“Things have happened in the past where it was too risky to do that [gestures firing a gun], and I’ve just pulled out a knife and stabbed the c*** to death,” he said.
In a later video call, Nesbitt showed off a shotgun, a pistol, and live ammunition to prove he had the means to follow through.
Weapons smuggling
The money paid for the murder would be used to arm the UVF in Northern Ireland, Nesbitt said.
“All the money gets raised in Scotland and the things get bought in Scotland and we smuggle them into Ireland.”
According to Nesbitt, he has been involved in this weapons smuggling for many years.
“It’s us that smuggled the stuff into Ireland for them to fight the war in there,” he said, referring to The Troubles.
During that period, which began in the late 1960s, Catholic and Protestant groups in Northern Ireland fought over whether Protestant-majority Northern Ireland should remain part of the UK or join the Catholic-majority Republic of Ireland.
Those in favour of Northern Ireland remaining a part of the UK are widely known as unionists or loyalists. Those seeking to break from the UK usually identify themselves as republicans or Irish nationalists.
The UVF belonged to the Protestant loyalist side and was responsible for some of the most infamous killings and murders during The Troubles, according to Patricia Devlin, a journalist who has been investigating the group for years.
“Between 1966 and 1999, the UVF killed over 500 people,” she told Al Jazeera.
“They went on to commit atrocities such as the 1971 McGurk’s bar bomb massacre, which killed 15 people, and the 1974 Dublin and Monaghan bombings, which killed 33 people”, she added.
But after the 1998 Good Friday Agreement that at least officially ended the Troubles, the UVF, like many other groups, transformed into a more traditional criminal gang.
“The movement has turned into drug gangs, while still using the name of the UVF,” Devlin said.
To Roy McComb, former deputy director of the UK’s National Crime Agency, Nesbitt’s claims are no surprise.
“The history of loyalism between Northern Ireland [and] Scotland is a very strong and very longstanding one.
“Operationally, there’s certainly evidence previously of firearms being trafficked, of intelligence being shared, of activists being moved between the two countries [Scotland and Northern Ireland].
“Firearms … are simply tools that can be sold and that could be sold onto the far right.”
Far-right groups
Besides links to the UVF, Al Jazeera’s investigation also shows links between Turning Point UK and other far-right agitators in the UK. These include groups that have been at the forefront of protests against migrants and LGBTQ+ rights.
“Turning Point UK are fanboys of these kinds of people. These people are obviously a lot more physically tough than Turning Point UK. Turning Point UK know that they put these little, no far right allowed at the bottom just to protect themselves,” Ciaran O’Connor, senior analyst at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue, told Al Jazeera.
“They use these events as wedge issues upon which to try and mobilise their support and try and attack the message or the meaning of the other side, and demonise the housing of asylum seekers in society,” he added.
A former member of the UVF told Al Jazeera that the “far right in the UK is a toothless tiger”, but links between the far right and groups like the UVF could change that.
“It changes whenever you make a connection to individuals who are behind a terrorist campaign for probably 40 years, and are still armed, and still have the ability to shoot and bomb,” the former UVF member said.
“Then you’re in trouble.”
Al Jazeera notified Scottish police about Allan Nesbitt and his weapons in the interest of public safety.
Jack Ross denied our findings “completely”, telling us that everything he said to our undercover reporter was not meant seriously.
The other parties featured did not respond to our inquiries.

Turkish forces prepare to deploy to Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:20:19 UTC
19:20:19 KST

- Türkiye is preparing to deploy military personnel to Saudi Arabia under its joint defense pact with the kingdom and Pakistan, Reuters reported.
- The Turkish parliament must first ratify the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement and then approve a separate deployment mandate.
Türkiye is preparing to deploy military personnel to Saudi Arabia under the new joint defense pact it signed with the kingdom and Pakistan, and the government will send a deployment mandate to the Turkish parliament once lawmakers ratify the agreement, Reuters reported.
Ankara has already submitted the pact, known as the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, to parliament, where Speaker Numan Kurtulmuş is expected to refer it to the foreign affairs commission for debate as soon as this week.
The two-step process follows the Turkish constitution, which requires separate parliamentary approval for any deployment of troops abroad even after an international treaty has been ratified. The Turkish Defense Ministry made the same point at its weekly briefing on Oct. 15, saying that any deployment of forces or military capabilities to Saudi Arabia must go through parliament and that the size of Türkiye’s contribution would depend on Saudi requests, conditions on the ground and agreement between Ankara and Riyadh.
Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed the pact in Mecca on Aug. 7, with President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif agreeing that an armed attack on one member will be treated as an attack on all three. The agreement commits the members to provide immediate assistance to any partner facing aggression, in language that mirrors NATO’s Article 5, while leaving each country to decide the scope of its support, and it also covers intelligence sharing, logistics and defense industry cooperation.
The three governments agreed at an emergency meeting in Riyadh earlier this month to ensure the rapid deployment of forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia, which has come under a widening campaign of Houthi missile and drone attacks from Yemen. The deadliest strike, on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Oct. 10, killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300, and the Houthis have also targeted oil facilities and claimed to have shot down a Saudi F-15 in September, a claim Riyadh has not confirmed.
Türkiye already has technical teams, air defense systems and electronic warfare equipment in Saudi Arabia, deployed last year under a 2010 military training agreement to help protect energy infrastructure. Turkish officials told Middle East Eye earlier this month that Ankara plans to add more personnel, technicians and emergency response teams with accompanying combat forces, as well as pilots, aircraft and a limited number of special forces once parliament grants approval, though officials stressed that Türkiye does not plan to send large numbers of soldiers or to intervene directly in Yemen.
Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said the pact is not an offensive agreement and that Türkiye will not send troops to attack another country’s territory, while another Turkish official told Reuters that Ankara’s contribution so far has been limited to military equipment, intelligence sharing and weapons systems. Türkiye has also agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition for shipping security in the Red Sea.
Turkish forces would join a growing number of foreign militaries helping defend the kingdom, after Pakistan sent fighter jets and support aircraft to King Abdulaziz Air Base in April and Britain announced on Oct. 20 that Royal Air Force Typhoons will fly defensive patrols over Saudi Arabia. Neither the size of the Turkish deployment nor its timing will be set until parliament votes on both the treaty and the separate troop mandate.

‘Jackdaw means we pay our mortgages’: relief in Aberdeen over gasfield approval
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:19:18 UTC
19:19:18 KST

As recently as 2012, Aberdeen boasted the highest concentration of millionaires in the UK. An ATM reportedly had the highest withdrawal rate in Europe in the 90s, as oil and gas wealth flowed through the city. House prices soared in the scramble for space as fossil fuel firms transformed the city’s grand granite houses into company offices. But that was then.
Today, “for sale” and “to let” signs punctuate the city’s main thoroughfares. Disposable income in Aberdeen has fallen by nearly 20% between 2013 and 2023 – more than any other large UK city – after a 2014 oil price shock sparked a brutal reversal in Aberdeen’s fortunes.
At the beginning of this year, demolition began on the former offices of Marathon Oil, once a base for hundreds of workers. Between 2010 and 2021, the number of people aged 20-29 fell by 16%. BP appears set to leave the city after announcing plans to divest from its North Sea business. On darker days, the spectre of former coalmining towns looms large in the minds of some residents.
“Years ago, a fund should have been set up that saved some of the oil money for Aberdeen. But that’s long gone,” said Scott, an assistant at a men’s clothing shop. “It’s a city centre like any other now. People blame the local council and the local government. I don’t know. It’s very different to how it was.”
“Twenty years ago this street was full. Now it is so quiet,” said one woman at a bus stop on Union Street.
For many Aberdonians, the government’s decision to approve the Jackdaw gasfield, located 150 miles offshore, came as a relief.
Critics point to the climate impact and the modest number of jobs that the new gasfield would likely support. Tessa Khan, the executive director of the anti-oil campaign group Uplift, said: “Jackdaw will provide around just 2% of our gas demand for roughly 10 years. It has been oversold and won’t stop the overall decline in North Sea jobs as it will be largely unmanned and operated remotely.”
The UN Environment Programme has said global carbon emission targets need to be cut by nearly a fifth in the next four years, and by close to half within a decade, to avoid overshooting climate targets by a disastrous margin.
But for oil and gas workers in the city, this is about keeping as many North Sea jobs for as long as possible, which have so far not been replaced by the renewables sector and tend to pay less.
At the heliport, offshore workers returning to dry land after a flight across stormy North Sea waters were in good spirits about the prospect of a new field.
“Jackdaw means we pay our mortgages. Without oil and gas, what am I supposed to do?” said one woman, who works offshore as a cleaner on a rig.
Another offshore worker said: “Short-term, the green industry isn’t going to replace this. It’s a slow process. You can’t expect it to happen overnight.”
Few think that the new gasfield will restore the city’s boomtown years. Unlike other oil cities such as Houston, Abu Dhabi and Stavanger, Aberdeen has not been able to recover from the 2014 price shock and there is growing acceptance that the decline is permanent. Many offshore oil and gas workers acknowledge that they are likely to be the last generation of their kind – and increasingly work away for weeks at a time on rigs in Africa and Asia.
More than 90% of the UK part of the North Sea basin has been exploited, compared with just over 50% in Norway, which has not outlawed new exploration licences. Jackdaw is projected to supply only 6% of the UK’s gas output at its peak. In the approval, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, pointed to national security reasons behind her decision to back the project.
“This decision will support the country’s energy security with homegrown gas this winter and help minimise the UK’s use of imported higher emission fuels as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear.
“The decision is compatible with our legally binding climate commitments, and we remain resolute in ending new licences for oil and gas and achieving net zero by 2050,” she said.
The rapidly growing renewables industry in the city has proved to be a boon for some firms: the shipping operator North Star once made all of its money from the oil and gas sector, but now nearly 80% of its operating profit comes from offshore wind. Great British Energy is headquartered in the city. Yet, the growth in the offshore wind industry has so far failed to offset the decline in oil and gas jobs in Aberdeen, and it is unclear it ever will. About 90% of offshore jobs in the northeast of Scotland remain in the oil and gas sector, supporting around 38,000 jobs compare to 4,200 in the renewables sector.
From the doldrums of the 2014 crash, Aberdeen has seen recent signs of recovery. Major regeneration works are taking place in the city centre. On a drive through the leafy west of the city, grand houses are not longer left on the market for months, said Joni Esson, a property lawyer with Simpson & Marwick.
“We’re seeing property sell for reasonable prices and a little bit of confidence coming back,” she said. “Loads of people who bought pre-2014 got in negative equity and then just couldn’t shift their homes.”
Our Union Street, a community group formed to reinvigorate the city’s main thoroughfare, has been filling empty shops after the vacancy rate reached 20%. For Bob Keiller, a former oil and gas CEO who oversees the effort, Jackdaw’s approval was a sign that the government was taking a more pragmatic approach to the fossil fuel sector – which would be a boost to the city.
“It’s symbolic. For a long time, it’s been ‘no, nothing, never, never again’. Whereas now there’s recognition that maybe it makes sense to produce your own fuel sources. It has to make economic and environmental sense, of course,” he said. “Before, it was, ‘No, not listening! Just stop oil.’ What does that mean? Everything we’ve got here just now relies on oil and gas at the moment.”

Less than a week before Israel's election, one in nine registered voters lives abroad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
10:19:08 UTC
19:19:08 KST

Approximately 7.3 million Israelis are registered to vote in next Tuesday's election for the 26th Knesset, but about 810,000 of them, roughly one in nine, live outside the country, according to figures released Tuesday by Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics (CBS). 
The data highlight a significant gap between the number of citizens on the electoral register and those actually residing in Israel. The bureau noted that some Israelis registered abroad may have died without their deaths being reported to the Population and Immigration Authority. Under Israel's election rules, most citizens living overseas cannot vote from abroad and must return to Israel to cast a ballot, with limited exceptions for eligible state representatives and their families. 
Since the previous Knesset election in November 2022, the number of eligible voters living in Israel has risen by approximately 333,000, an increase of 5.4%. Among registered voters residing in the country, 15.1% are between the ages of 18 and 24, while 27.6% are aged 25 to 39. The largest group, accounting for 31%, comprises voters aged 40 to 59, and another 26.3% are 60 or older.
The figures also reveal significant differences between Israel's population groups. Just over 5 million eligible voters living in Israel, or 77%, are Jewish, including approximately 684,000 ultra-Orthodox Jews. Arab citizens, including Muslims, Arab Christians and Druze, account for about 1.16 million eligible voters, or 18%. Another 346,000, representing 5%, are classified as members of other population groups, primarily non-Arab Christians and people without a registered religious affiliation, many of them immigrants and their families who are not registered as Jewish.
The CBS stressed that differences in age distribution help explain why some communities account for a smaller share of eligible voters than of the general population. Arab Israelis make up approximately 22% of the population but only 18% of the electorate, reflecting the community's relatively young population and the presence of residents without Israeli citizenship, particularly in East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights. Similarly, ultra-Orthodox Jews account for 13.9% of Israel's population but only 10.5% of registered voters, largely because of the community's high proportion of children.
The geographical differences are equally pronounced. The northern border town of Metula has the highest share of residents eligible to vote, at 83.8%, while Mas'ade, a Druze community in the northern Golan Heights, has the lowest, at just 30.1%. In most Israeli cities with more than 100,000 residents, the proportion of eligible voters ranges between 70% and 80%. Three cities fall significantly below that range: Jerusalem, where just 39.2% of residents are eligible to vote, Beit Shemesh at 47.1%, and Bnei Brak at 50.4%. Their relatively young populations contribute to the figures, while Jerusalem's rate is also affected by the substantial number of noncitizen residents.
By comparison, 79.5% of Bat Yam residents are eligible to vote, followed by Tel Aviv-Jaffa at 77.4%, Ramat Gan at 77.2%, Rishon LeZion at 76.7%, Haifa at 76.3%, Holon at 75.6% and Beersheba at 73.9%.
Israel's electorate has expanded dramatically since the country's first parliamentary election in 1949, when 506,567 citizens were registered to vote, all of them living in Israel. That figure nearly doubled by the second Knesset election. By the election held after the 1973 Yom Kippur War, the number of eligible voters had exceeded 2 million, rising to approximately 3.4 million in 1992 and surpassing 5 million by 2006.

Unknown

- Category
- World
US Navy P-8A Poseidon Returns to Black Sea Skies as Attacks on Commercial Ships Raise Alarm
A US Navy Boeing P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft conducted a surveillance mission over the western Black Sea near Bulgaria after arriving at Varna from Naval Air Station Sigonella, marking its first tracked appearance in the region in several months.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to ItaMilRadar on October 19, flight-tracking data showed the P-8A making several turns over the maritime area, with portions of its mission conducted at altitudes below 9,000 feet.
The aircraft’s extended flight at lower altitudes indicates that maritime patrol was likely a key objective of the operation, rather than intelligence collection alone. However, publicly available flight-tracking data does not provide enough information to determine the mission’s exact purpose.
According to ItaMilRadar, the mission comes amid heightened security concerns in the western Black Sea following a series of reported attacks against commercial shipping near Bulgaria and Romania.
In early October, two commercial ships were targeted by aerial and maritime drones within Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, with one vessel sinking following the attack. Further incidents were later reported near the Bulgarian and Romanian coastlines, including strikes against ships in Romanian territorial waters.
The incidents have also intensified concerns over Russia’s hybrid warfare activities in the Black Sea, as attacks on civilian vessels increasingly threaten maritime security and commercial shipping routes near NATO member states.
On October 5, a civilian cargo vessel was struck by two Russian drones near Romania’s coastline, killing two people, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, as cited by Reuters.
Romania’s Interior Ministry later confirmed that 11 crew members had been rescued after the vessel caught fire approximately 30 nautical miles south of Sfântu Gheorghe.
According to ItaMilRadar, while exclusive economic zones fall under a different legal framework than territorial waters, attacks on commercial vessels in these areas can still create serious maritime security risks.
However, the publication emphasized that there is no direct evidence connecting the US Navy P-8A’s latest mission to the recent attacks on commercial vessels.
The deteriorating security situation has also prompted Bulgaria to seek additional military assistance from NATO to strengthen its defenses and increase the alliance’s presence in the region.
On October 16, Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said Sofia had requested additional aircraft, air defense systems, counter-drone capabilities, and aerial patrols in response to the increasing frequency of maritime attacks.
Speaking to reporters, Stoyanov expressed concern over the worsening security environment in the Black Sea, pointing to recent strikes in Romanian territorial waters as further evidence of the threats facing countries in the region.
He added that deploying additional allied military resources would not only strengthen regional defenses but also demonstrate a more substantial NATO presence in the Black Sea.

Ukrainian Partisans Cut Moscow Military Comms to Help Drones Slip Through Russian Air Defenses
Agents of the ATESH partisan movement are sabotaging Russian military communications around IXcellerate, one of Moscow’s largest commercial data centers, in an effort to disrupt air-defense coordination and help Ukrainian drones reach their targets, the group said on October 21.
“We are disabling enemy channels, disrupting command and control, and helping UAVs reach their targets,” ATESH said.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
IXcellerate is a major part of Moscow’s digital infrastructure, supporting banking applications, card payments, telecommunications operators, and business services.
ATESH claims that Russia’s Defense Ministry also uses infrastructure connected to the facility for military communications and air-defense command systems, effectively embedding military traffic within civilian server networks.
According to the movement, drone strikes depend not only on the aircraft themselves but also on disrupting the communications networks that connect Russian air-defense crews and command posts.
Cutting those links on the ground, ATESH says, can delay target information and reduce coordination between air-defense units.
Without stable communications, Russian air-defense crews can lose situational awareness, receive targeting information too late, and struggle to cover the routes used by incoming drones, the group said.
ATESH claims its agents are identifying military communications infrastructure concealed within civilian facilities and disrupting those networks from inside Russia.
The group said Moscow’s attempts to hide military traffic inside civilian server infrastructure have not prevented partisan cells from locating and targeting the communications links supporting Russian military operations.
Previously, ATESH claimed responsibility for sabotaging a critical electrical substation in Azov, Russia’s Rostov region, disrupting power to a defense manufacturing facility that produces guidance systems and other components for Russian missiles.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade, 54 agreements with US companies were signed in Samarkand on October 19. Just one day later, Russian and Uzbek forces launched the Hamkorlik-2026 military exercises at the Termez training ground in southern Uzbekistan, according to Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Defense.
The American agreements cover critical minerals, energy, transportation, financial services, digital technologies, and industrial development. Companies involved include GE Aerospace, Wabtec, BlackRock, Citigroup, and Franklin Templeton.
The $12 billion figure represents the announced value of the agreements rather than funds already invested.
The deals come as Washington seeks to expand its economic influence in Central Asia, a region where Russia and China have traditionally maintained strong political, economic, and security ties.
Russian troops from the 201st Military Base in neighboring Tajikistan traveled more than 300 kilometers through mountainous terrain to reach the training ground near the Afghan border.
The Russian military column included BTR-82A armored personnel carriers, Ural military trucks, and specialized vehicles based on KamAZ chassis.
The exercises focus on detecting and eliminating simulated armed groups operating in border areas. Russian and Uzbek forces are expected to deploy reconnaissance and attack drones, ground robotic systems, mountain assault units, and Mi-24 attack helicopters.
The military cooperation reflects an established relationship between Moscow and Tashkent. The two countries conducted similar exercises at the same training ground in July 2025 and have agreed on a defense cooperation plan covering 2026–2030.
Earlier in October, Russia conducted the Center-2026 military exercises involving more than 47,000 troops, during which its forces rehearsed an offensive into a neighboring Central Asian country and the establishment of a “security zone” on its territory. North Korea Sends 12,000 Workers to Russia to Build Shahed Drones
North Korea has reportedly sent 12,000 workers to Russia to help manufacture Shahed-type attack drones at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan, expanding Pyongyang’s involvement in Russia’s military production supporting its war against Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to a joint report by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) and the George W. Bush Institute on October 14, North Korean workers receive approximately $2.50 per hour, while the North Korean government reportedly takes between 70% and 90% of their earnings.
The report identifies three main groups involved in drone manufacturing at Alabuga: Russian students and young workers, foreign recruits from other countries, and North Korean nationals. Researchers raised concerns about coercive labor practices affecting all three groups, particularly the systematic withholding of wages from North Korean workers.
Russian students are recruited through Alabuga’s educational programs, which combine technical training with industrial work. Some reportedly work shifts lasting up to 12 hours, with their pay tied to strict production targets.
Workers have also reportedly faced threats of financial penalties for disclosing details about the facility’s operations, including to family members.
The Alabuga industrial complex is a major Russian production site for Geran-2 drones, based on the Iranian-designed Shahed-136, which Russia regularly uses in attacks against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
Satellite imagery published in September showed additional production buildings and warehouses under construction at the site, indicating continued expansion of its manufacturing infrastructure.
North Korea’s involvement in Russian drone production comes amid growing military cooperation between Moscow and Pyongyang. Beyond providing personnel, North Korea has reportedly sought to incorporate lessons from Russia’s use of drones in Ukraine into its own military development programs.
Analysts have also indicated that Pyongyang is working to expand domestic production of Shahed-type drones and smaller unmanned aircraft, potentially benefiting from Russian technical expertise.
Earlier, Bloomberg reported on September 17 that approximately 25,000 North Korean nationals were working at Russian drone manufacturing facilities, including Alabuga. Many reportedly entered Russia on student visas to circumvent international sanctions, while North Korean authorities confiscated most of their earnings.

Russia Faces $10.5 Billion Regional Budget Deficit as 65 Regions Prepare Spending Cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21

19:16:56 KST

- Category
- World
Russia Faces $10.5 Billion Regional Budget Deficit as 65 Regions Prepare Spending Cuts
Around 65 Russian regions are planning to reduce spending on investment and infrastructure projects between 2027 and 2029 as stagnant revenues, rising financial obligations, and war-related expenditures put increasing pressure on local budgets, according to Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SZRU) on October 20.
The agency reported that regional authorities are being forced to scale back planned construction, infrastructure modernization, and investment programs as available funds become insufficient to cover social payments, public institutions, and expenditures associated with Russia’s war against Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Among the regions preparing budget reductions is Tatarstan, which plans to cut spending by 13% in 2027, bringing its budget to approximately $6.6 billion.
The Leningrad region is expected to reduce expenditures by 2.9% to $3.5 billion, while Yakutia plans a 2.7% reduction to approximately $4 billion.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, the reductions will primarily affect investment initiatives, repairs, and modernization of municipal infrastructure, potentially leaving local development projects without sufficient funding.
The financial pressure is also reflected in Russia’s broader regional budget projections.
According to forecasts from Russia’s Finance Ministry cited by SZRU, regional budgets are expected to generate approximately $331.4 billion in revenue in 2027, against projected expenditures of $342 billion. This would leave Russia’s regions facing a combined budget deficit of approximately $10.5 billion.
At the same time, Ukrainian intelligence reported that Moscow continues to transfer additional responsibilities to regional authorities without providing corresponding financial resources. As a result, local administrations must finance these obligations from their existing budgets, redirecting funds originally allocated to other programs.
The federal government is also reportedly preparing changes to financial assistance for economically weaker regions, potentially further restricting their access to budgetary support.
Under the proposed arrangements, Dagestan, Tuva, Ingushetia, and Altai Krai would be guaranteed no more than 90% of the subsidies allocated under existing budget legislation in 2027, rather than receiving the full amount with indexation.
Additionally, SZRU noted that even partial debt relief on regional budget loans would come with restrictions requiring local authorities to spend the freed-up funds on priorities established by Moscow.
Russian regions are losing control over their financial resources as their budgets become increasingly dependent on decisions made by Moscow. The Kremlin continues to dictate how funds are distributed, leaving local authorities with fewer resources to address pressing regional issues.
The growing financial pressure on Russia’s regions comes amid broader strains on the country’s federal budget, which have also prompted the Central Bank to draw down its gold reserves.
According to The Moscow Times on October 20, Russia’s Central Bank has been selling gold from its reserves for ten consecutive months to help cover a widening federal budget deficit, projected to reach 7.3 trillion rubles ($81.1 billion) this year, twice the amount initially anticipated.
The latest reduction brought the country’s total gold reserves to 72.8 million ounces, their lowest level since late 2019.
