Life before Barents: Russian scientists reiterate Spitsbergen discovery discussion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:07:21 UTC
16:07:21 KST

MOSCOW, October 21. /TASS Correspondents Maria Kartuz, Konstantin Malykh/. TASS correspondents visited the archipelago and gathered opinions about its discoverers. Why the discussion about the Pomors' early sites on Spitsbergen has faded away and how it may return to the scientific sphere - read about it in this material by TASS.
The archipelago discovery's stories vary. One of them, the most well-known and document-proven, is that the first discoverer was Dutch navigator Willem Barents in 1596. It is believed that he gave the name to the archipelago - Spitsbergen (Sharp mountains). Another story is related to Soviet archaeologist Vadim Starkov, who claimed that Russian hunters and fishers had known the land under the name of Grumant at least half a century before Barents. He proved the claim by results of own dendro-chronology analysis of wooden buildings' remains.
Scandinavian scientists insist the Vikings discovered the islands back in the 12th century, but any evidence is hidden in the depths of centuries and waters. Their claim is based on a single source - the Icelandic Chronicles of 1194, where the archipelago (Svalbard, or Cold Shores) was mentioned for the first time. This is exactly the name Norway uses for the archipelago nowadays. However, no traces of the Vikings have been found there, thus this story may be put aside for now.
As for the first two versions, historians are sure it is quite unreasonable that from the discussion stage they have moved into the stage of categorical claims. While Western critics used to study Starkov's conclusions, argued, offered reasons, nowadays the discussion has been artificially stopped, and the Norwegian museum ultimately presents the period of Grumant's Pomors as the term between 1700 and 1850.
"Nor should we take a hard line claiming the Pomors definitely were there in the middle of the 16th century. On the other hand, it is impossible to turn one version into an ultimate claim. There exist Starkov's conclusions, as well as a number of indirect arguments in favor of the Pomors' early presence on Spitsbergen, and there is also criticism of these data. We need to remain at the level of scientific discussion: double-checking arguments, searching for documents, and discussing methods," leader of the Russian Geographical Society's expedition to Spitsbergen Pavel Filin said.
The last great discovery
The discovery of Severnaya Zemlya in 1913 is commonly considered to be the last great geographical discovery on the planet. But the North's historical map still remains being incomplete. It contains territories of well-known routes, settlements, and even names of participants in events, but their sequence is not clear, and Spitsbergen is not an exception.
We talked with Pavel Filin at the Barentsburg Museum. The scientists have arrived in the archipelago on an expedition of the Russian Geographical Society to map the Russian cultural heritage on Spitsbergen. Collected artifacts are very numerous here. For example, a fragment of the Pomors vessel's hull - thick planks are connected by flexible bundles of steamed roots. The planks keep holes through which the "thread" passed, as well as the darkened surface, and traces of repair. Other museum showcases present fishing devices, household items, fragments of crosses. A map on the wall shows old settlements' locations.
Vadim Starkov's Spitsbergen expedition worked on the archipelago since the 1970s. The researchers managed to identify many monuments associated with Russian fishers and hunters, and the archeologist dated some of them to the middle of the 16th century. As for technical reasons of those who criticize Starkov - they may be shared or waived, but as for the logics - the story seems quite clear.
The Pomors' culture on the White Sea formed in the 15th-16th centuries, or even earlier. It was based on fishing, hunting sea animals, shipping, and seasonal sea navigation. The fishermen and hunters, guided by the approach "the sea is our field", traveled following the resources and developed fresh marine areas similar to the ways agricultural communities do.
The Pomors were sailing further on towards Spitsbergen to hunt walruses, arctic foxes, and to fish. People traveled and worked in teams, and brought supplies with them - they transported dismantled houses, bricks, and sometimes firewood. They used fins as fuel, but it was impossible to rely on them alone in the treeless archipelago. "Wintering is a specific technology," the scientist said. "They were to know how not to die there. Of course, many did die. But the Pomors had the experience of survival gained in the White Sea, on the Kola Peninsula, and Novaya Zemlya."
In the 17th century, Spitsbergen was a place of intensive European whaling. British, Dutch, French and German vessels entered the archipelago's waters in the summer, hunted whales, butchered the carcasses on the shore and left before the ice settled. Competition for fishing and hunting areas sometimes led to armed clashes. Noteworthy, European whalers did not practice wintering - only a few such cases are known, and those cases used to end tragically.
The Pomors' presence was different. For Russian hunters and fishermen, Spitsbergen was part of the northern economic area that required a long year-round stay. They were preparing for winter, hunted arctic foxes, repaired rigging and ships, and organizing life on the shore. The camps and settlements became a material trace of this approach.
There are many traces of the Pomors in the archipelago - settlements and camps, remains of crosses, burials, fragments of ships. Archaeologists have discovered about 70 camps, which is a significant number for the high-latitude territory. At the same time, the early period's documentary history remains fragmentary. According to the scientist, the earliest Russian document directly related to Spitsbergen, that he knows, dates back to 1710.
"This does not mean that Russians had not been there earlier. Documents from the early 18th century describe sailing to Grumant like a fully formed practice. Perhaps Russian documents from an earlier period are still to be found in archives. Besides, the Pomors' navigation is a traditional culture that has long existed in the oral form. People could understand from experience the winds, currents, prominent capes and landmarks. They could have not recorded such voyages in written sources," he explained.
The political formula
The dispute about who was the first acquired special importance back in the early 20th century. Norway gained independence in 1905, and in 1920 was signed the Treaty of Spitsbergen, which stipulated Norway's sovereignty over the archipelago with a special international regime of economic activity. In such a situation, the dispute about the discoverers reached an ideological level. Historical arguments have become part of discussions about cultural memory and national presence in the Arctic.
The expert believes that the history of Spitsbergen demonstrates most clearly how a research discussion may acquire a political sounding. "The historical science turns very easily into politics," he said. "The researchers, who argued with Starkov, presented counterarguments, and questioned the methods - this is a regular scientific process. But further on, the complex and interesting dispute has turned into a short museum formula."
What is permitted when nothing is permitted
Work with Spitsbergen's archaeological heritage continues under a strict regime of monument protection. Excavations, sampling, and removal of objects are significantly limited by the Norwegian legislation. Therefore, to re-test earlier stories, specialists need archives, museum collections, field reports, non-invasive examination methods and detailed fixation of objects on the ground. This is exactly the kind of data map that the Russian Geographical Society's expedition has been developing.
In the expedition, cartographer Alevtina Paramonova is responsible for the creation of the map's thematic basis. At first, she said, it is necessary to collect and compare various sources - archival plans, old maps, photographs, publications, field survey materials, and stories by local residents. "We have been working on maps of cultural and natural heritage. It's a special genre. We need to build a foundation, show periods, types of objects, and connections between them. The map must accumulate knowledge about the territory."
The map will present the archipelago's heritage as a linked system, said Egor Shevyakov of the Russian Academy of Sciences' Institute of Archaeology. "The map is needed to systematize knowledge: when Russia appeared on the archipelago, what types of activities it conducted there, and what objects have been preserved. This is the basis for conservation projects, educational programs, tourist routes, and for further research," he added.
The Pomors' wintering grounds on Spitsbergen will become the earliest and, perhaps, the most disputable layer of the future map. Anyway, the truth often lies somewhere inside layers of the kind.
The Russian Geographical Society has organized a comprehensive expedition to Spitsbergen to create a map of the archipelago's Russian historical and cultural heritage. The expedition participants are recording objects related to the Pomors ' culture, scientific expeditions, coal mining, and the history of Russian villages. They are working with archives and talk to local residents. The Russian Geographical Society has organized a press tour for Russian reporters to cover the expedition's work.

The right to enforce civil rights is under attack in the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:06:41 UTC
16:06:41 KST

The right to enforce civil rights is under attack in the US
The Trump administration and conservative courts are restricting the ability of individuals and advocacy groups to challenge rights violations.
This autumn, the Supreme Court will consider a question with potentially far-reaching consequences for civil rights in the United States: Who gets to enforce them? On November 30, the justices will hear a case over whether employees of federally funded universities can sue under Title IX over alleged workplace sex discrimination. The Trump administration has urged the court to rule that they cannot, arguing that Congress never gave university employees a private right to bring such claims.
The dispute is the latest front in a broader legal push to restrict the ability of individuals and advocacy groups to take rights violations to court themselves. In June, the Supreme Court declined to hear a challenge to a federal appeals court ruling that barred Arkansas United, an immigrant advocacy organisation, from suing to enforce protections for voters who need assistance at the polls. Across a growing number of cases, Republican-led states and the Trump administration are advancing the same basic principle: Unless Congress has clearly authorised private citizens to sue, enforcement should largely be left to the government.
That may sound like an arcane legal argument, but its implications are anything but. If individuals and civil rights groups cannot go to court when laws protecting them are violated, the power to decide which rights are actually enforced increasingly rests with the very government that may be violating, ignoring or choosing not to enforce them.
A private right of action allows individuals, or groups acting on their behalf, to file lawsuits to enforce rights protected by law. These lawsuits can seek compliance with the law or compensation for past violations. Private rights of action are not automatic under US federal and state law. Congress and state legislatures sometimes explicitly authorise private lawsuits. Where they have not, courts have had to determine whether a law implicitly allows individuals or groups to sue, or whether enforcement rests solely with government authorities.
In practice, private litigation has been an essential part of enforcing rights throughout much of US history. As University of Virginia School of Law Professor George Rutherglen writes in a 2015 law review article (PDF):
“The long history of civil rights, dating back to Reconstruction, makes them quintessentially private rights, whose exercise and enforcement should depend primarily on the initiative of the individuals who bear those rights. Public enforcement no doubt remains necessary, and it has an equally long and distinguished pedigree in civil rights law, but it cannot entirely displace individual control over individual rights.”
Proponents of private rights of action, such as AARP, consider them an effective tool for vulnerable individuals and groups to protect their rights when government agencies are unwilling or unable to act. Critics, such as the US Chamber of Commerce Institute for Legal Reform, however, argue that private lawsuits can encourage frivolous litigation.
These critics, often from the political right, have attempted to restrict private litigation through legal arguments against private causes of action. An example is the 2001 Alexander v Sandoval decision, in which a Supreme Court majority led by Justice Antonin Scalia ruled that Title VI did not provide a private right of action to enforce regulations prohibiting policies or practices with a disparate impact on protected groups – discrimination that can occur without clear evidence of intent.
The legal push against private rights of action has intensified in recent years. Republican-led states have increasingly challenged the doctrine of implied private rights of action, arguing that courts should reject private suits to enforce various types of rights. The Trump administration has also adopted this stance. When the court decided a 2021 voting rights case, Justice Neil Gorsuch submitted a one-paragraph concurrence, joined by Justice Clarence Thomas, questioning whether “the Voting Rights Act of 1965 furnishes an implied cause of action,” despite that issue not being raised in the case itself.
The conservative push to restrict private rights of action has extended to a variety of areas. In June, the Supreme Court ruled against Falun Gong practitioners who accused Cisco Systems of helping the Chinese government develop surveillance technology used to facilitate their persecution, concluding that they could not pursue those aiding-and-abetting claims under the federal laws they had invoked.
One of the most consequential implications of restricting private rights of action is the threat to voting rights. In the Arkansas United case, the Eighth Circuit ruled that the immigrant advocacy organisation did not have the right to sue on behalf of non-native English speakers over the right to have language assistance in the voting booth. The ruling concerned Section 208 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965. But it extended a much broader argument already adopted by the Eighth Circuit: that private individuals and advocacy organisations cannot sue to enforce key provisions of the Voting Rights Act. The Supreme Court’s refusal in June to hear Arkansas United left that ruling in place.
This argument has also been pushed by Republican-led governments in two redistricting and vote-dilution cases: Board of Election Commissioners v NAACP in Mississippi and Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians v Howe in North Dakota. In May, the Supreme Court vacated judgments in both cases and sent them back for reconsideration in light of its ruling in Louisiana v Callais, without resolving the private-enforcement question. That decision sharply raised the bar for some racial vote-dilution claims, endangering the voting power of Black, Hispanic and Native American communities across the US. At the same time, conservative-controlled governments are attempting to deny members and advocates for these communities the right to even bring some of these cases before the courts, arguing that only the Department of Justice can initiate action over such voting rights violations.
The broader danger is that, as private rights of action are curtailed, enforcement of federal law increasingly depends on decisions made by the executive branch.
The Trump administration is now pursuing a different means of restricting private enforcement. The Clean Air Act explicitly gives private citizens the right to bring certain lawsuits, yet the Justice Department has sought to intervene and dismiss a case brought against xAI over allegations that gas turbines at its power facility in Southaven, Mississippi, are violating federal environmental law and polluting surrounding communities. The facility powers xAI’s Colossus 2 data centre in nearby Memphis. In September, the Justice Department appealed to the Fifth Circuit and sought to halt the case. The department has argued that allowing the suit to proceed would threaten national security and the US pursuit of global leadership in AI. Here, the issue is not whether Congress created a private right to sue – it did – but whether the executive branch can nevertheless step in to stop such a case when it conflicts with its priorities.
Relying solely on the Justice Department to pursue such cases at the federal level is a particularly dubious proposition under the current administration. The department has also been weaponised to target political foes of President Trump. Its Civil Rights Division has been steered away from defending the rights of racial and ethnic minorities and refocused on cases brought by white plaintiffs alleging so-called “reverse discrimination”.
The Justice Department’s current politicisation may be reversed under a future administration. But even then, the erosion of private rights of action would leave the enforcement of civil and political rights increasingly dependent on a federal agency with limited resources and subject to political direction. For example, as Democracy Docket noted in 2024, of the 216 active voting rights and redistricting cases it was tracking at the time, only five were cases brought by the Justice Department. As Professor Rutherglen noted in his article, to rely primarily on government actors to enforce rights “is to transform the nature of those rights: from private to public, from individuals to groups, from legal control by plaintiffs to political control by administrators.”
Private rights of action are now being eroded, case by case. Politicians, civil liberties advocates and organisations must challenge this trend before more avenues for enforcement are closed off. Otherwise, protections won over decades may become increasingly dependent on the willingness of government authorities to uphold them, leaving those whose rights are violated with fewer ways to seek redress.

Reporting on Gaza is our duty, but who protects us?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:04:07 UTC
16:04:07 KST

Breadcrumb
Reporting on Gaza is our duty, but who protects us?
It is that time of year when we Palestinians seem relevant again.
My inbox is flooded with interview requests about 7 October. Media outlets are interested in hearing my thoughts on the anniversary, and journalists want to know whether I condemn Hamas or not.
But what difference does it make?
Growing up, I dreamed of the day I would wear the press vest and helmet and tell the stories of Gaza to the world through my own eyes. I wanted to tell stories about how Palestinians love life, how they try to create something out of nothing, and how they try to bounce back after Israeli aggression and continue. I wanted to tell the stories of the Gaza I know, instead of the Gaza the media focuses on only when there is Israeli aggression or genocide.
But shortly after I graduated, it was 7 October.
In no time, wearing press gear became risky. Instead of protecting journalists and media workers, it made them a target.
Since the genocide began, over 74,000 Palestinians have been killed, including over 21,000 children, and this only accounts for the official numbers. Nearly 2 million people have been displaced, and 80% of the infrastructure in the Gaza Strip has been destroyed. According to the Committee to Protect Journalists, 247 journalists have been killed, 174 injured, and 118 imprisoned.
Staying alive
For the first 45 days of the genocide, I was on the ground reporting closely with two colleagues, Hatem Rawagh and Mohammed Abu Safia. They were both fathers, carrying the responsibility of staying strong and, most importantly, alive for their children. They held on to the hope of watching them grow up, giving them a future, and seeing them live in a better world than the one they were reporting on.
I still remember how Nour, Mohammed’s youngest daughter, would call him while we were out in the field reporting. She would tell him “bahebak” (I love you) in her soft voice, still learning how to pronounce the word. I could see how those words affected him each time he heard them.
His family has always been his reason for living, but Mohammed’s desire to tell the world the truth in hopes that this carnage could end forced him to stay away from them. Every day, he wondered whether it was safe to visit his family, or whether going would put them at more risk of being targeted.
His biggest fear was that Israel would kill them because of his profession, and that he’d remain alive to bear that agony.
He thought a lot about what Wael Dahdouh endured. After learning that his family had been killed by an Israeli airstrike, the Al Jazeera journalist had to report on the tragedy.
This was not the only loss we shared.
Belal Jadallah, the founder of Press House Palestine, who was a father figure to all journalists in Gaza, was also targeted and killed by Israel. He trained so many of us, including how to stay safe and how to be careful with our language and terminology because of the weight they carried for the wider world.
I was with Hatem when he told us the news: “Belal got targeted with an Israeli tank shell, or an airstrike hit his car.”
If the person who taught us how to protect ourselves could not be protected, then the vest and helmet were certainly never going to be enough.
It always felt like the only certainty in Gaza was uncertainty.
We had watched Israel kill our colleagues one after the other. Many others had also been injured or imprisoned. Each time, we’d wonder who would be next as it became harder to escape.
We were surviving one day at a time, never knowing when our turn might come.
Duty
Hatem and Mohammed are still in Gaza, still reporting. They explain: “It’s our duty.”
Part of them still wants to believe that if the world learned more about what is happening in Gaza, the genocide would stop. But now, three years into it, we know it’s not enough. Knowledge without accountability and justice means nothing.
As journalists, our responsibility is to bear witness and tell the truth, and in Gaza, we risk our lives to do it. But the responsibility cannot rest on our shoulders alone. The rest of the world must also be willing to carry that truth forward, to turn what it knows into action.
I used to dream of telling the world how Palestinians love life, how they build something out of barely anything and keep going. Instead, I have spent the last three years telling the world how they are being killed.
Whenever I see the number of journalists killed on the news, I think of the families they left behind, and of the people who are still waiting for a call that will never come. Whenever I watch the news from far away, I imagine the journalists behind the footage, standing in the same streets in the same vests, wondering if today is their turn.
Now, three years into a genocide, there is less and less coverage coming out of Gaza, and it is because journalism itself has become a target.
Despite our colleagues around the world watching so many being killed in Gaza, which sets a dangerous precedent for the future of their own work, too many are contributing to the injustice through the so-called measured language they choose, the realities they obscure, and the violence they help justify and normalise.
So every year around this time, when those press requests come flooding in, I think about the journalists who are still in Gaza, still on the ground reporting, and who will never get an email asking for their expert opinion, their experiences of tragedy and destruction.
Hatem and Mohammed say it is their duty, but it should not be theirs alone.
Plestia Alaqad is an award-winning journalist and author who has emerged as a powerful voice in digital media. She gained international recognition for her heartfelt, on-the-ground reporting during the genocide on Gaza, where her raw, personal storytelling brought global attention to the human impact of the violence. She recently published her book The Eyes of Gaza, that became an instant New York Times, Indie, San Francisco, and Boston Global Bestseller.

Aussie mothers with postpartum psychosis 'falling through the cracks'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:03:35 UTC
16:03:35 KST

Report finds women with postpartum psychosis contact health services repeatedly
In short:
Many Australian women with postpartum psychosis actively seek help despite not understanding what is wrong with them, new research has found.
The rare mental health condition affects one to two in 1,000 new mothers and is considered a psychiatric emergency.
What's next?
The women interviewed by Flinders University researchers said healthcare staff needed more awareness of postpartum psychosis to identify it quickly.
Australian women with postpartum psychosis are "falling through the cracks", with some contacting health services dozens of times before getting care.
A new report by researchers at Flinders University found women were seeking help an average of seven times before receiving it.
The peer-reviewed report, published today in the Australian Journal of Advanced Nursing, interviewed 15 women diagnosed with postpartum psychosis.
The condition, which affects one to two in 1,000 mothers, is considered a psychiatric emergency, developing suddenly in the days or weeks after birth.
But many of the women interviewed said their symptoms were not met with urgent concern, lead author and provisional psychologist Donna McMahon said.
"One of the stand-out findings of the research for me was that all the women we interviewed recognised something felt wrong to them," she told the ABC.
"They all describe having this feeling soon after childbirth, but before other and more overt psychotic symptoms developed.
"None of the women thought to be disingenuous or hide their symptoms, they were actively seeking help.
"[But] they described feeling like their symptoms were going unheard and minimised when they were asking for help."
Women report a sense 'something was not right'
More than half of the 15 women interviewed by researchers had never been diagnosed with a mental health condition prior to developing postpartum psychosis.
The lowest number of contacts with the Australian healthcare system when seeking help was four times.
The highest number was 27.
Women often had recognised a "vague, yet persistent sense that something was not right soon after childbirth", the report said.
Many said they had requested to be taken to the hospital, identifying they needed "urgent" support.
"I can remember thinking I've got to get to the bottom of this," one woman told researchers.
"Like … I'm going to get everyone together. I need my doctor. I need my psychiatrist. I need to … work out what's going on."
But the process of getting help, according to the report, was "fragmented".
Many women found the healthcare professionals they spoke to were unfamiliar with postpartum psychosis, often underestimating or overlooking symptoms.
They found their symptoms were "invisible" until they deteriorated further.
"It was sort of determined that it was probably a bit of baby blues," one woman said.
"I had lost touch with reality in that next 24 hours."
More follow-up needed from healthcare staff
The report identified a "critical period" for detecting postpartum psychosis early in its onset.
Failure to get help when they first noticed something was not right, according to the women interviewed, left many of them experiencing worsened outcomes.
"We are very lucky to have a health system like we do in Australia … but just like any system there is room for improvements," Ms McMahon said.
"From our research, one of those areas is [that] we need to actively and carefully listen to women and families when they are presenting time and again, saying something isn't right.
"We found the women felt that healthcare professionals weren't asking enough follow-up questions or probing questions that could help [the women] articulate what this feeling was.
"One way that the system can improve on their detection of this disorder is by improving the awareness and knowledge of what postpartum psychosis is, how it may present."
The report noted some limitations, including that its small sample size had been recruited via social media support groups.
This, according to the report, may mean the women were "more engaged with services and willing to share their experiences".
"However the sample reflects the target population relevant to the study and provides a realistic snapshot of the help-seeking experiences of women within the Australian healthcare system," the report said.
The localised sample size also meant the findings were more specific to Australia, and should not be used to draw global conclusions.
Concerns among women put down as 'part of new motherhood'
Asked about the report, psychologist Ariane Beeston said having localised research was vital.
Ms Beeston was diagnosed with postpartum psychosis after the birth of her son, Henry, in 2011.
She has since written a book about her experience and now works for the Centre of Perinatal Excellence (COPE), Australia's peak perinatal mental health body.
"[Postpartum psychosis] has definitely been an under-researched area, so while the findings aren't surprising, it's so important ot have them documented," she said.
"One thing that stood out to me was just the fact [that] when we're at our most vulnerable, we're left navigating this really confusing, fragmented system that's often ill-equipped to meet our needs.
"The other thing [was] concerns being dismissed and minimised, or put down as simply being part of new motherhood."
She said the number of women in the report who had actively sought help had surprised her.
"[I] and other women found it really difficult to speak up and ask for help, and certainly were fighting [or] downplaying symptoms,"
she said.
"I think while there are women who are very proactive and presenting to health professionals … there's still a lot of stigma and shame around this condition.
"It's not the case that everyone feels comfortable enough to seek help."

Pollard gives figure for Albion class write-down
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
08:00:51 BST
16:00:51 KST

The remaining economic value written down when the Royal Navy’s two landing platform docks left service was about £195 million for HMS Albion and £233 million for HMS Bulwark, a combined figure of roughly £428 million, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked for a breakdown of the remaining economic value of each Albion class vessel at the time of the write-down recorded on page 139 of the department’s Annual Report and Accounts for 2024-25, published on 4 November 2025.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “The remaining economic value written down was approximately £195.3 million for HMS Albion and £233.2 million for HMS Bulwark. The hon. Gentleman will know that this is the write down value and not a cost or payment made from the Defence budget.”
A write-down is the accounting recognition that an asset the department still carried on its books no longer has the service life it was assumed to have, and no money moves when it happens. The figure measures what the Treasury’s accounts said the ships were still worth on the day the decision was taken to stop using them.
Bulwark carrying a higher residual value than Albion follows from her refit history, since she had been in extended readiness and had received investment that Albion’s longer operational run had already consumed. Both ships were commissioned in the early 2000s, Albion in 2003 and Bulwark in 2005, and both were designed for a service life running towards 2033 and 2034.
The withdrawal came in the fleet decisions announced in late 2024, when the department confirmed that the two assault ships would go alongside a frigate and other units, and this publication reported at the time that the Albion class assault ships and a frigate were to be scrapped. The crews were reassigned across the fleet in the months that followed.

The girl who fled Rhodesia but never let go of her African roots

The girl who fled Rhodesia but never let go of her African roots
Marina Biber was eight when her family fled Rhodesia and came to Switzerland. Decades later, she stumbled across old television footage of herself as a child after reading a Swissinfo article. Now she shares her story.
Sometimes, all it takes is a news headline to bring the past flooding back. Earlier this year, Biber was scrolling through the news when she spotted a Swissinfo article about a Swiss man put up for adoption as a child in what was then Rhodesia. Intrigued, she read the article and watched the accompanying video by Swiss public television, SRF, about Swiss people living in Rhodesia in the 1970s.
Then she spotted her late father in the footage.
“I took a screenshot and sent it to my mother,” she recalls. “Is that Daddy?” she wrote. Her mother confirmed it straight away.
The footage dates from a time that Biber only vaguely remembers. Watching the full television report from the SRF archives, she spotted another familiar face: her own, as a little girl in Rhodesia more than 40 years ago.
“It was really a bit of a shock,” she says.
Biber was born in Rhodesia (now Zimbabwe) in 1972. Her mother had moved there from Kenya as a young woman and soon became pregnant. During the pregnancy, her mother split up with her biological father. Later, she met and married a Swiss watchmaker who had settled in Rhodesia. He adopted Biber and became the man she called “Daddy”.
Biber’s family history stretches across several continents. She has Italian roots and a Scottish grandmother. Born and raised in Africa, she moved to Switzerland with her mother and adoptive father when she was eight.
She now lives in Kreuzlingen, in northeastern Switzerland. Yet part of her has never quite left Africa.
Horses, a big house and wide-open skies
Biber remembers horses, dogs, a large property and children running around outside. Most of all, she remembers the vast sky, which seemed to stretch further than in Switzerland.
“When I was young, I never understood why vast skies moved me so deeply,” she says. Even now, when the landscape opens up and the sky stretches out before her, she sometimes feels that same childhood emotion.
Only when she first returned to Africa at 24 did she begin to make sense of where that feeling might come from. “So much sky. And completely different stars and cloud formations,” Marina says, visibly moved. It is not just the landscape that moves her. African music has a similar effect.
Other memories are more troubling. She clearly recalls the shop shelves in Rhodesia gradually emptying. Certain goods became impossible to find. The security situation had deteriorated. She heard helicopters at night, a sound that still triggers flashbacks. Eventually, her father began keeping a pistol under his pillow in case he needed to protect the family. Still, most of her memories are happy ones.
The day everything changed
On Saturdays, Biber took regular riding lessons at the local stables, where white settler families often met. The children looked after the animals and played together.
That Saturday, the family had also been invited to a party elsewhere. After Biber’s riding lesson, they left. Later that day, the stables were attacked. People and animals were killed.
At the time, Marina did not know what had happened. Her father only told her the story many years later. He had kept a newspaper clipping showing a white girl, about Biber’s age, who had been killed in the attack.
“That could have been Marina. We have to get out of here,” her father had said. To this day, she does not know whether any of the victims were people she knew.
Within a week, the family was on a flight to Switzerland. For Biber, just eight years old, it all felt like an adventure at first. There was snow, and everything was new.
For her mother, it was a very different experience. She had lived in Africa her whole life and she did not want to leave. She was forced to abandon her home, friends, animals, and everything that had made up her life there.
“I think it was traumatic for my mother,” Biber says. As a child, she never thought of their departure as escaping danger. Only years later did she come to see her family’s arrival in Switzerland as refugees fleeing their home. Except that her stepfather was Swiss. He had parents and siblings in Switzerland who took them in when they arrived and he was able to make a fresh start.
“That was a privilege,” she says.
The painful reality of starting over
Biber’s family first settled in Interlaken before moving to the Zurich Oberland region. She went to school in Hinwil and learnt German. At home, she still speaks English with her mother.
Her parents coped with leaving Africa in very different ways. Her father built a new life in Switzerland and took over a watch shop, while her mother remained deeply attached to Africa. Their marriage fell apart a few years after their arrival.
Her mother became an alcoholic before eventually giving up drinking. She still lives in Switzerland but is terribly homesick, Biber says.
In the 1970s, Rhodesia was ruled by a white minority: 270,000 whites ruled over 5.8 million blacks. At that time, about 660 Swiss nationals lived in the country. But the armed conflict between the government and black liberation movements spread. For safety reasons, many whites left the country.
In 1980, the country gained independence as Zimbabwe. Since then, it has been governed by the ZANU-PF party. Political repression, corruption, and economic crises continue to plague the country to this day. According to the Federal Statistical Office, 166 Swiss nationals were living in Zimbabwe at the end of 2025.
Returning to Zimbabwe was no longer an option because of the dire political and economic situation there. Health problems and financial difficulties made matters worse. Even years after the divorce, Biber’s mother continued working for her ex-husband in the watch shop. No money was set aside for her pension which made life difficult in retirement.
Biber bears no resentment when telling her story, just a mixture of sympathy and sadness. Her mother had never really given up hope that they would one day return to Zimbabwe.
Searching with a name and a phone book
It was years before Biber began the search for her African roots. In 1996, she travelled to South Africa and Zimbabwe with a friend, hoping to find her biological father. All she had to go on was his name.
These days an online search would provide clues but back then, Biber had to trawl through telephone directories. Eventually, she found her father and learnt that she had a step-brother and two step-sisters. She still keeps in touch with the former.
It was more difficult with her biological father. Watching the old video footage has changed how Biber sees the place she comes from. She feels ashamed of how black people are referred to in the television programme. “I find it really disturbing,” she says.
Biber recognises that she grew up in a society dominated by a white minority. Yet her own family history does not fit neatly into categories. Her mother had friends and relationships with people from different racial backgrounds. Biber tries to cope with these conflicting memories.
An excerpt from the Swiss news report from 1978 in German:
Africa never really left her
After returning from her trip in 1996, Africa faded into the background. She married, raised three children and built a career, first as a radiographer and later in the social services sector. For the past two years, she has been working in medical imaging at the University of Zurich’s veterinary hospital. Now, her work is giving her a chance to return to Africa.
This autumn, Biber plans to take part in a veterinary project in Zimbabwe. She will spend two weeks on a farm helping to monitor and protect wildlife. Then she will take a week off to rediscover her roots. But many people have warned her that travelling alone in Zimbabwe as a woman is too dangerous. She is still unsure how much of her childhood home she will safely be able to see.
Biber hopes one day to take her three teenage children back to Zimbabwe to see where she grew up. So far, though, they have not had the chance.
Her children know about their mother’s past, but Zimbabwe feels distant to them. Biber never placed much emphasis on her African heritage when bringing them up. They talk about it, but it plays little part in their everyday lives. “I do not make a big thing of it,” she says.
Perhaps her children will join her on a trip to Zimbabwe someday. For now, Biber wants to make the journey herself.
“I feel a very strong need to set foot in Africa again and see how it makes me feel,” she says. Marina does not know whether the trip will live up to her expectations. Perhaps she will come back feeling that it was a wonderful experience and leave it at that. Or perhaps her longing for Africa will grow even stronger.

Pharma pushes for higher European drug prices, Trump or no Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Pharma pushes for higher European drug prices, Trump or no Trump
US President Donald Trump’s plan to align US drug prices with those in peer countries is expected to have less impact than originally intended. That hasn’t stopped pharma companies from calling for higher prices and wider reforms in Europe, including Switzerland. An analysis.
Just over a year ago, US President Trump issued an executive orderExternal link calling for US drug prices to align with so-called Most-Favoured Nation (MFN) prices – those paid in other developed countries. On average, Americans pay three to four times as much for brand-name drugs as patients in other wealthy countries, research showsExternal link.
Pharma companies argued that if US prices dropped to levels in peer countries, it would wipe out budgets for research into new drugs.
The simple answer to this problem, Trump concluded, was for peer countries to raise prices and pay what he saw as their fair share of innovation. The US makes up less than 5% of the world population but accountsExternal link for at least half the revenue for most large pharmaceutical companies. The US National Institutes of Health is also the largest public funder of biomedical research in the world.
Companies and industry groups agreed with Trump and warned companies could delay or avoid launching products altogether in peer countries if prices don’t rise.
“If Switzerland serves as a benchmark for the US, medicines will only be offered in this country [Switzerland] at prices comparable to those in the US or will not be on the market at all, or with a massive delay,” wroteExternal link the Swiss pharmaceutical association Interpharma back in November 2025.
Switzerland and other MFN reference countries scrambled to respond. Governments faced a dilemma: raise prices amid surging healthcare costs or face worsening access to medicine.
Fast forward
In the last month though it’s become clear that MFN’s implementation includes a host of exceptions and conditions that limit its scope and impact.
Some 26 pharma companies have signed confidential MFN deals with the US government pledging to adopt drug prices in line with other countries in exchange for immunity from tariffs that could reach as high as 100%.
What we know now is that if companies participate in a voluntary pilot called GENEROUS for Medicaid, the federal insurance programme for low-income individuals, which already receives the lowest prices of US payers, they are exempt from a mandatory MFN pilot for Medicare called GLOBE.
According to rules announcedExternal link on September 30, only four unnamed companies are subject to GLOBE.
More
Drugmakers reassess Europe as Trump overhauls drug-pricing rules
A Roche spokesperson confirmed by email that the company expects to be exempt from GLOBE and other pricing mandates as part of the agreement its California subsidiary Genentech signed with the US government in December 2025. This means they aren’t obliged to offer MFN prices for drugs sold to Medicare, which is the federal programme for seniors.
The GLOBE rules also exclude several major drug categories like cell and gene therapies. This drops the estimated savingsExternal link to $440 million (CHF366 million) through 2032 instead of the $11.9 billion originally expected last December.
In May the White House projectedExternal link $529 billion in domestic savings over a decade through the MFN executive order. Under the voluntary MFN framework, manufacturers commit to launch new drugs across all markets in the US at prices comparable to those in other high‑income countries. They can also offer MFN prices in the Medicaid programme GENEROUS.
There are also two mandatory MFN programmes for Medicare – GLOBE (clinic-administered drugs) and GUARD (retail pharmacy drugs). If companies participate in GENEROUS, they appear to be exempt from the mandatory Medicare MFN programmes. GUARD rules have not been released yet.
Each federal pilot uses a slightly different set of reference countries. The MFN price in GENEROUS is defined as the second-lowest net price adjusted for GDP per capita using a purchasing-power-parity (PPP) for a group of eight countries – Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Switzerland, and the UK.TrumpRxExternal link, launched in February 2026, offers discounted prices for some medicines direct to patients. However, it isn’t clear that these discounts are tied to specific international reference prices.
In addition, at least two heavily redacted MFN deals raise doubts that higher prices will fund research into new medicine. A provision in the deal with US firm Pfizer indicatesExternal link that the US Department of Health and Human Services is slated to receive some revenue from price increases overseas.
MFN also isn’t codified in any laws, and many of the MFN deals expire by 2030, raising questions about what happens when Trump’s term ends. The US pharma industry association PhRMA has already filed a lawsuitExternal link against the US government, arguing that GLOBE is unlawful and exceeds the government’s authority to impose nationwide price setting policies that Congress never authorised.
Although the MFN deals are confidential, companies claim that they are still obliged to align prices with peer countries for future drugs. However, there is no clarity on how this will be calculated and enforced, especially in the commercial insurance market which covers roughly 65% of the US population.
More than MFN
So, how worried should Switzerland, which is home to pharma giants Roche and Novartis, still be about MFN? Do prices in reference countries like Switzerland still matter?
“Even if MFN isn’t implemented fully in the US, it still has an impact on Switzerland,” Marcel Plattner, president of the Association of Pharmaceutical Companies in Switzerland (VIPS), told Swissinfo. “Companies can’t jeopardise their position in the US market in order to have a presence in Switzerland.”
A survey of Interpharma membersExternal link released in August found that, between January 2025 and June 2026, MFN concerns led companies not to submit seven of 22 new innovative medicines for Switzerland’s Specialties List, the list of medicines covered by compulsory insurance.
Whether MFN is implemented in its current form or another form may not matter. MFN has already done its job, by showing how much the world is dependent on high prices in the US.
“MFN may have achieved its ultimate objective by highlighting the issue of differential pricing between the US and Europe,” said Neil Grubert, an independent expert on market access who has been following MFN developments closely.
“It has concentrated minds in Europe on the issue and reinforced Trumps case that other countries have been free riding on the US for far too long.”
MFN has reignited a longstanding debate over whether Europe pays too little for innovative medicines, leaving the US to shoulder a disproportionate share of the cost of pharmaceutical innovation.
Pharmaceutical lobbies have now capitalised on Trump’s messages about free riding to argue that years of cost-cutting measures and drug pricing pressure have gone too far in Europe.
In an open letterExternal link published in late September, the chairs of nine European pharma companies including Novartis and Roche argued that Europe risked decline and dependency if it didn’t “rebalance decades of underinvestment in innovative medicines”. They point to a range of problems including low prices, weak intellectual property protection, and overregulation.
More
Swiss pharma’s global success meets worries at home
Roche announcedExternal link this week it is putting all future investment decisions on hold in Germany over the country’s healthcare cost-cutting policies.
As a small market with a huge pharmaceutical sector, Switzerland has a lot at stake. The pharmaceutical industry accounts for some 40% of exports, around 30% of which went to the US in 2025. The sector was responsible for 40% of economic growth over the past decade. Switzerland also prides itself on a top-notch healthcare system and rapid access to the latest therapies.
Swiss politicians appear to be heeding industry calls. A couple months ago health commissions in both chambers of the Swiss parliament suggestedExternal link holding off on volume-based discounts on high-priced medicine that had already been agreed by parliament in a cost containment package before Trump was re-elected.
They cited the new “international context” as a reason. The policy would have obliged companies to offer a rebate on any drug generating more than CHF15 million in annual sales. It’s now up to a new life sciences location working group formed by the Swiss government to determine the way forward.

Text description provided by the architects. YUKI office is the headquarters of a company in Kuki, Saitama, that sells organic vegetables under the philosophy of "thinking about food and health." The client asked for a building that would immediately convey the company's mission to anyone who visits: to deliver safe, trustworthy produce to consumers and to help preserve Japan's traditional food culture. After the Great East Japan Earthquake, the company used its own distribution network to support the affected areas, and it wanted a headquarters that could also support the local community in future disasters.

NEW DELHI: 
Supreme Court
 on Wednesday directed the Andhra Pradesh State Election Commission to decide by Thursday whether to extend nomination deadlines for urban local body polls in areas where candidates were allegedly prevented from filing nominations due to law and order issues.
The court asked the poll panel to defer publication of the final candidates’ list until October 25 and examine complaints of violence and obstruction by tomorrow. The court also ordered police protection and CCTV coverage at nomination centres and sought a compliance report. The matter will be heard next on October 27.

Pentagon chief denies directives restricting Starshield in Ukraine, points to priority of replenishing US air defense arsenals
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:57:01 EEST
15:57:01 KST

The US Department of War maintains an unchanged position on supporting Ukraine and has refrained from issuing any directives on restricting the operation of the Starshield satellite network, while on the supply of interceptor missiles Washington's priority is to provide its own armed forces with as many as possible, US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has said.
"We have not changed our position on the Ukrainians in any way, but on things like interceptor missiles, of course, we want to make sure our guys are also supplied with as many as possible. So that is the case, and President Zelenskyy knows it," Hegseth said.
According to Hegseth, press reports about a change in the Pentagon's approach to Ukraine are false. He noted the heroic efforts of Ukrainians and recalled that under the previous American administration Kyiv was given large volumes of military aid that drained American stockpiles, so the department is now replenishing these stocks on the instruction of US President Donald Trump.
Commenting on reports about reduced speeds and restricted coverage of the Starshield military satellite system in Ukraine, the Pentagon chief assured that the US defense department had left service volumes unreduced and had refrained from issuing such orders. Hegseth explained that the use of terminals is governed by the terms of service, and the authority to decide on compliance with them rests directly with the Starlink operator, and he wished the Ukrainian side success.
As reported, the administration of US President Donald Trump is holding back, without consideration, the transfer of anti-aircraft interceptor missiles for Patriot systems for Ukraine from partner countries, which coincides with a sharp deterioration in diplomatic relations between Washington and Kyiv over disagreements about strikes on Russian oil refineries.

U.S. Navy taps portable reactor to power Indiana base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
06:53:49 UTC
15:53:49 KST

- The U.S. Navy selected Radiant to install a 1-megawatt Kaleidos microreactor at Naval Weapons Station Crane in Indiana under the U.S. Army’s Janus Program.
- The Department of War wants the Navy’s first shore-based microreactor operating at Crane no later than September 2028.
The U.S. Navy has selected Radiant to install its Kaleidos nuclear microreactor at Naval Weapons Station Crane in Indiana, putting a commercial company in charge of the service’s first shore-based advanced reactor, which the Department of War wants running no later than September 2028.
Radiant announced the selection on Oct. 20, about six weeks after the Department of War named Crane as the site for the Navy’s first microreactor without saying which vendor would build it.
Kaleidos is a factory-built reactor that produces 1 megawatt of electricity and is designed to be moved by truck, ship or aircraft and set up at a customer’s site without cooling water, major excavation or extensive construction. Each unit runs for up to five years before it needs refueling, over a planned service life of 20 years, and at Crane it is meant to keep power flowing to the base independently of the regional grid, which matters for an installation where the Naval Surface Warfare Center, Crane Division, works on microelectronics, high-voltage systems and weapons.
The reactor will be installed under the U.S. Army’s Janus Program, the Pentagon effort to put commercially owned and operated microreactors on military bases so they can keep critical facilities running through grid outages. Before it reaches Crane, the project still has to move through design refinement, prototype testing, environmental review, site preparation and coordination with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, with technical support from the Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program, the organization that runs the reactors on the Navy’s carriers and submarines.
“The Janus Program was built from day one to deliver real, reliable hardware and systems to solve energy resilience challenges across all of the Services,” said Dr. Jeff Waksman, Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary of the Army for Installations, Energy and Environment. “We are excited to partner with the Navy to place a Janus reactor at NWS Crane, and by doing so to deliver the state of Indiana its first advanced microreactor.”
Crane is the second military base Radiant has lined up this year under Janus. In August, the U.S. Army awarded contracts worth up to $2.2 billion to five reactor makers, with Radiant receiving the largest share, up to $750 million to deploy 15 Kaleidos units by 2030, as we reported, starting with three reactors at Fort Benning in Georgia that will back up Lawson Army Airfield and other critical facilities, we reported in September. The company also has a deal with the Defense Innovation Unit and the Department of the Air Force to deliver a Kaleidos unit by 2028, and it now says it is the only nuclear company working with the U.S. Army, U.S. Navy and U.S. Air Force at once.
“Our installations are foundational warfighting platforms and ensuring their resilience is essential to supporting the Fleet,” said Vice Adm. Brad Collins, Commander, Navy Installations Command. “By investing in advanced capabilities like this microreactor at Crane, we are providing our Shore infrastructure with the resources needed to sustain the mission and empower our warfighters.”
Radiant has not yet proven the design at full scale, and the reactor is now going through a year-long test campaign at the Idaho National Laboratory’s DOME facility, where the Department of Energy gave the company exclusive access after a competitive selection. The company says the test uses the same reactor design and the same type of fresh fuel that will go to military customers, running at full power for an extended period to show the performance and reliability needed before deployment.
The Navy brings decades of reactor experience to the project, since the Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program, founded in 1948, has logged more than 7,500 reactor-years of operation and over 171 million miles under nuclear power without a reactor accident.

Ukraine hits Russian heavy rocket launcher near Black Sea coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
06:48:44 UTC
15:48:44 KST

- Ukraine’s Prymary drone unit destroyed a Russian Tornado-S rocket launcher near Skadovsk in occupied Kherson Oblast, hitting it with several kamikaze drones.
- OSINT analyst Dominik geolocated the strike to Ulyanivka, while HUR said the unit also hit a Buk-M3, an Orion drone and four radars.
Ukrainian drones have destroyed a Russian 9K515 Tornado-S heavy multiple launch rocket system in occupied Kherson Oblast, hitting the launcher with several different kamikaze drones in succession in a strike carried out by the Prymary unit of Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR), which released the footage on Oct. 20.
OSINT analyst Dominik geolocated the strike to the village of Ulyanivka just outside Skadovsk, at coordinates 46.189524, 32.964916, which places the launcher close to the Black Sea coast and well behind the Dnipro River front line.
The video shows the Tornado-S being struck by drones of different types one after another, a method Ukrainian operators use against high-value vehicles so that a second or third drone can finish off a target that survives the first hit before the crew can drive it away. HUR did not give the exact date of the strike, saying only that it took place over the past month, and Russia has not commented on the loss.
The Tornado-S is one of the most valuable launchers in Russia’s rocket artillery, since it is a modernized version of the Soviet 9A52 Smerch that fires 300 mm (11.8-inch) rockets from a 12-tube launcher mounted on an eight-wheeled Kamaz truck. Built by NPO Splav in Tula, part of the state-owned Rostec group, the system uses digital fire control and GLONASS satellite navigation so its three-person crew can prepare and fire a full salvo without leaving the cab, and its guided rockets can reach targets up to 120 km (75 miles) away.
That range lets Russian crews fire on Ukrainian cities from deep inside occupied territory, and in the south the system has repeatedly been used against Kherson and other towns along the Dnipro from positions in the occupied part of the region. Ukrainian units put a high price on each launcher they destroy, and after a drone strike on a Tornado-S in the Huliaipole sector in July, the Pomsta Border Guard Brigade estimated the vehicle’s value at more than $15 million.
The Skadovsk strike is the latest in a series of Tornado-S losses this year as Ukrainian drones reach further behind Russian lines. In February, the Ptahi unit of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces destroyed a launcher in occupied Zaporizhzhia Oblast with FP-2 strike drones guided by reconnaissance drones, we reported at the time, and in March a long-range Fire Point drone hit three Tornado-S launchers and a transport-loader near Karakul in occupied Crimea, as we reported. Two more launchers were hit near Melitopol within a few days in late April, followed by the July strike in the Huliaipole sector.
“Big names, formidable specifications and the millions invested in military equipment do not guarantee the occupiers’ immunity,” Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence said in its statement.
The Tornado-S was the centerpiece of a wider monthly report from Prymary, which HUR said also hit a Buk-M3 air defense system, an Orion reconnaissance and strike drone, a Kasta-2E low-altitude radar, a Nebo-U long-range surveillance radar and two P-18 early warning radars. The unit also struck a drone assembly and repair site and a building housing troops of the 4th Air Assault Battalion of the 108th Air Assault Regiment, although HUR gave no dates or locations for those strikes and did not say whether every target was destroyed or only damaged.

From November 17 to 19, 2026, interihotel MAD26 will bring together architects, interior designers, hospitality operators, and specialized brands at IFEMA Madrid. Organized by AMBIT Living Spaces Cluster, the event is expected to welcome more than 14,000 professionals, 350 exhibiting brands, and over 200 international speakers. Under the theme Creative Rebellion, it will combine talks, workshops, five specialized forums, and full-scale experimental spaces to explore new approaches to hotel and restaurant design.
Three Perspectives on Rethinking Hospitality
As many spaces increasingly resemble one another, Creative Rebellion champions creativity and optimism as tools for imagining hospitality with a distinctive identity. It invites professionals to reconsider how spaces connect with people and place, how materials are selected, and what possibilities new technologies offer.
The Inside Rebellion, on November 17, will examine identity, emotion and experience. Stefan Sagmeister, Nini Andrade Silva, Bruzkus Greenberg, and Astet Studio will share their perspectives, alongside sessions on lighting and workshops focused on color, floral art, and ceramics in architecture.
The Green Rebellion, on November 18, will address sustainability, circularity, and well-being. Participants will include Lyndon Neri and Rossana Hu, co-founders of Neri&Hu, alongside Lucas Muñoz Muñoz, Studio Animal, Beaumier, and Rockwell Group. The programme will explore material recovery, spatial flexibility, and the relationship between lighting and health.
The Future Rebellion, on November 19, will highlight innovation, creativity, and new business models. Dani García, the day's keynote speaker, will open the discussion on reinventing the guest experience. Other participants will be Laura Vall of Axel Hotels; Luca Pronzato, founder and artistic director of We Are Ona; and Kike Sarasola of Room Mate Hotels.
Knowledge for Design Practice
Five specialized forums will address challenges in designing and developing spaces. Future Living will explore new accommodation models; Circular Spaces, the transformation of existing spaces and resources; WellSpaces, neuroarchitecture and evidence-based design; Hospitality Building Systems, industrialized construction; and AI Interiors, artificial intelligence in architecture and interior design.
Featuring participants such as Bill Browning, Jana Crepon of Inside Outside, Jorge Alonso Rodríguez of Chapman Taylor, and Tim Fu, these forums will connect research, design, investment, and operations through shared tools and experiences.
Experiencing Spaces at Full Scale
Interiors Living Lab will translate these ideas into spaces that visitors can experience firsthand. The Sensory Explorer Concept Room, designed by HBA and inspired by Barceló Hotel Group, will present The Dome: Earth, Light and Memory, a hotel room that interprets Tunisia's identity through geometry, light and materiality.
The Social Playful Concept Restaurant, designed by Livit and inspired by Lamucca, will propose a flexible restaurant where different rhythms coexist: eating, working, meeting or lingering after a meal.
Materials Lab will feature two installations: Materials by AMBIT Cluster, a selection of innovative and sustainable materials contributed by exhibiting brands; and Materialidad adaptable, an exhibition conceived by MATTER exploring the evolution of six material families.
Craft Lab, curated by Tachy Mora, will explore contemporary ceramics through eight makers and brands, demonstrating how craftsmanship, memory, and local context can bring identity to hotel and restaurant design.
Xperience Lab will offer hands-on experiences with tools for designing in Virtual and Mixed Reality, co-creating with an AI agent, visualizing projects in Augmented Reality, and configuring industrialized building modules.
Design and Industry for a New Hospitality
The exhibition will showcase furniture, lighting, materials, textiles, and equipment, encouraging dialogue between those who design, manufacture, and operate spaces. Alongside the event, interi-off will extend activities throughout Madrid from November 16 to 20, with visits, installations, talks, workshops, and networking events.
interihotel MAD26 offers three days to challenge conventions, experiment, and discover new ways of designing hotels and restaurants. Admission is reserved for practising professionals in the sector. Discover the visitor information and register to attend.

DIU: Russia has accumulated up to 700 ballistic missiles and more than 6,000 drones
Kyiv • UNN
According to the DIU's assessment, Russia has accumulated up to 700 ballistic missiles, thousands of cruise missiles, and 6,200 drones. Its defense industry produces more than 200 missiles every month.
Russia has accumulated up to 700 ballistic missiles, several thousand cruise missiles, and more than 6,000 drones. This was reported by the Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) of Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence in response to an inquiry from NV, reports UNN.
As of October, the Russian Federation has up to 700 ballistic missiles and several thousand cruise missiles of various types in reserve. (...) As of autumn, Russia had accumulated an operational reserve of about 6,200 Geran drones of various modifications (including jet-powered ones). This is what allows the enemy to carry out massive combined strikes in several waves
According to an assessment by the HUR, Russia’s defence-industrial complex is capable of producing more than 200 such aerial terror weapons every month, 110 of which are ballistic missiles.
According to intelligence data, the current enemy stocks of "Iskander-M" ballistic missiles are estimated at approximately 115 units, while monthly production amounts to up to 65 missiles. At the same time, the Russian Federation continues active development of a modernised system with a projected range of 550–700 km (currently—up to 500 km).
According to intelligence information:
-  Kh-101 cruise missiles—the monthly production plan, according to HUR estimates, amounts to more than 80 units, but Russian factories exceed these figures; 
-  Kalibr sea-launched cruise missiles—stocks are estimated at more than 450 units, while the monthly production rate is approximately 29 missiles; 
-  RM-48U strike missiles for S-300PM/S-400-type air-defence systems—the estimated stocks of missiles adapted for strikes against ground targets amount to up to 400 units, with approximately 40 units manufactured each month; 
-  Oniks anti-ship and modernised missiles—Russia’s stockpile is estimated at more than 600 units; during the first 7 months of 2026, the Russian Federation manufactured more than 55 Oniks missiles; 
-  Tsirkon hypersonic missiles—the total stockpile, according to HUR estimates, exceeds 120 units; during the first 7 months of this year, slightly more than 30 units were produced; 
-  Kinzhal hypersonic systems—missile production has been temporarily suspended due to low accuracy figures. The available capacity has been redirected to the production of conventional ballistic weapons; 
-  Russia currently assembles about 4,000 jet-powered drones per month, аnd production lines are adapted for rapid scaling. The core consists of the Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered models; 
-  The “conventional” Geran-2 is manufactured at a rate of approximately 2,000 units per month.  
According to an intelligence assessment, this year the Russian Federation’s state order for Geran-type drones and associated reconnaissance drones and decoys, such as Gerbera, exceeded 100,000 units annually. As the HUR noted, this indicates the enemy’s systematic reliance on exhausting Ukraine’s air-defence system.

Ukraine using satellite data to prepare lawsuits in international courts – lawyer
Anna Hurova, who holds a PhD in law specializing in space law and is a postdoctoral researcher at the Chair of Space Studies (Chaire Espace) at the École normale supérieure (ENS–PSL) in Paris, said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
"They are already being used for demining, environmental impact assessments, and preparing claims for international courts. This is happening even during the war," Hurova said, commenting on how satellite data could help Ukraine obtain compensation.
According to her, obtaining compensation first requires proving the damage caused by collecting data, assessments, and evidence.
"People may not believe in these courts, but as a lawyer, I understand that if there is a document, an official record, it can help even several years later. To obtain compensation, the damage must first be proven. And that requires data, assessments, and evidence," the lawyer explained.
As an example, she cited the use of satellite data to compare information and verify claims concerning the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant.
"Take the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant – satellite data helped cross-check information and verify statements. This is also part of countering disinformation. Obtaining compensation will be a long process, but there must be a basis to rely on," Hurova said.
The legal expert stressed that Ukraine had already gained unique experience in applying space technologies in the military sphere, during evacuations, in crisis management, and in restoring agricultural land. This expertise could become a source of funding.

Source: Ukrainska Pravda sources
Details: On 19 August, NABU and SAPO released details of Operation Forrest Gump, an investigation into a criminal group that organised a money-laundering scheme in order to pay bail for former energy and justice minister Herman Halushchenko. They had used the state-owned Sense Bank for this purpose.
On 20 August, the anti-corruption agencies released details of the second part of the investigation, entitled Femida (after the Greek goddess of law and justice, Themis), which examined how the same criminal group had orchestrated the illegal seizure of properties and businesses in Kyiv.
On 2 September, the National Bank found that Sense Bank CEO Oleksii Stupak did not meet the professional suitability requirements for his position and demanded that he be replaced.
Meanwhile, appointments to the bank's management and supervisory board were overseen by Vasyl Veselyi, the government's behind-the-scenes power broker at Sense Bank, who officially held the position of adviser to the chairman of the bank's supervisory board.
The Operation Midas recordings captured a conversation between Oleksandr Tsukerman and Vasyl Veselyi. The members appointed to Sense Bank's supervisory board on 18 June 2025 were the same candidates that the individuals implicated in the Midas case had discussed more than a month before.
Former Sense Bank supervisory board chairman Şevki Acuner told a temporary parliamentary commission of inquiry that Veselyi had been appointed to Sense Bank on the recommendation of NBU Governor Andrii Pyshnyi.
Sources in political circles told Ekonomichna Pravda that Pyshnyi and Veselyi knew each other through the late Andrii Ivanchuk, an MP from the People's Front faction who had been at university with the current NBU governor.
Pyshnyi himself said he had not made any recommendations to the Sense Bank supervisory board regarding the appointment of Veselyi, a person of interest in the investigations.
Update: NABU reported at 10:40 that searches have been carried out at the NBU and at an employee's home.
No one has been detained.
The NBU has also confirmed the searches and said it continues to operate as usual.
Background: It was reported in August that President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was dissatisfied with National Bank Governor Andrii Pyshnyi and that the possibility of his dismissal had already been discussed.

UAE-made armored vehicles seen again in Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
06:39:31 UTC
15:39:31 KST

- Russia’s Gyurza SOBR unit in the Moscow region has been seen with a Cobra-LAMV armored vehicle made by Emirati company Streit Group.
- Ukraine, the European Union, Switzerland and Canada have sanctioned Streit Group over vehicles supplied to Russia’s National Guard.
Armored vehicles built by Emirati manufacturer Streit Group have been spotted again in Russian service, this time with Gyurza, the special rapid response unit (SOBR) of Rosgvardia’s Main Directorate for the Moscow region, which was photographed operating a Cobra-LAMV 4×4. The light armored vehicle is built on a Toyota Land Cruiser chassis and marketed by Streit to police and internal security forces. It continues to turn up with Russia’s National Guard even though Ukraine, the European Union, Switzerland and Canada have all sanctioned the company over its vehicles reaching Russia.
Cobra vehicles first appeared in Russia in October 2024, when a Russian military blogger published video of a shipment of more than 20 Streit-built Spartan, Cobra and Cougar armored vehicles bound for Russian forces, as we were first to report. In September 2025, Rosgvardia units were filmed training with Spartan SUT vehicles, including one fitted with an 82 mm (3.2-inch) mortar in the rear compartment, we reported at the time. Every one of these deliveries reached Russia well after the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Ukraine was the first to respond, listing Streit Group in 2023, and the European Union and Switzerland followed in October 2025 before adding founder Guerman Goutorov personally to their sanctions lists in May 2026. Canada sanctioned the company in August 2026 for supplying vehicles to Rosgvardia, a move Russia’s ambassador in Ottawa dismissed as having no practical effect, and the new Moscow-region sighting shows that the vehicles keep reaching Russian units regardless.
The Canadian measures carry particular weight because Streit started out as a Canadian business founded in Ontario in 1992 by Goutorov, a Russian-born businessman who served five years in the Soviet police before emigrating to Canada in the early 1990s. He later moved the company’s headquarters to the Ras Al Khaimah free trade zone in the United Arab Emirates, where Streit grew into one of the world’s largest armored vehicle makers with production sites on several continents. Goutorov’s Canadian citizenship shields him personally from Ottawa’s sanctions, and he has appealed his listing in the European Union.
Streit’s links to Russia go well beyond finished vehicles, since the company opened an armored vehicle plant east of Moscow and another in Tatarstan in 2009 and kept trading with Russian suppliers after both the 2014 and 2022 invasions. Customs records show that between 2015 and 2022 it imported 41 shipments of parts from Russian truckmaker Kamaz and 38 shipments of VPK-Ural vehicle kits, including six from the sanctioned Arzamas plant in the two weeks before Russian troops crossed into Ukraine. The company also worked with Russia’s Military-Industrial Company on armored vehicles that were later used by Wagner Group fighters in several conflict zones.
Russia is far from the only controversial destination for Streit vehicles, which have repeatedly surfaced in conflict zones under arms embargoes or in the hands of armed groups. In Yemen, Houthi military media released footage of armored vehicles captured from Saudi-backed forces. In Iran, a Toophan MRAP displayed at the Eghtedar 40 military exhibition in Tehran in 2019 was photographed and described as the same design as Streit’s Typhoon, although Iranian sources present the vehicle as a domestic development.
UN expert panels have accused Streit of breaking arms embargoes on Libya and Sudan and criticized the sale of hundreds of its vehicles into South Sudan, as we reported in 2016. Its vehicles have since been delivered to Khalifa Haftar’s forces in eastern Libya and seen with riot police in Belarus and with Guinea’s military junta. In 2015, Streit’s U.S. subsidiary paid a $3.5 million fine and Goutorov personally paid $250,000 over unlicensed exports of armored vehicles to Afghanistan, Iraq, Nigeria and other countries.
Streit has denied wrongdoing every time its vehicles have surfaced in such places, insisting that it follows UAE export law, ships its vehicles without weapons and bears no responsibility for how buyers modify or use them after sale. The company has never explained how its armored vehicles continue to reach Rosgvardia units more than four years into Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine.
