BEIJING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- China has achieved significant results in responding to climate change in recent years, gradually forging a green and low-carbon development path, a senior environment official said Wednesday.
Li Gao, vice minister of ecology and environment, made the remarks at a news conference, where an annual report on China's policies and actions on climate change was released by the Ministry of Ecology and Environment.
The report showed that in 2025, China's carbon dioxide emissions per unit of GDP fell 17.7 percent compared with 2020 levels. Non-fossil energy accounted for 21.7 percent of total energy consumption. Combined installed capacity of wind and solar power reached 1.84 billion kilowatts. Forest stock volume stood at 20.99 billion cubic meters.
The progress is backed by the country's sustained efforts to accelerate the green and low-carbon transformation.
China has built the world's largest and most complete clean energy industrial chain, with green and low-carbon industries becoming an important engine of economic growth, Li said.
By the first half of 2026, the country's total installed renewable energy capacity reached 2.46 billion kilowatts, accounting for 60.7 percent of total national power generation capacity. At the end of July, installed solar power capacity surpassed coal power for the first time in history, making it China's largest single power source.
Moreover, China's combined installed capacity of operational and approved nuclear power units has risen to first place in the world. New energy vehicle production and sales have ranked first globally for 11 consecutive years.
Li noted that the country has established the world's largest carbon emissions trading market, covering about 8.3 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide, or more than 65 percent of the country's total emissions. Cumulative allowance trading volume has recently surpassed 1 billion tonnes. ■

Feature: Germany's cost-of-living squeeze lays bare deeper economic strains
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:36:40 CST
15:36:40 KST

BERLIN, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- On a crisp October evening in Berlin, Manuela, a middle-class resident, leaves her living-room heating firmly off. In years past, a flick of the switch would have sufficed at the first hint of a chill; today, she reaches for a sweater instead.
"Before turning on the heating, we have to think twice and ask ourselves whether it is really necessary at this temperature," she said.
The family's annual outlay on power, heat and hot water runs to about 3,500 euros (3,920 U.S. dollars) -- a monthly burden of nearly 300 euros. As fuel, food and other essentials grow dearer, they have been compelled to rethink their household budget.
According to the Household Energy Price Index for European Capitals, residential natural gas prices in Berlin rose by about 22 percent between February and September 2026. For Manuela, the concern is that annual heating bills could mean unexpected additional costs, as payments are made in monthly installments and adjusted later.
Her prudence echoes a wider anxiety across Germany. According to "The Fears of Germans in 2026," a survey by insurer R+V, 59 percent of respondents cited a sharp rise in the cost of living as a primary concern.
Isabelle Borucki, a political scientist at Philipps University of Marburg, said rising prices for essentials such as energy, housing and food were squeezing household budgets for leisure, holidays and other spending.
Official data point to renewed inflationary pressure. According to Germany's Federal Statistical Office, the annual inflation rate rose to 3.3 percent in September, its highest level since December 2023. Energy prices increased 14.9 percent year on year, with motor fuels up 37.1 percent and heating oil up 74.9 percent.
As households cut back on discretionary spending, the effects can spread to retail, hospitality and tourism, weighing on domestic demand.
Cost-of-living concerns have also fueled protests elsewhere in Europe in recent days, notably in France, Italy and Portugal. The demonstrations, driven by concerns over rising prices, public services and austerity, reflect broader anxieties about purchasing power and living standards.
The economic implications are particularly significant in Germany, where manufacturing and exports face mounting pressure. Energy-intensive industries such as chemicals are directly exposed to high gas and electricity costs, while other manufacturers face rising transport and raw material expenses. Companies unable to pass on these costs may see profits shrink, curbing investment and job creation.
Volker Treier, chief analyst at the German Chambers of Industry and Commerce, has warned that high oil and gas prices could increase Germany's energy import bill by as much as 40 billion euros (44.8 billion dollars), equivalent to nearly 1 percent of the country's gross domestic product.
The pressures on Germany's industrial base are evident in the chemical sector. According to German industry publication KunststoffWeb, LEUNA-Polyamid, a producer of plastics for the automotive and electronics industries at the Leuna chemical complex in Saxony-Anhalt, is gradually shutting down production after failing to find an investor. The company reported an 80 percent increase in combined energy and raw material costs since filing for insolvency in June. Around 400 jobs are at risk.
Germany's energy-cost pressures are unfolding amid a major transformation of Europe's energy supply. Following the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine conflict, Germany reduced its reliance on Russian energy, while European countries increased imports of liquefied natural gas. Escalating tensions in the Middle East have added uncertainty to global energy markets.
For Germany, the task is to balance energy security, affordability and industrial competitiveness. Diversifying supplies and investing in cleaner energy can reduce exposure to fossil-fuel price shocks, but households and businesses must also cope with near-term costs. If energy prices remain high, companies may delay investment or cut production, while households may further reduce discretionary spending.
The pinch is already being felt in Manuela's home. During Germany's autumn school break, the family would customarily take their children abroad; this year, they have opted to stay put and squirrel away the savings for more pressing needs. ■

For the year ending June 2026, greenhouse gas emissions from industries and households fell 2.9 percent to 75,042 kilotons. S. Korea's corporate profitability hits 4-year high in 2025 amid widening polarization
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:36:26 CST
15:36:26 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's corporate profitability hit a four-year high last year on the back of strong performances in the semiconductor and shipbuilding sectors amid a widening polarization between large and small companies, central bank data showed Wednesday.
The average ratio of operating profit to revenue for 982,767 surveyed companies, including 187,804 manufacturers and 794,963 non-manufacturers, rose 0.6 percentage points from a year earlier to 5.2 percent in 2025, marking the highest profitability since 2021, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
The operating profit-to-sales ratio for manufacturers gained 1.2 percentage points to 6.3 percent, fueled by robust sales of high-value-added semiconductors and high-value vessels.
The ratio for non-manufacturers added 0.2 percentage points to 4.3 percent last year.
Despite the overall recovery, the gap between large conglomerates and smaller firms widened significantly.
The operating profit margin for large corporations climbed 1.1 percentage points to 6.7 percent in 2025, hitting the highest since 2021.
The margin for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) went down 0.2 percentage points to 2.8 percent, marking the lowest since the BOK began compiling the data in 2009.
Financial stability improved, with the overall debt-to-equity ratio sliding from 119.9 percent in 2024 to 116.2 percent in 2025, the lowest level since 2019.
However, top-line growth momentum slowed, with the overall revenue growth rate dropping 1.3 percentage points to 2.4 percent last year.
Manufacturing revenue growth decelerated from 4.6 percent in 2024 to 2.4 percent in 2025, and non-manufacturing growth slowed from 2.9 percent to 2.3 percent.
The interest coverage ratio, or the ratio of operating profit to financial expenses, advanced to 292.7 percent in 2025 from 244.1 percent in the previous year thanks to the enhanced operating profit margin.
Nevertheless, the proportion of financially vulnerable companies with the interest coverage ratio below 100 percent edged up 0.1 percentage points to 42.9 percent in 2025, reaching the highest since 2009.
It meant that nearly 43 percent of South Korean businesses failed to generate enough operating profit to cover the interest costs last year. ■

====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: A sweeter deal for Guangxi's sugarcane
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
14:36:09 CST
15:36:09 KST

NANNING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- The golden-yellow liquid carries a delicate fruity fragrance. A sip brings a tangy-sweet burst to the palate. Yet few would guess the vinegar beverage is made from sugarcane, as some companies in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region find new uses for a crop long associated with sugar production.
With a warm, humid climate well suited to sugarcane cultivation, Guangxi is China's largest sugarcane-growing base. The region has accounted for around 60 percent of the country's total sugar output for years.
Now, the value chain of the tall, jointed crop is evolving, with mechanized farming reshaping production and diverse products revealing its versatility.
Yu Caiku, 36, was walking between the rows of sugarcane in Guangxi's Laibin City. Leaves brushed against his body, making a soft rustle.
A sugarcane farmer himself, Yu also heads a farm machinery service cooperative in the city, providing mechanized farming services to more than 300 sugarcane-growing households each year, covering over 10,000 mu (about 667 hectares) of sugarcane fields.
After checking the condition of the sugarcane field, Yu opened an app on his phone to guide a drone, which took off and flew along a preset route, spraying pesticides over the field. "Manual spraying could cover only three to five mu per hour. Now, with the drone, we can spray hundreds of mu in a single morning," said Yu.
Changes are not limited to spraying. Laibin City has also introduced digital soil monitoring in some areas. By tailoring fertilizer application based on data collected on soil pH, moisture and nutrient levels, farmers have reduced fertilizer use by 15 percent per mu while increasing sugarcane yields by 200 kilograms per mu in some fields, said Wang Zeping, a researcher at the Guangxi Academy of Agricultural Sciences.
In the 2025-26 crushing season, Guangxi's sugarcane planting area reached 12.34 million mu, the highest in nearly a decade, the region's official data revealed.
The extensive sugarcane cultivation provides a backdrop for companies exploring new uses for the crop beyond sugar production. Vinegar-drink producer Haoqingchun offers one example.
Headquartered in the city of Chongzuo, where one-fifth of China's sugar is produced, the company focuses on sugarcane-based fermented beverages.
"The idea of developing fermented products, such as vinegar and beer, came from consumers' growing awareness of healthy eating and sugar intake," said Lu Mingshan, general manager of Haoqingchun Biotechnology Co., Ltd.
By combining traditional vinegar-making techniques with modern fermentation technology, the company reduces the sugar content of fresh local sugarcane juice during fermentation while retaining its iron content, according to Lu. He attributed the relatively high iron content of locally grown sugarcane to the reddish soil.
The refreshing vinegar drink has found a market not only in China but also overseas, including Vietnam and the Republic of Korea. Exports generated around 20 million yuan (about 3 million U.S. dollars) in 2025, accounting for roughly one-third of the company's total sales, Lu said.
Data show that Guangxi processed about 60.93 million tonnes of sugarcane in the 2025-26 crushing season, producing around 7.7 million tonnes of sugar, up about 19 percent year on year. Byproducts such as molasses and bagasse are used in various industries, forming a virtuous cycle.
In Chongzuo, over 200,000 tonnes of molasses are every year turned into high-activity dry yeast, yeast extracts and other products at the local branch of Angel Yeast, said Liu Peidong, assistant general manager of the branch. The products are sold in more than 160 countries and regions.
While in Laibin, an intelligent system at Guangxi Ecolink Technology Co., Ltd. automates the process of turning bagasse into smooth, cream-colored biodegradable tableware. Once fully operational, the project is expected to produce 100,000 tonnes of plant-fiber food containers and utensils annually, with a yearly output value of 1.5 billion yuan, said Zhu Min, deputy general manager of the company.
Elsewhere in Guangxi, bagasse is also used in papermaking and biomass power generation. The comprehensive utilization rate of bagasse and molasses in the region has reached 100 percent, according to a sugar industry development report from the regional government released in July.
Sugarcane-themed tourism is also taking root across Guangxi, creating new opportunities for local communities. In Buhua Village of Chongzuo's Xinhe Town, tourists are trying their hand at traditional sugar-making, stirring boiling sugarcane juice in a large pot with long wooden paddles. They can also take part in other activities, from sugarcane planting to the recycling and reuse of byproducts.
The town has developed a rural tourism area. In 2025, it attracted more than 500,000 visits and helped over 600 local households increase their annual income by an average of 2,000 yuan.
Getting more "sweetness" out of sugarcane reflects China's broader efforts to modernize the agriculture sector and unlock greater value from agricultural resources. The country's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) calls for strengthening agricultural science and technology, and promoting deeper integration of farming, processing and services in rural areas. ■

====================================================================================================

Global warming will breach 1.5°C – but deep, fast cuts can still bring it back
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
06:34:22 UTC
15:34:22 KST

Global warming will breach 1.5°C – but deep, fast cuts can still bring it back
With global temperature rise set to exceed 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, countries “must pull out all the stops” and urgently cut emissions to minimize the overshoot and return to the internationally agreed threshold by the end of this century.
The recommendation comes in the Emissions Gap Report 2026: The Point of Return, published on Wednesday by the UN Environment Programme (UNEP).
It outlines a “lowest possible” overshoot scenario in which peak warming by roughly mid-century is limited to 1.7 to 1.8°C.
Achieving this requires slashing emissions by 18 per cent by the end of the decade, 45 per cent by 2035, and 69 per cent five years later, compared with 2025 levels.
No surrender
“Overshoot is not surrender,” UN Secretary-General António Guterres said in a message accompanying the report. “We can still keep it as small and as short as possible – and bring temperatures back below 1.5 degrees by the end of the century.”
The report argues that there are more opportunities than ever to step up action.
Since adoption of the 2015 Paris Agreement on Climate Change, which set the 1.5-degree target, renewable energy has boomed, total energy supply from coal and oil has grown slower than projected and climate policies have cut emissions in many places.
UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen was clear about the cost of inaction.
“Every additional fraction of a degree and additional year of warming above 1.5°C increases climate impacts and risks, such as the deadly floods, heatwaves and wildfires that have plagued many nations this year,” she said.
“So, we must pull out all the stops to minimize peak warming and return to 1.5°C by the end of the century”, she added, stressing that “this is possible”.
Warmer planet, worse outcomes
If current policies continue, warming could reach 2.8°C within this century and increase thereafter, the report warned.
Under the Paris Agreement, countries are required to submit national climate action plans, or NDCs, and even if all are delivered and similar efforts continue, warming will be limited to 2.6°C.
These outcomes are worse than last year’s projections, the report said, due to the United States withdrawing from the climate deal and revised estimates of historical emissions.
Meanwhile, new NDCs submitted since the last emissions report have hardly made a difference.
Yet, returning to or below the 1.5 threshold can be done, particularly as evidence increasingly shows how climate policies have reduced emissions.
Take stock, take action
The report calls for accelerating implementation of goals outlined during the first-ever Global Stocktake (GST) – a process held from 2021 to 2023 to assess collective progress towards achieving the Paris Agreement.
These include:
- Tripling renewable energy capacity and doubling the annual rate of energy efficiency improvements by 2030
- Shifting away from fossil fuels in energy systems
- Reducing non-CO2 (carbon dioxide) emissions
- Halting and reversing deforestation and forest degradation
However, progress across most of these goals remains insufficient.
The second GST – which begins next month at the UN COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye – can build on this by reaffirming priority mitigation action areas, extending quantified goals to 2035 and 2040, and making existing action areas more tangible through clearer and, where possible, quantified targets.
The report sets out benchmarks that would have to be hit to be consistent with the lowest overshoot scenario.
For example, extending the goal on transitioning from fossil fuels would require reducing the share of coal, oil and gas in total energy supply by at least 55, 15 and five per cent respectively by 2035, relative to 2025 figures.
Reductions of at least 75, 30 and 35 per cent would be required in 2040.

What Accumulates? Lessons on Materiality, Memory, and Public Space from Amman Design Week 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

After a seven-year pause, Amman Design Week returned to Jordan with a premise that feels closely tied to the city itself: that nothing is ever entirely new. Under the theme "Accumulations," the fourth edition of the biennial event brought together more than 220 designers, makers, architects, and collectives across exhibitions, public interventions, talks, workshops, and performances from October 2 to 17. The premise was particularly relevant to Amman, a city whose architecture has been shaped by waves of construction, migration, adaptation, and reuse, where accumulation is not simply a metaphor.
Founded by Queen Rania Al Abdullah in 2016, Amman Design Week has developed into a platform connecting design practice with the wider cultural and urban life of Jordan. Its return comes under a new leadership structure, with architects Sarah Hejazin and Bisher Tabbaa, co-founders of the Jordanian architecture and design practice FADAA, serving as directors. Their appointment is significant not simply because it places architects at the center of the event's direction, but because FADAA's own practice is grounded in research into Jordan's cultural and material landscape.
The edition brought together an exhibition program curated by Faysal Tabbarah and a public program curated by Khaled Al-Bashir. Tabbarah, an architect, educator, and co-founder of Architecture + Other Things (A+OT), brings a research-driven interest in regional environments and place-based building practices. Al-Bashir, an architect, curator, researcher, and Arts and Culture Director at Darat al Funun, approaches the event through spatial, cultural, and political questions. The word "accumulations" is deliberately expansive. It refers to the way materials gather, but also to knowledge, labor, memory, social relationships, construction techniques, and everyday rituals. The exhibition framework asks how shared daily practices, material environments, and cultural memories accumulate to influence what people make, value, and live with.
Related Article
Amman Design Week 2026 Returns with "Accumulations," Exploring the Layers of Place, Material, and Memory
The program stretches across Ras El Ain, Jabal Al Lweibdeh, Jabal Amman, Iraq Al Amir, and Aqaba, giving the theme "Accumulations" a geographical dimension. At Qasr Al Abd in Iraq Al Amir, Dima Srouji's Natural Residents draws on historical accounts of the area's water abundance, while Kais Al Rawi and Julia Koerner's Lamella Series in Clay explores the possibilities of combining local clay with 3D-printing techniques. The program also extended to Aqaba through a collaboration with WUJŨD Art Foundation, bringing together works by bahraini-danish, NEW SOUTH, Tasneem Zraikat, and Yazeed Khaldoun Balqar.
This geographical spread became one of its most interesting propositions: if accumulation describes how a place is formed through layers of activity, memory, and material transformation, understanding it requires moving beyond the exhibition itself and encountering the city in which those layers have gathered. Rather than presenting the city's material and cultural histories as subjects contained within an exhibition, the event invited visitors to encounter them through the act of moving around Amman. The city became something to be read through its different layers, and the venues became points of entry into that reading.
Design for Aging, Decay, and Open-Ended Use
The idea of accumulation is introduced before visitors encounter any of the individual works. The main exhibition venue, the Hangar in Ras El Ain, is itself an example of the kind of layered history the edition asks audiences to consider. Built in the 1930s to house electricity generators during a period of rapid urban development, the industrial structure was later rehabilitated by TURATH: Architecture and Urban Design in collaboration with the Greater Amman Municipality. Its own history makes it an unusually appropriate setting for an exhibition about accumulation: the building has already passed through several economic, infrastructural, and cultural lives before becoming an exhibition space.
Inside, Laith Matarweh Studio for Architecture's "Al-Mastaba" and DA+SA's "Common Ground" approach continuity from different directions. Combining stone and concrete, "Al-Mastaba" is conceived as a future ruin, with gaps between its elements and gravel surrounding the structure anticipating the gradual emergence of vegetation. Weathering and ecological change become part of its intended life rather than evidence of its eventual failure. "Common Ground," meanwhile, uses modular blocks arranged on a grid to establish a setting for gathering without prescribing a single configuration or activity. One leaves room for material and ecological transformation; the other allows social use to shape the outcome, both questioning the expectation that design should determine a definitive result at the moment of completion. Also at the Hangar, Praxis's Infusing Green Infrastructure in Amman explores how everyday urban spaces, including a staircase, a park, and an undeveloped plot, might accommodate site-specific green infrastructure. Shifting from urban ecology to material knowledge and cultural memory, Abeer Seikaly's Uyun brings together wool spun by women in the Jordanian Badia and crocheted in Amman with recycled glass beads from Damascus, tracing the movement of materials and skills across places and generations.
Re-engaging the City's Existing Resources
The relationship between design and environmental resources extended beyond the Hangar, finding a more direct expression in interventions across the city. In a region where water scarcity, construction waste, and the pressures of urban growth are everyday realities, sustainability becomes difficult to discuss meaningfully without considering the particular materials and infrastructures through which people live. The projects that engaged these questions most directly were not necessarily those presenting a new technology, but those reconsidering the role of resources already present in the city.
At Paris Circle, FADAA's "A Brief Untaming" temporarily transformed a familiar roundabout through earth berms made from soil and stone salvaged from construction excavations, alongside mobile planters containing native flora and wild vegetation. By allowing landforms and planting to extend beyond the roundabout's formal boundaries, the intervention challenged the controlled appearance of conventional civic landscaping. Planting is often introduced into public space as a finished visual layer, expected to remain contained and subordinate to roads, sidewalks, and buildings. FADAA instead explored what might happen if vegetation and topography were allowed a less controlled presence, drawing attention to native ecologies and the relationship between urban development and natural habitats. The temporary nature of the installation gives the proposal an experimental quality, but it also leaves open the question of how such an approach might translate into longer-term public-space management.
EAST Architecture Studio's "Bracing Accumulations," installed at Darat Abu Adnan, addressed the similar relationship between existing resources and contemporary needs through a different scale of intervention. Working with a heritage house dating from the 1950s, the studio transformed its rooftop and facade into a system for collecting and redistributing rainwater. The building's existing fabric became the basis for an environmental infrastructure, connecting adaptive reuse to Jordan's long history of managing limited water resources. The distinction between these projects is productive. One works with excavated matter and native vegetation to reconsider a public landscape; the other adapts an existing building to participate in water management. Both move sustainability away from the level of an abstract aspiration and toward the conditions of a particular place. The venue also hosted part of the Nuzul, a birdhouse project curated by Faysal Tabbarah scattered across different venues, featuring works such as Dār Al ʿAwda by Mariam Arwa and Yasmine Mansour, Omar Darwish's Binayat Al-Douri, Jessica Azizeh and Yasmin Tams's In the Nectar of the Flower of Cities, and Nada Barqawi's Of Kin.
Designing for Existing Practice
Some of the edition's most revealing moments emerged where design encountered activities that already belonged to the city. In Ras El Ain Park, Civil Architecture's permanent installation "Folly" creates a shaded gathering place beneath a ceramic-tile canopy manufactured locally by Haswa. Small figures of people and animals placed along the roof introduce a degree of ambiguity, while the structure itself offers a straightforward public function: shelter and a place to pause among the trees. Nearby, Mohamad Nahleh's permanent installation Domes of the Rock brings architectural memory into the same everyday setting. Referencing Jerusalem's Dome of the Rock through a reduced-scale wooden and steel form integrated with seating and lighting, the work shifts a familiar architectural image away from the monumental context in which it is usually encountered.
At the Ash Shariah College Intersection in Jabal Al Lweibdeh, "Ard Al Sahn," a permanent intervention by Ziad Jamaleddine and Makram el Kadi of L.E.FT, with Iheb Guermazi and Beya Othmani, makes the relationship between design and existing practice even more tangible. Built using locally sourced stone waste, the intervention introduces a surface oriented toward the Qibla, with stone elements shaped to evoke prayer rugs. Across the intersection from the Shariah Mosque, the space has already begun to accommodate Friday prayers, when the mosque fills, and worshippers extend into the surrounding public realm.
What Accumulates, and What Comes Next?
Amman Design Week 2026 offered a way to consider design not as an isolated act of creation, but as part of a longer process shaped by cultural exchange, material knowledge, and changing ways of life. Across the program, existing buildings, overlooked resources, and everyday public spaces emerged not as remnants of the past, but as active starting points for new forms of use and interpretation. Accumulation, in this sense, is not simply about what a city retains, but how its inherited conditions can be reworked to accommodate changing needs while remaining connected to place.
The implications extend beyond the event, touching on how local knowledge and material traditions might inform contemporary building practices, and how design can leave room for future generations to adapt and reinterpret what they inherit. The interventions across Amman offered different ways of engaging with these questions, from reusing construction materials to creating spaces that respond to existing social practices. What accumulates, then, is never fixed: each intervention enters a longer history of making, inhabiting, and transforming the city, adding another layer to what is already there.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) urged supporters to vote in the Nov. 28 mayoral election after a poll released Tuesday showed him trailing DPP challenger Puma Shen (沈伯洋) by 17 percentage points.
The Taipei Trust in Democracy Association poll showed Shen with 50.3% support, compared with Chiang’s 33.3%. Shen led across all six of the city’s electoral districts, including Daan-Wenshan, a traditional stronghold of Chiang’s KMT, per CNA.
The results marked a sharp reversal from September, when Chiang led Shen by 41.7% to 40.5% in a survey by the same association, a gap within the poll’s margin of error. Since then, Shen’s support has risen by 9.8 percentage points, while Chiang’s has fallen by 8.4 points.
Shen also gained ground among voters without a party affiliation. His support among these voters reached 34.2%, up 8.3 percentage points from September.
However, the association’s estimates suggested a much closer race after accounting for voter turnout and past voting patterns. If voting were held now, the result could range from a 0.7-point victory for Chiang to a six-point win for Shen, depending on turnout, per Business Today.
Chiang said he would take every poll seriously and work harder to win over voters. He said different polling methods could produce different results and that his campaign would study the findings.
Chiang acknowledged that he had not expected the outcome. He said some supporters had become anxious about the race and that his team would step up publicity for his administration’s achievements, per TVBS News.
Chiang also defended his administration’s record, saying his four years in office had improved daily life for Taipei residents. He urged voters who approved of his performance to show their support at the ballot box and help spread his campaign message.
The survey interviewed 1,075 Taipei residents aged 20 and older by landline and mobile phone from Oct. 14 to 16. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points

Şimşek says algorithm traced gains from fund abuses

06:28:34 UTC
15:28:34 KST

Authorities have used an algorithm to identify those who profited from market abuse in troubled investment funds, Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek said, detailing efforts to recover money for investors.
The review covered the funds from their establishment through liquidation, Şimşek told a joint Bloomberg HT–Habertürk broadcast on Oct. 20.
Lists of those identified have been submitted to the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) and the Justice Ministry.
The two institutions are working with the Central Securities Depository (MKK).
A separate recovery account has been opened for each of the 131 funds, alongside a general repayment account, bringing the total to 132, he said.
Initial requests for voluntary repayments would target companies and individuals with at least 10 million Turkish Liras in inflation-adjusted gains.
Their possible involvement in market manipulation would be assessed, Şimşek said.
“If they do not return it voluntarily, the Justice Ministry will initiate legal proceedings,” he said.
Recovery efforts would also extend to the personal assets of managers, shareholders and others involved in coordinated wrongdoing, he said.
Authorities had largely identified the assets and passed the information to the TMSF and prosecutors.
Funds managed by Tera, Pusula and Atlas remained under extraordinary liquidation, Şimşek said.
Atlas’s owners were in talks with the institution overseeing liquidation and had expressed willingness to return assets removed from the funds.
Interim payments of up to 1 million liras would follow Parliament’s approval of the liquidation bill, depending on the resources available in each fund. Small investors and money market fund holders would receive priority.
The payments could cover around 390,000 accounts if sufficient resources were available, he said.
Investors would retain their claims to any remaining balances.
Şimşek said 66 of the 131 funds had completed ordinary liquidation.
He also outlined plans for stronger supervision and tougher penalties for market manipulation and insider trading, potentially transferring experienced tax inspectors to regulatory institutions. Implementation of existing fund guidelines would not be postponed.
Separately, Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz said efforts were continuing to recover unlawful gains and repay investors.
He cautioned against treating measures targeting troubled funds as restrictions on the wider market, saying funds operating within the rules accounted for more than 90 percent of the market.

Türkiye has welcomed Libya’s eastern-based House of Representatives’ unanimous approval of a 2019 maritime jurisdiction agreement, with President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and other officials describing the decision as a step toward strengthening bilateral ties and protecting mutual interests in the Mediterranean.
The Turkish Foreign Ministry said on Oct. 20 that the agreement, which has been in force since 2019, was based on international law and equity and safeguarded the rights and interests of both countries.
“Türkiye will continue working with all partners to promote trust, stability and peace in the Mediterranean basin,” the ministry said in a statement, reaffirming Ankara’s commitment to international law.
Libya’s House of Representatives approved the memorandum of understanding on Oct. 20, reversing its previous opposition to the deal and repealing a 2020 resolution rejecting the ratification of agreements signed with Türkiye.
The agreement was signed in November 2019 between Türkiye and Libya’s then-Government of National Accord to establish the boundaries of their respective maritime jurisdiction areas in the Mediterranean Sea.
Erdoğan welcomed the parliamentary decision on Oct. 21, telling a meeting of his ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) that he hoped it would prove beneficial.
Turkish officials also held talks with Libyan counterparts following the vote. Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan spoke by phone with Libyan Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibeh and Saddam Haftar, deputy commander of forces in eastern Libya, thanking them for the parliamentary decision, according to sources.
Ibrahim Kalın, head of Türkiye’s National Intelligence Organization, also met Dbeibeh in Tripoli to discuss efforts to maintain peace in Libya, unify the country’s eastern and western administrations and military forces and preserve its territorial integrity, reports said.
Kalın said Türkiye was ready to support efforts to unify Libya’s institutions and urged all parties to prioritize the country’s future and territorial integrity. Dbeibeh expressed appreciation for Türkiye’s efforts to support Libya’s security and said his government was ready to work with Ankara to protect the country’s unity.
Libyan officials from both the country’s eastern and western political camps welcomed the vote, describing it as an opportunity to strengthen ties with Türkiye and protect Libya’s maritime and economic interests.
Haftar said the agreement could open opportunities for greater cooperation, investment and a long-term partnership with Türkiye. He said Libya’s national interests, sovereignty and territorial integrity should guide its foreign relations.
Libya’s Foreign Ministry, operating under the Tripoli-based government, also welcomed the decision, saying it would strengthen bilateral cooperation and contribute to stability in the Mediterranean.
Türkiye’s Communications Director Burhanettin Duran described the approval as an important development for bilateral relations and the eastern Mediterranean. He said the agreement would help protect the countries’ shared interests and support regional cooperation.
AKP spokesperson Ömer Çelik said the vote affirmed what he described as Türkiye’s historical and legal rights in the region. He said Ankara would continue to defend its interests and those of Libya while supporting a regional order based on fairness and cooperation.
The agreement has long been a point of contention in the eastern Mediterranean, where overlapping maritime claims have fueled disputes over jurisdiction and access to resources. Its approval by Libya’s eastern-based parliament marks a shift in the legislature’s position on the 2019 deal.

Who owns India’s textile traditions in age of AI-enabled mass production?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
06:22:04 UTC
15:22:04 KST

Who owns India’s textile traditions in age of AI-enabled mass production?
Technological tools meant to preserve a craft are now able to digitally reproduce it without involving the craftsperson.
Bitupan Deka was out shopping for a “gamusa” (traditional scarf) with his mother in India’s northeastern state of Meghalaya when he noticed something unusual.
“Every shop selling the scarf had the same handful of patterns repeated over and over,” he told Al Jazeera over the telephone from Shillong, the capital of Meghalaya.
“When I asked around, I found that weavers in Sualkuchi [district in neighbouring Assam state] are paid a one-time fee of roughly 2,000 rupees [$21] for each design they develop, instead of royalties. Cutting down the number of designs they produce was a cost-saving practice followed by the manufacturers.”
This discovery prompted Deka, an assistant professor of computer technology at Shillong’s MIT University, to create a system that can produce infinite new designs for such fabrics.
“My work isn’t meant to replace the traditional designers. I hope, instead, that it will become a tool in their hands to create new and modern motifs more easily, so the consumers can have variety,” Deka said.
Once the patent, which is being applied for under the research and development department of his university, comes through, Deka plans to monetise the system by making it a commercial designing service that the textile industry can avail.
In India’s varied textile traditions, patterns and motifs carry the memory of a place and the mythology of its people – sometimes even the history of migrations.
The designs are imagined by weavers from things that exist around them, and then painted with locally available colours, mostly using carved clay and wooden frames. These weavers do not simply reproduce a pattern; they inherit it. Their hands hesitate where their grandmother’s did, and they know why a particular flower must face left.
A computer has no such inheritance or hesitation. It learns by analysing pictures and repeating them in endless variations. And yet, as Deka’s system shows, the computer can now draw and weave the same flower.
The Rekh Sanganeri Dataset is a similar system developed for hand-block printed Sanganeri textiles from the western Indian state of Rajasthan. It includes high-resolution images of printed patterns, annotated down to ink bleed and slight misalignment – the imperfections that are the hallmark of the handmade work.
Its developer, Reddy Sai Nivas C, says it should be used as a resource for research and art, not as a substitute for artisans.
But the disclaimer is the paradox: Tools built to preserve a craft are making its visual language easier to digitally reproduce without involving the craftsperson.
Dinesh Chhipa comes from one of the oldest Chhipa families, an artisan and merchant caste renowned for dyeing and block printing. He is a Bagru designer – a block printing technique from Bagru town in the western state of Rajasthan – and a textile businessman.
“Traditional craft is slow to produce. Even if someone offered us a fortune, we wouldn’t be able to produce these pieces in mass numbers, so I don’t fault those using digital technology and AI to fill the gap,” he told Al Jazeera.
“But don’t borrow craft and regional names like Bagru and Jaipuri [named after the capital city of Rajasthan]. These designs and motifs were born out of a culture and necessities of the communities they come from.”
Who owns culture when it turns into plain data?
India has been digitising its textile memory for years – from the Botanical Survey of India’s historical collections to the Bharatiya Vastra Shilpa Kosh, a national portal built by the state-run National Institute of Fashion Technology and the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC).
Without documentation, the fragile traditions and knowledge could disappear. But digitisation also allows the same archive to be used by an AI system seeking to reproduce these crafts at scale.
At the India AI Impact Summit in New Delhi in February this year, Indian software company Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) showcased Bridgital Loom, an AI system that converts textile designs into loom-ready instructions. LED lights on the loom guide a weaver through the thread sequences of intricate Banarasi and Kanchipuram patterns – named after the cities where these iconic arts grew.
TCS says the technology helps weavers execute complex designs faster and with fewer errors, and is meant to be a bridge between the artisans and technology. A pilot project that uses the loom is already under way at Kanchipuram, a town in southern Tamil Nadu state.
In an interview with the online platform Digit at the New Delhi summit, the head of AI strategy at Bridgital Loom, Muthulakshmi Nellaiappan, pointed out that a new weaver takes more than 15 years to master the art.
“With the technologies we have in hand … the younger weaver who has just entered the skill can become a master much sooner,” she said.
Technology flattens the master-apprentice hierarchy of traditional knowledge systems. The weaver no longer has to conceptualise or remember patterns, colours and codes; he blindly follows the machine’s instructions, handing creativity and memory to AI.
Nellaiappan said that since a large percentage of India’s looms are non-electronic, TCS has ensured its system works with handlooms as well and that it was essential for scaling up the technology.
But digital looms also raise another question: Who owns culture when it turns into plain data?
For generations, India’s textile knowledge sat outside intellectual property systems. It lived in community memory, passed from master to apprentice with no certificate of ownership. Kanchipuram, Mekhela-Sador, Sanganeri and Banarasi are names for places that these textiles helped shape, not merely emerged from.
Now, this knowledge is entering generative models that owe nothing to these traditions.
For designers and manufacturers, the possibilities are seductive: Motifs combined at will, colours changed with a command, and thousands of designs generated instantly. The machine offers abundance.
The artisan, on the other hand, has always lived with scarcity: Of money, bargaining power, or recognition.
Ananthalakshmi Vadivel, a third-generation weaver and owner of Vadivel Silk Looms in Kanchipuram, says their venture is already competing in the market with cheaper Kanchipuram sarees produced on electronic looms.
“Perhaps, with AI, these sellers can create trending designs faster and cheaper to attract mass consumers. But these imitations can never replace the original,” she told Al Jazeera.
“There will always be a market for authentic Kanchipuram and handcrafted textiles, no matter how much technology makes the imitation cheaper. True Kanchipuram weave, colour, and designs can only be created by hand, and discerning buyers know this.”
Then again, the question is no longer whether AI can recreate a textile. It sure can. The question is: Who gets paid when it does?
Legal gaps
In December 2025, the federal government’s Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade floated a statutory “blanket licence” – a system where AI developers could train models on lawfully obtained copyrighted material without seeking permission from each rights holder. Once commercialised, those systems would owe royalties to copyright owners at rates set by the government.
But intellectual property (IP) laws assume a traceable work with a traceable author. A motif, on the other hand, is communal property, its technique passed down through generations with no single originator.
In such cases, who is entitled to royalty and copyright? The artisan who first created the design? The photographer who documented it? The researcher who assembled the dataset? The developer who built the tool? India’s laws offer no clear answers. The artisan whose name never appeared on a label may once again be missing from the paperwork.
Meanwhile, the government is planning a dedicated AI-handloom research department under the Centre of Excellence for Handloom Technology at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) in the capital, New Delhi. Inaugurated in August, the $1.4m facility aims to modernise India’s handloom sector by combining traditional weaving heritage with contemporary technology.
The government also plans to register thousands of weavers and fit their handlooms with sensors that convert weave patterns into digital data, and issue QR-coded tags to trace provenance. Maharashtra’s Vingatha system does something similar at the state level by authenticating handloom sarees such as Paithani and Karvat Kathi.
The idea is simple: If a saree can tell you where it came from, the person who made it becomes harder to erase.
While these measures cannot stop AI-enabled design and mass production, they may give artisans more visibility and turn each piece into an archive.
‘Cannot separate names from community’
In art galleries, the traditional textiles are increasingly shedding the label of craft for the more lucrative category of contemporary art.
Gurjeet Singh, an artist from Chandigarh city, recently hosted a textile-based solo show in New York. His work transforms discarded fabrics, buttons and embroidered scraps into sculptures that explore queer identity and social prejudices surrounding gender and sexuality.
Sayan Chanda, an Indian artist based in London, works with cut and rewoven vintage Bengali quilts to question fixed notions of cultural belonging. Gurugram-based artist Sumakshi Singh uses delicate embroidery and suspended thread structures to reconstruct the architectural fragments of vanished homes, gardens and personal histories. There are many more.
In New Delhi, 20 such artisans and craft-led collectives featured last month at an art show celebrating the traditional textile crafts.
“Our aim is to present these traditional crafts as living practices that continue to evolve through contemporary artisans, rather than as heritage to be archived. Kanmai Payun, one of the artists featured in the show, for example, is the last practitioner of Fulor Saneki, a flower pattern used by Assamese weavers. We encouraged her to teach her 17-year-old son so the craft outlives her,” Aparupa Ray Ganguly, the curator of the show, told Al Jazeera.
But as textiles gain value in art galleries, their makers do not necessarily gain automatic control over their work.
In April, another art exhibition in New Delhi, titled No ‘One’ Maker, saw artisans missing from the show’s preview, exposing how traditional textiles are aestheticised, but the people who carry that knowledge remain unrecognised.
“You cannot separate the names from the community. Call your mass-produced work digital prints and leave the traditional names to the original artisans,” says Chhipa, the artisan and merchant from Rajasthan.

Terracotta warriors were mainly built by women and children, batch fingerprints show
Qin dynasty artisans included women and children assigned to pottery crafting, legal records and physical evidence show
3-MIN READ3-MIN
1
 Listen
Some 5 metres (16.4 feet) underground near one of China’s oldest cities lies the life-size army of thousands of terracotta warriors.
The purpose of the army, located 35km (22 miles) northeast of historic Xian, was to protect China’s first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, in the afterlife. The Terracotta Army was buried with him after his death in 210BC.
Now, a new study shows that a portion of the terracotta warriors was largely made by adult women and minors, not solely by men as previously thought.
“These findings challenge the long-held assumption that Terracotta Army production relied exclusively on adult male labour, providing the first quantitative biological evidence for a diverse workforce including women and children,” Shen Jingyi wrote in the paper published on October 13 in the peer-reviewed Journal of Cultural Heritage.

Turkish space technology company Fergani successfully deployed its sixth test satellite, FRG-100D4, into orbit as part of SpaceX's Bandwagon-5 mission, manufacturer Baykar announced.
The satellite separated from the launch vehicle approximately 63 minutes after liftoff and reached its target orbit at an altitude of 590 kilometers (367 miles) at 3.07 pm local time, according to a statement from Baykar.

The Federation of Trade Unions will be able to seek a review of the law on workplace safety even after it enters into force, a lawyer says
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
09:13:24 EEST
15:13:24 KST

The Federation of Trade Unions will be able to seek a review of the law on workplace safety even after it enters into force, a lawyer says
Kyiv • UNN
Even after the law enters into force, trade unions will be able to promote amendments to it and use legal mechanisms to protect workers.
The Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine will be able to continue seeking a review of the controversial provisions of the law on the safety of employees at work, even if it enters into force in its current wording. Legislative mechanisms are provided for this purpose, and where there are sufficient grounds, constitutional review and judicial protection are also available. Lawyer and founder of LLC "Law Firm \"LOGIC\"" Valeriia Odyntsova said this in an exclusive comment to UNN.
Why the FPU is demanding a review of the law
On October 12, the Verkhovna Rada adopted Bill No. 10147, "On the Safety and Health of Employees at Work," in its second reading. However, Serhii Byzov, head of the Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine, said that the bill passed by parliament contains provisions that could weaken employee protection. According to him, this concerns risks to workplace safety, compensation for victims, and social guarantees for people working in difficult and hazardous conditions.
On October 19, the Joint Representative Body of Trade Union Associations appealed to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, asking him to veto the law.
How trade unions can secure amendments to the law
If the law enters into force without amendments, trade unions will be able to promote its review through the Verkhovna Rada. To do so, they can prepare proposals concerning the controversial provisions and approach members of parliament, the relevant committee, or the Cabinet of Ministers.
Trade unions do not have the right of legislative initiative, but they may participate in discussions of legislative amendments, submit expert opinions, and seek to have their position taken into account. This mechanism makes it possible to amend or repeal individual provisions even in the absence of grounds for declaring them unconstitutional
According to her, another avenue is to initiate a review of the controversial provisions for compliance with the Constitution of Ukraine. In particular, this concerns Article 22, which prohibits narrowing the content and scope of existing rights and freedoms when adopting new laws or amending existing ones.
At the same time, trade unions do not have the right to independently apply to the Constitutional Court of Ukraine with a constitutional submission concerning the law. However, they may approach the authorized entities designated in Article 150 of the Constitution of Ukraine, including members of parliament of Ukraine, the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, or the Supreme Court, with a proposal to initiate a review of the relevant provisions
She also recalled the mechanism of a constitutional complaint. However, it has clearly defined conditions for application: in particular, the challenged provision of the law must have been applied in a final court decision in the case of the person applying to the Constitutional Court. Therefore, trade unions cannot use this mechanism to challenge the law abstractly in the interests of all employees.
According to Valeriia Odyntsova, if application of the law results in violations of labor rights, trade unions will be able to defend the interests of their members through the courts. Depending on the circumstances, this may involve challenging unlawful actions by an employer, recovering payments due, or restoring violated rights.
In addition, where there are sufficient grounds, trade unions may use international mechanisms for monitoring compliance with labor standards, including the procedures of the International Labour Organization.
Thus, the entry into force of Law No. 10147 will not deprive trade unions of the opportunity to demand a review of its provisions. At the same time, legislative procedure will be the primary mechanism for changing rules that narrow employees’ rights and social guarantees, while in cases of well-founded doubts about their constitutionality or an actual violation of rights, the relevant mechanisms of constitutional review and judicial protection may be used

Australia at 'crossroads' as police warn of 'tsunami' of radicalisation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
06:09:13 UTC
15:09:13 KST

Australia at 'crossroads' as police warn of 'tsunami' of youth radicalisation online
In short:
Police are warning of an incoming "tsunami" of radicalisation among young Australians.
Senior officials have told a parliamentary inquiry that children and teenagers are being radicalised faster than ever before.
What's next?
Police are considering proposing an expansion of their powers to allow officers to more actively disrupt harmful online chat groups.
Australia is at a "crossroads" and facing a "tsunami of youth crime", with police warning vulnerable children as young as 11 are being radicalised online at unprecedented speed, including a boy who allegedly planned a school shooting.
Acting Australian Federal Police (AFP) Deputy Commissioner Sandra Booth told a parliamentary inquiry the radicalisation of young people, which used to take "months or years", was now happening "within days".
She described an online world in which children were being targeted by "sadistic" predators, pointing to the case of a 13-year-old boy charged after police allegedly found a notebook at his home outlining plans to shoot classmates.
"This was not in the US. This was in Australia,"
Deputy Commissioner Booth said.
In another case, police charged an Australian teenager over child abuse material offences after alleging he joined a sadistic online network and requested his handle be written on a baby's face while the infant was forced to vape.
Speaking to the Joint Parliamentary Committee on Intelligence and Security (JPCIS), the AFP attributed the rapid escalation to artificial intelligence, a growing grievance generation, and "young people searching for purpose and belonging, and the sophistication of these online networks".
She said predators often turned "desperate victims into perpetrators".
"For example, youth are recording or live streaming animal crushing, physically or sexually assaulting their siblings to escape the hold their blackmailers have over them," she said.
"They think if they do what they are being asked, they will no longer be targeted".
Since 2020, counter-terrorism authorities have targeted 65 children aged between 12 and 17, with 35 of those investigations resulting in charges.
ASIO boss Mike Burgess has repeatedly said Australia faces an "unprecedented" threat environment, saying that while the national terrorism threat level remained at "probable", the overall security landscape justified describing the threat as unprecedented.
ASIO Deputy Director-General Claire McGinnis said the agency's counter-terrorism caseload was getting younger, with Home Affairs later confirming an 11-year-old child had taken part in a de-radicalisation program.
Children use AI bots to plan attacks
The inquiry heard potential offenders were using AI chatbots to research and plan attacks.
Ms McGinnis said while there was no single factor that made young people susceptible to extremism, the fact many were digital natives made them more susceptible.
"[An AI chatbot] can bypass hours of work, for example, making attack planning more efficient,"
Ms McGinnis said.
Encrypted apps were also an "enduring challenge" for ASIO, she said, because they "enabled anonymity".
"Privacy is obviously very important but should not be absolute when we're dealing with significant threats," she said.
Police want powers to disrupt online chat rooms
Acting Deputy Commissioner Sandra Booth said the AFP was considering proposing an expansion of its powers to allow officers to more actively disrupt harmful online chat groups, including by posting messages which alert users that police are present.
Ms Booth said police were keen to explore ways to move beyond merely monitoring extremist content online.
"We do want to scope out how we can move forward from just covertly accepting violent extremist communications to more overtly interrupting chat groups and websites where youth are being radicalised," she said.
The inquiry also heard concerns that some young people who completed behaviour-change and de-radicalisation programs later returned to extremist ideologies.
Representatives from the Department of Home Affairs said most referrals to de-radicalisation programs come from law enforcement agencies.
"I think that tells us we are picking too many people up too late in the piece,"
Home Affairs counter-terrorism coordinator Brendan Dowling said.
"What we look to in the future is to have people identified earlier in the process by parents, by educators, by bystanders."
He said young people entering de-radicalisation programs often did not fit traditional perceptions of violent extremists.
"Radicalised young people often do not look like what our community imagines," he said.

L3Harris opens plant to double GMLRS rocket motor output
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
06:09:00 UTC
15:09:00 KST

- L3Harris opened a solid rocket motor plant in Camden, Arkansas, designed to double motor production for the U.S. Army’s GMLRS rockets.
- The site is funded under a $216 million Defense Production Act agreement signed with the Department of War in 2023.
L3Harris Technologies opened a new solid rocket motor plant in Camden, Arkansas, on Oct. 20 that is built to double its production of motors for the U.S. Army’s Guided Multiple Launch Rocket System, the company said in a statement. GMLRS is the precision rocket fired from HIMARS and M270 launchers, and the new site, which L3Harris calls an “Arsenal of Freedom” facility, brings motor production for the weapon under one roof with room to expand further.
The company told Defense Daily the plant can turn out one rocket motor every nine minutes and will cut manufacturing lead time in half. L3Harris says it has already more than doubled GMLRS motor output in recent years, a growth driven by demand since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, where the rocket has been used heavily, and by a growing list of HIMARS buyers.
“Rocket propulsion is a vital national security capability. This state-of-the-art facility enhances L3Harris’ capabilities and represents a critical leap forward in solid rocket motor production capacity, ensuring the joint forces and our allies maintain a resilient, responsive, and secure supply chain for precision munitions to support our warfighters,” said Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment Michael P. Duffey.
The plant is the latest piece of a $216 million Defense Production Act Title III cooperative agreement that L3Harris signed with the Department of War in 2023 to raise output of tactical missile motors for Javelin, Stinger and GMLRS. The agreement also funds new buildings at the company’s Orange County, Virginia, site and equipment and digital upgrades in Huntsville, Alabama.
Work for the Camden line is already lined up. On Oct. 12, L3Harris won a $250 million follow-on contract from Lockheed Martin for standard-range GMLRS motors, which the company called the largest quantity ordered in the program’s history, as we reported last week. Lockheed Martin is the prime contractor and assembles the rockets in Camden, while L3Harris supplies the motor, the electronic safe-and-arm device and the proximity sensor.
“The opening of this state-of-the-art facility marks a major step forward in strengthening the solid rocket motor industrial base our nation and its allies urgently need,” said Ken Bedingfield, president of L3Harris Missile Solutions.
L3Harris became one of the main U.S. solid rocket motor suppliers when it bought Aerojet Rocketdyne in 2023, and Camden is now its largest construction site. Besides the GMLRS plant, the company is building the Arkansas Advanced Propulsion Facilities campus and two new facilities for PAC-3 interceptor propulsion there. Across Arkansas, California, Virginia and Alabama, L3Harris says it is investing billions to build about 60 new facilities, with the aim of doubling, tripling and in some programs quadrupling propulsion output.
Demand for the rocket keeps climbing: in August, the U.S. Army issued a Sources Sought notice for 133,014 GMLRS rockets by 2034, or about 19,000 a year from 2028, Defense News reported, while Lockheed Martin is ramping up toward 14,000 rockets a year.
Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, who attended the ribbon-cutting, said L3Harris will soon begin producing motors at the new facility.

Tokyo Container Terminal is seen in Tokyo, Feb. 19, 2025. (AP File Photo)
Japan’s trade deficit reached 2.81 trillion yen ($17.8 billion) for the first fiscal half, according to government data released on Oct. 21, as the war in Iran sent oil import prices soaring.
The Finance Ministry’s preliminary data showed that Japan’s exports for the April-September period grew 18.4 percent from the same period the previous year to 63.5 trillion yen, while imports soared to 66.3 trillion yen, up 20.4 percent year-over-year.
Both were record highs for Japan. The soaring price of oil affects a wide range of sectors, including plastic goods and shipping costs.
Resource-poor Japan imports virtually all its oil and has relied on access to the Strait of Hormuz in the Middle East for its oil shipments. That’s now basically blocked, and Japan has had to pay more to get shipments from other routes.
Brent crude, the international standard, has soared from $70 a barrel in February to about $100 a barrel lately, after shooting up to above $110 a barrel in recent months. Analysts say prices are unlikely to ease soon.
For the month of September, Japan’s trade deficit totaled 536.6 billion yen, marking the fifth month of deficits, but down from 1.1 trillion yen in August.
Japan’s September imports grew 18.9 percent from the previous year, while exports rose 16.7 percent.
One sore point is the weakening yen, which drives up the cost of imports. The U.S. dollar is lately trading at 150-yen levels.

Europe weighs giving utilities, infrastructure companies more powers to bring down drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
06:06:21 UTC
15:06:21 KST

Europe weighs giving utilities, infrastructure companies more powers to bring down drones
Oct 21 - At a former flight-test base south of Paris, drones swoop over fields and woodland as teams on the ground test systems designed to stop them — a response to a growing wave of drone incursions and "hybrid attacks" since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.
The potential clients for technology such as electronic jammers and interceptor drones tested at the Brétigny-sur-Orge site are no longer just governments, police and armies.
Private firms and state entities across Europe that operate critical infrastructure want to strengthen their defences, with some utilities asking for authorisation to shoot drones down themselves. From Paris to Berlin, governments are taking note.
They are worried that hybrid warfare or a drone attack could knock out power to millions of people — as has happened frequently in Ukraine after Russian strikes.
"It is a theoretical, and increasingly a practical, possibility that there could be heating outages this winter due to hybrid attacks," Kristian Ruby, secretary general of European energy body Eurelectric, told Reuters.
Some European governments are responding by starting to give firms powers traditionally confined to the military. Interviews by Reuters with over 30 company executives, officials and drone experts meanwhile show the technology to detect and bring down drones is maturing faster than the rules on who may use it.
Approaches vary widely across Europe and legal uncertainties remain, including over who has the right to order a response to a drone threat. Bringing down a drone could cause injury or death to people on the ground or damage property, raising questions for companies about liability and accountability.
'DEFENCELESS'
France is among countries that have led the way. Its parliament passed a law in August allowing approved operators of critical infrastructure and contractors to detect, jam and shoot down drones near designated facilities.
The law passed by the French parliament in August responded to a wave of drone incursions over critical and military sites, including flights over the Ile Longue nuclear submarine base near Brest in northwestern France in December 2025.
France wants a newly expanded list of sensitive sites deemed of vital importance equipped by 2027, a senior French official involved in the plans told Reuters, asking not to be named because details of the plan are not yet public.
"We were defenceless in the face of the (drone) threat," the official said, adding that concerns had been growing over the last decade as unmanned aerial vehicles became more accessible and more common.
The French government wants to give operators of critical infrastructure such as state-owned utility company EDF and state-owned railway company SNCF a catalogue of approved systems ranging from electronic jammers to interceptor drones, depending on different environments and situations.
Confirming important elements of the plan outlined by the French official, Systematic Paris-Region, which runs the government testing programme at Brétigny-sur-Orge, said evaluations launched this summer had so far catalogued three systems integrators — which combine different computer systems into a unified whole — and 17 counter-drone systems.
It said assessments were continuing and work was under way to accelerate procurement from among those solutions.
France's defence ministry said the law passed in August would help strengthen capabilities to counter the threat, though it said it could speak only for the critical infrastructure under its authority. EDF and SNCF declined comment.
WHO CAN BRING DOWN A DRONE?
The discovery of an explosives-laden drone near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany's Leipzig/Halle airport in August underlined how far the risks have spread.
Germany blamed Russia for the incident. Moscow denied it was behind it, and has repeatedly denied carrying out hybrid attacks in Europe, many of which have been in countries that support Kyiv in Russia's war in Ukraine.
But concerns are growing that national authorities cannot respond fast enough to protect widely dispersed infrastructure against such attacks, and that the damage caused by relatively cheap drones could bring hefty repair costs.
In Germany, where counter-drone operations remain a policing function, the interior ministry told Reuters it was reviewing how critical infrastructure operators and third parties could be legally involved in active counter-drone measures.
In September, Austria announced plans to give similar powers to critical infrastructure operators, including large energy firms. Defence Minister Klaudia Tanner told a press conference that the state could not protect every site on its own.
Poland has gone further. Operators told Reuters they have deployed counter-drone systems and trained with military and police units. Drone-restricted zones have been established around critical energy infrastructure, and designated security units working for operators have been authorised to destroy, disable or take control of drones entering them.
But two sources at energy transmission companies on NATO's eastern flank told Reuters that effective intervention still requires more assurances, and perhaps a judicial precedent, on who bears responsibility for collateral damage.
Without that certainty, they said, operators of critical infrastructure could remain reluctant to neutralise drones because bringing one down could itself cause injury or costly damage.
BUILT FOR RECOVERY
Having powers to bring down drones would be a change of approach for companies across Europe.
Executives, officials and energy analysts told Reuters that utilities have spent years hardening networks and preparing to restore disrupted services, rather than preventing attacks.
Leonhard Birnbaum, chief executive of German energy firm E.ON, said in September that operators must assume some attacks will succeed, rather than plan on stopping all of them. The company operates about 2,720 substations across Germany, he said.
Lithuania is building a fortified substation near its border with Russia as part of plans by the Baltic states and Poland to improve their defences that include constructing bunkers, installing anti-drone nets and building up stocks of hard-to-replace equipment for critical parts of the energy grid.
Poland's state-owned transmission operator PSE patrols parts of its about 16,500-km (10,250-mile) high-voltage network by helicopter and is preparing more powerful aircraft to help protect an undersea power link to Sweden.
Yet relatively inexpensive drones are challenging such defences. Essential equipment such as large transformers can take years to replace, while even a successful repair can leave infrastructure out of service for months.
Not all utility operators are seeking a bigger role in defending themselves.
Asta Sihvonen-Punkka, chief executive of Finland's national power grid operator Fingrid, told Reuters that responsibility for countering threats around critical infrastructure should remain with Finnish authorities and armed forces.
Any move to give such powers to utility operators would be "a very, very big change" requiring careful legal consideration, she said.
Jari Stenius, head of security of Finnish utility Fortum, said he was content for energy companies to focus on producing energy while police and military authorities handled security threats.
TECHNOLOGY READY, RULES ARE NOT
Security officials and counter-drone technology firms say systems are becoming increasingly automated because operators cannot station specialist teams at every site.
Modern counter-drone systems combine sensors, command-and-control software and countermeasures into a single chain designed to identify, classify and respond to threats within seconds.
Several companies told Reuters that uncertainty over who can authorise a response has slowed investment in the latter stages of that process. France is therefore trying to automate the process as much as possible, said the senior French official involved in France's plans.
The official said security workers at utilities should eventually be able to detect a threat and launch an automated response at the press of a button, because having operators trained to use military-grade solutions at every location was unrealistic.
German defence company Rheinmetall told Reuters the biggest hurdle for civilian operators was often the delay between detecting a drone and deciding whether to deploy a countermeasure, as legal responsibilities remain fragmented.
Rheinmetall said interest from private infrastructure operators in counter-drone systems was rising sharply.
The company said it was conducting workshops, site surveys and infrastructure assessments for operators and was preparing for what it described as a "very fast-growing" market segment. REUTERS

Nigeria's government said on Tuesday there was a case of Ebola in the capital, Abuja, after laboratory tests confirmed the viral infection.

"She is in isolation, and she is receiving quality medical care. Contact tracing has been conducted, and it's under way as we speak, with 44 contacts already identified," Pate told public broadcaster NTA.

Pate said in a statement that the patient had been admitted to a private hospital in Abuja, where she had received care for several days before the diagnosis was confirmed.
"Nigeria successfully contained Ebola in 2014, and we have the experience and public health systems to respond to this case," the minister said in the statement.
An Ebola outbreak was declared in the Democratic Republic of Congo in mid-May and has since grown into the world'ssecond-largestoutbreak ever, caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain.
Uganda declared Ebola-free in August

Kenya has reported nine Ebola cases this month, all linked to a person who had traveled from Congo.
Africa's top public health agency has started mobilizing support for Nigeria, said its head, Jean Kaseya.
"This Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak has already become the most geographically extensive in history, affecting ... countries spread across three regions of Africa," Kaseya said in a post on X.

The IDF's Southern Command, Israel Air Force, Military Intelligence Directorate, and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) are preparing for a range of potential threats originating from the Gaza Strip ahead of the election.
These scenarios include rocket launches, attacks on IDF positions along the Yellow Line, and infiltration attempts targeting military outposts along both the Yellow Line and the Hourglass Fence on the international border.
Security officials are concerned that such operations could be intended to disrupt Israel's public agenda ahead of the vote.
In response, Maj.-Gen. Itzik Cohen, head of the IDF Operations Directorate, has ordered reinforcements across air, sea, and ground operations in the coming days.
The reinforcements will include special forces units positioned as rapid-response and reserve forces, with the aim of preventing a surprise attack similar to the October 7 massacre.
Security officials acknowledged that intelligence coverage remains incomplete, emphasizing that the military is taking precautions across all operational domains to minimize the risk of an unexpected attack.
As part of these preparations, the IDF has examined potential vulnerabilities and areas where terrain or other conditions could limit surveillance capabilities.
Additional ambush positions and defensive measures are being prepared in these locations to strengthen the military's readiness ahead of the election.

WSJ: Elon Musk personally ordered Starlink restrictions for Ukraine
The Wall Street Journal has written that Elon Musk ordered the speed of the military version of Starlink to be reduced in Ukraine, leaving some Ukrainian attack and interceptor drones practically unusable.
Source: The Wall Street Journal, citing sources
Details: The WSJ noted that both Musk and US President Donald Trump have expressed dissatisfaction with Ukraine over its strikes on Russian oil refineries in recent weeks. Trump sees these attacks as a reason for high energy prices.
Sources told the WSJ that Musk was behind the restriction of the speed at which Ukrainian equipment could connect to the satellite network last week, rendering some attack and interceptor drones practically useless.
Two sources said Musk and Trump had discussed the decision on Starlink during a phone call shortly after news of the speed restrictions became public.
One source also claimed that Musk and Trump had discussed the issue even before the decision to restrict Starlink speeds was made.
Public complaints by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said Ukrainians could die if unrestricted access to the service was not restored, led to widespread confusion over who had ordered the speed reduction and an unofficial investigation at the White House.
According to the sources, as the controversy unfolded, SpaceX representatives contacted their counterparts at the White House in an attempt to reach a common understanding and issue a joint statement saying that the company and Trump's administration had coordinated their actions before Musk issued the order.
Hours after news of the speed reduction became public, Musk wrote on X (Twitter): "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," using the acronym for president of the United States.
Trump told journalists on 19 October that he did not know who was responsible for reducing Starlink speeds, "but I would like to find out".
Some US officials claim that Musk had acted unilaterally and that Trump had not specifically ordered any retaliatory measures against Ukraine.
However, a source familiar with the situation said Musk had spoken to several administration officials, including Trump, before introducing the new speed restriction. Ukrainian officials said the restriction had allowed Russian missiles to bypass their air defence systems.
Background:
- Reuters reported earlier that the order to restrict Starshield, a satellite system Ukraine uses for battlefield communications and to control interceptor drones, came directly from the White House.
- US Republican Senator Thom Tillis is seeking an investigation into the Pentagon's actions with regard to problems with Starlink satellite communications systems encountered by the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
