Britain sends Typhoons to guard Saudi cities from Houthis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
06:01:24 UTC
15:01:24 KST

- Britain will deploy Royal Air Force Typhoon jets to Saudi Arabia to intercept Houthi missiles and drones, without striking targets inside Yemen.
- The UK already supports Saudi Arabia with a Voyager refueling tanker, air defense equipment and personnel, and is extending the tanker mission by 90 days.
Britain will send Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets to Saudi Arabia to shoot down Houthi missiles and drones aimed at Saudi cities and critical infrastructure, the UK Defense Ministry said on Oct. 20.
CNN reported that the jets will fly defensive counter-air missions over the kingdom, and a spokesperson for the prime minister’s office said they will intercept incoming threats and will not carry out strikes inside Yemen.
The government has not said how many Typhoons are going, where they will be based or when patrols will begin. The jets join UK support already in place in the kingdom, including air defense equipment, British personnel helping counter missile and drone attacks, and a Royal Air Force Voyager tanker that has been refueling Saudi fighters since September.
“The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable. The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region,” said UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting.
Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport has been hit repeatedly this month. The deadliest strike, on Oct. 10, wounded more than 300 people, and while Saudi civil aviation authorities put the death toll at 12, CNN has since reported 13 killed, making it the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. The Houthis have also fired ballistic missiles and drones at oil facilities, and on Sept. 16 the group claimed to have shot down a Saudi F-15 over Marib, a claim Saudi authorities have not confirmed.
The fighting escalated after the Houthis announced in July that they would target Saudi shipping in the Red Sea and infrastructure inside the kingdom, following a Saudi strike on the Houthi-held airport in Sanaa. Last month the group pushed down Yemen’s western coast and took the port of Mocha and Mayyun Island in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the narrow southern entrance to the Red Sea.
Saudi Arabia has asked regional and Western partners for air defense help. France has agreed to send military personnel and equipment, and more than 100 U.S. military advisers are providing intelligence and targeting support under a newly formed joint forces command. Pakistan already has troops in the kingdom, and Egypt’s parliament is debating a deployment after President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi called an emergency session.
The Typhoon is a familiar aircraft in the region, since the Royal Saudi Air Force has flown it since buying 72 jets in a deal agreed in 2006. Britain previously sent its Sky Sabre ground-based air defense system to Saudi Arabia earlier this year during the war with Iran.
The Associated Press reported that Britain is also extending its Voyager refueling mission by 90 days. Downing Street has described the support as defensive and limited in scope, while Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces press a counteroffensive that has so far failed to dislodge the Houthis from key positions.

Gaza children face worsening food shortages as prices rise and aid is cut
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
06:00:47 UTC
15:00:47 KST

Gaza children face worsening food shortages as prices rise and aid is cut
Families say they are struggling to provide nutritious meals for their children as commercial supplies are disrupted.
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – It has been months since Huda Abu Leila had to resort to serving only tea and bread to her five daughters for breakfast. But this week, that’s what the 30-year-old has had to do, after Israel restricted the entry of goods into Gaza earlier this month.
After living through three years of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, and the accompanying blockade that often leaves markets partly empty and goods unaffordable, Huda is used to struggling to provide her children – aged between 18 months and 10 years – with a balanced and nutritious diet.
But the current situation, with shortages of commercial goods, rising food prices, and cuts to humanitarian assistance, has made it ever harder for her to put enough food on the table.
“We were affected immediately. We couldn’t find eggs or milk, and we don’t have the money to stock up on food,” Huda said.
She lives with her daughters in a tent in western Gaza City. Her husband was injured during the war and can no longer work, while she earns a little money by baking bread for other people.
Some days, the family eats canned beans with duqqa – a local spice blend – or za’atar. On days when food is not as readily available, like this week, they dip bread in tea.
What worries her most is how the worsening situation will affect her children’s health, particularly as she is already struggling to provide them with enough nutritious food.
Israel halted commercial shipments into Gaza on October 14, disrupting supplies of food and other essential goods as families already struggling with high prices faced further shortages.
The suspension came amid a dispute over a demand for merchants to pay 10,000 shekels ($3,225) per truck to bring goods into the enclave.
On October 19, Israel announced that commercial shipments would gradually resume.
The Israeli military body responsible for coordinating aid and commercial access to Gaza, COGAT, said merchants had reported that Hamas had withdrawn the demand. Hamas described the payment as a voluntary contribution to a fund supporting people affected by the war.
The disruption comes as humanitarian assistance is also reduced. On October 19, the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) announced that funding shortages had forced it to cut food assistance in Gaza.
The programme reduced the number of people it supports from 1.6 million in September to 1.1 million in October.
It has also halved food rations, with families receiving one food parcel instead of two, alongside a smaller bag of wheat flour. The number of hot meals WFP provides daily has been reduced from 250,000 to 150,000.
WFP said about 1.4 million people in Gaza, approximately two-thirds of the population, were facing acute food insecurity at crisis levels or worse.
Famine was declared in Gaza City in August 2025. The UN-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification said in December of the same year that it had receded after the beginning of the Gaza ceasefire two months earlier.
Families struggle to provide nutritious meals
For Huda, the crisis means she can no longer afford many of the foods her daughters need for a balanced and nutritious diet.
Eggs have become too expensive. A shopkeeper recently quoted her 60 shekels ($19.40) for a tray. She also said some shops appeared to be holding back stock.
Fresh vegetables have also become difficult to afford. When she goes to the market, which she usually does about once a week, she buys only small quantities.
“Onions cost about 10 shekels [$3.25] per kilogramme, while tomatoes cost between 10 and 15 shekels per kilogramme [$3.25 and $4.85],” she said.
The vast majority of Gaza’s population is unemployed as a result of Israel’s war and its restrictions on allowing the territory to rebuild its infrastructure and economy.
The lack of food is starting to have an impact on Huda’s children. She says that they are struggling to concentrate, and often become dizzy and exhausted.
The health of her eldest daughter, Salma, has become so poor that she is receiving follow-up care at al-Rantisi Hospital in Gaza, where a doctor advised Huda to improve her daughter’s diet.
“We have been through so much hardship over the past three years,” she said. “I worry that my daughters will get sick if I cannot provide them with enough nutritious food.”
Fears of malnutrition
For Raeda Soboh, 40, the struggle to feed her nine-member family means her children have gone months without some of the foods they need to stay healthy.
The displaced mother, originally from Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza but now living in Gaza City, said her family had long depended on community kitchens, known locally as tekkiya, even before the latest disruption to commercial supplies.
“When a kitchen has food, we eat from it,” she said.
Her children usually have tea for breakfast and a meal from a community kitchen for lunch. In the evening, they sometimes eat falafel, rice, lentils or pasta. But milk, meat, eggs and cheese have been absent from their diet for about eight months, she said. She last bought vegetables about a month ago.
“I don’t buy good-quality things. I buy only what we need and what we can manage to pay for,” Soboh said.
Her experience reflects wider concerns about children’s nutrition across Gaza.
According to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), more than 2,800 children were admitted for malnutrition treatment in September, including more than 360 with severe acute malnutrition.
About 3,000 children aged between six months and five years continued to be admitted for malnutrition treatment each month, OCHA said in a report published on October 19.
A UNICEF-supported nutrition survey published in August also found that 12.2 percent of children under five in areas accessible to researchers were affected by stunting, a sign of impaired growth associated with prolonged nutritional and health problems.
Dr Mohamed B Alraee, a paediatrician and nutrition specialist in Gaza City, warned that prolonged restrictions on food supplies entering Gaza could lead to a further increase in child malnutrition, with children already missing the balanced meals they need to grow and recover.
Despite improvements after earlier periods of famine, hospitals continue to receive children with moderate and severe malnutrition, he said. Cases are not limited to children under five, with older children, including those aged five to 17, also affected.
Alraee said some children were suffering from severe malnutrition accompanied by swelling in the legs, a condition associated with serious protein deficiency. He linked these cases to families surviving on a single meal dominated by carbohydrates without enough protein, because they cannot afford more nutritious food.
“Even when the crossings were open and food was entering, we were still seeing these cases. Children do not recover from malnutrition in a month or two. Some cases need three to six months to recover,” he said. “If the situation continues like this, we expect to see more cases of malnutrition.”
For Raeda, the consequences are already visible in her children’s daily lives. She said they had become weak and easily exhausted, leaving her worried about what months of inadequate food could mean for their health.
“They seem to spend the whole day sleeping. When I ask one of them to carry a water container, he might manage it once but cannot do it a second time,” she said. “I feel sorry for him and ask myself: is he getting proper nutrition? Is he eating like other children?”
The family has no reliable source of income, Raeda said. She also said the area where they live is not recognised as an official camp, leaving them without the same aid vouchers and hygiene supplies received by some other camps.
Like many parents in Gaza, she is left trying to meet their basic needs with whatever food she can find and afford.
“I hope someone will help us and stand with us in these difficult circumstances,” Raeda said. “I hope the war ends, the situation improves and the crossings open, so prices can come down.”

Childcare chain collapse highlights private credit risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
05:59:22 UTC
14:59:22 KST

Childcare chain's collapse into administration highlights private credit risks
In short:
Shared Beginnings, owned by private lender Finexia, is in administration.
Shares in Finexia have been suspended for months after the ASX-listed lender failed to file financial reports on time.
A former national children's commissioner says a lot of private providers are divesting childcare centres or pulling out of the sector altogether.
Childcare chain Shared Beginnings has hit financial strife, becoming the latest early education provider to run into trouble amid a wave of closures in the sector.
The childcare service, owned by private lender Finexia Financial Group, operates centres in Queensland, Victoria and the ACT.
Shared Beginnings entered administration on Monday.
Finexia wrote to staff, informing them the centres had been operating "at a loss".
The collapse highlights the risks of the private credit sector, with Finexia taking on ownership of the centres in the 2025 financial year after the previous owner, Genius Education, defaulted on substantial loans owed to Finexia.
The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) has recently said it was closely scrutinising private lending, which has typically been a much more lightly regulated sector than the banking industry, and was concerned "the first significant cracks" were appearing.
Centres still operating
The impact on childcare places and jobs at Shared Beginnings remains unclear as the administrators continue to operate the centres.
The firm said the decision came after exhausting all other options.
Finexia managing director Neil Sheather said placing Shared Beginnings into administration was not taken lightly, but was necessary.
"Finexia has committed to honour staff entitlements and continues to financially support the business as it continues to provide services to families,"
he said.
"Ultimately, the administrators are in control of Shared Beginnings."
In a letter to staff, Mr Sheather said the administration would affect all seven of its centres, including Sinnamon Park and Kenmore in Queensland, Reservoir, Mont Albert and Beaumaris in Victoria, and Bonython and Conder in the ACT.
In a separate letter to parents, Mr Sheather assured families that all centres remained open, and care would continue as normal.
Bill Karageozis and Nick Keramos of DVT McLeods have been appointed administrators to find suitable buyers.
Minister for Early Childhood Education Jessica Walsh said she acknowledged the news from Shared Beginnings would "cause disruption and uncertainty for families and educators".
"Since coming to government, we've seen 1,200 new centres, 52,000 more educators and 57,000 more children in early learning."
For-profit providers drive 'churn'
A September report by the Early Learning and Care Council Australia has found the rate of early childhood education and care (ECEC) service closures has continued to increase.
The report said 152 long daycare services had closed since 2024, with a further 276 services (both long day care and preschool/kindergarten) identified as at risk of closing in the next 12 months.
Former national children's commissioner Anne Hollonds AO said the childcare sector was undergoing a significant adjustment, driven by increased regulatory costs and a number of prominent crises.
"I think what we're seeing is a lot of private providers divesting centres or pulling out altogether,"
she said.
For-profit centres dominate the long daycare sector. Most of the growth in recent years has been in private for-profit providers, with a recent report from the Mitchell Institute finding they made up 74 per cent of long daycare places.
Ms Hollonds said the sector would be better if it were shared 50-50 between non-profit and for-profit organisations.
"We really need to focus on the safety and well-being of children as the priority," she said, adding that she had no problem with for-profit providers as long as their operation was up to scratch.
The Mitchell Institute also found substantial instability or "churn" in the long daycare sector was driven by for-profit centres.
"Since 2013, about one-third [32 per cent] of long day care services open in 2025 had changed approved provider," the report said.
"The rate is higher in for-profit centres where 40 per cent have changed provider, compared to 11 per cent of all other centres."
Have you been impacted by the closure of childcare centres or private lending? We would like to hear from you! Contact our journalist confidentially on li.yiying@abc.net.au or li.yiying@proton.me.
Finexia shares suspended
The seven Shared Beginnings centres arose from the ashes of Genius Early Learning, which operated more than 30 early childhood centres across the country and collapsed under massive debt in March 2025.
Finexia said it had since "provided significant financial and operational support, including rebranding, marketing, staffing support and substantial funding to cover working capital shortfalls".
The stock exchange suspended Finexia's securities on March 2 after it failed to file multiple periodic reports, including its half-yearly report which was due at the end of February.
The company had reported a $5.2 million net loss for the 2025 financial year, which it described as "one of the most challenging in Finexia's history".
The collapse of Genius, which had been a major borrower from Finexia, was described as a "troubling event for management and investors alike" and led to Finexia taking on ownership.
Earlier this week, the company told the market it had completed the divestment of its interest in the Stay Company Income Fund, offloading $25 million in debt from its balance sheet.
The fund was established to capitalise on the "demand for tourism and residential accommodations in Australia".
In early October, Finexia's former executive chairman, Robert Spano, resigned and transitioned to non-executive director and chairman of the board.

Spain gets its third Airbus tanker, completing 2021 order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
05:56:42 UTC
14:56:42 KST

- Airbus delivered Spain’s third A330 MRTT tanker, completing a 2021 order for three aircraft converted from former Iberia airliners.
- The tanker joins the Spanish Air and Space Force’s 45th Wing at Torrejón de Ardoz Air Base near Madrid.
Airbus has delivered the third A330 Multi Role Tanker Transport to Spain, completing the three-aircraft order the Spanish Ministry of Defense placed in 2021.
The company announced the handover on X, and Spanish media reported that the ceremony took place on Oct. 20 at its plant in Getafe, outside Madrid.
The tanker will join the 45th Wing of the Spanish Air and Space Force at Torrejón de Ardoz Air Base near Madrid, which already flies the first two. The first entered service in April 2025 and the second followed in October 2025, so the last aircraft arrived ahead of the November 2026 completion date set when the program was rescheduled in 2023.
Spain did not buy new-build jets. The ministry bought three secondhand A330-200 airliners from Iberia in November 2021, and Airbus converted them into tankers at Getafe under a program the Spanish cabinet had approved two months earlier at an estimated €810 million. Before conversion, the airframes flew transport missions for the air force in their original configuration, including evacuation flights from Niger and Sudan.
The Spanish tankers use a hose-and-drogue system, trailing a hose with a basket that receiving aircraft plug into with a refueling probe. Airbus says the aircraft can stay airborne for more than 18 hours, have a range of 16,000 km (9,940 miles) and carry 111 tonnes (245,000 pounds) of fuel in their standard tanks, enough to fly refueling missions without extra fuel tanks. The A330 MRTT can also carry up to 300 troops or 45 tonnes (99,000 pounds) of cargo, and it can be fitted for medical evacuation.
The Spanish crews have already started taking the aircraft abroad. In August 2026, the Spanish Air and Space Force brought an A330 MRTT to Exercise Pitch Black in northern Australia, where it refueled strike aircraft alongside Royal Australian Air Force KC-30As, a Royal Air Force Voyager and U.S. Air Force KC-135s.
The delivery closes out the 2021 contract, but Madrid has a larger tanker purchase in the works. On Aug. 25, the Spanish cabinet approved up to €5.4 billion ($6.3 billion) for a joint A330 MRTT buy with Poland, financed through the European Union’s SAFE defense loan program, as we reported in August. Spanish media have reported a split of three aircraft for Spain and four for Poland, though the official readout did not give a number, and the final contract has not yet been signed.
Airbus says its A330 MRTT order book stands at 91 aircraft, with 68 delivered to more than 18 countries, and that the global fleet has logged more than 375,000 flight hours.

Czech Skyfox jets will soon fly in Armenia, minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
05:52:31 UTC
14:52:31 KST

- Armenian Defense Minister Suren Papikyan visited Aero Vodochody on Oct. 20 and said L-39 Skyfox jets will soon fly in Armenia.
- Czech industry trackers reported Armenia ordered four Skyfox aircraft, but neither side has officially confirmed the number, value or delivery date.
Armenia’s Defense Minister Suren Papikyan toured Czech aircraft maker Aero Vodochody on Oct. 20 and said L-39 Skyfox jet trainers will soon be flying with Armenia’s armed forces. The country’s Ministry of Defense published a photo series from the visit showing Papikyan with the new aircraft, which can also fly light attack missions.
“These marvels will soon be flying in Armenian skies,” said Armenian Defense Minister Suren Papikyan.
Neither Yerevan nor Aero has announced how many jets Armenia is buying, what the deal is worth or when deliveries will start. Czech defense industry trackers reported in September that Armenia had ordered four Skyfox aircraft, a figure that has not been officially confirmed.
The visit came about six weeks after Armenian President Vahagn Khachaturyan toured the same plant at Vodochody, outside Prague, on Sept. 4 during an official trip to the Czech Republic. Armenia already flies the older L-39 Albatros, the Soviet-era Czechoslovak trainer that the Skyfox replaces on Aero’s production line.
The Skyfox, known as the L-39NG until Aero renamed it in October 2024, keeps the general layout of the Albatros but uses a new composite wing, modern avionics and a Williams FJ44-4M turbofan engine. The subsonic jet tops out at about 900 km/h (560 mph) and has five hardpoints for up to 1,640 kg (3,616 pounds) of gun pods, rockets and other stores, so it can fly ground attack and reconnaissance missions as well as train pilots for fourth- and fifth-generation fighters.
Aero has spent the past two years turning the design into a production aircraft. Hungary took delivery of its first three Skyfox jets in May 2025 under a 12-aircraft order, as we reported at the time, and the Czech flight training center at Pardubice had six of its eight aircraft by January 2026. Vietnam ordered 12, and in June 2026 Aero signed contracts with customers in Angola and North America.
In October, Aero also signed an agreement with Thales Belgium to arm the Skyfox with 70 mm FZ275 laser-guided rockets for shooting down drones, a version the company calls the Drone Hunter. There is no indication yet whether Armenia’s jets will receive that configuration or any particular weapons package.

Unknown Publisher

Anupam Kher slams BJP cabinet minister over ‘public humiliation’ of Daler Mehndi in Uttarkhand
NEW DELHI: Veteran actor Anupam Kher has backed singer Daler Mehndi after Uttarakhand cabinet minister Subodh Uniyal confronted him on stage during a cultural event, questioning his performance. Kher criticised the minister's conduct, asking whether it was necessary to publicly humiliate the singer instead of raising concerns privately.“Mantri ji...kya sabke saamne manch par jakar is tarah unhe apmanit karna zaruri tha?” Kher wrote in an Instagram post, expressing disappointment over the way the singer was addressed in front of an audience.
The controversy erupted after Mehndi's performance at the annual Siddhpeeth Maa Kunjapuri Tourism and Development Fair in Tehri Garhwal, Uttarakhand. Uniyal allegedly questioned the singer's presentation, claiming that he appeared disoriented and was lip-syncing. The minister also alleged that Mehndi was drunk.
What Anupam Kher said
In his post, Kher said he had known Mehndi for several years and was concerned about the singer's health. He said the singer had not been keeping well and deserved to be treated with dignity after decades of contributing to the music industry.“I watched a video in which a minister was speaking to Daler Mehndi ji on stage.
The way he spoke to him was deeply upsetting to see. I have known Daler ji for many years. I also know that he hasn’t been keeping well for some time now. Minister ji, you may have had complaints about his performance. You may even have been upset with him. But was it really necessary to go up on stage and humiliate him in front of everyone? Couldn’t the same thing have been said to him privately, with dignity and respect? (Mantri ji.....kya sabke saamne manch par jakar is tarah unhe apmanit karna zaruri tha?),” Kher wrote.He added that an artist's contribution should be acknowledged and respected, particularly after years of work.“An artist spends an entire lifetime earning the recognition and respect that comes through years of hard work. For the past 30–35 years, Daler ji has brought joy to all of us through his songs. Surely, his contribution deserves some appreciation and respect. Daler ji, I have always known you as a kind-hearted person who spreads love. As far as I know you, you don’t even drink alcohol. I am deeply sorry that you had to go through something like this.”
Mika Singh defends his brother
Earlier, singer Mika Singh came out in support of his brother, saying Mehndi had been unwell for the past two years and had undergone an operation recently. Mika suggested that his health could explain his speech during the performance and rejected allegations that the singer had consumed alcohol.
“I know my brother Daler Mehndi, and he does not drink alcohol. He has been unwell for the past two years and is still recovering, yet he continues to perform with his band. These days, many performers use backing tracks, but nobody questions them in the same way,” Mika said.Kher also urged members of the film industry to speak up in support of Mehndi, saying it should not be Mika's responsibility alone to defend his brother.The incident has triggered a debate over the treatment of performers at public events, with Kher questioning why any concerns about Mehndi's performance could not have been raised privately and respectfully.

Number of Australian occupations with workforce shortages declines
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:47:54 CST
14:47:54 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- The number of jobs in Australia with workforce shortages has fallen year-on-year, according to government data.
Jobs and Skills Australia on Wednesday released the annual occupation shortage list for 2026, revealing that 27 percent of assessed occupations have a national workforce shortage, down from 29 percent in 2025 and a record high of 36 percent in 2023.
The government agency said workforce shortages remained concentrated among professionals, technicians and trade workers, which accounted for 90 percent of occupations that have been in a workforce shortage every year since 2021.
It said that almost half of technician and trade worker occupations, and 37 percent of occupations filled by professionals, were assessed as being in a shortage in 2026.
An analysis by Jobs and Skills Australia identified supply pipeline constraints, a lack of suitable applicants and retention challenges as the key drivers of workforce shortages.
According to the list, occupations that have been in a national workforce shortage every year since 2021 include agricultural technicians, aircraft maintenance technicians, carpenters and diesel technicians.
Cyber security engineers, timber and wood production operators and vascular surgeons were among the occupations assessed as having no shortage in 2026 after having national shortages in 2025. ■

Across China: Metamorphosis of a city that coal built, and nearly buried
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:47:53 CST
14:47:53 KST

HEGANG, Heilongjiang, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Li Jianguo, 72, remembers the mountain of coal waste that once loomed outside his front door.
"Coal dust blew into the house with the wind all year round. You had to keep the windows shut even in summer," Li recalled. That was the nature of life in the city he knew for three decades as a coal miner.
Today, the retiree strolls through a lakeside park every morning, thermos of tea in hand, watching children run across well-trimmed lawns while elderly neighbors practice Tai Chi under birch trees.
The park is built on what was once a collapsed mining wasteland, a subsidence zone pockmarked with abandoned pits and shanties.
In many ways, it tells the story of an entire city and its transformation.
CITY BUILT ON "BLACK GOLD"
The city of Hegang is located in northeast China's Heilongjiang Province, near the Russian border, where forested hills give way to lowland plains. Though the city's name translates as crane ridge, it actually derives from an old word for the raccoon dogs that once roamed its wilderness.
In 1914, a hunter accidentally found coal while clearing land along a river. A mining company was established four years later, drawing waves of mine workers. By 1929, a town had taken shape. Hegang got its present name when the People's Republic was founded in 1949, and went on to become one of new China's four major "coal capitals," an engine fueling the country's industrialization.
But the "black gold" that gave birth to the city was finite. As reserves dried up and mines shut down one after another from the early 2000s onward, young people left, and Hegang became a city with far more homes than people.
In 2019, the internet turned this surplus into a punchline. In one of the most extreme cases, an old walk-up apartment sold for just 15,000 yuan (2,246 U.S. dollars). Netizens joked that homes in Hegang were selling for "cabbage prices," meaning dirt cheap.
"We were under huge pressure," said Xiao Yu, an official at the municipal bureau of housing and urban-rural development.
Rather than doubling down on cheap housing to attract bargain hunters, the city chose to reverse course. Officials traveled across the country studying advanced building techniques, developed new construction standards tailored to extreme cold, and urged local developers to pursue quality over volume.
Between 2019 and 2025, commercial housing sales grew nearly five-fold. Average prices at premium developments now exceed 4,800 yuan per square meter.
"This is just the beginning," said Li Baiyang, chief of the municipal bureau of housing and urban-rural development. "We plan to upgrade all of Hegang's old housing into decent homes."
This quiet, frigid city has its own appeal, especially for those fed up with the humid south or burned out by the whirlwind pace of life in megacities.
Yan Bo and his wife, from the bustling city of Hangzhou, east China's Zhejiang Province, drove more than 2,000 kilometers to Hegang for a taste of its slower rhythm. They bought an apartment here and never left.
Ivan, a Russian cross-border trader who asked that only his first name be used, settled here last year. He describes the city as "livable," and its people as "genuinely friendly."
METAMORPHOSIS OF A CITY
Hegang's transformation is even more dramatic than its housing market. A little over a decade ago, the city was still coated in soot. All its 16 waterways, including two rivers and 14 drainage channels, ran black with pollution. Years of systematic cleanup efforts have now turned them clear.
The city demolished over 4,100 old buildings along riverbanks, planted 96 hectares of riverside greenery, and converted former mining subsidence zones into 32 parks and public squares. The deserted mine pit of Xinling has been renovated into a scenic area, and the Dulu River wetland has become an important stopover for migratory birds and home to some endangered species.
A new economy is also taking shape underground. Hegang holds 2.3 billion tonnes of proven graphite ore, the raw material for lithium-ion battery anodes. More than 80 percent of China's natural graphite for battery production comes from here.
The city has partnered with China Minmetals to apply modern technologies such as the Internet of Things and cloud computing across the whole graphite industrial chain, including mining and processing, and to overcome key technical hurdles in achieving high-purity graphite. The former coal capital is aiming to build a technological innovation highland for the graphite new materials industry.
Chinese people have long held that food is the first pleasure of life. In Hegang, a traditional grain production base, that pleasure comes in the form of crayfish raised alongside rice paddies, and a signature street food: grilled meat skewers.
This snack, popular since the 1950s when it provided quick calories for miners emerging from shifts, has grown into a 4.5-billion-yuan industry, with more than 1,200 franchise outlets across China.
To foster further development, mayor Deng Weiyuan said the city will focus on upgrading traditional industries, cultivating emerging ones, and developing new quality productive forces tailored to local conditions.
With a population of 935,000 and a modest GDP of 37.6 billion yuan in 2024, Hegang still faces many challenges. The shadow of the coal era lingers in old infrastructure and in the collective memory of its people.
"Globally, resource-dependent cities face daunting transformation hurdles," said Sun Haojin, director of the Institute of Economics at the Heilongjiang Provincial Academy of Social Sciences. "Both economic restructuring and ecological improvement are difficult."
He described Hegang's push for green development as exemplary.
Like many rust-belt cities worldwide, Hegang is not so much reborn as it is being rebuilt. Its next chapter is being written by the people who stayed, and those who chose to arrive.
Zheng Siduo, 32, graduated from a university in the provincial capital Harbin, and returned to his hometown to start a business.
"Compared to the first-tier cities, Hegang's relaxed, livable and low-cost environment provides ideal soil for tech startups to grow," said Zheng, founder of Zhanhui Industrial Design, Hegang's first digital printing and creative design firm.
The company, established in May this year, makes customized 3D-printed models and industrial components, exporting them globally via cross-border e-commerce platforms like Amazon. ■

World Insights: China-Central Asia cooperation boosts SCO development
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:47:52 CST
14:47:52 KST

DUSHANBE, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- During his just-concluded official visits to Uzbekistan and Tajikistan and attendance at the 25th meeting of the Council of Heads of Government (Prime Ministers) of Member States of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), Chinese Premier Li Qiang called for closer cooperation with the two Central Asian countries and greater development of the SCO.
In recent years, China has deepened practical cooperation with Central Asian countries and injected fresh momentum into development of the SCO by enhancing connectivity, trade and exchanges in various fields. Analysts say these efforts will contribute to common prosperity and high-quality development in the region and beyond.
CONNECTIVITY BRINGS OPPORTUNITY
Enhancing connectivity between China and the landlocked countries of Central Asia is key to promoting development in the region and beyond. The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, now under construction, is a prime example of this effort.
In recent years, the railway project has remained high on the agenda of leaders of the countries involved. Most recently, during Li's official visit to Uzbekistan, the two sides pledged to advance the railway's high-quality construction.
The railway, launched at the end of 2024, is a flagship project of the Belt and Road Initiative, serving as a strategic link between China and Central Asia. The route will begin in Kashgar in northwest China and pass through the mountainous terrain of Kyrgyzstan to reach Uzbekistan.
High-quality construction and efficient operation of the railway will set a valuable example for countries across the region and beyond, said Kubanychbek Taabaldiev, a professor at Ala-Too International University in Bishkek.
"It has the potential to change the economic geography of Central Asia and transform Kyrgyzstan from a country located between major markets into an important link between China, Central Asia, and further on to European and Middle Eastern destinations," Taabaldiev said.
Beyond railway and road construction, the strengthening of transport cooperation between China and Central Asian countries also encompasses facilitating customs clearance at borders, digitizing transport permits and other efficiency-enhancing measures. Better connectivity has created new development opportunities for the region, boosting trade and exchanges in various fields.
Ulugbek Shermatov, chairman of the Committee on International Affairs, Defence and Security of the Legislative Chamber of the Oliy Majlis of Uzbekistan, noted that the creation of new transport arteries "not only expands economic opportunities, but also forms a solid material foundation for long-term interdependence and peaceful cooperation in the region."
This demonstrates China's commitment to developing friendly relations with neighboring states and promoting Belt and Road cooperation, Shermatov said.
PRACTICAL COOPERATION BEARS FRUIT
From trade and agriculture to cutting-edge technological innovation, practical cooperation between China and Central Asia has been a driving force behind regional growth and, more broadly, the development of the SCO as a whole.
Trade figures speak to the robust momentum in cooperation. China's trade with five Central Asian countries topped 100 billion U.S. dollars in 2025, hitting a record high. Meanwhile, trade structure continues to improve, with more Central Asian products entering the Chinese market.
"Stability in the region is inextricably linked with trade and economic development. The growth of the total trade turnover of Central Asian countries with China ... clearly demonstrates China's importance in ensuring stability in our region," said Shermatov.
Building on traditional merchandise trade, both sides are further expanding cooperation in digital trade, agriculture, energy, manufacturing, as well as scientific and technological innovation.
Take energy cooperation as an example. Cooperation has gradually expanded from traditional oil and gas to clean energy and related technologies.
At the Second China-Central Asia Summit in Astana, Kazakhstan last year, China and the five Central Asian nations pledged to support the establishment of a China-Central Asia energy development partnership to expand cooperation across the entire energy industry chains.
The countries also affirmed their commitment to promoting technological and talent exchanges and cooperation in areas such as the management and development of desertified and saline-alkali lands.
"China possesses rich technical expertise in renewable energy, electric mobility, digital infrastructure, telecommunications, artificial intelligence (AI) and industrial automation," said Mukhtor Umarov, chairman of the Economic Assembly of Uzbekistan.
At the broader SCO level, the establishment and development of cooperation platforms between China and other SCO members in emerging fields "have opened new avenues for countries in the region -- shifting the focus from simply purchasing equipment toward technology localization, joint R&D, engineer cultivation and the buildout of new production capacities," Umarov said.
SCO DEVELOPMENT STRENGTHENED
Leaders of China and Central Asian nations, together with their SCO colleagues, reaffirmed stronger cooperation within the SCO framework at the just-concluded 25th meeting of the Council of Heads of Government (Prime Ministers) of Member States of the SCO in the Tajik capital of Dushanbe.
China's coordination with Central Asia will help promote the high-quality development of the SCO by strengthening the foundation for regional security, expanding economic cooperation and connectivity, and cementing mutual trust among member states.
These efforts will further enhance the SCO's role in safeguarding regional security, promoting common development and improving global governance, experts said.
"In my view, the most prominent feature of China's current contribution to the development of the SCO lies in its tight integration of strategic concepts, multilateral rules and concrete development tools," said Uzbek expert Umarov.
"Against the backdrop of intensifying geoeconomic fragmentation, increasing trade restrictions, and chronic shortages of long-term financing, SCO member states urgently need predictable rules and institutions to mitigate risks faced by enterprises," he said.
China has been a key contributor to the SCO's evolution. At the Tianjin Summit last year, a milestone in the SCO's development, China and other member states jointly formulated a development strategy for the organization for the next decade and action plans to promote high-quality development.
Since the Tianjin Summit, a number of cooperation platforms have been launched, covering green industry, digital economy, scientific and technological innovation, energy, education and AI.
At the Bishkek Summit earlier this year, China brought more initiatives and projects supporting the SCO's development, including the establishment of a China-SCO port economic cooperation center in Tianjin, the launch of an international AI application cooperation center, and the training of more green industry professionals.
The SCO's international significance is "determined not only by its geographical reach or the combined potential of its member states, but also by its ability to translate political agreements into functioning mechanisms for security, economic cooperation, and diplomatic coordination," said Guzel Maitdinova, director of the Center for Geopolitical Studies at the Russian-Tajik (Slavonic) University.
"Looking ahead, linking SCO economic initiatives with national development strategies, China's Belt and Road Initiative, and the programs of international financial institutions could play a particularly important role," Maitdinova added.
Shermatov, meanwhile, offered an Uzbek perspective: "This is precisely how we see the responsibility of China and Uzbekistan for the future of the SCO -- to preserve the Shanghai Spirit while simultaneously adapting the organization to new global realities." ■

Mainland denounces Taiwan authorities for hindering cross-Strait exchanges
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21

14:47:27 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson on Wednesday criticized the Taiwan authorities for barring relevant people on the island from attending the commemorative event held on the mainland marking the 160th anniversary of the birth of Sun Yat-sen.
Sun, a founding figure of the Chinese Kuomintang (KMT) and a revered revolutionary leader who played a pivotal role in overthrowing imperial rule in China, died in 1925 in Beijing. His remains rest at the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum in Nanjing, east China's Jiangsu Province.
Zhang Han, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, noted that the grand commemoration of Sun's legacy is intended to inherit and carry forward his noble spirit of upholding national unity and striving for national rejuvenation.
She stressed that the move by Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party authorities to obstruct cross-Strait exchanges and suppress Taiwan compatriots fully exposes their vicious intentions of betraying the nation and history, seeking to split the country, and stoking confrontation across the Taiwan Strait.
The Taiwan question stems from China's civil war fought between the forces led by the Communist Party of China (CPC) and the KMT about eight decades ago. In 1949, the defeated KMT retreated to Taiwan, and the People's Republic of China was founded under the leadership of the CPC.
The unresolved civil war, combined with foreign interference, has kept the two sides of the Taiwan Strait in a prolonged state of political confrontation. However, the fact that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory has never changed. ■

Brazil's progress in curbing deforestation benefits global economy: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:47:15 CST
14:47:15 KST

RIO DE JANEIRO, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Brazil's progress in curbing deforestation across the Amazon rainforest and the Cerrado savanna over the past three years has spared the global economy an estimated 1.16 trillion reals (232 billion U.S. dollars), according to a study published on Tuesday.
The economic benefit stems from prevention, including curbing the release of harmful greenhouse gases and their damaging impact on climate change, said the study by Brazil's prestigious think tank, the Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV), whose findings were published by the state-run news agency Agencia Brasil.
Of the total estimated benefits, 67-192 billion reals (13.4-38.4 billion dollars) represent the prevention of climate-related damage to Brazil's own economy, according to the study.
The study compares deforestation in 2019-2022 with that in 2023-2026. Data from the National Institute for Space Research showed that from August 2025 to July 2026, deforestation fell by 41.8 percent in the Amazon and by 23.8 percent in the Cerrado.
Deforested area in the Amazon totaled 3,335 square km, the lowest figure since 1988, while in the Cerrado, it reached 5,516.69 square km, the lowest level since 2001.
Taken together, deforested area across both biomes dropped from 78,900 square km in 2019-2022 to 56,700 square km in 2023-2026. In other words, some 22,200 square km were spared from deforestation.
Cutting the deforestation rate prevented as much as 1.49 billion tons of greenhouse gases from polluting the atmosphere over the period studied.
The study employs a cost of 145 dollars per ton of carbon dioxide, placing the value of climate-related damage prevention at 1.16 trillion reals (232 billion dollars).
The calculation does not take into account the direct regional effects of Amazonian deforestation on rainfall, temperature and water availability in Brazil. Moisture transported by so-called "flying rivers," atmospheric currents fueled by the rain forest's "evapotranspiration," contributes to precipitation in the country's central-western, southeastern and southern regions.
"Reducing deforestation is not incompatible with expanding agricultural production, because the agribusiness sector itself is one of the primary beneficiaries of the rainfall generated by the forest," the report said.
According to the report, the economic benefits of keeping forests standing far outweigh financial compensation Brazil receives from other countries or international schemes. ■

Interview: China's biodiversity conservation offers valuable lessons for world, says UN biodiversity chief
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:47:07 CST
14:47:07 KST

YEREVAN, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- China's experience in biodiversity conservation offers valuable lessons for the world, particularly in combining ambitious commitments with sound science, effective institutions and long-term investment, the UN biodiversity chief said on Monday.
Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), made the remarks in an interview with Xinhua on the sidelines of the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the CBD (COP17), which began on Monday in Yerevan, capital of Armenia.
China's experience is particularly evident in the scale of its conservation efforts and its integration of biodiversity into national development planning, Schomaker said.
Its ecological conservation redline system, national parks network, ecological restoration programs and investments in biodiversity monitoring demonstrate practical approaches to implementing national commitments, she said.
In her eyes, three lessons stand out from China's experience: conservation must be integrated into broader economic and land-use planning; ecological restoration requires sustained investment; and effective monitoring is essential to measuring results.
China's contribution extends beyond its domestic efforts. "Its continued support for multilateral cooperation is especially valuable amid today's geopolitical challenges," Schomaker said.
China helped bring the world together around a common plan for nature, and its continued leadership will help turn that plan into results, she said.
Schomaker highlighted China's role in securing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF), one of the most significant international agreements for nature in decades.
As COP15 president, China helped guide complex negotiations among countries with different priorities and capacities. Working closely with Canada, host of the Montreal meeting, China helped build the consensus needed to adopt the framework and its 23 targets, she said.
"That was a landmark diplomatic achievement," Schomaker said. Four years later, the challenge is to turn the agreement into measurable results. "COP15 gave us the plan. COP17 is about making that plan work."
Financing is key to implementation. China established the Kunming Biodiversity Fund to help developing countries strengthen their capacity for biodiversity conservation. Schomaker described the fund as an important instrument for the CBD, created specifically to support implementation of the KMGBF.
The fund seeks to align its support with decisions made by parties under the convention and help developing countries implement them, Schomaker said.
She also highlighted the fund's ability to attract private-sector contributions alongside China's government funding. "So that is very good news for us," she said.
Schomaker deems South-South cooperation particularly valuable because countries facing similar challenges can share practical experience, technology and expertise.
The effectiveness of biodiversity finance should be measured by whether it strengthens national capacity, improves conservation and restoration outcomes, supports local communities and helps countries achieve their biodiversity targets, she said.
The first global review of progress in implementing the KMGBF, to be conducted at COP17, shows encouraging engagement, Schomaker said. Nearly 90 percent of parties have established national biodiversity targets, and more than 140 countries have submitted national reports. However, fewer than half of the aligned national targets assessed by parties themselves are currently on track.
The largest gaps concern targets requiring changes to economic systems, particularly those related to business impacts and disclosure, sustainable consumption, harmful subsidies and biodiversity finance. Significant shortfalls also remain in protected-area coverage and efforts to address invasive alien species, she said.
"The fundamental challenge is that biodiversity cannot remain the responsibility of environment ministries alone." Progress increasingly depends on decisions by finance, agriculture, energy and other economic ministries, Schomaker said.
A major challenge is ensuring that developing countries have adequate, predictable and accessible financial resources to implement their commitments, she said. Developing countries emphasize the need for greater international support, while developed countries stress mobilizing finance from a wider range of sources and improving its effectiveness. Both are essential.
Countries have agreed to mobilize at least 200 billion U.S. dollars annually for biodiversity by 2030. Yet the United Nations Environment Program estimates that for every dollar invested in protecting nature, approximately 30 dollars go toward activities that harm it.
"We cannot close the biodiversity finance gap simply by adding more money while continuing to finance biodiversity destruction," Schomaker said.
COP17 needs to make progress in delivering financial commitments, improving access to funding, strengthening capacity and reforming harmful subsidies and incentives, so that economic decisions support rather than undermine nature, she said. ■

AI driving acceleration of online radicalization: Australian authorities
China
Unknown Publisher

13:47:06 CST
14:47:06 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Australian authorities have warned that artificial intelligence (AI) is accelerating the speed at which people can be radicalized or manipulated online.
Sandra Booth, acting deputy commissioner of National Security Investigations at the Australian Federal Police (AFP), told a parliamentary inquiry into AI on Wednesday that youth radicalization and manipulation is one of the greatest challenges the agency has ever faced.
She told the inquiry that radicalizing or manipulating individuals online used to take months or years, but now it is happening within days in some cases.
"This can be attributed to artificial intelligence, a growing grievance generation, young people searching for purpose and belonging, and the sophistication of these online networks," Booth said.
"While technology and AI bring many opportunities to society, including for law enforcement agencies, the AFP is deeply concerned AI is accelerating and lowering the skills required to actively manipulate and radicalize victims online, and cause serious harm."
The bipartisan parliamentary inquiry into AI was established in August to examine the opportunities and risks presented by the emerging technology.
Booth told the committee that, without serious intervention, Australia's mental health, education, finance and judicial systems could be overwhelmed by younger generations and vulnerable people who are repeatedly victimized.
"Manipulation and the grievances criminals fuel can cause distrust in communities and fray our social fabric," she said.
The inquiry will release its final report by the end of November. ■

Full Text: Remarks by Chinese Premier Li Qiang at 25th Meeting of the Council of Heads of Government of Member States of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
13:47:01 CST
14:47:01 KST

DUSHANBE, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Tuesday delivered a speech at the 25th Meeting of the Council of Heads of Government of Member States of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) in Dushanbe, the capital of Tajikistan.
The following is the full text of the speech:
Remarks by H.E. Li Qiang
Premier of the State Council of the People's Republic of China
At the 25th Meeting of the Council of Heads of Government
Of Member States of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization
Dushanbe, October 20, 2026
Your Excellency Prime Minister Kokhir Rasulzoda,
Colleagues,
It is a great pleasure to join you in the beautiful city of Dushanbe. I would like to thank Prime Minister Rasulzoda and the government of Tajikistan for the meticulous preparations and thoughtful arrangements for this meeting.
This year marks the 25th anniversary of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, and the beginning of the implementation of the SCO development strategy for the next decade. The Bishkek Summit in September produced a series of important outcomes, which has enabled us to take our work forward on multiple fronts and added new momentum to peace and development in our region and beyond. That said, our world today is far from tranquil. Factors of instability and uncertainty are still on the rise. As President Xi Jinping pointed out at the Bishkek Summit, at such a crossroads with humanity's future at stake, the SCO should step forward to shoulder its historical responsibility and steer the course for the future. What should we do to undertake such a responsibility? In my view, SCO members should, at the conceptual level, build greater consensus in vision, philosophy and way of thinking, and at the practical level, be more effective in execution and operation.
At the conceptual level, we should have a clear understanding of some fundamental questions and stay sober-minded and clear-eyed. First, we should have a keen insight into the overarching trend. Currently in the world, different ideas are contending and even clashing with each other. In particular, some narratives that cling to the zero-sum mindset and clamor for power politics are gaining traction. Despite this, the underlying logic of history and the fundamental trend of the times will not change. Multipolarity and economic globalization represent the future, and multilateralism and free trade remain the shared popular aspiration. Second, we should have a grand vision that embraces the world. All countries live in the same global village, and share the same future. The interests of a country or a region can only be better realized, preserved and advanced when they are in harmony with the common interests of the international community. The SCO should continue to carry forward the Shanghai Spirit. We should work to promote stability and prosperity in our region and at the same time contribute our share to the common development of the world. Third, we should have the perseverance to forge ahead. SCO members share the aspiration of promoting friendship, ensuring security and pursuing development, but the realization of this vision will not be smooth sailing. There will be risks, challenges, and even disruptions and sabotage, which makes it all the more important for the SCO to stay the course, remain closely united, and forge ahead with fortitude.
At the practical level, we should strengthen coordination and adopt a pragmatic and innovative approach to keep improving our relevant working mechanisms. China is ready to work with fellow member states to push for higher-quality development of the SCO. First, the SCO should boost the efficiency of its operation. Taking the opportunity provided by the amendment of the SCO Charter, members should implement a package of organizational reform, increase resources input and enhance capacity building, optimize the cooperation mechanisms in all areas and at all levels, and improve and expand the functions of the permanent bodies including the Secretariat, so as to make the SCO better structured and its operation more efficient. China is ready to step up coordination with all parties to put in place the institutional frameworks of the four security centers as soon as possible, and lay a solid foundation for their high-standard operation. Second, the SCO should strive for concrete and robust outcomes in cooperation projects. Only when consensus and plans are translated into specific cooperation projects can their value be truly released and shared by all parties. We should put greater emphasis on development and people's livelihood, implement a number of priority cooperation projects in such areas as trade, energy, and digital and green development, and strive for concrete outcomes at an early date. China stands ready to build the branches of the Demonstration Base for Agricultural Technology Exchange and Training with relevant countries and provide funding for 1,000 medical workers from member countries to study in China via the China-SCO Cooperation Center for Metabolic Diseases, so as to continuously enhance the well-being of people in our region. Third, the SCO should lead by example. Through its participation in international and regional affairs, the SCO has accumulated rich experience and shown the Shanghai Spirit to the world. We should strengthen dialogue and coordination with the U.N., BRICS, the Eurasian Economic Union, ASEAN, and other multilateral institutions, encourage all parties to jointly implement the four global initiatives and build a community with a shared future for humanity.
In recent years, there have been increasingly stronger calls for enhancing multilateralism and reforming and improving global governance in the international community. During the Bishkek Summit, leaders had in-depth discussions on building a multipolar world and reached important consensus, demonstrating the SCO's sense of responsibility of our times. Under the current circumstances, the SCO should bring together more international partners and shoulder its responsibility on the global stage. In doing so, it is crucial to lay greater stress on seeking common ground and resolving differences, so as to pool wisdom and strength to the largest extent.
First, the SCO should enhance economic and trade cooperation based on different endowments. Countries vary in resources, technology and market. That is no obstacle to cooperation, but an advantage for complementarity. The SCO should further promote regional economic integration, work to build an open global economy and turn differences of endowment into drivers for win-win results. We need to step up connectivity of markets and industries. It's important to enhance trade and investment liberalization and facilitation, oppose building walls or creating barriers, and keep global industrial and supply chains stable and unimpeded. All parties are welcome to join the International Economic and Trade Cooperation Initiative on Green Mining and Minerals, boost digital trade and investment cooperation, and jointly build the Pilot Zone for Silk Road E-commerce Cooperation and the Smart Customs Cooperation Partnership. We need to build stable and resilient international transportation corridors. It's important to strengthen the building of Arctic waterways and the Trans-Caspian International Transport Corridor, and actively develop multimodal transport, so as to enhance transport capacity and grow industries along the routes. Participation in the United Nations Convention on Negotiable Cargo Documents enables better leverage of the transnational land logistics corridor.
Second, the SCO should pursue common interests among different needs. Countries differ in national condition and naturally have differences regarding interests and needs. The key to handling the differences lies in mutual respect and equal consultation, which enables a joint endeavor in the same direction to seek the broadest common ground. The SCO should encourage all parties to focus on common interests, replace confrontation and estrangement with dialogue and inclusion, seek viable solutions, and jointly safeguard world peace and stability. Amidst increasing attention on energy security in the international community, SCO countries should work together in producing and supplying traditional energy, and at the same time accelerate green and low-carbon transition. Joint efforts in building the China-SCO Energy Cooperation Platform and the China-SCO Platform for Green Industry Cooperation and sharing their benefits could help expand cooperation in such areas as green energy, new-type energy storage and digital grid.
Third, the SCO should promote coexistence and harmony among different cultures. The history of human development is also one of the development of diverse civilizations. The SCO should work with all parties to carry out more people-to-people exchanges and dialogue, and boost cooperation in culture and tourism, so as to strengthen the bond between people from different countries, and promote mutual learning between different civilizations. China is ready to enhance cooperation with all parties in talent cultivation, joint research and high-quality education at all levels, bring free clinic "Brightness Action" to cataract patients in more countries, and deliver greater benefits to more peoples.
Through solidarity we can achieve great success, and through cooperation we can open up the future. Pakistan has assumed the chairmanship of the SCO. China will work with all parties to fully support Pakistan in carrying out its plan under the theme "Turning Vision into Action", and to continuously improve the quality and efficiency of the SCO development. Let us join hands to build a better and stronger SCO, and thus a more beautiful future for humanity.
Thank you. ■

China and Russia push Japan’s jet scrambles to 4-year high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
05:45:08 UTC
14:45:08 KST

- Japan’s Air Self-Defense Force scrambled fighters 442 times from April to September 2026, up from 265 in the same period of 2025.
- Scrambles against Russian aircraft rose from 59 to 152, while those against Chinese aircraft and drones climbed from 198 to 285.
Japan’s Air Self-Defense Force scrambled fighter jets 442 times between April 1 and Sept. 30, about two-thirds more than the 265 scrambles in the same period last year, according to Joint Staff Office figures reported by USNI News. The rise came as Chinese and Russian military aircraft flew near Japan far more often, and the six-month total for the first half of Japan’s 2026 fiscal year is the highest first-half count since fiscal 2022, when JASDF fighters launched 446 times.
None of the flights crossed into Japanese sovereign airspace, and the report lists no airspace violations during the period. Japan scrambles fighters against foreign aircraft approaching the country and entering its Air Defense Identification Zone, a monitoring area that reaches well past the 12-nautical-mile (22 km) territorial limit into international airspace.
Chinese aircraft and drones accounted for 285 scrambles, or about 65 percent, up from 198 a year earlier. The sharper change came from Russia, as JASDF fighters launched 152 times against Russian aircraft compared with 59 in the first half of fiscal 2025, which is more than in the first half of any of the four previous fiscal years listed in the report. The remaining five scrambles were classed as “other.”
The Joint Staff Office pointed to three patterns behind the numbers: Russian Il-20 intelligence-gathering flights over the Sea of Japan and the Pacific, Chinese Y-9 intelligence flights over the East China Sea, and long-range joint flights by Chinese H-6 and Russian Tu-95 bombers. Japan reported Y-9 flights on five consecutive days from Sept. 3 to Sept. 7, after we reported on an Aug. 12 Y-9 sortie through the same corridor between the Danjo Islands and Okinawa.
The southwest, which faces Taiwan and the East China Sea, remained the busiest sector, with the Southwestern Air Defense Force logging 201 scrambles against 189 a year earlier. The Northern Air Defense Force, which covers Hokkaido and northern Honshu opposite Russia’s Sakhalin Island, more than doubled its count from 53 to 112. The Central Air Defense Force rose from nine to 27.
The steepest jump came in the Western Air Defense Force, which covers Kyushu, Shikoku and western Honshu and went from 14 scrambles to 102. USNI News, citing the Joint Staff flight-path map, attributed the increase to Chinese activity over the East China Sea and to Russian aircraft flying from the Sea of Japan to the East China Sea to link up with Chinese formations.
The largest single event came on June 27, when two H-6 bombers and two J-16 fighters flew from the East China Sea into the Sea of Japan. There they joined two Russian Tu-95 bombers, two Tu-142 maritime patrol aircraft and a Su-35 fighter. The combined group flew back to the East China Sea, where the Russian bombers and patrol aircraft met another two H-6s and four J-16s, passed between Okinawa and Miyako Island and continued on a long-range flight over the Pacific south of Shikoku.
South Korea also scrambled fighters that day after nearly 10 Chinese and Russian aircraft entered and left its own air defense zone, and Seoul lodged a protest with both countries the next day. It was the first joint bomber flight around Japan since a December 2025 mission that paired two Tu-95s with two H-6s and eight J-16s. Beijing and Moscow describe such patrols as normal cooperation, while Japan’s 2026 defense white paper says repeated joint activities are “obviously intended as demonstration activities against Japan.”
The report also lists 25 publicly announced cases of unusual flight activity during the six months. Chinese Y-9 flights account for 13 of them, twice accompanied by a TB-001 reconnaissance and strike drone, while Russian Il-20 flights appear 10 times. The only other bomber entry covers July 21, when a single Tu-95 and a Su-35 flew over the Sea of Japan.
The surge follows a quieter year. Japan recorded 595 scrambles in all of fiscal 2025, including 214 against Russian aircraft, and monthly counts climbed late in that year, reaching 79 in December 2025. That same month, Japan accused J-15 fighters from the carrier Liaoning of directing their radar at two JASDF F-15s southeast of Okinawa.
The pace held through the summer, with 90 scrambles in July and 76 in August, as Chinese intelligence aircraft and drones and Russian intelligence planes kept up flights around Japan.

Anticyclone will bring warmth and mostly dry weather - weather on October 21
Kyiv • UNN
On October 21, mostly dry weather is expected in Ukraine due to the strengthening anticyclone. Warm air will arrive from the southeast.
In Ukraine, an anticyclone will determine the weather on October 21. Warm temperatures of up to 20° are expected. It will be mostly dry, with fog in a number of regions in the morning. UNN reports this, citing the Ukrainian Hydrometeorological Center.
On October 21, the synoptic situation will be favorable for the formation of good weather: atmospheric pressure will rise rapidly as a high-pressure field from a powerful anticyclone to the northeast spreads toward us, so dry weather will prevail. As before, a warm air mass will arrive from the southeast, providing corresponding temperatures
According to the forecast, today will be cloudy with sunny intervals.
In Ukraine, except in the west and southwest, there will be light rain in places. At night and in the morning, fog is expected in Zakarpattia, the Carpathian foothills, the southern part of the country, and most central regions.
Winds will be southeasterly and easterly at 5–10 m/s, and 7–12 m/s in the western regions.
Temperatures will be 6–11° at night, and 0–5° above zero in the Carpathians; during the day, 12–17°, reaching 20° in Zakarpattia and the south of the country.

Anthropic posts $80bn loss in first half of 2026: WSJ
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21

Anthropic posts $80bn loss in first half of 2026: WSJ
The loss is up $13 billion more than last year, driven by accounting charges, the report said.
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) company known for creating the chatbot Claude, recorded a net loss of more than $80bn in the first half of 2026, according to the Wall Street Journal, as the market anticipates its looming initial public offering (IPO).
The corporation also indicated it could spend up to $750bn in coming years to acquire more computing capacity, including potential deals currently under discussion, the Journal said on Tuesday.
The main driver for the loss was the $72bn in accounting charges related to changes in the value of convertible notes and other financial instruments Anthropic issued to raise funding, the report said.
The loss figure was up from $13bn a year earlier, according to a draft prospectus, a legal document corporations submit to financial regulators, for its IPO.
The figures show the hefty costs of the AI race, even as investors look more closely at whether the money companies are pouring into chips and data centres will pay off.
Anthropic also shared a list of potential risk factors, including uncertainty over how to prevent its products from doing harm, whether through sophisticated cyberattacks or blackmail by uncontrolled models.
Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment, and the report on the non-public information could not be immediately verified.
Investors weigh loss
Reuters first reported in September that Anthropic posted a net loss of $42bn in 2025, as part of a series of exclusives from its IPO prospectus.
The company has benefited from the popularity of Claude Code, its coding assistant that developers use to write software and build apps.
But some current and prospective investors who attended Anthropic’s investor day in San Francisco, California, last week are weighing a lower valuation for the AI company after its latest financial disclosures, four people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
The investors who attended the event discussed a valuation of around $1.5 trillion, three of the people said, a significant step down from the roughly $2 trillion valuation previously expected for the November share sale.
Anthropic’s revenue jumped to $16.3bn in the six-month period that ended June 30, up from $1.1bn a year ago, while AI infrastructure spending nearly quadrupled to almost $9bn, the Journal reported.
Anthropic reported last week that AI could be months away from learning to self-replicate on everyday home devices.

OpenAI says its agents turned off own safeguards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

OpenAI says its agents turned off own safeguards
ChatGPT creator says AI agents disabled misalignment monitoring during two internal coding tasks.
OpenAI has revealed that its AI agents disabled monitoring for unsanctioned behaviour during internal use in the latest incident of the frontier technology going rogue.
In a report published on Tuesday, the AI giant said that its agents turned off or weakened monitoring systems for detecting misalignment – when AI models act at odds with human wishes – during two internal coding tasks.
The incidents involved a GPT-6.1 Sol agent disabling automatic alerts to the company’s security team, and a GPT-6 Astra agent removing a monitoring system and falsely claiming it had not done so, OpenAI said.
The ChatGPT creator said neither case met the threshold for a highest-priority incident necessitating immediate review by its security team.
OpenAI said it updated its systems to better detect attempts to disable misalignment monitoring and began investigating the cause.
“It is possible that this behavior is simply an example of ‘benign’ overpersistence, with models not understanding why monitoring is important or insisting that instructions be executed beyond what a reasonable person might expect,” the San Francisco-based firm said.
“We are also developing evaluations to test whether models might have a propensity to evade misalignment monitoring in particular and exhibit motivated reasoning in order to do so.”
Roman V Yampolskiy, an expert on AI and cybersecurity at the University of Louisville, described the revelations as “extremely concerning, but not surprising.”
“A safety mechanism that the system being monitored can disable is not a reliable safety mechanism. Particularly concerning is that one agent subsequently denied removing the monitor,” Yampolskiy told Al Jazeera.
“Monitoring cannot guarantee safety if the monitored system can undermine the monitor,” Yampolskiy said.
“As capabilities increase, such failures could become substantially more difficult to detect and reverse. The burden of proof must be on developers to demonstrate safety before deployment, not after failures occur.”
Rogue behaviour by AI models has been under heightened scrutiny since July, when OpenAI revealed that some of its agents broke out of a controlled testing environment and hacked the AI platform Hugging Face.
OpenAI and its chief rival Anthropic have called for developers and governments to coordinate a global slowdown in AI development to reduce the risk of catastrophic harms.
The US and China, the world’s leading AI powers, have displayed little appetite for cooperation on AI regulation, with coordination so far limited to pledges to improve communication on incidents with implications for safety or national security.
