Russia is selling off its gold reserves at the fastest pace since 1998 to cover the budget deficit
Kyiv • UNN
Russia’s central bank sold about 62 tonnes of gold over 10 months. The budget deficit in 2026 could rise to 7.3 trillion rubles.
Russia’s central bank has been selling gold from its reserves for 10 consecutive months amid a growing budget deficit. In 2026, it could reach 7.3 trillion rubles—twice as much as initially forecast. The Moscow Times reports, according to UNN.
Details
In September, Russia’s gold reserves fell by 6.2 tonnes, while the total volume of reserves declined to 72.8 million troy ounces—the lowest level since the end of 2019.
Since December last year, the central bank has sold around 62 tonnes of gold. This is more than during the entire crisis-ridden 1998, when Russia’s gold reserves fell by approximately 50 tonnes.
Why Russia is actively selling gold
According to Reuters, the sales are linked to the use of assets from the National Wealth Fund to cover the budget deficit. Due to declining oil and gas revenues, the Russian authorities have been forced to spend their accumulated reserves more actively.
At the same time, China is increasing its purchases of Russian gold. From January to July, around 100 tonnes of precious metal from Russia were imported through Hong Kong—three times more than during the same period last year.
After the London market was closed to Russian gold, exporters redirected shipments to Asia. According to Financial Times estimates, $35 billion worth of Russian gold has been exported through Hong Kong since the beginning of the full-scale war.

Unknown Publisher

21:11:18 UTC

Musk ordered slowdown of Starlink service used by Ukraine’s military: WSJ
WASHINGTON – Elon Musk in October ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite service that Ukraine relies on, The Wall Street Journal reported on Oct 20, citing US officials and sources familiar with the matter.
Musk, SpaceX and the White House did not immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comment. Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
Ukraine uses Starlink for battlefield communications and drone operations. Restricting the satellite service hampered the country’s attack and air defence drone missions against Russia.
Musk and US President Donald Trump discussed the Starlink decision in a call soon after the slowdown became public, while the President was campaigning earlier in October, according to the report, which added the two had also discussed the matter prior to the decision to throttle Starlink.
Reuters had reported exclusively that the order to limit the satellite system came from inside the White House.
Trump earlier said he did not think either he or Musk was responsible for Ukraine losing Starlink access, while Musk said any limits on speed or Starship use were decided by the US military or the President.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s relations with Washington have sunk to new lows after Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and waived new sanctions on Moscow.
Trump has also told Kyiv to stop attacking Russian refineries and urged Ukrainians to replace Zelensky.
Zelensky, who is in Oslo in a bid to repair US relations, said on Oct 20 he discussed issues including “the situation with Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored” with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Oct 20 Washington had not pulled back Ukraine’s ability to access Starlink’s satellite network, but signalled the problem lay with the terms of service Kyiv needed to comply with. REUTERS

06:09:13 KST

In short:
Townsville's Abbey Ellis has scored 47 points to defeat Adelaide in the WNBL.
Ellis's mammoth haul was the most scored by an individual in a WNBL match for 21 years.
What's next?
The second round of the WNBL season begins tomorrow as Southside Melbourne Flyers face Tasmania Jewels.
Townsville's Abbey Ellis has produced one of the all-time great WNBL individual performances with a mammoth 47-point effort in the Fire's 86-68 away win over Adelaide.
The defending champions trailed 35-21 in the second quarter but outscored Adelaide 27-10 in the last term.
They improved to 1-1 while Adelaide dropped to 0-2.
Ellis kept her team afloat in the first half, scoring 25 of their first 33 points and their first 16 of the second quarter.
Her club record individual score, eclipsing the 45 points by Chandi Jones in 2005, was the equal fifth-highest in WNBL history and the largest in 21 years.
She joined league legends Lauren Jackson, Penny Taylor and Belinda Snell among the only players to record 47 points and six steals in a game.
"It's a pretty cool feeling," Ellis said.
She hit 16 of 24 from the field, nailing seven of 13 from three-point range.
"Credit to our team, we used the ball really well and found the hot hand," Ellis said.
Townsville coach Shannon Seebohm said Ellis was one of the bravest players he had coached.
"Abbey had probably one of the best games that I know I've ever seen In the WNBL, making huge shots, making big plays," Seebohm said.
"I said to her probably the thing I was most proud of her wasn't all the scoring, [it was] that she was fighting as hard as she could and defending her butt off."
Adelaide led by seven at quarter-time and Townsville scored the last seven points of the second quarter to get within three at the half.
As the game progressed, Townsville's defence improved and Ellis got more scoring support from Courtney Woods (14) and German centre Marie Gulich (13).
Alicia Froling grabbed 11 rebounds and Alexandra Fowler 10 to help Townsville collect 11 more boards.
Adelaide were shooting at 62 per cent from the field at half-time, but that dropped to 45 per cent by the end, as they scored just 25 points after half-time.
"We had a tough second half," Lightning coach Aja Parham-Ammar said.
Tayla Brazel led Adelaide's offence with a personal WNBL career-high of 19, at 72 per cent from the field.
Shay Ciezki tallied 13 points, Zitina Aokuso 12 and Opals star Steph Talbot had 11 and nine assists in her first game back from WNBA duties.

21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday that Ukraine is not losing the war with Russia but is losing people and time as Russian attacks continue, stressing the need to end the conflict as soon as possible.
Speaking at a news conference in Oslo, Norway, alongside Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, Zelenskyy said Ukraine is ready for negotiations and hoped the US and European partners would help bring the war to an end.
“Of course, we are not losing this war, but we are losing people ... and because Russia attacks, we're losing people and time,” he said, adding that Ukrainian children are being deprived of their childhood.
Zelenskyy said US Envoy Steve Witkoff attended the meeting in Oslo, with President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner joining online to discuss various “sensitive points,” security guarantees, and Ukraine’s postwar reconstruction.
He added that Ukraine is ready for negotiations and supports exploring different ceasefire formats to achieve de-escalation, stressing: “We want to push as quick as possible to end this war."
He said Ukraine had supported a US proposal for an energy ceasefire but accused Russia of continuing attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Kyiv had offered not to strike sensitive parts of Russia's energy sector if Moscow stopped attacking Ukraine's, he added.
He said Ukraine and its European partners had developed proposals aimed at advancing peace efforts, including a potential trilateral meeting involving the leaders of Ukraine, Russia, and the US, saying Kyiv hopes Washington will convey its proposals to Moscow.
"We have some clear ideas on how to get to peace. And we are united with our European partners in this effort, and we want the Americans to take these ideas to the Russians. One of the important ideas is to move to a potential trilateral meeting of the leaders to address the issues that only the leaders can do," he said.
“Steve is going to Russia tomorrow, and let's see what (Russian President Vladimir) Putin has to say,” he added. 
Legitimacy only with Ukraine’s participation, says Zelenskyy
Zelenskyy also said he had held a “very positive” conversation with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier Tuesday, discussing sensitive issues including Starlink connectivity, air defense interceptor missiles, and intelligence sharing. He said the two agreed to speak again within 48 hours.
He said Ukraine is currently receiving intelligence from the US, including through an early warning system for Russian ballistic missile attacks, stressing that Washington’s support is important for protecting Ukrainian civilians.
On possible peace talks, Zelenskyy said no discussion of Ukraine's future without Kyiv’s participation can be legitimate.
“I don't know what about trilateral meeting will be between America, China, and Russia. It's up to them. But of course, if the issues are about Ukraine, our future, it can be acceptable only when we are at the table of negotiations. It's absolutely clear,” he said.
Asked whether Putin was using Moscow's ties with Iran as leverage over US President Donald Trump, Zelenskyy said he did not know but believes Russia has supported Tehran during the ongoing war, including through drone supplies and intelligence sharing.

====================================================================================================

Why do the US midterms matter for Trump and Congress?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
21:00:42 UTC
06:00:42 KST

Why do the US midterms matter for Trump and Congress?
Republicans and Democrats jockey for control of Congress, which will set course for Trump’s final two years in office.
The United States midterms on November 3 are dominating national and international headlines.
The stakes of the election are high. The midterm race will determine which party controls the US Congress, and in turn, shape the direction of Trump’s final two years in office. It will also decide key state and local positions.
But notching big wins in the midterm election may not be enough to shake up the balance of power in Washington, DC.
To understand the implications of this year’s midterm election and what may come next, Al Jazeera has put together this simple primer.
Here’s why the US midterms matter at the federal level.
Battle for the US House of Representatives and US Senate
Midterm elections fall at the halfway point of a president’s term, meaning the executive office will not be on the ballot.
Front and centre will be the battle for control of Congress. Two chambers make up the US legislature: the House of Representatives and the Senate.
Because members of the House serve two-year terms, all 435 seats in the chamber are up for election on November 3. However, most races are already considered formalities, with a clear frontrunner.
That leaves only a handful of races — about 50 — to decide who will win the House majority.
While subject to change, nearly every reputable election prognosticator has predicted that Democrats will win control of the House, some by as many as 15 seats.
The Democrats have a slimmer chance of winning a majority in the Senate, however.
That chamber has only 100 seats. But because senators have staggered six-year terms, only 35 seats are up for election. Only about a dozen of those races are considered competitive.
Still, Democrats have seen their odds of seizing the Senate increase, as the number of competitive races has grown.
Left-wing candidates have made inroads in deep-red states like Texas and Kansas, creating more opportunities for the Democratic Party to claim a Senate majority this election cycle.
Because the US vice president breaks ties in the Senate, Democrats would need 51 seats to control the chamber.
What does party control mean?
Congress passes laws and approves federal budgets. But even if a party secures a majority in both chambers of Congress, it may not be enough to control the country’s legislative agenda.
Laws can pass by a simple majority in the House, but they typically need a supermajority of 60 votes in the Senate to overcome a process known as the filibuster. That process can allow a minority group to stall legislation indefinitely, barring a supermajority.
Therefore, unless a party wins more than 60 seats in the Senate, most legislation will still require at least some level of bipartisan support to pass.
Even if legislation passes both chambers, the president can veto any bill that comes across his desk. Overriding a presidential veto requires a two-thirds supermajority in both the House and the Senate.
Achieving the broad bipartisan support needed to overcome a presidential veto is exceedingly rare.
The last time it happened was in January 2021, during Trump’s first term. At the time, the US president had lost the 2020 election, and he saw his support from Republican lawmakers dissipate when he attempted to veto a defence spending bill.
Still, there are instances when bipartisan support overcomes presidential objections. A bill to increase the housing supply passed both the House and Senate with veto-proof majorities earlier this year, despite Trump’s stated opposition.
So what happens if Republicans maintain control of Congress?
Republicans currently hold two majorities in Congress, with 53 seats in the Senate and 218 in the House.
With Trump in the White House, that means the party has held a so-called government “trifecta” over the last two years, with three levers of power under its command.
The Republican majorities in Congress have helped Trump pass some of his signature legislation, including surging funding to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and cleaving back some forms of publicly funded healthcare as part of a sweeping 2025 tax bill.
But Republicans’ numbers have not been enough to pass Trump’s entire legislative wishlist. Notably, he has been unable to pass his signature federal voter identification law, dubbed the “SAVE America Act“, amid Democratic opposition.
There have also been a handful of issues where Republicans have defied Trump, particularly on tariffs. A few Republicans have also voted to assert congressional authority over the US-Israel war with Iran.
If the Republican Party maintains control of both the House and Senate in November’s race, its majorities could continue to help Trump’s legislative agenda. But there is an important caveat.
Lawmakers will be keeping an anxious eye on voter sentiment as the 2028 elections approach. With Trump unable to seek a third term, some Republicans may have more appetite to publicly oppose the lame-duck president during the next two years, in order to boost their election prospects.
If Republicans maintain control of the Senate but lose the House, they would still be able to help Trump confirm his nominees for key federal roles.
Hundreds of federal positions require approval from a simple majority in the Senate, including roles in the judiciary, including Supreme Court justices.
What if Democrats take control?
The party in control of Congress, with a few exceptions, can determine what legislation is brought to a vote and when.
But for Democrats, the most significant outcome of winning a majority in one or both chambers would be the ability to block Trump from legislating his agenda over the next two years.
That said, analysts expect a Democrat-led Congress to take a largely defensive stance, batting down Trump’s proposals.
Going on offence — and passing their own legislative agenda — will be far more difficult, even if the party wins a majority in both the House and Senate. Democrat-led laws would still face Trump’s veto power.
However, holding majorities would help Democratic members slip policy priorities into “need-to-pass” funding legislation. The spectre of a government shutdown could pressure Republicans to pass budget bills, even if they do not agree on all the terms.
Democrats can also bring topics to a vote to force congressional Republicans to oppose popular policies or simply take a public stance on divisive issues.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has laid out a 100-day plan for if Democrats take control of the chamber. Topping the agenda are votes on Trump-backed healthcare funding cuts, asserting congressional authority over the US-Israel war with Iran and rolling back Trump’s tariff programme.
Those issues have split the Republican base and would pose thorny dilemmas for lawmakers already posturing for the 2028 vote.
Will Democrats impeach Trump?
As Trump rallies on behalf of Republicans in the run-up to November’s vote, he has repeatedly expressed concern that Democratic control of Congress could lead to one eventuality: his third impeachment.
Trump was already impeached twice during his first term. “If we don’t win, they’ll end up impeaching me,” he told a rally in Durant, Oklahoma, in early October.
If Democrats do take control of the House or the Senate, they will take over leadership of dozens of committees. Through those committees, they can launch investigations — with subpoena power — into an array of subjects.
Some Democrats have already said probing allegations of Trump family corruption will be a top priority.
House lawmakers can also introduce articles of impeachment and ultimately vote to impeach federal officials, including the president, with a simple majority.
However, the Senate would need to vote to convict the official with a two-thirds majority before they can be removed from office.
Perhaps more significantly, if Democrats win control of the Senate, they would be able to block the confirmation of Trump appointees in key roles during his final two years in office.
So what will change on the war with Iran and the economy?
A Democratic surge is likely to signal discontent with the Trump administration, but there will not be a swift, tangible change on many of the issues that have defined the election season.
For example, if Democrats secure both majorities in Congress, they could assert their leverage to seek to address affordability issues, drilling into topics like housing, healthcare and the cost of living.
But they can do little to immediately change the myriad factors that led to the high price of petrol and groceries. Any gains would most likely be hard-fought, slow-coming and incremental.
The same is true for the US-Israel war with Iran.
Under the US Constitution, only Congress can declare war, something it has not done since World War II. Presidents have long used various legal arguments to circumvent that constitutional requirement.
Most recently, the Trump administration argued that the US-Israel war with Iran did not require authorisation from Congress because the president has a duty to protect the American people.
Trump has also argued that the war has started and stopped several times, each time renewing the 60-day window he has to receive Congress’s authorisation.
To reassert Congress’s authority to declare war, Democrats could pass a legally binding “war powers resolution” to rein in Trump, but they would need two-thirds support to overcome the presidential veto.
Even if a resolution were able to overcome the veto, experts say it is unclear how the US judiciary would respond if Trump were to flout Congress’s will.
Still, Democrats could use control of Congress to attempt to stifle any funding for the war.

Spotify excludes over 50 million AI slop, spam tracks from recommendations in 2026

06:00:06 KST

Halis Sünnetci
21 October 2026•Update: 21 October 2026
Music streaming giant Spotify announced Tuesday that it has excluded more than 50 million tracks classified as AI slop or spam from its recommendations this year as part of efforts to protect listeners and promote human artists.
In a statement marking one year since introducing stronger protections against AI-related spam and impersonation, Spotify said it had also removed more than 75 million spam tracks from its platform for serious or repeated violations of its rules.
Unlike tracks deleted from the platform, the 50 million excluded from recommendations were not necessarily removed from Spotify's catalog.
"AI-generated slop and spam don't belong in your recommendations, and we've made changes to keep them out and protect the listening experience," the company said.
Spotify said it had updated its recommendation system over the past six months after identifying patterns among tracks that listeners frequently skipped, ignored or reported as unwanted.
To detect suspicious content, the company combines listener feedback, upload patterns, track metadata and third-party AI detection tools, while acknowledging the limitations of AI detection technology.
The company also highlighted measures introduced over the past year, including AI Credits that disclose the use of artificial intelligence in music production and badges identifying AI-generated artist identities.
More than 300,000 artists have received Spotify verification badges, while thousands of AI-generated artist identities have been labeled and excluded from recommendations by default.
Spotify said tracks considered highly likely to be AI-generated were 10 times more likely to fall below its annual 1,000-stream threshold for royalty payments, making large-scale attempts to exploit its payment system less profitable.
The company said it would continue updating its detection systems as generative AI technology evolves and spammers develop new tactics.

Uzbekistan and the US have agreed on 54 joint projects worth $12 billion in the energy, technology, aviation and mining sectors. Some of the agreements still need to be financed.
Uzbekistan announced 54 agreements and joint projects with the United States worth a total of $12 billion. The agreements became known after U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio held talks with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev in Samarkand. Euronews reports, UNN writes.
Details
The cooperation will cover several strategic areas, including energy, the extraction of critical minerals, the aviation industry, the financial sector, and advanced technologies.
The parties are paying particular attention to the development of renewable energy and electricity storage systems. Such projects are to become part of a broader economic partnership between Washington and Tashkent.
The U.S. and Uzbekistan plan to deepen their technological partnership
The priority areas of cooperation also include the creation of data centers and the development of artificial intelligence technologies. These areas have been included in the list of promising joint investment projects.
The extraction of strategic minerals used in high-tech manufacturing and energy will become a separate area of cooperation. The parties view this sector as one of the foundations of future economic interaction.
In addition, the countries are considering the possibility of preparing a long-term program of trade, investment, and technological cooperation through 2035. It is intended to define the main areas for developing bilateral economic relations.
The announced package of agreements envisages the implementation of projects worth $12 billion, but this amount does not mean that all the funds have already been invested. Further implementation of the agreements will depend on the specific projects and their financing.

‘I’m alive’: Paris street medic isn’t dead, despite viral claims he was killed by police
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
20:43:22 UTC
05:43:22 KST

'I'm alive': Paris street medic isn't dead, despite viral claims he was killed by police
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
A video showing French riot police violently beating a 26-year-old street medic in Paris has gone viral, with social media users falsely claiming he died from his injuries. But the street medic is alive, and spoke to FRANCE 24. The rumour was fuelled by confusion with a separate incident that same day: a man died of cardiac arrest in the same area, causing online users to conflate the two events. Vedika Bahl explains in Truth or Fake.
Antoine, a 26-year-old who volunteers as a "street medic" to provide first aid to injured protesters, spoke to the FRANCE 24 Observers about the incident after videos showing officers striking him, knocking him to the ground and dragging his apparently unconscious body circulated widely online.
In the footage from Saturday October 17, Antoine appears to lose consciousness after officers strike him with batons. Some versions of the video were later shared with claims that he had been "assassinated by police" or "beaten to death".
Antoine said he had stepped in front of a water cannon to identify himself as a medic, before being struck on the head with a baton: "I stepped in front of it to show I was harmless – I had "medic" written on an armband on my side. What I do remember is getting hit in the head from behind. I was half-unconscious, then something hit me in the back."
He regained consciousness in a fire engine, where emergency responders carried out a concussion test. Antoine said he continued to suffer severe headaches, planned to return to hospital for further examinations and intended to file a complaint. He also said his injuries had left him unable to work.
The false claims appear to have been fuelled by confusion surrounding a separate death in Paris on the same day.
French media and Paris police headquarters confirmed that a man had died from cardiac arrest on Boulevard Magenta, in the capital's 10th arrondissement. The incident occurred in the same general area as the street medic's incident, which was filmed near Place de la République, near the intersection with the road Rue du Faubourg du Temple.
With limited information initially available about the man who died, social media users began conflating the two incidents and wrongly identifying the street medic as the victim.
One viral clip, which amassed more than 5 million views, was taken from a six-hour livestream of Saturday's protests and reposted separately online. The caption initially described the man being dragged away as "unconscious", before other posts escalated the claim, alleging that he had been killed or died from his injuries.
This particular false claim shows how misinformation can develop in stages over time: genuine footage of a violent incident is shared with incomplete information, speculation follows, and separate events are wrongly linked. In this instance, a confirmed death elsewhere in Paris helped fuel a false claim about a man who is still alive.

The UN high commissioner for human rights on Tuesday voiced concern over human rights violations amid mass protests across several European countries, including France, Belgium, Italy, Portugal, and Albania.
"The mass protests across Albania, Belgium, France, Italy and Portugal are raising human rights concerns," Volker Turk said in a statement, condemning all acts of violence.

He called for prompt, effective, and independent investigations into allegations of unlawful use of force, emphasizing the need for accountability and effective remedies for victims.
Noting steps taken by some authorities to investigate incidents and ease tensions, Turk urged governments to engage protesters, particularly young people, in "meaningful, inclusive and constructive dialogue."

STG Design unveils upcoming “unconventional, sinuous” Houston skyscraper
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

20:40:36 UTC

STG Design unveils upcoming “unconventional, sinuous” Houston skyscraper
Texas architecture studio STG Design has released renderings of O27, an office skyscraper covered with triangular panels that is planned for Houston’s River Oaks area.
The 32-storey building will contain flexible office floors, as well as luxury amenities and a rooftop terrace on top of its nine-storey base.
It will have a parking garage block at its podium and a tower that rises in an undulating form.
The design is the result of an “intensive computational design process” by STG Design that sought to prioritise “highly efficient, repeatable floorplates” within the building’s curved geometry.
Renders show two, curving glass facades folded around either side of the building. They are divided at the middle, where a spine of terraces travel up its length.
“Its unconventional, sinuous form resists the rigid verticality that has come to dominate contemporary office buildings, resulting in a structure that feels fluid, expressive and perpetually in motion,” said the team.
Its facade will be made up of triangular glass panels to create a “shimmering skin” that will appear to shift in the changing light of the day.
Other elements include an entrance drive covered in a sculpted ceiling embedded with lights to “evoke a night sky” and a double-height, glass-clad lobby, both designed by international design practice Design ALT + TAB.
Interior renderings show spaces covered in a metallic bronze, with black-and-white marble surfaces and curved seating.
According to developers Broadview Capital, the project was informed by the admiration its founders, brothers Anish and Ashay Bavishi, have for Houston’s Williams Tower, designed by architects Philip Johnson and John Burgee.
The skyscraper symbolises “ambition, possibility and global sophistication” for Houston, said the team, an element the designers and developers hope to bring to the city’s “prestigious” River Oaks area, known for its historic estates and luxury shopping.
“O27 serves as both a geographic marker and a tribute to a neighbourhood whose century-long legacy has been defined by thoughtful planning, architectural distinction and enduring relevance,” said the team.
The building is expected to be completed in 2028.
STG Design is based in Austin, Texas and was founded in 1976.
Other projects recently announced for Houston include a coffee plant set to be converted into a music school by OMA and a performance space created by Theaster Gates and Studio Zewde.

====================================================================================================

'Can you imagine a soldier shooting a Jew?': Inside the IDF's plan to curb settler violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
20:40:20 UTC
05:40:20 KST

"The problem is that the IDF is the governing authority, but the solutions to nationalist crime are not military ones." That is how a senior security official summed up one of the most sensitive issues currently facing Israel's defense establishment.
Behind the scenes, amid escalating violence in the West Bank, IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir convened a high-level meeting with senior security officials. The meeting resulted in a series of operational measures aimed at curbing the violence, improving law enforcement and closing intelligence gaps that have developed over time.
The IDF recognizes that responsibility for security in the area rests largely with the military, while confronting Jewish rioters presents soldiers with a challenge fundamentally different from the missions for which they were trained.
"We don't have the tools to deal with them. You're deploying more soldiers when what's needed are police officers," the senior official explained. "Combat soldiers arrive after fighting in Lebanon and then have to deal with Israelis. They don't know how to handle Israelis. Can you imagine a situation in which a soldier from the 202nd Battalion might, God forbid, shoot Jews?"
According to the official, these are no longer isolated incidents that can be contained by deploying additional forces or through localized intervention. He stressed that the scale of the phenomenon and its consequences now extend well beyond the military's area of responsibility.
"These are criminals who have lost all restraint and are defying the authority of the state," he said. "This is a shared mission that requires joint efforts. It has become a national and international problem."
The meeting chaired by Zamir included senior representatives of the IDF, Shin Bet security agency and Israel Police. Among those attending were a representative of the Shin Bet division responsible for preventing Jewish extremism, a representative of the Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT), IDF Central Command chief Maj. Gen. Avi Bluth and Judea and Samaria District police commander Deputy Commissioner Moshe Pinchi.
Bringing all these officials together around one table reflects a growing recognition within the defense establishment that combating nationalist crime requires a change in approach: less reliance on military forces for policing duties and greater coordination between intelligence gathering, police enforcement and operational activities.
More forces, more command centers
Some of the measures were already implemented before the meeting. The IDF recently reinforced its presence in the West Bank with additional forces, including the headquarters of the 98th Division and the Paratroopers Brigade, which is operating in areas including the Shiloh Valley.
However, military reinforcements alone are not enough to provide the necessary response. The defense establishment is now seeking to change how responsibilities are divided on the ground so that police forces can focus on incidents of nationalist crime.
One of the central measures approved concerns preparations for November, when a new Border Police unit is expected to be established to focus exclusively on nationalist crime.
Until the unit is established, during the remaining days of October, IDF soldiers are expected to replace Border Police officers at some of the positions and checkpoints where they are permanently stationed in the West Bank.
The move is intended to free up additional Border Police personnel to concentrate on law enforcement and responding to violent incidents.
But deploying more soldiers is not necessarily the solution if they are required to handle situations that fall outside their training and designated responsibilities. The IDF wants combat soldiers to focus on security missions, while police forces assume a greater share of responsibility for crime prevention and law enforcement involving Israeli civilians.
Another measure ordered by Zamir is the reestablishment of a joint interagency command center to coordinate the activities of the IDF, police and Shin Bet.
The command center was originally established following a push by Pinchi but was later shut down because of insufficient personnel.
Under the new arrangements, Border Police forces equivalent to two companies will be assigned to the effort, including officers freed up when IDF soldiers take over some of their existing positions.
The goal is to create a joint framework that will improve coordination between the agencies, consolidate their efforts and enable faster information sharing among those responsible for identifying and preventing violent incidents.
The main gap: Intelligence
The defense establishment recognizes that the problem goes beyond the number of police officers and soldiers deployed on the ground.
One of the main shortcomings identified during the meeting concerns intelligence: the ability to identify organized groups, provide advance warnings of potential incidents and reach flashpoints before violence erupts.
Various measures are also expected to be introduced to strengthen intelligence gathering on Jewish rioters and their plans.
"There is an intelligence problem," one security official acknowledged. "There are incidents involving large crowds where additional rioters arrive to escalate the violence before security forces even become aware of what's happening. This is a gap we must close."
At the same time, Zamir instructed officials to promptly present him with the results of the use of administrative exclusion orders, along with a list of the main individuals involved in recent violent incidents and information on efforts to monitor them.
He also directed officials to expand the use of these orders if necessary, with the aim of determining whether administrative measures are effective in curbing the violence or whether changes are needed in how they are applied.
In doing so, Zamir is seeking to shift the response to nationalist crime from a primarily reactive approach to one whose effectiveness is also measured by results on the ground.
Military uniforms do not grant immunity
The meeting also addressed the conduct of IDF soldiers themselves.
Zamir ordered that instructions to soldiers be clarified and reinforced, with particular emphasis on soldiers on leave who become involved in incidents primarily connected to illegal outposts.
In cases where soldiers participate in such activities, the military has been instructed to impose tougher penalties, potentially including removal from combat service, depending on the circumstances and severity of their actions.
The message to soldiers is clear: Wearing a military uniform does not grant immunity, and being on leave does not exempt them from the obligations and restrictions that apply to them.
The defense establishment wants to make clear that soldiers cannot exploit their military status.
Ultimately, the meeting chaired by the IDF chief of staff signals an attempt to move beyond condemnations and isolated responses to violent incidents toward a coordinated action plan: reinforcing security forces, redistributing responsibilities between the IDF and Border Police, strengthening intelligence capabilities, establishing a dedicated police unit and reassessing enforcement and disciplinary measures.
The real test, however, will be implementation.
The question is not simply how many additional forces will be deployed to the West Bank or how many new units will be established. Rather, it is whether the defense establishment can identify potential incidents before violence erupts, respond quickly to violent confrontations and establish a credible deterrent that will reduce the likelihood of further attacks.
Senior security officials understand that allowing the current situation to continue is not merely an operational challenge. It is also a test of the state's ability to enforce the law equally and maintain its authority on the ground.

Feds hold back an additional $1.2 billion in California Medicaid reimbursements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
20:33:02 UTC
05:33:02 KST

Feds hold back an additional $1.2 billion in California Medicaid reimbursements
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- The move is the latest in a series of efforts by the administration to withhold federal money from California.
- Dr. Mehmet Oz did not provide any evidence of fraud.
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration is deferring an additional $1.2 billion in Medicaid reimbursements to California, citing concerns about potential fraud in a state program that helps older adults and people with disabilities with everyday tasks.
Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, said federal officials took action after they grew concerned about the rapid expansion of California’s personal care services program in recent years. State officials were notified of the decision Tuesday, he said.
“California has been growing that program 24% in the last three years. That is twice the rate of every other state average in the country,” Oz said. “Impossible for us to understand how that could be so we are taking major action in California.”
Oz did not provide any evidence of fraud but suggested the state was paying people too much taxpayer money to help with services that could be offered for free, like “paying somebody to carry groceries upstairs for your mom.”
“Many of you would carry groceries upstairs for your mom for free, but in California, they will pay you a lot of money for it,” he said.
Vice President JD Vance said Wednesday that the Trump administration is deferring $1.3 billion in Medicaid reimbursements to California over concerns the state is allowing “fraudsters” to drive up costs to taxpayers by pushing unnecessary medications on unsuspecting patients.
The move is the latest in a series of efforts by the administration to withhold federal money from California. In May, the administration held back $1.3 billion in Medicaid reimbursements to the state over concerns about “fraudsters” in the state’s hospice and in-home care programs. The actions have been part of a broad effort by the administration to rein in fraud in federal healthcare benefits programs, particularly in Democrat-led states.
Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla criticized the administration’s decision.
“This Administration’s track record speaks for itself: Fewer people have health insurance, premiums are up, and drug costs are higher. This decision will hurt older Californians, people with disabilities, and those recovering from illness or injury,” Padilla said in a statement. “The American people deserve better, and I’ll keep fighting against their attacks.”
Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. But the office has been critical of the administration’s past efforts.
In May, Newsom’s office called the action to withhold funds for in-home care programs a “sick” and politically motivated attack on services that are meant to “keep seniors and people with disabilities OUT of nursing homes.”
Those services usually cover assistants who help people with daily tasks such as bathing, laundry or cooking. They also provide needed care such as injections under the direction of a medical professional. A 2020 report by the California state auditor found that nearly three-quarters of In-home Supportive Services caregivers assist a family member.
Newsom’s office, however, has argued that the program saves taxpayers money, saying IHSS care costs $30,000 a year, while nursing home care costs $137,000 a year.
Medicaid Reckoning Awaits Next California Governor After Program’s Rapid Expansion
California’s hospice industry has had problems in the past and authorities have tried to crack down on the issue. A Times investigation in 2020 found that providers were billing Medicare for hospice services and equipment for patients who were not actually dying while the industry boomed.
The Trump administration, led by Vice President JD Vance, has tried to focus attention on the issue of waste, fraud and abuse as a centerpiece policy platform to bring down healthcare costs.
On Tuesday, Trump and Vance announced a $25-million whistleblower program designed to pay out cash to people who tip off the federal government about fraudsters. The program will offer a 1% commission for tips that lead to a successful conviction. Trump said he would be the sole arbitrator of who gets to keep the money.
“I’ll determine whether or not the person is deserving, and I will be very generous believe me. We are not looking to save on that,” Trump said. “I promise you I will be fair.”
Trump said the money will be handed out “expeditiously and fairly.”
“I promise there is nothing in this for me,” he said.
The White House referred comment about the decision to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. The federal agency did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Netflix reported third-quarter earnings above market expectations Tuesday, while revenue matched forecasts, as the streaming company sought to reassure investors about viewer engagement.
Earnings per share reached $0.87 for the quarter that ended on Sept. 30, exceeding analysts' expectations.
Revenue rose nearly 12% year-on-year to $12.87 billion, in line with estimates, supported by membership growth and subscription price increases introduced in March.

jean-baptiste fastrez turns an inflatable boat and a wall fixing into mirrors to look and to be looked at
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
20:30:45 UTC
05:30:45 KST

jean-baptiste fastrez turns an inflatable boat and a wall fixing into mirrors to look and to be looked at
'I like the paradox of an object that has such a strong physical presence, yet whose image is almost entirely made up of whatever surrounds it,' says the french designer, who has spent more than a decade of his practice reworking the mirror through different forms and materials.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
The mirror as an object to look and to be looked at
‘The mirror is, after all, a utopia, since it is a placeless place,’ said Michel Foucault in a 1967 lecture, explaining that in a mirror you see yourself where you are not, ‘in an unreal, virtual space that opens up behind the surface.’ He then called it a heterotopia as well, since the mirror does exist in reality, where it ‘exerts a sort of counteraction’ on the position you occupy. No other object in a house behaves this way, since everything else in a room is looked at while a mirror hands the room back with its viewer inside it. That duality, between what the object looks like and what it does to whoever stands in front of it, has given the mirror an unusual position in design. Creatives have worked on both halves of it, the form and the surface, which is why the object keeps producing experiments in both how it looks and how we see.
In Jean-Baptiste Fastrez’s case, the mirror is ‘one of the objects that offers the greatest freedom to explore ideas somewhere between design and sculpture.’ The French designer, who has spent more than a decade of his practice reworking this one object through different forms and materials, tells designboom that he likes the paradox ‘of an object that has such a strong physical presence, yet whose image is almost entirely made up of whatever surrounds it.’ Two of his recent designs for Paris-based design company Moustache push that paradox in two very different directions.
Jean-Baptiste Fastrez’s sculptural mirrors for Moustache
Both pieces Fastrez developed for Moustache begin from something that already exists. The Zodiac mirror borrows its form from the inflatable boat it is named after, so that what looks like an inflated tube is in fact high-gloss ceramic. Sphera, on the other hand, takes its cues from the hardware once used to hold mirrored walls together, reworking it into a set of oversized chrome spheres that clamp sheets of flat mirror to a wall.
‘With Zodiac, I was interested in the idea of the ready-made, or rather the fake ready-made,’ he says. ‘I wanted to create objects that looked as though they had been made by repurposing something else.’ The image was precise from the start, an inflatable boat whose inflated tube becomes a sort of floating frame, and the story he wanted was of a boat that had somehow ended up hanging on a wall and turned into a mirror. ‘I really enjoy these collisions between completely different types of objects,’ he says. ‘They can create narratives that are both strong and open-ended, with something almost mysterious about them.’
The idea for Sphera arrived in a particular room. ‘I remember very clearly that the idea came to me while visiting Carlo Mollino’s house in Turin,’ Fastrez says. ‘Some of the walls in his preserved apartment are covered with mirrors made up of several sections, held together by small chrome fittings. I found this fascinating, before realising that the system was actually nothing particularly unusual.’ The fitting was not a Mollino invention and was never rare, and he is precise about where it lived, ‘quite common throughout the twentieth century, in sophisticated architectural interiors as well as much more ordinary settings, like a bathroom or a student bedroom.’
What he saw in it was a frame with no shape of its own. ‘I started to see it as perhaps the most minimal frame imaginable, but also one of the most universal,’ he says. ‘It allows an enormous variety of formats, compositions and uses.’ His decision was then not to redesign the principle but to change its volume. ‘I wanted to take this principle almost exactly as it was, but give these little fixing elements a much stronger presence. I increased their size and transformed their geometry into something spherical, almost sculptural.’
THE GLASS AS STRUCTURE RATHER THAN AS SURFACE in ZODIAC & SPHERA
What makes a mirror worth more than a decade of a designer’s attention is how little it asks. ‘A mirror is an object whose function is reduced to its absolute minimum,’ Fastrez says. ‘As long as something has a reflective surface, it can essentially be considered a mirror.’ Hung on a wall it carries nobody’s weight and resists nothing, so it never faces the structural tests a chair or a table has to pass, and what remains is a single geometric demand, which is that it stay more or less flat.
He treats that as a paradox rather than a gift, one severe constraint in a single direction and almost total freedom in every other, and says constraints are what he finds stimulating in the first place. By his own account it is probably the object that leaves him the most room to work somewhere between design and sculpture, and the one most willing to carry a story.
Both of these pieces then do something that reverses what a mirror usually is, which is to use the glass as structure rather than as surface. Zodiac’s ceramic frame is half a ring, built from two moulded sections, and where the ceramic stops the reflection continues, so what the eye reads as two inflated tubes floating one above the other is a single tube and its image. ‘The reflection becomes an essential part of the object’s construction,’ Fastrez says, and in doing that work the mirror very nearly disappears. Sphera relies on the glass just as literally, since without the rigidity of a sheet of mirror the fixing system has nothing to hold and nothing to hold it. ‘With Sphera, the object is visually made of nothing but chrome and reflections,’ he says. ‘Its appearance depends entirely on its surroundings, which are reflected faithfully in the flat mirror and distorted across the chrome spheres.’
ORNAMENT AS FUNCTION IN ITS OWN RIGHT
‘I’m very interested in the idea of taking something as ordinary as a piece of hardware and reworking it until it becomes the strongest aesthetic feature of a project,’ Fastrez says. Both pieces end as arguments about ornament, and he makes the argument himself rather than leaving it to be inferred. ‘Ornament is something I actively pursue in my work as a designer, but I find it particularly interesting when it isn’t simply added to an object, but becomes part of its construction or the way it functions,’ he explains, and he describes that as possibly the most interesting form design can take, an object acquiring a sculptural character directly out of the logic that produced it. Sphera, by his account, began at the moment he realized that emphasising the small functional elements would generate ornament without costing the original system any of its functionalism.
The second half of the argument is about the word function itself. ‘I also think our definition of an object’s function is often far too restrictive,’ he notes. ‘An object never serves just one purpose. A mirror’s primary function might seem to be reflecting an image, but to me that’s a very incomplete definition. A mirror also serves to decorate an interior, to give it character, to place a space within a particular period, style or narrative.’ He then goes further than most designers would be willing to, and says that this ornamental function can be as important as the reflective one and is sometimes more so.
That produces a reversal of the sentence design students have been handed since Louis Sullivan wrote it in 1896, and of the century of suspicion toward ornament that followed. ‘If we accept ornament as a function in its own right,’ Fastrez says, ‘Zodiac and Sphera are, in their own way, functionalist objects whose form also follows their ornamental function.’ Zodiac arrives there through the relationship between a frame and its reflection, Sphera through the repetition of a fitting that spent fifty years being hidden, and in both cases the decoration is not sitting on the object but holding it up.
project info:
name: Zodiac and Sphera
designer: Jean-Baptiste Fastrez | @jeanbaptistefastrez
company: Moustache | @moustache_editions

At the high end of that range, it would bring United's 2026 adjusted earnings to no more than $7.22 per share. In mid-July, United said it was expecting full-year earnings of $9 to $11 a share.

A surge in fuel prices this year has added billions of dollars to airlines' costs, eating into profits, despite strong demand, and driving up airfares.
Here is what United Airlines reported for the quarter that ended Sept. 30 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on estimates compiled by LSEG:
- Earnings per share: $2.54 adjusted vs. $2.57 expected
- Revenue: $17.88 billion vs. $17.9 billion expected
United's third-quarter net income rose 8.5% from a year earlier to $1.03 billion, or $3.14 a share. During the same period last year its net income totaled $949 million, or $2.90 a share.
"Our employees met the challenge of our ever-changing environment and our results prove the resilience of focusing on building a brand-loyal airline for customers," Kirby said in an earnings release.
United's fuel bill rose close to 62% in the quarter from a year earlier to $4.84 billion.
Revenue for the three months ended Sept. 30 rose 17.4% from a year earlier to $17.88 billion, compared with $15.23 billion the year before.
Domestic passenger unit revenue rose 14.5% from a year earlier, while international unit revenue was up 17.4%, a sign of higher fares. Passengers continue to book, United said, with passenger counts up more than 2% from last year.
Adjusting for one-time items, United reported net income of $833 million or $2.54 a share.

UK police re-arrest two men on suspicion of assisting Iran’s intelligence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
20:17:53 UTC
05:17:53 KST

UK police rearrest two men on suspicion of assisting Iran’s intelligence
The duo was first arrested for a suspected link to an incident at a US-run airbase used for striking Iran during this year’s war.
Police in the United Kingdom have rearrested two men on suspicion of assisting Iran’s intelligence service after an incident at a United States-run airbase in England last month.
Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK said the men, a 24-year-old British national and a 25-year-old dual British-Iranian national, were arrested under the National Security Act.
One of the suspects was first arrested on September 27, when the suspected plot against RAF Fairford took place. The airbase in Gloucestershire in western England has been used to launch strikes on Iran during this year’s war.
The second suspect was first arrested on October 1. Until Tuesday, the men had been released on bail pending more investigation.
Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK, said the investigation was “hugely complex” and that detectives were looking at “many lines of enquiry”.
“This is very much a live investigation,” Taylor said in a statement, adding: “We consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement.”
“Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it,” he added.
Major incident
British police declared a major incident in the area around RAF Fairford after a member of the public reported seeing three “suspicious” vans driving near the base.
Residents were forced to leave their homes as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swarmed the rural area.
Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant – petrol – in three vans at the site, but no explosives.
The incident prompted the US to pull its bombers out of RAF Fairford, while British authorities blamed Iran.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the apparent plot was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
Not unique
Ken McCallum, the UK’s domestic intelligence spy chief, warned that Iran and Russia were expanding attacks against military bases in the UK, adding that the RAF Fairford incident was not unique.
In all, more than 50 people have been arrested over Iran-linked plots in the past year, McCallum said.
Iran has denied involvement, although it has previously said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.
Five other men in their 20s were arrested earlier then released on bail pending further investigation. No one has yet been charged.

A person was killed and 18 others injured in Russian attacks on Kyiv on October 20 — Klitschko
Kyiv • UNN
A person was killed and 18 injured as a result of Russian attacks on Kyiv. Twelve of those wounded remain in hospitals; medical facilities and an energy facility were damaged.
Throughout October 20, Russian forces carried out a series of attacks on Kyiv, killing one person and leaving another 18 people injured. Of them, 12 victims remain in inpatient wards of hospitals in the capital. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported this, UNN writes.
Details
During the day, Russian drones attacked several districts of the capital. In particular, in the Solomianskyi district, a drone struck the top floor of a medical facility, partially destroying the roof. Drone debris also fell onto railway tracks, but no fire broke out.
In the Holosiivskyi district, drone debris damaged the upper floors of another medical facility. As a result, two people were injured and received medical assistance at the scene. Debris also fell in an open area near residential buildings.
Strikes on energy facilities and other districts of the capital
One of the most serious episodes of the attack was the crash of a Russian drone near a gas station on the boundary between Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast. According to preliminary reports from the city authorities, one person was killed there and seven others were injured. Five of the wounded were hospitalized.
In the Shevchenkivskyi district, Russian forces struck one of the energy facilities. Following the strikes on the energy infrastructure, partial power outages occurred in several districts of the capital.
In addition, in the Desnianskyi district, a drone strike was recorded in an open area near a green zone, and later against a warehouse building. In the Sviatoshynskyi district, a Russian drone struck the grounds of a garage cooperative.
Following the attacks of October 20, the number of people injured in the capital rose to 18, 12 of whom require inpatient treatment. Emergency services worked at the strike sites, eliminating the aftermath of the shelling and inspecting the damaged facilities.

Gardner smashes 84 as Australia retains Rose Bowl over NZ
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
20:09:55 UTC
05:09:55 KST

Australia has retained the Rose Bowl following a 40-run victory in the second T20 against New Zealand.
Australia has a 2-0 lead in the three-match series, retaining the Rose Bowl, which it has held for 26 years.
What's next?
The third and final match of the series will be played on Thursday.
Australia has retained the Rose Bowl with a comfortable 40-run victory in the Twenty20 International against New Zealand at North Sydney Oval.
Led by a blazing 84 from vice-captain Ash Gardner, Australia scored a competitive 6-167 and held New Zealand to 8-127 on Tuesday night, claiming a 2-0 lead in the three-match series, with the remaining game on Thursday.
It was Australia's 12th T20 victory in a row, including an unbeaten run during the World Cup in the UK during June and July, prompting Gardner to credit surprise skipper Sophie Molineux with enhancing a winning culture.
"It's led by Soph, who has brought this different mantra to the group, and the fun aspect as well," Gardner said.
"When you're enjoying yourself, and you're having fun, it creates an environment of growth and wanting to learn and challenge yourself."
Australia has held the Rose Bowl for more than 26 years, and the trophy is on the line again in March for a three-match one-day series. This will be the first time it has been contested twice in the same season.
Gardner dominated an otherwise stuttering Australian batting performance, hitting 10 fours and four sixes in 45 balls on the compact North Sydney Oval.
Beth Mooney looked good for the second time in the series without pressing on, well caught by a diving Maddy Green at long on for 39 from 28 deliveries, lofting a slower ball from Jess Kerr.
Australia then smothered New Zealand. White Ferns captain Melie Kerr top scored with 32 from 38 balls, while Australia's most successful bowler was leg-spinner Georgia Wareham, who claimed 3-18 from her four overs.
New Zealand named an unchanged team after giving Australia a fright in the opening game, with the home side scrambling to victory by two wickets in a tense finish.
There was no such tension this time, with New Zealand never mounting a serious challenge.

The Russians had a thousand tanks moving along a concrete highway. They would have been in Ukraine in four hours. Nothing could have stopped them. The war would have ended in one day. And this very stupid general decided to turn onto farmland and then turn left and head toward Kyiv instead of staying on the highway. Eventually, he got stuck in the mud

EU revises Arctic strategy as pressure from Russia, US grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
20:05:39 UTC
05:05:39 KST

EU revises Arctic strategy as pressure from Russia, US grows
The new strategy shifts the bloc’s focus from long-term climate concerns to urgent security measures.
The European Commission has unveiled a new Arctic strategy for the European Union that lists security and resilience first among four priorities, alongside climate change, economic prosperity and opportunities for Arctic communities.
The strategy calls for a new maritime security hub to help member states and partners share information and monitor maritime activity in the Arctic, the Commission said on Tuesday.
The hub would later expand to track shadow fleet vessels, detect illegal fishing and pollution, and improve search and rescue coordination.
The Commission also said the EU will work to expand European icebreaker capacity. Icebreakers are specialised vessels designed to navigate ice-covered waters by breaking up sea ice and maintaining safe shipping routes.
“The Arctic is one place where the tectonic plates of geopolitics are colliding,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said, adding that sovereignty and territorial integrity can no longer be taken for granted.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Russia is expanding its military footprint in the high north, citing drone incursions, GPS jamming and cable sabotage, the AFP news agency reported.
Cutting reliance on Washington
Several measures appear aimed at reducing dependence on the United States. The Commission said the EU will back a strategic pan-Arctic fibre-optic telecommunications cable project linking Greenland directly to Europe. It is part of a wider plan that would also connect Canada, Japan and South Korea.
The EU will also provide secure satellite connectivity for government communications through the IRIS² constellation, a constellation AFP said is meant to rival US tech mogul Elon Musk’s Starlink.
The shift follows US President Donald Trump’s repeated demands to take control of Greenland, a Danish autonomous territory. Although his tone has softened this year, with a security deal signed with Greenland and Denmark, many in Europe remain wary, AFP said.
Member states press for action
The strategy follows last month’s meeting of leaders from 12 countries, including Germany, France, Finland and Denmark. Member states urged the EU to take a more strategic and proactive role, according to a joint statement.
Participants identified Russia as the largest threat while noting the ambitions of China and the US.
At the meeting, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the era of “high north, low attention” was over. Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo called Russia the most significant long-term threat and said the EU must treat the Arctic as a strategic frontier.
The Commission reiterated the EU’s position remains that oil, coal and gas should stay in the ground, including in the Arctic.
To combat increasing climate concerns, the Commission pledged to “strengthen climate research, observation and monitoring to better understand these changes and support effective responses”, while working in tandem with the people who live and work in the Arctic.

Bavuma's batting masterclass takes control away from Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
20:03:42 UTC
05:03:42 KST

A few days before this Test series began, a digitally manipulated image was doing the rounds on social media.
Modelling South Africa's new Test playing kit, a pensive expression on his face, Proteas skipper Temba Bavuma was flanked by teammates Ryan Rickelton and Marco Jansen.
The visual punchline, in this case, was that Bavuma had been shrunk even smaller than his already-diminutive self, dwarfed by his teammates, even though he was standing on a superimposed shoe-shine box. My sides!
Never mind that 5'4" Bavuma's batting inspiration, Sachin Tendulkar, stands only an inch taller, nor that the previous owner of India's "Little Master" moniker, Sunil Gavaskar, is the same height as Bavuma. Nor, indeed, that a certain lad from Bowral who did kind of OK in the 1930s and 40s was only 5'7". None faced quite the same level of condescension or fixation on their physical stature as Bavuma.
In reality, Bavuma is, by a few key measures, as big as anyone in the story of South African cricket in the post-apartheid decades. On the world stage he captained his country to victory in the 2025 World Test Championship decider, banishing years of big-tournament heartbreak.
Australians, apt to wipe such unexpected defeats in crunch games from the collective memory, are thus obliged to bracket Bavuma with a select group of figurehead skippers of recent decades — Clive Lloyd, Sourav Ganguly, Michael Vaughan, Virat Kohli — who've engineered famous and important victories against great Australian Test sides in their pomp.
Now Australia reckons with his batting. On day three of the second Test at Gqeberha, Bavuma played an innings that, for context and quality, ranks among the highest calibre; a towering and important century that any of the all-timers above would envy.
Beginning the day on 41, with his side wobbling away at 5-97, Bavuma finished it with a stunning set of numbers next to his name: 179 runs from 334 deliveries in a total of 9-425 declared.
Due to the rain and delays of the opening stages of this game, Bavuma's epic stretched across three days, clocked in at a shade under 10 hours and required nothing less than the total psychological and physical mastery of the most complete pace attack in world cricket. Australians scoff at the mere concept of moral victories, but here Bavuma and South Africa claimed a resounding one.
It was the highest score of Bavuma's career, his fourth century (out of five all up) since becoming captain and moving up the order, and it means that a game in which Australia fancied skittling the Proteas on a green pitch is very unlikely to be won by the tourists — and possibly worse.
The "possibly worse" part got its preview sequence in the final moments of the day, when South Africa's returning paceman Kagiso Rabada marauded his way through Nic Maddinson to leave Australia one wicket down at stumps. Had bad light not limited Bavuma to the use of spinners in the final three overs of the day, the carnage could have been worse.
It has been said that the Australians respect but don't particularly warm to Bavuma. By this theory, he is aloof, undemonstrative and unlikely to engage in banter, verbal sparring or fun. In that way, he is more like a bowler who always had Australia's measure, Curtly Ambrose. "Curtly talks to no-one," Ambrose once said. It worked out just fine for him, too.
Bavuma's knock was a masterpiece of the kind of tempo batting that makes Test cricket tragics swoon. His watchful first 50, comprised almost entirely of judicious nudges, nurdles and leaves, took 140 deliveries.
His second, which grew to encompass sumptuous on drives, square drives and a cracking pull shot off Pat Cummins to reach his century, took only 86 balls. His third, a by-product of an acceleration phase when he and Simon Harmer removed any thoughts of an Australian victory, came from just 73 balls.
It was hard to believe this was the same player who'd scratched around for a combined total of four runs in 45 tortured deliveries last week in Durban. But like Matt Renshaw in that game, it was not just Bavuma's own runs that turned this contest on its head but the partnerships he forged with his side's highly capable tailenders.
Loading Instagram content
There was a thrilling stand of 132 from 186 with Marco Jansen, whose 85 came at almost a run a ball and, to be fair, presented a truly arresting example of cricket's capacity to attract all shapes and sizes. Paired with the 6'8" beanpole, Bavuma brought to mind the famous photo of NBA basketballers Muggsy Bogues and Manute Bol.
Even more profitable — game-defining, most likely — was Bavuma's union with Harmer, the spinner whose surprising selection reprieve suddenly seemed completely sensible as he hammered his way through a sparkling knock of 82 from 157 deliveries. Their partnership of 183 traversed 46 overs and was South Africa's highest eighth-wicket stand ever — not the sort of record with which this Australian squad likes to be associated.
In the final analysis, 315 runs came after the fall of South Africa's sixth wicket. It was a total wipe-out for the Aussies.
What did Cummins get wrong? There were some indefensibly defensive field placements, in truth, especially in the crucial phase when Jansen went berserk and Bavuma fed him the strike with easy singles to men stationed in the deep.
But as Richie Benaud once said, the best attribute a captain can have is luck, and there wasn't much on offer here for Cummins. Josh Hazlewood, missing with illness on day two, was thus obliged not to bowl for the first two hours of the day. The green pitch, which had promised carnage early in the game, turned docile and offered minimal lateral movement even for Scott Boland. And after the second new ball brought the wicket of Jansen — Boland's fifth — very little else transpired, so the field spread again.
Of the Australian bowlers, Boland was clearly the pick with 5-81 from 29 overs, and the overall picture of gloom rather rubbished the claim that his otherworldly Test statistics could be attributed to being slotted into an attack that was always firing from the other end (and anyway, by that logic, Andy Bichel, as the last backup quick to receive acclaim like that heaped on Boland, would have easily maintained a bowling average far lower than 32).
In the Boland years, as in the Bichel ones, sometimes even great sides have to admit it has not been their day. That was Australia today; at the mercy of the biggest small man in cricket, who doesn't have to open his mouth to say something profound.

Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite Oslo optimism
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
21:00:57 BST
