Trump and Zelensky at loggerheads despite new optimism
- Published
The hug that Trump envoy Steve Witkoff offered Volodymyr Zelensky before talks in Oslo is unlikely to have dispelled the Ukrainian leader's misgivings about the current direction of US policy towards his war-ravaged country.
Zelensky posted a video of the moment on social media, with the message "Ukraine is working for peace. I thank our partners for their support!"
But given everything that's happened this month, does the Ukrainian leader still regard Donald Trump as a partner?
The two men have never been close – that much is obvious – but have they now fallen out once and for all?
Both in rhetoric and actions, the past 10 days have seen evidence of a rupture as deep as any in their fractious relationship.
Just listen to the way they talk about each other.
"Zelensky's not a good guy for us to deal with," Trump told Newsmax last week.
The verbal assault has continued this week.
"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump told a reporter on Monday when asked what he thought of the Ukrainian leader's suggestion that striking a diesel deal with Russia put the US on the wrong side of history.
Such personal attacks are typical of Trump's sledgehammer approach to diplomacy. It's hard to know when to take them seriously.
In June, he lashed out at Israel's prime minister, using an expletive while criticising Benjamin Netanyahu's judgement. Four months later, he endorsed Netanyahu enthusiastically, calling him a "great warrior prime minister".
"Trump can always do another U-turn," says Ian Bond of the Centre for European Reform. "But this does look bad."
For his part Zelensky has generally been circumspect in how he describes his unreliable but vital American counterpart.
But this month his frustration has been clear. Addressing a US congressional delegation, he spoke of "decisions on the American side that are hard to explain between friends" and voiced the fear that "some political decision has been made to slow down support for us."
Answering Trump's charge that he represented the principal obstacle to a negotiated settlement, Zelensky sounded more exasperated than ever.
"We have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to end this war with dignity," he wrote on Telegram on Monday.
But rhetoric aside, how bad is the relationship?
In some ways, we've been here before.
After their notorious televised bust up in the Oval Office in February 2025, at which Trump accused Zelensky of "gambling with World War III", the US suspended military assistance and restricted intelligence sharing.
The crisis only lasted a week. And when the Trump administration decided, later that year, that it no longer wanted to finance direct military assistance to Ukraine, a mechanism was put in place for European countries to pay for American equipment instead.
One exception, in the wake of this year's US war with Iran, has been badly needed US-made Patriot air defence missiles.
Amid a global shortage, the supply to Ukraine has slowed to a trickle, making it harder than ever for Kyiv to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles.
The Washington Post, quoting an unnamed Ukrainian official, said "only a couple" of Patriot interceptors remained in Ukraine's stockpile, and that the Trump administration had slowed down the process by which US allies seek approval to transfer their stocks.
Similar concerns have been voiced in the past, but the latest reports – not confirmed by US officials – come against an increasingly difficult backdrop for Kyiv.
Earlier this month, as Ukrainian negotiators arrived in Miami for talks with Trump's all-purpose envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner, they were blindsided by the news that the president had just struck a deal with Vladimir Putin to open US markets to Russian diesel.
Experts questioned whether it would do much to drive down US petrol prices, ahead of congressional mid-term elections (the apparent motive), but as a signal of US displeasure over Ukraine's campaign of long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and Washington's willingness to do deals with the Kremlin, it represented a stinging rebuke to Kyiv.
Last Friday, Trump went further, waiving wide-ranging sanctions on Russia just two days before they were due to take effect.
Trump said the sanctions contained in the Graham Act (named after the former South Carolina senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine who died in July) would hinder his efforts to broker peace. But for Kyiv and its supporters this was another alarming sign that the White House was siding with the Kremlin.
"What the Trump administration is doing is providing carrots to the Russians and sticks to the Ukrainians," former US ambassador to Kyiv William Taylor told the BBC.
"It's inexplicable and saddening."
Kiriil Dmitriev, a senior Putin envoy, called it "an important and truly historic moment".
For Moscow, this felt like a welcome return to the "spirit of Alaska", a phrase much touted by Russian officials in the wake of the Trump-Putin summit in Anchorage in August 2025.
Adding to the impression that Trump is turning his back on Ukraine is the allegation – again not confirmed by Washington – that the US has restricted the flow of intelligence and interfered with Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite internet service.
Amid an escalation in Russia's drone and missile war on Ukraine's cities, Kyiv says advance warning provided by US satellite intelligence has been lacking.
"We didn't receive it during ballistic attacks for three days," Zelensky told NBC News.
On 12 October five Russian S-400 missiles hit Kyiv, reportedly before air raid sirens or mobile alerts had sounded.
The US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, denied there had been any pause in intelligence sharing, blaming a "software problem" for the temporary lack of early warnings.
Similar uncertainty surrounds Ukraine's access to Starlink.
A week ago, Ukrainian officials reported that the system was being throttled, with terminals unable to maintain connections at high speeds, making it harder for Ukraine's military to intercept fast moving Russian drones.
Since the summer, Ukraine has struggled to cope with a wave of attacks by advanced, jet-powered drones.
It's not clear where any order to limit Ukraine's use of Starlink – or its military grade equivalent Starshield – originated. Reuters reported that it came from the White House.
Rubio said "no-one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet."
But the fact that such suspicions surface so frequently points to the lack of trust that continues to infect US-Ukrainian relations.
Much of this has its roots in Donald Trump's seemingly long-standing mistrust of Ukraine as a whole - and Zelensky in particular.
A decade ago, Trump became convinced that Ukraine had tried to prevent him from becoming US president. Among a number of unfounded allegations was the suggestion that the US Democratic National Committee had a server hidden somewhere in Ukraine.
When Zelensky became president, three years later, he resisted Trump's demands that he investigate charges of election interference.
During a notorious July 2019 telephone conversation, Trump also asked Zelensky to investigate Joe Biden, the man who went on to defeat him in the 2020 presidential election. Again, Zelensky refused.
At the time, the White House was withholding $391m (£290m) in military assistance to Ukraine, a juxtaposition that ultimately led to Trump's first impeachment.
Whether Trump's resentment over these historic slights continues to inform his current policy towards Ukraine is an open question, but it's clear that the roller coaster of US-Ukraine relations has taken another stomach-churning dip.
Following the talks in Oslo, Witkoff is taking a set of updated proposals to St Petersburg. All eyes will now be on Putin.
Jonas Gahr Støre, the Norwegian leader, said the talks in Oslo had helped "to straighten out a few things."
"There's nothing to gain from… digging into what was said yesterday or a week ago," he said diplomatically.
Zelensky said the day had begun with a productive conversation with the US Secretary of State and indicated that the issue of early warning had already been fixed. He also sounded optimistic about Patriot missiles and Starlink.
"I think we will have good results too," he said.
Yet despite the optimistic tone, it's hard to get around the fact that Volodymyr Zelensky and Donald Trump appear, once again, to be at loggerheads.

Brain scans map multiple “low road” fear pathways between the human thalamus and amygdala
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
20:00:28 UTC
05:00:28 KST

Researchers have mapped several direct routes between the human thalamus and amygdala that may help the brain respond rapidly to threatening information, according to a study published in NeuroImage. Connections involving the back of the thalamus were the most consistent, while others were weaker or harder to detect reliably.
Fear responses can begin quickly. When a person hears a sudden noise or sees a possible threat, the brain must evaluate the information and prepare the body to respond. Animal studies have identified short pathways that carry sensory information from the thalamus, a central relay station for incoming sensory signals, to the amygdala, a region involved in emotional learning and defensive responses.
These pathways have sometimes been described as “low roads” because they may transmit basic sensory information without first passing through the cerebral cortex, where more detailed analysis takes place. Although animal studies have characterized them, they had not been comprehensively mapped in the human brain.
Led by Emmanouela Kosteletou-Kassotaki of the University of Barcelona, the researchers studied 113 healthy right-handed volunteers (average age 24.5 years; 65 women).
The team used high-resolution diffusion-weighted MRI, a scanning method that estimates the direction of nerve fibers by tracking the movement of water through brain tissue. They then used tractography, a technique that reconstructs likely fiber pathways from these data, to map connections between several thalamic nuclei and the basolateral amygdala, a part of the amygdala central to fear learning. Their approach was designed to cope with the dense, crisscrossing fibers around these deep brain structures.
A smaller group of 24 participants underwent a second MRI scan about 15 days later on average. This allowed the researchers to examine whether the pathways could be reconstructed consistently across sessions.
The most reliable connections linked the posterior thalamus to the basolateral amygdala. One pathway ran from the inferior colliculus, an auditory hub in the midbrain, through the medial geniculate nucleus, a key auditory relay in the thalamus, to the amygdala, mirroring an auditory fear pathway well documented in rodents. This pathway was found in nearly all participants.
Connections between the amygdala and the medial, inferior and lateral portions of the pulvinar, a thalamic structure involved in visual attention and combining information across the senses, appeared in all 113 participants and were highly reproducible, particularly for the inferior pulvinar. By contrast, connections with the anterior pulvinar were sparse and inconsistent, and a direct route from the inferior colliculus to the amygdala that bypassed the medial geniculate nucleus could not be reliably reconstructed.
The mediodorsal nucleus, located in the medial thalamus, also showed a prominent connection with the basolateral amygdala, with a high number of reconstructed fiber paths and moderate-to-high reproducibility. The authors note, however, that this connection may mainly carry signals from the amygdala rather than to it.
Connections from intralaminar thalamic nuclei, a group of small nuclei near the center of the thalamus, were also identified, particularly from the parafascicular and central medial nuclei. However, these pathways varied more between people and between the first and second scans. This suggests that some connections are robust across people, while others may be weaker, more difficult to detect or more variable in their anatomy.
Different thalamic regions also tended to connect with different subregions of the basolateral amygdala, and several pathways showed more reconstructed fiber paths in the left hemisphere than in the right, although the authors caution that this asymmetry may partly reflect methodological factors. Overall, the results support the idea that humans possess several direct thalamus–amygdala pathways rather than one simple route. These pathways could help transmit sensory and emotional signals quickly, potentially supporting flexible defensive responses.
Kosteletou-Kassotaki and colleagues described the study as providing “a unifying anatomical framework for multiple direct thalamo-amygdala pathways in the human brain.”
Diffusion tractography has technical limitations that should be noted. It can mistakenly identify pathways that are not present or fail to detect pathways that are present, particularly where nerve fibers cross, so the connections will need to be confirmed with studies of brain tissue. The method also cannot show which direction signals travel and provides information about structure rather than real-time brain function, so the link to fear is inferred largely from animal research.
The study, “Mapping the subcortical pathways associated with fear in the human brain: multiple thalamo-amygdala connections revealed by high-resolution tractography,” was authored by Emmanouela Kosteletou-Kassotaki, Liu Mengxing, Martina T. Cinca-Tomás, Pedro M. Paz-Alonso and Judith Domínguez-Borràs.

Ministers set out who can stop a ship in British waters
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
21:00:25 BST
05:00:25 KST

Royal Navy Police may exercise specified maritime enforcement powers in defined circumstances, any exercise of such powers requires a legal basis and must be undertaken by authorised personnel, and the department supports government efforts to secure British territorial waters including primary legislation as necessary, according to answers given in Parliament.
Ian Roome, the Liberal Democrat member for North Devon, put five questions on the subject, asking whether the Royal Navy must obtain the agreement and authorisation of a civilian police force before intercepting or challenging a foreign military vessel suspected of posing a threat to national security, whether the requirement for Royal Navy Police to act only at the request of civilian forces should be reviewed, what assessment has been made of legislative change to give Royal Navy Police consistent powers across England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, how clear the division of responsibilities is between the Royal Navy, the Royal Navy Police and civilian forces, and whether the six-month review of the Maritime Enforcement Powers (Specification of the Royal Navy Police) Regulations 2020, announced on 17 December 2020, was completed.
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, gave the same answer to all five: “The Royal Navy works with the Home Office, civilian police and partners across government to protect UK territorial waters, and respond to threats.
“Responsibilities and authorisations depend on the circumstances and proposed action. Defence may support civilian authorities through established Military Aid to the Civil Authorities arrangements, while any exercise of maritime law-enforcement powers require a legal basis and must be undertaken by authorised personnel.
“Royal Navy Police may exercise specified maritime enforcement powers in defined circumstances. Any review or change must reflect operational needs, applicable law and the UK’s different jurisdictions. As the threat picture changes, the MOD supports HMG efforts to ensure the continued security of the UK and our territorial waters, including primary legislation as necessary.”
The maritime enforcement regime comes from the Policing and Crime Act 2017, which gave designated officers powers to stop, board, divert and detain ships, and the 2020 regulations specified Royal Navy Police as a body able to use them. Separate jurisdictions in England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland mean the powers do not apply identically around the coast.
Warships of another state carry sovereign immunity and cannot be boarded without consent, so intercepting and challenging a foreign military vessel is a naval task carried out under rules of engagement and not a policing one.
Britain took powers this year to board and detain shadow fleet vessels in its territorial waters, and this publication reported when the government announced the policy and again when British forces boarded a Russian shadow fleet tanker.

Forbo Flooring spotlights creative possibilities of custom flooring
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
20:00:00 UTC

Forbo Flooring spotlights creative possibilities of custom flooring
From digitally printed floral and graphic patterns to photographic images and precision-cut inlays, flooring brand Forbo Flooring Systems offers custom design possibilities to make flooring an “integral part of the identity and story of a space”.
Across Forbo’s Flotex, Vinyl, Entrance Flooring and Marmoleum collections, the brand offers customisation techniques that incorporate graphics, branding and messaging upon a floor.
Each technique creates custom floor designs that introduce graphic messaging in hospitality interiors, direct visitors to a certain space, or help support orientation in education or healthcare settings.
Forbo’s flooring can also be used in a museum setting, distinguishing one exhibition from another, or used to reinforce a brand identity in a retail or workplace environment.
“The result is a floor that does more than provide a surface,” said the brand.
“It can contribute to the character of an interior, communicate identity, support zoning and wayfinding, and connect different spaces through a coherent design language.”
The brand’s Flotex flooring has a densely flocked design, allowing detailed patterns, graphics and imagery to be reproduced at high resolution. In comparison, its vinyl collection is digitally printed, making it possible to translate more detailed bespoke patterns, graphics and imagery onto the material.
Across its Marmoleum collections, Forbo uses a specific Aquajet technology that uses high-pressure water to precisely cut material, which can then be combined to form detailed designs.
This enables Forbo to adapt flooring to specific colours and patterns to create individual graphics, imagery, logos or wayfinding.
“The technique makes it possible to translate a wide variety of ideas into the material, from geometric patterns and decorative elements to lettering, logos and intricate artwork,” said Forbo of its Aquajet technology.
“Designers can develop their own concept and work with colours from the Marmoleum palette to create an individual composition.”
Forbo also offers Coral Entrance Flooring, allowing a building’s entrance to connect visually with its identity while helping prevent dirt and moisture from entering.
“Digital printing creates extensive graphic possibilities for Flotex and vinyl,” said Forbo of its process. “Aquajet technology enables precise compositions in Marmoleum, while custom techniques for Coral bring individual design into the entrance area.”
Rather than presenting its collections as separate products, Forbo explained that projects often involve different flooring collections as part of one portfolio.
For example, a project might begin with a customised entrance, continue with an individual floor design and use colour, graphics or patterns to define different zones and destinations.
According to Forbo Flooring, the diversity of its collections allows designers the opportunity to choose the flooring material and technique that best suit both their creative vision and the functional requirements of the space.
“The flooring can therefore contribute to aesthetics, identity, orientation and the overall experience of a space, while different products continue to respond to the functional requirements of each area,” it added.
Forbo Flooring explained that customisation can start at different levels. For example, designers can build on an existing Forbo design, adapting its colours, or develop something entirely new.
“Depending on the flooring type, an original graphic, photograph, pattern, illustration, logo or other visual concept can be translated into the floor,” said the brand.
As a result, this flexibility allows flooring to respond more closely to the architecture, identity and purpose of a space.
To learn more about Forbo’s custom flooring, visit its website.

Israel Police reported 143 cases in which draft evaders detained during random encounters with police officers were released because IDF personnel allegedly failed to arrive within the required time, according to a document from the Attorney-General's Office dated Monday that summarized a meeting on draft enforcement.
Military Police representatives said at the meeting that they were unfamiliar with the figures.
The document, which summarized a meeting held on October 14 and chaired by Deputy Attorney-General Dr. Gil Limon, outlined shortcomings in enforcement operations and coordination between the authorities.
The meeting was held ahead of an update to the High Court of Justice in petitions concerning the implementation of its ruling on the conscription of yeshiva students.
According to figures provided by Israel Police, the 143 releases occurred between July 1 and October 12. The draft evaders were released with a "summons to report to the recruitment authorities," rather than being transferred to the Military Police.
Under the procedure described in the document, the IDF had committed to meeting police officers within half an hour.
Limon said the number of people released was high and "could indicate a failure in the implementation of the joint working procedure."
Police were instructed to provide the Military Police with details of the cases so the IDF could investigate them, draw lessons, and take steps to reduce the phenomenon. An update on the matter was requested by November 1.
At the same time, police reported that 14 draft evaders had been arrested during random encounters over the same period. The document does not explicitly clarify the relationship between that figure and the 143 release cases.
Joint arrest operation postponed as police demand for significant reinforcement
Another central finding concerns a joint IDF and police enforcement operation that had been scheduled for October but was postponed for the second time.
According to the document, the postponement followed a police demand for substantial reinforcements, including hundreds of IDF soldiers, as a condition of approving the operation.
IDF representatives said the demand was impractical and inconsistent with the division of responsibilities and authority between the two organizations.
According to the military representatives, the IDF is responsible for carrying out the arrests themselves, while dealing with disturbances of public order falls under the responsibility of Israel Police.
Major gaps in enforcement between Israel Police and the IDF were exposed by the document
Limon emphasized that Israel Police is responsible for maintaining public order during enforcement operations.
He further clarified that, under the court's ruling, enforcement operations cannot be made conditional on the allocation of IDF soldiers to public-order duties, as distinct from assigning the soldiers required to carry out the arrests.
"The situation described is inconsistent with the state's obligation to combat the phenomenon of draft evasion," the document stated.
The IDF and police were instructed to promptly formulate a framework to resume proactive enforcement operations and provide a detailed update by November 1.
Alongside the joint operations, which have not taken place for some time, the IDF said the Military Police conducts targeted arrest operations every week in various parts of the country as part of an organized work plan.
However, the document emphasized that "in practice, these amount to only a handful of arrests."
The document also identified enforcement gaps at border crossings.
According to figures already presented in the summary of the previous meeting, more than 200 people subject to mandatory military service were arrested in September.
In 64 cases, authorities arrested draft evaders at Ben-Gurion Airport upon their return to Israel after they were not identified as subject to military service when leaving the country.
Conflicting reports between authorities about 64 cases at Ben-Gurion Airport
The Population and Immigration Authority said the cases had been referred to the police for investigation on suspicion of "illegal border crossing."
However, in its response to the meeting summary, Israel Police said it was unaware of any such reports having been received from the authority.
The matter is expected to be examined at another meeting involving representatives of the Population and Immigration Authority, the IDF, and Israel Police.
The document further revealed that, despite a request included in the summary of an August meeting, the IDF has yet to provide a document detailing the criteria used to decide whether draft evaders are released at border crossings.
"It has not been clarified what criteria are used to determine which draft evader is permitted to travel abroad or return home and which draft evader is arrested," the document stated.
The IDF was again instructed to provide the document before the next meeting on the matter.

UN warns Gaza displacement sites at risk of flooding, collapse as winter nears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
19:52:26 UTC
04:52:26 KST

Merve Gül Aydoğan Ağlarcı
20 October 2026•Update: 20 October 2026
 
 The UN on Tuesday warned that displaced Palestinians in the Gaza Strip could face serious flood and collapse risks as winter approaches, with aid efforts hampered by funding shortfalls and supply restrictions.
Citing the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said at a news conference that "we assessed displacement sites hosting over 650 families in Khan Younis, including 160 families staying in a low-lying pit that used to collect rainwater and is now at risk of being flooded with both rain and sewage."
Dujarric said the UN and its partners assessed five other low-lying displacement sites on Monday hosting about 750 people, also in Khan Younis.
"We also assessed a sixth site hosting a number of families on the edge of a cliff overlooking the five low-lying sites," he said. "We are concerned that soil erosion this winter could cause the ground beneath the tents there to collapse."
Across Gaza, partners are undertaking "drainage clearance, sandbagging and ground-levelling to support such communities. But efforts are held back by funding shortfalls and restrictions on the entry of a range of critical supplies."
Dujarric added that shelter partners said that "the supplies currently available are only enough to partially support less than a fifth of the nearly 300,000 families in need of winter shelter assistance."
Israel's genocidal war on Gaza, launched with US support in October 2023, has killed more than 74,000 victims and injured over 175,000, while destroying 90% of civilian infrastructure.
Despite a ceasefire that has been in effect since Oct. 10, 2025, Israel has continued shelling, shooting and demolishing Palestinian structures, further expanding the destruction.

Germany news: AfD's Weidel calls for major EU reforms

Germany news: AfD's Weidel calls for major EU reforms
Published October 21, 2026last updated October 21, 2026
What you need to know
- One of Weidel's reforms is for European parliamentarians to no longer be directly elected
- Nvidia's Jensen Huang had words of encouragement for Europe's growing AI economy during a conference in Berlin
- Germany's Finance Ministry has erroneously introduced an approved tax hike on tobacco products months before it was scheduled to come into effect
- Germany's Bundesbank has forecast growth for the fourth quarter after a dip in the third quarter
Here is a round-up of top stories from and about Germany on Wednesday, October 21, 2026:
If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.
Weidel pitches 'three pillars' of EU reform at European Parliament
Alice Weidel, the co-leader of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, has presented her party's proposals for a European Union that she said was "in severe need of reform" during a visit to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, saying they rested on three core pillars.
"We would like to rebuild and reform the European Union," she said. "We would like to found the European Union on three major principles: the first one is subsidiarity, the second one is responsibility, and the third one is sovereignty."
On subsidiarity — the idea that power should reside as close to the grassroots level as possible as much as possible — she said it was important to put the "competences" on the "lowest level of decision-making," saying "we don't want the state, or the [European] Commission — that is not elected — to intrude and disturb your private life in decision-making."
"I'm an economist, and for me, the European Union is not a group of sovereign states any more," Weidel said. She said that in sovereign states' parliaments, leaders were elected, "and so the decision-making on the sovereign level should be made in the national parliaments and not here, to be very clear."
This is already the case in the vast majority of core EU public policy areas. National governments decide foreign and defense issues, finance and health policy, education policy and much more. The notable exceptions Weidel objects to are fiscal policy and the primacy of EU law, but only after sovereign member states agree to them.
She said the European Commission was not elected but had a "legislative right of initiative," saying this was a "huge disturbance of checks and balances" and of a "democratic decision-making process."
Weidel accused the EU of failing to follow its own rules, for instance on sovereign debt and whether the European Central Bank should or can guarantee it, citing issues like this as questions of responsibility.
Finally, she reiterated her desire for "sovereign states to protect their borders," saying that "if the European Union is not capable of protecting our borders, the outer borders ... then it is a decision of the sovereign states to protect our national borders."
"If Schengen is over, if Schengen doesn't work, then we need to get out of Schengen and protect our borders," she said of the open-border zone within much of the EU.
She said that if the EU fails to protect the bloc's external borders, "we should have a veto right to opt out of this chaos."
While the EU maintains a border management agency, Frontex, national authorities are responsible for the external borders of the Schengen zone and the EU.
WATCH — Journalist says Merz 'sounds very much like Trump'
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz criticized China for "unfair practices" in trade, and said he wants EU member states to balance out their trade deficits.
That elicited a bold comparison from a journalist who said, "You sound very much like Donald Trump."
Watch the exchange here:
Nvidia CEO Huang dazzles Berlin audience with AI pitch
A massive stage, all in black. A colorful laser light show. Upbeat music. AI-generated videos on a gigantic screen. On stage, just one man in a black leather jacket: Jensen Huang, the 63-year-old CEO of Nvidia, which manufactures superfast computer chips needed for AI data centers and happens to be the world's most valuable company.
The relaxed Nvidia boss set out his vision of the upcoming AI revolution and, of course, the products Nvidia has developed for the "second wave" of AI. The 4,000 attendees at Berlin's Tempodrom arena were thrilled by what Jensen Huang had to say (see entry below).
Huang said Germany and Europe could be part of the next industrial revolution — not as developers of AI language models or computer chips, but as producers of robots, machines, tools, and entire factories controlled by AI applications.
"You have to transfer AI into the real world of production," he said. Europe could use its data to train AI and develop customized models for automakers, pharmaceutical companies, and many small and medium-sized businesses.
Unsurprisingly, Nvidia offers all the AI software and hardware needed to get in on the action. A new addition to the Nvidia universe is a "Giga-Factory," which is housed in modular shipping containers and can be set up in just a few days or weeks anywhere with a suitable power grid.
There was also something for consumers: a high-performance laptop with a built-in AI agent that acts as a "friend and helper," capable of taking over tasks and programming new agents. Huang went on to demonstrate four small robot ducks that had been trained by this AI agent to perform cute tricks, which were met with laughter and applause.
But it wasn't all cheers. A woman in the audience interrupted a product demo to point out that AI is also used to control Russian drones. She was escorted out by security guards, but Huang assured the audience that he would speak with her later. He was keen to add that Nvidia has also developed a security system designed to keep AI agents in check and prevent misuse.
Nvidia is now valued at €5 trillion ($5.6 trillion) on the stock market. That is roughly equivalent to the total economic output of all of Germany in 2025.
German Bundeswehr sees 'significant' threat of sabotage
The German military, known as the Bundeswehr, has rated the threat of sabotage against it as "significant," according to a reports by the Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) and public broadcaster WDR.
A spokesperson for the Defense Ministry pointed to several recent cases, including the discovery of a drone close to an airbase in Wunstorf and acts of sabotage against Navy ships.
The military is looking to increase security to counter the threat, with the ministry spokesperson naming increased surveillance at airports and military docks by soldiers or infrared cameras.
"The incidents highlight the ability that Russia has almost certainly had for a while now, as well as very likely the increased intention, to act against Bundeswehr forces and facilities, as well as partners such as Ukraine in Germany," SZ reported based on internal military analysis.
The aim is therefore "very likely an intention to degrade the current political and society-wide German support for Ukraine."
The ministry spokesperson also pointed out that the incidents did not mark a major change, with the military facing similar challenges over the past decades.
He said "automatic defense concepts" are in place for acute terror threats, but "we are not at that point."
German imports from Russia plunge, but not to zero
German trade with Russia collapsed following the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, especially due to the decision to cut all imports of Russian gas. However, some trade has continued.
According to the German Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), German imports of Russian goods were down by 96.4% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period in 2021.
This amounted to €500 million ($561 million) in 2026, down from €15 billion. German exports to Russia were also down, but still significant, reaching €3.4 billion in the first six months of 2026. However, this was about a quarter of the exports in the same period in 2021.
Pharmaceutical products made up more than 40% of German exports to Russia, with machinery, food and animal feed also being exported in smaller quantities.
Nvidia CEO urges Europe to build more data centers
Jensen Huang, the head of chip manufacturing giant Nvidia, was speaking at a company conference for developers and investors in Berlin's Tempodrom auditorium on Wednesday.
He was seeking to encourage Europe to build out its data center infrastructure and touted Nvidia's modular tools to help speed up that process.
"Europe's AI economy is starting, and it's accelerating, and it's great to see," Huang said.
He promoted a new design for a ready-made modular computing center that comes in a box akin to a shipping container and that could make it possible to construct a data center in a matter of days. Huang said it "will change the way people build AI centers."
Nvidia has invested $10 billion (€8.9 billion) in European startups over the past year, the Nvidia boss said.
Europe has fallen behind the US and China in terms of building up data centers and is currently home to around 5% of the world's AI computing capacity in comparison to 75% in the US. This capacity is required to train AI models and its lack is seen as a major obstacle for European developers.
Most current data centers are reliant on Nvidia GPUs to run.
Financial Ministry admits mistake, says tobacco tax coming January 1 as planned
A spokesperson for Germany's Federal Financial Ministry on Wednesday addressed confusion surrounding the implementation of a new tobacco tax saying, "The tax increase in the law's wording was approved to go into effect on January 1, 2027, that remains the case."
The spokesperson confirmed that the mix-up over when the new law would take effect resulted from a technical error that put the law on the books immediately rather than January 1 as intended.
The issue stemmed from a mistake in the government's original writing of the law.
Customs officials have reportedly been informed and the Financial Ministry's website makes clear that the price increase will not be charged until the beginning of the new year.
German youth plans France-style mass protests
"Gen Z regelt" — or Gen Z's Got It — a youth initiative, has called for mass protests in 21 cities across Germany on Saturday, October 31; including Berlin, Cologne, Hamburg and Munich.
Thousands are expected to participate in demonstrations protesting "broken schools and austerity," as well as the cost of living, social injustice, military conscription and climate change.
French protests that exploded in violence and rampant destruction of private and public property this weekend also grew out of student frustration over the national school system and soon included numerous unions, groups and individuals voicing anger over a number of issues.
Gen Z regelt's website clearly states that the initiative is "against all violence," whether directed at people or property.
Police say they are "vigilant and relaxed," adding that they intend to protect people's right to congregate and express their opinions.
Still, images of massive damage and public violence from France, Italy and Spain have raised concerns among domestic policymakers and police, who have warned against allowing the protests to be hijacked by left-wing extremists.
Andreas Roßkopf, head of the German Federal Police's GdP union, made clear that officers would deal harshly with riots and rioters, telling the Rheinische Post newspaper on Wednesday, "State, but also federal police, will offer a firm and decisive response" to any trouble.
Roßkopf also warned that radicals and extremists could insert themselves among demonstrators in order to "attack police" or "simply be destructive."
Bundesbank forecasts German growth for Q4
The Bundesbank, Germany's central bank, has said it is expecting to see an uptick in growth for Europe's biggest economy in the fourth quarter.
"German economic output is likely to improve again markedly in the fourth quarter," the bank said in its monthly report on Wednesday. "However, the future economic recovery depends, not least, on the development of the war in the Middle East."
The optimistic outlook follows a dip in the third quarter, which the bank chalked up largely to this summer's drought that caused such low water levels in the Rhine River, an artery in western Germany for industry, that most ships could not travel.
"The low water levels are also likely to continue to have a negative impact on foreign trade via European ports as a result of restrictions on inland water transport," the bank wrote.
The forecast will be welcomed by the Merz government as it has struggled to boost the economy after two consecutive years of recession followed by weak growth in 2025.
Merz: EU doesn't want trade war with China
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said he does not think Europe is on course for a trade war with China while acknowledging what he called "unfair practice" on the part of Beijing.
Speaking at a business conference in Berlin, Merz said the imbalance did not mean "the beginning of a war, of a trade war with China. We are looking for peaceful solutions, but the level for that is fair trade."
The German chancellor has been pushing for the EU to be better prepared for trade disputes with China, including calling for a means to quickly exclude non-EU countries from the EU's single market if they flood it with cheap goods.
Merz said the EU needs to be able "to protect our markets and defend ourselves against those who don't play by the rules."
"Anyone who disrupts the functioning of the markets through unfair subsidies, overcapacities, aggressive pricing, or artificially undervalued currencies must expect a response," he said.
That includes tools that "enable us to respond swiftly and vigorously to targeted attacks on our industry and supply chain, with the idea being that in the best case we will not have to use it."
Ifo Institute questions savings target of parental allowance reform
Germany has a rather generous parental allowance system in comparison to many countries, with parents being able to take off 14 months, if each parent takes at least two months off, with the government paying up to €1,800 (just over $2,000) a month during that period.
However, this system has become the subject of a planned reform under the government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
The plan is to reduce the maximum amount of full-time paid parental leave to 12 months. With three months each reserved for both parents and the remaining six months free to be divided up however the parents choose. It also raises the minimum payment from €300 to €330 and the maximum from €1,800 to €1,900.
The government's aim is to make cuts to help the Ministry for Family Affairs reach its savings target of €1.6 billion, while also encouraging more fathers to take parental leave. Currently, fewer than half of fathers in Germany take parental leave.
Now the Ifo Institute for Economic Research has cast doubts on the government's savings plan.
"The savings target and the goal of increasing fathers’ participation in the planned parental allowance reform are at odds with each other. The higher the number of fathers who are motivated to participate by the reform, the less the government saves," Ifo researcher Kyra Puteanus said.
The institute estimates savings of around €880 million from November 2027, when the reform comes into effect. However, if more fathers, who generally earn more and thus are able to request the highest payment, do take up the parental leave, this will quickly reduce the savings, with Ifo predicting that even if the uptake by fathers only increases by 1%, savings will fall to €597 million. An increase of 3.1% would undo any savings from the reform, according to the institute.
"Since 2010, however, the share of fathers receiving parental allowance has almost doubled. A rapid increase can therefore not be ruled out, especially if months are otherwise forfeited," Ifo researcher Franziska Nuernbergk said.
IDF says it killed Hamas member involved in abduction of German dual national
The Israel Defense Forces (IFD) said in a post on X that they have killed Tamer Mohammad Ibrahim Al-Zabaq, a member of the Hamas terror group who was involved in the October 7 attacks.
The post said that al-Zabaq had been one of the men responsible for the abduction of Shani Louk, a dual German-Israeli national.
Louk was initially thought to have been taken hostage following the Hamas-led attacks but it was later confirmed that she had been killed.
In the immediate aftermath of the terror attacks, pictures and videos shared online showed a young woman, believed to be Shani, lying face down in a pick-up truck driven by militants. It was unclear from the footage whether she was alive.
The IDF also accused Al-Zabaq of operating to "restore Hamas' military capabilities, in systematic violation of the ceasefire."
"The terrorist was eliminated in order to remove the threat he posed," the IDF said.
The claims in the X post could not be independently verified.
Israel has carried out numerous deadly strikes on Gaza since the ceasefire came into effect just over a year ago.
Merz calls on Trump to make sure South Africa is at G20
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, addressing the Business Global Dialogue summit in Berlin on Wednesday, renewed calls for US President Donald Trump to invite South Africa (a G20 member) to the upcoming G20 summit that he will host in Miami this December.
"Whoever talks about the future of the global economy must include all important partners. Of course Africa belongs at the table," he said, adding: "The African Union is a G20 member, as is South Africa. That is why I urgently insist that South Africa be represented at the G20 summit."
Merz made a similar plea last year, when Trump angrily insisted that he would not invite South Africa to the annual summit of the 20 leading industrial and emerging economies.
Trump has accused South Africa of committing genocide on white farmers and dismissed South African pushback against his repeated claim. The anti-immigrant president also took the unusual step of offering South Africans political asylum in the US — as long as they are white.
The US President is apparently less bothered by wars of aggression, extending an invitation to President Vladimir Putin to come to Miami, despite Russia being thrown out of the G8 — now G7 — over its 2014 invasion and annexation of Ukraine's Crimea.
Beyond his plea for South Africa's inclusion, Merz said he would travel to the US with what he called a "Miami Growth Agenda" aimed at slashing bureaucracy, pushing structural reforms and making investment easier.
"Those" he said, "are the prerequisites for new economic growth and prosperity, not only in Germany, but globally."
Russia arrests German national, says he's a 'mercenary' — reports
Russian FSB agents have arrested a German national, accusing him of being a mercenary under contract with the Ukrainian army.
"The Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation has detained a German citizen who is a serving member of the Armed Forces of Ukraine," said a statement cited by Russian news agencies.
The FSB says the man, whom they described as a sniper, previously fought in Afghanistan and Syria as well as in Ukraine between 2016 and 2018.
They say he arrived in Ukraine last November and signed a three-year contract with the Ukrainian army before deserting over unpaid wages.
Last week, the FSB arrested a Swedish national whom Russian authorities also accused of fighting on Kyiv's behalf.
Russia has arrested hundreds of foreign nationals that it accuses of "espionage," "sabotage" or "treason" to long prison sentences since it began its invasion of neighboring Ukraine.
A number of foreign nationals have also been jailed over supposed "mercenary activity."
Feminist Alice Schwarzer announces closure of Emma magazine
Alice Schwarzer, Germany's most famous feminist, told DPA on Wednesday that the December 8 issue of her magazine Emma would be its last.
Schwarzer said despite dwindling circulation, the magazine is still turning a profit but the 83-year-old said "we are leaving because we think: Enough is enough!"
She said that Emma had stood up against "quite a bit of nonsense in the name of feminism," adding, "we are exhausted."
The first issue of Emma hit newsstands on January 26, 1977, with Schwarzer saying hostility against women in "men's media" had driven her to found a magazine that was produced by women, for women.
Schwarzer on Wednesday described Emma as the world's last professional, feminist-owned magazine still on newsstands.
Child sexual abuse and Islamism were among the issues that Emma began covering from the beginning. It later expanded to look at German tax law as regards married couples, breast cancer and female genital mutilation, among other topics. 
Among the controversial stances that Schwarzer has taken over the years, two that hurt sales were her seemingly pro-Russian calls for a quick peace deal with Ukraine after the start of Moscow's 2022 invasion — leading 20% of readers to cancel subscriptions — and her perceived hostility on transgender issues.
Schwarzer wholly rejects accusations that she has made transphobic, racist and misogynistic statements.
Emma's extensive archive will now be transferred to the German Literature Archive in Marbach, where it will be publicly accessible.
Asked about what people may not understand looking back, Schwarzer pointed to the hardships that women had to overcome in order to secure the rights enjoyed by women today.

Court acquits Polish soldier who accidentally shot Syrian refugee at Belarus border

A Polish soldier who accidentally shot a Syrian refugee who had entered Poland over the border from Belarus has been acquitted of negligent use of a weapon. The Syrian man had been seeking 50,000 zloty (€11,500) in compensation from the soldier.
The verdict was welcomed by defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, whose ministry had supported the soldier’s legal defence.

The incident in question took place in November 2023 in Poland’s northeastern Podlasie province. The soldier, named only as Adam Ł. under Polish privacy law and who holds the rank of second lieutenant, had only recently received his first posting to the border, reports legal news service Prawo.pl.
Since 2021, Belarus has been encouraging, assisting and in some cases coercing tens of thousands of migrants, mainly from Asia and Africa, to try to cross into Poland. Among those who make it over the border, most head westwards to Germany, while some have sought to claim international protection in Poland.
In response, Poland has posted thousands of soldiers to the border, where they provide support to the border guard and police. Officers have at times faced violence from migrants trying to cross. In one case, in June 2023, a Polish soldier died after being stabbed.
Poland has named a Moroccan man, Mohamed Addamrou, as the suspect in the 2024 murder of a Polish soldier, Mateusz Sitek, who was fatally stabbed while trying to stop a group of migrants from forcing their way through the border from Belarus to Poland https://t.co/mw8JuOPwcE
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 10, 2026
A few months after that tragedy, Adam Ł. took part in an operation to apprehend a group of migrants who had crossed from Belarus and were around 2 kilometres from the border.
After the soldiers called on the migrants to stop, one of them, a 23-year-old Syrian man, began to flee. As Adam Ł. chased him, the soldier slipped and fell, resulting in his gun, a PM-98 Glauberyt submachine gun, accidentally discharging two rounds.
One bullet hit the Syrian man in the back, close to his spine. The soldier immediately began providing him with first aid, before the Syrian was taken to hospital. He was discharged a few weeks later and, in May 2024, was granted asylum in Poland.
Initially, when it appeared possible that the Syrian could suffer partial paralysis, military prosecutors considered charging Adam Ł. with negligent use of a weapon resulting in serious injury, a crime carrying a prison sentence of up to eight years.
In the end, that was downgraded to a lower charge of negligent use of a weapon causing impairment or a health disorder, which is punishable by up to three years in prison.
The defence ministry provided the soldier with legal counsel from a special team set up in 2024 to defend military personnel. They advised him not to plead guilty.
Eventually, prosecutors asked only that the court impose an indemnity of 2,000 zloty on Adam Ł., to be paid to the Syrian. The Syrian’s lawyer, meanwhile, sought 50,000 zloty for his client.
The president has signed into law new rules removing criminal liability from officers who use firearms while serving on the border.
The measures were passed in response to a surge in aggression from some migrants seeking to cross the border from Belarus https://t.co/sBMaoYhoCw
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 16, 2024
In a ruling announced on Wednesday, a military court in Warsaw fully acquitted Adam Ł. Judge Michał Żak said that it remained unclear how the incident unfolded. He also pointed to expert evidence commissioned by the court that found the soldier’s gun could have had defects that caused it to fire when it hit the ground.
Those doubts, and a lack of convincing evidence to support the prosecutor’s version of events, meant the charge of negligence could not be proven, found Żak. The verdict can still be appealed. The Syrian’s lawyer said they would wait for the judge’s full written justification before deciding whether to appeal.
Kosiniak-Kamysz, meanwhile, welcomed the ruling in a social media post. “From the very beginning, we provided him with legal assistance,” wrote the defence minister. “A soldier who carries out his duties cannot be left alone, even in a difficult situation.”
In May this year, another soldier was acquitted over an incident in which he fired shots towards a group of migrants who had illegally crossed the Belarussian border. The judge found that, in fact, the soldier had been fulfilling his obligation to defend the Polish border.
A Polish soldier who fired shots towards migrants who had illegally crossed the border from Belarus has been acquitted of abusing his powers and threatening the lives of others
The military judge found he had been fulfilling his duty to protect the border https://t.co/ugxq5tkdFV
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 27, 2026
In 2024, Poland’s government introduced a new law making it easier for soldiers and other uniformed officers serving at the border to use firearms. They now no longer face criminal liability for employing their weapons in certain cases.
Since then, the government has also further strengthened physical border barriers and banned asylum claims by migrants who cross irregularly from Belarus.
That has been followed by a significant drop in attempted crossings by migrants from Belarus: in the first half of this year, only 250 attempts were recorded, down from 15,500 in the same period of 2025 – a 98% drop. Poland also now claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending those who do manage to cross.

How do we actually turn down the temperature in political debate?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:47:44 UTC
04:47:44 KST

analysis
After Helen Haines attack, how do we actually turn down the temperature?
Only two months ago, a group called Compassion in Politics Australia gained the first signatory to its "Civility Pledge".
Helen Haines.
The organisation, based on a similar foundation in the United Kingdom, aims to turn the tide of toxic debate and build a better politics.
As a start, it's asking elected officials to sign a simple pledge. "In my political life, I pledge to act with honesty, respect, and compassion," is all it states.
This week the independent MP was the victim of an attack widely described as shocking but unsurprising. Sadly predictable was the common reaction amongst MPs who have been at the receiving end of increasing threats and harassment.
Yesterday, security agencies briefed MPs on the risks to their safety. Security will no doubt be improved as much as practicable, without sacrificing MPs' ability to interact in their communities.
The more difficult question is what, if anything, can be done about the increasingly hostile political environment. What can be done to restore the "civility" that Haines, at least, pledged to pursue?
Civility was the word emphasised by the Governor-General late yesterday, who stood alongside the husband of Helen Haines in an effort to calm a worried nation.
"We don't have to all agree, but we can wrestle with the issue not the person," Sam Mostyn said from Melbourne's Alfred Hospital. Her message echoed the call to turn the temperature down.
"Words matter, whether spoken or in written form or increasingly in the virtual world."
This call for civility is something ASIO boss Mike Burgess has been going on about now for years.
"I genuinely believe the temperature of our security environment would be several degrees lower if we recommitted to conversing with civility, debating with respect and disagreeing with restraint," he said after the attack on Haines.
Burgess draws a line between words and actions: "ASIO has seen direct correlations between inflamed language, inflamed tensions and acts of violence."
The intelligence chief must feel at times he's talking to a brick wall. He warned against "inflamed language" and called for a return to civility after the October 7 Hamas attack on Israel in 2023, again after lifting the terrorism threat level to "probable" in 2024, and again after the Bondi terrorist attack in 2025.
Will anyone listen this time? Will an attack on one of their own force politicians to re-think their part in setting the tone of political discourse?
For some, the answer is clearly yes. There is a degree of self-reflection this week.
"We should all, every single one of us, me included, find ways to minimise the temperature of these debates," said shadow minister Jono Duniam, who will soon depart the Senate.
"We could all do better. I don't exclude myself or any political party," acknowledged the prime minister who, like Burgess, has repeatedly called for a more civil debate.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, by contrast, is worried about limiting robust argument. While condemning anything that intimidates or incites violence, he defended the role of vigorous debate.
"We have, like so few other countries in the world, avoided political violence. This is part of the great Australian achievement, and we've done that by having vigorous and rigorous debate and choice at the ballot box," he said.
"This is what's worked for us. We need to make sure it stays there."
It's certainly true — Australia has long enjoyed robust political debate while largely avoiding political violence.
But this misses the point being made by the ASIO boss. Times have changed.
We're now in an environment, according to Burgess, where "politically motivated violence is more likely than previous years".
Angus Taylor's own colleagues can recognise the deterioration, too.
"It's clear that the political environment has become more heated in recent years," said shadow minister James Paterson.
"In the last few years things have gotten much worse," said independent MP Monique Ryan, adding that "the 2025 election was completely different to 2022", with more aggression and anger. It's a common view, particularly among female politicians.
MPs are worried. For themselves, for their families, and for the fate of Australia's democracy.
So, what does it take to turn the temperature down?
"Gosh, if only I could say what the answer to that is," One Nation's Barnaby Joyce admitted on Radio National yesterday. "I don't know," he said.
It's rare to hear Barnaby Joyce stumped for an answer on anything. He's certainly not accepting any blame on the part of One Nation for raising the temperature.
Many might agree with Joyce that there are no easy solutions to counter the powerful domestic and global forces driving voter frustration, political polarisation, toxic online discourse and hate.
Politicians are certainly limited in what they can control. But they're not entirely powerless.
As Burgess says, language matters: "By all means, disagree. But consider how you disagree."
Signing a "Civility Pledge" might seem like a mere symbolic gesture, but it's something. If it's good enough for Helen Haines, why not others?
Compassion in Politics Australia issued a statement after the horrific attack on Monday, calling it "a stark reminder that compassion and civility in public life are not abstract ideals. They matter profoundly".
The attack on Helen Haines may prove to be just another brief interruption before regular political mud-slinging resumes. Or it could see all sides of politics try to course correct.
David Speers is national political lead and host of Insiders, which airs on ABC TV at 9am on Sunday or can be streamed anytime on ABC iview.

Quick hits: Sore Smith doesn't return as Marnus throws it away on horror day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:43:42 UTC
04:43:42 KST

Steve Smith doesn't return after reaching a major milestone and Marnus Labuschagne makes a mockery of an enormous reprieve as Australia is sent barrelling towards a chastening defeat in Gqeberha.
Here are the quick hits from day four of the second Test between Australia and South Africa.
1. Fiery Marco tears through the Aussies
Fresh from his swashbuckling 85 on day three, the towering Marco Jansen continued to terrorise the Australians on day four.
The left-arm seamer was at his fiery, probing best, with his aggression and accuracy proving all too much for the tourists in their first innings.
Jansen dismissed both Scott Boland and Travis Head early in the day, before a few tense exchanges with Marnus Labuschagne appeared to light a fuse somewhere deep in the big man.
He proceeded to treat Matt Renshaw to a send-off — seemingly in Afrikaans — upon having the Yorkshire-born Queenslander caught at short leg, before sending Alex Carey packing in a double breakthrough in the shadows of lunch.
Unfortunately for the Aussies, Jansen wasn't done there, with the South African having Beau Webster caught in the cordon to claim his fifth wicket and continue Australia's horror day.
2. Sore Smith reaches 11,000 and doesn't return
Amid the carnage up the other end, Steve Smith was just about hanging in there.
Struggling with a neck issue, the Australian received running repairs at multiple points during his innings and never quite looked his usual self.
Even so, Smith was at the crease long enough to become just the 12th batter to score 11,000 Test match runs, joining Ricky Ponting and Allan Border as the only Australians in that rare air.
But the Australia vice-captain was in serious discomfort throughout his innings, and departed promptly after joining that exclusive club.
The stiff-necked Smith was bowled through the gate by Wiaan Mulder for 28 as Australia was asked to follow on after being skittled for just 99, their fourth-lowest Test total against the Proteas.
And in a massive blow for his team, the Australia vice-captain did not recover in time to return to the crease as wickets started falling in the tourists' second dig, remaining in training gear in the dugout as Australia limped towards stumps.
3. Two remarkable grabs, two very different reactions
We have been treated to some seriously sensational slip catching in Gqeberha.
With Australia 3-45 in its first innings and already beginning to teeter, the desperately out-of-touch Labuschagne drove unconvincingly, sending his thick edge flying low and hard towards the cordon.
Harmer dived dramatically to his left, using his sizeable left hand to pluck the quickly dropping ball from the air in front of second slip.
And the off-spinner was absolutely pumped with his effort, throwing his head back and roaring as he got to his feet.
It provided quite some contrast to Renshaw's bewilderment after pouching his similarly excellent catch earlier in the Test.
4. Marnus throws it away after enormous reprieve
With Australia beginning its second innings needing 326 runs to just make South Africa bat again, Labuschagne had a golden opportunity to revive his sputtering Test career and make up for his rash dismissal earlier in the day.
Coming in after the early departure of Nic Maddinson, the signs were good for the Queenslander, who knuckled down with Head to push Australia towards 100.
And it was beginning to feel like Labuschagne might have finally been on for a score when he was the beneficiary of a huge reprieve in the 28th over.
Given out LBW to a Harmer off break, Labuschagne reviewed the decision in a blink and it was high drama as both camps waited for ball tracking to take an unusually long time to build.
Eventually, the technology projected the ball to be missing leg stump by what surely wasn't much more than a coat of paint.
Helmet off and head back, Labuschagne was making no secret of his relief.
But only moments later, he threw it all away, mistiming his slog and holing out to long-on for 39.
It was an ugly, ugly dismissal and one that left Australia once again on the rack with shadows lengthening in St George's.
5. Consecutive night shifts for Boland
With Australia proceeding to lose both Renshaw and Webster late on, Boland once again found himself batting in the dying embers of a day.
It was the second consecutive evening the Victorian had been called on as nightwatchman, and for the second consecutive evening, he made his way through to stumps.
Again, he betrayed no hint of annoyance with his sacrificial role, instead digging in and bravely finding his way through a couple of overs of twilight finger spin.
It was another committed shift from Boland — but boy, it's some reward for taking a five-wicket haul on his return to the team.
He'll begin day five alongside Head (87*) with Australia 4-156 and still 170 runs away from making South Africa bat again.

Hundreds sign letter supporting Irish author Sally Rooney, Faber over UK restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-21
19:42:12 UTC
04:42:12 KST

Hundreds of authors, actors and musicians have signed an open letter supporting Irish author Sally Rooney and her publisher, Faber, demanding an amendment to legislation that has prevented the sale of her books in the UK, Anadolu reports.
The letter, which was published in the New Statesman, argues that the decision to stop distributing Rooney’s works in the UK raises concerns about freedom of expression following the government’s designation of Palestine Action as a terror organization.
“Sally Rooney is a writer, not a terrorist. Her books must be available to the public,” said the letter.
Signatories include authors Zadie Smith, Patrick Ness, Damian Barr and Juno Dawson; actors Paul Mescal, Daisy Edgar-Jones and Tilda Swinton; musician Kate Nash; filmmaker Jonathan Glazer; and the Irish rap group Kneecap.
The letter describes removing Rooney’s books from shelves as an “affront to basic principles of free speech and expression so long taken for granted in this country,” and attributes the decision to “ill-conceived and draconian anti-terror legislation.”
“We categorically reject censorship – whether direct or indirect – and urge the government to change course, amending the legislation which has led us to this point of repressive absurdity,” it added.
Public support for Palestine Action and financial assistance to the group can constitute criminal offenses punishable by up to 14 years in prison under the legislation that designated it a terror organization.
Rooney previously said she would continue donating proceeds from her books to Palestine Action, arguing that the designation equated acts of vandalism, demonstrations and disruptions at military bases with terror crimes.
Earlier this month, Rooney said Faber had determined it could “no longer supply my work within the UK,” and that the decision had been made with her full agreement.
“I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions,” she said. “And I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences.”
